Name: Goserelin
Description: Goserelin (DrugBank DB00014) is a synthetic decapeptide gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist engineered from the native GnRH/LHRH peptide by strategic residue substitution, notably including a D-amino-acid at position 6 and a C-terminal azaglycine-derived modification that increase conformational stability, receptor affinity, and resistance to enzymatic degradation; structurally it is therefore a linear, highly polar, peptide-based endocrine modulator with amide-rich backbone functionality rather than a small heterocyclic organic compound. Chemically, it belongs to the class of peptide hormones and hormone analogs, more specifically GnRH agonists, and its core scaffold is the modified GnRH decapeptide scaffold shared across this therapeutic family. Similar drugs include leuprolide, triptorelin, histrelin, buserelin, and nafarelin, which also act as long-acting GnRH receptor agonists, whereas degarelix is a mechanistically related but antagonistic comparator within the broader GnRH-modulating space. Pharmacokinetically, goserelin is administered as a subcutaneous depot implant because oral delivery is not feasible for a peptide; systemic absorption occurs gradually from the depot, producing sustained exposure over weeks to months depending on formulation, distribution is largely confined to extracellular fluid with limited classic tissue partitioning expected for a hydrophilic peptide, protein binding is not typically the dominant determinant of disposition, metabolism occurs mainly through peptide hydrolysis and proteolytic degradation rather than CYP-mediated biotransformation, and elimination proceeds via metabolism followed by renal excretion of peptide fragments and some unchanged drug, with terminal disposition governed substantially by depot release kinetics. Its pharmacodynamic effect is an initial stimulation of the gonadotropin-releasing hormone receptor, now designated GNRHR, in the anterior pituitary causing a transient rise in luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone and a consequent testosterone or estradiol flare, followed by receptor desensitization and suppression of gonadotropin secretion with marked reduction in gonadal steroid production; GNRHR is the principal validated target protein. Toxicity is dominated by exaggerated hypoandrogenic or hypoestrogenic physiology rather than classic intrinsic cytotoxicity: examples include tumor flare with transient worsening of bone pain or urinary obstruction in prostate cancer, loss of bone mineral density and osteoporosis with prolonged use, metabolic effects such as impaired glucose tolerance, possible cardiovascular risk amplification in susceptible patients, and

Name: Gramicidin D
Description: Gramicidin D (DrugBank DB00027) is a naturally derived peptide antibiotic produced by Bacillus brevis and is best described structurally as a heterogeneous mixture of closely related linear hydrophobic pentadecapeptides, principally gramicidins A, B, and C, composed of alternating L- and D-amino acids that adopt a beta-helical conformation and dimerize head-to-head within lipid bilayers to form transmembrane ion channels; chemically it belongs to the polypeptide/peptide antibiotic class, more specifically the gramicidin family of ionophoric membrane-active agents, and its core scaffold is a linear alternating stereochemistry peptidic channel-forming scaffold enriched in hydrophobic residues such as valine, leucine, alanine, and tryptophan, which distinguishes it from cyclic peptide antibiotics. Similar drugs include other membrane-disrupting peptide antibiotics and topical polypeptides such as tyrothricin, bacitracin, polymyxin B, colistin, and to a mechanistically related extent amphotericin B as a channel-forming membrane-active anti-infective, although gramicidin is particularly associated with monovalent cation channel formation rather than detergent-like membrane dissolution. Its pharmacokinetics are limited by marked systemic toxicity, so it is used almost exclusively topically or locally: cutaneous, ophthalmic, otic, or oropharyngeal administration yields minimal intended systemic absorption across intact tissue, distribution is therefore largely confined to the site of application, classical hepatic metabolism is poorly characterized and probably limited because clinically relevant systemic exposure is ordinarily avoided, and excretion data are sparse for the same reason; if absorbed systemically, peptide degradation by proteolysis and tissue partitioning into membranes would be expected, but systemic use is not therapeutically acceptable. Toxicity is dominated by potent membrane injury in mammalian as well as bacterial cells, with marked hemolytic and cytolytic effects, irritation to skin or mucosa, and severe local tissue damage or systemic toxicity if inappropriately administered parenterally; examples include erythrocyte lysis, epithelial irritation, nephrotoxicity risk from membrane disruption, and dangerous effects on excitable tissues through altered ion conductance. Name: Desmopressin
Description: Desmopressin (DrugBank DB00035) is a synthetic vasopressin analog with a compact peptide structure characterized by a cyclic disulfide-bridged ring and a short C-terminal tail, distinguished from the natural antidiuretic hormone by deamination at the N-terminus and substitution of L-arginine with D-arginine near the C-terminus, modifications that increase metabolic stability, prolong antidiuretic action, and confer marked selectivity for vasopressin V2 receptors over vasopressor V1 receptors; chemically it belongs to the peptide hormone/oligopeptide class and more specifically to cyclic neurohypophyseal hormone analogs, with a vasopressin-like disulfide-constrained peptide scaffold. Similar drugs include vasopressin itself, lypressin, terlipressin, and other antidiuretic or vasopressinergic agents such as arginine vasopressin analogs used for diabetes insipidus, bleeding disorders, or vasodilatory shock, although desmopressin is notably more V2-selective and less vasoconstrictive than vasopressin. Pharmacokinetically, desmopressin is administered intranasally, orally, sublingually, or parenterally; oral absorption is low and variable because of peptide degradation and poor membrane permeability, intranasal absorption is better but still variable, and subcutaneous or intravenous dosing yields the most reliable exposure; it distributes mainly in extracellular fluid with limited tissue penetration typical of small peptides, shows relatively low plasma protein binding, and has a longer functional duration than native vasopressin because deamination and D-amino-acid substitution reduce susceptibility to aminopeptidases and other peptidases; metabolism occurs primarily through peptide catabolism rather than cytochrome P450 pathways, and elimination is largely renal with unchanged drug and peptide fragments excreted in urine, so exposure and toxicity risk can increase in renal impairment. Its principal target protein is the vasopressin V2 receptor, encoded by AVPR2, on renal collecting duct principal cells where receptor activation increases cAMP signaling and promotes aquaporin-2 trafficking to the apical membrane, enhancing water reabsorption; in endothelial cells, V2-mediated release of von Willebrand factor and factor VIII underlies hemostatic use, while much weaker activity at vasopressin V1a receptors may occur at higher

Name: Cyclosporine
Description: Cyclosporine (DrugBank DB00091) is a highly lipophilic, neutral, cyclic undecapeptide natural product originally isolated from Tolypocladium inflatum, characterized structurally by an 11-residue macrocyclic peptide ring rich in N-methylated amino acids and containing the unusual residue MeBmt, features that constrain conformation, reduce hydrogen-bond donor exposure, and enhance membrane permeability; chemically it belongs to the calcineurin-inhibitor immunosuppressants and more broadly to cyclic peptide fungal metabolites, with a macrocyclic N-methylated peptide scaffold that is closely related to other immunophilin-binding agents, while pharmacologically similar drugs include tacrolimus and pimecrolimus as calcineurin-pathway inhibitors and voclosporin as a structural analog of cyclosporine. Its principal target protein is cyclophilin A, with binding also described to other cyclophilin isoforms such as cyclophilin B and cyclophilin D; the cyclosporine-cyclophilin complex then functionally inhibits calcineurin, preventing NFAT dephosphorylation and suppressing IL-2 transcription and T-cell activation. Pharmacokinetically, oral absorption is incomplete and highly variable because of poor aqueous solubility and significant intestinal first-pass effects, though microemulsion formulations improve consistency; distribution is extensive with high partitioning into erythrocytes and tissues and substantial binding to lipoproteins and plasma proteins; metabolism occurs predominantly in the liver and intestinal wall via CYP3A4 and CYP3A5 with transport strongly influenced by P-glycoprotein, creating numerous clinically important drug-drug interactions; excretion is mainly biliary as metabolites with minimal unchanged renal elimination. Toxicity is dominated by dose- and exposure-related nephrotoxicity from afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction and chronic tubulointerstitial injury, with important additional toxicities including hypertension, neurotoxicity such as tremor or seizures, hepatotoxicity, hyperkalemia, hypomagnesemia, dyslipidemia, gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, and increased risks of serious infection and malignancy, especially lymphoma and skin cancer; overdose or interacting CYP3A inhibitors can accentuate renal failure and neurologic effects. Name: Octreotide
Description: Octreotide (DrugBank DB00104) is a synthetic cyclic octapeptide engineered as a long-acting somatostatin analog, characterized structurally by a compact peptide framework containing a disulfide bridge that constrains the molecule into the bioactive conformation required for high-affinity receptor binding, with strategically incorporated non-natural or modified residues that enhance enzymatic stability and prolong biologic activity relative to native somatostatin; chemically it belongs to the peptide therapeutic and peptidomimetic hormone class, and its core scaffold is the conformationally restricted cyclic somatostatin pharmacophore that preserves the key receptor-recognition motif while truncating the parent hormone to a metabolically robust octapeptide. Closely related or similar drugs include other somatostatin receptor ligands such as lanreotide and pasireotide, as well as the radiolabeled diagnostic or therapeutic congeners derived from octreotide-like scaffolds such as pentetreotide and lutetium Lu 177 dotatate-type receptor-targeting constructs. Pharmacokinetically, subcutaneous octreotide is rapidly absorbed with relatively high systemic bioavailability and reaches peak concentrations within hours, whereas long-acting intramuscular depot formulations release drug gradually over weeks; distribution is mainly within extracellular fluid with moderate plasma protein binding, receptor-rich tissue uptake, and limited penetration into the central nervous system; metabolism occurs largely through peptide degradation and hepatic biotransformation to smaller inactive fragments rather than classic CYP-dominant pathways; excretion is predominantly renal for unchanged drug and metabolites, with reduced clearance and prolonged exposure possible in renal impairment and altered elimination also reported in hepatic dysfunction. Its toxicity profile is generally dominated by exaggerated pharmacology rather than direct cytotoxicity, including inhibition of endocrine and gastrointestinal secretions, with clinically important examples such as dysglycemia from suppression of insulin and glucagon, cholelithiasis or biliary sludge from reduced gallbladder contractility and bile flow, steatorrhea and fat-soluble nutrient malabsorption from inhibition of pancreatic exocrine secretion, bradycardia or conduction abnormalities in susceptible patients, and rare severe hypersensitivity or pancreatitis. Name: Abarelix
Description: Abarelix (DB00106) is a synthetic decapeptide gonadotropin-releasing hormone antagonist built on a highly modified GnRH-like peptide framework in which multiple non-natural amino acid substitutions and terminal modifications increase receptor affinity, metabolic stability, and antagonistic activity; chemically it is classified as a peptide endocrine modulator and specifically an LHRH/GnRH antagonist, with a peptide backbone scaffold closely related to other depot GnRH antagonists such as degarelix and, more broadly, to cetrorelix and ganirelix. Its principal target is the gonadotropin-releasing hormone receptor, GNRHR, on pituitary gonadotrophs, where it rapidly suppresses luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone release, causing prompt reduction of testosterone without the initial flare seen with GnRH agonists. Pharmacokinetically, it is administered intramuscularly as a depot formulation, is slowly absorbed from the injection site, distributes mainly within extracellular fluid with limited oral bioavailability as expected for peptides, undergoes proteolytic peptide degradation rather than major CYP-mediated biotransformation, and is eliminated through metabolism with excretion of peptide fragments in urine and probably bile/feces. It was indicated for palliative treatment of advanced symptomatic prostate cancer, particularly when immediate chemical castration was desired. Toxicity is dominated by serious immediate systemic allergic or histamine-mediated reactions, including anaphylactoid events, hypotension, syncope, and urticaria, which restricted use; other adverse effects include QT-related concern secondary to androgen deprivation, hot flushes, erectile dysfunction, decreased libido, gynecomastia, injection-site pain, fatigue, and elevations in liver enzymes. Clinically, abarelix was used to achieve rapid testosterone suppression in men with metastatic or locally advanced prostate cancer, especially in patients at risk from tumor flare complications such as bone pain, urinary obstruction, or spinal cord compression.

Name: Choline
Description: Choline (DrugBank DB00122) is a small, highly polar quaternary ammonium alcohol composed of a permanently charged trimethylated nitrogen attached through a two-carbon linker to a terminal hydroxyl group, placing it in the class of essential nutrient-like ammonium compounds, specifically quaternary ammonium alcohols and lipotropic methyl-donor agents, with a minimal 2-hydroxyethyltrimethylammonium scaffold that also underlies related cholinergic or phospholipid-associated molecules. Similar compounds include acetylcholine, betaine, citicoline, alpha-glycerophosphocholine, and carnitine-like zwitterionic nutrients, which share cationic headgroup features or methyl-donor biology. Pharmacokinetically, choline is efficiently absorbed from the intestine by carrier-mediated and passive processes, distributed widely in plasma and tissues with high uptake in liver, kidney, brain, and placenta, incorporated into phosphatidylcholine and sphingomyelin pools, oxidized to betaine in liver and kidney, acetylated to acetylcholine in cholinergic neurons, and eliminated mainly as metabolized products with some urinary excretion; gut microbiota may also convert it to trimethylamine, later oxidized to trimethylamine N-oxide. Known biological targets include choline acetyltransferase, high-affinity choline transporter SLC5A7, choline kinase alpha and beta, acetylcholine receptors indirectly via acetylcholine biosynthesis, and phospholipid-synthesizing enzymes in the Kennedy pathway. Clinically, choline is used as a nutritional supplement or component of parenteral nutrition to prevent or treat deficiency, hepatic steatosis, liver dysfunction, muscle damage, and neurodevelopmental impairment, while adverse effects at higher doses include fishy body odor, sweating, salivation, gastrointestinal upset, hypotension, and rarely hepatotoxic or pro-atherogenic concern through excess trimethylamine N-oxide generation.

Name: Lysine
Description: Lysine (DrugBank DB00123) is a basic, essential α-amino acid whose structure consists of the canonical amino acid backbone bearing a flexible four-methylene side chain terminating in a primary ε-amino group, making it strongly cationic at physiologic pH; chemically it belongs to the proteinogenic essential amino acids, specifically the dibasic aliphatic amino acid class, and its scaffold is best described as a linear α-amino acid scaffold with an n-butylammonium side chain. Similar agents include other cationic amino acids such as arginine and ornithine, as well as amino acid formulations used in parenteral nutrition. After oral administration, lysine is generally well absorbed in the small intestine via sodium-independent cationic amino acid transport systems, distributed widely into extracellular and intracellular pools with extensive incorporation into proteins, limited direct metabolism through saccharopine and related catabolic pathways mainly in the liver, and excreted principally as metabolic products with some unchanged renal elimination; handling is influenced by renal tubular amino acid transport. Its pharmacology is mediated less by classic receptor action than by participation in protein synthesis and competition at cationic amino acid transporters, with relevant biological partners including SLC7A1/CAT-1, SLC7A2, and the heteromeric transporter SLC7A7/SLC3A2. Clinically, lysine is used for dietary supplementation and prevention or treatment of lysine deficiency, especially in malnutrition, restricted diets, and parenteral nutrition, and has also been used adjunctively for recurrent herpes simplex symptoms. Toxicity is generally low, but excessive intake may cause gastrointestinal intolerance such as nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and rare metabolic or renal complications in predisposed patients; clinical use therefore centers on nutritional repletion and supportive metabolic care.

Name: Arginine
Description: Arginine (DrugBank DB00125) is a basic, polar, proteinogenic α-amino acid whose structure consists of an α-carbon bearing a primary amine and carboxylate, with a three-methylene side chain terminating in a strongly basic guanidinium group that is protonated at physiologic pH; chemically it belongs to the cationic amino acids and amino acid/nitric oxide precursor class, and its core scaffold is the α-amino acid backbone with a terminal guanidino alkyl substituent. Closely related or similar agents include L-citrulline, ornithine, lysine, and nitric oxide donor strategies such as sodium nitroprusside or organic nitrates by functional analogy. Pharmacokinetically, oral arginine is absorbed in the small intestine via cationic amino acid transporters, undergoes substantial first-pass extraction in the gut and liver, distributes widely in extracellular and intracellular water, crosses into metabolically active tissues, and is metabolized primarily by arginase to ornithine and urea, and by nitric oxide synthases to nitric oxide plus citrulline; additional fates include protein incorporation and creatine/polyamine biosynthesis, with renal excretion of unchanged drug generally limited except at high loads or renal dysfunction. Known targets include nitric oxide synthases NOS1, NOS2, and NOS3, arginase 1 and 2, and cationic amino acid transporters such as SLC7A1/CAT-1. It is used for arginine deficiency states, urea cycle disorders, hyperammonemia, and as adjunctive therapy in some cardiovascular or endothelial dysfunction settings; adverse effects commonly include nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, bloating, headache, hypotension, and electrolyte disturbance, while toxicity at excessive doses may cause marked vasodilation, worsening asthma or herpes reactivation, hyperkalemia in susceptible patients, and concern in acute myocardial infarction settings. Clinically, it is given orally or intravenously for metabolic supplementation, ammonia-lowering support, and selected diagnostic or nutritional applications.

Name: Ascorbic acid
Description: Ascorbic acid (DrugBank DB00126) is a small, highly polar vitamin C molecule composed of a five-membered unsaturated lactone ring bearing an enediol motif and multiple hydroxyl groups, a structure responsible for its strong reducing and metal-chelating properties; chemically it is classified as a water-soluble carbohydrate-derived vitamin and enediol lactone, with a furanone-like ascorbate scaffold. Closely related agents include sodium ascorbate, calcium ascorbate, ascorbyl palmitate, and the oxidized congener dehydroascorbic acid, while erythorbic acid is a stereoisomer with similar redox behavior. Pharmacokinetically, oral absorption occurs in the small intestine through saturable sodium-dependent vitamin C transporters SLC23A1 and SLC23A2, with dehydroascorbic acid also entering cells via facilitative glucose transporters such as GLUT1/SLC2A1; distribution is wide, with high concentrations in leukocytes, adrenal glands, pituitary, and ocular tissues; metabolism involves reversible oxidation to dehydroascorbic acid and further breakdown to diketogulonic acid, oxalate, and other metabolites; renal reabsorption is saturable, so excess is excreted in urine. Known targets and functional protein interactions include prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases involved in collagen maturation, dopamine beta-hydroxylase, peptidylglycine alpha-amidating monooxygenase, and regulation of HIF hydroxylases through its role as a reductant. It is indicated for prevention and treatment of vitamin C deficiency and scurvy, and used clinically in supplementation states such as malnutrition, alcoholism, burn recovery, wound healing support, pregnancy, and dialysis. Adverse effects are usually dose related and include nausea, abdominal cramping, diarrhea, and headache; toxicity is generally low but excessive dosing may precipitate hyperoxaluria, calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis, rare oxalate nephropathy, and hemolysis in susceptible patients such as some with G6PD deficiency.

Name: Aspartic acid
Description: Aspartic acid (DrugBank DB00128) is a small, highly polar acidic proteinogenic amino acid whose structure consists of an α-amino group and an α-carboxylate attached to a two-carbon side chain terminating in a second carboxyl group, usually present clinically as the L-enantiomer; chemically it belongs to the aliphatic dicarboxylic amino acids, and its core scaffold is the aspartate amino-acid backbone, a simple succinic acid-derived α-amino acid motif. Similar drugs or closely related compounds include glutamic acid, asparagine, ornithine aspartate, potassium or magnesium aspartate salts, and the excitatory analogue N-methyl-D-aspartate. Pharmacokinetically, oral aspartic acid is absorbed in the small intestine by sodium-dependent amino-acid transporters, distributed widely in extracellular and intracellular pools, incorporated into proteins and intermediary metabolism, and participates in the urea cycle, transamination, gluconeogenesis, nucleotide biosynthesis, and the malate-aspartate shuttle; excess is metabolized to oxaloacetate and related intermediates, while renal handling involves extensive tubular reabsorption with limited urinary excretion unless intake is high or transport is saturated. Known biological targets include NMDA receptor subunits GRIN1, GRIN2A, GRIN2B, and related ionotropic glutamate receptors, although aspartate also functions broadly as an endogenous metabolite rather than a selective drug ligand. Toxicity is generally low at nutritional doses, but excessive exposure may cause excitotoxic neuronal injury, especially with parenteral overload or impaired clearance; adverse effects can include gastrointestinal discomfort, nausea, headache, and rarely neuroexcitation. Clinically, aspartic acid is used mainly as a nutritional supplement or electrolyte salt component and in metabolic support formulations, for example in amino-acid supplementation, fatigue states, and adjunctive correction of potassium or magnesium deficiency.

Name: L-Glutamine
Description: L-Glutamine (DrugBank DB00130) is the naturally occurring L-enantiomer of glutamine, a polar, neutral proteinogenic alpha-amino acid whose structure comprises an alpha-amino and alpha-carboxylate center with a four-carbon aliphatic side chain terminating in a carboxamide, making it a dicarboxylic acid amide derivative and conditionally essential amino acid; its core scaffold is the canonical alpha-amino acid backbone with a glutamate-like side chain capped as a primary amide. Chemically and pharmacologically related agents include other amino acid therapeutics and nutritional substrates such as L-glutamate, L-asparagine, glycine, and essential amino acid formulations. After oral administration, glutamine is absorbed in the small intestine by sodium-dependent neutral amino acid transporters, undergoes substantial first-pass utilization by enterocytes and liver, distributes widely to plasma, skeletal muscle, gut, kidney, and immune cells, crosses tissues via transport systems including SLC1A5/ASCT2 and SLC38 family members, is metabolized principally by glutaminase to glutamate and ammonia or by glutamine synthetase in reversible nitrogen shuttling, contributes carbon to the TCA cycle, nucleotide synthesis, and acid-base homeostasis, and is excreted mainly as metabolized products with limited unchanged renal elimination. Known biological targets or interacting proteins include glutaminase, glutamine synthetase, solute carriers such as SLC1A5 and SLC38A1/2, and enzymes using glutamine as an amide donor including CTP synthetase and GMP synthetase. Clinically, L-glutamine is used to reduce acute complications of sickle cell disease and as nutritional supplementation in catabolic states, mucositis, trauma, burns, critical illness, or short bowel settings; adverse effects are usually gastrointestinal, including nausea, abdominal pain, constipation, bloating, and headache, while toxicity is generally low but excessive dosing or impaired hepatic/renal function may increase nitrogen load, worsen hyperammonemia, or contribute to metabolic disturbances.

Name: Adenosine phosphate
Description: Adenosine phosphate (DrugBank DB00131), commonly referring to adenosine monophosphate, is an endogenous purine nucleotide composed of an adenine base linked to a ribofuranose sugar and a single phosphate ester, giving it a nucleoside-phosphate architecture with a ribosyl-purine scaffold and placing it in the chemical category of purine nucleotides and phosphate-containing metabolites. Its core scaffold is closely related to adenosine, ATP, ADP, and cyclic AMP, and similar drugs or biologically related agents include adenosine itself, ATP preparations, dipyridamole-potentiated adenosine signaling contexts, and other nucleotide analogs used diagnostically or therapeutically. Pharmacologically, adenosine phosphate is poorly membrane permeable and, when administered exogenously, is expected to undergo rapid extracellular and intracellular interconversion by ectonucleotidases, 5'-nucleotidases, kinases, and deaminases to adenosine, ADP, ATP, inosine, and uric acid pathway products; distribution is largely intravascular/interstitial with efficient cellular uptake via nucleoside transport systems after dephosphorylation, and elimination occurs mainly as renal excretion of downstream metabolites rather than unchanged parent compound. Known targets are indirect and include purinergic signaling systems, especially adenosine receptor subtypes ADORA1, ADORA2A, ADORA2B, and ADORA3 after conversion to adenosine, as well as enzymes of nucleotide metabolism. Toxicity is generally related to exaggerated purinergic or adenosinergic effects, with examples including hypotension, bradycardia, atrioventricular conduction disturbance, bronchospasm, flushing, and chest discomfort; excessive nucleotide load may also perturb urate metabolism. Indications and clinical use have historically centered on metabolic support or adjunctive use in states such as fatigue, ischemic symptoms, or cardiovascular dysfunction, but direct modern therapeutic use is limited compared with adenosine; adverse effects similarly include headache, dizziness, nausea, dyspnea, and transient arrhythmic symptoms.

Name: Serine
Description: Serine (DrugBank DB00133) is a small, highly polar proteinogenic α-amino acid whose structure consists of an amino group and carboxylate attached to the chiral α-carbon bearing a hydroxymethyl side chain, making it a hydroxy-substituted aliphatic amino acid; chemically it belongs to the class of neutral polar amino acids and is built on the canonical α-amino acid scaffold shared with glycine, alanine, threonine, and cysteine, with closest functional analogs including glycine, threonine, and the therapeutic amino acid preparations containing L-serine or related amino acids. Pharmacokinetically, exogenous serine is efficiently absorbed in the small intestine by sodium-dependent amino acid transporters, distributed widely in plasma and tissues including liver, kidney, muscle, and central nervous system, crosses cellular membranes through neutral amino acid carriers, undergoes extensive intermediary metabolism via serine hydroxymethyltransferase, phosphoserine phosphatase pathways, conversion to glycine, pyruvate, sphingolipids, phosphatidylserine, and one-carbon folate metabolism intermediates, and is not extensively excreted unchanged because it is readily incorporated into proteins or metabolized, with renal elimination mainly handling excess nitrogenous end products. Its relevant targets are metabolic enzymes and transport systems rather than a classic receptor, including serine hydroxymethyltransferases SHMT1 and SHMT2, phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase-associated biosynthetic enzymes, D-serine interactions at the NMDA receptor glycine site, and amino acid transporters such as SLC1 and SLC38 family members. Clinically, serine has been used mainly as a nutritional or metabolic supplement, particularly in serine biosynthesis defects, hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type 1, and investigational support in neurologic or metabolic states; adverse effects are usually mild and gastrointestinal, such as nausea, bloating, abdominal discomfort, or diarrhea, while toxicity is generally low but excessive amino acid loading may worsen metabolic imbalance, and altered serine metabolism has been linked to neurotoxicity or tumor metabolic adaptation rather than common direct poisoning.

Name: Calcitriol
Description: Calcitriol (DB00136) is the hormonally active 1,25-dihydroxylated metabolite of vitamin D3, structurally a secosteroid in which the B ring of the steroid nucleus is opened, bearing hydroxyl groups at C1, C3, and C25 and a flexible lipophilic side chain that distinguishes it from less active vitamin D congeners; it belongs to the vitamin D/sterol class and is built on a cholecalciferol-derived secosteroid scaffold. Similar drugs include vitamin D analogs and congeners such as alfacalcidol, doxercalciferol, paricalcitol, and calcifediol, which share the secosteroid framework but differ in activation requirements or substituent pattern. Calcitriol is generally well absorbed orally, circulates extensively bound to vitamin D-binding protein, distributes to intestine, bone, kidney, and parathyroid tissue, undergoes CYP24A1-mediated oxidation and other hydroxylation/catabolic steps in kidney and liver to less active metabolites, and is eliminated mainly through biliary/fecal routes with limited urinary excretion; its short biologic half-life supports careful titration. Its principal target is the vitamin D receptor, a nuclear receptor that heterodimerizes with RXR to regulate calcium/phosphate transport and parathyroid hormone-responsive genes; functional effects also involve proteins such as TRPV6, calbindin, and osteocalcin pathways. It is indicated for hypocalcemia and disordered mineral metabolism, especially hypoparathyroidism, secondary hyperparathyroidism in chronic kidney disease, and hypocalcemia associated with renal osteodystrophy, and is also used in some patients with vitamin D-dependent rickets or osteoporosis adjunctively. Major toxicity is exaggerated vitamin D activity causing hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, renal impairment, soft-tissue or vascular calcification, and arrhythmia risk, while common adverse effects include weakness, nausea, vomiting, constipation, headache, polyuria, polydipsia, and confusion.

Name: Lutein
Description: Lutein (DrugBank DB00137) is a naturally occurring oxygenated carotenoid xanthophyll characterized by a long, highly conjugated C40 polyene chain with alternating double bonds and terminal cyclic ionone-type rings bearing hydroxyl substituents, a structure that underlies its yellow pigment, antioxidant capacity, and membrane-localizing behavior; chemically it belongs to the tetraterpenoid carotenoid class, with a xanthophyll/polyene scaffold closely related to zeaxanthin, meso-zeaxanthin, beta-carotene, and other dietary carotenoids. After oral administration, lutein is absorbed in the small intestine in a fat-dependent manner via micellar solubilization, enters chylomicrons, distributes through plasma lipoproteins, and accumulates preferentially in the retina and macula as well as adipose tissue and liver; metabolism appears limited and involves oxidative cleavage and conversion to polar metabolites, with elimination occurring mainly through biliary/fecal routes and minimal renal excretion. Toxicity is generally low, but high chronic intake may cause benign carotenodermia-like yellowing of skin and has rarely been associated with crystalline maculopathy in heavily supplemented individuals; gastrointestinal discomfort can also occur. Known binding/target proteins include the macular carotenoid-binding proteins StARD3 and GSTP1, while pharmacologic effects are largely attributed to blue-light filtering and quenching of reactive oxygen species rather than classic receptor agonism. Lutein is used primarily as a nutritional/ophthalmic supplement for age-related macular degeneration, cataract risk reduction, and support of visual function, and is also studied in diabetic retinopathy and photic retinal stress; clinical use is typically as oral supplementation, often combined with zeaxanthin and antioxidant vitamins, with side effects usually mild and limited to dyspepsia, nausea, or skin discoloration.

Name: Succinic acid
Description: Succinic acid (DB00139) is a small endogenous aliphatic dicarboxylic acid composed of a saturated four-carbon chain terminated by two carboxyl groups, giving a simple linear butanedioic acid framework that is highly polar and readily ionized at physiological pH; chemically it belongs to the tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediates and broader organic dicarboxylic acid class, with a succinate scaffold shared by related compounds and therapeutically or chemically similar agents such as fumaric acid, malic acid, glutaric acid, and succinate salts or esters used as pharmaceutical counterions or metabolic supplements. Pharmacologically, succinic acid is primarily a metabolic substrate rather than a classic receptor-directed drug: it is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract as a small water-soluble organic acid, distributed widely in extracellular fluid and metabolically active tissues, enters intermediary metabolism via transport into cells and mitochondria, is converted through succinate dehydrogenase, which is also mitochondrial respiratory chain complex II, and is ultimately oxidized to fumarate with carbon flux ending largely as carbon dioxide and water; renal excretion of unchanged compound is expected to be limited at ordinary doses. Known molecular targets or interactors include succinate dehydrogenase subunits SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, and SDHD, and the succinate receptor SUCNR1/GPR91. Reported or proposed indications have included nutritional or metabolic support, correction of succinate deficiency states, and use in formulations aimed at fatigue, hypoxia, or mitochondrial dysfunction, although mainstream approved therapeutic indications are limited. Toxicity is generally low because it is endogenous, but excessive exposure may cause gastrointestinal irritation, acid-base disturbance, or local irritation; adverse effects can include nausea, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, and formulation-specific intolerance. Clinically, succinic acid is more often encountered as a metabolic intermediate, excipient-related moiety, or component of supplement and salt formulations than as a widely used standalone prescription drug.

Name: Riboflavin
Description: Riboflavin (DrugBank DB00140) is a water-soluble vitamin of the flavin class, chemically characterized by a tricyclic isoalloxazine ring system bearing methyl substituents and linked at the N-10 position to a reduced sugar alcohol side chain, ribitol; this confers a heteroaromatic flavin scaffold that underlies its redox activity and distinguishes it from related vitamers. It belongs to the vitamin B2 family and is closely related to the active coenzyme derivatives flavin mononucleotide and flavin adenine dinucleotide, as well as similar nutritional agents such as nicotinamide and other B-complex vitamins used in deficiency states. After oral administration, riboflavin is absorbed mainly in the proximal small intestine by saturable transport, distributed widely but stored only in limited amounts, converted intracellularly by riboflavin kinase and FAD synthetase to FMN and FAD, and excreted predominantly in urine, often imparting a bright yellow discoloration. Pharmacologically, its relevant targets are not classical receptors but flavoprotein-dependent enzymes that require FMN or FAD as cofactors, including mitochondrial electron transport proteins, glutathione reductase, xanthine oxidase, monoamine oxidase, and methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase. Riboflavin is indicated for prevention and treatment of ariboflavinosis, nutritional deficiency, and supplementation in malabsorption, alcoholism, pregnancy, and some inherited metabolic disorders; it is also used clinically in migraine prophylaxis and supportive care where deficient flavin-dependent metabolism is suspected. Toxicity is low because excess is renally cleared, with no well-defined severe overdose syndrome, though high doses may rarely cause diarrhea, polyuria, or pruritus; adverse effects are generally mild and include urine discoloration, gastrointestinal discomfort, and occasional hypersensitivity.

Name: Glycine
Description: Glycine (DrugBank DB00145) is the simplest proteinogenic amino acid, chemically characterized as a small neutral α-amino acid bearing a primary amino group and a carboxylate on a single methylene backbone; because its side chain is hydrogen, it is achiral and highly water soluble, placing it in the aliphatic amino acid and endogenous metabolite category with an aminoacetic acid scaffold. Structurally and pharmacologically related compounds include other amino acids and amino acid-derived agents such as serine, alanine, and the irrigant component glycine-containing urologic solutions. Its known targets include the inhibitory glycine receptor subunits GLRA1, GLRB, and related ligand-gated chloride channel complexes, as well as the glycine-binding co-agonist site of the NMDA receptor complex involving GRIN subunits; it also serves broadly as a metabolic substrate in one-carbon, porphyrin, purine, glutathione, and creatine biosynthesis. Pharmacokinetically, glycine is well absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract and by parenteral routes, distributes widely in total body water, crosses the blood-brain barrier to a limited but physiologically relevant extent, undergoes extensive endogenous utilization and interconversion via serine hydroxymethyltransferase, the glycine cleavage system, and other intermediary pathways, and is ultimately eliminated mainly as metabolized carbon units with only a small fraction excreted unchanged renally. Clinically, glycine has been used as a nutritional supplement, in specialized amino acid formulations, and as a nonconductive irrigant during transurethral procedures; investigated or supportive indications include nutritional deficiency states and adjunctive neuropsychiatric use. Toxicity is generally low at physiologic dosing, but excessive systemic absorption, especially from irrigant solutions, can cause hyperglycinemia, hypo-osmolality, visual disturbances, nausea, vomiting, encephalopathy, seizures, cardiovascular instability, and rarely death; routine adverse effects of supplementation are usually mild gastrointestinal symptoms such as soft stools, abdominal discomfort, or nausea.

Name: Calcifediol
Description: Calcifediol (25-hydroxyvitamin D3; DrugBank DB00146) is a secosteroidal vitamin D metabolite structurally characterized by a cholesterol-derived, lipophilic cholecalciferol skeleton in which the B-ring is opened, retaining the fused steroid-like A, C, and D rings, a 3β-hydroxyl group, a 25-hydroxylated side chain, and a conjugated triene system that underlies its vitamin D activity; it belongs to the vitamin D/sterol lipid class and is built on the vitamin D secosteroid scaffold. Closely related drugs include cholecalciferol, ergocalciferol, calcitriol, alfacalcidol, and paricalcitol, which share the same core scaffold but differ in side-chain unsaturation or hydroxylation pattern. After oral administration, calcifediol is efficiently absorbed with dietary fat, transported in chylomicrons and then tightly bound in plasma to vitamin D-binding protein, achieving higher and more predictable increases in circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D than cholecalciferol; it distributes predominantly to plasma and adipose compartments, undergoes renal and extra-renal 1α-hydroxylation by CYP27B1 to the active hormone calcitriol and catabolism mainly by CYP24A1, and is eliminated chiefly via biliary/fecal excretion with a relatively long circulating half-life. Its principal target pathway is the vitamin D receptor, mediated largely after conversion to calcitriol, with relevant proteins including VDR, CYP27B1, CYP24A1, and GC/DBP. Calcifediol is indicated for vitamin D deficiency and insufficiency, including osteomalacia, rickets, secondary hyperparathyroidism in chronic kidney disease, and osteoporosis-related states. Toxicity is dominated by hypervitaminosis D with hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, renal impairment, and soft-tissue or vascular calcification; adverse effects may include nausea, vomiting, constipation, weakness, polyuria, polydipsia, confusion, and arrhythmias. Clinically, it is used to rapidly replete vitamin D stores in patients with malabsorption, obesity, liver dysfunction, or chronic kidney disease, and as an adjunct in bone and mineral disorder management.

Name: Cysteine
Description: Cysteine (DrugBank DB00151) is a small, polar, sulfur-containing α-amino acid whose structure consists of the canonical amino acid backbone bearing a primary amine, a carboxyl group, and a thiol-containing side chain, making it chemically distinctive as a reduced aminothiol and conferring strong nucleophilic and redox activity; it belongs to the natural proteinogenic amino acid class, with an amino acid/aminothiol scaffold related to other sulfur amino acids. Similar drugs or close analogues include N-acetylcysteine, cystine, methionine, and glutathione precursors, which share thiol or sulfur-based redox chemistry. Pharmacokinetically, cysteine is absorbed in the small intestine through amino acid transport systems, distributed widely into plasma and tissues, incorporated into proteins, and used in glutathione, taurine, and coenzyme A biosynthesis; it undergoes extensive intermediary metabolism via transsulfuration and oxidation-reduction pathways, with excess sulfur metabolites and minor unchanged material excreted mainly in urine. Toxicity is generally low at nutritional doses, but excessive exposure may cause redox imbalance, gastrointestinal intolerance, neurotoxicity in susceptible settings, and, in parenteral use, metabolic disturbances such as acid-base abnormalities; high cysteine loads may also promote cystine stone formation in predisposed patients. Its biologic targets are not dominated by a single receptor but include amino acid transporters and enzymes such as cysteine dioxygenase, cystathionine β-synthase, cystathionine γ-lyase, glutamate-cysteine ligase, and proteins regulated through thiol-disulfide exchange. Clinically, cysteine is used primarily as a nutritional supplement in parenteral nutrition, especially for neonates or patients with limited synthetic capacity, and to support deficiency states, growth, nitrogen balance, and glutathione-dependent antioxidant defense; adverse effects can include nausea, vomiting, unpleasant sulfur odor or taste, infusion-related irritation, and rare hypersensitivity.

Name: Thiamine
Description: Thiamine (DrugBank DB00152), or vitamin B1, is a small, water-soluble cationic vitamin composed of a substituted aminopyrimidine ring linked by a methylene bridge to a thiazolium ring bearing a hydroxyethyl side chain; this places it in the vitamin/cofactor and quaternary heteroaromatic thiazolium class, with a pyrimidine-thiazolium scaffold that is conserved in its active coenzyme form, thiamine pyrophosphate. Closely related agents include thiamine phosphate and thiamine pyrophosphate, as well as lipophilic derivatives or analogs such as benfotiamine, fursultiamine, and sulbutiamine. It is absorbed mainly in the jejunum by carrier-mediated transport at physiologic doses and passive diffusion at high doses, distributed widely with appreciable uptake into liver, heart, kidney, and nervous tissue, converted intracellularly by thiamine pyrophosphokinase to thiamine pyrophosphate and other phosphate esters, stored only in limited amounts, and eliminated primarily in urine as unchanged thiamine and metabolites with rapid depletion during deficiency. Its principal functional targets are thiamine-dependent enzymes rather than classic receptors, especially pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex, branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase, transketolase, and 2-hydroxyacyl-CoA lyase 1. Thiamine is indicated for prevention and treatment of deficiency states including beriberi, Wernicke encephalopathy, Korsakoff syndrome, malnutrition, chronic alcoholism, prolonged vomiting, and refeeding risk. Toxicity is generally low, but parenteral administration can rarely cause hypersensitivity, urticaria, bronchospasm, hypotension, or anaphylactoid reactions; other adverse effects include injection-site pain, nausea, sweating, pruritus, and restlessness. Clinically it is used orally for nutritional supplementation and deficiency prevention, and intravenously or intramuscularly in suspected Wernicke encephalopathy, acute alcoholism-associated deficiency, and severe depletion in critically ill or malnourished patients.

Name: Ergocalciferol
Description: Ergocalciferol (DrugBank DB00153) is vitamin D2, a fat-soluble secosteroid characterized by a broken B-ring steroid nucleus, a conjugated triene chromophore, a 3β-hydroxyl group, and an ergosterol-derived side chain containing a C22-C23 double bond and C24 methyl substituent; chemically it belongs to the vitamin D secosteroids and is built on the calciferol/sterol-derived secosteroid scaffold. Closely related drugs include cholecalciferol (vitamin D3), calcifediol, calcitriol, alfacalcidol, paricalcitol, and doxercalciferol, which share the vitamin D receptor agonist paradigm with differing activation requirements. After oral administration, ergocalciferol is absorbed with dietary fat in the small intestine, incorporated into chylomicrons, distributed via lymph and blood bound mainly to vitamin D-binding protein, stored in adipose tissue and muscle, hydroxylated in the liver chiefly by CYP2R1 and other 25-hydroxylases to 25-hydroxyergocalciferol, then in the kidney by CYP27B1 to active 1,25-dihydroxyergocalciferol, with catabolism mediated largely by CYP24A1 and excretion predominantly through bile and feces. Its principal target is the vitamin D receptor, with downstream regulation of calcium/phosphate transport proteins and suppression of parathyroid hormone. It is indicated for vitamin D deficiency, hypocalcemia, nutritional rickets, osteomalacia, hypoparathyroidism, and prevention or treatment of deficiency in malabsorption or chronic kidney disease contexts. Toxicity is dominated by hypervitaminosis D and hypercalcemia, causing nausea, vomiting, constipation, polyuria, dehydration, nephrolithiasis, soft-tissue or vascular calcification, confusion, and renal impairment, especially with excessive dosing or concomitant calcium/thiazides. Clinically, it is used as oral capsules, tablets, drops, or fortified preparations for repletion and maintenance of vitamin D status and bone mineral homeostasis.

Name: Folic acid
Description: Folic acid (DrugBank DB00158) is a water-soluble B-vitamin and pteroylglutamic acid composed of a bicyclic pteridine ring linked through p-aminobenzoic acid to a terminal glutamate residue, giving a conjugated heteroaromatic folate scaffold with distinct hydrogen-bonding and ionizable carboxyl functionalities; chemically it belongs to the folates/antianemic vitamins, and its core scaffold is shared with reduced folates and antifolates. Closely related or similar drugs include folinic acid (leucovorin), levomefolate, methotrexate, pemetrexed, and pralatrexate, which exploit the same folate-recognition architecture. After oral administration, folic acid is absorbed mainly in the proximal small intestine via the proton-coupled folate transporter SLC46A1 and other folate carriers, undergoes reduction and methylation in intestinal mucosa and liver by dihydrofolate reductase and folate-cycle enzymes to tetrahydrofolate derivatives including 5-methyltetrahydrofolate, distributes widely with notable hepatic storage and placental transfer, circulates partly protein-bound, and is excreted primarily in urine as unchanged drug and metabolites, with biliary recycling contributing modestly. Key target proteins include DHFR, folate receptor alpha FOLR1, reduced folate carrier SLC19A1, and SLC46A1, while downstream pharmacology supports one-carbon transfer reactions required for thymidylate and purine synthesis. It is indicated for folate deficiency, megaloblastic anemia due to deficiency, prevention of neural tube defects in pregnancy, and supplementation in malnutrition, alcoholism, hemolytic states, or chronic anticonvulsant use. Toxicity is generally low, but excessive dosing may mask vitamin B12 deficiency and permit progression of irreversible neuropathy; uncommon adverse effects include nausea, abdominal discomfort, irritability, sleep disturbance, rash, pruritus, bronchospasm, and rare hypersensitivity. Clinically, it is used as oral or parenteral replacement therapy, routine prenatal supplementation, and supportive care when folate requirements are increased.

Name: Vitamin A
Description: Vitamin A (DrugBank DB00162) refers primarily to retinol and related retinoids, a fat-soluble isoprenoid micronutrient characterized by a substituted β-ionone ring linked to a conjugated polyene chain terminating in a primary alcohol; this places it in the retinoid/terpenoid class, with a carotenoid-derived vitamin A scaffold built on the β-ionone–polyene motif. Closely related or similar drugs include retinyl esters such as retinyl palmitate, the aldehyde retinal, the acid metabolite tretinoin, and synthetic or semisynthetic retinoids such as isotretinoin, acitretin, and adapalene. After oral administration, vitamin A is absorbed in the small intestine with dietary fat and bile, packaged into chylomicrons, stored mainly in the liver as retinyl esters, circulated bound to retinol-binding protein and transthyretin, converted intracellularly to retinal and retinoic acid, and eliminated slowly after hepatic metabolism via oxidation, conjugation, and biliary and urinary excretion. Its major targets are retinoic acid receptors RARA, RARB, and RARG, retinoid X receptors RXRA, RXRB, and RXRG, and visual cycle proteins including rhodopsin through 11-cis-retinal. Clinically, it is indicated for prevention and treatment of vitamin A deficiency, xerophthalmia, night blindness, keratomalacia, and deficiency associated with malnutrition, malabsorption, or measles; it is also used in nutritional supplementation and, via related retinoids, in dermatologic disease. Toxicity includes acute hypervitaminosis A with nausea, vomiting, headache, and dizziness, and chronic toxicity with hepatotoxicity, bone pain, alopecia, pseudotumor cerebri, teratogenicity, and skin desquamation; common adverse effects include dry skin, cheilitis, fatigue, irritability, and gastrointestinal upset.

Name: Vitamin E
Description: Vitamin E (DrugBank DB00163) is a lipid-soluble vitamin comprising a family of tocopherols and tocotrienols, with alpha-tocopherol the principal therapeutic form; structurally it contains a chromanol (benzopyran-6-ol) head with a phenolic hydroxyl that donates hydrogen to quench lipid radicals, attached to a long hydrophobic isoprenoid-derived side chain, saturated in tocopherols and unsaturated in tocotrienols, placing it in the fat-soluble vitamin, phenolic antioxidant, and prenylquinone-related natural product categories, with a chromanol/tocopherol scaffold. Similar drugs or related agents include other vitamin E congeners such as gamma-tocopherol and tocotrienols, and functionally overlapping antioxidants such as vitamin C, beta-carotene, and ubiquinone. After oral administration, absorption depends on dietary fat, bile, and pancreatic function; it is incorporated into chylomicrons, distributed via lymph and blood to adipose tissue, liver, muscle, and cell membranes, with hepatic alpha-tocopherol transfer protein (TTPA) preferentially retaining alpha-tocopherol, followed by CYP4F2-mediated omega-hydroxylation and beta-oxidation to carboxyethyl-hydroxychroman metabolites and mainly fecal, with some urinary metabolite, excretion. Its pharmacology is mediated primarily by chain-breaking antioxidant effects rather than a classic receptor, although TTPA is a key handling protein and vitamin E can influence PKC, PLA2, PTGS pathways, and oxidative stress signaling. It is indicated for prevention and treatment of vitamin E deficiency, especially in fat-malabsorption states, abetalipoproteinemia, cholestatic liver disease, and certain neuropathic or hemolytic manifestations of deficiency; clinically it is used as oral supplementation and in specialized deficiency syndromes. Toxicity is usually low but high doses may impair vitamin K-dependent coagulation and increase bleeding risk, particularly with warfarin, and may cause gastrointestinal upset, headache, fatigue, weakness, blurred vision, rash, or rare thrombophlebitis; overdose examples include hemorrhagic complications and increased all-cause or prostate cancer risk signals reported in some supplementation trials.

Name: Pyridoxine
Description: Pyridoxine (DrugBank DB00165) is vitamin B6, a small water-soluble pyridine derivative whose structure consists of a substituted aromatic pyridine ring bearing hydroxymethyl groups and a hydroxyl substituent, typically used clinically as the alcohol form and interconverted with pyridoxal and pyridoxamine; chemically it belongs to the B-vitamin/pyridine alcohol class and is built on a hydroxymethyl-substituted pyridine scaffold. Closely related and pharmacologically similar compounds include pyridoxal, pyridoxamine, and the active coenzyme pyridoxal 5-phosphate, as well as multivitamin B-complex formulations containing these vitamers. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed from the jejunum by passive diffusion, distributed widely to liver, muscle, and brain, crosses the placenta and enters breast milk, and is converted primarily in the liver by pyridoxal kinase and pyridoxine 5-phosphate oxidase to pyridoxal 5-phosphate, which circulates largely protein-bound, especially to albumin; elimination occurs mainly as renal excretion of 4-pyridoxic acid and other metabolites. Its functional targets are therefore vitamin B6-dependent enzymes rather than a single receptor, including aminotransferases, decarboxylases, glycogen phosphorylase, cystathionine beta-synthase, and aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase. Pyridoxine is indicated for prevention and treatment of vitamin B6 deficiency, isoniazid-, cycloserine-, hydralazine-, or penicillamine-induced neuropathy, pyridoxine-dependent seizures, sideroblastic anemia, some homocystinurias, and nausea/vomiting of pregnancy in combination with doxylamine. It is usually well tolerated, but adverse effects can include nausea, headache, somnolence, photosensitivity, and paradoxical sensory symptoms; chronic high-dose exposure is classically associated with dose-related sensory neuropathy, ataxia, and impaired proprioception. Clinically it is used as oral or parenteral replacement therapy, antidotal adjunct in isoniazid toxicity, and supportive treatment where enhanced PLP-dependent metabolism is required.

Name: Cholecalciferol
Description: Cholecalciferol (vitamin D3; DrugBank DB00169) is a fat-soluble secosteroid whose structure is defined by a cholesterol-derived steroid nucleus in which the B ring is photochemically opened, yielding a 9,10-secocholesta scaffold with a conjugated triene system and a flexible aliphatic side chain; chemically it belongs to the vitamin D family of sterols/secosteroids, and its core scaffold is the vitamin D seco-steroid framework closely related to ergocalciferol, calcifediol, calcitriol, alfacalcidol, and paricalcitol. After oral administration it is absorbed in the small intestine with dietary lipids and bile salts, enters lymph in chylomicrons, and is distributed predominantly to adipose tissue, muscle, and liver bound mainly to vitamin D-binding protein; it undergoes hepatic 25-hydroxylation primarily by CYP2R1 and CYP27A1 to calcifediol, then renal 1alpha-hydroxylation by CYP27B1 to the active hormone calcitriol, with catabolism largely via CYP24A1 and excretion mainly in bile/feces with limited urinary loss. Its principal target is the vitamin D receptor, a nuclear receptor that heterodimerizes with RXR to regulate calcium-phosphate homeostasis, bone remodeling, parathyroid suppression, and intestinal calcium transport. Clinically it is used for prevention and treatment of vitamin D deficiency, rickets, osteomalacia, hypocalcemia, osteoporosis adjunctive care, and deficiency states due to malabsorption or limited sun exposure. Toxicity is dominated by hypervitaminosis D with hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria, causing nausea, vomiting, constipation, weakness, confusion, nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, arrhythmias, and soft-tissue or vascular calcification, particularly with chronic excessive dosing.

Name: ATP
Description: ATP (adenosine triphosphate; DrugBank DB00171) is an endogenous purine ribonucleotide composed of an adenine base linked to a ribose sugar and a linear triphosphate chain with high-energy phosphoanhydride bonds at the 5-prime position; chemically it belongs to the nucleoside triphosphate and purine nucleotide class, with an adenosine scaffold extended by a triphosphate moiety. Closely related or functionally similar drugs include adenosine, adenosine diphosphate derivatives, and triphosadenine formulations used in some markets, as well as purinergic agents that act on overlapping pathways. Pharmacologically, exogenous ATP is not orally useful because it is rapidly degraded in blood and tissues by ectonucleotidases to ADP, AMP, and adenosine; after parenteral administration it remains largely extracellular, distributes briefly in plasma and the vascular/interstitial compartment, is metabolized extremely rapidly, and is eliminated mainly as downstream purine metabolites excreted in urine. Its principal targets are purinergic receptors, especially P2X ligand-gated ion channels and P2Y G-protein-coupled receptors, while many physiological effects also arise indirectly through adenosine generated from ATP breakdown acting at adenosine receptors. Clinically, ATP has been used as a vasodilatory and cardiomodulatory agent and for symptom-based treatment in settings such as supraventricular tachyarrhythmias, peripheral circulatory disorders, ischemic symptoms, fatigue, and some neuromuscular complaints, although modern use is limited and often superseded by adenosine. Toxicity is chiefly an extension of purinergic and vasodilator activity, with examples including hypotension, flushing, chest discomfort, dyspnea, bronchospasm, bradycardia, atrioventricular block, and precipitation of arrhythmias; other side effects include headache, nausea, dizziness, and local injection reactions.

Name: Pravastatin
Description: Pravastatin (DrugBank DB00175) is a hydrophilic, fungal-derived statin characterized structurally by a substituted decalin nucleus bearing the conserved 3,5-dihydroxyheptanoic acid pharmacophore that mimics the tetrahedral intermediate of HMG-CoA reduction; chemically it is a polyketide-like hydroxy acid antihyperlipidemic agent, and its core scaffold is the compact hexahydronaphthalene/decalin statin framework seen in natural-product statins. Closely related drugs include lovastatin and simvastatin, which share the decalin scaffold but are more lipophilic lactone prodrugs, as well as semisynthetic or synthetic statins such as fluvastatin, atorvastatin, and rosuvastatin that retain HMG-CoA reductase inhibition with different ring systems. Pravastatin targets primarily 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase (HMGCR), lowering hepatic cholesterol synthesis and upregulating LDL receptor-mediated clearance; hepatic uptake is mediated in part by SLCO1B1/OATP1B1. Orally, it has moderate absorption, relatively low bioavailability because of significant first-pass hepatic extraction, limited metabolism compared with CYP-dependent statins, low plasma protein binding relative to more lipophilic congeners, and elimination through both renal and biliary routes, with much of the dose excreted unchanged or as minor metabolites. It is indicated for primary hypercholesterolemia, mixed dyslipidemia, and prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular events such as myocardial infarction and stroke. Adverse effects include myalgia, creatine kinase elevation, mild gastrointestinal upset, headache, and transaminase increases; important toxicities include hepatotoxicity, immune-mediated or toxic myopathy, rare rhabdomyolysis with acute kidney injury, and fetal risk in pregnancy. Clinically, it is used as monotherapy or with diet and other lipid-lowering agents in patients with elevated LDL cholesterol, diabetes, established coronary disease, or high cardiovascular risk.

Name: Fluvoxamine
Description: Fluvoxamine (DrugBank DB00176) is a synthetic arylalkylamine antidepressant of the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor class, structurally characterized by an oxime ether scaffold linking a 2-aminoethyl side chain to a substituted aromatic system, notably a trifluoromethyl-substituted phenyl ring and a methoxy-bearing aliphatic ether moiety, giving a compact lipophilic SSRI pharmacophore rather than the bicyclic scaffold seen in older antidepressants. Its core chemical scaffold is commonly described as a phenylalkyl oxime ether, and it is chemically and pharmacologically related to other SSRIs such as fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine, citalopram, and escitalopram, although fluvoxamine is distinguished by its monocyclic oxime-derived architecture. Its principal target is the serotonin transporter SLC6A4, through which it inhibits presynaptic serotonin reuptake; sigma-1 receptor binding has also been described as a potentially relevant ancillary interaction. After oral administration it is well absorbed, undergoes significant first-pass hepatic metabolism with moderate absolute bioavailability, is widely distributed, moderately protein bound, and extensively metabolized in the liver primarily by CYP2D6 and other CYP pathways including CYP1A2, with notable inhibition of CYP1A2 and CYP2C19 creating interaction liability; metabolites are largely excreted in urine. It is indicated mainly for obsessive-compulsive disorder and major depressive disorder, and is used clinically for obsessions, compulsions, depressive symptoms, anxiety states, social anxiety disorder, and panic-related symptoms in selected settings. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, insomnia, somnolence, headache, dry mouth, dizziness, sweating, tremor, constipation, and sexual dysfunction. Toxicity concerns include serotonin syndrome, QT-related risk at high exposure or with interacting drugs, hyponatremia, bleeding tendency, activation of mania, seizure risk, and overdose manifestations such as vomiting, agitation, and CNS depression.

Name: Valsartan
Description: Valsartan (DrugBank DB00177) is a nonpeptide angiotensin II receptor blocker of the biphenyl-tetrazole class whose structure features a substituted biphenyl core bearing a tetrazole bioisostere and a valine-derived acyl side chain, giving a lipophilic acidic architecture characteristic of AT1 antagonists; its central chemical scaffold is therefore a biphenyl-tetrazole linked to an amino acid-like amide/alkyl fragment. It is closely related to other sartans such as losartan, irbesartan, candesartan, and olmesartan, which share AT1 receptor antagonism and overlapping biphenyl or heteroaryl acidic motifs. Its principal target is the angiotensin II type 1 receptor encoded by AGTR1, with pharmacologic blockade reducing vasoconstriction, aldosterone release, sympathetic activation, and adverse cardiac and renal remodeling. Orally administered valsartan has moderate absorption with relatively low absolute bioavailability, food may reduce exposure, protein binding is high, distribution is largely extracellular, metabolism is limited with most circulating drug remaining unchanged, and elimination occurs predominantly via biliary/fecal excretion with a smaller renal component and a terminal half-life generally around several hours. It is indicated for hypertension, heart failure, and reduction of cardiovascular mortality after myocardial infarction, and is used clinically alone or in combinations such as valsartan/hydrochlorothiazide or in heart-failure regimens, including sacubitril/valsartan. Adverse effects include dizziness, hypotension, fatigue, hyperkalemia, and renal function decline; important toxicities include acute kidney injury, severe hypotension in volume depletion, rare angioedema, and fetotoxicity including fetal renal injury and oligohydramnios, making it contraindicated in pregnancy.

Name: Ramipril
Description: Ramipril (DrugBank DB00178) is a lipophilic dicarboxylate-containing angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor prodrug built on a substituted proline-like bicyclic peptidomimetic framework, specifically a carboxyl-bearing octahydrocyclopenta[b]pyrrole scaffold linked through an amide/ester architecture to an alanine-derived side chain; chemically it is classified as an ACE inhibitor and ester prodrug, while its active metabolite ramiprilat is the corresponding diacid that more tightly coordinates the catalytic zinc in ACE. Its core scaffold and mechanism closely resemble other ACE inhibitors, especially enalapril, perindopril, quinapril, benazepril, trandolapril, and lisinopril, all of which mimic peptide substrates of the renin-angiotensin system. After oral administration ramipril is well absorbed, undergoes significant first-pass hepatic de-esterification to ramiprilat, reaches peak parent concentrations relatively early, and yields a longer-lasting active metabolite with extensive tissue ACE binding, moderate protein binding, renal-predominant elimination, and prolonged terminal pharmacodynamic effect despite multiphasic plasma decline. Its principal target is angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE, kininase II); reduced angiotensin II formation and impaired bradykinin degradation explain both efficacy and adverse effects. Clinically it is used for hypertension, heart failure, post-myocardial infarction risk reduction, and slowing progression of diabetic or non-diabetic nephropathy/proteinuric chronic kidney disease. Common adverse effects include cough, dizziness, hypotension, headache, fatigue, and hyperkalemia; important toxicities include renal function deterioration in renal artery stenosis, angioedema, syncope, and rare severe hypersensitivity. Like other RAAS blockers, it is fetotoxic in pregnancy, causing fetal renal injury, oligohydramnios, skull hypoplasia, and neonatal death, and overdose may produce marked hypotension.

Name: Masoprocol
Description: Masoprocol (DrugBank DB00179), also known as nordihydroguaiaretic acid, is a small-molecule polyphenolic lignan characterized structurally by a symmetric bis-catechol architecture in which two 3,4-dihydroxyphenyl rings are linked through a butane backbone bearing methyl substituents; chemically it belongs to the catechol-containing plant phenols and antioxidant lignans, and its core scaffold is a diarylbutane or bis-aryl aliphatic lignan framework. It is chemically and pharmacologically similar to other redox-active polyphenols and lipoxygenase inhibitors, with partial resemblance to caffeic acid derivatives, curcumin-like phenolics, and topical antineoplastics such as diclofenac in the sense of eicosanoid pathway modulation, though masoprocol is distinguished by its lignan scaffold. Its principal known targets include lipoxygenases, especially 5-lipoxygenase, with downstream suppression of leukotriene synthesis, and it has also been reported to affect epidermal growth factor receptor-linked signaling, cyclooxygenase-related oxidative pathways, and other proliferation-associated proteins in tumor cells. Pharmacokinetically, topical administration produces largely local exposure with limited systemic absorption, distribution expected to favor protein-rich tissues if absorbed, extensive hepatic phase I oxidation and phase II conjugation, and renal plus biliary excretion of metabolites. Toxicity is driven by its catechol redox chemistry and includes contact irritation, inflammation, and potential hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, and pro-oxidant cytotoxicity at higher systemic exposures. It was developed mainly for actinic keratosis, a premalignant UV-induced skin lesion, and clinically used as a topical antikeratotic/antineoplastic agent, though adverse effects such as erythema, burning, pruritus, rash, pain, and local edema limited its tolerability and broader adoption.

Name: Flunisolide
Description: Flunisolide (DrugBank DB00180) is a synthetic fluorinated corticosteroid built on the pregnane steroid nucleus, specifically a glucocorticoid framework with the characteristic four fused rings, a 6α-fluoro substituent, 11β- and 16α-hydroxyl groups, 17α-acetonide-type ketal functionality, and 3- and 20-keto groups that confer potent local anti-inflammatory activity and high glucocorticoid receptor affinity; chemically it is classified as an inhaled and intranasal corticosteroid, with a corticosteroid steroidal scaffold closely related to other anti-inflammatory glucocorticoids such as budesonide, triamcinolone acetonide, beclomethasone, fluticasone, and mometasone. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, through which it alters transcription of inflammatory mediators and suppresses cytokines, eosinophilic inflammation, and arachidonic acid-derived signaling. Pharmacokinetically, flunisolide is administered mainly by inhalation or intranasally, is absorbed across respiratory mucosa with some swallowed fraction, undergoes significant first-pass hepatic metabolism that limits systemic bioavailability from the swallowed portion, distributes primarily locally with moderate plasma protein binding, is metabolized mainly in the liver to less active metabolites, and is excreted predominantly in urine with some fecal elimination. It is indicated for maintenance treatment of asthma and for allergic rhinitis, including seasonal or perennial nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, sneezing, and mucosal inflammation. Adverse effects are largely local, including dysphonia, throat irritation, cough, epistaxis, nasal burning, candidiasis, and headache, while toxicities with excessive or prolonged exposure can include adrenal suppression, hypercortisolism, growth suppression in children, reduced bone density, cataracts, glaucoma, and increased infection risk; clinically it is used as a controller rather than rescue therapy in chronic airway inflammatory disease.

Name: Baclofen
Description: Baclofen (DrugBank DB00181) is a chlorinated aromatic amino acid analogue structurally characterized as β-(4-chlorophenyl)-γ-aminobutyric acid, consisting of a para-chlorophenyl ring attached to a butyric acid chain bearing a terminal primary amine, which places it in the organochlorine, amino acid derivative, and centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant classes; its core scaffold is an aryl-substituted GABA mimic, closely related pharmacologically to other GABAergic antispastic agents and muscle relaxants such as gabapentin, pregabalin, tizanidine, and diazepam, though baclofen is most specifically a GABAB receptor agonist targeting GABBR1 and GABBR2 receptor subunits to reduce excitatory neurotransmitter release and spinal reflex activity. It is used primarily for spasticity associated with multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, cerebral palsy, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and other upper motor neuron syndromes, and is also used intrathecally for severe refractory spasticity; off-label, it has been used for alcohol use disorder, trigeminal neuralgia, and intractable hiccups. Orally, baclofen is reasonably well absorbed, penetrates the CNS incompletely because of limited blood-brain barrier transfer, distributes modestly with relatively low protein binding, undergoes minimal hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by the kidneys, giving it greater toxicity risk in renal impairment. Adverse effects commonly include sedation, dizziness, weakness, fatigue, hypotonia, nausea, and confusion, while serious toxicity can produce encephalopathy, respiratory depression, seizures, coma, and profound hypotonia, especially in overdose, accumulation, or abrupt withdrawal, the latter potentially causing rebound spasticity, hallucinations, hyperthermia, and rhabdomyolysis.

Name: Amphetamine
Description: Amphetamine (DrugBank DB00182) is a small, chiral phenethylamine built on an alpha-methylated phenethylamine core consisting of a benzene ring linked through a two-carbon side chain to a primary amine, with the alpha-methyl substituent increasing lipophilicity, CNS penetration, and resistance to monoamine oxidase; chemically it belongs to the substituted amphetamine and sympathomimetic amine class, and its principal scaffold is the phenethylamine/amphetamine scaffold. Closely related drugs include dextroamphetamine, methamphetamine, lisdexamfetamine, methylphenidate as a mechanistically related stimulant, and other monoaminergic agents such as ephedrine. Its main targets are the plasma membrane monoamine transporters SLC6A3/DAT, SLC6A2/NET, and SLC6A4/SERT, with secondary interaction with VMAT2 and trace amine-associated receptor 1, producing enhanced synaptic release and reduced reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine, and to a lesser extent serotonin. Amphetamine is well absorbed orally, widely distributed, readily crosses the blood-brain barrier, shows pH-dependent renal handling, is hepatically metabolized partly by CYP2D6 and oxidative deamination/aromatic hydroxylation pathways, and is excreted in urine as unchanged drug and metabolites, with urinary acidification increasing clearance. Toxicity reflects excessive sympathomimetic and dopaminergic activity and includes tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, agitation, insomnia, anorexia, arrhythmia, seizures, psychosis, rhabdomyolysis, and dependence or abuse liability, with overdose causing stroke or cardiovascular collapse. Clinically it is used primarily for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and narcolepsy, and historically for exogenous obesity, with therapeutic benefits including improved attention, wakefulness, and impulse control, but adverse effects commonly include dry mouth, weight loss, anxiety, palpitations, and sleep disturbance.

Name: Nicotine
Description: Nicotine (DrugBank DB00184) is a naturally occurring tobacco alkaloid composed of a linked pyridine ring and a saturated five-membered pyrrolidine ring bearing a chiral center, giving a compact, basic, lipophilic heteroaromatic amine structure; chemically it is a plant alkaloid and tertiary amine, and its core scaffold is best described as a pyridyl-pyrrolidine framework. Similar drugs include other nicotinic acetylcholine receptor ligands such as varenicline, cytisine, epibatidine analogs, and the ganglionic agonist lobeline, as well as tobacco-related minor alkaloids like nornicotine and anabasine. Nicotine is rapidly absorbed across buccal, pulmonary, nasal, and transdermal surfaces, with inhaled delivery producing fast brain penetration; distribution is wide, including placental transfer and entry into breast milk; it is metabolized predominantly in the liver by CYP2A6 to cotinine, with additional oxidation and glucuronidation pathways; elimination is mainly renal, with urinary pH influencing clearance. Its principal targets are neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subtypes including CHRNA4/CHRNB2-containing receptors, CHRNA7, and autonomic ganglionic and adrenal medullary nAChRs, driving catecholamine release and central dopaminergic reinforcement. Therapeutically, nicotine is indicated for smoking cessation and relief of tobacco withdrawal symptoms such as craving, irritability, anxiety, and difficulty concentrating, and is used clinically in gums, patches, lozenges, inhalers, and nasal sprays. Common adverse effects include nausea, dyspepsia, hiccups, insomnia, vivid dreams, palpitations, and local irritation depending on formulation. Toxicity reflects cholinergic and sympathomimetic excess, causing vomiting, abdominal pain, hypertension followed by hypotension, tachycardia, seizures, respiratory failure, and potentially fatal poisoning, especially in children after concentrated liquid exposure.

Name: Lorazepam
Description: Lorazepam (DrugBank DB00186) is a 1,4-benzodiazepine anxiolytic-hypnotic characterized structurally by a fused benzene-diazepine ring system bearing a 3-hydroxy group, a 2-keto functionality, and a 5-aryl substituent with ortho-chloro substitution, features that support high affinity allosteric modulation of GABAA receptors; chemically it belongs to the benzodiazepine class, with the classic 1,4-benzodiazepin-2-one scaffold, specifically a 3-hydroxy benzodiazepine scaffold shared with oxazepam and temazepam. Similar drugs include diazepam, clonazepam, alprazolam, midazolam, oxazepam, and temazepam, which share related sedative, anxiolytic, anticonvulsant, and muscle-relaxant properties.
