Its principal target is the benzodiazepine site on pentameric GABAA receptor complexes, especially those containing GABRA1, GABRA2, GABRA3, GABRA5 together with GABRB and GABRG2 subunits, enhancing GABA-mediated chloride conductance. Lorazepam is well absorbed orally, also effective intravenously and intramuscularly, shows moderate protein binding and distribution into the CNS, undergoes minimal oxidative biotransformation and is primarily metabolized by hepatic glucuronidation to inactive lorazepam-glucuronide, which is excreted mainly in urine; this relatively oxidation-independent clearance makes it useful in hepatic impairment compared with some other benzodiazepines. It is indicated for anxiety disorders, acute agitation, insomnia related to anxiety, status epilepticus, alcohol withdrawal, and procedural or preanesthetic sedation. Common adverse effects include sedation, dizziness, ataxia, confusion, anterograde amnesia, and respiratory depression, while toxicity and overdose can cause profound CNS depression, hypotension, coma, and synergistic fatal respiratory suppression with opioids or alcohol; dependence, tolerance, and withdrawal phenomena including rebound anxiety and seizures are important clinical risks.

Name: Esmolol
Description: Esmolol (DB00187) is an ultra-short-acting, cardioselective beta-adrenergic antagonist built on the aryloxypropanolamine beta-blocker pharmacophore, with a para-substituted phenoxypropanolamine core bearing an ester-containing side chain that distinguishes it from longer-acting congeners by conferring rapid hydrolysis; chemically it is classified as an esterified beta1-selective phenoxypropanolamine, and its principal scaffold is the beta-amino alcohol linked through an aryl ether to a propanol backbone. It is structurally and pharmacologically related to other beta blockers such as metoprolol, atenolol, landiolol, propranolol, and acebutolol, with greatest similarity to other short-acting beta1-selective agents like landiolol. Its main targets are the beta1-adrenergic receptor, with weaker activity at beta2-adrenergic receptors at higher concentrations, producing rapid reductions in heart rate, atrioventricular nodal conduction, and myocardial contractility. Administered intravenously because it is intended for acute titratable use, it has immediate onset, a very small effective half-life of about 9 minutes, limited tissue persistence, metabolism predominantly by red-blood-cell esterases to an acid metabolite with much lower activity plus methanol, and renal excretion mainly of metabolites. Toxicity is largely an extension of beta blockade and includes profound bradycardia, hypotension, atrioventricular block, cardiogenic shock, bronchospasm, and worsening heart failure, especially in overdose or in patients with conduction disease or poor ventricular function. Adverse effects include dizziness, nausea, diaphoresis, infusion-site reactions, fatigue, dyspnea, and syncope. Clinically, esmolol is used for rapid control of supraventricular tachycardia, perioperative or emergency tachycardia and hypertension, rate control in atrial fibrillation or flutter, and reduction of sympathetic surges such as during anesthesia, thyrotoxicosis, or aortic dissection management.

Name: Bortezomib
Description: Bortezomib (DrugBank DB00188) is a dipeptidyl boronic acid antineoplastic whose structure consists of a modified hydrophobic dipeptide backbone terminating in a boronic acid warhead, a motif that enables high-affinity yet reversible covalent interaction with the catalytic threonine of the proteasome; chemically it is classified as a boronic acid peptide mimetic and its core scaffold is a pyrazinecarbonyl-leucyl-phenylalanine boronate framework. It is closely related to other proteasome inhibitors, especially ixazomib, another boronic acid inhibitor, and more distantly to epoxyketone-based agents such as carfilzomib. Its principal targets are the 26S proteasome catalytic beta subunits, particularly PSMB5 (beta5, chymotrypsin-like), with activity also affecting PSMB1 and PSMB2, leading to inhibition of ubiquitin-proteasome protein degradation, endoplasmic reticulum stress, and apoptosis in plasma cell malignancies. After intravenous or subcutaneous administration, absorption is complete for IV dosing and high for SC dosing, distribution is extensive with high tissue penetration and strong protein binding, metabolism occurs predominantly via hepatic oxidative deboronation through CYP3A4, CYP2C19, and CYP1A2, and excretion is mainly as metabolites rather than unchanged drug. Major toxicities include dose-limiting peripheral neuropathy, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, hypotension, hepatotoxicity, and occasionally serious cardiac, pulmonary, or posterior reversible encephalopathy events. Common adverse effects include fatigue, nausea, diarrhea or constipation, anorexia, herpes zoster reactivation, and sensory neuropathy. Clinically, bortezomib is used primarily for multiple myeloma and mantle cell lymphoma, for example in induction, relapse, and maintenance-oriented combination regimens such as bortezomib with dexamethasone, lenalidomide, cyclophosphamide, or melphalan.

Name: Ethchlorvynol
Description: Ethchlorvynol (DrugBank DB00189) is a small, highly lipophilic tertiary carbinol sedative-hypnotic whose structure is characterized by an acetylenic alcohol center bearing ethyl and chlorophenyl/vinyl-derived hydrophobic substituents, placing it within the older nonbarbiturate sedative-hypnotic carbinol class; its core scaffold is an acetylenic tertiary alcohol, closely related to other historical sedative-hypnotics such as meprobamate-era nonbarbiturates and especially glutethimide- or chloral-derived alternatives in clinical role, although structurally it is most often compared with other acetylenic carbinols such as ethinamate. Pharmacologically, it acts as a central nervous system depressant, with sedative-hypnotic effects believed to reflect positive modulation of GABAergic neurotransmission at GABAA receptor complexes rather than a single highly selective protein target; specific molecular targets are not as well definitively established as for modern hypnotics. It was indicated for short-term treatment of insomnia, particularly difficulty initiating sleep and transient situational sleeplessness. After oral administration it is well absorbed, widely distributed into lipid-rich tissues including brain, undergoes extensive hepatic oxidative and conjugative metabolism, and is excreted primarily as metabolites in urine, with clinically relevant accumulation and prolonged sedation possible in hepatic dysfunction or repeated dosing. Toxicity is typical of older sedative-hypnotics and includes dose-related respiratory depression, coma, hypotension, psychomotor impairment, and potentially fatal overdose, especially with alcohol, opioids, or other CNS depressants; tolerance, dependence, withdrawal, and abuse liability are well recognized. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, ataxia, confusion, nausea, headache, and hangover sedation. Clinically, it was used as an oral hypnotic for short-course management of insomnia but has largely been abandoned because of safety concerns and the availability of safer benzodiazepine and nonbenzodiazepine alternatives.

Name: Carbidopa
Description: Carbidopa (DB00190) is a peripherally acting aromatic L-amino acid and hydrazine-containing catechol derivative structurally characterized as the (-)-α-hydrazino-3,4-dihydroxy-α-methylbenzenepropanoic acid, featuring a catechol-substituted phenylalanine-like backbone with an α-methylated amino acid center and hydrazino functionality; chemically it belongs to catechols, amino acid analogs, and dopa decarboxylase inhibitors, with a scaffold best described as an α-substituted aromatic amino acid built on a 3,4-dihydroxyphenylpropionic acid framework. It is closely related to other peripheral decarboxylase inhibitors such as benserazide and is functionally paired with levodopa, while sharing mechanistic similarity with central aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase inhibitors. Its principal target is aromatic-L-amino-acid decarboxylase, also known as DOPA decarboxylase (DDC), which it inhibits mainly outside the blood-brain barrier, thereby reducing peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine. Orally administered carbidopa is absorbed variably, has limited penetration into the CNS, low to moderate protein binding, undergoes partial metabolism to inactive metabolites, and is eliminated primarily in urine as unchanged drug and metabolites. Clinically, it is indicated in Parkinson disease and parkinsonian syndromes to enhance levodopa bioavailability, lower required levodopa doses, and reduce peripheral dopaminergic symptoms such as nausea and vomiting. Adverse effects usually reflect combination therapy and include dyskinesia, orthostatic hypotension, nausea, confusion, hallucinations, sleep disturbance, and motor fluctuations. Toxicity is generally lower than with levodopa alone but may include severe dyskinesias, cardiovascular instability, and neuropsychiatric effects in overdose or susceptible patients.

Name: Phentermine
Description: Phentermine (DrugBank DB00191) is a sympathomimetic anorectic built on the substituted phenethylamine/amphetamine framework, structurally characterized as an alpha,alpha-dimethylated phenethylamine bearing a primary amine and a phenyl ring, which places it in the amphetamine-like monoamine-releasing amine class and gives it a simple aryl-alkylamine scaffold closely related to other anorectics and stimulants. Its nearest similar drugs include amphetamine, methamphetamine, diethylpropion, benzphetamine, and phendimetrazine, which share catecholaminergic stimulant or appetite-suppressant properties. Pharmacologically, phentermine acts mainly by increasing synaptic norepinephrine, with lesser effects on dopamine and serotonin, through interaction with monoamine transport systems including SLC6A2, SLC6A3, and to a smaller extent SLC6A4, and indirectly influences adrenergic signaling relevant to appetite suppression. It is indicated as a short-term adjunct to caloric restriction, exercise, and behavioral modification in exogenous obesity, for example in patients with overweight or obesity complicated by cardiometabolic risk factors. After oral administration it is well absorbed, distributed systemically including CNS access, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated largely unchanged in urine, with renal clearance strongly influenced by urinary pH and an elimination half-life typically around 20 hours. Toxicity reflects stimulant excess and abuse potential, with examples including tachycardia, hypertension, agitation, insomnia, tremor, psychosis, and overdose-associated arrhythmia or seizures; common adverse effects include dry mouth, constipation, palpitations, nervousness, and headache. Clinically it is used primarily for short-duration weight management, including fixed-dose combination use with topiramate in chronic obesity treatment.

Name: Tramadol
Description: Tramadol (DrugBank DB00193) is a centrally acting synthetic opioid analgesic of the aminocyclohexanol/phenylpropylamine class, structurally characterized by a substituted cyclohexanol core bearing a 3-methoxyphenyl group and a dimethylaminomethyl substituent, creating a flexible aryl-cyclohexanol scaffold related to atypical opioids rather than the rigid morphinan nucleus; it is most often used as a racemate, with enantiomers contributing differently to activity. Its closest pharmacologic analogs include codeine, tapentadol, oxycodone, hydrocodone, and the active metabolite O-desmethyltramadol, with tapentadol being especially similar as an opioid/noradrenergic analgesic. Tramadol targets the mu-opioid receptor primarily through its M1 metabolite and also inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake via SLC6A4 and SLC6A2-related transporter systems, underpinning its dual analgesic mechanism. It is indicated for moderate to moderately severe pain, including postoperative pain, musculoskeletal pain, neuropathic pain components, osteoarthritis, and chronic low back pain. Orally it is well absorbed, undergoes moderate first-pass metabolism, distributes widely including into the CNS, is metabolized mainly by CYP2D6 to O-desmethyltramadol and by CYP3A4/CYP2B6 to N-desmethyl metabolites, and is eliminated largely renally as parent drug and metabolites, with exposure prolonged in renal or hepatic impairment. Toxicities include dose-related CNS and respiratory depression, seizures, serotonin syndrome, dependence, withdrawal, and fatal overdose risk, especially with alcohol, benzodiazepines, SSRIs, MAO inhibitors, or CYP-interacting drugs. Common adverse effects include nausea, dizziness, constipation, somnolence, vomiting, headache, dry mouth, sweating, and confusion. Clinically, tramadol is used as an oral, immediate-release, extended-release, or parenteral analgesic when nonopioid therapy is inadequate but a full-potency opioid may be unnecessary.

Name: Vidarabine
Description: Vidarabine (adenine arabinoside, ara-A; DrugBank DB00194) is a synthetic purine nucleoside analog in which adenine is linked by a beta-N9-glycosidic bond to D-arabinofuranose rather than ribose or deoxyribose, giving a stereochemically altered 2-hydroxyl configuration that disrupts nucleic acid synthesis; chemically it belongs to the antimetabolite antiviral class, with a purine nucleoside/arabinose scaffold closely related to other arabinosyl nucleosides and broadly similar to acyclovir, ganciclovir, idoxuridine, trifluridine, and especially cytarabine by virtue of the arabinose sugar modification. Its antiviral activity depends on intracellular phosphorylation to ara-ATP, which inhibits viral DNA polymerase and can also interfere with host DNA synthesis; reported relevant targets include herpesvirus DNA polymerases, host kinases that activate it, and to a lesser extent host DNA polymerases. Pharmacokinetically, oral bioavailability is poor, so it has historically been used mainly by intravenous infusion or topical ophthalmic administration; distribution includes ocular tissues and cerebrospinal fluid to some extent, metabolism is rapid and extensive via adenosine deaminase to the less active metabolite arabinosyl hypoxanthine, and elimination is primarily renal as metabolites. Toxicity is largely dose limiting and reflects effects on proliferating tissues and the central nervous system, with examples including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, tremor, ataxia, confusion, hallucinations, seizures, myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity, and local irritation. Clinically, vidarabine was used for serious herpes simplex and varicella-zoster infections, including herpes encephalitis, neonatal HSV, disseminated HSV, and herpetic keratoconjunctivitis, but it has largely been supplanted by safer and more effective antivirals such as acyclovir.

Name: Betaxolol
Description: Betaxolol (DrugBank DB00195) is a cardioselective aryloxypropanolamine beta-adrenergic antagonist whose structure features the classic beta-blocker pharmacophore of an aromatic ring linked through an ether to a secondary alcohol–propylamine side chain, with a para-substituted cyclopropylmethoxy phenyl moiety that contributes lipophilicity and beta1 selectivity; chemically it is a phenoxypropanolamine and more broadly an aryl ether secondary alcohol amine, built on the prototypical aryloxypropanolamine scaffold shared by many beta blockers. Similar drugs include metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, esmolol, and propranolol, although betaxolol is relatively beta1-selective and is also used ophthalmically. Its principal targets are beta1-adrenergic receptor and, with lower affinity, beta2-adrenergic receptor; therapeutic effects derive from reduced cardiac rate and contractility and, in the eye, reduced aqueous humor production. Betaxolol is indicated for hypertension, chronic open-angle glaucoma, and ocular hypertension, with clinical use as oral therapy for blood-pressure control and topical ophthalmic drops to lower intraocular pressure. Oral absorption is generally good, with substantial bioavailability, wide tissue distribution, hepatic metabolism mainly via oxidative pathways including CYP-mediated biotransformation, and renal excretion of metabolites and some unchanged drug; it has a relatively long elimination half-life that supports once-daily systemic dosing. Toxicity resembles other beta blockers: overdose may cause severe bradycardia, hypotension, atrioventricular block, heart failure, dizziness, seizures, or bronchospasm, while adverse effects include fatigue, depression, insomnia, cold extremities, impotence, and in ophthalmic use ocular irritation or discomfort.

Name: Fluconazole
Description: Fluconazole (DrugBank DB00196) is a synthetic bis-triazole antifungal whose structure consists of a difluorophenyl ring linked to a hydroxylated propane backbone bearing two 1,2,4-triazole moieties, giving a relatively small, polar, weakly basic molecule with high aqueous solubility compared with older azoles. It belongs to the triazole antifungal class and is built on an azole-difluorophenyl alcohol scaffold closely related to other sterol biosynthesis inhibitors such as itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, and ketoconazole, with voriconazole being a particularly close structural and mechanistic analog. Its principal target is fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase, a cytochrome P450 enzyme encoded by ERG11/CYP51, leading to impaired ergosterol synthesis and altered fungal membrane integrity; inhibition of human CYP isoenzymes is weaker but clinically relevant for interactions. Fluconazole is well absorbed orally with bioavailability exceeding 90%, food-independent absorption, wide distribution into body fluids and tissues including cerebrospinal fluid, low protein binding, limited hepatic metabolism, and predominantly renal excretion of unchanged drug with a relatively long half-life that supports once-daily dosing. Toxicity is usually mild to moderate but includes hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevation or rare hepatic failure, QT prolongation and torsades risk, rash, and embryo-fetal toxicity at prolonged high doses. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, and reversible liver enzyme abnormalities. Clinically it is used for vulvovaginal candidiasis, oropharyngeal and esophageal candidiasis, candidemia in selected patients, cryptococcal meningitis treatment and suppression, and prophylaxis of fungal infection in immunocompromised hosts such as transplant recipients or patients with HIV/AIDS or chemotherapy-associated neutropenia.

Name: Troglitazone
Description: Troglitazone (DrugBank DB00197) is a synthetic thiazolidinedione antidiabetic characterized structurally by a 2,4-thiazolidinedione ring linked to a substituted chroman/tocol-like lipophilic moiety bearing phenolic and ether functionalities, giving an amphipathic architecture designed to combine the insulin-sensitizing thiazolidinedione pharmacophore with a vitamin E-like scaffold. Chemically it belongs to the glitazone class of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma agonists, with a thiazolidinedione scaffold as the core chemotype; related drugs include pioglitazone and rosiglitazone, and more distantly ciglitazone. Its principal target is PPARG, with lesser reported effects on PPARA and downstream regulation of insulin-responsive genes involved in glucose and lipid metabolism. After oral administration it is absorbed reasonably well, is highly protein bound, distributes extensively to tissues, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 and CYP2C8 to sulfate and glucuronide conjugates and active quinone-type metabolites, and is eliminated predominantly through the biliary-fecal route with minimal renal excretion. It was indicated for type 2 diabetes mellitus to improve glycemic control and insulin resistance, particularly in patients inadequately controlled by diet or other oral agents, and was used clinically as monotherapy or in combination with sulfonylureas, metformin, or insulin. Major toxicities include idiosyncratic severe hepatocellular injury, fulminant hepatic failure, cholestatic hepatitis, oxidative mitochondrial stress, and drug-drug interaction liability through CYP induction or inhibition; common adverse effects included weight gain, edema, anemia, headache, fatigue, and elevated transaminases, with class-related concern for heart failure exacerbation, leading ultimately to withdrawal from many markets.

Name: Oseltamivir
Description: Oseltamivir (DrugBank DB00198) is an orally active ethyl ester prodrug of oseltamivir carboxylate, a synthetic influenza antiviral built on a highly functionalized cyclohexene scaffold bearing a carboxylate bioisostere precursor, an amino group, and a lipophilic pentyl ether side chain that mimics the transition state of sialic acid cleavage; chemically it is classified as a neuraminidase inhibitor and, more broadly, as an esterified amino cyclohexene derivative. Its core scaffold and mechanism are closely related to other anti-influenza neuraminidase inhibitors such as zanamivir, peramivir, and laninamivir, although oseltamivir is distinguished by oral bioavailability. After oral administration it is well absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract and undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic and intestinal ester hydrolysis by carboxylesterase 1 to the active oseltamivir carboxylate; protein binding is low to moderate, distribution reaches respiratory tract secretions, metabolism beyond ester cleavage is limited, and elimination is predominantly renal via glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, with dose adjustment required in renal impairment. Its principal targets are influenza virus neuraminidases from influenza A and B, including N1 and N2 subtype enzymes. Clinically it is indicated for treatment and post-exposure or seasonal prophylaxis of acute uncomplicated influenza, including H1N1 and H3N2 infection, especially when initiated within 48 hours of symptom onset. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and headache, while less common but important toxicities include hypersensitivity reactions, rare hepatotoxicity, and neuropsychiatric events such as delirium or abnormal behavior, particularly reported in pediatric patients. In practice it is used in outpatient and hospitalized settings to shorten symptom duration, reduce viral shedding, and lower the risk of influenza complications in high-risk patients.

Name: Erythromycin
Description: Erythromycin (DrugBank DB00199) is a naturally derived macrolide antibiotic characterized by a 14-membered lactone macrocycle bearing multiple hydroxyl substituents and two deoxy sugars, desosamine and cladinose, a structural motif that defines its erythronolide/macrolide scaffold and confers weakly basic, amphiphilic properties. Chemically it belongs to the macrolide polyketide class; closely related or similar drugs include clarithromycin, azithromycin, roxithromycin, dirithromycin, and to some extent ketolides such as telithromycin, which retain the same ribosomal binding paradigm. Its principal target is the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit, specifically 23S rRNA within the peptidyl transferase/exit tunnel region, where it inhibits translocation and nascent peptide elongation, producing mainly bacteriostatic effects. Erythromycin is indicated for susceptible respiratory tract, skin and soft tissue, and atypical infections, including Streptococcus pyogenes pharyngitis, community-acquired pneumonia due to Mycoplasma pneumoniae or Legionella, pertussis, diphtheria carriage eradication, Campylobacter enteritis, chlamydial infection, and as an alternative in penicillin-allergic patients; it is also used as a prokinetic in gastroparesis via motilin receptor agonism. Oral absorption is formulation dependent and acid labile, distribution is wide with limited CSF penetration, hepatic concentration is substantial, metabolism occurs mainly in the liver with notable CYP3A4 inhibition, and excretion is predominantly biliary with minor renal elimination. Toxicities include dose-related gastrointestinal intolerance, cholestatic hepatitis especially with estolate, QT prolongation and torsades risk, reversible ototoxicity, and important drug-drug interactions increasing exposure to agents such as warfarin, theophylline, carbamazepine, and certain statins. Common adverse effects include nausea, abdominal cramping, diarrhea, vomiting, rash, and transient liver enzyme elevation, and clinically it remains a useful narrow-to-broad spectrum macrolide when susceptibility, allergy status, and interaction risk are carefully considered.

Name: Caffeine
Description: Caffeine (DrugBank DB00201) is a naturally occurring methylxanthine built on a planar purine-like xanthine core, specifically a 1,3,7-trimethyl-substituted 2,6-dioxopurine scaffold, with fused imidazole and pyrimidinedione rings that confer weak basicity, moderate lipophilicity, and facile central nervous system penetration; chemically it belongs to the xanthine alkaloids, and its core scaffold is shared with related methylxanthines such as theophylline and theobromine, while mechanistically similar stimulants include adenosine receptor antagonists and, more distantly, wake-promoting agents. Its principal targets are adenosine receptors ADORA1, ADORA2A, ADORA2B, and ADORA3, with additional pharmacology at phosphodiesterases, ryanodine receptors, and downstream catecholaminergic signaling at higher concentrations. After oral administration it is rapidly and nearly completely absorbed, has high bioavailability, wide distribution including placenta and breast milk, low protein binding, and a typical adult half-life of about 3 to 7 hours; it is extensively metabolized in the liver, primarily by CYP1A2, to paraxanthine, theobromine, and theophylline, then excreted mainly in urine as metabolites. Caffeine is indicated for apnea of prematurity as caffeine citrate and is widely used clinically or symptomatically for neonatal respiratory stimulation, reversal of fatigue or somnolence, and as an adjuvant in headache and migraine analgesic combinations. Common adverse effects include insomnia, tremor, palpitations, anxiety, diuresis, gastroesophageal irritation, and tachycardia, whereas toxicity may produce agitation, severe arrhythmias, vomiting, hypokalemia, seizures, rhabdomyolysis, and rarely death, especially in overdose, rapid ingestion of concentrated products, or in patients with reduced clearance such as neonates, pregnancy, or hepatic impairment.

Name: Sildenafil
Description: Sildenafil (DrugBank DB00203) is a synthetic small-molecule heteroaryl sulfonamide built around a pyrazolo[4,3-d]pyrimidin-7-one core bearing a piperazine substituent and an N-methyl group, with a propyl side chain and an ethoxyphenyl sulfonamide moiety that together confer potent phosphodiesterase binding; chemically it is classified as a PDE5 inhibitor and more broadly as a nitrogen-rich heterocyclic vasodilator, with a pyrazolopyrimidinone scaffold that mimics features of cyclic nucleotide recognition motifs. Closely related drugs include tadalafil, vardenafil, and avanafil, which share PDE5-directed activity but differ in core scaffold and pharmacokinetic behavior. Sildenafil is orally absorbed with moderate bioavailability of about 40%, reaches peak plasma concentrations in roughly 0.5-2 hours, is distributed widely with high plasma protein binding, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism predominantly by CYP3A4 and secondarily CYP2C9 to an active N-desmethyl metabolite, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in feces with lesser renal excretion. Its principal target is phosphodiesterase type 5, with weaker activity at PDE6 that helps explain visual adverse effects. Clinically it is indicated for erectile dysfunction and pulmonary arterial hypertension, improving penile erection and exercise capacity or hemodynamics in PAH. Common adverse effects include headache, flushing, dyspepsia, nasal congestion, dizziness, and visual color tinge; serious toxicities include symptomatic hypotension, syncope, priapism, rare non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, sudden hearing loss, and cardiovascular events in susceptible patients, especially with nitrate coadministration, which is contraindicated due to profound blood pressure reduction.

Name: Dofetilide
Description: Dofetilide (DB00204) is a synthetic class III antiarrhythmic built on a methanesulfonanilide framework, with a diaryl-substituted aromatic core linked through ether-containing alkyl chains to a tertiary sulfonamide/amine-containing motif; structurally it is best described as a sulfonanilide potassium-channel blocker with an aryl ether scaffold related to other IKr inhibitors. Its closest pharmacologic analogs include ibutilide, sotalol, and the withdrawn methanesulfonanilide dofetilide-like agents sematilide and d-sotalol, although dofetilide is comparatively more selective for the rapid delayed rectifier potassium current. The principal target is the cardiac hERG potassium channel encoded by KCNH2, mediating blockade of IKr and prolongation of action potential duration and effective refractory period with minimal effect on conduction velocity. Orally administered dofetilide is well absorbed with high bioavailability, low to moderate protein binding, distribution into total body water, limited hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4, and predominant renal elimination of unchanged drug through glomerular filtration and active tubular cationic secretion, making clearance highly dependent on kidney function and susceptible to transporter- or CYP3A4-mediated interactions. Its major toxicity is dose-related QT prolongation leading to torsades de pointes and syncope, especially with renal impairment, hypokalemia, bradycardia, baseline long QT, or coadministration with verapamil, cimetidine, ketoconazole, trimethoprim, hydrochlorothiazide, or other QT-prolonging drugs. Indications and clinical use center on conversion and maintenance of sinus rhythm in highly symptomatic atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter, including persistent AF, with inpatient initiation and ECG/creatinine-clearance-guided dosing. Common adverse effects include dizziness, headache, chest pain, dyspnea, and ventricular arrhythmia.

Name: Pyrimethamine
Description: Pyrimethamine (DrugBank DB00205) is a synthetic diaminopyrimidine antifolate built around a 2,4-diaminopyrimidine ring bearing a para-chlorophenyl substituent and an ethyl side chain, placing it in the aromatic heterocyclic antifolate class and defining its core scaffold as a chlorophenyl-substituted diaminopyrimidine, closely related to other dihydrofolate reductase inhibitors such as trimethoprim, cycloguanil, and to some extent proguanil-derived metabolites. Its principal target is protozoal dihydrofolate reductase, particularly in Toxoplasma gondii and Plasmodium species, with weaker activity on human DHFR accounting for dose-limiting toxicity. Orally administered pyrimethamine is generally well absorbed, widely distributed including into tissues and the CNS, highly protein bound, slowly metabolized hepatically, and eliminated gradually in urine, with a long half-life that supports intermittent dosing but also favors accumulation. It is indicated mainly for toxoplasmosis, including cerebral toxoplasmosis in immunocompromised patients, and for malaria in combination regimens, classically with sulfadoxine, because sequential folate-pathway blockade improves antiparasitic efficacy. Clinically it is used with sulfadiazine plus leucovorin for toxoplasmic encephalitis, congenital toxoplasmosis, and ocular toxoplasmosis, and historically for chloroquine-resistant falciparum malaria. Toxicity is dominated by folate deficiency-related bone marrow suppression, including megaloblastic anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia, with risk increased at high doses or without folinic acid rescue; gastrointestinal upset, glossitis, rash, headache, dizziness, and rarely severe cutaneous reactions or hepatotoxicity may occur. Common adverse effects therefore include nausea, vomiting, anorexia, and hematologic suppression, making blood count monitoring and leucovorin coadministration central to safe use.

Name: Reserpine
Description: Reserpine (DrugBank DB00206) is a naturally derived indole alkaloid of the Rauwolfia alkaloid class, structurally characterized as a highly oxygenated yohimban/ajmalan-type pentacyclic monoterpenoid indole framework bearing a trimethoxybenzoyl ester and multiple fused stereochemically defined rings that create a rigid lipophilic scaffold typical of VMAT-binding alkaloids; its chemical category is therefore an esterified indole alkaloid, and its core scaffold is the polycyclic yohimbine-like monoterpenoid indole nucleus. Closely related or mechanistically similar drugs include rescinnamine and deserpidine, with tetrabenazine and deutetrabenazine representing nonindole VMAT inhibitors of similar pharmacologic effect. Reserpine is generally well absorbed orally, widely distributed including into the central nervous system, strongly tissue bound, slowly metabolized mainly by ester hydrolysis and hepatic biotransformation, and eliminated gradually in urine and feces, with prolonged pharmacodynamic effects because vesicular monoamine depletion persists beyond plasma clearance. Its principal target is vesicular monoamine transporter 2, and less selectively VMAT1, causing irreversible or quasi-irreversible depletion of norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin from presynaptic vesicles. Historically it has been indicated for hypertension and, less commonly, psychotic agitation or refractory hyperadrenergic states; clinical use includes low-dose adjunctive antihypertensive therapy and rare use in older antipsychotic regimens. Toxicity reflects excessive monoamine depletion and includes severe depression, suicidality, parkinsonism, profound sedation, bradycardia, hypotension, nasal congestion, diarrhea, peptic ulcer exacerbation, and sexual dysfunction; overdose may produce respiratory depression, hypothermia, and cardiovascular collapse. Common side effects include fatigue, dizziness, orthostasis, gastrointestinal hypermotility, and depressive symptoms, which have markedly limited modern use.

Name: Azithromycin
Description: Azithromycin (DrugBank DB00207) is a semisynthetic azalide macrolide antibiotic structurally derived from erythromycin, characterized by a large 15-membered lactone macrocycle containing a methyl-substituted nitrogen inserted into the ring and glycosidically linked deoxy sugars, a modification that improves acid stability and tissue penetration relative to earlier macrolides. Chemically it belongs to the macrolide/azalide class and is built on the erythromycin-like macrolactone scaffold; closely related drugs include erythromycin, clarithromycin, roxithromycin, and other ribosome-targeting macrolides such as telithromycin. Its principal target is the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit, especially 23S rRNA within the peptidyl transferase/nascent peptide exit tunnel region, where it inhibits translocation and protein synthesis; resistance-associated target-related proteins include Erm methyltransferases and efflux determinants such as MefA. Pharmacokinetically, oral absorption is moderate, bioavailability is reduced by some aluminum- or magnesium-containing antacids, distribution is extensive with very high intracellular and tissue concentrations and a long terminal half-life, metabolism is limited compared with erythromycin, and elimination occurs predominantly as unchanged drug in bile with a smaller renal component. Toxicity is usually mild but includes dose-related gastrointestinal intolerance, hepatotoxicity including cholestatic hepatitis, QT-interval prolongation with risk of torsades de pointes, reversible hearing impairment, and rare hypersensitivity or severe cutaneous reactions. It is indicated for susceptible respiratory, skin and soft-tissue, and sexually transmitted infections, including community-acquired pneumonia, streptococcal pharyngitis in penicillin-allergic patients, acute bacterial sinusitis, COPD exacerbations, chlamydial urethritis/cervicitis, chancroid, and Mycobacterium avium complex treatment or prophylaxis, and is widely used clinically in short-course outpatient regimens because of convenient once-daily dosing and durable tissue exposure.

Name: Trospium
Description: Trospium (DrugBank DB00209) is a synthetic quaternary ammonium antimuscarinic built on a rigid tropane-like nortropane bicyclic scaffold esterified to a substituted aromatic alcohol moiety, giving a permanently charged, highly polar cationic structure that limits passive membrane penetration and blood-brain barrier entry; chemically it is classified as a quaternary ammonium anticholinergic/urinary antispasmodic, with a scaffold and pharmacology related to other bladder antimuscarinics such as oxybutynin, tolterodine, fesoterodine, darifenacin, solifenacin, and propiverine, although trospium is distinguished by its cationic tropanium character. Its principal targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially M1, M2, and functionally M3 receptors in bladder smooth muscle, where competitive antagonism reduces parasympathetic detrusor contraction. Clinically it is indicated for overactive bladder with urge urinary incontinence, urgency, and frequency, and is also used in some patients with neurogenic detrusor overactivity. Oral absorption is low and variable because of poor permeability, food reduces bioavailability, distribution is limited with relatively low CNS exposure, protein binding is moderate, metabolism is modest and not heavily CYP-dependent, and elimination is predominantly renal with a substantial fraction excreted unchanged, so exposure rises in renal impairment. Dose-limiting toxicity reflects exaggerated anticholinergic effects, including severe xerostomia, constipation, urinary retention, tachycardia, blurred vision, heat intolerance, and rarely ileus or precipitation of narrow-angle glaucoma; adverse effects commonly include dry mouth, constipation, dyspepsia, headache, and urinary hesitation. In practice, trospium is used as a non-CNS-penetrant antimuscarinic option when minimizing cognitive adverse effects is clinically desirable, particularly in older adults or polypharmacy settings.

Name: Pantoprazole
Description: Pantoprazole (DrugBank DB00213) is a substituted benzimidazole proton-pump inhibitor characterized structurally by a 5-difluoromethoxy-substituted benzimidazole linked through a sulfinyl bridge to a dimethoxy-substituted pyridine ring; this acid-labile heteroaromatic sulfoxide defines its chemical category as a benzimidazole PPI and its core scaffold as the pyridylmethyl-sulfinyl-benzimidazole framework shared across the class. Closely related drugs include omeprazole, esomeprazole, lansoprazole, rabeprazole, and dexlansoprazole, which differ mainly in ring substitution patterns but act similarly. Pantoprazole is absorbed in the small intestine after enteric delivery, reaches peak plasma concentrations in about 2-3 hours, is highly protein bound, accumulates functionally in the acidic secretory canaliculi of gastric parietal cells, and is extensively metabolized hepatically, primarily by CYP2C19 and CYP3A4, to inactive metabolites excreted mainly in urine with lesser fecal elimination; its plasma half-life is short, but antisecretory action is prolonged because it covalently and irreversibly inhibits the gastric H+/K+-ATPase alpha subunit ATP4A, functionally associated with ATP4B. Indications include gastroesophageal reflux disease, erosive esophagitis, peptic ulcer disease, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, and prevention or treatment of NSAID-associated acid injury, including use in Helicobacter pylori eradication regimens. Adverse effects commonly include headache, diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, and flatulence, while toxicities of concern with prolonged use include hypomagnesemia, vitamin B12 deficiency, fracture risk, acute interstitial nephritis, Clostridioides difficile infection, and rare cutaneous or hepatic hypersensitivity; overdose is usually limited by a relatively wide therapeutic index, with supportive management used clinically in oral and intravenous acid-suppression settings.

Name: Torasemide
Description: Torasemide (DrugBank DB00214) is a pyridine-sulfonylurea loop diuretic characterized structurally by a substituted pyridine ring linked through a sulfonylurea bridge to an arylamine-containing moiety, giving an amphipathic, weakly acidic small molecule optimized for renal tubular secretion and activity in the thick ascending limb; chemically it belongs to the sulfonylurea-containing high-ceiling diuretics and is often described as having a heteroaryl sulfonylurea scaffold. It is pharmacologically similar to other loop diuretics such as furosemide, bumetanide, and ethacrynic acid, though torasemide is generally more potent than furosemide on a milligram basis and has more predictable oral bioavailability. Its principal target is the renal Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter NKCC2, encoded by SLC12A1, with diuretic action dependent on access to the luminal transporter after proximal tubular secretion. Oral absorption is usually rapid and high, bioavailability is relatively consistent, protein binding is extensive, distribution volume is modest, hepatic metabolism occurs mainly via CYP2C9 to inactive or weakly active metabolites, and elimination is by both renal excretion of unchanged drug and metabolites and biliary/fecal routes, with a duration often longer than furosemide. Toxicity is chiefly an extension of pharmacology, including dehydration, hypovolemia, hypotension, prerenal azotemia, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, hyperuricemia, and less commonly ototoxicity or sulfonamide-associated hypersensitivity. Clinically it is used to treat edema associated with heart failure, renal disease, and hepatic cirrhosis, and also hypertension; common adverse effects include polyuria, dizziness, headache, muscle cramps, electrolyte disturbances, and orthostatic symptoms, while routine use includes outpatient or inpatient volume management, adjunctive antihypertensive therapy, and diuretic treatment of refractory fluid overload.

Name: Citalopram
Description: Citalopram (DrugBank DB00215) is a bicyclic phthalane derivative antidepressant structurally characterized by a 1,3-dihydroisobenzofuran scaffold bearing a 4-fluorophenyl group and a dimethylaminopropyl side chain with a nitrile substituent, features that confer high affinity for monoamine transport proteins; chemically it is classified as a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and more broadly as an arylalkylamine antidepressant, with a phthalane/isobenzofuran core scaffold. Closely related drugs include escitalopram, its therapeutically active S-enantiomer, and other SSRIs such as fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine, and fluvoxamine, which share serotonin transporter inhibition as the dominant mechanism. Its principal target is the serotonin transporter SLC6A4, with relatively weak activity at norepinephrine and dopamine transporters and minimal direct affinity for many receptor systems compared with tricyclic antidepressants. Citalopram is well absorbed orally, has moderate bioavailability, extensive tissue distribution, substantial protein binding, and a long elimination half-life that supports once-daily dosing; it undergoes hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP2C19, CYP3A4, and CYP2D6 to demethylated metabolites, followed by renal and fecal excretion. It is indicated primarily for major depressive disorder and is also used in anxiety-spectrum conditions such as panic disorder, generalized anxiety symptoms, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, and sometimes off-label for premenstrual dysphoric symptoms. Common adverse effects include nausea, dry mouth, somnolence, insomnia, sweating, tremor, sexual dysfunction, and headache. Important toxicities include dose-dependent QT prolongation, serotonin syndrome, hyponatremia from SIADH, bleeding risk, and overdose manifestations such as CNS depression, tachycardia, and arrhythmia; clinically it is used as a first-line SSRI in adults when a relatively selective serotonergic antidepressant with favorable tolerability is desired.

Name: Moxifloxacin
Description: Moxifloxacin (DrugBank DB00218) is a fourth-generation fluoroquinolone antibacterial built on a 4-quinolone-3-carboxylic acid scaffold bearing the class-defining C6 fluorine, a C7 diazabicyclonyl substituent, and an 8-methoxy group that broadens Gram-positive and anaerobic activity while reducing some resistance liability; chemically it belongs to the fluoroquinolone/carboxyquinolone class, with close structural and pharmacologic analogs including levofloxacin, ciprofloxacin, gemifloxacin, gatifloxacin, and delafloxacin. Its principal targets are bacterial DNA gyrase, composed of GyrA and GyrB, and topoisomerase IV, composed of ParC and ParE, whose inhibition blocks DNA supercoiling and segregation, producing rapid bactericidal activity. After oral administration it is well absorbed with high bioavailability, low sensitivity to food, wide tissue distribution including lung, sinus, skin, and epithelial lining fluid, moderate protein binding, limited CYP-mediated metabolism, phase II biotransformation mainly to inactive sulfate and glucuronide conjugates, and elimination through both renal and biliary/fecal routes with a terminal half-life supporting once-daily dosing. Toxicities include concentration-related QT interval prolongation with torsades risk, hepatotoxicity including rare fulminant liver injury, dysglycemia, CNS effects, peripheral neuropathy, and class-associated tendinopathy or tendon rupture, with heightened concern in older adults and corticosteroid users. Common adverse effects are nausea, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, rash, and transaminase elevation. Clinically it is used for community-acquired pneumonia, acute bacterial sinusitis, acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, complicated skin and skin-structure infections, complicated intra-abdominal infections in combination regimens, and some multidrug-resistant tuberculosis settings when alternative agents are needed.

Name: Nelfinavir
Description: Nelfinavir (DrugBank DB00220) is an orally active HIV protease inhibitor built on a peptidomimetic hydroxyethylamine core that mimics the tetrahedral transition state of peptide cleavage; structurally it contains a central secondary alcohol, amide and sulfonamide functionalities, and lipophilic aromatic/heteroaromatic substituents that confer high affinity for the viral aspartyl protease. Chemically, it is classified as an antiretroviral peptidomimetic protease inhibitor, with a hydroxyethylamine protease-inhibitor scaffold closely related to other first-generation HIV protease inhibitors such as saquinavir, indinavir, ritonavir, amprenavir, and lopinavir. Its principal target is HIV-1 protease, with activity also against HIV-2 protease, thereby preventing gag-pol polyprotein cleavage and formation of mature infectious virions. After oral administration, absorption is improved with food; the drug is highly protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A and CYP2C19 to several metabolites including the active M8 hydroxyl-tert-butylamide metabolite, and is eliminated predominantly in feces with limited renal excretion. Toxicity is dominated by gastrointestinal and metabolic effects, including dose-limiting diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevations, rash, hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, lipodystrophy, and hyperlipidemia; overdose or interacting CYP3A inhibitors/inducers can increase systemic toxicity. Clinically, nelfinavir was used in combination antiretroviral therapy for HIV-1 infection, including adults, children, and prevention of progression to AIDS-related immunodeficiency, but its use has declined because of pill burden, resistance, and newer better-tolerated agents.

Name: Diflorasone
Description: Diflorasone (DrugBank DB00223) is a highly potent fluorinated synthetic corticosteroid used topically; structurally it is a pregnane-based glucocorticoid built on the steroidal cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene nucleus, bearing the characteristic 3-keto-4-ene A-ring, 11β- and 17β-hydroxyl functionality, a 20-ketone, and halogen substitution including fluorine and chlorine that increase lipophilicity and anti-inflammatory potency, with the clinically used form commonly formulated as the diacetate ester. Chemically it belongs to halogenated corticosteroids, specifically topical glucocorticoids, and its core scaffold is the corticosteroid/pregnane steroid scaffold closely related to diflucortolone, fluocinonide, betamethasone, clobetasol, and fluocinolone derivatives. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor encoded by NR3C1, with downstream transrepression of NF-κB- and AP-1-driven inflammatory gene expression and reduced cytokine, prostaglandin, and leukotriene signaling. After topical administration, absorption depends on formulation, skin integrity, occlusion, and body site; systemic uptake is usually limited on intact skin but increases on inflamed, denuded, or intertriginous areas, after which the drug distributes like other corticosteroids, undergoes primarily hepatic biotransformation including ester hydrolysis and oxidative/reductive metabolism, and is eliminated as metabolites in urine and bile. Indications include corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses such as eczema, atopic dermatitis, contact dermatitis, seborrheic dermatitis, lichen simplex chronicus, and localized plaque psoriasis. Adverse effects include burning, irritation, dryness, folliculitis, acneiform eruption, striae, telangiectasia, skin atrophy, hypopigmentation, and delayed wound healing; excessive or prolonged exposure can cause HPA-axis suppression, hyperglycemia, Cushingoid features, and growth suppression in children, illustrating its local and systemic corticosteroid toxicity profile in clinical use.

Name: Indinavir
Description: Indinavir (DrugBank DB00224) is a synthetic peptidomimetic HIV protease inhibitor built around a hydroxyethylamine/hydroxyaminopentane transition-state-mimetic core that imitates the tetrahedral intermediate of peptide bond cleavage; structurally it is a highly functionalized polyheteroatom small molecule containing secondary alcohol, amide-like, amine, and aromatic/heterocyclic features that confer potent active-site binding to aspartyl proteases. Chemically it belongs to the antiretroviral protease inhibitor class, and its central scaffold is the hydroxyethylamine peptidomimetic motif seen across early HIV protease inhibitors; related drugs include ritonavir, saquinavir, nelfinavir, amprenavir, lopinavir, and atazanavir. Its principal target is the HIV-1 protease, with activity also against HIV-2 protease, thereby preventing gag-pol polyprotein processing and formation of mature infectious virions. Indinavir is orally active, absorbed relatively rapidly, shows moderate bioavailability with food effects, is extensively hepatically metabolized mainly by CYP3A4, exhibits substantial first-pass metabolism, moderate protein binding, a short elimination half-life requiring boosted or frequent dosing, and is excreted largely as metabolites in feces and urine with a smaller fraction unchanged renally. Toxicity is notable for nephrolithiasis, crystalluria, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, hepatotoxicity, metabolic disturbances such as insulin resistance and hyperglycemia, and lipodystrophy; overdose or interaction-mediated exposure increases risk of jaundice and renal complications. Common adverse effects include nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, headache, rash, dry skin, dizziness, asthenia, and flank pain. Clinically, it has been used in combination antiretroviral therapy for HIV-1 infection, including treatment of symptomatic AIDS, reduction of viral load, and delay of disease progression, often with nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitors or ritonavir boosting.

Name: Guanadrel
Description: Guanadrel (DrugBank DB00226) is a peripherally acting adrenergic neuron-blocking antihypertensive whose structure is characterized by a highly polar guanidinium-containing amine attached to a saturated cyclic hydrocarbon framework, giving it a strongly basic cationic center and limited membrane permeability; chemically it belongs to the aliphatic/cycloaliphatic guanidine class, and its core scaffold is a guanidine-substituted cycloalkylalkyl amine motif closely related to other postganglionic sympathetic inhibitors such as guanethidine and, more distantly, bethanidine and debrisoquine. Its pharmacologic effect depends on uptake into peripheral sympathetic nerve terminals primarily via the norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, followed by intraneuronal accumulation in storage granules through vesicular monoamine transport processes and progressive depletion or inhibition of norepinephrine release, with functional involvement of adrenergic pathways rather than a classic receptor antagonist mechanism; therefore known target-associated proteins include SLC6A2 and indirectly vesicular monoamine transporters and peripheral adrenergic neurons. Guanadrel is administered orally for hypertension, especially moderate to severe essential hypertension, historically when sympathetic suppression was desired. Absorption is oral but variable, distribution is largely peripheral with poor CNS penetration, metabolism is limited, and elimination is predominantly renal as unchanged drug, so duration may be prolonged in renal impairment. Toxicity is mainly an extension of sympatholysis, including marked orthostatic hypotension, exercise intolerance, diarrhea, nasal congestion, bradycardia, fluid retention, and impaired ejaculation; overdose may produce severe hypotension and syncope. Clinically, it was used as a second-line antihypertensive, often with a diuretic to counter sodium and water retention, but its use declined because of troublesome autonomic adverse effects.

Name: Lovastatin
Description: Lovastatin (DrugBank DB00227) is a naturally derived statin and fungal polyketide lactone characterized structurally as a lipophilic hexahydronaphthalene-containing prodrug with a substituted decalin core esterified to a methylbutyrate side chain and a closed beta-hydroxy acid lactone ring that is hydrolyzed in vivo to the active hydroxy acid; chemically it belongs to the HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor class, with a compact decalin-based statin scaffold shared with other type 1 natural-product statins. Closely related drugs include simvastatin, pravastatin, and mevastatin, while atorvastatin and fluvastatin are more distant synthetic analogs with the same therapeutic mechanism. Its principal target is 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase (HMGCR), producing reduced hepatic cholesterol synthesis, upregulation of LDL receptors, and lowering of LDL cholesterol and, to a lesser extent, triglycerides. Lovastatin is indicated for primary hypercholesterolemia, mixed dyslipidemia, and prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease such as myocardial infarction and stroke risk reduction in selected patients. Orally administered lovastatin is better absorbed with food, undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic extraction, is highly protein bound, is metabolized mainly by CYP3A4 to active and inactive metabolites, and is excreted predominantly in feces with lesser renal elimination. Major toxicities include dose-related hepatotoxicity and myopathy ranging from myalgias to rhabdomyolysis, especially with CYP3A4 inhibitors, cyclosporine, macrolides, azole antifungals, or grapefruit juice; adverse effects also include abdominal pain, dyspepsia, constipation, headache, transaminase elevations, and rare immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy. Clinically, it is used as adjunctive therapy to diet and lifestyle modification in outpatient lipid management and long-term cardiovascular risk reduction.

Name: Pregabalin
Description: Pregabalin (DrugBank DB00230) is a small, highly polar γ-aminobutyric acid analog built on an aliphatic amino acid-like framework, structurally characterized as an isobutyl-substituted GABA mimic with a flexible saturated carbon chain bearing a primary amine and a carboxylic acid; chemically it is classified as a gabapentinoid and more broadly as a substituted amino acid, with a simple acyclic GABA-related scaffold rather than a heteroaromatic core. It is closely related to gabapentin and is sometimes compared pharmacologically with mirogabalin, although pregabalin has distinct potency and pharmacokinetic properties. Its principal molecular target is the α2δ auxiliary subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, especially CACNA2D1 and CACNA2D2, through which it reduces presynaptic calcium influx and decreases release of excitatory neurotransmitters; it does not meaningfully act as a direct GABA receptor agonist. Pregabalin is rapidly and extensively absorbed orally with high bioavailability, low protein binding, broad distribution into total body water, minimal metabolism, and predominantly renal excretion as unchanged drug, with elimination closely tied to kidney function. Toxicity is usually dominated by dose-related CNS depression, dizziness, somnolence, ataxia, blurred vision, and cognitive slowing, with overdose often causing sedation and confusion; peripheral edema, weight gain, misuse liability, and respiratory depression can occur, particularly with opioids or other sedatives. Clinically it is used for neuropathic pain states such as diabetic peripheral neuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia, and spinal cord injury-related pain, as adjunctive therapy for partial seizures, for fibromyalgia, and in some regions for generalized anxiety disorder.

Name: Temazepam
Description: Temazepam (DrugBank DB00231) is a 3-hydroxylated 1,4-benzodiazepine whose structure consists of a fused benzene and seven-membered diazepine ring bearing a 2-keto group, a 5-phenyl substituent, a 7-chloro substituent, and a hydroxyl group at C3; chemically it is a benzodiazepine anxiolytic-sedative/hypnotic, and its core scaffold is the classical 1,4-benzodiazepin-2-one nucleus. It is closely related to other benzodiazepines, particularly oxazepam and diazepam, and shares pharmacologic similarity with nitrazepam, lorazepam, and triazolam as positive allosteric modulators of GABAA receptors, acting at the benzodiazepine site on receptor complexes containing subunits such as GABRA1, GABRA2, GABRA3, GABRA5, GABRB2, and GABRG2. Temazepam is used primarily for the short-term treatment of insomnia, especially sleep-onset difficulty and nocturnal awakenings, and has also been used as a nighttime sedative in severely agitated or anxious patients. After oral administration it is well absorbed, reaches peak plasma concentrations within a few hours, is moderately protein bound, distributes into the CNS, undergoes minimal oxidative biotransformation compared with many benzodiazepines, and is cleared mainly by hepatic conjugation to glucuronides followed by renal excretion; its elimination half-life is generally intermediate, supporting bedtime dosing. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related CNS and respiratory depression, psychomotor impairment, falls, confusion, and overdose risk that is heightened by alcohol, opioids, or other sedatives; side effects commonly include daytime drowsiness, dizziness, ataxia, anterograde amnesia, headache, tolerance, dependence, rebound insomnia, and withdrawal symptoms including anxiety or seizures after abrupt discontinuation.

Name: Methyclothiazide
Description: Methyclothiazide (DrugBank DB00232) is a thiazide diuretic characterized structurally by a chlorinated benzothiadiazine 1,1-dioxide core bearing sulfonamide functionality and a 3-methyl substituent, a compact heteroaromatic sulfonamide architecture that confers weak acidity and renal tubular activity; chemically it belongs to the benzothiadiazine sulfonamide class, and its defining scaffold is the 1,2,4-benzothiadiazine ring system shared with classic thiazides. Closely related drugs include hydrochlorothiazide, chlorothiazide, bendroflumethiazide, polythiazide, and hydroflumethiazide, which have similar saluretic mechanisms and structure-activity relationships. Its principal target is the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter SLC12A3 in the distal convoluted tubule, leading to increased urinary sodium and chloride excretion with secondary potassium and magnesium loss and reduced calcium excretion. After oral administration, methyclothiazide is absorbed adequately, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid with limited tissue accumulation, shows little clinically important biotransformation, and is eliminated predominantly by the kidney as unchanged drug, with a relatively prolonged duration of action compared with some older thiazides. It is indicated for hypertension and edema, including edema associated with congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, corticosteroid or estrogen therapy, and some renal disorders. Adverse effects and toxicity reflect excessive diuresis and electrolyte depletion, including hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, dehydration, orthostatic hypotension, hyperuricemia precipitating gout, hyperglycemia, rash, photosensitivity, and rare sulfonamide hypersensitivity; severe overdose may cause profound volume depletion, weakness, arrhythmia, or confusion. Clinically, it has been used as an oral antihypertensive and adjunct diuretic, often in patients needing chronic blood pressure control or mobilization of mild to moderate fluid retention.

Name: Aminosalicylic acid
Description: Aminosalicylic acid, DrugBank DB00233, usually referring to para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS), is a small aromatic aminophenol-carboxylic acid characterized by a benzoic acid ring bearing an amino substituent para to the carboxyl group and a hydroxyl group ortho to the amino group; chemically it is an aminosalicylate, a salicylic acid derivative, and more broadly an aromatic carboxylic acid with a simple substituted benzenoid scaffold. It is structurally related to salicylic acid and resembles folate-pathway antimetabolites, with similarity to sulfonamides and to other salicylates such as mesalamine and acetylsalicylic acid in scaffold class, though its antimycobacterial role is distinct. PAS is used primarily as a second-line antitubercular agent for multidrug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis, historically also in combination regimens for resistant pulmonary and extrapulmonary tuberculosis. Its best supported target is dihydropteroate synthase in the folate biosynthetic pathway, and it may also act through incorporation into folate intermediates affecting dihydrofolate synthase/folC-dependent metabolism. Orally administered PAS is absorbed variably from the gastrointestinal tract, distributed systemically with limited CNS penetration unless meninges are inflamed, extensively acetylated in the liver and intestinal mucosa to inactive metabolites, and excreted mainly in urine as parent drug and acetylated products, with a relatively short half-life requiring divided dosing. Toxicity is dominated by dose-limiting gastrointestinal intolerance, hepatotoxicity including hepatitis, hypersensitivity reactions, malabsorption, hypothyroidism especially with ethionamide, and occasional crystalluria or hemolytic complications. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, fever, rash, arthralgia, and elevated liver enzymes; clinically it is reserved for combination treatment of drug-resistant tuberculosis when first-line agents cannot be used or are ineffective.

Name: Reboxetine
Description: Reboxetine (DrugBank DB00234) is a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor built on an aryloxy-benzyl morpholine framework, structurally characterized by a substituted phenoxy ring linked through a chiral benzylic center and propoxy chain to a morpholine heterocycle; chemically it is an aryl ether, morpholine-containing antidepressant and belongs to the phenoxypropylamine-related norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor class, with a scaffold closely related to other NRIs such as atomoxetine and, more broadly, to dual reuptake inhibitors like viloxazine and duloxetine in pharmacologic behavior. Its principal target is the norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, with minimal activity at serotonin and dopamine transporters relative to classical tricyclics. Reboxetine is used primarily for major depressive disorder, particularly presentations marked by psychomotor retardation, low energy, and impaired concentration, and has also been used off-label in disorders such as panic disorder, ADHD, and treatment-resistant depression as an augmenting agent. It is well absorbed orally, has good systemic bioavailability, distributes widely with moderate protein binding, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 to less active metabolites, and is eliminated predominantly in urine with a terminal half-life supporting twice-daily or once-daily dosing in some patients. Adverse effects reflect noradrenergic excess and include dry mouth, insomnia, sweating, tachycardia, constipation, urinary hesitation, anorexia, and dizziness. Toxicity is generally less cardiotoxic than tricyclic antidepressants but may include hypertension, agitation, seizures in overdose, and worsening suicidality or mood instability in susceptible patients, with caution warranted in hepatic impairment, glaucoma, urinary retention, and concomitant CYP3A4 inhibitor exposure.

Name: Milrinone
Description: Milrinone (DrugBank DB00235) is a bipyridine-derived cardiotonic agent whose structure is centered on a substituted 2-pyridone ring system, specifically a 1,6-dihydro-2-methyl-6-oxo-[3,4-bipyridine]-5-carbonitrile framework, giving it a planar, heteroaromatic nitrogen-containing scaffold with a nitrile substituent and lactam-like carbonyl that are important for phosphodiesterase binding; chemically it is classified as a phosphodiesterase-3 inhibiting inodilator and more broadly as a bipyridine/pyridone nitrile heterocycle. Its core scaffold and pharmacology are closely related to other PDE3 inhibitors such as inamrinone (amrinone), enoximone, and cilostazol, although milrinone is used primarily for cardiac rather than antiplatelet or peripheral vascular indications. Its principal targets are phosphodiesterase 3A and 3B, with inhibition increasing intracellular cAMP in cardiomyocytes and vascular smooth muscle, thereby producing positive inotropy, lusitropy, and vasodilation. Milrinone is administered intravenously, with essentially complete systemic availability by that route, rapid onset, low-to-moderate protein binding, distribution largely in extracellular fluid, minimal hepatic metabolism, and predominant renal excretion of unchanged drug, so clearance is substantially prolonged in renal impairment. Clinically it is indicated for short-term management of acute decompensated heart failure, low-output states after cardiac surgery, and cardiogenic shock in selected settings. Major toxicities and adverse effects include dose-related ventricular and supraventricular arrhythmias, hypotension, headache, tachycardia, thrombocytopenia, and, with prolonged use of PDE3 inotropes, increased mortality in chronic heart failure, limiting use to monitored short-term hemodynamic support.

Name: Butabarbital
Description: Butabarbital (DrugBank DB00237) is a short- to intermediate-acting sedative-hypnotic barbiturate whose structure is based on a 2,4,6-trioxohexahydropyrimidine barbituric acid core substituted at the 5-position with ethyl and sec-butyl groups, making it a 5,5-disubstituted oxybarbiturate; chemically it belongs to the barbiturates, a cyclic ureide class, and its defining scaffold is the barbiturate pyrimidinetrione ring. Closely related drugs include other CNS-depressant barbiturates such as secobarbital, pentobarbital, amobarbital, phenobarbital, and butalbital, which share the same core scaffold but differ in 5-position substitution and duration of action. Its principal pharmacologic target is the GABAA receptor chloride channel complex, at which barbiturates act as positive allosteric modulators and, at higher concentrations, direct channel activators; secondary functional effects include generalized suppression of excitatory neurotransmission. Butabarbital is generally well absorbed orally, distributes widely into the CNS and other tissues, is variably protein bound, undergoes substantial hepatic biotransformation mainly by oxidation and related phase I pathways with some potential for enzyme induction, and is eliminated as metabolites and a smaller fraction of unchanged drug in urine. It has been used for short-term treatment of insomnia and as a preanesthetic sedative or anxiolytic for procedural anxiety. Adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, impaired coordination, cognitive slowing, hangover sedation, nausea, and paradoxical excitement; toxic effects include dose-dependent respiratory depression, hypotension, coma, dependence, withdrawal syndromes including seizures, and potentially fatal overdose, especially with alcohol, opioids, or other sedative-hypnotics.

Name: Nevirapine
Description: Nevirapine (DB00238) is a dipyridodiazepinone antiretroviral whose structure consists of a rigid, highly conjugated fused heteroaromatic tricyclic system containing two pyridine-like rings annelated to a seven-membered diazepinone core with a cyclopropyl substituent, giving a lipophilic, planar non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor chemotype; chemically it belongs to the NNRTI class and more broadly to heterocyclic aromatic diazepinones, with a dipyridodiazepinone scaffold shared conceptually with other HIV-1 NNRTIs such as efavirenz, delavirdine, etravirine, and rilpivirine, although those agents differ in ring system and flexibility. Its principal target is HIV-1 reverse transcriptase, to which it binds at the allosteric NNRTI pocket distinct from the polymerase active site, thereby inhibiting viral DNA synthesis; it has no meaningful activity against HIV-2 reverse transcriptase. Nevirapine is indicated for treatment of HIV-1 infection, including combination antiretroviral therapy in adults and children and, historically, prevention of mother-to-child transmission. It is well absorbed orally, has high bioavailability, distributes widely with moderate protein binding and good penetration into placenta and breast milk, undergoes extensive hepatic oxidation primarily via CYP3A4 and CYP2B6 to hydroxylated metabolites followed by glucuronidation, autoinduces its own metabolism over the first weeks of therapy, and is eliminated mainly in urine as conjugated metabolites with a terminal half-life that decreases after autoinduction. Major toxicities include severe rash, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and potentially fatal hepatotoxicity, especially in women with higher CD4 counts; common adverse effects include rash, fever, nausea, headache, fatigue, transaminase elevation, and hepatitis. Clinically, it has been used in multidrug HIV regimens, but use now requires careful monitoring for hepatic injury, cutaneous hypersensitivity, and CYP-mediated drug interactions.

Name: Oxiconazole
Description: Oxiconazole (DrugBank DB00239) is a topical imidazole antifungal whose structure is characterized by a substituted imidazole ring attached to a lipophilic diaryl ether framework bearing chlorinated phenyl groups and a dioxolane-containing side chain, a design that confers strong membrane affinity and potent inhibition of fungal sterol synthesis. Chemically, it belongs to the azole antifungals, specifically the imidazole subclass, and its core scaffold is an aryl-imidazole ether closely related to other topical imidazoles. Similar drugs include clotrimazole, miconazole, econazole, ketoconazole, and sulconazole, which share the azole pharmacophore and antifungal mechanism. Its principal target is fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase, a cytochrome P450 enzyme encoded by ERG11/CYP51, leading to depletion of ergosterol and disruption of fungal membrane integrity; off-target interaction with mammalian CYP enzymes is possible but clinically limited with topical use. Oxiconazole is indicated for superficial dermatophyte and yeast infections, including tinea pedis, tinea cruris, tinea corporis, and cutaneous candidiasis, and is used clinically as a cream or lotion for localized pruritic, erythematous, scaling lesions. Pharmacokinetically, systemic absorption through intact skin is minimal, distribution is largely confined to the stratum corneum and superficial epidermis, and because plasma exposure is negligible, metabolism and excretion are not well characterized but would be expected to follow limited hepatic biotransformation and biliary or renal elimination of small absorbed fractions. Toxicity is generally low and primarily local, with examples including irritation, burning, stinging, pruritus, erythema, maceration, and contact dermatitis; serious systemic toxicity is rare, and overdose is unlikely except with inappropriate extensive application or accidental ingestion.

Name: Alclometasone
Description: Alclometasone (DrugBank DB00240), used clinically as alclometasone dipropionate, is a synthetic halogenated corticosteroid with a pregnane steroid nucleus characterized by the classic four-ring cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene scaffold, a 3-keto-4-ene A-ring, 11β-hydroxyl and 17α/21-propionate ester substitution, and a 9α-chloro group that enhances topical anti-inflammatory potency; chemically it belongs to the glucocorticoid corticosteroid class and more specifically to medium-potency topical corticosteroid esters built on the hydrocortisone/prednisolone-like steroid scaffold. Structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include hydrocortisone butyrate, desonide, triamcinolone acetonide, betamethasone valerate, and clobetasol propionate, which share the same steroidal anti-inflammatory pharmacophore but differ in halogenation, esterification, and potency. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, with downstream repression of proinflammatory mediators including cytokines, prostaglandins, and leukotrienes through glucocorticoid-responsive gene regulation and lipocortin induction. After topical administration, systemic absorption is usually low but increases with damaged skin, occlusion, large treatment area, prolonged use, or pediatric exposure; absorbed drug is distributed systemically, extensively metabolized hepatically by ester hydrolysis and steroid biotransformation to less active metabolites, and excreted mainly in urine with some fecal elimination. It is indicated for corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses such as atopic dermatitis, allergic contact dermatitis, irritant dermatitis, eczema, and localized psoriasis, and is used clinically to reduce pruritus, erythema, scaling, and inflammation on sensitive areas including the face and intertriginous regions. Toxicities include local skin atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, acneiform eruption, perioral dermatitis, hypopigmentation, delayed wound healing, and secondary infection, while excessive systemic exposure can cause hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis suppression, hyperglycemia, Cushingoid features, and growth suppression in children.

Name: Butalbital
Description: Butalbital (DrugBank DB00241) is a short- to intermediate-acting barbiturate whose structure is a 5,5-disubstituted barbituric acid derivative built on a pyrimidine-2,4,6-trione ring bearing ethyl and sec-butyl substituents, conferring substantial lipophilicity and central nervous system depressant activity; chemically it belongs to the barbiturate sedative-hypnotics, with the classic barbituric acid scaffold shared by related agents such as phenobarbital, pentobarbital, secobarbital, amobarbital, and thiopental. Its pharmacology is mediated primarily through positive allosteric modulation of GABAA receptor chloride channels, with barbiturates also capable at higher concentrations of directly prolonging channel opening and broadly suppressing neuronal excitability; no single highly selective protein target defines its action beyond GABAA receptor subunit complexes. Orally administered butalbital is well absorbed, widely distributed including across the blood-brain barrier, moderately protein bound, hepatically metabolized mainly by microsomal oxidation and related biotransformation pathways, and eliminated predominantly in urine as metabolites with some unchanged drug; its relatively long elimination half-life supports prolonged sedative effects and risk of accumulation. Toxicity is typical of barbiturates and includes dose-related CNS and respiratory depression, coma, hypotension, impaired psychomotor performance, dependence, tolerance, withdrawal seizures, and potentially fatal overdose, especially with alcohol, opioids, or benzodiazepines. Adverse effects commonly include drowsiness, dizziness, nausea, sedation, confusion, and impaired coordination. Clinically, butalbital is used chiefly in combination products for tension headache and selected refractory headache syndromes, for example with acetaminophen, aspirin, caffeine, and sometimes codeine, although use is limited by abuse liability and medication-overuse headache.

Name: Cladribine
Description: Cladribine (DB00242) is a chlorinated purine nucleoside analog structurally defined as 2-chloro-2′-deoxyadenosine, consisting of a 2-chloroadenine base linked through a β-N9-glycosidic bond to a 2-deoxyribose sugar; chemically it belongs to the antimetabolite, purine analog, and deoxynucleoside analog classes, with a deoxyadenosine scaffold modified by halogen substitution that confers resistance to adenosine deaminase. Closely related drugs include fludarabine, clofarabine, nelarabine, and deoxyadenosine-derived cytotoxic nucleosides such as cytarabine by therapeutic analogy. Its activity depends on intracellular phosphorylation, primarily by deoxycytidine kinase, to cladribine triphosphate, which accumulates especially in lymphocytes and inhibits DNA synthesis and repair while promoting strand breaks and apoptosis; relevant targets and pathway proteins include deoxycytidine kinase, ribonucleotide reductase, DNA polymerases, and enzymes involved in DNA repair, with adenosine deaminase resistance being pharmacologically important. Oral absorption is clinically useful though variable, distribution is wide with intracellular trapping in lymphoid cells and some CNS penetration, protein binding is low, metabolism is limited relative to deamination-susceptible analogs, and elimination occurs through both renal excretion and intracellular nucleotide turnover. Major toxicities are dose-limiting myelosuppression and prolonged lymphopenia with opportunistic infections; neurotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, and embryo-fetal toxicity are less common but important examples. Adverse effects include neutropenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, fever, rash, headache, nausea, and herpes zoster. Clinically, cladribine is used in hairy cell leukemia and other lymphoid malignancies, and orally in relapsing multiple sclerosis to produce selective immune reconstitution.

Name: Ranolazine
