Description: Ranolazine (DrugBank DB00243) is a piperazine-derived antianginal agent built around a substituted anisole/aryl ether linked through a short hydroxypropyl chain to a basic piperazine nucleus, giving an amphiphilic structure with one aromatic methoxy-containing ring and a tertiary diamine motif; chemically it is classified as a small-molecule anti-ischemic cardiovascular drug and more specifically an aryl ether–piperazine derivative, with a phenoxypropanolamine-like scaffold related in broad medicinal-chemistry terms to other basic lipophilic antianginal or ion-channel–active agents, though it is not a nitrate or beta-blocker, and drugs sometimes considered pharmacologically similar or comparator antianginals include trimetazidine, ivabradine, amlodipine, metoprolol, and nitroglycerin. Its principal molecular target is the cardiac late inward sodium current, attributed mainly to inhibition of SCN5A/Nav1.5-mediated late INa, with secondary effects on intracellular calcium handling and modest IKr/hERG channel interaction that explains QT prolongation risk. Ranolazine is indicated for chronic stable angina, especially persistent anginal symptoms despite standard therapy, and is used clinically as add-on or second-line treatment to improve exercise tolerance and reduce angina frequency in ischemic heart disease. It is orally administered, well absorbed, extensively distributed, moderately protein bound, metabolized predominantly by CYP3A and to a lesser extent CYP2D6, is a substrate of P-glycoprotein, and is eliminated through both renal excretion of metabolites and fecal routes, with a half-life around 7 hours for extended-release dosing. Toxicity concerns include dose-related dizziness, nausea, constipation, headache, and asthenia, plus clinically important QT interval prolongation, elevated exposure in hepatic impairment, and interactions with strong CYP3A inhibitors or inducers; overdose may accentuate neurologic and cardiovascular adverse effects.

Name: Mesalazine
Description: Mesalazine (mesalamine; DrugBank DB00244) is a small aromatic anti-inflammatory agent structurally defined as 5-aminosalicylic acid, consisting of a benzoic acid scaffold bearing adjacent phenolic hydroxyl and carboxylic acid functionalities with an amino substituent on the ring, placing it in the aminosalicylate/5-ASA class and more broadly among salicylic acid derivatives; its core chemical scaffold is the salicylate nucleus, and related or mechanistically similar drugs include sulfasalazine, olsalazine, balsalazide, and to a lesser extent other salicylates such as aspirin. Its activity is largely topical within the intestinal lumen and mucosa rather than systemic, with incompletely absorbed oral drug, formulation-dependent release in the distal small bowel or colon, limited plasma protein binding of absorbed fractions, extensive presystemic and mucosal/hepatic N-acetylation to N-acetyl-5-ASA, and elimination mainly in urine as parent drug and acetylated metabolite, with some fecal excretion of unabsorbed drug. Pharmacologically, mesalazine is associated with inhibition of cyclooxygenase and lipoxygenase pathways, reduced prostaglandin and leukotriene production, scavenging of reactive oxygen species, and modulation of NF-kB/PPAR-gamma-linked inflammatory signaling; reported targets or pathway nodes include PTGS1, PTGS2, ALOX5, PPARG, and NFKB-related signaling. It is indicated primarily for induction and maintenance of remission in ulcerative colitis and for ulcerative proctitis or proctosigmoiditis via oral or rectal use, and is also used in selected inflammatory bowel disease settings. Adverse effects commonly include headache, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, flatulence, and rash, while important toxicities include interstitial nephritis and renal impairment, pancreatitis, hepatitis, paradoxical colitis exacerbation, blood dyscrasias, and rare myocarditis or pericarditis.

Name: Benzatropine
Description: Benzatropine (benztropine; DrugBank DB00245) is a synthetic tropane-based antimuscarinic whose structure consists of a rigid bicyclic tropane ring bearing a tertiary amine and a benzhydryl ether-like substituent with phenyl aromatic groups, giving a lipophilic, atropine/diphenhydramine-like architecture that supports central nervous system penetration; chemically it is classified as a tertiary amine anticholinergic/antiparkinsonian agent, and its core scaffold is the 8-azabicyclo[3.2.1]octane tropane framework linked to a diarylmethoxy motif. Similar drugs include trihexyphenidyl, biperiden, procyclidine, atropine, scopolamine, and the antihistamine diphenhydramine. Its main targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially central M1-class signaling, with reported secondary inhibition of the dopamine transporter SLC6A3 and weaker interactions with histaminergic pathways, helping restore striatal dopamine-acetylcholine balance. After oral or parenteral administration it is reasonably absorbed, widely distributed including into brain, extensively tissue bound, hepatically metabolized, and eliminated slowly through renal and likely biliary routes, producing a relatively prolonged duration of action. It is indicated primarily for idiopathic parkinsonism and drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms such as acute dystonia, rigidity, tremor, and akathisia, but it is less effective for tardive dyskinesia. Toxicity reflects anticholinergic excess, with examples including confusion, delirium, hallucinations, hyperthermia, tachycardia, urinary retention, constipation, ileus, and angle-closure glaucoma precipitation; overdose may cause severe CNS toxicity. Common adverse effects include dry mouth, blurred vision, sedation, cognitive impairment, and decreased sweating. Clinically, it is used as adjunctive symptomatic therapy in Parkinson disease and for prevention or treatment of antipsychotic-induced extrapyramidal reactions.

Name: Ziprasidone
Description: Ziprasidone (DrugBank DB00246) is an atypical antipsychotic of the benzisothiazolyl-piperazine class, structurally characterized by a fused benzisothiazole heteroaromatic ring linked through a piperazine moiety to an indolin-2-one-like cyclic lactam scaffold, a combination that defines its tricyclic-like heteroaryl antipsychotic chemotype and distinguishes it from simpler phenothiazine or butyrophenone agents. Its core scaffold is most closely related to other serotonin-dopamine antagonists, with similar drugs including lurasidone, risperidone, paliperidone, quetiapine, olanzapine, and aripiprazole by therapeutic class, and particularly lurasidone by heteroaryl-piperazine design. Pharmacokinetically, ziprasidone is orally absorbed with substantially increased bioavailability when taken with food, is highly protein bound, distributes widely, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism primarily via aldehyde oxidase and to a lesser extent CYP3A4, forms inactive or weakly active metabolites, and is eliminated through both fecal and renal routes with a terminal half-life of roughly 7 hours. Its principal targets include dopamine D2, serotonin 5-HT2A, 5-HT1A, and 5-HT2C receptors, with additional affinity for 5-HT1D and moderate interaction with histamine H1 and alpha1-adrenergic receptors, supporting antipsychotic and mood-stabilizing effects. It is indicated for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, including acute manic or mixed episodes and maintenance use adjunctively in some settings. Important toxicities include QT interval prolongation, torsades de pointes risk, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, tardive dyskinesia, somnolence, extrapyramidal symptoms, dizziness, akathisia, nausea, and orthostatic hypotension, while clinically it is used when a relatively weight-sparing second-generation antipsychotic is desired for hallucinations, delusions, agitation, or bipolar mania.

Name: Cabergoline
Description: Cabergoline (DrugBank DB00248) is a long-acting semisynthetic ergot derivative with an ergoline tetracyclic indole-based core derived from lysergic acid and bearing a substituted urea/carboxamide side chain that increases lipophilicity and prolonged receptor binding; chemically it is classified as an ergot alkaloid, dopaminergic agonist, and prolactin-inhibiting agent, with the ergoline scaffold as its defining pharmacophore. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other dopamine agonists, especially bromocriptine, pergolide, lisuride, and to a lesser extent non-ergot agents such as pramipexole and ropinirole. Its principal targets are dopamine D2 receptor isoforms, with additional activity at D3 and variable affinity for D4, 5-HT2B, and alpha-adrenergic receptors, explaining both efficacy and some toxicities. Cabergoline is well absorbed orally, reaches peak concentrations within hours, is highly distributed into tissues, is extensively metabolized mainly by hydrolysis of the acylurea moiety to less active metabolites with limited CYP dependence, and is eliminated slowly, chiefly via biliary/fecal routes with lesser renal excretion; its terminal half-life is prolonged, supporting once- or twice-weekly dosing in hyperprolactinemia. It is indicated for hyperprolactinemic disorders such as prolactinoma, galactorrhea, amenorrhea, infertility, and sometimes acromegaly or Parkinson disease. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, vomiting, constipation, dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, headache, somnolence, and nasal congestion; important toxicities include impulse-control symptoms, hallucinations, psychiatric destabilization, and dose-related valvular heart disease, fibrotic reactions, and rare vasospasm. Clinically, it is used primarily to suppress prolactin, restore gonadal function, shrink pituitary adenomas, and occasionally for refractory endocrine or neurologic indications.

Name: Idoxuridine
Description: Idoxuridine (DrugBank DB00249) is a halogenated pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside analog structurally defined as 5-iodo-2′-deoxyuridine, consisting of a uracil-derived base bearing an iodine substituent at the 5-position linked through a beta-N1-glycosidic bond to a 2-deoxyribose sugar; thus, it belongs to the antimetabolite, antiviral nucleoside analog class and has a thymidine/2′-deoxyribonucleoside scaffold closely related to pyrimidine DNA building blocks. Similar drugs include trifluridine, zidovudine, brivudine, and other halogenated or modified pyrimidine nucleosides, especially thymidine and deoxyuridine analogs used as antiviral or antineoplastic antimetabolites. Its principal pharmacologic target is viral DNA synthesis after intracellular phosphorylation by host and infected-cell kinases to mono-, di-, and triphosphate metabolites; these metabolites are incorporated into viral DNA and interfere with replication, particularly in herpes simplex virus, rather than acting through a single unique protein target, although viral DNA polymerase and cellular kinases are functionally relevant targets. Because systemic administration causes marked host toxicity and rapid metabolism, idoxuridine is used topically, with limited ocular absorption, local corneal distribution, intracellular activation, catabolism to iodinated uracil derivatives, and minimal clinically useful systemic exposure; excretion of absorbed drug is mainly renal as metabolites. Toxicity reflects nonselective incorporation into host DNA, with examples including mutagenicity, cytotoxicity, delayed epithelial healing, and bone marrow toxicity if systemic exposure occurs. Clinically, it is indicated mainly for herpetic keratitis, especially dendritic corneal ulcers due to HSV-1, and has also been used topically for cutaneous herpes lesions. Common adverse effects include ocular pain, irritation, lacrimation, photophobia, conjunctival inflammation, punctate keratopathy, eyelid edema, and corneal epithelial toxicity.

Name: Dapsone
Description: Dapsone (DrugBank DB00250) is a synthetic aromatic sulfone whose structure consists of a diphenyl sulfone core with two para-amino substituents, giving a rigid, symmetrical 4,4'-diaminodiphenyl sulfone framework; chemically it is classified as a sulfone and specifically a sulfone-based antibacterial and anti-inflammatory agent, with a diaryl sulfone scaffold that is closely related to sulfonamide pharmacophores. Similar drugs include other sulfones and sulfonamide-like antifolates such as sulfoxone, acedapsone, sulfadiazine, and sulfamethoxazole, which share antibacterial activity through interference with folate biosynthesis. Its principal antimicrobial target is bacterial dihydropteroate synthase, while its anti-inflammatory activity is linked to inhibition of neutrophil myeloperoxidase-mediated oxidant injury, suppression of neutrophil chemotaxis, and reduced inflammatory mediator generation. After oral administration, dapsone is well absorbed, widely distributed into skin, muscle, liver, and inflamed tissues, undergoes enterohepatic recirculation, is metabolized hepatically by N-acetylation and CYP-mediated N-hydroxylation, and is excreted mainly in urine as metabolites and some unchanged drug; its relatively long half-life supports once-daily use. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related hemolysis and methemoglobinemia, especially in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, and idiosyncratic dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome with fever, rash, hepatitis, lymphadenopathy, and eosinophilia can occur; agranulocytosis, peripheral neuropathy, and hepatotoxicity are less common serious examples. Indications and clinical use include multidrug therapy for leprosy, dermatitis herpetiformis, prophylaxis and treatment support in Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and toxoplasmosis in selected patients, and off-label neutrophilic dermatoses such as linear IgA bullous dermatosis, with common side effects including nausea, headache, rash, hemolytic anemia, cyanosis from methemoglobinemia, and dizziness.

Name: Phenytoin
Description: Phenytoin (DrugBank DB00252) is a hydantoin anticonvulsant whose structure consists of a five-membered imidazolidine-2,4-dione ring bearing two phenyl substituents at the 5-position, giving a rigid diphenylhydantoin core with weakly acidic imide functionality and high aromatic lipophilicity; thus its chemical category is the hydantoin/ureide class, and its defining scaffold is the 5,5-diphenyl-substituted hydantoin ring system. Structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include fosphenytoin as a water-soluble prodrug, mephenytoin and ethotoin as older hydantoin analogs, and more distantly other sodium-channel-blocking antiseizure agents such as carbamazepine and lamotrigine. Its principal targets are voltage-gated sodium channels, especially neuronal alpha subunits including SCN1A, SCN2A, SCN3A, and SCN8A, with state-dependent stabilization of the inactivated channel state reducing high-frequency firing. Oral absorption is generally good but formulation dependent and sometimes delayed; the drug is highly albumin bound, distributes widely including into the CNS, undergoes hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP2C9 and CYP2C19 to inactive hydroxylated metabolites, and is eliminated largely in urine after glucuronidation, with capacity-limited, nonlinear kinetics that make serum concentrations dose-sensitive. Indications include focal seizures, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, status epilepticus after benzodiazepines, and seizure prophylaxis in selected neurosurgical settings; it is also used intravenously for acute seizure control. Toxicity includes dose-related nystagmus, ataxia, diplopia, sedation, encephalopathy, and hypotension or arrhythmias with rapid IV infusion, plus chronic gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, osteopenia, folate deficiency, hepatotoxicity, blood dyscrasias, teratogenic fetal hydantoin syndrome, and severe rash including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and DRESS.

Name: Medrysone
Description: Medrysone (DrugBank DB00253) is a synthetic corticosteroid of the pregnane steroid class, structurally characterized by the classic four-ring cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene nucleus bearing the glucocorticoid-defining 3-keto-4-ene A-ring and 20-ketone side chain, with hydroxyl and methyl substitutions arranged to confer anti-inflammatory activity while limiting mineralocorticoid effects; chemically it is categorized as an ophthalmic glucocorticoid, and its core scaffold is the corticosteroid/pregnane steroid framework closely related to prednisolone, hydrocortisone, dexamethasone, fluorometholone, loteprednol, and rimexolone. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor, with downstream repression of phospholipase A2-dependent eicosanoid synthesis and inflammatory cytokine signaling, rather than highly selective binding to multiple discrete protein targets. In clinical use it has been formulated mainly for topical ophthalmic administration for steroid-responsive inflammatory disorders of the eye such as allergic conjunctivitis, anterior segment inflammation, postoperative ocular inflammation, and irritation involving the palpebral and bulbar conjunctiva, cornea, and anterior globe. After ocular instillation, absorption is primarily local into corneal and conjunctival tissues, with limited but possible systemic absorption via ocular tissues and nasolacrimal drainage; distribution is therefore concentrated in anterior ocular compartments, metabolism is presumed largely hepatic after systemic uptake as with other corticosteroids, and excretion is expected mainly as metabolites in urine and to a lesser extent bile. Toxicities and adverse effects are typical of ophthalmic steroids and include elevated intraocular pressure, glaucoma, optic nerve damage, posterior subcapsular cataract, delayed wound healing, secondary bacterial, वायरल, or fungal ocular infection, ocular burning, stinging, blurred vision, and local irritation; excessive or prolonged use may increase systemic corticosteroid effects, although these are generally uncommon with ophthalmic dosing.

Name: Doxycycline
Description: Doxycycline (DrugBank DB00254) is a semisynthetic tetracycline antibiotic built on a rigid, linearly fused four-ring naphthacene core bearing multiple keto-enol and phenolic hydroxyl functionalities with a characteristic dimethylamino substituent that supports metal chelation and ribosomal binding; chemically it belongs to the tetracycline class, with the tetracycline/polyketide-derived naphthacene scaffold, and is closely related to tetracycline, minocycline, demeclocycline, and tigecycline. Its primary pharmacologic target is the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit, especially 16S rRNA within the decoding region, where it inhibits aminoacyl-tRNA binding and suppresses protein synthesis; no single protein target is usually emphasized because binding is largely ribosomal RNA-mediated. Orally, doxycycline is well absorbed, with bioavailability typically high and less affected by food than older tetracyclines, although polyvalent cations reduce absorption; it distributes widely into respiratory secretions, skin, prostate, and intracellular compartments, is highly protein bound, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated mainly via biliary/fecal routes with some renal excretion, giving it a relatively long half-life that supports once- or twice-daily dosing. Toxicities include dose-related gastrointestinal irritation and esophagitis, photosensitivity, hepatotoxicity, intracranial hypertension, and permanent tooth discoloration with impaired bone growth in fetuses and young children. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, diarrhea, rash, candidiasis, and pill esophagitis. Clinically it is used for acne vulgaris, rosacea, community-acquired respiratory infections, atypical pathogens such as Chlamydia trachomatis and Mycoplasma pneumoniae, tick-borne diseases including Lyme disease, ehrlichiosis, and Rocky Mountain spotted fever, malaria prophylaxis, and as part of combination regimens for cholera, brucellosis, and anthrax.

Name: Clotrimazole
Description: Clotrimazole (DrugBank DB00257) is a lipophilic imidazole antifungal built around a triarylmethyl scaffold in which an imidazole ring is attached to a substituted triphenylmethyl-like core bearing chlorophenyl and diphenyl moieties, a structure that places it in the azole antifungal class, specifically the imidazole derivatives. Its key scaffold and physicochemical profile resemble other imidazole antifungals such as miconazole, econazole, ketoconazole, and bifonazole, all of which disrupt fungal sterol biosynthesis. The principal pharmacologic target is fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase, a cytochrome P450 enzyme encoded by ERG11/CYP51, leading to impaired ergosterol synthesis and altered membrane permeability; at higher concentrations, it may also directly disturb fungal membranes and inhibit some yeast ATPases. Clotrimazole is used primarily for topical treatment of dermatophytoses, cutaneous candidiasis, tinea pedis, tinea cruris, tinea corporis, pityriasis versicolor, and vulvovaginal candidiasis, and as an oral troche for oropharyngeal candidiasis. Systemic absorption after topical or intravaginal use is minimal, whereas oral troches produce limited gastrointestinal absorption with largely local activity; absorbed drug is widely distributed, extensively hepatically metabolized by oxidative pathways, and excreted mainly in bile and feces with minor urinary elimination. Toxicity is usually low in topical use but can include local irritation, burning, erythema, blistering, peeling, edema, pruritus, and contact dermatitis; oral use may cause nausea or abnormal liver enzymes, and excessive systemic exposure could theoretically produce azole-like hepatotoxicity and drug interaction liability through mammalian CYP inhibition. Clinically, it is widely used as creams, lotions, solutions, vaginal tablets, and troches for localized fungal infections and symptomatic relief of itching, scaling, inflammation, and discharge associated with susceptible mycoses.

Name: Calcium acetate
Description: Calcium acetate (DrugBank DB00258) is a simple inorganic-organic calcium salt composed of a divalent calcium cation coordinated by two acetate anions, giving a small, highly water-soluble ionic structure built on an acetate carboxylate scaffold rather than a complex heterocyclic pharmacophore; chemically it belongs to the class of mineral supplements and phosphate binders, with close therapeutic analogs including calcium carbonate, calcium citrate, sevelamer, lanthanum carbonate, ferric citrate, and sucroferric oxyhydroxide, which are similarly used to reduce gastrointestinal phosphate absorption. Its pharmacologic action is mediated primarily by calcium ion binding of dietary phosphate in the gut lumen to form insoluble calcium phosphate, so it has no conventional receptor-selective mechanism, although physiologically relevant targets include phosphate handling pathways and calcium-sensing systems such as the calcium-sensing receptor indirectly affected by calcium load. Oral absorption results in partial dissociation and variable gastrointestinal uptake of calcium, with greater relevance in patients with renal failure; distribution follows normal extracellular calcium homeostasis and bone exchange, acetate is rapidly metabolized through endogenous intermediary metabolism to bicarbonate and carbon dioxide, and absorbed calcium is eliminated mainly via feces when unabsorbed, with renal excretion of the absorbed fraction being limited in end-stage kidney disease. The principal indication is control of hyperphosphatemia in patients with chronic kidney disease, especially those on dialysis, and it is used clinically with meals to lower serum phosphate in conditions such as CKD-mineral and bone disorder. Toxicity is dominated by hypercalcemia and calcium overload, with examples including confusion, weakness, arrhythmia, constipation, nephrolithiasis, and vascular or soft-tissue calcification; common adverse effects are nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, and constipation.

Name: Sulfanilamide
Description: Sulfanilamide (DrugBank DB00259) is the prototypical sulfonamide antibacterial, structurally defined by a para-aminobenzenesulfonamide motif in which an aniline ring bears a primary amino group para to a sulfonamide group, placing it in the aryl sulfonamide and antifolate chemical category with a simple aniline-sulfonamide scaffold that underlies many later sulfa drugs. Closely related agents include sulfamethoxazole, sulfadiazine, sulfisoxazole, sulfadoxine, and sulfacetamide, all of which preserve the p-aminobenzenesulfonamide pharmacophore while varying heteroaryl substitution to alter solubility and disposition. Its antibacterial action results from competitive inhibition of bacterial dihydropteroate synthase, blocking incorporation of para-aminobenzoic acid into folate biosynthesis and thereby suppressing nucleic acid formation in susceptible organisms. After administration, sulfanilamide is generally well absorbed, distributes widely into extracellular fluids and some tissues, exhibits limited to moderate protein binding relative to later sulfonamides, undergoes hepatic biotransformation primarily by N4-acetylation and possibly glucuronidation, and is eliminated predominantly by renal excretion of unchanged drug and metabolites, with urinary pH influencing solubility and clearance. Toxicity is characteristic of sulfonamides and includes crystalluria, hematuria, acute kidney injury, hypersensitivity reactions, fever, rash, urticaria, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, hematologic injury such as hemolytic anemia or agranulocytosis, and rare hepatotoxicity; gastrointestinal upset and photosensitivity are also recognized adverse effects. Historically, it was used for streptococcal and other susceptible bacterial infections, topical management of infected wounds or vaginal infections, and uncomplicated urinary or skin infections, but modern clinical use is limited because safer and more effective sulfonamides and non-sulfonamide antibacterials have largely replaced it.

Name: Cycloserine
Description: Cycloserine (DrugBank DB00260) is a small, highly polar cyclic amino acid antibiotic whose structure consists of a strained five-membered 1,2-oxazolidin-3-one ring bearing an exocyclic amino substituent, making it a structural analogue of D-alanine; chemically it is classified as an oxazolidinone-derived antitubercular/antibacterial agent, with an oxazolidinone-like heterocyclic scaffold that underlies its antimetabolite action in bacterial cell-wall synthesis. Similar drugs include other second-line antitubercular agents such as ethionamide, para-aminosalicylic acid, and terizidone, the latter being a prodrug/dimeric derivative related most closely to cycloserine. Its principal targets are the bacterial enzymes alanine racemase and D-alanine-D-alanine ligase, inhibition of which blocks peptidoglycan precursor formation. Orally, cycloserine is well absorbed with high bioavailability, distributes widely into tissues and body fluids including cerebrospinal fluid, shows relatively low protein binding, undergoes limited metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by the kidney, so accumulation occurs in renal impairment and dose adjustment is required. It is indicated mainly for multidrug-resistant or refractory tuberculosis and has also been used in certain urinary tract infections caused by susceptible organisms. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related neurotoxicity, with examples including headache, irritability, tremor, confusion, psychosis, depression, and seizures; peripheral neuropathy may occur and pyridoxine is often coadministered to mitigate CNS toxicity. Other adverse effects include dizziness, somnolence, rash, gastrointestinal upset, and rarely severe psychiatric reactions, so clinical use is generally reserved for specialist combination regimens when first-line options are ineffective or contraindicated.

Name: Carmustine
Description: Carmustine (DrugBank DB00262) is a highly lipophilic bifunctional alkylating antineoplastic agent of the nitrosourea class, structurally characterized by a 2-chloroethyl group and a nitrosocarbamoyl moiety attached to a small urea-based scaffold, with the core chemical scaffold being a chloroethyl-substituted N-nitrosourea that undergoes spontaneous nonenzymatic decomposition to reactive intermediates. It is chemically related to other nitrosoureas such as lomustine, semustine, streptozocin, and fotemustine, which share DNA-alkylating and carbamoylating behavior but differ in lipophilicity and tissue distribution. Carmustine is administered parenterally or as intracranial wafer implants; oral absorption is not clinically relevant. Its marked lipophilicity enables broad distribution, including efficient penetration of the blood-brain barrier, an important feature in neuro-oncology. It is rapidly cleared from plasma because of spontaneous degradation and hepatic biotransformation, producing active electrophilic species that alkylate DNA at guanine-rich sites and form interstrand cross-links, while excretion occurs mainly as urinary metabolites with minor expired carbon dioxide. It has no single selective protein target; its pharmacologic targets are nucleic acids, although glutathione-related detoxification systems and DNA repair pathways such as MGMT influence response. Major indications include glioblastoma, anaplastic glioma, brain metastasis adjunctive therapy, Hodgkin lymphoma, multiple myeloma conditioning regimens, and other refractory malignancies. Toxicity is substantial and includes delayed cumulative myelosuppression, severe thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, pulmonary fibrosis, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, profound nausea and vomiting, mucositis, neurotoxicity, and infusion-related reactions. Clinically, it is used intravenously in combination chemotherapy or locally as biodegradable wafers after tumor resection.

Name: Sulfisoxazole
Description: Sulfisoxazole (DrugBank DB00263) is a short- to intermediate-acting sulfonamide antibacterial whose structure consists of a para-aminobenzenesulfonamide core linked through the sulfonamide nitrogen to a heteroaromatic isoxazole ring, placing it in the sulfonamide anti-infective class and more specifically within the p-aminobenzenesulfonamide scaffold family; this aniline-sulfonamide pharmacophore is shared with closely related drugs such as sulfamethoxazole, sulfadiazine, sulfisomidine, and sulfamethizole. Its antibacterial target is dihydropteroate synthase in susceptible bacteria, where it acts as a para-aminobenzoic acid mimic to inhibit folate biosynthesis and thereby suppress bacterial growth. Sulfisoxazole is generally well absorbed orally, distributes widely into body fluids and tissues including urine, crosses the placenta, and undergoes partial hepatic metabolism mainly by N4-acetylation and glucuronidation; elimination is predominantly renal via glomerular filtration and tubular secretion as unchanged drug and metabolites, with urinary pH influencing solubility and clearance. Toxicity is typical of sulfonamides and includes crystalluria, hematuria, obstructive nephropathy, hypersensitivity reactions, fever, rash, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, hepatotoxicity, and hematologic injury such as agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, thrombocytopenia, or hemolysis, especially in G6PD deficiency; kernicterus risk limits use near term and in neonates. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, photosensitivity, and urticaria. Clinically, it has been used for susceptible urinary tract infections, otitis media, cervicitis, and other infections due to susceptible gram-positive and gram-negative organisms, though modern use is limited by resistance and safety concerns.

Name: Metoprolol
Description: Metoprolol (DrugBank DB00264) is a cardioselective beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist of the aryloxypropanolamine class, structurally characterized by a substituted phenoxypropanolamine core bearing a secondary alcohol, a protonatable isopropylamino side chain, and a para-(2-methoxyethyl) substituent on the aromatic ring; its central chemical scaffold is the classic phenoxy-2-propanolamine beta-blocker framework. It is closely related to other beta1-preferring agents such as atenolol, bisoprolol, betaxolol, and esmolol, and more broadly to propranolol as a less selective analogue. Its principal targets are the beta1-adrenergic receptor and, at higher concentrations, beta2-adrenergic receptor, producing reduced heart rate, myocardial contractility, atrioventricular conduction, and renin release. Metoprolol is well absorbed orally but undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, giving moderate and CYP2D6-dependent bioavailability; it is distributed widely, is only modestly protein bound, crosses the blood-brain barrier to a limited but clinically relevant extent, is extensively metabolized in the liver mainly by CYP2D6 to less active metabolites, and is excreted primarily in urine as metabolites with only a small fraction unchanged. Toxicity is dominated by excessive beta-blockade, including bradycardia, hypotension, AV block, acute heart failure, cardiogenic shock, bronchospasm in susceptible patients, hypoglycemia masking, and CNS depression in overdose. Clinically it is indicated and widely used for hypertension, angina pectoris, rate control in supraventricular tachyarrhythmias including atrial fibrillation, secondary prevention after myocardial infarction, and chronic heart failure in selected extended-release formulations; common adverse effects include fatigue, dizziness, depression, exercise intolerance, cold extremities, sleep disturbance, and sexual dysfunction.

Name: Crotamiton
Description: Crotamiton (DrugBank DB00265) is a small synthetic antipruritic and scabicidal agent whose structure is an aromatic carboxamide/crotonamide derivative consisting of an o-methyl-substituted phenyl ring linked through an amide to a substituted unsaturated acyl fragment, giving a lipophilic aryl amide scaffold with an alkene-containing crotonamide core; chemically it is classified as a topical aromatic amide and can be viewed within the broader family of ectoparasiticides and antipruritics. Its scaffold is relatively simple and distinct from pyrethroids or organochlorines, but it is pharmacologically similar to other topical scabicides such as permethrin, benzyl benzoate, lindane, sulfur, and ivermectin used for related indications. The precise molecular target in humans or mites is not well defined, and no single validated target protein is firmly established; its effects are generally described as direct antipruritic action plus toxic activity against Sarcoptes scabiei. After topical application, systemic absorption is usually low but can increase with inflamed, abraded, or extensive skin exposure; distribution is therefore mainly local to the stratum corneum and superficial epidermis, with limited human data on metabolism, though absorbed drug is thought to undergo hepatic biotransformation and renal excretion of metabolites. Toxicity is usually mild and local, but excessive use or application to damaged skin may cause irritant dermatitis, contact hypersensitivity, and rarely systemic toxicity; accidental ingestion can produce gastrointestinal and neurologic symptoms. It is indicated for scabies and symptomatic relief of pruritus from conditions such as allergic, senile, or nonspecific itchy dermatoses. Common adverse effects include transient burning, stinging, erythema, rash, and worsening irritation. Clinically, it has been used as a topical cream or lotion when treating uncomplicated scabies or itch, although in many settings it has been superseded by permethrin or oral ivermectin because of variable efficacy and the need for careful reapplication.

Name: Dicoumarol
Description: Dicoumarol (DrugBank DB00266) is a naturally derived synthetic-use anticoagulant built as a bis-4-hydroxycoumarin in which two 4-hydroxycoumarin rings are linked through a methylene bridge, creating a rigid, highly conjugated aromatic system with lactone carbonyls and phenolic hydroxyl groups; chemically it belongs to the coumarin/4-hydroxycoumarin anticoagulant class, and its core scaffold is the dicoumarin or biscoumarin scaffold. It is closely related to vitamin K antagonists such as warfarin, acenocoumarol, and phenprocoumon, which share the 4-hydroxycoumarin pharmacophore. Dicoumarol acts primarily by inhibiting vitamin K epoxide reductase complex subunit 1 (VKORC1), thereby impairing hepatic gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X and the anticoagulant proteins C and S; it has also been reported to inhibit NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1). It is orally active, absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, highly plasma protein bound, distributed mainly within the intravascular compartment, metabolized hepatically by oxidative and conjugative pathways, and excreted predominantly as metabolites in urine and bile/feces, with a relatively prolonged effect reflecting interference with clotting-factor turnover rather than direct clearance alone. Its principal indication and clinical use have been prevention and treatment of thromboembolic disorders such as deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and other hypercoagulable states, although it has largely been replaced by safer agents. Toxicity is dominated by excessive anticoagulation and hemorrhage, including epistaxis, hematuria, gastrointestinal bleeding, ecchymoses, and intracranial hemorrhage; additional adverse effects can include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, hepatic dysfunction, and rare tissue necrosis.

Name: Ropinirole
Description: Ropinirole (DrugBank DB00268) is a non-ergoline dopaminergic agonist built on an aminotetralin-like/indoline-derived bicyclic heteroaromatic scaffold, specifically an oxindole-related core bearing a dipropylamino substituent that confers affinity for dopamine receptors; chemically it is classified as a synthetic dopamine agonist and more broadly as a nitrogen-containing heterocyclic CNS agent. Its closest pharmacologic analogs include pramipexole, rotigotine, bromocriptine, and apomorphine, with ropinirole most closely resembling other non-ergot D2/D3-preferring agonists used in Parkinsonian and restless legs syndromes. It acts primarily at dopamine D2 and D3 receptors, with lesser activity at D4 and minimal affinity for D1-like receptors, and these dopamine receptors are the principal known targets. After oral administration it is well absorbed, though absolute bioavailability is limited by first-pass metabolism; peak concentrations occur within about 1-2 hours for immediate-release products, protein binding is low to moderate, distribution is systemic with CNS penetration, metabolism occurs predominantly in the liver via CYP1A2 to inactive metabolites, and excretion is mainly renal as metabolites with a terminal half-life of roughly 6 hours. Toxicity is dominated by dopaminergic excess, including nausea, vomiting, orthostatic hypotension, hallucinations, sedation, dyskinesia, and overdose-associated agitation or severe hypotension; impulse-control disorders and sudden sleep attacks are clinically important examples. It is indicated for Parkinson disease and moderate-to-severe restless legs syndrome, where it is used to reduce bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor, nocturnal leg discomfort, and urge to move, either as monotherapy in early Parkinson disease or adjunctively with levodopa in fluctuating disease.

Name: Topiramate
Description: Topiramate (DrugBank DB00273) is a sulfamate-substituted monosaccharide derivative structurally based on a fructopyranose-like hexose ring, specifically a highly oxygenated carbohydrate scaffold in which the 2,3:4,5 positions are protected as isopropylidene ketals and the primary hydroxyl is converted to a sulfamate ester; chemically it is classified as a sulfamate sugar anticonvulsant, with a ketalized pyranose scaffold that distinguishes it from classical aromatic antiepileptic agents. Similar drugs by therapeutic or mechanistic proximity include zonisamide, acetazolamide, valproate, lamotrigine, and other broad-spectrum antiseizure medicines, although topiramate is structurally most notable for sharing carbonic anhydrase inhibitory properties with sulfonamide-related agents. Its pharmacokinetics are characterized by good oral absorption, relatively low protein binding, broad tissue distribution including CNS penetration, limited hepatic metabolism with some hydroxylation, hydrolysis, and glucuronidation, and predominantly renal excretion of unchanged drug; elimination half-life is prolonged and shortened by enzyme-inducing antiepileptics. Known targets and mechanisms include voltage-gated sodium channels, GABA-A receptor modulation, AMPA/kainate glutamate receptor inhibition, and weak inhibition of carbonic anhydrase isoenzymes such as CA2 and CA12. It is indicated for epilepsy including focal-onset seizures, primary generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, and for migraine prophylaxis; it is also used clinically off-label for weight management, binge-eating disorder, essential tremor, neuropathic pain, and alcohol use disorder. Adverse effects commonly include paresthesia, cognitive slowing, word-finding difficulty, dizziness, somnolence, anorexia, dysgeusia, and weight loss, while important toxicities include metabolic acidosis, nephrolithiasis, oligohidrosis with hyperthermia, acute myopia and angle-closure glaucoma, teratogenic risk such as oral clefts, and overdose manifestations including CNS depression and severe acidosis.

Name: Cefmetazole
Description: Cefmetazole (DrugBank DB00274) is a semisynthetic cephamycin antibacterial whose structure is based on the cephem nucleus, a fused beta-lactam and dihydrothiazine ring system, bearing the characteristic 7-alpha-methoxy substitution that enhances beta-lactamase stability, along with acylamino and heterocyclic thio substituents that shape spectrum and pharmacokinetics; chemically it is a beta-lactam, specifically a second-generation cephamycin cephalosporin, and its core scaffold is the 7-aminocephalosporanic acid/cephamycin cephem framework. Closely related drugs include cefoxitin, cefotetan, and broader cephalosporin comparators such as cefuroxime. Its antibacterial action results from binding bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, especially transpeptidases involved in peptidoglycan cross-linking, leading to inhibition of cell-wall synthesis and bacterial lysis; relevant targets therefore include PBPs from susceptible Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms. Cefmetazole is administered parenterally, with good systemic bioavailability by intravenous or intramuscular routes, distribution into extracellular fluids and many tissues, limited metabolism, and predominant renal excretion of unchanged drug, giving a relatively short elimination half-life and need for dose adjustment in renal impairment. It is used for susceptible infections such as intra-abdominal, gynecologic, urinary tract, skin/soft tissue, and postoperative or surgical prophylactic settings, particularly where anaerobes or beta-lactamase-producing Enterobacterales are considerations. Adverse effects include hypersensitivity reactions, rash, fever, diarrhea, nausea, injection-site pain, transient hepatic enzyme elevation, eosinophilia, neutropenia, and superinfection including Clostridioides difficile colitis. Toxicities of note include class-related anaphylaxis, seizure risk with accumulation in severe renal dysfunction, bleeding or hypoprothrombinemia, and disulfiram-like reactions with alcohol due to its N-methylthiotetrazole-associated toxicity profile.

Name: Olmesartan
Description: Olmesartan (DrugBank DB00275) is an angiotensin II receptor blocker built around a biphenyl-tetrazole pharmacophore linked to an imidazole-containing core, with a hydroxylated side chain and, in marketed form, commonly administered as the medoxomil ester prodrug to enhance oral delivery; chemically it belongs to the sartans, a class of nonpeptide antihypertensive agents, and its core scaffold is the biphenyl-tetrazole/imidazole ARB framework shared with related agents such as losartan, valsartan, candesartan, irbesartan, and azilsartan. After oral administration of olmesartan medoxomil, the prodrug is rapidly and extensively hydrolyzed in the intestinal mucosa to active olmesartan; absorption is moderate, peak plasma concentrations occur within hours, protein binding is high, distribution is limited to extracellular fluid, metabolism is minimal, and elimination occurs largely as unchanged drug through both renal and biliary/fecal routes, supporting once-daily dosing. Its principal target is the angiotensin II type 1 receptor encoded by AGTR1, where antagonism reduces vasoconstriction, aldosterone signaling, and blood pressure. It is indicated primarily for hypertension, including essential hypertension and blood-pressure reduction to lower cardiovascular risk, and is used clinically alone or in combination with hydrochlorothiazide or amlodipine. Common adverse effects include dizziness, headache, fatigue, diarrhea, and hypotension, while important toxicities include hyperkalemia, renal function decline or acute kidney injury in renovascular disease, fetal toxicity in pregnancy, and the notable rare sprue-like enteropathy associated with severe chronic diarrhea and weight loss.

Name: Theophylline
Description: Theophylline (DrugBank DB00277) is a small, planar dimethylxanthine composed of a xanthine purine-dione core bearing methyl substituents at the 1 and 3 positions, giving a fused imidazole-pyrimidinedione heterobicyclic structure with moderate lipophilicity and weak basicity; chemically it belongs to the methylxanthine class and is built on the xanthine scaffold shared with caffeine and theobromine, with closely related or functionally similar drugs including aminophylline, dyphylline, caffeine, and doxofylline. Its principal pharmacology reflects nonselective inhibition of phosphodiesterases, especially PDE3 and PDE4, antagonism of adenosine receptors such as ADORA1 and ADORA2A, and downstream effects on histone deacetylase activity and inflammatory signaling, producing bronchodilation and mild respiratory stimulant activity. It is well absorbed orally, distributes widely into total body water, crosses the placenta and enters breast milk, shows variable protein binding, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP1A2 with contributions from CYP2E1 and CYP3A4 to methyluric acid and related metabolites, and is excreted primarily renally as metabolites with only a small unchanged fraction; clearance is increased by smoking and reduced in liver disease, heart failure, fever, and extremes of age. Toxicity is concentration dependent and narrow-therapeutic-index, with nausea, vomiting, tremor, insomnia, reflux, palpitations, and headache at modest excess and serious toxicity causing persistent emesis, hypokalemia, tachyarrhythmias, hypotension, and seizures. Clinically it is used chiefly as a second-line bronchodilator for asthma and COPD, and occasionally for apnea of prematurity or difficult nocturnal bronchospasm.

Name: Liothyronine
Description: Liothyronine (DrugBank DB00279) is the pharmaceutical form of triiodothyronine, a halogenated iodothyronine thyroid hormone characterized structurally by two phenyl rings linked through an ether oxygen, an alanine-derived amino acid side chain on the inner ring, phenolic and amino acid functional groups, and three iodine substituents that confer high lipophilicity and receptor affinity; chemically it belongs to the thyroid hormone/iodinated amino acid class and is built on an iodinated diphenyl ether amino acid scaffold. It is closely related to levothyroxine (T4), dextrothyroxine, and tiratricol, which share the thyronine core but differ in iodination pattern or side-chain biology. Liothyronine is well absorbed orally, with relatively rapid onset and higher potency than T4, is extensively protein bound in plasma to thyroxine-binding globulin, transthyretin, and albumin, distributes widely into tissues, undergoes hepatic and extrahepatic deiodination, conjugation by glucuronidation and sulfation, and is eliminated through both biliary/fecal and renal routes, with a shorter half-life than levothyroxine. Its principal targets are thyroid hormone receptors THRA and THRB, which regulate transcription at thyroid response elements. It is indicated for hypothyroidism, myxedema coma, TSH suppression in selected thyroid cancer or goiter settings, and occasionally for diagnostic thyroid suppression testing. Toxicity reflects hyperthyroid excess, including tachyarrhythmia, angina, myocardial ischemia, tremor, agitation, heat intolerance, weight loss, diarrhea, and long-term bone loss; overdose can precipitate thyroid storm-like states. Clinically it is used when rapid thyroid hormone action is desired, such as severe hypothyroidism, myxedema coma, or selected patients with impaired T4-to-T3 conversion.

Name: Lidocaine
Description: Lidocaine (DrugBank DB00281) is an amide-type local anesthetic and class Ib antiarrhythmic built on a xylidine/anilide scaffold, consisting of a 2,6-dimethylphenyl aromatic ring linked through an amide to a flexible aminoethyl side chain terminating in a tertiary diethylamino group, a structure that confers both lipophilicity for membrane penetration and a protonatable center for sodium channel blockade. Chemically it belongs to amino amide local anesthetics; its core scaffold is closely related to other anilide anesthetics such as mepivacaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine, prilocaine, and etidocaine, while pharmacologically similar sodium-channel blockers include mexiletine and tocainide. Its principal targets are voltage-gated sodium channels, especially SCN5A in cardiac tissue and neuronal sodium channel isoforms including SCN9A, SCN10A, and SCN11A, with blockade stabilizing inactivated channels and suppressing impulse initiation and conduction. Lidocaine is well absorbed from mucosa and by injection but undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism, so oral bioavailability is low; it distributes rapidly to highly perfused tissues, is moderately protein bound mainly to alpha-1-acid glycoprotein, crosses the blood-brain barrier and placenta, and is metabolized largely by CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 to active monoethylglycinexylidide and glycinexylidide before renal excretion of metabolites. It is indicated for local and regional anesthesia and analgesia in procedures, neuropathic pain, and ventricular arrhythmias such as post-myocardial-infarction ventricular tachycardia. Toxicity is concentration dependent, with CNS excitation or depression, seizures, coma, hypotension, bradycardia, conduction block, and cardiac arrest, especially after inadvertent intravascular injection or overdose; common adverse effects include dizziness, paresthesia, drowsiness, confusion, nausea, tinnitus, and local irritation. Clinically it is used as injectable infiltration, nerve block, epidural, spinal, and intravenous antiarrhythmic therapy, as well as topical creams, gels, sprays, and transdermal patches for pain states such as postherpetic neuralgia.

Name: Pamidronic acid
Description: Pamidronic acid (DrugBank DB00282) is a second-generation nitrogen-free bisphosphonate built on a P-C-P bisphosphonate core in which a central carbon bears two phosphonic acid groups and a 3-amino-1-hydroxypropyl side chain, giving a highly polar, strongly anionic hydroxybisphosphonate structure optimized for avid calcium binding in hydroxyapatite; chemically it belongs to the aminobisphosphonate-related class of antiresorptives, with a simple aliphatic bisphosphonate scaffold, and is structurally similar to other bone-seeking bisphosphonates such as etidronate, clodronate, alendronate, ibandronate, risedronate, and zoledronic acid. After intravenous administration, oral bioavailability is negligible in practice, plasma protein binding is modest, and the drug distributes rapidly to mineralized bone surfaces at sites of active remodeling, where it can persist for prolonged periods; it is not appreciably metabolized and is eliminated largely unchanged by renal excretion, with clearance reduced in renal impairment. Its principal pharmacologic target is bone mineral-associated osteoclast resorption machinery, with inhibition of osteoclast function and survival linked to interference with ATP-dependent pathways in non-nitrogen bisphosphonate pharmacology, although farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase is often discussed as a related bisphosphonate target class comparator. It is indicated for hypercalcemia of malignancy, Paget disease of bone, osteolytic bone metastases, and multiple-myeloma-associated bone disease, and is used clinically to reduce skeletal pain, lower serum calcium, and decrease pathologic fractures or other skeletal-related events. Toxicities include nephrotoxicity, hypocalcemia, acute-phase infusion reactions, and rare osteonecrosis of the jaw or atypical femoral fracture; common adverse effects include fever, myalgia, bone pain, nausea, fatigue, anemia, infusion-site reactions, and transient electrolyte disturbances.

Name: Clemastine
Description: Clemastine (DrugBank DB00283) is a first-generation ethanolamine antihistamine built around a lipophilic diaryl ether/benzhydryl-like scaffold in which a chlorinated aromatic ring and a substituted phenyl ring are linked through an ether-containing side chain to a tertiary aminoethyl moiety, a structural motif that confers strong H1 receptor antagonism and substantial central nervous system penetration; chemically it is classified as an H1-antihistamine of the ethanolamine class, with close similarity to other sedating antihistamines such as diphenhydramine, doxylamine, carbinoxamine, and dimenhydrinate. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, where it acts as an inverse agonist/antagonist, and it also exhibits clinically relevant antimuscarinic activity that contributes both to efficacy against rhinorrhea and to adverse effects. Clemastine is used for symptomatic treatment of allergic rhinitis, urticaria, pruritus, conjunctival allergy, and other histamine-mediated allergic states, and in clinical practice has been given for hay fever, hives, itchy dermatoses, and adjunctive management of mild allergic reactions. After oral administration it is well absorbed, widely distributed, crosses the blood-brain barrier, is extensively hepatically metabolized mainly by oxidative pathways, and is eliminated as metabolites in urine with a relatively prolonged duration of action compared with some older antihistamines. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related CNS depression and anticholinergic effects, with examples including marked sedation, confusion, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, and tachycardia; overdose may cause agitation, seizures, or arrhythmias, especially in children or with coingestants. Common side effects include drowsiness, dizziness, impaired psychomotor performance, fatigue, and mucosal dryness, so clinical use is generally as a sedating antiallergic agent when nighttime symptom control or a low-cost first-generation antihistamine is acceptable.

Name: Venlafaxine
Description: Venlafaxine (DrugBank DB00285) is a bicyclic arylalkylamine antidepressant of the phenethylamine-derived serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor class, structurally characterized by a 1-cyclohexanol core bearing a 4-methoxyphenyl substituent and a dimethylaminomethyl side chain; its scaffold is commonly described as an arylcyclohexanol/phenethylamine-like framework rather than a tricyclic or tetracyclic antidepressant nucleus. It is chemically and pharmacologically similar to desvenlafaxine, its major active O-desmethyl metabolite, and shows class similarity to duloxetine and milnacipran, while retaining some structural resemblance to tramadol among arylcyclohexanol analogs. Venlafaxine is well absorbed orally, undergoes limited first-pass loss, is moderately protein bound, distributes widely, and is extensively metabolized in the liver primarily by CYP2D6 to desvenlafaxine and by CYP3A4 to lesser metabolites; elimination is mainly renal as parent drug and metabolites, with extended-release formulations smoothing peak-trough fluctuations. Its principal targets are the serotonin transporter SLC6A4 and norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, with weak dopamine transporter SLC6A3 inhibition at higher concentrations. It is indicated for major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, social anxiety disorder, and panic disorder, and is used clinically for depressed mood, anhedonia, anxiety, autonomic hyperarousal, and sometimes neuropathic pain or vasomotor symptoms off label. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, insomnia, somnolence, dry mouth, constipation, sweating, sexual dysfunction, and dose-related hypertension; important toxicities include serotonin syndrome, tachycardia, agitation, seizures, mydriasis, arrhythmia risk, hyponatremia, abnormal bleeding, manic switching, and a recognized discontinuation syndrome, with overdose usually producing CNS and cardiovascular manifestations.

Name: Travoprost
Description: Travoprost (DrugBank DB00287) is a synthetic prostaglandin F2α analog formulated mainly as an isopropyl ester prodrug; structurally it contains a substituted cyclopentane core bearing α- and ω-side chains, a terminal phenyl group with trifluoromethyl substitution that increases lipophilicity, and multiple stereodefined hydroxyl/alkenyl functionalities characteristic of prostanoid signaling molecules. It belongs to the prostaglandin analog and ophthalmic hypotensive agent class, with a prostanoid lipid scaffold derived from the PGF2α framework. Similar drugs include latanoprost, tafluprost, bimatoprost, and unoprostone, all used to lower intraocular pressure by related mechanisms. After topical ocular administration, travoprost is absorbed through the cornea and rapidly hydrolyzed by esterases to travoprost acid, the active metabolite; systemic exposure is low, distribution is largely local to anterior segment tissues, metabolism occurs further via β-oxidation and oxidative/reductive pathways, and metabolites are eliminated predominantly renally. Its principal target is the prostaglandin F receptor, PTGFR (FP receptor), activation of which increases uveoscleral outflow and to a lesser extent trabecular outflow, thereby reducing intraocular pressure. It is indicated for open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension, including chronic pressure elevation refractory to first-line therapy. Toxicity is usually ocular rather than systemic, with examples including conjunctival hyperemia, eyelash growth, periocular skin darkening, iris pigmentation changes, ocular irritation, pruritus, dry eye, and rare uveitis or cystoid macular edema in susceptible patients; overdose is generally limited by minimal systemic absorption. Clinically, travoprost is used as once-daily topical therapy, alone or with agents such as timolol, especially when durable intraocular pressure reduction and convenient adherence are desired.

Name: Amcinonide
Description: Amcinonide (DrugBank DB00288) is a highly potent synthetic fluorinated corticosteroid built on the pregnane glucocorticoid steroid nucleus, specifically a hydrocortisone-derived 21-carbon tetracyclic framework modified by a 9α-fluoro substituent, an 11β-hydroxyl group, a 16,17-acetonide ketal, and a 17-side-chain bearing the characteristic corticosteroid carbonyl/alcohol functionality; chemically it is classified as a topical corticosteroid and more specifically a halogenated glucocorticoid, with a corticosteroid steroidal scaffold closely related to fluocinonide, fluocinolone acetonide, triamcinolone acetonide, and betamethasone derivatives. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor encoded by NR3C1, leading to altered transcription of anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive mediators, with downstream suppression of phospholipase A2 activity, cytokine production, and inflammatory cell recruitment. Clinically, amcinonide is used topically for corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses such as atopic dermatitis, allergic or contact dermatitis, eczema, lichen simplex chronicus, and localized psoriasis, particularly pruritic, erythematous, or lichenified inflammatory lesions. Percutaneous absorption is generally limited but increases with high potency use, damaged skin, occlusion, large surface area application, prolonged therapy, and pediatric exposure; after absorption it distributes systemically in a manner typical of corticosteroids, is metabolized mainly hepatically to inactive metabolites, and is excreted predominantly in urine with some biliary/fecal elimination. Toxicity is dominated by local cutaneous atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, acneiform eruption, rosacea, delayed wound healing, and secondary infection, while excessive systemic exposure can cause reversible hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis suppression, hyperglycemia, glucosuria, and Cushingoid features. Common adverse effects include burning, stinging, dryness, irritation, folliculitis, hypertrichosis, and hypopigmentation, and clinical use is therefore typically short-course, localized topical therapy with avoidance of prolonged occlusive application on the face, groin, axillae, or extensive body surfaces.

Name: Bleomycin
Description: Bleomycin (DrugBank DB00290) is a mixture of closely related glycopeptide antitumor antibiotics, principally bleomycin A2 and B2, characterized by a metal-chelating bithiazole-containing peptide framework linked to a carbohydrate-rich, highly polar cationic domain and a terminal amine side chain; chemically it belongs to the bleomycin/phleomycin family of glycopeptide natural products, with a distinctive bithiazole–pseudopeptide scaffold that intercalates DNA and binds Fe2+ to generate oxygen radicals. Similar drugs include other bleomycin congeners and the related antibiotic phleomycin, while clinically analogous DNA-damaging antineoplastics include dactinomycin, mitomycin C, and cisplatin. Its principal pharmacologic target is genomic DNA, with no single canonical protein target; activity depends on iron complexation and oxidative single- and double-strand DNA cleavage, with intracellular handling influenced by bleomycin hydrolase, the major inactivating enzyme. After parenteral administration, absorption is route-dependent, distribution is broad but uneven with relatively high skin and lung exposure, protein binding is low, metabolism is limited except for enzymatic hydrolysis by bleomycin hydrolase, and elimination is predominantly renal, so exposure rises in kidney impairment. Major toxicities include dose-related pulmonary injury ranging from pneumonitis to irreversible interstitial fibrosis, plus mucocutaneous toxicity such as hyperpigmentation, flagellate erythema, stomatitis, and alopecia; fever, chills, nausea, and rare anaphylactoid reactions also occur, while myelosuppression is usually modest. Bleomycin is indicated for Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, testicular germ-cell tumors, and palliative treatment of malignant pleural effusions, and is used clinically in combination regimens such as ABVD for Hodgkin lymphoma and BEP for testicular cancer.

Name: Chlorambucil
Description: Chlorambucil (DrugBank DB00291) is a bifunctional aromatic nitrogen mustard whose structure consists of a para-substituted phenyl ring bearing a bis(2-chloroethyl)amino alkylating moiety and a butyric acid side chain, placing it in the antineoplastic alkylating agent class; its core scaffold is the phenylalanine-like aryl-alkyl carboxylic acid nitrogen mustard framework. It is closely related to other nitrogen mustards and DNA-alkylating agents such as melphalan, cyclophosphamide, mechlorethamine, and bendamustine, with melphalan being especially similar structurally and mechanistically. Chlorambucil acts primarily through nonenzymatic formation of reactive aziridinium intermediates that covalently alkylate DNA, especially at the N7 position of guanine, producing interstrand and intrastrand crosslinks; accordingly, it is not highly selective for a single protein target, though its pharmacologic effect functionally engages DNA and downstream DNA damage response proteins such as TP53, ATM, ATR, and checkpoint/repair pathways. It is well absorbed orally, widely distributed, moderately protein bound, extensively hepatically metabolized by beta-oxidation to the active metabolite phenylacetic acid mustard, and eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites with a relatively short plasma half-life. Major toxicities include dose-limiting myelosuppression, cumulative marrow injury, immunosuppression, infertility, mutagenicity, teratogenicity, and secondary leukemia risk. Adverse effects include neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, mucositis, rash, hepatotoxicity, and rarely seizures or pulmonary toxicity. Clinically, it has been used mainly in chronic lymphocytic leukemia and indolent non-Hodgkin lymphomas such as follicular lymphoma, and also in selected autoimmune or nephrotic disorders, often as an oral palliative or combination regimen in older or less fit patients.

Name: Morphine
Description: Morphine (DrugBank DB00295) is a naturally occurring phenanthrene opioid alkaloid characterized by a rigid pentacyclic morphinan framework with a fused aromatic ring system, a 4,5-epoxy bridge, tertiary amine, and key hydroxyl substituents at the 3- and 6-positions that govern receptor binding, polarity, and conjugative metabolism; chemically it belongs to the opiate/benzylisoquinoline-derived alkaloid class, and its core scaffold is the morphinan phenanthrene nucleus. Closely related or pharmacologically similar drugs include codeine, hydromorphone, oxycodone, oxymorphone, heroin, and the semisynthetic antagonist naloxone. Morphine acts primarily as an agonist at the mu-opioid receptor OPRM1, with weaker activity at delta and kappa opioid receptors, altering nociceptive transmission in the CNS and gut. It is used for moderate to severe acute and chronic pain, including postoperative pain, trauma, cancer pain, myocardial infarction-associated pain, and palliative dyspnea. Oral bioavailability is limited by substantial first-pass metabolism and varies widely; distribution is moderate with CNS penetration less rapid than more lipophilic opioids; metabolism occurs mainly by hepatic UGT2B7 to morphine-3-glucuronide and the analgesically active morphine-6-glucuronide, with minor CYP-mediated pathways; elimination is predominantly renal, so metabolite accumulation occurs in kidney impairment. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related respiratory depression, profound sedation, miosis, hypotension, bradycardia, ileus, and coma, with overdose risking fatal apnea; chronic use can produce tolerance, physical dependence, neonatal withdrawal, and histamine-mediated pruritus. Common adverse effects include constipation, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, urinary retention, and confusion. Clinically, morphine remains a prototypical strong opioid administered orally, intravenously, subcutaneously, epidurally, or intrathecally for individualized analgesia and symptom relief.

Name: Bupivacaine
Description: Bupivacaine (DrugBank DB00297) is a long-acting amide-type local anesthetic built on an anilide/arylamide architecture consisting of a lipophilic 2,6-dimethylphenyl ring linked through an amide bond to a pipecolyl tertiary amine side chain bearing an N-butyl substituent; this places it in the amino-amide local anesthetic category, with a xylidine-anilide and piperidine-based scaffold closely related to mepivacaine, ropivacaine, levobupivacaine, and lidocaine, although its butyl substitution contributes to higher potency and longer duration. Its principal targets are voltage-gated sodium channels, especially neuronal NaV isoforms such as SCN9A, SCN10A, and SCN11A, with less selective effects on cardiac sodium channels including SCN5A; it blocks impulse initiation and conduction in peripheral nerves. After local or regional administration, absorption depends on dose, vascularity, and epinephrine use; it is widely distributed, highly protein bound mainly to alpha-1-acid glycoprotein, crosses the placenta, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism primarily via CYP3A4 and CYP1A2 to pipecolylxylidine and other metabolites, and is excreted mainly in urine as metabolites with little unchanged drug. It is indicated for surgical, dental, obstetric, epidural, spinal, peripheral nerve, and infiltration anesthesia and for postoperative analgesia, for example labor analgesia, cesarean section anesthesia, and nerve block for orthopedic procedures. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related CNS and cardiovascular injury, including circumoral numbness, tinnitus, seizures, hypotension, conduction block, ventricular arrhythmias, and potentially refractory cardiac arrest; clinically important adverse effects also include bradycardia, nausea, urinary retention, motor block, and rare hypersensitivity, making careful dose selection and monitoring essential.

Name: Penciclovir
Description: Penciclovir (DB00299) is an acyclic guanine nucleoside analog antiviral whose structure consists of a 2-aminopurine-6-one guanine base attached to a flexible hydroxyalkyl side chain terminating in diol functionality, lacking the complete ribose ring of natural nucleosides; chemically it belongs to the purine nucleoside analog/acyclic guanosine analog class and is built on an acyclic guanine scaffold closely related to acyclovir, ganciclovir, and the oral prodrug famciclovir, with additional similarity to valacyclovir through shared anti-herpes pharmacology. Its principal targets are viral thymidine kinase, which mediates initial phosphorylation in herpes simplex virus and varicella-zoster virus infected cells, and viral DNA polymerase, which is inhibited by penciclovir triphosphate after intracellular activation. Pharmacokinetically, topical penciclovir has minimal systemic absorption, whereas systemic exposure is generally discussed via famciclovir, which is well absorbed orally and rapidly converted to penciclovir; the active metabolite distributes into tissues, has low protein binding, undergoes little further metabolism, persists intracellularly as triphosphate longer than acyclovir in infected cells, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by the kidney. Toxicity is usually low with topical use, but class-related concerns include renal accumulation in impairment, neurotoxicity or crystalluria rarely with systemic exposure, and embryofetal toxicity only at high animal doses. Indications include recurrent herpes labialis and, via famciclovir-derived penciclovir exposure, genital herpes and herpes zoster. Adverse effects include local burning, erythema, numbness, headache, rash, nausea, and rare hypersensitivity. Clinically, penciclovir is used mainly as a topical cream for cold sores to shorten lesion duration and reduce pain, while famciclovir serves as the practical oral route for systemic anti-herpes therapy.

Name: Tenofovir disoproxil
Description: Tenofovir disoproxil (DB00300) is the oral diester prodrug of tenofovir, an acyclic nucleoside phosphonate analog structurally characterized by an adenine purine base linked through a propyl ether side chain to a phosphonate masked as two isopropyloxycarbonyloxymethyl ester groups to enhance lipophilicity and intestinal uptake; chemically it belongs to the nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor class and more broadly to antiviral acyclic nucleoside phosphonates, with an adenine-phosphonomethoxypropyl scaffold closely related to tenofovir alafenamide, adefovir dipivoxil, cidofovir, and nucleoside/nucleotide analogs such as emtricitabine and lamivudine used in combination therapy. After oral administration, it is absorbed and rapidly hydrolyzed to tenofovir, with improved bioavailability when given as fumarate; tenofovir distributes systemically, has low plasma protein binding, enters cells, and is phosphorylated to the active diphosphate that inhibits HIV-1 reverse transcriptase and hepatitis B virus polymerase as a chain terminator. It undergoes minimal CYP-mediated metabolism and is eliminated mainly unchanged by glomerular filtration and active renal tubular secretion. Major toxicity centers on proximal renal tubulopathy, increased creatinine, Fanconi syndrome, hypophosphatemia, and reduced bone mineral density/osteomalacia, with overdose or chronic exposure increasing nephrotoxicity risk. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, flatulence, headache, dizziness, rash, and asthenia. Its principal targets are HIV-1 reverse transcriptase and HBV DNA polymerase. Clinically, it is used for treatment of HIV-1 infection in combination antiretroviral regimens, for chronic hepatitis B, and in HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis when paired with emtricitabine.

Name: Tranexamic acid
Description: Tranexamic acid (DrugBank DB00302) is a synthetic antifibrinolytic agent structurally defined as a trans-4-(aminomethyl)cyclohexane-1-carboxylic acid, a conformationally restricted lysine analogue in which a cyclohexane ring presents spatially separated amino and carboxyl groups that mimic the side-chain pharmacophore of lysine; chemically it belongs to the amino acid derivative class, and its core scaffold is a substituted cyclohexane carboxylic acid. Closely related drugs include epsilon-aminocaproic acid, another lysine mimetic antifibrinolytic, and the serine protease inhibitor aprotinin, which is mechanistically related through inhibition of fibrinolysis. Its principal targets are the lysine-binding sites on plasminogen and plasmin, thereby blocking plasminogen activation and plasmin interaction with fibrin; indirect effects on tissue plasminogen activator-mediated fibrinolysis are central to action. Orally it is reasonably well absorbed, with low protein binding apart from plasminogen, limited metabolism, broad extracellular distribution, passage into synovial fluid and cerebrospinal fluid, and predominant renal excretion as unchanged drug, so exposure increases in renal impairment. Toxicity is chiefly dose-related and mechanistically linked to excessive antifibrinolysis or off-target neuroexcitation, with examples including thromboembolic events, postoperative seizures at high intravenous doses, visual disturbances, and hypotension after rapid injection. Indications include prevention and treatment of bleeding associated with surgery, trauma, postpartum hemorrhage, menorrhagia, epistaxis, dental procedures in hemophilia, and hereditary angioedema in some settings. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness, headache, and less commonly thrombotic complications or hypersensitivity. Clinically it is used intravenously or orally in cardiac and orthopedic surgery, major trauma protocols, obstetric hemorrhage, and heavy menstrual bleeding to reduce blood loss and transfusion requirements.

Name: Ertapenem
Description: Ertapenem (DrugBank DB00303) is a parenteral 1-beta-methyl carbapenem beta-lactam antibiotic whose structure is defined by a fused beta-lactam and unsaturated five-membered carbapenem ring bearing a trans-hydroxyethyl substituent, a carboxylate required for antibacterial activity, and a distinctive acidic benzoate-like side chain that increases lipophilicity and high protein binding; chemically it belongs to the carbapenem subclass of beta-lactams, with a penem-like bicyclic carbapenem scaffold. It is closely related to other carbapenems such as imipenem, meropenem, doripenem, and biapenem, though it differs by its prolonged half-life and lack of useful activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter spp. Its antibacterial targets are penicillin-binding proteins, especially PBPs 2 and 3 and also PBP1 variants, thereby inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-linking and bacterial cell-wall synthesis. After intravenous or intramuscular administration, absorption from IM dosing is high, distribution is mainly extracellular with good penetration into skin, soft tissue, intra-abdominal sites, and female pelvic tissues, protein binding is very high, metabolism is limited to hydrolysis of the beta-lactam ring to an inactive metabolite, and elimination is primarily renal with both unchanged drug and metabolite excreted in urine, supporting once-daily dosing. Indications include complicated intra-abdominal infection, complicated skin and soft tissue infection, community-acquired pneumonia, complicated urinary tract infection including pyelonephritis, and acute pelvic infections. Adverse effects commonly include diarrhea, nausea, infusion-site reactions, headache, rash, and transaminase elevations; important toxicities include hypersensitivity reactions, Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea, seizures or CNS effects especially in predisposed patients, and superinfection risk. Clinically, it is used as broad-spectrum empiric or targeted therapy for mixed aerobic-anaerobic infections, diabetic foot infections, pelvic infection, and step-down outpatient parenteral antimicrobial therapy when once-daily carbapenem coverage is advantageous.

Name: Mitomycin
Description: Mitomycin (DrugBank DB00305) is a naturally derived antitumor antibiotic isolated from Streptomyces caespitosus, characterized structurally by a densely functionalized mitosane core containing a fused aziridine ring, quinone moiety, carbamate functionality, and methoxy substitution that together enable bioreductive activation and DNA alkylation; chemically it is classified as an antineoplastic antibiotic and quinone-containing aziridine alkylating agent, with a mitomycin or mitosane scaffold. Similar drugs include other bioreductive DNA cross-linking agents and antitumor antibiotics such as porfiromycin, doxorubicin, daunorubicin, and to some mechanistic extent cisplatin because of shared DNA-damaging cytotoxicity. After intravenous or intravesical administration, mitomycin is rapidly distributed into tissues, exhibits limited oral utility, undergoes predominantly hepatic and extrahepatic enzymatic reduction to reactive intermediates, has a short plasma half-life, and is eliminated mainly by metabolic clearance with urinary excretion of parent drug and metabolites. Its pharmacologic effect is mediated primarily through reductive activation followed by covalent DNA binding and interstrand cross-link formation, so it lacks a single canonical receptor target, though NADPH-cytochrome P450 reductase, NQO1, xanthine oxidase, and other cellular reductases contribute functionally to activation. Major toxicities include delayed, cumulative myelosuppression, mucositis, nephrotoxicity, pulmonary toxicity, extravasation injury, and the serious hemolytic-uremic syndrome. Adverse effects commonly include leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, nausea, vomiting, stomatitis, fatigue, rash, and bladder irritation with intravesical use. Clinically, mitomycin is used for gastric and pancreatic adenocarcinomas, anal cancer in combination chemoradiation, superficial bladder cancer intravesically, and as an ophthalmic antifibrotic adjunct in glaucoma or pterygium procedures.

Name: Talbutal
