Description: Talbutal (DrugBank DB00306) is a short- to intermediate-acting barbiturate sedative-hypnotic whose structure is based on a 5,5-disubstituted barbituric acid nucleus, specifically a pyrimidine-2,4,6-trione ring bearing allyl and sec-butyl substituents at C5, a pattern that imparts substantial lipophilicity and central nervous system depressant activity; it belongs to the barbiturate class and more broadly to cyclic ureides, with the classic barbiturate scaffold shared by related drugs such as pentobarbital, secobarbital, amobarbital, butabarbital, and phenobarbital. Pharmacologically, talbutal acts primarily as a positive allosteric modulator of the GABAA receptor-chloride channel complex, and at higher concentrations can directly gate the channel, with likely interaction across receptor assemblies containing common GABAA subunits rather than a single unique protein target. After oral administration it is expected to be well absorbed, widely distributed including rapid brain penetration because of lipophilicity, variably protein bound, metabolized predominantly in the liver by oxidative biotransformation and related phase I/II pathways, and excreted mainly as metabolites in urine. Its indication has historically been the short-term treatment of insomnia and the use of sedation or hypnosis in anxious, agitated, or preprocedural patients. Adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, ataxia, cognitive slowing, hangover sedation, respiratory depression, hypotension, and paradoxical excitement; toxicity may manifest as profound coma, suppressed respiration, impaired cardiovascular function, and death in overdose, especially with alcohol, opioids, or other sedatives, and chronic use carries risks of tolerance, dependence, withdrawal, and abuse. Clinically, talbutal has been used as an older hypnotic-sedative, but like similar barbiturates it has largely been displaced by safer agents such as benzodiazepines and nonbenzodiazepine hypnotics.

Name: Vindesine
Description: Vindesine (DrugBank DB00309) is a semisynthetic vinca alkaloid derived from the Catharanthus roseus alkaloid vinblastine and characterized by a complex polycyclic bisindole structure composed of catharanthine- and vindoline-derived subunits linked into a dimeric indole-dihydroindole framework bearing multiple fused rings, tertiary nitrogen functionality, methoxy and ester substituents, and a modified side chain that distinguishes it from vinblastine and vincristine; chemically it belongs to the antineoplastic vinca alkaloids, with a monoterpenoid indole alkaloid scaffold. Closely related drugs include vincristine, vinblastine, vinorelbine, and vinflunine, which share the tubulin-binding vinca scaffold but differ in substitution pattern and toxicity profile. Vindesine acts primarily by binding β-tubulin in microtubules, disrupting tubulin polymerization, mitotic spindle formation, and M-phase progression; tubulin heterodimers, especially TUBB-family proteins, are its principal targets. It is administered intravenously because oral absorption is poor and unreliable, distributes widely into tissues with limited central nervous system penetration, shows substantial protein and tissue binding, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism likely involving CYP3A-mediated pathways, and is eliminated mainly via biliary/fecal excretion with lesser renal clearance. Its major toxicities are dose-limiting myelosuppression and neurotoxicity, with examples including leukopenia, granulocytopenia, peripheral neuropathy, paresthesias, and autonomic dysfunction; vesicant injury can occur with extravasation. Other adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, mucositis, constipation, alopecia, fatigue, and infection risk secondary to marrow suppression. Clinically, it has been used in acute lymphoblastic leukemia, malignant lymphoma, melanoma, lung cancer, and other refractory solid tumors, usually as combination chemotherapy in specialist oncology practice.

Name: Chlorthalidone
Description: Chlorthalidone (DrugBank DB00310) is a thiazide-like sulfonamide diuretic whose structure is distinguished by a chlorinated benzene ring fused to a bicyclic phthalimidine/isoindoline-like system bearing a sulfamoyl group and carbonyl functionality, giving a rigid aromatic sulfonamide scaffold rather than the classic benzothiadiazine core of true thiazides; chemically it is categorized as a sulfamyl benzophenone-related, thiazide-like antihypertensive/diuretic, with a scaffold most often described as a chloro-substituted aromatic sulfonamide fused bicyclic imide. Similar drugs include hydrochlorothiazide, bendroflumethiazide, indapamide, metolazone, and quinethazone, which share distal convoluted tubule natriuretic activity. Its principal target is the sodium/chloride cotransporter SLC12A3 in the distal convoluted tubule, indirectly affecting renal handling of sodium, chloride, potassium, magnesium, calcium, and water. Orally, chlorthalidone is well absorbed, has a relatively slow onset and very long duration due to extensive erythrocyte carbonic anhydrase binding and a large apparent distribution compartment, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged in urine with a long half-life that supports once-daily dosing. Toxicity is dominated by excessive diuresis and electrolyte disturbances, especially hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, hypercalcemia, dehydration, hypotension, and prerenal azotemia; hyperuricemia precipitating gout and worsening glucose tolerance can occur. Indications include hypertension, edema associated with heart failure, renal disease, or hepatic disease, and reduction of calcium nephrolithiasis risk in hypercalciuric patients. Common adverse effects include dizziness, orthostasis, weakness, polyuria, muscle cramps, photosensitivity, rash, and rare sulfonamide hypersensitivity. Clinically it is widely used alone or in combination antihypertensive therapy, particularly when prolonged blood-pressure control or edema management is desired.

Name: Pentobarbital
Description: Pentobarbital (DrugBank DB00312) is a short-acting oxybarbiturate whose structure is based on a 1,3-diazinane-2,4,6-trione barbituric acid core bearing 5-ethyl and 5-(1-methylbutyl) substitutions, features that increase lipophilicity and confer rapid central nervous system penetration; chemically it belongs to the barbiturates, specifically sedative-hypnotic pyrimidinetriones, and its key scaffold is the 5,5-disubstituted barbituric acid nucleus. It is closely related to other barbiturates such as secobarbital, phenobarbital, amobarbital, thiopental, and methohexital, which share the same core but differ in C5 substituents or oxygen/sulfur substitution. Pentobarbital acts primarily as a positive allosteric modulator and, at higher concentrations, direct activator of GABAA receptor chloride channels; reported targets center on GABAA receptor subunits including GABRA1, GABRB2, and GABRG2, with broader CNS depressant effects. It is generally well absorbed after oral or parenteral administration, widely distributed with significant brain uptake, variably protein bound, metabolized mainly hepatically by microsomal oxidation and hydroxylation with some enzyme induction, and excreted predominantly as inactive urinary metabolites with a smaller fraction unchanged. Toxicity is dominated by dose-dependent respiratory depression, coma, hypotension, bradycardia, impaired airway reflexes, and fatal overdose, especially with alcohol, opioids, or benzodiazepines. Indications and clinical uses include short-term treatment of severe insomnia, preoperative sedation, emergency control of refractory seizures or status epilepticus, induction of medically supervised coma for intracranial hypertension, and veterinary euthanasia formulations. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, ataxia, confusion, paradoxical agitation, nausea, rash, and cognitive or psychomotor impairment.

Name: Valproic acid
Description: Valproic acid (DB00313) is a simple branched short-chain aliphatic carboxylic acid whose structure is commonly described as a valeric acid derivative with a tertiary-like branching pattern, specifically the 2-propylpentanoic acid framework, placing it in the fatty acid/short-chain carboxylic acid anticonvulsant class and giving it an acyclic alkyl-carboxylate scaffold rather than a heteroaromatic antiepileptic core. Structurally and pharmacologically related drugs include divalproex sodium and sodium valproate as direct valproate formulations, and more distantly other broad-spectrum antiseizure agents such as carbamazepine, lamotrigine, and topiramate. Its known targets and mechanisms are pleiotropic, including enhancement of GABAergic tone through inhibition of GABA transaminase and succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase, modulation of voltage-gated sodium channels and T-type calcium channels, and inhibition of histone deacetylases, especially class I/II HDACs. Oral absorption is generally rapid and extensive, bioavailability is high, distribution is systemic with high but concentration-dependent albumin binding, CNS penetration is clinically relevant, metabolism is predominantly hepatic via glucuronidation and mitochondrial beta-oxidation with a smaller CYP-mediated fraction, and excretion occurs mainly in urine as metabolites. It is indicated for epilepsy, including absence, myoclonic, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, bipolar disorder, especially acute mania, and migraine prophylaxis. Major toxicities include hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, hyperammonemic encephalopathy, thrombocytopenia, and major teratogenicity such as neural tube defects. Common adverse effects include nausea, tremor, sedation, weight gain, alopecia, menstrual disturbance, and cognitive dulling. Clinically, it is used as a broad-spectrum antiseizure and mood-stabilizing drug, often when mixed seizure types, bipolar mania, or recurrent migraine require a multipurpose agent.

Name: Zolmitriptan
Description: Zolmitriptan (DrugBank DB00315) is a synthetic indole-based antimigraine agent of the triptan class, structurally characterized as a substituted tryptamine/indole ethylamine bearing a 5-position hydroxyl group and a dimethylaminoethyl side chain constrained by a fused oxazolidinone-like ring system, giving a compact serotonin-mimetic architecture; its core chemical scaffold is therefore a 1H-indole/tryptamine scaffold modified to enhance oral activity and central penetration. It is closely related to other 5-HT1B/5-HT1D agonist triptans such as sumatriptan, rizatriptan, naratriptan, eletriptan, and almotriptan. Pharmacologically, zolmitriptan acts primarily at HTR1B and HTR1D, with additional activity reported at HTR1A, producing cranial vasoconstriction and inhibition of trigeminovascular neuropeptide release. It is indicated for the acute treatment of migraine with or without aura and is also used intranasally for acute cluster headache, relieving headache pain, photophobia, phonophobia, and nausea in selected patients. Oral absorption is good, bioavailability is moderate because of first-pass metabolism, distribution includes CNS access, metabolism occurs mainly in the liver via CYP1A2 to the active N-desmethyl metabolite, and elimination is predominantly renal as parent drug and metabolites, with a terminal half-life of roughly 3 hours. Toxicity is generally dose-related and includes serotonergic and vasospastic risk; examples include chest pressure, hypertension, coronary vasospasm, myocardial ischemia, serotonin syndrome when combined with serotonergic drugs, and rare cerebrovascular events. Common adverse effects include paresthesia, dizziness, somnolence, asthenia, dry mouth, nausea, and throat or chest tightness. Clinically, it is used as an abortive, not preventive, migraine therapy in adults, with oral, orally disintegrating, and intranasal formulations chosen according to speed of onset and nausea severity.

Name: Acetaminophen
Description: Acetaminophen (paracetamol; DrugBank DB00316) is a small aniline-derived analgesic and antipyretic whose structure consists of a para-hydroxylated phenyl ring bearing an acetamide substituent, giving a p-hydroxyacetanilide framework with a simple phenyl-acetamide scaffold typical of para-aminophenol derivatives. Chemically it is classified as an anilide and non-opioid analgesic/antipyretic, and it is closely related to acetanilide and phenacetin, with broader therapeutic similarity to NSAID analgesics such as ibuprofen and aspirin despite weaker peripheral anti-inflammatory activity. Its pharmacology is attributed mainly to central inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis, historically linked to cyclooxygenase proteins PTGS1 and PTGS2, with additional evidence implicating endocannabinoid-related signaling and TRPA1 via the metabolite AM404. After oral administration it is rapidly and well absorbed, has moderate distribution with limited protein binding, readily crosses the blood-brain barrier, and undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism predominantly by glucuronidation and sulfation; a minor CYP-mediated pathway, especially via CYP2E1 and to lesser extents CYP1A2 and CYP3A4, forms the reactive intermediate NAPQI, which is detoxified by glutathione, and metabolites are excreted mainly in urine. It is indicated for mild to moderate pain and fever, including headache, myalgia, osteoarthritis pain, postoperative pain, and febrile viral illnesses. Adverse effects are usually mild, such as nausea, rash, and transient liver enzyme elevation, but overdose can cause severe centrilobular hepatic necrosis, acute liver failure, and sometimes renal tubular injury, with heightened risk in alcohol use, fasting, or enzyme induction; clinically it is widely used alone and in combination products, including pediatric antipyresis and multimodal perioperative analgesia.

Name: Codeine
Description: Codeine (DB00318) is a naturally derived opiate analgesic of the phenanthrene alkaloid class, structurally characterized as the 3-O-methyl ether of morphine with a rigid pentacyclic morphinan/phenanthrene scaffold bearing a tertiary amine, a 6-hydroxyl group, and an ether bridge that confers opioid receptor activity while reducing intrinsic potency relative to morphine. It belongs to the opioid analgesics and antitussives, specifically the methylated morphine congeners, and is chemically and pharmacologically similar to morphine, hydrocodone, dihydrocodeine, oxycodone, and heroin, with morphine being its principal active metabolite. Its main target is the mu-opioid receptor OPRM1, with weaker functional interactions in opioid systems involving delta and kappa receptors; antitussive effects are mediated centrally in the brainstem. Codeine is generally well absorbed orally, undergoes first-pass hepatic metabolism, distributes broadly including across the blood-brain barrier and placenta, and is metabolized chiefly by CYP2D6 to morphine, by CYP3A4 to norcodeine, and by UGT2B7 to glucuronides; elimination is predominantly renal as metabolites and conjugates, and pharmacokinetic variability is strongly influenced by CYP2D6 genotype. It is indicated for mild-to-moderate pain and cough suppression, for example postoperative dental pain, musculoskeletal pain, and nonproductive cough. Toxicity is opioid-typical and includes dose-related respiratory depression, profound sedation, miosis, constipation, nausea, and hypotension, with overdose causing coma or death; ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolizers, children after tonsillectomy, and patients using other CNS depressants are at particular risk. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, vomiting, pruritus, and constipation, and clinically it is used alone or in combination products such as with acetaminophen or aspirin when nonopioid therapy is insufficient.

Name: Piperacillin
Description: Piperacillin (DrugBank DB00319) is a semisynthetic ureidopenicillin characterized by the conserved penam nucleus, a fused beta-lactam and thiazolidine ring system bearing the acylamino side chain typical of extended-spectrum antipseudomonal penicillins; structurally, its key scaffold is the 6-aminopenicillanic acid beta-lactam core elaborated with a polar ureido side chain that broadens Gram-negative activity. It belongs to the beta-lactam antibiotic class, specifically the acylureidopenicillins, and is chemically and pharmacologically similar to other penicillins such as ampicillin, amoxicillin, mezlocillin, azlocillin, ticarcillin, and the fixed combination piperacillin-tazobactam. Its principal targets are bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, including transpeptidases such as PBP1a, PBP1b, PBP2, and PBP3, thereby inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-linking and cell-wall synthesis. Piperacillin is administered parenterally because oral absorption is inadequate; it distributes well into extracellular fluids and inflamed tissues, has modest protein binding, limited CNS penetration unless meninges are inflamed, undergoes minimal metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by renal excretion with contribution from biliary clearance, requiring dose adjustment in renal impairment. Toxicities include hypersensitivity reactions up to anaphylaxis, beta-lactam-associated interstitial nephritis, neurotoxicity including seizures at high concentrations, hematologic effects such as thrombocytopenia or neutropenia, and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea. Common adverse effects include rash, diarrhea, nausea, injection-site reactions, fever, eosinophilia, and transaminase elevation. Clinically it is used for moderate to severe susceptible infections, especially hospital-acquired pneumonia, complicated intra-abdominal infection, complicated urinary tract infection, skin and soft-tissue infection, gynecologic infection, bacteremia, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections, often with tazobactam to extend activity against beta-lactamase-producing organisms.

Name: Dihydroergotamine
Description: Dihydroergotamine (DrugBank DB00320) is a semisynthetic hydrogenated ergot alkaloid derived from ergotamine, characterized structurally by a rigid tetracyclic ergoline/lysergic acid-like fused indole scaffold linked through an amide to a substituted tripeptide-like moiety; hydrogenation of the 9,10-double bond reduces some vasospastic liability relative to ergotamine while preserving potent serotonergic activity. It belongs to the ergopeptine ergot alkaloid class, with an ergoline scaffold shared by related antimigraine agents such as ergotamine, methysergide, bromocriptine, cabergoline, and lisuride. Pharmacologically, it acts primarily as an agonist/partial agonist at 5-HT1B and 5-HT1D receptors, with additional activity at 5-HT1F, alpha-adrenergic receptors, and dopamine D2 receptors, producing cranial vasoconstriction and inhibition of trigeminovascular neuropeptide release. After intranasal, parenteral, or oral inhalation-type delivery, absorption is route dependent; oral bioavailability is poor because of extensive first-pass metabolism, plasma protein binding is substantial, distribution is broad, metabolism is predominantly hepatic via CYP3A4, and excretion occurs mainly in bile/feces with a smaller renal component. Its principal indication is acute treatment of migraine with or without aura and refractory cluster headache, especially prolonged or recurrent attacks. Adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, rhinitis with nasal use, dizziness, paresthesias, and chest tightness. Toxicity includes excessive vasoconstriction, hypertension, myocardial or peripheral ischemia, stroke risk, and ergotism, with heightened danger in pregnancy, sepsis, vascular disease, and during coadministration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors such as macrolides or azole antifungals. Clinically it is used as injectable or intranasal rescue therapy when triptans fail, when migraine recurs, or when a longer-acting nonopioid abortive option is needed.

Name: Amitriptyline
Description: Amitriptyline (DrugBank DB00321) is a tertiary amine tricyclic antidepressant built on a dibenzocycloheptene scaffold, consisting of two fused benzene rings linked through a seven-membered central ring and bearing a flexible three-carbon side chain terminating in a dimethylamino group; this highly lipophilic, cationic arylalkylamine architecture places it in the tricyclic antidepressant and dibenzazepine-like chemical family, with close structural and pharmacologic similarity to nortriptyline, imipramine, doxepin, clomipramine, and cyclobenzaprine. Its principal targets are the serotonin transporter SLC6A4 and norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, with additional clinically relevant antagonism at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors such as CHRM1, histamine H1 receptor HRH1, and alpha1-adrenergic receptors including ADRA1A, explaining both efficacy and adverse effects. Amitriptyline is well absorbed orally but undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, is extensively distributed with high protein binding and CNS penetration, is metabolized mainly by CYP2C19, CYP2D6, and CYP3A4 to active nortriptyline and other hydroxylated metabolites, and is excreted predominantly in urine as metabolites. Toxicity is characteristic of TCAs and includes dose-related anticholinergic delirium, seizures, coma, and potentially fatal cardiotoxicity with QRS widening, QT prolongation, and ventricular arrhythmias in overdose. Indications include major depressive disorder, neuropathic pain, postherpetic neuralgia, migraine prophylaxis, chronic tension-type headache, fibromyalgia, and some functional gastrointestinal pain syndromes. Common side effects include sedation, dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, orthostatic hypotension, tachycardia, weight gain, and sexual dysfunction; clinically it is used both as an antidepressant and, often at lower doses, as an analgesic adjuvant and sleep-promoting agent in chronic pain practice.

Name: Floxuridine
Description: Floxuridine (DB00322) is a fluorinated pyrimidine antimetabolite structurally defined as 5-fluoro-2′-deoxyuridine, consisting of a uracil-like pyrimidine base bearing a fluorine at the 5-position and linked to a 2-deoxyribose sugar; it therefore belongs to the fluoropyrimidine nucleoside analog class and is built on a deoxyuridine/thymidine-like nucleoside scaffold. Closely related drugs include fluorouracil, capecitabine, tegafur, trifluridine, and the deoxycytidine analog gemcitabine as a broader antimetabolite comparator. Its principal pharmacologic action follows intracellular conversion to active metabolites, especially 5-fluoro-2′-deoxyuridine monophosphate, which inhibits thymidylate synthase, with additional incorporation of fluorinated nucleotides into DNA; relevant targets and pathway proteins include thymidylate synthase, thymidine phosphorylase, thymidine kinase, deoxyuridine triphosphatase, and DNA polymerase-associated DNA synthesis pathways. Floxuridine is poorly suited to routine oral use because of extensive first-pass conversion to fluorouracil, and in practice is most often delivered by continuous intra-arterial hepatic infusion, achieving high regional liver exposure; it distributes into rapidly proliferating tissues, is metabolized mainly to fluorouracil and downstream catabolites by pyrimidine metabolic enzymes including dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase, and is eliminated predominantly as urinary metabolites. Clinically it has been used mainly for hepatic metastases from colorectal adenocarcinoma and other gastrointestinal tumors. Toxicity is characteristic of fluoropyrimidines, including severe myelosuppression, mucositis, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, dermatitis, alopecia, hepatotoxicity, biliary sclerosis with hepatic arterial infusion, and potentially fatal toxicity in dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase deficiency. Side effects commonly include stomatitis, anorexia, abdominal pain, fever, rash, and catheter- or infusion-related hepatic complications.

Name: Tolcapone
Description: Tolcapone (DrugBank DB00323) is a nitrocatechol catechol-O-methyltransferase inhibitor structurally characterized by a substituted benzophenone framework bearing a catechol ring, a para-methyl group, and a strongly electron-withdrawing nitro substituent on the opposing aryl ring, giving a lipophilic nitrocatechol diaryl-ketone architecture; thus, it belongs to the nitrocatechol antiparkinson class and is built on a benzophenone-like scaffold. Closely related drugs include the peripheral COMT inhibitors entacapone and opicapone, which share nitrocatechol pharmacophoric features, although tolcapone is distinguished by central as well as peripheral activity. It targets COMT as its principal protein target, inhibiting methylation of levodopa and dopamine and thereby prolonging levodopa exposure. After oral administration it is rapidly absorbed with moderate bioavailability, is highly protein bound, distributes into peripheral tissues and the central nervous system, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly by glucuronidation with minor oxidative pathways, and is eliminated predominantly in urine as metabolites with a relatively short plasma half-life, necessitating repeated dosing alongside levodopa/carbidopa. Its major indication is Parkinson disease, especially end-of-dose wearing-off and motor fluctuations in levodopa-treated patients, where it is used as adjunctive therapy to improve on-time and reduce bradykinesia, rigidity, and fluctuation-related disability. Important adverse effects include dyskinesia, nausea, diarrhea, orthostatic hypotension, hallucinations, insomnia, and orange urine discoloration. The major toxicity concern is potentially severe idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity, including fatal acute liver failure, with additional risks such as rhabdomyolysis or hyperpyrexia during dopaminergic destabilization, so clinical use is restricted to carefully selected, liver-monitored patients inadequately controlled with other adjuncts.

Name: Fluorometholone
Description: Fluorometholone (DrugBank DB00324) is a synthetic fluorinated corticosteroid built on the pregnane steroid nucleus, specifically a hydrocortisone-like four-ring cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene scaffold bearing the characteristic 11beta-hydroxyl, 3-keto, 20-keto, 21-hydroxyl, a 6alpha-methyl substituent, and a 9alpha-fluoro group that increases glucocorticoid potency while limiting mineralocorticoid activity; chemically it is a corticosteroid anti-inflammatory ophthalmic glucocorticoid, with a steroidal glucocorticoid scaffold shared with related drugs such as prednisolone, dexamethasone, loteprednol etabonate, rimexolone, and fluorometholone acetate. Its principal pharmacologic target is the glucocorticoid receptor encoded by NR3C1, with downstream suppression of phospholipase A2-mediated eicosanoid generation and reduced expression of inflammatory cytokines, adhesion molecules, and COX-2. In ophthalmic use, systemic absorption is usually low but can occur through corneal, conjunctival, and nasolacrimal routes; distribution is primarily local to anterior ocular tissues, metabolism occurs mainly after systemic uptake via hepatic steroid-reducing and conjugative pathways, and excretion is largely renal as metabolites. It is indicated for steroid-responsive inflammatory conditions of the palpebral and bulbar conjunctiva, cornea, and anterior segment, including allergic conjunctivitis, superficial punctate keratitis, episcleritis, postoperative ocular inflammation, and anterior uveitic irritation. Adverse effects and toxicities include elevated intraocular pressure, steroid-induced glaucoma, posterior subcapsular cataract, delayed corneal epithelial healing, secondary bacterial, viral, or fungal ocular infection, corneal thinning or perforation in susceptible eyes, blurred vision, irritation, hyperemia, and rare systemic corticosteroid effects with prolonged intensive use. Clinically, it is used as ophthalmic suspension or ointment when a relatively lower-penetration steroid is preferred for short-term control of external eye inflammation, especially after surgery or in allergic and inflammatory ocular surface disease.

Name: Nitroprusside
Description: Nitroprusside (DrugBank DB00325), used clinically as sodium nitroprusside, is a nitrosyl-transition-metal coordination complex composed of an octahedral iron center ligated by five cyanide groups and one linear nitrosyl ligand, making it a metal nitrosyl cyanide complex within the broader class of inorganic vasodilators and nitric oxide donors; its core scaffold is the nitrosyl pentacyanoferrate framework, which distinguishes it from organic nitrate and nitrite vasodilators, although it is pharmacologically similar to nitric oxide–releasing or cGMP-elevating agents such as nitroglycerin, isosorbide dinitrate, isosorbide mononitrate, and to some extent inhaled nitric oxide. After intravenous administration it has immediate onset and very short duration because it is not orally used, distributes rapidly in the vascular compartment, undergoes biotransformation through reaction with oxyhemoglobin and intracellular reductants to release nitric oxide or related nitrosyl species while liberating cyanide, with detoxification of cyanide by rhodanese to thiocyanate in the presence of sulfur donors, and is cleared mainly renally as thiocyanate. Its principal functional target is the soluble guanylate cyclase pathway, likely via nitric oxide activation of GUCY1A1/GUCY1B1, increasing cGMP in vascular smooth muscle and producing balanced arterial and venous dilation. It is indicated for hypertensive emergencies, acute decompensated heart failure with elevated afterload, and controlled intraoperative hypotension. Major toxicities include profound hypotension, cyanide toxicity with lactic acidosis, altered mental status, arrhythmias, and thiocyanate accumulation causing weakness, tinnitus, psychosis, or hypothyroid effects, while common adverse effects include headache, nausea, vomiting, diaphoresis, palpitations, abdominal pain, and excessive blood pressure reduction; accordingly, clinical use is restricted to closely monitored IV infusion, often in intensive care or operative settings, with dose limitation and surveillance of acid-base status and renal function.

Name: Hydromorphone
Description: Hydromorphone (DrugBank DB00327) is a semisynthetic opioid analgesic structurally derived from morphine and characterized by the rigid morphinan or 4,5-epoxymorphinan polycyclic phenanthrene-like framework bearing a 3-hydroxyl group, a ketone at the 6-position, a reduced 7,8 bond relative to morphine, and a tertiary N-methyl amine, features that increase potency and alter lipophilicity; it is therefore classified as a phenanthrene opioid within the morphinan alkaloid family, with a classic morphine-like scaffold closely related to morphine, oxymorphone, codeine, hydrocodone, and oxycodone. Its principal pharmacologic target is the mu-opioid receptor encoded by OPRM1, with weaker functional interaction at delta and kappa opioid receptors, producing central analgesia, sedation, miosis, reduced gastrointestinal motility, and respiratory depression. Hydromorphone is used for moderate to severe acute and chronic pain, including postoperative pain, trauma, cancer pain, and palliative or end-of-life symptom control. It is generally well absorbed orally but undergoes substantial first-pass metabolism, is also used parenterally and epidurally, distributes widely into highly perfused tissues including the CNS, is metabolized mainly by hepatic glucuronidation via UGT2B7 to hydromorphone-3-glucuronide, and is excreted predominantly in urine as metabolites. Toxicity is opioid-typical and dose related, with overdose causing profound respiratory depression, apnea, coma, bradycardia, hypotension, and death; neuroexcitatory metabolite accumulation may contribute to agitation or myoclonus, especially in renal impairment. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, constipation, pruritus, dizziness, somnolence, urinary retention, and confusion, while clinically it is used as immediate- and extended-release formulations or injection when potent opioid titration is required or morphine is poorly tolerated.

Name: Indomethacin
Description: Indomethacin (DrugBank DB00328) is a potent nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug of the indoleacetic acid class, structurally characterized by an indole nucleus bearing a 4-chlorobenzoyl substituent, a 5-methoxy group, a 2-methyl substituent, and an acetic acid side chain that confers acidic cyclooxygenase-binding properties; its core chemical scaffold is therefore an aryl-substituted indole-acetic acid pharmacophore. It is chemically related to other acidic NSAIDs, with similar drugs including sulindac, etodolac, diclofenac, ketorolac, and tolmetin, which share prostaglandin synthesis inhibition despite differing heteroaryl scaffolds. Indomethacin primarily targets prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthase 1 and 2, COX-1 and COX-2, reducing prostaglandin formation and thereby inflammation, pain, and fever. It is well absorbed orally, highly protein bound, widely distributed including synovial fluid and the central nervous system, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism via O-demethylation, N-deacylation, and glucuronidation, and is eliminated through both renal and biliary routes as parent drug and metabolites. Its major toxicities reflect strong COX-1 inhibition and include gastrointestinal ulceration, bleeding, perforation, renal insufficiency, sodium retention, hyperkalemia, hypertension, hepatotoxicity, and increased cardiovascular thrombotic risk; overdose may produce severe headache, confusion, dizziness, seizures, or metabolic disturbances. Indications include rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute gouty arthritis, bursitis, tendinitis, dysmenorrhea, pain, and fever, and it is also used for patent ductus arteriosus closure in neonates. Common adverse effects include nausea, dyspepsia, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, and edema, while clinical use spans oral, rectal, and intravenous formulations for short-term anti-inflammatory and analgesic therapy where potent prostaglandin suppression is desired.

Name: Ethambutol
Description: Ethambutol (DrugBank DB00330) is a small, highly polar, symmetric aliphatic diamine alcohol composed of a butane-like linker bearing two terminal primary alcohols and two secondary amino functionalities, usually administered as the dextrorotatory active enantiomer or as the dihydrochloride salt; chemically it is classified as a synthetic polyamino alcohol, specifically an ethylenediamine-related antimycobacterial, with a simple flexible aminoalkanol scaffold rather than a fused heterocycle or macrocycle. Structurally and pharmacologically similar agents include other first-line antitubercular drugs such as isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and rifampin, although these are not close structural analogs; more proximate antimycobacterial comparators include diamine-containing compounds with cationic aminoalcohol character. Its principal targets are mycobacterial arabinosyltransferases EmbA, EmbB, and EmbC involved in arabinan synthesis of the cell wall arabinogalactan and lipoarabinomannan, thereby increasing cell-wall permeability and impairing growth. Ethambutol is orally well absorbed, distributes widely including into lungs, kidneys, erythrocytes, and inflamed meninges, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism to inactive aldehyde and dicarboxylic acid metabolites, and is eliminated mainly unchanged in urine with partial fecal excretion; dose adjustment is therefore important in renal impairment. It is indicated primarily for active tuberculosis, including pulmonary and extrapulmonary disease, always in combination regimens to reduce resistance, and is also used in some nontuberculous mycobacterial infections such as Mycobacterium avium complex. Its major dose-limiting toxicity is optic neuropathy with decreased visual acuity, central scotoma, and red-green color discrimination defects, usually dose- and duration-related but potentially reversible; other adverse effects include hyperuricemia, arthralgia, rash, gastrointestinal upset, dizziness, headache, and rare hepatotoxicity or peripheral neuropathy.

Name: Metformin
Description: Metformin (DrugBank DB00331) is a small, highly polar biguanide composed of a dimethyl-substituted biguanide chain with multiple nitrogen atoms that confer strong basicity, hydrophilicity, and cationic character at physiological pH; chemically it belongs to the biguanide class of antihyperglycemic agents and is built on a biguanide scaffold related to guanidine derivatives. Closely similar drugs include phenformin and buformin, older biguanides with similar glucose-lowering mechanisms but greater toxicity, especially lactic acidosis. Metformin is absorbed mainly from the small intestine with incomplete oral bioavailability of roughly 50–60%, negligible plasma protein binding, distribution into liver, kidney, and intestinal tissues via organic cation transporters, essentially no hepatic metabolism, and renal elimination as unchanged drug through glomerular filtration and active tubular secretion, giving a plasma half-life of about 4–8 hours. Its principal molecular pharmacology involves reduced hepatic gluconeogenesis and improved insulin sensitivity, linked to mitochondrial respiratory-chain complex I inhibition and AMP-activated protein kinase signaling; relevant transport or interaction proteins include SLC22A1/OCT1, SLC22A2/OCT2, SLC47A1/MATE1, SLC47A2/MATE2-K, and mitochondrial complex I components. It is indicated primarily for type 2 diabetes mellitus, especially in insulin resistance, and is also used in prediabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome, and sometimes gestational diabetes. Toxicity is dominated by rare but serious lactic acidosis, with heightened risk in severe renal impairment, hypoxia, sepsis, liver disease, or overdose; vitamin B12 deficiency may emerge with chronic use. Common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, anorexia, metallic taste, and weight neutrality or modest loss. Clinically, it is widely used as first-line therapy alone or combined with agents such as sulfonylureas, DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, or insulin.

Name: Ipratropium
Description: Ipratropium (DrugBank DB00332) is a quaternary ammonium antimuscarinic bronchodilator structurally derived from atropine, consisting of a tropane bicyclic ester scaffold bearing a permanently charged isopropyl-substituted quaternary nitrogen and an aromatic acid ester, a motif that limits membrane permeability and central nervous system penetration; chemically it belongs to the anticholinergic parasympatholytic bronchodilators, with a belladonna alkaloid-derived tropane scaffold closely related to atropine, scopolamine, and the inhaled analog tiotropium, and more broadly similar to other muscarinic antagonists such as aclidinium and umeclidinium. Its principal targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially CHRM1, CHRM2, and CHRM3 in airway smooth muscle and secretory glands, where blockade of vagally mediated bronchoconstriction reduces bronchospasm and mucus secretion. After inhalation or intranasal administration, systemic absorption is low, oral bioavailability from swallowed drug is minimal, distribution is largely extracellular because of poor lipid penetration, metabolism is limited and includes ester hydrolysis, and elimination occurs mainly via renal excretion of unchanged drug and metabolites, with a relatively short systemic half-life but longer local airway action. It is indicated for maintenance treatment of bronchospasm in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, including chronic bronchitis and emphysema, and is also used for asthma, particularly in combination with beta2-agonists during acute exacerbations, as well as for rhinorrhea in allergic or nonallergic rhinitis. Adverse effects reflect anticholinergic activity and local administration, commonly including dry mouth, throat irritation, cough, bitter taste, headache, and nausea; clinically important toxicities include paradoxical bronchospasm, urinary retention, tachycardia, precipitation of narrow-angle glaucoma after ocular exposure, and additive antimuscarinic effects in overdose or susceptible elderly patients.

Name: Methadone
Description: Methadone (DrugBank DB00333) is a fully synthetic diphenylpropylamine opioid built around a flexible 4,4-diphenylheptan-3-one scaffold bearing a tertiary dimethylamino substituent, giving a lipophilic cationic structure that differs from morphinan opiates yet preserves strong opioid activity; chemically it is classified as a diphenylheptane or diphenylpropylamine analgesic, with related or similar drugs including levomethadyl acetate, propoxyphene, dextropropoxyphene, loperamide, and other long-acting mu-opioid receptor agonists. Its principal target is the mu-opioid receptor encoded by OPRM1, while additional pharmacology includes weaker activity at NMDA receptors and inhibition of serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake, features relevant to analgesia and toxicity. Methadone is well absorbed orally, has high but variable bioavailability, extensive tissue distribution, high protein binding, and a long, highly variable elimination half-life that exceeds its analgesic duration, predisposing to accumulation; it is metabolized mainly by CYP3A4, CYP2B6, and CYP2D6 to inactive metabolites and excreted in urine and feces, with urinary pH influencing renal clearance. Clinically it is indicated for severe chronic pain and opioid use disorder, especially maintenance therapy, detoxification, and suppression of heroin or prescription opioid withdrawal and craving. Important adverse effects include sedation, constipation, nausea, sweating, miosis, hypogonadism, respiratory depression, and dependence, while major toxicities include fatal overdose, profound respiratory arrest, QT prolongation and torsades de pointes, especially with high doses, CYP inhibitors, electrolyte abnormalities, or coadministration of benzodiazepines, alcohol, or other CNS depressants.

Name: Olanzapine
Description: Olanzapine (DrugBank DB00334) is an atypical antipsychotic of the thienobenzodiazepine class, characterized by a tricyclic dibenzodiazepine-like scaffold in which a thiophene ring is fused to a benzodiazepine core and bears a piperazine-containing side chain, a structure closely related to clozapine and broadly similar to other second-generation antipsychotics such as quetiapine and loxapine in polycyclic heteroaromatic architecture. Its pharmacology reflects multi-receptor antagonism, with principal targets including dopamine D1, D2, D3, and D4 receptors, serotonin 5-HT2A, 5-HT2C, 5-HT3, and 5-HT6 receptors, histamine H1, muscarinic M1-M5, and alpha1-adrenergic receptors, supporting efficacy in psychosis, mania, and agitation. Olanzapine is indicated for schizophrenia, bipolar I disorder including acute manic or mixed episodes, maintenance treatment, and in some settings treatment-resistant mood or psychotic syndromes, with clinical use as oral tablets, orally disintegrating tablets, and long-acting intramuscular formulations; it is also used with fluoxetine for bipolar depression or depressive episodes associated with treatment-resistant depression. It is well absorbed orally, undergoes moderate first-pass metabolism, is widely distributed with high protein binding, and is metabolized mainly by CYP1A2 and to a lesser extent CYP2D6 and direct glucuronidation, with inactive metabolites excreted primarily in urine and partly in feces; smoking increases clearance. Major toxicities include dose-related sedation, marked weight gain, dyslipidemia, insulin resistance, hyperglycemia, anticholinergic effects, orthostatic hypotension, hepatic enzyme elevation, lowered seizure threshold, and rare neuroleptic malignant syndrome, DRESS, tardive dyskinesia, and post-injection delirium/sedation syndrome with depot use.

Name: Atenolol
Description: Atenolol (DrugBank DB00335) is a cardioselective beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist of the aryloxypropanolamine class, structurally characterized by a para-substituted phenyl ring linked through an ether to a 2-hydroxy-3-isopropylaminopropyl side chain and bearing a para-acetamide substituent that increases polarity and limits central nervous system penetration; its core scaffold is the phenoxypropanolamine/beta-blocker pharmacophore. It is closely related to other beta1-preferring blockers such as metoprolol, bisoprolol, betaxolol, and esmolol, and more broadly to propranolol despite lower lipophilicity. Its principal targets are beta1-adrenergic receptor (ADRB1) and, at higher concentrations, beta2-adrenergic receptor (ADRB2), producing negative chronotropic, inotropic, and renin-suppressing effects. Atenolol is used in hypertension, chronic stable angina, acute and post-myocardial infarction management, and is also used off-label for symptomatic tachyarrhythmias, palpitations, and somatic symptoms of anxiety. Oral absorption is incomplete but reliable, bioavailability is roughly 40-50%, protein binding is low, distribution is limited with poor blood-brain barrier penetration, hepatic metabolism is minimal, and elimination is predominantly renal as unchanged drug with a half-life typically about 6-7 hours but prolonged in renal impairment. Toxicity is dominated by excessive beta-blockade, including bradycardia, hypotension, atrioventricular block, acute heart failure, and bronchospasm in susceptible patients, with overdose potentially causing cardiogenic shock or hypoglycemia. Common adverse effects include fatigue, dizziness, cold extremities, exercise intolerance, depression or sleep disturbance less often than with lipophilic beta-blockers, and sexual dysfunction. Clinically, it is prescribed to lower blood pressure, reduce anginal episodes, decrease myocardial oxygen demand, and improve outcomes after infarction in appropriately selected patients.

Name: Nitrofural
Description: Nitrofural (DrugBank DB00336), also known as nitrofurazone, is a synthetic nitrofuran antibacterial characterized structurally by a 5-nitrofuran heteroaromatic ring linked through a Schiff-base hydrazone motif to a semicarbazone/urea-like carboxamide side chain, placing it in the nitrofuran anti-infective class and defining its core scaffold as a nitrofuran-semicarbazone pharmacophore. It is chemically and pharmacologically related to other nitrofuran derivatives such as nitrofurantoin, furazolidone, nifuroxazide, and furaltadone, which share reductively activated nitroheterocyclic motifs. Its antimicrobial action is not highly target-selective; rather, bacterial nitroreductases, including oxygen-insensitive nitroreductase enzymes such as NfsA and NfsB, reduce the nitro group to reactive intermediates that damage multiple macromolecules, including DNA, ribosomal proteins, and other cellular enzymes. Nitrofural is used primarily as a topical anti-infective for prevention and treatment of superficial bacterial infections in burns, skin grafts, ulcers, wounds, and some postoperative lesions, with activity against organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus spp., Escherichia coli, and Enterococcus spp. Systemic pharmacokinetic data are limited because clinical use is largely topical; absorption through intact skin is low but can increase markedly over large denuded or burned surfaces, distribution is expected to remain mainly local unless substantial absorption occurs, metabolism involves reductive biotransformation and further hepatic conjugative handling, and excretion is mainly renal as metabolites. Toxicity includes local irritation, allergic contact dermatitis, rash, pruritus, edema, and delayed hypersensitivity; with extensive exposure, systemic toxicity is possible, including polyneuropathy, hemolysis risk, and experimental mutagenic or carcinogenic concern typical of nitrofuran derivatives. Clinically, it has been used as a topical cream or soluble dressing adjunct in burn care and contaminated wound management, though use has declined in some settings because of sensitization risk and availability of safer alternatives.

Name: Omeprazole
Description: Omeprazole (DrugBank DB00338) is a substituted benzimidazole proton-pump inhibitor characterized structurally by a 5-methoxy benzimidazole ring linked through a sulfoxide bridge to a substituted pyridine, a chiral sulfur-containing motif that underlies its acid-activated prodrug behavior; chemically it belongs to the benzimidazole sulfoxide class, with a benzimidazole-pyridine scaffold shared by related proton-pump inhibitors such as esomeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole, rabeprazole, and dexlansoprazole. After oral administration, usually as an enteric-coated formulation because of acid lability, absorption occurs in the small intestine with moderate bioavailability that increases on repeated dosing, extensive plasma protein binding, and broad tissue distribution with selective accumulation in acidic secretory canaliculi of gastric parietal cells, where protonation converts it to reactive sulfenamide/sulfenic intermediates that covalently inhibit the gastric H+/K+-ATPase, principally ATP4A and ATP4B; metabolism is predominantly hepatic via CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 to inactive metabolites, with urinary and biliary/fecal excretion of metabolites and a short plasma half-life but prolonged pharmacodynamic effect. It is indicated for gastroesophageal reflux disease, erosive esophagitis, peptic ulcer disease, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, Helicobacter pylori eradication regimens, and prevention of NSAID-associated ulcers. Adverse effects commonly include headache, abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, constipation, and flatulence, while toxicities with longer use include hypomagnesemia, vitamin B12 deficiency, fractures, interstitial nephritis, cutaneous lupus, fundic gland polyps, and increased risk of Clostridioides difficile infection or pneumonia; overdose is usually mild but may cause confusion, drowsiness, tachycardia, and visual disturbance. Clinically, omeprazole is widely used for acid suppression, ulcer healing, symptom control of heartburn, and adjunctive therapy in upper gastrointestinal bleeding risk reduction.

Name: Pyrazinamide
Description: Pyrazinamide (DrugBank DB00339) is a simple nicotinamide analogue built on a pyrazine carboxamide framework, consisting of a six-membered aromatic diazine ring bearing a carboxamide substituent; chemically it is classified as a pyrazine derivative, heteroaromatic carboxamide, and first-line antitubercular agent, with a compact pyrazinamide scaffold closely related to pyrazinoic acid, its active metabolite, and structurally similar to other nicotinamide-like antimycobacterial agents, though not closely interchangeable with isoniazid, ethionamide, or nicotinamide itself. It is well absorbed orally, distributes widely into tissues and body fluids including cerebrospinal fluid, undergoes hepatic deamidation by microsomal amidases to pyrazinoic acid followed by further hydroxylation, and is eliminated mainly by the kidney as metabolites with a relatively short plasma half-life that is prolonged in renal or hepatic impairment. Its principal mycobacterial target is linked to conversion by the Mycobacterium tuberculosis pyrazinamidase/nicotinamidase PncA to pyrazinoic acid, which is thought to disrupt membrane energetics and trans-translation through ribosomal protein S1/RpsA, with additional evidence for interference with aspartate decarboxylase PanD. Clinically, pyrazinamide is indicated primarily for active tuberculosis, including pulmonary and extrapulmonary disease such as tuberculous meningitis, and is used in combination regimens during the intensive phase to shorten therapy. Dose-limiting toxicity includes hepatotoxicity ranging from asymptomatic transaminase elevation to hepatitis, plus hyperuricemia and gouty arthralgia; common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, anorexia, rash, fever, photosensitivity, and polyarthralgia.

Name: Cetirizine
Description: Cetirizine (DrugBank DB00341) is a second-generation piperazine-derived antihistamine structurally characterized by a diphenylmethyl-substituted piperazine core bearing a para-chlorophenyl ring and a terminal acetic acid side chain, making it a zwitterionic, polar carboxylated metabolite of hydroxyzine with limited central nervous system penetration. Chemically, it is classified as a piperazine antihistamine and arylalkyl carboxylic acid; its dominant scaffold is the diaryl-piperazine/phenylenyl-piperazine antihistamine framework. Closely related or similar drugs include hydroxyzine, levocetirizine, meclizine, cyclizine, and other H1 antagonists such as loratadine and fexofenadine by therapeutic similarity. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor encoded by HRH1, at which it acts as a selective peripheral inverse agonist/antagonist to suppress histamine-mediated wheal, flare, pruritus, rhinorrhea, and sneezing. After oral administration it is rapidly and well absorbed, with high bioavailability, peak concentrations in about 1 hour, moderate protein binding, limited blood-brain barrier distribution, minimal hepatic metabolism, and predominantly renal excretion largely as unchanged drug, with an elimination half-life typically around 8 hours but prolonged in renal impairment and in some elderly patients. Indications include seasonal and perennial allergic rhinitis, chronic spontaneous urticaria, allergic conjunctival symptoms, and pruritic allergic dermatoses. Adverse effects are usually mild and include somnolence, fatigue, dry mouth, dizziness, headache, and occasional gastrointestinal upset; toxicity in overdose is generally limited to sedation, tachycardia, irritability, or anticholinergic-like symptoms, though dose reduction is clinically important in renal dysfunction. Clinically, it is widely used in adults and children for symptomatic relief of hay fever, hives, and itch, often as a once-daily oral agent when a low-sedation antihistamine is preferred.

Name: Terfenadine
Description: Terfenadine (DrugBank DB00342) is a lipophilic, non-sedating second-generation H1-antihistamine built on a substituted piperidine scaffold linked to a bulky diaryl tertiary alcohol framework, with a para-substituted aromatic system and butanol side chain that confer high peripheral H1 receptor affinity and limited central nervous system penetration under normal conditions; chemically it is classified as a piperidine antihistamine and more broadly as an arylalkylamine-derived antiallergic agent, with a scaffold closely related to other piperidine antihistamines such as fexofenadine, its active carboxylated metabolite, and with pharmacologic similarity to astemizole, loratadine, and cetirizine as second-generation antihistamines. After oral administration it is absorbed but undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism, mainly by CYP3A4, so parent-drug bioavailability is low and systemic activity is mediated largely by fexofenadine; distribution is substantial because of high lipophilicity and protein binding, metabolism is vulnerable to inhibition by erythromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, and grapefruit juice, and elimination occurs predominantly as metabolites in feces with lesser renal excretion. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, while major toxicity arises off-target from blockade of the cardiac hERG/KCNH2 potassium channel, producing QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, ventricular arrhythmias, syncope, and sudden death, especially in overdose, hepatic impairment, or CYP3A4 inhibition. It was indicated for seasonal allergic rhinitis and chronic idiopathic urticaria, relieving sneezing, rhinorrhea, pruritus, and wheals; adverse effects include headache, dry mouth, dizziness, gastrointestinal upset, and palpitations. Clinically, it was once widely used as a peripheral antihistamine but was withdrawn or severely restricted in many countries because of its proarrhythmic risk, with fexofenadine replacing it in practice.

Name: Diltiazem
Description: Diltiazem (DrugBank DB00343) is a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker of the benzothiazepine class, characterized structurally by a 1,5-benzothiazepine ring scaffold fused to an aromatic system and bearing ester, acetyloxy, methoxy, dimethylaminoethyl, and sulfur-containing substituents that confer lipophilicity and ionizable basicity important for membrane penetration and channel binding. Its core chemical scaffold distinguishes it from related L-type calcium channel antagonists such as the phenylalkylamine verapamil and the dihydropyridines nifedipine, amlodipine, and nicardipine, which are pharmacologically similar but chemically distinct. Diltiazem primarily targets the alpha-1 subunit of voltage-dependent L-type calcium channels, especially Cav1.2 encoded by CACNA1C in cardiac and vascular smooth muscle, reducing calcium influx, slowing atrioventricular nodal conduction, decreasing heart rate, and promoting coronary and peripheral vasodilation. It is well absorbed orally but undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, giving moderate bioavailability; it is widely distributed, highly protein bound, metabolized mainly by CYP3A4 to deacetylated and other metabolites, and excreted chiefly in urine with some fecal elimination. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related cardiovascular depression, including bradycardia, hypotension, AV block, worsening heart failure, and overdose-associated shock; hepatotoxicity and drug interactions with beta-blockers, digoxin, and CYP3A4 substrates are notable examples. Indications and clinical uses include hypertension, chronic stable and vasospastic angina, and supraventricular tachyarrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation or flutter with rapid ventricular response and paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia. Common adverse effects include edema, dizziness, headache, flushing, constipation, fatigue, nausea, and sinus bradycardia.

Name: Protriptyline
Description: Protriptyline (DrugBank DB00344) is a tricyclic antidepressant of the dibenzocycloheptadiene family, structurally characterized by a rigid tricyclic ring system composed of two fused benzene rings linked through a seven-membered central ring and bearing a propylidene side chain terminating in a secondary amine, a motif that confers strong monoamine reuptake inhibition and prominent anticholinergic activity; its core chemical scaffold is closely related to other classical TCAs such as amitriptyline, nortriptyline, imipramine, desipramine, and trimipramine, with particularly close resemblance to nortriptyline. Pharmacologically, it primarily targets the norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2 and serotonin transporter SLC6A4, while also antagonizing muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, histamine H1 receptors, and alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, which explains both therapeutic and adverse effects. It is used mainly for major depressive disorder, especially depression accompanied by psychomotor retardation, fatigue, or hypersomnia, and has also been used clinically for refractory depressive symptoms and occasionally off-label for attention-related symptoms or narcolepsy-associated fatigue because of its relatively activating profile. Oral absorption is generally good, distribution is extensive with high protein binding and CNS penetration, metabolism occurs largely in the liver via oxidative pathways including CYP2D6-mediated biotransformation, and elimination is mainly as metabolites in urine with a relatively long half-life permitting once- or divided-daily dosing. Toxicity resembles that of other TCAs and includes dose-related cardiotoxicity with tachycardia, QRS widening, conduction block, and potentially fatal arrhythmias in overdose, as well as seizures, coma, and severe anticholinergic effects. Common side effects include dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, orthostatic hypotension, sweating, tremor, insomnia, agitation, and weight change.

Name: Alfuzosin
Description: Alfuzosin (DrugBank DB00346) is a quinazoline-based, piperazine-containing aryl ether characterized structurally by a substituted 6,7-dimethoxyquinazoline core linked through an amino side chain to a tetrahydrofuran-containing moiety, placing it in the class of selective alpha-1 adrenergic receptor antagonists and more specifically within the quinazoline antihypertensive/urologic scaffold shared with related alpha-blockers such as prazosin, doxazosin, and terazosin, while being pharmacologically comparable though structurally distinct from tamsulosin and silodosin. Its principal targets are alpha-1 adrenergic receptor subtypes, especially ADRA1A, ADRA1B, and ADRA1D, through which it relaxes smooth muscle in the prostate, bladder neck, and lower urinary tract. Clinically, it is indicated primarily for symptomatic benign prostatic hyperplasia, improving urinary hesitancy, weak stream, incomplete bladder emptying, and frequency; it is used as an oral extended-release formulation and is not generally used as first-line antihypertensive therapy despite class ancestry. Pharmacokinetically, alfuzosin is well absorbed orally, with food increasing bioavailability of extended-release products; it is highly protein bound, widely distributed, extensively metabolized in the liver mainly by CYP3A4, and eliminated predominantly as metabolites in feces with a lesser urinary component, with exposure increased in hepatic impairment. Toxicity is mainly an extension of alpha-1 blockade and includes orthostatic hypotension, syncope, dizziness, and tachycardia, with clinically relevant risk of QT prolongation and exaggerated exposure when combined with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ketoconazole or ritonavir. Common adverse effects include dizziness, headache, fatigue, postural hypotension, upper respiratory symptoms, and occasional gastrointestinal discomfort, and clinical use focuses on reducing lower urinary tract symptoms in men with BPH while monitoring blood pressure, hepatic function, and drug interactions.

Name: Nitisinone
Description: Nitisinone (DB00348) is a synthetic triketone/1,3-dicarbonyl aromatic ketone herbicide-derived small molecule built around a nitro-substituted benzoylcyclohexane-1,3-dione framework, specifically a cyclohexane-1,3-dione scaffold bearing a 2-nitro-4-(trifluoromethyl)benzoyl group; chemically it is classified as a diketo/triketone inhibitor and is closely related to other 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (HPPD) inhibitors such as mesotrione, sulcotrione, and tembotrione, although nitisinone is the principal approved human therapeutic in this class. Its pharmacologic target is HPPD, encoded by HPD, and inhibition blocks tyrosine catabolism upstream of homogentisic acid, thereby reducing formation of fumarylacetoacetate-derived toxic metabolites. Orally administered nitisinone is well absorbed, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, is highly protein bound, distributes mainly in extracellular fluids, undergoes limited oxidative biotransformation, and is eliminated slowly by combined renal and fecal routes with a long terminal half-life on the order of about two days, supporting once-daily dosing. It is indicated primarily for hereditary tyrosinemia type 1, where it lowers succinylacetone and prevents progressive hepatic failure, renal tubular dysfunction, and neurologic crises; it is also used in alkaptonuria to reduce homogentisic acid production. Its major toxicity is mechanism-based hypertyrosinemia, which can cause corneal keratopathy, photophobia, eye pain, and cognitive or dermatologic effects if dietary tyrosine restriction is inadequate; additional adverse effects include thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, elevated liver enzymes, conjunctivitis, headache, and abdominal symptoms. Clinically, it is used with a tyrosine/phenylalanine-restricted diet in infants, children, and adults with HT-1 and increasingly in adults with alkaptonuria.

Name: Clobazam
Description: Clobazam (DrugBank DB00349) is a 1,5-benzodiazepine characterized by a fused benzene-diazepine ring system bearing keto functionality and aryl substitution, a structure that distinguishes it from the more common 1,4-benzodiazepines and contributes to its anticonvulsant profile; chemically it is a benzodiazepine anxiolytic and antiepileptic, built on a 1,5-benzodiazepin-2-one scaffold. Similar drugs include diazepam, clonazepam, lorazepam, and nitrazepam, although clobazam is often considered somewhat less sedating at therapeutic anticonvulsant doses than some 1,4-benzodiazepines. Its principal pharmacologic targets are the GABAA receptor benzodiazepine allosteric sites, especially receptor complexes containing α and γ subunits such as GABRA1, GABRA2, GABRA3, GABRA5, GABRG2, and associated chloride channel assemblies, thereby enhancing inhibitory neurotransmission. Clobazam is well absorbed orally, widely distributed including CNS penetration, substantially protein bound, hepatically metabolized mainly by CYP3A4 and CYP2C19 to the active metabolite N-desmethylclobazam, with further biotransformation involving CYP2B6, and is eliminated primarily as urinary metabolites with a relatively long half-life for both parent and active metabolite that supports twice-daily or once-daily use in some patients. It is indicated for anxiety in some jurisdictions and, more importantly, for seizure disorders including Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and refractory epilepsies as adjunctive therapy. Adverse effects include somnolence, sedation, dizziness, fatigue, ataxia, behavioral changes, drooling, constipation, and cognitive slowing; toxicity includes dose-related CNS and respiratory depression, impaired psychomotor performance, paradoxical agitation, tolerance, dependence, withdrawal seizures, and enhanced overdose risk with opioids, alcohol, or other sedatives. Clinically, it is used as chronic adjunctive antiseizure treatment and sometimes for acute anxiety symptom control.

Name: Minoxidil
Description: Minoxidil (DrugBank DB00350) is a small, highly polar pyrimidine-derived vasodilator whose structure is centered on a 2,4-diamino-substituted pyrimidine N-oxide ring bearing a piperidinyl substituent at the 6-position, giving a heteroaromatic aminopyrimidine scaffold with an N-oxide pharmacophore that distinguishes it from simple potassium channel openers. It is classified chemically as a piperidinopyrimidine and more broadly as a direct-acting arteriolar vasodilator; structurally and pharmacologically related drugs include diazoxide and, more distantly, other KATP-channel modulators, while topical use for alopecia is often compared clinically with finasteride. Minoxidil is well absorbed orally, undergoes hepatic sulfation to minoxidil sulfate, the active metabolite, distributes systemically to vascular tissue, and is eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites and unchanged drug with a relatively short plasma half-life, although hemodynamic effects may persist longer; topical absorption is limited but increases with barrier disruption. Its principal target is the ATP-sensitive potassium channel complex, especially sulfonylurea receptor-containing Kir6.x channels in vascular smooth muscle, with pharmacologic activation believed to depend on sulfotransferase-mediated bioactivation; follicular effects are linked to KATP signaling in dermal papilla and perifollicular tissues. It is indicated orally for severe or refractory hypertension and topically for androgenetic alopecia and sometimes other hair-loss disorders. Toxicity reflects excessive vasodilation and fluid retention, including reflex tachycardia, edema, worsening angina, pericardial effusion, and rare ECG changes; hypertrichosis is characteristic. Common adverse effects include scalp irritation, pruritus, dermatitis, unwanted facial hair growth, dizziness, and orthostatic symptoms. Clinically, oral minoxidil is typically reserved for resistant hypertension with a diuretic and beta-blocker, whereas topical formulations are widely used to promote hair regrowth in male and female pattern hair loss.

Name: Megestrol acetate
Description: Megestrol acetate (DB00351) is a synthetic steroidal progestin structurally derived from the pregnane/17α-hydroxyprogesterone series, characterized by the classic four-ring cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene steroid nucleus, conjugated 3-keto and 6-methyl substitution, a double bond in the A/B ring region, and an acetate ester at the 17-position that increases lipophilicity and oral activity; chemically it is categorized as a progestational corticosteroid-like sex hormone analog, with a progesterone-type pregnane scaffold. Closely related or pharmacologically similar agents include medroxyprogesterone acetate, hydroxyprogesterone derivatives, norethindrone, and progesterone itself. Its principal targets are the progesterone receptor and, to a lesser extent, the glucocorticoid receptor, explaining both antineoplastic/endocrine and orexigenic effects. Orally administered megestrol acetate is reasonably well absorbed, highly protein bound, widely distributed into tissues, hepatically metabolized mainly by oxidative and conjugative pathways, and eliminated predominantly in urine with some fecal excretion; it has a relatively long half-life that supports once-daily or divided dosing. Toxicity is dominated by endocrine and thromboembolic risk, with examples including adrenal suppression, hyperglycemia, Cushingoid features, deep-vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and fetal harm in pregnancy. Common adverse effects include marked weight gain, increased appetite, edema, hypertension, nausea, breakthrough vaginal bleeding, hypogonadism, and mood changes. Clinically, it is used as an appetite stimulant and palliative endocrine agent, especially for anorexia, cachexia, or significant weight loss in patients with AIDS or cancer, and for hormone-responsive advanced endometrial carcinoma or palliative treatment of selected breast cancers.

Name: Tioguanine
Description: Tioguanine (thioguanine; DrugBank DB00352) is a thiolated purine antimetabolite structurally defined as a guanine analog in which the 6-oxo group of the purine ring is replaced by sulfur, giving a planar bicyclic thiopurine heteroaromatic system that closely mimics endogenous purine bases; chemically it belongs to the antineoplastic antimetabolite and thiopurine class, with a 6-thioxopurine scaffold shared across sulfur-substituted purine drugs. Closely related drugs include mercaptopurine, azathioprine, and to a lesser extent fluorouracil as another antimetabolite used in leukemia therapy. After oral administration, absorption is variable and incomplete, systemic distribution is broad with intracellular accumulation of active nucleotides, metabolism occurs mainly through hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase to thioguanine nucleotides that are incorporated into DNA and RNA and inhibit de novo purine synthesis, while thiopurine S-methyltransferase and xanthine oxidase contribute to inactivation; elimination is primarily as metabolites in urine. Its principal molecularly relevant proteins include HPRT1, TPMT, XDH/xanthine oxidase, and enzymes of purine synthesis and DNA replication indirectly affected by thioguanine nucleotide incorporation. Tioguanine is indicated mainly for acute nonlymphocytic leukemias, especially acute myeloid leukemia, and has been used in remission induction or maintenance regimens. Major toxicities are dose-limiting myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity including sinusoidal obstruction syndrome and nodular regenerative hyperplasia, gastrointestinal toxicity, and infection risk; common adverse effects include neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomatitis, transaminase elevation, and jaundice. Clinically it is used chiefly in combination chemotherapy protocols for leukemia, with careful pharmacogenetic consideration of TPMT deficiency because severe, sometimes life-threatening hematologic toxicity can occur.

Name: Methylergometrine
Description: Methylergometrine (methylergonovine; DrugBank DB00353) is a semisynthetic ergot alkaloid characterized structurally by a rigid tetracyclic ergoline/indole-derived nucleus with a lysergic acid framework and an amide side chain bearing an N-methyl-substituted alcohol functionality, features that confer potent uterotonic activity; chemically it belongs to the ergot alkaloids, specifically the amide derivatives of lysergic acid, and its core scaffold is the ergoline ring system. Closely related drugs include ergometrine/ergonovine, ergotamine, dihydroergotamine, bromocriptine, cabergoline, and lisuride, which share the ergoline scaffold but differ in receptor selectivity and clinical use. Methylergometrine acts mainly at serotonergic 5-HT2 receptors and alpha-adrenergic receptors on uterine and vascular smooth muscle, with lesser dopaminergic interactions, producing sustained uterine contraction and vasoconstriction. It is used primarily for prevention and treatment of postpartum or postabortion hemorrhage due to uterine atony or subinvolution, especially after delivery of the placenta. After oral, intramuscular, or intravenous administration it is absorbed relatively rapidly, with faster and more reliable exposure parenterally; distribution is systemic with uterine and vascular smooth-muscle effects, hepatic metabolism is the principal route of biotransformation, and elimination occurs mainly via biliary/fecal excretion with a smaller renal component. Toxicity reflects excessive vasoconstriction and uterine stimulation, including severe hypertension, coronary vasospasm, myocardial ischemia or infarction, stroke, seizures, and ergotism; overdose may cause intense abdominal pain and persistent tetanic uterine contractions. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramping, headache, dizziness, sweating, chest pain, and elevated blood pressure. Clinically, it is used in obstetrics as a second-line uterotonic when oxytocin alone is inadequate, but is avoided in patients with hypertension, preeclampsia, significant cardiovascular disease, or peripheral vascular disease.

Name: Buclizine
Description: Buclizine (DrugBank DB00354) is a first-generation piperazine antihistamine whose structure consists of a diarylmethyl-substituted piperazine bearing bulky lipophilic aryl groups, including chlorinated benzhydryl and para-tert-butylbenzyl features, making it a highly hydrophobic cationic amine at physiologic pH; chemically it belongs to the piperazine-class H1 receptor antagonists, and its core scaffold is the diphenylmethyl-piperazine framework shared with related agents such as cyclizine, meclizine, hydroxyzine, and cetirizine precursors, with especially close similarity to cyclizine and meclizine as antiemetic antivertigo drugs. Its principal known target is the histamine H1 receptor, with clinically relevant ancillary antimuscarinic activity and central vestibular suppressant effects likely contributing to antiemetic efficacy. Buclizine is used for prevention and treatment of nausea, vomiting, motion sickness, and vertigo, and has also been used as an appetite stimulant in some settings. After oral administration it is absorbed adequately, distributes widely into tissues including the central nervous system because of its lipophilicity, is expected to undergo hepatic metabolism typical of piperazine antihistamines, and is eliminated as metabolites through renal and probably biliary routes, although modern quantitative pharmacokinetic data are limited. Toxicity is generally that of sedating antihistamines, with dose-related CNS depression, psychomotor impairment, anticholinergic toxicity such as dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention, and in overdose agitation, confusion, or rarely seizures may occur, especially in children or with alcohol and other sedatives. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, fatigue, impaired concentration, and gastrointestinal discomfort, and clinically it has been used as an oral antiemetic or antivertigo agent for travel sickness, labyrinthine disorders, and symptomatic nausea.

Name: Aztreonam
Description: Aztreonam (DB00355) is a synthetic monobactam beta-lactam antibiotic characterized by a monocyclic azetidin-2-one core rather than the fused bicyclic penam or cephem nucleus, bearing an N-sulfonated beta-lactam, a carboxylate, and an aminothiazolyl-oxime side chain that helps confer potent Gram-negative activity and beta-lactamase stability; chemically it belongs to the monobactam subclass of beta-lactams, and its defining scaffold is the sulfonated monocyclic beta-lactam ring. Structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include other beta-lactams active against Gram-negative bacteria such as ceftazidime, cefepime, ceftriaxone, imipenem, and meropenem, although true monobactam comparators are limited. Its principal targets are bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, especially PBP3 in susceptible aerobic Gram-negative organisms, leading to inhibition of peptidoglycan cross-linking and cell lysis. Aztreonam is used for infections caused by susceptible Gram-negative bacilli, including urinary tract infection, lower respiratory tract infection, intra-abdominal infection, septicemia, skin and soft tissue infection, and gynecologic infection, with clinical use in Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, complicated UTI, hospital-acquired pneumonia, and as inhaled therapy in cystic fibrosis patients with chronic Pseudomonas airway colonization. It is poorly absorbed orally, so it is given intravenously, intramuscularly, or by inhalation; distribution is mainly extracellular with therapeutic levels in lung, urine, bile, and peritoneal fluid; protein binding is low to moderate; metabolism is minimal with limited hydrolysis; and elimination is predominantly renal as unchanged drug, requiring dose adjustment in renal impairment. Toxicities include hypersensitivity reactions, gastrointestinal disturbance, transaminase elevation, hematologic abnormalities, local injection-site reactions, and neurotoxicity or accumulation-related adverse effects in severe renal dysfunction; common side effects include diarrhea, nausea, rash, phlebitis, cough or bronchospasm with inhaled use, while cross-reactivity with penicillin allergy is generally low except in patients with ceftazidime-specific side-chain sensitivity.

Name: Chlorzoxazone
Description: Chlorzoxazone (DrugBank DB00356) is a centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant whose structure is a small, chlorinated benzoxazolone consisting of a fused benzene-oxazolone bicyclic ring bearing a 5-chloro substituent; chemically it belongs to the benzoxazolone/oxazolidinone-related heteroaromatic carbamate class, and its core scaffold is the 1,3-benzoxazol-2-one nucleus. It is structurally and therapeutically similar to other centrally acting antispasmodics such as methocarbamol, carisoprodol, metaxalone, and cyclobenzaprine, although it is chemically distinct from them. Its precise molecular target is not well defined; no single high-confidence target protein fully explains activity, and the drug is generally understood to act within subcortical and spinal interneuronal pathways to depress polysynaptic reflexes and reduce muscle spasm. After oral administration it is readily absorbed, undergoes moderate distribution, and is cleared predominantly by hepatic metabolism, especially CYP2E1-mediated oxidation to 6-hydroxychlorzoxazone followed by glucuronide conjugation, with urinary excretion mainly as metabolites and a relatively short elimination half-life.
