Chlorzoxazone is indicated as an adjunct to rest, physical therapy, and analgesic measures for painful acute musculoskeletal conditions such as muscle spasm from lumbar strain, cervical strain, sprain, or other minor traumatic injury. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, lightheadedness, malaise, and gastrointestinal upset, while toxicity may include CNS depression, confusion, and rare but clinically important idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity ranging from transaminase elevation to acute hepatitis or liver failure, especially with overdose, alcohol use, or underlying liver disease; thus clinical use is typically short-term symptomatic relief rather than chronic therapy.

Name: Aminoglutethimide
Description: Aminoglutethimide (DB00357) is a synthetic aromatic glutarimide derivative whose structure consists of a substituted phenyl ring linked to a cyclic piperidine-2,6-dione (glutarimide) core, with an amino substituent conferring weak basicity and enabling interaction with steroidogenic enzymes; chemically it is classified as an endocrine-modulating steroidogenesis inhibitor and more specifically an aromatase and adrenal steroid synthesis inhibitor, built on a glutarimide scaffold related to other cyclic imide drugs. Similar drugs include the aromatase inhibitors letrozole, anastrozole, and exemestane, as well as the adrenolytic agent ketoconazole in the broader functional sense of suppressing steroid biosynthesis. Its principal targets are CYP19A1 aromatase, cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme CYP11A1, and functionally other adrenal cytochrome P450-dependent steroidogenic enzymes, leading to reduced estrogen and corticosteroid synthesis. Aminoglutethimide is orally absorbed, distributed systemically, hepatically metabolized with enzyme-inducing properties, and excreted mainly in urine as parent drug and metabolites; its half-life is moderate and clearance may increase during chronic therapy due to autoinduction. Toxicity reflects adrenal suppression and CNS effects, with examples including adrenal insufficiency, lethargy, ataxia, rash, and rarely hematologic toxicity such as agranulocytosis. Adverse effects commonly include dizziness, drowsiness, nausea, weakness, skin eruptions, hypothyroidism, and orthostatic symptoms. Clinically it has been used in hormone-responsive breast cancer, Cushing syndrome, and other states of pathologic hypercortisolism, often with glucocorticoid replacement when used to block adrenal steroid synthesis.

Name: Mefloquine
Description: Mefloquine (DrugBank DB00358) is a synthetic quinoline-methanol antimalarial characterized structurally by a lipophilic 4-quinolinemethanol core bearing a 2-piperidyl alcohol side chain and strongly electron-withdrawing trifluoromethyl substituents on the quinoline ring, placing it in the aryl amino alcohol/quinoline antimalarial chemical category with a quinoline-methanol scaffold closely related to quinine and more distantly to other quinoline antimalarials such as chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine, and halofantrine. Its antiplasmodial action is not fully resolved but is associated with accumulation in the parasite food vacuole and interference with heme detoxification; proposed interacting proteins include Plasmodium multidrug resistance transporter 1 and other parasite membrane transport systems rather than a single validated human target. Orally, mefloquine is well absorbed, highly protein bound, extensively distributed into tissues, and has a very long elimination half-life on the order of weeks, enabling weekly prophylaxis; it undergoes hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 to inactive metabolites and is eliminated predominantly through biliary/fecal excretion with limited renal clearance. It is indicated for treatment and chemoprophylaxis of malaria, especially uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum and chloroquine-resistant malaria in travelers or endemic settings. Major toxicities include dose-related neuropsychiatric and neurologic reactions such as anxiety, depression, vivid dreams, psychosis, seizures, dizziness, and vestibular disturbance, with gastrointestinal intolerance, headache, insomnia, rash, and palpitations also common; clinically it has been used alone or in combination for malaria treatment and for weekly prevention when regional resistance patterns and patient neuropsychiatric risk make its benefit acceptable.

Name: Sulfadiazine
Description: Sulfadiazine (DrugBank DB00359) is a synthetic sulfonamide antibacterial whose structure consists of a para-aminobenzenesulfonamide core linked through the sulfonamide nitrogen to a 2-pyrimidinyl heteroaryl ring, giving a classical p-aminobenzenesulfonamide pharmacophore with a pyrimidinyl-substituted aniline-sulfonamide scaffold. It belongs to the sulfonamide anti-infective class and shares close structural and pharmacological similarity with sulfamethoxazole, sulfisoxazole, sulfadoxine, and sulfapyridine. Its principal target is bacterial dihydropteroate synthase, which it inhibits as a competitive analog of para-aminobenzoic acid, thereby blocking folate biosynthesis; in Toxoplasma gondii, antifolate activity is exploited clinically in combination with pyrimethamine. Orally, sulfadiazine is generally well absorbed, widely distributed to body fluids and tissues including cerebrospinal fluid and placenta, is moderately protein bound, undergoes partial hepatic acetylation and glucuronidation, and is eliminated mainly by the kidney via glomerular filtration and tubular processes, with urinary pH influencing solubility and crystalluria risk. Toxicity is characteristic of sulfonamides and includes hypersensitivity reactions, rash, fever, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, hepatotoxicity, bone marrow suppression, and renal injury from crystalluria. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, photosensitivity, and allergic skin eruptions. Clinically, it has been used for susceptible streptococcal, pneumococcal, staphylococcal, Haemophilus, and urinary tract infections, but its most established modern use is treatment of toxoplasmosis, especially cerebral toxoplasmosis, usually with pyrimethamine and leucovorin.

Name: Sapropterin
Description: Sapropterin (DrugBank DB00360) is the synthetic 6R-diastereomer of tetrahydrobiopterin, an endogenous reduced pterin built on a bicyclic pteridine scaffold bearing a 2-amino-4-oxo core with a reduced 5,6,7,8-tetrahydro ring system and a chiral 1,2-dihydroxypropyl side chain, placing it in the pterin/biopterin class of redox-active enzyme cofactors; structurally and pharmacologically it is most similar to natural tetrahydrobiopterin and related pterin cofactors or precursor analogs such as sepiapterin and, more distantly, folate-like heterocyclic cofactors. Its principal target is phenylalanine hydroxylase, for which it functions as a pharmacologic cofactor and stabilizing chaperone in BH4-responsive variants, while endogenous tetrahydrobiopterin biology also supports tyrosine hydroxylase, tryptophan hydroxylase, and nitric oxide synthases. After oral administration, sapropterin is absorbed enterally with improved exposure when taken with food, distributed systemically as a small polar endogenous-cofactor analog, metabolized largely through normal biopterin turnover and oxidative recycling pathways, and excreted mainly in urine as biopterin-related metabolites. It is indicated for hyperphenylalaninemia associated with phenylketonuria and for tetrahydrobiopterin deficiency, where it lowers blood phenylalanine and may improve dietary tolerance; clinically it is used with dietary phenylalanine restriction, monitoring of plasma phenylalanine, and in selected BH4-deficient states alongside neurotransmitter replacement. Adverse effects are usually mild and include headache, rhinorrhea, diarrhea, vomiting, abdominal pain, cough, and pharyngolaryngeal symptoms, whereas toxicities of concern include excessive phenylalanine lowering causing hypophenylalaninemia, gastrointestinal irritation, and potential interaction-related hypotension or altered vascular tone through nitric oxide pathways.

Name: Anidulafungin
Description: Anidulafungin (DrugBank DB00362) is a semisynthetic echinocandin antifungal characterized structurally as a large cyclic hexapeptide lipopeptide bearing multiple hydroxylated amino acid residues and an N-linked lipophilic aryl-alkyl side chain, a motif that confers high protein binding and potent antifungal activity; chemically it belongs to the echinocandin class and is built on the echinocandin/nucleus-type cyclic peptide scaffold derived from fermentation products related to pneumocandins. Similar drugs include caspofungin and micafungin, which share the same antifungal class, macrocyclic peptide core, and inhibition of fungal cell-wall biosynthesis. Its principal target is the fungal 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase complex, especially Fks catalytic subunits, leading to impaired glucan formation and osmotic instability in Candida and Aspergillus species. Pharmacokinetically, anidulafungin is administered intravenously because it is not orally bioavailable, distributes largely within extracellular fluid with extensive plasma protein binding, undergoes negligible hepatic CYP-mediated metabolism, and is uniquely degraded slowly by nonenzymatic chemical breakdown to inactive products, with elimination mainly via feces and minimal renal clearance, so dose adjustment in renal impairment is generally unnecessary. It is indicated for candidemia, invasive candidiasis including intra-abdominal abscess and peritonitis, esophageal candidiasis, and other serious Candida infections, and is used clinically in hospitalized patients requiring systemic echinocandin therapy, especially when azole resistance, organ dysfunction, or critical illness is present. Adverse effects include infusion-related reactions, phlebitis, rash, pruritus, fever, nausea, diarrhea, hypokalemia, elevated transaminases, and occasional hypersensitivity or anaphylactoid reactions; toxicity is generally moderate but includes hepatic laboratory abnormalities and rare severe infusion or allergic events.

Name: Grepafloxacin
Description: Grepafloxacin (DB00365) is a synthetic fluoroquinolone antibacterial built on the 4-quinolone/1,4-dihydroquinoline-3-carboxylic acid scaffold, characterized by the class-defining 6-fluoro substituent, a 4-oxo-3-carboxyl pharmacophore required for metal-ion-mediated binding to bacterial topoisomerases, and a lipophilic substituted amine at C7 that enhances Gram-positive and atypical respiratory pathogen activity; chemically it belongs to the quinolone carboxylic acid class, with close structural and pharmacologic similarity to ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin, levofloxacin, sparfloxacin, and trovafloxacin. Its principal targets are bacterial DNA gyrase, especially GyrA/GyrB, and topoisomerase IV, especially ParC/ParE, producing inhibition of DNA replication and transcription. Grepafloxacin was developed for respiratory tract infections such as community-acquired pneumonia, acute bacterial exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, and sinusitis, including infections caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, and atypical organisms such as Mycoplasma and Chlamydia. Orally it is well absorbed, achieves good pulmonary and intracellular distribution, is moderately protein bound, undergoes limited hepatic biotransformation relative to some other fluoroquinolones, and is eliminated by both biliary/fecal and renal routes with a sufficiently long half-life to support once-daily dosing. Its major toxicologic liability is dose-related QT interval prolongation with risk of torsades de pointes and sudden death, which led to market withdrawal; additional toxicities include class effects such as CNS stimulation, hepatotoxicity, phototoxicity, dysglycemia, arthropathy, and tendinopathy. Common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, insomnia, rash, and taste disturbance, while clinical use historically centered on outpatient treatment of lower and upper respiratory infections when broad coverage of typical and atypical bacteria was desired.

Name: Doxylamine
Description: Doxylamine (DrugBank DB00366) is a first-generation ethanolamine antihistamine whose structure consists of a substituted diaryl ether framework linked through an ethoxy spacer to a tertiary dimethylamino group, with a chiral center and an o-methyl-substituted aromatic ring that contributes to lipophilicity and strong central nervous system penetration; chemically it belongs to the H1 receptor antagonist class and more specifically the ethanolamine antihistamines, with an aryloxyethyl-dimethylamine scaffold shared with related sedating antihistamines. Similar drugs include diphenhydramine, carbinoxamine, clemastine, and dimenhydrinate, which show overlapping H1-antagonist and anticholinergic properties. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, with clinically relevant off-target muscarinic cholinergic receptor antagonism and likely minor activity at other CNS receptors typical of older antihistamines. After oral administration it is well absorbed, widely distributed, crosses the blood-brain barrier and placenta, is extensively hepatically metabolized mainly by CYP-mediated N-demethylation and N-oxidation, and is excreted primarily in urine as metabolites with a terminal half-life generally in the range of about 10 hours, prolonged in some patients. Toxicity reflects excessive antihistaminic and antimuscarinic exposure, causing marked sedation, confusion, delirium, mydriasis, tachycardia, dry mucosa, urinary retention, seizures, rhabdomyolysis, and coma in overdose, with heightened risk in children and older adults. It is indicated for allergic rhinitis and other histamine-mediated symptoms, short-term management of insomnia, and in combination with pyridoxine for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, impaired psychomotor performance, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, and paradoxical excitation; clinically it is used as an over-the-counter nighttime sleep aid, as an antiallergic agent, and as part of Diclegis or Bonjesta for pregnancy-related nausea.

Name: Levonorgestrel
Description: Levonorgestrel (DrugBank DB00367) is a synthetic 19-nortestosterone-derived progestin whose structure is a highly lipophilic tetracyclic pregnane/estrane steroid nucleus bearing a 3-keto group, a 17β-hydroxyl substituent, and a 17α-ethynyl group, features that confer potent oral progestational activity; chemically it belongs to the gonane class of anabolic-androgenic steroid derivatives and is built on the estrane/gonane steroid scaffold closely related to other contraceptive progestins such as norethindrone, desogestrel’s active metabolite etonogestrel, norgestrel, and gestodene. Its principal target is the progesterone receptor (nuclear receptor subfamily 3 group C member 3, PGR), with weaker interaction with the androgen receptor and minimal estrogenic activity; pharmacologically it suppresses the luteinizing hormone surge and ovulation, thickens cervical mucus, and alters the endometrium. After oral administration it is rapidly and well absorbed with high bioavailability, is extensively bound to sex hormone-binding globulin and albumin, distributes widely, undergoes hepatic reduction, hydroxylation, and conjugation largely via CYP3A4-dependent pathways, and is eliminated mainly as glucuronide and sulfate metabolites in urine and feces with an elimination half-life typically around one day. Toxicity is generally low at therapeutic doses but may include menstrual irregularity, nausea, headache, breast tenderness, abdominal pain, mood change, and acne; serious adverse events include rare thromboembolic events, ectopic pregnancy after method failure, and intracranial hypertension or hepatic dysfunction in susceptible patients. Clinically it is used for routine hormonal contraception in combined or progestin-only pills, emergency contraception after unprotected intercourse, and long-acting intrauterine systems for contraception and treatment of heavy menstrual bleeding.

Name: Norepinephrine
Description: Norepinephrine (noradrenaline; DrugBank DB00368) is an endogenous catecholamine and phenethylamine built on a 3,4-dihydroxybenzene catechol ring linked to a β-hydroxylated ethylamine side chain, making it a highly polar, protonatable sympathomimetic amine; chemically it is classified as a catecholamine vasopressor, and its core scaffold is the arylethanolamine/phenethylamine catechol scaffold shared with other adrenergic agonists. Closely related drugs include epinephrine, dopamine, phenylephrine, ephedrine, and isoproterenol, which differ in ring substitution or N-alkylation but overlap pharmacodynamically. Norepinephrine acts primarily at adrenergic receptors ADRA1A, ADRA1B, ADRA1D, ADRA2A, ADRA2B, ADRA2C, and to a lesser extent ADRB1, producing potent vasoconstriction with modest cardiac inotropy. Because of extensive first-pass metabolism and poor oral bioavailability, it is used by continuous intravenous infusion; distribution is limited by rapid tissue uptake and poor central nervous system penetration, metabolism occurs mainly by catechol-O-methyltransferase and monoamine oxidase to normetanephrine, 3-methoxy-4-hydroxymandelic derivatives, and vanillylmandelic acid, and urinary excretion is primarily as metabolites. Major indications are acute hypotensive states such as septic shock, vasodilatory shock, neurogenic shock, and severe perioperative hypotension. Toxicity is dominated by excessive adrenergic stimulation, including severe hypertension, reflex bradycardia, arrhythmias, myocardial ischemia, pulmonary edema, anxiety, headache, and reduced renal or mesenteric perfusion; extravasation can cause intense local vasoconstriction, tissue ischemia, and necrosis, a classic example of its dose-limiting toxicity. Clinically, it is a first-line ICU vasopressor titrated to restore mean arterial pressure and end-organ perfusion in distributive shock.

Name: Mirtazapine
Description: Mirtazapine (DrugBank DB00370) is a tetracyclic antidepressant of the piperazinoazepine class whose structure consists of a dibenzocycloheptene-like fused aromatic system linked to a partially saturated azepine/piperazine-containing ring, giving a rigid tricyclic/tetracyclic noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressant scaffold; it is chemically related to mianserin and is often compared with other antidepressants such as mianserin, amitriptyline, and trazodone, although its receptor profile is distinctive. Its principal targets are central presynaptic alpha-2 adrenergic autoreceptors and heteroreceptors, whose antagonism enhances norepinephrine and serotonin release, and it also potently antagonizes serotonin 5-HT2A, 5-HT2C, and 5-HT3 receptors and histamine H1 receptors, with relatively weak muscarinic and peripheral alpha-1 activity. After oral administration it is well absorbed, with moderate first-pass metabolism and bioavailability around 50%, extensive tissue distribution, high protein binding, hepatic metabolism mainly by CYP1A2, CYP2D6, and CYP3A4 to demethylated, hydroxylated, and conjugated metabolites, and elimination primarily in urine with some fecal excretion; the half-life typically supports once-daily dosing. It is indicated for major depressive disorder, especially when insomnia, poor appetite, weight loss, nausea, or anxiety coexist, and is also used clinically for depression in medically ill patients and off-label for sleep disturbance. Toxicity is usually characterized by marked sedation, cognitive impairment, weight gain, increased appetite, dry mouth, constipation, and dizziness, while examples of more serious adverse effects include neutropenia or agranulocytosis, serotonin toxicity in combinations, mania induction, QT prolongation, and overdose-associated CNS depression and tachycardia.

Name: colchicine
Description: Colchicine (DrugBank DB00371) is a tricyclic tropolone alkaloid natural product characterized by a 7-membered aromatic tropolone ring fused to a methoxy-substituted trimethoxyphenyl system and an acetamide-containing ring, giving a rigid, highly oxygenated scaffold that underlies its strong tubulin-binding activity; chemically it belongs to the colchicinoid/tropolone alkaloid class, with a colchicine scaffold shared by related microtubule inhibitors such as demecolcine and thiocolchicoside, and it is mechanistically similar in part to other tubulin-directed agents including vinca alkaloids, although structurally distinct. Its principal target is tubulin beta chains within the alpha/beta-tubulin heterodimer, where binding disrupts microtubule polymerization, impairing neutrophil chemotaxis, inflammasome signaling, and mitosis; secondary pharmacology has been linked to suppression of NLRP3-inflammasome-dependent inflammatory pathways. Colchicine is well absorbed orally, undergoes extensive tissue distribution with leukocyte concentration, is metabolized predominantly by CYP3A4 and transported by P-glycoprotein/ABCB1, has important enterohepatic recirculation, and is eliminated through both fecal/biliary and renal routes, with exposure rising in hepatic or renal impairment and during coadministration with strong CYP3A4 or P-glycoprotein inhibitors such as clarithromycin. It is indicated for acute gout flares, gout prophylaxis, familial Mediterranean fever, and recurrent pericarditis, and is also used clinically in Behçet-associated mucocutaneous disease and selected cardiovascular inflammation settings. Common adverse effects include dose-limiting diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain, while serious toxicity includes myelosuppression, rhabdomyolysis, axonal neuropathy, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, and potentially fatal multiorgan failure in overdose.

Name: Thiethylperazine
Description: Thiethylperazine (DrugBank DB00372) is a piperazine-substituted phenothiazine antiemetic whose structure consists of the tricyclic phenothiazine nucleus with sulfur and nitrogen in the central ring, bearing a 2-ethylthio substituent and a three-carbon side chain terminating in a substituted piperazine, features that confer strong antidopaminergic and antiemetic activity with relatively less emphasis on antipsychotic use. Chemically it belongs to the phenothiazine class, specifically the piperazine phenothiazines, and its core scaffold is the phenothiazine tricycle linked to a basic piperazine side chain; closely related drugs include prochlorperazine, perphenazine, trifluoperazine, chlorpromazine, and promethazine. Its principal known pharmacologic target is dopamine D2 receptor antagonism in the chemoreceptor trigger zone, with additional lower-affinity activity at histaminergic, muscarinic, and alpha-adrenergic receptors contributing to both efficacy and adverse effects. After oral, rectal, or parenteral administration it is absorbed variably, undergoes extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism, distributes widely including into the central nervous system due to lipophilicity, is metabolized mainly by hepatic oxidative pathways and conjugation, and is excreted predominantly as metabolites in urine and bile/feces. It is indicated for prevention and treatment of nausea and vomiting, including postoperative emesis, medication-induced nausea, migraine-associated vomiting, and vertigo-related symptoms. Adverse effects include sedation, dizziness, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, orthostatic hypotension, and extrapyramidal reactions such as acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, and, rarely, tardive dyskinesia or neuroleptic malignant syndrome; overdose or susceptible patients may develop QT-related arrhythmia, seizures, or severe CNS depression. Clinically, thiethylperazine has been used as a symptomatic antiemetic rather than a primary psychiatric agent in hospital and ambulatory settings.

Name: Timolol
Description: Timolol (DrugBank DB00373) is a nonselective beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist built on the aryloxypropanolamine beta-blocker pharmacophore, with a substituted aromatic heterocycle linked through an ether to a propanolamine side chain bearing a secondary alcohol and secondary amine; chemically it is classified as a synthetic beta-blocker and more specifically an oxypropanolamine, with an aryloxypropanolamine scaffold shared across many ophthalmic and cardiovascular beta antagonists. Structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include propranolol, nadolol, metipranolol, levobunolol, carteolol, and betaxolol, although betaxolol is relatively beta1-selective whereas timolol blocks both ADRB1 and ADRB2. Its principal targets are the beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptors, and reduction of aqueous humor production in the ciliary body underlies its antiglaucoma action. After oral dosing timolol is well absorbed but undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, while ophthalmic dosing can still produce systemic absorption through conjunctival and nasolacrimal routes; distribution is systemic with clinically relevant cardiopulmonary exposure, metabolism occurs mainly in the liver including CYP2D6-mediated pathways, and metabolites plus unchanged drug are excreted predominantly in urine. Toxicity reflects exaggerated beta-blockade, with overdose causing severe bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm, heart block, hypoglycemia, and CNS depression. Adverse effects include ocular burning, dry eye, blurred vision, fatigue, dizziness, depression, impotence, bradycardia, and worsening asthma or COPD. Clinically, timolol is used mainly as ophthalmic therapy for open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension and has also been used orally for hypertension, angina, post-myocardial infarction risk reduction, and migraine prophylaxis.

Name: Treprostinil
Description: Treprostinil (DrugBank DB00374) is a chemically stable tricyclic benzindene-based prostacyclin analogue designed to mimic prostaglandin I2 while resisting rapid hydrolysis; structurally it contains a fused polycyclic hydrophobic core bearing a secondary alcohol, a carboxylic acid, and a pendant alkyl side chain that reproduces key prostanoid pharmacophores. It belongs to the prostaglandin/prostacyclin class of eicosanoid mimetics, with a prostacyclin-mimetic benzindene scaffold distinct from the native enol-ether prostacyclin ring system. Closely related drugs include epoprostenol, iloprost, beraprost, and selexipag as another prostacyclin-pathway agent. Its principal targets are the prostacyclin IP receptor, with additional activity reported at EP2 and DP1 prostanoid receptors, producing vasodilation, inhibition of platelet aggregation, and antiproliferative effects in pulmonary vascular smooth muscle. Treprostinil is used primarily for pulmonary arterial hypertension to improve exercise capacity and symptoms, and in some settings pulmonary hypertension associated with interstitial lung disease; clinical use includes continuous subcutaneous or intravenous infusion, inhalation, and extended-release oral therapy. Pharmacokinetically, it is well absorbed by inhaled and oral routes, highly protein bound, widely distributed, hepatically metabolized mainly by CYP2C8 with minor CYP2C9 contribution, and excreted predominantly as urinary metabolites with some fecal elimination; its half-life is markedly longer than epoprostenol, supporting practical outpatient administration. Toxicity is chiefly dose-related vasodilatory and infusion-related toxicity, including hypotension, flushing, headache, jaw pain, diarrhea, nausea, and extremity pain; serious examples include catheter-related bloodstream infection with IV use, infusion-site pain with SC use, bleeding risk from platelet inhibition, and potential worsening in severe hepatic impairment.

Name: Trihexyphenidyl
Description: Trihexyphenidyl (DrugBank DB00376) is a centrally acting synthetic antimuscarinic antiparkinsonian agent with a tertiary amino alcohol structure composed of a bulky hydrophobic cyclohexyl-phenyl substituted carbinol linked through a short propyl chain to a piperidine ring; chemically it is classified as a piperidine-containing anticholinergic and more broadly an arylcyclohexyl tertiary alcohol, with an amino alcohol antimuscarinic scaffold related to other centrally active antiparkinsonian anticholinergics. Its closest similar drugs include benztropine, procyclidine, biperiden, atropine, and to some extent diphenhydramine-like anticholinergics, all sharing lipophilicity and CNS muscarinic receptor antagonism. Trihexyphenidyl primarily targets muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially central M1 receptor-mediated signaling, though clinically it is often described as a relatively nonselective muscarinic antagonist affecting CHRM1, CHRM2, CHRM3, CHRM4, and CHRM5. It is used mainly for symptomatic treatment of Parkinson disease and drug-induced extrapyramidal syndromes such as acute dystonia, rigidity, tremor, and sialorrhea, particularly in antipsychotic-associated parkinsonism. Oral absorption is generally good, CNS penetration is substantial because of its tertiary amine and lipophilicity, distribution is wide, hepatic metabolism appears extensive, and elimination occurs mainly as metabolites in urine with a relatively short plasma half-life but longer clinical effect. Toxicity reflects anticholinergic excess, including agitation, confusion, hallucinations, hyperthermia, tachycardia, urinary retention, ileus, and mydriasis; overdose may produce delirium, especially in older adults. Common adverse effects include dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, cognitive impairment, dizziness, and decreased sweating. Clinically, it is most often reserved for tremor-predominant parkinsonism or younger patients who tolerate anticholinergic therapy better than elderly patients.

Name: Palonosetron
Description: Palonosetron (DrugBank DB00377) is a second-generation serotonin 5-HT3 receptor antagonist built as a rigid, conformationally restricted tricyclic isoquinoline-derived amine, featuring a fused ring system with a quinuclidine-like bicyclic tertiary amine appended to an aromatic heterocycle that supports high-affinity receptor binding. Chemically, it is categorized as a selective 5-hydroxytryptamine type 3 antagonist and can be viewed as belonging to the azabicyclic/isoquinolinone antiemetic scaffold class; it is structurally and pharmacologically related to other setron antiemetics such as ondansetron, granisetron, dolasetron, and tropisetron, although palonosetron is distinguished by greater receptor affinity and a substantially longer elimination half-life. Its principal target is the 5-hydroxytryptamine receptor 3, especially the HTR3A-containing ligand-gated ion channel complex. After intravenous administration and, in some regions, oral dosing, it is well absorbed, widely distributed with moderate plasma protein binding, metabolized hepatically mainly by CYP2D6 with contributions from CYP3A4 and CYP1A2 to inactive or weakly active metabolites, and eliminated through both renal excretion of unchanged drug and metabolites and nonrenal routes; the terminal half-life is about 40 hours, supporting prolonged antiemetic activity. It is indicated primarily for prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, including acute and delayed phases, and for prevention of postoperative nausea and vomiting. Toxicity is generally low at therapeutic doses, but examples include headache, constipation, dizziness, and rare hypersensitivity, bradyarrhythmia, or QT-related concerns, although QT prolongation risk is lower than with some older 5-HT3 antagonists; clinically it is used alone or with dexamethasone, NK1 antagonists, or olanzapine in highly and moderately emetogenic chemotherapy regimens and perioperative antiemetic prophylaxis.

Name: Mexiletine
Description: Mexiletine (DrugBank DB00379) is an orally active class IB antiarrhythmic that is structurally a lipophilic lidocaine analog built on a 2,6-dimethylphenoxy scaffold linked through an ether to a chiral propylamine side chain, giving a small aromatic ether–primary amine structure best described as an aryloxypropanamine; chemically it belongs to the amino-ether local anesthetic/antiarrhythmic family, with a xylidine-related phenoxyalkylamine scaffold shared conceptually with lidocaine and related sodium-channel blockers such as tocainide and, more distantly, flecainide and phenytoin in terms of Na+ channel modulation. Its principal targets are voltage-gated sodium channels, especially the cardiac channel Nav1.5 encoded by SCN5A, with broader activity across skeletal muscle sodium channels including Nav1.4 encoded by SCN4A, where it reduces abnormal repetitive firing by use-dependent blockade of open and inactivated channels. Mexiletine is well absorbed orally with high bioavailability, reaches peak concentrations in about 2 to 3 hours, distributes widely into tissues, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP2D6 and CYP1A2 to hydroxylated and dealkylated metabolites, and is eliminated predominantly in urine as metabolites with a terminal half-life typically around 10 to 12 hours but variable in liver disease or with enzyme-modifying drugs. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related neurologic and gastrointestinal effects, including tremor, dizziness, ataxia, nausea, and vomiting, while serious adverse events include conduction disturbances, bradyarrhythmia, hypotension, hepatotoxicity, and proarrhythmia, particularly in patients with structural heart disease. Clinically it is used for documented life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias and, in practice, for symptomatic nondystrophic myotonias such as myotonia congenita and paramyotonia congenita, and it is also used in some patients with long QT syndrome type 3 to shorten QT-related arrhythmic risk.

Name: Amlodipine
Description: Amlodipine (DrugBank DB00381) is a long-acting dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker whose structure is centered on a 1,4-dihydropyridine ring bearing ester substituents and a lipophilic chlorophenyl group, with a basic aminoethoxy side chain that is commonly present as the besylate salt; chemically it belongs to the dihydropyridine antihypertensive class and is built on the classic 1,4-dihydropyridine scaffold shared with related agents such as nifedipine, felodipine, nicardipine, isradipine, and lercanidipine. Its principal targets are L-type voltage-dependent calcium channel subunits in vascular smooth muscle and myocardium, especially Cav1.2 encoded by CACNA1C, with functional activity also involving cardiac L-type channels containing CACNA1D in some tissues; inhibition reduces transmembrane calcium influx, producing arterial vasodilation and reduced afterload. It is indicated for hypertension, chronic stable angina, and vasospastic angina, and is widely used clinically alone or in combination regimens for blood pressure control, ischemic symptom reduction, and prevention of anginal episodes, including in patients with coronary artery disease. Oral absorption is good, bioavailability is moderate to high, peak concentrations are delayed, protein binding is high, distribution is extensive, hepatic metabolism occurs primarily via CYP3A4 to inactive metabolites, and elimination is mainly renal as metabolites with a prolonged terminal half-life supporting once-daily dosing. Toxicity is usually dose-related and reflects excessive vasodilation, with overdose causing marked hypotension, reflex tachycardia, dizziness, and rarely shock. Common adverse effects include peripheral edema, flushing, headache, palpitations, fatigue, gingival hyperplasia, and nausea.

Name: Tacrine
Description: Tacrine (DrugBank DB00382) is a small, planar, tricyclic aromatic amine built on a rigid acridine framework, specifically a 9-amino-substituted tetrahydroacridine system in which a partially saturated central ring is fused to two benzene-like rings, giving a compact heteropolycyclic cationic scaffold that supports cholinesterase binding; chemically it is classified as a centrally acting aminoacridine and reversible cholinesterase inhibitor, with the tacrine/tetrahydroacridine scaffold shared conceptually with other acetylcholinesterase-directed cognitive enhancers, although structurally distinct from related anti-Alzheimer drugs such as donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine. Its principal targets are acetylcholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase, with additional reported weak interactions at muscarinic and nicotinic cholinergic systems and possible effects on monoamine handling. Tacrine was indicated for symptomatic treatment of mild to moderate Alzheimer disease to improve cognition, attention, and activities of daily living, but its clinical use became limited and largely obsolete because of safety concerns and the need for frequent dosing and liver-function monitoring. It is orally absorbed, undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism with variable bioavailability, distributes into the CNS, is metabolized mainly by CYP1A2 to hydroxylated metabolites, and is excreted predominantly in urine as metabolites. Major toxicities include dose-related hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevation and occasional clinically significant liver injury; overdose or excessive cholinergic exposure may produce bradycardia, salivation, bronchospasm, diarrhea, and seizures. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, dyspepsia, diarrhea, dizziness, headache, sweating, anorexia, and confusion.

Name: Oxyphencyclimine
Description: Oxyphencyclimine (DrugBank DB00383) is a synthetic tertiary-amine antimuscarinic built on an amino alcohol/ester-like anticholinergic motif in which a bulky hydrophobic cyclohexyl-phenyl substituent is linked to a dimethylaminoethyl side chain, giving the amphiphilic cationic architecture typical of gastrointestinal antispasmodics. It is classified chemically as an anticholinergic parasympatholytic and is most closely associated with the classical atropine-like antimuscarinic scaffold, with similarity to dicyclomine, oxybutynin, propantheline, atropine, and scopolamine in both structure-activity logic and pharmacology. Its principal targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially peripheral M1 and M3 receptor populations in the gastrointestinal tract, where receptor antagonism reduces smooth-muscle tone, motility, and secretory activity. After oral administration it is absorbed to a clinically useful extent, distributes systemically with some penetration into tissues and limited but relevant CNS exposure expected for a tertiary amine, undergoes hepatic biotransformation, and is eliminated through renal excretion of metabolites and some unchanged drug; as with related agents, precise human ADME parameters are limited in older literature. Toxicity is that of antimuscarinics: dose-related dry mouth, mydriasis, blurred vision, tachycardia, urinary retention, constipation, decreased sweating, and CNS confusion or agitation at higher exposures, with particular risk in angle-closure glaucoma, prostatic hypertrophy, obstructive gastrointestinal disease, and heat stress. Clinically it has been used as an adjunct for peptic ulcer disease, irritable bowel symptoms, and other gastrointestinal hypermotility or spastic disorders, especially abdominal cramping, pylorospasm, and functional bowel spasm.

Name: Triamterene
Description: Triamterene (DrugBank DB00384) is a synthetic potassium-sparing diuretic built on a 2,4,7-triaminopteridine heteroaromatic core bearing a phenyl substituent, giving a rigid, weakly basic, nitrogen-rich fused bicyclic scaffold characteristic of pteridine analogs. Chemically it is classified as an acylation-independent epithelial sodium channel inhibitor and an aminopteridine derivative; its scaffold is closely related to other potassium-sparing diuretics, most notably amiloride, which is mechanistically similar though structurally based on a pyrazinoylguanidine motif rather than a pteridine nucleus. Its principal target is the epithelial sodium channel ENaC, especially in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct, where it reduces luminal sodium reabsorption and secondarily limits potassium and hydrogen ion loss. After oral administration, triamterene is absorbed to a moderate extent with variable bioavailability, is distributed systemically with some plasma protein binding, undergoes hepatic metabolism chiefly to active and inactive hydroxylated sulfate-conjugated metabolites including hydroxytriamterene sulfate, and is excreted in urine and bile/feces. It is indicated for edema associated with congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, and for hypertension, especially in combination with thiazides to prevent hypokalemia. Clinical use commonly includes fixed-dose combinations such as triamterene with hydrochlorothiazide. Important adverse effects include hyperkalemia, nausea, dizziness, headache, dehydration, azotemia, and megaloblastic changes rarely in folate-deficient patients; toxicity is dominated by potentially life-threatening hyperkalemia, particularly in renal impairment, diabetes, the elderly, or with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium supplements, or spironolactone, and it may also cause crystalluria, nephrolithiasis, and rare acute kidney injury.

Name: Valrubicin
Description: Valrubicin (DrugBank DB00385) is a semisynthetic anthracycline antineoplastic structurally derived from doxorubicin, characterized by the planar tetracyclic anthraquinone/anthracyclinone core linked glycosidically to an amino sugar and further modified by N-trifluoroacetylation and 14-valerate esterification, changes that increase lipophilicity and favor local urothelial tissue penetration. Chemically it belongs to the anthracycline antibiotics, with an anthracyclinone scaffold closely related to doxorubicin, daunorubicin, epirubicin, and idarubicin. Like related anthracyclines, it is believed to act primarily through DNA intercalation and inhibition of topoisomerase II, with generation of oxidative and DNA-damaging stress; topoisomerase II alpha and beta are the principal recognized target proteins, although broader nucleic acid interactions contribute. Valrubicin is used intravesically, so systemic absorption is usually minimal in patients with intact bladder mucosa; distribution is therefore predominantly local to the bladder wall, while absorbed drug undergoes hepatic deacylation and carbonyl reduction to metabolites including N-trifluoroacetyladriamycin and other anthracycline derivatives, followed mainly by biliary/fecal elimination, with limited renal contribution. Its approved clinical role is treatment of bacillus Calmette-Guérin-refractory carcinoma in situ of the urinary bladder in patients for whom immediate cystectomy would be associated with unacceptable morbidity or is declined. Toxicity is dominated by local chemical cystitis and urothelial irritation rather than classic systemic anthracycline cardiotoxicity, though systemic anthracycline toxicities remain theoretical with substantial absorption; adverse effects include hematuria, dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, bladder spasm, suprapubic pain, and occasional nausea or urinary tract infection.

Name: Procyclidine
Description: Procyclidine (DrugBank DB00387) is a synthetic tertiary amine antimuscarinic built around a benzhydryl- or diaryl-substituted cyclohexyl scaffold, specifically a cyclohexanol framework bearing phenyl rings and a pyrrolidine-containing propyl side chain, a structure that confers marked lipophilicity and central nervous system penetration; chemically it is classified as an anticholinergic antiparkinson agent within the amino alcohol/tertiary amine class, and its core scaffold is closely related to other centrally acting muscarinic antagonists such as trihexyphenidyl, benztropine, biperiden, and to some extent orphenadrine. Its principal pharmacologic targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially central M1-class signaling pathways in the striatum, where it reduces relative cholinergic overactivity in dopamine-deficient states. After oral administration it is well absorbed, distributes widely including into the brain, is moderately protein bound, undergoes hepatic metabolism with first-pass processing, and is eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites with a smaller fraction unchanged; clinically its duration permits divided daily dosing. Procyclidine is indicated for idiopathic Parkinson disease and particularly for drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms such as acute dystonia, rigidity, tremor, akathisia, and parkinsonism caused by antipsychotics or antiemetics. Adverse effects are typical of antimuscarinics and include dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, tachycardia, decreased sweating, mydriasis, and cognitive impairment; confusion, agitation, hallucinations, and delirium are especially important in older adults. Toxicity reflects anticholinergic excess, with examples including hyperthermia, severe urinary retention, paralytic ileus, and CNS excitation or coma in overdose, so clinical use is generally individualized and cautious in elderly patients, glaucoma, and obstructive uropathy.

Name: Phenylephrine
Description: Phenylephrine (DrugBank DB00388) is a small-molecule sympathomimetic phenethylamine whose structure consists of a substituted benzene ring bearing one phenolic hydroxyl group and a β-hydroxylated ethylamine side chain with N-methyl substitution, making it a chiral, non-catechol adrenergic agonist; chemically it is classified as a phenylethanolamine and specifically a selective alpha-1 adrenergic receptor agonist, built on a phenethylamine/arylethanolamine scaffold closely related to other decongestant and vasopressor agents such as epinephrine, norepinephrine, pseudoephedrine, ephedrine, and methoxamine. Its principal targets are alpha-1A, alpha-1B, and alpha-1D adrenergic receptors, with minimal direct beta-adrenergic activity, producing vasoconstriction, mydriasis, and increased peripheral vascular resistance. Orally, phenylephrine has limited bioavailability because of substantial first-pass metabolism, whereas intravenous, intranasal, and ophthalmic routes yield more reliable local or systemic exposure; it distributes in extracellular tissues, undergoes hepatic and intestinal metabolism largely by monoamine oxidase and sulfate conjugation, and is excreted mainly in urine as metabolites and a minor unchanged fraction. Toxicity is primarily an extension of its pharmacology, including hypertension, reflex bradycardia, arrhythmia, ischemia, and rare tissue necrosis with extravasation; overdose may cause severe headache, intracranial hemorrhage, or end-organ hypoperfusion. Clinically it is used for hypotension, especially anesthesia-associated vasodilation or shock states, nasal congestion in rhinitis or upper respiratory illness, and ophthalmic mydriasis without cycloplegia. Common adverse effects include hypertension, bradycardia, palpitations, anxiety, tremor, urinary retention, headache, and rebound nasal congestion with prolonged topical use.

Name: Carbimazole
Description: Carbimazole (DrugBank DB00389) is a thioimidazole antithyroid prodrug characterized structurally by an imidazole/imidazoline-like heterocycle bearing a thione sulfur and a carbethoxy substituent, making it the ethoxycarbonyl derivative that is rapidly converted in vivo to the active metabolite methimazole; chemically it belongs to the thioamide or thioureylene class, with a compact mercaptoimidazole scaffold central to its activity. It is closely related to methimazole and functionally similar to propylthiouracil, all of which inhibit thyroid hormone biosynthesis. After oral administration, carbimazole is well absorbed and undergoes rapid presystemic and systemic metabolism to methimazole, which distributes into body water and concentrates in the thyroid, crosses the placenta, and appears in breast milk; metabolism is primarily hepatic with renal excretion of metabolites and some unchanged drug, and the effective half-life reflects thyroidal accumulation more than plasma persistence. Its principal pharmacologic target is thyroid peroxidase, thereby blocking iodide oxidation, organification of tyrosyl residues in thyroglobulin, and coupling of iodotyrosines to form thyroxine and triiodothyronine. It is indicated for hyperthyroid states such as Graves disease, toxic multinodular goiter, and preparation for thyroidectomy or radioiodine therapy, and is also used to control thyrotoxic symptoms before definitive treatment. Important toxicities include agranulocytosis, leukopenia, hepatotoxicity including cholestatic jaundice, vasculitic reactions, pancreatitis, and fetal thyroid suppression or teratogenic risk with early pregnancy exposure. Common adverse effects include rash, pruritus, urticaria, arthralgia, gastrointestinal upset, altered taste, fever, and reversible hair loss, while clinical use requires thyroid function and blood count monitoring with urgent evaluation of sore throat, fever, or jaundice.

Name: Digoxin
Description: Digoxin (DrugBank DB00390) is a naturally derived cardenolide cardiac glycoside built on a rigid steroid-like cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene nucleus bearing a characteristic unsaturated five-membered butenolide at C17 and three digitoxose sugar residues glycosidically linked at C3, a structural arrangement that defines its polar glycoside/lipophilic steroid balance and underlies its classification as a cardiotonic steroid and cardiac glycoside; its core scaffold is the cardenolide aglycone digoxigenin, and closely related drugs include digitoxin, ouabain, deslanoside, and lanatoside C. Pharmacologically, digoxin binds and inhibits the alpha subunits of the Na+/K+-ATPase pump, principally ATP1A1, ATP1A2, and ATP1A3, increasing intracellular sodium, secondarily reducing Na+/Ca2+ exchange, and thereby increasing intracellular calcium and myocardial contractility while also enhancing vagal tone and slowing atrioventricular nodal conduction. Oral absorption is variable to moderate, distribution is extensive with large tissue binding especially in heart and skeletal muscle, protein binding is relatively low, metabolism is limited, and elimination is predominantly renal as unchanged drug, making half-life prolonged in renal impairment and requiring dose adjustment; P-glycoprotein-mediated transport contributes to important drug interactions. Clinically it is used for symptomatic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and for ventricular rate control in atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter, especially when hypotension limits beta-blockers. Its narrow therapeutic index is central to toxicity, with examples including anorexia, nausea, vomiting, confusion, xanthopsia or other visual disturbances, bradycardia, AV block, premature ventricular beats, and life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias, particularly with overdose, renal failure, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia, or interacting drugs such as amiodarone, verapamil, quinidine, and macrolides.

Name: Beclomethasone dipropionate
Description: Beclomethasone dipropionate (DrugBank DB00394) is a highly lipophilic synthetic corticosteroid prodrug built on the pregnane glucocorticoid scaffold, specifically a halogenated 21-carbon steroid nucleus bearing the characteristic fused four-ring cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene framework, a 9α-chloro substituent, an 11β-hydroxyl group, and propionate esterification at the 17 and 21 positions that enhance topical potency and tissue retention. Chemically it is a glucocorticoid corticosteroid ester, closely related to other inhaled or topical corticosteroids such as beclomethasone, budesonide, fluticasone, mometasone, and triamcinolone derivatives. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, with downstream transrepression of proinflammatory transcription factors and reduced cytokine, eosinophil, mast-cell, and arachidonic acid mediator activity. After inhalation or intranasal administration, systemic bioavailability of the parent drug is limited by first-pass metabolism, while pulmonary and nasal esterases rapidly convert it to the more active metabolite beclomethasone-17-monopropionate; distribution is extensive due to lipophilicity and protein binding, metabolism proceeds mainly via esterase hydrolysis with further hepatic biotransformation, and excretion occurs predominantly in feces with a smaller urinary component. It is indicated for persistent asthma, allergic rhinitis, and inflammatory nasal symptoms, and has also been used in certain inflammatory bowel formulations. Adverse effects are largely local, including dysphonia, cough, throat irritation, oral candidiasis, epistaxis, and nasal dryness, whereas excessive systemic exposure can cause adrenal suppression, growth retardation in children, cataracts, glaucoma, skin thinning, hypercorticism, and reduced bone density; overdose or prolonged high-dose use therefore raises classic corticosteroid toxicities and infection risk.

Name: Carisoprodol
Description: Carisoprodol (DrugBank DB00395) is a centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant built as a substituted propanediol dicarbamate, structurally characterized by a 1,3-propanediol backbone bearing two carbamate ester groups and an isopropyl-substituted carbon center, placing it in the carbamate class with a meprobamate-like carbamate scaffold. Its closest similar drugs are meprobamate, its major active metabolite, and other centrally acting antispasmodics such as methocarbamol, chlorzoxazone, cyclobenzaprine, and metaxalone, although the strongest structural similarity is to meprobamate and related sedative carbamates. Pharmacokinetically, carisoprodol is rapidly and well absorbed orally, reaches peak plasma concentrations within a few hours, distributes systemically including into the central nervous system, and is extensively metabolized in the liver, primarily by CYP2C19, to meprobamate; both parent drug and metabolites are then excreted mainly in urine, with a relatively short half-life for carisoprodol and longer persistence of meprobamate. Its pharmacology is attributed mainly to CNS depressant effects, with no single definitively established molecular target, but functional activity is commonly linked to modulation of GABAergic signaling, especially at GABAA receptor systems, and carisoprodol is often indexed to CYP2C19 as a key biotransformation protein. It is indicated for short-term treatment of acute painful musculoskeletal conditions such as low back strain, neck spasm, and other muscle spasm-associated injuries, generally alongside rest and physical therapy. Adverse effects commonly include drowsiness, dizziness, headache, and impaired psychomotor performance, while toxicity can produce profound sedation, respiratory depression, tachycardia, hypotension, seizures, coma, and abuse, dependence, or withdrawal, especially in overdose or when combined with alcohol, opioids, or benzodiazepines.

Name: Progesterone
Description: Progesterone (DrugBank DB00396) is a naturally occurring pregnane steroid hormone characterized by the cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene nucleus with a 3-keto-4-ene A-ring and a 20-ketone side chain, placing it in the progestogen class and more specifically among endogenous C21 steroid ketones; its core scaffold is the pregn-4-ene-3,20-dione steroid framework. Closely related or pharmacologically similar agents include hydroxyprogesterone, medroxyprogesterone acetate, megestrol acetate, dydrogesterone, and norethindrone, which share progestogenic activity with varying androgenic, glucocorticoid, or pharmacokinetic properties. Progesterone acts primarily via the nuclear progesterone receptors PGR/PR-A and PR-B, with additional reported interactions with membrane progesterone receptors such as PAQR7, PAQR8, and PAQR5, progesterone receptor membrane component proteins PGRMC1 and PGRMC2, and weak functional modulation of the mineralocorticoid receptor and GABAA receptor through neuroactive metabolites. Pharmacokinetically, oral progesterone undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism and variable bioavailability, while intramuscular, vaginal, and micronized formulations improve systemic or local exposure; it is highly protein bound, widely distributed, extensively metabolized in the liver to pregnanediols and neurosteroids such as allopregnanolone, and excreted mainly in urine as glucuronide and sulfate conjugates, with some biliary/fecal elimination. Clinically it is used for luteal support in infertility treatment, prevention of endometrial hyperplasia during estrogen therapy, secondary amenorrhea, dysfunctional uterine bleeding, and support of pregnancy in selected progesterone-deficient states, with examples including assisted reproduction and menopausal hormone therapy. Adverse effects include sedation, dizziness, somnolence, breast tenderness, bloating, headache, mood change, nausea, and vaginal irritation with local products; toxicity is generally low in acute overdose but excessive exposure can produce marked CNS depression, cholestatic jaundice, fluid retention, thromboembolic risk in susceptible patients, and rare hypersensitivity or hepatic dysfunction.

Name: Phenylpropanolamine
Description: Phenylpropanolamine (DrugBank DB00397) is a small synthetic sympathomimetic amine built on a phenylpropane backbone, consisting of a substituted benzene ring attached to a three-carbon side chain bearing a beta-hydroxyl group and a primary amine, with stereochemical similarity to ephedrine-type agents; chemically it is classified as a phenylpropanolamine/amphetamine-related adrenergic agonist and more broadly as a phenethylamine-derived decongestant, with an aryl-aliphatic amino alcohol scaffold. Similar drugs include ephedrine, pseudoephedrine, norepinephrine, amphetamine, and other nasal decongestants such as phenylephrine, reflecting shared sympathomimetic pharmacology. Its principal targets are adrenergic system proteins, especially alpha-adrenergic receptors, with indirect promotion of norepinephrine release from presynaptic terminals and lesser activity at beta-adrenergic receptors. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed, distributes into highly perfused tissues, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged in urine; renal clearance is pH dependent, with faster excretion in acidic urine and a relatively short elimination half-life. Clinically it has been used as a nasal decongestant for rhinitis, sinus congestion, and common cold symptoms, and historically as an anorectic in weight-loss therapy. Adverse effects are typical of sympathomimetics and include hypertension, tachycardia, palpitations, insomnia, anxiety, tremor, headache, and urinary retention. Toxicity is dominated by excessive adrenergic stimulation, with overdose or susceptible patients developing severe hypertension, arrhythmias, agitation, seizures, myocardial ischemia, and notably hemorrhagic stroke, a risk that led to major withdrawal or restriction of human use in many jurisdictions.

Name: Sorafenib
Description: Sorafenib (DrugBank DB00398) is an orally active small-molecule biaryl urea multikinase inhibitor whose structure is characterized by a diaryl-substituted urea core linking a chlorinated trifluoromethyl phenyl ring to a pyridyl-oxy aryl system, giving a lipophilic heteroaromatic kinase-binding pharmacophore; chemically it is classified as a diphenyl urea/biaryl urea antineoplastic agent, with a diaryl urea scaffold closely related to other type II kinase inhibitors such as regorafenib, linifanib, and dovitinib, and more distantly to sunitinib and pazopanib as multitargeted antiangiogenic tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Its principal targets include RAF kinases, especially RAF1 and BRAF including mutant forms, and receptor tyrosine kinases involved in tumor proliferation and angiogenesis such as VEGFR1, VEGFR2, VEGFR3, PDGFRB, FLT3, KIT, and RET. Sorafenib is indicated for unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma, advanced renal cell carcinoma, and radioactive iodine-refractory differentiated thyroid carcinoma, and is used clinically to slow tumor growth and angiogenesis in these settings. Pharmacokinetically, it has moderate oral absorption, high protein binding, a large distribution tendency, hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 oxidation and UGT1A9 glucuronidation, enterohepatic recirculation, a relatively long terminal half-life, and predominant fecal excretion with lesser urinary elimination. Toxicity is mechanism-based and includes hepatotoxicity, hypertension, cardiac ischemia, hemorrhage, impaired wound healing, and embryo-fetal toxicity; common adverse effects include hand-foot skin reaction, rash, diarrhea, fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, abdominal pain, and hypertension, with dose reduction or interruption often required in practice.

Name: Zoledronic acid
Description: Zoledronic acid (DrugBank DB00399) is a highly potent third-generation nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate built on a geminal bisphosphonate P-C-P backbone in which a hydroxylated central carbon and an imidazole-containing side chain confer strong calcium-binding and antiresorptive activity; chemically it belongs to the heteroaryl amino-bisphosphonate class, and its core scaffold is best described as a hydroxybisphosphonate linked to an imidazolyl substituent. It is structurally and pharmacologically related to other bisphosphonates such as pamidronate, alendronate, ibandronate, risedronate, and less potent non-nitrogen congeners such as clodronate. After intravenous administration, oral bioavailability being negligible in routine practice, it rapidly partitions from plasma to bone mineral at sites of active remodeling, shows minimal protein binding relative to many lipophilic drugs, is not appreciably metabolized, and is eliminated unchanged by renal excretion, with a short plasma half-life but very prolonged skeletal retention. Its principal molecular target is farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway within osteoclasts, leading to impaired prenylation of small GTPases and osteoclast apoptosis; effects are mediated functionally through hydroxyapatite binding in bone. Indications include osteoporosis, Paget disease of bone, hypercalcemia of malignancy, multiple myeloma, and prevention of skeletal-related events from bone metastases, including breast and prostate cancer. Important toxicities include nephrotoxicity, severe hypocalcemia, acute phase reactions, uveitis, osteonecrosis of the jaw, and atypical femoral fractures; common adverse effects include fever, myalgia, arthralgia, bone pain, nausea, fatigue, and infusion-related symptoms. Clinically, it is used as intermittent IV therapy such as annual treatment for osteoporosis and more frequent oncology dosing for metastatic bone disease or malignant hypercalcemia.

Name: Griseofulvin
Description: Griseofulvin (DrugBank DB00400) is a naturally derived antifungal benzo-furanone/polyketide-like spirocyclic compound characterized by a chlorinated, highly oxygenated aromatic system fused to a rigid grisan scaffold, classically described as a spirocyclic benzofuranone linked to a cyclohexenone ring with methoxy substituents that confer lipophilicity and crystal-binding behavior; chemically it is categorized as a fungal antimitotic antifungal, and its core scaffold is the grisan spirobenzofuran-cyclohexenone framework. Structurally or therapeutically similar drugs include systemic and topical antifungals used in dermatophytosis such as terbinafine, itraconazole, ketoconazole, and fluconazole, although these differ in scaffold and direct molecular target. Griseofulvin is absorbed variably after oral administration, with markedly improved bioavailability when given as ultramicrosize formulations or with fatty meals; it distributes preferentially to keratin precursor cells in skin, hair, and nails, binds keratin, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly by demethylation and glucuronidation with cytochrome P450 induction potential, and is excreted primarily in urine as metabolites with lesser fecal elimination. Its principal target is fungal tubulin, disrupting microtubule function and mitosis, with secondary effects on mitotic spindle formation. It is indicated for dermatophyte infections such as tinea capitis, tinea corporis, tinea cruris, tinea pedis, and onychomycosis when caused by susceptible Trichophyton, Microsporum, or Epidermophyton species. Toxicities include hepatotoxicity, leukopenia, granulocytopenia, peripheral neuropathy, severe cutaneous hypersensitivity, and photosensitivity; common adverse effects include headache, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, dizziness, fatigue, and insomnia. Clinically, it has been used especially for scalp ringworm in children and refractory keratinized tissue infections where prolonged oral therapy is required.

Name: Alprazolam
Description: Alprazolam (DrugBank DB00404) is a triazolobenzodiazepine characterized by a fused benzene-diazepine core annelated with a triazole ring and bearing a chloro-substituted aryl group, a structure that confers high affinity for benzodiazepine modulatory sites on GABAA receptors; chemically it belongs to the benzodiazepine anxiolytic-sedative class, with a triazolobenzodiazepine scaffold closely related to triazolam and mechanistically and structurally similar to other benzodiazepines such as diazepam, lorazepam, clonazepam, and midazolam. Its principal targets are the benzodiazepine allosteric binding interface on pentameric GABAA receptor complexes, especially those containing α1, α2, α3, or α5 subunits together with γ2 and β subunits, thereby enhancing GABA-mediated chloride conductance and inhibitory neurotransmission. Alprazolam is indicated mainly for generalized anxiety disorder, short-term relief of anxiety symptoms, and panic disorder with or without agoraphobia, and is used clinically for acute panic attacks, severe situational anxiety, and anxiety associated with depressive states. It is well absorbed orally, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, is widely distributed with substantial protein binding, undergoes extensive hepatic CYP3A4 metabolism to active and inactive metabolites including alpha-hydroxyalprazolam, and is excreted primarily in urine as metabolites. Toxicity includes dose-related CNS and respiratory depression, psychomotor impairment, anterograde amnesia, overdose potentiation with opioids or alcohol, tolerance, dependence, withdrawal seizures, and neonatal toxicity with in utero exposure. Common adverse effects include sedation, dizziness, fatigue, impaired coordination, cognitive slowing, dysarthria, and rebound anxiety.

Name: Dexbrompheniramine
Description: Dexbrompheniramine (DrugBank DB00405) is the dextrorotatory active isomer of brompheniramine, a first-generation alkylamine antihistamine characterized structurally by a substituted propylamine bearing a tertiary dimethylamino group linked to a diaryl system composed of a para-bromophenyl ring and a 2-pyridyl ring; this places it in the ethanolamine/alkylamine-like H1-antihistamine chemical category, with a classic aryl-alkyl-amine scaffold typical of propylamine antihistamines. Closely related drugs include brompheniramine, chlorpheniramine, dexchlorpheniramine, pheniramine, and triprolidine, which share similar diarylpropylamine pharmacophores and H1-receptor antagonism. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, functioning as an inverse agonist/antagonist, with clinically relevant ancillary anticholinergic activity likely mediated through muscarinic receptors and possible weak CNS effects due to blood-brain barrier penetration. It is generally well absorbed orally, distributed widely including into the CNS, moderately protein bound, metabolized hepatically primarily by oxidative pathways including CYP2D6-dependent biotransformation, and excreted as parent drug and metabolites in urine, with elimination prolonged in hepatic impairment or urinary alkalinization. Dexbrompheniramine is indicated for symptomatic relief of allergic rhinitis, vasomotor rhinitis, urticaria, conjunctival irritation, pruritus, and uncomplicated allergic skin manifestations. Adverse effects commonly include sedation, dizziness, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention; paradoxical excitation may occur in children. Toxicity in overdose resembles other first-generation antihistamines, with marked anticholinergic effects, tachycardia, agitation, hallucinations, seizures, coma, and rare arrhythmias. Clinically, it is used alone or in combination cold/allergy products for hay fever, rhinorrhea, sneezing, itching, and watery eyes.

Name: Loxapine
Description: Loxapine (DrugBank DB00408) is a dibenzoxazepine antipsychotic structurally defined by a tricyclic ring system in which two benzene rings are fused to a seven-membered oxazepine heterocycle bearing a piperazine substituent, giving it close structural and pharmacologic relatedness to clozapine and other tricyclic antipsychotics; its chemical category is therefore a first-generation, medium-potency tricyclic antipsychotic, and its core scaffold is the dibenzoxazepine nucleus. Similar drugs include clozapine, amoxapine, olanzapine, quetiapine, and older typical agents such as chlorpromazine by therapeutic class. Loxapine acts primarily through antagonism of dopamine D2 receptors and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors, with additional affinity reported for DRD1, DRD3, DRD4, HTR2C, H1 histamine, alpha1-adrenergic, and muscarinic cholinergic receptors. It is indicated mainly for schizophrenia and acute agitation associated with schizophrenia or bipolar I disorder, including use of inhaled loxapine for rapid control of agitation in monitored settings. Pharmacokinetically, it is well absorbed orally, undergoes extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism, distributes widely into the CNS, and is metabolized mainly by CYP1A2, CYP3A4, and CYP2D6 to metabolites including 7-hydroxyloxapine and amoxapine-like derivatives, with elimination via urine and feces as metabolites. Toxicity includes dose-related CNS depression, extrapyramidal toxicity, seizures, hypotension, anticholinergic burden, QT-related cardiac risk, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, tardive dyskinesia, and boxed-risk bronchospasm with the inhaled formulation. Common adverse effects include sedation, dizziness, dry mouth, constipation, akathisia, parkinsonism, tremor, weight gain, orthostasis, and somnolence. Clinically, loxapine is used as an antipsychotic for chronic psychotic illness and as a fast-acting agent for severe agitation when rapid tranquilization is required.

Name: Mupirocin
Description: Mupirocin (DB00410) is a naturally derived topical antibacterial from Pseudomonas fluorescens, chemically classified as a monoxycarbolic acid polyketide and pseudomonic acid antibiotic; its structure is distinguished by a highly oxygenated unsaturated fatty-acid-like backbone linked through an ester to a substituted tetrahydropyran/monic acid moiety, giving a flexible polyketide scaffold often described as the pseudomonic acid or monic acid ester scaffold. It is structurally and mechanistically related to other topical antibacterials that inhibit bacterial protein synthesis, though it is chemically distinct from fusidic acid, retapamulin, and bacitracin; the closest analogs are pseudomonic acid derivatives such as mupirocin calcium. Its principal target is bacterial isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase, encoded by ileS, with resistance arising through target mutation or acquisition of alternate IleRS proteins such as MupA/MupB. Pharmacokinetically, systemic exposure after intact-skin topical use is minimal; limited absorbed drug is rapidly hydrolyzed to inactive monic acid, with negligible distribution and primarily renal excretion of metabolites, whereas intranasal application also yields low systemic levels. Toxicity is generally low because of poor systemic absorption, but excessive exposure on damaged skin or large surface areas may increase absorption; formulations containing polyethylene glycol can pose risk in severe renal impairment, and overdose may cause local irritation rather than systemic poisoning. Mupirocin is indicated for superficial skin infections caused by susceptible Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes, including impetigo, infected minor wounds, secondary infected eczema, and for nasal eradication of methicillin-resistant S. aureus colonization. Adverse effects are mainly local, including burning, stinging, pruritus, erythema, dryness, contact dermatitis, and with intranasal use headache, rhinitis, cough, or altered taste; clinically it is used as a short-course topical or intranasal agent to treat localized Gram-positive infections and to support infection-control decolonization protocols.

Name: Carbamoylcholine
Description: Carbamoylcholine, also known as carbachol, is a synthetic choline ester structurally defined by a permanent quaternary ammonium ethyl group linked through oxygen to a carbamoyl ester, making it a carbamic acid ester analog of acetylcholine in which the acetyl moiety is replaced by carbamyl, a change that markedly increases resistance to cholinesterase hydrolysis; chemically it belongs to the choline ester and direct-acting cholinergic agonist class, with an acetylcholine-like quaternary ammonium–ethylene–ester scaffold. Closely related drugs include acetylcholine, bethanechol, methacholine, and the more receptor-selective muscarinic agonist pilocarpine. Its pharmacology reflects nonselective agonism at muscarinic receptors CHRM1, CHRM2, CHRM3, CHRM4, and CHRM5 and, to a lesser extent, nicotinic cholinergic receptors including neuronal and neuromuscular subtypes such as CHRNA-containing receptor complexes. Because of its permanent charge, systemic absorption and blood-brain barrier penetration are poor; in ophthalmic use distribution is largely local to anterior ocular tissues, metabolism is slow relative to acetylcholine because it is a poor substrate for acetylcholinesterase, and elimination of absorbed drug is believed to occur mainly by renal excretion of unchanged compound. Toxicity is that of excessive cholinergic stimulation, with miosis, lacrimation, sweating, salivation, bronchospasm, bradycardia, hypotension, diarrhea, abdominal cramping, and, in severe poisoning, bronchorrhea or cardiovascular collapse. Clinically it is used primarily in ophthalmology to induce miosis during intraocular surgery and to lower intraocular pressure in glaucoma; adverse effects include brow ache, accommodative spasm, blurred vision, conjunctival irritation, headache, and, rarely, systemic parasympathomimetic reactions.

Name: Pramipexole
Description: Pramipexole (DB00413) is a non-ergoline aminobenzothiazole dopamine agonist whose structure is centered on a compact bicyclic thiazole-fused aromatic scaffold, specifically a tetrahydrobenzothiazole core bearing a primary amino substituent and a propylamino side chain that confer basicity and high affinity for dopamine receptors; chemically it is classified as a synthetic heterocyclic amine and more specifically a benzothiazole-derived dopaminergic agent. Its principal scaffold is the aminotetralin-like tetrahydrobenzothiazole motif, and it is pharmacologically similar to other dopamine agonists such as ropinirole, rotigotine, bromocriptine, and cabergoline, though it is structurally distinct from the ergolines. Pramipexole targets dopamine receptors with highest affinity for D3 and substantial activity at D2 and D4 receptors, with D3>D2 selectivity underlying antiparkinsonian and antiprolactin-sparing effects. It is well absorbed orally with high bioavailability, reaches peak plasma concentrations within a few hours, displays low protein binding and broad distribution into the central nervous system, undergoes minimal hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated largely unchanged by active renal tubular secretion, giving it a half-life that lengthens in renal impairment. Toxicity is dominated by dopaminergic excess, including nausea, vomiting, orthostatic hypotension, somnolence, hallucinations, confusion, dyskinesia, and overdose manifestations such as agitation or profound sedation; clinically important behavioral toxicity includes impulse-control disorders such as pathological gambling, hypersexuality, compulsive shopping, and eating. It is indicated for Parkinson disease and moderate-to-severe primary restless legs syndrome, and in practice is used to reduce motor fluctuations, rigidity, bradykinesia, tremor, nocturnal symptoms, and unpleasant leg sensations.

Name: Acetohexamide
Description: Acetohexamide (DrugBank DB00414) is a first-generation sulfonylurea oral hypoglycemic agent whose structure consists of a para-substituted benzenesulfonylurea core bearing a cyclohexyl group on the terminal urea nitrogen and an acetyl substituent on the aromatic ring, placing it in the aryl-sulfonylurea class with a classic sulfonylurea scaffold linking a lipophilic aryl ring to a urea pharmacophore. It is chemically and pharmacologically similar to other first-generation sulfonylureas such as tolbutamide, chlorpropamide, tolazamide, and, more distantly, second-generation agents like glipizide and glyburide, all of which share insulin secretagogue activity. Its principal target is the ATP-sensitive potassium channel of pancreatic beta cells, specifically the sulfonylurea receptor SUR1/ABCC8 within the Kir6.2-KCNJ11 channel complex, leading to channel closure, membrane depolarization, calcium influx, and insulin release. Acetohexamide is used in type 2 diabetes mellitus, particularly non-insulin-dependent hyperglycemia inadequately controlled by diet alone. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed, distributed systemically with protein binding typical of sulfonylureas, metabolized hepatically to active hydroxyhexamide and other metabolites, and excreted primarily in urine, so prolonged effects may occur in hepatic or renal impairment. Important toxicities include dose-related and sometimes prolonged hypoglycemia, especially in older adults, malnourished patients, or those with renal insufficiency; class-related concerns also include rare cholestatic jaundice, blood dyscrasias, and hypersensitivity reactions. Common adverse effects include sweating, tremor, dizziness, hunger, weight gain, nausea, dyspepsia, rash, and photosensitivity. Clinically, it has been used as an adjunct to dietary management for chronic glycemic control, though it has largely been superseded by newer antidiabetic agents with safer pharmacokinetic and hypoglycemia profiles.

Name: Ampicillin
Description: Ampicillin (DrugBank DB00415) is a semisynthetic aminopenicillin characterized by the penam core, consisting of a strained beta-lactam ring fused to a thiazolidine ring and bearing an acyl side chain with a primary amino-substituted phenylacetamido group that increases hydrophilicity and extends activity toward some Gram-negative organisms; thus, it belongs to the beta-lactam antibiotic class, specifically the penicillins, and its defining scaffold is the 6-aminopenicillanic acid nucleus. Structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include amoxicillin, penicillin G, penicillin V, bacampicillin, pivampicillin, and broader-spectrum beta-lactams such as piperacillin. Its antibacterial action results from covalent acylation of bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, notably transpeptidases including PBP1A, PBP1B, PBP2, and PBP3, thereby inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-linking and promoting cell lysis.
