Ampicillin is acid stable enough for oral use, although oral bioavailability is moderate and reduced by food; parenteral administration achieves higher serum concentrations. Distribution is wide into bile, lung, middle ear fluid, and inflamed meninges, with limited protein binding. Metabolism is minimal, and elimination is predominantly renal via glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, with dose adjustment needed in renal impairment. Toxicity is generally low but includes hypersensitivity reactions up to anaphylaxis, severe cutaneous eruptions, antibiotic-associated colitis, seizures at high concentrations or with renal failure, and selection for superinfection. Adverse effects commonly include rash, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, candidiasis, and injection-site irritation. Clinically, ampicillin is used for susceptible respiratory, urinary, gastrointestinal, biliary, skin and soft tissue infections, otitis media, sinusitis, salmonellosis, shigellosis, listeriosis, enterococcal infections, and bacterial meningitis, often combined with aminoglycosides or beta-lactamase inhibitors in serious infections.

Name: Phenoxymethylpenicillin
Description: Phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V; DrugBank DB00417) is an orally active natural penicillin characterized structurally by the penam nucleus, a strained bicyclic system composed of a β-lactam fused to a thiazolidine ring, bearing the acyl side chain phenoxyacetyl that confers improved acid stability relative to benzylpenicillin; chemically it belongs to the beta-lactam antibiotics, specifically the natural penicillins, and its core scaffold is the 6-aminopenicillanic acid penam framework. Closely related drugs include penicillin G, amoxicillin, ampicillin, cloxacillin, and other β-lactams such as cephalosporins that share the β-lactam pharmacophore. Its antibacterial effect results from covalent inhibition of bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, especially transpeptidases including PBPs such as PBP1A, PBP1B, PBP2, and PBP3 in susceptible organisms, thereby blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking and causing cell lysis. It is indicated mainly for mild to moderate infections due to susceptible streptococci and oral anaerobes, including streptococcal pharyngitis, tonsillitis, scarlet fever, erysipelas, mild skin and soft tissue infection, and prophylaxis against recurrent rheumatic fever. Oral absorption is moderate and variable but adequate in the fasting state, distribution is good to many tissues though limited in cerebrospinal fluid without meningeal inflammation, protein binding is modest, metabolism is limited, and elimination occurs predominantly by rapid renal tubular secretion and glomerular filtration, giving a short half-life and requiring repeated dosing. Toxicity is generally low but includes hypersensitivity ranging from rash and urticaria to anaphylaxis, gastrointestinal intolerance with nausea, diarrhea, and rare antibiotic-associated colitis, candidiasis, eosinophilia, hemolytic anemia, interstitial nephritis, and seizures mainly with excessive exposure or renal impairment. Clinically, it is used as a narrow-spectrum oral agent when pathogen susceptibility is likely or documented, especially for community streptococcal infections and long-term secondary prophylaxis.

Name: Secobarbital
Description: Secobarbital (DrugBank DB00418) is a short-acting barbiturate sedative-hypnotic built on a substituted barbituric acid core, specifically a 2,4,6-trioxohexahydropyrimidine ring bearing lipophilic 5-position alkyl substituents that confer rapid central nervous system penetration; chemically it belongs to the barbiturate class and more broadly to cyclic ureides, with a barbiturate pyrimidinedione scaffold. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other barbiturates such as pentobarbital, amobarbital, phenobarbital, and thiopental, which share the same sedative-hypnotic scaffold but differ in substituent-driven duration of action. Its principal targets are GABAA receptor chloride channel complexes, particularly allosteric sites on receptor subunits that prolong chloride channel opening and enhance inhibitory neurotransmission; at higher concentrations it can directly gate the channel and depress excitatory signaling. Secobarbital is well absorbed orally, highly lipophilic, rapidly distributed to the brain and then redistributed to peripheral tissues, extensively protein bound, metabolized mainly in the liver by oxidative pathways and ring-side-chain transformations, and excreted predominantly in urine as metabolites with a smaller fraction as unchanged drug. Clinically it has been used for short-term treatment of severe insomnia, preoperative sedation, procedural anxiolysis, and historically as an anticonvulsant or sedative in acute agitation. Toxicity is dominated by dose-dependent CNS and respiratory depression, coma, hypotension, impaired psychomotor function, tolerance, dependence, withdrawal seizures, and potentially fatal overdose, especially with alcohol, opioids, or benzodiazepines. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, confusion, ataxia, headache, nausea, paradoxical excitement, and cognitive impairment.

Name: Miglustat
Description: Miglustat (DrugBank DB00419) is a small iminosugar composed of a six-membered polyhydroxylated piperidine-like ring in which the ring oxygen of a monosaccharide is replaced by nitrogen, specifically an N-alkylated deoxynojirimycin analog with multiple hydroxyl groups that mimic glucose transition-state geometry; chemically it is classified as an iminosugar and glycosidase/glycosyltransferase inhibitor, built on the deoxynojirimycin scaffold. Similar drugs include eliglustat, another substrate reduction therapy for Gaucher disease, and other iminosugars such as miglitol and voglibose, which share carbohydrate-mimetic pharmacology. Its principal target is UDP-glucose:ceramide glucosyltransferase (UGCG), reducing glycosphingolipid synthesis; it also inhibits intestinal disaccharidases and has off-target activity toward nonlysosomal glucosylceramidase GBA2, which may contribute to adverse neurologic effects. Orally administered miglustat is well absorbed, has low protein binding, distributes into total body water with penetration into tissues including the CNS, undergoes minimal metabolism, and is eliminated largely unchanged in urine, so exposure rises with renal impairment. It is indicated for type 1 Gaucher disease, particularly in adults unsuitable for enzyme replacement therapy, and for progressive neurologic manifestations of Niemann-Pick disease type C. Toxicity is dominated by gastrointestinal carbohydrate malabsorption causing diarrhea, weight loss, and flatulence, and by dose-related tremor, peripheral neuropathy, and possible cerebellar or sperm effects seen clinically or preclinically. Common side effects include diarrhea, abdominal pain, tremor, paresthesia, decreased appetite, and weight loss. Clinically, it is used as an oral substrate reduction therapy to lower glucosylceramide burden in Gaucher disease and to help stabilize swallowing, ambulation, or eye movement abnormalities in Niemann-Pick type C.

Name: Promazine
Description: Promazine (DrugBank DB00420) is a first-generation phenothiazine antipsychotic whose structure consists of a tricyclic phenothiazine core containing sulfur and nitrogen heteroatoms, substituted at the ring nitrogen and bearing a dimethylaminopropyl side chain that confers basicity and dopamine-receptor affinity; chemically it belongs to the aliphatic phenothiazine neuroleptic class, with the phenothiazine tricycle as its defining scaffold. It is closely related to other phenothiazines such as chlorpromazine, levomepromazine, promazine sulfoxide derivatives, and more distantly to other typical antipsychotics with dopamine D2 antagonism. Its principal targets are dopamine D2 receptors, with additional antagonist activity at D1, 5-HT2, histamine H1, muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, and alpha1-adrenergic receptors, explaining both antipsychotic and sedative effects. Promazine is used for schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders, agitation, anxiety states, behavioral disturbance, and as a sedative or antiemetic in selected settings. After oral or parenteral administration it is variably but generally well absorbed, undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism, is widely distributed into lipid-rich tissues and the central nervous system, is highly protein bound, and is eliminated mainly as hepatic metabolites in urine and bile. Toxicity reflects CNS depression and autonomic and cardiac effects, including overdose-associated coma, hypotension, anticholinergic delirium, seizures, and QT-related arrhythmia risk, as well as rare cholestatic jaundice or hematologic dyscrasias. Common adverse effects include sedation, orthostatic hypotension, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention, weight gain, extrapyramidal symptoms, hyperprolactinemia, and tardive dyskinesia with prolonged use; clinically, it has been used mainly when a strongly sedating, lower-potency typical antipsychotic is desired.

Name: Spironolactone
Description: Spironolactone (DrugBank DB00421) is a synthetic steroidal antimineralocorticoid built on an androstane-derived 17-lactone scaffold with a 3-keto group, a 7alpha-thioacetyl substituent, and a characteristic spirolactone ring, placing it in the potassium-sparing diuretic and steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist category; its core scaffold is closely related to other steroidal MR antagonists such as eplerenone and canrenone, and it also shows structural and pharmacologic kinship to older steroid hormones and antiandrogens. Its principal target is the mineralocorticoid receptor encoded by NR3C2, with additional clinically relevant antagonism at androgen receptors and weaker interactions with progesterone and glucocorticoid signaling pathways. After oral administration it is reasonably well absorbed, extensively protein bound, rapidly and extensively metabolized in the liver to active metabolites including canrenone, 7alpha-thiomethylspironolactone, and 6beta-hydroxy-7alpha-thiomethylspironolactone, and eliminated mainly in urine with some biliary/fecal excretion; the parent drug has a short half-life but active metabolites prolong effect. It is indicated for primary hyperaldosteronism, edema and ascites in heart failure, cirrhosis, or nephrotic syndrome, resistant hypertension, and prevention of hypokalemia, and is also used clinically in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and off-label for acne, hirsutism, and polycystic ovary syndrome. Toxicity is dominated by hyperkalemia, especially with renal impairment or concomitant ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or potassium supplements, and may include dehydration or hyponatremia; adverse effects include gynecomastia, breast tenderness, menstrual irregularities, decreased libido, impotence, gastrointestinal upset, dizziness, and rash.

Name: Methylphenidate
Description: Methylphenidate (DrugBank DB00422) is a piperidine-derived central nervous system stimulant built around a phenethylamine-like arylacetic acid ester framework, specifically a substituted piperidine bearing a phenyl ring and a methyl ester, with the clinically used material consisting mainly of the threo racemate or enriched dexmethylphenidate stereoisomer; chemically it is classified as a piperidine stimulant and indirectly sympathomimetic aminergic reuptake inhibitor, with a scaffold closely related to other DAT/NET blockers such as dexmethylphenidate, ethylphenidate, serdexmethylphenidate-derived products, and more distantly cocaine, although it is structurally distinct from amphetamine. Its principal targets are the dopamine transporter SLC6A3 and norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, with limited direct serotonergic activity, leading to increased synaptic dopamine and norepinephrine, particularly in frontostriatal circuits. It is indicated primarily for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and narcolepsy, with clinical use spanning pediatric, adolescent, and adult ADHD, improvement of inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity, and daytime sleepiness, and use in immediate-release, extended-release, chewable, liquid, transdermal, and prodrug-based formulations. Oral absorption is generally rapid, but extensive first-pass metabolism limits bioavailability and produces variable exposure; distribution is moderate with low tissue accumulation, metabolism occurs predominantly via hepatic carboxylesterase 1 to inactive ritalinic acid, and excretion is mainly renal as metabolites. Toxicity includes dose-related sympathomimetic and neuropsychiatric effects such as tachycardia, hypertension, agitation, insomnia, appetite suppression, growth attenuation in children, misuse liability, and in overdose arrhythmias, hyperthermia, hallucinations, seizures, and rarely serious cardiovascular or cerebrovascular events.

Name: Methocarbamol
Description: Methocarbamol (DrugBank DB00423) is a centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant structurally defined as a guaifenesin carbamate derivative, specifically a 1,2-propanediol ether bearing a 2-methoxyphenoxy aryl-oxy scaffold and terminal dicarbamate functionality; chemically it is categorized as a carbamate and aryloxy alcohol derivative built on the guaifenesin/phenoxypropanediol scaffold. It is closely related to other centrally acting muscle relaxants, particularly chlorphenesin carbamate, carisoprodol, mephenoxalone, and in broader therapeutic similarity to cyclobenzaprine and metaxalone, although these differ structurally. Its precise molecular target is not well defined; it is generally considered to depress polysynaptic reflex pathways within the central nervous system rather than act directly at the neuromuscular junction or on skeletal muscle, and no single validated high-affinity target protein is established, though functional effects involve CNS inhibitory circuitry. Methocarbamol is indicated as an adjunct to rest, physical therapy, and analgesia for acute painful musculoskeletal conditions such as muscle spasm, low back pain, cervical strain, and traumatic or postoperative muscle injury; it is also used clinically, especially parenterally, for tetanus-related spasm control. It is well absorbed orally, distributed systemically with CNS penetration sufficient for sedation, extensively metabolized in the liver mainly by dealkylation, hydroxylation, and conjugation, and excreted predominantly in urine as metabolites with a relatively short elimination half-life. Toxicity is usually dose-related CNS depression, including somnolence, dizziness, ataxia, confusion, hypotension, and respiratory depression in overdose, with rare seizures or coma; common adverse effects include drowsiness, lightheadedness, blurred vision, nausea, flushing, and urine discoloration, while caution is warranted in renal or hepatic impairment and when combined with alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, or other sedatives.

Name: Hyoscyamine
Description: Hyoscyamine (DrugBank DB00424) is a naturally occurring belladonna alkaloid and tertiary amine antimuscarinic characterized structurally as the levorotatory isomer of atropine, consisting of a tropane bicyclic nitrogenous ring esterified to tropic acid, giving a compact lipophilic tropane ester scaffold typical of parasympatholytic natural products. Chemically it belongs to the tropane alkaloid class, with a muscarinic antagonist scaffold closely related to atropine, scopolamine, homatropine, dicyclomine, and other anticholinergic/antispasmodic agents. Its principal targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially CHRM1, CHRM2, CHRM3, CHRM4, and CHRM5, where competitive antagonism reduces smooth muscle tone, glandular secretions, and vagal effects. Orally, hyoscyamine is generally well absorbed, also effective sublingually and by other conventional routes, distributes widely including into the central nervous system because it is a tertiary amine, shows variable hepatic metabolism with a substantial fraction excreted unchanged in urine, and has renal elimination influenced by urinary pH. Toxicity reflects exaggerated antimuscarinic activity, including mydriasis, tachycardia, urinary retention, ileus, hyperthermia, agitation, delirium, and potentially coma, with heightened risk in children, older adults, and patients with angle-closure glaucoma or obstructive uropathy. Common adverse effects include dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, decreased sweating, palpitations, dizziness, and confusion. Clinically, hyoscyamine is used as an antispasmodic and antisecretory agent for irritable bowel syndrome, functional gastrointestinal cramping, peptic ulcer adjunctive care, neurogenic bladder or bladder spasm, infant colic in selected settings, and reduction of excessive salivation or other parasympathetic symptoms.

Name: Zolpidem
Description: Zolpidem (DrugBank DB00425) is a nonbenzodiazepine sedative-hypnotic of the imidazopyridine class whose structure features a fused imidazo[1,2-a]pyridine bicyclic heteroaromatic core bearing a p-methylphenyl substituent and an N,N-dimethylacetamide side chain, giving a compact lipophilic scaffold distinct from classical 1,4-benzodiazepines yet pharmacologically related as a positive allosteric modulator of GABAA receptors. Its core chemical scaffold is therefore the imidazopyridine hypnotic motif, and similar drugs include zaleplon, eszopiclone, and benzodiazepines such as temazepam or triazolam, which share GABAergic hypnotic effects despite different chemotypes. Zolpidem binds the benzodiazepine site on GABAA receptor complexes, with functional selectivity for α1-subunit-containing receptors; relevant targets include GABRA1, GABRB2, and GABRG2 within pentameric GABAA channels. It is indicated primarily for short-term treatment of insomnia, especially sleep-onset difficulty, and in some formulations for sleep maintenance or middle-of-the-night awakening. Pharmacokinetically, it is rapidly absorbed orally with relatively fast onset, is highly protein bound, distributes into the CNS, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 with contributions from CYP2C9, CYP1A2, CYP2D6, and CYP2C19 to inactive metabolites, and is excreted largely in urine with some fecal elimination; its short elimination half-life supports nocturnal use. Toxicity includes dose-related CNS depression, psychomotor impairment, falls, respiratory depression when combined with opioids, alcohol, or other sedatives, and overdose causing profound somnolence or coma, though often less severe than barbiturates. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, headache, amnesia, ataxia, hallucinations, complex sleep behaviors such as sleep-driving, and next-day impairment. Clinically, it is used as an oral hypnotic in adults with acute or chronic insomnia when sleep initiation or maintenance is the principal symptom, generally at the lowest effective dose and for limited-duration, carefully monitored therapy.

Name: Famciclovir
Description: Famciclovir (DB00426) is an orally active antiviral nucleoside analogue and the diacetyl 6-deoxy prodrug of penciclovir, structurally characterized by a substituted guanine base attached to an acyclic side chain rather than a complete ribose ring, with acetylated hydroxyl functionality and a 2-aminopurine-like heterobicyclic purine nucleus that places it in the acyclic guanine analogue class; its core scaffold is therefore a purine/guanine mimic on an acyclic sugar surrogate, closely related to penciclovir and similar antiviral congeners such as acyclovir, valacyclovir, and ganciclovir. After oral administration it is well absorbed and rapidly converted by first-pass deacetylation and oxidation to penciclovir, giving substantially improved bioavailability over penciclovir itself; penciclovir distributes into body tissues and infected cells, is only modestly protein bound, undergoes limited further metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged in urine by renal excretion, so dose reduction is required in renal impairment. Its antiviral activity depends on initial phosphorylation mainly by viral thymidine kinase in herpes simplex virus and varicella-zoster virus infected cells, followed by host kinases to penciclovir triphosphate, which inhibits viral DNA polymerase and suppresses viral DNA synthesis; relevant targets therefore include viral thymidine kinase and viral DNA polymerase. Indications include herpes zoster, recurrent genital herpes, and herpes labialis. Adverse effects are usually mild, especially headache, nausea, diarrhea, fatigue, and abdominal pain, while toxicity is generally limited but may include confusion or hallucinations in elderly or renally impaired patients and rare hypersensitivity or hepatic enzyme elevations. Clinically, it is used as short-course oral therapy for shingles, episodic treatment or suppression of recurrent HSV infection, and treatment of cold sores.

Name: Triprolidine
Description: Triprolidine (DrugBank DB00427) is a first-generation sedating H1-antihistamine of the alkylamine/propylamine class, structurally characterized by a substituted pyridine ring linked through an alkenyl side chain to a tertiary dimethylamino moiety and an aryl group, giving a lipophilic, conformationally restricted diaryl-alkenyl amine architecture; its core scaffold is therefore an alkylamine antihistamine scaffold incorporating a pyridyl-aryl vinyl framework. It is chemically and pharmacologically similar to other first-generation H1 antagonists, especially chlorpheniramine, brompheniramine, dexchlorpheniramine, and pheniramine. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, at which it acts as an inverse agonist/antagonist; like related older antihistamines, it may also show weak anticholinergic activity contributing to adverse effects. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed, with onset within hours, broad distribution including central nervous system penetration that explains sedation, hepatic metabolism likely involving oxidative biotransformation, and renal excretion of metabolites and some unchanged drug. Triprolidine is indicated for symptomatic relief of allergic rhinitis, hay fever, urticaria, conjunctival irritation, and common-cold symptoms such as sneezing and rhinorrhea, often in combination products such as triprolidine with pseudoephedrine. Toxicity resembles other first-generation antihistamines: dose-related CNS depression or paradoxical excitation, antimuscarinic effects, impaired psychomotor performance, and in overdose agitation, hallucinations, seizures, tachycardia, and potentially arrhythmias, with heightened risk in children, older adults, and when combined with alcohol or other sedatives. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention, and clinically it has been used as an oral antiallergic and cold-symptom reliever where a rapid, inexpensive H1-blocking agent is desired.

Name: Streptozocin
Description: Streptozocin (DB00428) is a naturally derived nitrosourea antineoplastic whose structure consists of an N-methyl-N-nitrosourea warhead linked to a 2-deoxy-D-glucopyranose-like sugar, making it a glucose-conjugated alkylating agent; chemically it is categorized as a nitrosourea and broader DNA-alkylating cytotoxic antibiotic, with a glucosamine/sugar-nitrosourea scaffold that distinguishes it from non-glycosylated nitrosoureas. Similar drugs include carmustine, lomustine, and semustine as nitrosourea congeners, although streptozocin is notable for pancreatic islet tropism related to glucose transporter uptake. Its principal pharmacologic target is DNA, with cell entry facilitated particularly by SLC2A2/GLUT2 in pancreatic beta cells and some neuroendocrine tumor cells; downstream injury includes DNA alkylation, strand damage, and activation of PARP-dependent stress pathways, leading to inhibition of tumor cell proliferation. Pharmacokinetically, streptozocin is administered intravenously, distributes rapidly into extracellular fluid with uptake in kidney, liver, and pancreas, undergoes limited metabolic transformation relative to many cytotoxics, and is cleared predominantly by renal excretion, with a short plasma half-life but prolonged biologic effects from DNA damage. Major toxicities include dose-limiting nephrotoxicity, severe nausea and vomiting, hepatotoxicity, myelosuppression, and diabetogenic pancreatic beta-cell destruction; animal use as an experimental diabetogenic agent exemplifies this beta-cell toxicity. Adverse effects commonly include proteinuria, elevated creatinine, fatigue, diarrhea, transaminase elevation, anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia. Clinically, it is used mainly for metastatic or unresectable pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, especially islet-cell carcinoma, often alone or in combination regimens such as streptozocin with fluorouracil or doxorubicin for symptom control and tumor burden reduction.

Name: Carboprost tromethamine
Description: Carboprost tromethamine (DB00429) is the tromethamine salt of carboprost, a synthetic 15-methyl analog of prostaglandin F2alpha characterized by a prostanoic acid eicosanoid framework with a cyclopentane core, hydroxyl substituents, a ketone, and two aliphatic side chains, one bearing the 15-methyl modification that increases metabolic stability; chemically it belongs to the prostaglandins, specifically prostaglandin F analogs and oxylipin lipid mediators, and its core scaffold is the prostaglandin/prostanoic acid cyclopentane lipid scaffold. Closely related drugs include dinoprost, dinoprostone, misoprostol, latanoprost, travoprost, and bimatoprost, although the latter ophthalmic agents are used for different indications. Its principal pharmacologic target is the prostaglandin F receptor PTGFR on uterine smooth muscle, with downstream stimulation of myometrial contraction and vasoconstriction; off-target prostanoid receptor activity may contribute to adverse effects. Administered mainly by intramuscular injection, it is rapidly absorbed, distributes largely in extracellular fluids with local uterine action, undergoes hepatic and tissue metabolism including oxidation and beta-oxidation-like pathways, and is eliminated predominantly as metabolites in urine. It is indicated for refractory postpartum hemorrhage due to uterine atony and for abortion induction in the second trimester, including missed abortion or intrauterine fetal demise. Toxicity reflects exaggerated prostaglandin effects, with dose-related bronchospasm, severe diarrhea, vomiting, hypertension or hypotension, fever, and rarely uterine rupture, especially in susceptible patients. Common adverse effects include nausea, abdominal cramping, flushing, pyrexia, and transient tachycardia. Clinically, it is used as a uterotonic when oxytocin or ergometrine are ineffective and in specialist obstetric protocols requiring controlled uterine evacuation.

Name: Lindane
Description: Lindane (DB00431), the gamma isomer of hexachlorocyclohexane, is a highly chlorinated cycloalkane composed of a saturated six-membered cyclohexane ring bearing six chlorine substituents in a stereochemically defined arrangement that confers marked lipophilicity and persistence; chemically it belongs to the organochlorine insecticides, with a hexahalogenated cyclohexane scaffold closely related to other chlorinated antiparasitics and pesticides such as other hexachlorocyclohexane isomers, aldrin, dieldrin, and chlordane. Its principal pharmacologic target is the ligand-gated GABA_A receptor chloride channel in arthropods, where antagonism produces neuronal hyperexcitation and parasite death; mammalian toxicity is also linked to GABAergic inhibition, and interaction with voltage-gated ion channel systems has been discussed. After topical administration for scabies or pediculosis, absorption is usually limited but can become clinically significant with damaged skin, excessive application, prolonged contact, infants, or low body weight; distribution is favored into lipid-rich tissues and the central nervous system, metabolism occurs predominantly in the liver via cytochrome P450-mediated oxidation and dechlorination, and elimination proceeds through urinary excretion of metabolites with some fecal clearance. Major toxicities include dose-related neurotoxicity, especially seizures, ataxia, dizziness, tremor, confusion, and in severe poisoning coma, with additional concerns for hematologic, hepatic, and possible carcinogenic effects after substantial exposure. Adverse effects in routine use include pruritus, burning, dry skin, rash, paresthesia, headache, and rarely convulsions. Clinically, lindane has been used as a second-line topical scabicide and pediculicide for infestations such as Sarcoptes scabiei scabies and Pediculus humanus capitis or pubis when safer agents such as permethrin fail or cannot be used.

Name: Trifluridine
Description: Trifluridine (DB00432) is a fluorinated pyrimidine nucleoside analog structurally defined as a thymidine derivative in which the uracil/thymine base bears a trifluoromethyl substituent at the 5-position and is linked to a 2-deoxyribose sugar, placing it in the antimetabolite, antiviral, and antineoplastic nucleoside class with a deoxythymidine scaffold closely related to idoxuridine, floxuridine, thymidine, and other pyrimidine analogs such as fluorouracil-derived agents. Its pharmacologic activity depends on intracellular phosphorylation to mono-, di-, and triphosphate metabolites; the triphosphate is incorporated into DNA and inhibits DNA synthesis, while antiviral effects are associated with interference in viral DNA replication, especially through inhibition of herpesvirus DNA synthesis. Known target biology includes thymidine kinase-mediated activation, DNA polymerases including viral DNA polymerase, and in oncology thymidylate synthase is functionally relevant in the trifluridine/tipiracil setting. Pharmacokinetically, ophthalmic trifluridine is absorbed locally into corneal tissues with limited systemic exposure, distributed primarily in ocular compartments, and undergoes rapid catabolism if systemically available, which historically limited systemic use because of extensive metabolism and short persistence; excretion occurs mainly as metabolites via renal pathways. Toxicity is dominated by damage to rapidly dividing tissues and local ocular irritation; examples include punctate keratopathy, eyelid edema, burning, conjunctival inflammation, and with systemic exposure potentially myelosuppression and gastrointestinal toxicity. It is indicated mainly for primary keratoconjunctivitis and recurrent epithelial keratitis due to herpes simplex virus, and clinically used as topical ophthalmic therapy for dendritic corneal ulcers and other superficial HSV ocular infections.

Name: Prochlorperazine
Description: Prochlorperazine (DrugBank DB00433) is a piperazine-substituted phenothiazine built on a tricyclic phenothiazine core containing sulfur and ring nitrogen, typically bearing a 2-chloro substituent and a three-carbon side chain terminating in a piperazine moiety, a structure that confers potent dopamine antagonism and distinguishes it from aliphatic phenothiazines. Chemically it is classified as a first-generation antipsychotic, antiemetic, and phenothiazine derivative, with the phenothiazine tricyclic scaffold as its defining chemotype; closely related or mechanistically similar drugs include chlorpromazine, perphenazine, fluphenazine, trifluoperazine, promethazine, and the non-phenothiazine dopamine antagonist metoclopramide. Its principal targets are dopamine D2 receptors, with additional antagonism at D1-like dopamine receptors, alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, histamine H1 receptors, and muscarinic cholinergic receptors, explaining both therapeutic and adverse effects. It is used primarily for severe nausea and vomiting, migraine-associated nausea, vertigo, and schizophrenia or short-term control of psychotic symptoms. Oral and rectal absorption is variable, parenteral dosing has faster onset, distribution is extensive with substantial CNS penetration and high protein binding, metabolism is predominantly hepatic via oxidative and conjugative pathways, and elimination occurs mainly as metabolites in urine and feces, with clinically important first-pass metabolism. Toxicity includes dose-related CNS depression, hypotension, anticholinergic burden, hepatotoxicity, lowered seizure threshold, extrapyramidal toxicity such as acute dystonia, akathisia and parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia with chronic exposure, QT prolongation, and rare neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Common side effects include sedation, dizziness, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, orthostasis, and hyperprolactinemic effects. Clinically, it is widely used in emergency, inpatient, and outpatient settings as an antiemetic and adjunct in migraine care, and less commonly as a conventional antipsychotic.

Name: Cyproheptadine
Description: Cyproheptadine (DrugBank DB00434) is a first-generation antihistamine with antiserotonergic activity built on a tricyclic dibenzocycloheptene/piperidine architecture, in which a fused bicyclic aryl system is linked through a seven-membered ring to a tertiary piperidine-containing side chain; chemically it is a piperidine-substituted tricyclic H1-receptor antagonist and is often classified among sedating antihistamines with serotonin antagonism. Its core scaffold is closely related to other tricyclic antihistamine and serotonin-antagonist chemotypes, and similar drugs include ketotifen, azatadine, promethazine, diphenhydramine, and the serotonin antagonist pizotifen. Pharmacologically, cyproheptadine acts primarily at histamine H1 receptors and serotonin 5-HT2A and 5-HT2C receptors, with additional antimuscarinic effects; reported targets include HRH1, HTR2A, HTR2C, and to a lesser extent cholinergic muscarinic receptors. It is used orally, is well absorbed, widely distributed including CNS penetration, undergoes substantial hepatic metabolism likely involving CYP-mediated biotransformation, and is excreted mainly as metabolites in urine, with some biliary/fecal elimination. Clinically it is indicated for allergic conditions such as seasonal allergic rhinitis, urticaria, and pruritus, and is also used for appetite stimulation, migraine prophylaxis, and management of serotonin syndrome. Adverse effects commonly reflect CNS and anticholinergic activity, including sedation, dizziness, confusion, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention, with increased appetite and weight gain being notable. Toxicity in overdose may produce marked somnolence, anticholinergic delirium, tachycardia, hypotension, agitation, seizures, and respiratory depression, particularly in children or with coadministered CNS depressants.

Name: Nitric Oxide
Description: Nitric oxide (DrugBank DB00435) is an endogenous, diatomic free-radical gas composed of one nitrogen and one oxygen atom with a linear bond arrangement and an unpaired electron, making it a highly reactive, diffusible molecule rather than a conventional complex small-molecule scaffold; chemically it is classified as a gaseous signaling mediator, reactive nitrogen species, and vasodilator, with a minimal inorganic radical scaffold shared conceptually with related nitrogen oxide therapeutics and nitric oxide–donating agents. Similar drugs include inhaled pulmonary vasodilators or NO donors such as nitroglycerin, sodium nitroprusside, isosorbide dinitrate, and isosorbide mononitrate, although these are structurally distinct prodrugs or donors rather than nitric oxide itself. After inhalation, nitric oxide is delivered directly to ventilated lung units, rapidly diffuses across the alveolar-capillary membrane, and is functionally confined to the pulmonary circulation because it binds avidly to hemoglobin, forming nitrosylhemoglobin and methemoglobin and being oxidized to nitrite and nitrate, which are subsequently distributed in blood and eliminated mainly in urine. Its principal pharmacologic target is soluble guanylate cyclase, especially the heme-containing beta-1 subunit GUCY1B1 with the alpha subunit GUCY1A1, increasing cGMP and relaxing pulmonary vascular smooth muscle; downstream effects may also involve platelet and mitochondrial signaling. It is indicated primarily for hypoxic respiratory failure with pulmonary hypertension in term and near-term neonates, and clinically used for perioperative or critical-care pulmonary hypertension, acute right ventricular failure, and vasoreactivity testing. Major toxicities and adverse effects include methemoglobinemia, nitrogen dioxide-mediated airway injury, rebound pulmonary hypertension after abrupt withdrawal, hypotension, platelet inhibition with bleeding risk, headache, and worsening oxygenation in susceptible patients.

Name: Bendroflumethiazide
Description: Bendroflumethiazide (DrugBank DB00436) is a thiazide diuretic characterized structurally by a benzothiadiazine 1,1-dioxide core bearing sulfonamide functionality, with halogenated and lipophilic ring substitution including trifluoromethyl and benzyl-type substituents that increase potency and duration relative to older congeners; chemically it belongs to the sulfonamide-containing benzothiadiazine class, and its defining scaffold is the 1,2,4-benzothiadiazine ring system shared with classical thiazides. Closely related drugs include hydrochlorothiazide, chlorothiazide, methyclothiazide, polythiazide, and hydroflumethiazide, which share the same natriuretic pharmacology. Its principal target is the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter SLC12A3 in the distal convoluted tubule, with downstream effects on renal sodium, chloride, potassium, magnesium, calcium, and water handling. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed, distributed in extracellular fluid with meaningful plasma protein binding, has limited biotransformation, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged in urine, so diuretic efficacy depends on renal delivery and is prolonged in renal impairment. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related electrolyte and volume disturbances such as hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, dehydration, and prerenal azotemia, with less common hyperuricemia provoking gout, hyperglycemia, photosensitivity, rash, and rare sulfonamide-associated hypersensitivity or pancreatitis. It is indicated mainly for hypertension and edema, including edema associated with heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, corticosteroid therapy, or renal disease, and clinically is used alone or with other antihypertensives to control blood pressure, reduce fluid overload, and mitigate symptoms such as peripheral swelling and dyspnea.

Name: Allopurinol
Description: Allopurinol (DrugBank DB00437) is a small, planar purine-like heteroaromatic compound structurally characterized as a pyrazolo-pyrimidinone, specifically an isomeric analog of hypoxanthine in which a fused pyrazole-pyrimidine scaffold mimics endogenous purines and enables tight interaction with xanthine oxidoreductase; chemically it belongs to the antimetabolite/purine analog and antihyperuricemic class, with a bicyclic aza-heterocyclic scaffold shared conceptually with other purine-mimetic agents. Similar drugs include febuxostat, a nonpurine xanthine oxidase inhibitor, and uricosurics such as probenecid, though these differ in scaffold and mechanism. Allopurinol is well absorbed orally, distributed widely including into tissues, and rapidly converted by xanthine oxidase and aldehyde oxidase to the active metabolite oxypurinol, which has a longer half-life and is largely responsible for sustained xanthine oxidase inhibition; parent drug and metabolite are cleared mainly by the kidney, so accumulation occurs in renal impairment. Its principal target is xanthine oxidoreductase/xanthine oxidase, reducing uric acid formation and increasing hypoxanthine and xanthine salvage. It is indicated for chronic gout, recurrent uric acid nephrolithiasis, hyperuricemia associated with malignancy or chemotherapy-induced tumor lysis, and hyperuricosuria. Toxicity ranges from gastrointestinal intolerance and rash to severe cutaneous adverse reactions including allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis, with risk heightened in renal dysfunction and certain HLA backgrounds such as HLA-B*58:01. Common adverse effects include rash, nausea, diarrhea, transaminitis, and acute gout flares on initiation. Clinically, it is used for long-term urate lowering in tophaceous gout, prevention of urate nephropathy during cancer therapy, and management of uric acid stone disease.

Name: Ceftazidime
Description: Ceftazidime (DrugBank DB00438) is a parenteral third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic built on the cephem/beta-lactam scaffold, consisting of a fused beta-lactam and dihydrothiazine ring system bearing a syn-oxime aminothiazolyl acyl side chain that enhances Gram-negative stability and a positively charged pyridinium substituent that improves antipseudomonal activity and water solubility. Chemically it is a beta-lactam, specifically an oxyimino cephalosporin, and is structurally similar to other advanced cephalosporins such as cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, cefepime, and cefoperazone, with closest functional similarity to antipseudomonal agents like cefepime. Its antibacterial action results from binding bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, especially PBP3 and related transpeptidases, thereby inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-linking and cell-wall synthesis. Ceftazidime is not orally absorbed and is given intravenously or intramuscularly; it distributes well into extracellular fluids, urine, lung, bone, skin, and inflamed meninges, has low protein binding, minimal metabolism, an elimination half-life of about 1.5 to 2 hours in normal renal function, and is excreted largely unchanged by glomerular filtration, requiring dose reduction in renal impairment. Toxicity is generally low but includes beta-lactam hypersensitivity, positive Coombs test, gastrointestinal injury including C. difficile-associated diarrhea, hematologic abnormalities, and neurotoxicity such as encephalopathy, myoclonus, or seizures, particularly with renal accumulation. Indications and clinical use include serious susceptible Gram-negative infections, especially Pseudomonas aeruginosa pneumonia, bacteremia, febrile neutropenia, complicated urinary tract infection, intra-abdominal infection when combined for anaerobic coverage, skin and soft tissue infection, bone and joint infection, and meningitis; common adverse effects include rash, nausea, diarrhea, injection-site reactions, transaminase elevations, eosinophilia, and candidiasis.

Name: Cerivastatin
Description: Cerivastatin (DrugBank DB00439) is a synthetic statin characterized structurally by a substituted pyridine-containing heptenoic acid pharmacophore that mimics the endogenous HMG-CoA reduction intermediate, bearing fluorophenyl, methoxy, isopropyl, and heteroaryl substituents that increase potency and lipophilicity; chemically it belongs to the statin class, specifically a fully synthetic HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor, and its core scaffold is commonly described as a dihydroxyheptenoic acid side chain appended to a highly substituted aromatic/heteroaromatic pyridine system. It is closely related pharmacologically to other statins such as atorvastatin, fluvastatin, simvastatin, lovastatin, pravastatin, and rosuvastatin, though it was notably more potent on a milligram basis. Its primary target protein is 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase (HMGCR), with downstream effects on LDL receptor upregulation and plasma LDL lowering. Cerivastatin was indicated for hypercholesterolemia and mixed dyslipidemia, including elevated LDL cholesterol in patients at risk for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. After oral administration it is well absorbed but undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic uptake, is highly protein bound, distributed preferentially to the liver, extensively metabolized mainly by CYP2C8 and CYP3A4 to active and inactive metabolites, and excreted predominantly via bile/feces with limited renal elimination. Its major toxicity is dose-related myopathy progressing to rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury, especially with gemfibrozil or other interacting CYP2C8 inhibitors; hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevation also occurs. Common adverse effects include myalgia, weakness, abdominal pain, dyspepsia, headache, rash, and liver enzyme abnormalities. Clinically, it was used as adjunctive therapy to diet and lifestyle modification for LDL reduction, but was withdrawn in many markets because of severe, sometimes fatal rhabdomyolysis.

Name: Trimethoprim
Description: Trimethoprim (DrugBank DB00440) is a synthetic diaminopyrimidine antibacterial whose structure consists of a 2,4-diaminopyrimidine ring linked through a methylene bridge to a 3,4,5-trimethoxybenzyl moiety, placing it in the antifolate class and giving it a diaminopyrimidine–trimethoxybenzyl scaffold closely related to other bacterial dihydrofolate reductase inhibitors such as pyrimethamine, brodimoprim, tetroxoprim, and the combination partner sulfamethoxazole. Its principal target is bacterial dihydrofolate reductase, encoded in many organisms by folA or homologous DHFR proteins, with much lower affinity for human DHFR, thereby blocking tetrahydrofolate synthesis and impairing thymidine and purine production. Pharmacokinetically, oral absorption is generally rapid and high, bioavailability is substantial, tissue penetration is broad including kidney, lung, prostate, sputum, saliva, and cerebrospinal fluid to a limited extent, protein binding is moderate, and the drug distributes well into urine where concentrations exceed plasma; it undergoes limited hepatic metabolism by oxidation and conjugation, while most elimination is renal via glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, with dose adjustment needed in renal impairment. Trimethoprim is indicated mainly for susceptible urinary tract infections, prostatitis, and respiratory or gastrointestinal infections, and is used clinically alone or more commonly with sulfamethoxazole for cystitis, pyelonephritis, otitis media, shigellosis, traveler’s diarrhea, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia treatment or prophylaxis, and nocardiosis. Toxicities reflect folate antagonism and include megaloblastic anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and teratogenic concern, while adverse effects commonly include nausea, rash, pruritus, hyperkalemia, and rises in serum creatinine from inhibited tubular secretion, with severe examples including Stevens-Johnson syndrome when given in combination products.

Name: Gemcitabine
Description: Gemcitabine (DB00441) is a difluorinated deoxycytidine analog antimetabolite whose structure consists of a cytosine base linked by a beta-N-glycosidic bond to a modified 2-deoxyribose bearing two fluorine atoms at the 2′ position, making it a pyrimidine nucleoside analog in the antineoplastic antimetabolite class with a deoxycytidine scaffold. It is closely related to other nucleoside analog drugs such as cytarabine, decitabine, azacitidine, and fluorinated analogs including clofarabine, although gemcitabine is distinguished by its 2′,2′-difluoro sugar substitution and strong self-potentiating effects on nucleotide metabolism. After intravenous administration it has negligible oral bioavailability, distributes rapidly into tissues, shows low plasma protein binding, and is transported into cells mainly by SLC29A1/ENT1 and other nucleoside transporters; intracellularly it is activated by deoxycytidine kinase to mono-, di-, and triphosphate metabolites, while it is inactivated primarily by cytidine deaminase to 2′,2′-difluorodeoxyuridine, with renal excretion of metabolites and some parent drug. Its principal targets are DNA synthesis pathways through incorporation of dFdCTP into DNA and inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase via RRM1 and RRM2, with deoxycytidine kinase, cytidine deaminase, and nucleoside transporters acting as key determinants of activity. Gemcitabine is indicated for pancreatic adenocarcinoma, non-small cell lung cancer, urothelial carcinoma, breast cancer, ovarian cancer, and biliary tract cancers, often in combination regimens. Dose-limiting toxicity is myelosuppression, especially neutropenia and thrombocytopenia; other toxicities include anemia, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, capillary leak, hemolytic uremic syndrome, interstitial pneumonitis, and radiosensitization. Common adverse effects include fatigue, nausea, vomiting, fever, rash, transaminase elevation, dyspnea, edema, and mucositis. Clinically, it is used as monotherapy or combined with agents such as cisplatin, carboplatin, nab-paclitaxel, or erlotin

Name: Entecavir
Description: Entecavir (DrugBank DB00442) is a carbocyclic 2'-deoxyguanosine nucleoside analog in which a guanine base is attached to a conformationally constrained cyclopentyl methylene scaffold bearing hydroxymethyl and exocyclic unsaturation features that mimic the natural sugar-phosphate geometry of purine nucleosides; chemically it is classified as an antiviral guanosine analog, with a carbocyclic nucleoside scaffold related to other anti-HBV nucleos(t)ide agents, and it is most similar in therapeutic class and mechanistic logic to lamivudine, telbivudine, adefovir, and tenofovir, although structurally it is especially comparable to other purine nucleoside analogs. After oral administration, entecavir is absorbed with relatively good bioavailability that is reduced by food, distributes widely with low plasma protein binding, undergoes minimal hepatic metabolism and little cytochrome P450 involvement, and is eliminated largely unchanged by the kidney through glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, giving a terminal half-life that supports once-daily dosing despite a longer intracellular triphosphate persistence. Its active triphosphate inhibits hepatitis B virus polymerase/reverse transcriptase, including priming, negative-strand reverse transcription, and positive-strand DNA synthesis; the principal target is therefore HBV polymerase. Clinically it is indicated for chronic hepatitis B infection, including compensated liver disease, active viral replication with elevated transaminases, histologic inflammation, and selected decompensated cases. Toxicity is usually limited but includes class-associated mitochondrial risk such as rare lactic acidosis and hepatomegaly with steatosis, plus severe hepatitis flares after discontinuation; resistance can emerge, particularly in prior lamivudine-resistant HBV. Common adverse effects include headache, fatigue, dizziness, nausea, abdominal discomfort, and transient ALT elevations. In practice it is used as first-line suppressive therapy for nucleoside-naive chronic HBV, in cirrhosis, and in patients needing potent long-term viral suppression with a high genetic barrier to resistance.

Name: Betamethasone
Description: Betamethasone (DrugBank DB00443) is a highly potent synthetic fluorinated corticosteroid built on the pregnane steroid nucleus, characterized by the classic four-ring cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene scaffold with key 9α-fluoro substitution, 11β- and 17α-hydroxyl groups, a 3-keto-4-ene system, a 20-ketone, and a 16β-methyl group; it is the 16β-epimer of dexamethasone and belongs chemically to the glucocorticoid class of corticosteroids. Its core scaffold is the corticosteroid/pregnane framework, shared with structurally related drugs such as dexamethasone, prednisolone, prednisone, triamcinolone, and hydrocortisone, although betamethasone has relatively strong glucocorticoid and minimal mineralocorticoid activity. It primarily targets the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, with downstream transrepression of proinflammatory transcription factors including NF-κB and AP-1 and reduced expression of cytokines, prostaglandins, and leukocyte adhesion mediators. Pharmacokinetically, absorption depends on formulation and route, with good systemic absorption orally and after parenteral, topical, intra-articular, or antenatal use; it is widely distributed, significantly protein bound, crosses the placenta, undergoes mainly hepatic CYP3A4-mediated metabolism, and is excreted predominantly as metabolites in urine. Toxicity reflects dose and duration, including HPA-axis suppression, hyperglycemia, infection risk, psychosis, myopathy, osteoporosis, cataracts, glaucoma, skin atrophy, poor wound healing, and fetal or neonatal effects after repeated exposure. Indications and clinical uses include inflammatory and allergic disorders such as asthma exacerbations, dermatitis, psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, and allergic reactions, as well as antenatal fetal lung maturation, local musculoskeletal injections, and topical treatment of corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses; common adverse effects include edema, mood change, insomnia, dyspepsia, hypertension, acne, and Cushingoid features.

Name: Teniposide
Description: Teniposide (DB00444) is a semisynthetic podophyllotoxin derivative in the epipodophyllotoxin class, structurally characterized by the polycyclic aryltetralin lignan core of podophyllotoxin with a trans-fused lactone-containing framework, multiple methoxy and hydroxyl substituents, and a glycosidic thiophene-containing moiety that distinguishes it from related congeners; thus its core chemical scaffold is the epipodophyllotoxin or aryltetralin lignan scaffold. It is closely related to etoposide and, more broadly, to topoisomerase II poisons such as etopophos, while differing from anthracyclines despite partial mechanistic overlap. Its principal target is topoisomerase II, especially TOP2A and TOP2B, with cytotoxicity arising from stabilization of the DNA-topoisomerase II cleavable complex, leading to DNA strand breaks and apoptosis. Pharmacokinetically, teniposide is administered intravenously because oral absorption is poor and variable; it is highly protein bound, distributes widely into tissues but has limited cerebrospinal fluid penetration, undergoes substantial hepatic metabolism including CYP3A-mediated biotransformation, and is eliminated by both biliary/fecal and renal routes, with a relatively prolonged terminal half-life and clearance reduced in hepatic dysfunction. Major toxicities include dose-limiting myelosuppression, especially leukopenia and thrombocytopenia, mucositis, hepatotoxicity, and risk of secondary leukemia related to topoisomerase II inhibition; examples of adverse effects also include nausea, vomiting, alopecia, hypersensitivity reactions, and infection from neutropenia. Clinically, teniposide is used as an antineoplastic agent primarily in pediatric oncology, especially refractory or relapsed acute lymphoblastic leukemia, and it has also been used in combination regimens for lymphomas, brain tumors, and other hematologic malignancies.

Name: Epirubicin
Description: Epirubicin (DrugBank DB00445) is an anthracycline antineoplastic antibiotic structurally characterized by a tetracyclic anthraquinone-like anthracycline aglycone with quinone and hydroquinone functionalities, a C-13 keto side chain, and an O-glycosidically linked amino sugar, daunosamine; it is specifically the 4′-epimer of doxorubicin, placing it within the anthracycline/anthracenedione-related cytotoxic class and on the doxorubicin-daunorubicin anthracycline scaffold. Closely related drugs include doxorubicin, daunorubicin, idarubicin, and valrubicin, which share DNA-intercalating and topoisomerase-directed properties. Its principal targets are topoisomerase II alpha and beta (TOP2A, TOP2B), with additional pharmacologic effects mediated through DNA intercalation, inhibition of nucleic acid synthesis, and iron-dependent free-radical generation. After intravenous administration, epirubicin shows rapid and extensive tissue distribution, high protein binding, triphasic elimination, predominant hepatic metabolism to epirubicinol and glucuronidated metabolites, and mainly biliary/fecal excretion with a lesser renal component; hepatic impairment reduces clearance. Clinically it is used for breast cancer, including adjuvant treatment of early breast cancer with nodal involvement and metastatic disease, and has also been used in bladder, gastric, ovarian, and soft-tissue sarcoma regimens. Dose-limiting and clinically important toxicities include cumulative cardiotoxicity with cardiomyopathy and heart failure, severe myelosuppression, mucositis, alopecia, nausea, vomiting, extravasation-related tissue necrosis, and secondary leukemia; common adverse effects include neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, stomatitis, diarrhea, infection risk, and transient red discoloration of urine.

Name: Chloramphenicol
Description: Chloramphenicol (DrugBank DB00446) is a small, highly lipophilic nitroaromatic antibacterial built on a dichloroacetamide-linked propanediol scaffold bearing a para-nitrophenyl ring and stereochemically defined 1,3-propanediol substituents; chemically it is classified as an amphenicol broad-spectrum antibiotic, with the chloramphenicol scaffold closely related to thiamphenicol and florfenicol, which are key similar drugs and semisynthetic analogs. Its antibacterial action is mediated by binding to the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit, primarily the peptidyl transferase center of 23S rRNA within ribosomes encoded by rrn operons, thereby inhibiting peptide bond formation and protein synthesis; resistance-associated targets and modifiers include chloramphenicol acetyltransferases. Pharmacokinetically, chloramphenicol is well absorbed orally, penetrates extensively into tissues, cerebrospinal fluid, and ocular compartments, exhibits moderate protein binding, undergoes predominant hepatic glucuronidation with some reduction pathways, and is excreted mainly in urine as inactive metabolites, with prolonged half-life in neonates and patients with hepatic impairment. Major toxicities include dose-related reversible bone marrow suppression and rare idiosyncratic aplastic anemia, as well as gray baby syndrome from impaired neonatal metabolism; neurotoxicity, optic neuritis, and peripheral neuropathy may occur with prolonged exposure. Adverse effects also include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, candidiasis, and hypersensitivity reactions. Clinically, it has been used for severe infections such as bacterial meningitis, typhoid fever, rickettsial disease, anaerobic brain abscess, and serious ocular infections, particularly when safer agents are unsuitable or resistance patterns necessitate its use.

Name: Loracarbef
Description: Loracarbef (DrugBank DB00447) is a semisynthetic oral beta-lactam antibacterial in the carbacephem/second-generation cephalosporin-related class, structurally characterized by the cephem-like bicyclic beta-lactam fused ring system in which the usual sulfur of the dihydrothiazine ring is replaced by carbon, with side-chain features closely paralleling cefaclor and conferring acid stability and oral activity; thus its core scaffold is a carbacephem nucleus bearing aminophenylglycyl-type substitution typical of orally active cephalosporin analogs. Similar drugs include cefaclor, cephalexin, cefuroxime axetil, cefprozil, and other oral cephalosporins with overlapping spectrum and pharmacology. Its antibacterial effect is mediated by binding bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, especially transpeptidases involved in peptidoglycan cross-linking, leading to inhibition of cell-wall synthesis and bacterial lysis. Loracarbef is generally well absorbed after oral administration, achieves therapeutic concentrations in respiratory and urinary tissues and fluids, shows relatively low protein binding, undergoes minimal metabolism, and is eliminated largely unchanged by the kidney via glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, so exposure increases in renal impairment. Toxicity is typical of beta-lactams and includes hypersensitivity reactions ranging from rash and urticaria to rare anaphylaxis, gastrointestinal toxicity such as antibiotic-associated diarrhea and rare Clostridioides difficile colitis, and uncommon hematologic or hepatic laboratory abnormalities; overdose would be expected mainly to accentuate GI and neurotoxic risk in renal dysfunction. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, candidiasis, and rash. Clinically, it has been used for susceptible mild-to-moderate infections including acute otitis media, sinusitis, pharyngitis/tonsillitis, acute bacterial exacerbations of bronchitis, community-acquired lower respiratory tract infection, uncomplicated skin and soft-tissue infection, and uncomplicated urinary tract infection.

Name: Lansoprazole
Description: Lansoprazole (DrugBank DB00448) is a substituted benzimidazole proton-pump inhibitor characterized structurally by a 2-pyridylmethylsulfinyl linkage connecting a benzimidazole ring to a substituted pyridine, with the sulfoxide center and electron-donating substituents enabling acid-activated conversion to reactive sulfenamide intermediates in the gastric canaliculus; chemically it belongs to the benzimidazole sulfoxide class, and its core scaffold is the benzimidazole–sulfoxide–pyridine PPI pharmacophore shared with related agents such as omeprazole, esomeprazole, pantoprazole, rabeprazole, and dexlansoprazole. Its principal target is the gastric H+/K+-ATPase proton pump, primarily ATP4A and functionally the ATP4A/ATP4B complex, which it inhibits covalently after activation in acidic conditions. Lansoprazole is indicated for acid-related disorders including gastroesophageal reflux disease, erosive esophagitis, peptic ulcer disease, NSAID-associated ulcer risk reduction, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, and Helicobacter pylori eradication regimens in combination therapy. It is acid-labile and therefore given as delayed-release formulations; absorption occurs in the small intestine, protein binding is high, distribution is moderate, hepatic metabolism is extensive via CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 to inactive metabolites, and excretion occurs through both urine and feces. Toxicity is generally low in overdose, but prolonged use is associated with hypomagnesemia, vitamin B12 deficiency, fracture risk, interstitial nephritis, Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea, and possible pneumonia risk. Common adverse effects include headache, diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea, constipation, and dizziness. Clinically it is used for short-course ulcer healing, maintenance of reflux control, eradication protocols with amoxicillin and clarithromycin, and high-dose acid suppression in hypersecretory states.

Name: Dipivefrin
Description: Dipivefrin (DB00449) is a lipophilic diester prodrug of epinephrine in which both catechol hydroxyls are esterified with pivaloyl groups, preserving the phenethylamine/β-amino alcohol core of adrenaline while masking the polar catechol to enhance ocular penetration; chemically it is a sympathomimetic catecholamine derivative, specifically an adrenergic prodrug, built on the arylethanolamine (phenethylamine) scaffold. It is closely related to epinephrine and other ophthalmic adrenergic antiglaucoma agents such as epinephrine itself and, more distantly, apraclonidine or brimonidine by therapeutic class rather than scaffold. After topical ocular administration, dipivefrin is absorbed across the cornea more efficiently than epinephrine, distributes mainly to anterior segment tissues, and is rapidly hydrolyzed by ocular and systemic esterases to active epinephrine; the released epinephrine undergoes further metabolism largely by catechol-O-methyltransferase and monoamine oxidase, with urinary excretion of metabolites. Its principal pharmacologic targets are adrenergic receptors, especially alpha-1, alpha-2, beta-1, and beta-2 adrenoceptors, through locally generated epinephrine, reducing intraocular pressure by decreasing aqueous humor production and increasing outflow. It is indicated for open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension, particularly when topical reduction of elevated intraocular pressure is needed. Adverse effects are commonly ocular burning, stinging, conjunctival hyperemia, lacrimation, blurred vision, eyelid irritation, and mydriasis; systemic sympathomimetic effects such as tachycardia, palpitations, hypertension, headache, tremor, and anxiety may occur but are less common. Toxicity reflects excessive adrenergic stimulation, with examples including arrhythmias, marked hypertension, or angle-closure precipitation in predisposed patients. Clinically, it has been used as an ophthalmic solution, often when improved corneal penetration over epinephrine was desired, although use has declined with newer glaucoma therapies.

Name: Droperidol
Description: Droperidol (DrugBank DB00450) is a butyrophenone antipsychotic and antiemetic whose structure consists of a fluorinated aromatic ring linked through a ketone-containing butyl chain to a tertiary piperidine, further substituted with a benzimidazolone-like heterocyclic moiety, giving a compact haloperidol-related scaffold optimized for high dopamine receptor affinity; chemically it belongs to the butyrophenone class and is built on the aryl-butyrophenone–piperidine scaffold seen in related agents such as haloperidol, benperidol, and trifluperidol. Its principal pharmacologic targets are dopamine D2 receptors, with additional antagonist activity at D1, D3, D4, 5-HT3, alpha1-adrenergic, histamine H1, and to a lesser extent muscarinic receptors, explaining its sedative, antiemetic, and neuroleptic effects. Clinically, droperidol is used for prevention and treatment of postoperative nausea and vomiting, acute nausea in emergency care, and rapid tranquilization of agitation, including severe migraine-associated nausea or acute psychomotor agitation. After parenteral administration it has rapid onset, extensive tissue distribution, high protein binding, hepatic metabolism mainly via oxidative pathways including CYP3A4-mediated biotransformation, and urinary plus fecal excretion of metabolites, with a terminal half-life of several hours. Its major toxicity is dose-related QT prolongation and torsades de pointes risk, especially in patients with electrolyte abnormalities, bradycardia, structural heart disease, or concomitant QT-prolonging drugs; other adverse effects include excessive sedation, hypotension, extrapyramidal symptoms such as dystonia or akathisia, restlessness, dizziness, and rare neuroleptic malignant syndrome, so present-day clinical use emphasizes low-dose monitored antiemetic administration or carefully supervised control of acute agitation.

Name: Levothyroxine
Description: Levothyroxine (DrugBank DB00451) is the synthetic levo-isomer of thyroxine, an iodinated amino acid derivative structurally characterized by a diphenyl ether core linking two iodinated phenyl rings and an L-tyrosine-like alanine side chain bearing amino and carboxyl groups; chemically it belongs to the thyroid hormone class, specifically iodothyronines, with a halogenated phenoxyphenylalanine scaffold. Closely related drugs include liothyronine (T3), liotrix, and desiccated thyroid preparations, as well as the endogenous hormone thyroxine. Its principal targets are thyroid hormone receptors THRA and THRB, with biological activity largely mediated after peripheral deiodination to triiodothyronine by deiodinases such as DIO1 and DIO2; transport proteins including transthyretin, albumin, and thyroxine-binding globulin are also pharmacologically relevant for disposition. Oral absorption is incomplete and variable, typically occurring in the small intestine and reduced by food, calcium, iron, bile acid sequestrants, and proton pump-related gastric pH changes; distribution is extensive but highly protein bound, metabolism occurs mainly by stepwise deiodination plus conjugation in liver and other tissues, and elimination is primarily renal and biliary as metabolites, with a long half-life of about 7 days in euthyroid adults, shortened in hyperthyroidism and prolonged in hypothyroidism. Toxicity reflects excessive thyroid hormone effect, including tachyarrhythmia, angina, heart failure exacerbation, tremor, insomnia, weight loss, heat intolerance, diarrhea, and with chronic overtreatment, osteoporosis; severe overdose can cause thyrotoxicosis or thyroid storm. Clinically, levothyroxine is used for replacement in primary, secondary, or congenital hypothyroidism, for TSH suppression in differentiated thyroid cancer or goiter, and for myxedema-related states, with adverse effects generally representing overreplacement rather than idiosyncratic toxicity.

Name: Meperidine
Description: Meperidine (pethidine; DrugBank DB00454) is a synthetic opioid analgesic built on a 4-phenylpiperidine structure, consisting of a tertiary piperidine ring bearing a phenyl substituent and an esterified carboxylate side chain, a motif that confers lipophilicity and distinguishes it from morphinan opioids; chemically it is classified as a phenylpiperidine opioid, with a piperidine scaffold shared across related agents. Similar drugs include other opioid analgesics, especially phenylpiperidines such as fentanyl, alfentanil, sufentanil, and loperamide, as well as more broadly morphine and methadone as mechanistically related analgesics. Its principal target is the mu-opioid receptor encoded by OPRM1, with weaker activity at kappa and delta opioid receptors reported. Meperidine is indicated for moderate to severe acute pain, including postoperative pain, trauma-related pain, and obstetric analgesia, and has also been used for control of postoperative shivering and rigors. It is generally well absorbed after oral or parenteral administration, widely distributed including CNS penetration, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly by hydrolysis and N-demethylation to normeperidine, and is excreted primarily in urine as metabolites and conjugates; its duration of analgesia is shorter than many opioids. Toxicity is clinically important because normeperidine is neurotoxic and can accumulate, particularly in renal impairment, causing tremor, myoclonus, agitation, delirium, and seizures; like other opioids, overdose can produce respiratory depression, miosis, coma, hypotension, and death. Common adverse effects include sedation, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, constipation, sweating, and orthostatic effects, and clinical use is now typically limited to short-term analgesia in selected settings due to seizure risk, serotonergic interactions, and dependence liability.

Name: Loratadine
Description: Loratadine (DrugBank DB00455) is a second-generation tricyclic antihistamine whose structure comprises a lipophilic dibenzocycloheptane-like fused aryl system linked to a substituted piperidine/carbamate-containing moiety, giving a conformationally restricted, peripherally selective H1-receptor antagonist profile; chemically it is a piperidine derivative and tricyclic antihistamine, with a benzo-cycloheptapyridine/piperidine scaffold related to other modern H1 blockers. Similar drugs include desloratadine, its active metabolite, as well as cetirizine, levocetirizine, fexofenadine, and older tricyclic antihistamines such as azatadine. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor (HRH1), where it acts as an inverse agonist/antagonist to reduce histamine-mediated vasodilation, pruritus, sneezing, and rhinorrhea. After oral administration, loratadine is rapidly absorbed, undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 to desloratadine, is highly protein bound, distributes largely to peripheral tissues with limited CNS penetration, and is eliminated as metabolites in urine and feces, with parent and metabolite half-lives supporting once-daily dosing. It is indicated for allergic rhinitis, seasonal and perennial allergy symptoms, and chronic idiopathic urticaria, and is used clinically for sneezing, nasal itching, watery eyes, hives, and pruritus. Adverse effects are usually mild and include headache, somnolence or fatigue, dry mouth, dizziness, and gastrointestinal discomfort; toxicity is generally low, but overdose may cause tachycardia, agitation, drowsiness, and anticholinergic-like effects, while hepatic impairment or strong CYP3A4/CYP2D6 inhibitors can increase exposure and rarely contribute to QT-related cardiac risk.

Name: Cefalotin
Description: Cefalotin, also known as cephalothin, is a first-generation cephalosporin beta-lactam antibiotic built on the 7-aminocephalosporanic acid scaffold, featuring a fused beta-lactam–dihydrothiazine bicyclic nucleus with a 2-thiopheneacetamido substituent at the 7-position and an acetoxymethyl group at the 3-position, structural elements that confer susceptibility to some beta-lactamases and define its early cephalosporin profile. Chemically it belongs to the cephalosporin subclass of beta-lams, with a cephem scaffold closely related to cefazolin, cephaloridine, cephalexin, and cefapirin, and more distantly to penicillins through the shared beta-lactam pharmacophore. Its antibacterial action is mediated by binding bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, particularly transpeptidases such as PBP1, PBP2, and PBP3, thereby inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-linking and causing cell-wall instability and lysis. Cefalotin is administered parenterally because oral absorption is poor; it distributes mainly in extracellular fluid with useful concentrations in skin, soft tissue, bone, pleural fluid, and urine, shows limited CSF penetration unless meninges are inflamed, undergoes partial hepatic deacetylation to desacetylcephalothin, and is eliminated predominantly by rapid renal tubular secretion and glomerular filtration, giving a short half-life and requiring dose adjustment in renal impairment. It has been used for susceptible staphylococcal and streptococcal infections, pneumococcal respiratory infections, skin and soft-tissue infection, osteomyelitis, urinary tract infection, and perioperative prophylaxis. Adverse effects include hypersensitivity reactions, rash, urticaria, fever, eosinophilia, diarrhea, nausea, injection-site pain, phlebitis, positive Coombs test, and superinfection; important toxicities include nephrotoxicity, especially with high doses or aminoglycosides, rare interstitial nephritis, hematologic abnormalities, and Clostridioides difficile-associated colitis.

Name: Prazosin
Description: Prazosin (DrugBank DB00457) is a quinazoline-derived piperazine antihypertensive whose structure features a 4-amino-6,7-dimethoxyquinazoline aromatic heterobicycle linked through a piperazine ring to a furan-containing acyl side chain, placing it in the alpha1-adrenergic receptor antagonist class and more specifically within the quinazoline-piperazine scaffold family shared by related alpha blockers. Similar drugs include terazosin, doxazosin, alfuzosin, and to a lesser extent tamsulosin, which differ in subtype selectivity and pharmacokinetic behavior but retain the alpha1-adrenoceptor blocking pharmacology. Its principal targets are alpha1-adrenergic receptor subtypes ADRA1A, ADRA1B, and ADRA1D, producing peripheral arterial and venous vasodilation and reduced smooth-muscle tone. Prazosin is well absorbed orally but undergoes first-pass hepatic metabolism, yielding moderate bioavailability; it is widely distributed, is substantially protein bound, reaches peak plasma concentrations within a few hours, has a relatively short elimination half-life requiring repeated dosing in many settings, is metabolized mainly in the liver by demethylation and conjugative pathways, and is excreted predominantly in bile/feces with a smaller renal component. Clinically it is indicated for hypertension and is also used for symptomatic benign prostatic hyperplasia and, off-label, trauma-related nightmares or PTSD-associated sleep disturbance. Adverse effects and toxicity reflect exaggerated alpha1 blockade, including first-dose syncope, orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, headache, palpitations, weakness, nasal congestion, edema, and occasionally severe falls or hypotensive episodes, particularly with dose initiation, rapid titration, dehydration, or concomitant antihypertensives or phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors.

Name: Imipramine
Description: Imipramine (DrugBank DB00458) is a dibenzazepine tricyclic antidepressant built on a rigid tricyclic aromatic system in which two benzene rings are fused to a seven-membered central ring and substituted with a three-carbon side chain terminating in a dimethylamino group, a motif that confers a lipophilic cationic amphiphile profile; chemically it belongs to the tertiary amine tricyclic antidepressants, with a dibenzazepine scaffold closely related to desipramine, amitriptyline, clomipramine, doxepin, and nortriptyline. Its principal targets are the serotonin transporter SLC6A4 and norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, with additional antagonist activity at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, histamine H1 receptor, and alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, explaining both efficacy and adverse effects. Imipramine is well absorbed orally, undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism, distributes widely into tissues including the central nervous system, is highly protein bound, and is metabolized mainly by CYP2D6, CYP2C19, and related oxidative pathways to active desipramine and other metabolites that are subsequently conjugated and excreted primarily in urine. It is indicated for major depressive disorder and has also been used for nocturnal enuresis, panic disorder, chronic neuropathic pain, and some anxiety syndromes. Common adverse effects include dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, sedation, weight gain, orthostatic hypotension, tremor, and sexual dysfunction. Toxicity is clinically important, especially in overdose, producing seizures, delirium, coma, anticholinergic syndrome, and potentially fatal cardiac conduction abnormalities such as QRS widening, ventricular arrhythmias, and hypotension; therefore its clinical use requires cautious dosing, monitoring, and attention to drug interactions and suicide risk.

Name: Acitretin
Description: Acitretin (DB00459) is a second-generation aromatic retinoid and active metabolite of etretinate, structurally characterized by a highly conjugated polyene side chain attached to a substituted benzoic acid ring bearing methoxy and tetramethyl groups, giving a lipophilic retinoic acid-like framework with geometric isomerism and a retinoid scaffold based on an aryl-polyene carboxylic acid motif. It belongs to the retinoid class, more specifically systemic synthetic vitamin A analogs used in keratinization disorders, and is chemically similar to etretinate, isotretinoin, tretinoin, adapalene, and tazarotene, although acitretin is distinguished by its aromatic retinoid backbone and free carboxylic acid. Its pharmacologic activity is mediated primarily through retinoic acid receptors RAR-alpha, RAR-beta, and RAR-gamma, with downstream modulation of gene transcription affecting keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation; indirect effects on RXR-regulated pathways may also be relevant. Orally administered acitretin shows variable but improved absorption with food, extensive tissue distribution due to high lipophilicity, high plasma protein binding, hepatic isomerization and metabolism, and elimination mainly as metabolites in urine and feces; importantly, co-ingestion of alcohol can promote reverse esterification to etretinate, markedly prolonging persistence.
