Major toxicity includes profound teratogenicity, mucocutaneous toxicity, hepatotoxicity, hypertriglyceridemia, pancreatitis risk, and skeletal or ligamentous calcification with long-term use. Adverse effects commonly include cheilitis, xerosis, epistaxis, alopecia, pruritus, photosensitivity, headache, and elevated liver enzymes or lipids. Clinically, acitretin is used chiefly for severe psoriasis, especially pustular, erythrodermic, and extensive plaque psoriasis, and is also used in disorders of keratinization such as ichthyosis, palmoplantar keratoderma, and Darier disease.

Name: Nabumetone
Description: Nabumetone (DrugBank DB00461) is a nonacidic arylalkanone nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug characterized structurally by a 6-methoxy-substituted naphthalene ring linked through a methylene bridge to a butan-2-one side chain, giving it a neutral ketone prodrug architecture rather than the carboxylate motif typical of many NSAIDs; its chemical category is therefore a naphthylalkanone NSAID, and its core scaffold is a methoxynaphthalene aryl-butanone framework. It is chemically and pharmacologically related to other cyclooxygenase-inhibiting NSAIDs such as naproxen, diclofenac, ibuprofen, indomethacin, and sulindac, although nabumetone is distinguished by conversion to the active acidic metabolite 6-methoxy-2-naphthylacetic acid (6-MNA). After oral administration it is well absorbed, undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism to 6-MNA, reaches peak active-metabolite concentrations within hours, is highly protein bound, distributes systemically to inflamed tissues, is further metabolized by hepatic oxidation and conjugation, and is excreted mainly in urine with a smaller fecal component; the parent drug has a short half-life, whereas 6-MNA has a longer elimination half-life that supports once- or twice-daily dosing. Its principal targets are cyclooxygenase enzymes PTGS1 and PTGS2, with anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antipyretic effects mediated predominantly by inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis. Indications include osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and symptomatic relief of musculoskeletal pain, stiffness, and inflammation. Toxicities and adverse effects are those of the NSAID class, including dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, edema, hypertension, renal impairment, peptic ulceration, gastrointestinal bleeding, hepatotoxicity, hypersensitivity, and increased thrombotic cardiovascular risk, with overdose potentially causing lethargy, vomiting, and acute kidney injury. Clinically, it is used as an oral anti-inflammatory analgesic when longer action and somewhat improved gastric tolerability relative to some acidic NSAIDs are desired.

Name: Methscopolamine bromide
Description: Methscopolamine bromide (DrugBank DB00462) is a semisynthetic quaternary ammonium antimuscarinic derived from the belladonna alkaloid scopolamine, structurally characterized by the tropane bicyclic 8-azabicyclo[3.2.1]octane nucleus esterified to a substituted aromatic acid and bearing a permanently charged N-methyl quaternary nitrogen as the bromide salt; thus, it belongs to the anticholinergic/parasympatholytic tropane ester class and is built on the scopolamine/atropine-like tropane scaffold. Closely related drugs include scopolamine, atropine, homatropine, hyoscyamine, butylscopolamine, glycopyrrolate, and propantheline, which share antimuscarinic pharmacology with differing CNS penetration and duration. Its principal targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially CHRM1, CHRM2, CHRM3, CHRM4, and CHRM5, with therapeutic effects largely attributable to peripheral antagonism at M1 and M3 receptors in the gastrointestinal tract and secretory glands. Because the quaternary ammonium limits membrane permeability, oral absorption is incomplete and variable, CNS penetration is poor, distribution is largely peripheral, metabolism is limited or only partial, and elimination occurs mainly via renal and fecal routes as unchanged drug and metabolites. Methscopolamine is used to reduce gastric acid secretion, intestinal spasm, and hypermotility in peptic ulcer disease, irritable bowel symptoms, abdominal cramping, and other functional gastrointestinal disorders, and sometimes as an adjunct to reduce secretions. Typical adverse effects are dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, tachycardia, urinary retention, decreased sweating, and mydriasis; toxicity reflects excessive antimuscarinic exposure, producing severe ileus, marked urinary retention, hyperthermia, confusion or agitation less commonly than tertiary amines, and worsening of angle-closure glaucoma or obstructive uropathy.

Name: Metharbital
Description: Metharbital (DrugBank DB00463) is a long-acting barbiturate anticonvulsant and sedative-hypnotic whose structure is a 5,5-disubstituted barbituric acid derivative built on a pyrimidine-2,4,6-trione ring, with two methyl substituents at C5 and N-methylation that increase lipophilicity relative to unsubstituted barbiturates; thus, its core chemical category is the barbiturates and its defining scaffold is the barbiturate or malonylurea heterocycle. It is closely related to other barbiturates such as mephobarbital, phenobarbital, primidone, pentobarbital, and secobarbital, sharing GABAergic CNS-depressant pharmacology. Like other agents in this class, metharbital is generally well absorbed orally, distributes widely including across the blood-brain barrier, shows meaningful plasma protein binding, undergoes predominant hepatic biotransformation via oxidative and N-dealkylation pathways with contribution from CYP-mediated metabolism, and is eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites with a relatively prolonged duration consistent with a long half-life. Its principal pharmacologic targets are the GABAA receptor chloride channel complex, where it acts as a positive allosteric modulator and at higher concentrations a direct channel activator, with broader suppression of excitatory neurotransmission. Clinically it has been used for epilepsy, especially generalized tonic-clonic and focal seizure disorders, and historically as a sedative. Toxicity reflects dose-dependent CNS and respiratory depression, coma, hypotension, impaired cognition, paradoxical agitation, dependence, and overdose risk, with examples including respiratory failure and enhanced toxicity with alcohol, opioids, or benzodiazepines. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, ataxia, dizziness, nystagmus, lethargy, rash, nausea, and behavioral changes; accordingly, clinical use has largely been limited or replaced by safer antiepileptic and sedative alternatives.

Name: Ketorolac
Description: Ketorolac (DrugBank DB00465) is a potent nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug of the heteroaryl acetic acid class, structurally characterized by a pyrrolizine core bearing an aryl ketone and a terminal carboxylic acid, with marketed ketorolac tromethamine as a water-soluble salt; its scaffold is the aryl-substituted pyrrolizine/acetic acid NSAID motif that supports strong cyclooxygenase binding. It is chemically and pharmacologically related to other nonselective NSAIDs such as diclofenac, indomethacin, ibuprofen, naproxen, and tolmetin, although ketorolac is distinguished by unusually strong analgesic efficacy relative to its anti-inflammatory use. Its principal targets are prostaglandin G/H synthase 1 and 2, namely PTGS1 (COX-1) and PTGS2 (COX-2), leading to reduced prostaglandin synthesis and analgesic, antipyretic, and anti-inflammatory effects. After oral, intramuscular, intravenous, or ophthalmic administration, absorption is efficient, protein binding is very high, distribution volume is low to moderate, hepatic metabolism occurs mainly via glucuronidation and some hydroxylation, and elimination is predominantly renal with an adult half-life of roughly 5 to 6 hours, prolonged in renal impairment and the elderly. It is indicated for short-term management of moderately severe acute pain, especially postoperative pain, and ophthalmically for ocular inflammation, pain, and pruritus. Clinical use commonly includes opioid-sparing perioperative analgesia, emergency treatment of renal colic or musculoskeletal pain, and postoperative ophthalmic care. Toxicity is typical of COX inhibition and dose- and duration-dependent, with serious examples including gastrointestinal ulceration, bleeding, perforation, acute kidney injury, fluid retention, hypertension, bronchospasm, and impaired platelet aggregation; overdose may cause severe abdominal pain, vomiting, metabolic disturbances, and renal dysfunction. Common adverse effects include nausea, dyspepsia, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, somnolence, edema, injection-site pain, and ocular irritation with topical formulations.

Name: Enoxacin
Description: Enoxacin (DrugBank DB00467) is a synthetic fluoroquinolone antibacterial built on a 4-quinolone-3-carboxylic acid core bearing the characteristic 6-fluoro substituent, a 7-piperazinyl ring, and an N-1 ethyl group, features that define a planar heteroaromatic zwitterion-forming structure optimized for bacterial enzyme binding and tissue penetration; chemically it belongs to the quinolone/fluoroquinolone carboxylic acid class, and its central scaffold is the fluoro-substituted quinolone nucleus closely related to nalidixic acid-derived antibacterial pharmacophores. Similar drugs include ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin, ofloxacin, pefloxacin, and lomefloxacin, which share the same DNA topoisomerase-targeting chemotype. Its principal targets are bacterial DNA gyrase subunits GyrA/GyrB and topoisomerase IV subunits ParC/ParE, leading to inhibition of DNA replication and bactericidal activity. Enoxacin is orally active with generally good gastrointestinal absorption, moderate protein binding, wide distribution into urine and genitourinary tissues, limited biotransformation, and predominantly renal excretion of unchanged drug, so elimination is prolonged in renal impairment. It has been used mainly for susceptible urinary tract and genitourinary infections such as cystitis, prostatitis, gonorrhea, and other lower urinary infections. Adverse effects resemble those of other fluoroquinolones and include nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, insomnia, rash, and photosensitivity; clinically important toxicities include CNS stimulation and seizure risk, especially with theophylline or NSAIDs, tendinopathy, hypersensitivity, and QT-related or class-associated dysglycemic concerns. In practice, its historical clinical use centered on oral treatment of uncomplicated and complicated urinary infections when pathogen susceptibility supported use.

Name: Quinine
Description: Quinine (DrugBank DB00468) is a naturally occurring cinchona alkaloid with a rigid quinoline–quinuclidine architecture, consisting of a methoxy-substituted aromatic quinoline ring linked through a secondary alcohol-bearing carbon to a bicyclic tertiary amine quinuclidine system, giving a stereochemically defined, lipophilic weak base; chemically it is classified as a quinoline alkaloid and its core scaffold is the 4-quinolinemethanol antimalarial pharmacophore, closely related to quinidine, chloroquine, mefloquine, and quinacrine, with quinidine being its stereoisomer and most structurally similar comparator. Quinine is well absorbed orally, distributed widely including to erythrocytes and inflamed tissues, is moderately protein bound, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 to hydroxylated metabolites, and is excreted predominantly in urine, with elimination influenced by urinary pH and prolonged in severe malaria. Its principal pharmacologic activity is against Plasmodium species, especially blood schizonts, likely through inhibition of heme detoxification in the parasite food vacuole; no single human protein target defines its antimalarial effect, although it also interacts clinically with cardiac ion conductance and neuromuscular transmission. It is indicated for treatment of uncomplicated malaria, particularly chloroquine-resistant Plasmodium falciparum, and has also been used for nocturnal leg cramps, although that use is restricted because of toxicity. Adverse effects include cinchonism with tinnitus, headache, nausea, dizziness, and visual disturbance, as well as hypoglycemia, QT prolongation, arrhythmias, hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, hypersensitivity, and rare blackwater fever or thrombotic microangiopathy; overdose may cause severe cardiotoxicity, blindness, and death. Clinically, it has been used orally or parenterally for falciparum malaria, often in combination regimens such as with doxycycline or clindamycin.

Name: Dronabinol
Description: Dronabinol (DB00470) is synthetic trans-delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, a highly lipophilic tricyclic terpenoid cannabinoid characterized by a dibenzopyran/benzochromene core bearing a phenolic hydroxyl group, a pentyl side chain, and stereochemically defined fused ring substituents that drive cannabinoid receptor affinity; chemically it belongs to the classical cannabinoids and its core scaffold is the THC benzochromene scaffold. Closely related drugs include nabilone, a synthetic cannabinoid antiemetic, cannabidiol as a phytocannabinoid comparator with distinct receptor pharmacology, and nabiximols, a THC/cannabidiol combination product. Its principal targets are cannabinoid receptor 1 (CNR1/CB1) and cannabinoid receptor 2 (CNR2/CB2), acting mainly as a partial agonist, with central CB1 activation underlying orexigenic, antiemetic, analgesic, and psychoactive effects. Oral dronabinol is variably absorbed because of extensive first-pass metabolism, has delayed and erratic peak concentrations, distributes extensively into highly perfused and adipose tissues owing to marked lipophilicity and high protein binding, is metabolized hepatically mainly by CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 to active 11-hydroxy-THC and further inactive carboxy metabolites, and is eliminated slowly in feces and urine with prolonged terminal disposition due to tissue redistribution. Toxicity is primarily dose-related neuropsychiatric and cardiovascular toxicity, including euphoria, anxiety, paranoia, somnolence, cognitive impairment, ataxia, tachycardia, and orthostatic hypotension, with severe intoxication potentially causing hallucinations or psychosis-like reactions. It is indicated for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting refractory to conventional antiemetics and for anorexia-associated weight loss in AIDS, and clinically is used as an oral cannabinoid when appetite stimulation or antiemesis is needed, though common adverse effects include dizziness, dry mouth, confusion, mood changes, and fatigue.

Name: Montelukast
Description: Montelukast (DrugBank DB00471) is a synthetic, orally active leukotriene receptor antagonist with a lipophilic diaryl scaffold characterized by a substituted quinoline nucleus linked through a thioether-containing side chain to aromatic phenyl groups and a terminal carboxylic acid, a structure that supports high affinity antagonism at cysteinyl leukotriene receptors; chemically it is classified as a leukotriene modifier and more specifically an arachidonic acid pathway antagonist, with a quinoline-diaryl thioether scaffold related pharmacologically to zafirlukast and pranlukast, and mechanistically similar to zileuton only in pathway focus, although zileuton inhibits 5-lipoxygenase rather than the receptor. Its principal target is the cysteinyl leukotriene receptor 1, CysLT1 or CYSLTR1, with inhibition of LTD4-mediated bronchoconstrictive and pro-inflammatory signaling. Montelukast is well absorbed after oral administration, is highly protein bound, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP2C8 with contributions from CYP3A4 and CYP2C9, has minimal renal elimination, and is excreted predominantly in bile as metabolites. It is indicated for prophylaxis and chronic treatment of asthma, prevention of exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, and relief of allergic rhinitis symptoms such as rhinorrhea and nasal congestion. Clinical use includes adjunctive therapy in mild to moderate persistent asthma and as a steroid-sparing option when inhaled therapy is insufficient or poorly tolerated. Adverse effects include headache, abdominal pain, diarrhea, cough, and upper respiratory symptoms; important toxicities include rare hepatobiliary abnormalities, hypersensitivity, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis in susceptible patients, and notable neuropsychiatric reactions such as agitation, insomnia, depression, and suicidal ideation, which have become a major limitation on routine use.

Name: Fluoxetine
Description: Fluoxetine (DrugBank DB00472) is a diphenhydramine-related arylalkylamine antidepressant structurally characterized by a substituted phenoxyphenylpropylamine framework containing a para-trifluoromethyl phenoxy ring linked through an ether to a chiral three-carbon side chain terminating in a secondary N-methylamine, placing it in the phenoxyphenylpropylamine class of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and defining its core scaffold as a trifluoromethyl-substituted diaryl ether with an aminopropyl chain. Closely related or pharmacologically similar drugs include other SSRIs such as paroxetine, sertraline, citalopram, escitalopram, and fluvoxamine, as well as the active metabolite norfluoxetine. Its principal target is the serotonin transporter SLC6A4, with weaker activity reported at 5-HT2C receptors and sigma-1 sites in some systems; therapeutically it inhibits presynaptic serotonin reuptake, enhancing serotonergic neurotransmission. Fluoxetine is well absorbed orally, undergoes extensive distribution with high protein binding, is hepatically metabolized mainly by CYP2D6 and also CYP2C9/CYP2C19 to norfluoxetine, and has unusually long elimination half-lives for both parent and metabolite, with excretion predominantly as urinary metabolites. It is indicated for major depressive disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, panic disorder, bulimia nervosa, premenstrual dysphoric disorder, and commonly used for anxiety-spectrum symptoms. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, insomnia, headache, tremor, anxiety, sexual dysfunction, diaphoresis, and decreased appetite, while toxicities include serotonin syndrome, QT-related risk in susceptible patients, hyponatremia, bleeding tendency, switch to mania, seizures in overdose, and important CYP2D6-mediated drug interactions; clinically it is used as a first-line SSRI in outpatient psychiatry because of once-daily dosing and persistence of effect during missed doses.

Name: Chlordiazepoxide
Description: Chlordiazepoxide (DB00475) is a classical 1,4-benzodiazepine anxiolytic whose structure consists of a fused benzene and seven-membered diazepine ring bearing a 5-phenyl substituent, a 7-chloro electron-withdrawing group, and an N-oxide functionality, features that define it as a benzodiazepine derivative and place it within the benzodiazepine heteroaryl anxiolytic-sedative chemical class; its core scaffold is the 5-phenyl-1,4-benzodiazepine nucleus, shared with related agents such as diazepam, clonazepam, lorazepam, oxazepam, and prazepam. Pharmacologically, it acts as a positive allosteric modulator of GABAA receptors at the benzodiazepine site, with target proteins including receptor complexes containing GABRA1, GABRA2, GABRA3, GABRA5, GABRB2, and GABRG2 subunits, thereby enhancing GABA-mediated chloride conductance. It is well absorbed orally, distributed widely including into the CNS, is highly protein bound, undergoes extensive hepatic oxidative metabolism and N-demethylation to active metabolites such as desmethylchlordiazepoxide, demoxepam, desmethyldiazepam, and oxazepam, and is eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites, giving it a prolonged effect and potential accumulation in older adults or liver impairment. Toxicity is characterized by dose-related CNS depression, psychomotor impairment, respiratory depression when combined with opioids or alcohol, dependence, withdrawal seizures, and overdose manifestations such as somnolence, ataxia, confusion, and coma. Clinically, it is indicated for anxiety disorders, short-term relief of acute anxiety symptoms, preoperative apprehension, and acute alcohol withdrawal, where it is used to reduce agitation, tremor, autonomic hyperactivity, and risk of withdrawal seizures; common adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, ataxia, fatigue, confusion, impaired coordination, and paradoxical agitation.

Name: Duloxetine
Description: Duloxetine (DrugBank DB00476) is a lipophilic aryloxypropylamine antidepressant structurally characterized by a naphthalene-containing aromatic system linked through an ether to a three-carbon side chain bearing a secondary amine, with marketed drug substance commonly used as the hydrochloride salt; chemically it is classified as a phenoxy/aryloxypropylamine serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, and its core scaffold is a naphthyl-oxy-propanamine motif related to other monoamine reuptake inhibitors. Similar drugs include venlafaxine, desvenlafaxine, milnacipran, levomilnacipran, and to a lesser extent fluoxetine or atomoxetine by mechanistic overlap. Its principal targets are the serotonin transporter SLC6A4 and norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, with weak functional influence on dopamine uptake at therapeutic exposure but no major direct receptor binding profile. Duloxetine is indicated for major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia, and chronic musculoskeletal pain such as chronic low back pain or osteoarthritis-related pain. It is well absorbed orally but undergoes substantial first-pass metabolism, is highly protein bound, widely distributed, extensively metabolized in the liver mainly by CYP1A2 and CYP2D6 to inactive metabolites, and is excreted predominantly in urine with some fecal elimination. Toxicities include hepatotoxicity, serotonin syndrome, suicidality risk in younger patients, discontinuation syndrome, hypertension, tachycardia, and overdose manifestations such as somnolence, vomiting, agitation, and seizures. Common adverse effects include nausea, dry mouth, constipation, decreased appetite, sweating, dizziness, insomnia, fatigue, and sexual dysfunction. Clinically, it is used when a dual antidepressant and analgesic effect is desired, for example in depressed patients with neuropathic pain or anxious patients with chronic pain syndromes.

Name: Chlorpromazine
Description: Chlorpromazine (DrugBank DB00477) is a first-generation antipsychotic of the phenothiazine class, structurally characterized by a tricyclic phenothiazine core containing sulfur and nitrogen heteroatoms and a 2-chloro substituent, linked through a three-carbon chain to a dimethylaminopropyl side chain that confers cationic amphiphilic behavior; its core scaffold is the chlorinated phenothiazine nucleus, shared with related typical antipsychotics. Similar drugs include other phenothiazines such as thioridazine, fluphenazine, perphenazine, and prochlorperazine, as well as the mechanistically related dopamine antagonists haloperidol and levomepromazine. Chlorpromazine acts primarily through antagonism of dopamine D2 receptors, but also blocks DRD1, DRD3, DRD4, 5-HT2A/5-HT2C, histamine H1, muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, and alpha1-adrenergic receptors, explaining its broad CNS and autonomic effects. It is used for schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders, acute mania, severe behavioral disturbance, intractable nausea and vomiting, hiccups, and preoperative sedation. Oral absorption is variable because of extensive first-pass metabolism; distribution is wide with high protein binding and brain penetration; metabolism is predominantly hepatic via CYP2D6 and CYP1A2 with formation of active and inactive sulfoxide, demethylated, and hydroxylated metabolites; excretion occurs in urine and bile/feces. Toxicity includes dose-related CNS depression, hypotension, anticholinergic toxicity, QT prolongation and arrhythmia, hepatotoxicity including cholestatic jaundice, seizures, and rare neuroleptic malignant syndrome or agranulocytosis. Common adverse effects include sedation, orthostasis, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, weight gain, hyperprolactinemia, and extrapyramidal symptoms including dystonia, parkinsonism, akathisia, and tardive dyskinesia. Clinically, it has been used as a low-potency antipsychotic when strong sedative and antiemetic properties are desired, for example in agitated psychosis, refractory vomiting, tetanus adjunct care, and severe persistent hiccups.

Name: Amikacin
Description: Amikacin (DrugBank DB00479) is a semisynthetic aminoglycoside antibiotic structurally derived from kanamycin A, built on a 2-deoxystreptamine aminocyclitol core glycosidically linked to multiple amino sugars and distinguished by an L-hydroxyaminobutyryl side chain that sterically protects it from many aminoglycoside-inactivating enzymes; chemically it belongs to the aminoglycoside/aminocyclitol class, with a kanamycin-like 2-deoxystreptamine scaffold. Closely related drugs include gentamicin, tobramycin, kanamycin, netilmicin, plazomicin, and neomycin. Its antibacterial target is the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit, especially 16S rRNA and associated ribosomal proteins, causing mistranslation and inhibition of protein synthesis, with concentration-dependent bactericidal activity against aerobic Gram-negative bacilli and some mycobacteria. Amikacin is not absorbed orally, so it is given intravenously, intramuscularly, or by inhalation in selected settings; distribution is mainly to extracellular fluid with limited CNS penetration unless meninges are inflamed, low protein binding, and accumulation in renal cortex and inner ear; it undergoes essentially no metabolism and is excreted unchanged by glomerular filtration, with half-life prolonged in renal impairment. Major toxicities are nephrotoxicity, irreversible or partly reversible ototoxicity affecting cochlear and vestibular function, and neuromuscular blockade with respiratory depression, particularly with high troughs or concomitant vancomycin, cisplatin, loop diuretics, or neuromuscular blockers. Adverse effects include tinnitus, hearing loss, vertigo, rising creatinine, rash, and injection-site pain. Clinically, it is used for severe infections such as complicated urinary tract infection, hospital-acquired pneumonia, intra-abdominal sepsis, bacteremia, neonatal sepsis, and multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, often in combination regimens for Pseudomonas, Enterobacterales, or nontuberculous mycobacterial disease.

Name: Celecoxib
Description: Celecoxib (DrugBank DB00482) is a diaryl-substituted pyrazole NSAID whose structure features a central 1,5-diarylpyrazole core bearing a para-sulfonamide phenyl ring and a trifluoromethyl-substituted phenyl ring, a motif that confers selective cyclooxygenase-2 binding; chemically it belongs to the coxib class of selective COX-2 inhibitors, with a diarylheterocyclic pyrazole scaffold. Closely related or pharmacologically similar drugs include other coxibs such as valdecoxib, etoricoxib, rofecoxib, and parecoxib, as well as less selective NSAIDs like diclofenac and meloxicam for therapeutic comparison. Its principal target is prostaglandin G/H synthase 2 (PTGS2, COX-2), with much weaker inhibition of PTGS1 (COX-1). Orally administered celecoxib is reasonably well absorbed, with peak plasma concentrations typically reached in a few hours; it is highly protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism primarily via CYP2C9 to inactive hydroxylated and carboxylated metabolites, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in feces and urine, with an elimination half-life of about 11 hours. It is indicated for osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute pain, primary dysmenorrhea, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, and reduction of colorectal polyps in familial adenomatous polyposis. Adverse effects include dyspepsia, abdominal pain, diarrhea, edema, hypertension, headache, and rash, while important toxicities include serious cardiovascular thrombotic events, renal impairment, fluid retention, gastrointestinal ulceration or bleeding despite relative COX-2 selectivity, hepatotoxicity, and severe sulfonamide-associated hypersensitivity reactions. Clinically, celecoxib is used when anti-inflammatory and analgesic efficacy is desired with reduced endoscopic GI toxicity relative to nonselective NSAIDs, for example in chronic arthritic pain or short-course postoperative and menstrual pain management.

Name: Brimonidine
Description: Brimonidine (DrugBank DB00484) is a lipophilic, halogenated imidazoline derivative whose structure consists of a 2-imidazoline ring linked to a 2,6-dibromophenyl moiety through an anilino-type connection, making it an aromatic heterocycle with a brominated aryl-imidazoline scaffold characteristic of selective alpha2-adrenergic agonists. It belongs chemically to the imidazoline/guanidine-like sympathomimetic class, and its closest analogs include apraclonidine, clonidine, and dexmedetomidine, which share alpha-adrenergic agonist pharmacology but differ in receptor selectivity and clinical use. Brimonidine primarily targets alpha2A-, alpha2B-, and alpha2C-adrenergic receptors, with ophthalmic activity mediated by reduced aqueous humor production and increased uveoscleral outflow, while topical dermatologic use reflects peripheral vasoconstriction. After ocular administration, systemic absorption is limited but measurable; distribution includes ocular tissues and some CNS penetration, metabolism occurs mainly hepatically via aldehyde oxidation and cytochrome P450-related pathways to inactive metabolites, and excretion is predominantly renal as metabolites. Toxicity is usually dose-related and formulation-dependent: ocular overdosing may cause marked hypotension, bradycardia, sedation, miosis, hypothermia, or apnea, especially in infants and young children, while chronic topical use can cause local intolerance. Major indications are open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension, and the topical gel is also used for persistent facial erythema of rosacea. Common adverse effects include conjunctival hyperemia, ocular pruritus, dry mouth, fatigue, headache, blurred vision, allergic conjunctivitis, and skin irritation; clinically, it is used as eye drops alone or with other antiglaucoma agents and as a cutaneous vasoconstrictor to transiently reduce rosacea-associated redness.

Name: Dicloxacillin
Description: Dicloxacillin (DrugBank DB00485) is a semisynthetic, acid-stable, penicillinase-resistant beta-lactam antibiotic whose structure consists of the 6-aminopenicillanic acid nucleus, featuring a strained bicyclic beta-lactam fused to a thiazolidine ring, substituted with a bulky isoxazolyl-containing aromatic acyl side chain bearing two chlorine atoms that sterically protects the beta-lactam from staphylococcal penicillinases; chemically it belongs to the isoxazolyl penicillins within the beta-lactam antibacterial class, and its core scaffold is the penam scaffold. Closely related drugs include oxacillin, cloxacillin, flucloxacillin, and nafcillin, which share antistaphylococcal activity and beta-lactamase stability. Its main targets are bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, particularly transpeptidases such as PBP1, PBP2, and PBP3 in susceptible Gram-positive organisms, leading to inhibition of peptidoglycan cross-linking and cell-wall synthesis. Dicloxacillin is indicated primarily for infections caused by penicillinase-producing, methicillin-susceptible staphylococci and other susceptible bacteria, including skin and soft-tissue infections, cellulitis, impetigo, wound infections, osteomyelitis, and some respiratory tract infections. Orally administered dicloxacillin is absorbed moderately and variably, with food reducing absorption; it distributes into many tissues but has limited cerebrospinal fluid penetration unless meninges are inflamed, is highly protein bound, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated mainly by renal tubular secretion and glomerular filtration, with some biliary excretion. Toxicity is generally similar to other penicillins and includes hypersensitivity reactions up to anaphylaxis, gastrointestinal injury including antibiotic-associated diarrhea, rare hepatotoxicity, interstitial nephritis, neutropenia, and seizures at very high exposures; common side effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, urticaria, and candidiasis. Clinically, it is used as an oral antistaphylococcal agent for targeted outpatient treatment and step-down therapy when susceptible methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus is confirmed or strongly suspected.

Name: Nabilone
Description: Nabilone (DrugBank DB00486) is a synthetic cannabinoid structurally derived from the dibenzopyran/tetrahydrocannabinol family, featuring a tricyclic benzochromene-like core with a ketone at C9, a phenolic hydroxyl group, and a dimethylheptyl side chain that increases lipophilicity and receptor potency relative to delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol; it is therefore classified as a cannabinoid antiemetic and fits the classical cannabinoid scaffold. Closely related drugs include dronabinol, delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, and the endocannabinoid-system modulators levonantradol and nabiximols. Its principal targets are cannabinoid receptors CB1 (CNR1) and CB2 (CNR2), acting mainly as a receptor agonist, with antiemetic and central neuromodulatory effects mediated predominantly through CB1 signaling in the CNS. After oral administration, nabilone is well absorbed but undergoes significant first-pass metabolism; it is highly lipophilic, widely distributed including into the brain, extensively metabolized hepatically by reduction and oxidative biotransformation into multiple metabolites, and eliminated through both feces and urine, with a terminal half-life sufficient to support dosing every 8 to 12 hours in some settings. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related CNS and autonomic effects such as marked sedation, dizziness, confusion, ataxia, orthostatic hypotension, dry mouth, tachycardia, and in susceptible patients hallucinations, dysphoria, or psychosis-like reactions; overdose may produce profound somnolence and cardiovascular instability. Clinically, it is indicated primarily for refractory chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, especially when conventional antiemetics fail, and it has also been used off-label for pain, spasticity, and appetite-related symptoms, though adverse neuropsychiatric effects often limit broader use.

Name: Sotalol
Description: Sotalol (DrugBank DB00489) is a synthetic arylsulfonamide aryloxypropanolamine composed of a para-substituted phenyl ring bearing a methanesulfonamide and a 2-hydroxy-3-isopropylamino-propoxy side chain, placing it within the beta-adrenergic receptor blocker class while also functioning as a class III antiarrhythmic; its core scaffold is the phenoxypropanolamine/beta-blocker pharmacophore combined with a sulfonamide-substituted aniline-like aromatic system. It is structurally and pharmacologically related to other beta-blockers and antiarrhythmics such as propranolol, timolol, nadolol, and to the d,l-sotalol class of QT-prolonging agents, though sotalol is distinguished by substantial potassium channel blockade. Its principal targets are beta-1 adrenergic receptor, beta-2 adrenergic receptor, and the cardiac rapid delayed rectifier potassium current mediated mainly by hERG/KCNH2 channels, producing rate slowing and action potential prolongation. Orally, sotalol is well absorbed with high bioavailability, low protein binding, minimal metabolism, broad distribution into extracellular water, and predominant renal excretion as unchanged drug, so clearance is closely linked to kidney function and the half-life is prolonged in renal impairment. Clinically it is indicated for documented life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias, maintenance of sinus rhythm in atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter, and suppression of symptomatic supraventricular or ventricular tachyarrhythmias. Its major toxicities are dose-related QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, bradycardia, hypotension, heart block, worsening heart failure, and bronchospasm, with common adverse effects including fatigue, dizziness, dyspnea, weakness, and nausea; accordingly, initiation often requires ECG and renal monitoring, especially in patients with electrolyte abnormalities, structural heart disease, or reduced creatinine clearance.

Name: Buspirone
Description: Buspirone (DrugBank DB00490) is an azapirone anxiolytic with a nonbenzodiazepine structure built around a substituted piperazine linked by a butyl chain to a bicyclic imide-like heteroaromatic system, specifically a pyrimidinyl/pyridinyl-type carbonyl-containing scaffold, giving it a flexible arylpiperazine pharmacophore rather than the fused benzodiazepine ring system; chemically it is categorized as an anxiolytic arylpiperazine and its core scaffold is the azaspirodecanedione/arylpiperazine-related azapirone motif. Similar drugs include other azapirones such as gepirone and ipsapirone, and mechanistically related serotonergic anxiolytics are sometimes compared, though buspirone is distinct from benzodiazepines like diazepam. Its principal target is the serotonin 5-HT1A receptor, where it acts as a partial agonist; it also shows affinity for dopamine D2, D3, and D4 receptors and weak interactions at alpha-adrenergic sites. Buspirone is indicated mainly for generalized anxiety disorder and for short-term relief of anxiety symptoms such as excessive worry, tension, irritability, and autonomic hyperarousal; clinically it is used as a scheduled daily anxiolytic rather than an as-needed sedative, and is sometimes used off-label as augmentation in depression or for SSRI-associated sexual dysfunction. It is well absorbed orally but undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism, yielding low absolute bioavailability; it is widely distributed, highly protein bound, metabolized primarily by CYP3A4 to active and inactive metabolites including 1-pyrimidinylpiperazine, and excreted in urine with some fecal elimination. Toxicity is usually mild to moderate, with overdose more often causing nausea, dizziness, drowsiness, miosis, and gastric distress than severe respiratory depression; adverse effects commonly include dizziness, headache, nervousness, lightheadedness, nausea, and insomnia, while rare concerns include serotonin toxicity with serotonergic combinations and increased exposure with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors.

Name: Cefotaxime
Description: Cefotaxime (DrugBank DB00493) is a semisynthetic third-generation cephalosporin built on the cephem/7-aminocephalosporanic acid scaffold, comprising a strained beta-lactam fused to a dihydrothiazine ring, with a syn-methoxyimino aminothiazolyl acyl side chain at the 7-position that enhances Gram-negative stability to many beta-lactamases and an acetoxymethyl substituent at the 3-position that influences hydrolysis and disposition; chemically it is a beta-lactam antibacterial, specifically an oxyimino cephalosporin. Its closest analogs include ceftriaxone, ceftazidime, cefixime, cefpodoxime, and the active metabolite-related cephalosporin class members sharing the aminothiazolyl-oxime motif. Cefotaxime targets bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, particularly transpeptidases such as PBP1A, PBP1B, PBP2, and PBP3 in susceptible organisms, thereby inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-linking and causing cell lysis. It is given parenterally because oral absorption is negligible; distribution is wide into lung, bone, skin, peritoneal fluid, urine, and inflamed meninges/CSF; metabolism is partial hepatic deacetylation to active desacetylcefotaxime; and excretion is predominantly renal, with both parent drug and metabolite eliminated in urine and a short half-life requiring repeated dosing, prolonged in renal impairment. Indications include pneumonia, sepsis, meningitis, gonorrhea, intra-abdominal infection, urinary tract infection, skin/soft tissue infection, bone and joint infection, and febrile neutropenia. Toxicities and adverse effects include hypersensitivity reactions up to anaphylaxis, rash, fever, eosinophilia, diarrhea and Clostridioides difficile colitis, injection-site pain, transient transaminase elevation, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, positive Coombs test, and rare neurotoxicity such as encephalopathy or seizures, especially with renal dysfunction; clinically it is widely used empirically and pathogen-directed for serious susceptible Gram-negative and selected streptococcal infections, often in hospitalized patients and sometimes in combination regimens.

Name: Darifenacin
Description: Darifenacin (DrugBank DB00496) is a synthetic, lipophilic tertiary amine antimuscarinic built around a substituted diarylmethyl framework linked through a propyl chain to a pyrrolidine ring, giving a rigid aromatic–basic amine architecture characteristic of bladder-selective muscarinic antagonists; chemically it is classified as a benzhydryl/pyrrolidine anticholinergic and its core scaffold is an aryl-alkyl-tertiary amine antimuscarinic motif related to other overactive bladder agents such as tolterodine, fesoterodine, oxybutynin, solifenacin, and trospium, with darifenacin distinguished by relatively high functional selectivity for the muscarinic M3 receptor. Its principal target is the human muscarinic acetylcholine receptor M3 (CHRM3), with lesser activity at other muscarinic receptor subtypes including CHRM1 and CHRM2, and blockade of detrusor M3 signaling reduces involuntary bladder contractions. Darifenacin is indicated for overactive bladder with urge urinary incontinence, urgency, and increased urinary frequency, and in practice is used to improve continence episodes and voiding interval in symptomatic adults. Orally administered as an extended-release product, it is well absorbed, undergoes significant first-pass hepatic metabolism, is highly protein bound, distributes systemically with moderate central penetration, and is metabolized predominantly by CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 to less active metabolites that are eliminated in urine and feces; exposure rises with hepatic impairment or strong CYP3A4 inhibition. Adverse effects and dose-limiting toxicity reflect anticholinergic activity, especially dry mouth, constipation, dyspepsia, nausea, headache, blurred vision, urinary retention, and occasional tachycardia, while important toxicities include severe constipation, heat intolerance, and worsening gastric retention or narrow-angle glaucoma in susceptible patients.

Name: Oxycodone
Description: Oxycodone (DrugBank DB00497) is a semisynthetic opioid analgesic structurally derived from thebaine and characterized by the rigid morphinan/phenanthrene opioid nucleus with a 4,5-epoxy bridge, ketone at C6, methoxy substitution at C3, and hydroxyl group at C14, features that distinguish it from morphine and contribute to high mu-opioid receptor agonist activity; chemically it belongs to the phenanthrene opioids and more specifically the morphinan scaffold class. Closely related or similar drugs include morphine, hydrocodone, oxymorphone, codeine, and hydromorphone, which share the same opioid polycyclic core but differ in oxygenation and methylation patterns. Oxycodone is well absorbed orally with moderate to high bioavailability, distributed systemically with CNS penetration and moderate protein binding, metabolized primarily in the liver by CYP3A4 to noroxycodone and by CYP2D6 to oxymorphone, followed by conjugation, and excreted mainly in urine as metabolites and smaller amounts of unchanged drug; exposure is increased by hepatic impairment and CYP3A4 inhibitors. Its principal targets are the mu-opioid receptor OPRM1, with weaker activity at kappa and delta opioid receptors. It is indicated for moderate to severe acute and chronic pain, including postoperative pain, cancer pain, traumatic injury pain, and severe musculoskeletal or neuropathic pain when opioid therapy is warranted. Toxicity is typical of opioids and includes dose-dependent respiratory depression, profound sedation, miosis, constipation, hypotension, overdose coma, dependence, abuse, neonatal opioid withdrawal, and potentially fatal interactions with alcohol, benzodiazepines, or other CNS depressants. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, pruritus, dizziness, somnolence, headache, dry mouth, and constipation; clinically it is used in immediate-release and extended-release formulations, alone or combined with acetaminophen or aspirin, for carefully titrated analgesia in opioid-naive or opioid-tolerant patients.

Name: Flutamide
Description: Flutamide (DB00499) is a first-generation, nonsteroidal antiandrogen built on a substituted anilide scaffold, chemically characterized as a nitroaromatic trifluoroacetyl anilide with a para-nitro phenyl ring linked through an amide to an isobutyramide-like side chain, a structure that confers lipophilicity and androgen receptor antagonism; it belongs to the anilide/nonsteroidal antiandrogen chemical category, and its core scaffold is closely related to other androgen receptor antagonists such as bicalutamide and nilutamide, with broader mechanistic similarity to newer antiandrogens including enzalutamide and apalutamide. Its principal target is the androgen receptor, which it inhibits competitively, with much of its activity mediated by the active metabolite hydroxyflutamide. After oral administration flutamide is well absorbed, extensively distributed, highly protein bound, and undergoes rapid first-pass hepatic metabolism, chiefly via CYP1A2 to hydroxyflutamide and other inactive metabolites, followed by predominant renal excretion of metabolites and a relatively short parent half-life requiring divided dosing. It is indicated mainly for metastatic or locally advanced prostate cancer, typically in combination with a GnRH agonist or after orchiectomy to achieve combined androgen blockade, and has also been used off-label for hyperandrogenic states such as hirsutism or acne in women. Major toxicities include hepatotoxicity ranging from transaminase elevation to fulminant hepatic failure, along with endocrine and gastrointestinal adverse effects; common side effects include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, gynecomastia, breast tenderness, hot flashes, decreased libido, impotence, and rare methemoglobinemia or photosensitivity. Clinically, flutamide is now used less often than newer antiandrogens because of liver toxicity and dosing burden, but remains a historically important oral androgen receptor antagonist in prostate cancer pharmacotherapy.

Name: Tolmetin
Description: Tolmetin (DrugBank DB00500) is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug of the arylacetic acid subclass whose structure is centered on a heteroaromatic pyrrole scaffold bearing a para-methylbenzoyl group, a methyl substituent, and an acetic acid side chain, a motif that confers acidic character and cyclooxygenase inhibitory activity; chemically it is categorized as a pyrrole-acetic acid NSAID, with a scaffold related to other arylacetic acid anti-inflammatory agents, and it shows pharmacologic similarity to indomethacin, sulindac, diclofenac, ketorolac, and to some extent other COX-inhibiting NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and naproxen. Its principal targets are cyclooxygenase-1 and cyclooxygenase-2, leading to reduced prostaglandin synthesis and consequent analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antipyretic effects. Tolmetin is used for symptomatic treatment of rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, and other painful inflammatory musculoskeletal conditions; clinically it has been used to reduce joint pain, swelling, stiffness, and fever. It is generally well absorbed orally, reaches peak plasma concentrations within a few hours, is highly protein bound, distributes mainly within extracellular fluids, undergoes hepatic metabolism with formation of inactive metabolites including conjugates, and is eliminated predominantly in urine with a smaller fecal component, with a relatively short elimination half-life necessitating multiple daily dosing. Toxicity is typical of nonselective NSAIDs and includes dose-related gastrointestinal irritation, ulceration, bleeding, and perforation, renal hypoperfusion or acute kidney injury, fluid retention, hypertension, hepatotoxicity, and hypersensitivity including bronchospasm in aspirin-sensitive patients; common adverse effects include dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, rash, and edema.

Name: Cimetidine
Description: Cimetidine (DrugBank DB00501) is a synthetic histamine H2-receptor antagonist built on a substituted imidazole scaffold, structurally characterized by a 5-methyl-1H-imidazole ring linked through a thioether-containing ethyl chain to a cyanoguanidine terminus, a polar basic arrangement that mimics histamine while conferring receptor selectivity and acid-suppressing activity; chemically it is classified as an imidazole-derived antiulcer agent and H2-blocker, with the imidazole-thioether-cyanoguanidine framework serving as its core chemical scaffold. Closely related drugs include other H2 antagonists such as ranitidine, famotidine, and nizatidine, which share antisecretory pharmacology but differ in heterocyclic cores and interaction liabilities. Its principal target is the histamine H2 receptor, encoded by HRH2, on gastric parietal cells, where antagonism reduces basal and stimulated gastric acid secretion. After oral administration, cimetidine is reasonably well absorbed, has moderate bioavailability limited partly by first-pass handling, distributes into body tissues with relatively low protein binding, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism including sulfoxidation and related biotransformation, and is eliminated predominantly by the kidney as unchanged drug with a short half-life that is prolonged in renal impairment. Toxicity is usually mild but may include CNS effects such as confusion in elderly or renally impaired patients, reversible endocrine effects such as gynecomastia or impotence from antiandrogenic interactions at high doses, and clinically important inhibition of CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2D6, and CYP3A4 causing drug interactions, for example with warfarin, phenytoin, and theophylline. Indications and clinical use include duodenal and gastric ulcer disease, gastroesophageal reflux disease, erosive esophagitis, dyspepsia, and hypersecretory states such as Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, while common adverse effects include headache, diarrhea, dizziness, rash, and constipation.

Name: Haloperidol
Description: Haloperidol (DrugBank DB00502) is a high-potency first-generation antipsychotic of the butyrophenone class built on a piperidine-containing butyrophenone scaffold, characterized structurally by a para-fluorobenzoyl moiety linked through a three-carbon ketone chain to a tertiary alcohol-bearing piperidine ring that is further substituted with a para-chlorophenyl group; this fluorobutyrophenone/pharmacophoric scaffold is shared with related dopamine antagonists, and similar drugs include droperidol, benperidol, trifluperidol, and, more distantly in pharmacologic effect, phenothiazines such as chlorpromazine and fluphenazine. Its principal targets are dopamine D2 receptors, with additional activity at D3, D4, sigma receptors, 5-HT2 receptors, and weaker alpha1-adrenergic and H1 histamine sites, explaining its antipsychotic and antiemetic actions. Clinically it is indicated for schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders, acute agitation, delirium, Tourette syndrome, severe behavioral disturbance, and nausea or vomiting in selected settings, and is widely used orally, intramuscularly, and as long-acting decanoate for maintenance therapy in chronic psychosis. Pharmacokinetically, oral absorption is good but limited by substantial first-pass metabolism, protein binding is high, distribution is extensive with CNS penetration, metabolism occurs mainly in the liver via CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 with carbonyl reduction and oxidative N-dealkylation, and elimination is slow through urinary and fecal excretion of metabolites, supporting once- or twice-daily dosing and depot use. Major toxicities include dose-related extrapyramidal symptoms, tardive dyskinesia, hyperprolactinemia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, QT prolongation and torsades risk, sedation, orthostatic hypotension, and overdose manifestations such as severe rigidity, arrhythmia, and coma.

Name: Ritonavir
Description: Ritonavir (DrugBank DB00503) is a peptidomimetic HIV protease inhibitor built on a hydroxyethylene-like transition-state-mimetic scaffold, with a central secondary alcohol flanked by amide/urea-like linkages and lipophilic thiazolyl, phenyl, and isopropyl-substituted groups that confer high affinity for the viral aspartyl protease; chemically it is categorized as an antiretroviral protease inhibitor and more broadly a peptidomimetic small molecule. Its scaffold and pharmacology resemble other HIV protease inhibitors such as lopinavir, saquinavir, indinavir, atazanavir, and darunavir, although ritonavir is now used predominantly as a pharmacokinetic enhancer rather than for its intrinsic antiviral effect. It targets HIV-1 protease and HIV-2 protease, and it is also a potent inhibitor of CYP3A4 and CYP2D6, with effects on P-glycoprotein that explain many interactions. Oral absorption is variable but improved with food; the drug is highly protein bound, widely distributed, extensively hepatically metabolized mainly by CYP3A and CYP2D6, exhibits nonlinear pharmacokinetics because it inhibits its own metabolism, and is eliminated chiefly in feces with limited renal excretion. Indications include combination therapy for HIV-1 infection and boosting of agents such as lopinavir, atazanavir, or darunavir; it has also been used in combination with nirmatrelvir for COVID-19. Toxicities include hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, hypertriglyceridemia, hypercholesterolemia, insulin resistance, and major drug-drug interactions that can precipitate arrhythmia, sedation, or ergot toxicity with contraindicated substrates. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, dysgeusia, circumoral paresthesia, fatigue, rash, and transaminase elevations.

Name: Tridihexethyl
Description: Tridihexethyl (DrugBank DB00505) is a synthetic antimuscarinic anticholinergic built on a tertiary amino alcohol ester architecture, characterized by a bulky hydrophobic diaryl-substituted glycolate-like core linked through an ester functionality to a tertiary amine-containing side chain bearing cyclohexyl and alkyl substituents; chemically it is classified as an anticholinergic tertiary amine ester, and its principal scaffold is the aryl-substituted aminoalkyl ester motif shared by many centrally and peripherally active muscarinic antagonists. Structurally and pharmacologically, it resembles agents such as trihexyphenidyl, benztropine, procyclidine, and dicyclomine, although tridihexethyl has been used mainly for gastrointestinal and smooth-muscle antispasmodic effects rather than antiparkinsonian therapy. Its known targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially M1 and M3 receptor populations in the gastrointestinal tract and other smooth muscle tissues, where antagonism reduces cholinergic tone, secretions, motility, and spasm. After oral administration it is expected to be reasonably absorbed, distributed into peripheral tissues with some central nervous system penetration because of its tertiary amine character, metabolized predominantly in the liver by ester hydrolysis and oxidative biotransformation, and eliminated as metabolites and a smaller fraction of unchanged drug in urine. Toxicity is typical of antimuscarinics and includes dose-related dry mouth, mydriasis, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, tachycardia, reduced sweating, confusion, agitation, and in overdose severe delirium or hyperthermia, with particular risk in elderly patients, those with angle-closure glaucoma, prostatic hypertrophy, or paralytic ileus. Clinically it has been used as an antispasmodic for peptic ulcer disease, irritable bowel symptoms, intestinal hypermotility, and painful gastrointestinal cramping.

Name: Nitazoxanide
Description: Nitazoxanide (DrugBank DB00507) is a synthetic nitrothiazolyl-salicylamide derivative whose structure consists of a 5-nitro-1,3-thiazole ring linked through an amide bond to an acetylated salicylamide aromatic system, placing it in the nitrothiazole antiparasitic class and giving it a nitroheteroaryl benzamide/salicylamide scaffold. It is closely related to its active circulating metabolite tizoxanide and is chemically or pharmacologically similar to other nitroheterocyclic anti-infectives such as metronidazole, tinidazole, furazolidone, and nifuroxazide, although its scaffold is distinct. After oral administration, nitazoxanide is rapidly deacetylated to tizoxanide, the principal active moiety; absorption is improved with food, plasma protein binding is very high, distribution is mainly systemic as metabolite, metabolism proceeds largely by conjugation to glucuronides, and excretion occurs predominantly in urine and feces with a relatively short elimination half-life for tizoxanide. Its best characterized molecular target is pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase-dependent electron transfer in susceptible protozoa and anaerobic microorganisms, with broader host-directed and antiviral effects reported, including modulation of viral protein maturation. Indications include treatment of Cryptosporidium parvum and Giardia lamblia diarrhea and, in some settings, off-label use for helminthic, anaerobic, or viral gastroenteritis syndromes. Adverse effects are usually mild and gastrointestinal, including abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, and yellow discoloration of urine or sclera; toxicity is generally low, but hypersensitivity, hepatic enzyme elevations, and greater risk of intolerance in overdose or severe hepatic impairment have been described. Clinically, it is used mainly as an oral antiparasitic and antidiarrheal anti-infective in adults and children, particularly for protozoal enteric infections.

Name: Triflupromazine
Description: Triflupromazine (DrugBank DB00508) is a first-generation antipsychotic of the phenothiazine class, specifically an aliphatic side-chain phenothiazine, built on a tricyclic phenothiazine scaffold containing sulfur and nitrogen heteroatoms and bearing a ring trifluoromethyl substituent with a 3-dimethylaminopropyl side chain that confers lipophilicity, cationic character at physiologic pH, and strong CNS penetration. It is chemically and pharmacologically similar to chlorpromazine, promazine, acepromazine, levomepromazine, and other low-potency phenothiazines. Its principal targets are dopamine D2 receptors, with additional antagonism at dopamine D1-like receptors, histamine H1 receptors, muscarinic cholinergic receptors, alpha1-adrenergic receptors, and likely serotonin 5-HT2 receptors, explaining its antipsychotic, sedative, antiemetic, and autonomic effects. After oral or parenteral administration it is variably but generally well absorbed, extensively distributed into brain and other tissues, highly protein bound, and undergoes substantial hepatic first-pass metabolism via oxidative and conjugative pathways to multiple metabolites, with elimination occurring mainly in urine and bile and a clinically relevant duration prolonged by tissue sequestration. It has been used for schizophrenia and other psychoses, severe agitation, anxiety states, preoperative sedation, and control of nausea and vomiting. Adverse effects include marked sedation, orthostatic hypotension, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, weight gain, hyperprolactinemia, and extrapyramidal symptoms such as parkinsonism, dystonia, akathisia, and tardive dyskinesia. Important toxicities include overdose-related CNS depression, seizures, arrhythmias or QT prolongation, severe hypotension, cholestatic jaundice, blood dyscrasias, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and rare sudden death.

Name: Dextrothyroxine
Description: Dextrothyroxine (DrugBank DB00509) is the dextrorotatory stereoisomer of thyroxine, a halogenated diphenyl ether amino acid structurally characterized by two iodinated phenyl rings linked through an ether bridge and bearing an alanine-like side chain with amino and carboxyl functions; chemically it belongs to the iodothyronine thyroid hormone class and is built on a thyroid-hormone diphenyl ether scaffold. It is closely related to levothyroxine (L-thyroxine), liothyronine, and endogenous thyroxine, with stereochemical inversion accounting for altered biologic and metabolic effects. Historically, it was used primarily as a lipid-lowering agent rather than for thyroid replacement, particularly in hypercholesterolemia and some atherosclerotic states, because it can reduce serum cholesterol and beta-lipoproteins. Its pharmacology is mediated mainly through thyroid hormone receptor targets, especially THRA and THRB, with downstream effects on hepatic lipid metabolism; plasma transport is expected via thyroxine-binding globulin, transthyretin, and albumin. Orally absorbed, it is extensively protein bound, distributed widely, metabolized chiefly by sequential deiodination and conjugation in liver and peripheral tissues, and eliminated through biliary/fecal and renal routes, with a relatively prolonged half-life typical of thyroxine analogs. Toxicity resembles thyrotoxic excess and includes tachyarrhythmias, angina, palpitations, weight loss, tremor, nervousness, insomnia, sweating, diarrhea, and heat intolerance; examples of serious adverse outcomes include atrial fibrillation and exacerbation of ischemic heart disease. Clinical use became limited and largely obsolete because of concerns about cardiovascular toxicity, despite historical use in dyslipidemia management.

Name: Acetyldigitoxin
Description: Acetyldigitoxin (DB00511) is a semisynthetic cardiotonic cardiac glycoside closely related to digitoxin, built on the classic cardenolide scaffold consisting of a steroidal aglycone nucleus with cis-trans fused rings, a characteristic butenolide ring at C17, and a trisaccharide chain of digitoxose residues at C3, with acetyl substitution increasing lipophilicity relative to some congeners; it belongs to the broader chemical category of digitalis glycosides and shares strong structural and pharmacologic similarity with digitoxin, digoxin, methyldigoxin, and deslanoside. Its principal target is the Na+/K+-transporting ATPase alpha subunit, especially ATP1A1 and related cardiac isoforms, leading secondarily to increased intracellular sodium, reduced Na+/Ca2+ exchange, higher intracellular calcium, and positive inotropy, with additional vagomimetic effects on atrioventricular nodal conduction. Pharmacokinetically, it is generally well absorbed orally, extensively distributed with substantial tissue binding, relatively highly protein bound, metabolized mainly hepatically with possible deacetylation and enterohepatic recycling, and eliminated through both biliary/fecal and renal pathways, giving a comparatively prolonged duration of action. Toxicity is typical of digitalis compounds and may be narrow-therapeutic-index toxicity manifesting as nausea, vomiting, anorexia, confusion, xanthopsia, bradycardia, AV block, ventricular ectopy, atrial tachycardia with block, and potentially fatal ventricular arrhythmias, especially with hypokalemia, renal or hepatic impairment, or interacting drugs. Clinically it has been used for congestive heart failure and for supraventricular tachyarrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter when rate control and increased myocardial contractility are desired.

Name: Vancomycin
Description: Vancomycin (DrugBank DB00512) is a complex, highly functionalized tricyclic glycopeptide antibiotic composed of a rigid, cross-linked heptapeptide aglycone decorated with carbohydrate moieties and multiple phenolic, amide, hydroxyl, and chlorine-substituted aromatic groups that create a cup-shaped binding pocket; chemically it belongs to the glycopeptide antibiotics, with a vancomycin-type glycopeptide scaffold closely related to other cell-wall active lipoglyco/glycopeptides such as teicoplanin, telavancin, dalbavancin, and oritavancin. Its pharmacologic target is not a classical protein receptor but the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of peptidoglycan precursors, thereby sterically blocking transglycosylation and transpeptidation steps in bacterial cell-wall synthesis; functionally associated bacterial enzymes affected downstream include penicillin-binding proteins and cell-wall biosynthetic machinery. Vancomycin is indicated for serious Gram-positive infections, especially methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infections, coagulase-negative staphylococcal infections, enterococcal infections when susceptible, bacteremia, endocarditis, osteomyelitis, pneumonia, skin and soft tissue infection, and, by oral administration, Clostridioides difficile colitis. It is poorly absorbed orally, so systemic therapy is given intravenously; distribution is moderate with penetration into inflamed tissues and variable cerebrospinal fluid entry, protein binding is modest, metabolism is minimal, and elimination is predominantly unchanged by glomerular filtration, necessitating renal dose adjustment and therapeutic drug monitoring. Major toxicities include nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, infusion-related histamine release with red man syndrome, neutropenia, thrombophlebitis, rash, fever, and rare DRESS or Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Clinically, it is widely used empirically and definitively for severe hospital-acquired or device-associated Gram-positive infections, often in combination regimens when broad resistant-pathogen coverage is needed.

Name: Dextromethorphan
Description: Dextromethorphan (DrugBank DB00514) is a dextrorotatory morphinan derivative whose structure consists of a rigid polycyclic phenanthrene-like morphinan framework bearing a tertiary N-methyl amine and a 3-methoxy substituent, lacking the analgesic 4,5-epoxy bridge and key stereochemical features of opioid analgesics; chemically it is classified as a synthetic morphinan antitussive and its core scaffold is the levorphanol/codeine-like morphinan nucleus. Closely related or pharmacologically similar drugs include levomethorphan, levorphanol, codeine, pholcodine, and the active metabolite dextrorphan, as well as combination product partners such as quinidine in dextromethorphan/quinidine. It is well absorbed orally, undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, distributes widely including to the CNS, and is metabolized primarily by CYP2D6 to dextrorphan and by CYP3A4 to 3-methoxymorphinan, followed by conjugation and renal excretion; exposure is highly CYP2D6-genotype dependent, with poor metabolizers showing higher parent-drug concentrations and prolonged effects. Its principal targets include sigma-1 receptor, NMDA-type glutamate receptor ion channel, serotonin transporter, norepinephrine transporter, nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, and to a lesser extent opioid sigma-related binding systems historically described in older literature. It is indicated mainly for symptomatic relief of nonproductive cough in upper respiratory infections or bronchitic irritation, and clinically is also used with quinidine for pseudobulbar affect. Toxicity includes dose-related CNS depression, dissociation, tachycardia, hypertension, serotonin syndrome with SSRIs or MAOIs, and abuse-related hallucinations; common adverse effects include dizziness, drowsiness, nausea, vomiting, and confusion, while overdose may cause ataxia, psychosis, respiratory depression, and rarely death.

Name: Albendazole
Description: Albendazole (DrugBank DB00518) is a benzimidazole carbamate anthelmintic whose structure consists of a fused benzene-imidazole bicyclic nucleus bearing a methyl carbamate at the 2-position and a propylthio substituent at the 5-position, placing it in the benzimidazole/thiabendazole-like heteroaromatic antiparasitic class with a benzimidazole carbamate scaffold. Closely related drugs include mebendazole, thiabendazole, fenbendazole, flubendazole, and triclabendazole, which share the tubulin-binding benzimidazole core but differ in peripheral substituents and spectrum. Its principal pharmacologic target is parasite beta-tubulin, with inhibition of microtubule polymerization leading to impaired glucose uptake, depletion of glycogen stores, and parasite death; mammalian tubulin has lower affinity. Albendazole is poorly water-soluble and variably absorbed orally, with absorption enhanced by fatty meals; it undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism to the active metabolite albendazole sulfoxide, which is widely distributed, including into bile, hydatid cyst fluid, cerebrospinal fluid, and other tissues, then is further converted to albendazole sulfone and other inactive metabolites that are eliminated mainly in urine and partly in bile. It is indicated for intestinal nematode infections and tissue helminthiases, including neurocysticercosis due to Taenia solium, echinococcosis or hydatid disease due to Echinococcus granulosus, ascariasis, hookworm, pinworm, whipworm, strongyloidiasis, and cutaneous larva migrans. Adverse effects are usually gastrointestinal upset, abdominal pain, nausea, headache, dizziness, and transient transaminase elevation, while important toxicities include hepatotoxicity, leukopenia, pancytopenia, alopecia, hypersensitivity, and embryo-fetal toxicity; inflammatory reactions can also occur during treatment of neurocysticercosis from dying parasites, sometimes provoking seizures or raised intracranial pressure, so corticosteroids and anticonvulsants are often coadministered in clinical practice.

Name: Trandolapril
Description: Trandolapril (DrugBank DB00519) is a lipophilic dicarboxylate angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor prodrug characterized structurally by a substituted tetrahydroisoindole/proline-like bicyclic core bearing esterified carboxyl functionality and an amide linkage that is hydrolyzed in vivo to the active diacid trandolaprilat; chemically it belongs to the ACE inhibitor class, specifically the non-sulfhydryl, non-phosphonate ester prodrugs, with a peptidomimetic scaffold designed to mimic angiotensin I transition-state interactions at ACE. Closely related drugs include enalapril, ramipril, perindopril, quinapril, and benazepril, which share esterified prodrug motifs and diacid active metabolites. After oral administration, trandolapril is absorbed with conversion by hepatic esterases to trandolaprilat; food may reduce absorption modestly, protein binding is moderate to high, tissue ACE binding contributes to a prolonged effect, and elimination occurs through both renal and biliary/fecal routes, with the active metabolite showing a longer terminal half-life than the parent. Its principal target is angiotensin-converting enzyme, with consequent reduction in angiotensin II generation and aldosterone secretion and increased bradykinin activity. It is indicated mainly for hypertension and for reduction of cardiovascular risk or improved survival after myocardial infarction with left ventricular dysfunction. Adverse effects include cough, dizziness, hypotension, headache, fatigue, hyperkalemia, and renal function decline; important toxicities include first-dose syncope, angioedema, acute kidney injury in renal artery stenosis, rare hepatotoxicity, and fetotoxicity/teratogenicity in pregnancy. Clinically, it is used alone or with diuretics, calcium channel blockers, or other antihypertensives for blood pressure control and post-MI ventricular remodeling management.

Name: Caspofungin
Description: Caspofungin (DrugBank DB00520) is a semisynthetic echinocandin antifungal characterized structurally as a large cyclic hexapeptide lipopeptide bearing multiple hydroxylated and amide-containing residues and an N-linked long-chain fatty acyl side chain that confers amphipathic membrane-interacting properties; chemically it belongs to the echinocandin/lipopeptide natural-product-derived antifungals, and its core scaffold is the pneumocandin-derived cyclic hexapeptide macrolactam framework. Closely related drugs include micafungin and anidulafungin, with older mechanistically similar members derived from pneumocandin or echinocandin natural products. Its principal pharmacologic target is fungal beta-1,3-D-glucan synthase, especially the Fks catalytic subunits of the cell-wall synthase complex, leading to impaired glucan synthesis and osmotic instability in Candida and Aspergillus species. Caspofungin is administered intravenously because oral absorption is negligible; it distributes widely into tissues with high protein binding, undergoes slow hepatic biotransformation by peptide hydrolysis and N-acetylation rather than major CYP-dependent oxidation, and is eliminated gradually via both urinary and fecal routes with a terminal half-life supporting once-daily dosing. Toxicity is generally moderate but includes dose-related histamine-mediated infusion reactions, transaminase elevation, hepatotoxicity risk increased with cyclosporine, hemolysis in preclinical settings, and embryo-fetal toxicity in animals. Adverse effects commonly include fever, phlebitis, rash, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, hypokalemia, and elevated liver enzymes. Clinically, it is used for invasive candidiasis including candidemia and intra-abdominal candidiasis, esophageal candidiasis, and salvage or empiric therapy for invasive aspergillosis or febrile neutropenia, particularly in critically ill or immunocompromised patients.

Name: Carteolol
Description: Carteolol (DrugBank DB00521) is a nonselective beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity, structurally characterized as an aryloxypropanolamine bearing the classic beta-blocker pharmacophore of a protonatable secondary amine linked through a 2-hydroxy-3-isopropylaminopropoxy side chain to a heteroaromatic bicyclic ring system, specifically a carbazole-like scaffold incorporating oxygen-containing unsaturation; chemically it is classified as an aryloxypropanolamine and more broadly as a sympatholytic beta blocker, with a scaffold closely related to other ophthalmic or cardiovascular beta blockers such as timolol, propranolol, pindolol, levobunolol, and nadolol. Its principal targets are beta-1 adrenergic receptor and beta-2 adrenergic receptor, with ocular hypotensive and cardiodepressant effects mediated by reduction of aqueous humor production and blockade of sympathetic cardiac stimulation. After oral administration carteolol is well absorbed, and after ophthalmic dosing it can still undergo clinically relevant systemic absorption through conjunctival and nasolacrimal routes; distribution is moderate, metabolism is limited to partial hepatic biotransformation with a substantial fraction excreted unchanged, and elimination is primarily renal, so systemic exposure may rise in renal impairment. Toxicity reflects exaggerated beta blockade, including bradycardia, hypotension, atrioventricular conduction delay, bronchospasm, worsening heart failure, hypoglycemia masking, and overdose-associated cardiogenic shock; local ocular toxicity includes irritation and blurred vision. It is indicated for open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension and has also been used as an antihypertensive agent, with clinical use centered on topical intraocular pressure reduction in patients requiring chronic glaucoma management.

Name: Metolazone
Description: Metolazone (DrugBank DB00524) is a quinazoline-derived sulfonamide-like thiazide-related diuretic whose structure consists of a chlorinated aromatic system fused to a quinazoline core bearing a keto functionality and a sulfonamide substituent, giving a lipophilic heteroaromatic scaffold distinct from classical benzothiadiazine thiazides but pharmacologically similar to them; it is therefore categorized as a thiazide-like diuretic with a quinazoline/sulfonamide scaffold. Closely related or mechanistically similar drugs include chlorothiazide, hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, indapamide, and quinethazone, with metolazone often grouped among thiazide-type natriuretics despite its non-benzothiadiazine framework. Its principal target is the renal sodium/chloride cotransporter NCC encoded by SLC12A3 in the distal convoluted tubule, where inhibition increases sodium, chloride, potassium, and water excretion; clinically it is used for edema associated with congestive heart failure, chronic kidney disease, nephrotic syndrome, and for hypertension, especially resistant or volume-overloaded states, often in combination with loop diuretics such as furosemide to augment diuresis. Oral absorption is generally good, onset occurs within hours, protein binding is substantial, distribution is sufficient to maintain prolonged activity, metabolism is limited, and elimination occurs largely via renal excretion with some nonrenal clearance, supporting once-daily dosing in many patients. Toxicities and adverse effects reflect exaggerated diuresis and electrolyte loss, including hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, dehydration, orthostatic hypotension, prerenal azotemia, hyperuricemia with gout, and less commonly rash or other sulfonamide-associated hypersensitivity; severe examples include arrhythmia from potassium depletion and acute kidney injury from volume contraction.

Name: Tolnaftate
Description: Tolnaftate (DrugBank DB00525) is a synthetic topical antifungal with a thiocarbamate chemical structure characterized by an O-aryl,N-aryl-substituted thiocarbamate core linking a lipophilic naphthalene ring system to a p-tolyl group through a sulfur-containing carbamothioate functionality; chemically it belongs to the thiocarbamate antifungals, and its principal scaffold is an aromatic biaryl-like lipophilic thiocarbamate framework. It is structurally and pharmacologically related to other topical antifungals used for superficial dermatophyte infection, with somewhat similar clinical niches to allylamines such as tolciclate, naftifine, and terbinafine and to some azole topicals, although it is distinguished by its thiocarbamate scaffold. Its antifungal activity is generally attributed to inhibition of fungal squalene epoxidase, a key enzyme in ergosterol biosynthesis, with fungal squalene epoxidase regarded as the main target protein. Pharmacokinetically, tolnaftate is intended for topical use and shows minimal intact-skin systemic absorption, activity localized mainly to the stratum corneum, negligible distribution beyond superficial tissues, poorly characterized but likely limited hepatic metabolism if absorbed, and predominant elimination after minor systemic uptake via hepatic biotransformation and biliary or urinary excretion. It is indicated for tinea pedis, tinea cruris, tinea corporis, and sometimes pityriasis versicolor, and is used clinically as creams, powders, sprays, and solutions for interdigital scaling, pruritus, and superficial ringworm. Toxicity is low because of limited absorption, but excessive exposure may cause local irritation, erythema, burning, dryness, or allergic contact dermatitis; serious systemic toxicity is rare, while accidental ocular or oral exposure may provoke more significant irritation.

Name: Cinchocaine
