Description: Cinchocaine (dibucaine; DrugBank DB00527) is a highly lipophilic amide-type local anesthetic whose structure consists of a quinoline aromatic system bearing a butoxy substituent and linked through a carboxamide to a tertiary aminoalkyl diethylamino side chain, placing it within the amino amide anesthetic class and giving it a quinoline-carboxamide scaffold rather than the simpler anilide scaffold of lidocaine. It is chemically and pharmacologically related to other sodium-channel blocking local anesthetics such as lidocaine, bupivacaine, tetracaine, and procaine, although cinchocaine is notably more potent and longer acting, especially in topical and spinal use. Its principal targets are voltage-gated sodium channels, including neuronal NaV isoforms such as SCN9A, SCN10A, and SCN11A, where it stabilizes the inactivated state and prevents impulse conduction. After topical, rectal, or spinal administration, systemic absorption depends on dose, formulation, and tissue vascularity; distribution is favored to highly perfused tissues with substantial protein binding because of marked lipophilicity; hepatic metabolism is the main route of biotransformation, likely via oxidative N-dealkylation and amide-related metabolism; and metabolites and parent-related products are excreted predominantly in urine. It is indicated for local anesthesia and symptomatic relief of pain and pruritus, for example in hemorrhoids, anal fissures, minor anorectal inflammation, and historically spinal anesthesia. Adverse effects include local burning, irritation, rash, and hypersensitivity, while excessive systemic exposure can produce classic local anesthetic toxicity with circumoral numbness, tinnitus, seizures, hypotension, arrhythmias, respiratory depression, and cardiovascular collapse, making overdose and inadvertent intravascular absorption the major toxicologic concerns in clinical use.

Name: Lercanidipine
Description: Lercanidipine (DrugBank DB00528) is a highly lipophilic 1,4-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker whose structure is centered on a substituted dihydropyridine ring bearing ester functions and a bulky aryl group that confer marked membrane affinity and vascular selectivity; chemically it belongs to the dihydropyridine antihypertensive class, and its core scaffold is the 1,4-dihydropyridine ester framework shared with related agents such as amlodipine, nifedipine, felodipine, nicardipine, and lacidipine. Its principal pharmacologic target is the L-type voltage-dependent calcium channel, especially Cav1.2 encoded by CACNA1C in vascular smooth muscle, leading to reduced calcium influx, arteriolar vasodilation, and lowering of peripheral resistance. After oral administration it is absorbed but undergoes substantial first-pass metabolism, giving relatively low bioavailability that increases with food; it is extensively distributed because of high lipophilicity and high protein binding, is metabolized predominantly by hepatic CYP3A4 to inactive metabolites, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine and feces, with a duration of action supporting once-daily dosing. It is indicated primarily for mild to moderate essential hypertension, including long-term blood-pressure control in adults, either alone or with other antihypertensives. Adverse effects are typical of vasodilatory dihydropyridines and include headache, flushing, dizziness, palpitations, peripheral edema, tachycardia, and fatigue; examples of toxicity or overdose include excessive hypotension, reflex tachycardia, syncope, and rarely myocardial ischemia in susceptible patients, while drug interactions with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors can raise exposure. Clinically, lercanidipine is used as a well-tolerated once-daily antihypertensive, particularly when a vascular-selective calcium antagonist with relatively gradual onset is desired.

Name: Foscarnet
Description: Foscarnet (DB00529) is a small, highly polar inorganic pyrophosphate analog, structurally characterized as phosphonoformic acid with a one-carbon carboxylate-phosphonate scaffold that mimics the pyrophosphate leaving group of nucleotide polymerization reactions; chemically it belongs to the organophosphonate/pyrophosphate analog class, with a minimal phosphonate-carboxylate scaffold rather than a nucleoside core. Closely related or mechanistically similar antivirals include cidofovir, ganciclovir, acyclovir, and phosphonoacetic acid, although foscarnet is distinguished by direct pyrophosphate-site binding and lack of required phosphorylation. Its principal targets are viral DNA polymerases, including cytomegalovirus UL54 DNA polymerase, herpes simplex virus DNA polymerase, varicella-zoster virus DNA polymerase, and HIV reverse transcriptase, where it noncompetitively inhibits pyrophosphate cleavage and DNA chain elongation. Pharmacokinetically, foscarnet is poorly absorbed orally and is therefore given intravenously; it distributes largely in extracellular fluid, can accumulate in bone, has negligible metabolism, and is excreted unchanged by glomerular filtration, with elimination prolonged in renal impairment. It is indicated mainly for CMV retinitis in patients with AIDS and for acyclovir-resistant or refractory HSV mucocutaneous infections, with occasional use in resistant VZV or CMV disease. Major toxicities are dose-limiting nephrotoxicity and electrolyte disturbances, especially hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hypokalemia, and phosphate abnormalities, which may produce paresthesias, tetany, seizures, or arrhythmias. Common adverse effects include genital ulceration, nausea, anemia, fever, rash, and infusion-related symptoms. Clinically, it is used as a salvage antiviral for drug-resistant herpesvirus infections, particularly when resistance to thymidine kinase-dependent nucleoside analogs is present.

Name: Erlotinib
Description: Erlotinib (DrugBank DB00530) is a small-molecule, orally active 4-anilinoquinazoline derivative whose structure consists of a planar quinazoline heteroaromatic core bearing a 3-ethynyl phenylamino substituent and two alkoxy side chains that support ATP-pocket binding within receptor tyrosine kinases; chemically it belongs to the quinazoline class of tyrosine kinase inhibitors and is built on the classic anilinoquinazoline scaffold shared with related EGFR inhibitors such as gefitinib, afatinib, and osimertinib, although the latter agents differ in reversibility and kinase selectivity. Its principal target is epidermal growth factor receptor EGFR/ERBB1, with inhibition of downstream RAS-RAF-MAPK and PI3K-AKT signaling; clinically it is used mainly in EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer and, in combination with gemcitabine, pancreatic adenocarcinoma. After oral administration, absorption is variable but clinically significant, bioavailability is influenced by food and gastric pH, distribution is extensive with high plasma protein binding, metabolism occurs predominantly in the liver via CYP3A4 with contributions from CYP1A2 and extrahepatic CYP1A1, and elimination is mainly through feces with limited renal excretion; smoking can increase clearance and reduce exposure. Toxicity is dominated by mechanism-based epithelial injury, especially acneiform rash and diarrhea, with examples including severe dehydration, interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis, hepatotoxicity, corneal ulceration, and rare gastrointestinal perforation. Common adverse effects include rash, pruritus, stomatitis, anorexia, fatigue, and elevated liver enzymes. In practice, erlotinib is used as targeted therapy in advanced or metastatic EGFR-driven lung cancer, including first-line treatment and maintenance settings in appropriately selected patients.

Name: Cyclophosphamide
Description: Cyclophosphamide (DB00531) is a bifunctional oxazaphosphorine nitrogen mustard alkylating agent whose structure consists of a cyclic phosphamide ring, specifically a 1,3,2-oxazaphosphorine 2-oxide scaffold, bearing two 2-chloroethyl arms that generate reactive alkylating intermediates after bioactivation; chemically it belongs to alkylating antineoplastic and immunosuppressive agents, with the oxazaphosphorine mustard scaffold closely related to ifosfamide and more broadly similar in activity to other nitrogen mustards such as melphalan, chlorambucil, and mechlorethamine. It is a prodrug well absorbed orally and also widely used intravenously, distributes broadly into tissues and body fluids with clinically relevant protein binding, crosses into some extravascular compartments, and undergoes extensive hepatic CYP-mediated activation, especially via CYP2B6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, and CYP3A4, to 4-hydroxycyclophosphamide/aldophosphamide, which yield phosphoramide mustard, the principal DNA-crosslinking cytotoxin, and acrolein; inactive metabolites are then predominantly renally excreted. Its pharmacologic targets are not classical receptors but genomic DNA, producing interstrand crosslinks and apoptosis, although biotransformation depends on hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes and detoxification involves aldehyde dehydrogenase and glutathione pathways. Major toxicities include dose-limiting myelosuppression, immunosuppression, hemorrhagic cystitis from acrolein, gonadal toxicity and infertility, cardiotoxicity at high dose, SIADH, pulmonary injury, mutagenicity, teratogenicity, and secondary malignancies such as therapy-related leukemia or bladder cancer. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, vomiting, alopecia, mucositis, fatigue, infection risk, and hematuria. Clinically, cyclophosphamide is used in leukemias, lymphomas, multiple myeloma, breast and ovarian cancers, conditioning for hematopoietic transplantation, and severe autoimmune diseases such as lupus nephritis, ANCA-associated vasculitis, and refractory nephrotic syndromes.

Name: Mephenytoin
Description: Mephenytoin (DrugBank DB00532) is an older hydantoin anticonvulsant built on a 5,5-disubstituted imidazolidine-2,4-dione ring, specifically a hydantoin core bearing phenyl and ethyl substituents and an N-methyl group, giving a lipophilic weakly acidic structure related to classic seizure drugs. Chemically it belongs to the hydantoin/antiepileptic class, and its principal scaffold is the substituted hydantoin ring shared with structurally and pharmacologically similar agents such as phenytoin, ethotoin, and fosphenytoin. Its antiseizure activity is generally attributed to modulation of neuronal voltage-gated sodium channels, with sodium channel alpha subunits considered the main functional targets, although older literature is less target-resolved than for modern antiepileptics. Mephenytoin is absorbed orally, distributed systemically with central nervous system penetration, and undergoes extensive hepatic biotransformation, notably 4-hydroxylation that is strongly influenced by CYP2C19 polymorphism, making it a classic probe substrate for poor versus extensive metabolizer phenotypes; metabolites are then excreted predominantly in urine. It was used for epilepsy, particularly generalized tonic-clonic and partial seizure disorders, and in practice served as an alternative when other anticonvulsants were ineffective or poorly tolerated. Adverse effects include sedation, dizziness, ataxia, nystagmus, nausea, cognitive slowing, and rash. Toxicity can be clinically significant, with dose-related CNS depression and idiosyncratic hypersensitivity reactions reported, including fever, dermatitis, lymphadenopathy, hematologic toxicity such as agranulocytosis, and hepatic injury, which contributed to its decline in routine clinical use.

Name: Rofecoxib
Description: Rofecoxib (DrugBank DB00533) is a diaryl-substituted furanone nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug built on a 2(5H)-furanone lactone scaffold bearing a cis-styryl aryl group and a para-methylsulfonyl phenyl ring, a structural motif that confers high cyclooxygenase-2 selectivity; chemically it belongs to the coxib class of selective COX-2 inhibitors, with close analogs and therapeutically similar drugs including celecoxib, valdecoxib, etoricoxib, and the withdrawn parecoxib/valdecoxib lineage. Its principal target is prostaglandin G/H synthase 2 (PTGS2, COX-2), with relative sparing of PTGS1 (COX-1), thereby reducing inflammatory prostaglandin synthesis. Rofecoxib was indicated for osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, acute pain, primary dysmenorrhea, and pain states such as postoperative dental pain. It was well absorbed orally, with high bioavailability, moderate plasma protein binding, hepatic metabolism predominantly via non-CYP reductive pathways with minor CYP3A4 contribution, and elimination mainly as inactive metabolites in urine with some fecal excretion; its terminal half-life supported once-daily dosing. Distribution was systemic with limited accumulation at standard doses. Toxicity is dominated by mechanism-based cardiovascular risk, including increased rates of myocardial infarction, stroke, hypertension, edema, and heart failure exacerbation, likely from suppression of endothelial prostacyclin without offsetting platelet thromboxane inhibition; gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding still occurred, though generally less than with nonselective NSAIDs, and renal toxicity included sodium retention and acute kidney injury. Common adverse effects included dyspepsia, diarrhea, nausea, headache, dizziness, peripheral edema, and elevated blood pressure. Clinically, it was used as an anti-inflammatory and analgesic agent when reduced upper gastrointestinal toxicity relative to traditional NSAIDs was desired, but it was withdrawn in many markets because excess cardiovascular events outweighed its benefits in chronic use.

Name: Cefdinir
Description: Cefdinir (DrugBank DB00535) is an orally active third-generation cephalosporin antibacterial whose structure is defined by the cephem nucleus, a strained beta-lactam fused to a dihydrothiazine ring, bearing an aminothiazolyl oxime side chain at the 7-position that enhances Gram-negative activity and beta-lactamase stability, and a vinyl substituent at the 3-position that helps distinguish it from related oral cephalosporins. It belongs chemically to the beta-lactam cephalosporin class, with a cephalosporanic acid–derived cephem scaffold. Similar drugs include cefixime, cefpodoxime proxetil, ceftibuten, cefuroxime axetil, and parenteral third-generation analogs such as ceftriaxone and cefotaxime. Its pharmacologic targets are bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, especially transpeptidases involved in peptidoglycan cross-linking, leading to inhibition of cell-wall synthesis and bacterial lysis. Cefdinir is moderately absorbed after oral dosing, with reduced absorption when coadministered with iron products or some antacids, low to moderate protein binding, distribution into respiratory tract tissues, tonsils, sinus mucosa, skin, and middle-ear fluid, minimal metabolism, and predominantly renal excretion as unchanged drug, so exposure rises in renal impairment. Toxicity is generally low but includes hypersensitivity reactions typical of beta-lactams, gastrointestinal toxicity including antibiotic-associated diarrhea and Clostridioides difficile colitis, rare severe cutaneous reactions, and occasional hematologic or hepatic laboratory abnormalities. It is indicated for susceptible infections such as community-acquired pneumonia, acute bacterial sinusitis, acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, pharyngitis or tonsillitis, uncomplicated skin and skin-structure infections, and acute otitis media. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, rash, candidiasis, and the notable red discoloration of stool when taken with iron. Clinically, it is used as an oral outpatient cephalosporin for mild to moderate respiratory, ENT, and skin infections when susceptibility patterns support its use.

Name: Guanidine
Description: Guanidine (DrugBank DB00536) is the parent amidine-like strong organic base built around a minimal carboxamidine scaffold, consisting of a central carbon bound to three nitrogens in a planar, resonance-stabilized cationic guanidinium system that is highly polar and predominantly protonated at physiologic pH; chemically it belongs to the guanidines, a class of small aliphatic nitrogen-rich bases, and it serves as the core scaffold for related agents such as guanadrel, guanethidine, metformin, phenformin, and other guanidinium- or biguanide-containing drugs. Pharmacologically, guanidine has no highly selective single receptor target and is understood mainly to act at the neuromuscular junction by enhancing acetylcholine release, partly through effects on presynaptic ion handling and potassium conductance, with indirect functional involvement of voltage-gated calcium and potassium channel systems rather than a uniquely defined protein target. It is orally absorbed but variably tolerated, distributes largely in extracellular water with limited passive tissue penetration because of its persistent positive charge, undergoes little metabolic transformation, and is eliminated chiefly unchanged by the kidney, making accumulation more likely in renal impairment. Historically it was used for Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome and occasionally other disorders of impaired neuromuscular transmission to improve weakness and fatigability, but clinical use has been largely abandoned in favor of safer alternatives. Toxicity is substantial and dose-limiting, including bone marrow suppression, nephrotoxicity, gastrointestinal irritation, neurotoxicity, and potential cardiac effects; adverse effects include paresthesias, tremor, diarrhea, nausea, anorexia, weakness, and hematologic complications such as leukopenia or aplastic anemia.

Name: Ciprofloxacin
Description: Ciprofloxacin (DrugBank DB00537) is a synthetic second-generation fluoroquinolone antibacterial built on a 4-quinolone/1,4-dihydroquinoline core bearing the characteristic 3-carboxyl and 4-keto pharmacophore, a 6-fluoro substituent that enhances bacterial penetration and potency, a 7-piperazinyl moiety that broadens Gram-negative activity, and a cyclopropyl group at N-1 that strengthens overall spectrum; thus its chemical category is a fluorinated quinolone anti-infective and its principal scaffold is the fluoroquinolone quinolone-carboxylic acid nucleus. Closely related drugs include norfloxacin, ofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, and delafloxacin. It acts by inhibiting bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, with major target proteins including GyrA, GyrB, ParC, and ParE. Oral absorption is generally good though reduced by polyvalent cations, distribution is wide with high concentrations in urine, kidney, prostate, lung, and some intracellular compartments, protein binding is low to moderate, metabolism is limited, and elimination is primarily renal through glomerular filtration and tubular secretion with partial biliary/fecal excretion and a half-life of about 4 hours in normal renal function. Toxicity includes dose-related gastrointestinal and CNS effects, tendinopathy and tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, dysglycemia, QT prolongation, hepatotoxicity, and rare seizures or aortic aneurysm risk; overdose may cause crystalluria or neurotoxicity. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, diarrhea, rash, headache, dizziness, insomnia, and photosensitivity. Clinically it is used for susceptible urinary tract infections, pyelonephritis, bacterial prostatitis, infectious diarrhea, typhoid fever, intra-abdominal infection in combination regimens, bone and joint infections, certain respiratory infections due to Gram-negative pathogens, skin infections, and post-exposure prophylaxis or treatment of inhalational anthrax.

Name: Vincristine
Description: Vincristine (DrugBank DB00541) is a complex dimeric indole-dihydroindole alkaloid of the vinca alkaloid class, structurally derived from Catharanthus roseus and characterized by coupling of the vindoline and catharanthine moieties into a polycyclic, highly oxygenated bisindole framework containing multiple fused and bridged ring systems, tertiary amine functionality, and ester/acetal-like substituents; its core chemical scaffold is the vinca bisindole scaffold, closely related to similar antimicrotubule agents such as vinblastine, vinorelbine, vindesine, and semisynthetic analogues of the same family. Pharmacologically, vincristine binds β-tubulin in microtubules, disrupting tubulin polymerization and mitotic spindle formation; tubulin proteins, especially TUBB isoforms, are the principal targets, while transport and disposition are influenced by ABCB1/P-glycoprotein and metabolism primarily by CYP3A4 and CYP3A5. It is given intravenously because oral absorption is negligible/unreliable, distributes extensively into tissues but penetrates the CNS poorly, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated mainly via biliary/fecal excretion with limited renal clearance and a prolonged terminal elimination phase. Its major dose-limiting toxicity is neurotoxicity, including peripheral neuropathy, autonomic dysfunction with severe constipation or ileus, cranial neuropathies, and rarely SIADH; myelosuppression is typically less prominent than with vinblastine, but extravasation injury and fatal toxicity after intrathecal administration are classic hazards. Common adverse effects include paresthesias, weakness, neuropathic pain, constipation, abdominal cramping, alopecia, and mild marrow suppression. Clinically, vincristine is used in combination chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia, Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphomas, Wilms tumor, rhabdomyosarcoma, neuroblastoma, Ewing sarcoma, and other pediatric or hematologic malignancies, where its antimicrotubule action contributes to remission induction and disease control.

Name: Benazepril
Description: Benazepril (DrugBank DB00542) is a dicarboxylate-containing, nonsulfhydryl angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor of the prodrug class, structurally characterized by a substituted proline-like amino acid core bearing an esterified carboxyl group, an amide linkage, and a lipophilic aromatic side chain that is converted in vivo to the active diacid benazeprilat; chemically it belongs to the ACE inhibitor class and is built on a proline/carboxyalkyl peptidomimetic scaffold typical of renin-angiotensin system antagonists. Similar drugs include enalapril, ramipril, quinapril, perindopril, and trandolapril, which share related prodrug ester motifs and ACE-binding dicarboxylate pharmacophores. Its principal target is angiotensin-converting enzyme, with consequent reduction of angiotensin II formation and aldosterone secretion and increased bradykinin tone. After oral administration, benazepril is absorbed reasonably well, undergoes hepatic esterase-mediated de-esterification to benazeprilat, reaches peak active-metabolite concentrations within hours, distributes moderately with protein binding, and is eliminated by both renal and biliary routes, with prolonged exposure in renal impairment. Toxicity is largely an extension of pharmacology and includes hypotension, azotemia, hyperkalemia, and rarely angioedema; overdose may produce marked blood-pressure reduction, and fetotoxicity in later pregnancy is a major concern. Indications include hypertension, heart failure in some practice settings, and reduction of proteinuric renal disease progression, especially in chronic kidney disease. Adverse effects commonly include cough, dizziness, headache, fatigue, nausea, creatinine rise, and hyperkalemia, while serious reactions include angioedema and acute kidney injury. Clinically, it is used alone or with thiazides or calcium channel blockers for blood-pressure control and renal protection in hypertensive patients, including those with diabetes or proteinuria.

Name: Amoxapine
Description: Amoxapine (DrugBank DB00543) is a dibenzoxazepine tricyclic antidepressant whose structure consists of two fused benzene rings linked through a seven-membered oxazepine ring and bearing a piperazine substituent, giving it a rigid tricyclic aromatic framework with a basic tertiary amine that supports CNS penetration and monoamine transporter binding; chemically it belongs to the tetracyclic/tricyclic antidepressant-related class, with a dibenzoxazepine scaffold closely related to loxapine and broadly similar pharmacologically to other older antidepressants such as imipramine, amitriptyline, doxepin, and maprotiline. Its principal targets are the norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2 and serotonin transporter SLC6A4, with additional dopamine D2 receptor antagonism, a feature that distinguishes it from many other TCAs and likely reflects activity of its major metabolite 7-hydroxyamoxapine; it also interacts to varying degrees with histaminergic, muscarinic, and adrenergic receptors. Amoxapine is used for major depressive disorder, especially depression with anxiety, agitation, or insomnia, and has historically been employed in endogenous depression and treatment-resistant depressive states. It is well absorbed orally, undergoes hepatic first-pass metabolism to active metabolites including 7-hydroxyamoxapine and 8-hydroxyamoxapine, is widely distributed with substantial tissue and protein binding, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine with a moderate elimination half-life permitting divided or once-daily dosing. Toxicity resembles that of TCAs but includes relatively prominent extrapyramidal risk: overdose may cause sedation, seizures, coma, tachycardia, anticholinergic effects, hypotension, and potentially fatal arrhythmias, while adverse effects include drowsiness, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, weight gain, orthostasis, sexual dysfunction, tardive dyskinesia, akathisia, and hyperprolactinemia.

Name: Fluorouracil
Description: Fluorouracil (5-fluorouracil; DrugBank DB00544) is a halogenated pyrimidine antimetabolite structurally defined as a uracil analog bearing fluorine at the C5 position of a planar 2,4-dioxopyrimidine ring, placing it in the fluorinated nucleobase class with a uracil/pyrimidinedione scaffold; it is closely related to other fluoropyrimidines and antimetabolites such as capecitabine, tegafur, floxuridine, cytarabine, and gemcitabine. After intravenous or topical administration, systemic absorption is route dependent, distribution is broad including tumor tissue, protein binding is low, and the drug undergoes extensive first-pass and systemic catabolism mainly by dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase to inactive metabolites, with anabolic conversion intracellularly to FdUMP, FUTP, and FdUTP; elimination is predominantly respiratory as carbon dioxide and renal as metabolites, with a short plasma half-life but marked pharmacogenetic variability. Its principal targets are thymidylate synthase, with secondary effects through RNA and DNA misincorporation, and enzymes in pyrimidine metabolism including dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase and orotate phosphoribosyltransferase that influence response and toxicity. Indications include colorectal, gastric, pancreatic, breast, anal, and head and neck cancers, and topical treatment of actinic keratoses and superficial basal cell carcinoma. Dose-limiting and clinically important toxicities include severe myelosuppression, mucositis, diarrhea, hand-foot syndrome, neurotoxicity, cardiotoxicity such as angina or coronary vasospasm, and potentially fatal toxicity in DPD deficiency. In practice it is used alone, topically, or in regimens such as FOLFOX, FOLFIRI, and chemoradiation protocols.

Name: Desoximetasone
Description: Desoximetasone (DrugBank DB00547) is a high-potency synthetic topical corticosteroid whose structure is based on the pregnane steroid nucleus with the characteristic four fused cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene rings, bearing 11β- and 17α-hydroxyl groups, a 3-keto-4-ene system, a 20-ketone, fluorination at C9, methyl substitution at C16, and deoxygenation at C21, features that increase glucocorticoid potency and topical anti-inflammatory activity. Chemically, it belongs to the fluorinated corticosteroids, specifically nonhalogenated-at-side-chain topical glucocorticoid derivatives, and its core scaffold is the dexamethasone-like corticosteroid scaffold modified to enhance cutaneous activity. Similar drugs include betamethasone, dexamethasone, fluocinonide, clobetasol propionate, halobetasol, and diflorasone, which share related steroid pharmacophores and glucocorticoid receptor activity. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, with downstream suppression of phospholipase A2-mediated eicosanoid synthesis and broad inhibition of proinflammatory cytokine transcription. After topical administration, absorption is usually limited but increases with inflamed skin, large surface area, prolonged use, occlusion, or pediatric application; distributed mainly within skin and, when systemically absorbed, protein-bound in plasma; metabolized hepatically like other corticosteroids; and excreted largely as urinary metabolites with some fecal elimination. Toxicity reflects local and systemic corticosteroid excess, including skin atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, delayed wound healing, secondary infection, reversible hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis suppression, hyperglycemia, glucosuria, and Cushingoid features. It is indicated for corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses such as plaque psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, allergic/contact dermatitis, and eczema, and is used clinically as cream, ointment, gel, or spray to reduce erythema, pruritus, scaling, and inflammation, with common adverse effects including burning, stinging, dryness, folliculitis, acneiform eruption, and perioral dermatitis.

Name: Azelaic acid
Description: Azelaic acid (DB00548) is a saturated straight-chain nine-carbon dicarboxylic acid with terminal carboxyl groups linked by a flexible polymethylene spacer, placing it in the aliphatic dicarboxylic acid and naturally occurring organic acid category; its core scaffold is the nonanedioic acid backbone, which is closely related to other therapeutic carboxylic acids such as sebacic acid, adipic acid, and the acne-active dicarboxylic acid analogs used in topical dermatology, although azelaic acid is the principal marketed member for direct pharmacologic use. Its pharmacology is largely topical and multifactorial, involving inhibition of microbial protein synthesis in Cutibacterium acnes and Staphylococcus epidermidis, antiproliferative effects on abnormal keratinocytes, and inhibition of mitochondrial oxidoreductases and tyrosinase, with tyrosinase regarded as a relevant functional target in pigment reduction. After topical administration, percutaneous absorption is limited, systemic exposure is low, distribution is minimal beyond skin, absorbed drug undergoes fatty-acid-type beta-oxidation to shorter chain dicarboxylic acids, and elimination is mainly renal as unchanged drug and metabolites. Toxicity is generally low, with no major systemic organ toxicity expected at therapeutic topical doses, though irritation can be dose-limiting; excessive exposure may produce burning, erythema, scaling, pruritus, or rarely hypopigmentation, especially in sensitive skin. It is indicated for acne vulgaris and inflammatory papulopustular rosacea, and is also used clinically for dyschromias such as melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Common adverse effects include transient stinging, dryness, peeling, and local irritation. In practice, it is used as a topical gel, cream, or foam for comedonal and inflammatory acne, rosacea-associated papules and pustules, and pigmentary disorders when a keratolytic, anti-inflammatory, and depigmenting agent is desired.

Name: Zafirlukast
Description: Zafirlukast (DrugBank DB00549) is an orally active leukotriene receptor antagonist with a lipophilic diaryl thioether/sulfonamide-derived structure built around an indole-containing aromatic scaffold linked to substituted phenyl rings and heteroatom-rich acidic functionality that supports high receptor affinity; chemically it is categorized as an anti-asthmatic eicosanoid-modulating agent and more specifically a cysteinyl leukotriene receptor antagonist, with a scaffold broadly similar to other leukotriene pathway drugs such as montelukast and pranlukast, although zileuton is mechanistically related only at the pathway level as a 5-lipoxygenase inhibitor. Its principal target is the cysteinyl leukotriene receptor 1, CYSLTR1, through which it blocks LTD4-mediated bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion, vascular permeability, and eosinophilic airway inflammation. Zafirlukast is indicated for prophylaxis and chronic treatment of asthma, including prevention of bronchospasm and improvement of symptoms such as wheeze, cough, and nocturnal asthma, but it is not used for acute rescue. After oral administration it is absorbed moderately well, with food reducing bioavailability; it is highly protein bound, distributes mainly in plasma, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism predominantly via CYP2C9 with contribution from CYP3A4, and is eliminated chiefly as metabolites in the feces with limited renal excretion; the half-life is roughly in the 8-10 hour range. Important toxicities include hepatotoxicity ranging from asymptomatic transaminase elevation to rare hepatitis or hepatic failure, plus drug interactions such as potentiation of warfarin. Common adverse effects include headache, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and infection-like upper respiratory symptoms; rare hypersensitivity, rash, and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis have been reported, particularly during corticosteroid tapering. Clinically, it is used as a non-steroidal controller option in persistent asthma, especially when aspirin-sensitive or exercise-related leukotriene-mediated symptoms are suspected.

Name: Propylthiouracil
Description: Propylthiouracil (DrugBank DB00550) is a small, sulfur-containing antithyroid agent built on a thiouracil nucleus, specifically a 2-thioxo-4-hydroxypyrimidine ring bearing a propyl substituent at the 6-position; chemically it belongs to the thioamide/thiourea-derived antithyroid drugs and its core scaffold is the substituted thiouracil heterocycle. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other thionamides such as methimazole and its prodrug carbimazole, which share thyroid hormone synthesis inhibition but differ in scaffold and toxicity profile. Propylthiouracil acts primarily by inhibiting thyroid peroxidase, thereby blocking iodination of tyrosyl residues and coupling reactions in thyroglobulin, and it also inhibits peripheral iodothyronine deiodinase, reducing T4-to-T3 conversion; relevant target proteins include thyroid peroxidase and deiodinase enzymes, especially type 1 5-deiodinase. After oral administration it is well absorbed, though bioavailability may be incomplete due to first-pass handling; it is moderately protein bound, concentrates functionally in the thyroid, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via glucuronidation, and is excreted predominantly in urine as metabolites with a relatively short plasma half-life, necessitating divided dosing. It is indicated for hyperthyroidism, particularly Graves disease, toxic multinodular goiter, and thyroid storm, and is used when rapid reduction of T3 formation is desired, before thyroidectomy, or when radioiodine is unsuitable, including selected early-pregnancy cases. Major toxicities include severe hepatotoxicity, cholestatic or hepatocellular injury, agranulocytosis, neutropenia, aplastic anemia, ANCA-associated vasculitis, and hypersensitivity reactions; common adverse effects include rash, pruritus, urticaria, arthralgia, gastrointestinal upset, fever, and hypothyroidism with overtreatment.

Name: Acetohydroxamic acid
Description: Acetohydroxamic acid (DrugBank DB00551) is a small, highly polar acetylated hydroxamic acid composed of a methyl-substituted carbonyl linked to an N-hydroxylamide functionality, giving a simple amide-like structure with strong metal-chelating capacity; chemically it belongs to the hydroxamic acid class and is built on a minimal acetyl hydroxamate scaffold, a motif shared with other metal-binding and enzyme-inhibitory agents. Similar drugs include other hydroxamate-containing compounds and urease-directed agents, such as hydroxyurea in a broad functional sense and investigational hydroxamic acid derivatives, although acetohydroxamic acid is distinctive for clinical urease inhibition. Its principal target is bacterial urease, a nickel-dependent enzyme produced by organisms such as Proteus, Klebsiella, and some Staphylococcus species, and inhibition reduces ammonia generation and urinary alkalinization. Orally administered, it is reasonably well absorbed, distributed systemically including into urine where activity is therapeutically relevant, undergoes limited metabolism with some hydrolysis, and is eliminated mainly by renal excretion as unchanged drug and metabolites; dose adjustment may be necessary in renal impairment. It is indicated as adjunctive therapy in chronic or recurrent infection-induced struvite stone disease associated with urease-producing bacteria, for example persistent alkaline urine, hyperammonuria, and recurrent magnesium ammonium phosphate calculi when surgery or antibiotics alone are insufficient. Toxicities include teratogenicity in animals, hemolytic anemia, phlebitis, and neuropsychiatric effects; adverse effects commonly include headache, tremor, gastrointestinal upset, rash, alopecia, and rarely thrombosis or anemia. Clinically, it is used as an adjunct rather than sole therapy to suppress stone growth and recurrence in complicated urinary tract infection settings.

Name: Methoxsalen
Description: Methoxsalen (8-methoxypsoralen; DrugBank DB00553) is a tricyclic, planar furocoumarin composed of a coumarin core fused to a furan ring with a methoxy substituent at the 8-position, giving an aromatic, highly conjugated, lipophilic psoralen framework that readily intercalates into nucleic acids; chemically it is classified as a linear psoralen and more broadly an oxygenated heterocyclic coumarin, with the psoralen/furo[3,2-g]chromen-7-one scaffold as its defining chemotype. Closely related drugs include trioxsalen and aminolevulinic acid-based phototherapies in a broader photomedicine context, while naturally occurring or pharmacologically similar psoralens include bergapten and xanthotoxin. Its principal pharmacologic action is as a photosensitizer rather than a classic receptor ligand: after UVA exposure it forms covalent mono-adducts and interstrand crosslinks with pyrimidine bases in DNA, altering keratinocyte proliferation and exerting immunomodulatory effects; no single canonical protein target defines its activity, though downstream effects involve suppression of epidermal DNA synthesis and modulation of T-cell function. Methoxsalen is administered orally or topically for PUVA therapy, is variably absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, distributes into skin and ocular tissues, undergoes extensive hepatic oxidative metabolism largely via cytochrome P450 enzymes such as CYP3A4, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine. It is indicated for severe psoriasis, vitiligo, and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma such as mycosis fungoides. Toxicities include dose-related phototoxic erythema, blistering, burns, nausea, and long-term photoaging, cataract risk without eye protection, and increased nonmelanoma skin cancer risk with cumulative PUVA exposure. Common side effects include pruritus, hyperpigmentation, headache, dizziness, and edema. Clinically, it is used to sensitize skin before controlled UVA irradiation to induce repigmentation in vitiligo plaques, reduce psoriatic scaling, and palliate early-stage CTCL lesions.

Name: Piroxicam
Description: Piroxicam (DrugBank DB00554) is an oxicam nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug characterized structurally by a 1,2-benzothiazine 1,1-dioxide core bearing a 4-hydroxyl enolic function, a 3-carboxamide, and a 2-pyridyl substituent, a heteroaromatic enolic sulfonamide-like framework that defines the oxicam scaffold and distinguishes it from arylacetic and arylpropionic acid NSAIDs; closely related and chemically similar drugs include meloxicam, tenoxicam, lornoxicam, and droxicam. Its principal pharmacologic targets are cyclooxygenase enzymes PTGS1 (COX-1) and PTGS2 (COX-2), whose inhibition reduces prostaglandin synthesis, accounting for anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antipyretic effects. Piroxicam is well absorbed orally with high bioavailability, reaches peak concentrations within hours, is highly albumin bound, distributes broadly into inflamed synovial tissues, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP2C9-mediated hydroxylation and conjugation, and is eliminated slowly in urine and feces with a long half-life of about 45-50 hours, supporting once-daily dosing. Toxicity is typical of NSAIDs and includes dose-related gastrointestinal erosion, peptic ulceration, bleeding, renal hypoperfusion or acute kidney injury, sodium and water retention, hypertension, hepatotoxicity, and rare severe cutaneous adverse reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis. Common side effects include dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, edema, dizziness, headache, rash, and occult or overt GI blood loss. Clinically, it is used for symptomatic treatment of rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute musculoskeletal pain, and primary dysmenorrhea, especially when prolonged anti-inflammatory activity and once-daily oral administration are desired.

Name: Lamotrigine
Description: Lamotrigine (DrugBank DB00555) is a synthetic phenyltriazine anticonvulsant whose structure consists of a 1,2,4-triazine heteroaromatic core bearing two exocyclic amino groups and a dichlorophenyl substituent, giving a relatively planar, weakly basic, halogenated aryl-heterocycle; chemically it is classified as a triazine derivative and specifically an aryltriazine, with a diaminotriazine scaffold analogous in broad antiseizure pharmacology to agents such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, and to some extent lacosamide, although it is structurally distinct from those sodium-channel modulators. Its principal pharmacologic targets are voltage-gated sodium channels, especially neuronal SCN family channels such as SCN1A, SCN2A, and SCN8A, with consequent inhibition of pathologic high-frequency firing and reduced presynaptic glutamate release; functional effects on high-voltage-activated calcium currents are also described. Lamotrigine is well absorbed orally with high bioavailability, modest protein binding, wide tissue distribution including CNS penetration, predominant hepatic metabolism by UGT-mediated N-glucuronidation, and mainly renal excretion of glucuronide metabolites; its half-life is prolonged by valproate and shortened by enzyme-inducing antiepileptics such as carbamazepine or phenytoin. Major toxicities include serious cutaneous hypersensitivity reactions, notably Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, with risk increased by rapid titration, coadministration with valproate, and pediatric use; overdose may cause ataxia, nystagmus, seizures, QRS widening, and reduced consciousness. Clinically, lamotrigine is indicated for focal seizures, primary generalized tonic-clonic seizures, Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, and maintenance treatment of bipolar I disorder, especially for prevention of depressive episodes; common adverse effects include dizziness, diplopia, blurred vision, headache, nausea, somnolence, insomnia, tremor, and rash, and in practice it is widely used as a broad-spectrum antiseizure drug and mood stabilizer when a comparatively weight-neutral, cognitively sparing option is desired.

Name: Hydroxyzine
Description: Hydroxyzine (DrugBank DB00557) is a first-generation piperazine antihistamine with a flexible diaryl-ether architecture consisting of a diphenylmethyl/benzhydryl-substituted phenoxyethyl chain linked to a tertiary piperazine ring, placing it in the H1 receptor antagonist class and more specifically among piperazine-derived sedating antihistamines; its core chemical scaffold is the hydroxyzine/cetirizine-type benzhydryl-phenoxyethyl-piperazine framework. Closely related or similar drugs include cetirizine, its major active carboxylated metabolite, as well as levocetirizine, cyclizine, meclizine, and other sedating H1 blockers such as diphenhydramine in functional terms. Hydroxyzine is generally well absorbed orally, with onset within minutes to hours, wide tissue distribution including central nervous system penetration that accounts for sedation, high protein binding, hepatic metabolism mainly by CYP3A4 and CYP3A5 to cetirizine and other minor metabolites, and elimination through renal and fecal routes with an elimination half-life that is shorter in children and prolonged in the elderly or hepatic dysfunction. Its principal pharmacologic target is histamine H1 receptor blockade, with additional antimuscarinic and likely 5-HT2A antagonistic activity contributing to antiemetic, anxiolytic, and antipruritic effects. Indications include anxiety and tension, pruritus associated with urticaria or atopic dermatitis, adjunctive sedation, and nausea or vomiting. Adverse effects commonly include somnolence, dry mouth, dizziness, blurred vision, constipation, and impaired psychomotor performance; toxicity may produce marked CNS depression, anticholinergic effects, seizures, hypotension, and QT prolongation with torsades de pointes risk, especially in overdose or when combined with other QT-prolonging drugs. Clinically, hydroxyzine is used as a non-benzodiazepine anxiolytic, antipruritic, sedative, and perioperative adjunct.

Name: Zanamivir
Description: Zanamivir (DrugBank DB00558) is a rationally designed sialic acid analog neuraminidase inhibitor whose structure is based on a highly polar 4-guanidino-substituted unsaturated N-acetylneuraminic acid framework, containing multiple hydroxyl groups and a carboxylate that mimic the transition-state interactions of the natural neuraminidase substrate; chemically it is categorized as a carbohydrate-like antiviral, specifically a sialic acid analog, and its core scaffold is the modified neuraminic acid/cyclohexene-like scaffold shared by influenza neuraminidase inhibitors. Similar drugs include oseltamivir, peramivir, and laninamivir, which also target influenza neuraminidase but differ in lipophilicity, route, and residence time. Zanamivir acts on influenza virus neuraminidase proteins from influenza A and B, inhibiting virion release and spread. It is indicated for treatment and prophylaxis of uncomplicated influenza, particularly seasonal influenza A and B in patients presenting early after symptom onset or in exposed contacts. Pharmacokinetically, zanamivir is administered mainly by oral inhalation because oral bioavailability is poor; systemic absorption after inhalation is low to moderate, distribution is limited with meaningful drug levels in the respiratory tract, plasma protein binding is minimal, metabolism is negligible, and elimination occurs largely unchanged via renal excretion with a short plasma half-life. Toxicity is generally low because of limited systemic exposure, but bronchospasm and decline in respiratory function can occur, especially in asthma or COPD; overdose experience suggests mainly exaggerated local or mild systemic effects. Common adverse effects include cough, throat irritation, nasal symptoms, headache, nausea, and rare hypersensitivity or neuropsychiatric events. Clinically, it is used as an inhaled antiviral for early outpatient influenza treatment and for post-exposure prophylaxis in household or institutional outbreaks.

Name: Bosentan
Description: Bosentan (DB00559) is an orally active, dual endothelin receptor antagonist built on a substituted pyrimidine scaffold bearing tert-butyl, methoxyphenoxy, hydroxyethylamino, and sulfonamide functionalities, giving an amphiphilic, highly aromatic small-molecule structure characteristic of nonpeptide endothelin antagonists. Chemically, it is classified as a sulfonamide-containing heteroaryl vasomodulator, with a diaryl-heterocycle pharmacophore related to other endothelin receptor antagonists such as ambrisentan, macitentan, and the intravenous agent sitaxsentan-like congeners, although receptor selectivity differs across the class. Its principal targets are endothelin receptor type A and type B, through which it blocks endothelin-1-mediated vasoconstriction and vascular smooth muscle proliferation. Bosentan is indicated primarily for pulmonary arterial hypertension, including idiopathic and connective tissue disease-associated PAH, where it improves exercise capacity and delays clinical worsening; it has also been used to reduce new digital ulcer formation in systemic sclerosis. After oral administration, absorption is moderate with peak concentrations in a few hours and bioavailability limited by first-pass effects; the drug is highly protein bound, distributed mainly in plasma, extensively metabolized hepatically by CYP3A4 and CYP2C9 to active and inactive metabolites, induces hepatic enzymes and transport processes, and is excreted predominantly via the biliary-fecal route with minimal renal elimination. Major toxicities include dose-related hepatotoxicity with aminotransferase elevations, teratogenicity, reduced hemoglobin, and clinically relevant drug interactions. Common adverse effects include headache, flushing, peripheral edema, nasal congestion, palpitations, dizziness, and liver function abnormalities. Clinically, bosentan is used as chronic oral therapy in PAH patients requiring endothelin pathway blockade, often with regular liver monitoring and pregnancy prevention measures.

Name: Tigecycline
Description: Tigecycline (DrugBank DB00560) is a semisynthetic glycylcycline antibiotic structurally derived from minocycline, built on the classic four linearly fused-ring tetracycline naphthacene core with multiple keto, hydroxyl, and amide-related functionalities and a distinctive 9-glycylamido side chain that increases ribosomal affinity and helps overcome common tetracycline resistance mechanisms; chemically it belongs to the tetracycline-class polyketide-derived antibacterials, with a tetracycline/glycylcycline scaffold, and it is most closely related to tetracycline congeners such as minocycline, doxycycline, tetracycline, and newer tetracycline-like agents including omadacycline and eravacycline. Its principal target is the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit, especially 16S rRNA-associated binding sites, where it blocks aminoacyl-tRNA entry and inhibits protein synthesis. Pharmacokinetically, tigecycline is administered intravenously because oral absorption is not clinically useful; it shows a large volume of distribution with extensive tissue penetration, moderate protein binding, limited metabolism, and elimination mainly via biliary/fecal excretion with a smaller renal component, supporting loading-dose then maintenance dosing. It is indicated for complicated skin and soft tissue infections, complicated intra-abdominal infections, and community-acquired bacterial pneumonia, with clinical use against susceptible MRSA, VRE, anaerobes, and many multidrug-resistant Gram-negative organisms, though not ideally for bacteremia because serum concentrations are relatively low. Toxicity includes dose-limiting gastrointestinal intolerance, hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, coagulopathy, hypersensitivity, superinfection including Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea, and tetracycline-class risks such as fetal toxicity and tooth discoloration; common adverse effects are nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, transaminase elevation, and infusion-related reactions.

Name: Doxapram
Description: Doxapram (DrugBank DB00561) is a synthetic respiratory stimulant built on a substituted piperidine framework, structurally characterized as a keto-amide bearing a 2-pyrrolidinyl substituent and aromatic ring system, giving it a lipophilic, conformationally restricted heterocyclic architecture; chemically it is classified as a piperidine derivative and central nervous system/respiratory analeptic, with a piperidine-carboxamide scaffold related in broad pharmacologic space to older analeptics and respiratory stimulants such as nikethamide, almitrine, and historically bemegride, although it is structurally most distinctive for its piperidyl amide core. Its pharmacologic action is attributed mainly to stimulation of peripheral carotid body chemoreceptors and, at higher concentrations, central medullary respiratory centers; identified molecular targets/mechanisms include inhibition of background potassium channels, particularly TASK-1 and TASK-3 channels in carotid body type I cells, with downstream enhancement of ventilatory drive. After intravenous administration, onset is rapid; distribution is brisk to highly perfused tissues including brain, metabolism occurs primarily in the liver to active metabolites such as 2-ketodoxapram, and elimination is mainly renal as metabolites, with a relatively short clinical duration necessitating titration or infusion. Toxicity is dose-related and dominated by excessive CNS and cardiorespiratory stimulation, including hypertension, tachyarrhythmia, agitation, hyperreflexia, and seizures. Adverse effects commonly include anxiety, sweating, nausea, vomiting, dyspnea, flushing, and increased blood pressure. Clinically, doxapram has been used to treat postoperative or drug-induced respiratory depression, to stimulate breathing during recovery from anesthesia, and as a short-term adjunct in acute hypercapnic exacerbations or apnea settings where temporary ventilatory stimulation is desired, though use is limited by its narrow therapeutic window and toxicity.

Name: Methotrexate
Description: Methotrexate (DrugBank DB00563) is a folate antimetabolite and classical antifolate structurally characterized by a 2,4-diaminopteridine ring system linked through a para-aminobenzoic acid moiety to a terminal glutamate residue, giving a pteridine–p-aminobenzoate–glutamate scaffold that mimics folic acid but with substitutions that favor tight enzyme binding. It belongs to the antineoplastic and immunomodulatory antimetabolite class, with a folate analog scaffold closely related to aminopterin and mechanistically similar to pralatrexate and pemetrexed, while leucovorin is a reduced folate used for rescue rather than a direct analog. Its principal target is dihydrofolate reductase; functionally relevant secondary intracellular targets after polyglutamation include thymidylate synthase and transformylases such as ATIC and GART, contributing to impaired purine and thymidylate synthesis and increased adenosine-mediated anti-inflammatory effects. Methotrexate is variably absorbed orally, especially at lower doses, is partly protein bound, distributes into tissues and third spaces, enters cells via reduced folate carriers, undergoes intracellular polyglutamation, has limited hepatic metabolism including formation of 7-hydroxymethotrexate, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by renal glomerular filtration and active tubular secretion, so clearance falls with renal dysfunction and drug interactions. Toxicity includes dose-dependent myelosuppression, mucositis, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity from crystal precipitation at high doses, pulmonary toxicity, severe infection risk, and teratogenicity. Common adverse effects include nausea, stomatitis, fatigue, transaminase elevation, cytopenias, rash, and alopecia. Clinically it is used in acute lymphoblastic leukemia, osteosarcoma, lymphomas, gestational trophoblastic disease, psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, Crohn disease, and ectopic pregnancy.

Name: Carbamazepine
Description: Carbamazepine (DrugBank DB00564) is a dibenzazepine anticonvulsant whose structure consists of a tricyclic iminostilbene-like framework with two fused benzene rings linked through a seven-membered azepine ring and a carboxamide substituent, making it a neutral, lipophilic aromatic amide; chemically it is classified as an iminostilbene-derived anticonvulsant and mood-stabilizing agent, with a dibenz[b,f]azepine scaffold closely related to tricyclic psychotropics. Similar drugs include oxcarbazepine and eslicarbazepine acetate, which are structurally related sodium-channel-active anticonvulsants, as well as the older tricyclic agent imipramine by scaffold analogy. Its principal pharmacology is use-dependent inhibition of voltage-gated sodium channels, especially neuronal SCN1A, SCN2A, and SCN8A-containing channels, reducing high-frequency firing; other reported targets include adenosine receptors and possible effects on calcium and glutamate signaling. It is well absorbed orally but variably and relatively slowly, is extensively distributed with moderate protein binding, crosses the blood-brain barrier, and undergoes hepatic CYP3A4 metabolism to the active carbamazepine-10,11-epoxide, followed by epoxide hydrolase-mediated conversion; autoinduction increases clearance over time, and elimination occurs mainly as urinary metabolites with limited unchanged drug excretion. Clinically it is indicated for focal and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, trigeminal neuralgia, and bipolar disorder, and is also used in glossopharyngeal neuralgia and some neuropathic pain states. Important adverse effects include dizziness, diplopia, ataxia, somnolence, nausea, hyponatremia, leukopenia, and rash, while major toxicities include hepatic injury, aplastic anemia, agranulocytosis, overdose-related CNS and cardiac toxicity, and severe cutaneous adverse reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, particularly in HLA-B1502-positive patients.

Name: Cephalexin
Description: Cephalexin (DrugBank DB00567) is a first-generation cephalosporin, a semisynthetic beta-lactam antibacterial whose structure consists of the conserved cephem nucleus with a strained four-membered beta-lactam fused to a six-membered dihydrothiazine ring, bearing a 7-amino side chain related to D-phenylglycine and a 3-methyl substituent that together support acid stability and oral activity; chemically it is categorized as a beta-lactam cephalosporin antibiotic, and its core scaffold is the 7-aminocephalosporanic acid/cephem scaffold. Similar drugs include cefadroxil, cefazolin, cephradine, and more broadly other beta-lactams such as amoxicillin that share cell-wall inhibitory pharmacology. Cephalexin targets bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, especially transpeptidases such as PBP1, PBP2, and PBP3, inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-linking and causing bacterial lysis. It is well absorbed orally with high bioavailability, reaches therapeutic concentrations in skin, soft tissue, bone, urine, and respiratory secretions, has low protein binding, limited metabolism, a short half-life of roughly 1 hour, and is eliminated largely unchanged by renal excretion via glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, requiring dose adjustment in renal impairment. Toxicity is generally low but includes hypersensitivity reactions up to anaphylaxis, gastrointestinal toxicity including antibiotic-associated diarrhea and rare Clostridioides difficile colitis, interstitial nephritis, hemolytic anemia, eosinophilia, and rarely seizures at high exposure or with renal failure. Indications and clinical use include streptococcal pharyngitis, uncomplicated skin and soft-tissue infections, methicillin-susceptible staphylococcal infections, urinary tract infections, otitis media, and selected respiratory tract infections; common adverse effects are nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, rash, urticaria, candidiasis, and dizziness.

Name: Cinnarizine
Description: Cinnarizine (DrugBank DB00568) is a lipophilic diphenylmethyl-substituted piperazine derivative whose structure consists of a tertiary piperazine core bearing a cinnamyl group and a benzhydryl moiety with chlorophenyl substitution, placing it in the piperazine-class antihistamine/calcium-entry blocker family with a diarylmethyl-piperazine scaffold; structurally and pharmacologically related drugs include cyclizine, hydroxyzine, meclizine, buclizine, and the fluorinated analog flunarizine. Its principal targets are histamine H1 receptors and voltage-gated calcium channels, with additional anti-vestibular and vasomodulatory effects that may involve reduced sensory hair-cell excitability and improved microcirculatory rheology. After oral administration it is absorbed variably, undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP2D6-mediated N-dealkylation and related oxidative pathways, is highly protein bound and widely distributed into lipid-rich tissues including the CNS, and is eliminated predominantly as metabolites in feces and urine with a several-hour terminal half-life. Clinically, it is used for vertigo, Ménière-associated vestibular symptoms, motion sickness, nausea, vomiting, labyrinthine disorders, and peripheral vascular insufficiency symptoms such as intermittent claudication or acrocyanosis in some regions. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, fatigue, dry mouth, gastrointestinal discomfort, and weight gain, while important toxicities include CNS depression, anticholinergic effects, hypotension, and especially extrapyramidal reactions or drug-induced parkinsonism with prolonged use, particularly in older adults; rare cholestatic hepatic injury and overdose-related sedation have also been described. Overall, cinnarizine is used as a symptomatic anti-vertigo and anti-motion-sickness agent and as an adjunct in selected peripheral circulatory disorders.

Name: Fondaparinux
Description: Fondaparinux (DrugBank DB00569) is a fully synthetic sulfated pentasaccharide anticoagulant structurally modeled on the minimal antithrombin-binding sequence of heparin, consisting of five highly oxygenated monosaccharide units linked in a defined linear arrangement and densely substituted with sulfate and carboxylate functionalities that confer a strong polyanionic charge; chemically it belongs to the heparin-derived glycosaminoglycan mimetic class, with a sulfated pentasaccharide scaffold. It is most closely related to indirect factor Xa inhibitors and heparinoid anticoagulants such as unfractionated heparin, low-molecular-weight heparins including enoxaparin and dalteparin, and the longer heparin mimetic idraparinux. Its principal target is antithrombin III, to which it binds selectively and with high affinity, inducing a conformational change that potently enhances inhibition of coagulation factor Xa without direct thrombin inhibition. After subcutaneous administration it is essentially completely absorbed, has predictable linear pharmacokinetics, limited distribution largely within the blood volume, negligible plasma protein binding apart from antithrombin, no meaningful hepatic metabolism, and is excreted largely unchanged by the kidney with a relatively long half-life permitting once-daily dosing. Toxicity is dominated by bleeding, including major gastrointestinal, postoperative, retroperitoneal, and intracranial hemorrhage, with accumulation and increased risk in renal impairment; anemia, thrombocytopenia, injection-site hematoma, and rare hypersensitivity can occur, while heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is less frequent than with heparin. Clinically it is used for prevention and treatment of venous thromboembolism, including deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, especially after orthopedic or abdominal surgery and in selected acute coronary syndrome settings such as unstable angina or non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction.

Name: Vinblastine
Description: Vinblastine (DrugBank DB00570) is a complex dimeric indole-dihydroindole alkaloid of the vinca alkaloid class, composed of catharanthine- and vindoline-derived polycyclic subunits linked into a highly oxygenated, nitrogen-containing bisindole framework with multiple fused/bridged rings, ester and methoxy substituents, and a characteristic vindoline-catharanthine scaffold that defines its tubulin-binding pharmacophore; it is therefore categorized chemically as a natural-product-derived antimitotic microtubule inhibitor, closely related to similar vinca agents such as vincristine, vinorelbine, vindesine, and semisynthetically to vinflunine. Its principal target is tubulin, especially the vinca-binding site on beta-tubulin within alpha/beta-tubulin heterodimers, leading to inhibition of microtubule polymerization, mitotic arrest, and apoptosis. Pharmacokinetically, vinblastine is administered intravenously because oral absorption is poor and unreliable, distributes extensively into tissues with high protein and cellular binding, undergoes predominant hepatic CYP3A4-mediated metabolism to active and inactive metabolites including desacetylvinblastine, and is eliminated mainly via biliary/fecal excretion with lesser renal clearance; dose reduction is important in hepatic impairment. Major toxicities include dose-limiting myelosuppression, especially neutropenia and leukopenia, along with mucositis, ileus, SIADH, vesicant local tissue injury after extravasation, and neurotoxicity that is generally less prominent than with vincristine. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, constipation, stomatitis, alopecia, fatigue, fever, and peripheral neuropathic symptoms. Clinically, vinblastine is used in Hodgkin lymphoma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, testicular germ cell tumors, Kaposi sarcoma, histiocytosis, and selected breast or bladder cancer regimens, often in combination protocols such as ABVD or cisplatin-based therapy.

Name: Propranolol
Description: Propranolol (DrugBank DB00571) is a lipophilic aryloxypropanolamine composed of a naphthalene ring linked through an ether to a chiral 2-hydroxy-3-isopropylaminopropyl side chain, placing it in the beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist class and more specifically the nonselective beta-blocker subclass built on the classic aryloxypropanolamine scaffold; structurally and pharmacologically similar agents include nadolol, timolol, pindolol, metoprolol, and atenolol, although propranolol is distinguished by its high membrane permeability and central nervous system penetration. Its principal targets are beta-1 adrenergic receptor and beta-2 adrenergic receptor, with lesser activity reported in relation to beta-3 adrenergic receptor and ancillary membrane-stabilizing sodium channel-blocking effects at higher concentrations. It is well absorbed orally but undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism, yielding variable bioavailability, is widely distributed with high protein binding, crosses the blood-brain barrier, is metabolized mainly by CYP2D6, CYP1A2, and CYP2C19 to active and inactive metabolites including 4-hydroxypropranolol, and is excreted predominantly in urine as metabolites. Toxicity reflects exaggerated beta-blockade, including bradycardia, hypotension, atrioventricular block, bronchospasm, hypoglycemia, seizures, and coma in overdose, with particular risk in asthma, diabetes, and severe conduction disease. Indications and clinical uses include hypertension, angina, rate control in supraventricular tachyarrhythmias, secondary prevention after myocardial infarction, essential tremor, migraine prophylaxis, hyperthyroid symptom control, performance anxiety, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, portal hypertension, and infantile hemangioma; common adverse effects include fatigue, dizziness, depression, sleep disturbance, cold extremities, exercise intolerance, sexual dysfunction, and gastrointestinal upset.

Name: Fenoprofen
Description: Fenoprofen (DrugBank DB00573) is a propionic acid derivative nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug of the arylalkanoic acid class, structurally characterized by a 2-phenylpropionic acid core bearing a biphenyl-like aryl ether arrangement in which a propionic acid side chain is attached to a substituted phenyl ring linked through oxygen to a second phenyl ring; thus its principal scaffold is the profen, specifically aryl-propionic acid, scaffold. It is chemically and pharmacologically similar to other profen NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, ketoprofen, flurbiprofen, and naproxen, which share cyclooxygenase inhibition and anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antipyretic effects. Fenoprofen is generally well absorbed orally, reaches peak plasma concentrations within a few hours, is highly albumin bound, distributes mainly within the vascular/extracellular compartment, undergoes substantial hepatic metabolism primarily by conjugation and oxidative biotransformation to inactive metabolites, and is excreted predominantly in urine as metabolites with a relatively short elimination half-life requiring repeated dosing. Its main targets are prostaglandin G/H synthase 1 and 2, namely PTGS1/COX-1 and PTGS2/COX-2, leading to reduced prostaglandin synthesis. It is indicated for symptomatic treatment of rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, and mild-to-moderate pain, including musculoskeletal pain and dysmenorrhea in some settings. Adverse effects include dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, edema, and rash; serious toxicity includes peptic ulceration, gastrointestinal bleeding, renal impairment, fluid retention, hypertension exacerbation, hypersensitivity reactions including bronchospasm, hepatotoxicity, and class-associated cardiovascular thrombotic risk. Clinically, it has been used as an oral anti-inflammatory and analgesic when reduction of joint pain, stiffness, and inflammatory symptoms is required.

Name: Fenfluramine
Description: Fenfluramine (DB00574) is a fluorinated substituted amphetamine characterized structurally as N-ethyl-alpha-methyl-3-(trifluoromethyl)phenethylamine, a lipophilic aromatic amine bearing a phenethylamine/amphetamine core with a meta-trifluoromethyl phenyl substituent and a secondary amine; chemically it belongs to the amphetamine-related anorectic and serotonergic agent class, with a substituted phenethylamine scaffold. Closely related drugs include dexfenfluramine, phentermine, amphetamine, and other monoaminergic appetite suppressants, although fenfluramine is distinguished by strong serotonergic activity. Its principal pharmacology involves increasing extracellular serotonin through interaction with the serotonin transporter SLC6A4 and promoting 5-HT release; norfenfluramine, its active metabolite, also has agonist activity at serotonin receptors including HTR2B, HTR2C, and to a lesser extent HTR2A, a profile relevant to both efficacy and toxicity. Fenfluramine is orally absorbed, widely distributed with CNS penetration, hepatically metabolized mainly by cytochrome P450 enzymes including CYP1A2, CYP2B6, and CYP2D6 to norfenfluramine and other metabolites, and eliminated primarily in urine as parent drug and metabolites. Historically it was indicated for obesity as an anorectic, and more recently, at lower controlled doses, for seizures associated with Dravet syndrome and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. Toxicities include serotonergic and sympathomimetic adverse effects, CNS depression or agitation in overdose, and especially valvular heart disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension linked to HTR2B activation. Common adverse effects include decreased appetite, weight loss, diarrhea, fatigue, somnolence, pyrexia, and reduced growth velocity in children. Clinically, its use has shifted from withdrawn anti-obesity combinations such as fen-phen to tightly monitored antiseizure therapy requiring cardiac surveillance.

Name: Clonidine
Description: Clonidine (DrugBank DB00575) is a centrally acting imidazoline derivative whose structure consists of a 2,6-dichlorophenyl ring linked through an anilino nitrogen to a cyclic amidine/imidazoline moiety, giving a compact, basic, lipophilic aryl-imidazoline architecture; chemically it is categorized as an antihypertensive sympatholytic and alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonist, with an imidazoline scaffold shared with related agents such as guanfacine, guanabenz, dexmedetomidine, tizanidine, and the topical analogue brimonidine. Its principal targets are alpha-2A, alpha-2B, and alpha-2C adrenergic receptors, with clinically important central alpha-2A agonism reducing sympathetic outflow, and it also shows affinity for imidazoline-binding sites, particularly nischarin/IRAS-related imidazoline receptors. Clonidine is well absorbed orally, has substantial bioavailability, readily crosses the blood-brain barrier, distributes widely with moderate protein binding, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated largely by the kidney as unchanged drug with a half-life that typically supports twice-daily dosing but is prolonged in renal impairment. It is indicated for hypertension and is also used for ADHD, opioid, nicotine and alcohol withdrawal symptoms, menopausal flushing, diarrhea related to autonomic dysfunction, and adjunctive analgesia or sedation; clinical use includes oral tablets, transdermal patches, and epidural formulations. Toxicity reflects excessive alpha-2 agonism and includes hypotension, bradycardia, sedation, miosis, respiratory depression, and CNS depression, while abrupt withdrawal can precipitate rebound hypertension and tachycardia. Common adverse effects include dry mouth, constipation, dizziness, fatigue, somnolence, sexual dysfunction, and orthostatic symptoms.

Name: Sulfamethizole
Description: Sulfamethizole (DrugBank DB00576) is a short-acting synthetic sulfonamide antibacterial built on the p-aminobenzenesulfonamide core, in which an aniline ring bearing a para-amino group is linked through a sulfonamide to a 5-membered nitrogen- and sulfur-containing heteroaryl substituent, giving the classic sulfonamide pharmacophore with a thiazolyl/isothiazolyl-type scaffold that governs antibacterial activity and physicochemical behavior. Chemically, it belongs to the sulfonamide anti-infectives, with a sulfanilamide scaffold closely related to sulfisoxazole, sulfamethoxazole, sulfadiazine, sulfathiazole, and sulfamethazine, all of which act as structural analogs of para-aminobenzoic acid. Its principal target is bacterial dihydropteroate synthase, whose inhibition blocks folate biosynthesis and thereby suppresses nucleotide synthesis and bacterial growth. Sulfamethizole is generally well absorbed orally, distributes mainly in extracellular fluids with variable protein binding, undergoes limited hepatic biotransformation including N4-acetylation, and is eliminated predominantly by the kidneys via glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, achieving high urinary concentrations but requiring caution in renal impairment. Toxicities are those typical of sulfonamides, including crystalluria, hematuria, interstitial nephritis, hypersensitivity reactions, fever, rash, urticaria, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, hepatotoxicity, and hematologic injury such as hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, thrombocytopenia, or megaloblastic effects, with kernicterus risk in neonates. Clinically it has been used mainly for susceptible urinary tract infections such as cystitis and pyelonephritis, and historically for other uncomplicated infections when organisms are sulfonamide-sensitive, though use has declined because of resistance and safer alternatives.

Name: Valaciclovir
Description: Valaciclovir (DrugBank DB00577) is the L-valyl ester prodrug of aciclovir, structurally defined by an acyclic guanine nucleoside analogue scaffold in which a 2-aminopurine-6-one base is attached to a hydroxyethoxymethyl side chain and esterified with L-valine to enhance intestinal transport; chemically it belongs to the purine nucleoside analogue antivirals and more specifically the carbocyclic/acyclic guanosine analogue class, with an aciclovir-like guanine-acyclic side-chain scaffold. Closely related drugs include aciclovir itself, famciclovir/penciclovir, ganciclovir, and valganciclovir, which share nucleoside analogue antiviral pharmacology. After oral administration, valaciclovir is rapidly absorbed, partly via peptide transport mechanisms, and undergoes extensive first-pass hydrolysis by valaciclovir hydrolase to aciclovir and L-valine, producing substantially greater oral bioavailability than aciclovir; aciclovir distributes widely into body fluids and tissues including cerebrospinal fluid, has low protein binding, undergoes minimal further metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by renal glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, so dose reduction is required in renal impairment. Its principal pharmacologic target is viral DNA polymerase after intracellular conversion of aciclovir to the triphosphate, with initial phosphorylation mainly by herpesvirus thymidine kinase in HSV-1, HSV-2, and VZV infected cells. It is indicated for herpes zoster, genital herpes, herpes labialis, and suppression or treatment of recurrent HSV infections. Adverse effects commonly include headache, nausea, abdominal pain, and dizziness; important toxicities include crystal nephropathy, acute kidney injury, neurotoxicity such as confusion or hallucinations, and rare thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura/hemolytic uremic syndrome, particularly at high doses or in immunocompromised patients. Clinically, it is widely used for shingles treatment, episodic and suppressive genital herpes therapy, cold sore treatment, and reduction of HSV transmission risk.

Name: Carbenicillin
Description: Carbenicillin (DrugBank DB00578) is a semisynthetic antipseudomonal beta-lactam antibiotic of the penicillin class whose structure consists of the canonical penam nucleus, a fused beta-lactam and thiazolidine bicyclic system, bearing an acylamino side chain with a carboxybenzyl substituent that increases activity against gram-negative bacilli; chemically it is categorized as a carboxypenicillin, and its core scaffold is the 6-aminopenicillanic acid penam framework. Closely related drugs include ticarcillin and other extended-spectrum penicillins such as ampicillin and piperacillin, which share the beta-lactam mechanism but differ in side-chain-driven spectrum. Carbenicillin acts by covalently acylating bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, especially transpeptidases such as PBP1 and PBP3, thereby blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking and cell-wall synthesis. It was used mainly for susceptible Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Proteus infections, including urinary tract infection, bacteremia, pneumonia, and other serious gram-negative infections. Orally, the indanyl ester prodrug improves absorption, whereas parenteral carbenicillin distributes mainly in extracellular fluid, reaches urine well, has limited intracellular penetration, low protein binding relative to some penicillins, minimal metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by renal tubular secretion and glomerular filtration, with dose adjustment in renal impairment. Toxicities include hypersensitivity reactions up to anaphylaxis, dose-related sodium load and fluid retention, hypokalemia, platelet dysfunction with bleeding, neurotoxicity including seizures at high concentrations or renal failure, and superinfection such as Clostridioides difficile colitis. Common adverse effects include rash, fever, diarrhea, nausea, phlebitis, eosinophilia, and laboratory evidence of renal or electrolyte disturbance. Clinically, it was historically used as a hospital antipseudomonal agent, sometimes in combination with aminoglycosides for severe systemic infections.

Name: Mazindol
