Description: Mazindol (DrugBank DB00579) is a tricyclic imidazoisoindole-derived anorectic with a rigid polycyclic aromatic structure containing a fused imidazole-like heterocycle linked to an isoindole framework and a chlorophenyl substituent, features that confer lipophilicity and potent central monoamine reuptake inhibition; chemically it is categorized as a sympathomimetic anorexiant and central nervous system stimulant, and its core scaffold is best described as a substituted tricyclic imidazoisoindole/isoindoline system rather than a classical phenethylamine, although it is pharmacologically similar to appetite suppressants such as phentermine, diethylpropion, amphetamine, and related catecholaminergic stimulants. Its principal targets are the norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2 and dopamine transporter SLC6A3, with weaker effects on the serotonin transporter SLC6A4, producing appetite suppression through enhanced synaptic catecholamine signaling. After oral administration mazindol is absorbed adequately, distributes systemically including to the CNS, undergoes limited to moderate hepatic biotransformation to inactive or less active metabolites, and is eliminated primarily in urine as parent drug and metabolites, with a relatively prolonged effect permitting once-daily dosing in some regimens. It is indicated for short-term management of exogenous obesity as an adjunct to caloric restriction, for example in obese patients requiring temporary appetite control. Toxicity reflects stimulant and sympathomimetic excess, including tachycardia, hypertension, agitation, insomnia, dependence liability, and, in overdose, arrhythmia, seizures, or psychosis; common adverse effects include dry mouth, constipation, nervousness, palpitations, headache, dizziness, and urinary retention. Clinically, it has been used as a short-course anti-obesity agent and has also been explored in disorders such as narcolepsy and attention-related symptoms, though obesity treatment remains its canonical use.

Name: Lactulose
Description: Lactulose (DrugBank DB00581) is a synthetic, nonabsorbable disaccharide composed of galactose linked to fructose through a β-1,4 glycosidic bond, making it a highly hydroxylated carbohydrate with a flexible polyol-like sugar framework; chemically it belongs to the laxative saccharides and osmotic cathartics, and its core scaffold is a keto-disaccharide closely related to lactose, from which it is derived by isomerization of the glucose moiety to fructose. Similar drugs include other osmotic laxatives such as lactitol, sorbitol, polyethylene glycol, and the disaccharide-derived agent lactulose analog lactitol, as well as nonabsorbable agents used for hepatic encephalopathy. Pharmacokinetically, lactulose is minimally absorbed in the small intestine, remains largely confined to the gut lumen, and reaches the colon intact, where bacterial fermentation converts it to low-molecular-weight organic acids including lactic, acetic, and formic acids; this acidification traps ammonia as ammonium, alters the colonic microbiome, increases osmotic water retention, and promotes peristalsis, with negligible systemic distribution and excretion primarily in feces, while small absorbed fractions may be excreted unchanged in urine. Its pharmacology is mediated mainly by physicochemical and microbiome-dependent effects rather than high-affinity human protein targets, so no definitive canonical target protein is typically assigned. Indications include chronic constipation and prevention or treatment of portal-systemic encephalopathy or hepatic encephalopathy with hyperammonemia. Toxicity is usually dose related and gastrointestinal, including diarrhea, abdominal cramping, flatulence, dehydration, and electrolyte disturbances such as hypokalemia or hypernatremia; excessive use can cause severe fluid loss, and caution is warranted in diabetics and patients requiring restricted galactose intake. Clinically, it is widely used orally or rectally to produce 2–3 soft stools daily in hepatic encephalopathy and as a titratable osmotic laxative for constipation.

Name: Voriconazole
Description: Voriconazole (DrugBank DB00582) is a second-generation synthetic triazole antifungal whose structure is characterized by a fluoropyrimidine-containing azole with a central chiral secondary alcohol, a 1,2,4-triazole ring, and fluorinated aryl substituents that increase lipophilicity and antifungal potency; chemically it belongs to the triazole antifungal class and is built on an azole–aryl alcohol scaffold closely related to fluconazole, with similar drugs including fluconazole, itraconazole, posaconazole, isavuconazole, and ketoconazole. Its principal antifungal target is fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase, the CYP51 enzyme encoded by ERG11/CYP51, causing depletion of ergosterol and disruption of fungal membrane integrity; voriconazole also inhibits human CYP2C19, CYP2C9, and CYP3A4, which underlies many interactions. It is well absorbed orally with high bioavailability, distributes widely into tissues including lung and central nervous system, is moderately protein bound, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism predominantly via CYP2C19 with contributions from CYP2C9 and CYP3A4, shows nonlinear pharmacokinetics and major pharmacogenetic variability, and is eliminated mainly as inactive metabolites in urine with minimal unchanged renal excretion. It is indicated for invasive aspergillosis, candidemia and other serious Candida infections, esophageal candidiasis, and difficult infections due to Scedosporium apiospermum and Fusarium species. Toxicities include hepatotoxicity, neurotoxicity, visual disturbance, phototoxicity, QT prolongation, hallucinations, and with prolonged use periostitis and increased cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma risk. Common adverse effects include blurred vision, color perception changes, rash, nausea, vomiting, elevated transaminases, headache, and edema. Clinically, it is used as first-line therapy for invasive aspergillosis and as oral step-down or targeted therapy in severe mold and yeast infections, especially when CNS penetration or broad mold coverage is needed.

Name: Levocarnitine
Description: Levocarnitine (DrugBank DB00583) is the naturally occurring L-isomer of carnitine, a small highly polar quaternary ammonium hydroxy acid whose structure consists of a trimethylated ammonium headgroup linked through a short carbon chain to a chiral secondary alcohol and a terminal carboxylate; chemically it is classified as a carnitine derivative, zwitterionic betaine, and endogenous amino acid-like nutrient, with a butyrobetaine/carnitine scaffold. Closely related agents include acetyl-L-carnitine, propionyl-L-carnitine, and the racemate D,L-carnitine, while mechanistically analogous metabolic therapies are sometimes compared with coenzyme Q10. Its principal functional targets are the mitochondrial carnitine shuttle components SLC22A5/OCTN2, CPT1A/CPT1B, CPT2, and the carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase SLC25A20, through which it facilitates transport of long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria and buffers acyl-CoA/acylcarnitine balance. Oral absorption is variable and saturable, bioavailability decreases at higher doses, distribution is extensive to skeletal and cardiac muscle, metabolism is limited with substantial conversion by gut microbiota to trimethylamine and hepatic trimethylamine N-oxide, and elimination is mainly renal with efficient tubular reabsorption that is impaired in deficiency states or dialysis. It is indicated for primary systemic carnitine deficiency and secondary carnitine deficiency, including in hemodialysis patients and valproate-associated depletion, and is used clinically for cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy, hypoketotic hypoglycemia, hyperammonemia, and fatigue related to deficiency. Toxicity is generally low, but high doses may cause gastrointestinal intolerance, fishy body odor, seizures in predisposed patients, and concern for TMAO-associated cardiovascular risk; common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhea, and restlessness.

Name: Enalapril
Description: Enalapril (DrugBank DB00584) is a dicarboxylate-containing angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor built as an L-alanyl-L-proline-derived peptidomimetic ester prodrug, structurally characterized by a substituted proline core, a secondary amide linkage, a phenethyl side chain, and an ethyl ester that enhances oral delivery before hydrolysis to the active diacid enalaprilat; chemically it belongs to the peptide-mimetic ACE inhibitor class, with a proline-based amino acid scaffold closely related to other ACE inhibitors such as ramipril, perindopril, lisinopril, quinapril, benazepril, and the prototype captopril, though unlike captopril it lacks a thiol group. Its principal target is angiotensin-converting enzyme, reducing formation of angiotensin II and secondarily lowering aldosterone signaling, with downstream effects on the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and bradykinin metabolism. After oral administration, enalapril is moderately absorbed, undergoes hepatic de-esterification to enalaprilat, reaches peak enalaprilat concentrations within hours, shows low-to-moderate protein binding, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid, and is eliminated predominantly by the kidney, so exposure is prolonged in renal impairment. Toxicity is largely mechanism-based and includes excessive hypotension, hyperkalemia, acute kidney injury, fetopathy in pregnancy, and rare but serious angioedema. Indications and clinical use include hypertension, symptomatic heart failure, asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction, and reduction of cardiovascular strain in patients with diabetic or proteinuric kidney disease. Common adverse effects include cough, dizziness, headache, fatigue, syncope, creatinine increase, rash, and gastrointestinal discomfort.

Name: Nizatidine
Description: Nizatidine (DrugBank DB00585) is a ranitidine-like histamine H2-receptor antagonist whose structure is characterized by a polar nitroethenediamine/guanidine-like pharmacophore linked through a thioether to a substituted thiazole ring, giving a heteroaromatic sulfur-containing scaffold with both basic and hydrogen-bonding functionalities; chemically it is classified as an H2 antihistamine and antiulcer agent, and its core scaffold is best described as a thiazolyl-thioethyl nitroethenediamine framework. It is closely related to other H2 blockers such as ranitidine, cimetidine, famotidine, and roxatidine, which share the strategy of mimicking histamine at the H2 receptor while reducing cholinergic activity. Its principal target is the histamine H2 receptor, encoded by HRH2, on gastric parietal cells, where antagonism suppresses basal and stimulated gastric acid secretion. Orally, nizatidine is rapidly and well absorbed with relatively high bioavailability, low to moderate protein binding, broad extracellular distribution, limited hepatic metabolism compared with some earlier H2 antagonists, and predominantly renal excretion of unchanged drug, so dose reduction is important in renal impairment. Toxicity is generally low but can include CNS effects such as confusion or somnolence, especially in older adults or renally impaired patients, reversible liver enzyme elevations, hypersensitivity reactions, and rare hematologic events; overdose is usually expected to exaggerate these effects rather than produce unique organ toxicity. Indications and clinical use include duodenal ulcer, benign gastric ulcer, gastroesophageal reflux disease, erosive esophagitis, dyspepsia, and pathological hypersecretory states, with common adverse effects including headache, dizziness, diarrhea, nausea, abdominal discomfort, and less commonly rash or fatigue.

Name: Diclofenac
Description: Diclofenac (DrugBank DB00586) is an arylacetic acid nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug characterized structurally by a dichlorinated aniline linked through a secondary amino bridge to a phenylacetic acid moiety, giving a lipophilic diarylamine/acetic acid architecture with a 2-anilino-phenylacetic acid scaffold; it is therefore classified within the phenylacetic acid NSAID subclass, with related or similar drugs including aceclofenac, indomethacin, sulindac, ketorolac, and to a lesser extent other cyclooxygenase inhibitors such as ibuprofen and naproxen. Its principal pharmacologic targets are prostaglandin G/H synthase 1 and 2, COX-1 and COX-2, with consequent suppression of prostaglandin synthesis, and ancillary effects on lipoxygenase-linked pathways and ion channels have been described. Diclofenac is indicated for pain and inflammatory disorders such as osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute musculoskeletal pain, dysmenorrhea, migraine, and postoperative or ophthalmic inflammation. It is usually well absorbed orally but undergoes substantial first-pass metabolism, is highly albumin bound, distributes well into synovial fluid, is metabolized predominantly in the liver by CYP2C9 with glucuronidation and oxidative hydroxylation, and is excreted mainly as urinary and biliary metabolites with a short plasma half-life but longer tissue effect. Toxicity is typical of NSAIDs and includes dose-related gastrointestinal ulceration or bleeding, renal hypoperfusion and acute kidney injury, hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevation or rare severe liver injury, fluid retention, hypertension, and increased thrombotic cardiovascular risk. Common adverse effects include dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, rash, and edema. Clinically, it is widely used as oral, topical, injectable, and ophthalmic formulations for short-term analgesia and chronic anti-inflammatory therapy when risk-benefit is carefully assessed.

Name: Fluticasone propionate
Description: Fluticasone propionate (DrugBank DB00588) is a highly lipophilic, synthetic trifluorinated corticosteroid built on the pregnane steroid nucleus, featuring the characteristic four-ring glucocorticoid scaffold with a 6α-fluoro substituent, a 9α-fluoro/halogenated steroid pattern, a 16α-methyl group, hydroxyl and ketone functionalities, and a 17α-propionate ester with a thiofluoromethyl-containing side chain that enhances topical potency and receptor affinity while limiting systemic exposure; chemically it is classified as an inhaled and intranasal glucocorticoid corticosteroid, closely related to fluticasone furoate and broadly similar to other anti-inflammatory steroids such as budesonide, beclomethasone dipropionate, mometasone furoate, triamcinolone acetonide, and ciclesonide. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, with downstream repression of proinflammatory cytokines, eosinophil recruitment, and inflammatory gene transcription. After inhalation or intranasal use, oral absorption of swallowed drug is negligible because of very low gastrointestinal bioavailability and extensive first-pass metabolism; pulmonary or nasal deposition provides local action, plasma protein binding is high, distribution is tissue extensive, metabolism occurs mainly via CYP3A4 to inactive metabolites, and excretion is predominantly fecal with minimal renal elimination. It is indicated for persistent asthma, allergic rhinitis, nasal polyposis, and sometimes COPD in combination inhalers; common adverse effects include oropharyngeal candidiasis, dysphonia, throat irritation, epistaxis, headache, and cough, whereas excessive or prolonged exposure can cause adrenal suppression, hypercorticism, reduced growth velocity in children, decreased bone mineral density, cataracts, glaucoma, skin bruising, and increased infection risk. Clinically, it is used as maintenance inhalation therapy for asthma control and as intranasal therapy for seasonal or perennial rhinitis symptoms such as congestion, rhinorrhea, sneezing, and itching.

Name: Lisuride
Description: Lisuride (DrugBank DB00589) is a semisynthetic ergoline dopamine agonist whose structure is built on the rigid tetracyclic ergoline/lysergic acid-derived scaffold, incorporating an indole-containing fused ring system with a basic tertiary amine and urea-like amide substitution that confers high affinity at monoaminergic receptors; chemically it is classified as an ergot derivative and dopaminergic antiparkinson agent, with the ergoline scaffold placing it close to related drugs such as bromocriptine, cabergoline, pergolide, and the hallucinogenic ergoline analog LSD, although lisuride is distinguished by potent dopaminergic activity without prominent psychedelic effects at therapeutic doses. Its principal targets are dopamine D2, D3, and D4 receptors, with activity also reported at D1-family receptors, serotonin receptors including 5-HT1A and 5-HT2 subtypes, and alpha-adrenergic receptors, consistent with antiparkinsonian and prolactin-lowering actions. Lisuride is used for Parkinson disease, hyperprolactinemia, prolactinoma-related galactorrhea or amenorrhea, and sometimes migraine prophylaxis or restless legs symptoms. After oral administration it is absorbed but undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, resulting in relatively low bioavailability; it is widely distributed, extensively metabolized in the liver to less active metabolites, and excreted mainly in urine and partly in feces, with a short plasma half-life that may necessitate repeated dosing or transdermal delivery in some settings. Adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, headache, somnolence, dyskinesia, nasal congestion, hallucinations, confusion, and impulse-control disturbances; toxicity may present as severe hypotension, psychosis, or excessive dopaminergic stimulation, while ergot-related vasospasm is a theoretical or occasional concern. Clinically, it has been used as monotherapy or adjunctive therapy with levodopa in Parkinsonism and as an endocrine dopamine agonist to suppress prolactin secretion.

Name: Doxazosin
Description: Doxazosin (DrugBank DB00590) is a quinazoline-derived piperazine sulfonamide antihypertensive and urologic agent whose structure is centered on a 6,7-dimethoxyquinazoline aromatic heterobicycle linked through a piperazine ring to a benzodioxinyl carboxamide-containing moiety, giving it the characteristic quinazoline–piperazine scaffold shared by selective alpha-1 adrenergic antagonists. Chemically, it belongs to the arylpiperazine/quinazoline class, and its closest similar drugs include prazosin, terazosin, and alfuzosin, with mechanistic overlap also with tamsulosin and silodosin as alpha-1 blockers used in lower urinary tract symptoms. Its principal targets are alpha-1 adrenergic receptor subtypes ADRA1A, ADRA1B, and ADRA1D, producing peripheral vasodilation and relaxation of smooth muscle in the bladder neck and prostate. Orally administered doxazosin is well absorbed, has high bioavailability, extensive plasma protein binding, a relatively long elimination half-life permitting once-daily dosing, undergoes substantial hepatic metabolism mainly via O-demethylation and hydroxylation, including CYP3A-mediated pathways, and is excreted predominantly in feces with a smaller urinary component. It is indicated for hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia, including symptoms such as hesitancy, weak stream, incomplete emptying, and nocturia. Toxicity is dominated by exaggerated pharmacology, especially first-dose syncope, orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, and reflex tachycardia; overdose may cause marked hypotension. Common adverse effects include fatigue, headache, somnolence, edema, palpitations, and gastrointestinal upset. Clinically, it is used as monotherapy or adjunctive therapy for blood pressure control and to improve urinary flow and symptom burden in men with BPH.

Name: Fluocinolone acetonide
Description: Fluocinolone acetonide (DrugBank DB00591) is a synthetic fluorinated corticosteroid characterized by the classic pregnane steroid nucleus with fused cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene rings, a 1,4-diene-3,20-dione glucocorticoid framework, a 6α-fluoro substituent, 11β- and 21-hydroxyl groups, and a 16α,17α-acetonide ketal that increases lipophilicity and topical potency; it belongs to the chemical category of halogenated glucocorticoids and is built on the corticosteroid/prednisolone-like scaffold. Structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include triamcinolone acetonide, fluocinonide, fluticasone, betamethasone, dexamethasone, and hydrocortisone derivatives. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, with downstream repression of NF-κB, AP-1, PLA2-mediated eicosanoid synthesis, and multiple proinflammatory cytokines and adhesion pathways. Pharmacokinetically, topical, otic, intravitreal, and implant formulations are designed for local exposure; percutaneous absorption rises with inflamed skin, occlusion, larger treatment area, and prolonged use, distribution is largely tissue-local with systemic corticosteroid distribution when absorbed, metabolism occurs mainly hepatically via steroid-reductive and oxidative pathways with conjugation, and excretion is primarily renal as metabolites with some biliary elimination. It is indicated for corticosteroid-responsive inflammatory and pruritic dermatoses such as eczema, atopic dermatitis, seborrheic dermatitis, psoriasis, otic inflammation, and diabetic macular edema or chronic noninfectious posterior uveitis in ophthalmic implant use. Toxicities include local skin atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, delayed wound healing, superinfection, cataract and glaucoma in ocular use, and systemic HPA-axis suppression, hyperglycemia, Cushingoid features, and growth suppression in children when exposure is excessive; common adverse effects include burning, irritation, dryness, folliculitis, acneiform eruption, hypopigmentation, and secondary infection. Clinically it is used as a low- to medium-potency topical anti-inflammatory steroid and as a sustained-release intraocular corticosteroid for chronic retinal inflammatory disease.

Name: Piperazine
Description: Piperazine (DrugBank DB00592) is a small, highly water-soluble cyclic diamine composed of a six-membered saturated heterocycle containing two opposing secondary nitrogens, giving a flexible basic 1,4-diazacyclohexane structure that is readily protonated and forms pharmaceutically useful salts; chemically it belongs to the piperazine class of aliphatic nitrogen heterocycles and serves as the parent piperazine scaffold found widely in medicinal chemistry. Structurally related drugs include anthelmintic piperazine salts such as piperazine citrate and adipate, and the broader piperazine-containing drug family includes hydroxyzine, cetirizine, cyclizine, and fluphenazine, although these are pharmacologically distinct derivatives rather than direct equivalents. Piperazine acts primarily at helminth neuromuscular systems, with evidence for agonist-like effects at parasite inhibitory GABA-gated chloride channels and functional interference with cholinergic transmission, producing flaccid paralysis of susceptible worms such as Ascaris lumbricoides and Enterobius vermicularis; no single human therapeutic protein target is central to its classic use. After oral administration it is well absorbed, distributed mainly in extracellular water, undergoes limited metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged in urine, with renal function strongly influencing exposure and duration. Its main indication is treatment of ascariasis and enterobiasis, historically also used for other nematode infestations. Adverse effects are usually gastrointestinal or neurologic, including nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, dizziness, headache, drowsiness, and urticaria; toxicity at high doses or in renal impairment may cause tremor, ataxia, confusion, hallucinations, or seizures, with heightened risk in patients with epilepsy. Clinically, it has been used as an oral anthelmintic, often as piperazine citrate, to facilitate expulsion of paralyzed worms in uncomplicated intestinal roundworm and pinworm infection.

Name: Ethosuximide
Description: Ethosuximide (DrugBank DB00593) is a small cyclic imide anticonvulsant structurally defined as an alpha-ethyl, alpha-methyl-substituted succinimide, consisting of a five-membered pyrrolidine-2,5-dione ring bearing two carbonyls and lipophilic alkyl substituents that confer moderate CNS penetration; chemically it belongs to the succinimide class, with a succinimide/imide heterocycle scaffold that is closely related to methsuximide and phensuximide, and more distantly to other older anti-seizure agents such as trimethadione by shared use in absence epilepsy. Its principal pharmacologic target is the low-voltage-activated T-type calcium channel, especially thalamic Cav3 family currents implicated in corticothalamic oscillations underlying absence seizures, although precise binding to specific channel subunits is less completely defined than for many receptor-directed drugs. It is indicated primarily for uncomplicated absence seizures in epilepsy, particularly childhood absence epilepsy, and is used clinically as monotherapy or in combination when absence events predominate. Orally, it is well absorbed with high bioavailability, distributes widely including into cerebrospinal fluid, shows relatively low protein binding, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A-mediated oxidation to inactive metabolites, and is excreted predominantly in urine as metabolites with a smaller unchanged fraction; its long half-life supports once- or twice-daily dosing. Toxicity is usually dose-related and neurologic or gastrointestinal, but rare serious events include blood dyscrasias, lupus-like reactions, severe cutaneous reactions, and hepatotoxicity. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, anorexia, weight loss, fatigue, dizziness, headache, drowsiness, ataxia, hiccups, behavioral changes, and sleep disturbance.

Name: Amiloride
Description: Amiloride (DB00594) is a small, highly polar pyrazine-derived potassium-sparing diuretic built on a substituted pyrazine scaffold, specifically a pyrazinoyl-guanidine–like framework bearing amino and chloro substituents that confer strong basicity and activity at epithelial sodium transport pathways; chemically it is categorized as an acylguanidine/pyrazine diuretic and is closely related to other potassium-sparing agents and epithelial sodium channel blockers, with clinically relevant similar drugs including triamterene and the amiloride analog benzamil, and it is often pharmacodynamically compared with mineralocorticoid pathway potassium-sparing agents such as spironolactone and eplerenone. Its principal targets are the epithelial sodium channel ENaC subunits SCNN1A, SCNN1B, and SCNN1G in the distal nephron, with additional inhibitory activity reported against Na+/H+ exchangers such as SLC9A1 at higher concentrations. After oral administration, absorption is moderate and incomplete, distribution is limited by hydrophilicity and low protein binding, metabolism is minimal, and elimination occurs largely as unchanged drug in urine, so renal impairment prolongs exposure. Toxicity is dominated by hyperkalemia, which may produce weakness, paresthesias, arrhythmias, or fatal conduction abnormalities, with increased risk in kidney disease, diabetes, and combination therapy with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or potassium supplements; gastrointestinal intolerance and dehydration may also occur. Major adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, rash, and electrolyte disturbances. Clinically, amiloride is used for hypertension and edema, especially to prevent diuretic-induced hypokalemia when combined with thiazides or loop diuretics, and it is also used in heart failure-associated fluid retention, cirrhotic or nephrotic edema, lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, and Liddle syndrome.

Name: Oxytetracycline
Description: Oxytetracycline (DrugBank DB00595) is a naturally derived tetracycline antibiotic characterized by a rigid, linearly fused four-ring naphthacene core bearing multiple keto-enol and phenolic hydroxyl functionalities, an amide, and the characteristic C4 dimethylamino substituent, with an additional hydroxyl group distinguishing it from tetracycline; it belongs to the polyketide tetracycline class and shares the classic tetracycline scaffold found in tetracycline, doxycycline, demeclocycline, and minocycline. Similar drugs include other 30S ribosomal inhibitors such as tetracycline and doxycycline, and more distantly glycylcyclines such as tigecycline. Its antibacterial action is mediated primarily by binding the 30S bacterial ribosomal subunit, especially 16S rRNA within the A-site region, blocking aminoacyl-tRNA access and inhibiting protein synthesis; relevant target annotations therefore include the bacterial 30S ribosome and associated 16S rRNA-containing complexes. Oral absorption is moderate and reduced by food, dairy, and polyvalent cations; distribution is wide into many tissues but variable into cerebrospinal fluid, with deposition in bone and teeth, limited metabolism, and predominantly renal excretion with some biliary/fecal elimination, leading to prolonged exposure in renal impairment. Indications include susceptible infections such as acne vulgaris, chlamydial infections, rickettsial disease, respiratory tract infections, and certain zoonoses. Toxicities include tooth discoloration, enamel hypoplasia, growth inhibition in children, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity including outdated Fanconi-like syndrome from degraded products, and photosensitivity. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, esophagitis, candidiasis, rash, and superinfection. Clinically, oxytetracycline has been used orally and topically for acne, ocular or skin infections, and other susceptible Gram-positive, Gram-negative, atypical, and intracellular bacterial infections when resistance patterns permit.

Name: Ulobetasol
Description: Ulobetasol (DrugBank DB00596), also known as halobetasol, is a highly potent topical synthetic corticosteroid whose structure is based on the pregnane glucocorticoid nucleus, specifically a hydrocortisone-like steroid scaffold modified by 9-fluoro, 11β-hydroxyl, 16β-methyl, 17-propionate, 20-keto, and 21-chloro substituents that enhance lipophilicity, receptor affinity, and topical anti-inflammatory potency. It belongs chemically to the halogenated corticosteroids and more specifically the super-high-potency topical glucocorticoids, with a corticosteroid cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene scaffold. Similar drugs include clobetasol propionate, betamethasone dipropionate, fluocinonide, and diflorasone diacetate, which share a halogenated topical steroid pharmacophore. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor encoded by NR3C1, with downstream suppression of phospholipase A2-mediated eicosanoid formation, cytokine transcription, and inflammatory cell activity. After topical administration, absorption is generally limited but increases with inflamed or occluded skin, large treatment area, prolonged use, or impaired barrier function; distribution is mainly local to skin with systemic exposure possible, metabolism occurs primarily hepatically after systemic absorption as with other corticosteroids, and excretion is mainly via renal elimination of metabolites with some biliary/fecal contribution. It is indicated for corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses such as plaque psoriasis, eczema, and dermatitis, particularly when severe, localized, and refractory. Adverse effects include burning, stinging, pruritus, dryness, folliculitis, acneiform eruption, telangiectasia, striae, skin atrophy, and secondary infection; toxicities include reversible hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis suppression, Cushingoid features, hyperglycemia, glucosuria, and rare growth suppression in children. Clinically, it is used short term as cream, ointment, or lotion for thick inflammatory plaques or recalcitrant lesions, with avoidance of long duration, occlusion, and extensive body-surface application to minimize systemic corticosteroid toxicity.

Name: Labetalol
Description: Labetalol (DrugBank DB00598) is a lipophilic aryloxypropanolamine antihypertensive with a salicylamide-related aromatic system, characterized structurally by a substituted phenyl ring linked through an ether-containing propanolamine chain to a secondary amine and bearing an amide and hydroxyl functionality; it is administered as a racemate whose stereoisomers contribute differently to pharmacology. Chemically it is a mixed alpha- and beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist in the beta-blocker class, built on the classic phenoxypropanolamine/beta-amino alcohol scaffold seen in related adrenergic antagonists. Similar drugs include carvedilol, propranolol, metoprolol, and timolol, although carvedilol most closely resembles labetalol in combined alpha1- and beta-blocking activity. Its principal targets are adrenergic receptors ADRB1, ADRB2, and ADRA1, producing reduced peripheral vascular resistance with limited reflex tachycardia. After oral administration, labetalol is well absorbed but undergoes substantial first-pass metabolism, giving moderate bioavailability; it distributes widely, is moderately protein bound, is extensively metabolized in the liver mainly by glucuronidation to inactive metabolites, and is excreted predominantly in urine with some fecal elimination, with an elimination half-life typically around 5 to 8 hours. Toxicity is dominated by exaggerated adrenergic blockade, including hypotension, bradycardia, heart block, bronchospasm, dizziness, and overdose-related cardiogenic shock or seizures; rare but important hepatotoxicity has been reported. Indications include chronic hypertension, hypertensive urgency or emergency, and pregnancy-associated hypertension such as preeclampsia. Common adverse effects include fatigue, orthostatic hypotension, nausea, scalp tingling, sexual dysfunction, and nasal congestion. Clinically, it is used orally for long-term blood-pressure control and intravenously for rapid treatment of severe hypertension, including perioperative and obstetric settings.

Name: Thiopental
Description: Thiopental (DrugBank DB00599) is an ultrashort-acting sulfur-containing barbiturate whose structure is a substituted barbituric acid core in which the C2 carbonyl oxygen is replaced by sulfur, forming a thiobarbiturate ring, with lipophilic alkyl substituents at the 5-position that drive rapid central nervous system penetration; chemically it belongs to the barbiturate sedative-hypnotics and is built on the barbituric acid/thiobarbituric acid scaffold. Closely related drugs include methohexital, pentobarbital, secobarbital, and phenobarbital, with thiopental distinguished by especially rapid onset and brief hypnotic effect after intravenous administration. Its principal pharmacologic target is the GABAA receptor chloride channel complex, where it acts as a positive allosteric modulator and, at higher concentrations, a direct agonist; it may also inhibit excitatory AMPA-type glutamate signaling. After IV dosing, onset occurs within seconds because of high lipid solubility, distribution is initially to brain then rapidly redistributes to muscle and fat, terminating anesthesia after a bolus; it is extensively protein bound, hepatically metabolized mainly by oxidative desulfuration and other biotransformation pathways to less active metabolites, and excreted primarily in urine. Toxicity is dominated by dose-dependent respiratory depression, apnea, hypotension, myocardial depression, prolonged coma, and accumulation with repeated dosing, with greater risk in shock, hepatic dysfunction, or porphyria, which it can precipitate. Adverse effects include laryngospasm, bronchospasm, nausea, delirium, tissue necrosis after extravasation, and severe injury with intra-arterial injection. Clinically, thiopental has been used for induction of general anesthesia, brief procedural hypnosis, control of refractory status epilepticus, and reduction of intracranial pressure in neurocritical care.

Name: Linezolid
Description: Linezolid (DrugBank DB00601) is a fully synthetic oxazolidinone antibacterial whose structure is defined by a 2-oxazolidinone ring bearing an aryl substituent and an acetamidomethyl side chain, linked to a fluorinated phenyl ring and a morpholine moiety that together confer potent Gram-positive activity and oral bioavailability. Chemically, it belongs to the oxazolidinone class, and its core scaffold is the aryl-substituted 2-oxazolidinone pharmacophore exemplified by linezolid and related agents such as tedizolid; more distant similar drugs include other anti-MRSA agents like chloramphenicol, clindamycin, and quinupristin/dalfopristin, which also inhibit bacterial protein synthesis though by different binding interactions. Linezolid targets the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit, binding 23S rRNA within the peptidyl transferase center of the 50S/70S initiation complex and thereby preventing formation of the functional initiation complex; resistance determinants include methyltransferase-mediated ribosomal modification such as Cfr. It is well absorbed orally with near-complete bioavailability, distributes widely into lung, skin, soft tissue, and cerebrospinal fluid to a modest extent, undergoes predominantly non-CYP oxidation to inactive metabolites, and is eliminated by both renal and nonrenal routes with a half-life of about 4 to 6 hours. Indications and clinical use include pneumonia, complicated and uncomplicated skin and soft tissue infections, diabetic foot infection, and vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus or methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infections. Important toxicities and adverse effects include myelosuppression, especially thrombocytopenia, peripheral and optic neuropathy with prolonged use, lactic acidosis, gastrointestinal upset, headache, serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs, and mild monoamine oxidase inhibition-related pressor reactions.

Name: Ivermectin
Description: Ivermectin (DrugBank DB00602) is a semisynthetic avermectin composed primarily of 22,23-dihydroavermectin B1a with a minor B1b component; structurally it is a highly lipophilic 16-membered macrocyclic lactone bearing a fused spiroketal-like polyether region, multiple hydroxyl substituents, olefinic functionality, and a disaccharide at C13, placing it in the macrocyclic lactone antiparasitic class and specifically the avermectin scaffold. Closely related drugs include abamectin, doramectin, eprinomectin, selamectin, and the milbemycins such as moxidectin, which share a similar macrocyclic endectocide framework. Its principal pharmacologic targets are glutamate-gated chloride channels in nematodes and arthropods, with secondary activity at ligand-gated chloride channels related to GABAA signaling; mammalian P-glycoprotein, encoded by ABCB1/MDR1, is important in limiting CNS penetration. Oral absorption is variable but enhanced by fatty food, distribution is extensive because of high lipophilicity and protein binding, metabolism occurs mainly hepatically via CYP3A4-dependent oxidation, and excretion is predominantly biliary/fecal with minimal renal clearance and an elimination half-life on the order of about 12 to 36 hours depending on formulation and host factors. It is indicated for onchocerciasis, strongyloidiasis, lymphatic filariasis control, scabies, pediculosis, and other ectoparasitic or nematode infections, and is used clinically as single-dose or repeated oral therapy and as topical formulations. Adverse effects include pruritus, rash, dizziness, nausea, diarrhea, and edema, while toxicity may manifest as neurotoxicity, ataxia, confusion, hypotension, seizures, or coma, especially in overdose, increased CNS exposure, or heavy parasite burden with inflammatory Mazzotti-type reactions.

Name: Medroxyprogesterone acetate
Description: Medroxyprogesterone acetate (DrugBank DB00603) is a semisynthetic 17alpha-hydroxyprogesterone derivative in which the pregnane steroid nucleus retains the 3-keto-4-ene motif and bears a 6alpha-methyl substituent with acetylation of the 17alpha-hydroxyl group, features that increase oral activity and progestational potency; chemically it is a progestin, more specifically an acetylated pregnane steroid, built on the progesterone/17alpha-hydroxyprogesterone scaffold. Closely related or pharmacologically similar drugs include progesterone, megestrol acetate, hydroxyprogesterone caproate, cyproterone acetate, chlormadinone acetate, and depot medroxyprogesterone formulations. Its principal target is the progesterone receptor, with lesser activity at the glucocorticoid receptor and weak androgen receptor interactions, producing antigonadotropic effects through hypothalamic-pituitary suppression. After oral administration it is reasonably absorbed but undergoes first-pass metabolism; after intramuscular depot injection absorption is slow and prolonged, with wide tissue distribution, high protein binding, hepatic metabolism mainly via reduction and CYP3A4-associated biotransformation, and excretion predominantly as urinary metabolites with some fecal elimination. It is indicated for contraception, abnormal uterine bleeding, secondary amenorrhea, endometriosis, menopausal hormone therapy combinations, and palliative treatment of endometrial or renal carcinoma. Adverse effects commonly include menstrual irregularity, amenorrhea, weight gain, edema, mood changes, headache, decreased bone mineral density, and delayed return of fertility; serious toxicity can include thromboembolic events, hypertension, hepatic dysfunction, depression, and fetal harm if used in pregnancy, while overdose is usually limited to nausea or withdrawal bleeding. Clinically it is used as oral tablets and long-acting depot injections for contraception, menstrual suppression, and gynecologic or oncologic indications.

Name: Cisapride
Description: Cisapride (DrugBank DB00604) is a substituted piperidinyl benzamide gastroprokinetic agent whose structure consists of an anisamide-like aromatic benzamide core bearing methoxy substitution and a fluorinated aromatic moiety linked through a piperidine-containing side chain, giving it the characteristic scaffold of a serotonergic prokinetic benzamide rather than a dopamine antagonist scaffold. Chemically, it is classified as a serotonin 5-HT4 receptor agonist/prokinetic substituted benzamide, with related or similar drugs including metoclopramide, mosapride, renzapride, clebopride, and the withdrawn agent tegaserod in the broader serotonergic prokinetic class. Its principal target is HTR4, where agonism enhances acetylcholine release from enteric neurons and promotes upper and lower gastrointestinal motility; weaker interactions with other serotonergic sites have also been described. Cisapride is orally absorbed, undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism predominantly by CYP3A4 to norcisapride and other metabolites, is distributed systemically with moderate protein binding, and is eliminated mainly via feces and urine as metabolites, with exposure markedly increased by CYP3A4 inhibitors or hepatic impairment. It was indicated for symptomatic gastroesophageal reflux disease, diabetic and idiopathic gastroparesis, chronic constipation, dyspepsia, and other motility disorders, and clinically used to improve nocturnal heartburn, regurgitation, postprandial fullness, delayed gastric emptying, and sometimes pseudo-obstructive symptoms. Its major toxicity is dose- and exposure-related QT prolongation leading to torsades de pointes, ventricular arrhythmias, syncope, and sudden death, especially with macrolides, azole antifungals, protease inhibitors, grapefruit juice, electrolyte disturbance, or baseline cardiac disease. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, abdominal cramping, nausea, headache, and borborygmi.

Name: Sulindac
Description: Sulindac (DrugBank DB00605) is an indene-acetic acid nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug structurally characterized by a substituted indene core bearing a para-methylsulfinylbenzylidene moiety and an acetic acid side chain, making it a member of the arylalkanoic acid NSAID class; its core scaffold is best described as an indene/indenylidene acetic acid framework related to other acidic cyclooxygenase inhibitors. Similar drugs include indomethacin, diclofenac, etodolac, tolmetin, and other nonselective NSAIDs, although sulindac is distinctive as a prodrug sulfoxide that is reversibly reduced to the active sulfide metabolite and oxidized to an inactive sulfone. After oral administration it is well absorbed, highly protein bound, widely distributed, undergoes extensive hepatic and extrahepatic redox cycling, and is eliminated through both renal and biliary/fecal routes, with enterohepatic recirculation contributing to persistence of metabolites. Its principal targets are prostaglandin G/H synthase 1 and 2, also known as PTGS1/COX-1 and PTGS2/COX-2, leading to reduced prostaglandin synthesis; additional pharmacology relevant to chemoprevention has been linked in some studies to effects on apoptosis and Wnt/beta-catenin signaling. Clinically, it is indicated for osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute gouty arthritis, and painful inflammatory musculoskeletal conditions, and has also been used in familial adenomatous polyposis to reduce colorectal adenoma burden. Adverse effects and toxicities resemble other NSAIDs, including dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, peptic ulceration, gastrointestinal bleeding, hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, renal impairment, edema, hypertension, rash, dizziness, and rare severe hypersensitivity or Stevens-Johnson syndrome, with overdose or high-risk use increasing the likelihood of serious GI, renal, and cardiovascular complications.

Name: Nafcillin
Description: Nafcillin (DrugBank DB00607) is a semisynthetic, penicillinase-resistant beta-lactam antibiotic whose structure consists of the conserved penam nucleus, a fused beta-lactam and thiazolidine bicyclic system bearing the usual carboxylate and acylamino substituents, decorated with a bulky lipophilic naphthyl-containing side chain that sterically protects the beta-lactam from staphylococcal penicillinases; chemically it is an antistaphylococcal isoxazolyl-adjacent penicillin-class beta-lactam, with the core penam scaffold shared across penicillins. Similar drugs include oxacillin, cloxacillin, dicloxacillin, methicillin, and flucloxacillin, which likewise target penicillin-resistant staphylococci. Its main targets are bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, especially transpeptidases such as PBP1, PBP2, and PBP3, leading to inhibition of peptidoglycan cross-linking and cell-wall synthesis. Nafcillin is used primarily for infections caused by methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus, including bacteremia, endocarditis, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, pneumonia, cellulitis, and skin/soft-tissue infection. It is usually given parenterally because oral absorption is limited or unreliable; it distributes widely into extracellular fluids and inflamed tissues, shows substantial protein binding, undergoes partial hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated largely via biliary excretion with some renal clearance, making it useful when renal dysfunction limits other antistaphylococcal penicillins. Toxicities include hypersensitivity reactions up to anaphylaxis, hepatotoxicity such as cholestatic hepatitis or transaminase elevation, interstitial nephritis, neutropenia, phlebitis, electrolyte load issues, and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea. Common side effects include rash, fever, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, eosinophilia, and local infusion reactions, and clinically it remains a standard narrow-spectrum choice for serious MSSA infections when susceptibility is confirmed.

Name: Chloroquine
Description: Chloroquine (DB00608) is a synthetic 4-aminoquinoline antiprotozoal and immunomodulatory agent built on a planar quinoline heteroaromatic ring scaffold bearing a 7-chloro substituent and a 4-amino side chain that terminates in a basic diethylaminoalkyl moiety, a cationic amphiphilic architecture that promotes lysosomal trapping and heme-binding activity; chemically it belongs to the aminoquinoline class, with the 7-chloro-4-aminoquinoline scaffold shared by related drugs such as hydroxychloroquine, amodiaquine, quinacrine, and the structurally more distant quinine/mefloquine antimalarials. It is generally well absorbed orally, widely distributed with a very large volume of distribution, accumulates extensively in liver, spleen, kidney, lung, melanin-containing tissues, and retina, is partially metabolized hepatically mainly by CYP2C8 and CYP3A4/5 to desethylchloroquine and related metabolites, and is eliminated slowly through the kidney with a prolonged terminal half-life measured in days to weeks. Its principal targets/mechanistic effectors include ferriprotoporphyrin IX in Plasmodium food vacuoles, with inhibition of heme detoxification, and in human cells lysosomal acidification pathways and endosomal toll-like receptors TLR7 and TLR9. Indications include treatment and prophylaxis of chloroquine-sensitive malaria, extraintestinal amebiasis, and inflammatory disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus. Toxicity is clinically important and includes dose-related retinopathy, cardiomyopathy, QT prolongation and ventricular arrhythmias, hypoglycemia, neuropsychiatric effects, myopathy, and severe overdose toxicity with seizures and cardiovascular collapse; common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, headache, pruritus, dizziness, blurred vision, and skin hyperpigmentation. Clinically, it has been used for acute malaria attacks, malaria suppression in endemic travel, lupus rash and arthritis control, and selected hepatic amebiasis regimens, although resistance and safety concerns have limited use in many settings.

Name: Ethionamide
Description: Ethionamide (DrugBank DB00609) is a small, lipophilic thioamide antimycobacterial agent structurally defined as a nicotinamide analog in which the pyridine ring bears an ethyl substituent and the carboxamide oxygen is replaced by sulfur, giving a 2-ethylpyridine-4-carbothioamide framework; chemically it belongs to the thioamide/isonicotinic acid derivative class and is built on a substituted pyridine carbothioamide scaffold closely related to isoniazid and particularly the analog prothionamide, with functional similarity to other second-line antitubercular drugs such as para-aminosalicylic acid and cycloserine in multidrug-resistant regimens. It is a prodrug activated in Mycobacterium tuberculosis mainly by the flavin monooxygenase EthA, after which it forms an NAD adduct that inhibits the enoyl-acyl carrier protein reductase InhA, thereby blocking mycolic acid synthesis; EthR is a transcriptional repressor regulating EthA and is an indirect mechanistic protein of interest. Oral absorption is generally good, tissue distribution is broad including cerebrospinal fluid penetration, hepatic metabolism is extensive via oxidation to active and inactive sulfoxide and other metabolites, and renal excretion occurs mainly as metabolites with limited unchanged drug. Toxicity is dominated by dose-limiting gastrointestinal intolerance, hepatotoxicity ranging from transaminase elevation to hepatitis, neurotoxicity including peripheral neuropathy and psychotic reactions, and metabolic/endocrine effects such as hypothyroidism, especially with para-aminosalicylic acid. Indications are active tuberculosis, especially multidrug-resistant or refractory pulmonary and extrapulmonary disease, sometimes including meningeal infection because of CNS penetration. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, anorexia, metallic taste, weight loss, dizziness, depression, rash, and hepatotoxicity. Clinically, ethionamide is used only in combination regimens as a second-line antitubercular drug when first-line therapy cannot be used because of resistance or intolerance.

Name: Metaraminol
Description: Metaraminol (DrugBank DB00610) is a synthetic phenethylamine sympathomimetic whose structure is a substituted benzene ring bearing a benzylic hydroxyl group and a β-aminoethyl side chain with an additional ring hydroxyl substituent, giving a norepinephrine-like arylethanolamine architecture; chemically it is classified as a catecholamine-related adrenergic agonist/vasopressor, built on a phenylethanolamine scaffold closely related to metaraminol’s endogenous analogs and to other pressor amines such as norepinephrine, epinephrine, phenylephrine, ephedrine, and dopamine-derived vasopressors. Its principal pharmacology is direct and indirect adrenergic stimulation, acting mainly at alpha-1 adrenergic receptors and also promoting norepinephrine release from sympathetic nerve terminals; relevant targets therefore include ADRA1A, ADRA1B, ADRA1D, with lesser functional involvement of adrenergic pathways linked to norepinephrine transport and storage. After parenteral administration, especially intravenous use, onset is rapid; distribution is largely extracellular with limited CNS penetration relative to more lipophilic amines; metabolism occurs partly through hepatic and extrahepatic biotransformation including oxidative deamination and conjugative pathways, and elimination is mainly renal, with a clinically useful pressor duration longer than norepinephrine because of mixed direct/indirect action. It is indicated for acute hypotensive states, especially perioperative hypotension, spinal anesthesia-associated hypotension, and shock with low vascular tone. Toxicity reflects excessive adrenergic stimulation, including severe hypertension, reflex bradycardia, ventricular arrhythmias, myocardial ischemia, headache, pulmonary edema, and tissue necrosis after extravasation; adverse effects commonly include palpitations, anxiety, tremor, urinary retention, nausea, and reduced peripheral or renal perfusion. Clinically, metaraminol is used as an injectable vasopressor to restore blood pressure in anesthesia, critical care, and other settings of symptomatic hypotension.

Name: Butorphanol
Description: Butorphanol (DrugBank DB00611) is a semisynthetic morphinan opioid derived from the levorphanol series, characterized structurally by a rigid fused polycyclic phenanthrene-like/morphinan nucleus bearing a tertiary amine, a phenolic hydroxyl group, and a 14-hydroxyl substitution with an N-cyclobutylmethyl moiety that helps confer mixed opioid agonist-antagonist properties; thus it is classified as an opioid analgesic, specifically a morphinan derivative, with a morphinan scaffold closely related to levorphanol, nalbuphine, pentazocine, and other mixed-action opioids such as buprenorphine in pharmacologic behavior. Its principal targets are the kappa opioid receptor and mu opioid receptor, acting predominantly as a kappa agonist and partial agonist/antagonist at mu receptors, with downstream CNS analgesic and sedative effects. Pharmacokinetically, butorphanol is well absorbed after parenteral and intranasal administration, undergoes significant first-pass metabolism that limits oral utility, distributes broadly including to the CNS, is metabolized mainly hepatically by hydroxylation and conjugation to inactive metabolites, and is excreted primarily in urine with some fecal elimination; elimination half-life is typically a few hours, though effects may outlast plasma decline. It is indicated for moderate to severe pain, preoperative or postoperative analgesia, adjunctive anesthesia, and migraine treatment in intranasal form. Adverse effects include sedation, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, sweating, dysphoria, confusion, constipation, and respiratory depression, while toxicity may present as profound CNS depression, apnea, hypotension, dependence, and precipitated withdrawal in opioid-dependent patients; clinically it is used for perioperative pain control, labor analgesia in selected settings, and rescue treatment of severe headache or breakthrough pain.

Name: Bisoprolol
Description: Bisoprolol (DrugBank DB00612) is a cardioselective beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist of the aryloxypropanolamine class, structurally characterized by the classic beta-blocker scaffold consisting of a substituted phenoxy-2-propanolamine core with a secondary alcohol, protonatable secondary amine, and a para-substituted aromatic ring bearing a 2-isopropoxyethoxy side chain that contributes to high beta1 selectivity; its chemical scaffold is therefore the phenoxypropanolamine/beta-aryloxy alcohol framework shared with related agents such as metoprolol, atenolol, betaxolol, and esmolol. Its principal targets are the beta1-adrenergic receptor (ADRB1) in the heart and juxtaglomerular apparatus, with weaker activity at beta2-adrenergic receptors (ADRB2) at therapeutic doses, leading to reduced heart rate, contractility, cardiac output, and renin release. Pharmacokinetically, bisoprolol is well absorbed orally with high bioavailability due to limited first-pass metabolism, distributes moderately with relatively low plasma protein binding, undergoes mixed hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 and to a lesser extent CYP2D6 to inactive metabolites, and is eliminated by both renal excretion of unchanged drug and renal clearance of metabolites, supporting once-daily dosing and an elimination half-life of about 10-12 hours. It is indicated for hypertension, chronic stable angina, and chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and is used clinically to control symptomatic tachycardia, reduce myocardial oxygen demand, improve survival in heart failure, and prevent cardiovascular events in selected patients. Toxicity is dominated by excessive beta-blockade, including bradycardia, atrioventricular block, hypotension, acute heart failure decompensation, bronchospasm in susceptible patients, hypoglycemia masking, fatigue, dizziness, depression, and sexual dysfunction; overdose may produce cardiogenic shock and severe conduction disturbances.

Name: Rifabutin
Description: Rifabutin (DB00615) is a semisynthetic rifamycin antibacterial characterized by a highly lipophilic ansamycin architecture built on a naphthohydroquinone aromatic core bridged by a long aliphatic ansa chain, with multiple hydroxyl, acetyl, and spiro-piperidyl substituents that distinguish it from rifampin and increase tissue penetration; chemically it belongs to the rifamycin class of macrocyclic polyketide-derived antibiotics, and its core scaffold is the rifamycin ansa macrocycle. Closely related drugs include rifampin, rifapentine, and rifaximin, which share the same RNA polymerase-targeting pharmacophore but differ in lipophilicity, half-life, and interaction profiles. Rifabutin targets the bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase beta subunit encoded by rpoB, thereby suppressing transcription and exerting bactericidal activity particularly against mycobacteria. It is used primarily for prophylaxis and treatment of Mycobacterium avium complex infection in advanced HIV disease and as an alternative rifamycin in tuberculosis, especially when drug-drug interactions with antiretrovirals are a concern. Oral absorption is moderate and enhanced by lipophilicity, distribution is extensive with high intracellular and tissue penetration, protein binding is substantial, metabolism occurs mainly in the liver via CYP3A to active and inactive metabolites, and elimination is prolonged with a relatively long half-life and excretion through both feces and urine. Toxicities include dose-related uveitis, leukopenia, hepatotoxicity, and rare severe hypersensitivity; adverse effects commonly include orange discoloration of body fluids, nausea, abdominal pain, rash, arthralgia, and neutropenia. Clinically, rifabutin is often selected in HIV-associated mycobacterial disease or multidrug regimens where CYP3A induction is still relevant but less pronounced than with rifampin.

Name: Paramethadione
Description: Paramethadione (DrugBank DB00617) is an oxazolidinedione anticonvulsant characterized structurally by a five-membered 2,4-dione heterocycle, the oxazolidine-2,4-dione ring, bearing methyl substitution at the 3 and 5 positions; thus, its core scaffold is the dimethyloxazolidinedione ring system, a classic cyclic imide motif associated with older absence-seizure therapies. It belongs chemically to the oxazolidinedione class and is closely related to trimethadione and conceptually to other historical nonhydantoin anticonvulsants used for petit mal epilepsy. Its antiseizure effect is attributed primarily to depression of thalamocortical rhythmicity through reduction of T-type voltage-gated calcium currents, although no single highly selective target protein has been definitively established; Cav3 calcium channel family members are the most commonly implicated functional targets. Paramethadione is administered orally, is reasonably well absorbed, distributes systemically including penetration into the central nervous system, undergoes hepatic biotransformation to active and inactive metabolites, and is eliminated mainly via renal excretion of metabolites, with a relatively prolonged effect due to metabolite persistence. It was indicated chiefly for absence seizures, especially petit mal epilepsy refractory to simpler measures, and was used clinically as an older second-line antiepileptic in selected patients. Toxicity is significant and historically limiting, including teratogenicity with fetal trimethadione/paramethadione syndrome, sedation, ataxia, photophobia, visual disturbance, nausea, rash, and hematologic or renal adverse reactions; severe examples include aplastic anemia, agranulocytosis, nephrosis, and potentially fatal hypersensitivity, which largely account for its abandonment in modern practice.

Name: Demeclocycline
Description: Demeclocycline (DrugBank DB00618) is a semisynthetic tetracycline antibiotic built on the classic rigid, linearly fused four-ring naphthacene core bearing multiple keto, phenolic, and hydroxyl functionalities with a dimethylamino substituent and chlorine substitution that distinguishes it from tetracycline; chemically it belongs to the tetracycline class, with a polyketide-derived tetracyclic scaffold closely related to tetracycline, doxycycline, minocycline, oxytetracycline, and chlortetracycline. Its antibacterial action is mediated primarily by binding the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit, especially 16S rRNA within the ribosome, thereby blocking aminoacyl-tRNA accommodation and inhibiting protein synthesis. Oral absorption is moderate and variably reduced by food, dairy, and polyvalent cations; distribution is wide into many tissues but not optimally into cerebrospinal fluid; protein binding is moderate; metabolism is limited; and elimination occurs largely as unchanged drug through renal and biliary/fecal routes, with persistence prolonged in renal dysfunction. Toxicity resembles that of other tetracyclines and includes dose-related gastrointestinal irritation, hepatotoxicity, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus from reduced renal response to vasopressin, photosensitivity, and class effects such as tooth discoloration, enamel hypoplasia, and inhibition of bone growth in the fetus or child. Adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, esophagitis, rash, candidiasis, dizziness, and superinfection. Clinically, it has been used for susceptible infections such as acne, respiratory tract infections, and atypical bacterial infections, but it is particularly notable for off-label treatment of chronic hyponatremia due to syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, where it induces a reversible antidiuretic hormone-resistant state.

Name: Imatinib
Description: Imatinib (DrugBank DB00619) is a small-molecule 2-phenylaminopyrimidine tyrosine kinase inhibitor whose structure consists of a substituted aminopyrimidine core linked to a benzamide and N-methylpiperazine moiety, with chlorophenyl and other aryl substituents that support ATP-site binding in inactive kinase conformations; chemically it is classified as an aminopyrimidine/aryl amide anticancer agent, and its core scaffold is the phenylamino-pyrimidine kinase-inhibitor scaffold. Closely related or mechanistically similar drugs include nilotinib, dasatinib, bosutinib, ponatinib, and earlier lead compounds such as STI-571 analogs. Imatinib is orally well absorbed with high bioavailability, reaches peak plasma levels within hours, is extensively distributed and highly protein bound, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism mainly by CYP3A4 to an active N-desmethyl metabolite, and is eliminated chiefly via biliary-fecal excretion with a relatively long terminal half-life permitting once-daily dosing. Its principal targets are BCR-ABL1, ABL1, ABL2, KIT, PDGFRA, PDGFRB, and CSF1R. It is indicated for Philadelphia chromosome-positive chronic myeloid leukemia and acute lymphoblastic leukemia, as well as KIT-positive gastrointestinal stromal tumors, myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasms with PDGFR rearrangements, aggressive systemic mastocytosis lacking certain resistant KIT mutations, dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, and hypereosinophilic syndrome. Toxicities include myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity, fluid retention and edema, gastrointestinal irritation, rash, and less commonly cardiotoxicity or severe cutaneous reactions; common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, muscle cramps, fatigue, periorbital edema, anemia, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia. Clinically, it is used as frontline targeted therapy, chronic maintenance treatment, and adjuvant or metastatic therapy in molecularly selected kinase-driven malignancies.

Name: Triamcinolone
Description: Triamcinolone (DrugBank DB00620) is a synthetic fluorinated corticosteroid built on the pregnane steroid nucleus, characterized by the canonical four-ring cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene scaffold with key 1,4-diene unsaturation, 9α-fluoro substitution, 11β- and 21-hydroxyl groups, a 3-keto function, and a 16α-hydroxyl substituent that help confer potent glucocorticoid activity with relatively limited mineralocorticoid effect; chemically it is a corticosteroid, specifically a synthetic glucocorticoid, and its core scaffold is closely related to prednisolone, dexamethasone, betamethasone, methylprednisolone, and hydrocortisone. It acts primarily through the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, altering transcription of anti-inflammatory and immunoregulatory genes, with downstream effects on NF-κB, AP-1, cytokines, and phospholipase A2 pathways. Pharmacokinetically, absorption depends on formulation and route, being well absorbed orally and locally from intra-articular, intralesional, inhaled, intranasal, topical, and injectable products; distribution is systemic with plasma protein binding mainly to albumin and corticosteroid-binding globulin; metabolism occurs largely in the liver via CYP3A4-mediated oxidation and reduction; and metabolites plus some parent drug are excreted mainly in urine. Indications include allergic rhinitis, asthma, eczema, psoriasis, rheumatoid and osteoarthritis flares, bursitis, uveitis, and other inflammatory, autoimmune, or dermatologic disorders. Toxicities reflect glucocorticoid excess, including HPA-axis suppression, hyperglycemia, infection risk, osteoporosis, myopathy, cataracts, glaucoma, mood changes, skin atrophy, impaired wound healing, and growth suppression; adverse effects commonly include edema, dyspepsia, hypertension, acne, candidiasis with inhaled use, and local tissue atrophy after injection. Clinically, triamcinolone is used systemically or locally as triamcinolone, triamcinolone acetonide, or related formulations for targeted anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive therapy.

Name: Nicardipine
Description: Nicardipine (DrugBank DB00622) is a lipophilic 1,4-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker whose structure features a 1,4-dihydropyridine ring bearing ester substituents and aryl functionality, a motif that confers potent vascular smooth-muscle selectivity; chemically it belongs to the dihydropyridine class of L-type calcium channel antagonists, with the classic nifedipine-like dihydropyridine scaffold as its core. Closely related drugs include nifedipine, amlodipine, felodipine, isradipine, nimodipine, and clevidipine, which share similar vasodilatory pharmacology. Its principal targets are L-type voltage-dependent calcium channels, especially Cav1.2 channels encoded by CACNA1C in vascular smooth muscle and, to a lesser extent, cardiac tissue, where blockade reduces transmembrane calcium influx and lowers arterial tone. Nicardipine is indicated primarily for hypertension, hypertensive emergencies when given intravenously, and angina pectoris, including chronic stable and vasospastic forms. Clinically it is used for rapid blood-pressure control in perioperative hypertension, acute neurologic settings such as intracerebral hemorrhage or ischemic stroke requiring BP management, and outpatient antihypertensive therapy in oral form. Pharmacokinetically, oral nicardipine is well absorbed but undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, giving moderate bioavailability; it is highly protein bound, widely distributed, hepatically metabolized mainly by CYP3A4 to less active metabolites, and excreted chiefly as metabolites in urine with some fecal elimination. Toxicity is largely an extension of vasodilation and calcium-channel blockade, with overdose causing profound hypotension, reflex tachycardia, dizziness, flushing, headache, and possible myocardial ischemia; adverse effects commonly include peripheral edema, palpitations, nausea, and hypotension, while excessive exposure may produce syncope or worsening angina in susceptible patients.

Name: Fluphenazine
Description: Fluphenazine (DrugBank DB00623) is a first-generation antipsychotic of the phenothiazine class, specifically a piperazine-substituted phenothiazine, with a tricyclic phenothiazine core bearing an electron-withdrawing trifluoromethyl group and a three-carbon side chain terminating in a piperazine ring, a structural arrangement that underlies its high antipsychotic potency; its central chemical scaffold is therefore the phenothiazine tricycle with a piperazine side chain, and it is closely related to other typical antipsychotics such as perphenazine, trifluoperazine, prochlorperazine, chlorpromazine, and thioridazine. Pharmacologically, it acts primarily as an antagonist at dopamine D2 receptors, with additional activity at D1-like receptors, 5-HT2 receptors, alpha1-adrenergic receptors, histamine H1 receptors, and muscarinic cholinergic receptors to varying degrees; reported targets include DRD2, DRD1, DRD3, DRD4, HTR2A, HRH1, CHRM receptors, and ADRA1 receptors. It is indicated mainly for schizophrenia and other chronic psychotic disorders, particularly for hallucinations, delusions, agitation, and thought disorder, and it has also been used for severe behavioral disturbance and intractable nausea in some settings. Fluphenazine is well absorbed orally, undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism, is highly lipophilic and protein bound with broad tissue distribution including CNS penetration, is metabolized mainly by hepatic oxidative pathways including CYP2D6, and is excreted as metabolites in urine and feces; long-acting decanoate formulations provide depot release over weeks. Major toxicities and adverse effects include dose-related extrapyramidal symptoms such as acute dystonia, parkinsonism, akathisia, and tardive dyskinesia, as well as sedation, anticholinergic effects, orthostatic hypotension, hyperprolactinemia, QT-related arrhythmia risk, seizures, rare cholestatic jaundice, blood dyscrasias, and potentially fatal neuroleptic malignant syndrome; clinically it is used orally or as depot injection for maintenance treatment in patients with chronic schizophrenia, especially when adherence is poor.

Name: Testosterone
Description: Testosterone (DrugBank DB00624) is the principal endogenous androgen, a lipophilic C19 steroid characterized structurally by the classic cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene nucleus with a 3-keto group, a Δ4 double bond in the A ring, and a 17β-hydroxyl substituent, placing it in the androstane class of steroid hormones and specifically among androgenic-anabolic steroids; its core scaffold is the androst-4-en-17β-ol-3-one steroid framework. Closely related or pharmacologically similar agents include methyltestosterone, testosterone enanthate, testosterone cypionate, nandrolone, dihydrotestosterone, and oxandrolone. Its primary target is the androgen receptor, with important biologic conversion to dihydrotestosterone by steroid 5α-reductase types 1 and 2 and aromatization to estradiol by aromatase; binding to sex hormone-binding globulin and albumin strongly influences disposition. Pharmacokinetically, testosterone is variably absorbed depending on formulation, with poor oral bioavailability of unmodified drug because of extensive first-pass metabolism, while intramuscular esters, transdermal gels/patches, buccal, nasal, and subcutaneous products improve systemic exposure; it distributes widely into androgen-responsive tissues, is metabolized mainly hepatically to androsterone, etiocholanolone, DHT, and estradiol, and is excreted predominantly in urine as glucuronide and sulfate conjugates. It is indicated for male hypogonadism, delayed puberty in selected cases, gender-affirming masculinizing therapy, and certain catabolic states. Toxicities and adverse effects include erythrocytosis, acne, edema, gynecomastia, infertility with testicular atrophy, mood changes, worsening sleep apnea, dyslipidemia, hepatic injury with some oral derivatives, and potential prostate enlargement or stimulation of occult prostate cancer; clinical use therefore spans replacement in primary or secondary testosterone deficiency using injectable or transdermal preparations with monitoring of hematocrit, prostate parameters, lipids, and liver function where relevant.

Name: Bacitracin
Description: Bacitracin (DrugBank DB00626) is a polypeptide antibiotic composed of a closely related mixture of cyclic dodecapeptides, chiefly bacitracin A, featuring a branched, conformationally constrained peptide macrocycle with unusual amino acid residues and a thiazoline-containing peptide scaffold that enables high-affinity binding to the lipid carrier undecaprenyl pyrophosphate. Chemically, it is classified as a peptide natural product antibiotic, specifically a cyclic polypeptide, and its core scaffold is a metal-binding, thiazoline-bearing cyclic peptide distinct from but broadly similar in functional class to other membrane-active or cell-wall-directed peptide antibiotics such as polymyxin B, colistin, gramicidin, and the glycopeptides vancomycin and teicoplanin, although the latter are structurally different. Its principal pharmacologic target is bacterial bactoprenol pyrophosphate, thereby functionally inhibiting peptidoglycan precursor dephosphorylation and cell-wall synthesis rather than acting through a human protein target; activity is greatest against Gram-positive organisms including Staphylococcus and Streptococcus species. Bacitracin is indicated mainly for topical treatment or prevention of localized skin, աչքի, and minor wound infections, often in combination products such as bacitracin-neomycin-polymyxin for abrasions, burns, or postoperative superficial infection prophylaxis. Systemic absorption through intact skin is minimal, but absorption can increase across damaged skin or mucosa; distribution after systemic exposure is limited, metabolism is not clinically important, and elimination is predominantly renal. Because parenteral use is associated with substantial nephrotoxicity, systemic use is now rare; toxicities include acute tubular injury, renal failure, neurotoxicity, and hypersensitivity, while topical adverse effects more commonly include allergic contact dermatitis, rash, pruritus, and local irritation.

Name: Niacin
Description: Niacin (DrugBank DB00627), also known as nicotinic acid, is a simple water-soluble pyridinecarboxylic acid composed of an aromatic six-membered pyridine ring bearing a carboxylic acid substituent at the 3-position, placing it in the vitamin B3 and heteroaromatic carboxylic acid chemical categories and giving it a nicotinic acid/pyridyl monocarboxylate scaffold. Structurally and pharmacologically related compounds include nicotinamide, acipimox, and in broader lipid-modifying context fibrates and statins, although these latter agents are mechanistically distinct. Niacin is rapidly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, widely distributed, and converted intracellularly to nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide and related coenzymes; at pharmacologic doses it also undergoes substantial hepatic first-pass metabolism through conjugative and amidation pathways, with urinary excretion of parent drug and metabolites, and formulation strongly affects peak exposure and tolerability. Its best-characterized target is hydroxycarboxylic acid receptor 2 (HCAR2/GPR109A), with downstream effects that reduce adipose lipolysis and alter hepatic lipoprotein handling, while its vitamin function reflects precursor roles in NAD/NADP biosynthesis rather than classical receptor pharmacology. Niacin is indicated for niacin deficiency states such as pellagra and has been used to treat dyslipidemia, including elevated LDL cholesterol, elevated triglycerides, and low HDL cholesterol. Adverse effects commonly include intense cutaneous flushing, pruritus, warmth, and gastrointestinal upset; clinically important toxicities include hepatotoxicity, hyperuricemia with gout, hyperglycemia or worsened insulin resistance, and rarely hypotension or arrhythmia, with sustained-release products posing greater liver risk. In practice, it is used as nutritional replacement and, more selectively today, as an adjunct lipid-lowering agent in mixed dyslipidemia or severe hypertriglyceridemia when individualized risk-benefit assessment supports use.

Name: Clorazepic acid
Description: Clorazepic acid (DrugBank DB00628), better known as clorazepate or clorazepate dipotassium in clinical formulations, is a 1,4-benzodiazepine derivative characterized structurally by a fused benzene-diazepine ring system bearing a 7-chloro substituent, a 5-phenyl ring, and a 3-carboxylate function that distinguishes it from many other benzodiazepines and renders it an acid-labile prodrug; chemically it belongs to the benzodiazepine anxiolytic-anticonvulsant class, with a classic 1,4-benzodiazepine scaffold closely related to nordazepam-type agents. Similar drugs include diazepam, nordazepam, chlordiazepoxide, prazepam, and lorazepam, especially those used for anxiety, seizure control, or alcohol withdrawal. After oral administration, clorazepic acid is rapidly decarboxylated in the acidic stomach to the active metabolite nordazepam, which is well absorbed, highly protein bound, widely distributed into the CNS, metabolized hepatically to oxazepam and other conjugated metabolites, and eliminated mainly in urine with a long effective half-life that can promote accumulation, particularly in elderly patients or hepatic impairment. Its principal pharmacologic target is the benzodiazepine allosteric site on GABAA receptor complexes, especially receptors containing alpha, beta, and gamma subunits, enhancing GABAergic inhibitory neurotransmission. Indications include anxiety disorders, acute alcohol withdrawal, and adjunctive management of partial seizures.
