Adverse effects and toxicity are typical of benzodiazepines, including sedation, dizziness, ataxia, cognitive slowing, respiratory depression in overdose or with opioids/alcohol, dependence, withdrawal seizures, and impaired psychomotor performance; clinically it has been used as an oral long-acting anxiolytic, anticonvulsant adjunct, and withdrawal-symptom suppressant.

Name: Guanabenz
Description: Guanabenz (DrugBank DB00629) is a centrally acting antihypertensive of the amidine/guanidine-derived imidazoline-related class, structurally characterized by a dichlorobenzylidene-substituted aminoguanidine motif in which an aromatic ring bearing two chlorine atoms is linked through an imine-like bridge to a hydrazinecarboximidamide functionality; this places it within aryl-imine guanidines and gives it a clonidine-like sympatholytic scaffold. Similar drugs include clonidine, guanfacine, methyldopa, and other central alpha-adrenergic agonists, with clonidine being the closest pharmacologic analogue. Its principal target is the alpha-2 adrenergic receptor, especially central presynaptic alpha-2 receptors in the brainstem, reducing sympathetic outflow and peripheral vascular resistance; interaction with imidazoline-associated pathways has also been discussed. Guanabenz is used primarily for hypertension, particularly essential hypertension, and has also been investigated in other settings such as modulation of stress-response pathways, although routine clinical use is antihypertensive. After oral administration it is reasonably absorbed, undergoes first-pass hepatic metabolism, is distributed systemically with CNS penetration sufficient for central action, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine with a relatively short duration compared with some analogues, necessitating repeated dosing. Toxicity is dominated by excessive pharmacology, including hypotension, marked sedation, bradycardia, dizziness, and CNS depression; overdose may produce profound hypotension and coma. Common adverse effects include dry mouth, drowsiness, कमजोरी/fatigue, constipation, and orthostatic symptoms. Clinically, it was used as an oral second-line antihypertensive, especially when reduction of sympathetic tone was desired, but tolerability concerns and the availability of newer agents have limited its modern use.

Name: Alendronic acid
Description: Alendronic acid (DrugBank DB00630) is a second-generation, nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate characterized structurally by a nonhydrolyzable P-C-P backbone with two phosphonic acid groups attached to the same carbon and a 4-amino-1-hydroxybutyl side chain, a motif that mimics pyrophosphate and confers strong affinity for hydroxyapatite in bone; chemically it belongs to the aminobisphosphonate class, and its core scaffold is the geminal bisphosphonate pharmacophore linked to a primary alkylamine. Closely related drugs include pamidronate, risedronate, ibandronate, and zoledronic acid, which share the bisphosphonate scaffold but differ in side-chain heterocycle or amine substitution and potency. Its principal molecular target is farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway of osteoclasts, with downstream inhibition of protein prenylation and suppression of osteoclast-mediated bone resorption. Oral absorption is very poor, typically well under 1% and further reduced by food, calcium, antacids, or polyvalent cations; absorbed drug distributes selectively to mineralized bone, shows negligible metabolism, and is eliminated unchanged by the kidney, while skeletal retention may persist for years. Toxicities include severe upper gastrointestinal irritation, esophagitis, esophageal ulceration, hypocalcemia, musculoskeletal pain, osteonecrosis of the jaw, atypical femoral fractures, and renal risk in susceptible patients. Common adverse effects include abdominal pain, dyspepsia, nausea, constipation, and bone or joint pain. Clinically it is used to prevent and treat postmenopausal osteoporosis, glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, osteoporosis in men, and Paget disease of bone, reducing vertebral and hip fracture risk when administered with strict dosing instructions and adequate calcium and vitamin D supplementation.

Name: Clofarabine
Description: Clofarabine (DB00631) is a second-generation halogenated purine nucleoside antimetabolite structurally defined as a 2-chloro-2′-fluoro-deoxyadenosine analog in which a chlorinated adenine base is linked by a beta-N9-glycosidic bond to an arabinofuranosyl-like sugar bearing a strategically placed fluorine that increases acid stability and resistance to phosphorolysis; chemically it belongs to the purine nucleoside analog and antineoplastic antimetabolite class, with a deoxyadenosine/arabinonucleoside scaffold closely related to fludarabine and cladribine, and more distantly to nelarabine and cytarabine as mechanistically related nucleoside analogs. After intravenous administration, it has predictable systemic exposure, distributes into total body water with intracellular trapping after phosphorylation, shows low to moderate protein binding, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism, is activated intracellularly by deoxycytidine kinase to clofarabine triphosphate, and is eliminated primarily by the kidney as unchanged drug, so exposure rises in renal impairment. Its principal pharmacologic targets are ribonucleotide reductase subunits RRM1 and RRM2 and DNA polymerases, with incorporation into DNA causing chain termination, inhibition of DNA synthesis and repair, mitochondrial membrane disruption, and apoptosis. It is indicated mainly for relapsed or refractory acute lymphoblastic leukemia in pediatric patients, and has also been used in acute myeloid leukemia regimens. Toxicity is dominated by dose-limiting myelosuppression, severe infections, hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevation or veno-occlusive patterns, nephrotoxicity, capillary leak/systemic inflammatory response, and gastrointestinal toxicity; common adverse effects include febrile neutropenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, fatigue, pyrexia, mucositis, and elevated liver enzymes. Clinically, it is used as an IV salvage leukemia agent, alone or in combination with cytarabine and other cytotoxics, particularly where rapid cytoreduction is needed.

Name: Docosanol
Description: Docosanol (DrugBank DB00632) is a saturated 22-carbon primary fatty alcohol with a linear, unbranched hydrocarbon chain terminating in a single hydroxyl group, giving it an amphipathic long-chain aliphatic structure; chemically it is classified as a very long-chain fatty alcohol and belongs to the broader lipid-like alkanol class, with a simple n-docosane-derived alcohol scaffold that lacks rings, unsaturation, or heteroatom-rich pharmacophores. It is structurally similar to other long-chain aliphatic alcohols and antiviral lipid-like agents such as eicosanol, tetracosanol, and to some extent acyclovir-class topical antiherpetics by therapeutic use rather than close scaffold homology. Its principal pharmacology is believed to involve interaction with host cell plasma membrane components to inhibit fusion between the herpes simplex virus envelope and the cell membrane rather than binding a classic high-affinity protein target; accordingly, no single definitive molecular target protein is well established, though membrane fusion machinery and viral entry processes are implicated. After topical administration, systemic absorption is minimal, distribution is largely confined to the application site, metabolism likely follows endogenous fatty alcohol oxidation pathways to fatty acids and further lipid intermediates, and excretion of any absorbed fraction is expected through normal metabolic disposal routes rather than unchanged renal elimination. Docosanol is indicated for recurrent herpes labialis, particularly early treatment of cold sore symptoms such as tingling, pain, and lesion development. It is generally well tolerated, with low systemic toxicity; adverse effects are usually mild local reactions including irritation, rash, dryness, burning, headache, and pruritus, while serious toxicity is uncommon in routine clinical topical use.

Name: Sulfacetamide
Description: Sulfacetamide (DB00634) is a synthetic sulfonamide antibacterial whose structure consists of a para-aminobenzenesulfonamide core bearing an N-acetyl substituent on the sulfonamide nitrogen, making it a relatively simple aniline-sulfonamide derivative; chemically it belongs to the sulfonamide anti-infective class and is built on the p-aminobenzenesulfonamide, or sulfa-drug, scaffold that mimics para-aminobenzoic acid. Closely related drugs include sulfamethoxazole, sulfadiazine, sulfisoxazole, and sulfadoxine, which share the same antifolate pharmacophore but differ in heterocyclic or N-substituted groups. Its principal target is bacterial dihydropteroate synthase, which it inhibits competitively, blocking folate biosynthesis and thereby suppressing susceptible organisms such as Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Chlamydia trachomatis in ophthalmic use. Sulfacetamide is used mainly topically in bacterial conjunctivitis, blepharitis, trachoma adjunctive therapy, and dermatologic conditions such as acne vulgaris and seborrheic dermatitis, including sulfacetamide-sulfur products. Pharmacokinetically, topical ocular or cutaneous administration leads to limited but measurable systemic absorption, distribution into local tissues and ocular fluids, hepatic acetylation and related sulfonamide biotransformation if absorbed, and primarily renal excretion of parent drug and metabolites. Toxicity is generally lower with topical use than with systemic sulfonamides but includes local irritation, burning, stinging, dermatitis, and hypersensitivity; serious examples, though rare, include Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, hemolysis in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, crystalluria, and hematologic dyscrasias. Clinically, it is chiefly valued as a topical anti-infective when sulfonamide-susceptible bacterial eye or skin disease is present.

Name: Prednisone
Description: Prednisone (DrugBank DB00635) is a synthetic corticosteroid of the glucocorticoid class built on the pregnane steroid nucleus, characterized structurally as a 17-hydroxy corticosteroid with a conjugated 1,4-diene-3-ketone A-ring, an 11-keto group, and 20-ketone/21-hydroxyl side chain; it is therefore a prodrug closely related to prednisolone, differing by oxidation at C11. Its chemical scaffold is the cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene steroid framework, and similar drugs include prednisolone, methylprednisolone, hydrocortisone, dexamethasone, and cortisone. After oral administration prednisone is generally well absorbed, extensively distributed with substantial plasma protein binding to albumin and corticosteroid-binding globulin, rapidly converted in the liver by 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase to the active metabolite prednisolone, further metabolized hepatically by reduction and conjugation, and excreted mainly in urine as inactive metabolites; biologic effects outlast the plasma half-life because of genomic signaling. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, with downstream suppression of NF-κB- and AP-1-regulated inflammatory pathways and limited mineralocorticoid-related effects. Prednisone is indicated for inflammatory, autoimmune, allergic, dermatologic, pulmonary, gastrointestinal, renal, rheumatologic, hematologic, and oncologic disorders, including asthma exacerbations, COPD flares, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, inflammatory bowel disease, nephrotic syndrome, immune thrombocytopenia, and certain leukemias or lymphomas. Toxicities and adverse effects include immunosuppression and infection risk, hyperglycemia, hypertension, edema, mood change or psychosis, peptic ulceration, myopathy, cataracts, glaucoma, skin thinning, osteoporosis, adrenal suppression, growth retardation in children, and Cushingoid features, with chronic high-dose use carrying particular risk; clinically it is widely used for short-course acute symptom control and longer-term immunomodulation, often with tapering to reduce hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis suppression.

Name: Clofibrate
Description: Clofibrate (DB00636) is an aryloxyisobutyric acid derivative and classic fibrate antihyperlipidemic administered as the ethyl ester prodrug of clofibric acid; structurally it consists of a chlorophenoxy group linked through an ether to a branched isobutyrate motif, giving the characteristic phenoxyisobutyric acid scaffold that defines this chemical class. It belongs to the fibric acid derivatives, with close structural and pharmacologic analogs including clofibric acid, fenofibrate, bezafibrate, and gemfibrozil, all of which modulate lipid metabolism primarily through peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARA), with downstream effects on lipoprotein lipase, apolipoprotein A-I/A-II, and suppression of apoC-III. Clofibrate is well absorbed orally, rapidly hydrolyzed by esterases to the active metabolite clofibric acid, distributed substantially in plasma with high albumin binding, undergoes limited further biotransformation including glucuronidation, and is eliminated mainly by the kidney as clofibric acid and conjugates, with a relatively prolonged half-life that can increase in renal impairment. It was used for hypertriglyceridemia, mixed dyslipidemia, type III hyperlipoproteinemia, and prevention of pancreatitis associated with severe triglyceride elevation, and clinically served to lower triglycerides and very-low-density lipoprotein while modestly increasing high-density lipoprotein. Important adverse effects include dyspepsia, nausea, diarrhea, rash, fatigue, myalgia, and elevations in transaminases; notable toxicities include hepatotoxicity, gallstone formation from increased biliary cholesterol excretion, myopathy or rhabdomyolysis particularly with statins or renal dysfunction, and rare hematologic or arrhythmic events.

Name: Astemizole
Description: Astemizole (DrugBank DB00637) is a lipophilic, second-generation H1-antihistamine built around a substituted benzimidazole/piperidine-derived diaryl scaffold, featuring a heteroaromatic benzimidazole core linked through flexible alkyl spacers to aromatic fluorophenyl functionality and a basic tertiary nitrogen that supports high receptor affinity and extensive tissue partitioning; chemically it is classified as a benzimidazole antihistamine within the piperidine-like nonsedating H1-receptor antagonists, and its scaffold and pharmacology resemble terfenadine, loratadine, ebastine, mizolastine, and other peripheral H1 blockers. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, although it is also clinically notable for potent off-target blockade of the cardiac hERG potassium channel encoded by KCNH2, which underlies its proarrhythmic liability. Astemizole was indicated for allergic rhinitis, chronic idiopathic urticaria, and other histamine-mediated pruritic or rhinoconjunctival symptoms such as sneezing, rhinorrhea, and wheal-and-flare reactions. After oral administration it is well absorbed but undergoes extensive first-pass CYP3A4-mediated metabolism to active and persistent metabolites including desmethylastemizole, is highly protein bound, widely distributed, penetrates the CNS poorly relative to older antihistamines, and is eliminated slowly mainly via hepatic metabolism with biliary/fecal excretion, giving a very long effective half-life and risk of accumulation. Toxicity is dominated by QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, ventricular arrhythmias, and sudden death, especially with overdose, hepatic impairment, electrolyte abnormalities, or CYP3A4 inhibitors such as erythromycin, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, or itraconazole. Adverse effects include dry mouth, headache, dizziness, mild sedation, palpitations, and gastrointestinal discomfort. Clinically, although once used as a nonsedating antiallergic, its use became severely restricted or withdrawn in many markets because cardiac risk outweighed benefit.

Name: Adenosine
Description: Adenosine (DrugBank DB00640) is an endogenous purine nucleoside composed of an adenine base linked through a beta-N9-glycosidic bond to ribofuranose, giving a compact, highly polar heteroaromatic nucleoside structure rich in hydrogen-bonding functionality; chemically it belongs to the purine nucleosides and its core scaffold is the adenine-ribose adenosine scaffold shared by several nucleoside drugs and analogues. Closely related or pharmacologically similar agents include adenosine phosphate congeners such as ATP, receptor-active analogues such as regadenoson and adenosine monophosphate derivatives, and antiarrhythmic AV nodal blockers with overlapping clinical effects such as verapamil. Its principal targets include adenosine receptors ADORA1, ADORA2A, ADORA2B, and ADORA3, and it also functionally acts on cardiac AV nodal tissue via A1-receptor-mediated suppression of adenylate cyclase, reduced cAMP, potassium current activation, and slowed calcium-dependent conduction. Pharmacokinetically, adenosine is given intravenously because oral delivery is impractical; it distributes rapidly in extracellular fluid and has an ultrashort plasma half-life of less than 10 seconds due to rapid cellular uptake by erythrocytes and endothelial cells, metabolism by adenosine deaminase to inosine and by adenosine kinase to AMP, with downstream purine metabolites ultimately excreted renally. It is indicated primarily for acute conversion of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia and diagnostically to unmask atrial activity, and is also used in pharmacologic stress testing to provoke coronary vasodilation. Toxicity is usually brief but can include profound bradycardia, transient asystole, hypotension, bronchospasm, chest pain, and flushing; adverse effects commonly include dyspnea, chest pressure, lightheadedness, headache, nausea, and a sense of impending doom, with heightened risk in asthma, high-grade AV block, or concomitant dipyridamole exposure.

Name: Simvastatin
Description: Simvastatin (DrugBank DB00641) is a lipophilic, semisynthetic statin derived from a fungal polyketide framework and chemically characterized as an inactive lactone prodrug bearing a substituted hexahydronaphthalene ring system linked to a methylbutanoate side chain; after hydrolysis, the opened β,δ-dihydroxyheptanoic acid pharmacophore mediates activity. It belongs to the HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor class, with a decalin-like polyketide scaffold closely related to lovastatin and structurally/pharmacologically similar to pravastatin, atorvastatin, fluvastatin, rosuvastatin, and pitavastatin. Its principal target is 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase (HMGCR), leading to reduced hepatic cholesterol synthesis, upregulation of LDL receptors, and lowering of LDL cholesterol and, to a lesser extent, triglycerides. Orally administered simvastatin is well absorbed but undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic extraction, has low systemic bioavailability of active acid, is highly protein bound, and is metabolized mainly by CYP3A4 to active and inactive metabolites; elimination occurs predominantly via the bile/feces with limited renal excretion, and the plasma half-life of active inhibitors is short though pharmacodynamic effects persist. It is indicated for primary hypercholesterolemia, mixed dyslipidemia, familial hypercholesterolemia, and prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular events such as myocardial infarction and stroke. Common adverse effects include myalgia, abdominal pain, constipation, nausea, headache, and mild transaminase elevation; important toxicities include dose-related myopathy, rhabdomyolysis with renal injury, hepatotoxicity, and increased risk with CYP3A4 inhibitors, gemfibrozil, or cyclosporine. Clinically, it is used adjunctively with diet and lifestyle modification for long-term LDL lowering and cardiovascular risk reduction in high-risk patients.

Name: Mebendazole
Description: Mebendazole (DrugBank DB00643) is a benzimidazole carbamate anthelmintic built on a fused bicyclic benzimidazole scaffold bearing a methyl carbamate at the 2-position and an aromatic benzoyl substituent that contributes lipophilicity and high affinity for helminth tubulin; chemically it belongs to the benzimidazole class and is closely related to other tubulin-binding antiparasitic agents such as albendazole, thiabendazole, flubendazole, and fenbendazole. Its principal pharmacologic target is parasite beta-tubulin, with inhibition of microtubule polymerization leading to impaired glucose uptake, depletion of glycogen stores, and degenerative changes in intestinal cells of susceptible worms; mammalian tubulin is less avidly affected at therapeutic exposure. After oral administration, absorption is relatively low and variable because of poor aqueous solubility, but increases with fatty meals; the absorbed fraction is widely distributed, undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism mainly to inactive or less active hydroxy and amino metabolites, is highly protein bound, and is eliminated predominantly via bile and feces with minor urinary excretion. It is indicated for intestinal nematode infections including enterobiasis, ascariasis, trichuriasis, and hookworm, and is also used in some tissue helminthiases such as echinococcosis in selected regimens. Adverse effects are usually gastrointestinal, including abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, and flatulence, but prolonged or high-dose therapy may cause hepatotoxicity, neutropenia, agranulocytosis, alopecia, rash, urticaria, and rare severe cutaneous reactions; embryotoxic and teratogenic signals in animals support caution in pregnancy. Clinically, it is used as a short-course oral deworming agent for pinworm and mixed soil-transmitted helminth infections, and in prolonged specialist-directed courses for hydatid disease when surgery is unsuitable or adjunctive therapy is needed.

Name: Gonadorelin
Description: Gonadorelin (DB00644) is a synthetic or purified form of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, a short linear decapeptide built on a peptide backbone with an N-terminal pyroglutamyl residue and a C-terminal amidated glycinamide, features that stabilize the native hypothalamic hormone and define its compact peptide scaffold; chemically it belongs to the GnRH agonist class within oligopeptide hormones, and its core scaffold is the conserved L-amino-acid decapeptide neuroendocrine motif recognized by pituitary GnRH receptors. Closely related drugs include other GnRH receptor agonists or analogs such as leuprolide, triptorelin, goserelin, nafarelin, histrelin, and buserelin, which share the same hormonal signaling axis but often incorporate substitutions that prolong activity. Gonadorelin acts primarily at the gonadotropin-releasing hormone receptor, GNRHR, on anterior pituitary gonadotrophs to stimulate release of luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone. After parenteral administration it is rapidly absorbed, distributed mainly within extracellular fluid, subject to swift enzymatic proteolysis in blood and tissues, and cleared largely as inactive peptide fragments and metabolites in urine, giving it a very short plasma half-life of minutes and limiting sustained systemic exposure. Toxicity is generally low but may include endocrine overstimulation, ovarian hyperstimulation risk in susceptible women, and rare hypersensitivity; adverse effects can include headache, nausea, abdominal discomfort, flushing, injection-site reactions, altered blood pressure, and transient menstrual or gonadal effects. Clinically it has been used diagnostically to assess pituitary-gonadal function and therapeutically in conditions such as hypothalamic hypogonadism, delayed puberty, infertility due to deficient GnRH secretion, and evaluation of amenorrhea or pubertal disorders.

Name: Dyclonine
Description: Dyclonine (DrugBank DB00645) is a synthetic topical local anesthetic with an aryl-alkyl ketone structure characterized by a lipophilic substituted aromatic ring linked through a ketone-containing carbon chain to a tertiary amino group, placing it in the ketone-type amino local anesthetic class rather than the ester- or amide-type agents; its core scaffold is commonly described as a butyrophenone-like amino-ketone framework with a piperidine-containing side chain. Chemically and pharmacologically it is related to other topical local anesthetics such as benzocaine, lidocaine, tetracaine, and dyclonine-containing throat lozenges, although it is structurally most distinct from the classic ester and amide subclasses. Its principal action is believed to involve reversible inhibition of voltage-gated sodium channels in peripheral sensory neurons, reducing initiation and conduction of nerve impulses; specific molecular targets are not usually formalized beyond neuronal sodium channel proteins. After topical oral or pharyngeal administration, systemic absorption is generally limited but can increase with damaged mucosa or excessive dosing; distribution is expected to favor well-perfused tissues, metabolism occurs largely hepatically, and excretion is primarily renal as metabolites. Toxicity is usually low at recommended doses but excessive exposure may produce local irritation, CNS symptoms such as dizziness or numbness, or rarely systemic local-anesthetic toxicity; aspiration risk may increase if pharyngeal sensation is overly suppressed. It is indicated for temporary relief of sore throat, minor mouth and pharyngeal pain, and discomfort from mucosal irritation, and clinically used in lozenges or topical preparations for conditions such as viral pharyngitis, stomatitis, and procedure-related oral discomfort. Common adverse effects include transient oral numbness, stinging, burning, altered taste, nausea, and hypersensitivity reactions.

Name: Nystatin
Description: Nystatin (DrugBank DB00646) is a polyene macrolide antifungal composed of a large 38-membered macrolactone ring bearing a rigid conjugated polyene chromophore on one face and multiple hydroxyl substituents plus a mycosamine sugar on the other, creating a strongly amphipathic structure that underlies its membrane-binding activity; it is classified chemically as a polyene antifungal antibiotic and more specifically shares the macrolide-polyene scaffold typical of sterol-binding antifungals. Closely related drugs include amphotericin B and natamycin, with amphotericin B being the most pharmacologically similar example. Its principal target is fungal membrane ergosterol rather than a classical protein target, with membrane pore formation and permeability disruption leading to leakage of intracellular ions and metabolites. Pharmacokinetically, nystatin is essentially not absorbed from intact skin, mucous membranes, or the gastrointestinal tract, so systemic distribution is negligible after oral, topical, or oral cavity administration; it undergoes little meaningful metabolism and is eliminated largely unchanged in feces after oral use. This poor absorption explains its utility for localized Candida infections and also limits systemic efficacy. Indications include oropharyngeal candidiasis, oral thrush, intestinal candidiasis suppression, cutaneous candidiasis, diaper rash with Candida involvement, and vulvovaginal candidiasis in some formulations. Adverse effects are usually local or gastrointestinal, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal irritation, unpleasant taste, and mouth irritation, while rash, contact sensitivity, and rare hypersensitivity reactions may occur. Toxicity is generally low because of minimal absorption, but excessive local exposure can worsen irritation, and systemic toxicities typical of amphotericin B are not expected in routine nystatin use. Clinically, it is used as oral suspension, pastilles, topical creams, ointments, and powders for noninvasive mucocutaneous Candida infections.

Name: Mitotane
Description: Mitotane (DB00648) is an adrenolytic organochlorine derivative structurally related to the insecticide DDT, consisting of a dichlorodiphenyl scaffold with a substituted ethane/ethylene core bearing multiple para-chloro aryl substituents; chemically it is classified as a halogenated aromatic hydrocarbon and more specifically a diphenylmethane- or DDT-like chlorinated hydrocarbon, with a lipophilic chlorinated diaryl scaffold that underlies its persistence and adrenal tropism. Similar drugs are limited, but close chemical analogs include o,p'-DDD and the broader DDT-related organochlorine series; functionally, it may be compared with other adrenal-directed therapies such as ketoconazole, metyrapone, and osilodrostat, although these are not close structural congeners. Mitotane is orally administered, variably and incompletely absorbed but better absorbed with fatty meals, extensively distributed into adipose tissue because of extreme lipophilicity, highly protein bound, slowly released from tissue stores, hepatically metabolized largely by oxidative pathways to inactive and active acid/alcohol metabolites, and excreted mainly in bile/feces with a very prolonged and variable terminal half-life measured in weeks. Its principal targets are incompletely defined but include adrenal mitochondrial functions and steroidogenic pathways, with reported effects on CYP11A1, CYP11B1, CYP11B2, CYP17A1, CYP21A2, sterol-O-acyltransferase 1, and adrenal mitochondrial membranes, producing selective zona fasciculata/reticularis cytotoxicity. It is indicated primarily for inoperable, recurrent, or metastatic adrenocortical carcinoma and for control of severe hypercortisolism/Cushing syndrome due to adrenal malignancy. Toxicity includes dose-limiting gastrointestinal and neurologic effects, adrenal insufficiency, hepatotoxicity, dyslipidemia, and possible teratogenic or endocrine-disrupting effects; common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia, dizziness, ataxia, lethargy, confusion, rash, and gynecomastia. Clinically, it is used as adjuvant or palliative therapy after adrenalectomy, in advanced adrenocortical carcinoma, and with glucocorticoid replacement and therapeutic drug monitoring to balance efficacy against systemic toxicity.

Name: Stavudine
Description: Stavudine (DB00649) is a synthetic thymidine analog antiretroviral with a modified 2,3-didehydro-2,3-dideoxyribose sugar, lacking the 3′-hydroxyl group required for DNA chain elongation; structurally it belongs to the nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor class and is built on a pyrimidine nucleoside scaffold closely related to thymidine. Similar drugs include other NRTIs such as zidovudine, didanosine, lamivudine, emtricitabine, abacavir, and zalcitabine, which share intracellular activation to triphosphate metabolites and inhibition of viral reverse transcription. After oral administration stavudine is rapidly and well absorbed, has relatively low protein binding, distributes broadly into body fluids and tissues including cerebrospinal fluid, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism, and is cleared predominantly by renal excretion as unchanged drug, giving it potential for accumulation in renal impairment. Its principal pharmacologic target is HIV reverse transcriptase, specifically HIV-1 and HIV-2 reverse transcriptase after conversion intracellularly to stavudine triphosphate, which competitively inhibits the enzyme and terminates proviral DNA synthesis. It is indicated for treatment of HIV infection, historically in combination antiretroviral regimens for AIDS and symptomatic or progressive HIV disease. Clinical use has markedly declined because of important toxicities, notably mitochondrial toxicity with lactic acidosis and severe hepatomegaly with steatosis, dose-related peripheral neuropathy, pancreatitis, lipoatrophy, and metabolic complications; other adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, rash, insomnia, headache, fatigue, and hepatic enzyme elevations. Thus, although effective against HIV, stavudine is now generally reserved for limited settings where safer alternatives are unavailable.

Name: Leucovorin
Description: Leucovorin (folinic acid; 5-formyl-tetrahydrofolate, DrugBank DB00650) is a reduced folate antimetabolite rescue agent structurally characterized by a pteridine ring linked through p-aminobenzoate to an L-glutamate residue, retaining the classical folate scaffold but existing in a tetrahydro, one-carbon substituted form that bypasses dihydrofolate reductase; chemically it is a folate analog within the pterin-based antifolate/folate derivative class, with a glutamylated pteroyl scaffold shared by related agents such as folic acid, methotrexate, levoleucovorin, pemetrexed, and pralatrexate. Its principal pharmacologic targets are indirect rather than high-affinity receptor mediated, chiefly folate-dependent enzymes including thymidylate synthase, whose inhibition by 5-fluorouracil is stabilized by leucovorin-derived reduced folates, and it functionally circumvents blockade of dihydrofolate reductase during methotrexate rescue. After oral or parenteral administration, absorption is dose dependent and saturable orally, distribution is broad to tissues, intracellular conversion yields active reduced folate cofactors such as 5-methyltetrahydrofolate, metabolism occurs mainly in liver and intestinal mucosa, and elimination is primarily renal with biliary contribution. Toxicity is usually limited but may include excessive rescue diminishing methotrexate efficacy, potentiation of fluoropyrimidine toxicity with severe diarrhea, mucositis, and myelosuppression, and rare hypersensitivity or seizures in susceptible patients. Indications include rescue after high-dose methotrexate, treatment of folate-deficient megaloblastic anemia, and combination therapy with 5-fluorouracil in colorectal and other gastrointestinal cancers; adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, rash, fever, insomnia, and, in combination regimens, enhanced gastrointestinal and hematologic toxicity.

Name: Dyphylline
Description: Dyphylline (DrugBank DB00651) is a synthetic xanthine derivative and methylxanthine bronchodilator characterized structurally by a substituted purine-2,6-dione (xanthine) core bearing two N-methyl groups and a hydroxyethyl side chain, placing it within the theophylline-related ethylenediamine-free xanthines; its central chemical scaffold is therefore the methylxanthine/xanthine bicyclic purinedione nucleus. It is chemically and pharmacologically similar to theophylline, aminophylline, caffeine, and oxtriphylline, sharing adenosine receptor antagonism and weak nonselective phosphodiesterase inhibition as class-related mechanisms, although specific high-affinity target assignment is often generalized to adenosine receptor subtypes and PDE enzymes rather than a single dominant protein target. Dyphylline is indicated for relief of bronchospasm in bronchial asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, and other reversible obstructive airway diseases, and has been used clinically as an oral or parenteral bronchodilator when xanthine therapy is desired. Pharmacokinetically, it is reasonably well absorbed after oral administration, distributes in total body water, shows relatively limited protein binding, undergoes less extensive hepatic biotransformation than theophylline, and is eliminated largely unchanged in urine, giving it a comparatively shorter and somewhat more predictable disposition profile in some patients. Toxicity is typical of methylxanthines and includes dose-related gastrointestinal and CNS stimulation, with nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, tremor, insomnia, headache, palpitations, and tachycardia; severe overdose may produce marked arrhythmias, hypotension, agitation, or seizures. Its adverse-effect profile and clinical usage therefore resemble other older methylxanthine bronchodilators, mainly as symptomatic therapy for reversible airway obstruction rather than first-line long-term anti-inflammatory control.

Name: Magnesium sulfate
Description: Magnesium sulfate (DrugBank DB00653) is a simple inorganic salt composed of a divalent magnesium cation electrostatically paired with a tetrahedral sulfate dianion, most commonly encountered clinically as the heptahydrate; structurally it lacks an organic ring system and is best described as an ionic mineral electrolyte rather than a classical small-molecule scaffold, with an elemental ionic scaffold centered on Mg2+ coordination chemistry. It belongs to the chemical category of inorganic sulfate salts and is pharmacologically similar to other magnesium salts such as magnesium chloride, magnesium oxide, magnesium citrate, and magnesium gluconate, as well as functionally related to calcium channel-modulating or anticonvulsant agents in some settings. After intravenous or intramuscular administration it is rapidly bioavailable, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid with limited protein binding, crosses the placenta, is not metabolized, and is eliminated almost entirely by the kidney, so accumulation occurs in renal impairment. Its molecular actions are pleiotropic rather than receptor-selective, with known functional targets including voltage-gated calcium channels, NMDA-type glutamate receptors, and ion transport processes involved in neuromuscular transmission and cardiac excitability. Clinically it is indicated for prevention and treatment of seizures in preeclampsia and eclampsia, correction of hypomagnesemia, torsades de pointes, severe asthma exacerbations, and as an osmotic cathartic in some formulations. Toxicity reflects hypermagnesemia, causing flushing, nausea, hypotension, loss of deep tendon reflexes, muscle weakness, respiratory depression, bradycardia, heart block, paralysis, and cardiac arrest; accordingly, common adverse effects include warmth, injection-site pain, somnolence, and dizziness. In practice it is widely used in obstetrics, emergency medicine, cardiology, and electrolyte replacement, with calcium gluconate or calcium chloride serving as physiologic antidotal therapy in overdose.

Name: Latanoprost
Description: Latanoprost (DrugBank DB00654) is a lipophilic isopropyl ester prodrug of a prostaglandin F2α analog characterized structurally by a substituted cyclopentane core bearing two aliphatic side chains, one terminating in an aromatic phenyl group and the other in an ester that is rapidly hydrolyzed to the active carboxylic acid; the molecule contains defined stereochemistry and a 15-hydroxyl typical of prostanoid pharmacophores. Chemically, it belongs to the eicosanoid/prostanoid class, specifically prostaglandin analog ophthalmic hypotensives, with a prostaglandin F2α scaffold as its core chemical framework. Closely related drugs include travoprost, tafluprost, bimatoprost, and unoprostone, which share prostanoid-like ocular hypotensive properties. After topical ocular administration, latanoprost is absorbed through the cornea, where esterases convert it to latanoprost acid; systemic exposure is low, distribution is mainly local to anterior ocular tissues with some access to the ciliary body, metabolism occurs primarily in the liver via fatty acid β-oxidation and related oxidative pathways, and metabolites are excreted predominantly in urine. Its principal target is the prostaglandin F receptor, encoded by PTGFR, activation of which increases uveoscleral outflow and lowers intraocular pressure. It is indicated mainly for open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension, including chronic elevation of intraocular pressure in adults. Toxicity is usually local rather than systemic, with examples including irreversible iris hyperpigmentation, eyelash growth, periocular skin darkening, conjunctival hyperemia, ocular irritation, and rare cystoid macular edema or uveitis; overdose is generally associated with limited systemic toxicity but may cause headache, dizziness, or bronchospasm in susceptible patients. Clinically, it is widely used as once-daily first-line topical therapy, either alone or in combination regimens, to reduce glaucoma progression and preserve visual function.

Name: Estrone
Description: Estrone (DrugBank DB00655) is a naturally occurring endogenous estrogen steroid characterized by the rigid cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene nucleus with an aromatic A-ring, a phenolic hydroxyl group at C3, and a C17 ketone, making it less potent than estradiol but structurally distinct from estriol by its 17-keto functionality; chemically it belongs to the steroidal estrogens, specifically an estrane-derived phenolic sex hormone, and its core scaffold is the estrane tetracyclic steroid framework. Closely related or similar drugs include estradiol, estriol, conjugated estrogens, ethinyl estradiol, and esterified estrogen preparations, which share estrogen receptor agonist activity but differ in potency, metabolism, and formulation. Estrone acts primarily through estrogen receptors ESR1 and ESR2, with downstream modulation of gene transcription, and can also interact indirectly with sex hormone-binding globulin and steroid-converting enzymes such as 17beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases and aromatase-linked pathways. Pharmacokinetically, estrone is absorbed after oral or parenteral administration, is extensively protein bound in plasma, undergoes interconversion with estradiol, and is metabolized hepatically by reduction, oxidation, hydroxylation, and conjugation to sulfate and glucuronide metabolites, with biliary and renal excretion and notable first-pass effects. Clinically it has been used for menopausal symptoms, hypoestrogenism, vulvovaginal atrophy, and sometimes palliative treatment of selected hormone-responsive cancers such as prostate cancer or breast cancer. Adverse effects and toxicity resemble other estrogens and include nausea, breast tenderness, edema, headache, breakthrough bleeding, endometrial hyperplasia, thromboembolism, cholestatic effects, and increased risk of estrogen-dependent neoplasia, with overdose typically causing gastrointestinal symptoms or vaginal bleeding rather than acute lethal toxicity.

Name: Metaxalone
Description: Metaxalone (DrugBank DB00660) is a centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant whose structure is defined by a 1,3-oxazolidin-2-one carbamate-like heterocycle bearing a 3,5-dimethylphenoxy methyl substituent, placing it in the oxazolidinone/oxazolidinone-related muscle relaxant chemical category with an aryloxy-substituted oxazolidinone scaffold. It is structurally and therapeutically similar to other centrally acting antispasmodic agents such as methocarbamol, chlorzoxazone, carisoprodol, cyclobenzaprine, and orphenadrine, although it is chemically distinct from these classes. Its precise molecular target is not well established; no single validated target protein fully explains its action, and its clinical effect is generally attributed to central nervous system depression within polysynaptic pathways rather than direct action at the neuromuscular junction or on skeletal muscle, so specific target proteins remain undefined or incompletely characterized. Pharmacokinetically, metaxalone is well absorbed orally, with exposure increased by food, is distributed systemically with moderate protein binding, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism primarily via cytochrome P450 enzymes including CYP1A2, CYP2D6, CYP2E1, and CYP3A4, and is excreted mainly in urine as metabolites with little unchanged drug. It is indicated as an adjunct to rest, physical therapy, and other measures for acute painful musculoskeletal conditions such as lumbar strain, cervical spasm, and other muscle spasm syndromes. Adverse effects commonly include drowsiness, dizziness, headache, nausea, irritability, and gastrointestinal upset, while toxicity may involve excessive CNS depression, respiratory compromise in overdose, hepatotoxicity, hemolytic anemia, leukopenia, and serotonin syndrome risk when combined with serotonergic drugs; clinically it is used short term to reduce discomfort from acute muscle spasm rather than to treat spasticity from upper motor neuron disorders.

Name: Verapamil
Description: Verapamil (DrugBank DB00661) is a phenylalkylamine calcium-channel blocker characterized structurally by a lipophilic tri-substituted aromatic system linked through a flexible aliphatic chain to a tertiary aminoalkyl nitrile, with methoxy-substituted phenyl rings forming the key recognition elements for L-type calcium-channel binding; chemically it belongs to the non-dihydropyridine calcium antagonist class and is built on a phenylalkylamine scaffold. Closely related or pharmacologically similar drugs include other non-dihydropyridines such as gallopamil and diltiazem, and functionally similar calcium-channel blockers such as nifedipine or amlodipine despite their distinct dihydropyridine scaffold. Its principal targets are L-type voltage-dependent calcium channel subunits, especially CACNA1C, with additional inhibition of cardiac conduction through effects at the AV node and recognized interaction with the drug transporter ABCB1/P-glycoprotein. Verapamil is well absorbed orally but undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, yielding active norverapamil; it is widely distributed, highly protein bound, metabolized mainly by CYP3A4 with contributions from CYP1A2 and CYP2C enzymes, and excreted predominantly as metabolites in urine with a smaller fecal component. Clinically, it is indicated for hypertension, chronic stable and vasospastic angina, and supraventricular tachyarrhythmias such as PSVT and atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. Typical adverse effects include constipation, bradycardia, hypotension, dizziness, headache, flushing, edema, and fatigue. Toxicity is dominated by excessive calcium-channel blockade, causing severe bradycardia, AV block, cardiogenic shock, hyperglycemia, and death in overdose; risk is heightened in heart failure, conduction disease, or when combined with beta-blockers or digoxin, making careful cardiovascular monitoring central to clinical use.

Name: Trimethobenzamide
Description: Trimethobenzamide (DrugBank DB00662) is a substituted benzamide antiemetic whose structure is centered on a 3,4,5-trimethoxybenzamide aromatic core linked through an amide bond to a branched amino side chain, giving a lipophilic methoxy-substituted phenylcarboxamide scaffold with a terminal tertiary amine that is commonly formulated as the hydrochloride salt. Chemically it belongs to the benzamide class of antiemetics and more broadly to aromatic carboxamides; its core scaffold is closely related to other substituted benzamides such as metoclopramide, procainamide-derived benzamides, and antiemetic/prokinetic congeners including domperidone in functional similarity, although trimethobenzamide lacks the strong prokinetic profile of some analogs. Its precise molecular target has not been fully defined, but antiemetic activity is generally attributed to central dopamine D2 receptor antagonism within the chemoreceptor trigger zone, with no single validated high-affinity target profile as well established as for newer agents. After oral or intramuscular administration it is absorbed reasonably well, distributed systemically with clinically relevant CNS access, undergoes hepatic biotransformation including oxidation and conjugative pathways, and is eliminated primarily in urine as metabolites and some unchanged drug; the elimination half-life is on the order of several hours. It is indicated for nausea and vomiting, especially postoperative nausea, drug-induced emesis, and acute gastroenteritis-associated symptoms. Adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, headache, diarrhea, blurred vision, and local injection-site reactions, while toxicity may involve excessive sedation, hypotension, confusion, and extrapyramidal reactions such as dystonia, particularly in children, older adults, or overdose. Clinically, it has been used as an oral capsule, suppository, or injectable antiemetic when phenothiazines or more sedating agents are undesirable.

Name: Flumethasone
Description: Flumethasone (DrugBank DB00663) is a highly fluorinated synthetic corticosteroid built on the pregnane steroid nucleus, featuring the characteristic four fused rings of the glucocorticoid scaffold with a 1,4-diene-3-keto motif, 11β- and 17α-hydroxyl substituents, a 20-ketone, and halogenation including fluorine that increases glucocorticoid potency and lipophilicity. Chemically, it is a fluorinated corticosteroid, specifically a glucocorticoid anti-inflammatory steroid, and its core scaffold is closely related to prednisolone- and dexamethasone-like corticosteroid frameworks. Similar drugs include dexamethasone, betamethasone, triamcinolone, fluocinolone, and prednisolone, which share steroidal anti-inflammatory pharmacology with differing halogenation and substitution patterns. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor encoded by NR3C1, with downstream transrepression of proinflammatory transcription factors such as NF-κB and AP-1 and reduced cytokine, prostaglandin, and leukotriene production. Pharmacokinetically, flumethasone is absorbed after topical, otic, or systemic administration to an extent dependent on formulation and tissue integrity, distributes widely with plasma protein binding typical of corticosteroids, undergoes hepatic biotransformation largely via reduction and oxidative metabolism followed by conjugation, and is excreted mainly in urine as metabolites with some biliary/fecal elimination. It is indicated for corticosteroid-responsive inflammatory and allergic disorders, including dermatitis, eczema, otitis externa, and other localized inflammatory states, and in practice has been used topically or in combination products such as otic anti-infective preparations. Toxicity reflects glucocorticoid excess: prolonged or high exposure can cause hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal suppression, hyperglycemia, infection risk, skin atrophy, impaired wound healing, osteoporosis, mood changes, cataracts, and glaucoma; common adverse effects include local burning, irritation, dryness, folliculitis, and with systemic absorption Cushingoid features and edema.

Name: Nafarelin
Description: Nafarelin (DrugBank DB00666) is a synthetic peptide gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist built on the decapeptide GnRH scaffold, structurally characterized as an LHRH analog with strategic substitutions that increase receptor affinity and resistance to enzymatic degradation, notably a D-amino-acid substitution in the central region and a modified C-terminal residue that enhance potency relative to native GnRH. Chemically it belongs to the class of peptide hormone analogs, specifically synthetic GnRH/LHRH agonists, and its core scaffold is shared with related agents such as leuprolide, goserelin, triptorelin, buserelin, and histrelin. Its principal target is the gonadotropin-releasing hormone receptor, GNRHR, on anterior pituitary gonadotrophs, where initial stimulation transiently increases luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone release, followed by receptor desensitization and suppression of gonadal steroidogenesis. Nafarelin is administered mainly intranasally, is absorbed through the nasal mucosa with relatively low but pharmacologically effective systemic bioavailability, distributes systemically as a peptide, undergoes proteolytic metabolism to inactive fragments, and is eliminated primarily as peptide metabolites in urine. Toxicity is largely mechanism-based and reflects hypoestrogenism or hypogonadism rather than major intrinsic organ toxicity; examples include bone mineral loss with prolonged use, mood changes, and potential fetal harm in pregnancy. Indications include endometriosis, central precocious puberty, and other sex steroid-dependent conditions. Common adverse effects include hot flashes, headache, decreased libido, vaginal dryness, menstrual irregularity, emotional lability, acne, and local nasal irritation. Clinically, it is used to induce reversible pituitary-gonadal suppression, for example to relieve endometriosis-associated pelvic pain or to delay premature pubertal progression.

Name: Epinephrine
Description: Epinephrine (adrenaline; DrugBank DB00668) is an endogenous catecholamine whose structure consists of a catechol ring bearing two adjacent phenolic hydroxyls linked to a β-hydroxylated ethylamine side chain with an N-methyl substituent, making it a small, highly polar sympathomimetic phenethylamine; chemically it belongs to the catecholamine/adrenergic agonist class and is built on a catechol-ethanolamine, phenethylamine-derived scaffold. Closely related drugs include norepinephrine, dopamine, isoproterenol, dobutamine, and phenylephrine, which share adrenergic pharmacology but differ in receptor selectivity and substitution pattern. Epinephrine is a nonselective agonist at alpha-1, alpha-2, beta-1, and beta-2 adrenergic receptors, encoded by ADRA1A/ADRA1B/ADRA1D, ADRA2A/ADRA2B/ADRA2C, and ADRB1/ADRB2/ADRB3, respectively, with principal clinical effects mediated especially through alpha-1, beta-1, and beta-2 receptors. It is used for anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest, severe acute bronchospasm, and as a vasoconstrictor adjunct to local anesthetics or for superficial bleeding control. After intramuscular, subcutaneous, inhaled, or intravenous administration, absorption is rapid but variable with local vasoconstriction; distribution is limited by polarity and poor CNS penetration; metabolism is rapid via COMT and MAO in liver and extrahepatic tissues to metanephrine, normetanephrine-related metabolites, and vanillylmandelic acid; urinary excretion is mainly as metabolites, yielding a short plasma half-life of only minutes. Toxicity reflects excessive adrenergic stimulation, including severe hypertension, tachyarrhythmias, myocardial ischemia, stroke, pulmonary edema, hyperglycemia, hypokalemia, and tissue necrosis after extravasation; common adverse effects include palpitations, tremor, anxiety, headache, diaphoresis, nausea, and pallor. Clinically, it is given intramuscularly for community or emergency treatment of anaphylaxis, intravenously during resuscitation or refractory shock, by inhalation for croup or bronchospasm, and locally to prolong anesthetic action and reduce mucosal

Name: Sumatriptan
Description: Sumatriptan (DrugBank DB00669) is a small-molecule indole-sulfonamide tryptamine derivative whose structure comprises an indole ring system bearing a 5-substituted methanesulfonamide and a 3-(2-dimethylaminoethyl) side chain, making it a serotonin-like, basic, heteroaromatic antimigraine agent; chemically it belongs to the triptan class of selective 5-HT1 receptor agonists, with an indole/ethylamine scaffold that mimics serotonin. Closely related drugs include zolmitriptan, rizatriptan, naratriptan, eletriptan, almotriptan, and frovatriptan, which share the same general serotonergic antimigraine pharmacophore. Its principal targets are 5-hydroxytryptamine receptor 1B, 1D, and to a lesser extent 1F, where agonism promotes cranial vasoconstriction and inhibition of trigeminal neuropeptide release. Pharmacokinetically, oral sumatriptan is rapidly but incompletely absorbed with low bioavailability due to substantial first-pass metabolism; intranasal and subcutaneous formulations provide faster exposure, protein binding is low, distribution is moderate, metabolism occurs mainly via monoamine oxidase A to an indole acetic acid analogue, and elimination is predominantly renal as metabolites with a short terminal half-life of about 2 hours. It is indicated for acute treatment of migraine with or without aura and cluster headache, including attacks with photophobia, phonophobia, nausea, or severe unilateral pulsatile pain. Adverse effects commonly include paresthesia, flushing, dizziness, fatigue, somnolence, nausea, and chest or throat pressure; toxicities include hypertension, coronary vasospasm, myocardial ischemia, serotonin syndrome risk with serotonergic drugs, and medication-overuse headache. Clinically, it is used as oral tablets, nasal spray, or subcutaneous injection for rapid abortive therapy, particularly when early intervention or nonoral dosing is needed.

Name: Pirenzepine
Description: Pirenzepine (DB00670) is a tricyclic antimuscarinic agent of the selective M1 muscarinic receptor antagonist class, built on a dibenzodiazepine-like heterotricyclic scaffold in which two aromatic rings are fused through diazepine/piperazine-related nitrogen-containing ring elements, giving a rigid, bulky, weakly basic structure that distinguishes it from simpler tertiary amine anticholinergics. It is chemically related to other antimuscarinics and shares pharmacologic similarity with atropine, scopolamine, telenzepine, trihexyphenidyl, and dicyclomine, although pirenzepine is relatively more selective for CHRM1 than for CHRM2 or CHRM3. Its principal targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially CHRM1, with lower affinity at other muscarinic subtypes. Clinically it has been used primarily to reduce gastric acid secretion in peptic ulcer disease, including gastric and duodenal ulcer, and has also been explored for dyspeptic symptoms and other hypersecretory gastrointestinal states. After oral administration it is absorbed incompletely, has modest bioavailability, limited penetration into the central nervous system because of its polar cationic character, distributes mainly extracellularly, undergoes relatively limited hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated largely unchanged in urine with some fecal excretion; its duration supports divided daily dosing. Toxicity is typical of anticholinergics and includes dose-related dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, tachycardia, urinary retention, and reduced sweating, while overdose may produce pronounced antimuscarinic syndrome with ileus, confusion, or precipitation of angle-closure glaucoma, though CNS toxicity is generally less marked than with more lipophilic agents. In practice, its clinical use has centered on ulcer management and symptomatic antisecretory therapy where a selective antimuscarinic effect was desired.

Name: Cefixime
Description: Cefixime (DrugBank DB00671) is an orally active semisynthetic third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic whose structure is defined by the cephem/beta-lactam core fused to a dihydrothiazine ring, bearing the 7-beta acylamino substituent with an aminothiazolyl-oxyimino side chain that enhances Gram-negative activity and beta-lactamase stability, and a 3-vinyl group characteristic of its oral cephalosporin scaffold. Chemically it is a beta-lactam, specifically an expanded-spectrum cephalosporin, built on the cepham/cephem scaffold shared with related agents such as cefpodoxime, cefdinir, cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, and ceftibuten. Its primary targets are bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, especially transpeptidases involved in peptidoglycan cross-linking, leading to inhibition of cell-wall synthesis and bacterial lysis. Cefixime is absorbed moderately after oral dosing, with bioavailability roughly 40 to 50 percent, limited metabolism, low to moderate protein binding, distribution into respiratory, urinary, and middle-ear tissues, and predominant renal excretion of unchanged drug with a several-hour elimination half-life that supports once- or twice-daily use. Toxicity is generally low but includes hypersensitivity reactions up to anaphylaxis, severe cutaneous reactions, Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea, seizure risk in renal impairment or overdose, and hematologic abnormalities such as eosinophilia or thrombocytopenia. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, dyspepsia, rash, pruritus, headache, and candidiasis. Clinically, cefixime is used for susceptible infections including uncomplicated urinary tract infection, otitis media, pharyngitis/tonsillitis, acute bronchitis exacerbations, and uncomplicated gonorrhea, particularly when an oral third-generation cephalosporin is appropriate.

Name: Aprepitant
Description: Aprepitant (DrugBank DB00673) is a highly lipophilic, nonpeptide trifluoromethyl-substituted morpholine derivative whose structure is centered on a 3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)phenyl group linked to a chiral morpholine-acetal/ether-rich framework with fluorophenyl substitution, placing it in the neurokinin-1 receptor antagonist class and more specifically within the diaryl morpholine scaffold family; structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include fosaprepitant, its water-soluble phosphono prodrug, and other NK1 antagonists such as rolapitant, netupitant, and casopitant. Its principal target is the tachykinin neurokinin 1 receptor encoded by TACR1, where it blocks substance P signaling in central emetic pathways. After oral administration, aprepitant is well absorbed, has moderate bioavailability limited by first-pass metabolism, reaches peak concentrations within hours, is extensively distributed with high plasma protein binding, penetrates the CNS, and is metabolized predominantly by CYP3A4 with minor roles for CYP1A2 and CYP2C19; elimination occurs mainly as metabolites in feces with a smaller urinary component, and the terminal half-life supports once-daily use. Toxicity is generally modest but includes clinically important CYP3A4-mediated drug interactions, increased exposure to coadministered substrates, reduced warfarin effect via INR lowering, and reduced hormonal contraceptive efficacy; overdose or susceptibility may increase dizziness, somnolence, or hepatic enzyme abnormalities. Approved indications include prevention of acute and delayed chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting and postoperative nausea and vomiting, commonly in cisplatin-based chemotherapy or perioperative settings. Adverse effects include fatigue, hiccups, constipation, diarrhea, dyspepsia, anorexia, headache, dizziness, and transient transaminase elevation. Clinically, it is used in combination antiemetic regimens with 5-HT3 antagonists and dexamethasone, and fosaprepitant is used intravenously when oral administration is unsuitable.

Name: Galantamine
Description: Galantamine (DrugBank DB00674) is a naturally derived tertiary isoquinoline alkaloid of the phenanthrene/benzazepine-type acetylcholinesterase inhibitor class, structurally characterized by a rigid fused tricyclic dibenzofuran-like scaffold with a bridged azepine ring, a tertiary amine, and a methoxy and hydroxyl substituent that support central nervous system penetration and cholinergic activity; its core scaffold is commonly described as the galanthamine-type Amaryllidaceae alkaloid framework. Chemically and pharmacologically it is related to other anti-dementia cholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezil, rivastigmine, and tacrine, although galantamine is distinguished by additional allosteric potentiation of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. Its principal targets are acetylcholinesterase, butyrylcholinesterase to a lesser extent, and neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subtypes including alpha4beta2 and alpha7 as positive allosteric sites. After oral administration it is well absorbed with high bioavailability, widely distributed including into brain tissue, exhibits relatively low protein binding, undergoes hepatic metabolism primarily via CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 with O-demethylation, N-oxidation, and glucuronidation, and is eliminated through both renal excretion of unchanged drug and metabolites; extended-release formulations prolong absorption without altering major metabolic pathways. It is indicated for mild to moderate Alzheimer disease to improve cognition, global function, and activities of daily living, and has also been used symptomatically for memory impairment associated with cholinergic deficit. Adverse effects are predominantly cholinergic and dose related, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia, weight loss, dizziness, headache, bradycardia, syncope, insomnia, and muscle cramps; toxicity and overdose may produce a cholinergic crisis with severe emesis, bronchospasm, hypotension, seizures, and arrhythmias, with greater risk in renal or hepatic impairment or when combined with other cholinomimetics.

Name: Tamoxifen
Description: Tamoxifen (DrugBank DB00675) is a nonsteroidal triphenylethylene derivative characterized structurally by a triarylethylene core bearing two phenyl rings and a substituted ethylene linked to a dimethylaminoethoxy side chain, a configuration that confers lipophilicity and selective estrogen receptor modulation; it belongs to the selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) class and is built on a triphenylethylene scaffold closely related to other antiestrogens such as toremifene and the active metabolites endoxifen and 4-hydroxytamoxifen, with more distant pharmacologic analogs including raloxifene and clomifene. Its principal targets are estrogen receptor 1 (ESR1) and estrogen receptor 2 (ESR2), acting predominantly as an antagonist in breast tissue and partial agonist in bone and endometrium. Orally administered tamoxifen is well absorbed, highly protein bound, widely distributed, and extensively hepatically metabolized by CYP3A4/5 and especially CYP2D6 to active metabolites including endoxifen; elimination is slow, with a long terminal half-life and predominantly fecal excretion via biliary pathways. It is indicated for estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer treatment and recurrence prevention, including adjuvant therapy, metastatic disease, ductal carcinoma in situ risk reduction, and breast cancer chemoprevention in high-risk patients. Toxicities include endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma, venous thromboembolism, stroke risk, hepatotoxicity including fatty liver, ocular toxicity such as cataracts, and fetal harm; common adverse effects include hot flashes, vaginal discharge or bleeding, menstrual irregularity, nausea, edema, rash, and mood changes. Clinically, it is used in premenopausal and postmenopausal patients, often for 5 to 10 years in adjuvant endocrine therapy, and sometimes in male breast cancer.

Name: Losartan
Description: Losartan (DrugBank DB00678) is a nonpeptide angiotensin II receptor blocker built on a biphenyl-tetrazole scaffold, with an imidazole core bearing chlorinated and hydroxymethyl-substituted aryl functionality that mimics key angiotensin II binding determinants; chemically, it belongs to the sartan class of antihypertensive biaryl tetrazoles, and its closest similar drugs include valsartan, irbesartan, candesartan, olmesartan, telmisartan, and eprosartan, which share related AT1 receptor antagonism but differ in scaffold substitutions and pharmacokinetic behavior. Its principal target is the angiotensin II type 1 receptor encoded by AGTR1; pharmacologically relevant downstream effects also involve suppression of aldosterone signaling and modulation of renal hemodynamics. After oral administration, losartan is reasonably absorbed but undergoes first-pass metabolism, with modest absolute bioavailability; it is highly protein bound, distributed largely in extracellular fluid, and oxidized mainly by CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 to an active carboxylic acid metabolite, EXP3174, which is more potent and longer acting than the parent drug, with elimination via both renal and biliary/fecal routes. Clinically it is indicated for hypertension, reduction of stroke risk in hypertensive patients with left ventricular hypertrophy, and diabetic nephropathy in type 2 diabetes with proteinuria, and is used broadly for blood pressure control, renal protection, and off-label in heart failure or chronic kidney disease when renin-angiotensin blockade is desired. Adverse effects include dizziness, hypotension, hyperkalemia, renal function decline, fatigue, and less commonly angioedema; major toxicities include fetal toxicity in pregnancy, acute kidney injury in renovascular disease or volume depletion, and clinically important potassium elevation, especially with potassium-sparing agents or renal impairment.

Name: Moricizine
Description: Moricizine (DB00680) is a phenothiazine-derived antiarrhythmic whose structure consists of a tricyclic phenothiazine-like heteroaromatic scaffold bearing sulfur and nitrogen atoms and substituted with a carboxamide-containing aminoalkyl side chain, features that place it in the class I antiarrhythmic group, historically categorized mainly as class IC with some class IA/IB-like electrophysiologic properties; its core scaffold is the phenothiazine nucleus, and it is chemically and pharmacologically related to other sodium-channel-blocking antiarrhythmics such as flecainide, propafenone, encainide, and, more distantly, disopyramide and quinidine. Its principal target is the cardiac fast voltage-gated sodium channel, especially Nav1.5 encoded by SCN5A, through which it depresses phase 0 depolarization, slows conduction, and suppresses ventricular ectopy. After oral administration, moricizine is absorbed reasonably well but undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, yielding variable bioavailability; it is distributed systemically, is likely moderately protein bound, is extensively metabolized in the liver to multiple metabolites, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine with some biliary or fecal excretion, giving a relatively short half-life that may require divided dosing. It has been used primarily for symptomatic ventricular arrhythmias, including premature ventricular complexes and sustained or nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, and more selectively for serious rhythm disturbances when alternative therapy is unsuitable. Toxicity includes dose-related and idiosyncratic proarrhythmia, QRS widening, conduction block, worsening heart failure, hypotension, dizziness, nausea, and CNS effects; serious examples include induction of more dangerous ventricular arrhythmias and increased mortality in post-myocardial-infarction patients with asymptomatic ventricular ectopy, which markedly limited clinical use.

Name: Amphotericin B
Description: Amphotericin B (DrugBank DB00681) is a polyene macrolide antifungal natural product characterized by a large 38-membered macrolactone ring bearing a rigid heptaene conjugated polyene segment on one face and a densely hydroxylated polyol region on the other, with a mycosamine sugar appended to the macrocycle, creating a strongly amphipathic sterol-binding structure; chemically it belongs to the polyene macrolide class, and its core scaffold is the amphoteronolide/macrolactone polyene framework glycosylated with mycosamine. Closely related drugs include nystatin and natamycin, and functionally similar systemic antifungals include azoles and echinocandins, although these differ structurally. Its principal target is fungal membrane ergosterol rather than a classical protein target, causing membrane permeabilization and ion leakage, with additional oxidative and immunomodulatory effects; mammalian cholesterol binding contributes to toxicity. Amphotericin B is not orally bioavailable for systemic therapy and is given mainly by intravenous infusion, shows extensive tissue distribution with high protein and lipoprotein binding, limited CSF penetration unless inflamed, slow terminal elimination, minimal defined hepatic metabolism, and predominantly biliary/fecal with some renal excretion. It is indicated for severe invasive fungal infections such as cryptococcosis, candidemia, invasive aspergillosis, histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, mucormycosis, and coccidioidomycosis, and is also used for visceral leishmaniasis, especially in lipid formulations. Toxicity is dominated by nephrotoxicity with azotemia, tubular acidosis, hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia, infusion reactions with fever, chills, rigors and hypotension, anemia from reduced erythropoietin, thrombophlebitis, and occasional arrhythmias; clinically it is reserved for life-threatening mycoses, empiric antifungal treatment in high-risk neutropenic patients, cryptococcal meningitis induction with flucytosine, and treatment when rapid fungicidal activity or activity against resistant molds is required.

Name: Warfarin
Description: Warfarin (DrugBank DB00682) is a synthetic 4-hydroxycoumarin anticoagulant composed of a coumarin-like benzopyran-2-one core bearing a 4-hydroxyl group and a 3-substituted chiral side chain with a phenyl and ketone-containing alkyl moiety; it is therefore classified as a vitamin K antagonist and coumarin derivative, with a 4-hydroxycoumarin scaffold that is shared with related oral anticoagulants such as acenocoumarol, phenprocoumon, and the rodenticide superwarfarins brodifacoum and difenacoum. Its principal pharmacologic target is vitamin K epoxide reductase complex subunit 1 (VKORC1), functionally reducing activation of the vitamin K-dependent coagulation proteins factors II, VII, IX, and X and the endogenous anticoagulants protein C and protein S; CYP2C9, CYP3A4, CYP1A2, and CYP2C19 are major metabolic proteins influencing disposition, with CYP2C9 especially important for the more potent S-enantiomer. Warfarin is well absorbed orally, is highly albumin bound, has a small apparent distribution volume, crosses the placenta, undergoes extensive hepatic oxidative metabolism and subsequent conjugation, and is eliminated mainly in urine as inactive metabolites, with a long half-life supporting once-daily dosing. Major toxicity is hemorrhage, ranging from epistaxis and hematuria to gastrointestinal or intracranial bleeding, with additional risks including skin necrosis, purple toe syndrome, teratogenic fetal warfarin syndrome, and numerous pharmacogenetic and drug-drug interaction liabilities. It is indicated and widely used for prevention and treatment of venous thromboembolism, pulmonary embolism, stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation, and thromboprophylaxis in patients with mechanical prosthetic heart valves; common adverse effects include bruising, bleeding, nausea, rash, alopecia, and elevated INR-related complications.

Name: Midazolam
Description: Midazolam (DrugBank DB00683) is a short-acting imidazobenzodiazepine whose structure consists of a fused benzene-diazepine core annulated with an imidazole ring, bearing halogenated and aryl substituents that confer high lipophilicity at physiologic pH and permit a water-soluble open-ring formulation under acidic conditions; chemically it belongs to the benzodiazepine sedative-hypnotics, with an imidazobenzodiazepine scaffold closely related to other benzodiazepines such as diazepam, lorazepam, triazolam, alprazolam, and clonazepam. Its principal pharmacologic targets are the benzodiazepine allosteric sites on GABAA receptor complexes, especially receptors containing alpha1, alpha2, alpha3, alpha5 and gamma2 subunits, where it enhances GABA-mediated chloride channel opening frequency to produce anxiolytic, sedative, hypnotic, amnestic, anticonvulsant, and muscle-relaxant effects. After intravenous, intramuscular, oral, intranasal, or buccal administration, absorption is rapid, distribution is extensive with high CNS penetration and substantial protein binding, metabolism occurs mainly by hepatic CYP3A4 and CYP3A5 to 1-hydroxymidazolam and related glucuronidated metabolites, and elimination is primarily renal as metabolites, with clearance prolonged in neonates, older adults, obesity, hepatic impairment, critical illness, and during CYP3A inhibition. Toxicity is characterized by dose-related CNS and respiratory depression, apnea, hypotension, paradoxical agitation, delirium, and coma, especially with opioids, alcohol, or other sedatives; adverse effects commonly include drowsiness, anterograde amnesia, impaired coordination, confusion, and injection-site reactions. Clinically, midazolam is used for procedural sedation, anesthesia induction, ICU sedation, preoperative anxiolysis, and treatment of acute seizures or status epilepticus, including buccal or intranasal use for seizure clusters and sedation for endoscopy, bronchoscopy, and minor surgery.

Name: Tobramycin
Description: Tobramycin (DrugBank DB00684) is a highly polar aminoglycoside antibiotic composed of a central 2-deoxystreptamine aminocyclitol core glycosidically linked to multiple amino sugars, creating a densely hydroxylated, polycationic structure that lacks substantial lipophilicity and underlies strong ribosomal RNA binding; chemically it belongs to the aminoglycoside class, with a 2-deoxystreptamine-containing aminocyclitol scaffold closely related to other antipseudomonal aminoglycosides such as gentamicin, amikacin, kanamycin, and netilmicin. Its principal target is the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit, especially 16S rRNA and associated ribosomal proteins within the decoding site, where it disrupts initiation and causes mRNA misreading, giving concentration-dependent bactericidal activity, particularly against aerobic Gram-negative bacilli including Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Tobramycin is not absorbed orally, is therefore given parenterally, by inhalation, or topically/ophthalmically, distributes mainly into extracellular fluid with limited CNS penetration unless meninges are inflamed, shows negligible protein binding and essentially no metabolism, and is eliminated almost entirely unchanged by glomerular filtration with a renal-function-dependent half-life. Major toxicities are nephrotoxicity from proximal tubular accumulation, ototoxicity affecting cochlear and vestibular function, and less commonly neuromuscular blockade and fetal auditory toxicity; adverse effects include rising creatinine, tinnitus, hearing loss, vertigo, dizziness, and local irritation. Clinically it is used for severe susceptible infections such as hospital-acquired pneumonia, bacteremia, sepsis, complicated urinary tract and intra-abdominal infections, and in inhaled form for chronic P. aeruginosa infection in cystic fibrosis, as well as ophthalmic treatment of bacterial conjunctivitis and keratitis.

Name: Trovafloxacin
Description: Trovafloxacin (DB00685) is a broad-spectrum fluoroquinolone antibacterial built on the 4-oxo-1,4-dihydroquinoline-3-carboxylic acid core, bearing the quinolone-defining 3-carboxyl and 4-keto pharmacophore, a 6-fluoro substituent that enhances antibacterial potency, and a bulky fused heterocyclic amine at C7 that broadens Gram-positive and anaerobic activity; chemically it is classified as a fluoroquinolone, with a quinolone/quinolone-carboxylic acid scaffold closely related to other agents such as ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, ofloxacin, grepafloxacin, and moxifloxacin. Its antibacterial effect results from inhibition of bacterial type II topoisomerases, principally DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, causing impaired DNA replication and cell death. After oral administration, trovafloxacin is well absorbed with high bioavailability; the prodrug alatrofloxacin was developed for intravenous use and is rapidly converted to active drug. Trovafloxacin distributes widely into tissues, has moderate protein binding, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism with both biliary/fecal and renal elimination, and supports once-daily dosing because of a relatively long half-life. It was indicated for serious infections including community-acquired pneumonia, complicated intra-abdominal infections, gynecologic and pelvic infections, skin and soft-tissue infections, and certain sexually transmitted or mixed aerobic-anaerobic infections. Adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness, headache, and rash, while serious toxicities include idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity, hepatitis, liver failure, QT-related concerns typical of the class, tendinopathy, CNS effects, and hypersensitivity.
