Because of severe liver toxicity, its clinical use became highly restricted and was generally reserved for life-threatening, serious infections when alternative therapies were unsuitable.

Name: Pentosan polysulfate
Description: Pentosan polysulfate sodium (DB00686) is a semisynthetic, highly sulfated polysaccharide composed of β-(1→4)-linked xylopyranose units derived from beechwood hemicellulose, bearing dense O-sulfate substitution that creates a strongly polyanionic, heparin-like structure; chemically it belongs to the sulfated glycosaminoglycan mimetic/carbohydrate polyanion class, with a pentosan sulfate scaffold characterized by a linear sulfated xylan backbone. Closely related or mechanistically similar drugs include heparin, low-molecular-weight heparins such as enoxaparin, and other sulfated polysaccharides used for anticoagulant or mucosal-protective purposes. After oral administration, systemic absorption is low, with only a small fraction bioavailable; absorbed drug distributes largely within the vascular/extracellular compartment, shows limited tissue penetration, undergoes partial desulfation and depolymerization in the liver and reticuloendothelial system, and is excreted mainly in urine with some fecal elimination of unabsorbed material. Its pharmacology is linked less to a single receptor than to interactions with coagulation and extracellular matrix proteins, including antithrombin III, thrombin, factor Xa-related pathways, fibroblast growth factors, selectins, and bladder-surface proteoglycan components, supporting its proposed urothelial protective effect. It is indicated primarily for interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome to reduce bladder pain, urgency, frequency, and discomfort. Toxicities reflect weak anticoagulant activity and chronic exposure risks, including bleeding, ecchymosis, thrombocytopenia, elevated hepatic enzymes, alopecia, gastrointestinal upset, and the now well-recognized pigmentary maculopathy associated with long-term cumulative use. Clinically, it is used orally for chronic interstitial cystitis symptom control, with monitoring for ocular toxicity and bleeding risk, especially in patients receiving concomitant anticoagulants or with coagulopathy.

Name: Fludrocortisone
Description: Fludrocortisone (DrugBank DB00687) is a synthetic fluorinated corticosteroid, usually used clinically as the acetate ester prodrug, built on the pregnane steroid nucleus with the characteristic four fused rings of the hydrocortisone scaffold and distinguished structurally by a 9α-fluoro substituent, 11β-hydroxyl, 17α-hydroxyl, and 20-ketone/21-hydroxyl side chain that confer potent mineralocorticoid activity with modest glucocorticoid effect; chemically it is a corticosteroid, specifically a fluorinated mineralocorticoid, and its core scaffold is the hydrocortisone/cortisol steroid framework. Closely related drugs include hydrocortisone, cortisone acetate, prednisone/prednisolone, dexamethasone, and the mineralocorticoid-active analog deoxycorticosterone acetate. Its principal target is the mineralocorticoid receptor NR3C2, with some activity at the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, altering transcription of epithelial sodium transport and other corticosteroid-responsive genes. After oral administration it is well absorbed, widely distributed with plasma protein binding to albumin and corticosteroid-binding globulin, hepatically metabolized by steroid-reducing and conjugative pathways, and excreted mainly as urinary metabolites. Toxicity reflects mineralocorticoid excess and chronic corticosteroid exposure: hypertension, edema, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, heart failure exacerbation, hyperglycemia, infection risk, myopathy, osteoporosis, growth suppression, adrenal suppression, and rarely psychiatric disturbance. Adverse effects commonly include fluid retention, weight gain, headache, supine hypertension, muscle weakness, and electrolyte disturbances. It is indicated for primary and secondary adrenal insufficiency, especially Addison disease and congenital adrenal hyperplasia requiring mineralocorticoid replacement, and is also used for orthostatic hypotension or autonomic failure to expand intravascular volume and improve symptomatic blood pressure maintenance.

Name: Mycophenolate mofetil
Description: Mycophenolate mofetil (DrugBank DB00688) is the 2-morpholinoethyl ester prodrug of mycophenolic acid, built on a substituted phthalide-like fungal polyketide scaffold consisting of a methoxy-substituted aromatic ring linked to a dihydrofuranone/lactone core with an appended unsaturated side chain; chemically it is classified as an ester immunosuppressant and antimetabolite, with mycophenolic acid and the enteric formulation mycophenolate sodium as the closest analogous drugs, and broader mechanistic comparators including azathioprine and mizoribine. After oral administration it is rapidly and extensively absorbed and presystemically hydrolyzed to active mycophenolic acid, which is highly albumin bound, distributes largely in extracellular fluids, undergoes predominant hepatic glucuronidation via UGT enzymes to the inactive phenolic glucuronide and a minor acyl glucuronide, exhibits enterohepatic recirculation that can produce a secondary concentration peak, and is excreted mainly in urine as glucuronide metabolites with limited unchanged drug elimination. Its principal target is inosine-5-monophosphate dehydrogenase, especially IMPDH2 in activated T and B lymphocytes, thereby suppressing de novo guanosine nucleotide synthesis and lymphocyte proliferation. It is indicated for prophylaxis of organ rejection in kidney, heart, and liver transplantation and is also widely used off-label in lupus nephritis, vasculitis, autoimmune hepatitis, and other immune-mediated disorders. Toxicity is dominated by teratogenicity and embryo-fetal loss, dose-related myelosuppression, serious infections, gastrointestinal mucosal injury, and increased lymphoma and skin cancer risk; common adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, leukopenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and opportunistic infections such as cytomegalovirus or BK virus. Clinically it is used with calcineurin inhibitors and corticosteroids as a maintenance immunosuppressant and as a steroid-sparing agent in systemic autoimmune disease.

Name: Flurazepam
Description: Flurazepam (DrugBank DB00690) is a long-acting 1,4-benzodiazepine hypnotic whose structure consists of a fused benzene-diazepine core bearing the characteristic 5-aryl substituent and a 7-chloro electron-withdrawing group, with a dialkylaminoethyl side chain that contributes to lipophilicity and formation of active metabolites; chemically it is classified as a benzodiazepine anxiolytic-sedative and more specifically a triazole-free classical benzodiazepine scaffold built on the 1,4-benzodiazepin-2-one/related benzodiazepine hypnotic framework. Closely related drugs include diazepam, temazepam, quazepam, nitrazepam, triazolam, and estazolam, which share GABAA receptor positive allosteric modulation. Its principal targets are the benzodiazepine site on GABAA receptor complexes containing α1, α2, α3, or α5 subunits together with γ2, indirectly enhancing chloride conductance and inhibitory neurotransmission. Flurazepam is well absorbed orally, extensively distributed into the CNS, highly protein bound, and undergoes hepatic oxidative N-dealkylation and hydroxylation, mainly via CYP3A4 and CYP2C19, to active metabolites such as desalkylflurazepam that markedly prolong effect; elimination is primarily renal as metabolites, producing prolonged half-life and next-day residual sedation, especially in older adults. Toxicity is typical of benzodiazepines and includes dose-related CNS and respiratory depression, psychomotor impairment, falls, paradoxical agitation, dependence, withdrawal seizures after chronic use, and dangerous potentiation with alcohol, opioids, or other sedatives; overdose examples commonly involve somnolence, ataxia, confusion, and coma. It is indicated for short-term management of insomnia, particularly difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep, and clinically used as a bedtime hypnotic, though adverse effects such as drowsiness, dizziness, amnesia, impaired coordination, cognitive slowing, and rebound insomnia limit prolonged use.

Name: Moexipril
Description: Moexipril (DrugBank DB00691) is an esterified, orally active angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor of the dicarboxylate class, structurally characterized as a prodrug bearing a substituted tetrahydroisoquinoline/proline-like peptidomimetic scaffold with a carboxylic acid functionality masked as an ethyl ester to enhance absorption; after activation it yields moexiprilat, which contains the zinc-binding dicarboxylate pharmacophore typical of this class. Chemically it belongs to small-molecule antihypertensive peptidomimetic ACE inhibitors, and its core scaffold is closely related to other non-sulfhydryl ACE inhibitors such as enalapril, quinapril, benazepril, ramipril, perindopril, and trandolapril, which are considered similar drugs by class and mechanism. Its principal target is angiotensin-converting enzyme, with downstream reduction of angiotensin II formation and aldosterone secretion and enhancement of bradykinin signaling. Moexipril is absorbed orally but food can reduce bioavailability, is converted hepatically and systemically to the active metabolite moexiprilat, shows moderate protein binding, and is eliminated by both renal and biliary/fecal routes; like other ACE inhibitors, impaired renal function can prolong exposure. It is indicated primarily for hypertension, especially essential hypertension, and is used clinically as monotherapy or in combination with thiazide diuretics to reduce blood pressure and related cardiovascular risk. Adverse effects include cough, dizziness, fatigue, headache, hypotension, hyperkalemia, renal function deterioration, rash, and rare but serious angioedema. Toxicity concerns include excessive first-dose hypotension, acute kidney injury in renovascular disease, fetal toxicity in pregnancy, and increased potassium-related arrhythmia risk when combined with potassium-sparing agents.

Name: Phentolamine
Description: Phentolamine (DB00692) is a synthetic imidazoline-derived, nonselective alpha-adrenergic antagonist whose structure consists of a substituted phenyl ring linked through a thioether-containing side chain to an imidazoline/imidazoline-like cationic heterocycle, giving it the classic aryl-alkyl-imidazoline vasoactive scaffold seen in older sympatholytic agents; chemically it is classified as an antiadrenergic imidazoline and more broadly as a reversible alpha-blocker, with related or pharmacologically similar drugs including phenoxybenzamine, tolazoline, prazosin, doxazosin, and terazosin, although these differ in selectivity or reversibility. Its principal targets are alpha-1 adrenergic receptors and alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, antagonism of which produces peripheral vasodilation and enhanced norepinephrine release with reflex tachycardia. Phentolamine is used for diagnosis and management of pheochromocytoma, prevention or treatment of catecholamine-induced hypertensive crises, treatment of dermal ischemia after extravasation of vasopressors such as norepinephrine, and in some settings erectile dysfunction or reversal of local soft-tissue anesthesia. Pharmacokinetically, it is active after parenteral or local infiltration administration, has rapid onset, distributes mainly in extracellular tissues, undergoes hepatic biotransformation, and is eliminated relatively quickly in urine, supporting short duration of action. Toxicity is chiefly an extension of alpha-blockade and includes marked hypotension, severe tachyarrhythmia, myocardial ischemia, and shock, especially with excessive dosing or in patients with coronary disease. Common adverse effects include orthostatic hypotension, flushing, nasal congestion, dizziness, headache, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, palpitations, and reflex tachycardia, which shape its predominantly monitored acute-care clinical use.

Name: Daunorubicin
Description: Daunorubicin (DrugBank DB00694) is an anthracycline antineoplastic antibiotic characterized by a planar tetracyclic anthraquinone-like aglycone, daunomycinone, bearing quinone and hydroquinone functionalities and linked through a glycosidic bond to the amino sugar daunosamine, a structure that supports DNA intercalation and redox cycling; chemically it belongs to the anthracycline/anthracycline glycoside class, with an anthracycline polyketide scaffold closely related to doxorubicin, idarubicin, epirubicin, and valrubicin, and more distantly to mitoxantrone as a functionally similar DNA-topoisomerase poison. Its principal targets are DNA and topoisomerase II isoforms TOP2A and TOP2B, with additional injury mediated by iron-dependent reactive oxygen species generation and effects on chromatin-associated nucleic acids. Pharmacokinetically, daunorubicin is administered intravenously because oral absorption is poor and unreliable; it distributes rapidly into highly perfused tissues, shows extensive tissue binding and limited CNS penetration, undergoes hepatic and tissue carbonyl reduction to the active metabolite daunorubicinol and other minor metabolic transformations, and is eliminated mainly via the biliary/fecal route with a smaller renal component, such that hepatic impairment can increase exposure. Its major dose-limiting toxicities include myelosuppression and cumulative cardiotoxicity, including cardiomyopathy and congestive heart failure, with additional toxicities such as severe mucositis, vesicant extravasation injury, hepatotoxicity, and rare therapy-related leukemia. Common adverse effects include neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, nausea, vomiting, stomatitis, alopecia, infection, fever, and red discoloration of urine. Clinically, daunorubicin is used primarily in acute leukemias, especially induction regimens for acute myeloid leukemia and acute lymphoblastic leukemia, often in combination with cytarabine or other cytotoxics.

Name: Furosemide
Description: Furosemide (DrugBank DB00695) is a sulfonamide-derived anthranilic acid loop diuretic with a substituted benzoic acid core bearing a sulfamoyl group, a chlorine substituent, and a furfurylamino moiety, giving it an aromatic acidic scaffold often described as a sulfamoylbenzoic acid/anthranilate framework. Chemically, it belongs to the loop diuretic class and more broadly to arylsulfonamides; its scaffold is closely related to other high-ceiling diuretics such as bumetanide, torsemide, and ethacrynic acid, although ethacrynic acid is non-sulfonamide. Its principal target is the Na+/K+/2Cl− cotransporter NKCC2 encoded by SLC12A1 in the thick ascending limb of Henle, with inhibition reducing sodium, chloride, and potassium reabsorption; secondary renal effects involve altered medullary concentration gradients and increased calcium and magnesium excretion. Oral absorption is variable and incomplete, while intravenous administration produces rapid onset; it is highly protein bound, distributed mainly in extracellular fluid, undergoes limited metabolism including some glucuronidation, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by renal excretion with tubular secretion, with a shorter half-life than torsemide. Toxicity includes profound volume depletion, hypotension, prerenal azotemia, electrolyte disturbances such as hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, hyperuricemia with gout, and dose-related ototoxicity, especially with rapid IV dosing or concomitant aminoglycosides. Adverse effects commonly include dehydration, dizziness, muscle cramps, photosensitivity, rash, and rare severe sulfonamide-associated hypersensitivity. Clinically, furosemide is used to treat edema due to congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, and chronic kidney disease, as well as acute pulmonary edema and hypertension, particularly when rapid natriuresis or diuresis is required.

Name: Ergotamine
Description: Ergotamine (DrugBank DB00696) is a semisynthetic/ergot-derived indole alkaloid of the ergopeptine subclass, built on the rigid tetracyclic ergoline nucleus with an indole-fused lysergic acid framework amide-linked to a tripeptide-like cyclic peptide moiety, giving a polycyclic, conformationally constrained scaffold characteristic of peptide ergot alkaloids; chemically it is categorized as an ergot alkaloid, specifically an ergopeptide and serotonergic/adrenergic ligand, and its closest structural and pharmacological analogues include dihydroergotamine, methysergide, ergometrine, bromocriptine, and the triptans as mechanistically related antimigraine agents. Its principal targets are serotonin receptors HTR1B and HTR1D, with additional activity at HTR1A, HTR1F, alpha-1 and alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, and dopaminergic receptors, producing cranial vasoconstriction and inhibition of trigeminovascular neuropeptide signaling. Orally and rectally absorbed but with low and variable bioavailability because of extensive first-pass metabolism, ergotamine is highly protein bound, widely distributed, hepatically metabolized mainly by CYP3A4, and eliminated predominantly via biliary/fecal routes with limited renal excretion. It is indicated primarily for acute migraine attacks, with or without aura, and historically for cluster headache, but not for prophylaxis. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related ergotism, including severe peripheral and coronary vasospasm, ischemia, hypertension, myocardial infarction, stroke, and rarely gangrene, with risk markedly increased by CYP3A4 inhibitors. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, paresthesias, dizziness, weakness, and chest tightness. Clinically, it has been used alone or with caffeine for abortive treatment of refractory migraine when early vasoconstrictive therapy is desired, but use is limited by cardiovascular contraindications, drug interactions, and medication-overuse headache.

Name: Tizanidine
Description: Tizanidine (DrugBank DB00697) is a centrally acting imidazoline-derived muscle relaxant whose structure consists of a fused benzothiadiazole ring system linked through an amino bridge to an imidazoline moiety, giving a heteroaromatic, basic nitrogen-rich framework optimized for alpha-2 adrenergic receptor binding; chemically it is classified as an imidazoline/adrenergic agonist and its core scaffold is an imidazoline attached to a benzothiadiazole heterobicycle. It is structurally and pharmacologically related to other central alpha-2 agonists such as clonidine, guanfacine, dexmedetomidine, and xylazine, with clonidine being the closest clinical analogue. Its main targets are alpha-2A, alpha-2B, and alpha-2C adrenergic receptors, with functional reduction of excitatory interneuronal transmission in the spinal cord and consequent suppression of polysynaptic reflex activity. Orally, it is rapidly absorbed, but extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism limits bioavailability; it is moderately distributed systemically, is highly dependent on CYP1A2-mediated metabolism, and is excreted mainly in urine as metabolites with a relatively short elimination half-life, supporting repeated daily dosing. It is indicated for spasticity associated with multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, stroke, and other upper motor neuron syndromes, and is used clinically for relief of painful muscle spasms, nocturnal spasticity, and functional impairment from increased tone. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related CNS depression, hypotension, bradycardia, xerostomia, and hepatotoxicity, with overdose causing profound sedation, coma, miosis, and cardiovascular instability; common adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, weakness, dry mouth, fatigue, nausea, and transient liver enzyme elevations.

Name: Nitrofurantoin
Description: Nitrofurantoin (DB00698) is a synthetic nitrofuran antibacterial whose structure consists of a 5-nitrofuran aromatic heterocycle linked through a methylene-imine/hydrazone-type connection to a hydantoin (imidazolidine-2,4-dione) ring, placing it in the nitrofuran anti-infective class and defining a nitrofuran-hydantoin scaffold. It is chemically and pharmacologically related to other nitrofuran derivatives such as furazolidone, nitrofurazone, nifuroxazide, and, more distantly, other urinary antibacterials used for lower urinary tract infection. Its activity depends on enzymatic reduction by bacterial nitroreductases, notably oxygen-insensitive nitroreductases such as NfsA and NfsB, generating reactive intermediates that damage bacterial DNA, ribosomal proteins, and other macromolecules; no single dominant human protein target is established. Pharmacokinetically, oral absorption is moderate and formulation dependent, increased with food, with low plasma protein binding, limited tissue penetration, and therapeutically high urinary concentrations; it undergoes partial hepatic and tissue metabolism and is eliminated rapidly mainly by renal excretion via glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, giving a short half-life and restricting utility to the lower urinary tract. It is indicated primarily for treatment and prophylaxis of uncomplicated urinary tract infections, especially cystitis caused by susceptible Escherichia coli, Enterococcus faecalis, and Staphylococcus saprophyticus, but not pyelonephritis or prostatitis. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, vomiting, anorexia, headache, and diarrhea; important toxicities include acute or chronic pulmonary hypersensitivity/fibrosis, hepatotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy, and hemolytic anemia, particularly in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency or neonates. Clinically, it is widely used as first-line oral therapy for acute uncomplicated cystitis and as suppressive prophylaxis in recurrent UTI.

Name: Eplerenone
Description: Eplerenone (DB00700) is a selective steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist built on a 9,11-epoxy pregnene-derived steroid nucleus with a 3-keto group, a 17-carbomethoxy substituent, and a 7alpha-methoxy modification that reduces off-target androgen and progesterone receptor binding relative to older agents. Chemically, it is a cardenolide-like steroidal spirolactone-related antimineralocorticoid, and its core scaffold is the epoxy-substituted corticosteroid-like tetracyclic steroid framework closely related to spironolactone; similar drugs include spironolactone, finerenone, canrenone, and other mineralocorticoid receptor blockers. Its principal target is the mineralocorticoid receptor, encoded by NR3C2, through which it blocks aldosterone-mediated sodium retention, potassium wasting, vascular remodeling, and myocardial fibrosis. After oral administration, eplerenone is reasonably absorbed, reaches peak plasma concentrations in about 1.5 to 2 hours, is moderately protein bound, has a relatively small to moderate distribution volume, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 to inactive metabolites, and is eliminated through both urine and feces with a terminal half-life of roughly 4 to 6 hours. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related hyperkalemia, especially in renal impairment, diabetes, heart failure, or with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium supplements, or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors; hypotension and worsening renal function are also important examples. It is indicated for hypertension and for improving outcomes in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, particularly post-myocardial infarction left ventricular dysfunction. Common adverse effects include hyperkalemia, dizziness, diarrhea, cough, fatigue, and increased creatinine. Clinically, it is used as a potassium-sparing antihypertensive and cardioprotective aldosterone antagonist in resistant hypertension, post-MI heart failure, and selected chronic HFrEF patients when a more receptor-selective alternative to spironolactone is desired.

Name: Amprenavir
Description: Amprenavir (DrugBank DB00701) is a peptidomimetic HIV protease inhibitor built around a nonhydrolyzable hydroxyethylamine core that mimics the tetrahedral transition state of protease-mediated peptide cleavage, with a sulfonamide-linked tetrahydroxy-substituted framework and aromatic/heteroaromatic substituents that optimize occupancy of the viral protease active site; chemically it is classified as an antiretroviral aspartyl protease inhibitor, and its principal scaffold is the hydroxyethylamine-sulfonamide peptidomimetic motif. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other HIV protease inhibitors such as darunavir, fosamprenavir (its phosphate prodrug), ritonavir, indinavir, lopinavir, and saquinavir. Its main target is the HIV-1 protease, with activity also against HIV-2 protease to a lesser extent, thereby blocking gag-pol polyprotein processing and preventing maturation of infectious virions. Orally administered amprenavir is reasonably absorbed, highly protein bound, widely distributed, extensively metabolized in the liver primarily by CYP3A4, and eliminated mainly as metabolites in feces with a smaller urinary component; ritonavir coadministration historically increased exposure by CYP3A4 inhibition. Toxicity includes rash, including occasional severe cutaneous hypersensitivity, gastrointestinal toxicity, hepatotoxicity, hyperglycemia, lipodystrophy, and metabolic disturbances such as hypertriglyceridemia, with sulfonamide-related reactions as a recognized concern. Its indication is treatment of HIV-1 infection, typically in combination antiretroviral therapy for adults and selected pediatric patients, especially where protease inhibitor-based regimens are desired. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, oral paresthesia, headache, and rash. Clinically, amprenavir was used as part of multidrug ART, often boosted or replaced by fosamprenavir to improve formulation and pill burden.

Name: Methazolamide
Description: Methazolamide (DrugBank DB00703) is a heterocyclic sulfonamide carbonic anhydrase inhibitor built on a 1,3,4-thiadiazole scaffold bearing a sulfonamide pharmacophore and methylated substituents that increase lipophilicity relative to older congeners; chemically it is classified as a sulfonamide, nonantimicrobial carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, with the thiadiazole-sulfonamide core serving as its defining scaffold. It is closely related to acetazolamide, dichlorphenamide, dorzolamide, brinzolamide, and other carbonic anhydrase inhibitors used in ophthalmology and neurology. Its principal targets are carbonic anhydrase isoenzymes, especially CA II and CA IV, with broader activity across other carbonic anhydrase family members in ocular and renal tissues, leading to reduced bicarbonate formation, decreased aqueous humor secretion, and lower intraocular pressure. After oral administration it is well absorbed, distributes systemically including erythrocytes and ocular tissues, is moderately protein bound, undergoes limited hepatic biotransformation compared with acetazolamide, and is eliminated mainly by the kidney as unchanged drug and metabolites, with a duration of action sufficient for divided daily dosing. Toxicities reflect carbonic anhydrase inhibition and sulfonamide liability, including metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, renal stone risk, crystalluria, and rare severe hypersensitivity reactions such as rash, fever, blood dyscrasias, or Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Common adverse effects include paresthesias, fatigue, gastrointestinal upset, anorexia, dysgeusia, polyuria, and electrolyte disturbances. Clinically, methazolamide is used primarily for chronic open-angle glaucoma and secondary glaucomas, and sometimes as a short-term adjunct when rapid lowering of intraocular pressure is needed or topical therapy is insufficient or poorly tolerated.

Name: Naltrexone
Description: Naltrexone (DrugBank DB00704) is a semisynthetic morphinan opioid antagonist structurally derived from oxymorphone, characterized by a rigid fused pentacyclic 4,5-epoxymorphinan nucleus bearing a 3-phenolic hydroxyl, 14-hydroxyl, 6-keto functionality, and an N-cyclopropylmethyl substituent that confers antagonist activity; chemically it belongs to the morphinans/phenanthrene opioids, with an epoxymorphinan scaffold closely related to naloxone, nalmefene, oxymorphone, and other opioid ligands. Its principal targets are the mu-opioid receptor OPRM1, with high-affinity antagonism, and also kappa and delta opioid receptors, OPRK1 and OPRD1. Orally, naltrexone is well absorbed but undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, yielding the active metabolite 6-beta-naltrexol; distribution is systemic with moderate protein binding, metabolism is mainly non-CYP hepatic reduction and conjugation, and elimination occurs largely via the urine as parent drug and conjugated metabolites, with a longer apparent activity for extended-release intramuscular formulations. Clinically it is indicated for opioid use disorder to prevent relapse after detoxification and for alcohol use disorder to reduce craving and heavy drinking; examples include maintenance therapy after heroin or prescription opioid dependence and relapse prevention in alcohol dependence. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related hepatotoxicity, nausea, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, insomnia, anxiety, and injection-site reactions with depot products; severe precipitated opioid withdrawal can occur if given to opioid-dependent patients, and overdose risk may increase if patients attempt to surmount receptor blockade. In practice it is used as oral daily therapy or monthly extended-release injection in addiction medicine, sometimes off-label in low-dose regimens for investigational immunomodulatory or pain-related indications.

Name: Tamsulosin
Description: Tamsulosin (DrugBank DB00706) is a uroselective α1-adrenergic receptor antagonist built on an aryloxyethylamine/sulfonamide chemotype, featuring a methoxy-substituted benzenesulfonamide linked through an ethoxy spacer to a chiral propylamine bearing a 2-methoxyphenoxyethyl substituent; chemically it is classified as a sulfonamide-containing phenoxyethylamine and its recognizable scaffold is an arylsulfonamide-oxyethyl-amine framework typical of selective α1A/α1D blockers. It is structurally and pharmacologically related to other α1 antagonists such as alfuzosin, doxazosin, terazosin, and the less uroselective quinazoline-based agents prazosin and silodosin as another highly uroselective comparator. Its principal targets are adrenergic alpha-1A, alpha-1D, and to a lesser extent alpha-1B receptors, where antagonism relaxes smooth muscle in the prostate, bladder neck, and lower urinary tract. Orally administered tamsulosin is well absorbed, with bioavailability increased and rate moderated by food; it is highly protein bound, distributed mainly in plasma, extensively hepatically metabolized primarily by CYP3A4 and CYP2D6, and excreted largely in urine as metabolites with a smaller unchanged fraction, supporting once-daily dosing. It is indicated chiefly for benign prostatic hyperplasia and lower urinary tract symptoms such as hesitancy, weak stream, incomplete emptying, and nocturia, and is also used off-label to facilitate ureteral stone passage. Toxicity is usually extension of α-blockade, including orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, syncope, and interaction-mediated adverse effects with strong CYP inhibitors; other adverse effects include headache, asthenia, nasal congestion, palpitations, ejaculatory dysfunction including retrograde or absent ejaculation, and intraoperative floppy iris syndrome in cataract surgery patients. In clinical practice it is used as chronic symptomatic therapy for BPH, particularly in older men in whom uroselectivity is desired to minimize blood-pressure effects relative to nonselective α1 blockers.

Name: Sufentanil
Description: Sufentanil (DrugBank DB00708) is a highly lipophilic synthetic opioid analgesic structurally characterized as an anilidopiperidine bearing a substituted piperidine core, an anilide moiety, and a thienyl-containing side chain, features that increase receptor affinity and potency relative to fentanyl; chemically it belongs to the phenylpiperidine/anilidopiperidine opioid class, with a fentanyl-like 4-anilidopiperidine scaffold. Closely related drugs include fentanyl, alfentanil, remifentanil, and carfentanil, which share the same general opioid pharmacophore but differ in potency, onset, and duration. Its principal target is the mu-opioid receptor, encoded by OPRM1, with much weaker activity at delta- and kappa-opioid receptors. After intravenous, epidural, intrathecal, or transmucosal administration, sufentanil is rapidly absorbed where applicable, extensively distributed because of high lipophilicity, strongly partitions into the CNS, and is highly protein bound; it undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism via oxidative N-dealkylation and O-demethylation, mainly involving CYP3A4, to less active metabolites that are eliminated largely in urine and partly in feces, with a short context-sensitive analgesic profile despite terminal redistribution. It is indicated for severe acute pain, perioperative analgesia, balanced general anesthesia, and analgesia in mechanically ventilated or critically ill patients, as well as neuraxial labor or postoperative analgesia. Toxicity is typical of potent mu-agonists and includes dose-dependent respiratory depression, apnea, profound sedation, bradycardia, chest wall rigidity, hypotension, coma, and potentially fatal overdose, especially with benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, pruritus, constipation, dizziness, miosis, urinary retention, and postoperative respiratory compromise. Clinically, it is used as an anesthetic adjunct during major surgery such as cardiac or neurosurgical procedures, for ICU sedation-analgesia, and in epidural or intrathecal regimens where intense analgesia with hemodynamic stability is desired.

Name: Lamivudine
Description: Lamivudine (DB00709) is a synthetic nucleoside analogue of the 2′,3′-dideoxythiacytidine type, structurally characterized by a cytosine base linked to an oxathiolane ring that replaces the usual ribose oxygen-carbon framework, with the clinically used enantiomer conferring potent antiviral selectivity; chemically it belongs to the nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor class and is built on a thiacytidine/oxathiolane scaffold closely related to other antiviral nucleoside analogues such as emtricitabine, zalcitabine, and, more distantly, cytarabine-derived pyrimidine analogues. Its principal targets are viral reverse transcriptases, especially HIV-1 reverse transcriptase and hepatitis B virus polymerase/reverse transcriptase, after intracellular phosphorylation to lamivudine triphosphate, which competitively inhibits deoxycytidine incorporation and causes chain termination. Orally, lamivudine is well absorbed with high bioavailability, distributes widely into body fluids including cerebrospinal fluid, undergoes minimal hepatic metabolism, has low protein binding, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by renal excretion through filtration and active tubular secretion, so clearance is prolonged in renal impairment. It is indicated for HIV infection and chronic hepatitis B, for example as part of combination antiretroviral therapy or HBV suppression in patients with active viral replication. Toxicity is generally lower than with older NRTIs but can include class-associated mitochondrial toxicity, lactic acidosis, hepatomegaly with steatosis, pancreatitis, and rare severe hepatic exacerbations after discontinuation in HBV. Common adverse effects include nausea, headache, fatigue, cough, diarrhea, and rash. Clinically, lamivudine is widely used in fixed-dose HIV combinations and in HBV treatment, although resistance can emerge rapidly in HBV and via the HIV M184V/I mutation.

Name: Ibandronate
Description: Ibandronate (DrugBank DB00710) is a nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate characterized structurally by a geminal P-C-P bisphosphonate core attached to a hydroxylated central carbon and a basic nitrogen-bearing alkyl side chain, a motif that confers strong hydroxyapatite binding and potent antiresorptive activity; chemically it belongs to the aminobisphosphonate class, with a simple non-ring alkyl-amino bisphosphonate scaffold related to other osteoclast inhibitors such as alendronate, risedronate, pamidronate, and zoledronic acid. Its principal pharmacologic target is farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway within osteoclasts, leading to impaired prenylation of small GTPases, osteoclast dysfunction, and apoptosis; bone mineral is also a functional binding site driving skeletal selectivity. Oral absorption is very low and markedly reduced by food, calcium, or polyvalent cations, whereas intravenous dosing bypasses this limitation; distribution is rapid to bone and extracellular fluid, plasma protein binding is low to moderate, metabolism is negligible, and elimination occurs largely unchanged by renal excretion plus prolonged skeletal retention with a very long terminal bone phase. It is indicated primarily for postmenopausal osteoporosis, including prevention of vertebral fractures and treatment of low bone mineral density, and has also been used in other high bone-turnover states. Toxicities include upper gastrointestinal irritation and esophagitis with oral use, acute-phase reactions after infusion, hypocalcemia, renal toxicity with excessive intravenous exposure, osteonecrosis of the jaw, atypical femoral fractures, and embryo-fetal risk; common adverse effects include dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, musculoskeletal pain, back pain, headache, and flu-like symptoms. Clinically it is used as monthly oral therapy or intermittent intravenous therapy in patients requiring long-interval antiresorptive treatment, especially when adherence to daily or weekly bisphosphonates is problematic.

Name: Diethylcarbamazine
Description: Diethylcarbamazine, DrugBank ID DB00711, is a small synthetic piperazine derivative whose structure consists of a six-membered diamine piperazine ring bearing a carbamoyl substituent and N,N-diethyl groups, making it a moderately basic, lipophilic anthelmintic in the piperazine carboxamide class; its core chemical scaffold is therefore a substituted piperazine/carbamazine framework related more broadly to older antihelminthic piperazines, with mechanistically comparable antiparasitic drugs including ivermectin, albendazole, thiabendazole, and suramin, although these are chemically distinct. It is well absorbed orally, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, distributes widely in body fluids, undergoes partial hepatic biotransformation with pH-dependent handling, and is eliminated predominantly by the kidney as unchanged drug and metabolites, with urinary acidification increasing excretion and shortening half-life. Its precise molecular target is not fully defined, but known pharmacologic action involves alteration of filarial parasite membrane function and arachidonic acid metabolism, enhanced host immune clearance, and effects on parasite susceptibility to phagocytosis; no single validated human protein target is established, though cyclooxygenase- and lipoxygenase-related pathways have been implicated. Clinically, it is indicated chiefly for lymphatic filariasis caused by Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, and Brugia timori, as well as tropical pulmonary eosinophilia and loiasis. Toxicity is usually moderate and often relates either to dose or parasite killing, with examples including headache, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, fever, arthralgia, and proteinuria, while important adverse reactions include Mazzotti-type inflammatory responses, pruritus, rash, lymphangitis, edema, eosinophilic inflammation, and severe ocular or neurologic reactions in heavy Loa loa infection. In practice it is used as individual therapy and in mass drug administration programs, sometimes in combination regimens for filarial control.

Name: Oxacillin
Description: Oxacillin (DrugBank DB00713) is a semisynthetic, penicillinase-resistant β-lactam antibiotic whose structure consists of the penam nucleus, a fused β-lactam and thiazolidine bicyclic ring system, bearing the characteristic carboxylate and an acylamino side chain containing an isoxazolyl-substituted aromatic moiety that sterically shields the β-lactam from staphylococcal β-lactamase hydrolysis. Chemically, it belongs to the isoxazolyl penicillins within the broader class of beta-lactam antibacterials, and its core scaffold is the 6-aminopenicillanic acid penicillin scaffold. Closely related drugs include methicillin, cloxacillin, dicloxacillin, flucloxacillin, and nafcillin, which share antistaphylococcal activity and penicillinase stability. Oxacillin targets bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, especially transpeptidases such as PBP1, PBP2, and PBP3 in susceptible Gram-positive organisms, thereby blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking and causing cell wall failure. It is indicated primarily for infections caused by methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus and other susceptible bacteria, including skin and soft tissue infections, osteomyelitis, endocarditis, pneumonia, and bacteremia. Pharmacokinetically, oxacillin may be given orally or parenterally, although serious infections are usually treated intravenously; absorption is incomplete and reduced by food, distribution is mainly extracellular with moderate protein binding and variable penetration into inflamed tissues, metabolism is limited and partly hepatic, and elimination occurs through both renal tubular secretion and biliary routes, with a short half-life necessitating repeated dosing. Toxicities include hypersensitivity reactions, cholestatic or hepatocellular liver injury, interstitial nephritis, neutropenia, and rarely seizures at very high exposures; common adverse effects include rash, fever, diarrhea, nausea, phlebitis, and superinfection. Clinically, it is used as a targeted antistaphylococcal agent for MSSA cellulitis, MSSA endocarditis, postoperative wound infection, and bone or joint infection when susceptibility is known or strongly suspected.

Name: Paroxetine
Description: Paroxetine (DrugBank DB00715) is a phenylpiperidine antidepressant of the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor class, structurally characterized by a substituted piperidine ring bearing a 4-fluorophenyl group and a benzodioxole-containing oxy-methyl side chain, giving a rigid arylpiperidine scaffold with a fluorophenyl and methylenedioxyaryl pharmacophore that supports high serotonin transporter affinity. It is chemically related to other SSRIs such as fluoxetine, sertraline, citalopram, escitalopram, and fluvoxamine, though its piperidine-based scaffold distinguishes it from several non-piperidine analogs. Its principal target is the serotonin transporter SLC6A4, with weaker activity reported at the norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, nitric oxide synthase 1, muscarinic cholinergic receptors, and CYP2D6 as a clinically important inhibitory off-target. Orally administered paroxetine is well absorbed, undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, is highly protein bound, widely distributed, extensively metabolized mainly by CYP2D6 into largely less active metabolites, and is eliminated through both renal and fecal routes; nonlinear pharmacokinetics can occur because of CYP2D6 inhibition. Clinically it is used for major depressive disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, panic disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, social anxiety disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, premenstrual dysphoric disorder, and vasomotor symptoms such as menopausal hot flashes in selected formulations. Common adverse effects include nausea, somnolence, insomnia, sweating, dry mouth, constipation, tremor, sexual dysfunction, and weight gain, while important toxicities include serotonin syndrome, discontinuation syndrome, hyponatremia, abnormal bleeding, QT-related concerns in overdose, seizures, suicidality in younger patients, and teratogenic concern signals such as fetal cardiac malformations from first-trimester exposure.

Name: Nedocromil
Description: Nedocromil (DrugBank DB00716) is a synthetic anti-inflammatory antiasthmatic built on a rigid pyranoquinoline dicarboxylate scaffold, specifically a fused bicyclic chromone-like heteroaromatic system bearing two carboxyl functionalities as sodium salt substituents, a structure that confers high polarity, low lipophilicity, and limited systemic penetration; chemically it is classified as a mast-cell stabilizer and cromone-related agent, with a scaffold closely related to other cromoglycate-like drugs such as cromolyn sodium, lodoxamide, and to some extent ketotifen in therapeutic role though not close structurally. Its pharmacology is characterized by inhibition of inflammatory cell activation and mediator release from mast cells, eosinophils, sensory nerves, and possibly airway epithelial cells, with no single dominant high-affinity protein target firmly established, although modulation of chloride channels, GPR35, and inflammatory signaling pathways has been proposed. After inhalation or ophthalmic administration, absorption is low to modest, oral bioavailability is poor, tissue distribution is limited, protein binding is not a major defining feature, metabolism is minimal, and elimination occurs largely as unchanged drug via renal and biliary/fecal routes, yielding a relatively short systemic half-life but prolonged local airway or ocular action. Toxicity is generally low because of limited systemic exposure; overdose is uncommon and usually mild, while irritative effects such as cough, throat irritation, bronchospasm, bitter taste, nausea, headache, and ocular burning can occur. Clinically, it has been used for prophylaxis of bronchial asthma, exercise-induced bronchospasm, allergic rhinitis, and allergic conjunctivitis, especially as maintenance therapy to reduce wheeze, chest tightness, and hyperresponsiveness rather than for acute bronchospasm rescue.

Name: Norethisterone
Description: Norethisterone (norethindrone; DrugBank DB00717) is a synthetic 19-nortestosterone-derived progestin whose structure is characterized by the cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene steroid nucleus, a 3-keto-4-ene A-ring, a 17β-hydroxyl group, and a distinctive 17α-ethynyl substituent that enhances oral activity and metabolic stability; chemically it belongs to the estrane anabolic/sex steroid family, with an estrane steroid scaffold typical of first-generation orally active progestogens. Closely related drugs include norethynodrel, lynestrenol, levonorgestrel, ethynodiol diacetate, and medroxyprogesterone acetate, which share progestational activity but differ in androgenic and metabolic profiles. Its principal target is the progesterone receptor, with weaker binding to the androgen receptor and minimal indirect effects on gonadotropin-regulating pathways via hypothalamic-pituitary feedback. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed, undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, is distributed bound mainly to albumin and partly to sex hormone-binding globulin, is metabolized by hepatic reduction and conjugation pathways, including CYP3A4-associated biotransformation, and is excreted as urinary and fecal metabolites. Toxicities reflect class effects, including thromboembolic risk, cholestatic jaundice, hepatic dysfunction, adverse lipid changes, and potential worsening of hormone-sensitive neoplasia; overdose is usually limited to nausea, vomiting, or withdrawal bleeding. Indications include contraception, abnormal uterine bleeding, secondary amenorrhea, endometriosis, dysmenorrhea, and menstrual postponement. Common adverse effects include breakthrough bleeding, amenorrhea, headache, breast tenderness, nausea, edema, mood change, acne, and weight gain. Clinically, norethisterone is used alone or with estrogens in oral contraceptives and in gynecologic practice to suppress ovulation, transform endometrium, regulate cycles, and control progesterone-responsive bleeding disorders.

Name: Adefovir dipivoxil
Description: Adefovir dipivoxil (DrugBank DB00718) is an orally active diester prodrug of adefovir, structurally characterized as the bis-pivaloyloxymethyl ester of an acyclic adenine phosphonate in which an adenine purine base is linked to a flexible hydroxypropyl side chain terminating in a phosphonate masked to enhance membrane permeability; chemically it belongs to the antiviral acyclic nucleoside phosphonate class, with an adenine phosphonate scaffold closely related to other nucleotide analogs such as adefovir, tenofovir disoproxil, tenofovir alafenamide, cidofovir, and more distantly entecavir and lamivudine as anti-HBV comparators. After oral administration, it is absorbed and rapidly hydrolyzed by esterases to adefovir, has relatively low but clinically useful bioavailability, limited plasma protein binding, distribution into extracellular fluid and hepatocytes, minimal CYP-mediated metabolism, intracellular phosphorylation to the active diphosphate, and predominant renal elimination by glomerular filtration and active tubular secretion. Its principal target is hepatitis B virus reverse transcriptase/DNA polymerase, which is inhibited after active metabolite incorporation causes viral DNA chain termination. It is indicated for chronic hepatitis B, including active viral replication with hepatic inflammation or fibrosis, and has been used in nucleoside-resistant HBV infection. Dose-limiting toxicity is nephrotoxicity, especially proximal tubular injury, Fanconi-like syndrome, and serum creatinine elevation, with less common lactic acidosis and hepatomegaly with steatosis as class risks. Common adverse effects include asthenia, headache, abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, flatulence, and renal laboratory abnormalities. Clinically, it has been used as once-daily oral therapy for chronic HBV, particularly when resistance to older agents such as lamivudine is present, although use has declined because safer, more potent alternatives are available.

Name: Azatadine
Description: Azatadine (DB00719) is a first-generation tricyclic antihistamine whose structure consists of a rigid dibenzocycloheptene-like polycyclic aromatic system bearing a basic tertiary amine side chain, a motif that confers strong H1-receptor affinity, marked lipophilicity, and central nervous system penetration; chemically it is classified as a tricyclic H1 receptor antagonist of the benzo-cycloheptene/dibenzocycloheptene family, with a scaffold closely related to classical sedating antihistamines and structurally similar agents such as cyproheptadine, ketotifen, and, more distantly, other tricyclic antiallergic or antidepressant-like compounds sharing a fused aryl ring system and protonatable amine. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, with additional clinically relevant antimuscarinic activity and possible weak interactions at serotonergic sites typical of this class. Azatadine was used for symptomatic relief of allergic rhinitis, urticaria, pruritus, conjunctival symptoms, and other histamine-mediated allergic states. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed, distributes widely into tissues including the brain because of high lipophilicity, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism likely via oxidative biotransformation to inactive or less active metabolites, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine with lesser fecal excretion. Toxicity reflects exaggerated H1-blockade and anticholinergic effects, including sedation, confusion, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, and tachycardia; overdose may produce marked CNS depression or paradoxical excitation, especially in children. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, impaired psychomotor performance, xerostomia, nausea, and headache. Clinically, it was used as an oral antiallergic agent when rapid symptomatic control of itching, sneezing, rhinorrhea, or hives was needed, but its use became limited by sedation and anticholinergic burden compared with newer second-generation antihistamines.

Name: Lisinopril
Description: Lisinopril (DrugBank DB00722) is a lysine-containing dicarboxylate angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor characterized structurally as a peptidomimetic derivative of the enalaprilat class, with a proline-like bicyclic peptide-surrogate motif, multiple hydrogen-bonding carboxyl groups, and a basic lysyl side chain that confer strong ACE binding and high polarity; chemically it belongs to the ACE inhibitor class, specifically the non-sulfhydryl, dicarboxylate subclass, and its core scaffold is a substituted dipeptide/proline peptidomimetic optimized to chelate the catalytic zinc in ACE. Closely related drugs include enalapril, ramipril, benazepril, quinapril, perindopril, captopril, and fosinopril, which share ACE inhibition but differ in zinc-binding group, lipophilicity, and prodrug status. Lisinopril targets angiotensin-converting enzyme, reducing conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II and decreasing bradykinin degradation. Orally absorbed with relatively low bioavailability of about one quarter, it is not protein bound to a major extent, is minimally distributed into lipophilic tissues, is not metabolized, and is excreted unchanged in urine with a prolonged effective half-life permitting once-daily dosing, while renal impairment reduces clearance. Toxicities include hypotension, hyperkalemia, and dose-related worsening renal function, with serious examples including angioedema, fetal toxicity in pregnancy, and rare severe renal failure in bilateral renal artery stenosis. Indications include hypertension, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and reduction of mortality after acute myocardial infarction. Common adverse effects include cough, dizziness, headache, fatigue, syncope, increased creatinine, and gastrointestinal upset. Clinically, it is widely used alone or with diuretics, calcium channel blockers, or beta-blockers for blood pressure control, afterload reduction, cardiorenal protection in high-risk patients, and guideline-directed heart failure therapy.

Name: Methoxamine
Description: Methoxamine (DrugBank DB00723) is a synthetic sympathomimetic amine built on a substituted phenethylamine/phenylpropanolamine framework, characterized by an anisole-type aromatic ring bearing a methoxy substituent and a side chain containing a beta-hydroxyl group and a primary amine, features that confer direct vasopressor activity; chemically it is classified as an adrenergic agonist and pressor agent within the phenylethanolamine or phenylpropanolamine family, with a compact aryl-ethanolamine scaffold related to other alpha-adrenergic agonists. Similar drugs include phenylephrine, metaraminol, norepinephrine, midodrine, and mephentermine, which share vasoconstrictive sympathomimetic properties. Its principal pharmacologic target is the alpha-1 adrenergic receptor, especially ADRA1A, ADRA1B, and ADRA1D, with minimal clinically relevant beta-adrenergic activity, producing peripheral vasoconstriction and reflex bradycardia. Historically it has been administered parenterally for acute hypotensive states, including anesthesia-associated hypotension, postoperative hypotension, and shock with reduced vascular tone. Pharmacokinetic data are limited, but as a catecholamine-like pressor with parenteral use it has rapid onset, distribution mainly in extracellular fluid, hepatic and possibly monoamine oxidase-related biotransformation with conjugative metabolism, and renal excretion of metabolites and some unchanged drug. Toxicity is largely an extension of exaggerated alpha-adrenergic stimulation, with severe hypertension, cerebral hemorrhage, myocardial ischemia, arrhythmia, and peripheral ischemia reported or anticipated in overdose. Adverse effects include headache, reflex bradycardia, palpitations, anxiety, nausea, urinary retention, piloerection, and chest discomfort. Clinically, methoxamine has mainly been used as an injectable vasopressor to restore blood pressure transiently rather than as chronic therapy.

Name: Imiquimod
Description: Imiquimod (DrugBank DB00724) is a small, synthetic imidazoquinoline amine whose structure consists of a fused imidazole-quinoline bicyclic heteroaromatic core bearing an amino substituent and an isobutyl side chain, giving a rigid, lipophilic, nitrogen-rich pharmacophore typical of heteroaromatic immune response modifiers; chemically it is classified as an imidazoquinoline and more broadly a topical immunomodulatory Toll-like receptor agonist, with an imidazo[4,5-c]quinoline scaffold shared by related agents such as resiquimod and, more distantly, other nucleic-acid-sensing innate immune agonists. Its principal known targets are TLR7, with downstream activation of MyD88-, NF-kappaB-, and IRF7-dependent signaling and induction of interferon-alpha, TNF-alpha, IL-6, and other cytokines; some literature also discusses indirect effects on adenosine receptor signaling and immune effector cells. Pharmacokinetically, imiquimod is intended for topical use, with generally minimal but measurable percutaneous absorption, low systemic exposure, local skin retention, hepatic metabolism to hydroxylated and conjugated metabolites, and predominant renal excretion of metabolites with minor fecal elimination. Toxicity is dominated by exaggerated local and systemic immune stimulation: erythema, erosion, edema, ulceration, and pain at application sites are common, while flu-like reactions, headache, myalgia, and rare severe inflammatory responses or worsening of autoimmune/inflammatory dermatoses can occur. It is indicated for external genital and perianal warts caused by HPV, actinic keratosis, and superficial basal cell carcinoma, and clinically used as a 5% or 3.75% topical cream to treat visible lesions and field cancerization, particularly where a non-surgical, immune-mediated local therapy is preferred.

Name: Trimipramine
Description: Trimipramine (DrugBank DB00726) is a dibenzazepine/tricyclic antidepressant characterized structurally by a three-ring tricyclic hydrophobic core with a central seven-membered azepine ring fused to two benzene rings and bearing a three-carbon side chain terminating in a tertiary dimethylamino group, making it a highly lipophilic cationic amine; chemically it belongs to the tricyclic antidepressant class, with a dibenzazepine scaffold closely related to imipramine and other TCAs such as desipramine, clomipramine, amitriptyline, doxepin, and doxepin-like sedating antidepressants. Unlike strongly reuptake-selective TCAs, trimipramine has relatively weak inhibition of serotonin and norepinephrine transporters but significant receptor antagonism, with known targets including SLC6A4, SLC6A2, HRH1, CHRM1, ADRA1A, HTR2A, and likely HTR2C, contributing to its antidepressant, anxiolytic, and hypnotic profile. It is used mainly for major depressive disorder, especially depression with anxiety, agitation, or insomnia, and has also been used clinically for sleep disturbance and psychovegetative symptoms. After oral administration it is reasonably well absorbed, undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, is widely distributed with high protein binding and CNS penetration, and is metabolized primarily by CYP2D6 and other hepatic oxidative pathways to active and inactive metabolites that are excreted mainly in urine. Toxicity resembles that of other TCAs: dose-related CNS depression, anticholinergic toxicity, orthostatic hypotension, seizures, and potentially fatal cardiac conduction abnormalities or arrhythmias in overdose. Common adverse effects include sedation, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention, weight gain, dizziness, tachycardia, and QT-related ECG changes, which shape its modern use as a second-line antidepressant when prominent insomnia or anxiety favors a sedating TCA.

Name: Nitroglycerin
Description: Nitroglycerin (glyceryl trinitrate; DrugBank DB00727) is a small organic nitrate ester consisting of a three-carbon glycerol scaffold in which all three hydroxyl groups are esterified with nitrate moieties, making it a highly lipophilic, nitric oxide-donating vasodilator in the nitrate/nitrite class; its core chemical scaffold is therefore a glycerol triester bearing nitrate esters, and it is closely related to other antianginal nitrates such as isosorbide dinitrate, isosorbide mononitrate, erythrityl tetranitrate, and pentaerythritol tetranitrate. Pharmacologically, nitroglycerin is bioactivated mainly by mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase ALDH2, with contribution from glutathione S-transferases and related reductive pathways, to generate nitric oxide or related nitrosating species that activate soluble guanylate cyclase GUCY1A1/GUCY1B1 in vascular smooth muscle, increasing cGMP and promoting venodilation more than arteriolar dilation. It is rapidly absorbed across sublingual, buccal, transdermal, and intravenous routes, undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism after oral dosing, distributes widely into vascular-rich tissues, is converted to dinitrate and mononitrate metabolites, and is excreted mainly in urine as metabolites. Toxicity includes dose-related profound hypotension, reflex tachycardia, syncope, headache, methemoglobinemia, and rare severe overdose with shock; tolerance and cross-tolerance develop with continuous exposure. Clinically it is indicated for acute relief and prophylaxis of angina pectoris, adjunctive treatment of acute coronary syndromes, acute pulmonary edema, hypertensive emergencies, and perioperative blood pressure control. Common adverse effects include throbbing headache, flushing, dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, nausea, and palpitations, with major contraindicated interactions with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil and tadalafil due to potentially life-threatening hypotension.

Name: Thiabendazole
Description: Thiabendazole (DrugBank DB00730) is a synthetic benzimidazole-thiazole anthelmintic whose structure consists of a fused benzene-imidazole benzimidazole nucleus bearing a 2-substituted thiazolyl group, giving a rigid, heteroaromatic, weakly basic framework optimized for helminth tubulin binding; chemically it belongs to the benzimidazole antiparasitic class, with a benzimidazole scaffold functionally extended by a thiazole ring. It is closely related to other benzimidazole antiparasitics such as albendazole, mebendazole, fenbendazole, and carbendazim, which share microtubule-disrupting properties. Its principal pharmacologic target is parasite beta-tubulin, with inhibition of microtubule polymerization and downstream impairment of glucose uptake and energy metabolism; flavin-containing monooxygenases and cytochrome P450 enzymes are relevant to its biotransformation rather than primary efficacy. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed, distributed systemically, extensively metabolized in the liver mainly to 5-hydroxythiabendazole and conjugated metabolites, and eliminated predominantly in urine with limited unchanged drug excretion. It has been used for strongyloidiasis, cutaneous larva migrans, trichinosis, ascariasis, and other nematode infections, and has also been applied as an agricultural antifungal. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, vomiting, anorexia, abdominal pain, dizziness, headache, and drowsiness, while toxicity may include hepatotoxicity, cholestatic jaundice, hypersensitivity reactions, visual disturbances, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and rarely severe skin reactions or hematologic abnormalities. Clinically, its use has largely been supplanted by better tolerated agents, but it remains a historically important systemic benzimidazole for susceptible helminth infections.

Name: Nateglinide
Description: Nateglinide (DrugBank DB00731) is an orally active, non-sulfonylurea insulin secretagogue structurally characterized as a D-phenylalanine-derived amino acid analog bearing a substituted benzyl side chain and a carboxylic acid-linked cyclohexylcarbonyl amide, giving a compact amphipathic architecture with aromatic, alicyclic, and acidic functionalities important for receptor binding; chemically it is classified as a meglitinide-like glinide antidiabetic, with a phenylalanine/amino-acid amide scaffold rather than a sulfonylurea core. Related drugs include repaglinide and mitiglinide, which share rapid prandial insulinotropic action via the pancreatic beta-cell KATP channel. Its principal target is the ATP-sensitive potassium channel complex, especially the sulfonylurea receptor 1 subunit ABCC8 with functional coupling to KCNJ11, leading to channel closure, depolarization, calcium influx, and glucose-dependent insulin release. Nateglinide is rapidly absorbed after oral dosing, reaches peak concentrations in about 1 hour, has high but not extreme protein binding, a short elimination half-life of roughly 1.5 hours, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 to less active metabolites, and is excreted predominantly in urine with a smaller fecal component. It is indicated for type 2 diabetes mellitus, particularly postprandial hyperglycemia, and is used alone or with metformin alongside diet and exercise. Adverse effects include hypoglycemia, dizziness, nausea, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, headache, and weight gain; toxicity is dominated by dose-related hypoglycemia, especially with missed meals, hepatic impairment, alcohol use, or combination therapy, while overdose may produce neuroglycopenic symptoms requiring prompt carbohydrate or dextrose administration.

Name: Pralidoxime
Description: Pralidoxime (DrugBank DB00733) is a quaternary pyridinium aldoxime composed of a positively charged pyridine ring bearing an aldoxime substituent and typically administered as the chloride or methanesulfonate salt; structurally it is a small, highly polar oxime designed as a nucleophilic reactivator of phosphorylated cholinesterases. It belongs to the oxime antidote class and more specifically to cationic pyridinium acetylcholinesterase reactivators, with a monopyridinium oxime scaffold that is closely related to other antidotal oximes such as obidoxime, trimedoxime, and asoxime/HI-6. Its principal target is organophosphate-inhibited acetylcholinesterase, and it can also reactivate butyrylcholinesterase to a lesser extent, restoring synaptic transmission at nicotinic and muscarinic sites after organophosphate exposure. Pharmacokinetically, pralidoxime is poorly absorbed orally, so it is usually given intravenously or intramuscularly; because of its permanent positive charge it distributes mainly in extracellular fluid, penetrates the blood-brain barrier poorly, undergoes limited metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by the kidneys with a relatively short plasma half-life, requiring repeated dosing or infusion in severe poisoning. It is indicated for organophosphate pesticide poisoning and nerve agent intoxication, especially when muscle weakness, fasciculations, bronchorrhea, and respiratory compromise are present, and is used adjunctively with atropine and ventilatory support. Toxicity and adverse effects include tachycardia, hypertension, diplopia, blurred vision, dizziness, headache, nausea, transient neuromuscular weakness, injection-site pain, and, at excessive doses, possible worsening of cholinergic or neuromuscular dysfunction; clinical use is greatest when administered early, before enzyme aging limits reactivation.

Name: Risperidone
Description: Risperidone (DrugBank DB00734) is an atypical antipsychotic of the benzisoxazole-derived piperidine class, characterized structurally by a 6-fluoro-1,2-benzisoxazole aromatic heterocycle linked through a short carbon chain to a substituted piperidine/pyridopyrimidinone-containing tertiary amine system, giving a rigid heteroaryl-piperidine scaffold typical of serotonin-dopamine antagonists. Its core scaffold is closely related to other benzisoxazole or benzisazole antipsychotics, especially paliperidone, its major active 9-hydroxy metabolite, and it also shows pharmacologic similarity to ziprasidone, iloperidone, and lurasidone as mixed 5-HT2A/D2 antagonists. Risperidone targets primarily dopamine D2 receptors and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors, with additional affinity for 5-HT7, 5-HT2C, alpha1- and alpha2-adrenergic receptors, and histamine H1 receptors, while having relatively low muscarinic cholinergic activity. It is indicated for schizophrenia, acute manic or mixed episodes of bipolar I disorder, irritability associated with autistic disorder, and is also used for psychosis, aggression, severe behavioral dysregulation, and tic-related symptoms in selected settings. After oral administration it is well absorbed, has high bioavailability, moderate protein binding, wide distribution including CNS penetration, and undergoes hepatic metabolism mainly by CYP2D6 and to a lesser extent CYP3A4 to paliperidone, with renal excretion of parent drug and metabolites and an elimination half-life prolonged in poor metabolizers or renal impairment. Toxicities include dose-related extrapyramidal symptoms, hyperprolactinemia, sedation, weight gain, orthostatic hypotension, QT prolongation, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, cerebrovascular adverse events in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis, and overdose manifestations such as somnolence, tachycardia, dystonia, and impaired consciousness; common side effects include akathisia, parkinsonism, tremor, dizziness, increased appetite, sexual dysfunction, and metabolic abnormalities. Clinically, it is widely used as oral tablets, solution, orally disintegrating tablets, and long-acting injectable formulations for maintenance antipsychotic therapy, relapse prevention, acute agitation control

Name: Naftifine
Description: Naftifine (DrugBank DB00735) is a synthetic allylamine antifungal characterized structurally by a lipophilic aromatic framework containing a naphthalene ring linked through a benzylic methylene to a tertiary allylamine side chain, giving an aryl-allylamine scaffold that is central to its antifungal activity; chemically it belongs to the allylamine class, with a scaffold closely related to other squalene epoxidase inhibitors such as terbinafine and butenafine, which are considered similar drugs by mechanism and topical use. Its principal molecular target is fungal squalene epoxidase, a key enzyme in ergosterol biosynthesis, and inhibition causes ergosterol depletion with intracellular squalene accumulation, disrupting fungal membrane integrity. Naftifine is used primarily as a topical agent for dermatophyte and some yeast-associated skin infections, including tinea pedis, tinea cruris, tinea corporis, and occasionally cutaneous candidiasis or pityriasis versicolor-related presentations, especially when pruritus and inflammation are prominent. Pharmacokinetically, systemic absorption after topical application is low but measurable, with drug concentrating in the stratum corneum and superficial epidermis; distribution is therefore mainly local, hepatic metabolism likely contributes to biotransformation of the small absorbed fraction, and excretion occurs predominantly as metabolites in urine and feces. Toxicity is generally limited because of minimal systemic exposure, but local intolerance can occur, including burning, stinging, erythema, dryness, irritation, and contact dermatitis; examples of uncommon adverse effects include pruritus and worsening inflammation at the application site. Clinically, naftifine is applied once or twice daily for localized superficial mycoses, valued for fungicidal activity against dermatophytes and concurrent antipruritic, anti-inflammatory benefit in symptomatic fungal dermatoses.

Name: Esomeprazole
Description: Esomeprazole (DrugBank DB00736) is the S-enantiomer of omeprazole and is a substituted benzimidazole proton-pump inhibitor built from a benzimidazole ring linked through a sulfoxide bridge to a substituted pyridine, giving a chiral sulfoxide-containing heteroaromatic structure whose core scaffold is the benzimidazole-sulfoxide-pyridine motif characteristic of this class. Chemically it belongs to gastric acid-suppressing benzimidazole sulfoxides, and close analogs include omeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole, rabeprazole, and dexlansoprazole. After oral administration, it is acid labile and therefore formulated as enteric-coated granules or tablets; absorption occurs in the small intestine with high but variable bioavailability that increases with repeated dosing, extensive plasma protein binding, and distribution mainly in extracellular fluids, followed by hepatic metabolism primarily via CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 to inactive hydroxy- and desmethyl-related metabolites, with excretion chiefly in urine and the remainder in feces. Its principal target is the gastric H+/K+-ATPase alpha subunit, which it inhibits irreversibly after acid-activated conversion to a reactive sulfenamide in parietal cell canaliculi. It is indicated for gastroesophageal reflux disease, erosive esophagitis, nonerosive heartburn, peptic ulcer disease, Helicobacter pylori eradication regimens, and prevention of NSAID-associated ulcers, and is also used in hypersecretory states such as Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. Adverse effects are usually mild and include headache, abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, constipation, and flatulence; important toxicities and longer-term risks include hypersensitivity, interstitial nephritis, hypomagnesemia, vitamin B12 deficiency, Clostridioides difficile infection, pneumonia, fractures, and possible CYP2C19-mediated drug interactions, for example with clopidogrel.

Name: Meclizine
Description: Meclizine (DB00737) is a first-generation piperazine antihistamine whose structure consists of a diaryl-substituted tertiary amine built on a piperazine core, typically described as a diphenylmethyl/p-chlorobenzhydryl-like lipophilic motif linked to an N-methylated piperazine, giving it the hydrophobic arylamine architecture characteristic of centrally acting H1 antagonists. Chemically it belongs to the piperazine-class antihistamines and more broadly to antiemetic/antivertigo agents; its principal scaffold is the aryl-substituted piperazine framework. Closely related or pharmacologically similar drugs include cyclizine, hydroxyzine, cetirizine, cinnarizine, dimenhydrinate, and diphenhydramine, especially among vestibular suppressants and sedating H1 blockers. Meclizine acts primarily at the histamine H1 receptor and also has clinically relevant antimuscarinic activity, reducing vestibular excitation and signaling to the vomiting center; muscarinic acetylcholine receptors are therefore also considered functionally relevant targets. After oral administration it is well absorbed, with onset in about 1 hour, extensive tissue distribution including CNS penetration, substantial hepatic metabolism, and relatively prolonged action with an elimination half-life generally reported around 5 to 6 hours but with longer clinical effect; excretion occurs mainly as metabolites in urine and feces. Toxicity is usually dose-related CNS and anticholinergic toxicity, with overdose causing marked drowsiness, confusion, hallucinations, hypotension, tachycardia, dry mouth, urinary retention, and rarely seizures, particularly in children or older adults. It is indicated for motion sickness, vertigo, and nausea/vomiting associated with vestibular disorders such as Ménière disease or labyrinthitis, and clinically is used prophylactically before travel and symptomatically for dizziness, nausea, and balance disturbance; common adverse effects include sedation, fatigue, blurred vision, constipation, and impaired psychomotor performance.

Name: Riluzole
Description: Riluzole (DB00740) is a small, lipophilic benzothiazole derivative whose structure is centered on a fused bicyclic 1,3-benzothiazole aromatic scaffold bearing a 2-amino substituent and a ring trifluoromethoxy group, features that confer weak basicity, CNS penetration, and glutamatergic modulating activity; chemically it is classified as a heteroaromatic aminobenzothiazole and its core scaffold is shared broadly with other benzothiazole-based neuroactive agents, although no close therapeutic analog is identical, with mechanistically or pharmacologically similar drugs including edaravone, gabapentin, lamotrigine, and memantine. Riluzole is well absorbed orally, undergoes significant first-pass hepatic metabolism with moderate bioavailability, distributes widely including into the central nervous system, is highly protein bound, and is metabolized predominantly by CYP1A2 to hydroxylated and conjugated metabolites that are excreted mainly in urine, with a terminal half-life of roughly half a day. Toxicity is driven chiefly by hepatotoxicity and neurotoxicity, with clinically relevant examples including transaminase elevations, hepatitis, dizziness, somnolence, and in overdose tachycardia, methemoglobinemia, or coma; caution is heightened in hepatic impairment and with CYP1A2 inhibitors. Its known or proposed targets include voltage-gated sodium channels, high-voltage-activated calcium channels, glutamatergic neurotransmission systems including presynaptic glutamate release machinery, excitatory amino acid signaling pathways, and potassium channels such as TREK-family channels. It is indicated primarily for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis to modestly prolong survival or delay tracheostomy, and clinically it is used as chronic oral disease-modifying therapy in ALS, with adverse effects commonly including nausea, asthenia, elevated liver enzymes, abdominal pain, vertigo, and neutropenia.

Name: Hydrocortisone
Description: Hydrocortisone (DrugBank DB00741) is the natural glucocorticoid cortisol, a C21 pregnane corticosteroid built on a rigid cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene steroid nucleus with ketone groups at C3 and C20, a Δ4 double bond, and characteristic hydroxyl substituents at C11β, C17α, and C21 that confer glucocorticoid and modest mineralocorticoid activity. Chemically it belongs to the corticosteroid and steroid alcohol class, with a hydrocortisone/cortisol steroid scaffold closely related to prednisone, prednisolone, cortisone, methylprednisolone, dexamethasone, and fludrocortisone. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, with lesser activity at the mineralocorticoid receptor NR3C2; downstream effects include transcriptional suppression of proinflammatory mediators such as NF-κB- and AP-1-regulated cytokines. Hydrocortisone is used in adrenal insufficiency, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, severe allergy, asthma exacerbations, septic shock adjunctive therapy, inflammatory dermatoses, rheumatoid and other autoimmune disorders, and ulcerative colitis, with topical, oral, rectal, and parenteral use. Oral absorption is generally good, distribution is wide with substantial plasma protein binding to corticosteroid-binding globulin and albumin, metabolism occurs mainly in the liver via reduction and 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase interconversion plus CYP3A4-mediated pathways, and excretion is primarily renal as inactive metabolites.
