Toxicity is dominated by dose- and duration-related hypercortisolism, including hyperglycemia, hypertension, edema, hypokalemia, osteoporosis, myopathy, skin atrophy, impaired wound healing, infection risk, psychosis, cataracts, glaucoma, growth suppression, and adrenal suppression; acute excess may cause fluid retention and gastrointestinal irritation. Common adverse effects include insomnia, mood change, dyspepsia, acne, bruising, and candidiasis with topical or mucosal use.

Name: Mannitol
Description: Mannitol (DrugBank DB00742) is a highly polar acyclic hexitol composed of a six-carbon straight-chain sugar alcohol scaffold with one hydroxyl group on each carbon, making it a stereochemically defined polyol and a close structural reduction product of mannose; chemically it belongs to the carbohydrate-derived polyol/osmotic diuretic class, with related drugs including sorbitol, glycerol, isosorbide, and the urea-like osmotic agent urea. Its pharmacologic action is largely target-independent and physicochemical rather than receptor-mediated, although no single canonical protein target is established; instead, it increases extracellular and tubular fluid osmolality, thereby extracting water from tissues and limiting renal tubular water reabsorption, with downstream effects influenced by renal handling proteins such as aquaporins and tubular solute transport systems. Mannitol is administered mainly intravenously, is poorly absorbed orally, distributes largely to the extracellular space with limited blood-brain barrier penetration unless disrupted, undergoes minimal metabolism, and is excreted predominantly unchanged by glomerular filtration, with elimination prolonged in renal impairment. It is indicated for reduction of elevated intracranial pressure and cerebral edema, lowering intraocular pressure in acute glaucoma, and promotion of diuresis in settings such as impending acute kidney injury, toxin clearance, or perioperative renal protection. Toxicity is mainly osmotic and volume-related, including dehydration, hypernatremia or hyponatremia, hyperosmolality, headache, nausea, and acute kidney injury; serious examples include pulmonary edema or heart failure exacerbation from transient intravascular expansion, especially in anuric or cardiac patients. Clinically, mannitol is used in neurocritical care, ophthalmologic emergencies, and selected nephrologic or toxicologic scenarios.

Name: Zileuton
Description: Zileuton (DB00744) is a synthetic small-molecule leukotriene pathway inhibitor whose structure is characterized by an N-hydroxyurea zinc/iron-chelating pharmacophore linked to a substituted benzothiophene-containing aromatic system, placing it in the hydroxyurea class of anti-inflammatory agents and more specifically among 5-lipoxygenase inhibitors; its core chemical scaffold can be described as an aryl-substituted hydroxyurea built on a benzothiophene framework. Structurally and mechanistically similar drugs include other antileukotriene agents such as montelukast, zafirlukast, and pranlukast, although these are cysteinyl leukotriene receptor antagonists rather than direct 5-lipoxygenase inhibitors; zileuton is also conceptually related to investigational lipoxygenase inhibitors. Its principal target is arachidonate 5-lipoxygenase, encoded by ALOX5, thereby reducing formation of leukotrienes including LTB4, LTC4, LTD4, and LTE4. After oral administration, zileuton is reasonably well absorbed, undergoes significant hepatic first-pass metabolism mainly via CYP1A2, CYP2C9, and CYP3A4 with glucuronidation also contributing, is distributed systemically with moderate protein binding, and is eliminated predominantly as urinary metabolites with a relatively short half-life that historically necessitated multiple daily dosing, although extended-release formulations reduced dosing frequency. The main indication is prophylaxis and chronic treatment of asthma, especially in patients with leukotriene-driven bronchoconstriction, nocturnal asthma, or aspirin-sensitive asthma, but it is not useful for acute bronchospasm. Toxicity is dominated by hepatotoxicity, including asymptomatic transaminase elevation and rare clinically significant liver injury, with additional risks of drug interactions through CYP inhibition, notably increasing theophylline and warfarin exposure. Common adverse effects include dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, headache, upper respiratory symptoms, myalgia, and sleep disturbance. Clinically, it is used as a controller medication to reduce asthma symptoms, improve pulmonary function, and decrease rescue bronchodilator use in selected patients requiring leukotriene suppression.

Name: Modafinil
Description: Modafinil (DrugBank DB00745) is a diphenylmethyl sulfinyl acetamide derivative whose structure features a benzhydryl core bearing two phenyl rings linked through a sulfoxide to an acetamide side chain; it is a racemic wake-promoting agent classified chemically as a eugeroic and more broadly as a central nervous system stimulant-like sulfoxide amide, with a modafinil/adrafinil benzhydryl sulfinyl scaffold. Closely related or pharmacologically similar agents include armodafinil, the R-enantiomer of modafinil, and adrafinil, its prodrug, as well as mechanistically overlapping wake-promoting stimulants such as methylphenidate and amphetamine. Its best-supported target is the dopamine transporter SLC6A3, which it inhibits weakly to moderately, increasing extracellular dopamine; other implicated targets or systems include the norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, orexin/hypocretin pathways, histaminergic neurons, and possibly GABAergic and glutamatergic signaling, although these are less definitively direct. Modafinil is well absorbed orally, reaches peak plasma concentrations in about 2 to 4 hours, is moderately protein bound, distributes systemically including into the CNS, undergoes primarily hepatic metabolism via amide hydrolysis, S-oxidation, and CYP-mediated pathways including CYP3A4, with potential inhibition of CYP2C19 and induction of CYP3A4, and is excreted mainly in urine as metabolites with an elimination half-life of roughly 12 to 15 hours. It is indicated for excessive sleepiness in narcolepsy, obstructive sleep apnea residual sleepiness, and shift-work sleep disorder, and is also used off-label in fatigue states and disorders of vigilance. Adverse effects commonly include headache, nausea, decreased appetite, insomnia, anxiety, dizziness, and dry mouth; important toxicities include hypertension, tachycardia, agitation, psychosis or mania in susceptible patients, and rare serious cutaneous hypersensitivity reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and DRESS, as well as rare hepatotoxicity and abuse liability lower than classical stimulants but still clinically relevant.

Name: Scopolamine
Description: Scopolamine (DrugBank DB00747) is a naturally occurring belladonna alkaloid with a tropane ester structure composed of a bicyclic nortropane/scopine core bearing a 6,7-epoxide bridge and esterified with tropic acid, placing it in the antimuscarinic parasympatholytic class; its core scaffold is the tropane alkaloid framework, closely related to atropine, hyoscyamine, homatropine, and other muscarinic antagonists such as ipratropium, although the latter are more extensively modified analogs. It acts primarily as a nonselective competitive antagonist at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially CHRM1, CHRM2, CHRM3, CHRM4, and CHRM5, with central penetration that distinguishes it from quaternary antimuscarinics. Scopolamine is well absorbed by oral, transdermal, parenteral, and ophthalmic routes; transdermal delivery provides sustained systemic exposure for about 72 hours. It is widely distributed, readily crosses the blood-brain barrier and placenta, undergoes hepatic metabolism largely by hydrolysis and conjugative or oxidative pathways, and is excreted mainly in urine as metabolites and a smaller unchanged fraction. Major indications include prevention of motion sickness, postoperative nausea and vomiting, and off-label control of vestibular nausea, drooling, or gastrointestinal spasm. Typical adverse effects reflect anticholinergic activity and include dry mouth, blurred vision, mydriasis, constipation, urinary retention, tachycardia, decreased sweating, and sedation; central toxicity may produce confusion, agitation, hallucinations, delirium, and amnesia, especially in older adults or overdose, while severe poisoning can cause hyperthermia and anticholinergic syndrome. Clinically, it is widely used as a transdermal patch before travel or surgery and less commonly by injection or ophthalmic administration when muscarinic blockade is desired.

Name: Carbinoxamine
Description: Carbinoxamine (DrugBank DB00748) is a first-generation ethanolamine antihistamine built around a diaryl ether scaffold in which a substituted pyridyl-aryl system is linked through an oxygen-containing propyl chain to a terminal dimethylamino moiety; structurally it is a lipophilic, weakly basic amine typically used clinically as the maleate salt. Chemically, it belongs to the H1 receptor antagonist class of alkylamine/ethanolamine-like sedating antihistamines, with a classic aryl-oxy-propanamine antihistamine pharmacophore shared by related agents such as doxylamine, clemastine, diphenhydramine, brompheniramine, and chlorpheniramine. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, at which it acts as an inverse agonist/antagonist, and it also shows clinically relevant anticholinergic activity through off-target muscarinic receptor blockade. After oral administration it is well absorbed, distributes widely including into the central nervous system, has moderate protein binding, undergoes hepatic biotransformation likely involving oxidative N-dealkylation and related microsomal pathways, and is eliminated primarily in urine as metabolites and some unchanged drug, with a duration consistent with multiple daily dosing. It is indicated for symptomatic relief of allergic rhinitis, vasomotor rhinitis, conjunctival allergy, urticaria, angioedema, pruritic dermatoses, and common-cold symptoms such as rhinorrhea and sneezing. Adverse effects reflect CNS and antimuscarinic actions, including sedation, dizziness, impaired psychomotor performance, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention. Toxicity is most notable in overdose or young children, where profound CNS depression or paradoxical excitation, anticholinergic syndrome, seizures, respiratory compromise, and potentially fatal outcomes have been reported; consequently, clinical use is mainly short-term symptomatic allergy treatment in carefully selected patients.

Name: Etodolac
Description: Etodolac (DrugBank DB00749) is a small-molecule nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug of the heteroaryl acetic acid class, structurally characterized by an indole-like fused pyranocarboxylic acid scaffold bearing an ethyl substituent and a para-substituted benzyl group, giving it a lipophilic aromatic framework linked to the acidic pharmacophore typical of NSAIDs; its core chemical scaffold is commonly described as a tetrahydropyranoindole or pyranocarboxylic acid NSAID scaffold. It is pharmacologically related to other COX-inhibiting anti-inflammatory agents, with broadly similar drugs including diclofenac, indomethacin, sulindac, nabumetone, ibuprofen, naproxen, and the relatively COX-2-selective oxicam and coxib-like comparators such as meloxicam and celecoxib. Its principal targets are cyclooxygenase-2 and cyclooxygenase-1, encoded by PTGS2 and PTGS1, with functional preference for COX-2 at therapeutic concentrations, reducing prostaglandin synthesis and thereby inflammation, pain, and fever. Etodolac is well absorbed orally, reaches peak plasma concentrations within a few hours, is highly protein bound, distributes mainly in the vascular/extracellular compartment, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism including oxidation and glucuronidation, and is eliminated primarily in urine as metabolites with a smaller fecal component; the terminal half-life generally supports twice-daily dosing, with extended-release formulations enabling once-daily use. Clinically it is indicated for osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and acute pain, including musculoskeletal pain, postoperative pain, and dysmenorrhea. Adverse effects resemble other NSAIDs and include dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, edema, hypertension, renal function impairment, and rash, while serious toxicity may include peptic ulceration, gastrointestinal bleeding or perforation, hepatotoxicity, fluid retention, cardiovascular thrombotic events, and hypersensitivity reactions including bronchospasm in aspirin-sensitive patients. In practice, it is used as an oral analgesic and anti-inflammatory agent when sustained symptom control is needed, particularly in chronic arthritic disease or short-term treatment of moderate nociceptive inflammatory pain.

Name: Prilocaine
Description: Prilocaine (DrugBank DB00750) is an amide-type local anesthetic structurally characterized by an o-toluidine-derived aromatic ring linked through a carboxamide to a propylamino side chain, giving a moderately lipophilic anilide architecture with a tertiary amine that is protonated near physiologic pH; chemically it belongs to the amino amide local anesthetics and is built on an anilide/amidopropyl scaffold closely related to lidocaine, mepivacaine, bupivacaine, and articaine in pharmacologic class, with lidocaine as a particularly similar comparator. Its principal targets are voltage-gated sodium channels in peripheral nerves, especially Nav channel alpha subunits such as SCN9A, SCN10A, and related neuronal and muscle sodium channel isoforms, where it stabilizes the inactivated state and blocks impulse conduction. Prilocaine is used for local and regional anesthesia, including infiltration anesthesia, peripheral nerve block, intravenous regional anesthesia, and topical dermal anesthesia in eutectic combination with lidocaine for procedures such as venipuncture, minor dermatologic interventions, and superficial surgery. It is absorbed variably depending on dose, route, vascularity, and coadministration with vasoconstrictors; it distributes into well-perfused tissues and crosses the placenta; hepatic and extrahepatic amidase-mediated metabolism produces ortho-toluidine and other metabolites; and renal excretion is mainly as metabolites with limited unchanged drug. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related CNS and cardiovascular effects, including circumoral numbness, tinnitus, seizures, hypotension, conduction disturbances, and rare collapse, but prilocaine is especially notable for methemoglobinemia due to ortho-toluidine formation, particularly in infants, high-dose exposure, or patients with G6PD deficiency, anemia, or oxidant stress. Common adverse effects include injection-site pain, pallor, edema, paresthesia, dizziness, somnolence, and hypersensitivity reactions, while clinical use favors it when relatively lower vasodilation and intermediate duration of action are desirable.

Name: Epinastine
Description: Epinastine (DrugBank DB00751) is a second-generation antiallergic agent whose structure is characterized by a rigid tricyclic dibenzazepine-like scaffold incorporating an annulated seven-membered azepine ring fused to aromatic rings and bearing a basic amidine/guanidine-like functionality that is protonated at physiologic pH, a feature important for high histamine H1 receptor affinity and limited central nervous system penetration. Chemically, it is classified as a tricyclic antihistamine and antiallergic piperidine-free H1 receptor antagonist with mast-cell stabilizing activity; its core scaffold is closely related in overall topology to other tricyclic antihistamines and antiallergic agents, with functional similarity to ketotifen, olopatadine, azelastine, cetirizine, and loratadine, although it is structurally distinct from each. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, and it has also been reported to inhibit mediator release from mast cells, reducing histamine-driven allergic inflammation. After topical ophthalmic administration, systemic absorption is low, plasma concentrations are typically minimal, distribution is therefore limited, metabolism appears modest, and elimination is primarily through renal excretion of unchanged drug, supporting a low burden of systemic biotransformation. Toxicity is generally mild at therapeutic exposure, with low cardiotoxic and sedative liability relative to first-generation antihistamines, though excessive exposure may produce somnolence, headache, dry mouth, or local irritation. It is indicated mainly for allergic conjunctivitis, especially pruritus, hyperemia, tearing, and seasonal ocular allergy symptoms, and clinically it is used as ophthalmic drops for rapid symptomatic relief and ongoing control of allergen-induced ocular itching and redness.

Name: Tranylcypromine
Description: Tranylcypromine (DrugBank DB00752) is a small, rigid phenylcyclopropylamine composed of a substituted cyclopropane ring bearing a primary amine and directly attached phenyl group, a structural design that mimics amphetamine-like monoamine substrates while constraining conformation; chemically it is classified as a nonhydrazine monoamine oxidase inhibitor and arylcyclopropylamine, with a phenylcyclopropylamine scaffold. Similar drugs include other MAO inhibitors such as phenelzine, isocarboxazid, moclobemide, and selegiline, although tranylcypromine is distinguished by irreversible nonselective MAO inhibition and its cyclopropyl core. Its principal targets are monoamine oxidase A and monoamine oxidase B, which it inhibits irreversibly, increasing synaptic norepinephrine, serotonin, and dopamine. Orally administered tranylcypromine is well absorbed, distributes systemically including into the CNS, undergoes hepatic biotransformation with relatively short plasma persistence despite prolonged pharmacodynamic action due to enzyme inactivation, and is eliminated mainly as urinary metabolites. It is indicated primarily for major depressive disorder, especially atypical, treatment-resistant, or anergic depression, and has also been used in refractory anxiety states or depressive syndromes with hypersomnia and mood reactivity. Adverse effects commonly include insomnia, agitation, orthostatic hypotension, dry mouth, dizziness, constipation, tachycardia, and headache. Toxicity is clinically important and includes hypertensive crisis precipitated by tyramine-containing foods or sympathomimetics, serotonin syndrome with serotonergic co-medications, and overdose manifestations such as hyperthermia, seizures, arrhythmias, and severe blood pressure instability. Clinically, it is reserved for patients who fail first-line antidepressants and requires strict dietary control, washout periods, and careful drug-interaction monitoring.

Name: Ethotoin
Description: Ethotoin (DrugBank DB00754) is a first-generation anticonvulsant of the hydantoin class, structurally characterized by a 2,4-imidazolidinedione hydantoin ring bearing 3-ethyl and 5-phenyl substitution, giving a relatively simple aromatic hydantoin scaffold closely related to other sodium channel–modulating antiepileptics. Its core chemical category is therefore a cyclic ureide, and its principal scaffold is the 5-phenyl-substituted hydantoin nucleus shared with similar drugs such as phenytoin, mephenytoin, and fosphenytoin as a prodrug analogue of phenytoin. Pharmacologically, ethotoin is believed to act mainly through voltage-gated sodium channels, especially neuronal sodium channel alpha subunits such as SCN1A, SCN2A, and SCN8A, stabilizing the inactivated state and limiting high-frequency repetitive firing, although its target assignment is less extensively defined than for phenytoin. After oral administration it is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, distributed systemically with moderate plasma protein binding, undergoes extensive hepatic biotransformation to inactive metabolites, and is excreted primarily in urine as metabolites; its half-life is shorter and pharmacokinetics generally less predictable than phenytoin. It is indicated for epilepsy, particularly tonic-clonic and focal seizures, often as adjunctive therapy when better-established agents are unsuitable. Adverse effects include dizziness, sedation, nausea, vomiting, ataxia, diplopia, and rash. Toxicity may include dose-related CNS depression, nystagmus, gait disturbance, and hypersensitivity reactions, with rare but important hematologic or dermatologic events such as leukopenia or severe rash. Clinically, it has been used for chronic seizure suppression in patients with recurrent generalized convulsive seizures or partial seizure disorders, though it is now used infrequently.

Name: Tretinoin
Description: Tretinoin (all-trans-retinoic acid; DrugBank DB00755) is a first-generation retinoid structurally characterized by a lipophilic β-ionone cyclohexenyl ring linked to a conjugated polyene side chain terminating in a carboxylic acid, making it a vitamin A-derived unsaturated monocarboxylic acid; chemically it belongs to the retinoic acids and more broadly the retinoid/isoprenoid lipid class, with a retinoid polyene-carboxylate scaffold. Closely related drugs include isotretinoin, acitretin, adapalene, tazarotene, and alitretinoin, which share retinoid-like receptor activity or similar hydrophobic aromatic/polyene frameworks. Tretinoin acts primarily through nuclear retinoic acid receptors RARA, RARB, and RARG, with downstream transcriptional effects mediated via RXR heterodimerization; in acute promyelocytic leukemia it functionally targets the PML-RARA fusion oncoprotein to restore differentiation. Topically, absorption is limited but variable and increases with damaged skin; systemically, oral tretinoin is well absorbed, highly protein bound, widely distributed, rapidly metabolized hepatically by CYP26 isoenzymes and other oxidative pathways to 4-oxo and related metabolites, and excreted mainly in urine and feces as metabolites, with a short plasma half-life. Major toxicities include teratogenicity, mucocutaneous inflammation, hepatotoxicity, hyperlipidemia, pseudotumor cerebri, and in APL differentiation syndrome with fever, pulmonary infiltrates, edema, and hypotension. Indications include topical treatment of acne vulgaris, photodamaged skin, and certain keratinization disorders, and oral use for induction of remission in acute promyelocytic leukemia. Common adverse effects are erythema, peeling, dryness, burning, photosensitivity, headache, bone pain, and leukocytosis; clinically it is used as topical cream, gel, or lotion for comedonal/inflammatory acne and as systemic differentiation therapy in APL, often combined with anthracyclines or arsenic trioxide.

Name: Dolasetron
Description: Dolasetron (DB00757) is an indole-based carbazole derivative antiemetic formulated clinically as the mesylate salt and characterized structurally by a rigid tricyclic pyridoindole/carbazole-like aromatic scaffold bearing a carbonyl-containing ester functionality and a basic piperidine-substituted side chain that is readily biotransformed to the active metabolite hydrodolasetron; chemically it belongs to the selective serotonin 5-HT3 receptor antagonist class, sharing a pharmacophore and therapeutic similarity with ondansetron, granisetron, tropisetron, and palonosetron. Its principal target is the 5-hydroxytryptamine type 3 receptor, including peripheral receptors on vagal afferents and central receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone, thereby suppressing nausea and vomiting induced by cytotoxic therapy or surgery. After oral or intravenous administration, dolasetron is well absorbed and rapidly converted by carbonyl reductase to hydrodolasetron, the major active species; distribution is moderate with systemic exposure sufficient for central and peripheral receptor blockade, metabolism also involves CYP2D6 and, to a lesser extent, CYP3A and CYP2C9 pathways, and elimination occurs mainly through renal excretion of metabolites with a clinically relevant half-life driven largely by hydrodolasetron. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related cardiac electrophysiologic effects, especially PR, QRS, and QTc prolongation, with examples including ventricular arrhythmia, torsades de pointes risk, and worsened conduction disturbance in patients with electrolyte abnormalities or underlying heart disease. Common adverse effects include headache, constipation, diarrhea, dizziness, fatigue, and asymptomatic ECG changes. Clinically, dolasetron has been used primarily for prevention and treatment of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting and postoperative nausea and vomiting, although use has become more restricted in some settings because of cardiac safety concerns.

Name: Clopidogrel
Description: Clopidogrel (DrugBank DB00758) is a thienopyridine-class antiplatelet prodrug with a chlorophenyl-substituted, partially saturated thieno[3,2-c]pyridine core bearing a methyl ester and a stereogenic center, giving a concise scaffold of a 2-chlorophenyl thienopyridine ester related to other P2Y12 inhibitors such as ticlopidine and prasugrel, and mechanistically distinct but clinically similar agents such as ticagrelor and cangrelor. After oral administration it is rapidly absorbed, with food having limited clinical impact, is highly protein bound in circulation, and undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism: most of the dose is hydrolyzed by carboxylesterase-1 to an inactive carboxylic acid derivative, while a smaller fraction is bioactivated via CYP2C19, with contributions from CYP3A4, CYP2B6, and CYP1A2, to a reactive thiol metabolite that irreversibly antagonizes the platelet ADP receptor P2RY12; downstream signaling functionally involves platelet GPIIb/IIIa integrin activation inhibition. Elimination occurs mainly as urinary and fecal metabolites, with antiplatelet effects lasting the lifespan of exposed platelets despite a short-lived active metabolite. It is indicated for prevention of atherothrombotic events in acute coronary syndrome, recent myocardial infarction, recent ischemic stroke, and established peripheral arterial disease, and is widely used in dual antiplatelet therapy after percutaneous coronary intervention with stent placement. Major toxicities center on bleeding, including gastrointestinal, intracranial, and procedure-related hemorrhage; rarer examples include thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, severe neutropenia, and hypersensitivity. Common adverse effects include bruising, epistaxis, dyspepsia, diarrhea, rash, and bleeding at any site.

Name: Tetracycline
Description: Tetracycline (DrugBank DB00759) is a naturally derived polyketide antibiotic characterized by a rigid, linearly fused four-ring naphthacene core bearing multiple keto, enol, phenolic hydroxyl, and amide-like functionalities that confer metal-chelating capacity and amphoteric behavior; it belongs to the tetracycline class and is built on the classic tetracycline/naphthacene scaffold shared by closely related agents such as doxycycline, minocycline, oxytetracycline, demeclocycline, and glycylcycline derivatives such as tigecycline. Its antibacterial action is mediated primarily by binding the 30S bacterial ribosomal subunit, especially 16S rRNA within the A-site region, thereby blocking aminoacyl-tRNA accommodation and inhibiting protein synthesis; functionally relevant target annotations therefore include the bacterial 30S ribosome and associated rRNA binding site. Orally administered tetracycline is absorbed moderately, with reduced bioavailability in the presence of food, calcium, iron, magnesium, or aluminum; it distributes widely into tissues and inflamed fluids but variably into cerebrospinal fluid, crosses the placenta, enters breast milk, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated mainly unchanged by renal excretion with some biliary/fecal elimination. It is indicated for susceptible infections including acne vulgaris, chlamydial infections, rickettsial disease, Mycoplasma pneumonia, cholera, brucellosis, and certain zoonoses. Important adverse effects include gastrointestinal upset, esophagitis, photosensitivity, candidiasis, and vestibular complaints less commonly than with minocycline. Toxicities include permanent tooth discoloration, enamel hypoplasia, and reversible inhibition of bone growth in fetuses and children, plus hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, and intracranial hypertension in susceptible patients. Clinically it has been used in outpatient oral therapy for acne, atypical respiratory infections, and selected tick-borne or sexually transmitted infections when organism susceptibility supports use.

Name: Meropenem
Description: Meropenem (DB00760) is a broad-spectrum carbapenem beta-lactam antibiotic whose structure is defined by a highly strained bicyclic carbapenem nucleus consisting of a beta-lactam ring fused to a five-membered unsaturated ring, with a 1-beta-methyl substituent that improves stability to renal dehydropeptidase I and a C-2 thioether side chain bearing a dimethylcarbamoyl-pyrrolidinyl moiety that enhances Gram-negative activity and penetration; chemically it belongs to the beta-lactam, carbapenem, and antibacterial anti-infective classes, and its core scaffold is the penem/carbapenem bicyclic beta-lactam framework. Closely related drugs include imipenem, doripenem, ertapenem, and biapenem, with imipenem as a classic structural and pharmacologic comparator. Meropenem targets bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, especially PBP2, PBP3, and PBP4 in susceptible organisms, inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-linking and causing cell lysis. It is given parenterally because oral absorption is negligible; distribution is good into extracellular fluids and many tissues including lung, bile, peritoneal fluid, CSF when meninges are inflamed, and skin, with low protein binding, minimal hepatic metabolism, and predominant renal excretion largely as unchanged drug, giving a short elimination half-life of about 1 hour and requiring dose adjustment in renal impairment. Toxicity is generally lower for seizure liability than imipenem but includes neurotoxicity, hypersensitivity up to anaphylaxis, severe cutaneous reactions, and antibiotic-associated colitis. Indications and clinical use include complicated intra-abdominal infection, meningitis, complicated skin and soft tissue infection, severe pneumonia, febrile neutropenia, and other serious polymicrobial or resistant Gram-negative infections such as those caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, rash, headache, thrombocytosis, transaminase elevation, and injection-site inflammation.

Name: Potassium chloride
Description: Potassium chloride (DrugBank DB00761) is a simple inorganic ionic salt composed of monovalent potassium cations and chloride anions arranged in a classic alkali halide crystal lattice, placing it in the electrolyte/mineral replacement category with an alkali metal halide scaffold rather than an organic pharmacophore; closely related agents include other potassium salts such as potassium citrate, potassium bicarbonate, and potassium phosphate, as well as sodium chloride as a physicochemically similar electrolyte replacement. Its pharmacologic action reflects replacement of total body potassium and restoration of transmembrane electrochemical gradients rather than selective receptor binding, although its functional targets are the broad set of potassium-dependent membrane proteins including Na+/K+-ATPase, cardiac and neuronal potassium channels, and transport systems governing excitability and acid-base balance. Orally, potassium chloride is generally well absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract; intravenously it is completely bioavailable, distributes mainly to the intracellular compartment under insulin, catecholamine, and acid-base regulation, is not metabolized, and is excreted primarily by the kidney with urinary elimination tightly controlled by distal tubular secretion and aldosterone. It is indicated for prevention and treatment of hypokalemia, for example in patients receiving loop or thiazide diuretics, with vomiting, diarrhea, hyperaldosteronism, or digitalis-associated arrhythmia risk. Toxicity is dominated by hyperkalemia, which may cause weakness, paresthesias, conduction disturbances, peaked T waves, ventricular arrhythmias, and cardiac arrest; oral products can also cause nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and esophageal, gastric, or intestinal ulceration, while IV use may cause infusion-site pain and dangerous rapid potassium loading. Clinically it is used as oral tablets, capsules, liquids, and IV supplementation for electrolyte repletion in hospitalized, cardiac, renal, and general medical patients.

Name: Irinotecan
Description: Irinotecan (DB00762) is a semisynthetic camptothecin derivative characterized by a pentacyclic quinoline-containing alkaloid core with a critical α-hydroxy-δ-lactone E-ring required for activity, bearing a bulky dipiperidino carbamate substituent at the 10-position that improves solubility and functions as a prodrug handle; chemically it is an antineoplastic topoisomerase I inhibitor in the camptothecin alkaloid class, built on the camptothecin scaffold shared with related agents such as topotecan, belotecan, and exatecan, while its active metabolite SN-38 is the closest pharmacologic analog. After intravenous administration, irinotecan shows extensive tissue distribution and high protein binding, undergoes esterase-mediated activation to SN-38, oxidative metabolism by CYP3A4/3A5 to inactive APC and NPC metabolites, and glucuronidation of SN-38 primarily by UGT1A1 to SN-38G, with biliary and fecal excretion predominating and a lesser renal component. Its main target protein is topoisomerase I (TOP1), with cytotoxicity resulting from stabilization of the TOP1-DNA cleavable complex and replication-associated DNA strand breaks. Major toxicities include severe delayed diarrhea, acute cholinergic syndrome, profound neutropenia, febrile neutropenia, mucositis, nausea, vomiting, and less commonly interstitial lung disease or hepatotoxicity; risk is increased in patients with reduced UGT1A1 activity such as UGT1A1*28 homozygotes. Clinically, it is indicated mainly for metastatic colorectal cancer, especially in FOLFIRI-based regimens, and is also used in small-cell lung cancer, pancreatic, gastric, and other gastrointestinal malignancies, with common adverse effects including diarrhea, myelosuppression, fatigue, alopecia, and anorexia.

Name: Methimazole
Description: Methimazole (DB00763) is a small, sulfur- and nitrogen-containing heteroaromatic antithyroid agent built on a 1,3-imidazole ring bearing a thione/thiol tautomeric functionality and a methyl substituent, making it a thioimidazole; chemically it belongs to the thiourea-related antithyroid drugs, with a methimazole/thioimidazole scaffold closely related to carbimazole, its prodrug, and mechanistically similar to propylthiouracil and other thyroid peroxidase inhibitors. Its principal target is thyroid peroxidase (TPO), which it inhibits to block iodide oxidation, organification of iodine, and coupling of iodotyrosines during thyroid hormone biosynthesis; unlike propylthiouracil, it has little direct effect on peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion. Methimazole is well absorbed orally, has high bioavailability, low plasma protein binding, concentrates in the thyroid, undergoes hepatic metabolism to inactive products, and is eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites and some unchanged drug; its serum half-life is shorter than its intrathyroidal action, permitting once-daily use in many patients. It is indicated for hyperthyroidism, especially Graves disease, toxic multinodular goiter, and preoperative or pre-radioiodine control of thyrotoxicosis. Major toxicities include agranulocytosis, severe neutropenia, hepatotoxicity with cholestatic jaundice, vasculitic reactions, and teratogenicity including aplasia cutis and congenital malformations when used in early pregnancy. Common adverse effects include rash, pruritus, urticaria, arthralgia, gastrointestinal upset, altered taste, and hypothyroidism with overtreatment. Clinically, it is widely used as first-line medical therapy for nonpregnant adults and many children with Graves disease, as bridge therapy before thyroidectomy or radioactive iodine, and for symptomatic biochemical control of excess thyroid hormone production.

Name: Mometasone
Description: Mometasone (DrugBank DB00764) is a highly lipophilic synthetic corticosteroid, usually used clinically as the furoate ester, built on the pregnane steroid nucleus with the characteristic four fused rings of glucocorticoids and distinguished by 9α-chloro, 11β-hydroxyl, 16α-methyl, 17-furoate ester, and 21-chloro/21-substituted functionalities that enhance receptor affinity and topical potency while limiting systemic exposure. Chemically it belongs to halogenated corticosteroids, specifically topical and inhaled glucocorticoid anti-inflammatory agents, and its core scaffold is the cortisol/prednisolone-like corticosteroid framework. Similar drugs include fluticasone, beclomethasone, budesonide, triamcinolone, and betamethasone, which share the glucocorticoid steroid scaffold and anti-inflammatory pharmacology. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, with downstream transrepression of NF-κB- and AP-1-dependent inflammatory signaling and reduced cytokine, chemokine, eosinophil, and mast-cell activity. Pharmacokinetically, mometasone shows low oral bioavailability because of poor gastrointestinal absorption and extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism; after intranasal, inhaled, or topical administration it is mainly retained locally, is highly protein bound when systemically absorbed, is metabolized predominantly by CYP3A4 to multiple inactive metabolites, and is excreted chiefly in feces with a smaller urinary fraction. It is indicated for allergic rhinitis, nasal polyposis, asthma maintenance therapy, and corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses such as eczema, psoriasis, and atopic dermatitis. Adverse effects are usually local, including epistaxis, nasal irritation, pharyngitis, headache, oral candidiasis, dysphonia, burning, pruritus, and skin atrophy; toxicities with excessive or prolonged exposure include HPA-axis suppression, hypercorticism, growth suppression in children, glaucoma, cataracts, and increased infection risk. Clinically it is used as nasal spray, inhalation powder, and topical cream/ointment/lotion for chronic inflammatory airway and skin disease control.

Name: Metyrosine
Description: Metyrosine (alpha-methyl-para-tyrosine; DrugBank DB00765) is a synthetic aromatic amino acid analog structurally based on the tyrosine/phenylalanine framework, consisting of a para-hydroxylated phenyl ring attached to an alpha-methyl-substituted amino acid side chain, making it a small polar catecholamine-biosynthesis inhibitor rather than a peptide or alkaloid; chemically it is categorized as an amino acid derivative and phenolic aromatic compound, with a substituted phenylalanine scaffold that resembles endogenous tyrosine, and it is structurally and pharmacologically related to tyrosine analogs and catecholamine-modulating agents such as levodopa, carbidopa, methyldopa, and phenoxybenzamine in the broader management of pheochromocytoma. Its principal target is tyrosine hydroxylase, the rate-limiting enzyme in catecholamine synthesis, leading to reduced formation of dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine. After oral administration it is reasonably absorbed, distributes mainly in total body water with some central nervous system penetration, undergoes limited metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged in urine, giving renal function an important role in clearance. Metyrosine is indicated chiefly for pheochromocytoma, especially to control excess catecholamine symptoms such as severe hypertension, tachycardia, diaphoresis, headache, and palpitations, including preoperative preparation and patients with unresectable or metastatic disease. Toxicity is dominated by excessive catecholamine depletion and CNS effects, with examples including marked sedation, anxiety, depression, extrapyramidal symptoms, crystalluria, and diarrhea; common adverse effects include somnolence, fatigue, dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, nasal congestion, and gastrointestinal upset. Clinically, it is typically used as an adjunct to alpha-adrenergic blockade, for example with phenoxybenzamine, to reduce perioperative risk and improve symptomatic control in catecholamine-secreting tumors.

Name: Clavulanic acid
Description: Clavulanic acid (DrugBank DB00766) is a naturally derived beta-lactam compound from Streptomyces clavuligerus characterized structurally by an oxazolidine ring fused to a beta-lactam nucleus, lacking the thiazolidine side-chain architecture of penicillins and bearing an enol-like oxygenated substituent that confers high reactivity toward beta-lactamases; it is therefore classified as a beta-lactamase inhibitor within the clavam family, with a clavulanate or bicyclic beta-lactam-oxazolidine scaffold. It is chemically and pharmacologically similar to other beta-lactamase inhibitors such as sulbactam, tazobactam, avibactam, and relebactam, although clavulanate is a classical suicide inhibitor most active against many class A serine beta-lactamases. Its principal targets are bacterial beta-lactamases, especially penicillinase-type enzymes, with covalent irreversible or quasi-irreversible acylation restoring activity of partner beta-lactams rather than exerting strong standalone antibacterial action. Orally, usually as amoxicillin-clavulanate, it is well absorbed, widely distributed into respiratory tissues, middle ear fluid, skin, urine, and bile, shows low to moderate protein binding, limited metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly by renal excretion with a short half-life. It is indicated for infections caused by beta-lactamase-producing organisms, including acute otitis media, sinusitis, community-acquired pneumonia, bite wounds, skin and soft-tissue infection, urinary tract infection, and some polymicrobial intra-abdominal or gynecologic infections. Adverse effects commonly include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, candidiasis, and rash; important toxicities include hypersensitivity, antibiotic-associated colitis, cholestatic hepatitis or mixed liver injury, and rare severe cutaneous reactions, particularly with prolonged or repeated exposure.

Name: Olopatadine
Description: Olopatadine (DrugBank DB00768) is a tricyclic dibenzoxepin-derived antihistamine whose structure consists of a rigid fused aromatic system incorporating an oxepin ring and a substituted piperidine side chain bearing a carboxyl functionality, a motif that supports potent peripheral H1-receptor antagonism with additional mast-cell stabilizing activity. Chemically, it is classified as a second-generation antiallergic agent and piperidine-containing antihistamine, with a dibenzoxepin scaffold related to other tricyclic antiallergic compounds; pharmacologically similar drugs include ketotifen, epinastine, azelastine, cetirizine, and loratadine, although olopatadine is particularly noted for dual antihistamine and anti-inflammatory effects. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, and it also functionally inhibits mediator release from mast cells, reducing histamine, leukotriene, and cytokine-driven allergic responses. Olopatadine is used mainly for allergic conjunctivitis, seasonal allergic rhinoconjunctivitis, ocular pruritus, and in some formulations allergic rhinitis and urticaria-associated symptoms. After topical ophthalmic or intranasal administration, systemic absorption is limited but measurable; oral absorption is good, protein binding is modest, distribution is largely peripheral with minimal CNS penetration, metabolism is limited, and elimination occurs predominantly via renal excretion of unchanged drug, with an elimination half-life generally in the several-hour range. Toxicity is usually low at therapeutic exposure, with overdose or systemic exposure potentially causing somnolence, tachycardia, dry mouth, or agitation; serious toxicity is uncommon. Common adverse effects include bitter taste, headache, fatigue, dry eye, blurred vision, nasal discomfort, epistaxis, and local irritation. Clinically, it is widely used as ophthalmic drops for rapid relief of itchy allergic eyes and as intranasal or oral therapy when histamine-mediated allergic symptoms require a relatively non-sedating agent.

Name: Alprostadil
Description: Alprostadil (DrugBank DB00770) is prostaglandin E1, an endogenous eicosanoid built on a 20-carbon prostanoic acid framework with a cyclopentane core, trans and cis alkenyl side chains, a terminal carboxylic acid, and characteristic secondary hydroxyl and ketone functionality that confer high lipid bioactivity; chemically it is a prostaglandin and more broadly an oxygenated unsaturated fatty-acid derivative, with the classic prostaglandin prostane/prostanoic acid scaffold. Closely related drugs include other prostaglandin analogs such as dinoprostone, misoprostol, epoprostenol, iloprost, and latanoprost, which share eicosanoid signaling features but differ in substitution and receptor selectivity. Its main targets are prostaglandin E receptors, especially EP2, EP3, and EP4 encoded by PTGER2, PTGER3, and PTGER4 on vascular and smooth muscle tissue, leading predominantly to adenylate cyclase activation, increased cAMP, vasodilation, and inhibition of platelet aggregation. Pharmacokinetically, alprostadil is given intracavernosally, intraurethrally, or by intravenous infusion because it is not orally practical; it is rapidly distributed locally or intravascularly, extensively metabolized on first pass through the lungs and other tissues by oxidation of the 15-hydroxyl group and beta- and omega-oxidation, and excreted mainly as urinary metabolites with a very short plasma half-life of minutes. It is indicated for erectile dysfunction and for maintaining ductus arteriosus patency in neonates with congenital heart disease. Adverse effects include penile pain, urethral burning, hypotension, flushing, dizziness, apnea in neonates, diarrhea, and tachycardia; important toxicities include excessive vasodilation, syncope, priapism, local fibrosis, and rarely bleeding or cardiovascular instability. Clinically, it is used as Caverject or Muse for erectile dysfunction and as prostaglandin E1 infusion in ductal-dependent cardiac lesions such as transposition of the great arteries or pulmonary atresia.

Name: Clidinium
Description: Clidinium (DrugBank DB00771) is a synthetic quaternary ammonium antimuscarinic whose structure consists of a permanently charged pyridinium-linked amino alcohol ester built around a substituted aromatic glycolate/carboxylate motif, giving it the classic cationic anticholinergic architecture that limits central nervous system penetration. Chemically, it is classified as an anticholinergic antispasmodic, specifically a quaternary ammonium muscarinic antagonist, and its core scaffold is most closely related to pyridinium or tropate/glycolate-type antimuscarinic esters. Similar drugs include glycopyrrolate, propantheline, methantheline, mepenzolate, and other atropine-like peripheral antimuscarinics. Its pharmacologic action is mediated by competitive antagonism at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, principally CHRM1, CHRM2, and CHRM3 in gastrointestinal smooth muscle and secretory tissues, reducing motility, tone, and glandular secretion. After oral administration, absorption is generally limited and variable because the quaternary cation reduces membrane permeability; distribution is largely peripheral with minimal blood-brain barrier entry; metabolism is incompletely characterized but likely involves partial ester hydrolysis and hepatic biotransformation; and elimination occurs via renal and biliary/fecal routes, with some drug excreted unchanged. Toxicity is the expected antimuscarinic syndrome, including severe dry mouth, tachycardia, urinary retention, constipation, blurred vision, decreased sweating, and precipitation of angle-closure glaucoma, with overdose causing ileus, hyperthermia, and marked autonomic blockade. It is indicated for adjunctive treatment of peptic ulcer disease and functional gastrointestinal disorders such as irritable bowel syndrome, intestinal hypermotility, abdominal cramping, and spasm, and has been used clinically, often in combination products such as clidinium with chlordiazepoxide, to reduce gastrointestinal spasm, secretions, pain, and anxiety-associated dyspeptic symptoms.

Name: Malathion
Description: Malathion (DrugBank DB00772) is a lipophilic organophosphate thioate insecticide and pediculicide built on a phosphorodithioate scaffold, consisting of a diethyl phosphorodithioate core esterified to a substituted succinate moiety, specifically a dimethoxycarbonyl ethyl side chain that distinguishes it from more persistent or more potent organophosphates. Chemically it belongs to the carboxylate-containing organophosphorus insecticides; its closest structural and pharmacologic analogs include parathion, diazinon, chlorpyrifos, and dimethoate, although malathion is generally less toxic to mammals because it is more readily detoxified by carboxylesterases. Its principal target is acetylcholinesterase, with toxicity mediated mainly by metabolic oxidation to malaoxon, a more potent cholinesterase inhibitor; butyrylcholinesterase is also functionally affected. After topical, inhalational, oral, or occupational exposure, absorption is variable but increased by solvents and damaged skin; distribution is systemic with limited persistence because rapid hepatic and plasma esterase hydrolysis predominates, while cytochrome P450 oxidation generates malaoxon, and urinary excretion of hydrolysis products is the major elimination route. Malathion is indicated primarily for treatment of Pediculus humanus capitis infestation and is also used in public health and agricultural vector control programs, for example against mosquitoes and fruit flies. Adverse effects and toxicity reflect cholinergic excess and may include scalp irritation, rash, conjunctival irritation, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramping, diarrhea, bronchospasm, bradycardia, miosis, muscle fasciculations, weakness, confusion, seizures, and respiratory depression; severe poisoning can produce coma or death, while chronic high exposure has been associated with neurobehavioral effects and possible genotoxic or carcinogenic concern.

Name: Etoposide
Description: Etoposide (DrugBank DB00773) is a semisynthetic podophyllotoxin-derived antineoplastic agent whose structure consists of a polycyclic aryltetralin lignan core bearing a trans-fused lactone-like framework, multiple methoxy and phenolic oxygen substituents, and a glycosidic moiety that distinguishes it from podophyllotoxin and modulates solubility and topoisomerase binding; chemically it belongs to the epipodophyllotoxin class, with an aryltetralin lignan scaffold. Closely related drugs include teniposide, another epipodophyllotoxin, and more broadly topoisomerase poisons such as doxorubicin and irinotecan by mechanistic analogy. Its principal target is DNA topoisomerase II, especially TOP2A and TOP2B, stabilizing the cleavable complex and causing double-strand DNA breaks, cell-cycle arrest, and apoptosis. Pharmacokinetically, oral bioavailability is variable and incomplete, while intravenous dosing avoids absorption variability; distribution is moderate with substantial plasma protein binding, limited CNS penetration, and broad tissue exposure; metabolism occurs mainly in the liver via CYP3A4 and conjugative pathways; excretion is through both renal elimination of unchanged drug and biliary/fecal routes, with dose adjustment often required in renal or hepatic dysfunction. Etoposide is indicated for small cell lung cancer, testicular germ cell tumors, leukemias, lymphomas, and selected solid tumors, commonly in combination regimens such as BEP or platinum-based protocols. Major toxicities include dose-limiting myelosuppression, especially leukopenia and thrombocytopenia, mucositis, alopecia, nausea, hypotension with rapid infusion, and hypersensitivity reactions; serious examples include severe infection from neutropenia, secondary therapy-related acute myeloid leukemia linked to TOP2-mediated genotoxicity, and hepatic or renal toxicity in susceptible patients.

Name: Hydroflumethiazide
Description: Hydroflumethiazide (DB00774) is a thiazide diuretic characterized structurally by a benzothiadiazine 1,1-dioxide core bearing sulfonamide functionality, with halogen substitution and hydrogenation of the heterocycle that increase lipophilicity and diuretic potency relative to older congeners; chemically it belongs to the thiazide/benzothiadiazine sulfonamide class, and its central scaffold is the chlorinated, fluorinated benzothiadiazine dioxide ring system typical of saluretic antihypertensives. Closely related drugs include hydrochlorothiazide, bendroflumethiazide, chlorothiazide, trichlormethiazide, and cyclothiazide, which share the same thiazide pharmacophore. Its principal target is the renal sodium-chloride cotransporter SLC12A3 (NCC) in the distal convoluted tubule, where inhibition promotes natriuresis, chloruresis, kaliuresis, and secondary reduction in plasma volume and blood pressure. After oral administration it is reasonably well absorbed, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid with limited metabolism, has a moderate duration of action, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by the kidney, so effects may be prolonged in renal impairment. Therapeutically it is used for hypertension and edema, including edema associated with congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, corticosteroid therapy, or renal disease. Adverse effects and toxicities reflect excessive diuresis and electrolyte loss, notably hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, dehydration, orthostatic hypotension, hyperuricemia precipitating gout, hyperglycemia, and occasional dyslipidemia; as a sulfonamide, it can also rarely cause rash, photosensitivity, pancreatitis, blood dyscrasias, or hypersensitivity reactions. Clinically, hydroflumethiazide is used alone or in combination with other antihypertensives to provide chronic blood-pressure control and symptomatic mobilization of fluid retention.

Name: Tirofiban
Description: Tirofiban (DrugBank DB00775) is a small, nonpeptide antiplatelet agent whose structure is built around a tyrosine-like arylsulfonamide framework bearing a basic amine and carboxylate functionality that together mimic the arginine-glycine-aspartate recognition motif involved in fibrinogen binding; chemically it is classified as a synthetic glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor antagonist and more broadly as an antithrombotic platelet aggregation inhibitor, with an arylsulfonamide amino acid-mimetic scaffold. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors such as eptifibatide and abciximab, though unlike the peptide-derived or antibody-based agents it is a small molecule. Its principal target is the platelet integrin alphaIIb beta3 receptor, also known as glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (ITGA2B/ITGB3 complex), through which it blocks fibrinogen-mediated platelet cross-linking. Tirofiban is administered intravenously, producing immediate systemic availability, a small extracellular distribution volume, minimal protein binding of practical consequence, little to no hepatic metabolism, and predominant renal excretion of unchanged drug, with a short elimination half-life that supports rapid offset after infusion cessation and dose adjustment in renal impairment. Its major toxicity is bleeding, including access-site hemorrhage, gastrointestinal bleeding, hematuria, and less commonly intracranial hemorrhage; thrombocytopenia, including acute profound thrombocytopenia, is an important additional toxicity. Indications and clinical use center on acute coronary syndromes, especially unstable angina and non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction, and as an adjunct during percutaneous coronary intervention to reduce thrombotic cardiovascular events; common adverse effects include bleeding, nausea, fever, dizziness, hypotension, bradycardia, and platelet count reduction.

Name: Oxcarbazepine
Description: Oxcarbazepine (DrugBank DB00776) is a dibenzazepine carboxamide anticonvulsant structurally characterized by a tricyclic iminostilbene-like framework in which two fused benzene rings are linked through a seven-membered azepine ring, bearing a keto substituent at the 10-position and a carboxamide at the 5-position; chemically it is a ketone analog of carbamazepine and belongs to the carboxamide antiepileptic class built on a dibenzazepine/iminostilbene scaffold. Closely related drugs include carbamazepine, eslicarbazepine acetate, and licarbazepine, which share similar sodium-channel-modulating pharmacology. Oxcarbazepine is rapidly and extensively absorbed orally, undergoes prompt first-pass cytosolic reduction to its pharmacologically active monohydroxy derivative (mainly S-licarbazepine), distributes with relatively low plasma protein binding compared with carbamazepine, is further conjugated largely by glucuronidation, and is eliminated predominantly in urine as metabolites with only minor unchanged drug excretion. Its principal target is considered voltage-gated sodium channels, especially neuronal SCN family channels such as SCN1A, SCN2A, and SCN8A, with functional suppression of high-frequency repetitive firing rather than a single highly selective binding protein. It is indicated for focal seizures and partial-onset epilepsy, including monotherapy or adjunctive treatment in adults and children. Adverse effects commonly include dizziness, somnolence, diplopia, ataxia, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, headache, and rash. Important toxicities include dose-related CNS depression, clinically significant hyponatremia from SIADH-like effects, hypersensitivity reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis, and rare hepatic or hematologic toxicity. Clinically, it is widely used as a carbamazepine alternative when seizure control is desired with fewer CYP-mediated drug interactions, and it is also used off-label in some neuropathic pain or bipolar-spectrum settings.

Name: Nalidixic acid
Description: Nalidixic acid (DrugBank DB00779) is a first-generation quinolone antibacterial built on a 1,8-naphthyridine/4-quinolone-like bicyclic aromatic scaffold bearing a 3-carboxylic acid and 4-keto pharmacophore essential for metal chelation and interaction with bacterial type II topoisomerases, with an N-1 ethyl substituent and a 7-methyl group that distinguish it from later fluoroquinolones. It belongs to the quinolone carboxylic acid class, and its closest similar drugs include oxolinic acid, cinoxacin, pipemidic acid, and the later fluoroquinolones such as norfloxacin and ciprofloxacin, which retain the same core topoisomerase-targeting scaffold but have broader spectra. Its principal targets are bacterial DNA gyrase, especially GyrA/GyrB, and topoisomerase IV, producing inhibition of DNA replication and transcription. Orally, nalidixic acid is reasonably well absorbed, achieves therapeutically useful urinary concentrations, is moderately protein bound, distributes mainly to the urinary tract with limited systemic tissue penetration, undergoes hepatic metabolism to active and inactive metabolites including hydroxynalidixic acid, and is eliminated primarily by renal excretion as parent drug and metabolites. It was classically indicated for uncomplicated urinary tract infections caused by susceptible Gram-negative organisms, particularly Escherichia coli, Enterobacter, Klebsiella, and Proteus species, and has also been used for chronic or recurrent bacteriuria. Toxicity includes dose-related CNS stimulation, seizures, hemolytic risk in G6PD deficiency, hepatotoxicity, crystalluria, rash, photosensitivity, and arthropathy concerns in pediatric patients; overdose may produce metabolic acidosis and convulsions. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, visual disturbances, and hypersensitivity reactions. Clinically, it is an older, largely superseded urinary antiseptic antibiotic used when narrow urinary Gram-negative coverage is sufficient and susceptibility is documented.

Name: Phenelzine
Description: Phenelzine (DrugBank DB00780) is a small, highly polar arylalkylhydrazine monoamine oxidase inhibitor whose structure consists of a phenethylamine-like scaffold bearing a terminal hydrazine moiety on a two-carbon linker attached to a phenyl ring; chemically it is classified as a nonselective, irreversible hydrazine MAOI, with a phenethylhydrazine scaffold that relates it to other classic MAOIs such as isocarboxazid, tranylcypromine, and older hydrazine antidepressants. Its principal pharmacologic targets are monoamine oxidase A and monoamine oxidase B, which it inhibits covalently after metabolic activation, thereby increasing synaptic serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine; indirect effects on GABA metabolism have also been described. Phenelzine is orally absorbed, undergoes substantial first-pass metabolism, distributes systemically including into the CNS, and is metabolized mainly by acetylation and oxidative pathways to inactive and reactive metabolites, with urinary excretion of metabolites predominating and a pharmacodynamic effect that outlasts plasma clearance because enzyme activity recovers only after new MAO synthesis. It is indicated for major depressive disorder, especially atypical, treatment-resistant, or anxious depression, and has also been used for panic disorder, social anxiety disorder, and other refractory anxiety states. Common adverse effects include orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, insomnia or sedation, dry mouth, constipation, nausea, weight gain, edema, sexual dysfunction, and paresthesias; serious toxicity includes hypertensive crisis with tyramine ingestion, serotonin syndrome with serotonergic co-medications, hepatotoxicity, and rarely overdose-related hyperthermia, seizures, or coma. Clinically, its use is now specialized, generally reserved for patients who fail first-line antidepressants and managed with strict dietary and drug-interaction precautions.

Name: Polymyxin B
Description: Polymyxin B (DrugBank DB00781) is a cationic cyclic lipopeptide antibiotic composed of closely related polymyxin B1 and B2 components, characterized structurally by a heptapeptide macrocycle, a tripeptide side chain, multiple positively charged diaminobutyric acid residues, and an N-terminal fatty acyl tail that confers amphipathic membrane activity. It belongs to the polymyxin class of polypeptide antibiotics and is built on the polymyxin cyclic lipopeptide scaffold, closely related to colistin (polymyxin E), and more distantly to other membrane-active peptide antibiotics. Its principal pharmacologic target is the lipopolysaccharide-rich outer membrane of susceptible Gram-negative bacteria, especially binding lipid A of LPS, displacing divalent cations and disrupting membrane integrity; no single human protein target is central to efficacy. Polymyxin B is poorly absorbed orally and is therefore used parenterally or topically; after intravenous administration it distributes mainly in extracellular fluid with limited penetration into some tissues including the CNS, undergoes minimal metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly by nonrenal pathways with partial renal excretion and a relatively narrow therapeutic window. It is indicated for serious infections caused by multidrug-resistant Gram-negative organisms such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, and Klebsiella pneumoniae, and is also used topically for ocular, otic, or skin infections. Major toxicities include dose-limiting nephrotoxicity from acute tubular injury and neurotoxicity such as paresthesias, dizziness, ataxia, weakness, or rarely neuromuscular blockade and apnea; common adverse effects include renal dysfunction, electrolyte abnormalities, rash, and local irritation. Clinically, it is reserved for severe hospital-acquired pneumonia, bacteremia, urinary tract infection, and wound infection when safer agents are ineffective or resistance is extensive.

Name: Propantheline
Description: Propantheline (DrugBank DB00782) is a synthetic quaternary ammonium antimuscarinic built on a substituted diaryl tertiary alcohol/ester-like anticholinergic scaffold in which a permanently charged isopropyl quaternary nitrogen is linked through a three-carbon chain to a xanthene-derived tertiary carbinol center bearing phenyl and hydroxyl substituents; chemically it is classified as a quaternary ammonium parasympatholytic agent and is structurally related to other antimuscarinics such as methantheline, oxyphenonium, glycopyrrolate, and atropine-like agents used to reduce gastrointestinal and genitourinary smooth-muscle tone. Its principal pharmacologic targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially peripheral CHRM1, CHRM2, and CHRM3 receptor populations in gastrointestinal, salivary, bronchial, and bladder tissues, where receptor antagonism decreases secretions, motility, and spasm. Oral absorption occurs but is incomplete and variable because the permanent positive charge limits membrane permeability; distribution is largely peripheral with poor blood-brain barrier penetration, modest tissue penetration, and reduced CNS exposure relative to tertiary amines; metabolism is limited or partial, with a clinically important fraction eliminated unchanged, mainly in urine and to a lesser extent feces. Toxicity reflects exaggerated anticholinergic effects, including severe xerostomia, ileus, urinary retention, tachyarrhythmia, hyperthermia, precipitation of angle-closure glaucoma, and confusion at high exposure, particularly in older adults or those with obstructive uropathy. Adverse effects commonly include dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, mydriasis, decreased sweating, palpitations, and difficulty voiding. Clinically, propantheline has been used to treat peptic ulcer disease, irritable bowel syndrome, intestinal hypermotility, abdominal cramping, hyperhidrosis, and bladder spasm, and historically as an adjunct to reduce gastrointestinal secretions and motility.

Name: Estradiol
Description: Estradiol (DB00783) is the principal endogenous estrogen, a natural steroidal sex hormone built on the rigid cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene estrane nucleus with four fused rings, an aromatic A ring, and hydroxyl groups at C3 and 17β that are critical for high-affinity estrogen receptor binding; chemically it belongs to the estrogen subclass of steroid hormones and uses the estrane steroid scaffold shared by related estrogens. Similar drugs include estrone, estriol, ethinyl estradiol, conjugated estrogens, mestranol, and synthetic nonsteroidal estrogenic agents such as diethylstilbestrol by pharmacologic similarity. Its main targets are estrogen receptor alpha (ESR1) and estrogen receptor beta (ESR2), with downstream genomic and non-genomic signaling and functional effects on the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, bone, breast, endometrium, liver, and vasculature; membrane-associated estrogen signaling proteins such as GPER may also contribute. Pharmacokinetically, estradiol is well absorbed but oral bioavailability is limited by extensive first-pass metabolism; transdermal, vaginal, and parenteral routes bypass part of this effect, it is highly protein bound mainly to albumin and sex hormone-binding globulin, widely distributed, metabolized primarily in the liver to estrone, estriol, and sulfate/glucuronide conjugates via hydroxylation and dehydrogenation pathways including CYP3A4, and excreted mainly in urine with some biliary/fecal elimination. It is indicated for menopausal vasomotor symptoms, vulvovaginal atrophy, hypoestrogenism, female hypogonadism, osteoporosis prevention, and gender-affirming hormone therapy. Toxicities include endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma when unopposed in women with a uterus, venous thromboembolism, stroke, cholestasis, gallbladder disease, and possible stimulation of estrogen-sensitive malignancies; overdose or excessive exposure may cause nausea, uterine bleeding, and breast tenderness. Common adverse effects include headache, fluid retention, nausea, breast pain, leg cramps, mood changes, and breakthrough bleeding. Clinically, estradiol is used as oral tablets, transdermal patches or gels, vaginal creams, rings, and injectable esters, often combined with a progestogen for endometrial protection in non-hyst

Name: Mefenamic acid
Description: Mefenamic acid (DrugBank DB00784) is an anthranilic acid derivative NSAID of the fenamate class characterized structurally by a substituted aminobenzoic acid core in which the aniline nitrogen links a 2,3-dimethylphenyl ring to a benzoic acid moiety, giving a biaryl arylamino carboxylic acid framework; its principal chemical scaffold is therefore the N-arylanthranilic acid, closely related to other fenamates such as flufenamic acid, meclofenamate, tolfenamic acid, and etofenamate, and more broadly pharmacologically similar to nonselective NSAIDs like ibuprofen or naproxen. Its main targets are cyclooxygenase enzymes PTGS1 and PTGS2, with consequent reduction in prostaglandin synthesis underlying analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antipyretic effects. Orally, mefenamic acid is well absorbed, is highly protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP2C9 to hydroxymethyl and carboxyl metabolites that may be conjugated, and is eliminated through both urine and feces with a relatively short half-life that supports repeated dosing. It is indicated for mild to moderate pain, primary dysmenorrhea, and short-term treatment of inflammatory painful states, for example menstrual pain, dental pain, musculoskeletal pain, and postoperative pain. Toxicity is typical of NSAIDs and includes dose-related gastrointestinal irritation, ulceration, bleeding, renal impairment, fluid retention, and rare hepatotoxicity or severe hypersensitivity; overdose may produce seizures, metabolic disturbance, and CNS depression. Common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, dyspepsia, headache, dizziness, rash, and edema, and clinically it is used chiefly as a short-course oral analgesic when prostaglandin-mediated pain or uterine cramping is prominent.

Name: Acyclovir
Description: Acyclovir (DrugBank DB00787) is a synthetic acyclic guanine nucleoside analog whose structure consists of a 2-aminopurine-6-one guanine base linked not to a ribose or deoxyribose ring but to an open-chain 2-hydroxyethoxymethyl side chain, placing it in the purine nucleoside analog and antiviral antimetabolite category; its core scaffold is best described as an acyclic guanosine scaffold, closely related to similar antiherpetic agents such as valacyclovir, penciclovir, ganciclovir, and famciclovir. It is absorbed orally with relatively low bioavailability, improved by the prodrug valacyclovir, distributes widely into body fluids including cerebrospinal fluid, exhibits low protein binding, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism to inactive metabolites such as 9-carboxymethoxymethylguanine, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by renal glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, with half-life prolongation in renal impairment. Its principal pharmacologic targets are viral thymidine kinase, which selectively phosphorylates acyclovir in infected cells, and viral DNA polymerase encoded by herpes simplex virus type 1, herpes simplex virus type 2, and varicella-zoster virus, where the triphosphate form competitively inhibits polymerase and terminates DNA chain elongation. Clinically, it is indicated for genital herpes, herpes labialis, herpes simplex encephalitis, neonatal HSV infection, varicella, and herpes zoster, and is widely used orally, intravenously, and topically for treatment and suppression of mucocutaneous and systemic herpesvirus infections. Toxicity is generally modest but includes crystalluria, acute kidney injury, and neurotoxicity such as confusion, tremor, hallucinations, or seizures, especially with intravenous dosing or renal dysfunction; common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, headache, rash, phlebitis, and local topical irritation.

Name: Naproxen
Description: Naproxen (DrugBank DB00788) is a propionic acid–derived nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug built on an arylacetic/arylpropionic acid-like anti-inflammatory pharmacophore, specifically a 2-arylpropionic acid scaffold featuring a naphthalene bicyclic aromatic system substituted with a methoxy group and a chiral propionic acid side chain; clinically it is used as the active S-enantiomer or as naproxen sodium. Chemically it belongs to the arylpropionic acid NSAID class, with a naphthalene-based profen scaffold closely related to ibuprofen, ketoprofen, flurbiprofen, and fenoprofen, while sharing functional similarity with diclofenac and indomethacin as cyclooxygenase inhibitors. Its principal targets are prostaglandin G/H synthase 1 and 2, COX-1 and COX-2, leading to reduced prostaglandin synthesis and consequent anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antipyretic effects. Naproxen is well absorbed orally, has high bioavailability, reaches peak plasma concentrations within a few hours, is extensively albumin bound, distributes mainly within extracellular fluids, undergoes hepatic metabolism largely by demethylation and conjugation, and is eliminated predominantly in urine as unchanged drug and metabolites, with an elimination half-life of roughly 12 to 17 hours. It is indicated for osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute gout, dysmenorrhea, musculoskeletal pain, headache, and fever. Toxicities include dose-related gastrointestinal ulceration, bleeding and perforation, renal impairment, sodium and fluid retention, hypertension, hepatotoxicity, and increased cardiovascular thrombotic risk; overdose may cause nausea, vomiting, drowsiness, metabolic disturbances, and rarely seizures. Common adverse effects include dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, heartburn, edema, dizziness, and rash. Clinically, naproxen is widely used for chronic inflammatory arthritides and short-term relief of acute pain, menstrual cramps, dental pain, and migraine-associated symptoms.

Name: Perindopril
Description: Perindopril (DrugBank DB00790) is a synthetic, orally active angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor of the dicarboxylate-containing, proline-derived peptidomimetic class; structurally it is an ethyl ester prodrug built on an L-proline-like bicyclic/heterocyclic peptide-mimetic scaffold with a secondary amine, carboxyl functionality, and lipophilic side chain, and it is hydrolyzed in vivo to the active diacid perindoprilat. Its core scaffold and pharmacology closely resemble other ACE inhibitors such as enalapril, ramipril, trandolapril, quinapril, lisinopril, and captopril, although captopril is distinguished by a sulfhydryl motif rather than a dicarboxylate zinc-binding group. Perindopril is well absorbed orally as the ester, with conversion by hepatic and systemic esterases to perindoprilat; food may reduce biotransformation efficiency, protein binding is moderate, tissue ACE binding contributes to a prolonged terminal effect, and elimination occurs predominantly via the kidney as perindoprilat, necessitating dose adjustment in renal impairment. Its principal target is angiotensin-converting enzyme, inhibiting angiotensin II formation and decreasing bradykinin degradation. Clinically it is indicated for hypertension, stable coronary artery disease, and reduction of cardiovascular risk, with use also in patients with heart failure or left ventricular dysfunction depending on jurisdiction and formulation. Common adverse effects include cough, dizziness, headache, hypotension, fatigue, nausea, and hyperkalemia; important toxicities include first-dose syncope, renal function decline, angioedema, severe hypotension in volume depletion, fetotoxicity in pregnancy, and rare cholestatic or hematologic reactions. In practice it is used alone or with diuretics, calcium channel blockers, or indapamide for blood pressure control and long-term vascular protection.

Name: Uracil mustard
Description: Uracil mustard (DrugBank DB00791) is a classic bifunctional alkylating antineoplastic agent built on a uracil pyrimidine ring substituted at the 5-position with a bis(2-chloroethyl)amino moiety, a structure that combines a nucleobase-recognition element with a nitrogen mustard warhead capable of intramolecular aziridinium formation and DNA cross-linking. Chemically it belongs to the nitrogen mustard class of alkylating agents and more specifically to antimetabolite-like pyrimidine mustards; its core scaffold is therefore a 5-substituted uracil linked to an N,N-bis(2-chloroethyl)amino pharmacophore. Closely related drugs include mechlorethamine, chlorambucil, melphalan, estramustine, and other nucleobase-linked mustards such as tegafur analog concepts, although uracil mustard is distinguished by its uracil scaffold. Its principal pharmacologic target is not a single protein but genomic DNA, especially N7 guanine sites, producing interstrand and intrastrand cross-links, replication arrest, and apoptosis; no highly specific protein target is generally assigned. Pharmacokinetic data are limited, but it has been used orally, is expected to undergo systemic absorption, broad distribution to proliferative tissues, nonenzymatic and hepatic biotransformation with reactive intermediates, and primarily renal excretion of metabolites. It was historically indicated for chronic leukemias and lymphomas, particularly chronic myelocytic leukemia and related hematologic malignancies. Toxicity is dominated by dose-limiting myelosuppression with leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and anemia, along with gastrointestinal injury, mucositis, nausea, vomiting, alopecia, infection risk, hemorrhage, and potential mutagenic, teratogenic, and secondary malignancy hazards. Clinically, it was used as an older cytotoxic chemotherapeutic when prolonged oral alkylating therapy was desired, but its use has largely been superseded by safer and more selective regimens.

Name: Tripelennamine
Description: Tripelennamine (DrugBank DB00792) is a first-generation ethanolamine-class antihistamine characterized structurally by a pyridine ring linked through a flexible ethylenediamine-like side chain to a substituted aromatic amine, yielding a lipophilic cationic base that is readily protonated at physiologic pH and capable of central nervous system penetration; chemically it is best categorized as an H1-receptor antagonist within the older arylalkylamine antihistamine family, and its core scaffold is commonly described as a pyridyl-arylaminoalkyl framework related to classical sedating antihistamines. Similar drugs include pyrilamine, diphenhydramine, doxylamine, chlorpheniramine, and other early H1 blockers that share anticholinergic and sedative properties. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, where it acts as an inverse agonist/antagonist; like many first-generation agents, it may also exhibit weak off-target muscarinic cholinergic antagonism.
