Tripelennamine is used for symptomatic relief of allergic rhinitis, urticaria, pruritus, conjunctival irritation, and other histamine-mediated allergic states, and historically has also been used in cough/cold preparations and as an antipruritic adjunct. After oral or parenteral administration it is absorbed reasonably well, distributed widely including to the brain, undergoes hepatic biotransformation with relatively short duration compared with newer antihistamines, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine. Adverse effects and toxicity reflect CNS depression and antimuscarinic activity, including drowsiness, dizziness, impaired psychomotor performance, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention; overdose may produce marked sedation, confusion, agitation, tachycardia, hypotension, seizures, or respiratory depression, especially in children, older adults, or when combined with alcohol, opioids, or other sedatives.

Name: Haloprogin
Description: Haloprogin (DB00793) is a halogenated topical antifungal with a compact aromatic structure consisting of a highly substituted phenyl ring bearing bromine and chlorine atoms linked through a propargyl alcohol side chain, placing it in the class of halogenated acetylenic phenyl alcohols; its core scaffold can be described as a haloaryl-propargyl alcohol pharmacophore, distinct from but functionally analogous to other older topical antifungals such as tolnaftate, undecylenic acid derivatives, clotrimazole, and miconazole. Its antifungal action has historically been attributed to direct disruption of fungal cell function and inhibition of fungal growth, although no single well-validated human or fungal target protein has been definitively established in DrugBank-style summaries; specific molecular targets are therefore generally listed as unknown or not clearly characterized. Haloprogin was used primarily for superficial dermatophyte and yeast infections including tinea pedis, tinea corporis, tinea cruris, and some cases of cutaneous candidiasis. Because it is administered topically, systemic pharmacokinetic data are limited; percutaneous absorption appears low under usual conditions, distribution is expected to remain largely confined to the stratum corneum and superficial epidermis, and any absorbed fraction is presumed to undergo hepatic biotransformation with renal elimination of metabolites, though these parameters were not extensively defined clinically. Toxicity is mainly local rather than systemic, with irritation, burning, stinging, erythema, pruritus, contact dermatitis, and maceration reported, while excessive use on inflamed or occluded skin could increase irritation. Clinically, it was applied as a topical treatment for uncomplicated superficial fungal infections, but its use declined as newer azole and allylamine agents with better tolerability and clearer pharmacology became available.

Name: Primidone
Description: Primidone (DrugBank DB00794) is a barbiturate-related anticonvulsant built on a 2,4-dioxohexahydropyrimidine nucleus, specifically a deoxybarbiturate scaffold in which the pyrimidinedione ring bears 5-ethyl and 5-phenyl substituents, giving a rigid cyclic ureide framework closely related to phenobarbital but lacking the 2-oxo pattern of classic barbiturates; it is therefore classified as a pyrimidinedione/deoxybarbiturate antiepileptic with a phenyl-ethyl substituted barbiturate-like scaffold. Structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include phenobarbital, mephobarbital, and to a lesser extent other older antiseizure sedative-hypnotics. Primidone is well absorbed orally, reaches peak concentrations within hours, distributes widely including into the CNS, shows relatively modest protein binding, and undergoes hepatic metabolism chiefly to phenobarbital and phenylethylmalonamide, both pharmacologically active, with elimination via renal excretion of parent drug and metabolites and an effective half-life influenced by autoinduction and coadministered enzyme inducers. Its main molecular action is enhancement of inhibitory GABAergic neurotransmission, largely attributed to barbiturate-sensitive modulation of GABAA receptor chloride channels, although no single highly selective protein target fully explains its antiseizure activity. Clinically it is indicated for generalized tonic-clonic seizures, focal seizures, and essential tremor, for example in patients with refractory epilepsy or disabling action tremor. Adverse effects commonly include sedation, dizziness, ataxia, diplopia, nausea, cognitive slowing, and nystagmus, while toxicity may produce profound CNS depression, respiratory suppression, coma, paradoxical agitation, hepatic dysfunction, megaloblastic anemia, osteopenia, and dependence risk; accordingly, clinical use centers on chronic seizure control and tremor reduction when newer agents are ineffective, contraindicated, or not tolerated.

Name: Sulfasalazine
Description: Sulfasalazine (DB00795) is a synthetic azo-linked prodrug composed of 5-aminosalicylic acid covalently joined to sulfapyridine through an aryl azo bond, giving a bifunctional structure that combines a salicylate ring bearing hydroxyl and carboxyl substituents with a sulfonamide-containing pyridyl aromatic system; chemically it is classified as an azo compound, sulfonamide, and aminosalicylate derivative, with an azo-aryl sulfonamide/salicylate scaffold. It is structurally related to other 5-aminosalicylate prodrugs and anti-inflammatory bowel agents such as olsalazine, balsalazide, and mesalamine, and by its sulfonamide fragment is distantly related to sulfonamide antibacterials. After oral administration, a limited fraction is absorbed intact in the small intestine, while most reaches the colon where bacterial azoreductases cleave it to sulfapyridine and mesalamine; sulfapyridine is well absorbed, widely distributed, hepatically metabolized mainly by acetylation, hydroxylation, and glucuronidation, and renally excreted, whereas mesalamine acts largely topically in the gut with partial acetylation and fecal/urinary elimination. Its pharmacologic effects are linked less to a single high-affinity target than to suppression of prostaglandin and leukotriene synthesis, inhibition of NF-kB-dependent inflammatory signaling, and modulation of cytokines including TNF, IL-1, and IL-6; reported protein-level associations include PTGS1, PTGS2, ALOX5, NF-kB pathway components, and DHFR-related folate pathways. Indications include ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, and sometimes other inflammatory bowel or spondyloarthritic disorders. Toxicities include dose-related gastrointestinal intolerance, hepatotoxicity, leukopenia, hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, oligospermia, hypersensitivity, severe cutaneous reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and crystalluria; common adverse effects are nausea, abdominal pain, headache, rash, fever, and reversible orange-yellow discoloration of urine or skin. Clinically, it is used for induction and maintenance of remission in ulcerative colitis and as a conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drug for peripheral joint inflammation.

Name: Candesartan cilexetil
Description: Candesartan cilexetil (DB00796) is an orally active ester prodrug of candesartan characterized structurally by a biphenyl-tetrazole angiotensin II antagonist core bearing a benzimidazole-derived acidic heteroaromatic system and a cilexetil ester moiety that enhances lipophilicity and gastrointestinal uptake; chemically it belongs to the angiotensin II receptor blocker class and more specifically to biphenyl-tetrazole benzimidazole derivatives, with a scaffold closely related to other sartans such as losartan, valsartan, olmesartan medoxomil, irbesartan, and telmisartan. After oral administration, it is rapidly hydrolyzed in the intestinal wall to active candesartan; absolute bioavailability is low to moderate, peak concentrations occur within hours, protein binding is high, distribution volume is modest, metabolism is limited with little CYP involvement, and elimination occurs largely as unchanged drug via both renal and biliary/fecal routes, supporting once-daily use and explaining increased exposure in renal or hepatic impairment. Its principal target is the angiotensin II type 1 receptor encoded by AGTR1, with pharmacologic blockade reducing vasoconstriction, aldosterone release, and adverse cardiovascular remodeling. It is indicated for hypertension and heart failure, for example essential hypertension, left ventricular systolic dysfunction, and reduction of heart-failure hospitalization risk. Adverse effects commonly include dizziness, hypotension, hyperkalemia, fatigue, and renal function deterioration, with rarer toxicities such as symptomatic renal failure, syncope, and angioedema; class-defining fetal toxicity can cause oligohydramnios, fetal renal injury, skull hypoplasia, or death if used during pregnancy. Clinically it is used alone or with diuretics or calcium-channel blockers for blood-pressure control and in guideline-based chronic heart failure management.

Name: Tolazoline
Description: Tolazoline (DrugBank DB00797) is a synthetic imidazoline derivative whose structure consists of an aromatic benzyl/aryl-substituted imidazoline ring system, giving it a basic heterocyclic vasoactive profile; chemically it is classified as a nonselective alpha-adrenergic antagonist and peripheral vasodilator, built on the imidazoline scaffold shared with related sympatholytic or vasoactive agents. Similar drugs include phentolamine and phenoxybenzamine as nonselective alpha blockers, and the structurally related imidazoline derivative naphazoline, although the latter differs pharmacologically by acting primarily as an alpha agonist. Tolazoline acts mainly by antagonizing alpha-1 and alpha-2 adrenoceptors, with additional histamine-like vasodilatory effects described in older literature; adrenergic receptor proteins ADRA1A, ADRA1B, ADRA1D, ADRA2A, ADRA2B, and ADRA2C are therefore the principal known targets. It has historically been administered parenterally or orally, is absorbed reasonably well, distributes systemically to vascular beds, undergoes limited hepatic biotransformation, and is cleared largely by renal excretion of parent drug and metabolites, with a relatively short duration of hemodynamic action requiring monitored dosing. Its main indications have been peripheral vasospastic disorders and pulmonary hypertension, especially persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, with past use in Raynaud-type ischemia and diagnostic or therapeutic reversal of vasoconstriction. Adverse effects reflect systemic vasodilation and alpha blockade, including hypotension, reflex tachycardia, flushing, arrhythmias, headache, dizziness, nasal congestion, and gastrointestinal irritation. Toxicity can include profound hypotension, myocardial ischemia from tachyarrhythmia, and shock-like cardiovascular collapse in overdose or susceptible patients, so current clinical use is limited and specialist supervised.

Name: Gentamicin
Description: Gentamicin (DrugBank DB00798) is a naturally derived aminoglycoside antibiotic produced by Micromonospora, marketed as a mixture of closely related congeners such as C1, C1a, C2, and C2a, all built on a highly polar, polycationic oligosaccharide framework consisting of a central 2-deoxystreptamine aminocyclitol linked by glycosidic bonds to multiple amino sugars richly substituted with hydroxyl and amino groups; this places it in the aminoglycoside/aminocyclitol class with a 2-deoxystreptamine scaffold shared by similar drugs including tobramycin, amikacin, kanamycin, netilmicin, and neomycin. Its principal target is the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit, especially 16S rRNA and associated ribosomal proteins within the decoding site, causing mistranslation and inhibition of protein synthesis, with concentration-dependent bactericidal activity. Gentamicin is not meaningfully absorbed orally, is therefore given mainly intravenously, intramuscularly, topically, or ophthalmically, distributes largely to extracellular fluid with limited CNS penetration but renal cortical and inner ear accumulation, undergoes negligible metabolism, and is excreted unchanged by glomerular filtration, giving a half-life prolonged in renal impairment. Major toxicities are dose- and exposure-related nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity affecting cochlear and vestibular function, and less commonly neuromuscular blockade, with fetal auditory toxicity a concern in pregnancy. Adverse effects include rising creatinine, proteinuria, hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo, and rare respiratory weakness. Clinically it is used for severe aerobic Gram-negative infections such as sepsis, complicated urinary tract infection, intra-abdominal infection, pneumonia, and bacteremia, often in combination with beta-lactams or vancomycin, and also for synergistic treatment of enterococcal endocarditis and for selected topical ocular or skin infections.

Name: Tazarotene
Description: Tazarotene (DB00799) is a third-generation acetylenic topical retinoid prodrug whose structure features a lipophilic aromatic system built around a thiochromene-like heteroaromatic ring linked through an ethynyl bridge to a substituted pyridyl moiety and terminated as an ethyl ester that is rapidly hydrolyzed to the active carboxylic acid, tazarotenic acid; chemically it is categorized as a synthetic retinoid, specifically an aromatic acetylenic retinoid, with a rigid retinoid scaffold designed to confer receptor selectivity. Similar drugs include other topical or systemic retinoids such as adapalene, tretinoin, isotretinoin, bexarotene, and acitretin, although tazarotene is distinguished by relative selectivity for retinoic acid receptors RAR-beta and RAR-gamma, with downstream modulation of keratinocyte differentiation, proliferation, and inflammatory gene expression; retinoid X receptors are not primary targets. After topical administration, absorption is limited but increases with compromised skin barrier or larger treated surface area; the drug is highly protein bound after conversion to tazarotenic acid, distributed systemically at low concentrations, metabolized mainly by ester hydrolysis and subsequent oxidation/sulfoxidation, and eliminated predominantly in urine and feces as inactive metabolites. Its major toxicology concerns are dose-related local irritation and class-associated teratogenicity, with examples including fetal risk, severe erythema, and animal developmental toxicity. Approved indications include plaque psoriasis, acne vulgaris, and photodamage such as fine wrinkling and mottled hyperpigmentation. Common adverse effects include burning, pruritus, peeling, dryness, erythema, desquamation, and photosensitivity. Clinically, it is used as topical cream, gel, foam, or lotion, often once daily, either alone or with moisturizers, corticosteroids, or acne combination regimens.

Name: Fenoldopam
Description: Fenoldopam (DrugBank DB00800) is a synthetic benzazepine-derived catecholamine-mimetic vasodilator whose structure consists of a substituted 2,3,4,5-tetrahydro-1H-3-benzazepine core bearing a catechol-type dihydroxyphenyl ring and an arylsulfonamide substituent, features that confer potent dopaminergic agonism without direct alpha- or beta-adrenergic activity; chemically it is classified as a selective dopamine receptor agonist and more specifically a benzazepine/catechol arylsulfonamide, with a benzazepine scaffold related to other dopaminergic ligands. Similar drugs include dopamine itself, which is less receptor-selective, and other dopamine agonists such as SKF-38393-like benzazepines, although fenoldopam is distinctive for peripheral D1 selectivity and intravenous antihypertensive use. Its principal target is the dopamine D1 receptor encoded by DRD1, producing rapid arteriolar vasodilation, natriuresis, and increased renal blood flow; weak activity at alpha2 receptors has also been described in some pharmacologic sources. Fenoldopam is indicated for short-term reduction of severe hypertension, including hypertensive emergencies, postoperative hypertension, and situations where preservation of renal perfusion is desirable, such as severe hypertension with renal insufficiency. It is given by continuous intravenous infusion, with immediate systemic availability, rapid distribution, extensive hepatic conjugative metabolism, and predominantly urinary excretion of inactive metabolites; its elimination half-life is about 5 minutes, necessitating titration by infusion. Toxicity is mainly extension of pharmacology, including excessive hypotension, reflex tachycardia, headache, flushing, nausea, hypokalemia, and increased intraocular pressure, with caution in glaucoma, sulfite-sensitive patients, and ischemic cardiovascular states. Clinically, it is used in monitored hospital settings as a rapidly titratable vasodilator when quick blood-pressure control and maintenance of kidney perfusion are priorities.

Name: Halazepam
Description: Halazepam (DrugBank DB00801) is a classical 1,4-benzodiazepine anxiolytic whose structure consists of a fused benzene-diazepine core bearing the characteristic 5-phenyl substituent and a 7-chloro ring substitution, with additional functionality that makes it a prodrug-like member of the class and supports biotransformation to active benzodiazepine metabolites; chemically it belongs to the benzodiazepines, specifically the sedative-anxiolytic chlorinated 1,4-benzodiazepine family, and its core scaffold is the 5-aryl-1,4-benzodiazepin-2-one framework. Similar drugs include diazepam, prazepam, chlordiazepoxide, clorazepate, and alprazolam, especially other anxiolytic benzodiazepines that act through GABAergic modulation. Its principal target is the GABAA receptor benzodiazepine allosteric site, typically on receptor complexes containing alpha, beta, and gamma subunits, thereby enhancing GABA-mediated chloride conductance and neuronal inhibition. Pharmacokinetically, halazepam is orally active, well absorbed, distributed widely into the CNS and other tissues with significant protein binding, and undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism to active metabolites including nordiazepam, which contributes to prolonged clinical effect; elimination is mainly renal as conjugated metabolites after oxidative biotransformation. Toxicity is consistent with benzodiazepines and includes dose-related CNS depression, psychomotor impairment, ataxia, confusion, and respiratory depression when combined with alcohol, opioids, or other sedatives; overdose is usually less lethal than barbiturates but can cause profound sedation. It is indicated primarily for anxiety disorders and short-term relief of anxiety symptoms such as tension, autonomic hyperactivity, and agitation. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, fatigue, weakness, impaired coordination, memory disturbance, and dependence, with withdrawal phenomena after prolonged use. Clinically, it has been used as an oral anxiolytic in generalized anxiety states, situational anxiety, and anxiety associated with psychosomatic or medical illness, particularly when a longer-acting benzodiazepine effect is desired.

Name: Dicyclomine
Description: Dicyclomine (DrugBank DB00804) is a synthetic tertiary amine antimuscarinic whose structure is best described as a glycolate ester linking a substituted cyclohexyl-hydroxy acetic acid moiety to a 2-(diethylamino)ethyl alcohol fragment, giving an amphiphilic ester with a protonatable diethylamino side chain that supports membrane permeability and anticholinergic activity. Chemically it belongs to the anticholinergic antispasmodics, specifically tertiary amino alcohol esters, and its core scaffold is a substituted cyclohexyl glycolate/carbinol ester related to the muscarinic antagonist pharmacophore seen in atropine-like agents. Similar drugs include other antimuscarinic gastrointestinal antispasmodics such as hyoscyamine, atropine, scopolamine, propantheline, oxybutynin, and glycopyrrolate, although these differ in scaffold rigidity and CNS penetration. Dicyclomine is well absorbed orally, reaches peak concentrations within hours, distributes widely including some central nervous system penetration, is variably protein bound, undergoes hepatic biotransformation, and is eliminated through both renal excretion of metabolites and some unchanged drug, with a relatively short elimination half-life supporting multiple daily dosing. Its principal targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially functional antagonism at M1 and M3 receptor-mediated smooth-muscle signaling in the gastrointestinal tract. It is indicated for symptomatic treatment of irritable bowel syndrome and functional bowel/spastic colon states, reducing abdominal pain, cramping, intestinal hypermotility, and bowel spasm. Toxicity reflects classic anticholinergic excess, including tachycardia, hyperthermia, urinary retention, ileus, agitation, confusion, hallucinations, and severe CNS or respiratory effects in overdose; infants are particularly vulnerable, and use is contraindicated in obstructive uropathy, glaucoma, myasthenia gravis, and GI obstruction. Common adverse effects include dry mouth, blurred vision, dizziness, constipation, nausea, somnolence, palpitations, and difficulty urinating, and clinically it is used mainly as an oral adjunct for IBS symptom control, occasionally with dietary and other supportive measures.

Name: Pentoxifylline
Description: Pentoxifylline (DrugBank DB00806) is a synthetic methylxanthine derivative structurally characterized by a substituted xanthine/purine-2,6-dione core bearing multiple N-methyl groups and a polar oxohexyl side chain, a design that preserves the planar heterocyclic methylxanthine pharmacophore while increasing hemorheologic activity; chemically it is classified as a xanthine, methylxanthine, and hemorrheologic phosphodiesterase-modulating agent, with a caffeine/theophylline-like xanthine scaffold. Similar drugs include other methylxanthines such as theophylline, caffeine, and dyphylline, as well as the related xanthine derivative propentofylline. Its principal pharmacology involves nonselective phosphodiesterase inhibition, increased intracellular cAMP, improved erythrocyte deformability, reduced blood viscosity, decreased platelet aggregation, and modulation of inflammatory signaling including TNF-alpha suppression; reported target associations include phosphodiesterases, adenosine receptors, and cytokine-regulatory pathways rather than a single highly selective protein target. After oral administration it is well absorbed but undergoes substantial first-pass metabolism, producing active metabolites; it distributes widely, has moderate protein binding, is extensively metabolized in the liver, and is eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites with a relatively short parent half-life. It is indicated primarily for intermittent claudication from chronic peripheral arterial disease, improving walking distance and ischemic limb symptoms, and has also been used off-label in disorders such as venous leg ulcers, alcoholic hepatitis, radiation injury, and some microvascular complications. Adverse effects are commonly gastrointestinal and neurologic, including nausea, vomiting, dyspepsia, dizziness, and headache; toxicity may include flushing, hypotension, tachycardia, agitation, arrhythmia, or seizures in overdose, with bleeding risk heightened in patients receiving anticoagulants or with recent hemorrhage.

Name: Indapamide
Description: Indapamide (DrugBank DB00808) is an indoline-derived sulfonamide antihypertensive diuretic whose structure consists of a chlorobenzamide-like aromatic system linked through a sulfonamide to an indoline ring, giving a lipophilic, non-thiazide scaffold that is nevertheless thiazide-like in pharmacology; chemically it is classified as a sulfonamide diuretic and more specifically a thiazide-like diuretic, with an indoline-sulfonamide/chlorobenzenesulfonamide scaffold. Closely related or pharmacologically similar drugs include hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, metolazone, and xipamide, which share distal convoluted tubule natriuretic activity. Its principal target is the renal sodium/chloride cotransporter SLC12A3 in the distal convoluted tubule, with antihypertensive benefit also attributed to direct vascular effects, likely involving calcium flux modulation and reduced peripheral resistance. Indapamide is well absorbed orally, is highly protein and erythrocyte bound, distributes widely because of its lipophilicity, undergoes substantial hepatic metabolism to inactive metabolites, and is eliminated through both renal and fecal routes, with a relatively long half-life that supports once-daily dosing. It is indicated mainly for essential hypertension and edema associated with salt and water retention, and clinically is used alone or in combination regimens, for example with perindopril, in uncomplicated hypertension or hypertension in older adults. Toxicity is dominated by excessive diuresis and electrolyte loss, including hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia, dehydration, orthostatic hypotension, and possible arrhythmia risk; less common examples include hyperuricemia, gout precipitation, hyperglycemia, photosensitivity, rash, and rare sulfonamide-associated hypersensitivity or hepatic encephalopathy in severe liver disease.

Name: Tropicamide
Description: Tropicamide (DrugBank DB00809) is a synthetic antimuscarinic mydriatic whose structure consists of a substituted aromatic amide built from a tropic acid-derived 2-phenyl-2-hydroxyacetamide framework linked to an N-ethyl-N-(4-pyridylmethyl) tertiary carboxamide, giving an aryl hydroxy amide scaffold with a pyridylalkyl tertiary amide pharmacophore; chemically it is categorized as an anticholinergic parasympatholytic ophthalmic agent within the tropic acid derivative class, and its core scaffold is related to other muscarinic antagonists used in ophthalmology. Similar drugs include atropine, homatropine, cyclopentolate, and scopolamine, which share antimuscarinic ocular actions but differ in duration and potency. Its principal target proteins are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially M3 receptors on the iris sphincter and ciliary muscle, with functional antagonism also involving M1–M5 subtypes. After topical ocular administration, systemic absorption is limited but can occur through conjunctival and nasolacrimal mucosa; onset is rapid, ocular distribution is local, cycloplegia and mydriasis are relatively short-lived, hepatic metabolism is presumed for absorbed drug, and renal excretion is expected for metabolites and a minor fraction of unchanged drug. Toxicity reflects anticholinergic effects, with examples including tachycardia, dry mouth, urinary retention, confusion, hyperthermia, and CNS excitation, particularly in children or with excessive dosing. It is indicated for diagnostic mydriasis and cycloplegia, for example during fundoscopy and refraction testing, and is also used perioperatively in ophthalmic examination. Common adverse effects include transient stinging, photophobia, blurred vision, increased intraocular pressure, and rare precipitation of angle-closure glaucoma.

Name: Biperiden
Description: Biperiden (DrugBank DB00810) is a centrally acting synthetic antimuscarinic with a tertiary amino alcohol structure characterized by a bulky lipophilic bicyclic ring system, a piperidine tertiary amine, and a hydroxyl-bearing tertiary carbon that together define an aminoalcohol ester-like anticholinergic pharmacophore; chemically it is classified as an antiparkinson anticholinergic of the piperidine/tertiary amine class, and its core scaffold is best described as a substituted norbornyl- or bicycloheptane-containing piperidinol framework. It is structurally and pharmacologically related to other centrally acting antimuscarinics such as trihexyphenidyl, benztropine, procyclidine, and orphenadrine. Its principal targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, with therapeutic activity attributed mainly to central M1 receptor antagonism in the striatum, restoring dopaminergic-cholinergic balance in parkinsonism. After oral administration it is reasonably well absorbed, distributes widely including across the blood-brain barrier, undergoes substantial hepatic metabolism with formation of inactive metabolites, and is eliminated primarily in urine with some fecal excretion; the clinical half-life is sufficient for divided daily dosing, while intramuscular use provides relatively rapid symptomatic relief. Toxicity reflects dose-dependent anticholinergic excess, including agitation, delirium, hallucinations, hyperthermia, urinary retention, severe tachycardia, constipation or paralytic ileus, and precipitation of angle-closure glaucoma, with overdose resembling classic antimuscarinic poisoning. Indications include Parkinson disease, postencephalitic or arteriosclerotic parkinsonism, and especially treatment or prevention of drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms such as acute dystonia, rigidity, tremor, and akathisia caused by antipsychotics. Common adverse effects include dry mouth, blurred vision, dizziness, confusion, memory impairment, sedation, constipation, and urinary hesitancy. Clinically, biperiden is used as oral maintenance therapy for tremor-predominant parkinsonian symptoms and as injectable rescue therapy for acute neuroleptic-induced dystonic reactions.

Name: Ribavirin
Description: Ribavirin (DrugBank DB00811) is a synthetic triazole nucleoside analog composed of a ribofuranose sugar linked to a substituted 1,2,4-triazole carboxamide base, giving it the structural character of a guanosine mimic; chemically it is classified as a broad-spectrum antiviral nucleoside analog, with a ribosyl-triazole carboxamide scaffold that distinguishes it from classical purine bases while preserving nucleoside-like recognition. Related drugs include other antiviral nucleoside analogs such as guanosine analogs and agents used in viral hepatitis therapy, including sofosbuvir, acyclovir, and vidarabine, although ribavirin has a broader and less target-selective antiviral profile. Its pharmacology reflects intracellular phosphorylation to mono-, di-, and triphosphate metabolites that inhibit inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase, interfere with viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerases, disrupt RNA capping, and promote lethal mutagenesis; reported target proteins therefore include host inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase 1 and 2 and viral polymerase-associated replication machinery. Oral absorption is moderate, increases with food, distribution is extensive with notable accumulation in erythrocytes and a very large apparent volume of distribution, metabolism is limited but includes reversible deribosylation and intracellular trapping as phosphorylated metabolites, and excretion is primarily renal with a long terminal half-life due to tissue sequestration. Major toxicity is dose-limiting hemolytic anemia from red-cell accumulation, with examples including fatigue, dyspnea, and worsening cardiac ischemia; it is also teratogenic and embryotoxic. Adverse effects include anemia, cough, rash, insomnia, irritability, nausea, and depression. Clinically, ribavirin has been used in chronic hepatitis C in combination regimens, severe respiratory syncytial virus infection by aerosol, and selected viral hemorrhagic fevers such as Lassa fever.

Name: Fentanyl
Description: Fentanyl (DrugBank DB00813) is a highly lipophilic synthetic opioid built on a 4-anilidopiperidine structure, specifically an N-phenyl-N-[1-(2-phenylethyl)piperidin-4-yl]propanamide framework in which a tertiary piperidine ring bears an anilide and phenethyl substituent that strongly enhance μ-opioid receptor affinity; chemically it belongs to the phenylpiperidine/anilidopiperidine opioid class, with the 4-anilidopiperidine scaffold serving as the core motif shared by related agents such as sufentanil, alfentanil, remifentanil, and the older phenylpiperidine opioid meperidine. Its principal target is the μ-opioid receptor (OPRM1), with much weaker functional activity at δ- and κ-opioid receptors, producing potent G protein-coupled analgesic and sedative effects. Pharmacokinetically, fentanyl is rapidly absorbed by intravenous, transmucosal, intranasal, and transdermal routes, is extensively distributed because of high lipid solubility and tissue uptake, is highly protein bound, undergoes predominant hepatic CYP3A4-mediated N-dealkylation to norfentanyl and other inactive metabolites, and is excreted mainly in urine as metabolites. It is indicated for severe acute and chronic pain, perioperative analgesia, anesthesia adjunct use, breakthrough cancer pain, and sometimes analgesia in mechanically ventilated patients. Toxicity is dominated by dose-dependent respiratory depression, apnea, bradycardia, chest wall rigidity, coma, miosis, and fatal overdose, especially with other CNS depressants; adverse effects also include constipation, nausea, vomiting, sedation, dizziness, confusion, and physical dependence, tolerance, misuse, and withdrawal. Clinically, it is used in anesthesia induction and maintenance, postoperative analgesia, transdermal treatment of opioid-tolerant chronic cancer or noncancer pain, and transmucosal rescue therapy for episodic breakthrough pain.

Name: Meloxicam
Description: Meloxicam (DrugBank DB00814) is an enolic acid nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug of the oxicam class characterized by a 1,2-benzothiazine-3-carboxamide 1,1-dioxide core bearing a 4-hydroxyl/4-enol functionality, a 5-methyl substituent, and a thiazolyl amide side chain, giving a heteroaromatic sulfonamide-like scaffold that underlies its acidic, highly protein-bound behavior; thus its chemical category is oxicam NSAIDs and its principal scaffold is the benzothiazine enol-carboxamide oxicam nucleus. Structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include piroxicam, tenoxicam, lornoxicam, and to a lesser extent other COX-inhibiting NSAIDs such as diclofenac and celecoxib. Its main targets are prostaglandin G/H synthase 2 and prostaglandin G/H synthase 1, with relative COX-2 preference that reduces prostaglandin synthesis and thereby inflammation, pain, and fever. Meloxicam is indicated for osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, and symptomatic relief of musculoskeletal pain and inflammatory arthropathies. Orally it is well absorbed with high bioavailability, reaches peak concentrations in several hours, is extensively albumin bound, distributes into synovial fluid, undergoes hepatic metabolism predominantly via CYP2C9 and to a lesser extent CYP3A4 with additional peroxidase-mediated biotransformation to inactive metabolites, and is eliminated through both urine and feces with a long half-life permitting once-daily dosing. Toxicities are typical of NSAIDs and include gastrointestinal ulceration, bleeding or perforation, acute kidney injury, sodium and fluid retention, hypertension, cardiovascular thrombotic risk, hepatotoxicity, and hypersensitivity including bronchospasm or severe cutaneous reactions; common side effects include dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, edema, and rash. Clinically, it is used as a once-daily anti-inflammatory and analgesic in chronic arthritic disease and short-term pain states when a relatively COX-2 preferential NSAID is desired.

Name: Orciprenaline
Description: Orciprenaline (metaproterenol; DrugBank DB00816) is a synthetic sympathomimetic bronchodilator built on a phenylethanolamine/arylethanolamine structure featuring a resorcinol-substituted benzene ring linked to a beta-hydroxylated ethylamine side chain bearing an N-isopropyl group, a motif that confers preferential beta-adrenergic agonism and relative resistance to catechol-O-methyltransferase; chemically it is a resorcinol-type beta-adrenergic receptor agonist within the phenethylamine class, and its core scaffold is the substituted beta-phenylethanolamine shared with other bronchodilators such as isoproterenol, terbutaline, albuterol (salbutamol), and ritodrine. Its principal targets are the beta-2 adrenergic receptor and, less selectively, the beta-1 adrenergic receptor, leading to bronchial smooth-muscle relaxation and some cardiac stimulation. Orciprenaline is used primarily for reversible bronchospasm in asthma, chronic bronchitis, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and historically also as a cardiac stimulant in bradyarrhythmias or atrioventricular conduction disorders. It is generally well absorbed after oral, inhaled, or parenteral administration, distributed systemically including to the heart and lungs, metabolized mainly by phase II conjugation such as sulfate or glucuronide formation rather than extensive COMT degradation, and excreted largely in urine as unchanged drug and conjugates. Toxicity is characteristic of beta-agonist excess, including dose-related tachycardia, palpitations, tremor, nervousness, headache, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, and rarely angina, supraventricular arrhythmias, or paradoxical bronchospasm; overdose may produce marked sympathetic stimulation and hemodynamic instability. Clinically, it has been used as an acute reliever bronchodilator, although newer, more beta-2-selective agents have largely replaced it because of improved tolerability.

Name: Acetazolamide
Description: Acetazolamide (DrugBank DB00819) is a classic heteroaromatic sulfonamide carbonic anhydrase inhibitor whose structure consists of a 1,3,4-thiadiazole ring bearing an exocyclic amino group and a sulfonamide substituent, with an acetamide-derived substitution pattern that helps confer acidity and zinc-binding capacity at the enzyme active site; chemically it belongs to the sulfonamide, thiadiazole, and carbonic anhydrase inhibitor classes, and its core scaffold is the acetylamino-substituted 1,3,4-thiadiazole-2-sulfonamide pharmacophore. It is closely related to other carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as methazolamide, dorzolamide, brinzolamide, dichlorphenamide, and the less selective older sulfonamide diuretic analogs. Its main targets are carbonic anhydrase isoenzymes, especially CA II, with activity also reported at CA I, CA IV, CA IX, and CA XII, producing reduced bicarbonate reabsorption, decreased aqueous humor formation, and lower cerebrospinal fluid production. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed, distributes widely including into erythrocytes, is moderately protein bound, is not extensively metabolized, and is eliminated largely unchanged by the kidney, so duration and exposure increase in renal impairment. Clinically it is used for glaucoma, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, acute mountain sickness prevention and treatment, metabolic alkalosis, edema adjunctive therapy, and selected epilepsies such as absence seizures. Adverse effects commonly include paresthesias, fatigue, dysgeusia, polyuria, nausea, and electrolyte loss with metabolic acidosis or hypokalemia; important toxicities include nephrolithiasis, sulfonamide hypersensitivity, rare severe cutaneous reactions, blood dyscrasias, hepatic encephalopathy risk in cirrhosis, and worsening acidosis in overdose or advanced renal dysfunction.

Name: Tadalafil
Description: Tadalafil (DrugBank DB00820) is a synthetic small-molecule phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor built on a rigid fused bicyclic beta-carboline-like pyrazinopyridoindole core bearing a dioxolophenyl substituent and a methyl group, giving a lipophilic, conformationally constrained heteroaromatic structure; chemically it is categorized as a PDE5-inhibiting indole-derived heterocyclic compound, with a tetracyclic pyrazino[1’,2’:1,6]pyrido[3,4-b]indole scaffold that distinguishes it from related agents. Similar drugs include sildenafil, vardenafil, and avanafil, which share PDE5 inhibition but differ in scaffold, selectivity, and duration. Its principal target is phosphodiesterase 5A, with weaker activity at PDE11A and minimal clinically relevant effects on other PDE isoforms. By preventing cGMP degradation in corpus cavernosum, pulmonary vasculature, and lower urinary tract smooth muscle, tadalafil is used for erectile dysfunction, pulmonary arterial hypertension, and signs and symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia, including men with both ED and BPH. Orally absorbed with good bioavailability surrogates and a Tmax of about 2 hours, it is widely distributed, highly protein bound, and notable for a long terminal half-life near 17.5 hours that supports once-daily or on-demand dosing; it is metabolized predominantly by CYP3A4 to inactive catechol and methylcatechol glucuronide metabolites and eliminated mainly in feces with lesser urinary excretion. Toxicities reflect vasodilation and PDE cross-reactivity, including headache, flushing, dyspepsia, nasal congestion, back pain, myalgia, and dizziness; serious examples include symptomatic hypotension, syncope with nitrates or riociguat, rare non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, sudden hearing loss, and priapism. Clinically, it is used as needed before sexual activity, as daily low-dose therapy for ED or BPH, and as chronic therapy in PAH to improve exercise capacity.

Name: Levomenthol
Description: Levomenthol (DrugBank DB00825) is the naturally occurring levorotatory isomer of menthol, a cyclic monoterpene alcohol whose structure consists of a substituted cyclohexane ring bearing a hydroxyl group and isopropyl and methyl substituents in a defined stereochemical arrangement that confers its characteristic cooling sensation and odor. Chemically, it belongs to the terpene alcohol and monoterpenoid class, with a menthane scaffold typical of p-menthane derivatives. Similar drugs and related compounds include racemic menthol, peppermint oil constituents, menthone, eucalyptol, camphor, and other topical counterirritants or cooling agents such as methyl salicylate in combination products. Its principal pharmacologic targets include transient receptor potential channels, especially TRPM8 as the canonical cold receptor agonist, with additional effects reported on TRPA1, TRPV3, voltage-gated sodium channels, and kappa-opioid-related sensory modulation, supporting local antipruritic, analgesic, and antitussive effects. Levomenthol is used mainly topically or in inhaled/oromucosal formulations; systemic pharmacokinetic data are limited, but it is absorbed through skin and mucosa, distributes into lipid-rich tissues, undergoes hepatic phase I oxidation and phase II glucuronidation, and is excreted predominantly in urine as conjugated metabolites. Indications include relief of minor throat irritation, cough, nasal congestion, pruritus, mild musculoskeletal pain, and topical discomfort in conditions such as upper respiratory symptoms or itchy dermatoses. Adverse effects are usually local and dose related, including skin or mucosal irritation, burning, lacrimation, contact dermatitis, nausea, or dizziness, whereas excessive exposure may cause CNS depression, ataxia, abdominal pain, or rare seizures, especially in children; thus clinical use is primarily as an OTC topical, inhalational, or lozenge ingredient for symptomatic relief rather than disease modification.

Name: Natamycin
Description: Natamycin (DrugBank DB00826) is a polyene macrolide antifungal whose structure consists of a large 26-membered macrolactone ring bearing a conjugated tetraene polyene segment, multiple hydroxyl substituents, a carboxyl functionality, and a glycosidically linked mycosamine sugar, placing it in the polyene macrolide natural product class and more specifically on the tetraene macrolide scaffold shared in part with other membrane-active antifungals. Closely related or mechanistically similar drugs include amphotericin B and nystatin, which are larger polyene macrolides, while pimaricin is a synonym for natamycin itself. Its principal pharmacologic target is ergosterol in fungal cell membranes rather than a classical protein target; by binding ergosterol it disrupts membrane-associated transport and permeability processes and inhibits fungal growth, with reported activity against Candida, Fusarium, Aspergillus, Cephalosporium, and other filamentous fungi and yeasts. Natamycin is used primarily as a topical ophthalmic anti-infective, especially for fungal blepharitis, conjunctivitis, and keratitis, including fungal corneal ulceration, and is also used in some settings for superficial mucocutaneous candidiasis and as a food preservative because of its poor systemic penetration. Pharmacokinetically, it is minimally absorbed after topical, oral, or mucosal administration, remains largely confined to the application site, has negligible systemic distribution, limited metabolism, and is excreted largely unchanged in feces when swallowed. Toxicity is therefore mainly local rather than systemic; examples include ocular irritation, conjunctival hyperemia, foreign-body sensation, tearing, eyelid edema, pain, and blurred vision, while serious systemic toxicity is uncommon compared with amphotericin B. Clinically, it is valued for localized antifungal therapy where high surface exposure and minimal systemic adverse effects are desired.

Name: Cinoxacin
Description: Cinoxacin (DrugBank DB00827) is a first-generation quinolone antibacterial built on a fused bicyclic 1,8-naphthyridine/quinolone-like heteroaromatic scaffold bearing the characteristic 3-carboxylic acid and 4-oxo pharmacophore required for DNA gyrase inhibition, with additional ring substitution that distinguishes it from later fluoroquinolones. Chemically, it belongs to the synthetic quinolone carboxylic acids, and its closest structural and pharmacologic analogs include nalidixic acid, oxolinic acid, pipemidic acid, norfloxacin, and ciprofloxacin, although cinoxacin is an older non-fluorinated urinary anti-infective. Its principal targets are bacterial DNA gyrase, especially the GyrA/GyrB topoisomerase II complex, and secondarily topoisomerase IV in susceptible organisms, thereby blocking bacterial DNA replication. Cinoxacin was used primarily for uncomplicated urinary tract infections caused by susceptible Gram-negative bacteria such as Escherichia coli, Proteus mirabilis, Enterobacter, and Klebsiella, with clinical use centered on cystitis and other lower urinary tract infections. After oral administration it is absorbed reasonably well, achieves therapeutically useful urinary concentrations, distributes mainly in extracellular fluids with limited tissue penetration compared with newer quinolones, undergoes partial hepatic biotransformation, and is eliminated predominantly by the kidney as parent drug and metabolites, giving especially high urinary excretion. Adverse effects and toxicity are broadly quinolone-like and include nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, headache, dizziness, rash, pruritus, and photosensitivity, while more serious but less common events include CNS stimulation, confusion, seizures in predisposed patients, hypersensitivity reactions, crystalluria, and potential renal irritation; accordingly, clinical use historically emphasized short-course treatment of susceptible lower UTIs rather than severe systemic infections.

Name: Fosfomycin
Description: Fosfomycin (DrugBank DB00828) is a small, highly polar phosphonic acid antibiotic characterized structurally by a strained three-membered epoxide ring attached to a carbon-phosphorus phosphonate moiety, giving a simple but highly reactive phosphoenolpyruvate mimic; chemically it belongs to the phosphonic acid derivative class and, more specifically, to epoxide-containing phosphonate antibacterials, with a minimal fosfomycin scaffold defined by the epoxide-phosphonate pharmacophore. It is most similar to other cell-wall-active urinary antibiotics in clinical use such as nitrofurantoin and pivmecillinam, though it is structurally distinct, and it also has mechanistic kinship to phosphonate natural products. Its principal target is the bacterial enzyme UDP-N-acetylglucosamine enolpyruvyl transferase, MurA, which it irreversibly inhibits after uptake through glycerophosphate and glucose-6-phosphate transport systems, blocking early peptidoglycan biosynthesis. Orally, fosfomycin tromethamine is rapidly absorbed with moderate bioavailability, distributes largely in extracellular fluid, achieves very high urinary concentrations, undergoes negligible metabolism, and is eliminated primarily unchanged by glomerular filtration; the intravenous disodium salt provides broader systemic exposure. It is indicated mainly for uncomplicated urinary tract infection, especially acute cystitis caused by susceptible Escherichia coli or Enterococcus faecalis, and is also used in some multidrug-resistant or complicated infections, including prostatitis, osteomyelitis, and combination therapy for resistant Gram-negative infections. Adverse effects are usually gastrointestinal, including diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, headache, and vaginitis, while toxicity is generally low but may include hypersensitivity, sodium load and hypokalemia with IV use, and selection of resistance via impaired transport or altered MurA.

Name: Diazepam
Description: Diazepam (DrugBank DB00829) is a lipophilic 1,4-benzodiazepine characterized structurally by a fused benzene–diazepine ring system bearing a 2-keto group, a 5-phenyl substituent, a 7-chloro electron-withdrawing group, and an N-methyl substituent, placing it in the benzodiazepine anxiolytic-sedative class with a classical 1,4-benzodiazepin-2-one scaffold. It is closely related to other benzodiazepines such as chlordiazepoxide, lorazepam, clonazepam, oxazepam, alprazolam, and temazepam, which share the GABAergic positive allosteric modulator pharmacology but differ in potency and disposition. Diazepam acts primarily at the benzodiazepine site of GABAA receptor complexes, especially receptor assemblies containing GABRA1, GABRA2, GABRA3, GABRA5, GABRB2, and GABRG2 subunits, enhancing chloride channel opening frequency in response to GABA. It is well absorbed orally, also effective intravenously and rectally, is highly protein bound, rapidly distributes into the CNS and adipose tissue, and undergoes hepatic CYP2C19- and CYP3A4-mediated N-demethylation and hydroxylation to active metabolites including nordiazepam, temazepam, and oxazepam, followed by glucuronidation and mainly renal excretion of metabolites; its long half-life and active metabolites can cause accumulation. Toxicity includes dose-related CNS and respiratory depression, profound sedation, coma in overdose, heightened danger with opioids or alcohol, dependence, withdrawal seizures, and teratogenic or neonatal adaptation concerns. Indications and clinical uses include anxiety disorders, acute alcohol withdrawal, status epilepticus, skeletal muscle spasm, preprocedural sedation, and short-term relief of severe agitation; common adverse effects include drowsiness, ataxia, confusion, impaired memory, dizziness, weakness, paradoxical disinhibition, and falls, particularly in older adults.

Name: Phenmetrazine
Description: Phenmetrazine (DrugBank DB00830) is a synthetic sympathomimetic amine with a substituted phenylmorpholine structure, consisting of a 3-methyl-2-phenylmorpholine core in which a morpholine-like six-membered heterocycle containing oxygen and nitrogen is decorated by a phenyl ring and methyl substituent; chemically it is classified as a phenylalkylamine-related anorectic and central nervous system stimulant, with a morpholine scaffold that distinguishes it from simpler amphetamine analogues. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other appetite suppressants and stimulants such as phendimetrazine, amphetamine, methamphetamine, diethylpropion, and methylphenidate, sharing catecholaminergic activity. Its principal known targets are the monoamine transporters, especially the norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2 and dopamine transporter SLC6A3, with weaker effects on serotonin transport systems, leading to enhanced synaptic catecholamine signaling. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed, distributes systemically including into the CNS, undergoes hepatic biotransformation with urinary excretion of parent drug and metabolites, and has a duration compatible with short-term dosing for appetite suppression. Toxicity reflects stimulant excess and abuse liability, including tachycardia, hypertension, agitation, insomnia, tremor, psychosis, dependence, and overdose presentations such as arrhythmia or seizures. Adverse effects commonly include dry mouth, nervousness, palpitations, constipation, headache, and restlessness. Clinically, phenmetrazine was used primarily as an anorectic for short-term management of obesity and hyperphagic states, for example in patients requiring appetite reduction as an adjunct to caloric restriction, but its use became limited and largely abandoned because of misuse potential and cardiovascular and neuropsychiatric safety concerns.

Name: Trifluoperazine
Description: Trifluoperazine (DB00831) is a first-generation antipsychotic of the phenothiazine class, specifically a piperazine-substituted trifluoromethyl phenothiazine, whose structure consists of a tricyclic phenothiazine core bearing an electron-withdrawing trifluoromethyl group and a three-carbon side chain terminating in a piperazine ring; its principal chemical scaffold is therefore the phenothiazine nucleus, shared with related neuroleptics such as fluphenazine, perphenazine, prochlorperazine, chlorpromazine, and thioridazine, with especially close similarity to other piperazine phenothiazines. Pharmacologically, it acts primarily through antagonism of dopamine D2 receptors, with additional activity at D1-like receptors, 5-HT2 receptors, alpha1-adrenergic receptors, histamine H1 receptors, and muscarinic cholinergic receptors to a lesser extent, and calmodulin has also been described as a noncanonical binding target. It is indicated mainly for schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders and has also been used for short-term management of nonpsychotic anxiety, agitation, and severe behavioral disturbance. After oral administration it is absorbed variably, undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism, is highly protein bound and widely distributed including into the CNS, is metabolized largely by hepatic oxidative pathways including CYP1A2-mediated and conjugative routes to multiple metabolites, and is eliminated predominantly as metabolites in urine and feces; the terminal half-life is long enough to support divided daily dosing. Toxicity is characteristic of potent typical antipsychotics and includes dose-related extrapyramidal syndromes, acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia, hyperprolactinemia, sedation, orthostatic hypotension, anticholinergic effects, QT-related arrhythmia risk, seizures, hepatotoxicity, and rare but serious neuroleptic malignant syndrome; overdose may cause profound CNS depression, hypotension, and severe movement disorders. In clinical practice it has been used for chronic schizophrenia, acute psychotic exacerbations, and severe anxiety when alternative treatments are unsuitable, but its use is limited by adverse effects such as dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, dizziness, somnolence, restlessness, rigidity, tremor, and endocrine or autonomic complications.

Name: Phensuximide
Description: Phensuximide (DrugBank DB00832) is a small, lipophilic succinimide anticonvulsant built on a five-membered cyclic imide scaffold, specifically a pyrrolidine-2,5-dione core bearing phenyl substitution that distinguishes it from simpler dialkyl succinimides; chemically it belongs to the dicarboximide/succinimide class and shares the classic ethosuximide-type anticonvulsant scaffold, with related drugs including ethosuximide and methsuximide as close structural and therapeutic analogues. Its antiepileptic action is generally attributed to suppression of thalamocortical rhythmicity, likely through modulation of low-threshold T-type calcium currents in thalamic neurons, although a single definitive human target protein has not been firmly established; Cav3 family T-type calcium channels, especially CACNA1H and related channel isoforms, are commonly cited mechanistic targets. Phensuximide is orally absorbed, distributes into the central nervous system consistent with its anticonvulsant activity, undergoes extensive hepatic biotransformation to active and inactive metabolites, and is eliminated primarily in urine as metabolites with a relatively prolonged effective half-life that supports chronic dosing. Clinically it has been used mainly for absence seizures, particularly petit mal epilepsy, and occasionally in refractory generalized seizure syndromes when other agents are unsuitable. Adverse effects resemble those of other succinimides and include drowsiness, dizziness, ataxia, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, headache, and behavioral or mood changes. Toxicity may involve excessive CNS depression, confusion, gastrointestinal distress, hypersensitivity reactions, and rarely serious hematologic or hepatic adverse events, so clinical use has typically required monitoring and has largely been superseded by better-characterized modern antiepileptic therapies.

Name: Cefaclor
Description: Cefaclor (DrugBank DB00833) is an orally active second-generation cephalosporin characterized structurally by the cephem nucleus, a strained four-membered beta-lactam ring fused to a dihydrothiazine ring, with a 3-chloro substituent and a D-phenylglycyl-derived acylamino side chain at C7 that influences acid stability and antibacterial spectrum; chemically it belongs to the beta-lactam cephalosporin class and more specifically the aminocephalosporin scaffold. It is closely related to other oral cephalosporins such as cephalexin, cefprozil, cefuroxime axetil, and cefixime, and also shows class similarity to penicillins through the shared beta-lactam pharmacophore. Its principal targets are bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, including transpeptidases involved in peptidoglycan cross-linking, leading to inhibition of cell-wall synthesis and bacterial lysis. Cefaclor is indicated for susceptible respiratory, otolaryngologic, skin and soft-tissue, and urinary tract infections, including otitis media, sinusitis, pharyngitis, bronchitis, pneumonia, cellulitis, and cystitis. Oral absorption is generally good and rapid, food may slow but not abolish uptake, protein binding is moderate, distribution is mainly into extracellular fluids and inflamed tissues, metabolism is minimal, and elimination occurs predominantly as unchanged drug via renal excretion, giving a relatively short half-life and motivating divided daily dosing. Adverse effects commonly include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, rash, urticaria, pruritus, and candidiasis; important toxicities include immediate or delayed hypersensitivity, serum sickness-like reactions particularly in children, anaphylaxis, positive Coombs-associated hemolysis, interstitial nephritis, rare hepatotoxicity, and Clostridioides difficile-associated colitis. Clinically it has been used as an oral step-down or outpatient agent for mild-to-moderate community-acquired infections caused by susceptible streptococci, methicillin-susceptible staphylococci, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, and certain Enterobacterales.

Name: Brompheniramine
Description: Brompheniramine (DrugBank DB00835) is a first-generation alkylamine antihistamine built around a substituted propylamine framework in which a tertiary dimethylamino side chain is linked to a diaryl system containing a para-bromophenyl ring and a 2-pyridyl ring, giving a lipophilic, weakly basic arylalkylamine structure that readily crosses the blood-brain barrier; chemically it belongs to the propylamine/alkylamine H1-receptor antagonists, and its core scaffold is the diarylpropyl tertiary amine shared with related antihistamines. Similar drugs include chlorpheniramine, dexchlorpheniramine, pheniramine, triprolidine, and other first-generation H1 blockers such as diphenhydramine and doxylamine, although the latter differ in scaffold class. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, acting as an inverse agonist/antagonist, with clinically relevant off-target anticholinergic activity at muscarinic receptors that contributes to adverse effects. Brompheniramine is used for symptomatic relief of allergic rhinitis, seasonal hay fever, urticaria, conjunctival irritation, and common-cold symptoms such as rhinorrhea and sneezing, often in combination cough-and-cold products. Orally it is reasonably well absorbed, distributed widely including the CNS, undergoes hepatic metabolism likely involving CYP450-mediated oxidative pathways with first-pass conversion to metabolites, and is eliminated mainly in urine as parent drug and metabolites; duration is typically several hours. Toxicity is typical of sedating antihistamines: dose-related CNS depression or paradoxical excitation, antimuscarinic effects, impaired psychomotor performance, and in overdose agitation, hallucinations, seizures, tachycardia, hyperthermia, and coma, especially in children or with alcohol and other sedatives. Common side effects include drowsiness, dizziness, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, and palpitations. Clinically, it is used as an older, inexpensive symptomatic antiallergic agent when mild sedation is acceptable, for example in nighttime allergy preparations or short-term treatment of acute upper-respiratory allergy symptoms.

Name: Loperamide
Description: Loperamide (DrugBank DB00836) is a synthetic peripherally acting opioid antidiarrheal whose structure is characterized by a highly lipophilic piperidine core bearing a 4-hydroxylated tertiary carbon, N-substituted 4-chlorophenyl and N,N-dimethylamide-containing side chains, and multiple aryl rings that confer strong membrane affinity and limited central nervous system penetration under normal conditions; chemically it is classified as a phenylpiperidine opioid, with a diphenyl/piperidine antidiarrheal scaffold related to other phenylpiperidines. Similar drugs include diphenoxylate, difenoxin, fentanyl-class phenylpiperidines by scaffold relationship, and the peripheral opioid eluxadoline by functional similarity. Its principal target is the mu-opioid receptor (OPRM1) in the enteric nervous system, with reduced gut motility, increased intestinal transit time, enhanced fluid absorption, and reduced fecal volume; it is also a substrate of P-glycoprotein/ABCB1, which limits brain exposure. Oral absorption occurs but substantial first-pass extraction lowers systemic bioavailability; distribution is extensive but normally peripheral, metabolism is predominantly hepatic via CYP3A4 and CYP2C8 to inactive metabolites, and excretion is mainly fecal with minor urinary elimination. It is indicated for acute nonspecific diarrhea, chronic diarrhea including that associated with inflammatory bowel disease or short-bowel states, and reduction of ileostomy output. Adverse effects commonly include constipation, abdominal cramps, nausea, dizziness, and dry mouth. Toxicity is usually related to overdose or drug interactions and includes paralytic ileus, severe constipation, CNS and respiratory depression in extreme exposure, and notable cardiotoxicity with QT prolongation, QRS widening, torsades de pointes, and ventricular arrhythmias, especially with supratherapeutic misuse or coadministration of CYP3A4, CYP2C8, or P-glycoprotein inhibitors such as quinidine or azoles.

Name: Clocortolone
Description: Clocortolone (DrugBank DB00838) is a synthetic halogenated corticosteroid used primarily as the ester prodrug clocortolone pivalate; structurally it is a pregnane-based glucocorticoid built on the cyclopenta[a]phenanthrene steroid nucleus with the characteristic 3-keto-4-ene A-ring, 11β-hydroxyl and 20-ketone glucocorticoid pharmacophore, and lipophilicity-enhancing chlorine and pivalate substitution that support topical potency. It belongs to the corticosteroid, specifically topical glucocorticoid, chemical category, and its core scaffold is the hydrocortisone/prednisolone-like steroid framework. Similar drugs include hydrocortisone, triamcinolone, betamethasone, desoximetasone, fluocinonide, and clobetasol, which share related steroidal anti-inflammatory scaffolds but differ in halogenation and esterification. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, through which it alters transcription of inflammatory mediators, suppresses phospholipase A2-dependent eicosanoid formation, and reduces cytokine signaling; no highly specific non-GR targets are typically emphasized clinically. After topical administration, absorption through intact skin is limited but increases with inflammation, thin skin, large treatment area, occlusion, or prolonged use; distributed locally in epidermal and dermal tissues, absorbed drug is metabolized hepatically like other corticosteroids and excreted mainly in urine as metabolites. Indications include corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses such as atopic dermatitis, eczematous dermatitis, contact dermatitis, seborrheic dermatitis, and localized psoriasiform inflammation, with clinical use centered on relief of pruritus, erythema, scaling, and swelling. Toxicity is mainly local with skin atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, burning, folliculitis, acneiform eruption, hypopigmentation, and secondary infection; excessive systemic exposure can produce hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis suppression, hyperglycemia, Cushingoid features, and growth suppression in children.

Name: Tolazamide
Description: Tolazamide (DrugBank DB00839) is a first-generation sulfonylurea oral hypoglycemic agent characterized structurally by the classic aryl-sulfonylurea pharmacophore, consisting of a para-substituted benzenesulfonylurea core bearing a lipophilic alkyl/heterocyclic substituent that confers moderate potency and duration; chemically it belongs to the sulfonamide-derived sulfonylurea class, and its central scaffold is the p-tolyl-sulfonylurea motif. It is closely related to other first-generation sulfonylureas such as tolbutamide, chlorpropamide, acetohexamide, and tolazamide-like second-generation secretagogues including glyburide and glipizide, which share the same insulin-secretagogue framework but differ in side-chain complexity and potency. Its principal target is the ATP-sensitive potassium channel in pancreatic beta cells, specifically the sulfonylurea receptor SUR1/ABCC8 functionally coupled to Kir6.2/KCNJ11, leading to channel closure, membrane depolarization, calcium influx, and insulin release. Tolazamide is used in type 2 diabetes mellitus, especially in patients with residual beta-cell function when diet alone is inadequate. After oral administration it is well absorbed, highly protein bound, hepatically metabolized to active and inactive metabolites, and eliminated by both renal and, to a lesser extent, biliary routes, with an intermediate duration of action that can prolong hypoglycemic risk in susceptible patients. Major toxicities are dose-related hypoglycemia, particularly in elderly patients, those with hepatic or renal impairment, poor intake, or drug interactions, and less commonly sulfonamide-type hypersensitivity, cholestatic jaundice, hematologic dyscrasias, and disulfiram-like or flushing reactions. Common adverse effects include nausea, epigastric discomfort, weight gain, dizziness, rash, pruritus, and photosensitivity. Clinically, tolazamide has been used as monotherapy or combined with diet and sometimes other antihyperglycemics for non-insulin-dependent diabetes to reduce fasting and postprandial hyperglycemia.

Name: Dobutamine
Description: Dobutamine (DrugBank DB00841) is a synthetic catecholamine and phenylethanolamine derivative built around a substituted benzene ring bearing catechol-type hydroxyl functionality linked through a β-hydroxyl ethylamine side chain to a bulky arylalkyl-substituted secondary amine, giving a flexible sympathomimetic structure optimized for cardiac adrenergic activity; chemically it is classified as a direct-acting adrenergic agonist, specifically a catecholamine in the broader phenethylamine/ethanolamine class, with a catechol-ethanolamine scaffold closely related to dopamine, isoproterenol, epinephrine, and norepinephrine, and pharmacologically similar inotropic agents include dopamine and isoproterenol, while milrinone is functionally similar though structurally distinct. Its principal targets are beta-1 adrenergic receptors, with additional activity at beta-2 and alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, producing predominantly positive inotropy with less chronotropy than many other catecholamines. Dobutamine is given intravenously because it is not orally bioavailable and is rapidly inactivated; it distributes mainly in extracellular fluid, has a very short onset and plasma half-life of about 2 minutes, is metabolized in tissues and liver largely by catechol-O-methyltransferase and conjugation, and is excreted mainly in urine as metabolites. It is indicated for short-term treatment of acute heart failure, cardiogenic shock, low-output states after cardiac surgery, and decompensation in severe systolic dysfunction, and is also used in dobutamine stress echocardiography. Toxicity reflects excessive adrenergic stimulation, including tachyarrhythmias, angina, hypertension or hypotension, myocardial ischemia, and rare hypokalemia; common adverse effects include palpitations, tachycardia, ectopy, headache, nausea, dyspnea, chest pain, and blood pressure lability.

Name: Oxazepam
Description: Oxazepam (DrugBank DB00842) is a 3-hydroxy, 1,4-benzodiazepin-2-one characterized structurally by a fused benzene-diazepine ring system bearing a 2-keto group, a 3-hydroxyl substituent, a 5-phenyl ring, and a 7-chloro substituent, features that define it as a classical benzodiazepine anxiolytic-sedative; chemically it belongs to the benzodiazepine class and more specifically the 1,4-benzodiazepin-2-one scaffold, closely related to diazepam, lorazepam, temazepam, chlordiazepoxide, and nordazepam. Its principal pharmacologic target is the GABAA receptor benzodiazepine allosteric site, especially receptor complexes containing alpha, beta, and gamma subunits such as GABRA1, GABRA2, GABRA3, GABRA5, GABRB2, and GABRG2, where it enhances GABA-mediated chloride conductance and neuronal inhibition. Oxazepam is orally absorbed at a moderate rate, reaches peak plasma concentrations in a few hours, is substantially protein bound, distributes into the central nervous system, undergoes minimal oxidative biotransformation, and is cleared mainly by hepatic glucuronidation to inactive metabolites followed by renal excretion, making it less dependent on cytochrome P450 metabolism than many benzodiazepines. It is indicated for anxiety disorders, short-term relief of anxiety symptoms, and management of acute alcohol withdrawal, particularly tremor, agitation, and autonomic hyperactivity. Adverse effects include sedation, drowsiness, dizziness, ataxia, confusion, impaired psychomotor performance, and anterograde memory difficulty. Toxicity is characterized by dose-related CNS depression, especially in overdose or when combined with alcohol, opioids, or other sedatives, with risks of respiratory depression, falls, dependence, tolerance, and withdrawal phenomena including rebound anxiety, insomnia, and rarely seizures.

Name: Nalbuphine
Description: Nalbuphine (DrugBank DB00844) is a semisynthetic opioid analgesic of the morphinan/phenanthrene class, structurally derived from the rigid tetracyclic morphine scaffold and characterized by a 4,5-epoxymorphinan core bearing a phenolic hydroxyl, a ketone at the 6-position, a 14-hydroxyl substituent, and an N-cyclobutylmethyl group that helps confer mixed opioid agonist-antagonist behavior; its closest structural and pharmacologic analogs include naloxone, naltrexone, oxymorphone, butorphanol, and pentazocine. Pharmacologically, nalbuphine acts primarily as a kappa opioid receptor agonist and a mu opioid receptor antagonist or weak partial agonist, with OPRK1 and OPRM1 as the principal targets, and possible class-related engagement of opioid signaling pathways involving GIRK channels and adenylate cyclase inhibition. It is used for moderate to severe pain, including postoperative pain, obstetric analgesia, and preoperative or adjunct anesthesia settings, and is sometimes chosen when reduced euphorigenic liability or attenuation of mu-agonist adverse effects is desirable. It is usually administered parenterally because of substantial first-pass metabolism; distribution is systemic with CNS penetration, hepatic metabolism predominates, and elimination occurs mainly as metabolites in urine with a relatively short analgesic duration. Toxicities include dose-related sedation, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, sweating, dysphoria, and respiratory depression, although the latter shows a ceiling effect relative to pure mu agonists; hypotension, bradycardia, and impaired psychomotor performance can occur, and it can precipitate acute withdrawal in opioid-dependent patients. Clinically, nalbuphine has been used to treat surgical pain, labor pain, and opioid-induced pruritus, especially when balancing analgesia against respiratory safety is important.

Name: Clofazimine
Description: Clofazimine (DB00845) is a highly lipophilic riminophenazine dye whose structure consists of a tricyclic phenazine core bearing an imino substituent and chlorinated, aryl-rich hydrophobic groups, giving it a planar, redox-active, weakly basic framework; chemically it is classified as a phenazine derivative, specifically a riminophenazine antimycobacterial agent, with a phenazine scaffold as its defining chemotype. Structurally and pharmacologically related compounds include other phenazines and older antimycobacterial dyes, and it is often discussed alongside leprostatic or antimycobacterial agents such as dapsone, rifampicin, bedaquiline, and linezolid in multidrug regimens, although these are not close structural analogs. Its mechanism is not fully resolved, but proposed targets and pathways include mycobacterial membrane components, electron transport/redox cycling systems, and DNA template interference, with reported activity linked to generation of reactive oxygen species and disruption of respiratory function in Mycobacterium leprae and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Oral absorption is variable and improved by fatty meals; distribution is extensive, with marked accumulation in macrophages, skin, liver, spleen, adipose tissue, and reticuloendothelial tissues, producing an exceptionally long terminal half-life on the order of weeks; metabolism appears limited to slow hepatic biotransformation, and excretion is predominantly biliary/fecal with minimal renal clearance. Toxicities include dose- and duration-related tissue deposition, ichthyosis, gastrointestinal intolerance, enteropathy, and rare severe abdominal complications; characteristic adverse effects include red-brown to black skin discoloration, conjunctival and body-fluid pigmentation, xerosis, pruritus, abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, and possible QT prolongation. Clinically, it is used chiefly for multibacillary leprosy and erythema nodosum leprosum, and also as part of combination salvage therapy for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis and some nontuberculous mycobacterial infections.

Name: Flurandrenolide
Description: Flurandrenolide (DB00846) is a synthetic fluorinated corticosteroid designed for topical anti-inflammatory activity, built on the pregnane steroid nucleus with the characteristic four fused rings of the hydrocortisone scaffold and distinguished by a 6α-fluoro substituent and a 16,17-acetonide ketal that increases lipophilicity, cutaneous retention, and glucocorticoid potency; chemically it is a halogenated corticosteroid glucocorticoid and more specifically a prednisolone/hydrocortisone-derived acetonide steroid, with a scaffold closely related to triamcinolone acetonide, fluocinolone acetonide, fludroxycortide, and other topical fluorinated steroids. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor encoded by NR3C1, leading to altered transcription of anti-inflammatory proteins and suppression of cytokine, prostaglandin, and leukotriene pathways, with downstream reduction of PLA2 activity and inflammatory mediator expression. After topical administration, absorption depends on vehicle, skin integrity, body site, duration, and occlusion; distribution is largely local in skin but systemically absorbed drug is expected to be protein bound and distributed similarly to other corticosteroids, metabolized mainly hepatically by steroid-reducing and conjugative pathways, and excreted predominantly in urine as metabolites. Toxicity reflects corticosteroid excess: local atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, delayed wound healing, purpura, acneiform eruptions, and secondary infection, and with extensive use or occlusion systemic HPA-axis suppression, hyperglycemia, glucosuria, Cushingoid features, and growth suppression in children may occur. It is indicated for corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses such as eczema, atopic dermatitis, contact dermatitis, seborrheic dermatitis, psoriasis, and lichenified pruritic eruptions, and clinically used as creams, ointments, lotions, or tape preparations to relieve erythema, scaling, swelling, and pruritus.

Name: Cysteamine
Description: Cysteamine (DrugBank DB00847) is a small aminothiol composed of a two-carbon ethyl chain bearing a terminal primary amine and a terminal sulfhydryl group, making it the simplest stable aliphatic thiolamine; chemically it belongs to the aminothiol/mercaptan class and is built on a 2-aminoethane thiol scaffold that is closely related to coenzyme A and the disulfide metabolite cystamine, with similar thiol-containing drugs such as mesna, tiopronin, and penicillamine providing mechanistic analogies. Its principal pharmacologic action in nephropathic cystinosis is lysosomal cystine depletion: cysteamine enters lysosomes and reacts with cystine to form cysteine and a cysteine-cysteamine mixed disulfide that can exit via alternative transport systems, functionally bypassing defective cystinosin; it has also been associated with effects on somatostatin handling and cellular redox processes rather than a single classic receptor target. After oral administration it is absorbed reasonably rapidly, undergoes broad tissue distribution, is extensively metabolized by thiol-disulfide exchange and oxidation to disulfides and sulfate/taurine-related sulfur metabolites, and is eliminated mainly in urine as inorganic sulfate and other metabolites, with a relatively short half-life necessitating repeated dosing or delayed-release formulations. Toxicity is largely dose related and includes gastrointestinal intolerance, sulfurous body odor, CNS lethargy, seizures in overdose, and chronic concerns such as hypermobility, skin fragility, bruising, and rare ulcerative or vasculopathic complications. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, halitosis, headache, rash, and fatigue. Clinically, cysteamine is used primarily to treat nephropathic cystinosis, reducing intracellular cystine accumulation to preserve renal function and limit corneal, thyroid, muscular, and neurologic complications; topical ophthalmic cysteamine is also used for corneal cystine crystal deposition.

Name: Levamisole
