Description: Levamisole (DrugBank DB00848) is a synthetic imidazothiazole derivative with a compact bicyclic heteroaromatic structure in which an imidazoline-like ring is fused to a thiazole framework and bears a para-substituted phenyl group, placing it in the imidazothiazole class and defining its core scaffold as a phenyl-substituted imidazo[2,1-b]thiazole; it is closely related to the anthelmintic tetramisole, from which it is the levorotatory active isomer, and is sometimes discussed alongside nicotinic anthelmintics such as pyrantel because of mechanistic similarity in helminths. Pharmacokinetically, levamisole is well absorbed after oral administration, distributes systemically with hepatic first-pass metabolism, undergoes extensive liver biotransformation to multiple inactive or weakly active metabolites, and is eliminated through both urine and feces with a relatively short plasma half-life on the order of a few hours. Its best characterized targets are nematode nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subtypes, where it acts as an agonist causing spastic paralysis of parasites; in mammals, its immunomodulatory effects are less clearly mapped but have been associated with modulation of T-cell, monocyte, and neutrophil function rather than a single validated human receptor target. Clinically, it has been used as an anthelmintic for ascariasis and other nematode infections and historically as an immunomodulatory adjunct, for example with fluorouracil in colon cancer and in some autoimmune or dermatologic disorders. Important adverse effects include nausea, abdominal pain, vomiting, dizziness, rash, fever, arthralgia, and headache, while major toxicities include agranulocytosis, leukopenia, vasculitis, encephalopathy, hepatotoxicity, and, in cocaine-adulteration exposure, retiform purpura with ANCA-associated vasculopathy.

Name: Methylphenobarbital
Description: Methylphenobarbital (mephobarbital; DrugBank DB00849) is a barbiturate anticonvulsant and sedative-hypnotic whose structure consists of a 5-ethyl-5-phenyl-substituted barbituric acid ring bearing N-methyl substitution, making it the N-methyl analog and prodrug-like congener of phenobarbital; chemically it belongs to pyrimidine-2,4,6-trione derivatives, with the classic barbiturate heterocyclic scaffold that underlies related agents such as phenobarbital, primidone, pentobarbital, secobarbital, and amobarbital. Its principal pharmacology is enhancement of GABAergic inhibition, primarily through positive allosteric modulation of GABAA receptor chloride channels, with barbiturates also capable at higher concentrations of direct channel gating and reduction of excitatory neurotransmission; molecular targets are therefore GABAA receptor subunits rather than a single highly selective protein target. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed, distributed widely including into the CNS, and undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism, notably N-demethylation to phenobarbital, which contributes substantially to activity; elimination is mainly renal as metabolites and phenobarbital, with a relatively prolonged duration reflecting long half-life and tissue distribution. Clinically it has been used for epilepsy, especially generalized tonic-clonic and focal seizures, and historically for sedation and anxiolysis. Adverse effects include drowsiness, cognitive slowing, ataxia, dizziness, nystagmus, behavioral changes, rash, and dependence. Toxicity resembles other barbiturates, with overdose causing profound CNS and respiratory depression, hypotension, coma, and death; chronic use may produce tolerance, physical dependence, hepatic enzyme induction with drug interactions, and rarely severe hypersensitivity or megaloblastic anemia.

Name: Perphenazine
Description: Perphenazine (DrugBank DB00850) is a first-generation antipsychotic of the phenothiazine class, specifically a piperazinyl phenothiazine, built on a tricyclic phenothiazine scaffold containing two benzene rings fused to a sulfur- and nitrogen-containing central thiazine ring, with a chlorine substituent on the aromatic system and a three-carbon side chain terminating in a piperazine moiety that strongly influences dopamine receptor affinity and antiemetic activity. It is chemically related to other phenothiazines such as prochlorperazine, fluphenazine, chlorpromazine, trifluoperazine, and thiethylperazine, which share the same core scaffold but differ in side-chain substitution and potency. Its principal pharmacologic targets are dopamine D2 receptors, with additional activity at D1, D3, D4, 5-HT2A, alpha1-adrenergic, histamine H1, and muscarinic cholinergic receptors, accounting for both efficacy and adverse effects. Perphenazine is used mainly in schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders, and also as an antiemetic for severe nausea and vomiting. After oral administration it is reasonably absorbed but undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism; it is widely distributed, highly protein bound, penetrates the CNS, and is metabolized primarily by hepatic oxidative pathways including CYP2D6, with urinary and fecal excretion of metabolites. Toxicity includes dose-related extrapyramidal symptoms, tardive dyskinesia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, QT-related arrhythmia risk, CNS depression, hypotension, anticholinergic effects, hyperprolactinemia, cholestatic jaundice, and rare hematologic reactions such as leukopenia or agranulocytosis. Clinically, it has been used for acute psychosis, chronic schizophrenia maintenance, agitation, and refractory emesis, with common side effects including sedation, akathisia, parkinsonism, dystonia, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, dizziness, and orthostatic hypotension.

Name: Dacarbazine
Description: Dacarbazine (DrugBank DB00851) is a synthetic antineoplastic triazene whose structure consists of an imidazole-4-carboxamide core bearing a 3,3-dimethyltriazenyl substituent, making it an imidazole-containing alkylating prodrug in the methylhydrazine/triazene class with a triazene-linked imidazole carboxamide scaffold closely related to temozolomide and mitozolomide, and pharmacologically similar to other DNA-methylating agents such as procarbazine. It is administered intravenously because oral absorption is unreliable; distribution is moderate with limited protein binding and some tissue penetration but relatively poor CNS exposure; it undergoes extensive hepatic microsomal activation, mainly via CYP1A1, CYP1A2, and CYP2E1, to MTIC and then to the methyl diazonium species that methylates DNA, especially at O6- and N7-guanine positions, while the major inactive metabolite is 5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide; elimination is chiefly renal as metabolites and some unchanged drug, with a short plasma half-life. Dacarbazine has no conventional high-affinity protein receptor target, its functional targets being genomic DNA and the DNA damage response, with cytotoxicity modulated by O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase and mismatch repair pathways. It is indicated for metastatic malignant melanoma and Hodgkin lymphoma, particularly in ABVD-based regimens, and has also been used in soft tissue sarcoma and other salvage oncology settings. Toxicities are dominated by dose-limiting myelosuppression, severe nausea and vomiting, hepatotoxicity including rare hepatic necrosis or veno-occlusive injury, flu-like symptoms, and mutagenic, teratogenic, and carcinogenic risk; common adverse effects include leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, anorexia, alopecia, injection-site pain, and photosensitivity.

Name: Pseudoephedrine
Description: Pseudoephedrine (DrugBank DB00852) is a sympathomimetic phenethylamine with an ephedrine-like arylaliphatic amino alcohol structure, consisting of a substituted benzene ring attached to a chiral propanolamine side chain bearing a secondary alcohol and a methylamino group; chemically it is classified as a phenethylamine, amphetamine-related decongestant, and mixed-acting adrenergic agonist, built on the β-amino alcohol/phenylpropanolamine scaffold. Closely related drugs include ephedrine, phenylephrine, cathine, and amphetamine-like nasal decongestants, with ephedrine being the most structurally and pharmacologically similar. It is well absorbed orally, has good systemic bioavailability, distributes widely into tissues, undergoes only limited hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged in urine; renal clearance is pH-dependent, with acidic urine accelerating excretion and alkaline urine prolonging half-life. Its principal pharmacologic targets are adrenergic pathways, acting mainly by promoting norepinephrine release and to a lesser extent directly stimulating alpha-adrenergic receptors, especially ADRA1 family receptors, with weaker beta-adrenergic effects. It is indicated for temporary relief of nasal and sinus congestion associated with the common cold, allergic rhinitis, and sinusitis, and is used clinically in oral decongestant products alone or in combination with antihistamines, analgesics, or antitussives. Adverse effects commonly include insomnia, nervousness, tremor, palpitations, tachycardia, dry mouth, and urinary retention. Toxicity is characterized by sympathomimetic excess, including hypertension, arrhythmias, agitation, psychosis, and seizures, particularly in overdose or when combined with monoamine oxidase inhibitors or in patients with cardiovascular disease.

Name: Temozolomide
Description: Temozolomide (DrugBank DB00853) is a small, lipophilic imidazotetrazine derivative whose structure consists of a fused imidazole and tetrazine ring bearing a carboxamide substituent; this heteroaromatic, ring-strained methylating prodrug belongs to the alkylating antineoplastic class and is built on the imidazotetrazine scaffold exemplified by related agents such as dacarbazine and, more mechanistically, other DNA-methylating triazenes including procarbazine. At physiologic pH it undergoes spontaneous nonenzymatic conversion to the reactive intermediate MTIC and then to a methyldiazonium species that methylates DNA, primarily at O6- and N7-guanine, so it has no classic high-affinity receptor target, but its pharmacologic effect is closely linked to DNA and to resistance/response proteins including MGMT and mismatch-repair pathway components such as MSH2, MSH6, MLH1, and PMS2. Oral absorption is rapid and usually high, food may reduce peak concentration, protein binding is low, distribution is broad with clinically important penetration into cerebrospinal fluid and brain tissue, metabolism is largely chemical rather than CYP-mediated, and elimination occurs mainly via renal excretion of unchanged drug and metabolites with a short plasma half-life. Major toxicities are dose-limiting myelosuppression, especially thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, and lymphopenia, with opportunistic infection risk including Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia; nausea, vomiting, fatigue, constipation, headache, alopecia, transaminase elevation, rash, infertility risk, and rare therapy-related myelodysplasia or acute leukemia also occur. Clinically, temozolomide is used primarily for glioblastoma and anaplastic astrocytoma, including concurrent use with radiotherapy and adjuvant maintenance schedules, and is also used in selected refractory CNS tumors and some neuroendocrine neoplasms.

Name: Chlorphenesin
Description: Chlorphenesin (DB00856) is a chlorinated phenoxy alcohol whose structure consists of a 4-chlorophenoxy aromatic ring linked through an ether oxygen to a propane-1,2-diol side chain, making it an aryl ether, halogenated phenol derivative, and glyceryl ether; its core chemical scaffold is the p-chlorophenoxy-propanediol motif, closely related to other phenoxy alcohols and centrally acting muscle relaxants such as mephenesin, methocarbamol, and guaifenesin-like ether congeners. Pharmacologically, chlorphenesin has been used primarily as a centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant and, in topical formulations, as an antimicrobial preservative; however, no single high-affinity molecular target protein is firmly established, and its effects are generally attributed to depression of polysynaptic reflex activity within the spinal cord and subcortical CNS pathways rather than selective receptor binding. After administration it is absorbed systemically, distributed into well-perfused tissues including the CNS to a limited functional extent, undergoes hepatic biotransformation mainly by conjugative pathways, and is excreted predominantly in urine as metabolites with relatively short persistence. Toxicity is chiefly dose-related CNS depression, with examples including sedation, ataxia, hypotonia, respiratory depression, and impaired coordination; topical exposure may cause local irritation, and excessive systemic exposure can produce profound weakness. Adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, nausea, malaise, and rash. Clinically, chlorphenesin has been used for painful musculoskeletal spasm, spasticity-associated discomfort, and adjunctive symptomatic relief in acute muscle strain or low back pain, while in cosmetics and dermatologic preparations it is also used for preservative activity against bacteria and fungi.

Name: Terbinafine
Description: Terbinafine (DrugBank DB00857) is a synthetic allylamine antifungal whose structure is characterized by a lipophilic naphthalene ring system linked through a methylene bridge to a tertiary amine and a branched unsaturated aliphatic chain containing an internal alkyne/alkene-like allylamine motif, giving it a hydrophobic aromatic–alkyl amine architecture optimized for fungal membrane targeting. It belongs to the allylamine class of antifungals, with an aryl-allylamine scaffold centered on a naphthylmethylamine pharmacophore; related drugs include naftifine, butenafine, and mechanistically similar ergosterol-pathway inhibitors such as azoles including itraconazole and fluconazole. Its principal target is fungal squalene epoxidase, encoded by ERG1 in many fungi, causing depletion of ergosterol and intracellular accumulation of squalene, which is fungicidal against many dermatophytes. Orally, terbinafine is well absorbed but undergoes substantial first-pass metabolism, is highly protein bound, distributes extensively into sebum, stratum corneum, hair, and nails, is metabolized mainly by hepatic CYP isoenzymes including CYP2C9, CYP1A2, CYP3A4, CYP2C8, and CYP2C19, inhibits CYP2D6, and is excreted largely as inactive urinary metabolites with a long terminal tissue half-life. It is indicated for onychomycosis, tinea pedis, tinea corporis, tinea cruris, and tinea capitis. Adverse effects commonly include gastrointestinal upset, headache, rash, pruritus, and dysgeusia or ageusia, while important toxicities include hepatotoxicity, cholestatic hepatitis, neutropenia, severe cutaneous reactions, and rare rhabdomyolysis or depression; clinically it is used topically for localized dermatophyte infections and orally for nail, scalp, or extensive skin disease.

Name: Penicillamine
Description: Penicillamine (DB00859) is a small chiral aminothiol structurally derived from cysteine, consisting of an alpha-amino acid framework bearing a free thiol, a carboxylic acid, and a gem-dimethyl-substituted beta carbon; clinically the D-enantiomer is used, and this compact thiolated amino acid motif defines both its reactivity and metal-binding behavior. It is classified chemically as a thiol-containing amino acid derivative and metal chelator, with a cysteine-like aminothiol scaffold featuring a branched dimethylated backbone. Related or mechanistically similar drugs include other chelators such as trientine and dimercaprol, and to a lesser extent succimer, which also exploit soft-donor sulfur or amine functionality for metal complexation. After oral administration, absorption is variable and incomplete and is reduced by food, iron, antacids, and other polyvalent cations; distribution is moderate with significant protein binding through disulfide exchange, metabolism occurs largely via oxidation and mixed disulfide formation with cysteine and other endogenous thiols, and elimination is mainly renal as unchanged drug and disulfide metabolites. Its principal pharmacologic targets are not classic receptors but free copper and other heavy metals, and it also disrupts collagen cross-linking by reacting with aldehyde intermediates, while in cystinuria it forms a more soluble penicillamine-cysteine disulfide. Indications include Wilson disease, cystinuria with recurrent cystine nephrolithiasis, and severe active rheumatoid arthritis. Toxicity is substantial and includes proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome, bone marrow suppression, hepatotoxicity, autoimmune phenomena such as myasthenia gravis or lupus-like syndromes, and serious hypersensitivity. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, anorexia, rash, dysgeusia, stomatitis, and hematologic abnormalities. Clinically, it is used as a second-line or specialized agent for decoppering in Wilson disease, prevention of cystine stones, and selected refractory rheumatologic disease under close laboratory monitoring.

Name: Prednisolone
Description: Prednisolone (DrugBank DB00860) is a synthetic glucocorticoid corticosteroid built on the pregnane steroid nucleus, characterized by the classic four fused rings, a 1,4-diene-3-keto A-ring, hydroxyl groups typically at C11, C17, and C21, and a side chain at C17 that supports potent glucocorticoid activity with relatively limited mineralocorticoid effect; chemically it belongs to corticosteroids, specifically glucocorticoid steroids, and its core scaffold is the hydrocortisone/prednane steroid framework. Closely related drugs include prednisone, methylprednisolone, dexamethasone, hydrocortisone, and triamcinolone, which share the same steroidal pharmacophore with different substitutions affecting potency and duration. Prednisolone primarily targets the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, with downstream transrepression and transactivation effects on NF-kB, AP-1, and cytokine signaling pathways. It is generally well absorbed orally, widely distributed with plasma protein binding mainly to albumin and transcortin, penetrates inflamed tissues, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism via reduction and conjugation, and is excreted mainly in urine as metabolites; elimination half-life is short relative to its longer biological effect. It is indicated for inflammatory, allergic, autoimmune, and hematologic disorders such as asthma exacerbations, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, inflammatory bowel disease, dermatitis, nephrotic syndrome, and acute allergic reactions. Toxicity reflects dose and duration and includes hyperglycemia, adrenal suppression, infection risk, osteoporosis, myopathy, cataracts, glaucoma, psychosis, peptic irritation, hypertension, and growth suppression in children. Common adverse effects include weight gain, mood change, insomnia, fluid retention, dyspepsia, acne, and Cushingoid features. Clinically it is used as systemic or local immunosuppressive and anti-inflammatory therapy, for example in short courses for asthma or prolonged regimens for autoimmune disease and transplant-related inflammatory complications.

Name: Diflunisal
Description: Diflunisal (DrugBank DB00861) is a salicylic acid-derived nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug with a biphenyl scaffold, structurally characterized as 5-(2,4-difluorophenyl)-2-hydroxybenzoic acid, in which a salicylate core bearing a phenolic hydroxyl and carboxylic acid is linked to a difluorinated phenyl ring; it is therefore classified as an aromatic carboxylic acid NSAID and, more specifically, a difluorophenyl salicylate. Its closest similar drugs include aspirin and other salicylates, as well as NSAIDs with related cyclooxygenase inhibition such as salsalate, diclofenac, and fenoprofen. Diflunisal acts mainly by inhibiting prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthase 1 and 2, namely COX-1 and COX-2 (PTGS1, PTGS2), reducing prostaglandin synthesis and thereby producing analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects; it has also been used as a transthyretin kinetic stabilizer in amyloid disease contexts. Orally it is well absorbed, highly albumin bound, distributed largely within the vascular compartment, undergoes limited oxidative biotransformation with predominant hepatic glucuronidation to acyl and phenolic glucuronides, and is eliminated mainly in urine with a relatively long half-life that supports twice-daily dosing. Indications include mild to moderate pain, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and inflammatory musculoskeletal conditions, with off-label use in transthyretin amyloidosis. Toxicities resemble other NSAIDs and include gastrointestinal ulceration, bleeding, renal impairment, fluid retention, hypertension, hepatotoxicity, and hypersensitivity; overdose may cause tinnitus, nausea, vomiting, metabolic disturbance, and CNS effects. Common adverse effects include dyspepsia, abdominal pain, constipation, diarrhea, dizziness, headache, rash, and edema. Clinically, it has been used for chronic arthritic pain, postoperative or dental pain, and selected transthyretin-mediated cardiomyopathy or neuropathy settings where TTR stabilization is desired.

Name: Vardenafil
Description: Vardenafil (DrugBank DB00862) is a synthetic small-molecule phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor built around a heteroaromatic imidazo-triazinone core bearing an ethyl substituent, a piperazine-linked sulfonamide, and a 2-ethoxyphenyl group, a structure designed to mimic key binding features of cyclic GMP and confer high PDE5 affinity; chemically it is a nitrogen-rich heterocyclic sulfonamide and more specifically a PDE5 inhibitor of the guanine-mimetic imidazotriazinone class, with a scaffold closely related to other erectile-dysfunction agents such as sildenafil, avanafil, tadalafil, and udenafil, although tadalafil has a distinct beta-carboline-like scaffold. Its principal target is PDE5A, with lesser activity at other phosphodiesterases including PDE6 and PDE11 of potential tolerability relevance. Clinically, vardenafil is indicated mainly for erectile dysfunction, improving penile erection in men with vasculogenic, diabetic, post-prostatectomy, or mixed-etiology symptoms by enhancing nitric oxide-mediated cGMP signaling in corpus cavernosum smooth muscle. It is orally absorbed with relatively rapid onset, reaches peak plasma concentrations in roughly 1 hour, is moderately affected by high-fat meals depending on formulation, is highly protein bound, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism primarily by CYP3A4 with contributions from CYP3A5 and CYP2C isoforms to active and inactive metabolites, and is eliminated predominantly as metabolites in feces with a smaller urinary component; half-life is generally about 4 to 5 hours. Toxicity is largely extension of vasodilatory pharmacology and PDE cross-reactivity, including headache, flushing, nasal congestion, dyspepsia, dizziness, and visual disturbance, while serious risks include hypotension with nitrates or riociguat, syncope, priapism, non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, sudden hearing loss, and increased exposure in hepatic impairment or with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors.

Name: Ranitidine
Description: Ranitidine (DrugBank DB00863) is a substituted aminomethyl furan derivative and histamine H2-receptor antagonist whose structure features a furan heteroaromatic ring linked through a thioether-containing side chain to a nitroethenediamine-like amidine system, giving a polar, basic anti-secretory molecule; chemically it belongs to the H2 antihistamine/antiulcer class, with a furan-thioether-amidine scaffold distinct from the imidazole-containing scaffold of cimetidine but related in function to famotidine, nizatidine, and cimetidine. Its principal target is the histamine H2 receptor, encoded by HRH2, on gastric parietal cells, where it suppresses basal and stimulated gastric acid secretion. After oral administration it is rapidly absorbed with moderate bioavailability, reaches peak plasma concentrations within a few hours, distributes broadly with relatively low protein binding, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism to minor metabolites including N-oxide, S-oxide, and desmethyl products, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged in urine, so clearance falls in renal impairment. It was indicated for duodenal and gastric ulcer, gastroesophageal reflux disease, erosive esophagitis, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, dyspepsia, and prevention of stress ulceration or aspiration-related acid injury. Adverse effects are usually mild and include headache, nausea, constipation, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, dizziness, and fatigue, while uncommon but important toxicities include confusion or agitation in older or renally impaired patients, bradycardia or hypotension with rapid intravenous use, hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, thrombocytopenia, and rare hypersensitivity reactions. Clinically it was widely used orally and intravenously for short-term ulcer healing, maintenance acid suppression, reflux symptom control, and inpatient stress-ulcer prophylaxis, although later its use became heavily restricted or withdrawn in many markets because of concerns about N-nitrosodimethylamine contamination.

Name: Tacrolimus
Description: Tacrolimus (DB00864) is a highly lipophilic, fermentation-derived macrolide lactone immunosuppressant characterized structurally by a large 23-membered tricyclic macrolactam-like ring rich in ether linkages, multiple hydroxyl and methoxy substituents, a conjugated diene region, and stereochemically complex polyketide architecture; chemically it is classified as a calcineurin-inhibiting macrolide and its core scaffold is the FK506 polyketide macrolactone. It is closely related to other calcineurin inhibitors and macrolide immunosuppressants, especially pimecrolimus and voclosporin by functional similarity, and cyclosporine by mechanistic similarity despite a distinct cyclic peptide scaffold. Tacrolimus binds FKBP12 (FKBP1A) to form a complex that inhibits calcineurin catalytic subunits PPP3CA/PPP3CB, suppressing NFAT activation and T-cell cytokine transcription. Orally, absorption is variable and incomplete, food reduces bioavailability, distribution is extensive with high erythrocyte and tissue binding, metabolism is predominantly hepatic and intestinal via CYP3A4 and CYP3A5 with P-glycoprotein transport involvement, and excretion is mainly biliary/fecal with minimal unchanged renal elimination. Major toxicities include dose-related nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity, hypertension, hyperglycemia/post-transplant diabetes, hyperkalemia, infection risk, and malignancy risk such as lymphoma and skin cancer. Common adverse effects include tremor, headache, diarrhea, nausea, insomnia, paresthesias, and renal dysfunction. Clinically, tacrolimus is used primarily for prophylaxis and treatment of organ transplant rejection in kidney, liver, heart, and lung transplantation, and topically for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis; it is also used in selected immune-mediated disorders such as ulcerative colitis, myasthenia gravis, and refractory nephrotic syndromes.

Name: Benzphetamine
Description: Benzphetamine (DrugBank DB00865) is a sympathomimetic anorectic of the substituted amphetamine/phenethylamine class whose structure is an N-benzyl, N-methylated amphetamine derivative built on an alpha-methyl-2-phenethylamine core, giving it a lipophilic arylalkylamine architecture; its key scaffold is therefore the amphetamine phenethylamine framework with benzyl substitution on the amine. It is closely related to other anti-obesity stimulants and amphetamine-like agents such as phentermine, methamphetamine, amphetamine, diethylpropion, and phenmetrazine, with similarity driven by shared monoaminergic stimulant pharmacology. Benzphetamine is administered orally and is well absorbed, distributes systemically including into the CNS, undergoes extensive hepatic N-demethylation and other biotransformations to active metabolites including amphetamine and methamphetamine, and is eliminated largely in urine as parent drug and metabolites, with urinary pH influencing excretion. Its pharmacologic effects are mediated primarily through monoaminergic systems rather than a single receptor target, with recognized targets including the norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, dopamine transporter SLC6A3, serotonin transporter SLC6A4, and trace amine-associated receptor 1, leading to increased synaptic catecholamines and appetite suppression. It is indicated as a short-term adjunct in exogenous obesity, particularly for weight reduction in patients inadequately responsive to diet alone. Adverse effects include insomnia, restlessness, dry mouth, palpitations, tachycardia, hypertension, constipation, and dizziness. Toxicity reflects stimulant excess and abuse liability, with examples including dependence, psychosis, arrhythmia, severe hypertension, and overdose manifestations such as agitation, tremor, hyperthermia, and seizures; clinically it has been used with caloric restriction and behavioral measures for short-term management of obesity.

Name: Benzonatate
Description: Benzonatate (DrugBank DB00868) is a peripherally acting antitussive that is chemically a para-alkylaminobenzoate ester, structurally characterized as a polydisperse mixture of tetracaine-related molecules containing a 4-butylamino benzoate aromatic core linked through an ester to a polyethoxy side chain terminated by a tertiary amine; thus, its chemical category is that of non-narcotic ester local anesthetic derivatives, and its core scaffold is the p-aminobenzoate ester/anesthetic pharmacophore. It is chemically and pharmacologically similar to local anesthetics such as tetracaine, procaine, and benzocaine, although it is used for cough suppression rather than anesthesia. Its mechanism is thought to involve reversible inhibition of voltage-gated sodium channels, reducing excitability of pulmonary stretch receptors and vagal afferent fibers in the respiratory tract; no single definitive human target protein is uniquely assigned, but sodium channel family members are the relevant target class. After oral administration, it is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, distributed systemically, likely hydrolyzed by esterases to para-butylaminobenzoic acid and polyethoxy metabolites, and eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine, with antitussive effects beginning within about 15 to 20 minutes and lasting 3 to 8 hours. It is indicated for symptomatic relief of cough, for example in acute bronchitis, viral upper respiratory infections, or other nonproductive cough states. Adverse effects include sedation, dizziness, headache, nausea, constipation, nasal congestion, and dysphagia, while toxicity may include severe CNS excitation or depression, seizures, arrhythmias, cardiac arrest, bronchospasm, and fatal overdose, especially in children; chewing capsules can cause oropharyngeal anesthesia with choking or aspiration risk. Clinically, it is used as an oral prescription alternative to opioid antitussives when suppression of troublesome cough is desired without narcotic exposure.

Name: Dorzolamide
Description: Dorzolamide (DrugBank DB00869) is a topical heterocyclic sulfonamide carbonic anhydrase inhibitor whose structure is defined by a fused thieno[2,3-b]thiopyran scaffold bearing a sulfonamide zinc-binding group and a secondary amino substituent, features that confer high affinity for carbonic anhydrase active sites; chemically it is classified as a sulfonamide antiglaucoma agent and more specifically a thiophene-fused cyclic sulfonamide. Its closest similar drugs are other carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, especially brinzolamide, acetazolamide, methazolamide, and dichlorphenamide, with brinzolamide being the most therapeutically analogous topical ocular agent. Dorzolamide primarily targets carbonic anhydrase II and also inhibits carbonic anhydrase IV and, to a lesser extent, carbonic anhydrase XII in the ciliary processes, reducing bicarbonate formation, aqueous humor secretion, and intraocular pressure. After ophthalmic administration, systemic absorption is limited but measurable through the nasolacrimal and conjunctival route; the drug accumulates extensively in erythrocytes via carbonic anhydrase binding, has relatively low free plasma concentrations, undergoes hepatic N-deethylation to an active N-desethyl metabolite, and is eliminated mainly by the kidney, with prolonged terminal disposition due to red-cell sequestration. Toxicity is usually low and predominantly local, but sulfonamide hypersensitivity, corneal edema, metabolic acidosis, electrolyte disturbances, and worsening renal impairment may occur, particularly in susceptible patients. It is indicated for open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension, commonly used alone or with timolol to lower elevated intraocular pressure. Typical adverse effects include ocular burning, stinging, blurred vision, conjunctivitis, bitter taste, punctate keratitis, and eyelid reactions; clinically it is used as chronic topical therapy when beta-blockers are insufficient or contraindicated.

Name: Terbutaline
Description: Terbutaline (DrugBank DB00871) is a synthetic phenethylamine sympathomimetic built on a substituted ethanolamine framework, featuring a resorcinol-type aromatic ring with two phenolic hydroxyl groups and a tert-butylamino side chain on a beta-hydroxylated ethyl linker, a structure that confers relative selectivity for beta-2 adrenergic receptors; chemically, it is classified as a beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonist and bronchodilator within the phenylethanolamine/resorcinol subclass, and its core scaffold is closely related to other short-acting beta-2 agonists such as albuterol (salbutamol), fenoterol, metaproterenol, ritodrine, and to less selective adrenergic agonists like isoproterenol. Its principal target is the beta-2 adrenergic receptor encoded by ADRB2, with weaker activity at other beta-adrenergic receptors at higher exposures, producing bronchodilation and uterine smooth muscle relaxation via cAMP signaling. Terbutaline is used primarily for reversible bronchospasm in asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and acute wheezing, and has also been used clinically as a tocolytic for premature labor, though this use is limited by safety concerns. It is reasonably absorbed after oral, subcutaneous, and inhaled administration, distributes into extracellular tissues with limited CNS penetration, undergoes relatively modest hepatic metabolism compared with catecholamines because the resorcinol motif resists COMT degradation, and is eliminated mainly in urine as unchanged drug and sulfate conjugates. Toxicity is largely an extension of beta-adrenergic stimulation and includes tachycardia, palpitations, tremor, nervousness, headache, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, lactic acidosis, and, in overdose or prolonged tocolysis, arrhythmias, myocardial ischemia, pulmonary edema, and rare maternal-fetal cardiovascular complications.

Name: Conivaptan
Description: Conivaptan (DrugBank DB00872) is a nonpeptide vasopressin receptor antagonist of the vaptan class built on a tri-substituted benzazepine-like small-molecule scaffold with fused aromatic and heteroaromatic features, including lipophilic phenyl systems and polar amide/imidazole-type functionality that support high-affinity binding to vasopressin receptors; chemically it is categorized as a mixed V1A/V2 arginine vasopressin receptor antagonist, with related drugs including tolvaptan, lixivaptan, mozavaptan, and satavaptan, which share the broader aquaretic vasopressin-antagonist pharmacology but differ in receptor selectivity. Its principal targets are the vasopressin V1A receptor AVPR1A and vasopressin V2 receptor AVPR2, producing free-water excretion without major sodium loss and thereby correcting dilutional hyponatremia. Clinically, it is used primarily as an intravenous agent for euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia, especially in hospitalized patients with syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, heart failure, or other states of elevated vasopressin tone. Pharmacokinetically, conivaptan is given IV because oral bioavailability is limited by extensive first-pass metabolism; it is highly protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism predominantly via CYP3A4, and is eliminated mainly in feces with a smaller urinary component, so exposure rises with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors and in hepatic impairment. Toxicities include overly rapid serum sodium correction with risk of osmotic demyelination, hypotension from V1A blockade, infusion-site phlebitis, and potential drug-drug interactions. Common adverse effects include infusion reactions, headache, thirst, dry mouth, polyuria, hypokalemia, constipation, and orthostatic symptoms; thus its clinical use is generally short-term, monitored inpatient correction of significant hyponatremia rather than chronic outpatient therapy.

Name: Loteprednol
Description: Loteprednol (DrugBank DB00873), usually used as the etabonate prodrug loteprednol etabonate, is a synthetic ophthalmic corticosteroid built on a pregnane steroid nucleus with the characteristic four fused rings of glucocorticoids, modified by 17α-esterification, a 17β-chloromethyl substituent, and a 20-ketone replacement strategy that makes it an ester-based “soft steroid” designed for rapid inactivation after local effect. Chemically it belongs to the corticosteroid/glucocorticoid class, with a hydrocortisone/prednisolone-like steroid scaffold, and is structurally related to other ophthalmic steroids such as prednisolone acetate, dexamethasone, fluorometholone, and rimexolone. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor, with downstream suppression of phospholipase A2-mediated arachidonic acid signaling, cyclooxygenase products, cytokines, and leukocyte recruitment. After topical ocular administration, systemic absorption is low; distribution is mainly local to anterior segment tissues, while any absorbed drug is rapidly hydrolyzed by tissue and plasma esterases to inactive metabolites such as Δ1-cortienic acid etabonate, limiting systemic exposure; excretion occurs predominantly after metabolism, with minimal unchanged parent drug. Clinically, it is indicated for steroid-responsive inflammatory eye disorders including postoperative ocular inflammation and pain, allergic conjunctivitis, giant papillary conjunctivitis, anterior uveitis, and dry-eye-associated inflammation. Adverse effects include transient burning or stinging, blurred vision, foreign-body sensation, epiphora, headache, delayed wound healing, elevated intraocular pressure, glaucoma, posterior subcapsular cataract, and secondary ocular infection. Toxicity is dominated by corticosteroid class effects, especially ocular hypertension and infection masking, but compared with conventional ketone corticosteroids it was designed to reduce systemic and local steroid burden during short-course ophthalmic use.

Name: Guaifenesin
Description: Guaifenesin, DrugBank DB00874, is a small aromatic ether-alcohol structurally described as a guaiacol derivative bearing a 1,2-propanediol side chain, with a methoxy-substituted phenyl ring linked through an ether oxygen to a hydroxypropyl moiety; chemically it is a phenoxypropanediol in the broader guaiacol/glycerol ether class, and its core scaffold is a methoxyphenoxy propane-1,2-diol framework related to expectorant guaiacol ethers. Similar drugs include guaiacol, glyceryl guaiacolate itself as a synonymic reference, and combination-cold/cough expectorant congeners such as bromhexine or ambroxol by therapeutic similarity rather than close structural identity. Its mechanism is not attributed to a well-defined high-affinity molecular target protein, and no canonical DrugBank-style target protein is firmly established; pharmacologically it is thought to enhance respiratory tract fluid output and reduce mucus viscosity via vagally mediated gastric-respiratory reflex pathways and secretory effects on airway epithelium. After oral administration it is rapidly absorbed, widely distributed in body water, extensively metabolized hepatically mainly by oxidation and O-demethylation to inactive metabolites such as beta-(2-methoxyphenoxy)lactic acid, and excreted predominantly in urine with a short elimination half-life, necessitating repeated dosing or extended-release formulations. It is indicated for symptomatic relief of chest congestion and productive cough in acute upper respiratory tract infections, bronchitis, and common cold syndromes. Toxicity is generally low at therapeutic doses, but overdose may cause marked nausea, vomiting, dizziness, somnolence, agitation, and rarely nephrolithiasis or urinary tract concretions with chronic excessive exposure. Common adverse effects include gastrointestinal upset, headache, rash, dizziness, and drowsiness. Clinically, it is used as an oral expectorant alone or in multi-ingredient cough/cold products to facilitate mucus clearance and improve cough efficiency.

Name: Flupentixol
Description: Flupentixol (DB00875) is a thioxanthene antipsychotic whose structure consists of a tricyclic dibenzothiophene-like thioxanthene core containing sulfur in the central ring, substituted with a piperazine-containing three-carbon side chain at C9 and a trifluoromethyl group that increases lipophilicity; it is used clinically as a mixture of geometric isomers, with the Z isomer being primarily responsible for antipsychotic activity. Chemically it belongs to the typical neuroleptic thioxanthenes, and its core scaffold is the thioxanthene/tricyclic antipsychotic scaffold closely related to phenothiazines. Similar drugs include other thioxanthenes such as zuclopenthixol and chlorprothixene, and functionally related typical antipsychotics such as fluphenazine and haloperidol. Its principal targets are dopamine D1 and especially D2 receptors, with additional activity at D3, D4, 5-HT2A, 5-HT2C, histamine H1, alpha1-adrenergic, and possibly muscarinic receptors at clinically relevant concentrations. After oral or depot administration it is variably but adequately absorbed, widely distributed because of high lipid solubility and protein binding, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism including sulfoxidation, N-dealkylation, and conjugative pathways, and is eliminated slowly as metabolites in feces and urine, with depot esters producing prolonged release over days to weeks. Toxicity resembles other first-generation antipsychotics and includes dose-related extrapyramidal syndromes, akathisia, dystonia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia, sedation, orthostatic hypotension, anticholinergic effects, hyperprolactinemia, QT-related arrhythmia risk, seizures, and rare neuroleptic malignant syndrome or hepatic injury. It is indicated for schizophrenia and other chronic psychoses, particularly hallucinations, delusions, agitation, and thought disorder, and in low doses has also been used in some regions for depressive or anxiety-associated symptoms; clinically it is used orally for maintenance or symptom control and as long-acting depot formulations for relapse prevention in poorly adherent patients.

Name: Eprosartan
Description: Eprosartan (DrugBank DB00876) is a non-biphenyl, non-tetrazole angiotensin II receptor blocker whose structure is characterized by an imidazole-derived heteroaromatic core linked to a substituted thiophene ring and bearing acidic carboxyl functionality that mimics key binding elements of angiotensin II; chemically it is classified as an aryl heterocyclic antihypertensive and more specifically an angiotensin II type 1 receptor antagonist, with a scaffold distinct from the biphenyl-tetrazole motif of losartan, valsartan, irbesartan, candesartan, and olmesartan, though it is pharmacologically similar to those agents and somewhat closer in non-biphenyl design to telmisartan. Its principal target is the angiotensin II receptor type 1, encoded by AGTR1, through which it inhibits vasoconstriction and aldosterone-mediated sodium retention. After oral administration, absorption is moderate with relatively low absolute bioavailability, food having limited clinical impact; distribution is moderate with substantial plasma protein binding; metabolism is limited, with little cytochrome P450 involvement; and elimination occurs largely as unchanged drug via biliary/fecal routes with a lesser renal component, giving a half-life that supports once- or twice-daily use. It is indicated primarily for essential hypertension and used clinically to reduce blood pressure, including in patients intolerant of ACE inhibitors because it does not typically cause bradykinin-mediated cough. Adverse effects include dizziness, headache, fatigue, rhinitis, gastrointestinal upset, and hypotension; important toxicities include hyperkalemia, worsening renal function, acute kidney injury in renovascular disease, and rare angioedema, while overdose would be expected to produce marked hypotension, and like all renin-angiotensin system blockers it is fetotoxic in pregnancy, causing fetal renal injury, oligohydramnios, and skull or neonatal developmental complications.

Name: Sirolimus
Description: Sirolimus (DrugBank DB00877), also called rapamycin, is a complex lipophilic natural-product macrocyclic lactone with a large 31-membered polyketide ring bearing multiple conjugated double bonds, hydroxyl and methoxy substituents, and a pipecolate-containing region that helps define its binding pharmacophore; chemically it is a macrolide, more specifically a triene macrolide and mTOR inhibitor within the rapamycin/rapalog family, built on the rapamycin macrocyclic polyketide scaffold. Closely related drugs include the structural analogs everolimus and temsirolimus, and more distantly the FKBP-binding calcineurin inhibitor tacrolimus, which shares macrolide-like immunosuppressant features but differs mechanistically. Sirolimus is absorbed orally with variable, formulation- and food-dependent bioavailability, distributes extensively into erythrocytes and tissues, is highly protein bound, and has a long terminal half-life that supports once-daily dosing; it is metabolized mainly by CYP3A4 and CYP3A5 and is also a P-glycoprotein substrate, with elimination occurring predominantly via biliary/fecal excretion and minimal renal clearance. Its principal target is the FKBP12-encoded immunophilin FKBP1A, forming a complex that inhibits mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1, with downstream effects on p70S6 kinase and EIF4EBP1 signaling. Clinically it is used to prevent renal transplant rejection, and in selected settings for lymphangioleiomyomatosis and vascular proliferative disorders such as coronary stent restenosis. Toxicities include dose-related myelosuppression, hyperlipidemia, impaired wound healing, proteinuria, edema, hepatotoxicity, interstitial pneumonitis, and increased susceptibility to bacterial, viral, and fungal infections; common adverse effects include mouth ulcers, diarrhea, acneiform rash, thrombocytopenia, anemia, leukopenia, and hypertension.

Name: Chlorhexidine
Description: Chlorhexidine (DB00878) is a synthetic bisbiguanide antiseptic and disinfectant whose structure consists of two p-chlorophenyl rings linked symmetrically through hexamethylene chains to terminal biguanide groups, giving a dicationic, highly basic amphipathic molecule; chemically it belongs to the biguanide/polybiguanide antiseptic class, with a chlorophenyl-bisbiguanide scaffold closely related in function, though not identical in structure, to other cationic membrane-active antiseptics such as alexidine, polyhexanide, octenidine, and quaternary ammonium agents like benzalkonium. Its antimicrobial activity is mediated not by a single selective human receptor but primarily by electrostatic binding to negatively charged bacterial cell envelopes and oral pellicle, disrupting membrane integrity, increasing permeability, precipitating cytoplasmic contents, and at higher concentrations causing rapid cell death; no clinically relevant canonical human target protein is established. Pharmacokinetically, chlorhexidine is used mainly topically or as oral rinse, with minimal intact skin absorption, limited oral mucosal uptake, strong binding to skin, الأسنان, and mucosa with prolonged substantivity, negligible systemic distribution after routine use, little meaningful metabolism, and elimination largely via feces if swallowed, with trace urinary excretion. It is indicated for plaque and gingivitis control, preoperative skin disinfection, hand antisepsis, wound cleansing, catheter-site preparation, and prevention of healthcare-associated infection. Adverse effects include tooth and tongue staining, taste disturbance, calculus increase, oral irritation, xerostomia, contact dermatitis, and rare but important hypersensitivity or anaphylaxis; toxicity examples include ocular injury, ototoxicity with middle-ear exposure, neurotoxicity on meninges, and gastrointestinal irritation after ingestion. Clinically, it is widely used in mouthwashes, surgical scrubs, impregnated dressings, and central-line infection prevention protocols.

Name: Emtricitabine
Description: Emtricitabine (DrugBank DB00879) is a synthetic fluorinated nucleoside analog with a 1,3-oxathiolane ring that mimics deoxycytidine, distinguished structurally by a sulfur-containing oxathiolane sugar surrogate, a cytosine base, and a 5-fluoro substitution that improves antiviral potency; it belongs to the nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor class and more specifically to thiacytidine analogs, with a lamivudine-like oxathiolane nucleoside scaffold. Closely related drugs include lamivudine, which is its nearest structural analog, and other NRTIs such as zidovudine, abacavir, tenofovir, and stavudine by pharmacologic similarity. After oral administration it is rapidly and well absorbed with high bioavailability, low plasma protein binding, broad distribution into body fluids and intracellular conversion to the active triphosphate, minimal hepatic metabolism, and predominantly renal excretion as unchanged drug, with elimination prolonged in renal impairment. Its principal target is HIV-1 reverse transcriptase, with activity also against HIV-2 reverse transcriptase and hepatitis B virus polymerase through chain termination after incorporation into viral DNA. Emtricitabine is indicated for treatment of HIV-1 infection in combination antiretroviral therapy and is also used in HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis in fixed-dose combinations, while its anti-HBV activity is clinically relevant though not generally used alone for hepatitis B. Toxicity is usually mild relative to older NRTIs, but examples include hyperpigmentation, gastrointestinal intolerance, headache, rash, rare lactic acidosis and hepatomegaly with steatosis, pancreatitis, and HBV flare after discontinuation in coinfected patients. Common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, dizziness, fatigue, cough, and skin discoloration. Clinically, it is widely used once daily in combination regimens such as emtricitabine/tenofovir with integrase inhibitors for HIV treatment and prevention because of its potency, tolerability, and convenient pharmacokinetic profile.

Name: Chlorothiazide
Description: Chlorothiazide (DrugBank DB00880) is a classic benzothiadiazine sulfonamide diuretic whose structure consists of a chlorinated fused benzene-thiadiazine 1,1-dioxide ring system bearing sulfamyl functionality, making it a relatively polar thiazide with a 1,2,4-benzothiadiazine scaffold that defines the class. Chemically it belongs to the thiazide diuretics and more broadly to heterocyclic sulfonamides; closely related and pharmacologically similar drugs include hydrochlorothiazide, bendroflumethiazide, methyclothiazide, polythiazide, and chlorthalidone, although the latter is thiazide-like rather than a true benzothiadiazine. Its principal target is the thiazide-sensitive Na+/Cl− cotransporter SLC12A3 in the distal convoluted tubule, with downstream effects that increase sodium, chloride, potassium, magnesium, and water excretion while reducing calcium excretion. After oral administration, chlorothiazide is absorbed less completely than many newer thiazides, has limited lipid solubility and modest tissue distribution, is minimally metabolized, and is eliminated largely unchanged by the kidney through glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, so efficacy falls in severe renal impairment. Toxicity is chiefly an extension of its pharmacology and includes dehydration, hypotension, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, hyperuricemia with gout, and hyperglycemia; rare serious reactions include sulfonamide hypersensitivity, photosensitivity, pancreatitis, blood dyscrasias, and hepatic encephalopathy in susceptible cirrhotic patients. Clinically it is used to treat hypertension and edema, especially edema due to heart failure, cirrhosis, corticosteroid therapy, estrogen therapy, and renal disease, and it may also be used in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; common adverse effects include dizziness, weakness, polyuria, muscle cramps, nausea, and rash.

Name: Quinapril
Description: Quinapril (DrugBank DB00881) is a dicarboxylate-containing angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor of the nonsulfhydryl proline class, formulated as an ethyl ester prodrug whose structure features a substituted tetrahydroisoquinoline-like bicyclic moiety linked to an L-alanyl-L-proline-derived ACE inhibitor pharmacophore; its core chemical category is peptidomimetic antihypertensive, and its scaffold is closely related to the proline-based, esterified enalaprilat/ramiprilat-type ACE inhibitor framework. Similar drugs include enalapril, ramipril, benazepril, lisinopril, perindopril, and captopril, which share ACE inhibition but differ in zinc-binding groups, lipophilicity, and prodrug status. After oral administration, quinapril is absorbed and rapidly de-esterified hepatically to the active diacid quinaprilat; bioavailability of active metabolite is moderate, food may modestly reduce absorption, protein binding is substantial, tissue ACE binding contributes to an effective half-life supporting once- or twice-daily use, and elimination is predominantly renal with some biliary/fecal contribution, so exposure increases in renal impairment and in older adults. Its principal target is angiotensin-converting enzyme, with downstream suppression of angiotensin II formation and reduced bradykinin degradation. Clinically it is indicated for hypertension and congestive heart failure, including chronic blood-pressure control and adjunctive reduction of heart-failure symptoms. Adverse effects include cough, dizziness, hypotension, fatigue, headache, nausea, and hyperkalemia; important toxicities include first-dose syncope, renal function decline especially in renal artery stenosis, angioedema, rare neutropenia, and fetotoxicity in pregnancy, with overdose typically manifesting as marked hypotension.

Name: Clomifene
Description: Clomifene (clomiphene; DrugBank DB00882) is a nonsteroidal triphenylethylene derivative composed of a chlorinated aromatic ring linked through an ethylene bridge to two additional phenyl rings and a basic diethylaminoethoxy side chain, usually marketed as a mixed E/Z isomer preparation in which enclomifene and zuclomifene contribute differing pharmacology; chemically it is a selective estrogen receptor modulator in the triarylethylene class built on a triphenylethylene scaffold closely related to tamoxifen, toremifene, and other antiestrogenic fertility or breast-cancer–associated SERMs. Its principal targets are estrogen receptors ESR1 and ESR2, acting predominantly as an estrogen antagonist at the hypothalamus and pituitary to block negative feedback, increase GnRH pulsatility, and raise pituitary FSH and LH secretion, thereby inducing follicular development and ovulation. Orally administered clomifene is well absorbed, highly protein bound, extensively distributed, metabolized hepatically via oxidative and conjugative pathways to multiple active and persistent metabolites, and eliminated mainly through biliary/fecal excretion with prolonged terminal persistence, especially for the cis isomer, supporting accumulation over repeated cycles. It is indicated primarily for anovulatory infertility, particularly ovulatory dysfunction in polycystic ovary syndrome, and is also used in selected cases of menstrual irregularity, luteal dysfunction, and off-label male hypogonadism or infertility. Adverse effects commonly include hot flashes, abdominal or pelvic discomfort, nausea, breast tenderness, headache, mood change, and visual disturbances; important toxicities include ovarian enlargement, ovarian hyperstimulation, multiple gestation, rare thromboembolic events, and occasional hepatotoxicity, so clinical use centers on short-course ovulation induction with careful monitoring of response and pregnancy risk.

Name: Isosorbide dinitrate
Description: Isosorbide dinitrate (DrugBank DB00883) is an organic nitrate ester composed of the rigid bicyclic isosorbide core, a fused oxygen-containing sorbitol-derived scaffold, bearing two nitrate ester substituents that act as nitric oxide-donating functionalities; chemically it belongs to the nitrate vasodilators and more specifically the polyol nitrate ester class, with an isosorbide scaffold closely related to other nitrovasodilators such as nitroglycerin, erythrityl tetranitrate, and the mononitrate metabolite isosorbide mononitrate. Its pharmacologic effect is mediated by bioactivation to nitric oxide or related nitrosating species, with downstream activation of soluble guanylate cyclase, increased cGMP signaling, and functional modulation of protein kinase G pathways in vascular smooth muscle; the principal recognized target is soluble guanylate cyclase, although mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase and other reductases participate in nitrate bioactivation. After oral administration it is absorbed but undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, giving variable bioavailability; sublingual use produces faster onset, distribution is moderate with rapid entry into vascular tissues, metabolism yields active mononitrate metabolites, and elimination occurs mainly as urinary glucuronide and denitrated metabolites with a relatively short parent half-life but longer-lived active metabolites. It is indicated for prevention and treatment of angina pectoris, including chronic stable angina and acute ischemic chest discomfort, and is also used in heart failure or acute coronary syndromes in selected settings. Dose-related toxicity reflects excessive vasodilation, causing headache, flushing, dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, reflex tachycardia, and syncope; severe overdose may produce profound hypotension, myocardial ischemia from reduced perfusion, and rarely methemoglobinemia. Clinically, it is used orally for angina prophylaxis and sublingually for rapid symptomatic relief, often alongside beta-blockers or calcium-channel blockers, while tolerance with continuous exposure necessitates nitrate-free intervals.

Name: Risedronic acid
Description: Risedronic acid (DrugBank DB00884), usually administered as the sodium salt risedronate, is a nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate characterized structurally by a geminal bisphosphonate moiety attached to a carbon bearing a hydroxyl substituent and a heteroaromatic pyridyl side chain, a motif that confers strong calcium affinity and antiresorptive potency; chemically it belongs to the aminobisphosphonate class, and its core scaffold is the P-C-P bisphosphonate pharmacophore with a hydroxy-substituted central carbon and pyridine ring. It is closely related to other bone-targeting bisphosphonates such as alendronate, ibandronate, pamidronate, and zoledronic acid. After oral administration, absorption is very low and markedly reduced by food, calcium, or polyvalent cations; the absorbed fraction distributes selectively to bone mineral surfaces, especially sites of active remodeling, shows minimal plasma protein binding relative to many lipophilic drugs, is not appreciably metabolized, and is eliminated largely unchanged by renal excretion, while the skeletal fraction can persist for prolonged periods. Its principal molecular target is farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway within osteoclasts, leading to impaired prenylation of small GTPases and osteoclast apoptosis. It is indicated for osteoporosis in postmenopausal women and men, glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, and Paget disease of bone, and is used clinically to reduce vertebral and nonvertebral fracture risk and suppress excessive bone turnover. Toxicities and adverse effects include esophagitis, dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, musculoskeletal pain, hypocalcemia, rare osteonecrosis of the jaw, atypical femoral fractures, ocular inflammation, and potential renal concerns, particularly with improper administration or predisposed patients.

Name: Pemirolast
Description: Pemirolast (DrugBank DB00885) is a nonsteroidal antiallergic agent whose structure is characterized by a planar, highly conjugated heteroaromatic system centered on a pyrimidinone/oxo-pyrimidine-like core bearing acidic functionality that confers strong polarity and low lipophilicity; chemically it is best classified as a mast-cell stabilizer and antiallergic dicarboxylate-like heteroaromatic compound, with a scaffold related to other acidic antiallergy agents used in immediate hypersensitivity disorders. Similar drugs include cromolyn sodium, nedocromil, tranilast, ketotifen, and olopatadine, which share mast-cell inhibitory or broader antiallergic properties. Its principal pharmacology is inhibition of mast-cell degranulation with suppression of histamine and leukotriene release; no single high-affinity molecular target is universally established, but relevant reported target biology includes modulation of mast-cell signaling pathways and downstream effects on histamine H1-receptor-mediated allergic responses. Pemirolast has been used mainly topically in ophthalmology for allergic conjunctivitis, including seasonal allergic conjunctivitis with ocular itching, hyperemia, and tearing, and has also been studied in asthma and other atopic conditions. Systemic absorption after ocular administration is minimal, distribution is limited by hydrophilicity, metabolism is modest, and elimination is primarily renal, with much of absorbed drug excreted unchanged. Toxicity is generally low at therapeutic ophthalmic doses, though excessive exposure may increase local irritation; adverse effects commonly include transient burning or stinging, աչքի discomfort, blurred vision, headache, rhinitis, and unpleasant taste, while rare hypersensitivity or local inflammatory reactions can occur. Clinically, it is used as a prophylactic antiallergic eyedrop rather than an acute bronchodilator or antihistamine rescue agent.

Name: Bumetanide
Description: Bumetanide (DrugBank DB00887) is a potent sulfonamide loop diuretic whose structure is based on a substituted benzoic acid bearing a sulfamyl group, a phenoxy substituent, and an alkylamino side chain, giving an aromatic sulfonamide-carboxylic acid architecture optimized for high activity at the renal thick ascending limb; chemically it belongs to the sulfamylbenzoic acid class of loop diuretics, with a p-sulfamylbenzoic acid scaffold closely related to other high-ceiling diuretics. Similar drugs include furosemide, torsemide, ethacrynic acid, and piretanide, with greatest structural similarity to furosemide despite differences in heteroaryl substitution. Its principal target is the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter NKCC2 encoded by SLC12A1 in the luminal membrane of the thick ascending limb, and it also has pharmacologic relevance for NKCC1 encoded by SLC12A2 in extrarenal tissues. Orally, bumetanide is rapidly and fairly completely absorbed, is highly plasma protein bound, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid with renal tubular secretion required for effect, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly by renal excretion of unchanged drug with a short elimination half-life of about 1 to 1.5 hours. Toxicity is largely extension-of-action toxicity, including profound diuresis, dehydration, hypotension, prerenal azotemia, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia, hyperuricemia, and dose-related ototoxicity, especially with renal impairment or concomitant aminoglycosides. It is indicated for edema associated with congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, and renal insufficiency, and is used clinically when rapid, potent diuresis is needed or when patients are refractory to less potent agents; common adverse effects include dizziness, muscle cramps, weakness, volume depletion, rash, nausea, and electrolyte disturbances.

Name: Mechlorethamine
Description: Mechlorethamine (DrugBank DB00888), also known as nitrogen mustard, is a highly reactive bifunctional alkylating agent whose structure consists of a methyl-substituted tertiary amine bearing two 2-chloroethyl arms that cyclize to electrophilic aziridinium intermediates; chemically it belongs to the nitrogen mustard class of antineoplastic alkylators, with a bis(2-chloroethyl)amine scaffold that is shared with related drugs such as cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, chlorambucil, melphalan, and bendamustine, although mechlorethamine is among the least selective and most reactive members. Its pharmacologic effect is mediated not by a classical high-affinity receptor but by covalent attack on nucleophilic sites in DNA, especially N7 of guanine, producing interstrand and intrastrand crosslinks, replication arrest, and apoptosis; therefore no single target protein is primary, though downstream damage responses involve TP53 and DNA repair pathways. After intravenous or topical administration it is rapidly absorbed locally or systemically, distributes quickly, reacts extensively with tissues and plasma constituents, undergoes rapid nonenzymatic transformation and hepatic metabolism to less active products, and is eliminated mainly as urinary metabolites, with a very short plasma persistence due to chemical instability. Major toxicities include profound myelosuppression, severe vesicant tissue injury with extravasation, mutagenicity, carcinogenicity, infertility, and immunosuppression. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, vomiting, alopecia, mucositis, dermatitis with topical use, and leukopenia. Clinically, it has been used in Hodgkin lymphoma and other lymphoid malignancies, historically in MOPP-like regimens, and topically for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma such as mycosis fungoides, where its local cytotoxicity can control plaque or patch lesions.

Name: Granisetron
Description: Granisetron (DrugBank DB00889) is a potent, selective serotonin 5-HT3 receptor antagonist built on an indazole-containing, rigid bicyclic/tropane-like amine scaffold, structurally characterized by a fused aromatic heterocycle linked through a carbonyl to a basic azabicyclic ring that supports high-affinity recognition of ligand-gated 5-HT3 receptors; chemically it is classified as an indazole-derived antiemetic within the setron class, and its core scaffold is closely related pharmacophorically, though not identically, to other 5-HT3 antagonists such as ondansetron, dolasetron, palonosetron, and tropisetron. Its principal target proteins are 5-hydroxytryptamine receptor 3 subunits, especially HTR3A-containing receptor complexes, with antiemetic action mediated by blockade of peripheral vagal afferent and central chemoreceptor-trigger zone signaling. After oral administration it is well absorbed, but absolute bioavailability is limited by first-pass metabolism; it is also used intravenously and as a transdermal system, distributes widely with moderate protein binding, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 with minor contributions from other oxidative pathways and subsequent conjugation, and is eliminated in urine and feces as metabolites with only a small fraction excreted unchanged; the elimination half-life is typically several hours, but antiemetic effects may outlast plasma exposure. It is indicated for prevention and treatment of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, radiation-induced nausea and vomiting, and postoperative nausea and vomiting. Adverse effects commonly include headache, constipation, asthenia, dizziness, and injection-site reactions, while important toxicities include QT interval prolongation, rare arrhythmias, hypersensitivity, serotonin syndrome when combined with serotonergic agents, and occasional liver enzyme elevations; clinically, it is widely used in oncology supportive care, perioperative medicine, and in selected patients requiring sustained antiemetic prophylaxis via transdermal delivery.

Name: Dienestrol
Description: Dienestrol (DrugBank DB00890) is a synthetic nonsteroidal estrogen structurally characterized as a stilbene derivative composed of two para-hydroxylated phenyl rings linked by a conjugated trans-alkene system, giving a rigid diarylethylene framework that mimics the spatial pharmacophore of estradiol; chemically it belongs to the stilbestrol/triaryl- or diaryl-olefin estrogen class, with a stilbene scaffold closely related to diethylstilbestrol and hexestrol, and similar drugs include diethylstilbestrol, hexestrol, chlorotrianisene, and natural estrogens such as estradiol by shared estrogen receptor agonism. Its principal targets are estrogen receptor alpha and estrogen receptor beta, through which it produces transcriptional estrogenic effects in reproductive epithelium and other hormone-responsive tissues. Pharmacokinetically, dienestrol is used mainly topically or intravaginally, where local absorption restores estrogen-deficient mucosa, though some systemic absorption can occur; absorbed drug is distributed to estrogen-responsive tissues, undergoes hepatic oxidative and conjugative metabolism typical of phenolic estrogens, and is excreted primarily in urine and to a lesser extent bile as glucuronide and sulfate metabolites. It has been indicated chiefly for vulvovaginal atrophy, atrophic vaginitis, pruritus vulvae, dyspareunia, and other hypoestrogenic menopausal symptoms. Adverse effects resemble those of other estrogens and include local irritation, breast tenderness, nausea, edema, headache, and uterine bleeding; important toxicities include endometrial stimulation with hyperplasia or carcinoma risk if exposure is prolonged, thromboembolic risk with systemic absorption, and potential estrogen-dependent tumor promotion. Clinically, dienestrol has been used predominantly as a vaginal cream for symptomatic relief of postmenopausal urogenital atrophy and related inflammatory or irritative symptoms.

Name: Sulfapyridine
Description: Sulfapyridine (DB00891) is a classic sulfonamide antibacterial whose structure consists of a p-aminobenzenesulfonamide core linked through the sulfonamide nitrogen to a pyridine ring, giving a heteroaryl sulfonamide architecture with an aniline para-amino group that is important for antifolate activity; chemically it belongs to the sulfonamide anti-infectives and more specifically the arylsulfonamide/aminobenzenesulfonamide class, and its key scaffold is the para-aminophenyl-sulfonyl-pyridine motif. It is closely related to other sulfonamides such as sulfadiazine, sulfathiazole, sulfamethoxazole, and sulfisoxazole, and is also notable as the active moiety released from sulfasalazine in the colon. Its principal target is bacterial dihydropteroate synthase, causing competitive inhibition of para-aminobenzoic acid utilization and blockade of folate synthesis. After oral or colonic liberation it is generally well absorbed, distributes widely into tissues and inflammatory fluids, is variably protein bound, undergoes hepatic acetylation and glucuronidation, and is eliminated mainly by the kidney as parent drug and metabolites, with risk of accumulation in renal impairment. Historically it was used for susceptible bacterial infections and remains clinically relevant mainly through sulfasalazine therapy in ulcerative colitis, Crohn disease, and rheumatoid arthritis, where sulfapyridine contributes systemic exposure while 5-aminosalicylic acid mediates much of the colonic anti-inflammatory effect. Toxicities and adverse effects are those of sulfonamides, including hypersensitivity rash, urticaria, fever, photosensitivity, hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, agranulocytosis, hepatitis, crystalluria, nephrotoxicity, and rare severe reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, as well as gastrointestinal upset, headache, and dizziness.

Name: Testolactone
Description: Testolactone (DrugBank DB00894) is a steroidal antineoplastic and endocrine agent structurally characterized as a synthetic androstane derivative in which the usual C17 side-chain region is incorporated into a lactone ring, giving a 17a-oxa-D-homo steroid framework with a fused four-ring cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene nucleus; chemically it is classified as a steroidal aromatase inhibitor and its core scaffold is the androstanolactone/aromatizable androgen-like steroid skeleton. It is chemically and pharmacologically related to other endocrine therapies that suppress estrogen action or synthesis, including aminoglutethimide, formestane, exemestane, and, by therapeutic similarity, antiestrogens such as tamoxifen. Its principal target is aromatase, now known as cytochrome P450 19A1, thereby reducing peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogens. After oral administration it is absorbed with variable but clinically useful bioavailability, distributed systemically with expected steroid-like tissue penetration and likely plasma protein binding, extensively metabolized hepatically to hydroxylated and reduced metabolites, and excreted mainly in urine with some biliary/fecal elimination; its half-life is relatively short, historically requiring divided daily dosing. Toxicity is generally moderate but includes hepatotoxicity risk, endocrine disturbance, gastrointestinal intolerance, and virilizing effects at higher exposure. Adverse effects reported include nausea, vomiting, edema, rash, somnolence, hot flashes, increased appetite, acne, hirsutism, and menstrual irregularities. Clinically, it has been used primarily for estrogen-dependent breast cancer, especially advanced or metastatic disease in postmenopausal women, and has also been used in selected cases of precocious puberty or other hyperestrogenic states where estrogen suppression is desired.

Name: Rimexolone
Description: Rimexolone (DB00896) is a synthetic ophthalmic corticosteroid built on the pregnane steroid nucleus, a lipophilic four-fused-ring glucocorticoid scaffold bearing the characteristic 3-keto-Δ1,4 diene corticosteroid pharmacophore with hydroxyl and ketone substituents that tune receptor affinity and reduce some systemic corticosteroid liabilities; chemically it is a glucocorticoid corticosteroid and is most closely related to other topical ophthalmic steroids such as prednisolone acetate, loteprednol etabonate, fluorometholone, dexamethasone, and medrysone. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor, encoded by NR3C1, through which it modulates corticosteroid-responsive gene transcription, suppressing phospholipase A2-dependent eicosanoid formation, cytokine production, leukocyte migration, and vascular permeability. Rimexolone has been used primarily as an ophthalmic suspension for steroid-responsive inflammatory eye disorders, especially postoperative ocular inflammation after cataract extraction, anterior uveitis, and other inflammatory states presenting with pain, cell and flare, photophobia, and conjunctival hyperemia. After topical ocular administration, ocular tissue exposure is favored while systemic absorption is generally low; distribution is largely local to corneal, conjunctival, and anterior chamber tissues, metabolism is presumed to occur mainly via hepatic steroid-transforming pathways after any absorbed fraction reaches the circulation, and excretion occurs predominantly as metabolites in urine and possibly bile/feces. Toxicities are those of ocular corticosteroids, notably increased intraocular pressure, steroid-induced glaucoma, posterior subcapsular cataract with prolonged use, delayed wound healing, and masking or worsening of bacterial, viral, or fungal ocular infection. Common adverse effects include blurred vision, eye discomfort, tearing, foreign-body sensation, hyperemia, pruritus, and headache. Clinically, it has been used as a relatively lower-pressure-elevating ophthalmic steroid alternative when anti-inflammatory efficacy is desired with careful intraocular pressure monitoring.

Name: Triazolam
Description: Triazolam (DrugBank DB00897) is a short-acting triazolobenzodiazepine hypnotic whose structure consists of a fused benzene-diazepine core annelated with a triazole ring and bearing lipophilic halogenated aryl substituents, notably a chlorophenyl group, features that increase high-affinity binding at benzodiazepine sites on GABAA receptors; chemically it belongs to the benzodiazepine class, more specifically the triazolobenzodiazepines, and its core scaffold is the 1,4-benzodiazepine fused to a triazole heterocycle. Closely related drugs include alprazolam, midazolam, estazolam, temazepam, and diazepam, which share the benzodiazepine pharmacophore but differ in duration and substituent pattern. Triazolam is rapidly and well absorbed orally, reaches peak plasma concentrations within about 1 to 2 hours, is highly protein bound, distributes into the CNS because of substantial lipophilicity, undergoes extensive hepatic oxidative metabolism primarily via CYP3A4 to inactive or weakly active metabolites, and is excreted mainly in urine as conjugated metabolites, with a short elimination half-life that supports sleep-initiation use rather than sleep maintenance. Its main target is the benzodiazepine allosteric site on pentameric GABAA receptor complexes, commonly those containing alpha1, alpha2, alpha3, alpha5, and gamma2 subunits. It is indicated for short-term management of insomnia, especially difficulty falling asleep, and has been used for acute situational insomnia and, historically, procedural anxiolysis. Toxicity includes excessive CNS and respiratory depression, profound sedation, anterograde amnesia, falls, paradoxical agitation, dependence, withdrawal including rebound insomnia or seizures, and dangerous potentiation with alcohol, opioids, or CYP3A inhibitors. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, impaired coordination, confusion, memory impairment, and next-day psychomotor slowing. Clinically, it is used at low doses for brief treatment courses in severe transient insomnia, generally avoiding long-term use, use in older adults, and coadministration with strong CYP3A inhibitors such as ketoconazole or clarithromycin.

Name: Remifentanil
Description: Remifentanil (DrugBank DB00899) is a synthetic 4-anilidopiperidine opioid whose structure closely resembles fentanyl but is distinguished by a piperidine core bearing an anilide substituent and a metabolically labile ester side chain, giving it the concise scaffold of an anilidopiperidine ester. It belongs to the phenylpiperidine opioid analgesic class, with close structural and pharmacologic analogs including fentanyl, alfentanil, sufentanil, and carfentanil.
