Its principal target is the mu-opioid receptor, encoded by OPRM1, through which it produces potent analgesia, profound antinociception, sedation, and respiratory depression; weaker functional interactions with other opioid-system components may be pharmacologically less relevant clinically. Remifentanil is administered intravenously because it is not used for oral absorption, has a very rapid onset, small-to-moderate distribution volume, limited context-sensitive accumulation, and relatively low dependence on hepatic or renal clearance. Its defining pharmacokinetic feature is ultra-rapid metabolism by nonspecific blood and tissue esterases to a substantially less active carboxylic acid metabolite, with urinary excretion of metabolites and a very short terminal half-life that permits rapid titration and recovery. Toxicity is typical of potent mu agonists and includes dose-dependent apnea, severe respiratory depression, bradycardia, hypotension, chest wall rigidity, oversedation, and potentially fatal overdose, especially with other CNS depressants. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, vomiting, dizziness, pruritus, constipation, and postoperative hyperalgesia. Clinically, remifentanil is used as an analgesic adjunct during induction and maintenance of general anesthesia, for monitored anesthesia care, and for short procedures or mechanically ventilated intensive care patients where precise, rapidly reversible opioid effect is desired.

Name: Bitolterol
Description: Bitolterol (DrugBank DB00901) is a synthetic arylalkylamine sympathomimetic bronchodilator designed as the di-p-toluate ester prodrug of colterol; structurally it contains a phenylethanolamine/beta-adrenergic agonist core with a substituted aromatic ring, a beta-hydroxylated ethylamine side chain, and two lipophilic p-toluate ester moieties that increase oral/inhalational delivery characteristics before enzymatic activation. It belongs to the catecholamine-related beta-adrenergic agonist class, more specifically the resorcinol/phenylethanolamine scaffold family used in bronchodilators. Closely related or pharmacologically similar drugs include colterol, albuterol (salbutamol), terbutaline, metaproterenol, and isoproterenol, all sharing the beta-agonist bronchodilator paradigm. After administration, bitolterol is absorbed and rapidly hydrolyzed by esterases in the gastrointestinal tract, plasma, and tissues to the active metabolite colterol; distribution is expected to favor well-perfused tissues, with limited persistence of the parent compound, and elimination occurs mainly as metabolites in urine. Its principal target is the beta-2 adrenergic receptor, with possible lesser activity at beta-1 receptors at higher exposures, leading to adenylyl cyclase activation, increased intracellular cAMP, bronchial smooth-muscle relaxation, and reduced airway resistance. It has been indicated for reversible bronchospasm in asthma and obstructive airway disease, including symptomatic wheeze, dyspnea, and exercise-related bronchoconstriction. Toxicity reflects excessive beta-adrenergic stimulation, with examples including tachycardia, palpitations, tremor, nervousness, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, and, in overdose, arrhythmias or angina. Adverse effects seen clinically similarly include headache, restlessness, nausea, and paradoxical bronchospasm, and its clinical use has been as a rescue or symptomatic bronchodilator rather than an anti-inflammatory controller therapy.

Name: Methdilazine
Description: Methdilazine (DrugBank DB00902) is a first-generation phenothiazine antihistamine whose structure is built on a tricyclic phenothiazine nucleus containing sulfur and ring nitrogen, substituted at the 10-position by a dimethylaminoalkyl side chain and on the aromatic system by a methyl group, giving a lipophilic, cationic diaryl thioether architecture typical of sedating H1 blockers. Chemically it belongs to the phenothiazine class and more specifically to the aminoalkyl phenothiazine scaffold, closely related to promethazine, alimemazine, and other older sedating antihistamines with anticholinergic activity. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, with clinically relevant off-target antagonism at muscarinic cholinergic receptors and likely weaker anti-serotonergic and antiadrenergic sites that contribute to sedation and autonomic effects. Methdilazine is used for symptomatic relief of allergic conditions such as urticaria, pruritus, allergic rhinitis, and other histamine-mediated dermal or upper-airway symptoms, and in practice has also been used when nighttime sedation is acceptable or desirable. Like related phenothiazines, it is expected to be well absorbed orally, widely distributed with substantial central nervous system penetration, extensively metabolized hepatically by oxidative biotransformation and conjugation, and excreted mainly as metabolites in urine and bile/feces. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related CNS depression and anticholinergic burden, with examples including marked drowsiness, confusion, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention; overdose may produce agitation, hypotension, tachycardia, and respiratory depression. Clinical use has therefore been limited to short-term management of allergic symptoms where sedating antihistaminic therapy is appropriate.

Name: Etacrynic acid
Description: Etacrynic acid (DrugBank DB00903) is a non-thiazide loop diuretic built on an aryloxyacetic acid scaffold, specifically a chlorinated phenoxyacetic acid bearing an alpha,beta-unsaturated ketone on the aromatic ring, a Michael acceptor feature that contributes to its high chemical reactivity and distinguishes it from the sulfonamide-containing loop diuretics; chemically it is classified as a phenoxyacetic acid derivative and electrophilic enone. Its closest pharmacologic analogs are other loop diuretics such as furosemide, bumetanide, and torsemide, although etacrynic acid is notable for lacking a sulfonamide moiety and is therefore sometimes used when sulfonamide hypersensitivity is a concern. The principal target is the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter SLC12A1/NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb of Henle, with additional covalent interactions reported with sulfhydryl-containing proteins including glutathione-related pathways that may contribute to toxicity. After oral administration it is variably but substantially absorbed, is highly plasma-protein bound, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid, undergoes hepatic conjugation including glutathione adduct formation and other biotransformation, and is eliminated by both renal and biliary routes with a relatively short half-life. It is indicated for edema associated with congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, renal disease including nephrotic syndrome, and for short-term management of ascites or acute fluid overload. Adverse effects and toxicities include profound diuresis, dehydration, hypotension, hyponatremia, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia, hyperuricemia, renal dysfunction, gastrointestinal upset, and particularly dose-related ototoxicity that can be severe, especially with rapid intravenous use or concomitant aminoglycosides. Clinically, it is used orally or intravenously when potent loop diuresis is needed, especially in patients unable to tolerate sulfonamide loop diuretics.

Name: Ondansetron
Description: Ondansetron (DrugBank DB00904) is a synthetic carbazole-derived antiemetic whose structure is characterized by an indole-like fused aromatic heterocycle linked through a ketone-containing methylene bridge to a basic imidazole ring, placing it within the serotonin 5-HT3 receptor antagonist class and more specifically within the carbazole/imidzolyl ketone scaffold family; it is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other 5-HT3 antagonists such as granisetron, dolasetron, palonosetron, and tropisetron, which share aromatic heterocyclic cores and cationic features important for receptor binding. Its principal targets are the 5-hydroxytryptamine type 3 receptor subunits, including HTR3A and related receptor complexes in the chemoreceptor trigger zone and on vagal afferents, accounting for its antiemetic action. Ondansetron is indicated for prevention and treatment of nausea and vomiting associated with highly or moderately emetogenic chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and postoperative states, and is also widely used for refractory nausea in palliative care or gastroenteritis-related vomiting. It is well absorbed orally but undergoes first-pass metabolism, with additional intravenous use bypassing this effect; distribution is moderate with clinically relevant central and peripheral receptor access, protein binding is substantial, metabolism is primarily hepatic via CYP3A4, CYP2D6, and CYP1A2, and elimination occurs mainly as metabolites in urine with a terminal half-life of several hours. Toxicity is usually limited at therapeutic doses but includes dose-related QT prolongation, risk of torsades de pointes, serotonin syndrome in combination with serotonergic drugs, and hepatic impairment-related exposure increases. Common adverse effects include headache, constipation, dizziness, fatigue, transient liver enzyme elevation, and less commonly bradyarrhythmia or hypersensitivity. Clinically, it is used alone or with dexamethasone and neurokinin-1 antagonists in modern antiemetic regimens for cisplatin chemotherapy, perioperative prophylaxis, and symptomatic control of severe vomiting.

Name: Bimatoprost
Description: Bimatoprost (DrugBank DB00905) is a synthetic prostamide and prostaglandin F2α analog whose structure is characterized by a lipophilic eicosanoid scaffold with a cyclopentyl core, two aliphatic side chains, cis/trans alkene geometry, multiple hydroxyl substituents, and a terminal ethyl amide that distinguishes it from the isopropyl ester prostaglandin analogs; chemically it is categorized as an ophthalmic prostaglandin/prostamide derivative built on the prostanoid arachidonic-acid scaffold. Closely related drugs include latanoprost, travoprost, tafluprost, and unoprostone, which share the ocular hypotensive prostaglandin framework but differ in terminal substituents and receptor pharmacology. Its principal pharmacologic target is the prostaglandin F receptor system, especially PTGFR, although bimatoprost has also been described as acting via prostamide-sensitive pathways in ciliary body and trabecular tissues. After topical ocular administration, systemic absorption is low; the drug penetrates the cornea and conjunctiva, distributes mainly to anterior ocular tissues, is converted only to a limited extent compared with ester prodrugs, undergoes oxidation, N-deethylation, and glucuronidation, and is eliminated predominantly in urine with some fecal excretion. It is indicated for reduction of elevated intraocular pressure in open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension and is also used clinically to treat eyelash hypotrichosis by promoting lash growth. Adverse effects commonly include conjunctival hyperemia, pruritus, ocular irritation, dry eye, eyelash growth, iris and periocular pigmentation, and less commonly uveitis, cystoid macular edema, or periorbital fat atrophy; toxicity is generally local rather than systemic, with overdose rarely causing serious systemic effects but misuse potentially exacerbating inflammation, pigmentary change, or ocular surface intolerance.

Name: Tiagabine
Description: Tiagabine (DrugBank DB00906) is a lipophilic nipecotic acid derivative designed as a selective γ-aminobutyric acid reuptake inhibitor; structurally it contains a piperidine/nipecotic acid core bearing a carboxylic acid and an N-substituted bis(thiophene)-containing alkenylaryl side chain, giving an amphipathic arrangement that supports blood-brain barrier penetration while preserving affinity for the GABA transporter. Chemically it is classified as an antiepileptic amino acid derivative and specifically a GABA uptake inhibitor, with a nipecotic acid scaffold elaborated by a diaryl heteroaromatic thiophene motif. Similar drugs by mechanism or therapeutic class include vigabatrin, which inhibits GABA transaminase, and broader antiepileptics such as gabapentin and pregabalin, though these act through distinct targets. Its principal target is the sodium- and chloride-dependent GABA transporter 1, SLC6A1/GAT-1, leading to increased extracellular synaptic GABA. Orally administered tiagabine is well absorbed, highly protein bound, extensively distributed, and undergoes predominant hepatic CYP3A-mediated oxidation with subsequent fecal and renal elimination of metabolites; its half-life is shortened by enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs. It is indicated as adjunctive therapy for partial seizures, including focal seizures with or without secondary generalization, and has been explored off-label in anxiety or pain disorders. Adverse effects commonly include dizziness, somnolence, asthenia, tremor, difficulty concentrating, confusion, nervousness, nausea, and abdominal pain. Toxicity is chiefly neuropsychiatric, with excessive dosing or inappropriate use associated with nonconvulsive status epilepticus, new-onset seizures in nonepileptic patients, encephalopathy, and rare suicidal ideation, so clinical use emphasizes cautious titration, interaction monitoring, and avoidance in patients at elevated seizure risk outside approved epilepsy settings.

Name: Quinidine
Description: Quinidine (DrugBank DB00908) is a cinchona alkaloid and class IA antiarrhythmic built on the quinoline–quinuclidine scaffold, consisting of a methoxy-substituted quinoline aromatic system linked through a secondary alcohol to a rigid bicyclic quinuclidine amine, a stereochemically defined framework closely related to quinine and similar to other class I antiarrhythmics such as procainamide and disopyramide in electrophysiologic effect, though not in alkaloid structure. It acts primarily by blocking cardiac voltage-gated sodium channels, especially SCN5A/Nav1.5, and also inhibits several potassium currents including hERG/KCNH2, accounting for slowed phase 0 depolarization, prolonged action potential duration, and QT prolongation; ancillary interactions with P-glycoprotein/ABCB1 are clinically important. Quinidine is generally well absorbed orally, undergoes moderate first-pass hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 to active and inactive hydroxylated metabolites, is widely distributed with substantial tissue and protein binding, crosses the placenta, and is excreted in both urine and metabolized fecal/renal pathways, with urinary pH affecting clearance. Its major indication is treatment and suppression of supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmias, including atrial fibrillation/flutter conversion or maintenance of sinus rhythm and certain ventricular tachyarrhythmias; it has also been used in Brugada syndrome and, as quinidine sulfate, historically for malaria. Toxicity includes dose-related cardiotoxicity with torsades de pointes, conduction block, hypotension, and ventricular proarrhythmia, as well as cinchonism featuring tinnitus, headache, dizziness, visual disturbance, nausea, and hearing changes; other adverse effects include diarrhea, vomiting, thrombocytopenia, hepatotoxicity, hypersensitivity, and digoxin toxicity due to reduced P-glycoprotein-mediated digoxin clearance.

Name: Zonisamide
Description: Zonisamide (DrugBank DB00909) is a small-molecule anticonvulsant built on a 1,2-benzisoxazole ring system bearing a methanesulfonamide substituent, giving a compact aromatic heterocycle with a sulfonamide pharmacophore; chemically it is classified as a sulfonamide-containing benzisoxazole derivative, and its core scaffold is the benzisoxazole-sulfonamide framework. It is structurally and pharmacologically related to other sulfonamide or broad-spectrum antiseizure agents such as acetazolamide, topiramate, and to some extent lamotrigine and levetiracetam in clinical use for focal and generalized seizure disorders. Its principal targets and mechanisms include voltage-gated sodium channels, T-type calcium channels, and modulation of carbonic anhydrase isoenzymes, with downstream reduction in neuronal hypersynchrony and excitatory transmission. Zonisamide is well absorbed orally, has high bioavailability, moderate protein binding, broad tissue distribution including CNS penetration, and a relatively long elimination half-life that supports once-daily or divided dosing; it is metabolized mainly by CYP3A4, with contributions from acetylation and glucuronidation pathways, and excreted in urine as parent drug and metabolites. Clinically it is indicated primarily for focal epilepsy as monotherapy or adjunctive therapy, and is also used in some settings for generalized seizures, Parkinson disease adjunct therapy, and weight-related off-label applications. Important adverse effects include somnolence, dizziness, ataxia, anorexia, weight loss, cognitive slowing, irritability, nephrolithiasis, oligohidrosis, hyperthermia, and metabolic acidosis. Toxicity concerns include sulfonamide hypersensitivity, serious rash including Stevens-Johnson syndrome, hematologic abnormalities, depression or suicidality, and renal stone formation, especially in predisposed patients.

Name: Tinidazole
Description: Tinidazole (DrugBank DB00911) is a 5-nitroimidazole antimicrobial whose structure consists of a nitro-substituted imidazole heteroaromatic ring bearing an N-ethylsulfonylethyl side chain, placing it in the nitroimidazole class and on a compact 2-methyl-5-nitroimidazole scaffold closely related to metronidazole, ornidazole, and secnidazole. Its activity depends on reductive bioactivation in anaerobic protozoa and bacteria; although no single human target protein defines its effect, microbial low-redox-potential electron transport proteins such as ferredoxin-like systems and nitroreductases reduce the nitro group to reactive intermediates that damage DNA, inhibit nucleic acid synthesis, and cause strand breakage. Tinidazole is well absorbed orally with high bioavailability, wide tissue distribution including genital tissues and gastrointestinal sites, moderate protein binding, hepatic metabolism primarily by oxidation and conjugative pathways, an elimination half-life of roughly 12 to 14 hours, and excretion through both urine and feces, with some unchanged drug and metabolites recovered renally. It is indicated for anaerobic bacterial and protozoal infections, including trichomoniasis, giardiasis, intestinal and hepatic amebiasis, and bacterial vaginosis, and is also used clinically for susceptible mixed anaerobic infections. Toxicity is generally dose related and includes gastrointestinal irritation, metallic or bitter taste, headache, dizziness, and reversible leukopenia; more serious examples include peripheral neuropathy, seizures, hepatotoxicity, hypersensitivity reactions, and a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol. In practice, tinidazole is valued for short-course oral therapy, for example single-dose treatment of trichomoniasis or brief regimens for giardiasis and bacterial vaginosis.

Name: Amantadine
Description: Amantadine (DrugBank DB00915) is a small, rigid polycyclic primary amine built on the adamantane cage, specifically a tricycloalkyl hydrocarbon scaffold bearing an amino substituent at the 1-position; chemically it is classified as an adamantane derivative and aliphatic amine, with the adamantyl scaffold shared by related drugs such as rimantadine and memantine. Its best-characterized targets are the influenza A virus M2 proton channel, which it blocks to inhibit viral uncoating, and central nervous system glutamatergic signaling, where it acts as a weak uncompetitive NMDA receptor antagonist; dopaminergic effects, including increased dopamine release and reduced reuptake, are also implicated in its antiparkinsonian activity. Amantadine is generally well absorbed orally, shows relatively low protein binding and broad distribution including CNS penetration, undergoes minimal hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated largely unchanged by the kidney, giving it a prolonged half-life that is markedly extended in renal impairment and in older adults. Clinically, it has been used for treatment and prophylaxis of influenza A infection and for Parkinson disease, drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms, bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor, and sometimes fatigue in neurologic disorders. Toxicity is predominantly neurologic and anticholinergic-like, with examples including agitation, insomnia, confusion, hallucinations, delirium, myoclonus, and seizures in overdose or renal accumulation; livedo reticularis and peripheral edema are characteristic adverse effects, while common side effects include dizziness, dry mouth, nausea, constipation, and orthostatic symptoms.

Name: Metronidazole
Description: Metronidazole (DrugBank DB00916) is a small, lipophilic 5-nitroimidazole composed of a substituted imidazole ring bearing a nitro group at the 5-position, a 2-methyl substituent, and a 1-(2-hydroxyethyl) side chain, placing it in the nitroimidazole antimicrobial class with a 5-nitroimidazole heteroaromatic scaffold shared by related agents such as tinidazole, ornidazole, secnidazole, and, more distantly, other nitroheterocyclic anti-infectives. Its pharmacologic action depends on reductive activation in anaerobic microorganisms and certain protozoa; the reduced nitro radical intermediates damage DNA and other macromolecules, so the relevant biological targets are microbial nitroreductase/electron-transport proteins including ferredoxin-linked redox systems rather than a single human receptor. It is well absorbed orally with high bioavailability, distributes widely into saliva, bile, bone, vaginal secretions, cerebrospinal fluid, and hepatic abscesses, exhibits relatively low protein binding, is metabolized primarily in the liver by oxidation and glucuronidation to active and inactive metabolites, and is excreted mainly in urine with some fecal elimination. Clinically it is used for trichomoniasis, bacterial vaginosis, giardiasis, amebiasis, Clostridioides difficile infection, and anaerobic bacterial infections such as intra-abdominal, gynecologic, dental, brain, and aspiration-related infections, and it is also used in Helicobacter pylori combination regimens. Important adverse effects include nausea, metallic taste, abdominal discomfort, headache, dizziness, stomatitis, dark urine, and candidiasis; notable toxicities include peripheral neuropathy, encephalopathy or seizures with prolonged/high-dose exposure, rare hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, leukopenia, and a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol.

Name: Dinoprostone
Description: Dinoprostone (DrugBank DB00917) is prostaglandin E2, an endogenous eicosanoid built on a 20-carbon prostanoic acid framework with a cyclopentane core, terminal carboxylic acid, keto and hydroxyl substituents, and defined cis/trans alkenes that confer the classic PGE-series geometry; chemically it is a prostaglandin, i.e., a lipid-derived autacoid within the eicosanoid class, and its core scaffold is the prostane/prostanoid cyclopentylheptenoic acid skeleton. Closely related drugs include other prostaglandin analogs such as misoprostol, carboprost, alprostadil, and gemeprost, which share prostanoid signaling or uterotonic/cervical-ripening properties. Dinoprostone acts primarily at prostaglandin E receptors EP1, EP2, EP3, and EP4, expressed in uterine, cervical, and gastrointestinal tissues, producing cervical softening, uterine contraction, and smooth-muscle modulation. It is used mainly for cervical ripening and induction of labor in term or near-term pregnancy and for evacuation of uterine contents in missed abortion or intrauterine fetal death. Pharmacokinetically, it is rapidly absorbed from vaginal gel, insert, or suppository with predominantly local obstetric action, is widely but transiently distributed, and undergoes very rapid pulmonary and tissue metabolism by 15-hydroxyprostaglandin dehydrogenase and related reductases/oxidases to less active metabolites that are excreted mainly in urine. Toxicity is chiefly an extension of pharmacology, including uterine hyperstimulation, tachysystole, fetal distress, uterine rupture risk in predisposed patients, severe gastrointestinal effects, hypotension or fever, with overdose causing intense myometrial contractions. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramping, back pain, fever, chills, and uterine tachysystole; clinically it is used as a vaginal insert, gel, or suppository in supervised obstetric settings with fetal and uterine monitoring.

Name: Almotriptan
Description: Almotriptan (DB00918) is a synthetic antimigraine agent of the triptan class, chemically a substituted indole-sulfonamide that acts as a serotonin 5-HT1 receptor agonist; its structure features an indole core, the characteristic scaffold shared by many triptans, bearing a sulfonyl-linked pyrrolidine side chain and substitutions that confer oral activity and receptor selectivity. As an arylsulfonamide indole derivative, it is closely related to other triptans such as sumatriptan, rizatriptan, zolmitriptan, eletriptan, and naratriptan, which share the same general 5-HT1B/5-HT1D agonist pharmacophore. Its principal targets are 5-hydroxytryptamine receptor 1B and 1D, with some activity at 5-HT1F, producing cranial vasoconstriction and inhibition of trigeminal neuropeptide release, especially calcitonin gene-related peptide-mediated signaling. Almotriptan is indicated for acute treatment of migraine attacks with or without aura, including symptoms such as throbbing unilateral headache, photophobia, phonophobia, and nausea, but not for prophylaxis or hemiplegic/basilar migraine. After oral administration it is rapidly and fairly completely absorbed, has relatively high oral bioavailability of about 70%, low to moderate plasma protein binding, onset typically within 1 to 2 hours, and an elimination half-life of roughly 3 to 4 hours; it is metabolized by MAO-A and to a lesser extent CYP3A4 and CYP2D6, with renal and fecal excretion of parent drug and metabolites. Toxicity is usually limited at therapeutic doses but may include serotonin syndrome with serotonergic co-medication, medication-overuse headache, hypertension, coronary vasospasm, myocardial ischemia, and rare cerebrovascular events; common adverse effects include dizziness, somnolence, fatigue, paresthesia, nausea, dry mouth, and chest or throat tightness. Clinically, it is used as an oral abortive therapy in adults and some adolescents with episodic migraine, particularly when rapid functional recovery and good gastrointestinal tolerability are desired.

Name: Ketotifen
Description: Ketotifen (DrugBank DB00920) is a tricyclic benzocycloheptathiophene-derived antihistamine characterized structurally by a fused thiophene-benzocycloheptene core linked through a ketone-containing bridge to a substituted piperidine ring, placing it in the chemical category of second-generation H1 receptor antagonists with mast-cell stabilizing activity; its principal scaffold is therefore the dibenzocycloheptathiophene/piperidyl ketone motif seen in antiallergic agents, and it shows pharmacologic similarity to other H1 antihistamines and mast-cell stabilizers such as olopatadine, azelastine, epinastine, cetirizine, and cromolyn-like antiallergic therapies by functional profile. Its main target protein is the histamine H1 receptor, and it also inhibits release of inflammatory mediators from mast cells and may reduce eosinophil chemotaxis. Pharmacokinetically, oral ketotifen is well absorbed but undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, yielding moderate systemic bioavailability; it is widely distributed, sufficiently lipophilic to enter the central nervous system, extensively metabolized mainly by hepatic glucuronidation and related biotransformation, and eliminated primarily in urine as metabolites with a relatively long terminal half-life that supports twice-daily dosing. Clinically it is indicated for prophylaxis of allergic conditions including allergic conjunctivitis, allergic rhinitis, and asthma symptom prevention, although it is not useful for acute bronchospasm. Adverse effects commonly include sedation, somnolence, dizziness, dry mouth, increased appetite, and weight gain, while toxicity in overdose may produce marked CNS depression or, especially in children, confusion, tachycardia, excitability, or seizures; overall use is mainly chronic prevention of allergic symptoms, particularly as ophthalmic therapy for pruritic conjunctivitis and in some regions as an oral adjunct in atopic or asthma-related disease.

Name: Buprenorphine
Description: Buprenorphine (DrugBank DB00921) is a semisynthetic thebaine-derived opioid characterized by the morphinan/6,14-ethanomorphinan polycyclic phenanthrene-like core bearing a bridged ring system, a 7α side chain, a 6-methoxy substituent, a 3-hydroxyl group, and a bulky N-cyclopropylmethyl moiety that confers mixed opioid receptor activity; chemically it is classified as an oripavine-derived opioid analgesic and partial agonist, with the morphinan scaffold as its defining chemotype. Structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include thebaine derivatives and other opioids such as levorphanol, diprenorphine, etorphine, morphine, oxycodone, and methadone, although buprenorphine is distinguished by very high receptor affinity and slow dissociation. Its principal targets are the mu opioid receptor OPRM1 as a high-affinity partial agonist, the kappa opioid receptor OPRK1 as an antagonist or weak partial agonist, the delta opioid receptor OPRD1 with lower affinity, and the nociceptin receptor OPRL1 to a lesser extent. Buprenorphine is used for moderate to severe pain and opioid use disorder, including office-based maintenance therapy, withdrawal suppression, and perioperative or chronic cancer and noncancer pain management; it is administered sublingually, buccally, transdermally, parenterally, and as long-acting depot formulations, undergoes substantial first-pass metabolism if swallowed, is highly lipophilic and protein bound, distributes widely, is metabolized mainly by CYP3A4 to norbuprenorphine and by UGT1A1/UGT2B7 glucuronidation, and is excreted predominantly in bile/feces with lesser renal elimination. Toxicities include respiratory depression, especially with benzodiazepines, alcohol, or other CNS depressants, sedation, neonatal opioid withdrawal after in utero exposure, hepatic enzyme elevations, QT prolongation in some formulations, misuse, dependence, and precipitated withdrawal in patients actively using full agonists; common adverse effects include constipation, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, headache, somnolence, sweating, orthostatic symptoms, and application-site reactions.

Name: Levosimendan
Description: Levosimendan (DB00922) is a pyridazinone-dinitrile cardiotonic agent whose structure is centered on a 6-phenyl-substituted pyridazinone ring bearing two nitrile groups and an anilino-type substituent, giving a conjugated, aromatic, moderately lipophilic small molecule optimized for calcium sensitization and vasodilation; chemically it is classified as an inodilator and calcium-sensitizing positive inotrope, with a pyridazinone scaffold that distinguishes it from catecholaminergic inotropes and PDE3 inhibitors, although it is pharmacologically similar to milrinone, enoximone, dobutamine, and dopamine as an agent used to augment cardiac output. Its principal targets are cardiac troponin C, where it stabilizes the calcium-bound conformation to enhance contractility without major increases in myocardial oxygen demand, and ATP-sensitive potassium channels, especially in vascular smooth muscle and mitochondria, contributing to vasodilation and possible cardioprotection; weak phosphodiesterase III inhibition has also been described. Administered intravenously, it has rapid systemic availability, extensive protein binding, limited distribution, and a short parent half-life of about 1 hour, but undergoes intestinal/hepatic biotransformation with formation of the active metabolite OR-1896, which has a much longer half-life of roughly 70 to 80 hours and prolongs hemodynamic effects for days; elimination is mainly via metabolism with renal and fecal excretion of metabolites. It is indicated for short-term treatment of acutely decompensated severe heart failure, particularly low-output states despite conventional therapy, and is used clinically in settings such as advanced systolic heart failure, perioperative cardiac support, and occasionally cardiogenic shock. Important adverse effects and toxicities include dose-related hypotension, tachycardia, atrial or ventricular arrhythmias, headache, dizziness, nausea, hypokalemia, and potential myocardial ischemia in susceptible patients.

Name: Phenoxybenzamine
Description: Phenoxybenzamine (DB00925) is a haloalkylamine-derived, nonselective, irreversible alpha-adrenergic antagonist whose structure consists of a highly lipophilic triarylmethyl ether framework linking a phenoxy group and a benzyl-substituted tertiary amine to a 2-chloroethyl moiety, the latter serving as the reactive alkylating pharmacophore; chemically it is classified as an aromatic ether tertiary amine and beta-haloalkylamine, with a scaffold related to phenethylamine/benzylamine alpha-blockers bearing the characteristic nitrogen mustard-like 2-chloroethyl substituent. Similar drugs include other alpha-adrenoceptor antagonists such as phentolamine, doxazosin, prazosin, and terazosin, although phenoxybenzamine is distinguished by covalent, long-lasting receptor blockade. Its principal targets are alpha-1 adrenergic receptors and alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, with additional off-target antagonism reported at histaminergic, muscarinic, and serotonergic sites. After oral administration it is variably but adequately absorbed, extensively distributed into tissues because of high lipophilicity, metabolized predominantly hepatically, and excreted mainly in urine as metabolites; despite a relatively short plasma half-life, pharmacodynamic effects persist for days because receptor inactivation is irreversible until new receptors are synthesized. Toxicity is dominated by excessive alpha-blockade, causing marked orthostatic hypotension, reflex tachycardia, nasal congestion, miosis, fatigue, dizziness, and gastrointestinal irritation; overdose may produce profound shock. It is indicated chiefly for control of hypertension and catecholamine-related symptoms in pheochromocytoma, including preoperative preparation and chronic palliation, and has also been used in autonomic hyperreflexia and certain peripheral vasospastic states. Clinically, it is used when durable alpha blockade is desired, especially to prevent paroxysmal hypertension, headache, diaphoresis, and palpitations from catecholamine excess.

Name: Etretinate
Description: Etretinate (DrugBank DB00926) is a first-generation aromatic retinoid characterized structurally as a highly lipophilic polyene ester containing a conjugated all-trans retinoid chain linked to an aromatic ring system and terminated as an ethyl ester of acitretin, placing it in the retinoid, terpenoid-like, and carboxylic acid ester drug categories; its core scaffold is the aromatic retinoid scaffold shared with etretin and acitretin, built around a rigid conjugated isoprenoid-like chromophore that supports nuclear retinoid receptor binding. Similar drugs include acitretin, isotretinoin, tretinoin, adapalene, and bexarotene, with acitretin being the principal active metabolite and closest analogue. Etretinate acts mainly through retinoic acid receptor family proteins RARA, RARB, and RARG, with downstream effects on keratinocyte differentiation, epidermal proliferation, and inflammation. It was used primarily for severe, recalcitrant psoriasis, especially pustular and erythrodermic forms, and other disorders of keratinization such as ichthyosis and palmoplantar keratoderma. Oral absorption is variable but improved with الغذ fat; distribution is extensive because of extreme lipophilicity and tissue sequestration, especially in adipose tissue; metabolism occurs hepatically with hydrolysis to acitretin and further oxidative biotransformation; excretion is slow via biliary/fecal and renal routes, with an exceptionally prolonged terminal elimination phase due to fat storage. Its major toxicity is profound teratogenicity, with fetal craniofacial, cardiac, thymic, and CNS malformations, and it also causes hepatotoxicity, hypertriglyceridemia, mucocutaneous toxicity, and skeletal hyperostosis. Common adverse effects include cheilitis, xerosis, epistaxis, conjunctival dryness, alopecia, pruritus, photosensitivity, elevated transaminases, and dyslipidemia, which limited clinical use and led largely to replacement by acitretin in specialist dermatologic practice.

Name: Famotidine
Description: Famotidine (DrugBank DB00927) is a histamine H2-receptor antagonist built on a substituted thiazole scaffold linked through a thioether-containing amidino/sulfamoyl framework, giving a highly polar, basic, guanidine-like heteroaromatic structure designed to mimic histamine recognition while lacking the imidazole ring seen in some earlier agents. Chemically, it is classified as an H2 antihistamine and antiulcer agent; its core scaffold is commonly described as a thiazole-thioether-sulfamidine pharmacophore. Structurally and therapeutically similar drugs include cimetidine, ranitidine, and nizatidine, which share H2-blocking activity but differ in heteroaromatic ring systems and metabolic interaction profiles. Famotidine selectively targets the histamine H2 receptor, encoded by HRH2, on gastric parietal cells, thereby suppressing basal and stimulated gastric acid secretion. It is indicated for duodenal and gastric ulcer disease, gastroesophageal reflux disease, erosive esophagitis, heartburn, and pathological hypersecretory states such as Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. After oral administration, absorption is moderate with incomplete bioavailability, protein binding is low, distribution is largely extracellular, hepatic metabolism is minimal, and elimination is predominantly renal as unchanged drug, with prolonged half-life and dose adjustment required in renal impairment. Toxicity is generally low, but adverse effects can include headache, dizziness, constipation or diarrhea, nausea, and fatigue; rarer examples include confusion, especially in older adults or renally impaired patients, QT prolongation in severe renal dysfunction, thrombocytopenia, and hypersensitivity reactions. Clinically, famotidine is widely used orally or intravenously for ulcer healing, reflux symptom control, nocturnal acid suppression, stress-ulcer prophylaxis in selected hospitalized patients, and prevention of recurrence of acid-mediated upper gastrointestinal symptoms.

Name: Misoprostol
Description: Misoprostol (DrugBank DB00929) is a synthetic prostaglandin E1 analog structurally characterized by a substituted cyclopentane prostanoid core bearing hydroxyl groups and a methyl ester side chain, with modifications that increase oral stability relative to endogenous prostaglandins; chemically it belongs to the eicosanoid/prostanoid class, and its core scaffold is the prostaglandin cyclopentane lipid framework. Closely related or mechanistically similar drugs include dinoprostone, alprostadil, gemeprost, and carboprost, which share prostaglandin-like scaffolds and uterotonic or gastroprotective actions. Misoprostol is rapidly absorbed after oral administration and is de-esterified to the active metabolite misoprostol acid; bioavailability is influenced by route of administration, with oral, buccal, sublingual, and vaginal use producing different peak concentrations and durations, it is widely distributed, highly protein bound to a moderate extent, undergoes hepatic fatty-acid oxidation rather than CYP-dominant metabolism, and is eliminated mainly in urine as inactive metabolites. Its principal targets are prostaglandin E receptors, especially EP2, EP3, and EP4 on gastric parietal cells and uterine smooth muscle, reducing gastric acid secretion, increasing mucus and bicarbonate, and stimulating cervical ripening and myometrial contraction. Indications include prevention of NSAID-induced gastric ulcer, medical abortion with mifepristone, management of missed or incomplete abortion, cervical ripening before procedures, induction of labor in selected settings, and prevention or treatment of postpartum hemorrhage. Dose-related toxicity includes severe diarrhea, cramping, dehydration, fever, uterine hyperstimulation, fetal distress, and uterine rupture risk in pregnancy, while common adverse effects are abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, chills, headache, and vaginal bleeding.

Name: Metacycline
Description: Metacycline (DB00931) is a semisynthetic tetracycline antibiotic characterized by the classic linearly fused four-ring naphthacene core bearing multiple keto, enol, phenolic, and dimethylamino substituents that create a highly functionalized, amphoteric, metal-chelating structure; chemically it belongs to the tetracycline class within polyketide-derived broad-spectrum antibacterials, and its core scaffold is the tetracycline nucleus shared with related agents such as tetracycline, doxycycline, minocycline, demeclocycline, and oxytetracycline. Like other tetracyclines, it acts primarily by binding the 30S bacterial ribosomal subunit, especially 16S rRNA within the A-site region, thereby blocking aminoacyl-tRNA access and inhibiting protein synthesis; thus its key target is the bacterial ribosome rather than a human protein target. Orally administered metacycline is absorbed incompletely but clinically usefully, with reduced absorption in the presence of calcium, magnesium, aluminum, iron, or dairy products; it distributes widely into tissues and inflammatory exudates, shows variable protein binding, limited but relevant placental passage, and class-characteristic deposition in teeth and bone, undergoes minimal hepatic biotransformation, and is eliminated mainly by renal excretion with some biliary/fecal clearance. It has been used for susceptible respiratory, skin and soft-tissue, genitourinary, and atypical infections, including acne, bronchitis, chlamydial infection, and infections caused by tetracycline-sensitive organisms. Adverse effects and toxicity resemble those of other tetracyclines: gastrointestinal irritation, nausea, diarrhea, esophagitis, photosensitivity, candidiasis, superinfection, hepatotoxicity, azotemia in renal impairment, hypersensitivity reactions, and permanent tooth discoloration, enamel hypoplasia, and reversible inhibition of bone growth in fetuses and children, making it clinically useful but generally avoided during pregnancy and early childhood.

Name: Tipranavir
Description: Tipranavir (DrugBank DB00932) is a nonpeptidic HIV-1 protease inhibitor characterized structurally by a highly lipophilic dihydropyrone/sulfonamide-based architecture with multiple aromatic rings, a tetrahydroxy-containing substituent pattern, and fluorinated and thiazolyl functionalities that distinguish it from earlier peptidomimetic protease inhibitors; chemically it is categorized as a coumarin-like, nonpeptide arylsulfonamide protease inhibitor built on a dihydropyranone scaffold. It is broadly similar in therapeutic role to other HIV protease inhibitors such as darunavir, lopinavir, atazanavir, and ritonavir, but is structurally distinct and was developed to retain activity against many protease-inhibitor-resistant HIV strains. Its principal target is the HIV-1 protease enzyme, and it also inhibits HIV-2 protease to a lesser extent; clinically it is administered with ritonavir boosting to treat HIV-1 infection, especially treatment-experienced patients with multidrug-resistant virus. Oral absorption is enhanced by food and ritonavir coadministration; it is highly protein bound, widely distributed, extensively metabolized hepatically mainly via CYP3A4, and excreted predominantly in feces with minimal renal elimination. Major toxicities include hepatotoxicity, sometimes severe or fatal, and intracranial hemorrhage, with hyperlipidemia and metabolic disturbances also recognized. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fatigue, headache, rash, and elevations in transaminases, cholesterol, and triglycerides. In practice, tipranavir is used as part of combination antiretroviral therapy in salvage regimens for resistant HIV infection rather than first-line treatment, particularly when genotypic or phenotypic resistance limits other protease inhibitor options.

Name: Mesoridazine
Description: Mesoridazine (DB00933) is a piperidine phenothiazine antipsychotic and the major active sulfoxide metabolite of thioridazine, characterized structurally by a tricyclic phenothiazine core bearing a 2-methylthio-derived sulfoxide substituent and a three-carbon side chain terminating in an N-methylpiperidine ring; thus its chemical category is a typical first-generation antipsychotic, and its core scaffold is the phenothiazine tricycle with a piperidyl alkyl appendage. Closely related drugs include thioridazine, piperacetazine, and other phenothiazines such as chlorpromazine, perphenazine, and trifluoperazine, which share the same heterotricyclic antipsychotic framework but differ in side-chain electronics and receptor-binding profiles. Its principal targets are dopamine D2 receptors, with additional antagonism at D1, 5-HT2, alpha1-adrenergic, histamine H1, and muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, accounting for both efficacy and adverse effects. It was used for schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders, particularly for agitation, thought disorder, hostility, and severe behavioral disturbance when alternative agents were unsuitable. After oral administration it is absorbed variably, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism with contribution from CYP2D6 and related oxidative pathways, is highly tissue distributed and protein bound, penetrates the CNS, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine and bile/feces. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, sudden cardiac death, CNS depression, anticholinergic toxicity, hypotension, seizures, and overdose-associated arrhythmia. Common side effects include sedation, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, orthostasis, weight gain, hyperprolactinemia, extrapyramidal symptoms, and tardive dyskinesia. Clinically, its use became highly restricted and largely discontinued because of serious cardiotoxic risk despite antipsychotic efficacy.

Name: Oxymetazoline
Description: Oxymetazoline (DrugBank DB00935) is a direct-acting sympathomimetic built on an imidazoline-containing arylalkylamine framework, structurally characterized by a substituted benzene ring bearing tert-butyl and hydroxylated aromatic features linked through a methylene bridge to a dihydroimidazoline moiety; chemically it is an imidazoline derivative and topical alpha-adrenergic agonist, with an imidazoline-aryl scaffold closely related to other nasal decongestants such as xylometazoline, naphazoline, tetrahydrozoline, and to the systemic alpha-agonist clonidine by pharmacophoric similarity. Its principal targets are alpha-1 adrenergic receptors and alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, especially ADRA1A, ADRA1B, ADRA1D, ADRA2A, ADRA2B, and ADRA2C, producing vasoconstriction in nasal and conjunctival vessels and, in dermatologic use, reduction of persistent facial erythema. After intranasal, ophthalmic, or topical administration, systemic absorption is usually limited but can increase with damaged mucosa, excessive dosing, or pediatric exposure; distribution is sufficient to cause central and cardiovascular effects when absorbed, metabolism is believed to occur mainly hepatically through oxidative biotransformation, and excretion is predominantly renal as metabolites and some unchanged drug. It is indicated for temporary relief of nasal congestion in rhinitis, sinusitis, and upper respiratory infections, for ocular redness, and for rosacea-associated facial erythema. Adverse effects include local burning, dryness, छींखें, irritation, headache, and rebound congestion with prolonged intranasal use; toxicity from overdose or accidental ingestion can cause hypertension, reflex bradycardia, CNS depression, sedation, miosis, hypothermia, apnea, and coma, particularly in children. Clinically, it is used as a short-course intranasal decongestant, ophthalmic vasoconstrictor, and topical dermatologic vasoconstrictor.

Name: Salicylic acid
Description: Salicylic acid (DrugBank DB00936) is a small aromatic hydroxycarboxylic acid built on a benzoic acid nucleus bearing an ortho phenolic hydroxyl group adjacent to a carboxyl group, a motif that confers weak acidity, hydrogen-bonding capacity, and keratolytic reactivity; it is classified chemically as a salicylate and phenolic acid, with a simple salicylic acid scaffold that also underlies related drugs such as acetylsalicylic acid, methyl salicylate, sodium salicylate, diflunisal, and salsalate. Its pharmacology is dominated by topical keratolysis and anti-inflammatory effects, with salicylates also interacting functionally with cyclooxygenase pathways, especially PTGS1 and PTGS2, although salicylic acid itself is less potent than aspirin as a direct COX inhibitor; additional reported biological interactions include modulation of inflammatory signaling and epidermal desquamation. Absorption is substantial across skin, especially when applied to large, inflamed, or occluded surfaces, and after systemic exposure it distributes widely with albumin binding, undergoes hepatic conjugation mainly to salicyluric acid and glucuronides, and is excreted renally with urinary pH affecting clearance. Toxicity includes local irritation and salicylism, with tinnitus, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, metabolic acidosis, hyperventilation, and CNS toxicity in overdose or excessive topical use, particularly in children. It is indicated chiefly for hyperkeratotic and inflammatory skin disorders such as acne vulgaris, psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, corns, calluses, common warts, and ichthyotic scaling. Common adverse effects include burning, peeling, erythema, dryness, contact dermatitis, and rarely systemic salicylate poisoning. Clinically, it is used in topical creams, gels, shampoos, pads, and wart-removal preparations, often combined with sulfur, lactic acid, benzoyl peroxide, corticosteroids, or retinoids to enhance desquamation and lesion clearance.

Name: Diethylpropion
Description: Diethylpropion (DrugBank DB00937), also known as amfepramone, is a sympathomimetic anorectic built on a substituted phenethylamine/amphetamine-like framework and more specifically an arylalkyl ketone scaffold characterized by a propiophenone core bearing a para-unsubstituted phenyl ring, an alpha-methyl substituent, and a diethylamino side chain; chemically it is categorized as a synthetic cathinone-related aminoketone and centrally acting appetite suppressant. Structurally and pharmacologically it is similar to other anorectic stimulants such as phentermine, benzphetamine, phendimetrazine, and amphetamine derivatives. Its principal pharmacology reflects indirect catecholaminergic stimulation, with increased synaptic norepinephrine and, to a lesser extent, dopamine through interaction with monoamine transport systems, especially the norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2 and dopamine transporter SLC6A3, with weaker effects at SLC6A4. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed, distributed systemically including CNS penetration, extensively hepatically metabolized to active metabolites including ethcathinone, and eliminated mainly in urine; urinary pH can influence excretion of parent drug and metabolites, and the clinical half-life is relatively short, supporting divided or modified-release dosing. It is indicated as a short-term adjunct in exogenous obesity for weight reduction in patients inadequately controlled by diet and exercise, for example obese adults with hyperphagia or weight-related cardiometabolic risk. Toxicities include abuse liability, dependence, tachyarrhythmia, hypertension, psychosis, seizures, and rare pulmonary hypertension or valvular complications; overdose may cause marked CNS stimulation and cardiovascular instability. Common adverse effects include insomnia, nervousness, dry mouth, constipation, palpitations, headache, dizziness, and increased blood pressure, and clinical use has historically been restricted to short-course obesity management under careful cardiovascular and psychiatric monitoring.

Name: Salmeterol
Description: Salmeterol (DrugBank DB00938) is a long-acting aryloxyalkylamino phenethylamine bronchodilator whose structure consists of a substituted saligenin-like aromatic ring bearing hydroxymethyl and hydroxyl groups linked through an ethanolamine/phenylamino side chain to a long lipophilic aryloxyalkyl tail, a design that confers high affinity and prolonged residence at the beta-2 adrenergic receptor; chemically it is classified as a long-acting beta2-adrenergic receptor agonist (LABA), and its core scaffold is a phenylethanolamine/saligenin beta-agonist framework extended by a bulky lipophilic phenoxyalkyl substituent. Closely related or pharmacologically similar drugs include formoterol, vilanterol, indacaterol, and the shorter-acting beta2 agonists albuterol (salbutamol) and terbutaline. Its principal target protein is ADRB2, with functional downstream activation of adenylyl cyclase and cAMP-mediated airway smooth muscle relaxation. After inhalation, pulmonary delivery predominates but swallowed drug contributes to low systemic exposure because oral bioavailability is poor; distribution is extensive with substantial tissue partitioning and high protein binding, metabolism occurs mainly in the liver via CYP3A4-mediated aliphatic oxidation to alpha-hydroxysalmeterol and related inactive metabolites, and excretion is chiefly in feces with a lesser renal component, with bronchodilator activity lasting about 12 hours. Toxicity reflects excessive beta-adrenergic stimulation, including tachycardia, palpitations, tremor, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, QT-related arrhythmia risk, paradoxical bronchospasm, and overdose-associated cardiovascular instability; LABA monotherapy in asthma has been associated with increased serious asthma-related events, so salmeterol is indicated for maintenance treatment of asthma only with an inhaled corticosteroid, for prevention of exercise-induced bronchospasm, and for maintenance treatment of COPD including chronic bronchitis and emphysema. In clinical use it is employed as a scheduled controller rather than rescue therapy, commonly in fixed combinations such as fluticasone/salmeterol for persistent asthma and symptomatic COPD, with common adverse effects including headache, throat irritation, cough, nervousness, muscle cramps, and tremor.

Name: Meclofenamic acid
Description: Meclofenamic acid (DrugBank DB00939) is an anthranilic acid derivative of the fenamate class of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, characterized structurally as a substituted N-arylanthranilic acid in which an aminobenzoic acid core is linked to a halogenated, methyl-substituted phenyl ring, giving a diarylamine-like, lipophilic scaffold centered on the fenamate/N-phenylanthranilic acid framework. It is therefore chemically related to other fenamates such as mefenamic acid, flufenamic acid, tolfenamic acid, and etodolac-adjacent aryl acid NSAIDs in broader SAR terms, sharing with these agents inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis primarily through cyclooxygenase target proteins PTGS1 and PTGS2. After oral administration, meclofenamic acid is generally well absorbed, is highly albumin bound, distributes into inflamed tissues, undergoes substantial hepatic metabolism including hydroxylation and conjugation, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine with some biliary/fecal excretion; its half-life is short enough to require divided dosing in routine use. Clinically, it has been used for mild to moderate pain, primary dysmenorrhea, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and historically menorrhagia, where reduced endometrial prostaglandin production may lessen menstrual blood loss. Adverse effects are typical of NSAIDs and include dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, edema, and rash. Important toxicities include gastrointestinal ulceration, bleeding, and perforation, renal impairment, sodium and fluid retention, hypertension exacerbation, hepatotoxicity, hypersensitivity reactions including bronchospasm in aspirin-sensitive patients, and increased thrombotic cardiovascular risk; overdose or severe intolerance may present with vomiting, GI bleeding, acute kidney injury, or CNS symptoms.

Name: Methantheline
Description: Methantheline (DrugBank DB00940) is a synthetic quaternary ammonium antimuscarinic agent structurally characterized by a permanently charged trialkyl-substituted ammonium center linked through an ester-containing alkyl chain to a bulky aromatic hydrophobic moiety, a design that limits membrane permeability and central nervous system penetration; chemically it belongs to the quaternary ammonium parasympatholytic anticholinergics, and its core scaffold is the classic atropine-like antimuscarinic ester scaffold adapted into a cationic, peripherally restricted framework. Similar drugs include propantheline, glycopyrrolate, methscopolamine, and oxyphenonium, which share quaternary ammonium antimuscarinic pharmacology. Its principal targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially peripheral CHRM1, CHRM2, and CHRM3 receptor subtypes in gastrointestinal, secretory, and smooth muscle tissues, where receptor antagonism reduces vagally mediated tone, motility, and secretion. Orally administered methantheline is absorbed incompletely and variably, distributes mainly extracellularly with poor blood-brain barrier entry, undergoes limited hepatic biotransformation relative to tertiary amines, and is eliminated largely in urine as unchanged drug and metabolites. Toxicity is that of peripheral anticholinergic excess, including marked xerostomia, blurred vision from mydriasis/cycloplegia, tachycardia, constipation, urinary retention, decreased sweating with heat intolerance, and potential paralytic ileus or precipitation of angle-closure glaucoma; overdose may cause severe autonomic blockade. Historically, it has been indicated for peptic ulcer disease, gastrointestinal hypermotility, intestinal cramping, and adjunctive reduction of gastric secretion, and has also been used for functional bowel spasm and other hypersecretory or spastic gastrointestinal states. Clinically, its use has been limited by class adverse effects and replacement by safer or more effective antisecretory and antispasmodic therapies.

Name: Cycrimine
Description: Cycrimine (DrugBank DB00942) is a synthetic antimuscarinic antiparkinsonian agent with a tertiary amine structure built around a bulky lipophilic aryl-substituted carbinol/amine framework, characteristic of centrally active anticholinergics; chemically it is classified as an anticholinergic, specifically an antimuscarinic amine, and its scaffold is related to the diaryl or aryl-cycloalkanol tertiary-amine pharmacophore seen in older antiparkinsonian drugs. Similar drugs include benztropine, trihexyphenidyl, procyclidine, biperiden, and orphenadrine, which share central muscarinic receptor antagonism and comparable medicinal chemistry features. Its principal pharmacologic targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, particularly central M1-predominant signaling pathways in the striatum, although classical older agents are not highly subtype selective. Cycrimine is used to reduce parkinsonian tremor, rigidity, sialorrhea, and drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms such as antipsychotic-associated pseudoparkinsonism; clinically it has been used in idiopathic Parkinson disease and postencephalitic or medication-induced parkinsonian syndromes. As a lipophilic tertiary amine, it is expected to be orally absorbed, to cross the blood-brain barrier efficiently, to distribute widely into tissues, to undergo hepatic metabolism, and to be eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine, with limited unchanged renal excretion. Toxicity reflects dose-related antimuscarinic excess, including confusion, agitation, hallucinations, mydriasis, hyperthermia, urinary retention, constipation, and tachycardia, with overdose potentially causing severe delirium or arrhythmia. Common adverse effects include dry mouth, blurred vision, cognitive impairment, dizziness, nausea, and reduced sweating; therefore its clinical use has generally been limited to symptom control in selected patients, especially where tremor or extrapyramidal adverse effects predominate.

Name: Zalcitabine
Description: Zalcitabine (DB00943), also known as 2′,3′-dideoxycytidine or ddC, is a synthetic pyrimidine nucleoside analog structurally derived from cytidine in which the ribose-like sugar lacks both the 2′ and 3′ hydroxyl groups, creating a deoxyribose-deficient, chain-terminating architecture; chemically it belongs to the antiretroviral nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor class and is built on a dideoxynucleoside scaffold. It is closely related to other NRTIs such as didanosine, zidovudine, stavudine, lamivudine, emtricitabine, and abacavir, which share nucleoside-mimetic antiviral pharmacology. After oral administration, zalcitabine is absorbed with moderate bioavailability, distributes widely into tissues with limited protein binding, undergoes intracellular phosphorylation by host kinases to the active triphosphate metabolite, has minimal hepatic biotransformation, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by renal excretion, with dose adjustment needed in renal impairment. Its principal pharmacologic target is HIV-1 reverse transcriptase, and the triphosphate inhibits viral DNA synthesis by competing with deoxycytidine triphosphate and causing obligate chain termination. It was indicated for HIV infection, historically in combination therapy for advanced HIV disease or zidovudine-intolerant patients. Major toxicities include dose-limiting peripheral neuropathy and pancreatitis, with additional risks of oral and esophageal ulceration, hepatotoxicity, lactic acidosis with hepatic steatosis, and rare cardiomyopathy; common adverse effects include headache, nausea, diarrhea, rash, stomatitis, and fatigue. Clinically, zalcitabine was used as combination antiretroviral therapy but has largely been abandoned because of inferior efficacy and substantial mitochondrial toxicity relative to newer agents.

Name: Acetylsalicylic acid
Description: Acetylsalicylic acid (DrugBank DB00945), commonly known as aspirin, is a small aromatic carboxylic acid composed of a salicylic acid core bearing an O-acetyl ester, giving a benzene ring substituted ortho with a carboxyl group and an acetylated phenolic oxygen; chemically it is a salicylate and acetylated nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug built on the salicylic acid/benzoic acid scaffold. Closely related or mechanistically similar drugs include salicylic acid, salsalate, diflunisal, and other NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, naproxen, and ketorolac. Its principal targets are cyclooxygenase 1 and 2, encoded by PTGS1 and PTGS2, with irreversible acetylation of COX-1 in platelets underlying its antithrombotic effect; additional pharmacology includes reduced thromboxane A2 and prostaglandin synthesis. After oral administration it is rapidly absorbed from the stomach and proximal small intestine, hydrolyzed by esterases to salicylate, distributed widely with moderate to high albumin binding, metabolized hepatically mainly by glycine and glucuronide conjugation with dose-dependent, nonlinear elimination at higher concentrations, and excreted predominantly in urine, with renal clearance enhanced by urinary alkalinization. It is indicated for दर्द, fever, inflammatory disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis, and secondary prevention of myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, and other atherothrombotic events. Toxicity includes salicylism, gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding, tinnitus, respiratory alkalosis followed by metabolic acidosis in overdose, renal injury, and Reye syndrome in children with viral illness. Common adverse effects include dyspepsia, nausea, bruising, epistaxis, and hypersensitivity or aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease. Clinically, it is used as low-dose chronic antiplatelet therapy and at higher doses as an analgesic, antipyretic, and anti-inflammatory agent.

Name: Phenprocoumon
Description: Phenprocoumon (DrugBank DB00946) is a synthetic oral anticoagulant of the coumarin-derived 4-hydroxycoumarin class, structurally characterized by a benzopyran-2-one core bearing a 4-hydroxyl group and a lipophilic 3-substituent containing a phenylpropyl side chain, placing it within the vitamin K antagonist family and giving it the classic 4-hydroxycoumarin scaffold shared by related anticoagulants. Closely similar drugs include warfarin, acenocoumarol, dicoumarol, and related coumarin anticoagulants, which share the same general mechanism and scaffold variations. Its principal pharmacologic target is vitamin K epoxide reductase complex subunit 1 (VKORC1), with downstream functional effects on hepatic gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X and the endogenous anticoagulant proteins C and S; CYP2C9, CYP3A4, and other hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes are also important determinants of its disposition. Phenprocoumon is well absorbed after oral administration, is highly albumin bound, distributes mainly within the vascular compartment, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism with a notably long elimination half-life relative to some other coumarins, and is excreted primarily as inactive metabolites in urine and, to a lesser extent, bile/feces. Its major toxicity is bleeding, ranging from epistaxis, hematuria, and gastrointestinal hemorrhage to intracranial bleeding; rarer toxicities include skin necrosis, purple toe syndrome, hepatotoxicity, and embryofetal toxicity. It is indicated for prevention and treatment of thromboembolic disorders such as deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and prevention of systemic embolism in atrial fibrillation or mechanical heart valves. Common adverse effects include bruising, mucosal bleeding, anemia, nausea, and elevated INR, and clinically it is used for long-term anticoagulation with INR-guided dose adjustment, drug-food interaction monitoring, and reversal when needed with vitamin K or coagulation factor replacement.

Name: Mezlocillin
Description: Mezlocillin (DrugBank DB00948) is a broad-spectrum semisynthetic acylureidopenicillin whose structure consists of the conserved penam nucleus, a strained fused beta-lactam–thiazolidine bicyclic core bearing the usual carboxylate and amide functionalities, elaborated at the 6-acylamino side chain with a ureido-containing aromatic substituent that expands Gram-negative activity; chemically it belongs to the beta-lactam antibiotics, specifically the penicillins, and its core scaffold is the 6-aminopenicillanic acid/penam framework. Closely related drugs include other ureidopenicillins such as piperacillin and azlocillin, and more broadly ampicillin and amoxicillin as aminopenicillin analogs. Mezlocillin acts by binding bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, especially transpeptidases including PBP1 and PBP3 class targets, thereby inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-linking and cell-wall synthesis. It has been used for susceptible infections including complicated urinary tract infections, lower respiratory tract infections, intra-abdominal and biliary infections, gynecologic infections, septicemia, skin/soft-tissue infections, and infections caused by Enterococcus, Streptococcus, some Enterobacterales, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. It is administered parenterally, has negligible oral absorption, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid with useful penetration into bile and inflamed tissues, shows low to moderate protein binding, undergoes limited metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by renal tubular secretion and glomerular filtration, with some biliary excretion and dose adjustment in renal impairment. Toxicities are typical of high-dose penicillins and include hypersensitivity reactions up to anaphylaxis, rash, drug fever, eosinophilia, positive Coombs test, diarrhea, antibiotic-associated colitis, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, elevated transaminases, interstitial nephritis, and rarely seizures with accumulation; clinical use often included severe polymicrobial or nosocomial infections, sometimes in combination with aminoglycosides.

Name: Felbamate
Description: Felbamate (DB00949) is a synthetic dicarbamate antiepileptic whose structure is characterized by a 2-phenyl-1,3-propanediol backbone bearing two carbamate ester functions, making it a neutral, relatively small bis-carbamate with an aromatic phenyl-substituted propane scaffold; chemically it is classified as a carbamate derivative and more specifically a propanediol dicarbamate, with a scaffold related in broad physicochemical terms to other CNS-active carbamates such as meprobamate and carisbamate, though felbamate is structurally distinct and pharmacologically notable for mixed glutamatergic and GABAergic actions. Its known targets include the NMDA receptor, particularly inhibition at the glycine modulatory site on NR1/NR2-containing receptors, enhancement of GABAA receptor-mediated signaling, and inhibition of voltage-gated sodium and high-voltage-activated calcium currents. Orally, it is well absorbed with high bioavailability, low to moderate protein binding, broad distribution including CNS penetration, hepatic metabolism mainly by hydroxylation and conjugation, and predominant renal excretion of parent drug and metabolites; it also alters the disposition of coadministered antiepileptics through CYP-mediated interactions. Clinically it is indicated for refractory partial-onset seizures in adults and for seizures associated with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome in children, especially drop attacks and mixed seizure patterns. Its use is limited by severe toxicity, most importantly aplastic anemia and acute hepatic failure, with additional adverse effects including anorexia, weight loss, insomnia, nausea, dizziness, headache, diplopia, and somnolence. In practice, felbamate is reserved for severe drug-resistant epilepsy when the potential benefit outweighs these rare but life-threatening risks.

Name: Fexofenadine
Description: Fexofenadine (DrugBank DB00950) is a second-generation, peripherally selective H1-antihistamine and the active carboxylated metabolite of terfenadine, structurally characterized as a substituted piperidine bearing a biaryl framework, a terminal carboxylic acid, and a tertiary alcohol that together confer amphoteric, zwitterion-forming behavior and low central nervous system penetration. Chemically it belongs to the piperidine antihistamines and more broadly to arylalkyl carboxylic acid derivatives, with a terfenadine-like diarylpropyl/piperidine scaffold; closely related or mechanistically similar drugs include terfenadine, loratadine, desloratadine, cetirizine, levocetirizine, and ebastine. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, where it acts as a selective peripheral inverse agonist/antagonist; clinically relevant transport interactions involve P-glycoprotein/ABCB1 and uptake transporters such as OATP1A2 and OATP2B1 that influence disposition. After oral administration, absorption is moderate, bioavailability is limited in part by transporter effects, peak concentrations occur within a few hours, protein binding is moderate, distribution is largely peripheral, metabolism is minimal with little CYP involvement, and elimination occurs mainly as unchanged drug via biliary/fecal excretion with a lesser renal component, supporting a half-life on the order of about 14 hours. It is indicated for seasonal allergic rhinitis and chronic idiopathic urticaria, improving sneezing, rhinorrhea, pruritus, watery eyes, and wheals. Adverse effects are usually mild, including headache, dizziness, nausea, dyspepsia, back pain, cough, and fatigue, with relatively low sedation and anticholinergic burden. Toxicity is generally low and notably lacks the QT-prolonging cardiotoxicity associated with terfenadine, although overdose may still cause exaggerated CNS or gastrointestinal symptoms. Clinically, it is widely used as a non-sedating oral antihistamine in adults and children for daytime allergy control and chronic hives, particularly when avoidance of psychomotor impairment is important.

Name: Isoniazid
Description: Isoniazid (DrugBank DB00951) is a small, highly polar nicotinic acid hydrazide composed of a pyridine ring bearing a 4-carboxylic acid hydrazide substituent, making it a simple heteroaromatic hydrazide with a pyridyl acylhydrazone-forming pharmacophore; chemically it belongs to the antimycobacterial hydrazides and is built on a nicotinamide-like pyridine scaffold. Structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include ethionamide, prothionamide, and other antitubercular prodrugs that interfere with mycolic acid biosynthesis. Isoniazid is rapidly and usually well absorbed orally, distributes widely into tissues and body fluids including cerebrospinal fluid and caseous lesions, exhibits low protein binding, and is metabolized primarily in the liver by NAT2-dependent acetylation to acetylisoniazid, with subsequent hydrolysis and formation of metabolites such as acetylhydrazine; excretion is mainly renal as parent drug and metabolites, and half-life varies substantially with slow versus rapid acetylator genotype. Its key microbial target pathway involves KatG-mediated prodrug activation followed by inhibition of InhA, the enoyl-acyl carrier protein reductase required for mycolic acid synthesis; KasA and other mycobacterial fatty acid synthesis components have also been implicated. It is indicated for treatment and prophylaxis of tuberculosis, including latent tuberculosis infection and active drug-susceptible Mycobacterium tuberculosis disease in multidrug regimens. Major toxicities include hepatotoxicity ranging from asymptomatic transaminase elevation to hepatitis, peripheral neuropathy from pyridoxine depletion, seizures, lupus-like reactions, and, less commonly, optic neuritis or hematologic toxicity. Common adverse effects include nausea, rash, fatigue, paresthesias, and elevated liver enzymes. Clinically, it is used with rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for active TB, and alone or with rifapentine or rifampin in preventive regimens for exposed or high-risk patients.

Name: Dirithromycin
Description: Dirithromycin (DrugBank DB00954) is a semisynthetic macrolide antibiotic structurally derived from erythromycin, characterized by a 14-membered erythronolide lactone ring bearing desosamine and cladinose sugars and modified as a 9N,11O-oxazine prodrug of erythromycylamine, a feature that increases acid stability and oral tolerability; chemically it belongs to the macrolide class, more specifically the erythromycin-derived azalide-like erythromycylamine/oxazine scaffold family, and is closely related to erythromycin, erythromycylamine, clarithromycin, and azithromycin. Its antibacterial effect is mediated after rapid nonenzymatic conversion to erythromycylamine, which binds the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit, principally 23S rRNA in the peptidyl transferase/exit tunnel region, inhibiting translocation and protein synthesis; thus its relevant target is the bacterial 50S ribosome rather than a human protein. Dirithromycin is orally absorbed as a prodrug, hydrolyzed in intestinal fluid/plasma to active erythromycylamine, distributes well into respiratory tissues and phagocytes with relatively low plasma concentrations, undergoes limited further metabolism compared with erythromycin, and is cleared mainly via biliary/fecal excretion with a smaller renal component and an elimination half-life permitting once-daily dosing. It has been used for mild to moderate infections such as community-acquired respiratory tract infections, bronchitis, pharyngitis/tonsillitis, sinusitis, and uncomplicated skin and soft-tissue infections caused by susceptible organisms. Adverse effects are typical of macrolides, including nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, dyspepsia, and headache, while toxicities of concern include cholestatic hepatitis, QT-interval prolongation with arrhythmia risk, hypersensitivity reactions, superinfection, and potential CYP3A-mediated interactions analogous to erythromycin, although generally less prominent.

Name: Hydrocodone
Description: Hydrocodone (DrugBank DB00956) is a semisynthetic opioid analgesic structurally derived from the morphinan/phenanthrene family, characterized by a rigid fused polycyclic 4,5-epoxymorphinan scaffold with a tertiary N-methyl amine, a ketone at C6, and a methoxy-substituted aromatic ring, features that distinguish it from codeine and align it chemically with hydrogenated codeine derivatives; thus, its chemical category is narcotic opioid analgesics and antitussives, and its core scaffold is the morphinan opioid nucleus. Closely related drugs include codeine, oxycodone, hydromorphone, morphine, and dihydrocodeine, which share overlapping opioid pharmacology but differ in oxygenation and potency. Hydrocodone acts primarily as an agonist at the mu-opioid receptor OPRM1, with lesser functional relevance at delta and kappa opioid receptors and downstream modulation of Gi/o signaling, reducing nociceptive neurotransmission and cough reflex. It is well absorbed orally, undergoes first-pass hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 to norhydrocodone and via CYP2D6 to the more potent hydromorphone, distributes broadly including into the CNS, is moderately protein bound, and is eliminated largely in urine as parent drug and metabolites with an elimination half-life typically around 4 hours. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related respiratory depression, profound sedation, miosis, coma, dependence, misuse, neonatal opioid withdrawal, and fatal overdose, especially with alcohol, benzodiazepines, or other CNS depressants. Adverse effects commonly include constipation, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, somnolence, pruritus, and headache. Clinically, hydrocodone is used for moderate to moderately severe pain such as postoperative, musculoskeletal, dental, or injury-related pain, and in some formulations for symptomatic suppression of nonproductive cough.

Name: Norgestimate
Description: Norgestimate (DrugBank DB00957) is a synthetic progestin used primarily as an orally active contraceptive component; structurally it is a 19-nortestosterone-derived steroid with the classical tetracyclic cyclopenta[a]phenanthrene nucleus, bearing a 17α-ethynyl substituent, a 17β-acetoxy group, and an oxime functionality at C3, placing it in the gonane/estrane-derived progestogen category and giving it a norelgestromin-active-metabolite scaffold related to desogestrel, levonorgestrel, norethindrone, and norgestrel.
