It is considered a prodrug that is rapidly absorbed after oral administration and undergoes extensive first-pass deacetylation and biotransformation to norelgestromin and levonorgestrel, the principal active metabolites; these are highly protein bound, distributed systemically, further metabolized hepatically mainly by reductive and conjugative pathways with some CYP contribution, and eliminated via both urine and feces as metabolites, with pharmacokinetics influenced by coadministered estrogens and enzyme inducers. Its principal targets are the progesterone receptor and, through suppression of gonadotropin signaling at the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, functional modulation of luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone release; it also alters cervical mucus and endometrial receptivity. Clinically, norgestimate is indicated for prevention of pregnancy and is also used in combined oral contraceptives for acne vulgaris and menstrual-cycle regulation, including dysmenorrhea or irregular bleeding. Adverse effects include nausea, headache, breast tenderness, breakthrough bleeding, mood changes, and weight fluctuation, while important toxicities include venous thromboembolism, hypertension, cholestatic/hepatic effects, and rare arterial events, particularly when combined with ethinyl estradiol and in smokers or patients with thrombosis risk factors.

Name: Methylprednisolone
Description: Methylprednisolone (DrugBank DB00959) is a synthetic corticosteroid built on the pregnane-derived cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene steroid nucleus, specifically a 9-fluoro-free 11β,17α,21-trihydroxylated glucocorticoid with a 3-keto-4-ene A-ring and a characteristic 6α-methyl substitution that increases glucocorticoid potency while reducing mineralocorticoid activity relative to hydrocortisone. It belongs to the corticosteroid, glucocorticoid, and pregnane steroid classes, with a hydrocortisone/prednisolone-like scaffold. Closely related drugs include prednisolone, prednisone, dexamethasone, triamcinolone, hydrocortisone, and methylprednisolone sodium succinate or acetate formulations. It acts primarily through the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, altering transcription of inflammatory and immune mediators; downstream effects involve suppression of NF-κB- and AP-1-regulated pathways, with reduced cytokine production and leukocyte trafficking. Oral absorption is generally good, distribution is wide with moderate plasma protein binding, hepatic metabolism occurs mainly via CYP3A4 to inactive metabolites, and excretion is predominantly renal as conjugated metabolites; biologic effects outlast the plasma half-life because of genomic signaling. Toxicity is dose- and duration-dependent and includes adrenal suppression, severe hyperglycemia, infection risk, myopathy, peptic ulceration, osteoporosis, psychosis, cataracts, glaucoma, and, in overdose or pulse therapy, profound metabolic and neuropsychiatric disturbances. Indications include asthma and COPD exacerbations, autoimmune and inflammatory diseases such as lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis relapse, inflammatory bowel disease, dermatologic disorders, transplant rejection prophylaxis, and cerebral edema. Common adverse effects include insomnia, mood change, fluid retention, hypertension, dyspepsia, hyperglycemia, weight gain, and increased susceptibility to infection; clinically it is widely used orally, intravenously, and intra-articularly for acute immunosuppression and anti-inflammatory control.

Name: Pindolol
Description: Pindolol (DrugBank DB00960) is a lipophilic aryloxypropanolamine beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist characterized structurally by an indole-containing aromatic system linked through an ether to a 3-carbon propanolamine side chain bearing a secondary alcohol and isopropyl-substituted amine, placing it in the nonselective beta blocker class with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity; its core scaffold is the indole-oxypropanolamine/beta-amino alcohol pharmacophore shared with several adrenergic ligands. Similar drugs include propranolol, oxprenolol, alprenolol, timolol, and penbutolol, especially other nonselective beta blockers with partial agonist properties such as oxprenolol. Pindolol targets beta-1 adrenergic receptor and beta-2 adrenergic receptor, and has also been reported to interact with serotonin 5-HT1A receptors, a property explored in neuropsychiatric augmentation strategies. It is well absorbed orally with high bioavailability due to limited first-pass metabolism, reaches peak plasma concentrations within a few hours, distributes widely with moderate protein binding, undergoes partial hepatic metabolism including hydroxylation and conjugative pathways, and is eliminated by both renal excretion of unchanged drug and metabolites, with an elimination half-life generally in the several-hour range. Toxicity is typical of beta blockade and includes bradycardia, hypotension, atrioventricular conduction delay, acute heart failure exacerbation, and bronchospasm, with overdose potentially causing severe cardiovascular depression and hypoglycemia. Adverse effects include fatigue, dizziness, sleep disturbance, nausea, cold extremities, depression, and sexual dysfunction. Clinically, pindolol has been used mainly for hypertension and sometimes angina or arrhythmia control, particularly when a beta blocker with less resting bradycardia is desired, and it has also been investigated as an adjunct in treatment-resistant depression because of its 5-HT1A-related effects.

Name: Zaleplon
Description: Zaleplon (DrugBank DB00962) is a nonbenzodiazepine sedative-hypnotic whose structure consists of a pyrazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidine bicyclic heteroaromatic core bearing a 3-cyano substituent and a 5-ethylacetamide side chain linked to an N-methyl aniline moiety, giving a compact, lipophilic aza-heterocycle optimized for rapid central nervous system penetration. Chemically it is classified as a pyrazolopyrimidine and belongs to the Z-drug class; its key scaffold is the pyrazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidine hypnotic pharmacophore, which distinguishes it from benzodiazepines despite overlapping receptor pharmacology. Similar drugs include zolpidem and eszopiclone, and more broadly benzodiazepine-site GABAA receptor modulators such as triazolam or temazepam. Its principal targets are GABAA receptor benzodiazepine modulatory sites, with functional selectivity favoring receptors containing the alpha1 subunit, consistent with hypnotic over anxiolytic or myorelaxant effects. Zaleplon is indicated for short-term treatment of insomnia, particularly difficulty with sleep initiation and delayed sleep onset, and is used clinically for transient, situational, or chronic sleep-onset insomnia when rapid onset and minimal next-day residual sedation are desired. It is rapidly absorbed orally, reaches peak concentrations in about 1 hour, has low to moderate bioavailability due to first-pass metabolism, is widely distributed, is extensively metabolized hepatically mainly by aldehyde oxidase and partly by CYP3A4 into inactive metabolites, and is excreted predominantly in urine with a short elimination half-life of about 1 hour. Adverse effects include somnolence, dizziness, headache, nausea, impaired coordination, amnesia, and rare complex sleep behaviors; toxicity in overdose usually causes CNS depression, confusion, and ataxia, but risk is markedly increased with alcohol, opioids, or other sedative-hypnotics.

Name: Bromfenac
Description: Bromfenac (DrugBank DB00963) is a brominated arylacetic acid nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug characterized structurally by a substituted benzoyl-phenylamine framework bearing a para-bromo substituent and a carboxymethoxy side chain, giving it the typical acidic, lipophilic profile of cyclooxygenase-inhibiting NSAIDs; chemically it is classified as a halogenated amino-benzoyl arylacetic acid, and its core scaffold is closely related to fenamate/arylacetic acid anti-inflammatory chemotypes. Similar drugs include amfenac, nepafenac (the ophthalmic prodrug of amfenac), diclofenac, ketorolac, and flurbiprofen, which share ocular anti-inflammatory use and COX inhibition. Its principal targets are cyclooxygenase-2 and cyclooxygenase-1, with anti-inflammatory activity largely attributed to suppression of prostaglandin synthesis. In ophthalmic use, bromfenac is absorbed locally into ocular tissues, achieving therapeutically relevant anterior segment concentrations with limited systemic exposure; systemically absorbed drug is expected to be highly protein bound, hepatically metabolized mainly by oxidative and conjugative pathways, and excreted predominantly in urine as metabolites with minor fecal elimination. It is indicated for postoperative ocular inflammation and pain, especially after cataract extraction, and is used clinically as topical eye drops to reduce anterior chamber inflammation, pain, photophobia, and cystoid macular edema risk. Adverse effects include ocular irritation, burning, conjunctival hyperemia, headache, and inflammation; more serious toxicities include corneal epithelial damage, keratitis, corneal thinning or ulceration, delayed wound healing, bleeding tendency, and hypersensitivity reactions, particularly in NSAID- or aspirin-sensitive patients.

Name: Telmisartan
Description: Telmisartan (DrugBank DB00966) is a nonpeptide angiotensin II receptor blocker characterized structurally by a biphenyl-like aromatic system integrated with a benzimidazole core and a terminal carboxylic acid, plus lipophilic alkyl substituents that confer high receptor affinity and marked hydrophobicity; chemically it belongs to the benzimidazole-containing ARB class, with a biphenyl-benzimidazole acidic scaffold that distinguishes it from related sartans. Similar drugs include losartan, valsartan, irbesartan, candesartan, and olmesartan, which share angiotensin II type 1 receptor antagonism but differ in heterocyclic core and pharmacokinetic behavior. Its principal target is the angiotensin II receptor type 1 encoded by AGTR1; functional effects include blockade of vasoconstriction, aldosterone release, sympathetic facilitation, and renal sodium retention. Telmisartan is indicated mainly for hypertension and reduction of cardiovascular risk in high-risk patients intolerant to ACE inhibitors, with clinical use in essential hypertension, diabetic or proteinuric nephropathy risk management, and combination antihypertensive therapy. Pharmacokinetically, it is orally active with variable but clinically useful absorption, very high plasma protein binding, a large apparent distribution volume, minimal CYP-mediated metabolism, predominant glucuronidation, a long elimination half-life of about 24 hours, and mostly biliary/fecal excretion with limited renal clearance. Toxicity is generally dose-related and includes excessive hypotension, acute kidney injury in susceptible patients, hyperkalemia, and fetotoxicity from renin-angiotensin system blockade during pregnancy; overdose may produce dizziness, tachycardia, or bradycardia. Common adverse effects include dizziness, hypotension, fatigue, back pain, diarrhea, and increases in creatinine or potassium.

Name: Desloratadine
Description: Desloratadine (DrugBank DB00967) is a tricyclic, second-generation antihistamine that is the major active metabolite of loratadine; structurally it is a piperidine-containing dibenzocycloheptene derivative with a rigid fused aromatic tricyclic core linked to a substituted piperidine nitrogen, placing it in the class of peripherally selective H1-receptor antagonists and more specifically within the piperidine antihistamine scaffold related to loratadine, fexofenadine, and rupatadine. Its principal pharmacologic target is the histamine H1 receptor encoded by HRH1, where it acts as an inverse agonist/antagonist to suppress histamine-mediated vasodilation, pruritus, sneezing, rhinorrhea, and wheal formation; limited anti-inflammatory effects on cytokine release and eosinophil recruitment have also been described. After oral administration it is well absorbed, reaches peak plasma concentrations within a few hours, is highly protein bound, distributes mainly to peripheral tissues with minimal blood-brain barrier penetration, and has a relatively long elimination half-life that supports once-daily dosing; it undergoes hepatic metabolism, including hydroxylation to 3-hydroxydesloratadine followed by glucuronidation, with elimination through both urine and feces. Toxicity is generally low at therapeutic doses, with overdose usually causing somnolence, tachycardia, or anticholinergic-like complaints rather than severe cardiotoxicity, though caution is warranted in hepatic impairment. It is indicated for seasonal and perennial allergic rhinitis and chronic idiopathic urticaria, and is used clinically to relieve sneezing, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, itching, watery eyes, and urticarial wheals; common adverse effects include headache, dry mouth, fatigue, pharyngitis, and occasional mild sedation.

Name: Methyldopa
Description: Methyldopa (DB00968) is a centrally acting antihypertensive that is structurally an alpha-methylated analogue of L-DOPA, consisting of a catechol-substituted phenylalanine-like amino acid framework with a 3,4-dihydroxyphenyl ring, an alpha-methyl group, and amino acid carboxylate/amine functionality; chemically it belongs to the catecholamines-related aromatic amino acid class and more specifically to substituted phenylalanine derivatives, with a catechol amino acid scaffold. It is closely related to levodopa and has mechanistic similarity to other central sympatholytics such as clonidine and guanfacine, although those are structurally distinct; older related agents include carbidopa and dopamine-precursor analogues. Methyldopa is absorbed orally with variable, incomplete bioavailability, distributes systemically with limited protein binding, crosses the blood-brain barrier via amino acid transport, and is converted in tissues and the CNS by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase and dopamine beta-hydroxylase to alpha-methyldopamine and the active metabolite alpha-methylnorepinephrine; elimination is mainly renal as unchanged drug and sulfate conjugates, with a relatively short plasma half-life but longer pharmacodynamic effect due to central storage of active metabolite. Its principal targets are alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, especially central ADRA2A-mediated reduction of sympathetic outflow, with indirect dependence on DOPA decarboxylase and DBH for bioactivation. It is indicated for hypertension, particularly chronic hypertension in pregnancy and occasionally hypertensive urgency control. Important adverse effects include sedation, dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, dry mouth, edema, depression, and sexual dysfunction; notable toxicities include hepatotoxicity, fever, hemolytic anemia with positive Coombs test, and rare leukopenia, making it clinically useful mainly as a well-established oral option in pregnancy-associated hypertension when maternal-fetal safety is prioritized.

Name: Dactinomycin
Description: Dactinomycin (actinomycin D; DrugBank DB00970) is a highly cytotoxic chromopeptide antineoplastic antibiotic composed of a planar phenoxazone chromophore bearing two identical cyclic pentapeptide lactone side chains, a rigid aromatic-peptide architecture that enables strong DNA intercalation; chemically it is classified as an actinomycin, chromopeptide lactone, and DNA-binding polypeptide natural product, with a core scaffold defined by the actinocin/phenoxazone ring system linked to bis(cyclic pentapeptides). Closely related agents include other actinomycins such as actinomycin C variants, while functionally similar DNA-interacting antineoplastics include anthracyclines such as doxorubicin and daunorubicin. Its principal target is DNA itself, especially guanine-cytosine-rich regions, where it stabilizes the duplex and inhibits RNA polymerases, thereby suppressing transcription and secondarily DNA replication; no single protein target is dominant, though RNA polymerase machinery is functionally inhibited. After intravenous administration, absorption is not relevant; distribution is extensive but variable, with high tissue binding and limited central nervous system penetration; metabolism is minimal or incompletely characterized; elimination occurs slowly via both biliary/fecal and renal routes, with prolonged terminal persistence. Major toxicities include dose-limiting myelosuppression, severe mucositis/stomatitis, gastrointestinal injury, hepatotoxicity including veno-occlusive disease, potent vesicant extravasation injury, and radiation recall; overdose may cause profound marrow aplasia and multiorgan toxicity. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, alopecia, fever, rash, and infection risk. Clinically, dactinomycin is used mainly in pediatric and gestational malignancies, including Wilms tumor, rhabdomyosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, and testicular germ-cell cancer, typically in combination regimens.

Name: Selenium Sulfide
Description: Selenium sulfide (DrugBank DB00971) is a topical inorganic selenium compound composed of selenium and sulfide in a polymeric, poorly water-soluble sulfide lattice rather than a discrete small organic molecule, and is best classified as a metal-like inorganic anti-infective/keratolytic agent with an inorganic chalcogenide scaffold; structurally and pharmacologically it is most similar to other topical anti-seborrheic and antifungal agents such as zinc pyrithione, sulfur, ketoconazole, ciclopirox, and coal tar preparations, although it is chemically distinct from these organic azoles and hydroxypyridones. Its pharmacokinetics are dominated by minimal percutaneous absorption through intact skin, with increased uptake possible across inflamed, abraded, or occluded skin; distribution is therefore largely limited to the stratum corneum and hair-bearing scalp, systemic metabolism is negligible at usual topical doses, and any absorbed selenium is expected to enter endogenous selenium handling pathways with renal and, to a lesser extent, fecal excretion. The drug’s principal pharmacologic action is not mediated by a single canonical protein target; instead it exerts cytostatic effects on epidermal and follicular epithelial cells, reduces corneocyte turnover, and has direct activity against Malassezia species implicated in seborrheic dermatitis and dandruff. Indications include dandruff, seborrheic dermatitis of the scalp, and tinea versicolor. Toxicity is mainly local, including irritant dermatitis, burning, erythema, dryness, scaling, hair or scalp oiliness changes, and occasional hair discoloration or increased hair loss; mucosal or ocular exposure can cause marked irritation, and excessive or prolonged exposure on damaged skin raises concern for selenium toxicity, though this is uncommon in routine clinical use. Clinically, selenium sulfide is used as a shampoo, lotion, or suspension applied intermittently for chronic dandruff control, seborrheic dermatitis flares, and short-course treatment of pityriasis versicolor.

Name: Azelastine
Description: Azelastine (DrugBank DB00972) is a second-generation antiallergic agent built on a phthalazinone-based scaffold, structurally characterized by a fused aromatic diazine ketone core linked through a flexible side chain to a basic azepane ring and a chlorobenzyl substituent, features that confer lipophilicity, H1-receptor affinity, and local mucosal activity. It is classified chemically as a phthalazinone derivative and functionally as an antihistamine with additional mast-cell stabilizing and anti-inflammatory properties. Structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include other H1 antagonists such as olopatadine, ketotifen, levocabastine, and cetirizine, although azelastine is distinguished by its intranasal and ophthalmic use and multimodal local anti-allergic effects. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor; it also inhibits release of histamine, leukotrienes, and other inflammatory mediators from mast cells and may reduce eosinophil activation. After intranasal or ophthalmic administration, systemic absorption is limited but measurable; swallowed drug undergoes hepatic metabolism, chiefly via CYP3A4, to the active metabolite desmethylazelastine, with broad tissue distribution, high protein binding, and elimination mainly in feces with some renal excretion; terminal half-life is relatively prolonged, especially for the metabolite. It is indicated for allergic rhinitis, nonallergic vasomotor rhinitis, and allergic conjunctivitis, improving sneezing, rhinorrhea, nasal pruritus, congestion, and ocular itching. Adverse effects commonly include bitter taste, somnolence, fatigue, headache, nasal irritation, epistaxis, and dry mouth; toxicity is generally low but excessive exposure may cause CNS depression, anticholinergic-like symptoms, or local irritation, with caution in sedation-sensitive patients and when combined with alcohol or other CNS depressants. Clinically, it is used as an intranasal spray or ophthalmic solution for seasonal and perennial allergy management, either alone or in combination regimens, including use with intranasal corticosteroids for more refractory nasal symptoms.

Name: Ezetimibe
Description: Ezetimibe (DrugBank DB00973) is a synthetic azetidinone lipid-lowering agent whose structure is defined by a substituted 2-azetidinone four-membered lactam core bearing aryl groups, including fluorophenyl and hydroxyphenyl moieties, and a side chain that supports potent inhibition of intestinal sterol uptake; chemically it is best classified as a β-lactam-like azetidinone, with an aryl-substituted azetidinone scaffold distinct from statins but related to other cholesterol absorption inhibitors such as SCH58235 analogs, while clinically similar drugs by therapeutic effect include statins like atorvastatin and rosuvastatin, bile acid sequestrants, bempedoic acid, and PCSK9 inhibitors. Its principal target is Niemann-Pick C1-Like 1 protein (NPC1L1) on enterocytes and hepatocytes, reducing intestinal and biliary cholesterol absorption. After oral administration it is rapidly absorbed and extensively converted by intestinal and hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferases, especially UGT1A1, UGT1A3, and UGT2B15, to an active phenolic glucuronide; parent drug and metabolite undergo enterohepatic recycling, are highly protein bound, reach peak levels within hours, have an effective half-life of about 22 hours, and are eliminated mainly in feces with lesser urinary excretion. It is indicated for primary hypercholesterolemia, homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, and sitosterolemia, used alone or more often with statins to lower LDL cholesterol and reduce cardiovascular risk. Adverse effects are usually mild and include diarrhea, abdominal pain, fatigue, arthralgia, and upper respiratory symptoms; with statins, myalgia and transaminase elevations are more relevant. Toxicity is generally low, but examples include reversible hepatotoxicity, rare hypersensitivity, cholelithiasis with fibrates, and uncommon myopathy or rhabdomyolysis, particularly in combination regimens.

Name: Edetic acid
Description: Edetic acid (EDTA; DrugBank DB00974) is a small, highly polar aminopolycarboxylic acid built on an ethylenediamine scaffold bearing four acetic acid arms, creating a flexible hexadentate metal-binding structure with two tertiary amine nitrogens and four carboxylate donors that avidly chelate divalent and trivalent cations. Chemically it belongs to the polyaminocarboxylate chelators, with an ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid scaffold that is closely related to other metal-binding agents such as calcium disodium edetate, disodium edetate, and structurally analogous chelators including dimercaprol, succimer, and penicillamine, though these differ in donor atoms and metal selectivity. Its pharmacologic activity is largely non-receptor-mediated, with no classic protein target; instead it complexes free or protein-associated metal ions, especially lead and calcium, and can indirectly affect metalloprotein function and coagulation pathways by removing essential cations. Oral absorption is poor, so therapeutic use is typically parenteral; distribution is mainly extracellular with minimal membrane penetration, negligible metabolism, and rapid renal excretion largely as unchanged chelate. Toxicity is dominated by excessive metal depletion, particularly hypocalcemia with tetany, arrhythmia, and QT prolongation, as well as nephrotoxicity, zinc depletion, and local irritation; overdose or rapid infusion has caused renal failure and fatal calcium chelation. Adverse effects include nausea, fever, injection-site pain, headache, chills, thirst, and renal dysfunction. Clinically, edetic acid derivatives are used for heavy-metal poisoning, especially lead intoxication, and disodium edetate has also been used to treat severe hypercalcemia and as an anticoagulant additive in blood collection by sequestering calcium.

Name: Dipyridamole
Description: Dipyridamole (DrugBank DB00975) is a lipophilic piperidine-containing vasodilatory antiplatelet agent built on a substituted pyrimido-pyrimidine heteroaromatic core bearing two bis(2-hydroxyethyl)amino side chains and two piperidinyl substituents, a structure that places it in the pyrimido-pyrimidine antiplatelet/vasodilator chemical class with a fused aza-heterocyclic scaffold distinct from thienopyridines but pharmacologically related to other platelet inhibitors and coronary vasodilators such as aspirin, cilostazol, clopidogrel, ticlopidine, and adenosine-enhancing agents. Its principal targets and mechanisms include inhibition of phosphodiesterases, especially cGMP/cAMP-hydrolyzing activity, blockade of equilibrative nucleoside transporters SLC29A1/ENT1 and SLC29A2/ENT2 causing increased extracellular adenosine, and downstream modulation of platelet adenosine A2 receptors and vascular smooth muscle signaling. After oral administration, absorption is variable and formulation dependent, bioavailability is limited by poor aqueous solubility and first-pass metabolism, distribution is extensive with high protein binding, metabolism occurs predominantly in the liver via glucuronidation, and excretion is mainly biliary into feces with minimal renal elimination; the terminal half-life is on the order of about 10-12 hours. Clinically it is used for secondary prevention of thromboembolism, particularly ischemic stroke and transient ischemic attack in combination with aspirin, and historically with warfarin in patients with prosthetic heart valves; it is also used pharmacologically in myocardial perfusion stress testing because of coronary vasodilation. Common adverse effects include headache, dizziness, flushing, hypotension, nausea, diarrhea, and palpitations, while toxicity is largely an extension of vasodilatory and antiplatelet effects, including severe hypotension, worsening angina or coronary steal in susceptible coronary artery disease, and increased bleeding risk, especially with concomitant anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs.

Name: Telithromycin
Description: Telithromycin (DrugBank DB00976) is a semisynthetic ketolide antibacterial structurally derived from the macrolide erythromycin scaffold, characterized by a 14-membered lactone macrocycle bearing desosamine and a 3-keto substitution in place of the cladinose sugar, plus an extended carbamate-linked aryl-imidazolyl side chain that enhances ribosomal affinity and helps overcome some macrolide resistance mechanisms; thus it belongs to the ketolide subclass of macrolides and retains the classic erythromycin-like macrocyclic polyketide scaffold. Closely related or similar drugs include erythromycin, clarithromycin, azithromycin, roxithromycin, and other ketolide/macrolide analogs such as cethromycin. Its principal target is the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit, especially 23S rRNA domains within the peptidyl transferase/exit tunnel region, where it inhibits protein synthesis. After oral administration it is reasonably well absorbed, with bioavailability limited by first-pass metabolism, distributes widely into respiratory tissues and macrophages, is moderately protein bound, undergoes substantial hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 with potential for mechanism-based inhibition, and is eliminated through both biliary/fecal and renal routes. It is indicated primarily for mild to moderate community-acquired respiratory tract infections, including community-acquired pneumonia, acute bacterial sinusitis, and acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis caused by susceptible organisms. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, dizziness, dysgeusia, and visual disturbances, while serious toxicity includes hepatotoxicity with acute liver failure, QT prolongation, syncope, exacerbation of myasthenia gravis, and important CYP3A4-mediated drug interactions; accordingly, clinical use has been restricted and generally reserved for selected respiratory infections when alternative agents are unsuitable.

Name: Ethinylestradiol
Description: Ethinylestradiol (DrugBank DB00977) is a semisynthetic steroidal estrogen structurally defined by the estrane nucleus with an aromatic A-ring, a 17β-hydroxyl group, and a characteristic 17α-ethynyl substituent that blocks rapid oxidative inactivation and confers high oral potency; it belongs to the phenolic steroid estrogens and more specifically the ethinylated estradiol derivatives, built on an estradiol/estrane steroid scaffold. Closely related or pharmacologically similar drugs include estradiol, mestranol, quinestrol, diethylstilbestrol, and combined hormonal contraceptive estrogens used with progestins such as levonorgestrel or norethindrone. It is well absorbed orally but undergoes substantial first-pass metabolism; distribution is extensive with high plasma protein binding, metabolism occurs mainly via CYP3A4-mediated hydroxylation and conjugation pathways including glucuronidation and sulfation with enterohepatic recirculation, and excretion is through urine and feces predominantly as metabolites. Its principal targets are estrogen receptor alpha (ESR1) and estrogen receptor beta (ESR2), with downstream regulation of gonadotropin secretion and estrogen-responsive gene transcription. Clinically, it is indicated for contraception, treatment of hypoestrogenic states, menstrual cycle control, abnormal uterine bleeding, dysmenorrhea, acne in selected combined products, and palliative management of advanced prostate cancer or certain breast cancers. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, breast tenderness, headache, edema, melasma, and breakthrough bleeding, while major toxicities include venous thromboembolism, stroke, myocardial infarction, hypertension, cholestatic liver injury, and increased risk of some hormone-sensitive neoplasms, with overdose or excessive exposure potentially causing marked nausea, vomiting, and vaginal bleeding.

Name: Lomefloxacin
Description: Lomefloxacin (DrugBank DB00978) is a difluorinated fluoroquinolone antibacterial built on the 4-quinolone/1,4-dihydroquinoline-3-carboxylic acid scaffold, characterized by the quinolone ketone-carboxylate pharmacophore, fluorine substitution that enhances antibacterial potency, a piperazinyl group at C7 that broadens Gram-negative activity, and a methyl substitution on the ring nitrogen; chemically it belongs to the quinolone carboxylic acid class, with close structural and pharmacologic similarity to ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin, ofloxacin, enoxacin, and pefloxacin. Its principal targets are bacterial DNA gyrase, especially GyrA/GyrB, and topoisomerase IV, leading to inhibition of DNA replication, transcription, and chromosomal segregation. Lomefloxacin is used for susceptible bacterial infections, particularly uncomplicated and complicated urinary tract infections, cystitis, pyelonephritis, chronic bacterial bronchitis exacerbations, and some lower respiratory or skin/soft tissue infections depending on local susceptibility patterns. Orally it is generally well absorbed with moderate to high bioavailability, reaches therapeutic concentrations in urine, kidney, prostate, and respiratory tissues, has relatively low protein binding, undergoes minimal hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by renal excretion with a half-life that supports once- or twice-daily dosing; dose reduction is required in renal impairment. Important toxicities include class-associated tendinopathy and tendon rupture, CNS stimulation such as dizziness, insomnia, agitation, or seizures, QT-related proarrhythmic potential, dysglycemia, peripheral neuropathy, and particularly notable phototoxicity, a well-recognized liability of lomefloxacin. Common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, headache, rash, and photosensitivity reactions. Clinically, its use has been limited or displaced in many settings because of safety concerns and resistance despite historical utility in urinary and respiratory infections.

Name: Cyclopentolate
Description: Cyclopentolate (DrugBank DB00979) is a synthetic antimuscarinic ophthalmic agent structurally characterized as a tertiary amino alcohol ester composed of a substituted glycolate-like ester linking a cyclopentyl ring and a 2-dimethylaminoethyl moiety to an aromatic phenyl group, giving a lipophilic arylcyclopentyl tertiary amine ester architecture; chemically it is classified as an anticholinergic, specifically a parasympatholytic mydriatic and cycloplegic, with a scaffold closely related to amino alcohol ester antimuscarinics. Similar drugs include atropine, homatropine, tropicamide, scopolamine, and to some extent dicyclomine, which share muscarinic receptor antagonism but differ in onset and duration. Its principal pharmacologic targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially M3 on the iris sphincter and ciliary muscle, with broader nonselective antagonism across CHRM1-CHRM5 likely contributing to systemic effects. After topical ocular administration, absorption occurs through the cornea and conjunctiva with some nasolacrimal systemic uptake; distribution is mainly local to anterior ocular tissues but systemic penetration, including CNS exposure, can occur in children; metabolism is presumed largely hepatic ester hydrolysis and further biotransformation, with renal excretion of metabolites and some unchanged drug. It is indicated for diagnostic mydriasis and cycloplegia, particularly refraction in pediatric patients, amblyopia assessment, and preoperative ophthalmic examination. Adverse effects include transient stinging, blurred vision, photophobia, increased intraocular pressure, and conjunctival irritation, while toxicity may produce anticholinergic syndrome with tachycardia, flushing, dry mouth, fever, urinary retention, hallucinations, ataxia, and seizures, especially after excessive dosing or in infants; clinically, it is used as short-acting eye drops when rapid but not prolonged pupillary dilation and ciliary paralysis are desired.

Name: Ramelteon
Description: Ramelteon (DB00980) is a synthetic melatonin receptor agonist built on a compact tricyclic indane-like scaffold in which a fused cyclopropyl-tetrahydronaphthalene core is substituted with a propionamide side chain and an oxygen-containing substituent that helps mimic key melatonin pharmacophores; chemically it is a melatonin analog and heterotricyclic amide rather than a benzodiazepine or Z-drug hypnotic. Its scaffold and receptor-binding features make it broadly similar to other melatonergic agents such as melatonin, tasimelteon, and agomelatine, although ramelteon is more selective as a hypnotic chronobiotic. Its principal targets are the human melatonin receptors MT1 and MT2, encoded by MTNR1A and MTNR1B, with therapeutic activity mainly attributed to MT1-mediated sleep onset promotion and MT2-mediated circadian phase regulation. After oral administration it is rapidly absorbed but undergoes substantial first-pass metabolism, giving low absolute bioavailability; it is highly protein bound, distributed systemically, extensively metabolized in the liver primarily by CYP1A2 with lesser roles for CYP2C and CYP3A4, and eliminated mainly as inactive metabolites in urine. A notable active metabolite, M-II, circulates at higher exposure than parent drug but with lower potency. Toxicity is generally low at therapeutic doses, with major concerns including CNS depression, next-day impairment, endocrine effects such as prolactin elevation or reduced testosterone, and increased exposure with strong CYP1A2 inhibitors such as fluvoxamine. It is indicated for insomnia characterized by difficulty with sleep onset, and clinically used for patients needing a non-controlled-substance hypnotic, especially when abuse liability should be minimized. Common adverse effects include somnolence, dizziness, fatigue, nausea, headache, and exacerbation of abnormal sleep behaviors in susceptible patients.

Name: Physostigmine
Description: Physostigmine (DB00981), also known as eserine, is a naturally derived tertiary amine carbamate alkaloid with an indole-containing pyrroloindoline framework bearing a carbamate ester, placing it in the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor class and giving it a compact indole alkaloid scaffold distinct from simpler quaternary ammonium cholinesterase inhibitors. Chemically and pharmacologically it is related to other reversible cholinesterase inhibitors such as neostigmine, pyridostigmine, rivastigmine, and donepezil, although physostigmine is distinguished by being a tertiary amine that readily penetrates the blood-brain barrier. Its principal target protein is acetylcholinesterase (AChE), with lesser activity at butyrylcholinesterase (BCHE), producing increased synaptic acetylcholine at central and peripheral muscarinic and nicotinic sites. After parenteral or ophthalmic administration it is absorbed sufficiently to produce systemic effects, distributes widely including into the CNS and eye, undergoes relatively rapid hydrolytic and hepatic metabolism, and is excreted mainly as metabolites in urine; its onset is rapid and duration is short, often necessitating repeated dosing. Clinically it has been used for anticholinergic toxicity, especially delirium caused by atropine, scopolamine, antihistamines, or tricyclic-related antimuscarinic syndromes, and historically for glaucoma or postoperative ileus. Toxicity reflects cholinergic excess and may include bradycardia, bronchospasm, hypersalivation, miosis, sweating, vomiting, diarrhea, seizures, and potentially life-threatening cholinergic crisis or asystole, with caution warranted in asthma, cardiac conduction disease, bowel or urinary obstruction, and mixed overdoses where proconvulsant or cardiotoxic effects may be amplified.

Name: Isotretinoin
Description: Isotretinoin (DrugBank DB00982) is the 13-cis geometric isomer of retinoic acid, a highly lipophilic vitamin A derivative characterized by a conjugated polyene chain terminating in a carboxylic acid and linked to a substituted cyclohexenyl ring, placing it in the retinoid/apocarotenoid chemical category with a retinoic acid polyene scaffold; structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include tretinoin (all-trans-retinoic acid), acitretin, adapalene, tazarotene, and alitretinoin. Its activity is mediated largely through intracellular isomerization and modulation of retinoid signaling, with known targets functionally including retinoic acid receptors RAR-alpha, RAR-beta, and RAR-gamma and retinoid X receptors RXR-alpha, RXR-beta, and RXR-gamma, leading to reduced sebaceous gland size and sebum production, normalization of follicular keratinization, and anti-inflammatory effects. Oral absorption is variable but increases substantially with food, especially fat; the drug is highly protein bound, distributes widely into tissues, undergoes hepatic metabolism to 4-oxo-isotretinoin, tretinoin, and other oxidative metabolites via CYP enzymes including CYP2C8, CYP2C9, CYP3A4, and CYP2B6, and is eliminated through both urine and feces, with an elimination half-life in the range of about 10-20 hours for parent drug and longer for major metabolites. Clinically, it is used primarily for severe nodular or recalcitrant acne vulgaris and in some settings off-label for rosacea, folliculitis, hidradenitis suppurativa, or disorders of keratinization; major toxicities include profound teratogenicity with craniofacial, cardiac, thymic, and CNS fetal malformations, hepatotoxicity, hypertriglyceridemia, pancreatitis, mucocutaneous toxicity, and rare neuropsychiatric or musculoskeletal adverse events. Common side effects include cheilitis, xerosis, dry eyes, epistaxis, photosensitivity, myalgia, arthralgia, elevated transaminases, and lipid abnormalities, and its clinical use therefore requires strict pregnancy prevention, laboratory monitoring, and careful dose titration in dermatologic practice.

Name: Formoterol
Description: Formoterol (DrugBank DB00983) is a long-acting, highly potent phenylethanolamine bronchodilator characterized structurally by an aryloxypropanolamine-like sympathomimetic framework bearing a substituted formamide and two aromatic rings with phenolic functionality that supports strong β2-adrenoceptor binding and prolonged action; chemically it is classified as a selective long-acting β2-adrenergic receptor agonist, and its core scaffold is a substituted phenethylamine/phenoxyalkanolamine bronchodilator motif closely related to other β2-agonists. Similar drugs include salmeterol, indacaterol, olodaterol, vilanterol, and shorter-acting congeners such as albuterol and terbutaline. Its principal target is the β2-adrenergic receptor encoded by ADRB2, with lesser activity at β1 receptors at higher exposures, leading to adenylate cyclase activation, increased intracellular cAMP, and airway smooth-muscle relaxation. After inhalation, formoterol is rapidly absorbed from the lung with onset within minutes, exhibits moderate systemic bioavailability from pulmonary and swallowed fractions, distributes widely with clinically relevant protein binding, undergoes hepatic metabolism mainly by direct glucuronidation and O-demethylation followed by conjugation, and is excreted in urine and feces as parent drug and metabolites, with an elimination half-life compatible with twice-daily dosing. Toxicity reflects exaggerated sympathomimetic effects, including tremor, tachycardia, palpitations, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, QT prolongation, and, in overdose, arrhythmia or paradoxical bronchospasm. It is indicated for maintenance treatment of asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, including bronchospasm prevention and exercise-induced bronchospasm prophylaxis in selected formulations, and is used clinically as an inhaled maintenance bronchodilator, often in fixed-dose combinations with inhaled corticosteroids such as budesonide or mometasone for persistent asthma and with other agents in COPD.

Name: Dimenhydrinate
Description: Dimenhydrinate (DB00985) is a salt complex composed of diphenhydramine and 8-chlorotheophylline, in which the therapeutically dominant moiety is the ethanolamine-class first-generation H1 antihistamine diphenhydramine; structurally, it contains a benzhydryl diaryl ether linked through a dimethylaminoethoxy side chain, while the chlorinated xanthine component is included primarily to offset sedation. Its chemical category is therefore an antihistamine/antiemetic combination built on an ethanolamine antihistamine scaffold with a benzhydryl ether pharmacophore and an associated xanthine counterion. Closely related or similar drugs include diphenhydramine, doxylamine, clemastine, meclizine, cyclizine, and promethazine, which share antihistaminic and antiemetic properties. Pharmacologically, dimenhydrinate acts mainly at the histamine H1 receptor and also exhibits antimuscarinic activity, with antiemetic effects linked to suppression of vestibular stimulation and reduced signaling to the vomiting center; relevant targets include HRH1 and likely muscarinic acetylcholine receptors such as CHRM1. It is well absorbed orally, distributes widely including into the CNS, has an onset typically within 15 to 30 minutes, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism principally via cytochrome P450-mediated pathways similar to diphenhydramine, and is excreted mainly in urine as metabolites. It is indicated for prevention and treatment of motion sickness and for nausea, vomiting, and vertigo, including postoperative or vestibular symptoms. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention; toxicity reflects exaggerated CNS depression or anticholinergic effects, with agitation, confusion, tachycardia, hyperthermia, hallucinations, or seizures in overdose, particularly in children or older adults. Clinically, it is used orally, intramuscularly, or intravenously for travel-related motion sickness, acute nausea, and symptomatic control of vestibular disorders such as labyrinthitis or Ménière-like vertigo.

Name: Glycopyrronium
Description: Glycopyrronium (glycopyrrolate; DrugBank DB00986) is a synthetic quaternary ammonium antimuscarinic built around a permanently charged pyrrolidinium-containing ester that links a substituted cyclopentyl/hydroxycyclopentyl glycolate-like moiety to a tertiary alcohol-bearing carboxylate framework; chemically it is classified as an anticholinergic, specifically a quaternary ammonium muscarinic receptor antagonist, and its core scaffold is the quaternary pyrrolidinium ester scaffold shared with several inhaled long-acting muscarinic antagonists. Closely related or pharmacologically similar drugs include atropine, scopolamine, ipratropium, tiotropium, aclidinium, and umeclidinium, with glycopyrronium being distinguished by limited blood-brain barrier penetration due to its permanent positive charge. Its principal targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially CHRM1, CHRM2, and CHRM3, with therapeutic bronchodilation and antisecretory effects mainly reflecting M3 blockade in airway and exocrine tissues. Pharmacokinetically, oral absorption is incomplete and variable, inhaled delivery provides local pulmonary action with low systemic bioavailability, distribution is largely extracellular with minimal CNS entry, metabolism is limited or partial depending on route, and elimination is predominantly renal, with unchanged drug and metabolites excreted in urine. Toxicity is that of antimuscarinic excess, including tachycardia, urinary retention, decreased sweating, hyperthermia, ileus, blurred vision, and potential precipitation of angle-closure glaucoma; overdose may produce severe dry mouth and cardiovascular stimulation. Clinically it is used for maintenance treatment of COPD, as a bronchodilator in some asthma regimens, and perioperatively to reduce salivary and respiratory secretions or prevent vagally mediated bradycardia, while common adverse effects include xerostomia, constipation, dysuria, palpitations, cough, headache, and nasopharyngitis.

Name: Cytarabine
Description: Cytarabine (DB00987) is a synthetic pyrimidine nucleoside antimetabolite and deoxycytidine analog whose structure consists of a cytosine base linked by a beta-N-glycosidic bond to an arabinose sugar, distinguished from physiologic deoxycytidine by the 2′-hydroxyl stereochemistry of arabinose; chemically it belongs to antineoplastic antimetabolites, specifically nucleoside analogs, and its core scaffold is an arabinofuranosyl cytosine scaffold. It is closely related to other nucleoside analog drugs such as gemcitabine, decitabine, azacitidine, and fludarabine, which share pyrimidine or purine antimetabolite features. After intravenous, subcutaneous, or intrathecal administration, oral absorption is negligible because of rapid degradation; distribution is wide but central nervous system penetration is limited after systemic dosing, prompting intrathecal use for meningeal disease. Cytarabine is activated intracellularly by deoxycytidine kinase to ara-CTP, its active metabolite, and is inactivated mainly by cytidine deaminase in liver, blood, and other tissues to uracil arabinoside; elimination is predominantly renal, largely as inactive metabolite, with a short plasma half-life. Its main targets are functional rather than receptor-based, notably DNA polymerases, with incorporation into DNA causing chain termination and inhibition of DNA synthesis in S-phase; deoxycytidine kinase and cytidine deaminase are key determinants of response. It is indicated chiefly for acute myeloid leukemia, also acute lymphoblastic leukemia, blast crisis of chronic myeloid leukemia, and leptomeningeal leukemia/lymphoma. Toxicity is dominated by dose-limiting myelosuppression, severe infections, mucositis, hepatotoxicity, cerebellar and other neurotoxicity, conjunctivitis, and rare pulmonary or gastrointestinal toxicity; common adverse effects include neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, fever, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, and the cytokine-like cytarabine syndrome. Clinically, it is a backbone of AML induction and consolidation regimens, used in standard-dose continuous infusion, high-dose schedules, and intrathecal prophylaxis or treatment of CNS leukemia.

Name: Dopamine
Description: Dopamine (DrugBank DB00988) is an endogenous catecholamine and phenethylamine whose structure consists of a catechol ring bearing adjacent 3,4-dihydroxyl groups attached through a two-carbon ethyl chain to a primary amine, giving a compact catechol-ethylamine scaffold that underlies its identity as the immediate biosynthetic precursor of norepinephrine and epinephrine; chemically it belongs to the monoamine neurotransmitters and catecholamine sympathomimetics, and it is closely related to agents such as norepinephrine, epinephrine, dobutamine, and the dopamine agonists fenoldopam and apomorphine by shared catecholaminergic pharmacology or receptor engagement. Its principal targets are dopamine receptors D1-D5, with dose-dependent indirect or direct functional activity at adrenergic receptors, especially beta1 and alpha1, producing renal/mesenteric vasodilation at lower doses and increasing cardiac inotropy and vasoconstriction at higher doses. Because oral administration is ineffective owing to extensive first-pass metabolism and poor blood-brain penetration, clinical dopamine is given intravenously, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid, has a very short plasma half-life of only minutes, and is rapidly metabolized by monoamine oxidase and catechol-O-methyltransferase to inactive metabolites such as homovanillic acid that are excreted in urine. It is indicated for hemodynamic support in shock states with hypotension, low cardiac output, severe heart failure, and post–cardiac surgery circulatory collapse. Toxicity includes excessive vasoconstriction, tachyarrhythmias, myocardial ischemia, hypertension, and tissue necrosis after extravasation; common adverse effects include palpitations, headache, nausea, anxiety, dyspnea, and ventricular ectopy. Clinically, it is used as a titratable ICU vasopressor/inotrope to restore perfusion in cardiogenic or septic shock and refractory symptomatic hypotension.

Name: Rivastigmine
Description: Rivastigmine (DrugBank DB00989) is a small, lipophilic tertiary amine carbamate built on an N-ethyl-N-methylphenyl carbamate framework with a dimethyl-substituted aromatic ring, placing it in the phenyl carbamate class and more specifically within the pseudo-irreversible cholinesterase inhibitor category; its key scaffold is an aryl carbamate that covalently carbamylates catalytic serine residues in cholinesterases. It is chemically and pharmacologically related to other anti-dementia cholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezil, galantamine, and the older agent physostigmine, although rivastigmine is distinguished by dual inhibition of acetylcholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase, with primary targets ACHE and BCHE. After oral or transdermal administration it is well absorbed, crosses the blood-brain barrier, shows moderate protein binding and a relatively short plasma half-life, but its pharmacodynamic effect persists longer because enzyme recovery is slow; it undergoes extensive non-CYP hydrolytic metabolism to inactive or weakly active metabolites and is excreted predominantly in urine, making major CYP-mediated drug interactions less important. Its principal indication is symptomatic treatment of mild to moderate Alzheimer disease and Parkinson disease dementia, where it is used to improve cognition, attention, global function, and activities of daily living. Toxicity is mainly cholinergic and dose related, including severe nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia, weight loss, dehydration, bradycardia, syncope, tremor exacerbation, and, in overdose, marked cholinergic crisis with excessive secretions and conduction disturbances. In clinical practice it is given orally or as a transdermal patch, the latter often improving gastrointestinal tolerability.

Name: Exemestane
Description: Exemestane (DrugBank DB00990) is a steroidal, irreversible aromatase inhibitor structurally derived from the androstane nucleus, characterized by a rigid four-ring steroid scaffold with a 3-keto group and a distinctive 6-methylene substitution that confers mechanism-based, suicide-inhibitor behavior toward aromatase; chemically it is classified as a synthetic steroidal endocrine antineoplastic agent and belongs to the androstenedione-like aromatase inactivator scaffold, contrasting with nonsteroidal triazole aromatase inhibitors such as anastrozole and letrozole, while showing greatest similarity to other steroidal estrogen-lowering agents such as formestane. Its principal target protein is aromatase, encoded by CYP19A1, thereby blocking peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogens in postmenopausal tissues. Orally administered exemestane is well absorbed, with bioavailability increased by food, extensive tissue distribution, high protein binding, and substantial first-pass metabolism; it is metabolized mainly by CYP3A4 oxidation and aldoketoreductase-mediated reduction to active and inactive metabolites, then eliminated predominantly in urine and feces as metabolites, with a terminal half-life of roughly one day. It is indicated primarily for estrogen receptor-positive early or advanced breast cancer in postmenopausal women, including adjuvant therapy after tamoxifen and treatment of progressive metastatic disease. Common adverse effects reflect estrogen deprivation and include hot flashes, arthralgia, fatigue, insomnia, nausea, sweating, headache, and decreased bone mineral density; toxicities may include osteoporosis, fracture risk, dyslipidemia, hepatotoxicity, and rarely severe hypersensitivity. Clinically, it is used as sequential endocrine therapy, as monotherapy in advanced disease, and sometimes in selected fertility or gynecologic endocrine protocols where estrogen suppression is desired.

Name: Oxaprozin
Description: Oxaprozin (DrugBank DB00991) is a propionic acid–derived nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug structurally characterized by a diaryl-substituted oxazole core bearing a para-hydroxyphenyl group and a second phenyl ring linked to an acetic acid side chain, giving it an acidic, highly lipophilic heteroaryl arylacetic/propionic acid-like NSAID profile; chemically it is classified as an oxazole-containing NSAID within the arylalkanoic acid family, and its key scaffold is a 1,3-oxazole diaryl framework. Similar drugs include other COX-inhibiting NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, naproxen, ketoprofen, fenoprofen, and diclofenac, which share anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antipyretic pharmacology despite distinct scaffolds. Its principal targets are cyclooxygenase-1 and cyclooxygenase-2, with inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis underlying efficacy. Oxaprozin is well absorbed orally, reaches peak concentrations in several hours, is extensively albumin bound, distributes broadly in plasma and inflamed tissues, undergoes predominantly hepatic biotransformation including oxidation and conjugation, and is eliminated slowly through both renal and fecal routes, with a long half-life supporting once-daily dosing. It is indicated for osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and musculoskeletal pain or inflammatory symptoms such as joint swelling, stiffness, and tenderness. Clinical use includes chronic outpatient management of arthritic pain and inflammation in adults and selected pediatric juvenile idiopathic arthritis settings. Toxicities are typical of nonselective NSAIDs and include gastrointestinal ulceration, bleeding, and perforation, renal impairment, sodium and fluid retention, hypertension, hepatotoxicity, and elevated cardiovascular thrombotic risk; overdose may cause CNS depression, nausea, vomiting, and metabolic disturbances. Common side effects include dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, dizziness, headache, rash, edema, and somnolence.

Name: Azathioprine
Description: Azathioprine (DrugBank DB00993) is a thiopurine immunosuppressant and antimetabolite structurally defined as a 6-mercaptopurine prodrug in which the purine thione nucleus is linked through sulfur to a 1-methyl-4-nitroimidazole moiety, giving a sulfur-substituted purine scaffold that combines a thiolated hypoxanthine-like core with a nitroimidazole leaving group; chemically it belongs to purine analogs, thiopurines, and imidazolyl derivatives, and its closest related drugs include 6-mercaptopurine, thioguanine, and functionally similar antiproliferative immunosuppressants such as mycophenolate. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed, distributes widely, and is converted nonenzymatically and via glutathione-dependent processes to 6-mercaptopurine, which is then metabolized by hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase to active thioinosine and thioguanine nucleotides, while xanthine oxidase and thiopurine S-methyltransferase are major competing inactivation pathways; metabolites are eliminated primarily in urine. Its principal pharmacologic targets are not classic receptors but intracellular enzymes and pathways including HPRT, TPMT, xanthine oxidase, GMPS, IMPDH-related purine synthesis steps, Rac1 signaling, and DNA/RNA synthesis machinery in proliferating lymphocytes. Clinically it is used to prevent renal transplant rejection and to treat autoimmune diseases such as inflammatory bowel disease, Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, autoimmune hepatitis, lupus, and some vasculitides. Dose-limiting toxicity is chiefly myelosuppression, especially in TPMT or NUDT15 deficiency or with allopurinol/febuxostat coadministration; hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, severe infection, gastrointestinal intolerance, rash, alopecia, and increased long-term risk of lymphoma, nonmelanoma skin cancer, and rare hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma are important adverse effects.

Name: Auranofin
Description: Auranofin (DrugBank DB00995) is an orally active gold(I) coordination complex in which a linear Au(I) center is ligated by triethylphosphine and a tetra-O-acetyl-1-thio-β-D-glucopyranosato thiolate, giving a lipophilic organogold structure that functions as a thiol-reactive metal drug rather than a classical small organic inhibitor. Chemically it is an antirheumatic gold compound, specifically a monovalent organogold phosphine-thiolate, built on a gold-phosphine/thioglucose scaffold. Similar drugs include other chrysotherapeutic agents such as sodium aurothiomalate, aurothioglucose, and gold sodium thiomalate, although these are typically parenteral and less lipophilic. After oral administration, absorption is incomplete but clinically meaningful; circulating gold is extensively protein bound, especially to albumin and erythrocyte components, distributes slowly into synovial tissue and reticuloendothelial compartments, undergoes ligand exchange and biotransformation to protein-bound gold species rather than classic CYP-dependent metabolism, and is eliminated slowly in feces and urine with a prolonged terminal half-life reflecting tissue retention. Its major pharmacologic targets are thiol- and selenol-dependent proteins, especially thioredoxin reductase 1 and 2, with downstream effects on redox signaling, NF-κB-associated inflammatory pathways, and macrophage/lymphocyte function; inhibitory activity has also been reported against IKK-related signaling and some cysteine enzymes. It is indicated primarily for rheumatoid arthritis, particularly active inflammatory disease with pain, stiffness, and synovitis, and has also been explored experimentally for parasitic, bacterial, viral, and neoplastic disorders. Toxicity includes diarrhea and enterocolitis, rash, pruritus, stomatitis, conjunctivitis, proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, aplastic anemia, hepatotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy, and rare interstitial pneumonitis or severe hypersensitivity. Clinically, it has been used as a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug in patients with inadequate response to NSAIDs, though use has declined because of modest efficacy, slow onset, and significant monitoring requirements.

Name: Gabapentin
Description: Gabapentin (DrugBank DB00996) is a small, highly polar gamma-aminobutyric acid analog built on a substituted cyclohexane scaffold, specifically a cyclohexylacetic acid framework bearing a primary aminomethyl group and a carboxylic acid, giving a conformationally restricted amino acid-like structure despite not acting directly as a GABA receptor agonist; chemically it is classified as a gabapentinoid and aliphatic amino acid derivative, with the key scaffold being 1-(aminomethyl)cyclohexaneacetic acid. Similar drugs include pregabalin as the closest marketed analog, and more distantly mirogabalin and phenibut as related CNS-active GABA-analog ligands. Its principal known pharmacologic targets are the alpha-2-delta subunits of voltage-gated calcium channels, especially CACNA2D1 and CACNA2D2, which reduce excitatory neurotransmitter release. Oral absorption occurs by a saturable intestinal L-amino acid transport process, producing dose-dependent bioavailability that decreases at higher doses; distribution is relatively broad with negligible plasma protein binding, CNS penetration is modest but clinically sufficient, metabolism is minimal to negligible, and elimination is predominantly renal as unchanged drug with a half-life of about 5 to 7 hours, prolonged in renal impairment. Toxicity is generally low but includes dose-related CNS depression, ataxia, profound somnolence, dizziness, and overdose presentations such as lethargy and diplopia, with respiratory depression more likely when combined with opioids or other sedatives. It is indicated for partial seizures and neuropathic pain, particularly postherpetic neuralgia, and is widely used clinically for diabetic neuropathy, radicular pain, post-surgical neuropathic states, restless legs syndrome, and some anxiety or pruritus syndromes; common adverse effects include dizziness, somnolence, peripheral edema, fatigue, tremor, blurred vision, weight gain, and cognitive slowing.

Name: Doxorubicin
Description: Doxorubicin (DrugBank DB00997) is an anthracycline antineoplastic antibiotic characterized by a planar tetracyclic anthraquinone-like anthracycline aglycone, doxorubicinone, bearing quinone and hydroquinone functionalities and linked through a glycosidic bond to the amino sugar daunosamine; chemically it belongs to the anthracycline/anthracenedione-related natural product class and is built on the anthracycline aromatic polyketide scaffold. Closely related drugs include daunorubicin, epirubicin, idarubicin, and the anthracenedione mitoxantrone, which share DNA-intercalating and topoisomerase-targeting properties. Its principal targets are topoisomerase II alpha and beta (TOP2A, TOP2B), with pharmacologic effects also involving DNA intercalation, free-radical generation, and indirect engagement of proteasome- and chromatin-associated stress pathways. After intravenous administration, absorption is not relevant; distribution is extensive with high tissue uptake, partial plasma protein binding, poor CNS penetration, and hepatic accumulation; metabolism occurs mainly in the liver to doxorubicinol and other reductive or conjugated metabolites; excretion is predominantly biliary/fecal with a smaller renal component, and terminal elimination is prolonged and multi-compartmental. Major toxicities include cumulative dose-dependent cardiomyopathy and heart failure, severe myelosuppression, mucositis, vesicant extravasation injury, and rare therapy-related leukemia; mechanistically, cardiotoxicity is linked to oxidative injury and TOP2B effects in cardiomyocytes. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, alopecia, stomatitis, neutropenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and red discoloration of urine. Clinically, doxorubicin is used in leukemias, lymphomas, breast cancer, sarcomas, ovarian cancer, small-cell lung cancer, and pediatric solid tumors, including in regimens such as ABVD for Hodgkin lymphoma and AC-based therapy for breast cancer.

Name: Frovatriptan
Description: Frovatriptan (DrugBank DB00998) is a synthetic antimigraine agent of the triptan class, structurally characterized as an indole-derived serotonin analog bearing a fused tricyclic pyridoindole core with a basic piperidine-like side-chain functionality and a carboxamide substituent that support high affinity for cranial serotonergic receptors; chemically it is categorized as a selective 5-hydroxytryptamine receptor agonist, and its core scaffold is best described as a rigid azaindole/pyridoindole triptan scaffold. It is closely related to other triptans used for acute migraine, including sumatriptan, rizatriptan, zolmitriptan, naratriptan, eletriptan, and almotriptan, which share serotonergic vasoconstrictive and trigeminovascular actions. Its principal targets are 5-HT1B and 5-HT1D receptors, with activity also reported at 5-HT1F, leading to inhibition of trigeminal neuropeptide release and constriction of dilated intracranial vessels. Orally, frovatriptan is well absorbed, reaches peak concentrations in roughly 2 to 4 hours, has moderate bioavailability, low protein binding, broad tissue distribution, and an unusually long elimination half-life of about 26 hours; it undergoes hepatic metabolism primarily via CYP1A2 to less active metabolites and is cleared through both renal and fecal excretion. It is indicated for acute treatment of migraine with or without aura and is also used short-term for menstrual-associated migraine. Adverse effects commonly include dizziness, fatigue, paresthesia, flushing, dry mouth, nausea, and chest or throat pressure. Toxicity is generally dose-related and usually mild to moderate, but class-relevant serious risks include hypertension, coronary vasospasm, myocardial ischemia, arrhythmia, serotonin syndrome, and medication-overuse headache, especially in patients with cardiovascular disease or when combined with serotonergic drugs.

Name: Hydrochlorothiazide
Description: Hydrochlorothiazide (DrugBank DB00999) is a benzothiadiazine sulfonamide diuretic whose structure consists of a chlorinated, hydrogenated benzothiadiazine 1,1-dioxide ring system bearing sulfamyl functionality, giving a heteroaromatic sulfone-rich framework with weakly acidic sulfonamide groups that are important for activity; chemically it belongs to the thiazide diuretic class, and its core scaffold is the chlorobenzothiadiazine dioxide nucleus. It is closely related to other thiazide or thiazide-like agents such as chlorothiazide, bendroflumethiazide, methyclothiazide, chlorthalidone, indapamide, and metolazone, which share distal convoluted tubule natriuretic effects. Its principal target is the renal sodium/chloride cotransporter SLC12A3 (NCC) in the distal convoluted tubule, with downstream effects on electrolyte handling rather than broad receptor pharmacology. After oral administration it is moderately well absorbed, has an onset within hours, limited metabolism, modest plasma protein binding, distribution largely in extracellular fluid and kidney, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by renal excretion, so accumulation may occur in renal impairment. Clinically it is indicated for hypertension and edema, including edema associated with heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, corticosteroid use, nephrotic syndrome, and chronic kidney-related salt retention, and it is also used to reduce recurrent calcium nephrolithiasis in hypercalciuric patients and sometimes for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Toxicities reflect exaggerated diuresis and sulfonamide-related intolerance, including hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia, metabolic alkalosis, dehydration, hypotension, hyperuricemia with gout, hyperglycemia, photosensitivity, rash, and rarely pancreatitis or severe hypersensitivity. In practice it is widely used alone or combined with agents such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or beta-blockers for chronic blood pressure control and volume management.

Name: Cyclacillin
Description: Cyclacillin (DrugBank DB01000) is an orally active semisynthetic beta-lactam antibiotic of the aminopenicillin class, structurally defined by the conserved penam nucleus in which a strained four-membered beta-lactam ring is fused to a thiazolidine ring and substituted at the 6-position with an amino-containing side chain that increases acid stability and broadens gram-negative activity; its core chemical scaffold is therefore the 6-aminopenicillanic acid penicillin scaffold. It is closely related to ampicillin and amoxicillin, and more broadly similar to other beta-lactams such as penicillin G and certain oral cephalosporins in antibacterial spectrum and mechanism. Cyclacillin targets bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, particularly transpeptidases involved in peptidoglycan cross-linking, thereby inhibiting cell-wall synthesis and promoting lysis in susceptible organisms. Pharmacokinetically, it is absorbed after oral administration, distributed into many extracellular tissues and fluids with limited intracellular and cerebrospinal penetration unless meninges are inflamed, undergoes minimal hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by renal excretion via glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, giving a relatively short half-life and potential need for dose adjustment in renal impairment. Toxicity is generally low but includes class risks of hypersensitivity ranging from rash and urticaria to anaphylaxis, gastrointestinal irritation, antibiotic-associated diarrhea and rarely pseudomembranous colitis, superinfection, interstitial nephritis, eosinophilia, and occasional hepatic enzyme elevation or hematologic effects. Clinically it has been used for susceptible respiratory, urinary tract, skin and soft-tissue, and otorhinolaryngologic infections, including streptococcal pharyngitis, bronchitis, cystitis, and uncomplicated infections caused by non-beta-lactamase-producing organisms.

Name: Albuterol
Description: Albuterol (salbutamol; DrugBank DB01001) is a short-acting sympathomimetic bronchodilator built on a substituted phenethylamine/ethanolamine framework, with a saligenin-type aromatic ring bearing hydroxymethyl and phenolic hydroxyl substituents and a β-hydroxylated side chain terminating in a tert-butylamino group; chemically it is a β2-adrenergic receptor agonist in the phenylaminoethanol class, and its core scaffold is the arylethanolamine beta-agonist scaffold optimized for β2 selectivity. Closely related drugs include terbutaline, metaproterenol, fenoterol, and the longer-acting analogs salmeterol and formoterol, which share the same adrenergic bronchodilator pharmacophore. Its principal target is the beta-2 adrenergic receptor encoded by ADRB2, with downstream activation of Gs signaling, adenylate cyclase, and cyclic AMP-mediated bronchial smooth muscle relaxation; minor cardiovascular activity can reflect spillover at ADRB1. Albuterol is indicated for rapid relief and prevention of bronchospasm in asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and exercise-induced bronchospasm, and is also used adjunctively to shift potassium intracellularly in hyperkalemia. After inhalation, onset occurs within minutes, systemic bioavailability is limited by incomplete lung deposition and first-pass handling of swallowed drug, distribution is moderate, metabolism occurs mainly by sulfate conjugation, and elimination is primarily renal as parent drug and metabolites with a short plasma half-life of roughly 3 to 6 hours. Toxicity is usually dose-related and includes tachycardia, palpitations, tremor, nervousness, headache, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, and rarely lactic acidosis, arrhythmia, paradoxical bronchospasm, or ischemia in susceptible patients; overdose produces exaggerated β-adrenergic stimulation. Clinically it is used mainly as a rescue inhaler or nebulized therapy for acute wheeze and bronchospastic exacerbations.

Name: Cromoglicic acid
Description: Cromoglicic acid, also known as cromolyn, is a synthetic bis-chromone dicarboxylic acid composed of two substituted chromone (benzopyran-4-one) rings linked through an oxypropyl bridge, bearing terminal carboxylate functionalities that confer high polarity and poor membrane permeability; chemically it belongs to the chromone-derived mast cell stabilizers and more broadly to aromatic ether dicarboxylic acids, with a characteristic bischromone scaffold. Structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include nedocromil, lodoxamide, ketotifen, and to a lesser extent tranilast, all used as anti-allergic or mast cell–directed agents. Its best-established pharmacology is prevention of mast-cell degranulation with suppression of histamine, leukotriene, and other mediator release; no single high-affinity canonical target fully explains its action, but reported target associations include chloride channel–related pathways, GPR35, S100 proteins, and mast-cell signaling components. Pharmacokinetically, cromoglicic acid is very poorly absorbed orally and only limitedly absorbed after inhalation or topical administration, remains largely extracellular because of low lipophilicity and minimal protein binding, undergoes little to no metabolism, and is excreted mainly unchanged in urine and bile/feces. Systemic toxicity is low because bioavailability is low; overdose is uncommon, while local toxicities include throat irritation, cough, bronchospasm, unpleasant taste, nasal burning, and ocular stinging, with rare hypersensitivity reactions such as rash or anaphylaxis. It is indicated for prophylaxis of allergic asthma, exercise-induced bronchospasm, allergic rhinitis, allergic conjunctivitis, and mastocytosis-related gastrointestinal symptoms. Clinically it is used as an inhaled, nasal, ophthalmic, or oral preventive therapy rather than a reliever, for example in seasonal allergy prevention and long-term asthma control adjunctive to bronchodilators or corticosteroids.

Name: Ganciclovir
Description: Ganciclovir (DB01004) is a synthetic acyclic guanine nucleoside analog whose structure consists of a 2-amino-6-oxo purine base linked to a hydroxyalkoxy side chain that mimics the sugar of deoxyguanosine, placing it in the antiviral nucleoside analog class and more specifically among acyclic guanosine derivatives; its core scaffold is closely related to guanine/purine and is chemically and pharmacologically similar to acyclovir, valacyclovir, penciclovir, valganciclovir, and cidofovir as anti-herpesvirus agents. It is active after intracellular phosphorylation, initially by the cytomegalovirus UL97 kinase and in herpes simplex virus by viral thymidine kinase to the triphosphate, which inhibits viral DNA polymerase and can terminate or markedly slow viral DNA elongation; key targets therefore include CMV UL97 phosphotransferase, CMV DNA polymerase UL54, and HSV DNA polymerase. Oral ganciclovir has limited bioavailability, whereas intravenous dosing and the oral prodrug valganciclovir improve systemic exposure; it distributes widely, including into ocular tissues and cerebrospinal fluid, undergoes minimal metabolism, and is eliminated largely unchanged by renal excretion, so dose adjustment is required in renal impairment. Major toxicities are dose-limiting bone marrow suppression, especially neutropenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and less commonly pancytopenia, with reproductive toxicity, embryofetal toxicity, mutagenic and carcinogenic potential shown in animals. Adverse effects include fever, nausea, diarrhea, headache, rash, phlebitis, elevated creatinine, and CNS effects such as confusion or seizures. Clinically it is used mainly for treatment and prophylaxis of cytomegalovirus disease, including CMV retinitis in AIDS, CMV colitis or esophagitis, and prevention of CMV infection in solid-organ or hematopoietic transplant recipients.

Name: Hydroxyurea
Description: Hydroxyurea (DrugBank DB01005) is a small, highly polar hydroxylated urea derivative whose structure consists of a monosubstituted urea core bearing a carbonyl flanked by two nitrogens, one of which carries a hydroxyl group, giving a simple hydroxycarbamide scaffold that places it in the antimetabolite, ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor, and substituted urea chemical categories. Its minimal urea-based scaffold is shared mechanistically with other cytotoxic antimetabolites that impair DNA synthesis, and functionally similar drugs include cytarabine, gemcitabine, 5-fluorouracil, and thioguanine, although these are structurally distinct. The principal pharmacologic target is ribonucleoside-diphosphate reductase, especially the RRM1/RRM2 subunits, causing depletion of deoxyribonucleotide pools and S-phase inhibition; it also increases fetal hemoglobin in sickle cell disease, likely via nitric oxide-related and stress erythropoiesis mechanisms. Hydroxyurea is well absorbed orally with high bioavailability, distributes widely including into erythrocytes and cerebrospinal fluid, undergoes partial hepatic and extrahepatic metabolism with conversion to urea, carbon dioxide, and reactive nitrogen species, and is eliminated by both renal excretion of unchanged drug and metabolic clearance; its plasma half-life is short but exposure rises with renal impairment. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related myelosuppression, including neutropenia, anemia, and thrombocytopenia, with examples of severe infection risk, bleeding, and cumulative marrow suppression; other toxicities include mucocutaneous ulcers, gastrointestinal upset, cutaneous hyperpigmentation, leg ulcers, teratogenicity, and potential mutagenic or carcinogenic risk. Clinically it is used for chronic myeloid and other myeloproliferative neoplasms, recurrent or metastatic head and neck cancer in radiosensitizing regimens, and especially sickle cell disease to reduce painful vaso-occlusive crises, acute chest syndrome, transfusion need, and hospitalization.

Name: Letrozole
Description: Letrozole (DB01006) is a nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor built on a lipophilic triaryl scaffold in which a central benzonitrile ring is substituted with two para-cyanophenyl and 1,2,4-triazole-containing aryl features; chemically it is a triazole derivative and nitrile-containing aromatic heterocycle whose key scaffold is the azole-bearing diaryl/triaryl motif typical of third-generation aromatase inhibitors.
