It is closely related pharmacologically to anastrozole and, more distantly, exemestane, while other endocrine comparators include tamoxifen and fulvestrant. Its principal target is cytochrome P450 19A1 aromatase, which it inhibits reversibly and with high selectivity, thereby suppressing peripheral estrogen biosynthesis. Orally administered letrozole is rapidly and well absorbed with high bioavailability, broad tissue distribution, moderate protein binding, and a long elimination half-life of about 2 days that supports once-daily dosing; it is metabolized mainly in the liver by CYP3A4 and CYP2A6 to an inactive carbinol metabolite and is excreted predominantly in urine as metabolites, with limited unchanged drug. Clinically it is indicated mainly for hormone receptor-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women, including adjuvant therapy, extended adjuvant therapy after tamoxifen, and first- or second-line treatment of advanced or metastatic disease; it is also widely used off-label for ovulation induction in anovulatory infertility such as polycystic ovary syndrome. Toxicities reflect estrogen deprivation and include decreased bone mineral density, osteoporosis, fractures, arthralgia, myalgia, hypercholesterolemia, and rarely hepatotoxicity; common adverse effects include hot flashes, fatigue, nausea, headache, edema, dizziness, and sweating.

Name: Busulfan
Description: Busulfan (DB01008) is a bifunctional alkyl sulfonate antineoplastic whose structure consists of a symmetric butane linker terminated at both ends by methanesulfonate ester leaving groups, making it a small, highly electrophilic DNA-alkylating agent; chemically it belongs to the alkyl sulfonates within the broader alkylating-agent class, and its core scaffold is a 1,4-butanediol dimethanesulfonate framework. It is closely related pharmacologically to other bifunctional alkylators such as treosulfan and, more broadly, to nitrogen mustards including melphalan and cyclophosphamide, although it lacks the mustard motif. Busulfan is administered orally or intravenously, with oral absorption historically variable, wide tissue distribution including marrow, limited CNS penetration, extensive hepatic and extrahepatic metabolism primarily through glutathione conjugation catalyzed by GSTA1 and related glutathione S-transferases, downstream oxidation to inactive metabolites, and predominantly urinary excretion of metabolites with little unchanged drug eliminated. Its principal target is not a single receptor but genomic DNA, where it forms interstrand DNA crosslinks at nucleophilic sites such as N7 of guanine, causing myeloablation and cytotoxicity; proteins relevant to disposition and response include GSTA1, other GST isoenzymes, and DNA damage response pathways rather than a canonical drug target. Clinically, it is used for chronic myelogenous leukemia and, more importantly, as a conditioning or myeloablative agent before hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in disorders such as acute myeloid leukemia, thalassemia, and other marrow diseases. Major toxicities include profound dose-limiting myelosuppression, veno-occlusive disease of the liver, pulmonary fibrosis or busulfan lung, mucositis, seizures at high exposure, infertility, teratogenicity, and secondary malignancy risk; common adverse effects include neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, fatigue, and hepatic enzyme elevation.

Name: Ketoprofen
Description: Ketoprofen (DrugBank DB01009) is a propionic acid-derived nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug characterized structurally by a 2-arylpropionic acid framework bearing a benzoyl-substituted biphenyl-like arrangement, specifically a ketone linking one phenyl ring to a second aromatic ring attached to the chiral propionic acid center; it is therefore classified within the arylpropionic acid NSAIDs, with a profen scaffold closely related to ketoprofen’s 2-(3-benzoylphenyl)propionic acid core. Similar drugs include ibuprofen, flurbiprofen, naproxen, fenoprofen, and dexketoprofen, which share the profen motif and cyclooxygenase inhibition as the principal mechanism. Its major targets are prostaglandin G/H synthase 1 and 2, also known as COX-1 and COX-2 (PTGS1, PTGS2), leading to reduced peripheral prostaglandin synthesis and consequent analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antipyretic effects. Ketoprofen is generally well absorbed orally, is highly albumin bound, distributes well into inflamed tissues and synovial fluid, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly by glucuronidation with limited oxidative biotransformation, and is excreted predominantly in urine as conjugated metabolites with a relatively short elimination half-life that may necessitate repeated dosing or modified-release formulations. Toxicity is typical of NSAIDs and includes dose-related gastrointestinal erosion, ulceration, bleeding, renal hypoperfusion or acute kidney injury, fluid retention, hypersensitivity reactions including bronchospasm in aspirin-sensitive patients, and, less commonly, hepatotoxicity or severe skin reactions. Clinically it is used for rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute musculoskeletal pain, dysmenorrhea, postoperative pain, dental pain, and fever, while common adverse effects include dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, edema, and gastrointestinal bleeding.

Name: Clobetasol propionate
Description: Clobetasol propionate (DB01013) is a super-high-potency topical corticosteroid whose structure is a halogenated pregnane glucocorticoid built on the cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene steroid nucleus, characterized by a 3-keto-4-ene A-ring, 11beta-hydroxyl and 20-ketone functionalities, 21-propionate esterification, and distinctive 9-fluoro and 21-chloro substitution with a 16beta-methyl group that markedly enhances topical anti-inflammatory potency; chemically it is a synthetic corticosteroid ester, and its core scaffold is the hydrocortisone/prednisolone-like glucocorticoid steroid scaffold. Similar drugs include other potent topical corticosteroids such as betamethasone dipropionate, fluocinonide, halobetasol propionate, and diflorasone diacetate. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, with downstream transrepression of NF-kappaB- and AP-1-regulated inflammatory mediators and reduced cytokine, prostaglandin, and leukotriene signaling. After topical administration, absorption depends on formulation, body site, inflammation, and occlusion; percutaneous uptake is usually limited but can become clinically significant, distribution is largely tissue-local with systemic protein binding after absorption, metabolism occurs mainly hepatically to less active metabolites, and excretion is primarily renal with some biliary/fecal elimination. Toxicity reflects excessive local or systemic corticosteroid exposure, including skin atrophy, telangiectasia, striae, delayed wound healing, secondary infection, HPA-axis suppression, hyperglycemia, glucosuria, Cushingoid features, and, rarely, growth suppression in children. It is indicated for short-term relief of corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses such as plaque psoriasis, refractory eczema, lichen planus, discoid lupus erythematosus, and severe dermatitis with pruritus and erythema. Clinical use is typically limited to localized, thick, resistant inflammatory lesions, with adverse effects including burning, irritation, dryness, folliculitis, acneiform eruption, hypopigmentation, and perioral dermatitis.

Name: Balsalazide
Description: Balsalazide (DrugBank DB01014) is an azo-bonded prodrug of 5-aminosalicylic acid composed of a mesalamine moiety linked through an aromatic azo bridge to an inert carrier, 4-aminobenzoyl-β-alanine, giving it a bifunctional structure with salicylate, aniline, amide, carboxylate, and azo functionalities that favor colon-targeted delivery; chemically it is an aminosalicylate and aromatic azo compound built on an azobenzene-like scaffold. It is closely related to other 5-ASA prodrugs and formulations such as sulfasalazine, olsalazine, and mesalamine itself, which share colonic 5-ASA release as the therapeutic principle. After oral administration, balsalazide is minimally absorbed in the upper gastrointestinal tract and reaches the colon largely intact, where bacterial azoreductases cleave the azo bond to release active mesalamine and 4-aminobenzoyl-β-alanine; mesalamine then acts mainly topically in the colonic mucosa, with limited systemic distribution, partial acetylation to N-acetyl-5-ASA, and predominantly renal excretion of absorbed metabolites, while unabsorbed drug-derived material is eliminated in feces. Its molecular targets are not highly specific receptors but inflammatory pathways, with mesalamine reported to modulate peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma, cyclooxygenase- and lipoxygenase-related eicosanoid signaling, NF-κB activation, and scavenging of reactive oxygen species. It is indicated primarily for mild to moderate ulcerative colitis, especially active colonic inflammation presenting with diarrhea, rectal bleeding, and urgency, and is used clinically to induce symptom control and, in some settings, maintain remission. Adverse effects commonly include abdominal pain, diarrhea, headache, nausea, and exacerbation of colitis symptoms, while toxicities of concern include hypersensitivity reactions, pancreatitis, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity such as interstitial nephritis, and rare blood dyscrasias.

Name: Sulfamethoxazole
Description: Sulfamethoxazole (DrugBank DB01015) is a synthetic sulfonamide antibacterial whose structure consists of a para-aminobenzenesulfonamide core linked through the sulfonamide nitrogen to a heteroaromatic isoxazole ring, specifically a 5-methylisoxazolyl substituent, giving an aniline-sulfonamide architecture optimized for competitive inhibition of folate synthesis. It belongs to the sulfonamide anti-infective class, with a p-aminobenzenesulfonamide scaffold that is shared across related antifolate sulfonamides; similar drugs include sulfisoxazole, sulfadiazine, sulfamethizole, and sulfadoxine, while its most important therapeutic analogue-partner is trimethoprim in the fixed combination cotrimoxazole. Its principal microbial target is dihydropteroate synthase, blocking incorporation of para-aminobenzoic acid into dihydropteroate and thereby suppressing tetrahydrofolate-dependent nucleotide biosynthesis. Orally, sulfamethoxazole is well absorbed, widely distributed into tissues and body fluids including sputum and cerebrospinal fluid to a limited extent, is moderately protein bound, undergoes hepatic metabolism mainly by N4-acetylation and glucuronidation, and is eliminated predominantly by the kidney as parent drug and metabolites, with dose adjustment in renal impairment. Clinically it is used mainly with trimethoprim for urinary tract infections, acute otitis media, bronchitis exacerbations, shigellosis, traveler’s diarrhea, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia treatment and prophylaxis, and nocardiosis. Toxicities include hypersensitivity reactions, crystalluria, nephrotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, bone marrow suppression, hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, and severe cutaneous adverse reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis; common side effects include rash, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, photosensitivity, and hyperkalemia when combined with trimethoprim.

Name: Glyburide
Description: Glyburide (glibenclamide; DB01016) is a second-generation sulfonylurea oral antihyperglycemic built around a diaryl-substituted sulfonylurea core in which a para-substituted benzenesulfonylurea pharmacophore is linked to a lipophilic cyclohexylurea-like moiety and a chloromethoxybenzamide-containing aryl group, placing it in the sulfonylurea/aryl-sulfonamide category with the classic sulfonylurea scaffold responsible for pancreatic insulin secretagogue activity. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other sulfonylureas such as glipizide, gliclazide, tolbutamide, chlorpropamide, and glimepiride, although glyburide is relatively potent and longer acting than first-generation congeners. Its principal targets are the ATP-sensitive potassium channel complex, especially sulfonylurea receptor 1/ABCC8 with functional inhibition of the Kir6.2/KCNJ11 channel in pancreatic beta cells, leading to membrane depolarization, calcium influx, and insulin release. Glyburide is well absorbed orally, is highly albumin bound, distributes largely in plasma, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP2C9 to weakly active or inactive metabolites, and is eliminated by both biliary/fecal and renal routes, giving clinical relevance to liver and kidney impairment. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related, sometimes prolonged hypoglycemia, particularly in older adults, malnourished patients, or those with renal insufficiency; overdose may cause neuroglycopenia, seizures, or coma. It is indicated for type 2 diabetes mellitus when diet and exercise are insufficient, including use alone or with metformin, and adverse effects include hypoglycemia, weight gain, nausea, dyspepsia, rash, cholestatic or other hepatic dysfunction, hyponatremia, and rarely hematologic hypersensitivity reactions. Clinically, it has been used to improve fasting and postprandial hyperglycemia in ambulatory adults with preserved beta-cell function, but is generally avoided in type 1 diabetes and diabetic ketoacidosis.

Name: Minocycline
Description: Minocycline (DrugBank DB01017) is a semisynthetic, second-generation tetracycline characterized by a rigid four-linearly fused-ring naphthacene carboxamide core bearing multiple keto-enol and phenolic functionalities that support metal chelation, with dimethylamino substitution at C4 and enhanced lipophilicity from side-chain modification distinguishing it from older tetracyclines; it is therefore classified as a tetracycline antibiotic, more specifically a lipophilic semisynthetic broad-spectrum polyketide-derived antibacterial, built on the tetracycline/naphthacene scaffold. Closely related drugs include tetracycline, doxycycline, demeclocycline, sarecycline, and glycylcyclines such as tigecycline. Its principal target is the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit, especially 16S rRNA within the A-site region, where it functionally inhibits aminoacyl-tRNA binding and suppresses protein synthesis; proposed off-target or ancillary interactions relevant to anti-inflammatory effects include matrix metalloproteinases and microglial signaling pathways. Orally, minocycline is well absorbed, has high bioavailability, wide tissue penetration including skin, respiratory secretions, gingival crevicular fluid, and cerebrospinal fluid to a limited but greater extent than many tetracyclines, is moderately protein bound, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated by both biliary/fecal and renal routes with a relatively long half-life permitting once- or twice-daily dosing. It is indicated for acne vulgaris, rosacea, respiratory tract and skin/soft-tissue infections, sexually transmitted infections such as chlamydial disease, and certain atypical or rickettsial infections. Toxicities include vestibular dose-related dizziness and vertigo, hepatotoxicity, drug-induced lupus, hypersensitivity syndromes, pigmentation of skin or teeth, and class effects such as tooth discoloration and inhibition of bone growth in pregnancy or childhood; common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, photosensitivity, rash, headache, and candidiasis. Clinically, it is widely used in outpatient dermatology and infectious disease practice, for example in moderate inflammatory acne, community-acquired MRSA-suspected skin infection, and tetracycline-susceptible atypical bacterial infections.

Name: Guanfacine
Description: Guanfacine (DrugBank DB01018) is a centrally acting imidazoline-derived arylacetamidine whose structure consists of a 2,6-dichlorophenyl ring linked to a guanidine/amidine-like imino functionality, giving a compact chlorinated aromatic scaffold with a guanidine-centered cationic pharmacophore; chemically it is classified as a selective alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonist, within the phenylguanidine/iminoimidazoline-related sympatholytic class, and its core scaffold is closely related to other central antihypertensives such as clonidine and, more distantly, methyldopa and dexmedetomidine in terms of alpha-2 agonism. Its principal target proteins are alpha-2A adrenergic receptors, with lesser activity at alpha-2B and alpha-2C receptor subtypes, producing reduced sympathetic outflow and enhanced prefrontal cortical network regulation. Guanfacine is well absorbed orally, has moderate bioavailability, reaches peak concentrations within hours depending on formulation, is distributed systemically with modest protein binding, undergoes hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4-mediated oxidation, and is eliminated in urine as parent drug and metabolites with an elimination half-life that supports once-daily extended-release dosing. Toxicity is dominated by exaggerated pharmacology, including hypotension, bradycardia, sedation, dizziness, and overdose-associated CNS depression; rebound hypertension may occur after abrupt discontinuation. Approved and common clinical uses include hypertension and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, especially pediatric ADHD, with off-label use for tic disorders, impulsivity, hyperarousal, and adjunctive management of oppositional symptoms. Common adverse effects include somnolence, fatigue, dry mouth, constipation, headache, abdominal pain, orthostatic hypotension, and bradycardia.

Name: Isosorbide mononitrate
Description: Isosorbide mononitrate (DrugBank DB01020) is an organic nitrate antianginal composed of a rigid bicyclic isosorbide core, derived from a fused 1,4:3,6-dianhydrohexitol scaffold, bearing a single nitrate ester substituent and one free hydroxyl group; chemically it belongs to the nitrate vasodilators and more broadly to nitric oxide donor esters, with the isosorbide bicyclic polyol scaffold distinguishing it from related nitrate esters. Closely related drugs include isosorbide dinitrate, glyceryl trinitrate (nitroglycerin), erythrityl tetranitrate, and pentaerythritol tetranitrate, which share nitrate ester-mediated vasodilatory activity. Its principal pharmacologic effect reflects bioactivation to nitric oxide or related nitrosating species, leading to stimulation of soluble guanylate cyclase and increased cGMP in vascular smooth muscle, with consequent venodilation and reduced preload; soluble guanylate cyclase is therefore the key functional target system. Orally, it is well absorbed with high bioavailability because it largely escapes first-pass hepatic metabolism, distributes systemically with modest protein binding, undergoes hepatic denitration and glucuronidation to inactive metabolites, and is excreted mainly in urine as metabolites. It is indicated for prevention of angina pectoris due to coronary artery disease, including chronic stable angina, but not for rapid relief of acute attacks. Toxicity is largely extension of pharmacology, including severe headache, flushing, dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, syncope, reflex tachycardia, and, in overdose, profound hypotension, myocardial ischemia from reduced perfusion, and rare methemoglobinemia; dangerous interactions occur with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil. Clinically it is used as an oral maintenance nitrate in chronic angina regimens, often in patients needing sustained symptom prophylaxis and nitrate-free intervals to limit tolerance.

Name: Phylloquinone
Description: Phylloquinone (vitamin K1; DrugBank DB01022) is a fat-soluble 2-methyl-1,4-naphthoquinone bearing a long phytyl-derived aliphatic side chain at the 3-position, giving a lipophilic quinone structure optimized for membrane association; chemically it is a vitamin K naphthoquinone, and its core scaffold is the menadione-like naphthoquinone ring with an isoprenoid side chain. Closely related drugs include other vitamin K congeners such as menaquinone (vitamin K2, including menaquinone-4) and the synthetic analog menadione (vitamin K3), while pharmacologic antagonists with mechanistic relevance include warfarin and other coumarins. After oral administration, absorption is bile salt- and dietary fat-dependent and occurs mainly in the small intestine; parenteral administration bypasses this limitation. It is transported in chylomicrons and later lipoproteins, concentrates largely in liver, undergoes oxidative side-chain shortening and conjugation, and is excreted primarily in bile and urine as polar metabolites, with relatively limited body stores. Its principal pharmacologic target pathway is vitamin K epoxide reductase complex subunit 1 (VKORC1), which recycles reduced vitamin K used by gamma-glutamyl carboxylase (GGCX) to activate coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X and proteins C and S. Phylloquinone is indicated for prevention and treatment of hypoprothrombinemia due to vitamin K deficiency, malabsorption, antibiotic-associated deficiency, and reversal of excessive anticoagulation from warfarin. Adverse effects are usually mild and include injection-site reactions, flushing, dysgeusia, and rash, whereas rapid intravenous use has rarely caused severe hypersensitivity or anaphylactoid reactions; toxicity is generally low, though excessive correction can produce warfarin resistance and, rarely, hemolysis or hyperbilirubinemia in vulnerable neonates. Clinically it is used for routine neonatal prophylaxis against hemorrhagic disease of the newborn, treatment of elevated INR or bleeding related to vitamin K deficiency, and perioperative correction of coagulopathy.

Name: Felodipine
Description: Felodipine (DrugBank DB01023) is a lipophilic dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker built on a 1,4-dihydropyridine ring bearing ester groups at the 3 and 5 positions, aryl substitution at the 4 position, and halogenated alkyl/aryl functionality that increases vascular selectivity and membrane affinity; chemically it belongs to the dihydropyridine class of L-type calcium-channel antagonists and shares the classic nifedipine-like dihydropyridine scaffold found in similar drugs such as amlodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine, isradipine, and lacidipine. Its principal target is the L-type voltage-dependent calcium channel, especially Cav1.2 encoded by CACNA1C in vascular smooth muscle, where inhibition reduces calcium influx, causing arteriolar vasodilation and reduced peripheral resistance. Felodipine is indicated mainly for hypertension and chronic stable angina, including use in patients needing once-daily antihypertensive therapy or combination treatment with beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, or diuretics. Orally, it is well absorbed but undergoes substantial first-pass metabolism, giving moderate bioavailability; it is highly protein bound, widely distributed, extensively metabolized in the liver predominantly by CYP3A4 to inactive pyridine metabolites, and eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites with a smaller fecal component. Toxicity is largely an extension of pharmacology, with overdose producing marked hypotension, reflex tachycardia, dizziness, flushing, and potentially myocardial ischemia or conduction disturbances; CYP3A4 inhibitors or grapefruit juice can raise exposure. Common adverse effects include peripheral edema, headache, palpitations, flushing, fatigue, and gingival hyperplasia, while clinical use emphasizes blood-pressure control and antianginal benefit with attention to drug interactions and dose titration in hepatic impairment.

Name: Mycophenolic acid
Description: Mycophenolic acid (DrugBank DB01024) is a fermentation-derived fungal secondary metabolite and immunosuppressant built on a substituted phthalide-like aromatic polyketide scaffold featuring a 4-hydroxy-6-methoxy-7-methyl benzofuranone/lactone core linked to an unsaturated hexenoic acid side chain; chemically it is classified as a phenolic carboxylic acid natural product and polyketide-derived antimetabolite. Its closest related drugs are the prodrugs mycophenolate mofetil and mycophenolate sodium, which deliver the same active moiety, and it is mechanistically analogous to other antiproliferative immunosuppressants such as azathioprine in transplant medicine. Mycophenolic acid selectively and reversibly inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase, especially IMPDH1 and IMPDH2, suppressing de novo guanine nucleotide synthesis in activated T and B lymphocytes. After oral administration, exposure depends on formulation, with mycophenolate mofetil rapidly absorbed and hydrolyzed to active mycophenolic acid; the drug is highly albumin bound, distributes largely in plasma, undergoes hepatic glucuronidation mainly by UGT1A9 and UGT2B7 to inactive MPAG and minor acyl-glucuronide metabolites, shows enterohepatic recirculation, and is excreted predominantly in urine as glucuronides with little unchanged drug. Major toxicities include dose-related gastrointestinal injury such as diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and colitis, hematologic suppression with leukopenia, anemia, and thrombocytopenia, serious infections, teratogenicity causing miscarriage and congenital malformations, and occasional hepatotoxicity. Clinically it is used chiefly to prevent acute rejection in kidney, heart, and liver transplantation and is also used in autoimmune disorders such as lupus nephritis and vasculitis, where its adverse-effect profile and infection risk require careful monitoring.

Name: Amlexanox
Description: Amlexanox (DrugBank DB01025) is a small synthetic anti-inflammatory and anti-allergic agent whose structure is a tricyclic heteroaromatic system best described as a substituted 1,7-naphthyridine/oxo-pyridopyrimidine-like framework bearing a carboxylic acid and isopropyl substituent, giving a rigid, planar, weakly acidic fused-ring architecture suited to protein-kinase and inflammatory target engagement. Chemically it is classified as a heterocyclic aromatic carboxylic acid and immunomodulatory antiallergic drug, with a fused bicyclic aza-aromatic scaffold related broadly to other mast-cell stabilizing or antiallergic agents, although it is structurally distinct from cromolyn, nedocromil, tranilast, and ketotifen. Its recognized molecular targets include TANK-binding kinase 1 and IKK epsilon, and historically it has been associated with inhibition of mediator release from mast cells, neutrophils, and mononuclear cells, reducing histamine, leukotrienes, and inflammatory cytokine signaling. Pharmacokinetically, topical oral formulations used for aphthous ulcers produce mainly local exposure with limited systemic absorption, while orally administered amlexanox is absorbed to a moderate extent, distributes systemically, undergoes hepatic biotransformation with renal and fecal elimination of parent drug and metabolites; overall exposure is influenced by formulation and route. Toxicity is generally low at therapeutic topical doses, but adverse effects can include local burning, stinging, pain, contact irritation, nausea, diarrhea, and rash; higher systemic exposure has been associated with gastrointestinal intolerance and potential hepatic laboratory abnormalities in investigational settings. Clinically, it is used primarily for recurrent aphthous stomatitis to reduce ulcer pain, erythema, and healing time, and has also been explored in asthma, allergic inflammation, and metabolic disease contexts such as obesity and insulin resistance.

Name: Ketoconazole
Description: Ketoconazole (DrugBank DB01026) is a synthetic imidazole antifungal characterized structurally by a halogenated dioxolane-containing diaryl framework linked to a piperazine-acetamide side chain and an imidazole ring, giving a lipophilic azole architecture optimized for fungal cytochrome P450 binding; chemically it belongs to the azole antimycotics, specifically the imidazole subclass, and its core scaffold is an imidazole-dioxolane-diaryl-piperazine scaffold. It is closely related to other azole antifungals such as miconazole, clotrimazole, econazole, and, more distantly, triazoles such as itraconazole and fluconazole. Its principal target is fungal lanosterol 14alpha-demethylase, encoded by CYP51, thereby blocking ergosterol biosynthesis; in humans it also inhibits steroidogenic and drug-metabolizing CYP enzymes including CYP3A4, CYP17A1, CYP11A1, and CYP11B1, accounting for endocrine and interaction liabilities. Oral absorption is variable and enhanced by gastric acidity and food, reduced by acid-suppressive therapy; it is highly protein bound, widely distributed but with limited CNS penetration, extensively metabolized in the liver, and excreted mainly via bile and feces with minor renal elimination. Major toxicities include hepatotoxicity ranging from transaminase elevation to fulminant hepatic failure, QT prolongation risk through interactions, and adrenal suppression or gynecomastia from steroid synthesis inhibition. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, abdominal pain, pruritus, rash, headache, diarrhea, decreased libido, menstrual irregularities, and gynecomastia. Clinically, ketoconazole has been used topically for seborrheic dermatitis, dandruff, tinea, and cutaneous candidiasis, and historically orally for systemic or refractory fungal infections and, off-label, for Cushing syndrome due to cortisol-lowering effects.

Name: Irbesartan
Description: Irbesartan (DrugBank DB01029) is a nonpeptide angiotensin II receptor blocker characterized structurally by a biphenyl-tetrazole pharmacophore linked to a diazaspiro imidazolinone-type core, giving it a lipophilic aromatic region and an acidic tetrazole moiety that support high-affinity receptor binding; chemically it belongs to the sartan class of antihypertensive agents, and its core scaffold is the biphenyl-tetrazole ARB scaffold with a spirocyclic heterocyclic extension. It is closely related to other ARBs such as losartan, valsartan, candesartan, olmesartan, telmisartan, and eprosartan, which share blockade of angiotensin II signaling but differ in substituents, prodrug status, and pharmacokinetics. Its principal target is the angiotensin II type 1 receptor, AGTR1, with functional suppression of vasoconstrictive and aldosterone-mediated effects of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Orally, irbesartan is well absorbed with relatively high bioavailability, reaches peak plasma levels within hours, is highly protein bound, undergoes mainly hepatic metabolism including glucuronidation and CYP2C9-mediated oxidation with minimal CYP3A4 contribution, and is eliminated through both biliary/fecal and renal routes, supporting once-daily dosing. Toxicities are generally extension-of-pharmacology effects, including hypotension, renal impairment or acute kidney injury in susceptible patients, hyperkalemia, and fetal toxicity when used during pregnancy; overdose may produce marked dizziness or blood-pressure reduction. It is indicated for hypertension and diabetic nephropathy in type 2 diabetes with hypertension, and clinically used to lower blood pressure, reduce proteinuria, and slow progression of renal disease. Common adverse effects include dizziness, fatigue, orthostatic symptoms, gastrointestinal upset, and occasional increases in serum creatinine or potassium.

Name: Topotecan
Description: Topotecan (DrugBank DB01030) is a semisynthetic camptothecin analog whose structure consists of a planar pentacyclic fused quinoline-based alkaloid core with the characteristic α-hydroxylactone E-ring required for activity, plus a dimethylaminomethyl substitution that improves water solubility; chemically it is an antineoplastic topoisomerase I inhibitor and belongs to the camptothecin/monoterpene indole alkaloid family, with the camptothecin lactone scaffold as its defining pharmacophore. Closely related drugs include irinotecan, belotecan, exatecan, and the parent natural product camptothecin, all sharing the same topoisomerase I poison concept. Its principal target is DNA topoisomerase I (TOP1), stabilizing the covalent TOP1-DNA cleavage complex and causing replication-associated single- and double-strand DNA breaks. Pharmacokinetically, intravenous topotecan has predictable linear exposure, while oral absorption is moderate but incomplete; protein binding is low to modest, distribution is broad into tissues, and reversible pH-dependent conversion occurs between active lactone and less active hydroxy acid forms. Metabolism is limited, with minor hepatic transformation, and elimination is predominantly renal as unchanged drug and hydrolysis products, so clearance falls in renal impairment. Major dose-limiting toxicity is myelosuppression, especially neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and anemia, with serious examples including febrile neutropenia, sepsis, and hemorrhage; other adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, mucositis, fatigue, alopecia, and occasional interstitial lung disease. Clinically, topotecan is used for recurrent ovarian cancer, relapsed small cell lung cancer, and in combination regimens for advanced or recurrent cervical cancer, particularly when platinum-based therapy has failed or palliation is needed.

Name: Ethinamate
Description: Ethinamate (DrugBank DB01031) is a sedative-hypnotic carbamate characterized structurally as an ethynyl-substituted tertiary carbinol esterified as a carbamate, giving a small lipophilic molecule built on an acetylenic alcohol/carbamate framework rather than a barbiturate ring system; chemically it belongs to the nonbarbiturate carbamate hypnotics, with a scaffold closely related to other older sedative carbamates such as meprobamate, carisoprodol, and especially ethinamate-like acetylenic carbamates including emylcamate, all of which share CNS-depressant properties. Its pharmacology is attributed to central nervous system depression, most plausibly through positive allosteric modulation of GABAergic signaling at the GABAA receptor-chloride ionophore complex, although no single definitive molecular target has been as firmly established as for modern hypnotics. After oral administration it is reportedly well absorbed, distributed into the CNS because of moderate lipophilicity, metabolized extensively in the liver by hydrolytic and oxidative pathways, and excreted primarily as metabolites in urine, with limited unchanged drug recovery. Toxicity resembles other sedative-hypnotics: dose-related somnolence, ataxia, impaired psychomotor performance, respiratory depression, hypotension, coma in overdose, and potentiation by alcohol, opioids, or other depressants; dependence, abuse liability, and withdrawal may occur with prolonged use. Adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, confusion, headache, nausea, and impaired coordination. Clinically, ethinamate was used as a short-term hypnotic and sedative for insomnia, nighttime agitation, and anxiety-associated sleep disturbance, but its use has largely been abandoned because safer modern agents offer better therapeutic indices.

Name: Probenecid
Description: Probenecid (DrugBank DB01032) is a uricosuric agent with a relatively lipophilic aromatic sulfonamide-carboxylic acid structure built around a para-disubstituted benzene scaffold bearing a propyl substituent, a sulfonamide linkage, and a terminal carboxylic acid; chemically it is classified as an aryl sulfonamide benzoic acid derivative and more broadly an organic acid transporter inhibitor, with a simple substituted benzoic acid/sulfonamide scaffold that distinguishes it from xanthine oxidase inhibitors. Similar drugs include other urate-lowering agents such as sulfinpyrazone and benzbromarone, and mechanistically related uricosurics such as lesinurad. Its principal targets are renal and tissue organic anion transport systems, especially SLC22A12/URAT1 and SLC22A6/OAT1, SLC22A8/OAT3, with effects also described on ABCC transporters including MRP family members; inhibition of tubular urate reabsorption increases uric acid excretion, while blockade of renal organic anion secretion reduces excretion of drugs such as penicillins and some antivirals. Orally administered probenecid is well absorbed, extensively albumin bound, distributed mainly in extracellular fluids, hepatically metabolized to acyl glucuronide and other metabolites, and eliminated chiefly in urine as parent drug and metabolites, with a duration influenced by urinary pH and renal function. It is indicated for chronic gout and hyperuricemia, and clinically used to enhance and prolong beta-lactam exposure, for example with penicillin or cefazolin. Adverse effects include nausea, anorexia, headache, dizziness, rash, and gout flares early in therapy; important toxicities include uric acid nephrolithiasis, hematuria, hypersensitivity reactions, and rare severe renal or hematologic complications, with risk increased in patients with renal impairment or high urate burden.

Name: Mercaptopurine
Description: Mercaptopurine (6-mercaptopurine; DrugBank DB01033) is a thiolated purine antimetabolite structurally defined as a hypoxanthine/guanine-like bicyclic purine ring bearing a thione-thiol functionality at the 6-position, placing it in the thiopurine class and on a purine heteroaromatic scaffold closely related to azathioprine, thioguanine, and the endogenous purines hypoxanthine and guanine. It is administered orally, with variable and often incomplete absorption, wide tissue distribution, limited CNS penetration, and extensive first-pass and intracellular metabolism; it is activated by hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase to thioinosine monophosphate and downstream thioguanine nucleotides, while xanthine oxidase, thiopurine S-methyltransferase, and nudix hydrolase 15 are major determinants of inactivation, exposure, and pharmacogenetic toxicity, and metabolites are eliminated mainly in urine. Its principal pharmacologic targets are enzymes and pathways of de novo purine synthesis and nucleic acid replication, including amidophosphoribosyltransferase indirectly via thioinosinate metabolites, with clinically relevant interacting proteins including HPRT1, TPMT, NUDT15, and XDH/xanthine oxidase. Mercaptopurine is indicated primarily for acute lymphoblastic leukemia, especially maintenance therapy, and is also used as an immunosuppressive thiopurine in disorders such as inflammatory bowel disease through its prodrug relationship to azathioprine. Dose-limiting toxicities include myelosuppression, profound neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, hepatotoxicity with cholestasis or transaminitis, gastrointestinal toxicity, infection risk, pancreatitis, and rare veno-occlusive or long-term secondary malignancy risk, with markedly increased toxicity in TPMT- or NUDT15-deficient patients and with allopurinol or febuxostat coadministration.

Name: Tolterodine
Description: Tolterodine (DrugBank DB01036) is a synthetic tertiary amine antimuscarinic built around a substituted diphenylpropyl scaffold, structurally characterized by two aryl rings attached to a three-carbon chain terminating in a chiral alcohol and diisopropylamino moiety, placing it in the arylalkyl tertiary alcohol/amine class of bladder antispasmodics; its scaffold and pharmacology are closely related to other antimuscarinics used for overactive bladder, including fesoterodine, oxybutynin, solifenacin, darifenacin, trospium, and propiverine, with fesoterodine being especially similar as a prodrug yielding the same active metabolite, 5-hydroxymethyltolterodine. Tolterodine targets muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, principally CHRM2 and CHRM3 in the detrusor, reducing involuntary bladder contraction and urgency. It is indicated for overactive bladder with urge urinary incontinence, urinary urgency, and increased urinary frequency, and is used clinically as immediate- or extended-release oral therapy to improve continence episodes and voiding patterns. It is well absorbed orally, undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism mainly by CYP2D6 to the active 5-hydroxymethyl metabolite and by CYP3A4 in poor CYP2D6 metabolizers, is moderately protein bound, distributes systemically, and is eliminated through renal excretion of metabolites with some fecal contribution; exposure increases in hepatic impairment, renal dysfunction, and with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. Toxicity is dominated by anticholinergic effects, including dose-related dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention, and tachycardia, with examples of clinically important risks including CNS confusion in susceptible older adults, QT prolongation at high exposure, and worsened gastric retention or bladder outlet obstruction. Common adverse effects include xerostomia, dyspepsia, headache, dizziness, somnolence, and dry eyes.

Name: Selegiline
Description: Selegiline (DB01037) is a lipophilic, chiral propargylamine built on a phenethylamine/amphetamine-like backbone, specifically the R-enantiomer of N-methyl-N-2-propynylamphetamine, with a tertiary amine, an arylalkyl chain, and a terminal alkynyl group that is critical for mechanism-based monoamine oxidase inhibition; chemically it is classified as a propargylamine monoamine oxidase inhibitor and more broadly as a substituted amphetamine, with a simple phenethylamine scaffold related to other MAO inhibitors and antiparkinsonian agents such as rasagiline, safinamide, tranylcypromine, and the amphetamine-derived methamphetamine. Its principal target is monoamine oxidase B (MAOB), which it irreversibly inhibits at usual doses, while selectivity diminishes at higher exposure; reported pharmacology may also involve effects on dopamine handling and trace amine pathways, but MAOB is the dominant validated target. Selegiline is indicated for Parkinson disease, especially as adjunct therapy to levodopa to reduce wearing-off and improve bradykinesia and rigidity, and a transdermal formulation is used for major depressive disorder. It is well absorbed orally but undergoes substantial first-pass metabolism, is widely distributed with CNS penetration, and is metabolized mainly by hepatic CYP2B6, CYP2C19, and CYP3A4 to desmethylselegiline, L-methamphetamine, and L-amphetamine, with urinary excretion of metabolites predominating. Toxicity includes insomnia, agitation, orthostatic hypotension, nausea, dyskinesia, hallucinations, hypertension in overdose or drug interactions, and risk of serotonin syndrome with serotonergic agents; tyramine-related pressor reactions are uncommon at standard MAOB-selective doses but become more relevant with dose escalation or loss of selectivity.

Name: Carphenazine
Description: Carphenazine (DrugBank DB01038) is a first-generation antipsychotic of the phenothiazine class, structurally characterized by a tricyclic phenothiazine nucleus containing sulfur and nitrogen heteroatoms and bearing a substituted aminoalkyl side chain that confers basicity and dopamine-receptor affinity; its core chemical scaffold is the classic phenothiazine ring system used across many typical neuroleptics. It is therefore chemically related to other phenothiazines such as chlorpromazine, perphenazine, fluphenazine, prochlorperazine, trifluoperazine, and thioridazine, which share broadly similar receptor pharmacology and adverse-effect patterns. Pharmacologically, carphenazine is understood to act primarily through antagonism of dopamine D2 receptors in mesolimbic and mesocortical pathways, with possible additional activity at D1, alpha-1 adrenergic, histamine H1, and muscarinic cholinergic receptors, accounting for both efficacy and off-target effects. Like other lipophilic phenothiazines, it is expected to be reasonably absorbed after oral administration, extensively distributed into the CNS and peripheral tissues, highly protein bound, metabolized mainly in the liver by oxidative and conjugative pathways, and excreted as metabolites in urine and bile/feces, with first-pass metabolism contributing to variable bioavailability. Its principal indication has been control of psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia and related agitation, hallucinations, delusions, and severe behavioral disturbance. Clinical adverse effects and toxicities are typical of this class, including dose-related extrapyramidal symptoms, akathisia, dystonia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia, sedation, anticholinergic effects, orthostatic hypotension, hyperprolactinemia, weight gain, QT prolongation, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, seizures, hepatic dysfunction, and overdose-associated coma or arrhythmia; accordingly, clinical use has centered on antipsychotic treatment in carefully monitored patients, particularly where older dopamine-blocking agents are appropriate.

Name: Fenofibrate
Description: Fenofibrate (DrugBank DB01039) is a lipophilic aryloxy-isobutyric acid derivative of the fibrate class, structurally characterized as the isopropyl ester prodrug of fenofibric acid, built on a chlorobenzoyl-substituted phenoxy linkage attached to a branched propanoate moiety; its core chemical scaffold is the phenoxyisobutyric acid/fibric acid scaffold shared across PPAR-alpha agonists. Closely related drugs include fenofibric acid, gemfibrozil, bezafibrate, ciprofibrate, and older clofibrate, which share hypolipidemic activity but differ in substitution patterns and disposition. After oral administration, fenofibrate is absorbed variably but better with food in many formulations, rapidly hydrolyzed by esterases to the active metabolite fenofibric acid, extensively bound to albumin, distributed mainly in plasma, minimally metabolized further by glucuronidation, and excreted predominantly in urine as fenofibric acid and its glucuronide, with renal impairment prolonging elimination. Its principal target is peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARA), with downstream effects on lipoprotein lipase, apolipoprotein C-III suppression, fatty-acid oxidation genes, and triglyceride-rich lipoprotein clearance. It is indicated for primary hypercholesterolemia, mixed dyslipidemia, and severe hypertriglyceridemia, including prevention of pancreatitis risk in markedly elevated triglycerides. Toxicities include hepatotoxicity, myopathy and rhabdomyolysis, especially with statins or renal dysfunction, cholelithiasis from altered biliary cholesterol balance, reversible creatinine elevation, and rare hypersensitivity or pancreatitis. Common adverse effects include dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, headache, back pain, elevated transaminases, and rash. Clinically, it is used as adjunctive therapy to diet, weight reduction, and glycemic control in patients with atherogenic dyslipidemia, diabetic mixed dyslipidemia, or severe triglyceride elevation when triglyceride lowering and HDL improvement are prioritized.

Name: Thalidomide
Description: Thalidomide (DrugBank DB01041) is a synthetic glutamic acid derivative and immunomodulatory imide whose structure consists of a chiral phthalimide ring system linked to a glutarimide moiety, giving a compact bicyclic imide framework; chemically it is classified as a piperidine-2,6-dione/phthalimide derivative, and its core scaffold is the glutarimide-imide scaffold shared by the immunomodulatory drugs lenalidomide and pomalidomide, which are its closest approved analogs. Its principal pharmacologic target is cereblon (CRBN), the substrate receptor of the CRL4 E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, with downstream effects on IKZF1 and IKZF3 degradation, reduced TNF-alpha production, altered cytokine signaling, antiangiogenic activity, and broader immunomodulation; additional pathway-level effects involve T cells, natural killer cells, and angiogenic mediators such as VEGF and bFGF. Orally administered thalidomide is slowly but adequately absorbed, widely distributed, undergoes limited classic CYP-dependent metabolism with substantial spontaneous nonenzymatic hydrolysis to multiple inactive metabolites, and is eliminated mainly as hydrolytic products in urine, with relatively little unchanged drug excreted. Its major indication is erythema nodosum leprosum, and it is also used in multiple myeloma, typically in combination with dexamethasone or other antineoplastics. Toxicity is dominated by profound teratogenicity causing severe limb, ear, cardiac, and visceral malformations after fetal exposure; other serious toxicities include peripheral neuropathy, venous thromboembolism, bradycardia, neutropenia, and sedation. Common adverse effects include somnolence, constipation, rash, dizziness, fatigue, edema, and neuropathic symptoms. Clinically, it is used under strict pregnancy-prevention controls for refractory inflammatory complications of leprosy and as an immunomodulatory antimyeloma agent in newly diagnosed or relapsed disease.

Name: Melphalan
Description: Melphalan (DB01042) is a bifunctional nitrogen mustard alkylating agent structurally defined as an L-phenylalanine scaffold bearing a para-bis(2-chloroethyl)amino substituent on the aromatic ring, combining an amino acid backbone with a lipophilic aromatic mustard warhead that forms reactive aziridinium intermediates; chemically it belongs to the aromatic nitrogen mustards and phenylalanine-derived antineoplastic alkylators, with a core scaffold closely related to phenylalanine and mechanistically similar to other mustard agents such as chlorambucil, cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, and mechlorethamine, especially chlorambucil as another aromatic mustard. Its principal pharmacologic target is not a single protein but nucleophilic sites in DNA, especially N7 of guanine, producing interstrand and intrastrand crosslinks, inhibition of DNA replication and transcription, and apoptosis; glutathione-related detoxification systems and DNA repair pathways modulate sensitivity. Orally absorbed but with variable and incomplete bioavailability, melphalan is also widely given intravenously; it distributes into extracellular fluids with limited CNS penetration and moderate protein binding, undergoes little classic CYP-mediated metabolism, instead showing substantial spontaneous hydrolysis and some hepatic and nonenzymatic degradation, and is cleared by both chemical breakdown and renal excretion of parent drug and metabolites, with a relatively short plasma half-life. It is indicated mainly for multiple myeloma and ovarian carcinoma and is also used in conditioning regimens before hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, including high-dose therapy for myeloma and isolated limb perfusion for melanoma or soft-tissue sarcoma. Dose-limiting toxicity is myelosuppression, particularly neutropenia and thrombocytopenia; other toxicities include mucositis, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, alopecia, infertility, pulmonary fibrosis, hepatotoxicity including veno-occlusive disease at high dose, hypersensitivity, and secondary myelodysplastic syndrome or acute leukemia.

Name: Gatifloxacin
Description: Gatifloxacin (DrugBank DB01044) is a synthetic 8-methoxy fluoroquinolone antibacterial built on a quinolone-3-carboxylic acid core with the characteristic 4-oxo, 6-fluoro substitution pattern and a basic piperazinyl-type side chain that enhances Gram-negative activity, making it chemically a fourth-generation fluoroquinolone and structurally part of the fluoroquinolone scaffold closely related to moxifloxacin, levofloxacin, ciprofloxacin, gemifloxacin, and ofloxacin. Its antibacterial action derives from inhibition of bacterial DNA gyrase, composed of GyrA and GyrB, and topoisomerase IV, composed of ParC and ParE, thereby blocking DNA replication, transcription, and chromosome segregation. It was used for susceptible respiratory and nonrespiratory infections including community-acquired pneumonia, acute bacterial sinusitis, acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, uncomplicated skin infection, urinary tract infection, and bacterial conjunctivitis in ophthalmic form. Orally, gatifloxacin is well absorbed with high bioavailability, low to moderate protein binding, broad tissue penetration including respiratory tissues, limited hepatic metabolism, and predominantly renal excretion as unchanged drug, so elimination is prolonged in renal impairment and dose reduction is required. Toxicity is notable for dysglycemia, with both severe hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia reported particularly in older adults and patients with diabetes, contributing to restriction or withdrawal of systemic use in some markets; like other fluoroquinolones it may also cause QT prolongation, tendinopathy or tendon rupture, CNS effects, peripheral neuropathy, hepatotoxicity, and hypersensitivity. Common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, dizziness, headache, insomnia, rash, and local ocular irritation with eye-drop use. Clinically, it was valued for broad-spectrum activity against common respiratory pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, and atypical organisms, but its use became limited by safety concerns, especially glucose homeostasis disturbances.

Name: Rifampin
Description: Rifampin (DrugBank DB01045) is a rifamycin-class ansamycin antibiotic built on a naphthohydroquinone aromatic core bridged by a long aliphatic ansa macrocycle, richly substituted with hydroxyl, acetyl, methoxy, and piperazinyl-imine-related functionalities that confer high lipophilicity and potent transcriptional inhibition; its chemical scaffold is the rifamycin macrocyclic ansa framework, closely related to similar drugs such as rifabutin, rifapentine, rifaximin, and the parent natural product rifamycin SV. It targets bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase by binding the beta subunit encoded by rpoB, thereby blocking initiation of RNA synthesis; in mycobacteria this same enzyme is the principal target. Rifampin is well absorbed orally, although food can reduce absorption; it distributes widely into tissues, macrophages, lung, liver, bone, and inflamed meninges, is highly protein bound to a moderate extent, undergoes hepatic deacetylation with marked enterohepatic recirculation, strongly induces CYP3A4, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP1A2, UGTs, and P-glycoprotein, and is eliminated mainly in bile/feces with some renal excretion. Major toxicities include hepatotoxicity ranging from asymptomatic transaminase elevation to hepatitis, severe drug-drug interactions causing therapeutic failure of warfarin, oral contraceptives, antiretrovirals, and azoles, and rare hypersensitivity, thrombocytopenia, hemolysis, interstitial nephritis, and flu-like syndrome. Adverse effects commonly include orange-red discoloration of urine, sweat, tears, and contact lenses, nausea, abdominal pain, rash, pruritus, and fever. Clinically, it is used primarily for tuberculosis in combination regimens, latent tuberculosis infection, leprosy with multidrug therapy, and prophylaxis or treatment of susceptible infections such as meningococcal or Haemophilus influenzae type b carriage and selected serious staphylococcal device-associated infections.

Name: Lubiprostone
Description: Lubiprostone (DB01046) is a bicyclic, highly lipophilic prostaglandin E1 derivative and chloride channel activator whose structure is characterized by a substituted eicosanoid-like fatty acid framework bearing multiple oxygenated functional groups, including hydroxyl and carbonyl moieties, and a terminal carboxylic acid; chemically it is categorized as a prostone, with a prostaglandin scaffold modified to enhance local intestinal secretory activity and minimize systemic effects. It is structurally and pharmacologically related to other prostaglandin analogs and intestinal secretagogues, with examples of similar drugs including misoprostol, latanoprost, and the non-prostaglandin secretagogues linaclotide and plecanatide by therapeutic analogy. Its principal target is generally described as apical chloride channels in intestinal epithelium, especially ClC-2, with downstream stimulation of chloride-rich fluid secretion and possible indirect effects on CFTR-mediated transport and epithelial barrier function. Oral absorption is low and systemic exposure is minimal; the drug acts mainly within the gastrointestinal lumen, is rapidly reduced at the 15-keto position to an active metabolite, undergoes further local carbonyl and omega oxidation without meaningful CYP involvement, distributes poorly systemically, and is eliminated predominantly via metabolism with fecal and minor urinary excretion of metabolites. Clinically it is indicated for chronic idiopathic constipation, irritable bowel syndrome with constipation in adult women, and opioid-induced constipation in adults with chronic non-cancer pain. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, distension, headache, and flatulence, while toxicity is usually limited to exaggerated pharmacology such as severe diarrhea, dehydration, syncope, or dyspnea/chest tightness shortly after dosing; it is avoided in mechanical bowel obstruction and used in practice to increase spontaneous bowel movements, soften stool, and reduce straining and constipation-associated discomfort.

Name: Fluocinonide
Description: Fluocinonide (DrugBank DB01047) is a highly potent synthetic topical corticosteroid built on the pregnane corticosteroid framework, specifically a fluorinated glucocorticoid with the classic four-ring steroid nucleus, a 3-keto-4-ene A-ring, 11β-hydroxyl functionality, 17- and 21-hydroxyl-derived substitution, a 16,17-acetonide-type ketal motif, and a 6α-fluoro substituent that enhances anti-inflammatory potency; chemically it belongs to the halogenated corticosteroids and its core scaffold is the hydrocortisone/prednisolone-like glucocorticoid steroid scaffold. Similar drugs include fluocinolone acetonide, triamcinolone acetonide, betamethasone, clobetasol propionate, and diflorasone, which share closely related corticosteroid pharmacophores. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, with downstream suppression of phospholipase A2-mediated eicosanoid synthesis and transcriptional inhibition of proinflammatory cytokines, adhesion molecules, and immune mediators. Fluocinonide is indicated for corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses such as atopic dermatitis, allergic contact dermatitis, eczema, lichen simplex chronicus, and plaque psoriasis, and is used clinically as a cream, ointment, gel, or solution for short-course treatment of localized inflammatory and pruritic skin lesions. Percutaneous absorption is usually limited but rises with occlusion, inflamed or denuded skin, prolonged use, large surface area exposure, and pediatric application; absorbed drug distributes systemically via corticosteroid pathways, undergoes mainly hepatic biotransformation to inactive metabolites, and is excreted primarily in urine with some fecal elimination. Toxicity is dominated by local and systemic corticosteroid effects, including skin atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, delayed wound healing, secondary infection, HPA-axis suppression, hyperglycemia, Cushingoid features, and rarely growth suppression in children; common adverse effects include burning, irritation, dryness, folliculitis, acneiform eruptions, hypopigmentation, and perioral dermatitis.

Name: Abacavir
Description: Abacavir (DrugBank DB01048) is a synthetic carbocyclic guanosine analog antiretroviral whose structure consists of a substituted cyclopentene ring replacing the ribose moiety and a purine-like 6-aminopyrimidinyl system, giving it the character of a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor; chemically it is classified as a carbocyclic nucleoside analog, with a cyclopentenyl-purine scaffold closely related to other NRTIs, and it is most similar in therapeutic role to lamivudine, zidovudine, emtricitabine, didanosine, and tenofovir-containing agents used in combination HIV therapy. After oral administration it is rapidly and well absorbed with high bioavailability, distributes widely including into cerebrospinal fluid, shows relatively low protein binding, is hepatically metabolized primarily by alcohol dehydrogenase and UDP-glucuronosyltransferase to inactive metabolites rather than by major CYP pathways, and is excreted mainly in urine as metabolites with only a small fraction unchanged. Its active intracellular metabolite, carbovir triphosphate, targets HIV-1 and HIV-2 reverse transcriptase by competing with endogenous nucleotides and causing viral DNA chain termination. The major indication is treatment of HIV infection, including combination regimens for adults and children, such as fixed-dose combinations with lamivudine with or without dolutegravir. The most clinically important toxicity is the potentially fatal HLA-B*57:01-associated hypersensitivity reaction, often presenting with fever, rash, gastrointestinal and respiratory symptoms; other toxicities and adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, headache, fatigue, abdominal pain, elevated liver enzymes, rare lactic acidosis, hepatomegaly with steatosis, and occasional pancreatitis, so clinical use requires pre-treatment HLA-B*57:01 screening and prompt discontinuation if hypersensitivity is suspected.

Name: Ibuprofen
Description: Ibuprofen (DrugBank DB01050) is a small-molecule, orally active arylpropionic acid nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug characterized structurally by a hydrophobic isobutyl-substituted phenyl ring linked to a propionic acid moiety, with a single chiral center and marketed commonly as a racemate, the active pharmacology residing predominantly in the S-enantiomer after partial in vivo chiral inversion from R-ibuprofen. Chemically, it belongs to the profen subclass of NSAIDs, with an arylpropionic acid scaffold that is shared by similar drugs such as naproxen, ketoprofen, flurbiprofen, and fenoprofen. Its principal targets are cyclooxygenase enzymes PTGS1 (COX-1) and PTGS2 (COX-2), which it reversibly inhibits to reduce prostaglandin and thromboxane synthesis, accounting for analgesic, antipyretic, and anti-inflammatory effects. Ibuprofen is well absorbed after oral administration, is highly albumin bound, distributes widely but with limited penetration into the central nervous system, undergoes extensive hepatic oxidation primarily via CYP2C9 followed by glucuronidation, and is eliminated mainly in urine as inactive metabolites with a relatively short half-life requiring repeated dosing. It is indicated for pain, fever, dysmenorrhea, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and other musculoskeletal or inflammatory conditions, and is widely used in acute headache, dental pain, postoperative pain, and minor injury. Toxicity includes dose-related gastrointestinal erosion, ulceration and bleeding, renal hypoperfusion or acute kidney injury, fluid retention, hypertension, and overdose manifestations such as nausea, metabolic acidosis, seizures, or central nervous system depression; adverse effects commonly include dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, dizziness, rash, and edema. Clinically, it is used over the counter for mild to moderate pain and fever and by prescription for chronic inflammatory arthropathies and other higher-intensity inflammatory states.

Name: Benzylpenicillin
Description: Benzylpenicillin (penicillin G; DrugBank DB01053) is a natural penam antibiotic built on a strained bicyclic 6-aminopenicillanic acid core in which a four-membered beta-lactam ring is fused to a five-membered thiazolidine ring and bears a benzyl acyl side chain, a structure that defines it chemically as a beta-lactam, specifically a natural penicillin, with the penam scaffold as its characteristic chemical framework. Closely related drugs include phenoxymethylpenicillin, ampicillin, amoxicillin, nafcillin, and the repository salts benzathine penicillin G and procaine penicillin G. Its antibacterial action results from covalent acylation of bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, especially transpeptidases such as PBP1, PBP2, and PBP3, thereby inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-linking and causing cell lysis; susceptibility is limited by beta-lactamases. Benzylpenicillin is acid labile and therefore poorly suited to oral delivery, so it is commonly given parenterally; it distributes widely into extracellular fluids, reaches therapeutic levels in pleura, joints, and inflamed meninges, shows modest protein binding, undergoes minimal metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by renal tubular secretion and glomerular filtration, with a short plasma half-life prolonged in renal impairment and neonates. Major toxicities are hypersensitivity reactions ranging from rash and urticaria to anaphylaxis, with additional risks of hemolytic anemia, interstitial nephritis, seizures at very high doses or with renal failure, and electrolyte load effects with potassium or sodium salts. Adverse effects commonly include injection-site pain, diarrhea, nausea, candidiasis, and Jarisch-Herxheimer reactions during syphilis treatment. Clinically, it is used for highly susceptible streptococcal and pneumococcal infections, meningococcal disease, syphilis, actinomycosis, clostridial infections, leptospirosis, and selected endocarditis regimens.

Name: Tocainide
Description: Tocainide (DrugBank DB01056) is an orally active class IB antiarrhythmic that is structurally a primary aromatic amine amide closely related to lidocaine, featuring a xylidine-like 2,6-dimethylphenyl ring attached through an amino-containing propyl linkage that confers local anesthetic/antiarrhythmic physicochemical properties; chemically it is categorized as an amino amide antiarrhythmic, and its core scaffold can be described as a dimethyl-substituted anilide/xylidine framework bearing a basic side chain. Similar drugs include lidocaine, mexiletine, and to a lesser extent phenytoin in terms of sodium channel-blocking electrophysiology. Its principal pharmacologic target is the cardiac voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.5, encoded by SCN5A, with use-dependent blockade of fast inward sodium current in ventricular myocardium and Purkinje fibers. Tocainide was indicated mainly for suppression of serious symptomatic ventricular arrhythmias, especially recurrent ventricular tachycardia and frequent premature ventricular complexes when benefit outweighed risk. It is well absorbed orally, has relatively low first-pass metabolism, distributes systemically with moderate protein binding, undergoes limited hepatic biotransformation compared with lidocaine, and is eliminated substantially by renal excretion as unchanged drug and metabolites, giving a plasma half-life typically in the low double-digit hour range and requiring dose adjustment in renal impairment. Toxicity includes proarrhythmia, conduction slowing, CNS toxicity such as tremor or dizziness, and serious idiosyncratic hematologic or pulmonary reactions including agranulocytosis, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and interstitial pneumonitis/fibrosis. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, lightheadedness, ataxia, paresthesias, and rash. Clinically, it was used as an oral lidocaine congener for chronic outpatient management of life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias, but use declined because of safety concerns and the availability of better-tolerated alternatives.

Name: Echothiophate
Description: Echothiophate (DrugBank DB01057) is a quaternary ammonium organophosphorus cholinergic agent structurally characterized as a bis-quaternary phosphorothioate/organophosphate containing permanently charged trimethylammonium-substituted ethyl groups linked through a phosphate-thioate center, a motif that confers high polarity and strong affinity for cholinesterases; chemically it belongs to the organophosphate anticholinesterase class, with a phosphorothioate ester scaffold closely related to other irreversible or pseudo-irreversible cholinesterase inhibitors such as isoflurophate/diisopropyl fluorophosphate, demecarium, neostigmine, and physostigmine, although echothiophate is distinguished by its bis-quaternary cationic scaffold and topical ophthalmic use. Its principal target proteins are acetylcholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase, which it phosphorylates, producing prolonged inhibition and increased acetylcholine at muscarinic and nicotinic synapses. After ocular administration, systemic absorption is limited by its permanent charge but can still occur through conjunctival and nasolacrimal tissues; distribution is largely extracellular with poor blood-brain barrier penetration, metabolism is slow because enzyme reactivation depends on dephosphorylation or new enzyme synthesis, and elimination reflects gradual hydrolysis and excretion of metabolites in urine. Toxicity is that of organophosphate excess, including prolonged cholinesterase inhibition, miosis, ciliary spasm, lacrimation, salivation, diarrhea, bronchospasm, bradycardia, muscle weakness, and rarely respiratory compromise. Clinically it has been used mainly for chronic open-angle glaucoma and sometimes accommodative esotropia, where its miotic effect lowers intraocular pressure and alters accommodation; adverse effects include brow ache, blurred vision, induced myopia, cataract risk, conjunctival irritation, retinal detachment risk in susceptible patients, and prolonged apnea with succinylcholine due to plasma cholinesterase inhibition.

Name: Praziquantel
Description: Praziquantel (DB01058) is a synthetic anthelmintic built around a compact pyrazinoisoquinoline framework, specifically a bicyclic tetrahydroisoquinoline fused to a diketopiperazine-like pyrazinone core with a cyclohexanecarbonyl substituent, giving a lipophilic, conformationally constrained structure; chemically it is classified as a pyrazinoisoquinoline cestocidal and trematocidal agent, and its core scaffold is the praziquantel pyrazino[2,1-a]isoquinolin-4-one nucleus. Closely related or therapeutically similar antiparasitic drugs include epsiprantel, niclosamide, albendazole, mebendazole, and oxamniquine, although they differ structurally. Praziquantel is rapidly and usually well absorbed orally, undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism with increased exposure when taken with food, is widely distributed including into bile and likely CSF during inflammation, is extensively metabolized mainly by CYP3A4 with contributions from other CYP enzymes to hydroxylated inactive metabolites, and is excreted predominantly in urine as metabolites with a short parent half-life of roughly 1 to 2.5 hours. Its best-characterized pharmacologic target is parasite voltage-gated calcium channel machinery, particularly Ca2+-permeable channel subunits such as schistosome Cav beta-associated systems, with proposed interactions involving transient receptor potential melastatin-like channels; the result is rapid calcium influx, tegumental disruption, and spastic paralysis. It is indicated for schistosomiasis, clonorchiasis, opisthorchiasis, paragonimiasis, taeniasis, diphyllobothriasis, and neurocysticercosis. Adverse effects are usually dose-related and include abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, headache, dizziness, somnolence, urticaria, fever, and transient liver enzyme elevation, while toxicities may include seizure exacerbation, inflammatory reactions from dying parasites, and rare hypersensitivity; clinically it is used as first-line oral therapy for Schistosoma mansoni, S. haematobium, and S. japonicum infections, liver and lung fluke disease, and selected tapeworm infections, often in single-day or short-course regimens.

Name: Norfloxacin
Description: Norfloxacin (DrugBank DB01059) is a synthetic fluoroquinolone antibacterial built on a 4-quinolone-3-carboxylic acid core bearing a fluorine at C6 that enhances bacterial penetration and potency, a piperazine substituent at C7 that broadens Gram-negative activity, and an N1 ethyl group; chemically it is categorized as a fluorinated quinolone carboxylic acid, with the classic fluoroquinolone scaffold shared by related agents such as ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin, levofloxacin, enoxacin, and pefloxacin. Its antibacterial effect arises from inhibition of bacterial DNA gyrase subunits GyrA/GyrB and topoisomerase IV subunits ParC/ParE, blocking DNA supercoiling and segregation. Orally administered norfloxacin is absorbed incompletely with relatively low bioavailability, food and polyvalent cations reduce absorption, protein binding is modest, tissue distribution is moderate with high urinary concentrations but comparatively limited systemic exposure, metabolism is limited, and elimination occurs largely by renal excretion of unchanged drug with a smaller fecal component, giving a short elimination half-life that typically requires twice-daily dosing. It is indicated mainly for susceptible urinary tract infections, including cystitis, pyelonephritis, prostatitis, and some cases of uncomplicated gonorrhea or bacterial gastroenteritis such as traveler’s diarrhea. Toxicities and adverse effects include gastrointestinal upset, headache, dizziness, rash, photosensitivity, hepatotoxicity, dysglycemia, QT prolongation, central nervous system excitation or seizures, peripheral neuropathy, tendinopathy and tendon rupture, and worsening of myasthenia gravis; class warnings also include rare aortic aneurysm risk and C. difficile-associated diarrhea. Clinically, it has been used primarily for lower and complicated UTIs and chronic bacterial prostatitis when pathogen susceptibility and local resistance patterns support its use.

Name: Amoxicillin
Description: Amoxicillin (DrugBank DB01060) is a semisynthetic aminopenicillin characterized by the penam nucleus, a strained bicyclic beta-lactam fused to a thiazolidine ring, bearing an amino-substituted phenylacetamido side chain with a para-hydroxylated aromatic group that increases acid stability and broadens activity against some Gram-negative organisms; chemically it belongs to the beta-lactam antibiotics, specifically the penicillins, and its core scaffold is the 6-aminopenicillanic acid framework. Closely related drugs include ampicillin, penicillin V, dicloxacillin, and the beta-lactamase inhibitor combination product amoxicillin/clavulanate. Its principal targets are bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, including transpeptidases such as PBP1A, PBP1B, PBP2, and PBP3 in susceptible organisms, leading to inhibition of peptidoglycan cross-linking and cell-wall synthesis. Orally, amoxicillin is well absorbed, with better bioavailability than ampicillin, distributes widely into respiratory tissues, middle ear fluid, urine, bile, and inflamed meninges to a limited extent, shows low-to-moderate protein binding, undergoes minimal hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by the kidney via glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, with a short half-life prolonged in renal impairment. Toxicity is generally low but includes hypersensitivity reactions ranging from rash and urticaria to anaphylaxis, antibiotic-associated colitis, interstitial nephritis, crystalluria, rare hepatotoxicity, and neurotoxicity such as seizures at high exposure or with renal dysfunction. Indications and clinical use include otitis media, sinusitis, streptococcal pharyngitis, community respiratory tract infections, uncomplicated urinary tract infection, Helicobacter pylori eradication regimens, Lyme disease, and susceptible skin or dental infections. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, candidiasis, and maculopapular rash, especially in infectious mononucleosis.

Name: Azlocillin
Description: Azlocillin (DrugBank DB01061) is a semisynthetic acylureidopenicillin whose structure is built on the penam nucleus, consisting of a strained beta-lactam ring fused to a thiazolidine ring and bearing the characteristic penicillin carboxylate plus an extended ureido-acyl side chain that broadens Gram-negative activity, especially against Pseudomonas; chemically it belongs to the beta-lactam antibiotics, specifically the ureidopenicillin subclass, and its core scaffold is the 6-aminopenicillanic acid penicillin scaffold. Closely related drugs include mezlocillin, piperacillin, ampicillin, and carbenicillin, which share the beta-lactam/penam framework but differ in side-chain features and spectrum. Like other parenteral penicillins, azlocillin is poorly orally absorbed, is administered intravenously or intramuscularly, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid with useful penetration into urine, bile, lung, and inflamed tissues, shows low to moderate protein binding, undergoes limited metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by renal tubular secretion and glomerular filtration, with some biliary excretion and dose adjustment needed in renal impairment. Its principal targets are bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, especially transpeptidases involved in peptidoglycan cross-linking, leading to inhibition of cell-wall synthesis and bactericidal activity. It has been used for serious susceptible infections such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacterales, urinary tract infections, lower respiratory tract infections, intra-abdominal infections, gynecologic infections, septicemia, and complicated soft-tissue infections. Toxicity and adverse effects resemble other penicillins and include hypersensitivity reactions up to anaphylaxis, rash, fever, eosinophilia, diarrhea, antibiotic-associated colitis, interstitial nephritis, reversible cytopenias, elevated liver enzymes, seizures at high concentrations or with renal failure, and local injection-site reactions; clinically, it has often been used in hospitalized patients, sometimes with aminoglycosides, for severe polymicrobial or pseudomonal infections.

Name: Oxybutynin
Description: Oxybutynin (DrugBank DB01062) is a synthetic tertiary amine antimuscarinic built on a glycolate ester architecture in which a substituted cyclohexyl-phenyl tertiary alcohol-like motif is linked through an ester to a diethylaminoethyl side chain; chemically it is classified as an anticholinergic/antispasmodic amino-ester and is commonly described as having a diaryl-substituted glycolate or aminoalcohol ester scaffold. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other bladder antimuscarinics such as tolterodine, fesoterodine, propiverine, solifenacin, darifenacin, and older agents like dicyclomine. Its principal targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially M3 (CHRM3) and also M1, M2, M4, and M5, with functional reduction of detrusor smooth-muscle contractions. After oral administration it is well absorbed but undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism, giving low and variable bioavailability; it is widely distributed, crosses the blood-brain barrier, and is highly protein bound. It is metabolized mainly by CYP3A4 to active N-desethyloxybutynin and other metabolites, with elimination primarily in urine as metabolites and a shorter half-life for immediate-release than extended-release or transdermal formulations. Toxicity reflects excessive anticholinergic exposure, including dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, tachycardia, hyperthermia, agitation, confusion, hallucinations, and overdose-related central anticholinergic syndrome. It is indicated for overactive bladder, urge urinary incontinence, urgency, frequency, and neurogenic detrusor overactivity, including pediatric bladder instability in selected cases. Clinically it is used as immediate-release tablets, extended-release tablets, syrups, transdermal patches, and topical gels, with transdermal delivery often preferred to reduce first-pass metabolite-mediated xerostomia.

Name: Acetophenazine
