Description: Acetophenazine (DB01063) is a first-generation antipsychotic of the phenothiazine class, specifically a piperazine-substituted phenothiazine derivative built on a tricyclic phenothiazine scaffold containing sulfur and nitrogen heteroatoms, with a ring substituent and a three-carbon side chain terminating in a piperazine moiety that contributes to potent dopamine-receptor antagonism. Chemically it belongs to the typical neuroleptics and is closely related to other piperazine phenothiazines such as prochlorperazine, perphenazine, trifluoperazine, and fluphenazine, which share the same core scaffold and broadly similar receptor-binding profiles. Its principal pharmacologic target is dopamine D2 receptor blockade in the mesolimbic system, with additional lower-affinity actions at D1-like receptors, alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, histamine H1 receptors, and muscarinic cholinergic receptors that help explain both efficacy and adverse effects. It was used for schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders, particularly hallucinations, delusions, agitation, and severe behavioral disturbance. Like other oral phenothiazines, it is expected to be reasonably absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, extensively distributed into highly perfused tissues including the CNS, strongly protein bound, hepatically metabolized by oxidative pathways with likely CYP-mediated biotransformation and conjugation, and excreted as metabolites in urine and bile. Toxicity is typical of phenothiazines and includes dose-related CNS depression, severe extrapyramidal reactions, anticholinergic effects, orthostatic hypotension, QT-related arrhythmia risk, seizures, cholestatic jaundice, blood dyscrasias, and rare neuroleptic malignant syndrome or tardive dyskinesia. Clinical use historically centered on maintenance or symptomatic treatment of chronic psychosis when a potent typical antipsychotic was required.

Name: Isoprenaline
Description: Isoprenaline (isoproterenol; DrugBank DB01064) is a synthetic catecholamine and direct-acting sympathomimetic whose structure consists of a catechol ring bearing two vicinal phenolic hydroxyls linked to a β-hydroxyethylamine side chain with a bulky N-isopropyl substituent, a motif that confers potent, relatively nonselective β-adrenergic agonism; chemically it is a phenylethanolamine within the catecholamine class, built on the arylethanolamine/phenethylamine scaffold shared with endogenous adrenergic transmitters. Closely related drugs include epinephrine, norepinephrine, dobutamine, salbutamol, terbutaline, and orciprenaline/metaproterenol, which retain the adrenergic ethanolamine pharmacophore with differing receptor selectivity. Its principal targets are β1-, β2-, and to a lesser extent β3-adrenergic receptors encoded by ADRB1, ADRB2, and ADRB3, stimulating adenylyl cyclase via Gs to increase cAMP. Isoprenaline is used for symptomatic bradycardia, atrioventricular block, Adams-Stokes attacks, and occasionally bronchospasm or cardiogenic states requiring chronotropic support. It is rapidly active by parenteral, inhaled, or sublingual routes but has poor oral bioavailability; distribution is rapid, CNS penetration is limited, metabolism occurs largely by catechol-O-methyltransferase rather than efficient MAO deamination, and metabolites plus unchanged drug are excreted mainly in urine, yielding a short plasma half-life and brief duration of action. Toxicity reflects excessive β-stimulation, including tachyarrhythmias, palpitations, angina, myocardial ischemia, hypotension, tremor, nervousness, headache, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, and rarely serious ventricular arrhythmias or myocardial necrosis at high doses. Clinically, it has been used as an emergency temporizing agent to raise heart rate and improve cardiac output while definitive pacing or other interventions are arranged.

Name: Melatonin
Description: Melatonin (DrugBank DB01065) is an endogenous indoleamine hormone whose structure consists of a 5-methoxy-substituted indole ring bearing a 3-position ethylacetamide side chain, placing it in the tryptamine/indole alkylamine chemical category and on an indole scaffold closely related to serotonin and other biogenic amines. Similar drugs include the melatonin receptor agonists ramelteon, tasimelteon, and agomelatine, as well as the serotonin precursor tryptophan and the pineal hormone analogue prolonged-release melatonin formulations. Its principal targets are melatonin receptors MT1 and MT2, encoded by MTNR1A and MTNR1B, with lower-affinity interactions reported for quinone reductase 2/NQO2 and indirect chronobiologic effects on circadian signaling pathways. After oral administration, melatonin is rapidly absorbed but exhibits variable and often low bioavailability because of substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism; it is widely distributed, crosses the blood-brain barrier and placenta, is mainly metabolized by CYP1A2, with contributions from CYP2C19 and possibly CYP1A1, to 6-hydroxymelatonin followed by sulfate conjugation, and is excreted predominantly in urine as 6-sulfatoxymelatonin. Toxicity is generally low, with overdose usually causing somnolence, dizziness, headache, nausea, hypotension, confusion, or vivid dreams rather than severe organ toxicity, although interaction-based toxicity can occur with fluvoxamine, anticoagulants, or other sedatives. Indications and clinical uses center on insomnia, circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders such as jet lag and delayed sleep phase disorder, and non-24-hour sleep-wake disorder, particularly in blind individuals; adverse effects commonly include daytime drowsiness, fatigue, headache, dizziness, nausea, and abnormal dreams.

Name: Cefditoren
Description: Cefditoren (DB01066) is an orally active third-generation cephalosporin antibacterial administered clinically as the pivoxil ester prodrug; structurally, the active drug is a beta-lactam fused to a dihydrothiazine cephem nucleus bearing the cephalosporin-defining carboxylate, an aminothiazolyl-oxyimino acyl side chain at the 7-position that enhances stability to many beta-lactamases, and a thiazolyl-containing substituent at the 3-position, placing it within the oxyimino aminothiazolyl cephalosporin class and the broader beta-lactam/cephem scaffold family. It is chemically and pharmacologically similar to other advanced oral cephalosporins such as cefpodoxime, cefixime, cefdinir, ceftibuten, and parenteral analogs like cefotaxime or ceftriaxone in spectrum-related features. After oral administration as cefditoren pivoxil, absorption is improved with food, the prodrug is hydrolyzed during absorption to active cefditoren, protein binding is high, tissue distribution is adequate for respiratory and skin infections, metabolism of active cefditoren is minimal, and elimination occurs primarily as unchanged drug via the kidney, so exposure rises in renal impairment. Its antibacterial targets are penicillin-binding proteins involved in peptidoglycan cross-linking, notably PBPs from susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, and methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. Indications include community-acquired pharyngotonsillitis, acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, uncomplicated skin and soft-tissue infections, and other mild-to-moderate respiratory infections. Adverse effects commonly include diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, dyspepsia, candidiasis, rash, and headache, while toxicities of concern include hypersensitivity reactions, Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea, seizure risk with excessive beta-lactam exposure in severe renal dysfunction, positive Coombs-related hematologic effects, and carnitine depletion from the pivoxil moiety, making prolonged use or use in carnitine deficiency clinically important considerations.

Name: Glipizide
Description: Glipizide (DrugBank DB01067) is a second-generation sulfonylurea oral antihyperglycemic agent characterized structurally by an arylsulfonylurea core linking a substituted pyrazinecarboxamide-containing lipophilic moiety to a cyclohexyl group, giving a compact, moderately lipophilic architecture optimized for high-affinity pancreatic receptor binding; chemically it belongs to the sulfonylurea class, and its dominant scaffold is the sulfonylurea pharmacophore appended to a heteroaromatic amide system. It is closely related to other insulin secretagogues such as glyburide (glibenclamide), gliclazide, glimepiride, tolbutamide, and chlorpropamide, which share the same broad scaffold but differ in potency, duration, and substituent pattern. Its principal target is the ATP-sensitive potassium channel in pancreatic beta cells, specifically the sulfonylurea receptor SUR1/ABCC8, functionally coupled to Kir6.2/KCNJ11, where binding promotes channel closure, membrane depolarization, calcium influx, and insulin release. Glipizide is well absorbed orally, has relatively rapid onset, is highly protein bound, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly to inactive or weakly active metabolites, and is eliminated primarily in urine with some fecal excretion; compared with longer-acting sulfonylureas, its half-life is shorter, though glucose-lowering can outlast plasma exposure. It is indicated for type 2 diabetes mellitus when diet and exercise are insufficient, especially for fasting and postprandial hyperglycemia control, and is used as monotherapy or with metformin or insulin. Major toxicities and adverse effects include dose-related hypoglycemia, potentially severe in elderly patients, those with hepatic impairment, irregular food intake, or drug interactions, as well as weight gain; other side effects include nausea, dizziness, headache, rash, photosensitivity, and rare cholestatic, hematologic, or hypersensitivity reactions.

Name: Clonazepam
Description: Clonazepam (DrugBank DB01068) is a nitro-substituted benzodiazepine whose structure consists of a 1,4-benzodiazepin-2-one core fused to a benzene ring and bearing a 5-aryl substituent, a 7-nitro group, and a 2-keto functionality, features that define its high-potency anticonvulsant and anxiolytic profile; chemically it belongs to the benzodiazepine class, more specifically the nitrobenzodiazepines, with the classic 1,4-benzodiazepinone scaffold shared by related agents such as diazepam, nitrazepam, lorazepam, alprazolam, and clobazam. Its principal pharmacologic targets are the benzodiazepine modulatory sites on GABAA receptor complexes, especially those containing α1, α2, α3, and α5 subunits together with γ2, where it acts as a positive allosteric modulator to enhance GABA-mediated chloride conductance. Orally, clonazepam is well absorbed with high bioavailability, distributes widely including into the CNS, is substantially protein bound, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism primarily by CYP3A-mediated reduction and oxidation to less active metabolites, and is eliminated mainly as urinary metabolites with a relatively long half-life that supports intermittent or divided dosing. It is indicated for seizure disorders including absence seizures, myoclonic epilepsy, Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, and for panic disorder with or without agoraphobia; clinically it is used as maintenance anticonvulsant therapy and as an anxiolytic when prolonged benzodiazepine action is desired. Toxicities include dose-related CNS and respiratory depression, oversedation, psychomotor impairment, dependence, withdrawal seizures, and potentiation by alcohol or opioids; common adverse effects include drowsiness, ataxia, dizziness, fatigue, impaired coordination, cognitive slowing, depression, and behavioral disinhibition.

Name: Promethazine
Description: Promethazine (DB01069) is a first-generation phenothiazine antihistamine whose structure consists of a tricyclic phenothiazine core containing sulfur and nitrogen heteroatoms, substituted at the ring nitrogen-bearing framework with a three-carbon side chain terminating in a dimethylamino group; chemically it belongs to the phenothiazine class and more specifically the aminoalkyl phenothiazine scaffold, closely related to other sedating H1 antagonists and phenothiazines such as promazine, chlorpromazine, methdilazine, alimemazine, and prochlorperazine. Its principal pharmacology is strong antagonism/inverse agonism at histamine H1 receptors, with additional antimuscarinic activity and weaker antagonism at dopamine D2, alpha-1 adrenergic, and possibly serotonergic sites, accounting for antiemetic, sedative, and anticholinergic effects; relevant targets therefore include HRH1, muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, DRD2, and ADRA1-family receptors. It is used for allergic conditions such as rhinitis and urticaria, prevention and treatment of nausea and vomiting, motion sickness, short-term sedation, and adjunctive perioperative use. Promethazine is generally well absorbed orally, rectally, or parenterally, is widely distributed including CNS penetration, is highly protein bound, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism primarily via CYP2D6 with other oxidative pathways and sulfoxidation, and is excreted mainly in urine as metabolites with some biliary/fecal elimination. Toxicity is dominated by profound sedation, respiratory depression, delirium, hypotension, QT-related arrhythmia risk, anticholinergic poisoning, and tissue injury with IV extravasation; children are particularly susceptible to fatal respiratory depression. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, and orthostatic hypotension, and clinically it is used as tablets, syrup, suppositories, or injection for symptomatic allergy relief, postoperative nausea, motion-sickness prophylaxis, and nighttime sedation.

Name: Dihydrotachysterol
Description: Dihydrotachysterol (DrugBank DB01070) is a synthetic vitamin D analog structurally derived from tachysterol and closely related to ergocalciferol-type secosteroids; it is a sterol-like, unsaturated secosteroid in which the B-ring is opened, retaining the characteristic vitamin D triene-like hydrophobic framework with a rigid steroidal A/C/D ring system and aliphatic side chain, making its core scaffold a vitamin D secosteroid/sterane-derived scaffold. Chemically it is categorized as a fat-soluble antirachitic agent and vitamin D analog, with similar drugs including ergocalciferol, cholecalciferol, calcifediol, calcitriol, alfacalcidol, paricalcitol, and doxercalciferol. Its pharmacologic action is mediated primarily through the vitamin D receptor (VDR, NR1I1), with downstream effects on intestinal calcium transport proteins, bone, kidney, and parathyroid hormone regulation; calcium-sensing receptor and parathyroid hormone pathways are functionally relevant though not direct primary binding targets. Orally administered dihydrotachysterol is generally well absorbed, distributed in lipid-rich tissues and bound to plasma proteins, activated more rapidly than native vitamin D and less dependent on renal hydroxylation, metabolized hepatically to active hydroxylated metabolites, and eliminated slowly via bile/feces with prolonged biologic effects. It is indicated mainly for hypocalcemia due to hypoparathyroidism, post-surgical tetany, and selected refractory states of impaired calcium metabolism. Clinical use has historically included chronic replacement therapy in hypoparathyroidism and management of latent or overt tetany. Toxicity is dominated by exaggerated vitamin D effects, especially hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria, which can produce nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, renal impairment, soft-tissue/vascular calcification, and cardiac arrhythmias; adverse effects include weakness, headache, nausea, vomiting, constipation, polyuria, polydipsia, anorexia, and confusion.

Name: Atazanavir
Description: Atazanavir (DrugBank DB01072) is an azapeptide HIV protease inhibitor with a lipophilic peptidomimetic structure built around a hydroxyethylamine-like transition-state-mimicking core, decorated with multiple amide/carbamate functionalities and bulky aromatic heterocyclic substituents, including a bis-aryl/pyridyl-rich framework that enhances protease binding; chemically it is classified as an antiretroviral protease inhibitor and more specifically an aza-dipeptide peptidomimetic, with a hydroxyethylamine-derived protease-inhibitor scaffold related to other HIV protease inhibitors such as darunavir, lopinavir, indinavir, ritonavir, and saquinavir. Its principal target is the HIV-1 protease, with activity also against HIV-2 protease, thereby blocking Gag-Pol polyprotein cleavage and preventing maturation of infectious virions. Orally administered atazanavir is absorbed variably and requires an acidic gastric environment for optimal dissolution, is highly protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes extensive hepatic CYP3A-mediated metabolism, and is eliminated mainly via biliary/fecal excretion with lesser renal clearance; ritonavir or cobicistat boosting increases exposure. It is indicated for treatment of HIV-1 infection in combination antiretroviral therapy, including use in treatment-naive and selected treatment-experienced patients. Toxicities include dose-related indirect hyperbilirubinemia from UGT1A1 inhibition, hepatotoxicity, PR/QT interval effects, nephrolithiasis/cholelithiasis, and important CYP3A drug-drug interactions; overdose or susceptibility states may accentuate jaundice or conduction abnormalities. Common adverse effects include jaundice, scleral icterus, nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, headache, rash, and lipid or glucose disturbances. Clinically, it has been used in once-daily regimens, often boosted, especially when a protease-inhibitor-based HIV regimen is desired.

Name: Fludarabine
Description: Fludarabine (DrugBank DB01073) is a fluorinated purine antimetabolite nucleoside analog, administered clinically most often as the water-soluble phosphate prodrug fludarabine phosphate, whose structure consists of a 2-fluoro-substituted adenine base linked through a beta-N9 glycosidic bond to an arabinofuranose sugar with a 5-monophosphate in the prodrug; chemically it belongs to the purine nucleoside analog and antineoplastic antimetabolite class, with a vidarabine/adenosine-like arabinosyl purine scaffold. Closely related drugs include cladribine, clofarabine, nelarabine, vidarabine, and to a lesser extent cytarabine as another arabinose-containing antimetabolite. After intravenous administration, the phosphate is rapidly dephosphorylated in plasma to 2-fluoro-ara-A, enters cells via nucleoside transporters, and is sequentially phosphorylated to the active triphosphate 2-fluoro-ara-ATP; oral bioavailability exists but is incomplete, distribution is systemic with notable lymphocyte uptake, metabolism is limited apart from intracellular activation and minor deamination, and elimination is predominantly renal, making exposure sensitive to kidney impairment. Its principal functional targets are DNA polymerase alpha, delta, and epsilon, ribonucleotide reductase, DNA primase, DNA ligase, and indirectly DNA repair and apoptosis pathways, producing inhibition of DNA synthesis and chain elongation. It is indicated mainly for B-cell chronic lymphocytic leukemia and has also been used in indolent non-Hodgkin lymphomas, mantle cell lymphoma, and conditioning regimens before hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation. Major toxicities include profound myelosuppression, prolonged T-cell immunosuppression with opportunistic infections, neurotoxicity at high doses, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, tumor lysis syndrome, and renal dose-related toxicity; common adverse effects include neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, fever, nausea, diarrhea, fatigue, rash, and infection. Clinically, it is used as single-agent therapy or in combination regimens such as fludarabine-cyclophosphamide-rituximab for CLL and related lymphoid malignancies.

Name: Diphenhydramine
Description: Diphenhydramine (DrugBank DB01075) is a first-generation ethanolamine antihistamine characterized structurally by a diaryl ether scaffold in which a benzhydryl-type diphenylmethoxy moiety is linked through a short ethyl chain to a terminal dimethylamino group, creating a lipophilic, cationic tertiary amine that readily crosses the blood-brain barrier; chemically it is classified as an H1 receptor antagonist of the aminoalkyl ether/ethanolamine class, with a diarylmethane-diaryl ether pharmacophore shared with related sedating antihistamines such as doxylamine, carbinoxamine, clemastine, dimenhydrinate, and the mechanistically similar diphenylpyraline. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor (HRH1), where it acts as an inverse agonist/antagonist, but it also has clinically relevant antimuscarinic activity at cholinergic receptors and lesser sodium-channel blocking effects that contribute to local anesthetic and cardiotoxic properties. It is well absorbed orally, with onset typically within 15 to 60 minutes, wide tissue distribution including CNS penetration, extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism mainly via CYP2D6-mediated N-demethylation and oxidative pathways, and renal excretion of metabolites with an elimination half-life commonly around 4 to 9 hours but variable with age and metabolizer status. It is indicated for allergic rhinitis, urticaria, pruritus, conjunctival allergy, common cold symptoms, motion sickness, nausea, and short-term insomnia, and is also used clinically as an adjunct in acute dystonic reactions and occasional cough/cold formulations. Common adverse effects include sedation, impaired psychomotor performance, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention; toxicity is dominated by anticholinergic syndrome, delirium, seizures, hyperthermia, QRS/QT abnormalities, and ventricular arrhythmias, especially in overdose, children, older adults, or when combined with alcohol and other CNS depressants.

Name: Atorvastatin
Description: Atorvastatin (DrugBank DB01076) is a synthetic lipid-lowering agent of the statin class, specifically a type II HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor, built around a substituted pyrrole core bearing aryl groups, including a fluorophenyl moiety, and a dihydroxyheptanoic acid side chain that mimics the endogenous HMG-CoA/mevalonate transition-state pharmacophore responsible for enzyme binding; thus its key scaffold is the heptanoic acid statin pharmacophore linked to a heteroaryl diaryl framework. It is chemically related to other statins such as simvastatin, lovastatin, pravastatin, rosuvastatin, fluvastatin, and pitavastatin, with greatest mechanistic similarity across this class through competitive inhibition of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase (HMGCR), its principal target protein, while downstream pharmacodynamic effects include increased hepatic LDL receptor expression. Orally administered atorvastatin is rapidly absorbed but undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic extraction, has moderate absolute bioavailability, is highly protein bound, distributes preferentially to the liver, is metabolized mainly by CYP3A4 to active ortho- and para-hydroxylated metabolites, and is excreted predominantly via biliary elimination with minimal renal clearance. It is indicated for primary hypercholesterolemia, mixed dyslipidemia, familial hypercholesterolemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular events such as myocardial infarction and stroke. Toxicities include dose-related hepatotoxicity, myopathy, myositis, rhabdomyolysis, and rare immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, with higher risk from CYP3A4 inhibitors or interacting drugs. Common adverse effects include myalgia, arthralgia, gastrointestinal upset, headache, and transaminase elevation. Clinically, it is widely used for high-intensity LDL lowering in secondary prevention after acute coronary syndrome, in diabetes with elevated cardiovascular risk, and in patients with established coronary, cerebrovascular, or peripheral arterial disease.

Name: Etidronic acid
Description: Etidronic acid, also known as etidronate, is a first-generation non-nitrogen bisphosphonate built on a simple P–C–P bisphosphonate scaffold in which a hydroxyethylidene carbon bears a hydroxyl group and a methyl substituent, creating a highly polar pyrophosphate mimic that avidly chelates calcium and binds hydroxyapatite in bone; chemically it belongs to the diphosphonate/bisphosphonate class, with a minimal aliphatic hydroxyalkyl bisphosphonate scaffold shared in concept with related agents such as clodronate, tiludronate, pamidronate, alendronate, and risedronate, though the latter are structurally more substituted and often nitrogen-containing. Its principal pharmacologic target is the bone mineral surface rather than a single high-affinity receptor, but at the cellular level it is taken up by osteoclasts and can interfere with ATP-dependent pathways through formation of nonhydrolyzable ATP analogs, thereby inhibiting osteoclast-mediated bone resorption; no canonical protein target is as dominant as with later nitrogen bisphosphonates. Oral absorption is poor, typically a few percent and reduced further by food or divalent cations; distribution is largely extracellular with rapid uptake into mineralized bone, negligible metabolism, and renal excretion of unchanged drug, while the skeletal fraction may persist for prolonged periods. It is indicated for Paget disease of bone and for prevention or treatment of heterotopic ossification, with historical use in disorders featuring pathologic calcification. Toxicity includes osteomalacia with excessive or prolonged dosing, hypocalcemia, renal injury, and GI mucosal irritation; adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, esophagitis, musculoskeletal pain, and rarely atypical mineralization defects. Clinically, it has been used orally or intravenously in carefully scheduled regimens to suppress abnormal bone turnover while minimizing impairment of normal mineralization.

Name: Tegaserod
Description: Tegaserod (DB01079) is a substituted indole-carbazimidamide serotoninergic prokinetic agent whose structure is built around an indole/aza-aromatic scaffold bearing a guanidinium-like amidino functionality and alkoxy substituents that confer high polarity while preserving receptor recognition; chemically it is classified as an aminoguanidine-containing indole derivative and more specifically as a selective 5-hydroxytryptamine type 4 (5-HT4) receptor partial agonist, with a scaffold related pharmacologically to other serotonergic gastrointestinal prokinetics such as cisapride, prucalopride, and mosapride, although it is structurally distinct from these benzamide-like agents. Its principal target protein is HTR4, with weak activity reported at other serotonin receptors in some systems, and its therapeutic effect is enhancement of peristaltic reflexes, intestinal secretion, and gastrointestinal motility. Pharmacokinetically, oral absorption is incomplete with relatively low bioavailability because of first-pass metabolism, distribution is modest with limited tissue accumulation, metabolism occurs mainly in the liver through acid hydrolysis and oxidative biotransformation yielding less active metabolites, and excretion is primarily biliary/fecal with a smaller renal component. Tegaserod was indicated mainly for irritable bowel syndrome with constipation and chronic idiopathic constipation, especially in women with abdominal pain, bloating, and infrequent hard stools. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, abdominal cramping, nausea, flatulence, headache, and dizziness. Toxicity concerns center on excessive GI stimulation causing severe diarrhea, dehydration, or ischemic colitis-like presentations, and more importantly a debated signal for cardiovascular ischemic events such as angina, myocardial infarction, or stroke in susceptible patients, which has strongly shaped its restricted clinical use in carefully selected patients without major cardiovascular risk factors.

Name: Vigabatrin
Description: Vigabatrin (DB01080) is a small, highly polar γ-aminobutyric acid analog built on a simple amino-acid-like scaffold consisting of a terminal carboxylic acid and primary amine separated by a four-carbon chain containing a vinyl substituent; chemically it is an unsaturated aliphatic amino acid and mechanism-based enzyme inhibitor, with a GABA-mimetic scaffold related to other anticonvulsants that enhance GABA signaling, such as gabapentin, pregabalin, valproate, and tiagabine, although vigabatrin is distinguished by irreversible target engagement rather than transporter blockade or channel modulation. Its principal target is 4-aminobutyrate aminotransferase, also called GABA transaminase or ABAT, which it irreversibly inhibits, increasing central nervous system GABA concentrations. After oral administration it is well absorbed, has low protein binding, distributes mainly in total body water with entry into the CNS, undergoes minimal metabolism, and is eliminated largely unchanged in urine, so renal impairment reduces clearance and prolongs exposure. Toxicologically, the major serious risk is irreversible bilateral concentric visual field constriction with retinal toxicity, likely exposure-related; neurotoxicity may also present as sedation, confusion, or MRI signal abnormalities in infants, and overdose can produce marked CNS depression. It is indicated for refractory focal seizures and for infantile spasms, particularly West syndrome, including cases associated with tuberous sclerosis complex. Common adverse effects include somnolence, fatigue, dizziness, weight gain, tremor, ataxia, irritability, depression, and blurred vision. Clinically, it is used as adjunctive therapy in drug-resistant partial epilepsy and as a key option for infantile spasms when rapid seizure suppression is needed, with visual monitoring and dose adjustment in renal dysfunction.

Name: Diphenoxylate
Description: Diphenoxylate (DrugBank DB01081) is a synthetic opioid antidiarrheal structurally characterized as a piperidine-based meperidine congener bearing a 4-phenyl-substituted piperidine core, an ester functionality, and a nitrile-containing side chain, giving it the profile of a lipophilic diaryl-opioid-like gastrointestinal motility inhibitor; chemically it is classified as a phenylpiperidine opioid derivative, and its key scaffold is the 4-phenylpiperidine framework shared with related agents such as loperamide, meperidine, and difenoxin, the latter being its active metabolite and a close pharmacologic analog. Its principal target is the mu-opioid receptor, with antidiarrheal action mediated predominantly through enteric opioid receptor activation that reduces propulsive intestinal motility and prolongs transit time. After oral administration it is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism including ester hydrolysis to difenoxin, distributes systemically with some central nervous system penetration at higher doses, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in feces and urine. It is indicated for adjunctive treatment of diarrhea, especially acute nonspecific diarrhea and chronic diarrhea associated with inflammatory bowel conditions when infection or other reversible causes are addressed. Clinically it is commonly combined with atropine to deter abuse and used for symptomatic stool-frequency reduction. Adverse effects include constipation, abdominal discomfort, nausea, drowsiness, dizziness, dry mouth, and ileus, while toxicity resembles opioid excess, with CNS and respiratory depression, miosis, lethargy, paralytic ileus, and potentially fatal overdose, particularly in children or with supratherapeutic dosing.

Name: Streptomycin
Description: Streptomycin (DrugBank DB01082) is a naturally derived aminoglycoside antibiotic composed of a highly polar, polycationic aminocyclitol core, streptidine, linked by glycosidic bonds to streptose and N-methyl-L-glucosamine, giving a densely hydroxylated, strongly basic carbohydrate-like architecture that lacks oral bioavailability and favors ionic interactions with ribosomal RNA; chemically it belongs to the aminoglycoside/aminocyclitol class and its central scaffold is the streptidine-containing aminoglycoside nucleus. Similar drugs include other aminoglycosides such as gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin, kanamycin, and neomycin, which share polyhydroxylated cationic sugar frameworks and ribosomal inhibition as a class effect. Its principal target is the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit, especially 16S rRNA and associated ribosomal protein S12, where binding causes misreading of mRNA and inhibition of initiation, leading to bactericidal activity. Streptomycin is poorly absorbed orally, is therefore given parenterally, distributes mainly into extracellular fluid with limited CNS penetration unless meninges are inflamed, shows negligible metabolism, and is excreted largely unchanged by glomerular filtration, so accumulation occurs in renal impairment. Major indications include tuberculosis in combination regimens, plague, tularemia, and selected severe infections due to susceptible Enterobacterales or Brucella. Toxicity is dominated by ototoxicity, particularly vestibular dysfunction with vertigo and ataxia, nephrotoxicity, and neuromuscular blockade causing respiratory weakness; common adverse effects include rash, fever, injection-site pain, tinnitus, hearing loss, nausea, and hypersensitivity. Clinically, it is now used selectively rather than routinely, for example as a second-line antitubercular agent and as a treatment for tularemia or plague when organism susceptibility and patient factors support aminoglycoside use.

Name: Orlistat
Description: Orlistat (DB01083) is a highly lipophilic, saturated derivative of lipstatin characterized structurally by a substituted four-membered beta-lactone ring bearing a long aliphatic chain and an N-formyl-L-leucine-derived side chain, placing it in the beta-lactone fatty acid/lipase inhibitor class with a lipstatin-like beta-lactone scaffold that acts as a reactive serine-directed acylating pharmacophore. It is chemically related to lipstatin and functionally similar to other anti-obesity agents such as sibutramine and liraglutide, although those are mechanistically distinct. Its principal targets are gastrointestinal lipases, especially pancreatic lipase, gastric lipase, and carboxyl ester lipase, which it inhibits covalently at the catalytic serine to block hydrolysis and absorption of dietary triglycerides. Pharmacokinetically, oral absorption is minimal, systemic exposure is usually negligible, distribution is therefore limited, metabolism occurs mainly within the gastrointestinal wall to inactive beta-lactone-opened metabolites, and excretion is predominantly fecal as unchanged drug with only minor urinary elimination. It is indicated for chronic weight management in obesity and overweight patients with comorbidities such as type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, or hypertension, and is used clinically with caloric restriction to promote weight loss and reduce weight regain. Toxicity is dominated by gastrointestinal fat malabsorption, including steatorrhea, fecal urgency, oily spotting, flatulence with discharge, abdominal cramping, and reduced absorption of fat-soluble vitamins; rarer but important examples include severe liver injury, oxalate nephropathy, pancreatitis, and interactions reducing exposure to cyclosporine, levothyroxine, and some antiepileptics.

Name: Emedastine
Description: Emedastine (DrugBank DB01084) is a second-generation antiallergic antihistamine whose structure is characterized by a compact tricyclic, dibenzazepine-like heteroaromatic scaffold incorporating a fused benzene-pyridyl system linked to a basic tertiary amine side chain, a motif that supports high-affinity H1 receptor antagonism with relatively limited anticholinergic activity; chemically it is classified as a benzo[c]pyridine-derived piperidine/tetrahydroethano-bridged antihistamine, and its core scaffold places it among tricyclic H1 antagonists related in function, though not identical in structure, to agents such as ketotifen, azelastine, olopatadine, levocabastine, and epinastine. Its principal known target is the histamine H1 receptor encoded by HRH1, where it acts as an antagonist/inverse agonist to suppress histamine-mediated itching, vasodilation, conjunctival erythema, and tearing. Clinically, emedastine is used primarily as an ophthalmic antiallergic drug for seasonal allergic conjunctivitis and symptoms such as ocular pruritus, redness, and watering. After topical ocular administration, systemic absorption is low, distribution is consequently limited, and clinically relevant central exposure is minimal; absorbed drug undergoes hepatic biotransformation with renal excretion of parent drug and metabolites, and elimination is sufficiently prolonged to allow twice-daily ocular dosing in practice. Toxicity is generally low at therapeutic ophthalmic exposure, but excessive systemic exposure could plausibly produce antihistaminic adverse effects including somnolence, dry mouth, dizziness, and mild antimuscarinic-type symptoms; local intolerance is more typical, with burning, stinging, աչքի irritation, headache, blurred vision, and dysgeusia reported. Thus, its clinical use is focused, symptomatic, and well suited to allergic eye disease where selective H1 blockade is desired with limited systemic burden.

Name: Pilocarpine
Description: Pilocarpine (DrugBank DB01085) is a naturally derived parasympathomimetic alkaloid characterized structurally by a compact N-methyl imidazole heteroaromatic ring linked through a short side chain to a five-membered γ-lactone, giving a small, moderately polar, chiral muscarinic agonist framework; chemically it is classified as an imidazole alkaloid and more broadly as a direct-acting cholinergic agonist, with an imidazole-lactone scaffold that distinguishes it from other miotics. Similar drugs include other muscarinic agonists or cholinomimetics such as cevimeline, bethanechol, methacholine, carbachol, and acetylcholine analogs, although pilocarpine is particularly notable for ocular and secretagogue use. Its principal targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially M3 with activity also at M1 and M2, producing contraction of the iris sphincter and ciliary muscle and stimulation of exocrine glands. After topical ophthalmic or oral administration it is absorbed reasonably well; oral bioavailability is sufficient for secretory indications, distribution is systemic with access to peripheral muscarinic sites, metabolism occurs mainly hepatically, and elimination is primarily renal with a relatively short half-life requiring repeated dosing. It is indicated for open-angle glaucoma, acute angle-closure management adjunctively, and xerostomia, particularly in Sjögren syndrome or after head and neck radiotherapy. Clinical use includes ophthalmic drops for intraocular pressure reduction and oral tablets for salivary hypofunction. Adverse effects reflect cholinergic excess and include sweating, salivation, nausea, diarrhea, urinary frequency, bronchospasm, bradycardia, miosis, blurred vision, brow ache, and headache; toxicity may present as severe parasympathomimetic syndrome with hypotension, bronchoconstriction, vomiting, and excessive secretions, with heightened risk in asthma, cardiovascular disease, or peptic ulcer susceptibility.

Name: Benzocaine
Description: Benzocaine (DrugBank DB01086) is a para-aminobenzoic acid–derived ester local anesthetic whose structure consists of an aniline-type aromatic ring bearing a para-amino substituent and an ethyl ester, giving a compact lipophilic aryl ester optimized for topical membrane penetration; chemically it belongs to the amino ester local anesthetic class, with a p-aminobenzoate scaffold shared by related agents such as procaine, chloroprocaine, tetracaine, and the mechanistically similar but amide-linked lidocaine. Its principal pharmacologic target is voltage-gated sodium channels in peripheral sensory neurons, especially SCN family channels such as SCN9A, SCN10A, and SCN11A, where it stabilizes the inactivated state and reversibly blocks action potential propagation. Because of poor water solubility and limited systemic absorption from intact skin, benzocaine is used mainly topically on skin and mucosa for minor pain, pruritus, burns, oral ulceration, sore throat, hemorrhoids, otitis-related discomfort, and procedural anesthesia such as endoscopy or nasogastric tube placement. Absorption increases across inflamed, abraded, or highly vascular surfaces; distribution is largely local, with any absorbed fraction rapidly hydrolyzed by plasma and hepatic esterases to para-aminobenzoic acid and ethanol, then further conjugated and excreted renally. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related methemoglobinemia, particularly in infants or with excessive mucosal exposure, causing cyanosis, dyspnea, and hypoxia; additional adverse effects include contact dermatitis, hypersensitivity, local burning or stinging, edema, rash, and rarely systemic CNS or cardiovascular toxicity. Clinically, it is formulated in gels, sprays, lozenges, drops, and creams for short-term symptomatic relief rather than durable regional anesthesia.

Name: Primaquine
Description: Primaquine (DrugBank DB01087) is an 8-aminoquinoline antimalarial built on a planar quinoline heteroaromatic ring bearing a methoxy substituent and a terminal primary amine-containing alkyl side chain at the 8-position, a structure that confers redox activity and distinguishes it from blood-schizonticidal quinolines. Chemically it belongs to the aminoquinoline class, more specifically the 8-aminoquinolines, and its core scaffold is the methoxy-substituted quinoline nucleus shared with related tissue-active antimalarials. Similar drugs include tafenoquine, pamaquine, and to a lesser mechanistic relatives such as chloroquine, although the latter is a 4-aminoquinoline with different stage specificity. Primaquine is generally well absorbed orally, distributes widely including to hepatic tissue where dormant hypnozoites reside, is extensively metabolized in the liver by oxidative deamination and CYP-dependent bioactivation, especially involving CYP2D6, to multiple metabolites thought to mediate efficacy and hemolytic toxicity, and is excreted mainly as metabolites in urine with a relatively short parent half-life. Its major toxicities are dose-related hemolytic anemia and methemoglobinemia, classically severe in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, with examples including acute intravascular hemolysis and cyanosis. No single validated parasite protein target fully explains its action; implicated targets or pathways include Plasmodium mitochondrial function and redox homeostasis, while host CYP2D6 is pharmacologically important for activation. It is indicated for radical cure and relapse prevention of Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale malaria, terminal prophylaxis, and gametocytocidal treatment of Plasmodium falciparum to reduce transmission. Common adverse effects include abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, headache, and pruritus. Clinically, it is used after blood-stage treatment for vivax or ovale malaria and, in selected programs, as a single low dose adjunct to falciparum therapy, with G6PD screening central to safe use.

Name: Butenafine
Description: Butenafine (DrugBank DB01091) is a synthetic benzylamine antifungal whose structure is characterized by a highly lipophilic tertiary amine linking a p-tert-butylbenzyl group to an N-methyl naphthalene-containing arylalkyl moiety, giving a diaryl, allylic benzylamine-like architecture optimized for stratum corneum retention. Chemically it is classified as a benzylamine antifungal, closely related in mechanism to allylamines, and its core scaffold can be described as a lipophilic aryl-alkyl tertiary amine built on a butenyl/benzylamine framework fused to aromatic hydrophobes. Similar drugs include terbinafine and naftifine, with butenafine often regarded as mechanistically akin to the allylamine class. Its principal target is fungal squalene epoxidase, causing inhibition of ergosterol biosynthesis and intracellular squalene accumulation, with activity against dermatophytes such as Trichophyton rubrum and Epidermophyton floccosum, and some activity against Candida and Malassezia. Clinically, it is used topically for tinea pedis, tinea cruris, tinea corporis, and sometimes pityriasis versicolor, typically as a 1% cream applied once or twice daily. Pharmacokinetically, systemic absorption after topical administration is minimal, distribution is mainly limited to superficial skin layers with prolonged persistence in keratinized tissue, hepatic metabolism may occur for the small absorbed fraction, and excretion is presumed primarily via urinary and fecal routes after biotransformation. Toxicity is generally low because of limited systemic exposure, though local irritation, erythema, burning, pruritus, contact dermatitis, and scaling can occur; serious systemic toxicity is rare, but accidental ingestion or extensive application could theoretically increase adverse effects.

Name: Dimethyl sulfoxide
Description: Dimethyl sulfoxide (DrugBank DB01093) is a small, highly polar aprotic organosulfur molecule consisting of a sulfoxide sulfur atom doubly bonded to oxygen and substituted by two methyl groups, giving a compact dimethyl-substituted sulfinyl scaffold that serves as the archetypal sulfoxide chemical framework; chemically it is classified as a sulfoxide and dipolar solvent, with related or similar agents including other dialkyl sulfoxides and sulfur-containing penetration enhancers such as methylsulfonylmethane, though DMSO is distinctive in clinical use. It is rapidly absorbed across skin, mucosa, and the bladder, distributes widely into total body water and tissues including the central nervous system, undergoes partial hepatic and extrahepatic conversion mainly to dimethyl sulfide and dimethyl sulfone, and is excreted in urine, breath, and to a lesser extent feces, with breath excretion explaining the characteristic garlic- or oyster-like odor. Its pharmacology is pleiotropic rather than target-selective; reported molecular interactions include modulation of inflammatory signaling and membrane-associated processes, with no single canonical therapeutic protein target, although effects have been described on ion channels, cytokine pathways, and hydroxyl-radical-mediated injury. Clinically, it is indicated primarily for symptomatic relief of interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome, especially pain, urgency, and inflammation, and is also used as a pharmaceutical solvent, cryoprotectant for cellular products, and topical analgesic or anti-inflammatory adjunct in some settings. Adverse effects include bladder irritation, dysuria, nausea, headache, dizziness, pruritus, erythema, and odor, while toxicity at higher exposure may involve hemolysis, gastrointestinal upset, hepatic enzyme elevation, and rare ocular lens changes observed in animal studies.

Name: Fluvastatin
Description: Fluvastatin (DB01095) is a fully synthetic statin characterized by the pharmacophoric 3,5-dihydroxyhept-6-enoic acid side chain that mimics the tetrahedral intermediate of HMG-CoA reduction, attached to a lipophilic indole-based, fluorophenyl-substituted heteroaromatic core with an isopropyl substituent; chemically it is a fluorinated, acidic, amphipathic antihyperlipidemic agent in the statin class, and its core scaffold is best described as an indole-derived statin scaffold rather than the decalin scaffold seen in lovastatin or simvastatin. Closely related drugs include other HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors such as atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, pravastatin, simvastatin, lovastatin, and pitavastatin, which share the same dihydroxyheptanoic acid pharmacophore but differ in ring system and lipophilicity. Fluvastatin targets and inhibits HMG-CoA reductase (HMGCR), producing upregulation of hepatic LDL receptors and reduction of LDL cholesterol, total cholesterol, and triglycerides, with modest HDL increases; it is indicated for primary hypercholesterolemia, mixed dyslipidemia, and prevention of cardiovascular events such as myocardial infarction in selected patients with atherosclerotic risk. After oral administration it is well absorbed but undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic extraction, is highly protein bound, acts mainly in the liver, is metabolized predominantly by CYP2C9 with minor CYP3A4/CYP2C8 contribution, and is eliminated largely via biliary/fecal excretion with limited renal clearance. Toxicities include dose-related hepatotoxicity and statin-associated myopathy ranging from myalgias to rare rhabdomyolysis, with increased risk during interacting therapy or hepatic impairment; adverse effects commonly include dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, headache, insomnia, transaminase elevation, and muscle symptoms. Clinically, it is used as an adjunct to diet and lifestyle modification, often in patients needing LDL lowering or secondary prevention after coronary disease interventions.

Name: Oxamniquine
Description: Oxamniquine (DrugBank DB01096) is a semisynthetic tetrahydroquinoline antischistosomal agent structurally characterized by a 6-hydroxymethyl-2-isopropylaminomethyl-7-nitro-substituted tetrahydroquinoline core, making it a nitrogen-containing heteroaromatic derivative in the quinoline-related chemical category; its central scaffold is a reduced quinoline (tetrahydroquinoline) bearing nitro, hydroxymethyl, and aminomethyl substituents that are important for bioactivation and antiparasitic activity. It is chemically and therapeutically similar to other antischistosomal drugs such as praziquantel, metrifonate, and the older schistosomicides niridazole and hycanthone, although it is structurally distinct from them. Oxamniquine is orally active, generally well absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, distributed systemically with hepatic first-pass biotransformation, and extensively metabolized in the liver to inactive conjugated metabolites, including glucuronide and sulfate derivatives, which are eliminated predominantly in the urine; its plasma half-life is relatively short, but antiparasitic effects persist because of parasite-directed activation. Its key known target system is the Schistosoma mansoni sulfotransferase SULT-OR, which converts the drug to a reactive ester that alkylates parasite macromolecules, including nucleic acids and possibly proteins, leading to worm paralysis and tegumental damage. It is indicated primarily for intestinal schistosomiasis caused by Schistosoma mansoni and has been used clinically for hepatointestinal disease and control programs in endemic regions. Toxicity is usually moderate and dose related, with examples including dizziness, drowsiness, headache, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, and reddish urine discoloration; less common but important adverse effects include urticaria, fever, hallucinations, agitation, and seizure-like reactions, particularly in heavily infected patients or those with CNS vulnerability. In clinical use, it has historically served as a single-dose or short-course oral alternative where S. mansoni predominates, though it has largely been supplanted by praziquantel because of broader spectrum activity and easier deployment.

Name: Leflunomide
Description: Leflunomide (DB01097) is an isoxazole-derived small-molecule disease-modifying antirheumatic drug characterized structurally by a 5-methylisoxazole ring bearing a carboxamide linkage to a para-trifluoromethyl-substituted aniline, making it a lipophilic heteroaromatic immunomodulator within the isoxazole carboxamide and anilide class; its core scaffold is an isoxazolyl anilide, and it is chemically and pharmacologically similar to its active metabolite teriflunomide as well as other conventional DMARDs such as methotrexate and sulfasalazine in therapeutic use, though not close structural analogs. After oral administration it is well absorbed, rapidly and almost completely converted in the gut wall, plasma, and liver to the active metabolite teriflunomide (A771726), is highly protein bound, distributes widely, undergoes extensive enterohepatic recirculation, has a very long effective half-life often measured in weeks, and is eliminated slowly in urine and feces, with accelerated clearance achievable using cholestyramine or activated charcoal. Its principal target is dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, causing inhibition of de novo pyrimidine synthesis in activated lymphocytes; additional reported targets or effects include tyrosine kinases and cyclooxygenase-2-related inflammatory signaling. It is indicated mainly for rheumatoid arthritis and psoriatic arthritis to reduce synovitis, pain, stiffness, and radiographic progression. Important toxicities include hepatotoxicity, teratogenicity, embryofetal toxicity, myelosuppression, serious infection, interstitial lung disease, peripheral neuropathy, and severe cutaneous reactions; common adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, alopecia, rash, hypertension, elevated transaminases, and weight loss. Clinically, it is used as a steroid-sparing conventional DMARD alone or with methotrexate in selected patients requiring long-term control of inflammatory arthritis.

Name: Rosuvastatin
Description: Rosuvastatin (DrugBank DB01098) is a synthetic hydrophilic statin characterized structurally by a substituted pyrimidine core linked to a fluorophenyl group and a polar heptenoic acid side chain bearing the dihydroxy carboxylic acid pharmacophore that mimics the HMG-like tetrahedral intermediate; it also contains a sulfonamide moiety that contributes to potency and hepatoselectivity. Chemically, it is a sulfur-containing antilipemic agent in the statin class, built on the type II statin scaffold exemplified by a heteroaryl-pyrimidine/aryl framework rather than the decalin scaffold of fungal statins. Similar drugs include atorvastatin and pitavastatin as synthetic comparators, and simvastatin, pravastatin, lovastatin, and fluvastatin as related HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors. Its principal target is 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase, with downstream increased hepatic LDL receptor expression driving LDL clearance. Orally administered rosuvastatin has moderate bioavailability, limited metabolism, high hepatic uptake largely via OATP1B1 and BCRP-related transport processes, minimal CYP metabolism mainly through CYP2C9 with minor CYP2C19 contribution, partial protein binding, and predominant fecal excretion of unchanged drug with a terminal half-life of about 19 hours. It is indicated for primary hypercholesterolemia, mixed dyslipidemia, hypertriglyceridemia, familial hypercholesterolemia, and cardiovascular risk reduction, and is used clinically to lower LDL-C and non-HDL cholesterol and reduce myocardial infarction and stroke risk. Important toxicities and adverse effects include dose-related myalgia, myopathy, rhabdomyolysis, transaminase elevation, proteinuria/hematuria, and rare immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy; common side effects include headache, abdominal pain, constipation, nausea, and asthenia.

Name: Capecitabine
Description: Capecitabine (DrugBank DB01101) is an orally administered fluoropyrimidine carbamate designed as a tumor-activated prodrug of 5-fluorouracil; structurally, it is a lipophilic fluorinated pyrimidine nucleoside analogue bearing a 5-fluorocytosine-like base linked to a modified sugar and masked by a carbamate/ester functionality that enhances oral bioavailability. Chemically it belongs to the antimetabolite fluoropyrimidine class, with a fluoropyrimidine nucleoside/prodrug scaffold closely related to 5-fluorouracil, tegafur, doxifluridine, and fluorouridine analogues. After oral absorption, capecitabine is well absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, distributed systemically with limited protein binding, and undergoes sequential metabolic activation by hepatic carboxylesterase to 5-deoxy-5-fluorocytidine, cytidine deaminase to 5-deoxy-5-fluorouridine, and thymidine phosphorylase, often enriched in tumors, to 5-fluorouracil; the active metabolites are then further converted intracellularly to FdUMP and FUTP, which inhibit thymidylate synthase and disrupt DNA and RNA synthesis, while catabolism occurs mainly through dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase and urinary excretion of metabolites predominates. Known targets therefore include thymidylate synthase, with pathway relevance for thymidine phosphorylase, cytidine deaminase, carboxylesterases, and dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase. It is indicated mainly for colorectal cancer, metastatic breast cancer, and some gastroesophageal cancers, often as monotherapy or in combination regimens. Major toxicities include dose-limiting hand-foot syndrome, diarrhea, mucositis, myelosuppression, cardiotoxicity, and severe or fatal fluoropyrimidine toxicity in patients with DPD deficiency; common adverse effects also include nausea, vomiting, fatigue, abdominal pain, and hyperbilirubinemia. Clinically, it is used as an oral alternative to infusional 5-FU in adjuvant colon cancer, metastatic colorectal cancer combinations such as CAPOX/XELOX, and HER2-negative or taxane/anthracycline-pretreated breast cancer.

Name: Quinacrine
Description: Quinacrine (DrugBank DB01103) is a synthetic acridine derivative built on a planar tricyclic acridine nucleus bearing methoxy and chloro substitution and a flexible 9-amino side chain terminating in a diethylamino moiety, a cationic amphiphilic architecture that promotes nucleic acid intercalation and lysosomal accumulation; chemically it is an aminoacridine antiprotozoal and the core scaffold is the 9-aminoacridine chromophore. Closely related drugs include other quinoline or acridine antiprotozoals such as chloroquine, mepacrine, amodiaquine, and pyronaridine, which share aromatic heterocyclic, weakly basic scaffolds and overlapping lysosomotropic behavior. Quinacrine is well absorbed orally, distributes extensively into tissues with marked accumulation in liver, spleen, lung, skin, and blood cells, crosses some biological membranes, exhibits a large apparent volume of distribution and a prolonged terminal half-life, undergoes hepatic metabolism including oxidative and conjugative pathways, and is eliminated slowly via urine and bile/feces. Its pharmacology is multifactorial rather than target-selective, with reported interactions involving DNA and RNA, phospholipase A2, toll-like receptors TLR7 and TLR9, and parasite heme handling pathways. Historically it has been used for giardiasis, cutaneous lupus erythematosus, discoid lupus, and occasionally malaria or tapeworm infections, and has also served as a second-line dermatologic immunomodulator. Toxicity includes dose-related gastrointestinal irritation, neuropsychiatric reactions such as agitation, insomnia, psychosis, hepatotoxicity, hemolysis in susceptible patients, aplastic anemia rarely, and characteristic yellow discoloration of skin and mucosa. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, pruritus, dermatitis, and corneal deposits; clinically, its modern use is limited but persists when standard antiparasitic or antimalarial options are unsuitable or when refractory lupus requires adjunctive therapy.

Name: Sertraline
Description: Sertraline (DrugBank DB01104) is a lipophilic arylamine antidepressant of the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor class, structurally characterized by a rigid cis-substituted tetralin scaffold, specifically a dichlorophenyl-substituted aminotetraline in which a secondary methylamine is attached to a bicyclic naphthalene-like framework that constrains its bioactive conformation; thus its chemical category is an SSRI/phenylaminotetraline derivative and its core scaffold is cis-(1S,4S)-4-(3,4-dichlorophenyl)-1,2,3,4-tetrahydronaphthalen-1-amine. Similar drugs include other SSRIs such as fluoxetine, paroxetine, citalopram, escitalopram, and fluvoxamine, although sertraline is distinguished by its tetralin rather than aryloxypropyl or bicyclic ether motif. Its principal target is the serotonin transporter SLC6A4, with weaker activity reported at the dopamine transporter SLC6A3 and sigma-related binding sites, producing antidepressant and anxiolytic effects by inhibiting presynaptic serotonin reuptake. Orally administered sertraline is slowly but well absorbed, undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism, is highly protein bound, distributes widely, reaches steady state in about 1 week, and is metabolized mainly by CYP2B6, CYP2C19, CYP2C9, CYP2D6, and CYP3A4 to less active desmethylsertraline; elimination is predominantly as metabolites in feces and urine, with a parent half-life of roughly 24-26 hours. It is indicated for major depressive disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, panic disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, social anxiety disorder, and premenstrual dysphoric disorder. Common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, insomnia, somnolence, tremor, sexual dysfunction, sweating, and headache; important toxicities include serotonin syndrome, hyponatremia, abnormal bleeding, QT effects rarely, activation of mania, discontinuation symptoms, and increased suicidality risk in younger patients, while overdose may cause agitation, tachycardia, vomiting, and CNS depression. Clinically, it is widely used as a first-line oral antidepressant and anxiolytic in outpatient and long-term maintenance treatment, for example in recurrent

Name: Sibutramine
Description: Sibutramine (DrugBank DB01105) is a centrally acting anorectic built on a substituted phenethylamine/tertiary amine framework, structurally characterized by a chlorophenyl ring attached to a butyl chain bearing a dimethylamino group and a cyclobutyl-substituted tertiary carbon, placing it in the amphetamine-related monoamine reuptake inhibitor class with a phenethylamine-like scaffold. It is chemically related to other appetite suppressants and monoaminergic agents such as amphetamine, phentermine, diethylpropion, and in mechanistic terms to antidepressant reuptake inhibitors, although sibutramine itself acts primarily through its active metabolites rather than as a classic stimulant. Its principal targets are the norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, serotonin transporter SLC6A4, and to a lesser extent the dopamine transporter SLC6A3, producing enhanced satiety and modest thermogenic effects. After oral administration it is well absorbed, undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism mainly by CYP3A4 to active primary and secondary amine metabolites, is highly protein bound, distributes systemically including the CNS, and is eliminated chiefly as inactive metabolites in urine with some fecal excretion. It was indicated for obesity management, especially in patients with high BMI or obesity complicated by type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, or hypertension, and was used clinically as an adjunct to calorie restriction, exercise, and behavioral modification. Toxicity is dominated by sympathomimetic and cardiovascular risk, including tachycardia, hypertension, palpitations, arrhythmia, stroke, myocardial infarction, seizures, and serotonin toxicity in interacting regimens; common adverse effects include dry mouth, constipation, insomnia, headache, anxiety, and sweating, which led to major restrictions and market withdrawal in many regions.

Name: Levocabastine
Description: Levocabastine (DrugBank DB01106) is a potent, peripherally acting second-generation antihistamine whose structure is characterized by a substituted piperidine-containing heteroaryl framework bearing chlorinated aromatic features and polar functionalities that confer high H1-receptor affinity with limited central nervous system penetration; chemically it is classified as a piperidine antihistamine and can be viewed as built on a diaryl/heteroaryl-piperidine antiallergic scaffold related in broad pharmacophoric terms to other H1 antagonists such as cetirizine, azelastine, epinastine, olopatadine, and ketotifen, although it is distinguished by its high topical selectivity. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, where it acts as a selective antagonist/inverse agonist to suppress histamine-mediated vasodilation, pruritus, sneezing, and conjunctival irritation. Levocabastine is used primarily as a topical ophthalmic or intranasal agent for seasonal allergic conjunctivitis and allergic rhinitis, including symptoms such as itchy red eyes, tearing, sneezing, and rhinorrhea. After local administration, systemic absorption is limited but measurable; distribution is correspondingly low, protein binding is modest to moderate, metabolism is minimal, and elimination occurs largely as unchanged drug via the kidney, giving a relatively straightforward pharmacokinetic profile suited to local therapy. Toxicity is generally low at therapeutic doses because of limited systemic exposure, but excessive exposure may increase risk of sedation, dizziness, or anticholinergic-like discomfort; local intolerance such as ocular burning or nasal irritation is more typical. Adverse effects include transient eye irritation, headache, drowsiness, fatigue, bitter taste, nausea, and local nasal or conjunctival discomfort. Clinically, it has been used as monotherapy for mild to moderate allergic eye and nasal disease or as part of broader allergy management when topical, rapid-onset H1 blockade is preferred.

Name: Trilostane
Description: Trilostane (DrugBank DB01108) is a synthetic steroidal adrenal enzyme inhibitor built on an androstane/pregnane-like tetracyclic steroid nucleus bearing a 3-one, a 4,5-ene, a 17β-hydroxyl group, and a distinctive 17α-substituted nitrile-containing side chain, placing it in the steroid derivative class and more specifically among steroidogenesis inhibitors; its core chemical scaffold is therefore a substituted steroid framework closely related to other adrenal steroid biosynthesis modulators. Pharmacologically similar drugs include ketoconazole, metyrapone, aminoglutethimide, mitotane, and osilodrostat, all used to reduce cortisol synthesis by different enzymatic mechanisms. Trilostane acts primarily by inhibiting 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase/Δ5-4 isomerase, especially HSD3B1 and HSD3B2, thereby reducing synthesis of cortisol, aldosterone, and androstenedione. After oral administration it is absorbed variably, with improved bioavailability when given with food; it is distributed systemically, undergoes hepatic metabolism to active and inactive metabolites including ketotrilostane, and is eliminated mainly in urine with some biliary/fecal excretion, yielding a relatively short duration that may require once- or twice-daily dosing in veterinary practice. Toxicity reflects excessive adrenal suppression and includes hypocortisolemia, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, dehydration, weakness, collapse, and potentially life-threatening adrenal necrosis or Addisonian crisis; gastrointestinal toxicity such as vomiting and diarrhea is also common. It is indicated mainly for hyperadrenocorticism, especially pituitary- or adrenal-dependent Cushing syndrome, and has also been used historically for hormone-dependent breast cancer and hyperaldosteronism. Clinical use is now best established in dogs with Cushing disease, where it reduces polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, panting, abdominal distension, and dermatologic signs.

Name: Miconazole
Description: Miconazole (DrugBank DB01110) is a synthetic imidazole antifungal characterized structurally by a 1-substituted imidazole ring linked through an ether-containing, chlorinated diaryl framework to a dioxolane-like/alkoxy side chain, giving a highly lipophilic halogenated azole architecture; chemically it belongs to the imidazole azole antifungals, and its core scaffold is best described as a chlorinated diphenyl-imidazole ether scaffold. Closely related or mechanistically similar drugs include clotrimazole, econazole, ketoconazole, tioconazole, and other azole antifungals. Its principal target is fungal lanosterol 14alpha-demethylase, the cytochrome P450 enzyme CYP51 (ERG11), leading to impaired ergosterol biosynthesis and disruption of fungal membrane integrity; secondary membrane effects and inhibition of fungal oxidative and peroxidative enzymes have also been described. Miconazole is used mainly topically or mucosally for candidiasis, tinea pedis, tinea corporis, tinea cruris, pityriasis versicolor, and oropharyngeal fungal infection, including vaginal candidiasis and oral thrush. Systemic absorption is generally low after topical, dermal, or intravaginal administration but can occur from mucosal surfaces; absorbed drug is widely distributed, highly protein bound, hepatically metabolized via oxidative/dealkylative pathways, and excreted mainly as metabolites in bile and urine. Toxicity is usually local and dose-limited, with burning, irritation, pruritus, rash, and contact dermatitis; gastrointestinal upset may occur with buccal use, and rare serious effects include hypersensitivity, hepatotoxicity, and clinically relevant CYP-mediated drug interactions such as enhanced warfarin anticoagulation. Clinically, it is used as creams, powders, sprays, suppositories, and buccal tablets for superficial fungal infections and symptomatic relief of associated erythema, itching, and scaling.

Name: Cefuroxime
Description: Cefuroxime (DrugBank DB01112) is a semisynthetic second-generation cephalosporin antibiotic whose structure features the classic cephem nucleus, a strained four-membered beta-lactam fused to a dihydrothiazine ring, with an anti-methoxyimino aminothiazolyl acyl side chain at the 7-position that enhances beta-lactamase stability and a carbamoyloxymethyl-type substituent at the 3-position influencing antibacterial spectrum and pharmacokinetics; chemically it belongs to the beta-lactam cephalosporin class and is built on the cephalosporanic acid/cephem scaffold. Closely related or similar drugs include ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, cefaclor, cefoxitin, and the oral prodrug cefuroxime axetil. Its primary targets are bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, especially transpeptidases such as PBP1, PBP2, and PBP3, leading to inhibition of peptidoglycan cross-linking and cell-wall synthesis. Cefuroxime is used for susceptible infections including community-acquired pneumonia, acute bacterial sinusitis, otitis media, pharyngitis/tonsillitis, urinary tract infections, skin and soft-tissue infections, gonorrhea, early Lyme disease, and perioperative surgical prophylaxis. Parenteral cefuroxime has good tissue penetration, while oral bioavailability is mainly associated with cefuroxime axetil and is improved by food; protein binding is moderate, metabolism is minimal, and elimination occurs predominantly as unchanged drug via renal glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, with dose adjustment in renal impairment. Toxicities include hypersensitivity reactions up to anaphylaxis, Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea, neurotoxicity such as encephalopathy or seizures at high exposure, hemolytic anemia, and interstitial nephritis. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, rash, candidiasis, injection-site pain, and transient liver enzyme elevations.

Name: Papaverine
Description: Papaverine (DrugBank DB01113) is a benzylisoquinoline opium alkaloid and non-narcotic vasodilator characterized structurally by a highly methoxylated isoquinoline core linked to an anisyl-substituted benzyl moiety, giving a planar aromatic, lipophilic scaffold best described as a 1-benzylisoquinoline scaffold. It belongs to the isoquinoline alkaloid chemical class and is chemically related to other opium-derived benzylisoquinolines and smooth-muscle relaxants; relevant comparators include drotaverine, noscapine, and to some extent other vasodilatory antispasmodics with phosphodiesterase-inhibitory activity. Its principal pharmacology is nonselective phosphodiesterase inhibition with consequent elevation of intracellular cAMP and cGMP, reduced calcium-dependent contractility, and direct relaxation of vascular and visceral smooth muscle; reported target associations include phosphodiesterase enzymes, with less specific effects on calcium flux and mitochondrial respiration in some systems. Papaverine is absorbed after oral, rectal, or parenteral administration, undergoes extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism, distributes widely because of its lipophilicity, is highly protein bound, is metabolized mainly by hepatic demethylation/conjugation, and is excreted largely in urine as metabolites with a relatively short plasma half-life. Clinically it is used for vasospasm, visceral spasm, and selected ischemic states, including cerebral, coronary, peripheral, and mesenteric vasospasm, biliary or ureteral spasm, and intracavernosal treatment of erectile dysfunction. Adverse effects include hypotension, flushing, tachycardia, dizziness, nausea, constipation, sedation, and local injection-site reactions; toxicities include marked cardiovascular collapse, arrhythmias, hepatotoxicity with abnormal liver enzymes, and priapism or corporal fibrosis after intracavernosal use.

Name: Chlorpheniramine
Description: Chlorpheniramine (DrugBank DB01114) is a first-generation alkylamine antihistamine built around a substituted propylamine framework in which a chiral 3-carbon side chain links a dimethylamino group to a diaryl pharmacophore composed of a para-chlorophenyl ring and a 2-pyridyl ring; this places it in the ethanolamine/alkylamine-related H1-antihistamine chemical space, with a propylamine diaryl scaffold characteristic of classic sedating antiallergic agents. Structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include dexchlorpheniramine, brompheniramine, pheniramine, triprolidine, and other first-generation H1 antagonists such as diphenhydramine and promethazine. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, where it acts functionally as an inverse agonist/antagonist, and it also has modest antimuscarinic activity that contributes to both efficacy and adverse effects. Orally, chlorpheniramine is well absorbed, undergoes hepatic first-pass metabolism, distributes widely including into the central nervous system, is metabolized mainly by cytochrome P450 enzymes, especially CYP2D6, to demethylated metabolites, and is excreted primarily in urine as parent drug and metabolites; elimination is prolonged relative to many older antihistamines. It is indicated for symptomatic relief of allergic rhinitis, urticaria, conjunctival irritation, pruritus, and common-cold symptoms such as sneezing and rhinorrhea. Common adverse effects include sedation, psychomotor impairment, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention; toxicity in overdose may produce marked anticholinergic syndrome, agitation, hallucinations, seizures, arrhythmias, and respiratory depression, especially in children or with alcohol and other sedatives. Clinically it is used alone or in combination cough-and-cold products for seasonal allergies, hives, and upper respiratory symptom control.

Name: Nifedipine
Description: Nifedipine (DrugBank DB01115) is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker built on a 1,4-dihydropyridine scaffold bearing 2,6-dimethyl substitution, ester groups at the 3 and 5 positions, and a 4-(2-nitrophenyl) ring, a substitution pattern that confers potent vasoselective L-type calcium channel antagonism; chemically it belongs to the dihydropyridine class of organic heterocyclic aromatic nitro-containing ester drugs, and its closest analogs include other dihydropyridines such as amlodipine, felodipine, nicardipine, nimodipine, isradipine, and nitrendipine. Its principal targets are L-type voltage-dependent calcium channel alpha-1 subunits, especially CACNA1C in vascular smooth muscle and myocardium, with functional effects on related Cav1 family channels. Nifedipine is used primarily for hypertension and angina pectoris, including chronic stable angina and vasospastic angina, and is also used in selected settings such as Raynaud phenomenon and as an oral tocolytic for preterm uterine contractions. It is well absorbed orally but undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism, giving variable bioavailability; it is highly protein bound, widely distributed, metabolized mainly by CYP3A4 to inactive oxidative metabolites, and excreted predominantly in urine as metabolites, with a relatively short half-life for immediate-release products and prolonged exposure with extended-release formulations. Toxicity is dominated by exaggerated vasodilation and cardiovascular depression, with overdose causing profound hypotension, reflex tachycardia, dizziness, metabolic disturbances, myocardial ischemia, or shock. Common adverse effects include headache, flushing, peripheral edema, palpitations, nausea, lightheadedness, and gingival hyperplasia. Clinically, it is used as an oral immediate- or extended-release vasodilator, although immediate-release use is generally avoided for routine chronic hypertension because of rapid blood pressure reduction and reflex sympathetic activation.

Name: Trimethaphan
Description: Trimethaphan (DB01116) is a short-acting synthetic bis-quaternary ammonium ganglionic blocker whose structure consists of two permanently charged trimethylammonium heads linked by an ester-containing polymethylene/aryl-containing spacer, giving a flexible dicationic architecture characteristic of classic nicotinic antagonists; chemically it belongs to quaternary ammonium autonomic blockers, and its core scaffold is a methonium-like bis-cationic ganglion-blocking framework related conceptually to other nicotinic antagonists such as hexamethonium, mecamylamine, and tetraethylammonium derivatives, although trimethaphan is distinguished by its ultra-short action and intravenous use. Its principal targets are neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in autonomic ganglia, especially NN receptor complexes in sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia, where it acts as a competitive antagonist and thereby suppresses autonomic transmission. Because of its permanent positive charges, oral absorption is negligible and CNS penetration is minimal; it is therefore administered intravenously, remains largely extracellular, has a very rapid onset, and is inactivated quickly by hydrolysis with short distribution and elimination phases, with metabolites and parent-derived products excreted mainly in urine. Historically it has been indicated for rapid, controlled hypotension, hypertensive emergencies, reduction of blood pressure during surgery, and occasional management of acute pulmonary edema or aortic dissection when immediate autonomic blockade was desired. Toxicity reflects excessive ganglionic blockade, including profound hypotension, cardiovascular collapse, reflex tachycardia attenuation, paralytic ileus, urinary retention, mydriasis, cycloplegia, and severe constipation; common adverse effects include orthostatic hypotension, dry mouth, blurred vision, dizziness, tachycardia, decreased sweating, and gastrointestinal atony. Clinically, it has mainly been used in anesthesia and critical care settings when transient titratable blood-pressure reduction was needed.

Name: Amiodarone
