Description: Amiodarone (DrugBank DB01118) is a highly lipophilic benzofuran antiarrhythmic characterized structurally by a 2-butyl-3-benzofuranyl core linked to a diiodinated methoxybenzoyl moiety through a ketone and bearing a diethylaminoethoxy side chain, making it an iodinated aromatic ether and a cationic amphiphile; chemically it is classified as a class III antiarrhythmic, with a benzofuran diaryl ketone scaffold, and it is structurally and pharmacologically related to dronedarone and, more distantly, to other multichannel antiarrhythmics such as sotalol. Its pharmacology is broad, with blockade of cardiac potassium channels including KCNH2/hERG, sodium channels such as SCN5A, and L-type calcium channels including CACNA1C, plus noncompetitive antiadrenergic effects at beta-adrenergic receptors, producing action potential prolongation, slowed conduction, and reduced automaticity. Oral absorption is variable and incomplete, bioavailability is moderate, distribution is extensive with marked adipose and tissue accumulation and a very large volume of distribution, metabolism occurs hepatically mainly via CYP3A4 and CYP2C8 to active desethylamiodarone, and elimination is very slow, largely biliary/fecal, with a terminal half-life often measured in weeks. It is indicated for life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias, ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, and commonly used for atrial fibrillation or flutter rhythm control. Toxicity is notable for pulmonary fibrosis or pneumonitis, hepatotoxicity, thyroid dysfunction from iodine load, corneal deposits, optic neuropathy, bradyarrhythmia, QT prolongation, torsades risk though relatively low, neuropathy, photosensitivity, and blue-gray skin discoloration. Clinically it is used acutely intravenously for refractory ventricular arrhythmias and chronically orally for suppression of recurrent ventricular tachycardia and maintenance of sinus rhythm in symptomatic atrial fibrillation.

Name: Diazoxide
Description: Diazoxide (DB01119) is a non-diuretic benzothiadiazine derivative whose structure consists of a fused benzene–1,2,4-thiadiazine 1,1-dioxide ring system bearing a 3-methyl substituent and a 7-chloro group, giving a lipophilic heteroaromatic sulfonamide-like scaffold related to thiazide chemistry but lacking meaningful natriuretic activity; chemically it is classified as a potassium channel opener and benzothiadiazine, with a chlorinated benzothiadiazine dioxide core as its defining scaffold. Similar drugs include other KATP channel openers such as minoxidil and nicorandil, and structurally related thiazide-class benzothiadiazines such as chlorothiazide and hydrochlorothiazide, although their pharmacology differs. Diazoxide acts mainly on ATP-sensitive potassium channels by binding the sulfonylurea receptor regulatory subunits, particularly ABCC8/SUR1 in pancreatic beta cells and ABCC9/SUR2 in vascular smooth muscle, thereby inhibiting insulin release and producing arteriolar vasodilation; Kir6.x pore-forming partners such as KCNJ11/Kir6.2 are functionally involved. It is used primarily for hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia, including congenital hyperinsulinism and insulinoma-associated hypoglycemia, and historically for hypertensive emergencies. Oral absorption is generally good, protein binding is high, distribution is mainly extracellular with placental transfer possible, metabolism is limited, and elimination is predominantly renal with a relatively long half-life that may be prolonged in renal impairment. Important toxicities include marked fluid and sodium retention, pulmonary edema, worsening heart failure, severe hyperglycemia or ketoacidosis, hyperuricemia, and hypotension. Common adverse effects include edema, tachycardia, nausea, headache, dizziness, hypertrichosis, and rash. Clinically, it is used chronically to suppress insulin secretion in diazoxide-responsive hyperinsulinism, often with diuretic co-therapy and close monitoring of glucose, fluid status, and cardiac function.

Name: Gliclazide
Description: Gliclazide (DrugBank DB01120) is a second-generation sulfonylurea oral hypoglycemic agent whose structure consists of a sulfonylurea core linking a substituted p-tolylsulfonyl moiety to a nitrogen-containing bicyclic ring, specifically an azabicyclooctyl group, giving it a relatively lipophilic arylsulfonylurea architecture characteristic of insulin secretagogues; chemically it belongs to the sulfonylurea class and more broadly to arylsulfonamide antidiabetic agents, with a sulfonylurea scaffold shared by related drugs such as glibenclamide, glipizide, gliquidone, tolbutamide, and chlorpropamide. Its principal pharmacologic target is the ATP-sensitive potassium channel in pancreatic beta cells, especially the sulfonylurea receptor SUR1/ABCC8 complex functionally coupled to Kir6.2/KCNJ11, leading to channel closure, membrane depolarization, calcium influx, and insulin release. After oral administration, gliclazide is well absorbed, shows high but reversible plasma protein binding, distributes mainly within the vascular compartment, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism largely via CYP2C9 with formation of inactive or minimally active metabolites, and is eliminated primarily in urine as metabolites with limited unchanged renal excretion; modified-release formulations prolong absorption and support once-daily dosing. It is indicated for type 2 diabetes mellitus, particularly when diet and exercise alone are insufficient, and is used clinically as monotherapy or in combination with metformin, alpha-glucosidase inhibitors, or insulin in selected patients. Major toxicities and adverse effects include dose-related hypoglycemia, especially in the elderly, malnourished, or those with hepatic or renal impairment, as well as weight gain, gastrointestinal upset, dizziness, headache, rash, pruritus, and rare but important hepatic dysfunction, hematologic dyscrasias, and severe prolonged hypoglycemic episodes.

Name: Phenacemide
Description: Phenacemide (DrugBank DB01121) is an older anticonvulsant whose structure is a small aromatic acetamide composed of a phenyl ring attached through a methylene linker to an acetamide/urea-like amidic functionality, placing it in the carboxamide anticonvulsant class and more specifically among phenyl-substituted acyclic amide derivatives; its core chemical scaffold is therefore a phenyl-ethyl/benzyl-substituted amide rather than a cyclic hydantoin, oxazolidinedione, or barbiturate nucleus. It is chemically and pharmacologically related to other legacy antiepileptic agents, with partial similarity to acetylurea- or carboxamide-containing anticonvulsants such as phenytoin, mephenytoin, primidone, and carbamazepine in the broad sense of aromatic seizure-suppressing drugs, although it is structurally simpler than these. Its precise molecular target profile was never fully defined, but anticonvulsant activity is generally attributed to CNS depressant effects with likely modulation of neuronal excitability, historically discussed alongside voltage-gated sodium channel–stabilizing antiseizure mechanisms rather than a single validated protein target; no highly specific modern target assignment is firmly established. Phenacemide was used for refractory epilepsy, especially partial seizures and some generalized tonic-clonic seizures, but clinical use became limited because oral absorption appears adequate, CNS distribution is expected, hepatic metabolism is substantial, and renal excretion occurs mainly as metabolites, while pharmacokinetic characterization remains comparatively sparse by modern standards. Its major liabilities are serious toxicity, notably hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, bone marrow suppression, psychosis, and potentially fatal idiosyncratic reactions; adverse effects include drowsiness, ataxia, dizziness, nausea, rash, behavioral change, and cognitive impairment. Consequently, although once reserved for difficult-to-control seizure disorders, it is now largely obsolete or only of historical interest because its therapeutic utility is outweighed by severe safety concerns.

Name: Ambenonium
Description: Ambenonium (DrugBank DB01122) is a synthetic bisquaternary ammonium anticholinesterase characterized structurally by two permanently charged pyridinium-type nitrogen centers linked through a rigid aromatic-containing spacer with amidine/aminocarbonyl functionality, a design that confers high polarity, strong ionic binding to cholinesterases, and poor membrane penetration; chemically it belongs to the quaternary ammonium acetylcholinesterase inhibitor class, and its core scaffold is best described as a bisquaternary aromatic cholinesterase-inhibitor framework related to other peripherally acting reversible anticholinesterases such as pyridostigmine, neostigmine, and distigmine. Its principal pharmacologic target is acetylcholinesterase, with inhibition of butyrylcholinesterase also reported, thereby increasing acetylcholine concentrations at the neuromuscular junction. Because of its permanent cationic character, oral absorption is limited and variable, distribution is largely extracellular, central nervous system penetration is negligible, metabolism is limited relative to tertiary amines, and elimination occurs predominantly by renal excretion of unchanged drug, so duration may be prolonged in renal impairment. Clinically, ambenonium has been used mainly for symptomatic treatment of myasthenia gravis, improving fatigable skeletal muscle weakness, ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia, and limb weakness, and historically as an alternative when pyridostigmine was ineffective or not tolerated. Its toxicity reflects excessive cholinergic stimulation, with nausea, abdominal cramping, diarrhea, salivation, sweating, miosis, bronchospasm, bradycardia, muscle fasciculations, and weakness, and severe overdose can precipitate cholinergic crisis with respiratory compromise; adverse effects in routine use are correspondingly muscarinic and nicotinic, and caution is warranted in asthma, peptic ulcer disease, bradyarrhythmia, and renal dysfunction.

Name: Tolbutamide
Description: Tolbutamide (DrugBank DB01124) is a first-generation sulfonylurea oral hypoglycemic agent whose structure consists of a para-methyl-substituted benzenesulfonylurea linked to a butyl chain, giving an aryl-sulfonylurea architecture with a lipophilic tolyl ring and terminal aliphatic substituent; chemically it belongs to the sulfonylurea class of antidiabetic drugs, and its core scaffold is the sulfonylurea pharmacophore attached to a p-tolyl aromatic ring. Closely related drugs include other sulfonylureas such as chlorpropamide, acetohexamide, tolazamide, glibenclamide, glipizide, and gliclazide, which share ATP-sensitive potassium channel inhibition as a class mechanism. Tolbutamide targets the pancreatic beta-cell KATP channel, binding primarily to the sulfonylurea receptor SUR1/ABCC8 and functionally modulating the Kir6.2/KCNJ11 channel complex to promote insulin release. It is well absorbed orally, has relatively rapid onset and short duration compared with longer-acting congeners, is extensively protein bound, distributed mainly in extracellular fluids, metabolized predominantly in the liver by CYP2C9 to inactive or weakly active hydroxylated/carboxylated metabolites, and excreted chiefly in urine with some biliary/fecal elimination. Its major indication is type 2 diabetes mellitus, especially nonketotic diabetes with residual beta-cell function, historically used for fasting hyperglycemia control when diet alone is inadequate. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related or prolonged hypoglycemia, particularly in elderly, malnourished, hepatic-impaired, or renally impaired patients, with examples including confusion, seizures, and coma; other adverse effects include weight gain, nausea, dyspepsia, rash, pruritus, photosensitivity, cholestatic jaundice, hematologic dyscrasias, and rare hypersensitivity. Clinically, it has been used as an older oral insulin secretagogue, sometimes in patients needing a shorter-acting sulfonylurea to limit persistent hypoglycemia risk.

Name: Dutasteride
Description: Dutasteride (DB01126) is a synthetic 4-azasteroid built on an androstane-like steroid nucleus in which a ring carbon is replaced by nitrogen, bearing a characteristic 4-aza-3-keto steroid scaffold with bulky bis(trifluoromethyl) phenyl substitution that enhances potent, prolonged inhibition of steroid 5-alpha-reductase. It is classified as a steroidal 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor, closely related to finasteride and pharmacologically similar to other androgen-lowering approaches, although finasteride is the most direct structural comparator. Its principal targets are steroid 5-alpha-reductase type 1 and type 2, encoded by SRD5A1 and SRD5A2, thereby reducing conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone in prostate, skin, and hair follicles. Dutasteride is indicated primarily for benign prostatic hyperplasia, including reduction of prostate volume, improvement of urinary flow, and lowering risk of acute urinary retention or need for surgery; it is also used clinically, often off-label, in androgenetic alopecia. After oral administration it is well absorbed, highly protein bound, extensively distributed, and undergoes hepatic CYP3A4- and CYP3A5-mediated metabolism to several metabolites; elimination is mainly fecal, with minimal renal excretion and an exceptionally long terminal half-life of about 5 weeks, supporting sustained suppression of dihydrotestosterone. Toxicity is dominated by reproductive and endocrine effects, including teratogenic risk to a male fetus, decreased semen parameters, and exposure concerns via leaking capsules; overdose is usually limited by low acute toxicity but prolonged due to slow clearance. Common adverse effects include decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, ejaculation disorders, gynecomastia, breast tenderness, and less commonly mood changes, making it a standard long-acting antiandrogenic therapy in BPH, often used alone or with alpha-1 blockers such as tamsulosin.

Name: Econazole
Description: Econazole (DrugBank DB01127) is a topical imidazole antifungal whose structure is characterized by a substituted imidazole ring linked through an ether-containing framework to lipophilic chlorinated aromatic rings, giving an aromatic halogenated azole architecture optimized for membrane partitioning and antifungal activity. Chemically, it belongs to the azole antifungals, specifically the imidazole class, and its core scaffold is an aryl-imidazole diaryl ether motif closely related to other topical imidazoles such as miconazole, ketoconazole, clotrimazole, oxiconazole, and sulconazole. Its principal target is fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase, a cytochrome P450 enzyme encoded by ERG11/CYP51, leading to impaired ergosterol biosynthesis, altered membrane permeability, and growth inhibition; secondary membrane-disruptive effects have also been described. After topical administration, systemic absorption is generally minimal through intact skin, with greater uptake across inflamed or damaged skin; distribution is therefore mainly local within the stratum corneum and epidermis, while any absorbed fraction is expected to undergo hepatic oxidative metabolism and biliary or renal excretion of metabolites, although systemic pharmacokinetic data are limited because the drug is used predominantly topically. Toxicity is usually low and localized, but excessive exposure may cause marked irritation, erythema, burning, contact dermatitis, or rarely hypersensitivity; systemic toxicity is uncommon. It is indicated for superficial fungal infections including tinea pedis, tinea cruris, tinea corporis, cutaneous candidiasis, and tinea versicolor, and clinically it is used as creams, lotions, foams, or vaginal formulations for dermatophyte and Candida infections, with common adverse effects including pruritus, stinging, rash, and local discomfort.

Name: Rabeprazole
Description: Rabeprazole (DrugBank DB01129) is a substituted benzimidazole proton-pump inhibitor characterized structurally by a benzimidazole ring linked through a sulfinyl bridge to a substituted pyridine, with methoxypropoxy and methyl substituents that confer acid lability and enable conversion in the acidic secretory canaliculus to reactive sulfenamide intermediates; thus it belongs to the benzimidazole sulfoxide class and shares the canonical PPI scaffold of pyridylmethylsulfinyl benzimidazoles. Closely related drugs include omeprazole, esomeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole, and dexlansoprazole, which have analogous acid-activated antisecretory mechanisms. Its principal target is the gastric H+/K+-ATPase proton pump, primarily ATP4A and functionally the ATP4A/ATP4B complex, which it inhibits covalently at luminal cysteine residues of parietal cells. After oral administration, enteric-coated rabeprazole is rapidly absorbed in the small intestine, reaches peak concentrations within a few hours, is moderately protein bound, distributes systemically, and undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly by nonenzymatic reduction to thioether and by CYP3A4 and CYP2C19 to sulfone and demethylated metabolites, with elimination predominantly as urinary metabolites and the remainder in feces. It is indicated for gastroesophageal reflux disease, erosive esophagitis, duodenal ulcer, pathological hypersecretory states such as Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, and Helicobacter pylori eradication in combination regimens. Adverse effects commonly include headache, diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea, constipation, and flatulence; important toxicities include hypersensitivity, interstitial nephritis, Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea, hypomagnesemia, vitamin B12 deficiency, fracture risk with prolonged use, and rare severe cutaneous reactions. Clinically, it is used for short-term healing and maintenance of acid-related disorders and as part of triple therapy with antibiotics for H. pylori infection.

Name: Prednicarbate
Description: Prednicarbate (DrugBank DB01130) is a nonhalogenated synthetic corticosteroid designed for topical use, structurally based on the pregnane glucocorticoid nucleus with the characteristic four-fused-ring steroid scaffold and functionalization including 11β- and 17α-hydroxyl groups, a 3-keto-1,4-diene system, and lipophilicity-enhancing ester/carbamate substitution that supports cutaneous anti-inflammatory activity while limiting systemic burden. Chemically, it is classified as a topical glucocorticoid corticosteroid, within the prednisolone-derived steroid family, and its core scaffold is the hydrocortisone/prednisolone-like corticosteroid framework. Similar drugs include hydrocortisone, prednisolone, methylprednisolone aceponate, desonide, and clobetasone butyrate, which share related steroidal anti-inflammatory pharmacophores but differ in potency and skin penetration. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, with downstream repression of proinflammatory cytokines, arachidonic acid mediators, and immune cell activation. After topical administration, absorption through intact skin is limited but increases with inflammation, occlusion, large surface area exposure, or prolonged use; distribution is largely local to epidermal and dermal tissues, while absorbed drug undergoes rapid hepatic and cutaneous ester hydrolysis and other metabolic inactivation to less active metabolites, followed by renal and some biliary excretion. Prednicarbate is indicated for corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses, especially atopic dermatitis, eczematous dermatitis, irritant or allergic contact dermatitis, and inflammatory pruritic rashes. Adverse effects are mainly local, including burning, stinging, erythema, dryness, pruritus, folliculitis, acneiform eruption, telangiectasia, striae, hypopigmentation, and skin atrophy; excessive exposure may cause HPA-axis suppression, hyperglycemia, or Cushingoid features, particularly in children. Clinically it is used as a medium-potency topical anti-inflammatory steroid when a relatively favorable local tolerability profile is desired for subacute or chronic eczema and steroid-responsive inflammatory skin disease.

Name: Proguanil
Description: Proguanil (DrugBank DB01131) is a synthetic biguanide-derived antimalarial built around a chlorophenyl-substituted biguanide framework, specifically a p-chlorophenyl ring linked through a substituted carbon to a flexible biguanide moiety, placing it in the diaminobiguanide/antifolate chemical category with a chlorophenyl biguanide scaffold; it is structurally and pharmacologically related to cycloguanil, its active triazine metabolite, and to other antifolate antimalarials such as pyrimethamine and, more distantly, chlorproguanil. Its principal antimalarial target is Plasmodium dihydrofolate reductase-thymidylate synthase, inhibited mainly by cycloguanil, although the proguanil parent also contributes to activity and, in combination with atovaquone, enhances mitochondrial dysfunction linked to the parasite cytochrome bc1 complex. After oral administration it is well absorbed, widely distributed, hepatically metabolized primarily by CYP2C19 to cycloguanil with additional inactive metabolites, and eliminated mainly in urine as parent drug and metabolites; CYP2C19 polymorphism materially affects exposure and bioactivation. It is indicated for malaria prophylaxis and treatment, especially uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria when coformulated with atovaquone, and for chemoprophylaxis in travelers to endemic regions. Adverse effects are usually gastrointestinal and neurologic, including abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, and dizziness, with occasional mouth ulcers or rash. Toxicity is generally low at therapeutic doses but may include antifolate-related effects such as stomatitis or hematologic suppression in overdose or prolonged exposure, with greater caution warranted in renal impairment and in combination regimens.

Name: Pioglitazone
Description: Pioglitazone (DrugBank DB01132) is an oral insulin-sensitizing antidiabetic agent of the thiazolidinedione, or glitazone, class, structurally characterized by a 2,4-thiazolidinedione ring linked through a methylene bridge to a lipophilic ethoxybenzyl-substituted pyridyl aromatic system, giving it an acidic heterocyclic headgroup and hydrophobic tail typical of PPAR ligands. Its core chemical scaffold is therefore the thiazolidinedione pharmacophore appended to a substituted pyridine-phenyl ether framework, and it is closely related to other PPARgamma agonists such as rosiglitazone and the withdrawn troglitazone; more distantly, it shares insulin-sensitizing therapeutic space with non-TZD agents such as metformin. Pioglitazone acts primarily on peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARG), with lesser effects on PPARalpha, altering transcription of genes involved in glucose and lipid metabolism; downstream affected proteins include adiponectin-regulated pathways, GLUT4-related glucose handling systems, and inflammatory mediators. It is indicated mainly for type 2 diabetes mellitus, especially in patients with insulin resistance, as monotherapy or in combination with metformin, sulfonylureas, or insulin, and has also been used in selected patients with nonalcoholic steatohepatitis or metabolic syndrome. After oral administration it is well absorbed, highly protein bound, hepatically metabolized mainly by CYP2C8 and to a lesser extent CYP3A4 to active metabolites, and eliminated via bile/feces and urine predominantly as metabolites, with a parent half-life of several hours but longer pharmacologic effect due to active metabolites. Major toxicities and adverse effects include weight gain, edema, dilutional anemia, heart failure exacerbation from fluid retention, increased fracture risk, hepatotoxicity monitoring concerns, and occasional macular edema; hypoglycemia is uncommon unless combined with insulin or secretagogues. Clinically, it is used to improve glycemic control, lower HbA1c, and enhance peripheral insulin sensitivity in chronic outpatient management of type 2 diabetes.

Name: Tiludronic acid
Description: Tiludronic acid (DrugBank DB01133) is a first-generation, non-nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate characterized structurally by a geminal bisphosphonate P-C-P backbone attached to a substituted aromatic ring, specifically a chlorophenylthio side chain, giving it a stable, highly polar hydroxyapatite-binding osteotropic motif typical of antiresorptive phosphonate drugs. Chemically, it belongs to the bisphosphonic acid class, with a simple non-nitrogen bisphosphonate scaffold distinct from the nitrogen-containing heterocyclic bisphosphonates; closely related drugs include etidronate, clodronate, pamidronate, alendronate, risedronate, ibandronate, and zoledronic acid. Its principal pharmacology is inhibition of osteoclast-mediated bone resorption after adsorption to bone mineral, with intracellular conversion in osteoclasts to nonhydrolyzable ATP analogs proposed for non-nitrogen bisphosphonates; no single high-affinity protein target is universally assigned, but functional targets include osteoclast biochemical pathways involved in bone resorption and, more broadly for the class, enzymes in the mevalonate-related osteoclast survival network are often discussed. Oral absorption is poor and reduced by food or divalent cations, distribution is mainly to bone and extracellular fluid with limited soft-tissue penetration, metabolism is minimal to absent, and elimination occurs largely as unchanged drug by renal excretion plus prolonged skeletal retention. Indications center on Paget disease of bone, with clinical use to reduce elevated bone turnover, bone pain, deformity progression, and biochemical markers; adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, dyspepsia, musculoskeletal pain, and headache. Toxicities include esophagitis or upper gastrointestinal irritation, hypocalcemia, renal risk in predisposed patients, and class-associated concerns such as osteomalacia with excessive suppression, osteonecrosis of the jaw, and atypical femoral fractures, although these are less commonly emphasized for tiludronate than for later bisphosphonates.

Name: Carvedilol
Description: Carvedilol (DrugBank DB01136) is a lipophilic aryloxypropanolamine in which a propanolamine side chain bearing a secondary alcohol and amine is linked through an ether to a substituted aromatic system and further fused to a carbazole ring scaffold, placing it within the nonselective beta-adrenergic antagonist class with additional vasodilatory alpha1-blocking activity; chemically it is best described as a carbazole-containing beta-blocker built on the classic aryloxypropanolamine pharmacophore, and it is structurally and pharmacologically related to agents such as propranolol, labetalol, metoprolol, and nebivolol, although carvedilol is distinguished by combined beta1, beta2, and alpha1 antagonism and ancillary antioxidant effects. Its principal targets are ADRB1, ADRB2, and ADRA1 receptor subtypes, with downstream reduction in heart rate, myocardial contractility, and peripheral vascular resistance. After oral administration it is well absorbed but undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, giving moderate systemic bioavailability; it is highly protein bound, widely distributed, extensively metabolized mainly by CYP2D6 and CYP2C9 with contributions from glucuronidation, and excreted predominantly via bile and feces with limited renal elimination. Toxicity is dominated by exaggerated pharmacology, including bradycardia, hypotension, atrioventricular block, bronchospasm, hypoglycemia masking, and overdose-associated cardiogenic shock. Indications include hypertension, chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and left ventricular dysfunction following myocardial infarction. Common adverse effects include dizziness, fatigue, diarrhea, orthostasis, bradycardia, edema, and worsening heart failure during initiation. Clinically, it is used chronically to improve survival in systolic heart failure, reduce blood pressure, and provide neurohormonal blockade in post-MI patients with ventricular dysfunction.

Name: Levofloxacin
Description: Levofloxacin (DrugBank DB01137) is the S-(-) enantiomer of ofloxacin and a fluoroquinolone antibacterial built on a quinolone/4-oxo-1,4-dihydroquinoline core bearing the characteristic 3-carboxyl and 4-keto pharmacophore, a 6-fluoro substituent that enhances potency, and a 7-piperazinyl moiety that broadens gram-negative and atypical coverage; thus its chemical category is a fluorinated quinolone antibiotic and its scaffold is the fluoroquinolone bicyclic quinolone nucleus. Closely related drugs include ofloxacin, ciprofloxacin, moxifloxacin, norfloxacin, and gemifloxacin. It acts by inhibiting the bacterial type II topoisomerases DNA gyrase (GyrA/GyrB) and topoisomerase IV (ParC/ParE), producing bactericidal suppression of DNA replication and segregation. Orally it is well absorbed with high bioavailability, food having limited effect, distributes widely into lung, urinary tract, prostate, skin, and macrophage-containing tissues, undergoes minimal hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged in urine, so renal impairment prolongs half-life and requires dose adjustment. Toxicities include concentration-related CNS excitation, dysglycemia, QT prolongation, tendinopathy and tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, hepatotoxicity, and risk of Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea; overdose may accentuate neurotoxicity and cardiac repolarization effects. Common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, insomnia, rash, and transaminase elevations. Clinically it is used for community-acquired and nosocomial pneumonia, acute bacterial sinusitis, COPD exacerbations, complicated and uncomplicated urinary tract infections, pyelonephritis, chronic bacterial prostatitis, skin and soft tissue infections, and post-exposure prophylaxis or treatment of inhalational anthrax and plague.

Name: Sulfinpyrazone
Description: Sulfinpyrazone (DrugBank DB01138) is a pyrazolidinedione-derived sulfinyl diaryl compound structurally characterized by a central 2-pyrazoline-3,5-dione or pyrazolidinedione ring bearing two phenyl substituents and a para-methylsulfinylbenzyl side chain, making it a lipophilic weak organic acid closely related to phenylbutazone-like anti-inflammatory/uricosuric agents. Chemically it is classified as a uricosuric agent and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory-related pyrazolidinedione, with a phenylbutazone-type diaryl pyrazolidinedione scaffold. Similar drugs include phenylbutazone and oxyphenbutazone by scaffold, and the uricosurics probenecid and benzbromarone by therapeutic function. Its principal pharmacology is inhibition of renal tubular urate reabsorption, classically attributed to urate transport pathways such as URAT1/SLC22A12 and related organic anion transport systems, and it also inhibits platelet aggregation by reducing platelet release reactions. Orally it is well absorbed, highly plasma-protein bound, distributed largely in the vascular compartment, extensively hepatically metabolized to sulfone and other oxidative metabolites, and excreted mainly in urine as metabolites and some unchanged drug, with a moderate half-life permitting divided daily dosing. It is indicated primarily for chronic gout and hyperuricemia, especially recurrent gouty arthritis with urate underexcretion, and historically for reduction of thromboembolic risk after certain cardiovascular events. Toxicity includes gastrointestinal irritation, peptic ulceration, gastrointestinal bleeding, hepatotoxicity, renal stone formation from increased uricosuria, hypersensitivity reactions, and rare blood dyscrasias such as agranulocytosis or thrombocytopenia. Common adverse effects include dyspepsia, nausea, rash, dizziness, and exacerbation of ulcer disease. Clinically, it has been used as a second-line urate-lowering adjunct in gout management with hydration and urine alkalinization, and more rarely as an antiplatelet agent in selected patients.

Name: Cefapirin
Description: Cefapirin (DrugBank DB01139) is a first-generation semisynthetic cephalosporin antibiotic built on the cephem/7-aminocephalosporanic acid scaffold, consisting of a strained bicyclic beta-lactam fused to a dihydrothiazine ring, with a 7-acylamino side chain and a 3-substituent that tune antibacterial spectrum and stability; chemically it belongs to the beta-lactam cephalosporin class and shares its core scaffold and pharmacology with related first-generation agents such as cefazolin, cephalothin, cephaloridine, and cephalexin. Its principal targets are bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, especially transpeptidases involved in peptidoglycan cross-linking, leading to inhibition of cell-wall synthesis and bactericidal activity against many susceptible Gram-positive cocci and selected Gram-negative organisms. Cefapirin has historically been used mainly parenterally, and in veterinary medicine also by intramammary infusion; after administration it distributes largely to extracellular fluid and inflamed tissues, has limited intracellular penetration, low to moderate protein binding, minimal hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by the kidney through glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, so exposure rises in renal impairment. Toxicity is broadly typical of cephalosporins: hypersensitivity reactions including rash, urticaria, fever, and rare anaphylaxis, gastrointestinal disturbance, local injection-site pain, superinfection, and uncommon hematologic or renal adverse effects; examples include eosinophilia, positive Coombs test, interstitial nephritis, and antibiotic-associated diarrhea. Clinically, it has been used for susceptible skin and soft-tissue, respiratory, urinary, bone, and perioperative infections, and for bovine mastitis caused by susceptible staphylococci or streptococci.

Name: Cefadroxil
Description: Cefadroxil (DrugBank DB01140) is a first-generation cephalosporin β-lactam antibiotic built on the 7-aminocephalosporanic acid nucleus, featuring a fused β-lactam–dihydrothiazine bicyclic ring system with a para-hydroxyphenylglycyl side chain that increases acid stability and supports oral activity; chemically it belongs to the cephalosporin subclass of β-lactam antibacterials, and its core scaffold is the cephem nucleus. It is closely related to other first-generation cephalosporins such as cephalexin and cephradine, and more broadly resembles penicillins in mechanism. Cefadroxil targets bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, especially transpeptidases involved in peptidoglycan cross-linking, thereby inhibiting cell-wall synthesis in susceptible organisms. It is well absorbed after oral administration, has relatively high bioavailability, low to moderate protein binding, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid and tissues but not extensively into the central nervous system, undergoes minimal metabolism, and is eliminated largely unchanged by renal glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, giving a plasma half-life of roughly 1-2 hours that is prolonged in renal impairment. Its major toxicities are those typical of β-lactams, including hypersensitivity reactions ranging from rash and urticaria to rare anaphylaxis, gastrointestinal toxicity including diarrhea and occasional Clostridioides difficile-associated colitis, and rare interstitial nephritis, eosinophilia, or hematologic abnormalities. It is indicated for susceptible infections such as streptococcal pharyngitis, uncomplicated skin and soft tissue infections, urinary tract infections, and certain respiratory tract infections; in clinical use it is valued as an oral agent for mild to moderate community-acquired infections caused by susceptible Gram-positive cocci and selected Gram-negative organisms.

Name: Micafungin
Description: Micafungin (DB01141) is a semisynthetic echinocandin antifungal characterized structurally as a large cyclic lipohexapeptide bearing multiple hydroxylated amino acid residues and an N-linked aromatic sulfonyl-containing lipophilic side chain, a design that confers high protein binding and potent inhibition of fungal cell-wall synthesis; chemically it belongs to the echinocandin/lipopeptide class, with the core scaffold being the cyclic echinocandin hexapeptide macrocycle derived from a fungal natural-product nucleus. Closely related drugs include caspofungin and anidulafungin, which share the same general scaffold and mechanism. Its principal target is the fungal 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase complex, especially Fks catalytic subunits, leading to depletion of beta-glucan in the cell wall and fungicidal activity against most Candida species with fungistatic activity against Aspergillus. Because it is not orally bioavailable, micafungin is given intravenously; it distributes mainly in the extracellular space, is extensively albumin bound, undergoes limited hepatic biotransformation via arylsulfatase, catechol-O-methyltransferase, and minor CYP3A-related pathways, and is eliminated predominantly through feces with minimal renal excretion and no major dose adjustment for renal impairment. Indications include candidemia, acute disseminated candidiasis, Candida peritonitis and abscesses, esophageal candidiasis, and prophylaxis of Candida infection in hematopoietic stem-cell transplant recipients. Adverse effects include infusion reactions, phlebitis, nausea, fever, rash, headache, thrombocytopenia, elevated transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin; important toxicities include hepatotoxicity, hypersensitivity/anaphylactoid reactions, hemolysis, and rare renal dysfunction, with animal data raising concern for hepatic tumorigenic potential. Clinically, it is widely used for invasive candidiasis and empiric or prophylactic antifungal therapy in high-risk immunocompromised patients.

Name: Doxepin
Description: Doxepin (DrugBank DB01142) is a dibenzoxepin tricyclic antidepressant characterized by a fused tricyclic aromatic system in which two benzene rings are linked through a seven-membered oxepin ring and bear a dimethylaminopropylidene side chain; it is typically used as a mixture of E/Z geometric isomers and belongs to the broader class of tricyclic antidepressants with a dibenzoxepin scaffold, closely related to other TCAs such as amitriptyline, imipramine, clomipramine, and trimipramine, while also showing pharmacologic similarity to sedating H1-antihistamines. Its principal targets include the serotonin transporter SLC6A4 and norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, with strong antagonism at histamine H1 receptor HRH1 and additional affinity for muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, alpha1-adrenergic receptors, and serotonin receptors such as HTR2, explaining its antidepressant, anxiolytic, antipruritic, and hypnotic effects. Orally administered doxepin is well absorbed, extensively distributed, highly protein bound, undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 to active metabolites including nordoxepin, and is eliminated predominantly in urine as metabolites with a variable half-life that supports once-daily use in some settings. Clinically, it is indicated for major depressive disorder, anxiety states, insomnia at low doses, and pruritus such as that associated with eczema or chronic urticaria. Common adverse effects include sedation, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, dizziness, weight gain, and orthostatic hypotension; serious toxicity includes anticholinergic delirium, QT prolongation, seizures, respiratory depression, and potentially fatal overdose from cardiac conduction abnormalities, particularly when combined with other CNS depressants or in patients with suicidality risk.

Name: Diphenylpyraline
Description: Diphenylpyraline (DrugBank DB01146) is a first-generation ethanolamine antihistamine with an aryldiaryl ether architecture characterized by two phenyl rings linked through a benzhydryl-like carbon to a pyridine-containing side chain and a tertiary aminoethoxy substituent, giving it a lipophilic, cationic structure typical of centrally active H1 antagonists. Chemically, it belongs to the diphenylmethane/ethanolamine class of antihistaminic agents, and its core scaffold is a diaryl-substituted ether–tertiary amine pharmacophore closely related to other sedating H1 blockers such as doxylamine, carbinoxamine, clemastine, and pheniramine-like agents. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, where it acts as an inverse agonist/antagonist; like many older antihistamines it may also show clinically relevant antimuscarinic off-target activity. After oral administration it is expected to be well absorbed, distributed widely into tissues, and to cross the blood-brain barrier extensively because of high lipophilicity; hepatic biotransformation, likely involving oxidative N-dealkylation and related cytochrome P450-mediated metabolism, precedes renal excretion of metabolites and a smaller amount of unchanged drug. Toxicity is consistent with first-generation antihistamines and includes dose-related CNS depression, psychomotor impairment, anticholinergic toxicity, and in overdose agitation, delirium, seizures, or cardiac effects. It is indicated for symptomatic relief of allergic disorders such as allergic rhinitis, urticaria, pruritus, and common-cold rhinorrhea or sneezing. Common adverse effects include sedation, dizziness, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention. Clinically, it has been used as an oral or combination-product antihistamine for short-term management of seasonal allergies, itching, and other histamine-mediated upper respiratory symptoms.

Name: Cloxacillin
Description: Cloxacillin (DrugBank DB01147) is a semisynthetic, penicillinase-resistant isoxazolyl penicillin whose structure consists of the canonical penam nucleus, a fused beta-lactam and thiazolidine bicyclic system, bearing a carboxylate and an acylamino side chain containing a bulky chlorophenyl-isoxazolyl substituent that sterically protects the beta-lactam from staphylococcal beta-lactamase hydrolysis. It belongs to the beta-lactam antibiotic class, specifically the antistaphylococcal penicillins, and its core chemical scaffold is the 6-aminopenicillanic acid penam framework. Closely related drugs include dicloxacillin, oxacillin, flucloxacillin, and nafcillin, as well as broader penicillin comparators such as methicillin. Its principal targets are bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, especially transpeptidases involved in peptidoglycan cross-linking, leading to inhibition of cell-wall synthesis and bacterial lysis. Cloxacillin is used primarily for infections caused by methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus and other susceptible gram-positive organisms, including skin and soft-tissue infections, cellulitis, impetigo, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, endocarditis, and pneumonia. Orally it is absorbed variably and incompletely, with reduced absorption by food; it is distributed into many tissues but has limited cerebrospinal fluid penetration unless meninges are inflamed, is highly protein bound, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated mainly by renal tubular secretion and glomerular filtration, with some biliary excretion and a short half-life requiring repeated dosing. Toxicity includes hypersensitivity reactions ranging from rash to anaphylaxis, gastrointestinal irritation, antibiotic-associated colitis, interstitial nephritis, hepatotoxicity such as cholestatic hepatitis, neutropenia, eosinophilia, and, at high exposures, neurotoxicity including seizures; common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, rash, urticaria, and injection-site reactions. Clinically, it is used as targeted therapy for beta-lactamase-producing but methicillin-susceptible staphylococcal infections, for example treatment of MSSA bacteremia after susceptibility confirmation or oral step-down therapy for uncomplicated skin infection.

Name: Flavoxate
Description: Flavoxate (DrugBank DB01148) is a synthetic urinary antispasmodic built as an aromatic carboxylate ester in which a flavone-like xanthene/chromone-related lipophilic aromatic system is linked through an ester bond to a 2-piperidinoethyl side chain, giving a tertiary amine-containing ester that is both hydrophobic and weakly basic; chemically it is classified as a piperidine-containing aminoalkyl ester and smooth-muscle relaxant, with a scaffold centered on an aryl ester–ethyl–piperidine pharmacophore. It is structurally similar in broad pharmacologic space to other antimuscarinic or bladder antispasmodic agents such as oxybutynin, propiverine, dicyclomine, and tolterodine, although its precise chemotype differs. Flavoxate is administered orally, is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, distributes systemically with functional access to urinary tract smooth muscle, undergoes substantial first-pass hydrolysis and other hepatic biotransformation to active and inactive metabolites including 3-methylflavone-8-carboxylic acid derivatives, and is eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites with relatively limited unchanged drug excretion. Its mechanism is not fully defined; reported targets and pathways include muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, phosphodiesterase-related smooth-muscle signaling, and direct calcium antagonism/spasmolysis in detrusor muscle. Clinically it is indicated for symptomatic relief of overactive bladder states, dysuria, urgency, frequency, nocturia, suprapubic pain, and bladder spasm associated with cystitis, prostatitis, urethritis, neurogenic bladder, and instrumentation. Adverse effects and toxicity are largely anticholinergic and CNS/GI related, including dry mouth, nausea, vomiting, dyspepsia, constipation, blurred vision, dizziness, headache, somnolence, tachycardia, urinary retention, confusion in susceptible older adults, and overdose may accentuate antimuscarinic toxicity; accordingly, use is established as adjunctive symptomatic therapy rather than disease-modifying treatment.

Name: Nefazodone
Description: Nefazodone (DrugBank DB01149) is a phenylpiperazine antidepressant whose structure consists of an arylpiperazine linked through a flexible ethyl chain to a substituted phenoxyethyl group and a triazolone-containing heterocycle, giving it a diaryl/heteroaryl, lipophilic, weakly basic architecture typical of serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitor agents. Chemically it is categorized as a second-generation antidepressant, specifically a phenylpiperazine and triazolone derivative, built on an arylpiperazine scaffold related to trazodone and sharing mechanistic similarity with serotonin modulators such as trazodone, vilazodone, and, more distantly, SSRIs as comparator drugs. Its principal targets include the serotonin transporter SLC6A4, 5-HT2A and 5-HT2C receptors, with lesser activity at 5-HT1A, alpha1-adrenergic, and histamine H1 sites. Pharmacokinetically, nefazodone is well absorbed orally but undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism, resulting in moderate bioavailability; it is highly protein bound, widely distributed, metabolized mainly by CYP3A4 to active metabolites including hydroxynefazodone and m-chlorophenylpiperazine, and eliminated predominantly as urinary and fecal metabolites. It is indicated for major depressive disorder, particularly when depression is accompanied by anxiety or insomnia, and has been used clinically for depressive symptoms such as low mood, sleep disturbance, and psychomotor agitation. Adverse effects commonly include somnolence, dizziness, dry mouth, nausea, constipation, blurred vision, and orthostatic hypotension. Its major toxicity concern is idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity, including rare acute liver failure requiring transplantation or causing death; overdose may also produce CNS depression, vomiting, and cardiac conduction abnormalities, which has markedly limited routine clinical use.

Name: Cefprozil
Description: Cefprozil (DrugBank DB01150) is a semisynthetic, orally active second-generation cephalosporin antibiotic whose structure is defined by the cephem nucleus, a strained beta-lactam ring fused to a dihydrothiazine ring, bearing the characteristic 7-aminocephalosporanic acid scaffold with an aminophenylglycyl-type side chain at C7 and a substituted propenyl group at C3; it is used clinically as a cis/trans isomeric mixture, with antibacterial activity primarily associated with the beta-lactam pharmacophore. Chemically, it belongs to the beta-lactam cephalosporin class and more specifically the 2nd-generation oral cephalosporins; its closest scaffold analogs and similar drugs include cefaclor, cefuroxime axetil, cefixime, cephalexin, and cefadroxil. Cefprozil acts by binding bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, especially transpeptidases such as PBP1, PBP2, and PBP3, thereby inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-linking and causing cell-wall instability and lysis. It is indicated for susceptible mild-to-moderate infections including acute otitis media, pharyngitis/tonsillitis, acute bacterial sinusitis, uncomplicated skin and skin-structure infections, and acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis caused by organisms such as Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. Oral absorption is good, bioavailability is relatively high, protein binding is modest, tissue penetration is adequate for respiratory and skin infections, metabolism is minimal, and elimination occurs predominantly as unchanged drug in urine, with renal impairment prolonging half-life and increasing exposure. Toxicity is usually low but includes class effects such as hypersensitivity reactions, anaphylaxis, rash, diarrhea, antibiotic-associated colitis including Clostridioides difficile, rare hematologic abnormalities, interstitial nephritis, and seizures mainly with renal dysfunction or excessive exposure; common side effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, candidiasis, and dizziness. Clinically, cefprozil is used as an oral outpatient beta-lactam option when coverage is needed for common community-acquired respiratory or skin pathogens and when a broader spectrum than first-generation cephalosporins is desired.

Name: Desipramine
Description: Desipramine (DrugBank DB01151) is a dibenzazepine tricyclic antidepressant and the major active secondary-amine metabolite of imipramine, characterized structurally by a rigid three-ring fused aromatic system with a central seven-membered azepine ring and a propyl side chain terminating in a monomethylaminopropyl group; its core scaffold is the iminodibenzyl/dibenzazepine tricyclic framework typical of classic TCAs. Chemically and pharmacologically related drugs include imipramine, nortriptyline, amitriptyline, clomipramine, doxepin, and protriptyline, with desipramine being relatively norepinephrine-selective among TCAs. Its principal targets are the norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2 and, to a lesser extent, the serotonin transporter SLC6A4; it also shows clinically relevant antagonism at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, histamine H1 receptors, and alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, contributing both therapeutic and adverse effects. Desipramine is well absorbed orally, undergoes substantial hepatic first-pass metabolism, is widely distributed with high tissue and plasma protein binding, penetrates the CNS, and is metabolized mainly by CYP2D6 via hydroxylation and further conjugation, with genetic CYP2D6 variability affecting exposure and toxicity; elimination is primarily renal as metabolites, with a relatively long half-life permitting once-daily dosing in some patients. It is indicated mainly for major depressive disorder and has also been used for neuropathic pain, attention-deficit symptoms, panic disorder, and functional gastrointestinal pain. Common adverse effects include dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention, tachycardia, sweating, tremor, sedation or insomnia, orthostatic hypotension, and sexual dysfunction. Important toxicities include conduction delay, QT prolongation, ventricular arrhythmias, seizures, delirium, coma, and potentially fatal overdose, especially in children or with coadministration of other cardiotoxic or serotonergic agents; clinically, it has been used when a comparatively activating, less antihistaminic TCA is desired, particularly in depression with psychomotor retardation or chronic pain comorbidity.

Name: Gemifloxacin
Description: Gemifloxacin (DrugBank DB01155) is a synthetic broad-spectrum fluoroquinolone antibacterial whose structure is built on a 4-quinolone-3-carboxylic acid core bearing the characteristic C-6 fluorine, a C-7 substituted pyrrolidinyl/heterocyclic amine region that enhances Gram-positive activity, and an 8-methoxy substituent that helps distinguish it from earlier quinolones; thus it belongs to the fluoroquinolone carboxylic acid class and more specifically the quinolone scaffold. Closely related drugs include moxifloxacin, levofloxacin, ciprofloxacin, gatifloxacin, and sparfloxacin, which share the same DNA topoisomerase-directed pharmacophore but differ in ring substitution patterns and spectrum. Its principal targets are bacterial DNA gyrase, especially GyrA/GyrB, and topoisomerase IV, especially ParC/ParE, leading to inhibition of DNA replication and cell death. Gemifloxacin is orally active with generally good absorption, moderate protein binding, wide distribution into respiratory tissues, limited hepatic metabolism, and elimination through both renal and fecal pathways, with a terminal half-life permitting once-daily dosing. Toxicity is class-consistent and includes dose-related gastrointestinal and CNS effects, QT-interval prolongation, dysglycemia risk, tendinopathy and tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, hepatotoxicity, photosensitivity, and hypersensitivity; rash is notably more frequent in younger women and with longer courses. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, headache, dizziness, candidiasis, and rash. Clinically, it has been used mainly for mild to moderate community-acquired pneumonia and acute bacterial exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, particularly when respiratory pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, or atypical organisms are suspected.

Name: Bupropion
Description: Bupropion (DrugBank DB01156) is an aminoketone antidepressant structurally characterized as a substituted cathinone/phenethylamine with a chlorinated aromatic ring linked to a tert-butylamino side chain and a β-keto group, giving it a chlorophenyl aminoketone framework; chemically it is classified as a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor and nicotinic receptor antagonist, and its core scaffold is best described as a β-keto-phenethylamine (cathinone-like) scaffold. Structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include cathinone analogs such as amfepramone and pyrovalerone, while clinically it is often contrasted with other atypical antidepressants or smoking-cessation agents such as venlafaxine, nortriptyline, and varenicline. After oral administration, bupropion is well absorbed but undergoes substantial first-pass metabolism; it is widely distributed, highly hepatically metabolized mainly by CYP2B6 to active metabolites including hydroxybupropion, threohydrobupropion, and erythrohydrobupropion, and is excreted predominantly in urine as metabolites with a smaller fecal component. Toxicity is dominated by dose-dependent seizure risk, especially in overdose or predisposed patients, and may also include tachycardia, agitation, hallucinations, hypertension, and cardiotoxicity in severe intoxication. Known targets include the norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, dopamine transporter SLC6A3, and neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptors such as CHRNA4/CHRNB2-containing subtypes. It is indicated for major depressive disorder, seasonal affective disorder, and smoking cessation, and is used clinically as sustained- or extended-release therapy for depressive symptoms, anergia, nicotine dependence, and sometimes antidepressant-associated sexual dysfunction or fatigue. Common adverse effects include insomnia, dry mouth, tremor, anxiety, nausea, headache, and reduced appetite, with less common but important risks of seizures and neuropsychiatric reactions.

Name: Bretylium
Description: Bretylium (DB01158) is a small, highly polar quaternary ammonium antiarrhythmic whose structure consists of a permanently charged trimethylammonium ethyl side chain attached to a brominated aromatic ring, giving it the character of an aralkyl quaternary ammonium salt; chemically it is categorized as an adrenergic neuronal blocker and class III antiarrhythmic, built on a bromobenzyl-ethyl-trimethylammonium scaffold related in function, though not identical in structure, to other antiarrhythmics and adrenergic neuron blockers such as amiodarone, sotalol, guanethidine, and bethanidine. Its principal pharmacology reflects uptake into sympathetic nerve terminals via the norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, where it initially promotes norepinephrine release and subsequently inhibits further release, while also prolonging cardiac action potential duration and refractoriness through effects on potassium-dependent repolarization; thus relevant targets include SLC6A2 and cardiac ion-channel systems, especially delayed rectifier potassium currents, although no single molecular target fully explains its actions. Bretylium was used mainly intravenously for life-threatening ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation, particularly refractory arrhythmias during cardiac arrest or acute myocardial infarction. Because it is poorly absorbed orally, it is generally given parenterally, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid with accumulation in adrenergic neurons, undergoes limited metabolism, and is excreted largely unchanged by the kidney, with a prolonged effect relative to plasma clearance. Toxicity is dominated by exaggerated autonomic and cardiovascular effects, including severe orthostatic hypotension, marked initial hypertension from catecholamine release, bradycardia, and precipitation or worsening of arrhythmias; adverse effects also include nausea, vomiting, dizziness, syncope, and injection-related discomfort. Clinically, its historical use was restricted to monitored emergency settings because of these toxicities and the availability of safer modern antiarrhythmics.

Name: Dinoprost tromethamine
Description: Dinoprost tromethamine (DB01160) is the tromethamine salt of dinoprost, a naturally occurring prostaglandin F2alpha analog formulation whose structure consists of a substituted eicosanoid fatty-acid framework with a cyclopentane core, two aliphatic side chains, a terminal carboxylate, and hydroxyl/alkene functionalities that define the prostanoid stereochemistry; chemically it belongs to the prostaglandins, specifically prostanoids and lipid-derived autacoids, and its core scaffold is the prostane cyclopentane ring system characteristic of PGF-series agents. Similar drugs include other prostaglandin analogs such as carboprost, dinoprostone, latanoprost, travoprost, and bimatoprost, although these differ in receptor selectivity and clinical context. Its principal target is the prostaglandin F receptor, PTGFR, with downstream smooth-muscle contractile signaling in uterine and other tissues. Pharmacokinetically, dinoprost tromethamine is generally given by intra-amniotic, intramuscular, or veterinary parenteral routes because prostaglandins are rapidly inactivated; it distributes locally and systemically, undergoes extensive first-pass pulmonary and tissue metabolism by oxidation of hydroxyl groups and beta/omega oxidation to inactive metabolites, and is eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites, with a short effective half-life. Toxicity reflects exaggerated prostaglandin effects, including severe uterine hyperstimulation, bronchoconstriction, gastrointestinal cramping, vomiting, diarrhea, fever, hypotension or hypertension, and rarely cardiovascular collapse; overdose can intensify these reactions. Adverse effects commonly include abdominal pain, uterine cramping, nausea, flushing, headache, pyrexia, and diarrhea. Clinically, it is used primarily to induce abortion or evacuate the uterus in the second trimester, manage missed abortion or intrauterine fetal death, and in veterinary medicine to lyse the corpus luteum, synchronize estrus, and treat pyometra.

Name: Terazosin
Description: Terazosin (DrugBank DB01162) is a quinazoline-derived piperazine antihypertensive and urologic agent whose structure is centered on a 6,7-dimethoxy-substituted quinazoline ring linked through an exocyclic amino group to a piperazine moiety that is further acylated with a tetrahydrofuran-containing carbonyl side chain, giving an arylamino-piperazine scaffold characteristic of peripheral alpha-1 adrenergic antagonists. Chemically it belongs to the quinazoline alpha-1 adrenoceptor blocker class, with a scaffold closely related to prazosin, doxazosin, and alfuzosin, which are its most similar therapeutic analogs. Its principal targets are alpha-1 adrenergic receptor subtypes, especially ADRA1A, ADRA1B, and ADRA1D, producing relaxation of vascular smooth muscle and prostatic/bladder neck smooth muscle. After oral administration, terazosin is well absorbed, has relatively high bioavailability, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, is moderately protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism including demethylation/conjugative pathways, and is eliminated through both biliary/fecal and renal routes, with an elimination half-life compatible with once-daily dosing. It is indicated for hypertension and symptomatic benign prostatic hyperplasia, for example reduction of elevated blood pressure and improvement of urinary hesitancy, weak stream, and incomplete bladder emptying. Toxicity is largely pharmacodynamic, with dose-related orthostatic hypotension, first-dose syncope, dizziness, and reflex tachycardia; overdose can cause profound hypotension. Common adverse effects include headache, asthenia, nasal congestion, somnolence, palpitations, peripheral edema, and postural dizziness. Clinically, it is used as an oral titrated agent for blood-pressure control and relief of lower urinary tract symptoms in men with BPH, particularly when smooth-muscle relaxation is desired.

Name: Calcium chloride
Description: Calcium chloride (DrugBank DB01164) is a simple inorganic ionic salt composed of a divalent calcium cation electrostatically associated with two chloride anions, typically encountered as a highly water-soluble crystalline electrolyte; structurally it lacks a complex organic framework, so its chemical category is a mineral salt/calcium supplement/electrolyte replenisher and its scaffold is best described as a nonorganic mononuclear alkaline-earth halide ionic lattice. Similar drugs include other calcium salts such as calcium gluconate and calcium acetate, as well as electrolyte salts used for related indications, including sodium chloride and potassium chloride. Pharmacokinetically, intravenous calcium chloride dissociates immediately in plasma, providing bioavailable Ca2+ that distributes predominantly to extracellular fluid and avidly exchanges with bone mineral stores; it is not metabolized, and calcium is eliminated mainly by renal excretion with additional fecal loss, under regulation by parathyroid hormone, calcitonin, and vitamin D. Its pharmacologic targets are not classic receptors but endogenous calcium-binding and calcium-conducting systems, with functional effects on cardiac myocyte excitation-contraction machinery, voltage-gated calcium channels, troponin C, calmodulin-dependent pathways, and neuromuscular membrane stabilization. It is indicated for acute hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia with ECG changes, hypermagnesemia, calcium channel blocker overdose, and cardiac resuscitation settings such as severe electrolyte-mediated myocardial depression. Toxicity includes hypercalcemia, tissue necrosis from extravasation, local venous irritation, arrhythmias, bradycardia, vasoconstriction, and milk-alkali-related complications when calcium excess occurs. Common adverse effects include flushing, nausea, vomiting, chalky taste, hypotension or hypertension, and injection-site pain. Clinically, it is used primarily as an intravenous emergency calcium source, for example in symptomatic tetany, transfusion-related citrate toxicity, and membrane stabilization during life-threatening hyperkalemia.

Name: Ofloxacin
Description: Ofloxacin (DrugBank DB01165) is a second-generation fluoroquinolone antibacterial built on a quinolone-3-carboxylic acid core with a fluorine substituent that enhances Gram-negative activity, a 4-oxo group essential for target binding, and a fused bicyclic N-containing ring at C7 that distinguishes it structurally; it is the racemic parent of levofloxacin and belongs to the fluoroquinolone carboxyquinolone class with a fluorinated 4-quinolone scaffold. Closely related drugs include ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, norfloxacin, moxifloxacin, and lomefloxacin, which share the same DNA gyrase/topoisomerase inhibitory pharmacophore but differ in ring substitutions and spectra. Its principal targets are bacterial DNA gyrase subunits GyrA and GyrB and topoisomerase IV subunits ParC and ParE, leading to inhibition of DNA replication and transcription. Ofloxacin is well absorbed orally with high bioavailability, widely distributed into urine, kidney, prostate, lung, skin, and gynecologic tissues, shows relatively low protein binding, undergoes minimal hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by the kidney, giving it utility in urinary tract infection but requiring dose adjustment in renal impairment. Toxicities and adverse effects include class-associated tendinopathy and tendon rupture, QT prolongation, dysglycemia, peripheral neuropathy, CNS stimulation with dizziness, insomnia, agitation or seizures, hepatotoxicity, phototoxicity, and risk of Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea. Clinically, it has been used for urinary tract infections, prostatitis, gonorrhea, pelvic inflammatory disease, bronchitis, pneumonia, skin and soft tissue infections, and ophthalmic or otic infections, though use is generally reserved for situations where safer alternatives are unsuitable or resistance patterns support its selection.

Name: Cilostazol
Description: Cilostazol (DrugBank DB01166) is a quinolinone-derived antiplatelet and vasodilator agent whose structure is centered on a 4(1H)-quinolinone bicyclic heteroaromatic scaffold bearing a cyclohexyl substituent and a tetrazolylbutoxy side chain, a combination that confers lipophilicity and potent phosphodiesterase inhibition; chemically it is classified as a selective phosphodiesterase type 3 inhibitor and can be grouped with related PDE3-active antiplatelet or inodilator drugs such as milrinone, amrinone, and anagrelide, although cilostazol is distinguished by its quinolinone-tetrazole framework. Its principal target is phosphodiesterase 3, especially PDE3A in platelets and vascular smooth muscle, leading to increased intracellular cAMP, inhibition of platelet aggregation, and arterial vasodilation. It is indicated primarily for intermittent claudication in peripheral arterial disease to improve walking distance, and it has also been used in some settings for secondary prevention of non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke and other thrombotic vascular conditions. After oral administration it is well absorbed, with enhanced absorption by high-fat meals, is highly protein bound, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly by CYP3A4 and CYP2C19 to active metabolites, and is eliminated predominantly in urine as metabolites with a smaller fecal component. Toxicity is driven largely by pharmacology and includes tachycardia, palpitations, hypotension, bleeding risk, and headache; it carries a contraindication in heart failure because PDE3 inhibition has been associated with increased mortality in that setting. Common adverse effects include headache, diarrhea, dizziness, peripheral edema, and palpitations. Clinically, cilostazol is used as an oral adjunct to exercise and smoking cessation in peripheral arterial disease and selectively in antiplatelet regimens where a vasodilating, platelet-inhibitory profile is desired.

Name: Itraconazole
Description: Itraconazole (DrugBank DB01167) is a highly lipophilic triazole antifungal characterized by a dioxolane-containing azole core linked to a dichlorophenyl group and an extended aryl-piperazine/triazolone-rich side chain, placing it in the triazole class and more specifically on a substituted azole-dioxolane scaffold closely related to other systemic azoles such as ketoconazole, fluconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, and isavuconazole. Its principal pharmacologic target is fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase, encoded by CYP51, leading to inhibition of ergosterol biosynthesis and disruption of fungal membrane integrity; it also inhibits human CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, explaining many drug interactions. Orally, absorption is formulation- and food-dependent, generally improved by gastric acidity and capsules taken with food, while the oral solution is better absorbed fasting; it is extensively distributed into keratinous tissues, lung, and adipose, highly protein bound, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 to active hydroxy-itraconazole, and is eliminated slowly through biliary/fecal and lesser renal routes with a long terminal half-life that supports pulse therapy. Major toxicities include hepatotoxicity, negative inotropy with risk of congestive heart failure, QT-interval effects, and severe CYP3A4-mediated interactions that can raise concentrations of statins, benzodiazepines, or certain antiarrhythmics. Indications and clinical use include histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, aspergillosis, sporotrichosis, onychomycosis, dermatophytoses, and mucosal or systemic infections due to Candida where appropriate. Common adverse effects include nausea, dyspepsia, abdominal pain, diarrhea, rash, edema, headache, dizziness, and transaminase elevation, with rarer neuropathy or serious hepatic injury.

Name: Arsenic trioxide
Description: Arsenic trioxide (DB01169) is a simple inorganic arsenical composed of trivalent arsenic linked through oxygen in a small covalent oxide lattice that in aqueous solution generates arsenious acid and related AsIII species; chemically it belongs to the inorganic metalloid oxides and its scaffold is best described as a minimal arsenic oxide/arsenite framework rather than an organic pharmacophore. Similar drugs include other arsenicals such as arsenic acid, sodium arsenite, melarsoprol, and historically Fowler’s solution, although these differ in oxidation state or substitution. After intravenous administration, arsenic trioxide is systemically available, widely distributed into blood cells and highly perfused tissues including liver, kidney, heart, skin, hair, and nails, undergoes hepatic biomethylation by AS3MT to monomethylarsonic and dimethylarsinic metabolites, and is eliminated mainly in urine as unchanged arsenic and methylated species with multiphasic clearance and tissue accumulation during repeated dosing. Its pharmacology is pleiotropic rather than receptor-selective, with key targets and effectors including the PML-RARA fusion oncoprotein, promyelocytic leukemia protein, retinoic acid receptor alpha complex, thiol-rich proteins such as thioredoxin reductase, glutathione-related redox systems, mitochondrial apoptotic pathways, and ion channels relevant to QT prolongation. It is indicated primarily for acute promyelocytic leukemia, especially relapsed/refractory or frontline APL in combination with all-trans retinoic acid. Major toxicities include QTc prolongation, torsades risk, hepatotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy, encephalopathy, pancreatitis, and differentiation syndrome with fever, edema, pulmonary infiltrates, and leukocytosis; common adverse effects include fatigue, nausea, diarrhea, hyperglycemia, rash, dyspnea, and electrolyte disturbances. Clinically, it is used as a differentiation-inducing and proapoptotic antileukemic agent in monitored oncology settings with ECG, electrolyte, and hepatic surveillance.

Name: Kanamycin
Description: Kanamycin (DrugBank DB01172) is a naturally derived aminoglycoside antibiotic composed of a highly polar, polycationic aminocyclitol core, 2-deoxystreptamine, glycosidically linked to multiple amino sugars rich in hydroxyl and primary amino groups, a structure that confers strong basicity, water solubility, and avid binding to bacterial ribosomal RNA; chemically it belongs to the aminoglycoside/aminocyclitol class, and its central scaffold is the 2-deoxystreptamine nucleus substituted by sugar moieties characteristic of kanamycin A and related congeners. Closely related drugs include amikacin, gentamicin, tobramycin, neomycin, and paromomycin, with amikacin being a semisynthetic derivative designed to evade some aminoglycoside-inactivating enzymes. Its principal target is the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit, especially 16S rRNA and associated proteins within the decoding site, causing mistranslation and inhibition of protein synthesis with bactericidal activity. Kanamycin is not orally absorbed to a clinically useful extent for systemic therapy, is usually given parenterally, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid with poor CNS penetration unless meninges are inflamed, shows low protein binding, undergoes negligible metabolism, and is eliminated largely unchanged by glomerular filtration, so accumulation occurs in renal impairment. It is indicated for serious susceptible Gram-negative and some mycobacterial infections, including septicemia, pneumonia, urinary tract infection, intra-abdominal infection, and tuberculosis in selected multidrug-resistant regimens. Major toxicities are nephrotoxicity, irreversible ototoxicity involving cochlear and vestibular damage, and neuromuscular blockade; adverse effects include tinnitus, hearing loss, vertigo, rising creatinine, rash, and rare respiratory paralysis, so clinical use is generally reserved for severe infections requiring susceptibility-guided therapy and careful drug-level and renal monitoring.

Name: Orphenadrine
Description: Orphenadrine (DB01173) is a synthetic ethanolamine-class anticholinergic and centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant structurally characterized as a diphenyl-substituted tertiary amino ether, with a benzhydryl aryl-ether motif linked through a short aliphatic chain to a dimethylated tertiary amine; its core scaffold is the diarylmethoxyethylamine framework shared with several first-generation antihistamine and antimuscarinic agents. Chemically and pharmacologically, it is closely related to diphenhydramine and shows similarity to other centrally acting anticholinergic or muscle relaxant drugs such as benztropine, cyclobenzaprine, and methocarbamol in therapeutic space, although the scaffold is most analogous to ethanolamine antihistamines. It is generally well absorbed after oral administration, distributes widely including into the central nervous system, is substantially protein bound, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism through demethylation, hydroxylation, and conjugative pathways, and is eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites with a relatively prolonged half-life that supports repeated daily dosing. Known targets include muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, and it also has reported NMDA receptor antagonistic and sodium channel-blocking properties that may contribute to analgesic and antispasmodic effects. Clinically, it is indicated as an adjunct for acute painful musculoskeletal conditions such as muscle spasm, low back pain, cervical strain, and traumatic soft-tissue injury, and has also been used in parkinsonian syndromes and drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms. Dose-limiting toxicity reflects anticholinergic and CNS effects, including dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, tachycardia, confusion, hallucinations, and sedation; overdose may produce severe agitation, hyperthermia, arrhythmia, seizures, and coma.

Name: Phenobarbital
Description: Phenobarbital (DrugBank DB01174) is a long-acting 5-ethyl-5-phenyl substituted barbiturate built on a barbituric acid core, specifically a pyrimidine-2,4,6-trione ring bearing phenyl and ethyl groups at C5 that confer marked lipophilicity and anticonvulsant-hypnotic activity; it belongs to the barbiturate sedative-hypnotic and antiepileptic chemical category, with a classical barbiturate scaffold shared by related drugs such as primidone, mephobarbital, pentobarbital, secobarbital, and thiopental. Pharmacologically, it acts mainly as a positive allosteric modulator of GABAA receptor chloride channels, prolonging channel opening, and at higher concentrations can directly gate GABAA receptors while also suppressing excitatory glutamatergic signaling; relevant targets include GABAA receptor subunits such as GABRA1, GABRB2, and GABRG2, with broader CNS network effects. Oral absorption is generally good though not rapid, bioavailability is high, protein binding is modest, distribution is wide including CNS and placental transfer, metabolism occurs partly in the liver via CYP2C9, CYP2C19, and CYP2E1 with potent induction of CYP3A4 and other drug-metabolizing enzymes, and elimination is slow, largely renal as unchanged drug and metabolites, yielding a long half-life that supports once-daily use. Clinically it is indicated for generalized and focal seizures, status epilepticus, and neonatal seizures, and has also been used for sedation and historically for insomnia. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related CNS and respiratory depression, coma, hypotension, cognitive impairment, dependence, withdrawal seizures, teratogenic risk, and hepatic enzyme induction interactions; common adverse effects include drowsiness, ataxia, nystagmus, dizziness, behavioral changes, depression, rash, and impaired psychomotor performance.

Name: Escitalopram
Description: Escitalopram (DB01175) is the S-enantiomer of citalopram, a lipophilic bicyclic arylalkylamine whose structure is centered on a 1,3-dihydroisobenzofuran scaffold bearing a para-fluorophenyl group and a dimethylaminopropyl side chain, with a nitrile substituent that contributes to its physicochemical profile; chemically it is classified as a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), more specifically a phthalane-derived fluorinated aryl nitrile, and its core scaffold is closely related to the citalopram/phthalane antidepressant chemotype. Similar drugs include citalopram, sertraline, fluoxetine, paroxetine, and fluvoxamine, which share SSRI pharmacology, though escitalopram has high selectivity for the serotonin transporter. Its principal target is SLC6A4 (serotonin transporter, 5-HTT), with negligible clinically relevant affinity for muscarinic, histaminergic, adrenergic, or dopaminergic receptors. After oral administration it is well absorbed, has high bioavailability, reaches peak plasma levels in a few hours, distributes widely with moderate protein binding, undergoes hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP2C19 with contributions from CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 to desmethyl and didesmethyl metabolites, and is eliminated by both hepatic and renal routes with a terminal half-life of roughly 27-32 hours.
