It is indicated for major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder, and is also used clinically for panic disorder, social anxiety disorder, and obsessive-compulsive symptoms in some settings. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, insomnia or somnolence, headache, sexual dysfunction, dry mouth, sweating, and diarrhea. Important toxicities include serotonin syndrome, QT prolongation at higher exposure, hyponatremia from SIADH, abnormal bleeding, activation of mania, withdrawal symptoms on abrupt cessation, and overdose manifestations such as CNS depression, tachycardia, vomiting, and ECG changes, although fatal toxicity is generally lower than with tricyclic antidepressants.

Name: Cyclizine
Description: Cyclizine (DrugBank DB01176) is a first-generation piperazine antihistamine whose structure consists of a diphenylmethyl-substituted piperazine bearing a tertiary amine and a para-methylbenzyl group, giving a lipophilic, cationic diaryl piperazine architecture typical of centrally active antiemetics. Chemically it belongs to the piperazine-class H1 receptor antagonists, and its core scaffold is the diarylmethyl-piperazine/pharmacophore shared with related agents such as meclizine, hydroxyzine, buclizine, and to a lesser extent cinnarizine. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, with clinically relevant antimuscarinic activity also contributing to vestibular suppression and antiemesis; broader CNS depressant effects are consistent with penetration into the brain. After oral administration, cyclizine is well absorbed, undergoes significant first-pass hepatic metabolism, reaches systemic circulation within hours, distributes widely including the CNS because of high lipophilicity, is metabolized mainly by hepatic N-demethylation and related oxidative pathways, and is excreted predominantly as metabolites in urine. It is indicated for prevention and treatment of nausea, vomiting, and vertigo, including motion sickness, postoperative nausea and vomiting, opioid-associated nausea, and vestibular disorders such as labyrinthine disturbance. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, dizziness, and urinary retention; paradoxical excitation may occur, especially in children or older adults. Toxicity reflects its antihistaminic and anticholinergic properties, with overdose causing marked sedation, tachycardia, agitation, hallucinations, hyperthermia, seizures, and respiratory compromise. Clinically, it is used orally, intramuscularly, or intravenously as a symptomatic antiemetic and antivertigo agent in perioperative care, travel medicine, and palliative or analgesic support settings.

Name: Idarubicin
Description: Idarubicin (DrugBank DB01177) is a semisynthetic anthracycline antineoplastic derived from the doxorubicin/daunorubicin family, characterized structurally by a planar tetracyclic anthraquinone-like anthracyclinone aglycone linked glycosidically to an amino sugar, daunosamine; relative to daunorubicin it is 4-demethoxy, a change that increases lipophilicity and cellular uptake. Chemically it belongs to the anthracycline antibiotics and antitumor quinones, with an anthracycline/anthraquinone fused aromatic scaffold as its core pharmacophore. Similar drugs include daunorubicin, doxorubicin, epirubicin, and mitoxantrone as a related anthracenedione topoisomerase poison. Its principal targets are topoisomerase II alpha and beta, with additional DNA intercalation and free-radical mediated damage contributing to cytotoxicity. After intravenous administration, and orally in some regimens, absorption is high orally relative to other anthracyclines, distribution is extensive with good intracellular penetration, metabolism occurs mainly via hepatic and extrahepatic carbonyl reduction to the active metabolite idarubicinol, and elimination is prolonged through biliary/fecal and partial renal routes. It is indicated primarily for acute myeloid leukemia, including induction therapy in adults, and has also been used in acute lymphoblastic leukemia and other hematologic malignancies. Dose-limiting toxicity is myelosuppression; important toxicities include cumulative cardiomyopathy/heart failure, severe mucositis, hepatotoxicity, gastrointestinal toxicity, alopecia, and vesicant tissue necrosis with extravasation, with examples including profound neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, febrile sepsis, and reduced left ventricular ejection fraction. Clinically, it is used most often in combination regimens such as idarubicin plus cytarabine for AML induction.

Name: Chlormezanone
Description: Chlormezanone (DrugBank DB01178) is a centrally acting anxiolytic and skeletal muscle relaxant built on a substituted 1,3,4-thiadiazole scaffold, with a compact heteroaromatic ring bearing chlorophenyl and carbonyl-derived substitution that contributes to its lipophilicity and CNS penetration; chemically it is classified as a thiadiazole derivative and non-benzodiazepine sedative-muscle relaxant. Its scaffold and pharmacology place it near older centrally acting agents used for tension states and muscle spasm, with broadly similar clinical comparators including meprobamate, methocarbamol, carisoprodol, and to some extent benzodiazepines such as diazepam for symptomatic relief of anxiety-associated muscle tension, although it is structurally distinct from those classes. The precise molecular target has not been definitively established; no single well-validated target protein is universally accepted, and its effects are generally attributed to central depressant actions within polysynaptic spinal and supraspinal pathways rather than selective receptor binding. After oral administration it is absorbed adequately, distributed systemically with access to the CNS, metabolized hepatically to more polar metabolites, and eliminated mainly in urine, with adverse outcomes heightened in hepatic impairment. It was indicated for painful musculoskeletal spasm, contracture, low back pain, and anxiety or tension-related somatic symptoms. Common adverse effects included drowsiness, dizziness, ataxia, कमजोरी, nausea, and skin rash, while major toxicities included severe cutaneous hypersensitivity, cholestatic or mixed hepatitis, jaundice, and rare life-threatening Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis, leading to withdrawal or major restriction in many markets. Clinically, it was used short term as an adjunct to rest, physical therapy, and analgesics in acute musculoskeletal disorders rather than as definitive disease-modifying therapy.

Name: Podofilox
Description: Podofilox (DB01179), also known as podophyllotoxin, is a non-alkaloid aryltetralin lignan characterized by a rigid polycyclic podophyllotoxin core containing a trans-fused tetralin/lactone framework, multiple methoxy substituents, a secondary alcohol, and a trimethoxy-substituted aromatic ring that helps define its tubulin-binding pharmacophore; chemically it belongs to the lignan antimitotic agents and is built on the podophyllotoxin aryltetralin scaffold. It is closely related to podophyllin resin constituents and is structurally ancestral to semisynthetic epipodophyllotoxin analogs such as etoposide and teniposide, although those latter agents differ pharmacologically by primarily targeting topoisomerase II rather than microtubules. Podofilox binds tubulin, disrupting microtubule assembly and arresting mitosis, with tubulin regarded as its principal target protein. Used topically, systemic pharmacokinetic exposure is generally low when applied to limited wart areas; absorption increases with damaged skin or excessive application, distribution is therefore usually minimal, metabolism is presumed mainly hepatic after systemic uptake, and excretion likely occurs via biliary and renal routes, though detailed human ADME data are limited because it is intended for local therapy. Its principal indication is external genital and perianal warts caused by human papillomavirus, especially condyloma acuminata, and it is used clinically as a patient-applied topical solution or gel in cyclic courses. Toxicity is predominantly local and dose-related, with erythema, burning, pain, inflammation, erosion, pruritus, and ulceration common; severe overuse may cause marked tissue necrosis, and systemic poisoning from podophyllotoxin-containing products can produce gastrointestinal toxicity, neurotoxicity, and bone marrow suppression.

Name: Propafenone
Description: Propafenone (DrugBank DB01182) is a lipophilic class Ic antiarrhythmic built on an aryloxypropanolamine-like framework with a substituted propiophenone core, consisting structurally of a 3-phenylpropiophenone backbone bearing a 5-hydroxy group and a 2-[3-(propylamino)-2-hydroxypropoxy] side chain; chemically it is best categorized as a phenylpropylamine/propiophenone antiarrhythmic with beta-blocking properties, and its dominant scaffold is an aromatic ketone linked to a hydroxypropoxyamino side chain. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other sodium-channel-blocking antiarrhythmics such as flecainide, encainide, pilsicainide, and to some extent beta-blocking aryloxypropanolamines. Its principal targets are the cardiac voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.5 encoded by SCN5A, with additional activity at beta-adrenergic receptors, hERG/KCNH2 and other cardiac potassium channels, and weak calcium-channel effects, producing slowed conduction and reduced excitability. Propafenone is used for rhythm control in supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmias, especially paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, and selected life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias. It is generally well absorbed orally but undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism with marked CYP2D6 polymorphism-dependent variability; distribution is extensive with high protein binding, metabolism occurs mainly via CYP2D6, CYP3A4, and CYP1A2 to active 5-hydroxypropafenone and N-depropylpropafenone, and elimination is predominantly as urinary metabolites with little unchanged drug excreted. Important toxicities include dose-related QRS widening, PR prolongation, bradycardia, hypotension, negative inotropy, and proarrhythmia including ventricular tachycardia or worsened heart failure; common adverse effects include dizziness, metallic or bitter taste, nausea, constipation, fatigue, blurred vision, and bronchospasm. Clinically it is used chronically or as pill-in-the-pocket therapy in carefully selected patients without major structural heart disease, with ECG and drug-interaction monitoring because CYP inhibitors and poor-metabolizer status can substantially increase exposure

Name: Naloxone
Description: Naloxone (DrugBank DB01183) is a semisynthetic morphinan opioid antagonist structurally derived from the 4,5-epoxymorphinan/phenanthrene opioid framework, featuring a rigid fused tetracyclic scaffold with a 3-phenolic hydroxyl, 14-hydroxyl substitution, 6-keto functionality, and an N-allyl group that confers potent antagonist activity at opioid receptors; it is therefore classified as an opioid antagonist and more specifically a morphinan derivative with a naloxone/naltrexone-like scaffold. Closely related drugs include naltrexone, nalmefene, and the mixed antagonist agonist nalorphine, as well as opioid agonist congeners such as oxymorphone from which its structural logic is derived. Its principal targets are the mu opioid receptor OPRM1, with additional antagonism at kappa OPRK1 and delta OPRD1 receptors. Naloxone is indicated for emergency reversal of opioid-induced respiratory and central nervous system depression, including overdose from heroin, morphine, fentanyl, methadone, and prescription analgesics, and is also used to reverse postoperative opioid effects and in combination products to deter parenteral misuse. Pharmacokinetically, it is rapidly absorbed intranasally, intramuscularly, subcutaneously, or intravenously, but has very low oral bioavailability because of extensive first-pass hepatic glucuronidation, distributes quickly to highly perfused tissues including the brain, undergoes mainly hepatic metabolism to naloxone-3-glucuronide, and is excreted primarily in urine with a short elimination half-life that may necessitate repeat dosing. Toxicity is generally low in opioid-naive individuals, but in dependent patients it can precipitate acute withdrawal with agitation, pain, vomiting, hypertension, tachycardia, pulmonary edema, and rarely arrhythmias or seizures; common adverse effects include nausea, sweating, tremor, headache, dizziness, and injection-site reactions.

Name: Domperidone
Description: Domperidone (DrugBank DB01184) is a peripherally selective dopamine D2-like receptor antagonist built on a substituted benzimidazolone scaffold linked through a piperidine ring to aryl and haloalkyl substituents, giving a lipophilic, weakly basic structure typical of antidopaminergic gastroprokinetic agents; chemically it is classified as a benzimidazole/benzimidazolone derivative and is closely related in pharmacologic behavior to other dopamine antagonist antiemetics and prokinetics such as metoclopramide, bromopride, clebopride, and, more distantly, antipsychotic butyrophenones with D2 affinity. Its principal targets are dopamine D2 receptor (DRD2) and likely D3 receptor (DRD3), with antiemetic effects mediated at the chemoreceptor trigger zone outside the blood-brain barrier and prokinetic effects mediated by blockade of enteric dopaminergic inhibition, increasing acetylcholine-dependent upper gastrointestinal motility and accelerating gastric emptying. Oral absorption is relatively rapid but absolute bioavailability is low because of extensive first-pass intestinal and hepatic metabolism; protein binding is high, central nervous system penetration is limited, metabolism occurs mainly via CYP3A4 with contributions from CYP1A2 and CYP2E1, and excretion is through both feces and urine predominantly as metabolites. It is indicated for nausea and vomiting, gastroparesis, dyspepsia, reflux-related upper GI stasis, and sometimes to augment lactation via prolactin elevation. Adverse effects include dry mouth, abdominal cramps, diarrhea, headache, hyperprolactinemia, galactorrhea, gynecomastia, and menstrual disturbance. Major toxicity concerns are QT prolongation, ventricular arrhythmias, torsades de pointes, and sudden cardiac death, especially with high doses, older age, electrolyte imbalance, structural heart disease, or CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ketoconazole, erythromycin, or certain protease inhibitors, which is why clinical use is generally restricted to short-term treatment of refractory nausea or documented motility disorders.

Name: Fluoxymesterone
Description: Fluoxymesterone (DrugBank DB01185) is a synthetic fluorinated androgenic anabolic steroid structurally derived from testosterone, characterized by the classic androstane four-ring steroid nucleus with a 17β-hydroxyl group, a 3-keto-4-ene system, a 9α-fluoro substituent, and a 17α-methyl group that confers oral activity and resistance to first-pass hepatic inactivation. It belongs chemically to the androgen/ anabolic steroid class, with a 17α-alkylated testosterone scaffold; closely related drugs include methyltestosterone, oxandrolone, oxymetholone, nandrolone derivatives, and testosterone itself. Its principal target is the androgen receptor, with downstream modulation of androgen-responsive gene transcription in muscle, bone, skin, and reproductive tissues; indirect effects on the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis suppress gonadotropin secretion. After oral administration it is well absorbed, distributed systemically with plasma protein binding largely to albumin and sex hormone-binding globulin to a limited extent relative to testosterone, metabolized hepatically by steroid-transforming enzymes to active and inactive metabolites, and excreted mainly in urine as conjugated metabolites. Toxicity is typical of 17α-alkylated androgens, notably cholestatic jaundice, hepatocellular injury, peliosis hepatis, hepatic neoplasms, edema, erythrocytosis, adverse lipid changes, hypertension, and virilization; overdose or prolonged exposure may worsen hepatic and cardiovascular risk. Adverse effects include acne, hirsutism, menstrual disturbance, deepened voice, gynecomastia, decreased fertility, testicular atrophy, mood changes, and premature epiphyseal closure in children. Clinically, fluoxymesterone has been used for male hypogonadism, delayed puberty in selected males, and palliative treatment of androgen-responsive breast cancer in women, as well as for symptoms of androgen deficiency such as low libido, weakness, and loss of lean mass.

Name: Pergolide
Description: Pergolide (DB01186) is a semisynthetic ergot-derived dopamine agonist whose structure is built on the rigid tetracyclic ergoline/lysergic acid-related scaffold, bearing a brominated indole-like ergoline nucleus with a thioalkyl substituent and tertiary amine functionality that confer high affinity for monoamine receptors; chemically it is classified as an ergot alkaloid derivative and more specifically an ergoline dopaminergic agonist. Its closest structural and pharmacologic analogs include bromocriptine, cabergoline, lisuride, and to a lesser extent other dopamine agonists such as pramipexole and ropinirole, although the latter are non-ergot agents and lack the ergoline scaffold. Pergolide acts primarily at dopamine D2 and D1 receptor families, with activity also reported at D3, D4, D5 and serotonergic receptors including 5-HT2B, the latter being central to its valvulopathic risk. It was used mainly in Parkinson disease, especially as adjunctive therapy to levodopa for bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor, motor fluctuations, and sometimes restless legs syndrome. After oral administration it is well absorbed, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism with first-pass biotransformation including sulfoxidation, hydroxylation and conjugative pathways, is widely distributed, highly protein bound, and eliminated through both renal and fecal routes with a relatively long half-life permitting once-daily or divided dosing. Adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, somnolence, hallucinations, confusion, dyskinesia, edema, nasal congestion, and impulse-control symptoms. Major toxicities include ergot-related fibrotic reactions and particularly 5-HT2B-mediated cardiac valvular fibrosis/regurgitation, with examples involving mitral, aortic, and tricuspid valves, which led to major restriction or withdrawal of clinical use in many markets.

Name: Ciclopirox
Description: Ciclopirox (DB01188) is a synthetic hydroxypyridone antifungal whose structure is centered on a substituted 2-pyridone/1-hydroxypyridin-2-one ring bearing a 6-cyclohexyl group and a 4-methyl substituent, typically formulated clinically as the ethanolamine salt; chemically it belongs to the hydroxypyridone class and its core scaffold is the lipophilic hydroxy-pyridone chelating pharmacophore, distinct from azole and allylamine antifungals but broadly similar in use to agents such as amorolfine, terbinafine, clotrimazole, ketoconazole, and other topical nail or skin antifungals. Its principal mechanism is metal chelation, especially of trivalent cations, leading to inhibition of metal-dependent enzymes involved in fungal energy production, peroxide degradation, membrane transport, and macromolecular synthesis; no single canonical human target protein is usually assigned, but fungal catalase, peroxidases, and other metalloenzymes are implicated. After topical administration as cream, gel, shampoo, or nail lacquer, systemic absorption is low through intact skin but can increase modestly across diseased skin; absorbed drug distributes systemically to a limited extent, undergoes hepatic conjugative metabolism mainly to glucuronides, and is excreted predominantly in urine with minor fecal elimination. Toxicity is generally low and localized, with examples including erythema, burning, pruritus, irritation, scaling, and contact dermatitis; excessive exposure may produce more pronounced inflammatory reactions, while serious systemic toxicity is rare. Clinically, ciclopirox is indicated for tinea pedis, tinea corporis, tinea cruris, cutaneous candidiasis, seborrheic dermatitis, dandruff, and onychomycosis, and is used topically as a cream or lotion for dermatomycoses, shampoo for seborrheic dermatitis, and 8% nail lacquer for mild to moderate fungal nail infection.

Name: Clindamycin
Description: Clindamycin (DrugBank DB01190) is a semisynthetic lincosamide antibiotic structurally derived from lincomycin, characterized by an amino-octose sugar linked through an amide-containing framework to a substituted proline-like amino acid moiety, with chlorination at the 7-position enhancing lipophilicity and antibacterial potency; thus, it belongs to the lincosamide class and is built on the lincomycin/lincosamine scaffold. Closely related or similar drugs include lincomycin, its parent compound, and functionally overlapping protein synthesis inhibitors such as macrolides including erythromycin and azithromycin, which share partially overlapping ribosomal binding behavior. Clindamycin targets the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit, binding primarily to 23S rRNA within the peptidyl transferase center and inhibiting peptide-chain elongation, with relevant target context in susceptible organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and anaerobes including Bacteroides fragilis. It is generally well absorbed orally, distributes widely into skin, soft tissue, bone, and abscesses but penetrates cerebrospinal fluid poorly, is substantially hepatically metabolized to active and inactive sulfoxide and N-demethyl metabolites, and is eliminated through bile and urine with a several-hour half-life. Major toxicities include antibiotic-associated diarrhea and Clostridioides difficile pseudomembranous colitis, as well as hepatotoxicity, rash, neutropenia, and rare severe hypersensitivity. Its indications and clinical uses include skin and soft tissue infections, dental and oropharyngeal infections, osteomyelitis, intra-abdominal and pelvic anaerobic infections, aspiration pneumonia, bacterial vaginosis, and adjunctive use in toxin-suppressing therapy for invasive streptococcal or staphylococcal disease; common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and candidiasis.

Name: Oxymorphone
Description: Oxymorphone (DrugBank DB01192) is a semisynthetic morphinan opioid derived from thebaine and structurally characterized by the rigid pentacyclic 4,5-epoxymorphinan nucleus bearing a tertiary N-methyl amine, a ketone at C6, hydroxyl groups at C3 and C14, and reduced 7,8-unsaturation relative to oxycodone, features that confer high mu-opioid receptor affinity; it is classified chemically as a phenanthrene/morphinan opioid analgesic, with a classic morphinan scaffold closely related to morphine, hydromorphone, oxycodone, and naloxone-class congeners, and especially similar to hydromorphone and oxycodone. Its principal target is the mu-opioid receptor OPRM1, with weaker activity at delta and kappa opioid receptors. Clinically, oxymorphone is indicated for moderate to severe acute and chronic pain, including postoperative pain, cancer pain, and severe musculoskeletal or neuropathic pain when opioid therapy is warranted. After oral administration it undergoes substantial first-pass metabolism, giving low absolute bioavailability, while parenteral delivery is more efficient; distribution is moderate with limited protein binding, hepatic metabolism occurs mainly via phase II glucuronidation to oxymorphone-3-glucuronide with minor CYP-mediated reduction products, and elimination is primarily renal as conjugated metabolites with a plasma half-life of a few hours, extended by modified-release formulations. Major toxicities are dose-dependent respiratory depression, profound sedation, coma, miosis, hypotension, bradycardia, and fatal overdose, with increased risk in opioid-naive patients or when combined with alcohol, benzodiazepines, or other CNS depressants; common adverse effects include constipation, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, somnolence, pruritus, dry mouth, and urinary retention. In practice it is used as immediate-release and extended-release analgesia for carefully selected opioid-tolerant or closely monitored patients when alternatives are inadequate.

Name: Acebutolol
Description: Acebutolol (DrugBank DB01193) is a cardioselective aryloxypropanolamine beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist whose structure consists of a para-acetyl-substituted anilide linked through an ether to a 2-hydroxy-3-isopropylaminopropyl side chain, giving the classic beta-blocker pharmacophore with one chiral secondary alcohol and a moderately lipophilic aromatic amide domain; chemically it is an aromatic ether, secondary alcohol, and amide within the beta-blocker class, built on the phenoxypropanolamine/aryloxypropanolamine scaffold. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to metoprolol, atenolol, propranolol, betaxolol, and esmolol, though acebutolol is notable for relative beta1 selectivity and an active metabolite, diacetolol, with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity. After oral administration it is reasonably well absorbed but undergoes first-pass metabolism; distribution is moderate with partial protein binding and placental transfer reported; hepatic metabolism forms diacetolol, which prolongs pharmacologic effect; elimination is mainly renal as parent drug and metabolites, with half-life extended in renal impairment. Its principal targets are beta1-adrenergic receptor and, at higher exposure, beta2-adrenergic receptor. It is indicated for hypertension, chronic stable angina, and ventricular arrhythmias such as premature ventricular contractions, and is used clinically to reduce heart rate, myocardial oxygen demand, and ectopic cardiac activity. Adverse effects include bradycardia, hypotension, fatigue, dizziness, depression, sleep disturbance, nausea, and cold extremities; toxic effects in overdose include severe bradyarrhythmia, atrioventricular block, heart failure, bronchospasm, hypoglycemia, and cardiogenic shock, with greater risk in asthma, diabetes, conduction disease, and renal dysfunction.

Name: Flecainide
Description: Flecainide (DrugBank DB01195) is a fluorinated benzamide antiarrhythmic characterized structurally by a substituted aromatic amide bearing a trifluoroethoxy group and a basic piperidine-containing side chain, giving it an amphipathic, lipophilic weak-base profile typical of membrane-active sodium channel blockers; chemically it belongs to the class Ic antiarrhythmics and more broadly to fluorinated aromatic carboxamides, with a benzamide-aniline/piperidyl scaffold. It is structurally and pharmacologically related to other sodium channel-blocking antiarrhythmics such as propafenone, encainide, and to a lesser extent quinidine and disopyramide. Its principal targets are the cardiac voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.5 encoded by SCN5A, with use-dependent blockade of fast inward sodium current and secondary effects on conduction tissue; it may also inhibit RyR2-mediated calcium release in some arrhythmia settings. Flecainide is well absorbed orally with high bioavailability, low to moderate protein binding, wide tissue distribution, hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP2D6 with contribution from CYP1A2, and renal excretion of both unchanged drug and metabolites; its elimination half-life is commonly about 12-27 hours and is prolonged in renal impairment, heart failure, or poor CYP2D6 metabolizer status. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related electrophysiologic effects including QRS widening, PR prolongation, AV block, ventricular tachyarrhythmia, and negative inotropy, with classic risk of proarrhythmia after myocardial infarction or in structural heart disease as shown in CAST-like experience. Indications include paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, AV re-entrant tachycardia, AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia, and selected life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias. Common adverse effects include dizziness, visual blurring, dyspnea, nausea, tremor, edema, and fatigue. Clinically, it is used for rhythm control and suppression of symptomatic supraventricular arrhythmias, including pill-in-the-pocket cardioversion in carefully selected patients without significant structural heart disease.

Name: Estramustine
Description: Estramustine (DB01196) is a bifunctional estradiol–nitrogen mustard conjugate whose structure consists of an estradiol steroid nucleus esterified at the 17-position with a bis(2-chloroethyl)carbamate moiety and commonly administered as the phosphate prodrug, placing it in the antineoplastic alkylating-agent/estrogenic hybrid class; its core scaffold is therefore a steroidal estrane framework linked to a carbamate mustard pharmacophore. It is chemically and pharmacologically related to estramustine phosphate and to other nitrogen mustards such as chlorambucil and melphalan, while also sharing steroidal features with estradiol derivatives. Unlike classical DNA-alkylating mustards, its major antitumor action is associated with binding to microtubule-associated proteins and tubulin, disrupting microtubule assembly and mitotic function; reported targets include tubulin and microtubule-associated proteins, with additional estrogen-receptor-related tissue distribution effects. After oral administration, the phosphate form is dephosphorylated and extensively metabolized to estramustine and estromustine; absorption is variable and reduced by calcium-rich food, distribution is notable in prostate tissue and via plasma protein binding including estramustine-binding protein, metabolism is primarily hepatic with enterohepatic contribution, and excretion occurs through bile/feces and to a lesser extent urine. It is indicated mainly for palliative treatment of metastatic or progressive prostate cancer, especially hormone-refractory disease. Toxicities reflect both estrogenic and cytotoxic properties, including thromboembolism, fluid retention, hypertension, gynecomastia, hepatotoxicity, and rare serious cardiovascular events; common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, edema, decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, and breast tenderness. Clinically, it has been used alone or in combination regimens for advanced prostate carcinoma to reduce tumor burden, pain, and progression-related symptoms.

Name: Captopril
Description: Captopril (DrugBank DB01197) is a small-molecule sulfhydryl-containing angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor built on a proline-derived peptidomimetic scaffold, structurally characterized by an L-proline ring linked through an amide-like framework to a short acyl side chain terminating in a free thiol and carboxylic acid, features that enable high-affinity zinc coordination within ACE. Chemically, it is categorized as a thiol-containing ACE inhibitor and more broadly as an antihypertensive peptidomimetic carboxylic acid. Its core scaffold is distinct from later dicarboxylate or phosphinate ACE inhibitors, but it is closely related pharmacologically to enalapril, lisinopril, ramipril, benazepril, quinapril, fosinopril, and the thiol analog zofenopril. Its principal target is angiotensin-converting enzyme, with downstream suppression of angiotensin II formation and reduced bradykinin degradation. After oral administration, captopril is absorbed relatively rapidly, with moderate bioavailability that is reduced by food; it distributes mainly in extracellular fluids with limited protein binding, undergoes partial hepatic and nonenzymatic conversion to disulfide dimers and mixed disulfides, and is excreted predominantly in urine as unchanged drug and metabolites, with a short elimination half-life that is prolonged in renal impairment. Toxicities include excessive hypotension, renal dysfunction or acute kidney injury especially in renovascular disease, hyperkalemia, rare neutropenia or agranulocytosis, proteinuria, and fetotoxicity in pregnancy. Indications include hypertension, chronic heart failure, post-myocardial-infarction left ventricular dysfunction, and diabetic nephropathy, and in clinical use it is employed alone or with diuretics and other antihypertensives; common adverse effects include dry cough, dizziness, rash, dysgeusia or metallic taste, nausea, and rare but serious angioedema.

Name: Zopiclone
Description: Zopiclone (DrugBank DB01198) is a nonbenzodiazepine sedative-hypnotic of the cyclopyrrolone class whose structure is defined by a fused pyrrolopyrazine-like bicyclic core bearing a lactam and ester functionality, a substituted piperazine moiety, and a chlorinated aromatic ring, features that confer lipophilicity and high affinity for the benzodiazepine site of GABAA receptors; its core chemical scaffold is the cyclopyrrolone hypnotic pharmacophore, distinct from benzodiazepines but functionally similar to Z-drugs such as eszopiclone, zaleplon, and zolpidem, and more broadly analogous in clinical effect to benzodiazepines like temazepam. It acts primarily at GABAA receptor complexes, especially receptor assemblies containing α1, with binding mediated through the benzodiazepine modulatory site formed by subunits including GABRA1, GABRA2, GABRA3, GABRA5, GABRB2, and GABRG2. Orally, zopiclone is rapidly absorbed with good bioavailability, reaches peak plasma concentrations in about 1 to 2 hours, distributes widely including CNS penetration, is moderately protein bound, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 and CYP2C8 to N-oxide and N-desmethyl metabolites, and is eliminated largely in urine as metabolites with a terminal half-life of about 4 to 6 hours. It is indicated for short-term treatment of insomnia, particularly sleep-onset difficulty, nocturnal awakening, and poor sleep maintenance. Common adverse effects include dysgeusia or bitter taste, dry mouth, dizziness, somnolence, impaired coordination, and next-day psychomotor slowing; toxicities include CNS and respiratory depression, falls, anterograde amnesia, parasomnias, tolerance, dependence, withdrawal, and overdose potentiation with alcohol, opioids, or other sedatives. Clinically it is used as a short-course hypnotic in acute or transient insomnia when nonpharmacologic measures are inadequate.

Name: Bromocriptine
Description: Bromocriptine (DrugBank DB01200) is a semisynthetic ergot alkaloid derivative built on a rigid tetracyclic ergoline nucleus bearing a brominated peptide-like amide substituent, giving a conformationally constrained, lipophilic dopamine agonist structure; chemically it is classified as an ergot-derived dopaminergic agent, and its core scaffold is the ergoline/lysergic acid-related ergot framework. Closely related drugs include other ergot dopamine agonists such as cabergoline, pergolide, lisuride, and ergometrine/ergonovine analogs, while non-ergot functional comparators include pramipexole and ropinirole. Its principal targets are dopamine D2 receptors, with additional activity at D1, D3, D4, serotonin receptor subtypes including 5-HT2A/5-HT2B, and adrenergic receptors, explaining both efficacy and adverse effects. Bromocriptine is used for hyperprolactinemia and prolactinomas, acromegaly, and Parkinson disease, and has also been used in type 2 diabetes mellitus in quick-release form to improve glycemic control and in selected cases of galactorrhea, amenorrhea, infertility, or pituitary hormone excess. Orally, it is variably but often well absorbed, undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4, is highly protein bound, widely distributed, has a relatively prolonged terminal half-life despite modest bioavailability, and is excreted predominantly in bile and feces with limited renal elimination. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, constipation, orthostatic hypotension, headache, dizziness, somnolence, and nasal congestion; more serious toxicities include hallucinations, impulse-control or psychiatric effects, digital vasospasm, pleuropulmonary or retroperitoneal fibrosis with chronic ergot exposure, and rare valvular or ischemic complications, especially in overdose or susceptible patients.

Name: Rifapentine
Description: Rifapentine (DrugBank DB01201) is a semisynthetic rifamycin characterized by a large lipophilic ansa-macrocyclic scaffold in which an aliphatic bridge spans a substituted naphthohydroquinone aromatic core; structurally it is a cyclopentyl-substituted rifamycin derivative closely related to other rifamycins and belongs to the ansamycin antibiotic class. Its core chemical scaffold is the rifamycin ansa framework, and similar drugs include rifampin, rifabutin, rifaximin, and rifalazil, which share inhibition of bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase. The principal target is the beta subunit of mycobacterial RNA polymerase encoded by rpoB, leading to suppression of RNA synthesis and bactericidal activity against susceptible mycobacteria. Rifapentine is indicated primarily for pulmonary tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, including latent tuberculosis infection and selected drug-susceptible active disease regimens, for example once-weekly continuation therapy with isoniazid in some settings and short-course latent TB regimens with isoniazid. Orally administered rifapentine is absorbed better with food, is highly protein bound, widely distributed into tissues, undergoes hepatic deacetylation to an active metabolite, induces CYP3A4, CYP2C8, CYP2C9, and transport pathways, and is eliminated mainly via biliary-fecal routes with a long half-life that supports intermittent dosing. Toxicities include hepatotoxicity, hyperbilirubinemia, hypersensitivity, hematologic abnormalities, and orange-red discoloration of body fluids; overdose or coadministration can magnify liver injury or drug interactions. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, rash, pruritus, arthralgia, headache, transaminase elevation, and flu-like reactions. Clinically, it is used only in combination therapy to improve adherence and sterilizing activity in tuberculosis treatment while minimizing resistance emergence.

Name: Levetiracetam
Description: Levetiracetam (DrugBank DB01202) is a pyrrolidone-derived antiepileptic whose structure is the S-enantiomer of an alpha-ethyl substituted 2-oxo-1-pyrrolidine acetamide, giving a small, polar, neutral lactam-acetamide framework closely related to piracetam; chemically it is classified as a racetam and more broadly as a pyrrolidone anticonvulsant, with a 2-oxopyrrolidine scaffold as its core pharmacophore. Similar drugs include brivaracetam, a higher-affinity analog, as well as older racetams such as piracetam. Its principal known target is synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A), with binding believed to modulate synaptic neurotransmitter release and reduce hypersynchronous neuronal firing; no major sodium-channel or direct GABAergic mechanism predominates. Pharmacokinetically, levetiracetam is rapidly and almost completely absorbed orally with high bioavailability, minimal protein binding, broad distribution including CNS penetration, and linear dose-proportional kinetics; it undergoes little hepatic metabolism, with the major pathway being enzymatic hydrolysis of the acetamide to an inactive metabolite, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged in urine, so clearance falls in renal impairment and drug-drug interaction liability is low because CYP involvement is minimal. It is indicated for epilepsy, including focal-onset seizures, myoclonic seizures in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, and primary generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Clinical use includes oral and intravenous adjunctive therapy and, in many settings, monotherapy for partial epilepsy. Toxicity is generally modest, but overdose may cause marked somnolence, agitation, respiratory depression, or coma; important adverse effects include dizziness, asthenia, headache, and especially neuropsychiatric reactions such as irritability, anxiety, depression, aggression, and rarely suicidality or severe behavioral disturbance.

Name: Nadolol
Description: Nadolol (DrugBank DB01203) is a nonselective beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist of the aryloxypropanolamine class, structurally characterized by a naphthalene-derived aromatic ether linked to a propanolamine side chain and multiple hydroxyl groups that increase polarity and limit membrane penetration; its core scaffold is the classic beta-blocker phenoxy/aryloxypropanolamine pharmacophore, and it is closely related to other nonselective beta-blockers such as propranolol, timolol, pindolol, and sotalol, although nadolol is distinguished by low lipid solubility and long duration of action. Its principal targets are beta-1 adrenergic receptor and beta-2 adrenergic receptor, with therapeutic effects mediated by reduction in heart rate, myocardial contractility, atrioventricular conduction, and renin release. Pharmacokinetically, nadolol is absorbed orally with moderate and somewhat incomplete bioavailability, shows minimal hepatic metabolism, low protein binding, limited central nervous system distribution, and a relatively long elimination half-life that supports once-daily dosing; it is excreted largely unchanged by the kidney, so clearance is prolonged in renal impairment. Clinically it is indicated for hypertension and chronic stable angina, and is also used in settings such as rate control of tachyarrhythmias and prophylaxis of variceal bleeding in portal hypertension. Adverse effects include bradycardia, hypotension, fatigue, dizziness, cold extremities, depression, and sexual dysfunction; important toxicities include atrioventricular block, worsening heart failure, severe bronchospasm in asthma or COPD, masking of hypoglycemia in diabetes, and overdose manifestations such as profound bradycardia, shock, and hypoperfusion.

Name: Mitoxantrone
Description: Mitoxantrone (DrugBank DB01204) is a synthetic anthracenedione antineoplastic and immunomodulatory agent built on a planar tricyclic anthracene-9,10-dione-like aromatic core with two side chains bearing terminal hydroxyethylamino substituents, a structure that promotes DNA intercalation and electrostatic interaction with nucleic acids; chemically it belongs to the anthracenedione/topoisomerase II poison class, with an anthraquinone-related scaffold distinct from but mechanistically similar to anthracyclines. Similar drugs include doxorubicin, daunorubicin, epirubicin, idarubicin, and the anthracenedione pixantrone, all of which share DNA-binding cytotoxic properties. Its principal targets are topoisomerase II alpha and beta, with downstream inhibition of DNA replication and repair, induction of strand breaks, and suppression of proliferating lymphocytes. Pharmacokinetically, mitoxantrone is administered intravenously, exhibits extensive tissue distribution and high protein/tissue binding, has a large volume of distribution, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated slowly mainly via biliary/fecal routes with minor renal excretion, yielding a prolonged terminal half-life. Major toxicities include dose-dependent myelosuppression, cumulative cardiotoxicity with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction or heart failure, mucositis, hepatotoxicity, and therapy-related acute myeloid leukemia. Common adverse effects include neutropenia, infection risk, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, alopecia, fatigue, amenorrhea, blue-green urine or scleral discoloration, and infusion-related reactions. Clinically, it is used in acute myeloid leukemia, hormone-refractory or metastatic prostate cancer, and worsening relapsing or secondary progressive multiple sclerosis, where it is employed for cytoreduction or immunosuppression in carefully selected patients.

Name: Lomustine
Description: Lomustine (DrugBank DB01206) is a highly lipophilic nitrosourea alkylating agent whose structure consists of a 2-chloroethyl group and a nitrosourea pharmacophore attached to a cyclohexyl-substituted nitrogen, giving a small, neutral, nonpolar molecule able to cross the blood-brain barrier efficiently. Chemically it belongs to the N-nitrosourea class of antineoplastic alkylators, with a chloroethylnitrosourea scaffold; closely related drugs include carmustine, semustine, fotemustine, and streptozocin, which share DNA-reactive nitrosourea chemistry but differ in substituents and tissue distribution. Lomustine is administered orally and is well absorbed, undergoes extensive first-pass and systemic hepatic microsomal metabolism to reactive intermediates, distributes widely including into CNS tissue, and is eliminated mainly as urinary metabolites with a relatively short parent-plasma half-life but prolonged biologic effects because active species form covalent adducts. Its pharmacologic action is largely non-target-based: spontaneous and metabolic decomposition generates chloroethyl carbonium and isocyanate species that alkylate DNA at O6-guanine and other sites, causing interstrand crosslinks, strand damage, and carbamoylation of proteins; resistance is associated with O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase. Major toxicities include delayed, cumulative myelosuppression with thrombocytopenia and leukopenia, pulmonary fibrosis, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, infertility, mutagenicity, teratogenicity, and secondary leukemia risk. Known biologically relevant target proteins are therefore indirect, principally DNA and repair determinants such as MGMT rather than a single receptor. Clinically, lomustine is used for primary and recurrent brain tumors including glioblastoma and other high-grade gliomas, and for Hodgkin lymphoma in combination regimens; common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, stomatitis, anorexia, fatigue, and delayed bone marrow suppression, and its practical use emphasizes intermittent oral dosing with prolonged blood count monitoring.

Name: Sparfloxacin
Description: Sparfloxacin (DrugBank DB01208) is a synthetic fluoroquinolone antibacterial built on the 4-quinolone-3-carboxylic acid scaffold, specifically a difluorinated quinolone bearing the canonical 4-oxo and 3-carboxyl pharmacophore, a 6-fluoro substituent that enhances antibacterial potency, a 7-piperazinyl ring that broadens Gram-negative activity, and a 5-amino group that contributes to its distinctive spectrum and safety liabilities; chemically it belongs to the quinolone/fluoroquinolone class and is closely related to other DNA gyrase/topoisomerase inhibitors such as ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin, levofloxacin, lomefloxacin, and moxifloxacin. Its principal targets are bacterial DNA gyrase (gyrA/gyrB) and topoisomerase IV (parC/parE), producing concentration-dependent inhibition of DNA replication and transcription. Sparfloxacin is orally absorbed with good bioavailability, reaches wide tissue distribution including respiratory tissues, has relatively low protein binding, undergoes limited hepatic biotransformation, and is eliminated by both renal and biliary/fecal routes, with a comparatively long elimination half-life that supports once-daily dosing. It was used mainly for community-acquired respiratory infections such as pneumonia, acute bacterial exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, and sinusitis, particularly when susceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, or Chlamydia pneumoniae were suspected. Important toxicities include QT-interval prolongation with risk of torsades de pointes, phototoxicity/photosensitivity, hepatotoxicity, CNS effects, and class-associated tendinopathy; common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, headache, dizziness, insomnia, rash, and heightened sun sensitivity. Clinically, its use became restricted or discontinued in many settings because proarrhythmic and phototoxic risks often outweighed its utility despite favorable respiratory pharmacokinetics and broad antibacterial coverage.

Name: Dezocine
Description: Dezocine (DB01209) is a semisynthetic opioid analgesic with a rigid morphinan/benzomorphan-like polycyclic framework characterized by a fused aromatic-cycloalkane tertiary amine scaffold and a phenolic hydroxyl substituent, placing it within the opioid alkaloid-derived analgesic class and more specifically the morphinan family. Its core scaffold is closely related to pentazocine and other mixed opioid ligands, and it is also structurally and pharmacologically comparable in part to buprenorphine, butorphanol, and nalbuphine, while differing from classic pure mu agonists such as morphine. Dezocine primarily targets the mu-opioid receptor and kappa-opioid receptor, with reported activity as a partial mu agonist/antagonist and kappa antagonist or weak partial agonist depending on assay system; opioid receptor signaling underlies its analgesic effects. It is indicated for moderate to severe pain, especially postoperative pain, perioperative analgesia, and obstetric or trauma-related pain in some settings. After parenteral administration it has rapid onset, broad tissue distribution including CNS penetration, substantial hepatic metabolism likely involving conjugative and oxidative pathways, and renal excretion of metabolites with some unchanged drug; clinically its duration is intermediate and protein binding is moderate to high. Toxicities are those of opioids, including dose-related respiratory depression, excessive sedation, hypotension, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, and impaired psychomotor function; overdose may cause coma or ventilatory failure, though some studies suggest a ceiling effect on respiratory depression relative to full mu agonists. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, sweating, dry mouth, constipation, headache, and injection-site reactions. Clinically, dezocine has been used as an injectable analgesic and peri-anesthetic adjunct when effective pain control with potentially reduced abuse liability or less severe respiratory suppression than traditional opioids is desired.

Name: Levobunolol
Description: Levobunolol (DrugBank DB01210) is a nonselective beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist of the aryloxypropanolamine class, structurally characterized by a lipophilic aromatic naphthalenone-derived ring system linked through an ether to a propanolamine side chain bearing a secondary alcohol and isopropylamino substituent; its core scaffold is the classic beta-blocker aryloxypropanolamine pharmacophore fused to a tetrahydronaphthalenone framework. Chemically, it is closely related to other ophthalmic nonselective beta-blockers such as timolol, carteolol, metipranolol, and betaxolol, although betaxolol is relatively beta1-selective. Its principal targets are the beta-1 adrenergic receptor and beta-2 adrenergic receptor, with ocular hypotensive activity mediated by reduced aqueous humor production in the ciliary body. Levobunolol is used primarily as a topical ophthalmic agent for open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension, including chronic elevation of intraocular pressure requiring long-term pressure control. After ocular administration, systemic absorption can occur through conjunctival and nasolacrimal routes; distribution includes ocular tissues and limited systemic exposure sufficient to produce beta-blockade, metabolism occurs largely in the liver with formation of the active metabolite dihydrolevobunolol, and elimination is mainly renal as metabolites and drug-related material. Toxicity reflects systemic beta-blockade and excessive local exposure, with examples including bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm, heart block, worsening heart failure, and CNS fatigue, while ocular adverse effects include transient burning, stinging, irritation, blurred vision, dry eye, and reduced corneal sensitivity. Clinically, it is used as eye drops once or twice daily, particularly in patients needing effective intraocular pressure lowering when prostaglandin analogs are unsuitable or as adjunctive therapy.

Name: Clarithromycin
Description: Clarithromycin (DrugBank DB01211) is a semisynthetic 14-membered macrolide antibiotic derived from erythromycin, distinguished structurally by a large lactone ring bearing two deoxy sugars, desosamine and cladinose, with a 6-O-methyl substitution that improves acid stability and oral bioavailability; chemically it belongs to the macrolide polyketide class and is built on the erythromycin/macrolactone scaffold. Closely related drugs include erythromycin, azithromycin, roxithromycin, and telithromycin, which share ribosome-targeting antibacterial activity. Its principal target is the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit, especially 23S rRNA within the peptidyl transferase/exit tunnel region, where it inhibits translocation and protein synthesis. Clarithromycin is well absorbed orally, distributes extensively into respiratory tissues, tonsils, skin, and macrophages, has moderate plasma protein binding, and undergoes hepatic CYP3A-mediated metabolism to the active metabolite 14-hydroxyclarithromycin; elimination occurs through both biliary/fecal and renal pathways, with dose adjustment often needed in renal impairment. It is indicated for community-acquired respiratory infections such as pneumonia, acute bacterial sinusitis, pharyngitis, and bronchitis, for skin and soft-tissue infections, and in combination regimens for Helicobacter pylori eradication and treatment or prophylaxis of Mycobacterium avium complex. Toxicities include hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation with torsades risk, reversible hearing loss, and important CYP3A4-mediated drug interactions that can raise concentrations of statins, antiarrhythmics, or ergot derivatives. Common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, dysgeusia, and headache, and clinically it is widely used as an oral or intravenous macrolide when atypical pathogen coverage or H. pylori-directed combination therapy is desired.

Name: Ceftriaxone
Description: Ceftriaxone (DrugBank DB01212) is a third-generation cephalosporin, a semisynthetic beta-lactam antibacterial built on the cephem/7-aminocephalosporanic acid scaffold consisting of a fused beta-lactam and dihydrothiazine ring, with a 7-position aminothiazolyl-oxime side chain that enhances Gram-negative stability to many beta-lactamases and a 3-position thiotriazinedione-derived substituent that contributes to prolonged elimination; chemically it is a broad-spectrum oxyimino-cephalosporin within the beta-lactam class. Structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include cefotaxime, ceftazidime, cefixime, and cefepime. Its antibacterial action results from binding bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, particularly transpeptidases such as PBP1, PBP2, and PBP3, thereby inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-linking and cell wall synthesis. Ceftriaxone is not orally absorbed and is given IV or IM, has high but saturable albumin binding, distributes well into lung, bone, urine, bile, and inflamed meninges, achieves therapeutically useful CSF concentrations in meningitis, undergoes minimal metabolism, and is eliminated by both renal and biliary routes with a relatively long half-life that supports once-daily dosing. It is indicated for susceptible infections including community-acquired pneumonia, sepsis, meningitis, gonorrhea, pelvic inflammatory disease, pyelonephritis, intra-abdominal infection, skin and soft-tissue infection, bone and joint infection, and Lyme neuroborreliosis. Toxicities include hypersensitivity reactions up to anaphylaxis, biliary sludging or pseudolithiasis, cholestatic effects, diarrhea including Clostridioides difficile colitis, hematologic abnormalities such as eosinophilia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, and rare neurotoxicity or seizures, with clinically important calcium-ceftriaxone precipitation risk in neonates. Common adverse effects include injection-site pain, rash, nausea, diarrhea, and transaminase elevation. Clinically, it is widely used empirically and definitively for serious hospital and community infections, often in combination regimens such as with vancomycin for meningitis or with metronidazole for intra-abdominal se

Name: Fomepizole
Description: Fomepizole (4-methylpyrazole; DrugBank DB01213) is a small, heteroaromatic azole composed of a five-membered pyrazole ring bearing two adjacent nitrogens and a methyl substituent at the 4-position, making it a simple substituted pyrazole and classifiable within nitrogen-containing heterocyclic antidotes; its core chemical scaffold is the methylated pyrazole ring, a motif shared in part with other azole-like alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitors, although close therapeutic analogs are limited, with ethanol being the classic mechanistically similar comparator used historically for toxic alcohol poisoning and pyrazole derivatives such as pyrazole itself representing chemical relatives. Its principal target is alcohol dehydrogenase, especially hepatic ADH1 isoenzymes, which it inhibits competitively to prevent conversion of methanol to formic acid and ethylene glycol to glycolate, glyoxylate, and oxalate. Clinically, it is indicated for methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning, including patients presenting with metabolic acidosis, visual toxicity risk, nephrotoxicity risk, or elevated osmolar gap, and it is used with supportive care, bicarbonate, folinic/folic acid in methanol poisoning, thiamine or pyridoxine in ethylene glycol poisoning, and sometimes hemodialysis. Pharmacokinetically, it is well absorbed intravenously, distributes largely in total body water with low protein binding, undergoes hepatic metabolism predominantly via CYP2E1 to inactive metabolites, can induce its own clearance with repeated dosing, and is eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites, with removal increased during dialysis. Toxicity is generally modest compared with the poisoned substrates but includes headache, nausea, dizziness, somnolence, metallic taste, infusion-site reactions, transient transaminase elevation, rash, fever, eosinophilia, and rarely bradycardia or seizures; overdose may cause excessive CNS effects, but the major clinical toxicology relevance is mitigation of toxic alcohol metabolism rather than intrinsic severe organ toxicity.

Name: Metipranolol
Description: Metipranolol (DrugBank DB01214) is a nonselective beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist of the aryloxypropanolamine class, structurally characterized by the classic beta-blocker pharmacophore consisting of a lipophilic aromatic ring linked through an ether bond to a secondary alcohol–propylamine side chain; its scaffold is a substituted phenoxypropanolamine closely related to other ophthalmic beta blockers. Chemically, it belongs to the alkanolamine/aryloxypropanolamine beta-blocker family, and similar drugs include timolol, levobunolol, propranolol, carteolol, and betaxolol, with timolol and levobunolol being especially relevant ophthalmic comparators. Its principal targets are beta-1 adrenergic receptor and beta-2 adrenergic receptor, with ocular hypotensive activity mediated by blockade of ciliary body beta receptors and reduced aqueous humor production. After topical ocular administration, systemic absorption can occur via conjunctival and nasolacrimal routes; distribution is sufficient to produce occasional systemic beta-blockade, hepatic metabolism contributes to clearance, and excretion occurs primarily as metabolites in urine, although ophthalmic dosing limits overall exposure relative to oral beta blockers. It is indicated mainly for lowering elevated intraocular pressure in open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension. Clinical use has historically involved ophthalmic drops for chronic glaucoma management, often as monotherapy or adjunctive therapy. Adverse effects include ocular irritation, burning, blurred vision, lacrimation, conjunctival hyperemia, and reduced corneal sensitivity, while systemic effects may include bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm, fatigue, and depression. Toxicity resembles that of other nonselective beta blockers, with overdose or susceptible patients at risk for severe bradyarrhythmia, heart block, bronchoconstriction, and worsening heart failure; notably, metipranolol has also been associated with anterior uveitis in some patients.

Name: Finasteride
Description: Finasteride (DrugBank DB01216) is a synthetic 4-azasteroid built on the androstane steroid nucleus, characterized by a fused tetracyclic hydrophobic scaffold with a 4-aza substitution in the A ring and a carboxamide-containing side chain that confers potent enzyme inhibition; chemically it is classified as a steroidal 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor, with an azasteroid scaffold closely related to other antiandrogenic enzyme inhibitors such as dutasteride and, more distantly, epristeride. Its principal targets are steroid 5-alpha-reductase type 2 (SRD5A2) and, with lower affinity, type 1 (SRD5A1), thereby reducing conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone in prostate, scalp, and other androgen-responsive tissues. After oral administration, finasteride is well absorbed with good bioavailability, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, is substantially protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 to less active metabolites, and is eliminated through both urine and feces with a terminal half-life of roughly 5 to 8 hours in younger adults and longer in the elderly. It is indicated for benign prostatic hyperplasia and androgenetic alopecia, with clinical use including reduction of prostate volume, improvement of urinary flow and lower urinary tract symptoms, and treatment of male pattern hair loss. Toxicity is generally low at therapeutic doses but includes teratogenic risk to a male fetus from exposure in pregnancy, rare hypersensitivity reactions, possible hepatic adverse effects, and overdose is usually not associated with severe acute toxicity. Common adverse effects include decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, ejaculatory disorder, reduced semen volume, gynecomastia, breast tenderness, mood changes including depression, and occasional persistent sexual dysfunction after discontinuation.

Name: Anastrozole
Description: Anastrozole (DrugBank DB01217) is a nonsteroidal triazole aromatase inhibitor whose structure is centered on a 1,2,4-triazole ring linked to a bis-nitrile-substituted, branched aromatic framework, giving a compact lipophilic azole-containing architecture optimized for heme iron coordination within aromatase; chemically it is classified as a nitrogen-containing heteroaromatic endocrine agent, with a diaryl/triazole-rich azole scaffold related to other third-generation aromatase inhibitors such as letrozole and, more distantly by mechanism, exemestane. Its principal target is aromatase, the cytochrome P450 enzyme CYP19A1, which catalyzes peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogens; inhibition markedly lowers estradiol concentrations and underlies its use in hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, especially adjuvant treatment of postmenopausal early-stage disease, first-line or subsequent therapy for advanced or metastatic estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer, and occasionally ovulation induction in infertility settings. Orally administered anastrozole is well absorbed, has high bioavailability, reaches peak concentrations within a few hours, distributes widely with moderate protein binding, undergoes hepatic metabolism mainly by N-dealkylation, hydroxylation, and glucuronidation involving CYP3A4, CYP2C8, and UGT pathways, and is eliminated primarily in urine as metabolites with an elimination half-life of about 40-50 hours permitting once-daily dosing. Toxicity is dominated by estrogen depletion, with clinically important bone mineral loss, osteoporosis, arthralgia, myalgia, vasomotor symptoms, vaginal dryness, and possible hypercholesterolemia; less common adverse effects include hepatotoxicity, rash, nausea, fatigue, headache, mood changes, and rarely ischemic cardiovascular events, while overdose experience suggests no distinctive acute toxidrome beyond exacerbation of these effects.

Name: Halofantrine
Description: Halofantrine (DrugBank DB01218) is a synthetic phenanthrene-methanol antimalarial whose structure is defined by a rigid tricyclic phenanthrene aromatic core bearing a benzylic secondary alcohol side chain and a piperidine-containing aminoalkyl substituent, with lipophilic halogenated aryl features that drive high membrane partitioning; chemically it belongs to the aryl amino alcohol/phenanthrene methanol class, and its key scaffold is the phenanthrene-methanol framework, making it structurally and pharmacologically related to quinoline- or aryl-amino alcohol antimalarials such as quinine, mefloquine, and lumefantrine. It is active primarily against erythrocytic Plasmodium falciparum and also P. vivax, including some chloroquine-resistant infections, and is used for treatment of acute uncomplicated malaria rather than prophylaxis. Its antimalarial mechanism is not completely resolved but is generally linked to interference with parasite heme detoxification in the food vacuole; no single validated human target protein is central to efficacy, although cardiac hERG/KCNH2 potassium channels are clinically important off-targets underlying toxicity. Oral absorption is variable and markedly increased by fatty meals, distribution is extensive because of high lipophilicity and protein binding, hepatic metabolism occurs mainly via CYP3A4 to the active metabolite desbutylhalofantrine, and elimination is slow, predominantly biliary/fecal with a long terminal half-life. The major toxicity is dose-related cardiotoxicity, especially QT prolongation, ventricular arrhythmias, torsades de pointes, and sudden death, with risk increased by food, preexisting heart disease, electrolyte disturbance, or coadministration of QT-prolonging or CYP3A4-interacting drugs. Common adverse effects include abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, pruritus, rash, and palpitations; clinically, its use became highly restricted because safer alternatives such as artemisinin-based combinations are preferred.

Name: Dantrolene
Description: Dantrolene (DrugBank DB01219) is a direct-acting skeletal muscle relaxant with a substituted hydantoin structure, consisting of a 2,4-imidazolidinedione core linked through a hydrazone-like methylene bridge to a nitrophenyl-furan aromatic system; chemically it is classified as a hydantoin derivative and more specifically a nitrophenyl furfurylidene-imidazolidinedione, with a hydantoin scaffold serving as its defining chemotype. It is structurally related in broad class terms to other hydantoin-containing drugs such as phenytoin, although its pharmacology is distinct, and it is functionally similar to antispastic or anti-hyperthermic agents such as baclofen, tizanidine, and diazepam despite different scaffolds. Its principal target is the skeletal muscle ryanodine receptor calcium-release channel RyR1, with inhibition of sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release reducing excitation-contraction coupling; RyR3 is also reported as a lesser target. Oral absorption is variable and incomplete, peak concentrations occurring within hours, with substantial tissue distribution, hepatic metabolism likely involving oxidative and reductive biotransformation, and predominantly urinary excretion of metabolites with a relatively long elimination half-life that supports repeated dosing. Major toxicities include dose-related hepatotoxicity, occasionally severe or fatal, as well as muscle weakness and respiratory compromise in susceptible patients; overdose may produce profound weakness, CNS depression, and dysphagia. Adverse effects commonly include drowsiness, dizziness, fatigue, diarrhea, nausea, and generalized weakness. Clinically, dantrolene is indicated for malignant hyperthermia treatment and prophylaxis and for chronic spasticity associated with upper motor neuron disorders such as multiple sclerosis, cerebral palsy, stroke, and spinal cord injury, and it is also used in neuroleptic malignant syndrome and severe hypermetabolic rigidity states.

Name: Rifaximin
Description: Rifaximin (DrugBank DB01220) is a semisynthetic rifamycin antibiotic whose structure consists of the characteristic rifamycin ansa scaffold: a naphthohydroquinone or naphthalene-like aromatic core bridged by a long aliphatic ansa chain rich in hydroxyl, acetyl, and ether functionalities, with an imidazole-derived modification that increases chemical stability and maintains very low systemic absorption; chemically, it is classified as an ansamycin, specifically a rifamycin derivative, and is closely related to rifampin, rifabutin, rifapentine, and rifalazil. Its principal target is bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, binding the beta subunit encoded by rpoB and thereby inhibiting transcription initiation. Pharmacokinetically, rifaximin is minimally absorbed after oral administration, remains largely confined to the gastrointestinal lumen, exhibits negligible distribution to systemic tissues under normal conditions, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism with minor deacetylation, and is excreted predominantly unchanged in feces, with systemic exposure increasing somewhat in severe mucosal inflammation or hepatic impairment. Toxicity is generally low because of poor absorption, but examples include hypersensitivity reactions, C. difficile-associated colitis despite antibacterial use, and rare systemic rifamycin-like effects when absorption rises. It is indicated for travelers’ diarrhea caused by noninvasive Escherichia coli, reduction of recurrence of overt hepatic encephalopathy, and irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea; it is also used in some settings for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth. Common adverse effects include nausea, abdominal pain, flatulence, constipation, headache, peripheral edema, dizziness, and sometimes elevated liver enzymes. Clinically, it is valued as a gut-selective oral antimicrobial for luminal intestinal infections and microbiota-modulating therapy where broad local antibacterial activity with limited systemic exposure is desirable.

Name: Budesonide
Description: Budesonide (DrugBank DB01222) is a potent synthetic corticosteroid built on the pregnane steroid nucleus, specifically a glucocorticoid scaffold featuring the characteristic four fused rings, a 1,4-diene-3-ketone A-ring, 11β- and 21-hydroxyl groups, and a distinctive 16α,17α-butylidene acetal that increases topical anti-inflammatory activity and first-pass inactivation; it is therefore classified as a nonhalogenated corticosteroid and more specifically an inhaled, intranasal, and locally acting glucocorticoid. Structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include beclomethasone, fluticasone, mometasone, prednisolone, and hydrocortisone. Its primary target is the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, through which it modulates transcription of anti-inflammatory proteins and suppresses proinflammatory cytokines, with downstream effects on NF-κB- and AP-1-regulated pathways. Budesonide has route-dependent absorption: inhaled and intranasal drug is partly absorbed systemically, oral controlled-release preparations are absorbed in the intestine, and rectal formulations act largely locally; distribution includes substantial tissue uptake and high plasma protein binding. It undergoes extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism, mainly by CYP3A4, to metabolites with much lower glucocorticoid activity, and is excreted predominantly in urine as metabolites, with minor fecal elimination. Clinically it is used for asthma maintenance, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in combination products, allergic rhinitis, eosinophilic esophagitis, and inflammatory bowel diseases such as mild to moderate Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis. Adverse effects include oral candidiasis, dysphonia, cough, epistaxis, headache, nausea, and dyspepsia, while toxicities with high-dose or prolonged exposure include adrenal suppression, hypercortisolism, reduced bone density, cataracts, glaucoma, growth suppression in children, infection risk, and CYP3A4 inhibitor-mediated increases in systemic steroid exposure.

Name: Aminophylline
Description: Aminophylline (DrugBank DB01223) is a salt-like complex of the methylxanthine theophylline with ethylenediamine, formulated to improve aqueous solubility for parenteral and oral use; structurally, the active pharmacophore is theophylline, a planar purine-like xanthine nucleus bearing 1,3-dimethyl substitution on the imidazo-pyrimidinedione scaffold, so it is classified chemically as a methylxanthine bronchodilator and adenosine-antagonist/phosphodiesterase-inhibitor scaffold. Closely related drugs include theophylline, caffeine, dyphylline, and doxofylline, which share the xanthine core but differ in substitution and pharmacologic tolerability. Its principal targets are nonselective phosphodiesterases, especially PDE3 and PDE4, and adenosine receptors such as ADORA1, ADORA2A, ADORA2B, and ADORA3, producing bronchodilation, mild anti-inflammatory effects, and respiratory stimulant activity. Aminophylline is indicated for reversible airflow obstruction, particularly acute or chronic asthma, COPD with bronchospasm, and occasionally apnea of prematurity via theophylline exposure. It is usually well absorbed orally, distributes into total body water with modest protein binding, crosses the placenta and enters breast milk, is hepatically metabolized mainly by CYP1A2 with contributions from CYP2E1 and CYP3A4, and is excreted primarily as metabolites in urine; clearance varies with age, smoking, heart failure, liver disease, fever, and drug interactions, giving it a narrow therapeutic index. Toxicity is dose related and includes nausea, vomiting, tremor, insomnia, reflux, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, tachycardia, atrial or ventricular arrhythmias, and seizures, with severe overdose causing life-threatening neurocardiac toxicity. Clinically, aminophylline has been used intravenously for acute severe bronchospasm and orally as a second-line maintenance bronchodilator when inhaled therapies are inadequate or unavailable.

Name: Quetiapine
Description: Quetiapine (DrugBank DB01224) is a dibenzothiazepine-derived second-generation atypical antipsychotic whose structure consists of a tricyclic dibenzothiazepine core linked through a piperazine ring to a terminal 2-ethoxyethanol side chain, giving an amphiphilic, polyheterocyclic architecture typical of serotonin-dopamine antagonists; chemically it is categorized as a tricyclic antipsychotic and more specifically a dibenzothiazepine/piperazinyl ethanol derivative, with a scaffold closely related to clozapine-like multi-receptor ligands, and similar drugs include clozapine, olanzapine, risperidone, ziprasidone, and the active metabolite-related agent norquetiapine. It is well absorbed orally but undergoes substantial first-pass metabolism, is highly protein bound and widely distributed including CNS penetration, is extensively metabolized in the liver mainly by CYP3A4 to inactive and active metabolites including norquetiapine, and is excreted predominantly as metabolites in urine with lesser fecal elimination; its principal targets include DRD2, HTR2A, HTR1A, H1, ADRA1, ADRA2, CHRM1, and SLC6A2 via norquetiapine, explaining antipsychotic, sedative, and antidepressant properties. It is indicated for schizophrenia, acute manic and depressive episodes in bipolar disorder, maintenance bipolar therapy adjunctively, and major depressive disorder as adjunct treatment. Adverse effects commonly include somnolence, dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, dry mouth, constipation, tachycardia, weight gain, dyslipidemia, and hyperglycemia; important toxicities include overdose-related CNS depression, QT prolongation, seizures, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, tardive dyskinesia, and metabolic syndrome. Clinically, it is used across inpatient and outpatient psychiatry for psychosis, bipolar agitation or depression, and adjunctive treatment of treatment-resistant depressive symptoms.

Name: Levacetylmethadol
Description: Levacetylmethadol (LAAM; DrugBank DB01227) is a synthetic diphenylheptane opioid characterized structurally by a methadone-like flexible heptanone backbone bearing two aryl rings, a tertiary dimethylamino substituent, and an acetoxy group; chemically it belongs to the methadone/diphenylpropylamine-related opioid analgesic class, with a diphenylheptane scaffold closely related to methadone and congeners such as methadone itself, dextromoramide, and other long-acting mu-opioid receptor agonists. Its principal target is the mu-opioid receptor (OPRM1), through which it suppresses opioid withdrawal and reduces craving, with possible lesser activity at other opioid receptors of limited clinical importance. Pharmacokinetically, levacetylmethadol is well absorbed orally, extensively distributed into tissues because of high lipophilicity, and undergoes hepatic N-demethylation mainly via CYP3A4, CYP2B6, and CYP2D6 to active metabolites including nor-LAAM and dinor-LAAM, which prolong its effect; elimination is slow, occurring through hepatic metabolism with excretion of metabolites in urine and feces, supporting dosing less frequent than methadone. It was indicated for maintenance treatment of opioid dependence, particularly heroin use disorder, in supervised substitution programs. Its major toxicities are opioid-related respiratory depression, overdose, sedation, and dependence, but the most important serious example is QT interval prolongation with torsades de pointes and sudden death risk, especially with high doses, electrolyte abnormalities, or interacting QT-prolonging/CYP-inhibiting drugs. Common adverse effects include constipation, sweating, nausea, dizziness, somnolence, and hypotension. Clinically, it was used as a long-acting maintenance agent when reduced clinic visit frequency was desired, but its use became highly restricted or withdrawn in many settings because cardiac toxicity outweighed benefit.

Name: Encainide
Description: Encainide (DB01228) is a synthetic class Ic antiarrhythmic whose structure is characterized by a lipophilic aromatic amide/ester-like framework built around substituted anisidine- and benzamide-related aryl groups linked through a chiral amino alcohol side chain, giving a basic tertiary amine that is protonated at physiologic pH and supports high-affinity sodium-channel blockade; chemically it is best categorized as a phenylbenzamide-type membrane-active antiarrhythmic, with an anilide/aminoalcohol scaffold related in function, though not identical, to other class I agents such as flecainide, propafenone, moricizine, procainamide, and quinidine. Its principal targets are the cardiac fast voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.5 encoded by SCN5A, with consequent marked slowing of phase 0 depolarization and conduction in atrial, ventricular, and His-Purkinje tissue. Encainide was used for symptomatic ventricular arrhythmias, especially frequent premature ventricular complexes, nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, and other serious ventricular ectopy. It is well absorbed orally, undergoes substantial hepatic metabolism to active metabolites including O-demethylated derivatives, exhibits moderate protein binding and broad tissue distribution, and is eliminated through combined renal excretion of metabolites and parent drug plus biliary/fecal routes; accumulation may occur in hepatic or renal impairment.
