Toxicity is dominated by dose-related and exposure-related proarrhythmia, including QRS widening, heart block, worsening ventricular tachyarrhythmias, and excess mortality after myocardial infarction as highlighted by the CAST experience; noncardiac adverse effects include dizziness, visual disturbance, nausea, tremor, and hypotension. Clinically, it was reserved for refractory, potentially life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias under ECG monitoring, but its use became largely obsolete because safer alternatives are preferred.

Name: Paclitaxel
Description: Paclitaxel (DrugBank DB01229) is a complex, highly oxygenated diterpenoid natural product of the taxane class, characterized by a rigid tricyclic/bicyclic taxane core bearing multiple hydroxyl and ester functionalities, an essential oxetane ring, and a distinctive C13 side chain containing an N-benzoyl-3-phenylisoserine moiety; chemically it is an antimitotic taxoid and its core scaffold is the 6-8-6 fused taxane framework. Closely related or similar drugs include docetaxel, cabazitaxel, and albumin-bound paclitaxel formulations, as well as other microtubule-targeting agents such as ixabepilone by mechanistic analogy. Its principal targets are beta-tubulin isoforms within microtubules, including TUBB, TUBB2A, TUBB3, and related tubulin heterodimers, where it stabilizes polymerized microtubules, suppresses depolymerization, and induces mitotic arrest and apoptosis. Pharmacokinetically, paclitaxel is administered intravenously because of very poor oral bioavailability, displays extensive tissue distribution and high protein binding, undergoes primarily hepatic CYP2C8- and CYP3A4-mediated metabolism to hydroxylated metabolites such as 6-alpha-hydroxypaclitaxel, and is eliminated mainly by biliary/fecal excretion with nonlinear disposition at some dose ranges. Major toxicities include dose-limiting myelosuppression, especially neutropenia, peripheral sensory neuropathy, hypersensitivity reactions related to formulation vehicle, mucositis, hepatotoxicity, and less commonly bradyarrhythmias. Adverse effects commonly include alopecia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fatigue, arthralgia, myalgia, and nail changes. Clinically, paclitaxel is used for ovarian cancer, breast cancer, non-small cell lung cancer, AIDS-related Kaposi sarcoma, and in some regimens for head and neck, esophageal, endometrial, and bladder cancers, often in combination with platinum agents or trastuzumab-containing protocols.

Name: Pemoline
Description: Pemoline (DrugBank DB01230) is a central nervous system stimulant of the oxazolidinedione class, structurally defined by a 2,4-oxazolidinedione ring bearing a 5-phenyl substituent, giving a compact heterocyclic imide scaffold that is closely related to other diphenyl- or aryl-substituted stimulant chemotypes but distinct from amphetamine; its core scaffold is therefore a phenyl-substituted oxazolidinedione, and similar drugs discussed historically include methylphenidate, dextroamphetamine, methamphetamine, and modafinil as clinically comparable wakefulness- or attention-promoting agents rather than close structural analogs. Pemoline was used primarily for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and has also been employed in narcolepsy, fatigue, and occasionally refractory daytime somnolence. Its mechanism was not fully resolved, but pharmacologically it appears to enhance dopaminergic and possibly noradrenergic signaling, with weak interaction reported at the dopamine transporter and indirect effects on catecholamine transmission rather than a single well-validated high-affinity target protein. Orally administered pemoline is well absorbed, distributes into the CNS, undergoes limited hepatic biotransformation relative to many stimulants, and is eliminated over a relatively long half-life that supports once-daily dosing, with urinary excretion of parent drug and metabolites. The major toxicological concern is idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity, including asymptomatic transaminase elevation, hepatitis, hepatic failure, and cases requiring transplantation or causing death; other adverse effects include insomnia, anorexia, irritability, headache, nausea, abdominal pain, tachycardia, and weight loss. Clinically, because of its delayed onset and serious liver risk, pemoline became a second-line or obsolete ADHD therapy and was withdrawn or severely restricted in many markets.

Name: Saquinavir
Description: Saquinavir (DrugBank DB01232) is a peptidomimetic HIV protease inhibitor built around a hydroxyethylamine/hydroxyethylamine-like transition-state mimic scaffold that reproduces the tetrahedral intermediate of peptide bond cleavage; structurally it is a large lipophilic, conformationally constrained pseudopeptide containing amide and carbamate functionalities, a decahydroisoquinoline-derived P1 moiety, and tert-butyl-rich hydrophobic substituents that optimize binding in the viral protease active site. Chemically it is classified as an antiretroviral protease inhibitor, with a non-natural peptidomimetic scaffold related to other first-generation HIV protease inhibitors such as ritonavir, indinavir, nelfinavir, amprenavir, fosamprenavir, and lopinavir. Its principal target is the HIV-1 protease, with activity also against HIV-2 protease, thereby blocking gag-pol polyprotein processing and preventing maturation of infectious virions. Saquinavir is indicated for treatment of HIV-1 infection in combination antiretroviral therapy, historically for symptomatic HIV disease, advanced immunodeficiency, and viral suppression regimens. Oral absorption is limited by poor bioavailability and extensive first-pass metabolism, food increases exposure, protein binding is high, distribution is wide but CNS penetration is modest, metabolism occurs predominantly via CYP3A4, and excretion is mainly biliary/fecal with minimal renal elimination; ritonavir boosting markedly raises plasma concentrations. Toxicities include hepatotoxicity, PR-interval and QT-interval prolongation, metabolic complications such as hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia, lipodystrophy, and potential drug-drug interactions from CYP3A substrates/inhibitors. Common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, headache, fatigue, and rash. Clinically, saquinavir has been used mainly as ritonavir-boosted saquinavir in combination regimens for HIV suppression, though its use declined because of pill burden, interaction liability, and cardiac safety concerns.

Name: Metoclopramide
Description: Metoclopramide (DrugBank DB01233) is a substituted benzamide antiemetic and gastroprokinetic whose structure is centered on a 4-amino-5-chloro-2-methoxy benzamide ring linked through the amide to a flexible 2-diethylaminoethyl side chain, giving an anisamide-like aromatic benzamide scaffold with a basic tertiary amine that supports receptor binding and CNS penetration; chemically it belongs to the benzamide dopamine antagonist class, and its core scaffold is closely related to other prokinetic/antiemetic benzamides such as procainamide analogs in broad motif terms and more directly to domperidone, bromopride, clebopride, levosulpiride, and sulpiride. Its principal targets are dopamine D2 receptors, with additional activity at serotonin 5-HT3 receptors as an antagonist and 5-HT4 receptors as a weak agonist, actions that enhance acetylcholine release in the enteric nervous system, increase lower esophageal sphincter tone, and accelerate gastric emptying. It is well absorbed orally, also used intravenously or intramuscularly, distributes widely including across the blood-brain barrier and placenta, undergoes hepatic metabolism mainly by conjugation and oxidative pathways, and is excreted predominantly in urine with an elimination half-life typically about 5 to 6 hours but prolonged in renal impairment. Indications include nausea and vomiting from postoperative states, migraine-associated emesis, chemotherapy exposure, diabetic gastroparesis, and symptomatic gastroesophageal reflux. Adverse effects commonly include drowsiness, fatigue, diarrhea, agitation, and restlessness, while major toxicities include acute dystonia, parkinsonism, akathisia, hyperprolactinemia, depression, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and tardive dyskinesia, especially with high dose or prolonged use; clinically it is used short term as an antiemetic and prokinetic, for example in refractory gastroparesis, facilitation of gastric emptying before procedures, and control of severe vomiting when central dopamine antagonism is desired.

Name: Dexamethasone
Description: Dexamethasone (DrugBank DB01234) is a synthetic fluorinated corticosteroid whose structure is based on the pregnane steroid nucleus with the classic four-ring cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene scaffold, distinguished by a 9α-fluoro substituent, 16α-methyl group, and hydroxyl/ketone functionality that confers very high glucocorticoid potency with negligible mineralocorticoid activity; chemically it is classified as a glucocorticoid corticosteroid and more specifically a fluorinated pregnane steroid, with close analogs and similar drugs including prednisone, prednisolone, methylprednisolone, hydrocortisone, betamethasone, and triamcinolone. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, with downstream transcriptional repression of NF-κB- and AP-1-mediated inflammatory signaling and reduced expression of cytokines, prostaglandins, and adhesion molecules. Pharmacokinetically, dexamethasone is well absorbed orally, is also used intravenously, intramuscularly, intra-articularly, and topically, is widely distributed including CNS and placental compartments, is substantially protein bound, is metabolized mainly hepatically by CYP3A4, and is excreted primarily in urine as metabolites; it has a relatively long biologic half-life. Toxicity reflects dose and duration and includes adrenal suppression, severe hyperglycemia, infection risk, myopathy, peptic ulceration, osteoporosis, psychiatric disturbance, cataracts, and glaucoma, with examples such as opportunistic infection or steroid-induced diabetes. Indications and clinical use are broad, including cerebral edema, severe allergy, asthma and COPD exacerbations, autoimmune and rheumatologic disease, inflammatory dermatoses, inflammatory bowel disease, antiemetic regimens in chemotherapy, croup, COVID-19 requiring oxygen, and hematologic malignancies such as multiple myeloma; common adverse effects include insomnia, mood change, fluid retention, hypertension, dyspepsia, weight gain, and immunosuppression.

Name: Levodopa
Description: Levodopa (L-DOPA; DrugBank DB01235) is a small-molecule aromatic amino acid composed of a catechol-substituted phenyl ring bearing a two-carbon amino acid side chain in the L-configuration, making it a 3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine derivative and the immediate biosynthetic precursor of dopamine; chemically it belongs to the catecholamines-related aromatic amino acid class, with a catechol phenethylamine/amino acid scaffold that is closely related to dopamine, methyldopa, carbidopa, benserazide-associated therapy, and other dopaminergic antiparkinsonian agents such as bromocriptine or pramipexole by functional similarity. Its principal pharmacologic relevance derives from transport by large neutral amino acid transporters and enzymatic conversion by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase/DDC to dopamine, with downstream action at dopamine receptors; key proteins in its disposition or effect include DDC, solute carrier transporters SLC7A5/SLC3A2 at the gut and blood-brain barrier, catechol-O-methyltransferase, monoamine oxidase A and B, and dopamine receptors indirectly stimulated after conversion. Orally, levodopa is absorbed mainly in the proximal small intestine by carrier-mediated uptake, competes with dietary amino acids, has variable bioavailability due to extensive first-pass peripheral decarboxylation, crosses the blood-brain barrier, is metabolized peripherally and centrally to dopamine and by COMT to 3-O-methyldopa, and is excreted predominantly in urine as metabolites. Toxicity is chiefly dose-related and dopaminergic, including nausea, vomiting, orthostatic hypotension, confusion, hallucinations, dyskinesias, arrhythmias, and rare severe psychosis; long-term motor fluctuations and peak-dose choreiform movements are classic examples. It is indicated primarily for Parkinson disease and parkinsonian syndromes, especially bradykinesia, rigidity, and tremor, and is used clinically most often in combination with peripheral decarboxylase inhibitors such as carbidopa to improve central delivery and reduce peripheral adverse effects.

Name: Bromodiphenhydramine
Description: Bromodiphenhydramine (DrugBank DB01237) is a first-generation ethanolamine antihistamine structurally characterized as a diaryl-substituted tertiary amino ether in which a benzhydryl-like lipophilic core bears brominated aromatic substitution and is linked through a short ethoxy spacer to a dimethylamino moiety; this places it within the arylalkylamine H1-antihistamine class and on the classic diphenhydramine-type ethanolamine scaffold. Similar drugs include diphenhydramine, dimenhydrinate, doxylamine, carbinoxamine, and clemastine, which share H1-receptor antagonism and anticholinergic/sedative liabilities. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, with clinically relevant off-target antagonism at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors and likely central sedative activity due to ready blood-brain barrier penetration. Pharmacokinetically, bromodiphenhydramine is expected to be well absorbed orally, widely distributed into highly perfused tissues including the CNS, substantially protein bound, hepatically metabolized mainly by oxidative N-dealkylation and related CYP-mediated biotransformations, and excreted predominantly in urine as metabolites with some unchanged drug. Toxicity resembles other first-generation antihistamines: dose-related CNS depression or paradoxical excitation, strong anticholinergic toxicity with mydriasis, dry mouth, urinary retention, tachycardia, constipation, delirium, and in overdose possible seizures, coma, and arrhythmias. It is indicated for symptomatic relief of allergic rhinitis, urticaria, pruritus, conjunctival irritation, and other histamine-mediated symptoms, and has been used clinically as an antipruritic, antiallergic, and sedating agent. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, impaired psychomotor performance, blurred vision, xerostomia, constipation, and urinary hesitancy, making it most suitable for short-term symptomatic treatment where nighttime sedation is not undesirable.

Name: Aripiprazole
Description: Aripiprazole (DrugBank DB01238) is a quinolinone-derived atypical antipsychotic whose structure features a 3,4-dihydroquinolin-2-one core linked through a butoxy chain to a piperazine ring bearing a 2,3-dichlorophenyl substituent, giving an amphiphilic arylpiperazine architecture typical of CNS dopamine-serotonin modulators; chemically it is classified as a quinolinone/aryl-piperazine antipsychotic, and its central scaffold is the butoxy-quinolinone–piperazine pharmacophore. Similar drugs include brexpiprazole and cariprazine as dopamine-serotonin partial agonist antipsychotics, and more distantly other atypical antipsychotics such as risperidone, quetiapine, and olanzapine. Its principal targets are dopamine D2 and D3 receptors and serotonin 5-HT1A and 5-HT2A receptors, with additional activity at 5-HT2C, 5-HT7, alpha1-adrenergic, and histamine H1 receptors; mechanistically it acts mainly as a D2/5-HT1A partial agonist and 5-HT2A antagonist. Oral bioavailability is high, absorption is good with peak levels in several hours, protein binding is extensive, distribution is wide, and metabolism occurs primarily via CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 to the active metabolite dehydroaripiprazole; elimination is slow, with a long half-life supporting once-daily dosing, and excretion occurs through urine and feces mainly as metabolites. Indications include schizophrenia, bipolar I disorder including manic or mixed episodes and maintenance, adjunctive treatment of major depressive disorder, irritability associated with autism spectrum disorder, and Tourette disorder. Adverse effects commonly include akathisia, insomnia, anxiety, nausea, constipation, headache, dizziness, and weight gain, while toxicity concerns include extrapyramidal symptoms, tardive dyskinesia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, impulse-control disorders, orthostatic hypotension, somnolence, seizures, metabolic disturbances, and increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis. Clinically it is used as oral tablets, orally disintegrating tablets, solution, and long-acting injectable formulations for chronic psychotic and mood disorders.

Name: Chlorprothixene
Description: Chlorprothixene (DrugBank DB01239) is a first-generation antipsychotic of the thioxanthene class, structurally characterized by a tricyclic dibenzothiopyran-like thioxanthene core in which sulfur and an exocyclic double bond replace key features of the phenothiazine framework, bearing a three-carbon side chain terminating in a dimethylaminopropyl substituent that confers basicity and dopamine-receptor affinity; thus its principal chemical scaffold is the thioxanthene tricyclic neuroleptic scaffold, and it is closely related to other typical antipsychotics such as chlorprothixene analogs thiothixene, flupentixol, clopenthixol, and phenothiazines such as chlorpromazine. Pharmacologically, it acts mainly through antagonism of dopamine D2 receptors, with additional activity at D1, 5-HT2A, histamine H1, alpha1-adrenergic, and muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, which explains both efficacy and adverse effects. It is used for schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders, particularly when agitation, anxiety, aggression, or insomnia are prominent, and has also been used as a sedative or adjunct in severe behavioral disturbance. After oral administration it is variably but adequately absorbed, undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, is highly protein bound and widely distributed including CNS penetration, is metabolized predominantly by hepatic oxidative pathways including CYP2D6-mediated biotransformation to multiple metabolites, and is excreted mainly as metabolites in urine and feces. Toxicity includes dose-related CNS depression, anticholinergic toxicity, orthostatic hypotension, QT prolongation, seizures, extrapyramidal reactions, tardive dyskinesia, and rare neuroleptic malignant syndrome; common side effects include sedation, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, dizziness, weight gain, sexual dysfunction, and hyperprolactinemia.

Name: Epoprostenol
Description: Epoprostenol (DB01240) is a synthetic version of prostacyclin, an endogenous prostaglandin of the eicosanoid family, characterized structurally by a highly oxygenated prostanoid framework with a substituted cyclopentane core, pendant aliphatic side chains, multiple hydroxyl groups, and a labile enol ether/unsaturated motif that underlies its marked chemical instability; chemically it is classified as a prostaglandin vasodilator and platelet aggregation inhibitor, with a prostacyclin prostanoid scaffold closely related to other prostanoid drugs such as iloprost, treprostinil, beraprost, and related PGI2 analogs. Its principal target is the prostacyclin IP receptor, encoded by PTGIR, activation of which stimulates adenylate cyclase, raises intracellular cAMP, relaxes vascular smooth muscle, and inhibits platelet aggregation. Because epoprostenol is not orally bioavailable and is rapidly hydrolyzed at physiologic pH, it is administered by continuous intravenous infusion; distribution is largely intravascular with rapid tissue access, metabolism occurs predominantly through spontaneous hydrolysis and enzymatic degradation to inactive metabolites rather than CYP-dependent pathways, and excretion is mainly renal as metabolites, with an extremely short elimination half-life of only minutes. Clinically it is used primarily for pulmonary arterial hypertension to improve exercise capacity, hemodynamics, and symptoms, and also during renal dialysis when heparin is contraindicated. Toxicity is largely an extension of pharmacology, including dose-related hypotension, flushing, headache, tachycardia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, jaw pain, and bleeding risk from platelet inhibition; serious examples include syncope, catheter-related bloodstream infection from chronic infusion systems, rebound pulmonary hypertension after abrupt interruption, and rarely pulmonary edema in patients with occult pulmonary veno-occlusive disease.

Name: Gemfibrozil
Description: Gemfibrozil (DrugBank DB01241) is an aryloxyisobutyric acid derivative of the fibrate class, structurally characterized by a dimethyl-substituted phenoxy ring linked through an ether bond to a branched aliphatic chain terminating in a carboxylic acid, giving it the classic phenoxyisobutyric acid/fibric acid scaffold associated with lipid-modifying activity. It is chemically categorized as a fibrate antihyperlipidemic and is closely related to other PPAR-alpha agonist drugs such as fenofibrate, bezafibrate, clofibrate, and to a lesser extent pemafibrate. Its principal pharmacologic target is peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha, with downstream effects on lipoprotein lipase expression, apolipoprotein C-III suppression, and enhanced catabolism of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins. Orally administered gemfibrozil is well absorbed, highly protein bound, distributed largely within plasma, extensively metabolized hepatically mainly by oxidation and glucuronidation, and eliminated predominantly in urine as metabolites with a relatively short half-life that supports twice-daily dosing. It is indicated for hypertriglyceridemia, mixed dyslipidemia, and prevention of pancreatitis risk in severe triglyceride elevation, and has been used clinically in patients with low HDL and elevated very low-density lipoproteins, such as type IV and type V hyperlipoproteinemia. Toxicities include hepatotoxicity, cholelithiasis from increased biliary cholesterol excretion, and myopathy or rhabdomyolysis, especially with statins such as simvastatin or repaglinide-related interaction risk via enzyme/transporter inhibition. Common adverse effects include dyspepsia, abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, rash, headache, dizziness, and liver enzyme elevation. In practice, gemfibrozil is used as an adjunct to diet and lifestyle modification when triglyceride lowering is the primary therapeutic goal.

Name: Clomipramine
Description: Clomipramine (DrugBank DB01242) is a chlorinated tricyclic antidepressant of the dibenzazepine class, structurally characterized by a rigid tricyclic aromatic ring system bearing a 3-chloro substituent and a three-carbon side chain terminating in a tertiary dimethylamine, giving it a classic lipophilic tricyclic antidepressant scaffold related to iminodibenzyl/dibenzazepine frameworks. It is closely related to other tricyclics, especially imipramine, and has pharmacologic similarity to amitriptyline, desipramine, and doxepin, while its potent serotonin reuptake inhibition also makes it mechanistically comparable to SSRIs such as fluoxetine in obsessive-compulsive disorder. Its principal targets are the serotonin transporter SLC6A4 and the norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, with additional antagonistic activity at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, histamine H1 receptors, and alpha1-adrenergic receptors, accounting for both efficacy and adverse effects. Oral absorption is good but subject to substantial first-pass metabolism; the drug is widely distributed, highly protein bound, penetrates the CNS, and is extensively metabolized hepatically, mainly by CYP2D6, CYP2C19, and CYP3A4, to active desmethylclomipramine, with elimination occurring largely as urinary metabolites. It is indicated primarily for obsessive-compulsive disorder and has also been used for major depressive disorder, panic symptoms, cataplexy in narcolepsy, and chronic pain states. Common adverse effects include dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, sedation, orthostatic hypotension, sweating, sexual dysfunction, weight gain, and tremor. Toxicity resembles other TCAs, including dose-related seizures, delirium, coma, serotonin toxicity, and potentially fatal cardiac conduction abnormalities and arrhythmias in overdose. Clinically, it is used when strong anti-obsessional or antidepressant efficacy is needed, particularly in severe OCD or refractory depressive and anxiety syndromes.

Name: Chloroxine
Description: Chloroxine (DrugBank DB01243) is a halogenated hydroxyquinoline antiseptic and topical anti-infective whose structure consists of a quinoline bicyclic aromatic scaffold bearing a phenolic hydroxyl group and multiple halogen substituents, classifying it within the 8-hydroxyquinoline family; its core chemical scaffold is therefore the metal-chelating 8-hydroxyquinoline nucleus, a privileged heteroaromatic motif also seen in related drugs such as clioquinol, iodoquinol, broxyquinoline, and other halogenated quinoline antimicrobials. Pharmacologically, chloroxine is used primarily as a topical antibacterial and antifungal agent, especially in seborrheic dermatitis, dandruff, eczema complicated by secondary infection, and other superficial dermatoses associated with itching, scaling, or microbial overgrowth; its mechanism is not fully defined but is thought to involve chelation of essential metal ions and disruption of microbial enzyme systems and membrane-associated processes rather than a single highly validated human protein target, so no definitive canonical target proteins are established. Because it is mainly administered topically, systemic pharmacokinetic data are limited; dermal absorption is generally low under normal conditions, distribution is expected to remain largely local, any absorbed fraction is likely hepatically metabolized by conjugative pathways, and elimination would be expected through renal and possibly biliary excretion. Toxicity is correspondingly low in routine topical use but can include local irritation, burning, erythema, dryness, contact dermatitis, and hypersensitivity; excessive application, damaged skin, or accidental ingestion could increase systemic exposure and raise concern for gastrointestinal upset or broader hydroxyquinoline-class neurotoxicity, although such events are uncommon. Clinically, chloroxine has been used in shampoos, creams, and lotions to reduce microbial burden and improve inflammatory scalp and skin symptoms.

Name: Alimemazine
Description: Alimemazine (trimeprazine; DrugBank DB01246) is a phenothiazine derivative built on a tricyclic phenothiazine scaffold containing fused benzene rings flanking sulfur and nitrogen in the central thiazine ring, with a three-carbon side chain at the ring nitrogen terminating in a tertiary dimethylamino moiety and a branched substituent that contributes strong antihistaminic and sedative properties; chemically it is classified as a first-generation H1 antihistamine within the broader phenothiazine family, and it is structurally and pharmacologically similar to promethazine, methdilazine, chlorpromazine, and other sedating phenothiazines. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, with additional clinically relevant antagonism at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, alpha1-adrenergic receptors, and likely serotonergic and dopaminergic receptors at higher exposures, explaining its sedative, antiemetic, antipruritic, and antitussive effects. After oral administration it is reasonably absorbed, undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, is widely distributed including into the central nervous system, is highly protein bound, and is cleared mainly by hepatic oxidative and conjugative biotransformation with metabolites excreted predominantly in urine and to a lesser extent bile/feces. It is used for pruritus, urticaria, allergic rhinitis, nighttime cough, insomnia associated with allergy, and premedication or pediatric sedation in some settings. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention; toxicities include profound CNS depression, hypotension, paradoxical agitation in children, anticholinergic delirium, lowered seizure threshold, respiratory depression, and rare QT prolongation or neuroleptic-like extrapyramidal reactions.

Name: Docetaxel
Description: Docetaxel (DrugBank DB01248) is a semisynthetic taxane antineoplastic agent derived from the taxoid nucleus of precursors from yew species and is structurally characterized by a highly oxygenated, rigid tetracyclic diterpenoid core bearing an oxetane ring, multiple ester and hydroxyl substituents, and a distinctive C13 side chain that enhances tubulin binding and differentiates it from paclitaxel. Chemically, it belongs to the taxane diterpenes, with the taxane/baccatin scaffold as its defining pharmacophore; closely related drugs include paclitaxel, cabazitaxel, and other microtubule-stabilizing taxoids. Its principal target is beta-tubulin within the microtubule polymer, encoded by TUBB and related beta-tubulin isoforms, leading to promotion of microtubule assembly, inhibition of depolymerization, mitotic arrest, and apoptosis. Pharmacokinetically, docetaxel is administered intravenously because oral bioavailability is poor, exhibits extensive tissue distribution and high plasma protein binding, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism via CYP3A4 and CYP3A5 to less active oxidized metabolites, and is eliminated mainly through biliary/fecal excretion with limited renal clearance. Major toxicities include dose-limiting neutropenia, febrile neutropenia, mucositis, severe fluid retention, hepatotoxicity, and hypersensitivity reactions, partly related to formulation excipients. Common adverse effects include alopecia, fatigue, diarrhea, nausea, stomatitis, peripheral neuropathy, nail changes, edema, and myelosuppression. Clinically, docetaxel is used in breast cancer, non-small cell lung cancer, castration-resistant prostate cancer, gastric adenocarcinoma, and head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, often in combination regimens such as with prednisone, platinum agents, trastuzumab, cyclophosphamide, or fluoropyrimidines.

Name: Olsalazine
Description: Olsalazine (DrugBank DB01250) is a dimeric 5-aminosalicylic acid prodrug composed of two salicylate-like aromatic rings linked by an azo bond, each ring bearing amino and carboxylic acid substituents, making it a bis-aryl azo compound in the aminosalicylate class with an azobenzene-like salicylic acid scaffold. It is structurally and pharmacologically related to other 5-ASA–delivering agents used in inflammatory bowel disease, especially sulfasalazine and balsalazide, and to mesalamine as the active released moiety. After oral administration, olsalazine is minimally absorbed in the upper gastrointestinal tract, remains largely intraluminal, and reaches the colon where bacterial azoreductases cleave the azo linkage to liberate two molecules of mesalamine; systemic distribution of intact parent drug is limited, mesalamine undergoes mucosal and hepatic acetylation to N-acetyl-5-ASA, and drug-related material is excreted in feces and urine. Its principal pharmacologic targets are not a single high-affinity receptor but inflammatory pathways modulated by mesalamine, including inhibition of cyclooxygenase and lipoxygenase products, reduced prostaglandin and leukotriene formation, and suppression of NF-kB–linked cytokine signaling. It is indicated mainly for maintenance of remission in ulcerative colitis and other mild-to-moderate inflammatory colitides. Dose-limiting toxicity is predominantly gastrointestinal, especially secretory diarrhea, with abdominal pain, nausea, and cramping; headache and rash also occur. Rare but important toxicities reported with 5-ASA agents include hypersensitivity reactions, pancreatitis, hepatitis, worsening colitis, interstitial nephritis, and other renal impairment, so clinically olsalazine is used as a colon-targeted steroid-sparing maintenance therapy in patients intolerant of sulfasalazine or needing mesalamine delivery to the colon.

Name: Gliquidone
Description: Gliquidone (DrugBank DB01251) is a second-generation sulfonylurea oral antihyperglycemic characterized structurally by the canonical aryl-sulfonylurea pharmacophore linked to a bulky lipophilic heterocyclic acyl substituent, giving a molecule with one sulfonamide-like sulfuryl-urea bridge, aromatic rings, and a ketone-containing cyclic moiety that increases receptor affinity and modulates disposition; chemically it belongs to the sulfonylurea class, with a sulfonylurea scaffold decorated by an aryl group and a hydrophobic heterocycle, and it is closely related to other insulin secretagogues such as glibenclamide, gliclazide, glipizide, tolbutamide, and chlorpropamide. Its principal target is the ATP-sensitive potassium channel of pancreatic beta cells, specifically binding the sulfonylurea receptor SUR1/ABCC8 within the Kir6.2/KCNJ11 channel complex, thereby closing KATP channels, depolarizing the membrane, and stimulating insulin release. Gliquidone is indicated for type 2 diabetes mellitus, especially non-insulin-dependent hyperglycemia inadequately controlled by diet and exercise, and is used clinically as monotherapy or with other antidiabetic agents in patients with preserved beta-cell function. It is generally well absorbed orally, highly protein bound, extensively hepatically metabolized, and eliminated predominantly via the biliary/fecal route with relatively limited renal excretion, a feature historically considered useful in some patients with mild to moderate renal impairment. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related prolonged hypoglycemia, particularly with overdose, reduced caloric intake, hepatic dysfunction, alcohol use, or interacting drugs; additional adverse effects include weight gain, nausea, dyspepsia, rash, pruritus, photosensitivity, dizziness, headache, and rare cholestatic, hematologic, or hypersensitivity reactions.

Name: Mitiglinide
Description: Mitiglinide (DB01252) is a rapid-acting oral insulin secretagogue in the glinide class, chemically a benzylsuccinic-acid derivative bearing a substituted aromatic ring system and a chiral carboxylic acid-containing side chain that confers high affinity for the pancreatic ATP-sensitive potassium channel; its practical scaffold is the non-sulfonylurea meglitinide/benzylsuccinic acid pharmacophore rather than a sulfonylurea nucleus. It is therefore most similar to other prandial glinides such as nateglinide and repaglinide, and functionally related, though structurally distinct, to sulfonylureas including glibenclamide and gliclazide. Its principal target is the KATP channel complex on pancreatic beta cells, especially the sulfonylurea receptor 1 subunit ABCC8 in association with the inward rectifier potassium channel Kir6.2 encoded by KCNJ11, where binding closes the channel, depolarizes the membrane, and promotes glucose-dependent insulin release. Mitiglinide is indicated for type 2 diabetes mellitus, particularly postprandial hyperglycemia, and is used clinically as a premeal agent alone or with agents such as metformin or alpha-glucosidase inhibitors to improve mealtime glucose excursions. Pharmacokinetically, it is rapidly absorbed after oral dosing, reaches peak concentrations quickly, shows short duration of action, is moderately protein bound, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism with formation of inactive or weakly active metabolites, and is excreted mainly via biliary/fecal routes with some renal elimination. Toxicity is dominated by excessive pharmacology, especially hypoglycemia, which may present with sweating, tremor, palpitations, confusion, or severe neuroglycopenia; other adverse effects include weight gain, gastrointestinal discomfort, headache, dizziness, and occasional hepatic enzyme elevations, while overdose or use in frail patients, those with hepatic impairment, or when combined with other antihyperglycemics can increase hypoglycemic risk.

Name: Dasatinib
Description: Dasatinib (DrugBank DB01254) is an orally active, small-molecule antineoplastic tyrosine kinase inhibitor built on a 2-aminothiazole-containing heteroaromatic scaffold linked to a chloromethyl-substituted phenyl ring, a hydroxyethyl piperazine side chain, and an amide functionality, giving a relatively planar, lipophilic, weakly basic structure optimized for ATP-pocket binding; chemically it is classified as a multikinase inhibitor, particularly a BCR-ABL/Src-family kinase inhibitor, with an aminothiazole kinase-inhibitor scaffold related pharmacologically to imatinib, nilotinib, bosutinib, and ponatinib, and with overlap to Src-directed agents. Its principal targets include BCR-ABL1, SRC family kinases such as SRC, LYN, and FYN, as well as KIT, PDGFR, EPHA2, and some TEC-family kinases, explaining its potency in Philadelphia chromosome-positive malignancies. Dasatinib is indicated mainly for chronic myeloid leukemia and Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia, including newly diagnosed chronic-phase disease and imatinib-resistant or intolerant cases. After oral administration it is rapidly absorbed, reaches peak concentrations within hours, shows pH-dependent solubility with reduced exposure from acid suppressants, is highly protein bound, widely distributed, extensively metabolized in the liver primarily by CYP3A4, and eliminated mainly in feces with minimal renal excretion and a short terminal half-life despite sustained pharmacodynamic effects. Toxicities include myelosuppression, bleeding, fluid retention, pleural and pericardial effusions, pulmonary arterial hypertension, QT prolongation, hepatotoxicity, and embryo-fetal toxicity. Common adverse effects include thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, anemia, diarrhea, rash, headache, fatigue, nausea, edema, and dyspnea. Clinically, it is used as a targeted oral therapy requiring monitoring of blood counts, liver function, cardiopulmonary status, and drug-drug interactions, especially with CYP3A4 modulators and gastric acid-reducing agents.

Name: Lisdexamfetamine
Description: Lisdexamfetamine (DB01255) is a synthetic amphetamine-class central nervous system stimulant designed as the dimesylate salt of a prodrug in which d-amphetamine is covalently linked through an amide bond to the essential amino acid L-lysine, giving a peptidomimetic phenethylamine structure with an aryl-alkylamine amphetamine scaffold masked by amino acid conjugation; chemically it belongs to substituted phenethylamines and amphetamine derivatives, and its closest analogs include dextroamphetamine, mixed amphetamine salts, methamphetamine, and the methylphenidate-class stimulants as pharmacologically similar comparators. After oral administration it is well absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, is less dependent on gastric pH than immediate-release amphetamine products, and is converted mainly in blood by enzymatic hydrolysis in erythrocytes to active dextroamphetamine and L-lysine; dextroamphetamine then distributes widely, including to the CNS, undergoes limited hepatic biotransformation involving CYP2D6 and other oxidative pathways to active and inactive metabolites, and is excreted primarily in urine with elimination strongly influenced by urinary pH. Its principal pharmacologic targets are the dopamine transporter SLC6A3, norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, and to a lesser extent serotonin transporter SLC6A4, with indirect promotion of catecholamine release via trace amine-associated receptor 1. It is indicated for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and moderate to severe binge eating disorder, improving inattention, impulsivity, hyperactivity, and binge frequency. Common adverse effects include decreased appetite, insomnia, dry mouth, irritability, tachycardia, and weight loss; important toxicities include hypertension, arrhythmia, psychosis, mania, seizures, peripheral vasculopathy, serotonin toxicity with interacting drugs, growth suppression in children, and abuse, dependence, and overdose risks typical of sympathomimetic stimulants.

Name: Retapamulin
Description: Retapamulin (DrugBank DB01256) is a semisynthetic pleuromutilin antibiotic structurally characterized by a compact tricyclic mutilin core bearing a glycolate-derived C14 side chain and multiple oxygenated substituents that create a rigid, lipophilic diterpene-like framework optimized for ribosomal binding; thus, its chemical category is pleuromutilin antibacterial, and its core scaffold is the pleuromutilin/mutilin tricyclic diterpene nucleus. Closely related drugs include tiamulin and valnemulin, used mainly in veterinary medicine, and the human pleuromutilins lefamulin and, more distantly by scaffold class, azamulin. Retapamulin acts by binding the peptidyl transferase center of the 50S bacterial ribosomal subunit, principally interacting with 23S rRNA and ribosomal protein environments around L3, thereby inhibiting protein synthesis; the functional target is the bacterial 50S ribosome. It is indicated topically for impetigo and other minor superficial skin infections, especially those caused by methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes. Pharmacokinetically, after dermal application systemic absorption is minimal, plasma exposure is usually very low, distribution is therefore limited systemically, metabolism occurs mainly in the liver via CYP3A4 oxidation if absorbed, and excretion is expected predominantly through biliary/fecal routes with minor renal contribution. Toxicity is generally low because of limited absorption, but excessive exposure or use on damaged skin could theoretically increase systemic risk; local irritation, erythema, pruritus, burning, pain, and contact dermatitis are the most common adverse effects, while hypersensitivity reactions are uncommon. Clinically, it is used as a short-course topical agent for localized uncomplicated bacterial skin lesions when targeted Gram-positive coverage and reduced systemic exposure are desired.

Name: Lapatinib
Description: Lapatinib (DrugBank DB01259) is an orally active small-molecule 4-anilinoquinazoline derivative characterized by a planar quinazoline heteroaromatic core bearing substituted aniline, benzyloxy, sulfonyl, and chlorophenyl motifs that confer lipophilicity and ATP-pocket binding; chemically it is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor in the quinazoline/anilide class, with a classic EGFR-family inhibitory scaffold closely related to other HER/EGFR-directed kinase inhibitors such as gefitinib, erlotinib, afatinib, and neratinib, although lapatinib is a reversible dual inhibitor with principal targets ERBB2/HER2 and EGFR/ERBB1. It is indicated mainly for HER2-positive breast cancer, including advanced or metastatic disease, commonly in combination with capecitabine, letrozole, or trastuzumab, especially after progression on prior HER2-directed therapy. Pharmacokinetically, oral absorption is incomplete and variable but increases with food; the drug is highly protein bound, widely distributed into tissues, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism predominantly by CYP3A4 and CYP3A5 with lesser CYP2C19 and CYP2C8 contribution, and is excreted mainly in feces with minimal renal elimination, giving it interaction liability with strong CYP3A modulators. Toxicities include hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevation and rare severe liver injury, dose-related diarrhea and dehydration, QT prolongation, and reversible decreases in left ventricular ejection fraction reflecting HER2-pathway cardiac effects. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, rash, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia when combined with capecitabine, mucositis, and anorexia. Clinically, it is used as a targeted anti-HER2 therapy to suppress proliferative signaling in tumors overexpressing HER2 or co-dependent on EGFR-family pathways.

Name: Desonide
Description: Desonide (DrugBank DB01260) is a low-potency, nonfluinated synthetic corticosteroid structurally defined by the pregnane steroid nucleus with the characteristic four fused rings, 3-keto-4-ene functionality, 11β- and 21-hydroxyl groups, and a 16,17-acetal/ketal feature that increases topical anti-inflammatory activity while limiting systemic exposure relative to more potent halogenated analogs. Chemically it belongs to the glucocorticoid corticosteroid class, with a hydrocortisone-like corticosteroid scaffold; closely related drugs include hydrocortisone, prednisolone, alclometasone, fluocinolone acetonide, triamcinolone acetonide, and desoximetasone, which share the same steroidal anti-inflammatory pharmacophore but differ in halogenation and acetal substitutions. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, through which it alters transcription of anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory genes and suppresses phospholipase A2-derived mediator production, cytokine release, and leukocyte recruitment. After topical administration, percutaneous absorption is generally low but increases with damaged skin, occlusion, large surface area, prolonged use, and pediatric age; distributed mainly within skin with limited systemic bioavailability, it undergoes hepatic corticosteroid metabolism and is excreted primarily as metabolites in urine, with some biliary/fecal elimination. Desonide is indicated for corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses such as atopic dermatitis, eczema, seborrheic dermatitis, allergic/contact dermatitis, and inflammatory pruritic rashes, especially on sensitive areas like the face or intertriginous skin. Adverse effects include burning, stinging, dryness, erythema, folliculitis, acneiform eruptions, perioral dermatitis, telangiectasia, striae, skin atrophy, and secondary infection; excessive or prolonged exposure can cause HPA-axis suppression, hyperglycemia, Cushingoid features, and growth suppression in children. Clinically it is used as creams, ointments, lotions, foams, or gels for short-course control of mild inflammatory skin disease where lower corticosteroid potency is preferred.

Name: Sitagliptin
Description: Sitagliptin (DrugBank DB01261) is an orally active, small-molecule dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor built on a beta-amino acid/triazolopyrazine-derived scaffold, featuring a fused nitrogen-rich heteroaromatic core linked to a trifluorophenyl substituent and a chiral amino-containing side chain that promotes high-affinity binding to the catalytic site of DPP-4; chemically it is classified as a fluorinated heterocyclic antidiabetic agent and is structurally related to other gliptins such as vildagliptin, saxagliptin, linagliptin, and alogliptin, which share the same incretin-enhancing pharmacology but differ in scaffold and elimination pathways. Its principal target is DPP4/CD26, with therapeutic action arising from inhibition of GLP-1 and GIP degradation, thereby increasing glucose-dependent insulin secretion and lowering glucagon. After oral administration, sitagliptin is well absorbed with high bioavailability, reaches peak plasma levels within a few hours, shows low to moderate protein binding, limited distribution, minimal metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 and CYP2C8, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by the kidney through active tubular secretion, giving a terminal half-life that supports once-daily dosing. It is indicated for type 2 diabetes mellitus, especially for improvement of glycemic control as monotherapy or in combination with metformin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones, or insulin. Common adverse effects include nasopharyngitis, upper respiratory symptoms, headache, and gastrointestinal complaints; clinically important toxicities include hypoglycemia when combined with insulin secretagogues or insulin, hypersensitivity reactions such as angioedema or Stevens-Johnson syndrome, pancreatitis, severe arthralgia, and rare renal function concerns, so dose adjustment is used in renal impairment.

Name: Decitabine
Description: Decitabine (DrugBank DB01262) is a deoxycytidine analog antimetabolite in the pyrimidine nucleoside class, structurally characterized by a 2′-deoxyribose sugar linked through a beta-N-glycosidic bond to 5-aza-2′-deoxycytosine, in which a ring nitrogen replaces the carbon at the 5-position of the cytosine scaffold; thus its core scaffold is an azapyrimidine deoxynucleoside closely related to azacitidine, cytarabine, gemcitabine, and other cytidine-derived epigenetic or antineoplastic agents. After intravenous administration, decitabine shows rapid systemic distribution and a short plasma half-life on the order of minutes because it is extensively inactivated by cytidine deaminase in blood, liver, gut, and other tissues, with intracellular phosphorylation to active triphosphate metabolites that become incorporated into DNA; elimination occurs predominantly after metabolic degradation, with limited unchanged renal excretion. Its principal pharmacologic targets are DNA methyltransferases, especially DNMT1, with effects also involving DNMT3A and DNMT3B depletion or trapping, leading to hypomethylation, re-expression of silenced genes, impaired malignant progenitor survival, and cytotoxicity at higher exposures. It is indicated mainly for myelodysplastic syndromes, including refractory anemia and chronic myelomonocytic leukemia, and is also used in acute myeloid leukemia, particularly in older or unfit patients. Dose-limiting toxicity is myelosuppression, with clinically important neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, febrile neutropenia, and infection; other adverse effects include nausea, fatigue, constipation or diarrhea, mucositis, elevated liver enzymes, and less commonly renal or hepatic dysfunction, making it a standard hypomethylating therapy in hematologic oncology.

Name: Posaconazole
Description: Posaconazole (DrugBank DB01263) is a broad-spectrum triazole antifungal built on a highly lipophilic azole scaffold featuring a 1,2,4-triazole ring linked to a fluorinated phenyl moiety and a hydroxylated side chain attached to a substituted tetrahydrofuran/piperazine-containing framework, a structure closely related to other second-generation triazoles. Chemically it belongs to the triazole antifungal class, with a scaffold most similar to itraconazole and, to a lesser extent, voriconazole and fluconazole, all of which inhibit fungal sterol biosynthesis. Its principal target is fungal lanosterol 14alpha-demethylase, the CYP51 enzyme encoded by ERG11/CYP51, leading to depletion of ergosterol and disruption of fungal membrane integrity; inhibition of human CYP3A4 is also pharmacologically important for drug interactions. Posaconazole is indicated for prophylaxis of invasive Aspergillus and Candida infections in severely immunocompromised patients, such as those with prolonged neutropenia or graft-versus-host disease, and for treatment of invasive aspergillosis, oropharyngeal candidiasis, and refractory endemic mycoses including mucormycosis, coccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis, and chromoblastomycosis when alternatives are unsuitable. Pharmacokinetically, absorption is formulation dependent, improved with food for the oral suspension, and more reliable with delayed-release tablets or intravenous dosing; it is highly protein bound, widely distributed, minimally metabolized mainly by UDP-glucuronidation, and eliminated predominantly unchanged in feces with limited renal clearance. Toxicities include hepatotoxicity, QT-interval prolongation, electrolyte-associated arrhythmia risk, and rare adrenal steroid synthesis effects; common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, headache, fever, rash, and transaminase elevation. Clinically, it is used both as targeted salvage therapy and as antifungal prophylaxis in high-risk hematology and transplant populations.

Name: Darunavir
Description: Darunavir (DrugBank DB01264) is a nonpeptidic HIV-1 protease inhibitor with a compact peptidomimetic structure built around a hydroxyethylsulfonamide core that mimics the tetrahedral transition state of protease-mediated peptide cleavage, decorated with bis-tetrahydrofuran and sulfonamide-derived polar functionalities plus lipophilic aromatic moieties that optimize active-site binding; chemically it belongs to the antiretroviral aspartyl protease inhibitor class, and its principal scaffold is the hydroxyethylamine/hydroxyethylsulfonamide protease-inhibitor framework. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other HIV protease inhibitors such as amprenavir, fosamprenavir, lopinavir, atazanavir, and ritonavir, although darunavir is distinguished by high affinity and retained activity against many resistant viral variants. Its primary target is the HIV-1 protease, with activity also against HIV-2 protease in clinical practice. Orally administered darunavir is absorbed better when taken with food and is commonly boosted with ritonavir or cobicistat to inhibit CYP3A-mediated first-pass and systemic metabolism; it is highly protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4, and is eliminated predominantly in feces with limited renal excretion of unchanged drug. Toxicities include hepatotoxicity, severe rash, sulfonamide-associated hypersensitivity, and metabolic disturbances such as hyperlipidemia, with overdose or interaction risk increased by CYP3A modulators. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, headache, rash, transaminase elevation, and lipid abnormalities. Clinically, darunavir is indicated for treatment of HIV-1 infection, including antiretroviral-experienced patients with resistant virus, and is used in combination regimens for chronic HIV disease suppression and prevention of progression to AIDS.

Name: Telbivudine
Description: Telbivudine (DB01265) is a synthetic L-nucleoside analogue of thymidine characterized structurally by a thymine pyrimidine base linked to an unnatural beta-L-2-deoxyribose-like sugar, making it the L-enantiomer of a 2-deoxythymidine analogue and placing it in the antiviral nucleoside analogue class; its core chemical scaffold is therefore an L-pyrimidine nucleoside, closely related to other anti-hepatitis B nucleos(t)ide agents such as lamivudine, emtricitabine, entecavir, adefovir, and tenofovir, with especially strong structural similarity to other L-nucleosides. After oral administration it is well absorbed, has relatively low protein binding, distributes into total body water and hepatocyte compartments relevant to hepatitis B infection, undergoes minimal hepatic metabolism including little cytochrome P450 involvement, is phosphorylated intracellularly to the active triphosphate, and is eliminated largely unchanged by the kidney, so exposure increases in renal impairment. Its principal pharmacologic target is hepatitis B virus DNA polymerase/reverse transcriptase, which is inhibited after incorporation of the active metabolite into viral DNA, causing chain termination and suppression of HBV replication. It is indicated for chronic hepatitis B, particularly in adults with active viral replication and evidence of hepatic inflammation or fibrosis, and has been used to reduce serum HBV DNA and improve transaminases and liver histology. Important toxicities include myopathy with creatine kinase elevation, peripheral neuropathy, mitochondrial toxicity-related lactic acidosis, and rare hepatomegaly with steatosis; common adverse effects include fatigue, headache, cough, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, elevated CK, and upper respiratory symptoms. Clinically, it has been used as an oral anti-HBV monotherapy or as an alternative when treatment goals include durable viral suppression, though resistance can emerge, especially via HBV polymerase substitutions such as M204I.

Name: Paliperidone
Description: Paliperidone (DB01267) is an atypical antipsychotic and the major active metabolite of risperidone, structurally characterized as a benzisoxazole-derived piperidine compound bearing a fluorobenzisoxazole ring system linked through a short alkyl chain to a substituted piperidine with a hydroxyl group, placing it in the benzisoxazole antipsychotic class with a fluorobenzisoxazole-piperidine scaffold. Closely related drugs include risperidone, from which it is formed, and other mechanistically similar second-generation antipsychotics such as iloperidone, ziprasidone, and lurasidone. Its pharmacology is driven primarily by antagonism at dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors, with additional activity at 5-HT7, alpha1- and alpha2-adrenergic, and H1-histamine receptors, while having minimal muscarinic affinity. After oral administration, extended-release paliperidone is absorbed gradually with relatively high absolute bioavailability, limited hepatic metabolism, modest protein binding, and predominant renal excretion of unchanged drug; metabolism involves minor CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 contributions, making it less metabolism-dependent than risperidone, and long-acting palmitate esters provide sustained release for monthly or longer dosing. Toxicity is consistent with dopamine and autonomic blockade and includes dose-related extrapyramidal symptoms, hyperprolactinemia, QT prolongation, orthostatic hypotension, sedation, weight gain, and, more rarely, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, tardive dyskinesia, seizures, and cerebrovascular adverse events in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis. Clinically, it is indicated for schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder, including treatment of hallucinations, delusions, disorganized thought, agitation, and mood symptoms, and is used orally or as long-acting injectable maintenance therapy to improve adherence and reduce relapse.

Name: Sunitinib
Description: Sunitinib (DrugBank DB01268) is an orally active small-molecule antineoplastic tyrosine kinase inhibitor built on an indolinone/oxindole-derived heteroaromatic scaffold, specifically a substituted 5-fluoroindolin-2-one core linked through an exocyclic alkene to a pyrrole ring and terminating in a diethylaminoethyl side chain, a structure that confers lipophilicity, kinase hinge-binding capacity, and broad receptor promiscuity; chemically it is categorized as a multitargeted receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor within the indolinone class, and its scaffold is closely related to other VEGFR/PDGFR-directed agents such as semaxanib, with pharmacologic similarity to sorafenib, pazopanib, axitinib, cabozantinib, and regorafenib. Its principal targets include VEGFR1/FLT1, VEGFR2/KDR, VEGFR3/FLT4, PDGFRA, PDGFRB, KIT, FLT3, CSF1R, and RET, producing antiangiogenic and antiproliferative effects. It is used clinically for renal cell carcinoma, imatinib-resistant or intolerant gastrointestinal stromal tumor, and progressive, well-differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. Oral absorption is substantial, bioavailability functionally high, peak concentrations occur in roughly 6-12 hours, protein binding is extensive, tissue distribution is broad, metabolism is primarily hepatic via CYP3A4 to an active metabolite, and elimination is prolonged with terminal half-lives of about 40-60 hours for parent drug and longer for the metabolite, with excretion mainly in feces and partly in urine. Important toxicities include hepatotoxicity, hypertension, left ventricular dysfunction, QT prolongation, hemorrhage, thromboembolism, proteinuria, posterior reversible encephalopathy, and impaired wound healing; common adverse effects include fatigue, diarrhea, mucositis, nausea, anorexia, hand-foot syndrome, rash, hypothyroidism, cytopenias, and yellow skin discoloration.

Name: Arformoterol
Description: Arformoterol (DB01274) is the single active (R,R)-enantiomer of formoterol, a long-acting phenylaminoethanol beta2-adrenergic agonist whose structure features a substituted aromatic ring system linked through an ethanolamine side chain to a lipophilic formamide-containing aryl group, giving an aryloxy/aryl-ethanolamine bronchodilator pharmacophore optimized for high beta2-receptor affinity and prolonged airway residence; chemically it is classified as a sympathomimetic bronchodilator and selective long-acting beta2-adrenergic receptor agonist, with a phenethylamine/arylethanolamine scaffold related to other LABAs such as formoterol, salmeterol, indacaterol, olodaterol, and vilanterol, and more broadly to short-acting beta2 agonists such as albuterol. Its principal target is the beta2-adrenergic receptor, with lesser activity possible at beta1 receptors at higher exposure, leading through Gs-cAMP signaling to bronchial smooth muscle relaxation. After inhalation by nebulization it is absorbed from the lung, shows low systemic concentrations at therapeutic doses, distributes moderately into tissues, undergoes hepatic biotransformation mainly by direct conjugation and O-demethylation followed by conjugation, and is eliminated in urine and feces as parent drug and metabolites, with an effective duration near 12 hours. It is indicated for maintenance treatment of bronchoconstriction in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, including chronic bronchitis and emphysema, but not for acute bronchospasm rescue or asthma monotherapy. Toxicity reflects excessive beta-adrenergic stimulation, with overdose potentially causing tachycardia, tremor, palpitations, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, QT prolongation, ventricular arrhythmias, hypertension or hypotension, and rarely paradoxical bronchospasm; common adverse effects include headache, tremor, nervousness, back pain, diarrhea, sinusitis, rash, leg cramps, and chest discomfort. Clinically, arformoterol is used as a twice-daily nebulized LABA in COPD patients who need sustained bronchodilation, particularly those with persistent symptoms, poor inhaler technique, or preference for nebulized maintenance therapy.

Name: Hydralazine
Description: Hydralazine (DrugBank DB01275) is a small aromatic hydrazinophthalazine antihypertensive whose structure consists of a fused bicyclic phthalazine ring bearing a terminal hydrazine substituent, making it a nitrogen-rich heteroaromatic base; chemically it belongs to the phthalazine/hydrazine class and is built on a phthalazine scaffold functionalized with a reactive hydrazino group that is important for both activity and metabolism. It is most closely related pharmacologically to direct vasodilators such as dihydralazine, cadralazine, and, more distantly, minoxidil and sodium nitroprusside, although its heteroaromatic hydrazine scaffold distinguishes it. Hydralazine is generally well absorbed orally but undergoes substantial first-pass metabolism with marked acetylator-dependent variability in bioavailability, distributes widely, is metabolized mainly in the liver by N-acetylation, oxidation, and conjugation, and is excreted predominantly in urine as metabolites; its half-life is short, but hemodynamic effects may persist longer. Its principal pharmacologic action is direct relaxation of arteriolar smooth muscle, often linked to effects on intracellular calcium handling and vascular signaling, with no single definitive receptor target, though reported protein associations include myeloperoxidase and xanthine oxidase. It is indicated for essential hypertension, severe hypertension, hypertensive urgency in selected settings, and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction when combined with isosorbide dinitrate, particularly in patients intolerant of ACE inhibitors or ARBs, and has also been used in hypertension of pregnancy. Important adverse effects include headache, flushing, tachycardia, palpitations, fluid retention, angina exacerbation, nausea, and hypotension, while notable toxicities include dose-related peripheral neuropathy and a lupus-like syndrome, especially with prolonged use or slow acetylator status.

Name: Nelarabine
Description: Nelarabine (DB01280) is a synthetic purine nucleoside antimetabolite and prodrug of 9-β-D-arabinofuranosylguanine (ara-G), structurally characterized by a 6-methoxy guanine analog linked to an arabinose sugar, placing it in the deoxyguanosine-like nucleoside analog class with a purine N-glycoside scaffold; it is closely related to other antimetabolite nucleosides such as cytarabine, fludarabine, cladribine, clofarabine, and especially ara-G. After intravenous administration, nelarabine is rapidly O-demethylated by adenosine deaminase to ara-G, which is distributed into plasma and tissues and then phosphorylated intracellularly, particularly in T lymphoblasts, to ara-GTP, the active cytotoxic metabolite; ara-G and metabolites are eliminated mainly by the kidney, with relatively short plasma half-lives for parent drug and ara-G but longer intracellular retention of ara-GTP that supports antileukemic activity. Its principal pharmacologic targets are DNA synthesis and replication machinery rather than a single receptor, with activation by deoxycytidine kinase and mitochondrial deoxyguanosine kinase and cytotoxicity mediated by ara-GTP incorporation into DNA, inhibition of DNA polymerase-dependent elongation, and induction of apoptosis. Nelarabine is indicated primarily for relapsed or refractory T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia and T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma, including pediatric and adult settings. Major toxicities are dose-limiting neurotoxic effects such as somnolence, peripheral neuropathy, seizures, ataxia, ascending sensory-motor deficits, and rarely demyelinating or severe central nervous system events, along with myelosuppression, anemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, infection risk, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fatigue, and transaminase elevations. Clinically, it is used as salvage monotherapy or bridge-to-transplant therapy in heavily pretreated T-lineage hematologic malignancies.

Name: Carbetocin
Description: Carbetocin (DrugBank DB01282) is a long-acting synthetic oxytocin analogue built on a cyclic nonapeptide peptide framework with an intramolecular disulfide bridge and strategic substitutions, notably deamination and O-methyltyrosine incorporation, that increase enzymatic stability and prolong uterotonic action relative to oxytocin; chemically it belongs to the oxytocin/vasopressin neurohypophyseal peptide class, with a cyclic peptide scaffold closely related to oxytocin and broadly similar to other uterotonics such as oxytocin itself and, more distantly in therapeutic role rather than structure, ergometrine and misoprostol. Its principal pharmacologic target is the oxytocin receptor OXTR on uterine smooth muscle, where agonism increases intracellular calcium signaling and promotes sustained postpartum myometrial contraction. After intravenous or intramuscular administration, absorption is immediate by the IV route and rapid after IM dosing, distribution is largely extracellular, placental transfer is limited in postpartum use, protein binding is not a dominant feature, metabolism occurs mainly through peptide hydrolysis/proteolysis rather than cytochrome P450 pathways, and elimination is relatively slow for this class, with a terminal half-life notably longer than oxytocin and excretion occurring predominantly as peptide metabolites in urine. The main indication is prevention of postpartum hemorrhage due to uterine atony after cesarean delivery or vaginal birth, particularly in the immediate third-stage/postpartum setting. Adverse effects resemble oxytocin and include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, flushing, headache, pruritus, tremor, hypotension, tachycardia, and injection-site reactions; toxicity is chiefly an extension of uterotonic and vasodilatory effects, with examples including excessive uterine contraction, hemodynamic instability, and, less commonly, chest pain or hypersensitivity, so clinical use is typically restricted to supervised obstetric prophylaxis rather than labor induction.

Name: Lumiracoxib
Description: Lumiracoxib (DrugBank DB01283) is a diaryl-substituted arylacetic acid nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug characterized structurally by a chlorinated aniline-linked biphenyl-like aromatic system bearing a fluorophenyl ring and a terminal acetic acid moiety, a design that confers acidic NSAID behavior while favoring high cyclooxygenase-2 selectivity; chemically it belongs to the coxib-related selective COX-2 inhibitor class, although its core scaffold is better described as an arylacetic acid/diaryl-aniline scaffold rather than the sulfonamide or sulfone heterocycle seen in celecoxib or rofecoxib. Similar drugs include other selective COX-2 inhibitors such as celecoxib, etoricoxib, rofecoxib, and valdecoxib, as well as the related acidic COX-2-preferring agent diclofenac in terms of some structural and pharmacologic features. Its principal target is prostaglandin G/H synthase 2 (PTGS2, COX-2), with substantially less inhibition of PTGS1 (COX-1). After oral administration it is well absorbed, highly protein bound, distributed systemically including inflamed tissues, extensively metabolized hepatically mainly via CYP2C9-dependent oxidation and conjugation to inactive metabolites, and excreted predominantly in urine with some fecal elimination; the terminal half-life is generally in the low single-digit hours permitting once-daily use. It was indicated for osteoarthritis and other painful inflammatory musculoskeletal conditions, with clinical use including symptomatic relief of joint pain, stiffness, and inflammation. Adverse effects include headache, nausea, dyspepsia, abdominal pain, diarrhea, edema, and dizziness, while major toxicities include serious hepatotoxicity with marked transaminase elevation, hepatitis, jaundice, and rare acute liver failure, along with class-related cardiovascular and renal risks such as hypertension, fluid retention, and renal impairment, which led to severe restrictions and market withdrawals in multiple countries.

Name: Tetracosactide
Description: Tetracosactide (DrugBank DB01284) is a synthetic peptide drug corresponding to the biologically active N-terminal 24-residue segment of adrenocorticotropic hormone, built as a linear oligopeptide with amide-linked amino acids and a corticotropin-like amphipathic peptide backbone that preserves the receptor-binding and steroidogenic determinants of native ACTH; chemically it is classified as a peptide hormone analogue and more specifically a synthetic melanocortin receptor agonist, with an ACTH(1-24) peptide scaffold. Closely related agents include repository corticotropin injection, natural corticotropin, cosyntropin, and other ACTH analogues used diagnostically or therapeutically. Its principal target is the melanocortin 2 receptor on adrenal cortical cells, with consequent stimulation of adrenal steroidogenesis and secondary increases in cortisol and related corticosteroids. After parenteral administration, tetracosactide is absorbed rapidly, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid, is subject to proteolytic degradation in blood and tissues, has a short plasma half-life relative to the duration of adrenal stimulation, and is cleared as peptide fragments and amino acid metabolites largely via renal routes. It is used primarily for assessment of adrenocortical function in suspected primary or secondary adrenal insufficiency and has also been used clinically in some inflammatory or neurologic conditions such as infantile spasms or multiple sclerosis relapse settings where ACTH-like steroidogenic effects are desired. Toxicity and adverse effects resemble corticosteroid excess or ACTH stimulation and include hypertension, edema, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, mood changes, gastrointestinal upset, facial flushing, hypersensitivity, and with repeated use risk of Cushingoid features, infection exacerbation, and adrenal suppression.

Name: Glisoxepide
Description: Glisoxepide (DrugBank DB01289) is a first-generation sulfonylurea oral hypoglycemic agent whose structure consists of the characteristic arylsulfonylurea pharmacophore linked to a lipophilic substituted cyclohexyl-containing side chain and an isoxepide/isoxazole-related heterocyclic motif, placing it in the sulfonylurea class of insulin secretagogues; its core chemical scaffold is therefore the sulfonylurea bridge appended to a hydrophobic aromatic-heterocyclic framework that supports high affinity binding to the pancreatic ATP-sensitive potassium channel complex. It is closely related pharmacologically and structurally to other first-generation sulfonylureas such as tolbutamide, chlorpropamide, acetohexamide, and tolazamide, and more distantly to second-generation agents such as glibenclamide and glipizide. The principal target is the sulfonylurea receptor 1 subunit of the KATP channel, encoded by ABCC8, functionally coupled to Kir6.2 encoded by KCNJ11, leading to channel closure, beta-cell depolarization, calcium influx, and insulin release. It was used for type 2 diabetes mellitus, especially non-insulin-dependent hyperglycemia inadequately controlled by diet alone. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed, extensively protein bound, distributed mainly within extracellular and highly perfused tissues, hepatically metabolized by oxidative and related biotransformation pathways, and eliminated as metabolites in urine and to a lesser extent bile/feces. Its major toxicity is dose-related prolonged hypoglycemia, particularly in elderly patients, those with hepatic or renal impairment, or with poor caloric intake; other adverse effects include weight gain, nausea, epigastric discomfort, rash, pruritus, photosensitivity, and rare cholestatic, hematologic, or hypersensitivity reactions. Clinically it was used as an adjunct to dietary management of type 2 diabetes, but like other older sulfonylureas it has largely been superseded by agents with more favorable safety and pharmacokinetic profiles.

Name: Pirbuterol
Description: Pirbuterol (DrugBank DB01291) is a short-acting sympathomimetic bronchodilator built on a substituted phenylethanolamine/aryl-alkanolamine structure characterized by a pyridine-containing aromatic ring linked to a beta-amino alcohol side chain with hydroxyl and tert-butyl-like beta2-agonist features that favor receptor selectivity; chemically it is classified as an adrenergic beta2-receptor agonist and more specifically a resorcinol/saligenin-like bronchodilator analogue within the phenethylamine bronchodilator family, with a simple beta-amino alcohol scaffold shared broadly by inhaled SABA agents. Similar drugs include albuterol (salbutamol), terbutaline, metaproterenol, and fenoterol, which have related beta2-selective bronchodilating pharmacology. Its principal target is the beta2-adrenergic receptor, encoded by ADRB2, with pharmacologic activation increasing adenylate cyclase signaling and airway smooth-muscle relaxation. Pirbuterol is indicated for reversible bronchospasm in asthma and other obstructive airway diseases, and has been used clinically as an inhaled rescue medication for acute wheezing, episodic dyspnea, and bronchospasm associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. After inhalation, absorption is partly pulmonary and partly gastrointestinal from swallowed drug; systemic distribution is limited by inhaled dosing, metabolism is largely by conjugative pathways rather than extensive catechol-O-methyltransferase degradation, and elimination occurs mainly in urine as parent drug and metabolites. Toxicity reflects excessive beta-adrenergic stimulation, with tremor, tachycardia, palpitations, nervousness, headache, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, and rare arrhythmias or paradoxical bronchospasm, especially in overdose or when combined with other sympathomimetics; common adverse effects in clinical use include cough, throat irritation, dizziness, and nausea.

Name: Fosamprenavir
Description: Fosamprenavir (DB01319) is a phosphate ester prodrug of amprenavir, structurally characterized as a water-soluble phosphonooxy derivative built on the hydroxyethylsulfonamide HIV protease inhibitor pharmacophore, with a peptidomimetic, noncleavable transition-state-mimicking scaffold that includes tetrahydroxy-substituted and sulfonamide-linked aromatic/heteroaliphatic elements designed to occupy the viral protease active site; chemically it is classified as an antiviral, specifically an HIV-1 protease inhibitor prodrug, and its core scaffold is closely related to other hydroxyethylamine or hydroxyethylsulfonamide protease inhibitors such as amprenavir, darunavir, ritonavir, lopinavir, and atazanavir. After oral administration, fosamprenavir is rapidly hydrolyzed by intestinal epithelial phosphatases to active amprenavir; absorption is clinically useful with or without ritonavir boosting, distribution is moderate with substantial plasma protein binding, metabolism occurs mainly via hepatic CYP3A4, and excretion is predominantly as metabolites in feces with a smaller urinary component. Its principal target is HIV-1 protease, with activity also directed against HIV-2 protease to a lesser extent. Indicated for treatment of HIV-1 infection in combination antiretroviral therapy, including use in treatment-naive and some treatment-experienced adults, it reduces viral replication and plasma HIV RNA. Toxicities include hepatotoxicity, severe rash including Stevens-Johnson syndrome, sulfonamide-associated hypersensitivity, lipid abnormalities, insulin resistance, and rare nephrolithiasis; overdose or interaction-mediated exposure increases gastrointestinal and hepatic toxicity. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, headache, paresthesia, fatigue, and rash. Clinically, fosamprenavir has been used with ritonavir as a boosted protease inhibitor regimen and as an alternative when constructing suppressive combination therapy in HIV disease.

Name: Fosphenytoin
Description: Fosphenytoin (DrugBank DB01320) is a water-soluble phosphate ester prodrug of phenytoin in which the hydantoin anticonvulsant nucleus, specifically a 5,5-diphenyl-substituted imidazolidine-2,4-dione scaffold, is functionalized through a phosphonooxymethyl substituent to improve parenteral formulation; chemically it belongs to the hydantoin anticonvulsants and organophosphate prodrug class, with the core scaffold shared by phenytoin and related aromatic anticonvulsants. Similar drugs include phenytoin itself as the active metabolite, and more distantly other sodium channel-blocking antiseizure agents such as mephenytoin, ethotoin, carbamazepine, and lamotrigine. After intravenous or intramuscular administration, fosphenytoin is rapidly and extensively converted by plasma and tissue phosphatases to phenytoin, phosphate, and formaldehyde; it is effectively completely bioavailable as phenytoin equivalents, distributes as generated phenytoin with high plasma protein binding, enters the CNS, and is then hepatically metabolized mainly by CYP2C9 and CYP2C19 to inactive hydroxylated metabolites excreted in urine, while exhibiting capacity-limited phenytoin elimination. Its principal targets are voltage-gated sodium channels, especially neuronal SCN family channels such as SCN1A, SCN2A, and SCN8A, stabilizing the inactivated state and limiting repetitive firing. Indications include status epilepticus, seizure prophylaxis during neurosurgery or head trauma, and short-term replacement when oral phenytoin cannot be used.
