Toxicity mirrors phenytoin exposure and infusion-related effects, including hypotension, bradyarrhythmia, cardiovascular collapse, nystagmus, ataxia, CNS depression, and local paresthesia or pruritus; serious examples include purple glove syndrome, severe cutaneous reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, blood dyscrasias, hepatotoxicity, and teratogenicity. Clinically, it is used in emergency and inpatient settings for rapid loading or maintenance anticonvulsant therapy, particularly when safer, faster IV administration than phenytoin is desired.

Name: Polythiazide
Description: Polythiazide (DrugBank DB01324) is a thiazide diuretic of the benzothiadiazine class, structurally characterized by a chlorinated benzene ring fused to a 1,2,4-benzothiadiazine 1,1-dioxide core bearing sulfonamide functionality and lipophilic substituents that increase potency and duration relative to early thiazides; its key chemical scaffold is therefore the chlorobenzenesulfonamide-containing benzothiadiazine dioxide nucleus typical of thiazide saluretics. It is closely related to other thiazide or thiazide-like antihypertensives and diuretics such as hydrochlorothiazide, chlorothiazide, bendroflumethiazide, methyclothiazide, and cyclothiazide. Its principal pharmacologic target is the renal sodium/chloride cotransporter NCC encoded by SLC12A3 in the distal convoluted tubule, where inhibition reduces sodium reabsorption and promotes natriuresis, kaliuresis, and secondary water loss. After oral administration, polythiazide is absorbed sufficiently for clinical effect, distributed systemically with activity at the kidney, undergoes limited hepatic biotransformation compared with extensively metabolized drugs, and is eliminated predominantly by renal excretion, with a relatively prolonged duration consistent with once-daily use. It is indicated for hypertension and edema, including fluid retention associated with congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, corticosteroid therapy, or renal disorders. Adverse effects and toxicity reflect exaggerated diuresis and electrolyte loss, including hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia, dehydration, orthostatic hypotension, metabolic alkalosis, hyperuricemia precipitating gout, hyperglycemia, and occasional sulfonamide-type hypersensitivity such as rash or photosensitivity; severe overdose may produce profound volume depletion, weakness, arrhythmia, or confusion. Clinically, polythiazide has been used alone or with other antihypertensives to lower blood pressure and to mobilize edema when a long-acting oral thiazide is desired.

Name: Cefamandole
Description: Cefamandole (DrugBank DB01326) is a semisynthetic second-generation cephalosporin antibiotic, usually administered clinically as the water-soluble prodrug cefamandole nafate, and structurally characterized by the classical cephem nucleus: a strained beta-lactam fused to a dihydrothiazine ring, with an aminophenylacetamido-type acyl side chain at the 7-position and a heterocyclic substituent at the 3-position that modulates antibacterial spectrum and stability. Chemically it belongs to the beta-lactam/cephalosporin class, and its core scaffold is the 7-aminocephalosporanic acid cephem framework shared with related agents such as cephalothin, cefazolin, cefuroxime, and cefoxitin, which are considered pharmacologically similar comparators. Its antibacterial activity arises from covalent acylation of bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, particularly transpeptidases involved in peptidoglycan cross-linking, with inhibition of cell-wall synthesis and consequent bactericidal activity. Cefamandole is given parenterally, achieves broad distribution into extracellular fluids and many tissues, has limited oral bioavailability, minimal metabolism apart from prodrug conversion, low protein binding relative to some cephalosporins, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by the kidney with a short plasma half-life requiring repeated dosing; dose adjustment is therefore important in renal impairment. It has been used for susceptible respiratory tract infections, skin and soft tissue infections, urinary tract infections, intra-abdominal or gynecologic infections, septicemia, bone and joint infections, and perioperative prophylaxis. Adverse effects include hypersensitivity reactions, rash, fever, eosinophilia, diarrhea, phlebitis, and positive Coombs test, while important toxicities include bleeding or hypoprothrombinemia and disulfiram-like reactions with ethanol, reflecting its methylthiotetrazole-associated liability, with rare nephrotoxicity, superinfection, or Clostridioides difficile-associated colitis.

Name: Cefazolin
Description: Cefazolin (DrugBank DB01327) is a first-generation cephalosporin beta-lactam antibiotic whose structure consists of the characteristic cephem nucleus, a strained four-membered beta-lactam ring fused to a dihydrothiazine ring, bearing a tetrazolylacetamido side chain at the 7-position and a thiadiazolyl-thiomethyl substituent at the 3-position that enhance antistaphylococcal activity and parenteral stability; chemically it is a semisynthetic cephalosporin, and its core scaffold is the 7-aminocephalosporanic acid/cephem framework. Similar drugs include other first-generation cephalosporins such as cephalexin, cephradine, and cephalothin, as well as later cephalosporins that retain the same beta-lactam pharmacophore. Cefazolin targets bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, particularly transpeptidases including PBP1, PBP2, and PBP3 in susceptible organisms, thereby inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-linking and bacterial cell-wall synthesis. It is indicated for susceptible infections caused mainly by methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus and streptococci, including skin and soft-tissue infection, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, bacteremia, urinary tract infection, biliary tract infection, pneumonia, and perioperative surgical prophylaxis. Pharmacokinetically, cefazolin is not meaningfully absorbed orally and is administered intravenously or intramuscularly, distributes well into extracellular fluids, bone, skin, and synovial tissues with limited cerebrospinal fluid penetration, is minimally metabolized, is highly protein bound, and is eliminated largely unchanged by the kidney with dose adjustment in renal impairment. Toxicities include hypersensitivity reactions, beta-lactam anaphylaxis, interstitial nephritis, neurotoxicity or seizures with accumulation, hematologic abnormalities, and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea; common adverse effects include rash, pruritus, nausea, diarrhea, injection-site pain, transient transaminase elevation, eosinophilia, and positive Coombs test. Clinically, it is widely used as a narrow, MSSA-active parenteral agent and as a standard prophylactic antibiotic before orthopedic, cardiac, vascular, and abdominal surgery.

Name: Cefonicid
Description: Cefonicid (DrugBank DB01328) is a semisynthetic second-generation cephalosporin antibiotic built on the cephem beta-lactam scaffold, consisting of a strained four-membered beta-lactam ring fused to a dihydrothiazine ring and bearing side-chain substitutions that enhance beta-lactamase stability and confer prolonged plasma persistence; chemically it is an oxyimino aminothiazolyl cephalosporin and thus belongs to the beta-lactam/cephalosporin class. Its core scaffold and antibacterial profile make it structurally and pharmacologically similar to other parenteral cephalosporins such as cefamandole, ceforanide, cefuroxime, and ceftriaxone, although cefonicid is especially notable for a relatively long elimination half-life among older cephalosporins. Like other cephalosporins, it targets bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, particularly transpeptidases involved in peptidoglycan cross-linking, thereby inhibiting cell-wall synthesis and causing bacterial lysis. It is administered parenterally, is well distributed into extracellular fluids and many tissues, shows high plasma protein binding, undergoes minimal metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by the kidney, with dosage reduction typically required in renal impairment. Cefonicid has been used for susceptible infections of the respiratory tract, skin and soft tissue, bone and joint, and urinary tract, and for perioperative prophylaxis, for example in postoperative wound infection prevention. Adverse effects resemble those of other cephalosporins and include injection-site pain, rash, pruritus, diarrhea, nausea, eosinophilia, and transient hepatic enzyme elevations; toxicities include hypersensitivity reactions up to anaphylaxis, Clostridioides difficile-associated colitis, rare hematologic abnormalities, and potential neurotoxicity or drug accumulation in severe renal dysfunction.

Name: Cefotetan
Description: Cefotetan (DrugBank DB01330) is a semisynthetic second-generation cephamycin beta-lactam antibiotic whose structure is built on the 7-aminocephalosporanic acid–like cephem nucleus, featuring the fused beta-lactam–dihydrothiazine bicyclic core, a 7-alpha-methoxy substituent that confers cephamycin character and enhanced beta-lactamase stability, and a 3-position N-methylthiotetrazole-containing side chain associated with characteristic adverse effects; chemically it belongs to the cephalosporin/cephamycin class, and its core scaffold is the methoxy-substituted cephem beta-lactam. Similar drugs include cefoxitin, cefmetazole, cefotaxime, cefuroxime, and other broad-spectrum cephalosporins, especially cephamycins with anaerobic activity. Its antibacterial effect arises from binding bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, particularly transpeptidases involved in peptidoglycan cross-linking, thereby inhibiting cell-wall synthesis and causing lysis. Pharmacokinetically, cefotetan is given parenterally because oral absorption is negligible, distributes well into extracellular fluids and peritoneal and pelvic tissues, shows moderate protein binding, undergoes minimal metabolism, and is eliminated largely unchanged by the kidney with a relatively long cephamycin half-life, so dose reduction is required in renal impairment. Toxicity includes hypersensitivity reactions, positive Coombs test, hematologic effects, superinfection, and N-methylthiotetrazole-related hypoprothrombinemia/bleeding and disulfiram-like reactions with ethanol. Target proteins are bacterial PBPs rather than human proteins. Clinically it is used for susceptible intra-abdominal, gynecologic, urinary tract, skin/soft tissue, bone/joint, and lower respiratory infections, and for perioperative prophylaxis, especially where mixed aerobic-anaerobic flora such as Bacteroides fragilis are suspected; common side effects include diarrhea, nausea, rash, injection-site pain, fever, candidiasis, and transient liver enzyme elevation.

Name: Cefoxitin
Description: Cefoxitin (DrugBank DB01331) is a semisynthetic cephamycin β-lactam antibiotic structurally defined by the cephem nucleus, consisting of a fused β-lactam and dihydrothiazine ring system bearing a 7α-methoxy substituent that confers relative β-lactamase stability, a 7-acylamino side chain, and a 3-carbamoyloxymethyl substituent important for antibacterial activity; chemically it belongs to the second-generation cephalosporin/cephamycin class and is built on the cepham scaffold. Closely related or similar drugs include cefotetan and cefmetazole among cephamycins, and broader second-generation cephalosporin comparators such as cefuroxime. Its antibacterial effect results from binding bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, particularly transpeptidases such as PBP1A, PBP1B, PBP2, and PBP3, thereby inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-linking and cell-wall synthesis. Cefoxitin is administered parenterally because oral absorption is negligible; it distributes mainly in extracellular fluid with useful penetration into peritoneal fluid, soft tissues, bone, and urine, shows low to moderate protein binding, undergoes minimal metabolism, and is eliminated largely unchanged by the kidney with a short elimination half-life, so exposure is prolonged in renal impairment. It is indicated for susceptible infections including intra-abdominal and pelvic infections, gynecologic infections, skin and soft-tissue infections, bone and joint infections, urinary tract infections, lower respiratory tract infections, and perioperative prophylaxis, especially where anaerobes such as Bacteroides fragilis are concerns. Toxicities and adverse effects include hypersensitivity reactions, rash, urticaria, fever, anaphylaxis, gastrointestinal upset, diarrhea including Clostridioides difficile colitis, transient aminotransferase elevation, eosinophilia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, local phlebitis or pain at injection sites, and rare seizures with high levels or renal dysfunction.

Name: Ceftizoxime
Description: Ceftizoxime (DrugBank DB01332) is a semisynthetic third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic built on the cephem/beta-lactam scaffold, consisting of a fused beta-lactam and dihydrothiazine ring system with a syn-methoxyimino aminothiazolyl acyl side chain at the 7-position that enhances stability to many beta-lactamases, and a heterocyclic thio-substituent at the 3-position that influences antibacterial spectrum and pharmacokinetics; chemically it is a beta-lactam, specifically an oxyimino-cephalosporin, and is structurally similar to cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, ceftazidime, and cefmenoxime. Its antibacterial effect results from binding bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, particularly transpeptidases such as PBP1 and PBP3 in susceptible Gram-negative organisms, thereby inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-linking and cell-wall synthesis. Ceftizoxime is administered parenterally because oral absorption is negligible; it distributes well into extracellular fluids and many tissues, including peritoneal fluid, skin, lung, bone, urine, and inflamed cerebrospinal fluid, shows low to moderate protein binding, undergoes minimal metabolism, and is eliminated largely unchanged by the kidney via glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, giving a relatively short half-life that is prolonged in renal impairment. Toxicities are typical of cephalosporins and include hypersensitivity reactions up to anaphylaxis, positive Coombs test, eosinophilia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, rare interstitial nephritis, and antibiotic-associated colitis from Clostridioides difficile. Adverse effects commonly include rash, fever, diarrhea, nausea, injection-site pain, and transient elevations in hepatic enzymes. Clinically, it is used for susceptible respiratory tract, urinary tract, skin and soft-tissue, intra-abdominal, gynecologic, bone and joint, and bloodstream infections, for example pneumonia, pyelonephritis, pelvic inflammatory infection, peritonitis, cellulitis, and sepsis.

Name: Cefradine
Description: Cefradine (DrugBank DB01333) is a first-generation cephalosporin beta-lactam antibiotic whose structure consists of the canonical cephem nucleus, a bicyclic beta-lactam fused to a dihydrothiazine ring, bearing a 7-aminoacyl side chain closely related to that of cephalexin and a 3-methyl substituent that supports acid stability and oral activity; chemically it is classified as a semisynthetic cephalosporin, with a 7-aminocephalosporanic acid-derived scaffold. Its closest similar drugs include cephalexin, cefadroxil, cephalothin, and cefazolin, which share the same beta-lactam pharmacophore and broadly similar antibacterial spectrum against susceptible gram-positive cocci and some gram-negative organisms. Cefradine acts by binding bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, particularly transpeptidases involved in peptidoglycan cross-linking, thereby inhibiting cell-wall synthesis and causing bactericidal lysis. After oral administration it is well absorbed, and it can also be given parenterally; protein binding is low to moderate, tissue penetration is adequate for skin, soft tissue, respiratory, and urinary sites, metabolism is minimal, and elimination occurs largely as unchanged drug by renal glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, producing a short half-life that is prolonged in renal impairment. Toxicity is generally low but includes class-associated hypersensitivity reactions ranging from rash and urticaria to anaphylaxis, gastrointestinal intolerance, antibiotic-associated colitis, rare interstitial nephritis, eosinophilia, neutropenia, and very rarely seizures at high concentrations or in renal failure. Clinically it has been used for susceptible urinary tract infections, pharyngitis, tonsillitis, otitis media, bronchitis, pneumonia, and skin and soft tissue infections, with common adverse effects including nausea, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, candidiasis, and allergic rash.

Name: Cilazapril
Description: Cilazapril (DrugBank DB01340) is a dicarboxylate-containing angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor of the peptidomimetic, proline-derived class, administered as an ester prodrug whose structure features a bicyclic or conformationally constrained amino acid-like core with a hydrolyzable ester, a secondary amide, and terminal carboxyl functionality that, after activation to cilazaprilat, supports high-affinity zinc-dependent ACE binding; its chemical scaffold is closely related to other non-sulfhydryl ACE inhibitors built on a diacid/proline mimic framework, and similar drugs include enalapril, ramipril, perindopril, quinapril, benazepril, and lisinopril. Its principal target protein is angiotensin-converting enzyme, with consequent reduction of angiotensin II formation and aldosterone secretion and increased bradykinin tone. Pharmacokinetically, oral cilazapril is absorbed as a prodrug and rapidly hydrolyzed by esterases to the active metabolite cilazaprilat; bioavailability of active drug is moderate, protein binding is limited to moderate, tissue distribution includes vascular ACE sites, metabolism beyond ester cleavage is minimal, and elimination is predominantly renal, with prolonged exposure in renal impairment requiring dose adjustment. It is indicated mainly for hypertension and has also been used in chronic heart failure and other settings where renin-angiotensin system blockade is beneficial. Adverse effects are typical of ACE inhibition and include cough, dizziness, headache, hypotension, fatigue, hyperkalemia, and rises in serum creatinine; important toxicities include first-dose syncope, renal failure in bilateral renal artery stenosis, angioedema, and rare severe hypersensitivity, while overdose may produce marked hypotension. Clinically, cilazapril is used as monotherapy or with diuretics for blood-pressure control and for symptomatic improvement and afterload reduction in selected heart-failure patients.

Name: Spirapril
Description: Spirapril (DB01348) is a prodrug angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor of the dicarboxylate class, structurally characterized by a peptidomimetic, proline-containing framework bearing carboxylate and ester functionalities and a lipophilic bicyclic/aryl-substituted side chain that is hydrolyzed in vivo to the active diacid spiraprilat; chemically it belongs to antihypertensive ACE inhibitors and is built on the classic amino acid–derived ACE-inhibitor scaffold related to captopril-free sulfhydryl-lacking agents such as enalapril, ramipril, quinapril, perindopril, benazepril, cilazapril, and trandolapril. Its principal target is angiotensin-converting enzyme, with consequent reduction in angiotensin II formation and aldosterone secretion and increased bradykinin activity. After oral administration, spirapril is absorbed as the ester prodrug, converted by hepatic and plasma esterases to spiraprilat, distributed systemically with meaningful ACE binding in plasma and tissues, and eliminated by combined renal and biliary/fecal routes; like other agents in its class, food may modestly affect absorption, and renal impairment can increase exposure to the active metabolite. Clinically it is indicated primarily for essential hypertension, and has also been used in settings where ACE inhibition is desirable, such as hypertensive patients with cardiovascular risk or impaired ventricular function. Adverse effects resemble the class profile and include cough, dizziness, hypotension, headache, fatigue, nausea, hyperkalemia, and renal function deterioration; important toxicities include first-dose syncope, azotemia in renal artery stenosis, rare angioedema, cholestatic or hepatic reactions, neutropenia in susceptible patients, and marked fetotoxicity in pregnancy. In practice, spirapril has been used as oral long-term antihypertensive monotherapy or in combination with diuretics or other agents to improve blood pressure control and reduce afterload.

Name: Tasosartan
Description: Tasosartan (DB01349) is a nonpeptide angiotensin II receptor antagonist of the biphenyl-tetrazole antihypertensive class, built around the canonical sartan scaffold consisting of a lipophilic biphenyl core linked to an acidic tetrazole bioisostere and a heteroaryl imidazole-related moiety that confers high affinity for the angiotensin II type 1 receptor; structurally and pharmacologically it is closely related to other ARBs such as losartan, valsartan, irbesartan, candesartan, and eprosartan, with particular similarity to early biphenyl-tetrazole sartans. Its principal known target is AGTR1, with therapeutic action deriving from blockade of angiotensin II-mediated vasoconstriction, aldosterone release, sympathetic facilitation, and renal sodium retention; AGTR2 is not considered the main therapeutic target. It was investigated primarily for hypertension and potentially other renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system-driven states such as heart failure or diabetic nephropathy, where lowering blood pressure and reducing proteinuric renal stress would be clinically relevant. Pharmacokinetically, tasosartan is orally active, absorbed systemically, distributed in the vascular compartment with expected moderate to high protein binding, and undergoes hepatic biotransformation to an active metabolite that contributes materially to AT1 blockade, followed by elimination through combined biliary/fecal and renal routes. Adverse effects are generally ARB-like, including dizziness, headache, fatigue, hypotension, hyperkalemia, and renal function worsening in susceptible patients such as those with renal artery stenosis or volume depletion. Toxicity concerns include excessive hypotension, azotemia, potassium elevation, and class-associated fetofetal toxicity in pregnancy; development was also limited by safety findings including liver injury signals in some studies, which constrained broad clinical use.

Name: Amobarbital
Description: Amobarbital (DrugBank DB01351) is a medium-acting barbiturate whose structure is that of a 5,5-disubstituted barbituric acid, specifically a pyrimidine-2,4,6-trione ring bearing ethyl and isoamyl substituents at C5, which confers substantial lipophilicity and central nervous system depressant activity; it therefore belongs to the barbiturate sedative-hypnotic class and is built on the barbituric acid scaffold. Closely related drugs include phenobarbital, pentobarbital, secobarbital, butabarbital, and thiopental, which share the same core heterocycle but differ in C5 substitution and duration of action. Its principal pharmacologic targets are GABAA receptor chloride channel complexes, where it positively modulates inhibitory neurotransmission and, at higher concentrations, can directly gate the channel; functional effects may involve receptor subtypes containing GABRA, GABRB, and GABRG family subunits. Amobarbital is generally well absorbed after oral or parenteral administration, distributes widely including across the blood-brain barrier and placenta, is moderately protein bound, undergoes primarily hepatic oxidative biotransformation with some renal elimination of metabolites and unchanged drug, and has an intermediate elimination half-life consistent with medium duration of action. It has been used for short-term treatment of insomnia, preoperative sedation, and procedural anxiolysis, and historically in narcoanalysis or the amobarbital interview. Toxicity is typical of barbiturates and includes dose-dependent respiratory depression, coma, hypotension, impaired psychomotor function, paradoxical agitation, tolerance, dependence, and potentially fatal overdose, especially with alcohol, opioids, or other sedatives; common adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, confusion, ataxia, headache, nausea, and residual next-day sedation.

Name: Aprobarbital
Description: Aprobarbital (DrugBank DB01352) is a short- to intermediate-acting barbiturate sedative-hypnotic built on a 5,5-disubstituted barbituric acid core, specifically a pyrimidine-2,4,6-trione ring bearing alkyl substituents that increase lipophilicity and central nervous system penetration; chemically it belongs to the barbiturate class, and its defining scaffold is the substituted barbiturate or malonylurea nucleus shared with related agents such as amobarbital, pentobarbital, secobarbital, phenobarbital, and aprobarbital analogs used historically as sedatives, anticonvulsants, or anesthetic adjuncts. Like other barbiturates, it acts primarily as a positive allosteric modulator of GABAA receptor chloride channels, with functional targets centered on GABAA receptor subunit-containing complexes and, at higher concentrations, direct GABA-mimetic channel activation and suppression of excitatory neurotransmission. It was used clinically for insomnia, anxiety, and short-term sedation, including preoperative calming and relief of agitation. Pharmacokinetically, aprobarbital is generally well absorbed orally, distributes widely with substantial brain uptake and variable plasma protein binding, undergoes predominant hepatic biotransformation via oxidation and other microsomal pathways, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine with a smaller fraction of unchanged drug excreted renally; duration is influenced by lipophilicity, redistribution, liver function, and urinary pH. Toxicity is typical of barbiturates and includes dose-related CNS and respiratory depression, coma, hypotension, impaired psychomotor performance, and potentially fatal overdose, especially with alcohol, opioids, or other sedatives. Adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, ataxia, confusion, cognitive slowing, paradoxical excitement, tolerance, dependence, and withdrawal phenomena such as tremor, delirium, or seizures, which sharply limited modern clinical use.

Name: Butobarbital
Description: Butobarbital (DrugBank DB01353) is a short- to intermediate-acting sedative-hypnotic barbiturate built on a 5,5-disubstituted barbituric acid core, specifically a pyrimidine-2,4,6-trione ring bearing butyl and ethyl substituents at C5, which confer substantial lipophilicity and central nervous system depressant activity; chemically it belongs to the barbiturates, and its defining scaffold is the barbiturate ureide heterocycle shared with other sedative-hypnotics. Structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include secobarbital, pentobarbital, amobarbital, phenobarbital, and aprobarbital, which differ mainly in C5 substitution and duration of action. Its principal molecular target is the GABAA receptor chloride channel complex, at which barbiturates act as positive allosteric modulators and, at higher concentrations, direct channel activators; functional interactions with excitatory glutamatergic signaling may also contribute to CNS depression. After oral administration, butobarbital is generally well absorbed, distributes widely including across the blood-brain barrier, is moderately protein bound, undergoes hepatic biotransformation primarily by oxidation and related metabolic pathways, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine with some unchanged drug possible. Toxicity is characteristic of barbiturates and includes dose-dependent sedation, cognitive and psychomotor impairment, ataxia, hypotension, coma, and potentially fatal respiratory depression, especially in overdose or when combined with ethanol, opioids, or other sedatives; tolerance, dependence, and withdrawal seizures may occur with prolonged use. Clinically, it has been used for short-term management of insomnia and as a sedative for anxiety, agitation, or preprocedural calming, while common adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, headache, nausea, confusion, hangover effects, and impaired coordination.

Name: Mestranol
Description: Mestranol (DB01357) is a synthetic steroidal estrogen characterized structurally as the 3-methyl ether prodrug of ethinyl estradiol, built on the rigid estrane/gonane tetracyclic steroid nucleus with an aromatic A-ring, a 17β-hydroxyl group, and a 17α-ethynyl substituent that enhances oral activity; chemically it belongs to semisynthetic estrogenic hormones, with an estradiol-derived ethinyl estrane scaffold. Closely related drugs include ethinyl estradiol, estradiol, quinestrol, and other estrogenic oral contraceptive components such as mestranol-containing combinations with norethindrone. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed, undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic O-demethylation to the active metabolite ethinyl estradiol, is extensively protein bound in plasma, distributes broadly to estrogen-responsive tissues, is further metabolized by hepatic oxidation and conjugation pathways, and is excreted in urine and bile with enterohepatic recycling contributing to persistence of effect. Its principal pharmacologic targets are estrogen receptors ESR1 and ESR2, altering transcription of estrogen-responsive genes and suppressing gonadotropin-driven ovulation in contraceptive regimens. Indications have primarily included combined hormonal contraception and historically management of menstrual disorders, dysmenorrhea, and estrogen-responsive symptoms. Adverse effects are typical of estrogens and include nausea, breast tenderness, headache, fluid retention, breakthrough bleeding, melasma, and hypertension. Important toxicities include venous thromboembolism, stroke, myocardial infarction, cholestatic jaundice, hepatic dysfunction or rare hepatic adenoma risk, and stimulation of hormone-sensitive malignancies in susceptible patients; overdose may cause nausea or withdrawal bleeding. Clinically, mestranol has mainly been used in low-dose combination oral contraceptives rather than as a standalone estrogen.

Name: Penbutolol
Description: Penbutolol (DrugBank DB01359) is a lipophilic aryloxypropanolamine beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist whose structure consists of the classic beta-blocker pharmacophore, an aromatic ring linked through an ether oxygen to a 2-hydroxy-3-isopropylaminopropyl side chain, further distinguished by a bulky tert-butyl-substituted phenyl moiety that increases membrane permeability and contributes to partial agonist properties reported for the class; chemically it is categorized as a nonselective beta blocker and more specifically an aryloxypropanolamine, with an aryloxypropanolamine scaffold shared by related agents such as propranolol, pindolol, timolol, nadolol, and bopindolol. Its principal targets are beta-1 adrenergic receptor and beta-2 adrenergic receptor, with antihypertensive activity mediated by reduction in heart rate, cardiac output, and renin release. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed, but systemic availability is moderated by first-pass hepatic metabolism; it distributes widely because of high lipophilicity, is metabolized in the liver to inactive or less active metabolites, and is eliminated through both renal and biliary/fecal pathways, with a duration of action compatible with once-daily antihypertensive use. Toxicity is typical of beta blockade and includes excessive bradycardia, hypotension, atrioventricular block, acute worsening of heart failure, and bronchospasm, especially in asthma or COPD, while overdose may produce severe cardiovascular depression and hypoglycemia masking. Adverse effects include fatigue, dizziness, cold extremities, depression, sleep disturbance, sexual dysfunction, nausea, and exercise intolerance. Clinically, penbutolol has been used primarily for hypertension and occasionally for symptomatic states driven by adrenergic excess such as palpitations or tachycardia, particularly when long-acting nonselective beta blockade is desired.

Name: Ephedrine
Description: Ephedrine (DrugBank DB01364) is a naturally derived and synthetic phenylpropylamine sympathomimetic whose structure consists of a substituted benzene ring attached to a two-carbon side chain bearing a beta-hydroxyl group and a secondary N-methylamino center, creating a chiral phenethylamine/phenylpropanolamine framework with stereochemistry important for activity; chemically it belongs to the alkaloid-like arylalkanolamine class and is built on the phenethylamine scaffold closely related to phenylpropanolamine. Similar drugs include pseudoephedrine, norepinephrine, amphetamine, methamphetamine, and other mixed-acting adrenergic agonists such as metaraminol. Its pharmacology reflects direct and indirect sympathomimetic action at adrenergic targets, especially alpha-1, beta-1, and beta-2 adrenergic receptors via enhanced norepinephrine release and weaker direct receptor stimulation; relevant targets therefore include ADRA1 receptors, ADRB1, ADRB2, and presynaptic norepinephrine handling systems. Ephedrine is well absorbed orally and also active parenterally, distributes widely including across the blood-brain barrier, undergoes only limited hepatic metabolism with a substantial fraction excreted unchanged in urine, and has elimination strongly influenced by urinary pH, with acidification increasing renal clearance. Toxicity is primarily excessive sympathomimetic stimulation, causing hypertension, tachyarrhythmia, agitation, tremor, insomnia, psychosis, stroke, myocardial ischemia, and seizures, especially in overdose or with other stimulants or monoamine oxidase inhibitors. Clinically, ephedrine has been used for hypotension, particularly anesthesia-associated hypotension, bronchospasm in asthma, nasal congestion, and occasionally stress urinary incontinence, while common adverse effects include palpitations, nervousness, anxiety, headache, nausea, urinary retention, and reduced appetite.

Name: Mephentermine
Description: Mephentermine (DrugBank DB01365) is a synthetic sympathomimetic amine structurally characterized as an amphetamine-like phenethylamine bearing an alpha-methyl substituent and a N-methyl-N-(3-methylphenyl)-substituted side chain, giving a lipophilic aromatic amine framework that supports indirect adrenergic activity; chemically it is classified among substituted phenethylamines and pressor amines, with an amphetamine/phenylisopropylamine scaffold. It is closely related to other indirect-acting sympathomimetics such as methamphetamine, amphetamine, ephedrine, pseudoephedrine, and phentermine, which share catecholamine-releasing or adrenergic-stimulating properties. Its principal pharmacologic targets are not highly selective receptor-binding proteins but the adrenergic system functionally, especially norepinephrine handling at sympathetic nerve terminals, with downstream activation of alpha-1 adrenergic receptor-mediated vasoconstriction and beta-1 adrenergic receptor-mediated cardiac stimulation; monoamine transporters such as the norepinephrine transporter are also plausibly involved in its indirect mechanism. After parenteral administration, absorption is rapid, distribution is systemic with CNS penetration expected for a lipophilic amine, metabolism occurs mainly in the liver by oxidative and dealkylative pathways, and renal excretion eliminates parent drug and metabolites, with urinary pH influencing clearance as with related amines. Clinically, it is used primarily as a vasopressor for hypotension, especially anesthesia-associated, spinal anesthesia-related, or perioperative blood pressure collapse. Adverse effects and toxicity reflect excessive sympathomimetic stimulation, including hypertension, tachycardia, palpitations, arrhythmias, anxiety, tremor, insomnia, headache, urinary retention, and possible cerebral hemorrhage, myocardial ischemia, or pulmonary edema in overdose or susceptible patients.

Name: Rasagiline
Description: Rasagiline (DB01367) is a small, lipophilic propargylamine whose structure consists of an indane bicyclic aromatic scaffold bearing a chiral aminopropynyl substituent, typically used clinically as the R-enantiomer; chemically it is classified as a monoamine oxidase inhibitor, specifically a selective, irreversible MAO-B inhibitor, with an aminoindan/propargylamine scaffold that it shares conceptually with other antiparkinsonian MAO inhibitors and related propargylamine agents. Similar drugs include selegiline, another irreversible MAO-B inhibitor that also contains a propargyl motif, and safinamide, a reversible MAO-B inhibitor with broader ion-channel effects. Rasagiline is well absorbed orally, undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, distributes systemically including CNS penetration, and is metabolized mainly by CYP1A2 to 1-aminoindan and other inactive metabolites; elimination is predominantly renal as metabolites with only limited unchanged drug excretion, and its terminal half-life is short despite prolonged pharmacodynamic action due to irreversible enzyme inhibition. Its principal target protein is monoamine oxidase B, reducing dopamine catabolism in the striatum and thereby improving dopaminergic tone. It is indicated for idiopathic Parkinson disease, including early monotherapy and adjunctive use with levodopa for motor fluctuations such as wearing-off. Adverse effects include headache, arthralgia, dyspepsia, insomnia, nausea, orthostatic symptoms, and when combined with levodopa, dyskinesia or hallucinations. Toxicity concerns include serotonergic toxicity with serotonergic drugs, hypertensive reactions with sympathomimetics or excessive tyramine exposure, and increased adverse CNS effects in overdose; clinically it is used to improve bradykinesia, rigidity, and fluctuation control in ambulatory Parkinsonian patients.

Name: Quinupristin
Description: Quinupristin (DB01369) is a semisynthetic streptogramin B antibiotic derived from pristinamycin, characterized structurally by a highly functionalized macrocyclic depsipeptide/lactone framework with multiple amide, ester, ketone, and unsaturated substituents that create a rigid lipophilic peptidic ring optimized for ribosomal binding; chemically it belongs to the streptogramin class, specifically the group B streptogramins, and its core scaffold is a macrocyclic depsipeptide related to pristinamycin IA and other synergistic streptogramins. Similar drugs include dalfopristin, with which it is coformulated as quinupristin/dalfopristin, as well as other streptogramin agents such as pristinamycin and virginiamycin components. Its principal target is the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit, binding at the 23S rRNA region of the peptidyl transferase center to inhibit protein synthesis, particularly in combination with dalfopristin, which enhances affinity and bactericidal activity. Pharmacokinetically, quinupristin is given intravenously because oral bioavailability is not clinically used, distributes well into many tissues but has limited cerebrospinal fluid penetration, is extensively metabolized hepatically, and is eliminated mainly through biliary/fecal routes with lesser renal excretion. Toxicity is dominated by infusion-related venous irritation, arthralgia, myalgia, hyperbilirubinemia, and hepatic enzyme elevation, with severe examples including clinically significant hepatotoxicity and intolerance in critically ill patients. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, rash, pain at the infusion site, and musculoskeletal symptoms. Clinically, it has been used for serious infections caused by susceptible gram-positive organisms, especially vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium bacteremia and complicated skin and soft tissue infections due to methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes, generally as a reserve agent when resistance or intolerance limits alternatives.

Name: Cortisone acetate
Description: Cortisone acetate (DrugBank DB01380) is the 21-acetate ester prodrug of cortisone, a naturally derived corticosteroid built on the pregnane steroid nucleus with the characteristic four fused cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene rings, ketones at C3 and C20, a Δ4-ene, an 11-keto group, a 17α-hydroxyl, and an acetylated 21-hydroxyl that increases oral utility; chemically it is a glucocorticoid corticosteroid, and its core scaffold is the hydrocortisone/cortisone adrenal steroid framework. Closely related drugs include cortisone, hydrocortisone, prednisone, prednisolone, methylprednisolone, and dexamethasone, which share the same steroidal anti-inflammatory pharmacophore with differing oxidation, double-bond, or substitution patterns. After oral or intramuscular administration, cortisone acetate is absorbed and deacetylated to cortisone, then converted mainly in the liver by 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 to the active metabolite hydrocortisone; glucocorticoids distribute widely, are substantially protein bound to transcortin and albumin, undergo hepatic reduction and conjugation, and are excreted predominantly as urinary metabolites. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, with indirect suppression of NF-κB and AP-1 signaling and feedback inhibition of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis; mineralocorticoid receptor activity is weaker but clinically relevant. It is indicated for adrenal insufficiency and for inflammatory, allergic, rheumatic, dermatologic, and some hematologic disorders, such as rheumatoid arthritis, asthma exacerbations, severe dermatitis, and lupus. Toxicity and adverse effects reflect chronic glucocorticoid excess, including hyperglycemia, hypertension, sodium and fluid retention, hypokalemia, infection risk, peptic ulcer, myopathy, osteoporosis, cataracts, glaucoma, mood changes, growth suppression, and adrenal suppression, while acute overdose is usually less dramatic than prolonged high-dose exposure. Clinically, it has been used as systemic replacement therapy in Addison disease and as an anti-inflammatory or immunosuppressive agent when corticosteroid responsiveness is desired.

Name: Glymidine
Description: Glymidine (DrugBank DB01382) is a first-generation sulfonylurea oral antihyperglycemic agent characterized structurally by the classic sulfonylurea pharmacophore, in which a substituted arylsulfonyl moiety is linked through a urea bridge to a heterocyclic amidine-containing side chain; chemically it belongs to the sulfonylurea class and is built on the aryl-sulfonylurea scaffold shared by early insulin secretagogues. It is therefore closely related to other first-generation sulfonylureas such as tolbutamide, chlorpropamide, acetohexamide, and tolazamide, which have similar glucose-lowering mechanisms but differ in substituent pattern and duration of action. Its principal pharmacologic target is the ATP-sensitive potassium channel of pancreatic beta cells, functionally via binding to the sulfonylurea receptor SUR1, part of the KCNJ11/ABCC8 channel complex, leading to membrane depolarization, calcium influx, and insulin release. Glymidine was indicated for type 2 diabetes mellitus, particularly non-insulin-dependent hyperglycemia inadequately controlled by diet alone. Like related agents, it is absorbed orally, distributed systemically with meaningful plasma protein binding, undergoes hepatic biotransformation, and is eliminated through renal excretion of parent drug and metabolites, with hypoglycemia risk increased by reduced clearance, hepatic dysfunction, or renal impairment. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related or prolonged hypoglycemia, which may present with sweating, tremor, confusion, seizures, or coma; other adverse effects include weight gain, nausea, dyspepsia, rash, and occasional hematologic or hepatic intolerance. Clinically, it was used as an older oral antidiabetic for chronic glycemic control, but has largely been superseded by newer agents with improved safety and pharmacokinetic profiles.

Name: Mibefradil
Description: Mibefradil (DB01388) is a tetralol-derived benzimidazolyl-substituted calcium channel blocker whose structure features a fluorobenzimidazole-containing aromatic system linked through a tertiary aminoalkyl chain to a highly substituted tetraline/tetralol core with ester functionality, placing it in the non-dihydropyridine calcium antagonist class and more specifically among tetraline-based T-type calcium channel inhibitors; its central scaffold is best described as a benzimidazole–tetraline hybrid. It is chemically and pharmacologically related to other calcium channel blockers, especially verapamil and diltiazem by functional class, although it is distinguished by relative selectivity for low-voltage-activated T-type calcium channels; it also shows some overlap with agents such as amlodipine and nifedipine in antihypertensive use. Its principal targets are voltage-gated calcium channels, particularly Cav3 T-type channels and to a lesser extent L-type channels in vascular smooth muscle and myocardium. Mibefradil was developed for hypertension and chronic stable angina, with clinical use aimed at lowering blood pressure and reducing anginal symptoms. Orally administered, it is well absorbed, undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, is highly protein bound, distributes widely, has an elimination half-life compatible with once-daily dosing, and is cleared mainly by hepatic metabolism with biliary/fecal excretion and lesser renal elimination. Its major toxicologic liability is potent inhibition of CYP3A4 and CYP2D6, causing serious drug-drug interactions, elevated concentrations of coadministered agents, bradycardia, hypotension, conduction disturbances, and rare severe cardiovascular collapse; adverse effects include dizziness, headache, fatigue, nausea, edema, flushing, and sinus bradycardia. These interaction-driven toxicities ultimately led to withdrawal from routine clinical use despite efficacy as an antihypertensive and antianginal drug.

Name: Bezafibrate
Description: Bezafibrate (DrugBank DB01393) is an aryloxyisobutyric acid derivative of the fibrate class, chemically characterized by a chlorobenzamide-linked phenoxyalkyl carboxylic acid architecture in which a para-chlorobenzamido substituent is attached to a phenoxy-2-methylpropionic acid framework; thus its core scaffold is the phenoxyisobutyric acid/fibric acid motif shared with related hypolipidemic agents. It is chemically and pharmacologically similar to other fibrates such as fenofibrate, gemfibrozil, ciprofibrate, and clofibrate, although bezafibrate is often described as a relatively broad peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor agonist. Its principal targets are PPARA, with activity also reported at PPARD and PPARG, leading to increased lipoprotein lipase activity, enhanced fatty acid oxidation, reduced hepatic triglyceride synthesis, and modulation of apolipoprotein expression. Clinically, it is indicated for hypertriglyceridemia, mixed hyperlipidemia, and dysbetalipoproteinemia, for example in patients with elevated triglycerides, low HDL cholesterol, or atherogenic diabetic dyslipidemia. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed, distributed with moderate to high plasma protein binding, undergoes limited hepatic biotransformation relative to some other fibrates, and is eliminated predominantly by the kidney as unchanged drug and conjugated metabolites, so exposure rises in renal impairment. Important toxicities include myopathy and rhabdomyolysis, especially with statins or renal dysfunction, hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevations, cholelithiasis from altered biliary lipid composition, and reversible increases in serum creatinine. Common adverse effects include dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, headache, rash, and muscle pain. In practice, bezafibrate is used as an adjunct to diet, weight loss, glycemic control, and other cardiovascular risk reduction measures when triglyceride lowering or mixed dyslipidemia management is required.

Name: Colchicine
Description: Colchicine (DB01394) is a tricyclic, highly oxygenated tropolone alkaloid natural product characterized by a 7-membered tropolone ring bearing a methoxy-substituted aromatic system and an acetamide-containing fused aryl framework, giving a rigid colchicinoid architecture; chemically it is classified as an antimitotic alkaloid and anti-inflammatory agent, with the colchicinoid/tropolone scaffold defining its activity. Structurally and pharmacologically related compounds include colchicoside derivatives and other tubulin-binding antimitotics such as vinca alkaloids, although these are not close scaffold analogs. Its principal target is tubulin, especially beta-tubulin within the colchicine-binding site of microtubules, leading to inhibition of microtubule polymerization, neutrophil chemotaxis, inflammasome signaling, and crystal-induced inflammation. Colchicine is well absorbed orally, undergoes extensive tissue distribution with leukocyte accumulation, is metabolized predominantly in the liver by CYP3A4 and transported by P-glycoprotein/ABCB1, and is eliminated through both biliary/fecal and renal routes; accumulation is increased in renal or hepatic impairment and with strong CYP3A4 or P-glycoprotein inhibitors. It is indicated for acute gout flares, gout prophylaxis during urate-lowering therapy, familial Mediterranean fever, and recurrent pericarditis, with clinical use also extending to crystal arthropathies and selected autoinflammatory conditions. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain, while toxicity may cause severe myelosuppression, rhabdomyolysis, peripheral neuropathy, multiorgan failure, and potentially fatal poisoning; examples of high-risk interactions include clarithromycin, cyclosporine, and certain azole antifungals, which can markedly increase exposure.

Name: Drospirenone
Description: Drospirenone (DrugBank DB01395) is a synthetic steroidal progestin structurally characterized by a 17-spirolactone derivative built on the cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene steroid nucleus, with features related to spironolactone and a lactone ring that confers antimineralocorticoid and antiandrogenic properties; chemically it is classified as a progestogen and pregnane-derived steroid analogue, with a spirolactone steroid scaffold. Closely related or pharmacologically similar drugs include spironolactone, progesterone, dienogest, desogestrel, levonorgestrel, and other combined oral contraceptive progestins such as norethindrone. It acts primarily at the progesterone receptor, and also shows antagonistic activity at the mineralocorticoid receptor and androgen receptor, with clinical effects mediated mainly through PGR, NR3C2, and AR. After oral administration it is rapidly absorbed with high bioavailability, reaches peak plasma concentrations within a few hours, is highly albumin bound, is not appreciably bound to sex hormone-binding globulin, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism largely independent of CYP-mediated biotransformation with some contribution from CYP3A4, and is eliminated as metabolites in urine and feces with an elimination half-life around 30 hours. Its main indications are contraception, premenstrual dysphoric disorder, acne associated with hormonal contraception, and treatment of menopausal symptoms in combination with estrogens. Adverse effects include nausea, breast tenderness, headache, irregular uterine bleeding, mood changes, and hyperkalemia; important toxicities include venous thromboembolism risk when combined with ethinyl estradiol and potassium elevation, especially in renal impairment, adrenal insufficiency, hepatic disease, or with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs, or potassium-sparing diuretics. Clinically, it is widely used in combined oral contraceptives and in estrogen-drospirenone formulations for women needing contraception with reduced androgenic effects or menopausal hormone therapy.

Name: Salsalate
Description: Salsalate (DrugBank DB01399) is a nonacetylated salicylate NSAID chemically defined as the salicylic acid dimer salicylsalicylic acid, in which two benzene rings each bearing an ortho-hydroxyl group are linked through a salicylate ester, giving a diaromatic hydroxybenzoate structure; its chemical category is salicylates and more broadly aromatic carboxylic acid anti-inflammatory agents, and its core scaffold is a salicylic acid/2-hydroxybenzoic acid biaryl-ester framework. Closely related or mechanistically similar drugs include aspirin, diflunisal, choline magnesium trisalicylate, sodium salicylate, and other NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen, although salsalate differs by lacking aspirin’s acetyl group. After oral administration it is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract and hydrolyzed in the intestine, plasma, and liver to salicylic acid, the active moiety; salicylate distributes widely, is substantially albumin bound, undergoes dose-dependent hepatic conjugation to salicyluric acid and phenolic/acyl glucuronides, and is excreted primarily in urine, with renal clearance increased by urinary alkalinization. Its principal pharmacologic targets are prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthases PTGS1 and PTGS2 via salicylate-mediated inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis, with additional anti-inflammatory effects reported on NF-kB signaling. It is indicated for symptomatic relief of rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, and other musculoskeletal pain or inflammatory states. Adverse effects include dyspepsia, nausea, tinnitus, dizziness, headache, and rash; toxicities resemble salicylism, with overdose causing vomiting, tinnitus, hyperventilation, acid-base disturbance, dehydration, and rarely renal injury or gastrointestinal bleeding. Clinically, it has been used as an oral anti-inflammatory and analgesic when a salicylate is desired with relatively less direct gastric irritation than aspirin.

Name: Neostigmine
Description: Neostigmine (DrugBank DB01400) is a synthetic quaternary ammonium carbamate characterized structurally by a permanently charged trimethylammonium-substituted aromatic ring linked to a dimethylcarbamyl ester, placing it in the cholinesterase inhibitor class and more specifically among reversible carbamate acetylcholinesterase inhibitors; its core scaffold is an aryl carbamate bearing a quaternary anilinium/phenyltrimethylammonium motif that limits blood-brain barrier penetration. Closely related drugs include pyridostigmine, physostigmine, ambenonium, and the depolarizing-context comparator edrophonium, all used to enhance cholinergic transmission by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, with principal targets including acetylcholinesterase and, less selectively, butyrylcholinesterase. Pharmacokinetically, neostigmine is incompletely and variably absorbed after oral dosing, is more predictably effective when given intravenous, intramuscular, or subcutaneous, distributes largely in extracellular fluid with poor CNS entry because of its quaternary charge, undergoes partial hepatic metabolism and hydrolysis, and is eliminated substantially by the kidney, with a relatively short duration requiring repeated dosing or procedural use. It is indicated for myasthenia gravis, reversal of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade after anesthesia, and postoperative urinary retention or paralytic ileus in selected cases. Toxicity reflects excessive cholinergic stimulation, with examples including bradycardia, bronchospasm, hypersalivation, abdominal cramping, diarrhea, miosis, sweating, muscle fasciculations, weakness, and in overdose cholinergic crisis with respiratory compromise; accordingly atropine or glycopyrrolate is often coadministered perioperatively. Clinical use includes routine operating-room reversal of rocuronium- or vecuronium-induced blockade and symptomatic improvement of fatigable weakness in myasthenia gravis.

Name: Danazol
Description: Danazol (DrugBank DB01406) is a synthetic attenuated androgen derived from the steroid nucleus, structurally characterized as an isoxazole-fused 17α-ethinyl testosterone analogue with a rigid four-ring androstane scaffold, making it a heterocyclic anabolic-androgenic steroid and antigonadotropic agent. Its core chemical category is a synthetic steroid hormone derivative, and its scaffold is best described as an androstane steroid framework modified by an isoxazole ring fusion that distinguishes it from simpler testosterone congeners. Similar drugs include gestrinone, stanozolol, methyltestosterone, testosterone derivatives, and other endocrine modulators such as leuprolide in overlapping therapeutic settings. Danazol acts through interaction with the androgen receptor, progesterone receptor, and glucocorticoid receptor, while functionally suppressing pituitary output of luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone and reducing ovarian estrogen synthesis; it also increases C1 esterase inhibitor levels in hereditary angioedema. It is orally absorbed, highly protein bound, widely distributed, hepatically metabolized mainly by CYP3A4 to active and inactive metabolites including ethisterone-related products, and eliminated primarily in urine with some fecal excretion; the terminal half-life is typically in the low-to-mid teens of hours but can vary with formulation and dose. Clinically, it is used for endometriosis, fibrocystic breast disease, and prevention of hereditary angioedema attacks, with examples including pelvic pain and dysmenorrhea from endometriosis or recurrent laryngeal edema prophylaxis. Toxicities reflect androgenic and hepatic risk, including virilization, menstrual disturbance, weight gain, acne, edema, adverse lipid changes, thromboembolism, benign intracranial hypertension, and serious hepatotoxicity such as cholestatic jaundice, peliosis hepatis, and hepatic adenoma.

Name: Tiotropium
Description: Tiotropium (DrugBank DB01409) is a long-acting quaternary ammonium antimuscarinic bronchodilator whose structure is a tropane-based bicyclic ester bearing two thiophene-containing aromatic ester substituents and a permanently charged nitrogen, a feature that limits membrane penetration and contributes to prolonged airway residence; chemically it belongs to the anticholinergic bronchodilators, specifically long-acting muscarinic antagonists, and its core scaffold is a substituted N-quaternized tropane closely related to atropine-like alkaloid pharmacophores. Similar drugs include ipratropium, aclidinium, glycopyrrolate, umeclidinium, and older antimuscarinics such as atropine. Its pharmacological targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially CHRM3 and CHRM1, with slower dissociation from CHRM3 than from CHRM2, producing sustained bronchodilation. After inhalation, systemic absorption is limited but measurable, oral bioavailability is very low, protein binding is modest, distribution is largely extracellular, metabolism is limited with a substantial fraction excreted unchanged in urine, and terminal elimination is prolonged enough to support once-daily dosing; renal impairment increases exposure. Tiotropium is indicated primarily for maintenance treatment of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, including chronic bronchitis and emphysema, and is also used as maintenance therapy in asthma inadequately controlled on inhaled corticosteroids, improving airflow limitation, dyspnea, and exacerbation risk rather than relieving acute bronchospasm. Adverse effects and toxicity reflect anticholinergic activity, with dry mouth most common, plus constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, tachycardia, and possible precipitation of narrow-angle glaucoma; overdose can produce exaggerated peripheral antimuscarinic effects, though severe central toxicity is less prominent because of poor blood-brain barrier penetration.

Name: Ciclesonide
Description: Ciclesonide (DrugBank DB01410) is a nonhalogenated inhaled corticosteroid prodrug built on the pregnane glucocorticoid steroid nucleus, specifically a lipophilic corticosteroid scaffold bearing the characteristic four fused rings with a 16,17-acetal/butyryloxy-type substitution and a 21-isobutyrate ester that enhances airway delivery and local activation; chemically it belongs to corticosteroid esters and is closely related to other inhaled glucocorticoids such as budesonide, beclomethasone dipropionate, fluticasone propionate, and mometasone furoate. After oral inhalation or intranasal administration, pulmonary or nasal esterases rapidly convert ciclesonide to the active metabolite desisobutyryl-ciclesonide, which binds the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1 and modulates glucocorticoid-responsive genes, suppressing cytokine production and inflammatory cell recruitment; systemic exposure to parent drug is low because of extensive first-pass metabolism, high plasma protein binding, and relatively favorable lung deposition, while metabolism is primarily hepatic via CYP3A4 with biliary/fecal excretion predominating and minimal unchanged renal elimination. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor, with downstream effects on NF-kB- and AP-1-regulated inflammatory pathways. Clinically, it is indicated for maintenance treatment of persistent asthma and for allergic rhinitis, including symptoms such as wheeze, cough, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, and sneezing, but it is not appropriate for acute bronchospasm relief. Adverse effects are usually local and dose related, including oropharyngeal candidiasis, dysphonia, throat irritation, cough, epistaxis, and headache; important toxicities of chronic or excessive corticosteroid exposure include adrenal suppression, reduced growth velocity in children, glaucoma, cataracts, decreased bone mineral density, and increased infection risk, although these are generally less frequent than with more systemically bioavailable corticosteroids.

Name: Pranlukast
Description: Pranlukast (DrugBank DB01411) is an orally active leukotriene receptor antagonist whose structure is characterized by a highly lipophilic aromatic framework containing multiple phenyl rings linked through ether and amide/sulfonamide-like functionality, with an acidic terminal group that mimics endogenous cysteinyl leukotrienes and supports high-affinity receptor binding; chemically it is best classified as an anti-asthmatic cysteinyl leukotriene antagonist, and its core scaffold is an aryl-heteroatom-linked diaryl pharmacophore bearing a polar acidic headgroup typical of this drug class. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to montelukast, zafirlukast, and to some extent pobilukast, all of which antagonize cysteinyl leukotriene signaling. Its principal target is the cysteinyl leukotriene receptor 1, CysLT1, through which it blocks LTD4-mediated bronchoconstriction, vascular permeability, mucus secretion, and eosinophilic airway inflammation. After oral administration, pranlukast is absorbed sufficiently for chronic therapy but has variable bioavailability influenced by food, is extensively protein bound in plasma, distributes mainly within the vascular/extracellular compartment, undergoes hepatic metabolism with biliary predominance and limited renal elimination, and exhibits an elimination half-life compatible with twice-daily dosing. Toxicity is generally moderate and includes hepatic enzyme elevation, rare clinically significant hepatotoxicity, hypersensitivity reactions, and potential class-associated neuropsychiatric complaints; overdose experience is limited but would be expected to accentuate gastrointestinal and CNS symptoms. Indications include bronchial asthma, exercise- or allergen-related bronchospasm prevention, and allergic rhinitis symptoms such as rhinorrhea and nasal congestion. Common adverse effects include headache, nausea, dyspepsia, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, rash, and somnolence. Clinically, pranlukast is used as maintenance anti-inflammatory therapy, often as an adjunct or alternative to inhaled corticosteroids in mild to moderate asthma and in patients with concomitant allergic rhinitis.

Name: Cefepime
Description: Cefepime (DrugBank DB01413) is a parenteral fourth-generation cephalosporin beta-lactam whose structure consists of a cephem nucleus with a strained beta-lactam fused to a dihydrothiazine ring, bearing a 7-position oxyimino-aminothiazolyl acyl side chain that enhances stability to many beta-lactamases and a positively charged N-methylpyrrolidinium substituent at the 3-position that confers zwitterionic character and improves penetration into Gram-negative bacteria. Chemically it is an aminothiazolyl oxyimino cephalosporin, built on the cephalosporin/cephem scaffold, and is closely related to other extended-spectrum cephalosporins such as ceftazidime, cefpirome, cefotaxime, and ceftriaxone, with particularly notable similarity to cefpirome and ceftazidime in antipseudomonal use. Its antibacterial targets are penicillin-binding proteins, especially bacterial transpeptidases including PBP3 and other PBPs in susceptible Gram-negative and Gram-positive organisms, thereby inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-linking and cell-wall synthesis. Cefepime is indicated for pneumonia, febrile neutropenia, complicated urinary tract infection, pyelonephritis, intra-abdominal infection with metronidazole, skin and soft tissue infection, and severe sepsis caused by susceptible organisms including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacter spp., Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Streptococcus pneumoniae. It is not orally absorbed and is given IV or IM, distributes well into extracellular fluid, urine, lung, bile, peritoneal fluid, and inflamed CSF, undergoes minimal metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by renal excretion with dose reduction required in renal impairment. Toxicity is generally similar to other cephalosporins but includes hypersensitivity reactions, positive Coombs test, cytopenias, C. difficile-associated diarrhea, and dose-related neurotoxicity such as encephalopathy, myoclonus, seizures, and nonconvulsive status epilepticus, especially in elderly or renally impaired patients; common adverse effects include rash, gastrointestinal upset, phlebitis, fever, headache, and mild transaminase elevation.

Name: Ceftibuten
Description: Ceftibuten (DrugBank DB01415) is an orally active third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic whose structure is defined by the cephem/β-lactam scaffold fused to a dihydrothiazine ring, bearing an aminothiazolyl oxyimino acyl side chain that enhances Gram-negative activity and β-lactamase stability, and a vinyl-substituted carboxylic acid functionality characteristic of this agent; chemically, it is a β-lactam, specifically an aminothiazolyl cephalosporin, within the broader cephalosporanic acid family. Its closest analogs include other expanded-spectrum oral cephalosporins such as cefixime, cefpodoxime proxetil, cefdinir, and parenteral agents like ceftazidime, which share related oxyimino-cephalosporin motifs. Ceftibuten acts by binding bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, particularly transpeptidases involved in peptidoglycan cross-linking, thereby inhibiting cell-wall synthesis; relevant target proteins therefore include PBPs from susceptible organisms such as Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Proteus mirabilis. After oral administration it is well absorbed, has moderate protein binding, distributes mainly in extracellular fluids and respiratory/urinary tissues, undergoes minimal metabolism, and is eliminated largely unchanged by the kidney with a several-hour half-life, requiring dose adjustment in renal impairment. Toxicity is generally low but includes class-associated hypersensitivity reactions, gastrointestinal toxicity including diarrhea and possible Clostridioides difficile colitis, rare neurotoxicity or seizures in severe renal dysfunction, and occasional hepatic enzyme elevations. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, abdominal pain, headache, rash, and candidiasis. Clinically, it is used for susceptible respiratory and urinary infections, including acute bacterial exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, pharyngitis/tonsillitis, otitis media, and uncomplicated urinary tract infection.

Name: Cefpodoxime
Description: Cefpodoxime (DrugBank DB01416) is an orally active third-generation cephalosporin antibacterial, typically administered as the lipophilic prodrug cefpodoxime proxetil, whose structure is built on the cephem or beta-lactam–dihydrothiazine bicyclic nucleus bearing the characteristic 7-acylamino and 3-substituted side chains that enhance beta-lactamase stability and broaden Gram-negative activity; chemically it belongs to the beta-lactam cephalosporin class, with a cephalosporin/cephem scaffold closely related to other oxyimino aminothiazolyl cephalosporins such as cefixime, cefdinir, ceftriaxone, ceftibuten, and more distantly cefuroxime. Its antibacterial effect results from binding bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, especially transpeptidases including PBP1, PBP2, and PBP3 in susceptible organisms, thereby inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-linking and cell-wall synthesis. After oral dosing of cefpodoxime proxetil, the prodrug is absorbed in the intestine and hydrolyzed to active cefpodoxime; bioavailability is moderate and improved with food, protein binding is modest, tissue penetration is clinically useful in respiratory and urinary sites, metabolism beyond prodrug activation is minimal, and elimination is primarily renal as unchanged drug, so half-life is prolonged in renal impairment. Toxicity is generally low but includes class effects such as hypersensitivity reactions ranging from rash to anaphylaxis, gastrointestinal toxicity including antibiotic-associated diarrhea and Clostridioides difficile colitis, rare hematologic abnormalities, hepatic enzyme elevations, interstitial nephritis, and occasional neurotoxicity or seizures in severe renal dysfunction. It is indicated for susceptible infections including community-acquired pneumonia, acute bacterial sinusitis, pharyngitis/tonsillitis, acute otitis media, uncomplicated skin and soft tissue infection, uncomplicated urinary tract infection, and uncomplicated gonorrhea; in clinical use it serves as an oral step-down or outpatient cephalosporin when coverage of common respiratory pathogens and Enterobacterales is desired, with common adverse effects including diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, headache, vulvovaginal candidiasis, and rash.

Name: Acenocoumarol
Description: Acenocoumarol (DrugBank DB01418) is a synthetic oral anticoagulant of the 4-hydroxycoumarin class, structurally characterized by a coumarin benzopyran-2-one core bearing a 4-hydroxyl group and a substituted 3-side chain containing a phenyl ring and ketone functionality, giving it the classic vitamin K antagonist pharmacophore; its chemical scaffold is therefore the 4-hydroxycoumarin nucleus closely related to warfarin, phenprocoumon, dicoumarol, and other coumarin anticoagulants. It acts primarily by inhibiting vitamin K epoxide reductase complex subunit 1, VKORC1, thereby reducing hepatic activation of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X and the anticoagulant proteins C and S; pharmacodynamic response is also influenced by CYP2C9, the principal metabolic enzyme, and by CYP1A2 and CYP2C19 to lesser degrees. Acenocoumarol is generally well absorbed orally, is highly albumin bound, distributes mainly within plasma, has a relatively short elimination half-life compared with warfarin, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism including reduction and hydroxylation, and is excreted predominantly as metabolites in urine with some biliary or fecal elimination. Its major toxicity is hemorrhage, ranging from epistaxis, hematuria, gastrointestinal bleeding, and menorrhagia to intracranial hemorrhage, with risk amplified by overdose, liver disease, drug interactions, or vitamin K deficiency; rarer toxicities include skin necrosis and teratogenic fetal toxicity. It is indicated for prevention and treatment of thromboembolic disorders such as deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, atrial fibrillation-associated embolism, and thrombosis in patients with mechanical heart valves, and clinically it is used for long-term anticoagulation with INR-guided dose adjustment, while common adverse effects include bruising, bleeding, nausea, rash, alopecia, and hepatic enzyme abnormalities.

Name: Testosterone propionate
Description: Testosterone propionate (DrugBank DB01420) is a short-acting esterified androgen in which the natural steroid nucleus of testosterone, an androst-4-en-17β-ol-3-one framework, is modified by propionyl esterification at the 17β-hydroxyl group, increasing lipophilicity while preserving the classic fused four-ring cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene steroid scaffold; it belongs chemically to androgen esters, anabolic-androgenic steroids, and sex hormone derivatives. Closely related drugs include testosterone enanthate, testosterone cypionate, testosterone undecanoate, methyltestosterone, and nandrolone esters, which share the steroidal androgen scaffold but differ in ester chain, substitution pattern, and duration of action. After intramuscular administration, testosterone propionate is absorbed from the depot relatively rapidly, then hydrolyzed by esterases to free testosterone, which distributes widely with high protein binding to sex hormone-binding globulin and albumin, enters androgen-responsive tissues, undergoes hepatic and extrahepatic metabolism to dihydrotestosterone, estradiol, androsterone, etiocholanolone, and glucuronide or sulfate conjugates, and is excreted mainly in urine with minor fecal elimination. Its principal target is the androgen receptor; downstream biological effects also reflect conversion by steroid 5α-reductase to dihydrotestosterone and by aromatase to estradiol. It is indicated for male hypogonadism, delayed puberty, and selected cases of palliative treatment of metastatic breast cancer in women. Toxicities include erythrocytosis, edema, hypertension, dyslipidemia, hepatotoxicity less prominent than with oral 17α-ალკylated androgens, virilization, infertility, testicular atrophy, prostate enlargement, and potential cardiovascular or thromboembolic risk. Common adverse effects include acne, oily skin, injection-site pain, mood changes, gynecomastia, fluid retention, and altered libido; clinically it has been used for androgen replacement and symptom control in testosterone deficiency states.

Name: Paromomycin
Description: Paromomycin (DrugBank DB01421) is a highly polar aminoglycoside aminocyclitol antibiotic composed of a 2-deoxystreptamine core glycosidically linked to multiple amino sugar residues, creating a densely hydroxylated, polycationic structure that strongly binds ribosomal RNA; chemically it belongs to the aminoglycoside/aminocyclitol class and is built on the canonical 2-deoxystreptamine scaffold shared by several ribosome-targeting antibiotics. Closely related drugs include neomycin, kanamycin, gentamicin, tobramycin, and amikacin, which share similar cationic sugar-rich frameworks and antibacterial mechanisms. Its principal target is the prokaryotic 30S ribosomal subunit, especially 16S rRNA within the decoding site, where binding disrupts translational fidelity and inhibits protein synthesis; in protozoa, antileishmanial and antiamoebic activity is also linked to interference with parasite ribosomes. Pharmacokinetically, paromomycin is very poorly absorbed orally, remains largely within the intestinal lumen, distributes minimally systemically after oral administration, undergoes negligible metabolism, and is excreted primarily unchanged in feces, while any absorbed fraction is eliminated renally. Toxicity resembles that of other aminoglycosides, including nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, and rarely neuromuscular blockade, with risk increased by renal impairment or prolonged exposure; gastrointestinal cramping, nausea, diarrhea, and malabsorption can also occur. Clinically, it is used orally for intestinal amebiasis and as a luminal agent for hepatic encephalopathy to reduce ammonia-producing gut flora, and it is also used, including parenteral formulations in some settings, for visceral leishmaniasis; adverse effects commonly include abdominal discomfort and diarrhea, while systemic exposure raises concern for renal and auditory injury.

Name: Alizapride
Description: Alizapride (DrugBank DB01425) is a substituted benzamide antiemetic whose structure is centered on an anisamide-like aromatic benzamide ring bearing methoxy substitution and a basic amino side chain, giving a polar, protonatable molecule typical of dopamine antagonist gastroprokinetics; chemically it belongs to the ortho-/para-substituted benzamide class and is built on the metoclopramide/sulpiride-like benzamide scaffold. Closely related or pharmacologically similar drugs include metoclopramide, clebopride, levosulpiride, sulpiride, and to some extent domperidone, all sharing dopamine D2 receptor antagonism with varying gastrointestinal prokinetic and antiemetic profiles. Its principal known target protein is the dopamine D2 receptor, with antiemetic activity mainly attributed to blockade of D2 receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone and peripheral enteric sites; limited serotonergic interactions have been discussed but D2 antagonism is primary. Alizapride is used for the prevention and treatment of nausea and vomiting, especially postoperative emesis, drug-induced vomiting, and emesis associated with migraine or gastrointestinal dysmotility, and it has been used clinically as an antiemetic and prokinetic in acute care and perioperative settings. Pharmacokinetically, it is active after parenteral and oral administration, is reasonably well absorbed, distributes mainly in extracellular fluids with some CNS penetration, undergoes hepatic biotransformation to more polar metabolites, and is eliminated predominantly by the kidneys as parent drug and metabolites. Toxicity is broadly consistent with dopamine antagonists, including dose-related sedation, hypotension, and extrapyramidal reactions such as acute dystonia, akathisia, and parkinsonism; adverse effects also include diarrhea, abdominal cramping, dizziness, hyperprolactinemia-related endocrine effects, and rarely severe neurologic reactions such as tardive dyskinesia or neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

Name: Ajmaline
Description: Ajmaline (DrugBank DB01426) is a naturally derived antiarrhythmic alkaloid of the rauwolfia/monoterpenoid indole alkaloid class, characterized by a rigid polycyclic yohimban-like indole-containing framework with a tertiary amine and oxygenated substituents that confer weak basicity and membrane activity; its core chemical scaffold is the ajmalan or yohimban-type indole alkaloid nucleus. It is structurally and pharmacologically related to other class I antiarrhythmics and to alkaloid congeners such as quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide, and the rauwolfia alkaloid ajmalicine, although ajmaline is distinguished by its indole alkaloid scaffold rather than the arylaminoalkyl motifs of many synthetic sodium-channel blockers.
