Its principal target is the cardiac voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.5 encoded by SCN5A, with resultant slowing of phase 0 depolarization, reduced conduction velocity, and prolongation of impulse propagation in atrial, ventricular, and His-Purkinje tissue. Pharmacokinetically, ajmaline is typically administered intravenously for rapid effect, producing prompt distribution into well-perfused tissues, hepatic biotransformation, and renal excretion of metabolites and a smaller fraction of unchanged drug; elimination is relatively short, supporting its diagnostic and acute procedural use rather than chronic oral therapy. Clinically, it is used for acute supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmias and especially as a provocative test in suspected Brugada syndrome to unmask diagnostic ECG changes. Toxicity reflects excessive sodium-channel blockade, with hypotension, QRS widening, atrioventricular block, bradycardia, negative inotropy, and provocation of dangerous ventricular tachyarrhythmias including torsades-like or Brugada-related events; adverse effects can include dizziness, flushing, paresthesia, nausea, and syncope, so use is generally restricted to monitored hospital settings.

Name: Amrinone
Description: Amrinone (DrugBank DB01427), also known as inamrinone, is a bipyridine cardiotonic built on a 3,4-bipyridin-6-one scaffold, structurally characterized by two linked pyridine rings containing a lactam-like pyridone core and an amino substituent that contributes to its weakly basic, heteroaromatic profile; chemically it is classified as a bipyridine phosphodiesterase inhibitor and positive inotrope, and it is closely related to other inodilators such as milrinone and, more distantly, enoximone. Its principal pharmacologic target is phosphodiesterase 3, especially PDE3A and PDE3B, leading to increased intracellular cAMP in cardiac myocytes and vascular smooth muscle, with consequent enhanced calcium-mediated contractility and vasodilation; it may also secondarily influence platelet function through cAMP signaling. Clinically, amrinone has been used intravenously for short-term management of acute decompensated congestive heart failure, low-output states after cardiac surgery, and severe refractory systolic dysfunction where rapid inotropic support is needed. Pharmacokinetically, it is administered parenterally because oral use is limited, distributes into extracellular fluid with modest protein binding, undergoes limited hepatic biotransformation, and is eliminated predominantly by the kidney, so clearance falls in renal impairment and dose adjustment is prudent. Important toxicities include dose-related thrombocytopenia, hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevation, hypotension from vasodilation, and ventricular or supraventricular arrhythmias; common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, fever, infusion-site reactions, and headache. Because of these safety liabilities and the availability of better tolerated analogs, its clinical use has become relatively limited and is generally confined to monitored short-term hospital settings.

Name: Aprindine
Description: Aprindine (DrugBank DB01429) is a class Ib antiarrhythmic agent with local anesthetic-like membrane-stabilizing activity, built around a lipophilic diarylalkylamine structure in which a tertiary amino side chain is linked to a compact hydrophobic aromatic/cycloalkyl framework; chemically it is an antiarrhythmic aminoalkyl aryl compound and its core scaffold is commonly described as a bulky hydrophobic aryl-cycloalkyl tertiary amine related to other fast sodium-channel blockers. Similar drugs include lidocaine, mexiletine, tocainide, and in broader antiarrhythmic comparison flecainide and propafenone, although aprindine is structurally distinct and tends to show mixed class I electrophysiologic behavior. Its principal target is the cardiac voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.5, encoded by SCN5A, with use-dependent blockade of inward sodium current and consequent slowing of impulse conduction; secondary interactions with potassium currents have also been reported. Aprindine is used for ventricular and supraventricular tachyarrhythmias, including symptomatic premature ventricular contractions, ventricular tachycardia, paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, and atrial arrhythmias in selected patients. It is generally well absorbed orally, is highly tissue distributed because of marked lipophilicity, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism with a relatively long elimination half-life that can favor accumulation, and is excreted mainly as metabolites in urine with some biliary/fecal elimination. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related cardiotoxicity and neurotoxicity, including QRS widening, conduction block, proarrhythmia, dizziness, tremor, confusion, and at high exposure seizures; hepatotoxicity, leukopenia, and cholestatic jaundice have been described. Common adverse effects include nausea, dry mouth, visual disturbance, palpitations, bradycardia, and worsening heart failure. Clinically, it has been used as an oral antiarrhythmic when suppression of refractory ventricular or supraventricular rhythm disorders is needed, particularly where longer duration of action is advantageous but careful ECG and hepatic monitoring are required.

Name: Almitrine
Description: Almitrine (DrugBank DB01430) is a synthetic piperazine-derived respiratory stimulant characterized structurally by a highly lipophilic dihalogenated aromatic framework linked through a tertiary piperazine core, giving a substituted diphenyl-piperazine scaffold typical of peripheral chemoreceptor modulators; chemically it is classified as a piperazine derivative and more broadly as a vasomodulatory/respiratory stimulant agent. Its core scaffold and physicochemical profile resemble other diphenylpiperazine-containing drugs, although its pharmacology is distinct from examples such as cinnarizine and flunarizine, and it has also been discussed alongside other ventilatory stimulants such as doxapram because of overlapping therapeutic intent rather than close structural identity. Almitrine acts predominantly at peripheral carotid body chemoreception and has been associated with modulation of oxygen-sensitive potassium channel function in glomus cells, but no single highly specific canonical target protein is firmly established; proposed target classes include carotid body chemosensory ion channels and pulmonary vascular smooth muscle pathways. It was used to improve ventilation-perfusion matching and arterial oxygenation, especially in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with hypoxemia and sometimes other chronic respiratory insufficiency states. Pharmacokinetically, it is orally absorbed, extensively distributed into tissues because of marked lipophilicity, highly protein bound, slowly metabolized hepatically, and eliminated mainly via biliary-fecal routes with a long effective half-life permitting accumulation during chronic dosing. Major toxicities include dose- and duration-related peripheral neuropathy and weight loss, with additional concern for hepatic dysfunction and pulmonary vascular effects. Common adverse effects include paresthesias, distal sensory symptoms, gastrointestinal intolerance, insomnia, and fatigue. Clinically, it was used as an adjunct oral treatment for hypoxemic COPD, but its use became limited or withdrawn in many settings because toxicity outweighed modest oxygenation benefit.

Name: Alfacalcidol
Description: Alfacalcidol (DB01436) is a synthetic vitamin D analog structurally characterized as 1alpha-hydroxycholecalciferol, a secosteroid in which the B ring of the steroid nucleus is opened, retaining the cholestane-derived framework, a conjugated triene system, a 3beta-hydroxyl group, and a flexible lipophilic side chain; chemically it belongs to the vitamin D/ secosteroid class and is built on the calciferol scaffold. It is closely related to calcitriol, cholecalciferol, ergocalciferol, paricalcitol, and doxercalciferol, which share the vitamin D receptor agonist pharmacophore with differences in hydroxylation pattern or side-chain substitution. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed, transported in blood mainly bound to vitamin D-binding protein, distributed to liver and other tissues, and rapidly 25-hydroxylated in the liver to calcitriol, thereby bypassing the renal 1alpha-hydroxylation step; elimination occurs predominantly via biliary/fecal routes after further metabolism, with limited renal excretion. Its principal target is the vitamin D receptor, with downstream regulation of calcium- and phosphate-handling proteins such as TRPV6, calbindin, and osteocalcin-associated pathways. Clinically it is used for disorders of impaired calcium homeostasis including renal osteodystrophy, secondary hyperparathyroidism in chronic kidney disease, hypoparathyroidism, osteoporosis, rickets, and osteomalacia. Toxicity is dominated by exaggerated vitamin D effects, especially hypercalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, which may cause nausea, vomiting, constipation, polyuria, polydipsia, weakness, confusion, nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, and soft-tissue or vascular calcification; accordingly, adverse effects and clinical use require careful monitoring of serum calcium, phosphate, renal function, and parathyroid hormone.

Name: Glutethimide
Description: Glutethimide (DrugBank DB01437) is a sedative-hypnotic piperidinedione characterized structurally as a 2,6-dioxopiperidine ring bearing ethyl and phenyl substitution at the 3-position, giving a lipophilic cyclic imide architecture typical of older nonbarbiturate hypnotics. Chemically it belongs to the glutarimide class, and its core scaffold is the glutarimide or piperidine-2,6-dione nucleus, a motif shared with centrally acting depressants and some structurally related compounds. Similar drugs include other historical sedative-hypnotics such as thalidomide and aminoglutethimide by scaffold analogy, and barbiturates such as phenobarbital by pharmacologic effect rather than close structure. It is well absorbed orally, distributes widely with significant CNS penetration because of high lipophilicity, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism with microsomal enzyme induction, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine; its half-life is variable and chronic use can accelerate its own clearance and that of coadministered drugs. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related CNS and respiratory depression, coma, hypotension, ataxia, and dependence, with overdose resembling barbiturate poisoning; misuse with codeine in Ts and blues is a classic example of severe abuse liability. Its precise molecular target profile was historically incompletely defined, but its sedative action is generally attributed to positive modulation of GABAergic neurotransmission, functionally implicating the GABAA receptor-chloride channel complex and broader neuronal CNS depressant pathways. Clinically it was indicated for insomnia and short-term management of sleep disturbance, but adverse effects including drowsiness, dizziness, confusion, impaired coordination, nausea, rash, tolerance, withdrawal, and drug interactions sharply limited use, and it is now largely obsolete because safer hypnotics replaced it.

Name: Phenazopyridine
Description: Phenazopyridine (DrugBank DB01438) is a synthetic azo dye-derived urinary tract analgesic whose structure consists of a pyridine ring substituted with an azo linkage to a phenyl ring bearing amino groups, giving a planar, highly conjugated aromatic system with weakly basic character and intense orange-red pigmentation; chemically it is classified as an azo aromatic amine and more specifically a pyridine-containing azo dye, with an aminophenyl-azopyridine scaffold. It is most similar to other azo dye or urinary analgesic compounds, though few are used clinically; related comparators include azo dyes such as prontosil and symptomatic urinary agents used in overlapping settings such as methenamine combinations, although these are not close structural analogs. Its mechanism is not well defined and no single validated pharmacologic target protein is established; it is generally considered a locally acting analgesic on the urinary tract mucosa rather than a receptor-selective agent. After oral administration it is absorbed to a moderate extent, distributed systemically, undergoes partial hepatic metabolism, and is excreted largely by the kidneys as unchanged drug and metabolites, producing characteristic urine discoloration; renal impairment increases exposure. It is indicated for symptomatic relief of dysuria, burning, urgency, frequency, and suprapubic discomfort associated with lower urinary tract irritation, for example in cystitis, urethritis, prostatitis, catheter trauma, or after urologic procedures, and is used clinically only as short-term adjunctive therapy with definitive treatment such as antibiotics when infection is present. Adverse effects include orange-red discoloration of urine and tears, gastrointestinal upset, headache, and rash; important toxicities include methemoglobinemia, hemolytic anemia especially in G6PD deficiency, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, and rare hypersensitivity, particularly with overdose, prolonged use, or kidney disease.

Name: gamma-Hydroxybutyric acid
Description: Gamma-hydroxybutyric acid (GHB; DrugBank DB01440) is a small endogenous short-chain hydroxy carboxylic acid characterized structurally as a four-carbon aliphatic backbone bearing a terminal carboxylic acid and a gamma-position hydroxyl group, making it a highly polar fatty acid derivative and central nervous system depressant; chemically it falls within hydroxy acids and GABA-related neuroactive compounds, with a simple butanolic acid scaffold closely related to gamma-aminobutyric acid by functional-group substitution. Similar drugs include sodium oxybate, its sodium salt and principal pharmaceutical form, as well as mechanistically or clinically related sedative-hypnotics such as baclofen, ethanol, benzodiazepines, and other GABAergic depressants. GHB is rapidly absorbed orally, reaches peak plasma concentrations typically within about 30 to 60 minutes, distributes mainly in total body water with blood-brain barrier penetration via monocarboxylate transport processes, undergoes capacity-limited metabolism largely through conversion to succinic semialdehyde and then succinate entering the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and is eliminated primarily by biotransformation with only a small fraction excreted unchanged in urine; its half-life is short, roughly 30 to 60 minutes. Its known targets include the high-affinity GHB-binding site and the GABAB receptor, which mediates many sedative and anti-cataplectic effects. Clinically, sodium oxybate is indicated for narcolepsy with cataplexy and excessive daytime sleepiness, and has also been used in alcohol withdrawal or dependence in some settings. Toxicity is dose-dependent and includes profound sedation, bradycardia, respiratory depression, vomiting, seizures, coma, and death, especially with alcohol or opioids; common adverse effects include dizziness, nausea, enuresis, confusion, headache, somnolence, and parasomnias.

Name: Barbital
Description: Barbital (DrugBank DB01483) is a long-acting sedative-hypnotic barbiturate built on a 5,5-disubstituted barbituric acid core, specifically a pyrimidine-2,4,6-trione ring bearing two ethyl substituents at C5, making it a ureide derivative and classic oxybarbiturate within the barbiturate chemical category; its defining scaffold is therefore the barbiturate/pyrimidinetrione nucleus, a motif shared with structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs such as phenobarbital, amobarbital, pentobarbital, secobarbital, and thiopental, although the latter is a thiobarbiturate. Pharmacologically, barbital acts mainly as a positive allosteric modulator of the GABAA receptor-chloride channel complex, with barbiturates also capable at higher concentrations of directly enhancing inhibitory chloride conductance and suppressing excitatory neurotransmission; specific target assignment is therefore centered on GABAA receptor subunits rather than a single unique protein. It was historically indicated for insomnia, agitation, and anxiety-related states requiring sedation, and was also used as a general CNS depressant. Barbital is absorbed orally, distributes widely including into the CNS, shows relatively limited biotransformation compared with some later barbiturates, and is eliminated slowly, with substantial renal excretion of unchanged drug contributing to its prolonged duration and risk of accumulation. Toxicity is typical of barbiturates and includes dose-dependent CNS and respiratory depression, coma, hypotension, impaired psychomotor function, tolerance, dependence, and fatal overdose, especially with alcohol or other sedatives. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, ataxia, confusion, dizziness, cognitive slowing, and residual next-day sedation. Clinically, barbital is now largely obsolete, replaced by safer hypnotics, but remains historically important as an early prototype sedative-hypnotic.

Name: Difenoxin
Description: Difenoxin (DrugBank DB01501) is a synthetic opioid antidiarrheal structurally characterized as a diphenyl-substituted piperidine carboxylic acid derivative, specifically the active metabolite of diphenoxylate, bearing a 4-phenylpiperidine core with a quaternary carbon linked to two phenyl rings and a terminal carboxyl functionality that distinguishes it from more lipophilic opioid congeners; chemically it is classified as a phenylpiperidine opioid and more broadly as an opioid-related antiperistaltic agent, with a scaffold closely related to meperidine-like 4-phenylpiperidines. Similar drugs include diphenoxylate, loperamide, meperidine, and to some extent fentanyl-class opioids by shared phenylpiperidine ancestry, although difenoxin is used peripherally at therapeutic doses. Its principal target is the mu-opioid receptor, through which it decreases intestinal propulsive motility and prolongs transit time. After oral administration it is absorbed systemically, distributed sufficiently to exert gastrointestinal opioid effects, undergoes limited further biotransformation relative to its prodrug parent, and is eliminated through hepatic and renal routes, with enterohepatic contribution possible; central nervous system penetration increases with high doses. It is indicated for acute and chronic noninfectious diarrhea, commonly in combination with atropine to deter abuse, and is used clinically for symptomatic control of severe diarrhea refractory to simpler measures. Adverse effects include constipation, abdominal discomfort, nausea, drowsiness, dizziness, dry mouth, and at higher exposure euphoria or CNS depression. Toxicity resembles opioid poisoning, including respiratory depression, stupor, miosis or occasionally mydriasis, ileus, and abuse liability, with children particularly vulnerable to severe overdose.

Name: Ethyl loflazepate
Description: Ethyl loflazepate (DrugBank DB01545) is a long-acting anxiolytic benzodiazepine derivative whose structure is built on a 1,4-benzodiazepin-2-one core fused to a benzene ring and bearing the characteristic 5-aryl substituent, with additional halogenated/aromatic substitution and an ethyl ester functionality that contributes to its lipophilicity and prodrug-like behavior; chemically it is classified as a benzodiazepine anxiolytic/sedative-hypnotic, and its central scaffold is the classical 1,4-benzodiazepine ring system shared with related agents such as diazepam, clorazepate, prazepam, lorazepam, and other GABAergic sedative-anxiolytics. Like similar long-acting benzodiazepines, it is well absorbed orally, distributes widely into the CNS because of high lipid solubility and substantial plasma protein binding, undergoes hepatic biotransformation to active benzodiazepine metabolites including desalkyl species with prolonged elimination, and is then cleared mainly as glucuronidated or otherwise oxidized metabolites in urine, with a relatively long effective half-life that supports sustained anxiolysis but also next-day sedation. Its pharmacologic targets are the benzodiazepine allosteric recognition sites on GABAA receptor complexes, especially receptors containing α1, α2, α3, and α5 subunits associated with the GABRA, GABRB, and GABRG protein families, enhancing GABA-mediated chloride conductance. It is indicated chiefly for anxiety disorders, tension states, and psychosomatic symptoms, and has been used clinically for generalized anxiety, agitation, insomnia associated with anxiety, and stress-related autonomic complaints. Major adverse effects and toxicities include dose-related sedation, psychomotor impairment, ataxia, anterograde amnesia, confusion, falls, respiratory depression when combined with alcohol or opioids, and dependence, tolerance, withdrawal, and overdose-related CNS depression, with elderly patients particularly vulnerable to cognitive impairment and prolonged sedation.

Name: Fenproporex
Description: Fenproporex (DrugBank DB01550) is a synthetic sympathomimetic anorectic of the amphetamine family, structurally characterized as an N-substituted phenethylamine/propan-2-amine bearing an alpha-methylated chiral amphetamine core linked through the amino nitrogen to a 2-cyanoethyl group; thus, it belongs chemically to substituted amphetamines and more specifically anorexigenic phenylisopropylamines, with an amphetamine/phenethylamine scaffold. It is closely related to amphetamine and has pharmacologic similarity to other appetite suppressants such as phentermine, diethylpropion, benzphetamine, and mazindol, although fenproporex is distinguished by its nitrile-containing N-substituent and by acting largely as a prodrug of amphetamine. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed, distributes systemically including into the central nervous system, undergoes hepatic biotransformation with conversion to amphetamine as a major active metabolite alongside other minor metabolites, and is eliminated mainly in urine, with excretion influenced by urinary pH as for other weakly basic amines. Its principal targets are the monoamine transporters SLC6A2, SLC6A3, and SLC6A4, with indirect enhancement of synaptic norepinephrine and dopamine predominating. Clinically it has been used as a short-term adjunct in exogenous obesity and weight reduction programs, particularly for appetite suppression in overweight or obese patients refractory to diet alone. Adverse effects and toxicity resemble other stimulants, including insomnia, dry mouth, irritability, anxiety, tremor, palpitations, tachycardia, hypertension, and anorexia, while overdose or misuse may cause agitation, arrhythmias, severe hypertension, psychosis, seizures, dependence, and other amphetamine-like cardiovascular and neuropsychiatric harms.

Name: Dihydrocodeine
Description: Dihydrocodeine (DrugBank DB01551) is a semisynthetic opioid analgesic structurally derived from the morphinan/phenanthrene series, characterized by the rigid tetracyclic 4,5-epoxymorphinan nucleus with a tertiary N-methyl amine, a 3-methoxy substituent, a 6-hydroxyl group, and saturation of the 7,8-double bond relative to codeine, placing it in the opioid alkaloid analogue class and more specifically within the codeine-like morphinan scaffold. Closely related drugs include codeine, hydrocodone, oxycodone, morphine, and levorphanol, which share the same general opioid core but differ in oxidation state, O-methylation, and unsaturation. Its principal pharmacologic target is the mu-opioid receptor OPRM1, with weaker or less clinically relevant activity at delta and kappa opioid receptors such as OPRD1 and OPRK1; analgesia and antitussive effects arise from central opioid receptor agonism. After oral administration it is reasonably well absorbed, undergoes first-pass hepatic metabolism, distributes widely including into the central nervous system, and is metabolized mainly by CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 with UGT-mediated conjugation to active and inactive metabolites including dihydromorphine; elimination is predominantly renal as parent drug and conjugates, with pharmacokinetics influenced by CYP2D6 phenotype, age, and renal impairment. Toxicity is typical of opioids and includes dose-dependent respiratory depression, profound sedation, miosis, constipation, nausea, hypotension, coma, and potentially fatal overdose, with enhanced risk when combined with alcohol, benzodiazepines, or other CNS depressants. Clinically it is used for moderate to moderately severe pain, chronic cancer pain, postoperative pain, and sometimes troublesome nonproductive cough, while adverse effects commonly include dizziness, somnolence, vomiting, pruritus, urinary retention, dependence, tolerance, and withdrawal on abrupt cessation.

Name: Chlorphentermine
Description: Chlorphentermine (DrugBank DB01556) is a chlorinated amphetamine-derived sympathomimetic anorectic whose structure is characterized by an alpha-methyl phenethylamine core bearing a para-chloro substituted phenyl ring and a primary amine, placing it in the substituted amphetamine/phenethylamine class with an aryl-2-aminopropane scaffold. It is closely related to anorectic stimulants such as phentermine, amphetamine, methamphetamine, and diethylpropion, sharing a monoaminergic mechanism but differing in lipophilicity and tissue handling because of para-halogenation. Pharmacologically, it is understood to act mainly by promoting catecholaminergic, and to a lesser extent serotonergic, neurotransmission; reported target systems therefore include the norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, dopamine transporter SLC6A3, serotonin transporter SLC6A4, and trace-amine-associated monoaminergic signaling pathways rather than a single highly selective receptor target. It was used as an appetite suppressant in obesity and weight-management settings, particularly exogenous obesity with hyperphagia, to reduce caloric intake. Oral absorption is expected to be good, with broad tissue distribution including CNS penetration, slow elimination, partial hepatic metabolism, and substantial renal excretion of parent drug and metabolites, consistent with a relatively prolonged duration. Its major safety liability is toxicity from phospholipidosis, especially pulmonary accumulation associated with chronic exposure, producing concern for pneumonitis, pulmonary hypertension, dyspnea, and other organ lipid-storage changes; overdose or excessive sympathomimetic exposure may also cause tachycardia, hypertension, agitation, insomnia, tremor, and arrhythmia. Clinically, its use became limited and largely obsolete because benefit in short-term appetite suppression was outweighed by pulmonary and systemic toxicity concerns.

Name: Chloral hydrate
Description: Chloral hydrate (DrugBank DB01563) is a small halogenated aliphatic sedative-hypnotic whose structure consists of a geminal diol hydrate of trichloroacetaldehyde, with a two-carbon chloral-derived backbone bearing three chlorines on one carbon and two hydroxyl groups on the carbonyl-derived carbon, placing it in the organochlorine alcohol/aldehyde hydrate class; its core scaffold is therefore a trichloroethyl gem-diol chloral scaffold, closely related to chloral, trichloroethanol, and other older sedative-hypnotics such as paraldehyde and, mechanistically more distantly, barbiturates and benzodiazepines. Its pharmacology is mediated primarily through rapid conversion to the active metabolite trichloroethanol, which positively modulates GABA-A receptor function; additional reported targets include GABA-A receptor subunits and possible weak actions on glycine receptor and other CNS depressant pathways rather than a highly selective single protein target. It is generally well absorbed orally, widely distributed including CNS penetration, metabolized in the liver and erythrocytes by alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde reductive pathways to trichloroethanol, with further glucuronidation, and by oxidative metabolism to trichloroacetic acid; metabolites are excreted mainly in urine, and sedative effects may outlast parent drug because of active metabolite persistence. Toxicity includes dose-dependent respiratory depression, hypotension, coma, dysrhythmias, delirium, hepatic injury, and potentially fatal overdose, especially with alcohol or other sedatives. Adverse effects commonly include drowsiness, ataxia, confusion, gastric irritation, nausea, vomiting, headache, and paradoxical agitation in children. Clinically, chloral hydrate has been used for short-term treatment of insomnia, preprocedural or pediatric sedation, and to calm anxious or uncooperative patients during EEG, imaging, or dental procedures, although use has declined because of safety concerns and newer alternatives.

Name: Dextroamphetamine
Description: Dextroamphetamine (DrugBank DB01576) is the dextrorotatory enantiomer of amphetamine, a small chiral phenethylamine composed of a benzene ring linked through a two-carbon side chain to a primary amine with an alpha-methyl substituent, giving a compact lipophilic arylalkylamine structure that readily crosses the blood-brain barrier. Chemically it belongs to the amphetamine class of central nervous system stimulants and sympathomimetic amines, with a simple phenethylamine/alpha-methylphenethylamine scaffold. Closely related drugs include racemic amphetamine, lisdexamfetamine, methamphetamine, methylphenidate as a mechanistically related stimulant, and other monoaminergic sympathomimetics such as phentermine. It is well absorbed orally, has high bioavailability, distributes widely including into the CNS, shows limited protein binding, and is metabolized hepatically in part by CYP2D6 and related oxidative pathways to active and inactive metabolites such as 4-hydroxyamphetamine and norephedrine; elimination is primarily renal, strongly influenced by urinary pH, with acidic urine increasing clearance and an elimination half-life commonly around 10 to 12 hours but variable. Its principal targets are the dopamine transporter SLC6A3, norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, serotonin transporter SLC6A4 to a lesser extent, and vesicular monoamine transporter 2 SLC18A2, promoting catecholamine release and reuptake inhibition. Clinically it is indicated for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and narcolepsy, improving attention, wakefulness, and impulse control. Toxicity includes hypertension, tachyarrhythmia, hyperthermia, agitation, psychosis, seizures, rhabdomyolysis, and abuse dependence liability. Common adverse effects include insomnia, anorexia, weight loss, dry mouth, anxiety, tremor, palpitations, and gastrointestinal upset. In practice it is used as immediate- or extended-release stimulant therapy in carefully monitored patients, especially for ADHD with prominent inattentiveness or for excessive daytime sleepiness in narcolepsy.

Name: Metamfetamine
Description: Metamfetamine (methamphetamine; DrugBank DB01577) is a small, lipophilic phenethylamine/amphetamine derivative whose structure consists of a phenyl ring attached to a substituted ethylamine side chain bearing an alpha-methyl group and an N-methylated secondary amine, giving a simple aryl-alkylamine framework that enhances central nervous system penetration; chemically it is classified as a substituted amphetamine, sympathomimetic amine, and central stimulant built on the phenethylamine/amphetamine scaffold. Closely related drugs include amphetamine, lisdexamfetamine, phentermine, and the empathogen methylenedioxymethamphetamine, which share portions of the same stimulant pharmacophore. Its principal targets are the dopamine transporter SLC6A3, norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, and serotonin transporter SLC6A4, with indirect effects involving vesicular monoamine transporter 2 SLC18A2 and trace amine-associated receptor 1, producing increased synaptic monoamines. Oral bioavailability is high, absorption is rapid, distribution is extensive with efficient blood-brain barrier penetration, metabolism occurs mainly in the liver via CYP2D6 and related pathways to amphetamine and hydroxylated products, and elimination is primarily renal with urinary pH strongly influencing excretion and half-life. Clinically, methamphetamine has been used in ADHD and exogenous obesity, and historically for narcolepsy, fatigue, or refractory attentional symptoms, exemplified by the prescription product Desoxyn. Toxicity includes marked abuse liability, dependence, agitation, psychosis, seizures, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, stroke, myocardial infarction, arrhythmias, hypertension, and neurotoxicity to monoaminergic systems; common adverse effects include insomnia, anorexia, weight loss, tachycardia, dry mouth, anxiety, irritability, tremor, and increased blood pressure.

Name: Phendimetrazine
Description: Phendimetrazine (DrugBank DB01579) is a sympathomimetic anorectic of the phenethylamine/amphetamine-related class whose structure is characterized by a substituted phenylisopropylamine framework constrained into a morpholine ring, specifically a 2-phenyl-3,4-dimethylmorpholine scaffold that confers stereochemical complexity and serves as a prodrug-like precursor to the more active metabolite phenmetrazine; chemically it is categorized as a synthetic substituted amine and centrally acting appetite suppressant, with close structural and pharmacologic analogs including phenmetrazine, phentermine, amphetamine, diethylpropion, and benzphetamine. After oral administration it is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, distributed systemically with central nervous system penetration sufficient for anorectic action, and undergoes hepatic metabolism, notably N-demethylation and ring-related biotransformation to phenmetrazine and other metabolites; elimination is primarily renal, with urinary excretion enhanced by acidification and duration of action typically intermediate relative to other older anorectics. Its principal pharmacologic targets are not highly selective receptor proteins but catecholaminergic systems, especially promotion of norepinephrine release and, to a lesser extent, dopamine signaling through monoamine transport pathways including the norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2 and dopamine transporter SLC6A3, producing appetite suppression. It is indicated as a short-term adjunct in exogenous obesity management, for example in patients with obesity insufficiently responsive to caloric restriction alone. Toxicities reflect stimulant and abuse-liability properties, including tachycardia, hypertension, agitation, insomnia, psychosis, dependence, overdose-related arrhythmias or seizures, and rare serious cardiovascular or cerebrovascular events. Common adverse effects include dry mouth, constipation, nervousness, palpitations, headache, dizziness, and irritability. Clinically, phendimetrazine has been used short term alongside diet, exercise, and behavioral modification in weight-reduction programs, particularly for obesity with associated cardiometabolic risk factors.

Name: Oxprenolol
Description: Oxprenolol (DrugBank DB01580) is a lipophilic aryloxypropanolamine beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist characterized structurally by the classic beta-blocker pharmacophore of a protonatable secondary alcohol–amine side chain attached through an ether linkage to a substituted aromatic ring, specifically an indole-like/allyl-substituted aryloxy scaffold that confers membrane permeability and intrinsic sympathomimetic activity. Chemically it belongs to the nonselective beta-blocker class and more broadly to phenoxypropanolamine derivatives, with an aryloxypropanolamine scaffold shared by related agents such as propranolol, pindolol, alprenolol, timolol, and carteolol. Its principal targets are beta-1 adrenergic receptor and beta-2 adrenergic receptor, with antihypertensive, antianginal, and antiarrhythmic effects mediated by reduction of heart rate, myocardial contractility, and renin release; partial agonist properties may distinguish its hemodynamic profile from propranolol. Oxprenolol is generally well absorbed orally but undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, producing variable bioavailability; it distributes widely into tissues including the central nervous system, is metabolized in the liver mainly by oxidative biotransformation and conjugative pathways, and is excreted primarily as metabolites in urine with limited unchanged drug. Toxicity resembles that of other beta-blockers and includes bradycardia, hypotension, atrioventricular block, acute heart failure, bronchospasm in susceptible patients, hypoglycemia masking, and CNS effects in overdose. Adverse effects include fatigue, dizziness, cold extremities, depression, sleep disturbance, nausea, and exercise intolerance. Clinically, it has been used for hypertension, chronic stable angina, supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmias, and symptomatic control of adrenergic states such as palpitations or tremor, although use is limited in asthma, severe conduction disease, and decompensated heart failure.

Name: Ursodeoxycholic acid
Description: Ursodeoxycholic acid (DrugBank DB01586) is a naturally occurring hydrophilic secondary bile acid with a cholane steroid nucleus characterized by the rigid perhydrocyclopentanophenanthrene scaffold, a 5β-cholanic acid backbone, a terminal carboxylic acid side chain, and hydroxyl groups in the 3α and 7β positions, the 7β epimeric configuration distinguishing it from chenodeoxycholic acid. It belongs to the bile acids and bile salts class, more specifically a dihydroxy bile acid, and shares the same steroidal bile acid scaffold seen in chenodeoxycholic acid, cholic acid, and obeticholic acid; related or similar drugs include chenodeoxycholic acid for gallstone dissolution and obeticholic acid as an FXR-directed bile acid analogue. After oral administration it is variably but generally well absorbed in the small intestine, undergoes extensive enterohepatic recirculation, is highly concentrated in bile rather than systemically distributed, is conjugated in the liver mainly with glycine or taurine, is partially biotransformed by intestinal flora to lithocholic acid and other metabolites, and is excreted predominantly in feces with limited renal elimination. Pharmacologically it alters the bile acid pool toward a less cytotoxic composition and is associated with targets or mechanistic interactors including FXR, TGR5, bile salt export pump ABCB11, and hepatobiliary transport systems. It is indicated chiefly for primary biliary cholangitis and cholesterol gallstone dissolution, and is also used in cholestatic liver disorders such as intrahepatic cholestasis and some pediatric cholestatic diseases. Toxicity is usually low but may include dose-related diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, nausea, pruritus worsening, and rare hepatotoxicity or gallstone calcification; adverse effects commonly include loose stools, dyspepsia, rash, and headache. Clinically it is used chronically to improve cholestatic liver biochemistry, delay progression in primary biliary cholangitis, and reduce biliary cholesterol saturation in selected noncalcified gallstones.

Name: Prazepam
Description: Prazepam (DrugBank DB01588) is a 1,4-benzodiazepine anxiolytic whose structure consists of a fused benzene-diazepine ring system bearing the characteristic 5-phenyl substituent and a 7-chloro group, with an N-substituted side chain that contributes to its prodrug-like behavior; chemically it is a classical benzodiazepine derivative and belongs to the sedative-hypnotic/anxiolytic benzodiazepine class, built on the 1,4-benzodiazepine scaffold shared by many GABAergic modulators. Similar drugs include diazepam, clorazepate, chlordiazepoxide, lorazepam, and oxazepam, especially because prazepam is metabolically related to nordazepam. Its principal target is the GABAA receptor benzodiazepine allosteric site, particularly receptors containing alpha, beta, and gamma subunits, where it acts as a positive allosteric modulator to enhance GABA-mediated chloride conductance. After oral administration it is well absorbed, extensively distributed into the CNS and lipid-rich tissues, highly protein bound, and undergoes hepatic biotransformation, notably N-dealkylation to the active metabolite nordazepam, followed by further metabolism and renal excretion of conjugated metabolites; its long effective half-life reflects active metabolites. Toxicity is typical of benzodiazepines, including dose-related CNS and respiratory depression, psychomotor impairment, ataxia, coma in overdose, and heightened danger with alcohol, opioids, or other sedatives, while chronic use can produce tolerance, dependence, and withdrawal seizures. It is indicated mainly for anxiety disorders, tension states, and short-term relief of severe anxiety symptoms, and clinically has been used for generalized anxiety, agitation, and anxiety-associated insomnia; common adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, confusion, weakness, impaired coordination, memory impairment, and paradoxical disinhibition in susceptible patients.

Name: Everolimus
Description: Everolimus (DB01590) is a semisynthetic derivative of sirolimus built on a large lipophilic 31-membered triene macrolide lactone scaffold bearing multiple hydroxyl, ether, and ester functionalities and distinguished structurally by a 40-O-(2-hydroxyethyl) substitution, placing it in the rapamycin analog, macrolide, and mTOR inhibitor chemical category; its core scaffold is the rapamycin polyketide macrolactam/macrolide framework, and closely related drugs include sirolimus, temsirolimus, and other rapalogs. Pharmacologically, everolimus binds FKBP12 (FKBP1A) to form a complex that allosterically inhibits mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1, with downstream effects on MTOR signaling nodes such as RPTOR, EIF4EBP1, and RPS6KB1; oral absorption is moderate and variable, bioavailability is limited by first-pass metabolism and transporter effects, distribution is extensive with substantial erythrocyte and protein partitioning, metabolism occurs predominantly via CYP3A4 and CYP3A5 with P-glycoprotein involvement, and excretion is mainly biliary/fecal with minimal renal elimination. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related immunosuppression and antiproliferative effects, including serious infections, noninfectious pneumonitis, stomatitis, delayed wound healing, nephrotoxicity, cytopenias, hyperglycemia, and dyslipidemia, with embryo-fetal toxicity and interaction-driven toxicity seen with strong CYP3A modulators. Indications and clinical use include prophylaxis of organ rejection in kidney and liver transplantation and treatment of advanced renal cell carcinoma, hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer, pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, renal angiomyolipoma and subependymal giant cell astrocytoma in tuberous sclerosis complex, and certain refractory seizures in TSC; common adverse effects include oral ulcers, rash, diarrhea, fatigue, edema, anemia, thrombocytopenia, hypertriglyceridemia, and increased susceptibility to bacterial, viral, and fungal infections.

Name: Solifenacin
Description: Solifenacin (DrugBank DB01591) is a synthetic, lipophilic tertiary amine antimuscarinic built around a substituted quinuclidine-containing biaryl ester architecture, featuring a rigid bicyclic amine linked through an ester to an aromatic system bearing tetrahydroisoquinoline-like character; chemically it is categorized as a urinary antispasmodic and anticholinergic muscarinic receptor antagonist, with a quinuclidine ester scaffold that is closely related in pharmacophore terms to other bladder-selective antimuscarinics such as darifenacin, tolterodine, fesoterodine, oxybutynin, and trospium. Its principal targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially M3 (CHRM3), with activity also at M1 and M2 receptor subtypes, reducing detrusor smooth-muscle contraction and bladder urgency. Clinically, it is indicated for overactive bladder, including urge urinary incontinence, urgency, and urinary frequency, and is also used in neurogenic detrusor overactivity in selected pediatric patients. Orally administered solifenacin is well absorbed with high bioavailability, reaches peak concentrations within several hours, is extensively distributed and highly protein bound, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism via CYP3A4 to inactive and minor active metabolites, and is eliminated through both renal and fecal routes, with a relatively long half-life that supports once-daily dosing. Toxicity reflects exaggerated anticholinergic effects, including severe dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, tachycardia, heat intolerance, and CNS effects such as confusion, particularly in older adults; QT prolongation has been reported at high exposure. Common adverse effects include xerostomia, constipation, dyspepsia, nausea, blurred vision, and urinary tract infection. In practice it is used as chronic oral symptomatic therapy for adults with overactive bladder when behavioral measures alone are insufficient.

Name: Iron
Description: Iron (DrugBank DB01592) is an essential transition-metal drug and mineral supplement, administered clinically as ferrous or ferric salts or as carbohydrate-coordinated iron complexes; chemically, it is a redox-active metal center that cycles between Fe2+ and Fe3+ states and, in formulations, is typically embedded in simple ionic scaffolds such as ferrous sulfate, gluconate, or fumarate, or in macromolecular colloidal scaffolds such as iron sucrose, ferric carboxymaltose, and iron dextran. It belongs to the class of hematinic agents and trace-element therapeutics, with a metal-ion scaffold rather than a conventional organic pharmacophore; similar drugs include other oral and parenteral iron preparations such as ferrous fumarate, ferrous gluconate, ferric maltol, and iron sucrose. After oral administration, iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum via DMT1 after reduction, exported by ferroportin, bound in plasma to transferrin, distributed predominantly to bone marrow, liver, spleen, and muscle, incorporated into hemoglobin, myoglobin, and enzymes, stored as ferritin or hemosiderin, and lacks classic metabolism aside from physiologic recycling; excretion is limited and occurs mainly through epithelial loss, sweat, and bleeding. Key protein targets handling iron include transferrin, transferrin receptor 1, DMT1, ferroportin, ferritin, hephaestin, and ceruloplasmin. Iron is indicated for prevention and treatment of iron deficiency and iron-deficiency anemia, including pregnancy, chronic blood loss, postpartum states, chronic kidney disease, and malabsorption. Major adverse effects include nausea, epigastric pain, constipation, diarrhea, dark stools, infusion reactions, hypotension, and hypersensitivity with parenteral products. Toxicity is dominated by acute overdose causing corrosive gastrointestinal injury, metabolic acidosis, shock, hepatic failure, and death, and by chronic overload such as hemosiderosis or hemochromatosis, especially with repeated transfusions or excessive supplementation.

Name: Nitrazepam
Description: Nitrazepam (DrugBank DB01595) is a classic 1,4-benzodiazepine hypnotic whose structure consists of a fused benzene and seven-membered diazepine ring bearing a 2-keto group, a 5-phenyl substituent, and a characteristic 7-nitro substituent that increases electron withdrawal and helps define its sedative-anticonvulsant profile; chemically it is a nitrobenzodiazepinone within the benzodiazepine class, built on the 1,4-benzodiazepin-2-one scaffold. It is closely related to other benzodiazepines such as diazepam, clonazepam, flunitrazepam, temazepam, and lorazepam, with particularly strong similarity to other nitro-substituted congeners including clonazepam and flunitrazepam. Its principal targets are the benzodiazepine allosteric sites on GABAA receptor complexes, especially receptors containing α1, α2, α3, or α5 subunits with γ2, where it positively modulates GABA-mediated chloride currents to produce sedation, anxiolysis, muscle relaxation, and anticonvulsant effects. Nitrazepam is generally well absorbed orally, reaches peak plasma concentrations within a few hours, is substantially protein bound, distributes widely into the CNS, undergoes mainly hepatic nitroreduction and related biotransformation to less active metabolites, and is eliminated largely in urine with an intermediate-to-long elimination half-life that can support next-day effects. It is indicated for severe insomnia, nocturnal anxiety, and in some settings seizure disorders such as infantile spasms or myoclonic epilepsy. Adverse effects include drowsiness, ataxia, impaired coordination, confusion, amnesia, dizziness, respiratory depression, tolerance, dependence, and withdrawal phenomena; toxicity is typified by profound CNS depression, especially with alcohol, opioids, or other sedatives, and overdose may produce coma, hypotonia, and compromised ventilation. Clinically, it has been used as a short-term nighttime hypnotic and occasionally as an adjunct anticonvulsant where sustained sedative action is acceptable.

Name: Cilastatin
Description: Cilastatin (DrugBank DB01597) is a small-molecule dehydropeptidase-I inhibitor structurally characterized as a highly polar N-formimidoyl thioether-containing diacid with multiple carboxylate functionalities and a substituted heptenoic acid backbone designed to mimic peptide-like substrates of renal brush-border metalloprotease enzymes; chemically it is classified as a renal dehydropeptidase inhibitor and peptide-mimetic carboxylic acid, built on an unsaturated amino-diacid/thioether scaffold rather than a beta-lactam nucleus. Its closest pharmacologic analogs are not many marketed stand-alone agents, but it is most closely associated with imipenem in the fixed combination imipenem/cilastatin, and is conceptually similar to other enzyme-protective adjuncts such as relebactam in combination products, though relebactam is a beta-lactamase inhibitor rather than a dehydropeptidase inhibitor. Cilastatin acts primarily on renal dehydropeptidase I, also known as membrane metallo-endopeptidase-like 1 or DPEP1, inhibiting tubular metabolism of imipenem and reducing nephrotoxic metabolite formation. Pharmacokinetically, it is administered intravenously, has limited tissue penetration outside extracellular fluid, negligible metabolism, low protein binding, and is eliminated largely unchanged by glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, with a half-life prolonged in renal impairment. Toxicity is generally low but accumulation in kidney dysfunction may increase adverse reactions; examples include hypersensitivity, infusion reactions, and potentiation of seizure risk indirectly through altered imipenem exposure. Its indication is protection of imipenem from renal degradation in serious infections such as intra-abdominal infection, pneumonia, septicemia, urinary tract infection, gynecologic infection, and skin or bone infections. Adverse effects reported in clinical use of imipenem/cilastatin include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, phlebitis, elevated hepatic enzymes, eosinophilia, and rare anaphylactoid or CNS events. Clinically, cilastatin is used almost exclusively as a fixed companion drug with imipenem to enhance antibacterial efficacy, prolong urinary and systemic imipenem concentrations, and reduce renal metabolism during treatment of severe polymicrobial or nosocomial infections.

Name: Imipenem
Description: Imipenem (DrugBank DB01598) is a broad-spectrum carbapenem beta-lactam antibiotic whose structure consists of a highly strained bicyclic carbapenem nucleus with a fused beta-lactam and five-membered unsaturated ring, a trans-1-hydroxyethyl substituent that helps resist many beta-lactamases, and a basic thioether side chain that enhances Gram-negative penetration; chemically it belongs to the carbapenem subclass of beta-lactams and is built on the penem/carbapenem scaffold. Closely related drugs include meropenem, ertapenem, doripenem, and the older thienamycin scaffold from which it was derived. Its antibacterial targets are penicillin-binding proteins, especially PBP1A, PBP1B, PBP2, and PBP3 in susceptible organisms, leading to inhibition of peptidoglycan cross-linking and cell-wall synthesis. Imipenem is not orally bioavailable and is given intravenously or intramuscularly, usually with cilastatin to block renal dehydropeptidase I metabolism; it distributes well into extracellular fluids and many tissues, including urine, lung, abdomen, skin, and with inflamed meninges into CSF, undergoes limited nonrenal metabolism when protected by cilastatin, and is eliminated predominantly by the kidney, requiring dose reduction in renal impairment. It is indicated for complicated intra-abdominal, urinary tract, skin/soft tissue, bone/joint, gynecologic, lower respiratory, and polymicrobial nosocomial infections, including severe sepsis caused by susceptible Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and anaerobic bacteria. Important toxicities include dose-related seizures and CNS excitation, especially in renal dysfunction or CNS disease, as well as hypersensitivity and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea; common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, phlebitis, elevated transaminases, eosinophilia, and superinfection. Clinically, imipenem/cilastatin is used empirically or definitively for severe hospital-acquired mixed infections, resistant Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas aeruginosa in selected settings, aspiration-related polymicrobial infection, and complicated febrile neutropenia when broad coverage is required.

Name: Probucol
Description: Probucol (DrugBank DB01599) is a highly lipophilic bisphenolic hypolipidemic agent characterized structurally by two sterically hindered phenol rings linked through a sulfur-containing isopropylidene thioether bridge and decorated with bulky tert-butyl substituents, giving it the scaffold of a symmetrical hindered bisphenol antioxidant. Chemically, it belongs to phenolic antioxidants and sulfur-containing lipid-lowering agents, and its closest analog-like comparators are other antihyperlipidemic drugs with antioxidant or LDL-lowering intent, such as statins, cholestyramine, and older agents like clofibrate, although probucol is structurally more similar to lipophilic phenolic antioxidants than to these drugs. Its pharmacology is associated with enhancement of LDL catabolism and inhibition of oxidative modification of LDL, with reported effects involving cholesteryl ester transfer protein, apolipoprotein-associated pathways, and scavenger-related lipoprotein handling rather than a single dominant receptor target; no highly specific canonical protein target is firmly established, but CETP and pathways affecting LDL metabolism are commonly cited. Oral absorption is slow and variable, improved by food, distribution is extensive into adipose and lipoprotein-rich compartments, metabolism is limited and slow, and excretion occurs predominantly via the biliary-fecal route with a very long elimination half-life and tissue accumulation on chronic dosing. It has been used for hypercholesterolemia, especially familial forms and refractory dyslipidemia, and historically for reduction of LDL cholesterol and xanthomas. Major toxicities and side effects include QT prolongation with risk of ventricular arrhythmias such as torsades de pointes, marked lowering of HDL cholesterol, gastrointestinal upset including diarrhea and abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, and rash, which have limited or discontinued its clinical use in many settings.

Name: Tiaprofenic acid
Description: Tiaprofenic acid (DrugBank DB01600) is a propionic acid–derived nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug built around a 2-arylpropionic acid motif in which a thiophene ring serves as the principal heteroaryl core and is substituted by a benzoyl group, giving a lipophilic aromatic scaffold linked to the acidic propionate pharmacophore typical of profen NSAIDs. Chemically, it is classified as an arylpropionic acid NSAID, with a thiophene-benzoyl propionic acid scaffold related to other cyclooxygenase-inhibiting profens; similar drugs include ibuprofen, ketoprofen, flurbiprofen, fenoprofen, and naproxen, although tiaprofenic acid is distinguished by its thiophene-containing framework. Its principal targets are cyclooxygenase enzymes PTGS1 and PTGS2, with inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis accounting for analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antipyretic activity. It is used for symptomatic treatment of osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, musculoskeletal pain, and other inflammatory or painful conditions such as postoperative or dental pain. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed, reaches peak plasma concentrations within a few hours, is highly albumin bound, distributes mainly within the vascular/extracellular compartment, undergoes limited hepatic biotransformation with conjugative metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly in urine as unchanged drug and metabolites, with an elimination half-life in the low-hour range permitting divided daily dosing. Toxicities are those of NSAIDs, including gastrointestinal erosion, ulceration, bleeding, renal impairment, sodium and fluid retention, hypersensitivity reactions, and rare hepatotoxicity; tiaprofenic acid has also been notably associated with severe irritative cystitis and other urinary tract inflammation. Common adverse effects include dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, rash, and edema, and clinically it has been used as an oral anti-inflammatory analgesic when reduction of pain, stiffness, and inflammatory symptoms is required, although safety concerns have limited its favorability relative to other NSAIDs.

Name: Lopinavir
Description: Lopinavir (DrugBank DB01601) is a peptidomimetic HIV protease inhibitor built around a hydroxyethylene/hydroxyethylamine-like transition-state-mimetic core that replaces the scissile peptide bond and is decorated with lipophilic aryl, carbamate, and substituted amino alcohol functionalities, giving a flexible pseudopeptide structure optimized for binding the catalytic site of aspartyl proteases; chemically it is categorized as an antiretroviral protease inhibitor and its principal scaffold is a hydroxyethylene peptidomimetic protease-inhibitor framework closely related to ritonavir, darunavir, saquinavir, indinavir, atazanavir, and fosamprenavir/amprenavir. Its main target is the HIV-1 protease, with activity also against HIV-2 protease, thereby blocking Gag-Pol polyprotein cleavage and producing immature, noninfectious virions. Lopinavir is indicated for treatment of HIV-1 infection, typically in combination antiretroviral therapy, classically as lopinavir/ritonavir for adults, children, and postexposure contexts in selected protocols. Orally administered lopinavir has limited standalone bioavailability and is intentionally pharmacokinetically boosted by ritonavir via strong CYP3A and P-glycoprotein inhibition; it is highly protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes extensive hepatic CYP3A-mediated metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly in feces with limited renal excretion. Toxicities include hepatotoxicity, hypertriglyceridemia, hypercholesterolemia, insulin resistance/hyperglycemia, pancreatitis, PR/QT conduction effects, and major CYP3A-based drug interactions. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, rash, fatigue, and transaminase elevation. Clinically, it has been widely used in combination regimens for virologic suppression, including ritonavir-boosted oral tablets or solution in multidrug ART programs.

Name: Bacampicillin
Description: Bacampicillin (DrugBank DB01602) is an orally active ester prodrug of ampicillin built on the penam beta-lactam scaffold, consisting of the fused beta-lactam and thiazolidine bicyclic nucleus of aminopenicillins with a 6-side-chain bearing the alpha-aminobenzyl substituent characteristic of ampicillin, while the carboxyl group is masked as a lipophilic ester to enhance gastrointestinal uptake. It belongs to the beta-lactam antibiotic class, more specifically the aminopenicillin prodrugs, and its closest similar drugs include ampicillin, pivampicillin, talampicillin, amoxicillin, and other penicillins with related penam cores. After oral administration, bacampicillin is absorbed better than ampicillin and is rapidly hydrolyzed by esterases in the intestinal mucosa, blood, and liver to active ampicillin; the released drug distributes widely into many tissues and extracellular fluids but has limited cerebrospinal fluid penetration unless meninges are inflamed, undergoes minimal further metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by renal tubular secretion and glomerular filtration, with dose adjustment needed in renal impairment. Its antibacterial targets are penicillin-binding proteins, including transpeptidases such as PBP1, PBP2, and PBP3, thereby inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-linking and bacterial cell-wall synthesis. Clinically it has been used for susceptible respiratory, urinary, skin and soft tissue, and enteric infections, for example bronchitis, pneumonia, otitis, sinusitis, cystitis, and salmonellosis. Adverse effects and toxicities resemble those of ampicillin, including nausea, diarrhea, rash, candidiasis, antibiotic-associated colitis, hypersensitivity up to anaphylaxis, rare hepatitis or cholestatic jaundice, hematologic reactions, seizures at high exposure, and occasional ester-related carnitine depletion concerns seen with some pivampicillin-like prodrugs.

Name: Meticillin
Description: Meticillin (methicillin; DrugBank DB01603) is a semisynthetic, penicillinase-resistant beta-lactam antibiotic built on the 6-aminopenicillanic acid nucleus, comprising a strained beta-lactam ring fused to a thiazolidine ring and bearing a bulky 2,6-dimethoxybenzamido side chain that sterically protects the beta-lactam from many staphylococcal beta-lactamases; chemically it is an antistaphylococcal penicillin within the beta-lactam/penam class, with a penam scaffold as its core structural framework. Similar drugs include other penicillinase-resistant penicillins such as oxacillin, nafcillin, cloxacillin, dicloxacillin, and flucloxacillin, as well as the broader penicillin family. Its antibacterial effect results from covalent acylation of bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, especially transpeptidases such as PBP1, PBP2, and PBP3, thereby blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking and cell-wall synthesis; resistance classically emerged through altered PBP2a encoded by mecA in methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Meticillin was used primarily for infections caused by penicillinase-producing susceptible staphylococci, including skin and soft tissue infection, pneumonia, osteomyelitis, endocarditis, and bacteremia. Pharmacokinetically, it is acid labile and poorly absorbed orally, so it was administered parenterally, distributed mainly in extracellular fluid with variable tissue penetration, underwent limited metabolism, and was eliminated predominantly by renal excretion via glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, with a short half-life necessitating repeated dosing. Important toxicities include hypersensitivity reactions, interstitial nephritis, rash, fever, eosinophilia, gastrointestinal upset, and less commonly hematologic abnormalities or hepatotoxicity; because safer congeners replaced it, its clinical use is now largely historical.

Name: Tazobactam
Description: Tazobactam (DB01606) is a penicillanic acid sulfone beta-lactamase inhibitor whose structure consists of a bicyclic beta-lactam fused to a thiazolidine-like ring bearing a sulfone and carboxylate, preserving the penam scaffold while enhancing irreversible enzyme inhibition; chemically it is classified as a beta-lactamase inhibitor within the beta-lactam/penam sulfone class, with a penicillanic acid sulfone scaffold closely related to sulbactam and clavulanate, and broadly similar to other beta-lactamase inhibitors such as sulbactam, clavulanic acid, and the newer diazabicyclooctane inhibitors avibactam and relebactam, although the latter have distinct non-beta-lactam scaffolds. Its principal targets are bacterial serine beta-lactamases, especially class A enzymes and some class C species, through covalent acylation and suicide inhibition, thereby protecting partner beta-lactams such as piperacillin from hydrolysis. Pharmacokinetically, tazobactam is administered parenterally, has essentially complete systemic availability by intravenous use, low to moderate plasma protein binding, distribution mainly in extracellular fluids and infected tissues, minimal metabolism, and predominant renal excretion as unchanged drug with a short elimination half-life, requiring dose adjustment in renal impairment. Clinically it is used almost exclusively in combination, particularly piperacillin/tazobactam, for polymicrobial and susceptible Gram-negative or anaerobic infections including intra-abdominal infection, pneumonia, skin and soft tissue infection, gynecologic infection, and complicated urinary tract infection. Adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, rash, candidiasis, transaminase elevations, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, hypersensitivity, and infusion-site reactions; toxicity is generally low but can include beta-lactam allergy, hepatic enzyme abnormalities, hematologic suppression with prolonged therapy, and neurotoxicity or seizures mainly when combined therapy is excessive or renal clearance is impaired.

Name: Ticarcillin
Description: Ticarcillin (DrugBank DB01607) is a semisynthetic carboxypenicillin beta-lactam antibiotic whose structure consists of the penam nucleus, a strained bicyclic system formed by a beta-lactam fused to a thiazolidine ring, bearing the characteristic acylamino side chain and an additional thiophene-derived carboxylated substituent that broadens Gram-negative activity; chemically it belongs to the penicillin family, specifically the antipseudomonal carboxypenicillins, and its core scaffold is the 6-aminopenicillanic acid penam scaffold. Closely related drugs include carbenicillin and piperacillin, as well as broader beta-lactam comparators such as ampicillin and mezlocillin. Ticarcillin targets bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, especially transpeptidases such as PBP1A, PBP1B, PBP2, and PBP3 in susceptible organisms, thereby inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-linking and cell-wall synthesis. It has negligible oral absorption and is administered parenterally; distribution is mainly extracellular with penetration into urine, lung, pleural, peritoneal, and some inflamed meningeal compartments, low to moderate protein binding, minimal metabolism, and predominantly renal excretion by glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, giving a relatively short half-life prolonged in renal impairment. It is indicated for serious susceptible infections, particularly Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Proteus, Enterobacteriaceae, and mixed infections causing lower respiratory tract infection, septicemia, urinary tract infection, intra-abdominal infection, gynecologic infection, skin/soft tissue infection, and bone/joint infection, often clinically used with clavulanate or an aminoglycoside. Toxicities include hypersensitivity reactions, interstitial nephritis, sodium load–related fluid and electrolyte disturbances, platelet dysfunction and bleeding tendency, seizures at high concentrations or in renal failure, and antibiotic-associated colitis; common adverse effects include rash, fever, diarrhea, nausea, phlebitis, eosinophilia, elevated transaminases, and superinfection.

Name: Deferasirox
Description: Deferasirox (DrugBank DB01609) is an oral tridentate iron chelator built on a lipophilic bis-phenolic triazole framework, structurally characterized by a central 1,2,4-triazole-linked aromatic scaffold bearing two salicylamide-like phenolic rings and a benzoic acid substituent that together create oxygen- and nitrogen-donor sites for high-affinity ferric iron coordination; chemically it is categorized as a synthetic iron-complexing agent and triazole-containing chelator, with a diaryl-1,2,4-triazole scaffold. Closely related drugs with similar therapeutic intent include deferoxamine and deferiprone, which differ in denticity, route, and pharmacokinetics. Its pharmacological target is ferric iron rather than a canonical receptor, forming stable iron-deferasirox complexes that reduce non-transferrin-bound iron and labile plasma iron; no major specific protein target is central to efficacy, although iron removal secondarily affects iron-dependent pathways. After oral administration it is reasonably well absorbed, highly protein bound mainly to albumin, distributed largely in plasma, extensively metabolized predominantly by hepatic glucuronidation via UGT1A1 and UGT1A3 with minor oxidative metabolism, and excreted chiefly in feces with limited renal elimination and a relatively long half-life permitting once-daily dosing. It is indicated for chronic iron overload due to repeated transfusions, such as in beta-thalassemia, sickle cell disease, and myelodysplastic syndromes, and for non-transfusion-dependent thalassemia with iron overload. Important toxicities include renal impairment, proteinuria, acute kidney injury, hepatotoxicity, hepatic failure, gastrointestinal ulceration or hemorrhage, cytopenias, and rare severe cutaneous hypersensitivity; common adverse effects include nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, vomiting, rash, and increases in serum creatinine or transaminases. Clinically, it is used as long-term outpatient iron chelation to lower liver iron concentration and serum ferritin and to prevent end-organ complications of hemosiderosis, especially in chronically transfused patients.

Name: Hydroxychloroquine
Description: Hydroxychloroquine (DrugBank DB01611) is a synthetic 4-aminoquinoline bearing a planar quinoline heteroaromatic core with a 7-chloro substituent and a 4-amino side chain terminating in a hydroxylated tertiary aminoalkyl moiety, a structure that confers weakly basic, lysosomotropic behavior; chemically it is classified as an antimalarial aminoquinoline and more broadly a quinoline derivative, with a chloroquine-like 4-aminoquinoline scaffold. Closely related drugs include chloroquine, amodiaquine, primaquine, and quinacrine, with chloroquine being the most structurally and pharmacologically similar. Hydroxychloroquine is well absorbed orally, has a very large volume of distribution with extensive sequestration in melanin-containing tissues, liver, spleen, kidney, lung, and blood cells, is partially metabolized hepatically mainly by CYP2C8, CYP3A4, and CYP2D6 to active and inactive desethyl metabolites, and is eliminated slowly by the kidney with a prolonged terminal half-life measured in weeks. Its pharmacology involves endosomal and lysosomal alkalinization and interference with antigen processing and nucleic acid sensing, with reported targets or pathway mediators including TLR7, TLR9, cGAS-STING-associated signaling, and lysosomal processes rather than a single high-affinity receptor. It is indicated for malaria and for autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis, where it is used chronically for disease control, rash, arthralgia, and constitutional symptoms. Important toxicities include dose- and duration-related retinopathy, QT prolongation and cardiomyopathy, hypoglycemia, neuropsychiatric effects, myopathy, and hemolysis risk in susceptible patients; common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, pruritus, rash, and visual disturbance.

Name: Amyl Nitrite
Description: Amyl nitrite (DrugBank DB01612) is a small, highly volatile aliphatic nitrite ester consisting of a pentyl, historically often isoamyl, hydrocarbon chain linked through an oxygen atom to a nitroso-derived nitrite group, giving a simple alkyl nitrite structure with a flexible lipophilic C5 scaffold and an O–N=O pharmacophore responsible for rapid nitric oxide bioactivity; it belongs to the organic nitrites, with the alkyl-nitrite scaffold shared by related vasodilators such as butyl nitrite, isobutyl nitrite, and propyl nitrite, and is pharmacologically analogous in some respects to other nitrovasodilators such as nitroglycerin and sodium nitrite. Its principal functional targets are not classical high-affinity receptors but the nitric oxide–soluble guanylate cyclase signaling axis, with downstream activation of GUCY1A1/GUCY1B1 and increased cGMP in vascular smooth muscle, and it also oxidizes hemoglobin to methemoglobin. After inhalation it is absorbed extremely rapidly through the pulmonary alveoli, distributes quickly to highly perfused tissues, has a very short duration because it undergoes rapid enzymatic and nonenzymatic metabolism to nitrite, nitrate, and corresponding alcohol derivatives, with further renal elimination of inorganic metabolites. Clinically it has been used for acute relief of angina pectoris and as part of cyanide poisoning treatment by inducing methemoglobinemia to bind cyanide, and historically for transient coronary vasodilation or smooth-muscle relaxation. Adverse effects and toxicity reflect potent vasodilation and oxidant stress, including flushing, throbbing headache, dizziness, reflex tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension, syncope, and nausea; excessive exposure can cause severe methemoglobinemia, hypoxemia, hemolysis, and dangerous hypotension, especially with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors or in patients with anemia, G6PD deficiency, or cardiopulmonary disease.

Name: Aceprometazine
Description: Aceprometazine (DrugBank DB01615) is a sedating first-generation antihistamine of the phenothiazine family whose structure is characterized by a rigid tricyclic phenothiazine nucleus containing sulfur and ring nitrogen, substituted at the 10-position by a dimethylaminopropyl side chain and further ring substitution that supports strong central H1-antihistaminic and anticholinergic activity; chemically it is therefore classified as a phenothiazine antihistamine, with the phenothiazine tricycle serving as its core scaffold. It is closely related to other sedating phenothiazine or tricyclic antihistamines such as promethazine, alimemazine, methdilazine, and to some extent chlorpromazine-like phenothiazines, which share similar lipophilic cationic architecture and CNS penetration. After oral administration it is expected to be reasonably absorbed, widely distributed, highly protein bound, and to cross the blood-brain barrier effectively; like related agents it undergoes substantial hepatic biotransformation, likely including oxidative and conjugative metabolism, with metabolites and parent-related material excreted mainly in urine and to a lesser extent bile/feces. Its principal pharmacologic target is histamine H1 receptor antagonism/inverse agonism, with additional likely activity at muscarinic cholinergic receptors and possibly weaker interactions at alpha-adrenergic or serotonergic sites typical of phenothiazines. Clinically it has been used for symptomatic relief of allergic conditions such as rhinitis, urticaria, and pruritus, and as a sedative component in cough, cold, or nighttime allergy preparations. Adverse effects and toxicity resemble other sedating antihistamines: marked drowsiness, impaired psychomotor performance, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, hypotension, and paradoxical excitation in children; overdose may cause profound CNS depression, anticholinergic syndrome, seizures, arrhythmias, or respiratory compromise, especially with alcohol or other sedatives.

Name: Molindone
Description: Molindone (DrugBank DB01618) is a first-generation antipsychotic of the dihydroindolone class, structurally characterized by a substituted 3-ethyl-2-methylindolin-2-one core bearing a morpholineethyl side chain, giving it a compact heterocyclic ketone-containing framework with both lipophilic and basic tertiary amine features typical of centrally active dopamine antagonists. Chemically it is classified as a heterocyclic antipsychotic and is built on an indolone scaffold, distinguishing it from phenothiazines and butyrophenones, although it is pharmacologically similar to other typical antipsychotics such as haloperidol, thiothixene, loxapine, and perphenazine in its antidopaminergic effects. Its principal known targets are dopamine D2 receptors, with lesser activity at other central dopaminergic and possibly serotonergic sites, and its antipsychotic efficacy is mainly attributed to mesolimbic D2 blockade. Molindone has been used primarily for schizophrenia, especially for reduction of hallucinations, delusions, agitation, and disorganized thought, and historically in chronic psychotic illness requiring oral maintenance therapy. After oral administration it is absorbed variably, undergoes substantial hepatic first-pass metabolism, distributes into the CNS, is extensively metabolized in the liver to inactive or less active metabolites, and is eliminated mainly in urine with some fecal excretion; its relatively short half-life generally necessitates divided dosing. Adverse effects include extrapyramidal symptoms such as akathisia, parkinsonism, dystonia, and tardive dyskinesia, along with sedation, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, orthostatic hypotension, and endocrine effects related to dopamine blockade; unlike many antipsychotics it has been associated with weight loss rather than gain. Toxicity may include overdose-related CNS depression, seizures, severe EPS, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and potential cardiovascular instability, so clinical use has required careful dose titration and monitoring in vulnerable psychiatric patients.

Name: Phenindamine
Description: Phenindamine (DrugBank DB01619) is a first-generation H1-antihistamine of the alkylamine/ethylenediamine-related antihistamine family, structurally characterized by a lipophilic triaryl-like arrangement built around an indene scaffold linked to a dimethylaminoalkyl side chain; this compact benzhydryl-like pharmacophore, containing fused aromatic ring character and a basic tertiary amine, underlies its classification as a classical sedating antihistamine. Its core chemical scaffold is best described as an indene-derived antihistamine framework, and it is broadly similar to other older H1 antagonists such as tripelennamine, chlorpheniramine, brompheniramine, and pyrilamine, which share aromatic hydrophobic groups and a protonatable amine that enable histamine H1 receptor binding. Pharmacologically, its principal known target is the histamine H1 receptor, with likely additional weak antimuscarinic activity typical of the class. After oral administration it is expected to be reasonably well absorbed, distributed widely including into the central nervous system because of lipophilicity, metabolized predominantly in the liver by oxidative biotransformation, and excreted as metabolites and a smaller unchanged fraction in urine. Toxicity resembles that of other first-generation antihistamines, including dose-related CNS depression or paradoxical excitation, anticholinergic burden, impaired psychomotor performance, and in overdose delirium, tachycardia, seizures, or coma. It is indicated for symptomatic relief of allergic conditions such as allergic rhinitis, urticaria, conjunctival irritation, pruritus, and sneezing.
