Common adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention. Clinically, phenindamine has been used as an older oral antiallergic agent for hay fever, hives, and other histamine-mediated hypersensitivity symptoms, but its use is limited by sedation and anticholinergic effects.

Name: Pheniramine
Description: Pheniramine (DrugBank DB01620) is a first-generation alkylamine antihistamine built around a substituted propylamine framework in which a pyridyl ring and a phenyl ring are linked through a short carbon chain to a dimethylamino terminus, giving a lipophilic, basic aryl-alkyl tertiary amine structure typical of classical H1 antagonists; chemically it is categorized as an antihistaminic alkylamine and more broadly an aromatic amine, with an alkylarylamine/propylamine scaffold closely related to chlorpheniramine, brompheniramine, triprolidine, and other older H1 receptor blockers. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, where it acts as an inverse agonist/antagonist, and it may also show mild antimuscarinic activity that contributes to adverse effects. Pheniramine is used for symptomatic relief of allergic rhinitis, urticaria, conjunctival irritation, pruritus, and common cold symptoms such as sneezing and rhinorrhea, and in practice appears in oral, topical, and ophthalmic products, for example in hay fever, hives, and itchy eye preparations. It is generally well absorbed after oral administration, distributes widely including into the central nervous system because of blood-brain barrier penetration, undergoes hepatic metabolism with biotransformation typical of tertiary amines, and is excreted mainly in urine as metabolites and some unchanged drug. Toxicity is consistent with first-generation antihistamines and includes dose-related CNS depression or paradoxical excitation, anticholinergic effects, and in overdose agitation, delirium, seizures, or cardiac effects; common side effects include sedation, dizziness, impaired psychomotor performance, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention, with heightened risk in children, older adults, and when combined with alcohol or other sedatives.

Name: Pipotiazine
Description: Pipotiazine (DrugBank DB01621) is a typical antipsychotic of the phenothiazine class, specifically a piperidine-substituted phenothiazine, built on a tricyclic phenothiazine scaffold in which two benzene rings flank a sulfur- and nitrogen-containing central ring and a three-carbon side chain terminates in a substituted piperidine moiety; this architecture closely relates it to other phenothiazines such as thioridazine, periciazine, prochlorperazine, chlorpromazine, and fluphenazine, with shared dopamine-receptor antagonism but differing potency and adverse-effect balance. Its principal pharmacologic targets are dopamine D2 receptors in mesolimbic and nigrostriatal pathways, with additional antagonism reported at D1-like receptors, alpha1-adrenergic receptors, histamine H1 receptors, and muscarinic cholinergic receptors, accounting for both antipsychotic and autonomic effects. Clinically it has been used in schizophrenia and other chronic psychotic disorders, particularly for agitation, delusions, hallucinations, and behavioral disturbance, including depot formulations such as pipotiazine palmitate for maintenance therapy in poorly adherent patients. Pharmacokinetically, oral absorption is variable because of first-pass metabolism, while long-acting ester formulations are slowly absorbed intramuscularly, widely distributed into lipid-rich tissues and the CNS, highly protein bound, hepatically metabolized by oxidative pathways and ester hydrolysis, and eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine and bile with a prolonged apparent half-life for depot dosing. Toxicity resembles that of other low- to mid-potency phenothiazines: dose-related CNS depression, hypotension, anticholinergic burden, QT prolongation and arrhythmia risk, extrapyramidal syndromes, tardive dyskinesia, hyperprolactinemia, seizures, cholestatic jaundice, blood dyscrasias, and rare neuroleptic malignant syndrome; common side effects include sedation, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, orthostasis, weight gain, tremor, akathisia, parkinsonism, and sexual dysfunction.

Name: sirolimus
Description: Sirolimus (DrugBank DB01623), also called rapamycin, is a natural product-derived macrocyclic lactone characterized by a large highly functionalized 31-membered triene-containing macrolide ring with multiple hydroxyl, methoxy, ketone, and ester substituents and a pipecolate moiety, placing it in the macrolide polyketide immunosuppressant class and more specifically within the rapamycin/rapalog scaffold family. Closely related drugs include the mTOR-pathway analogs everolimus, temsirolimus, ridaforolimus, and the structurally/mechanistically related calcineurin-binding macrolide tacrolimus. Its primary pharmacologic target is FKBP1A (FKBP12); the sirolimus-FKBP12 complex inhibits mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 via MTOR, with downstream effects on RPTOR, p70S6K, and EIF4EBP1 signaling, thereby suppressing IL-2-driven T-cell proliferation. Orally administered sirolimus has variable, incomplete absorption, is highly erythrocyte- and protein-bound with a large apparent distribution volume, undergoes extensive hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4/3A5 metabolism and P-glycoprotein transport, has a long terminal half-life, and is eliminated predominantly in feces with minimal renal excretion. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related immunosuppression and antiproliferative effects, including serious infection, delayed wound healing, interstitial pneumonitis, proteinuria, thrombotic microangiopathy, hepatotoxicity, hyperlipidemia, and myelosuppression such as thrombocytopenia or leukopenia. Common adverse effects include mouth ulcers, edema, acne or rash, diarrhea, anemia, hypertension, and dyslipidemia. Clinically, sirolimus is used primarily to prevent renal transplant rejection, especially in calcineurin-sparing regimens, and is also used in lymphangioleiomyomatosis and selected vascular anomalies, with investigational or off-label use in certain cancers and restenosis-prevention devices.

Name: Zuclopenthixol
Description: Zuclopenthixol (DrugBank DB01624) is a first-generation antipsychotic of the thioxanthene class, structurally characterized by a tricyclic dibenzothiepin-like thioxanthene core in which the central ring contains sulfur and an exocyclic double bond, bearing a 2-chloro aromatic substitution and a three-carbon side chain terminating in a tertiary alcohol-linked piperazine-like amine functionality; its principal scaffold is the chlorinated thioxanthene neuroleptic framework closely related to other typical antipsychotics. Chemically and pharmacologically it is similar to other thioxanthenes such as flupenthixol and chlorprothixene, and more broadly to phenothiazine-type dopamine antagonists such as chlorpromazine. Its main targets are dopamine D1 and especially D2 receptors, with additional antagonism at serotonin 5-HT2, alpha1-adrenergic, and histamine H1 receptors, explaining both antipsychotic efficacy and adverse effects. It is indicated for schizophrenia, acute and chronic psychosis, severe agitation, aggression, and manic or behavioral disturbance, and in practice is used as oral zuclopenthixol or long-acting acetate and decanoate esters for rapid tranquilization or maintenance treatment in poorly adherent patients. Pharmacokinetically, it is well absorbed after oral or intramuscular administration, is highly lipophilic and extensively protein bound, distributes widely including into the CNS, undergoes hepatic metabolism mainly by oxidative pathways and conjugation, and is eliminated predominantly as metabolites in feces and urine, with depot esters producing prolonged release. Toxicity is typical of potent dopamine antagonists and includes dose-related extrapyramidal syndromes, tardive dyskinesia, hyperprolactinemia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, QT-related cardiac risk, sedation, hypotension, anticholinergic effects, weight gain, and overdose manifestations such as coma, respiratory depression, and severe cardiovascular instability.

Name: Isopropamide
Description: Isopropamide (DrugBank DB01625) is a synthetic quaternary ammonium antimuscarinic agent whose structure consists of a permanently charged pyridinium-containing ester linking a bulky diaryl-substituted glycolate-like moiety to an isopropyl group, a design that confers strong peripheral anticholinergic activity and poor central nervous system penetration; chemically it is categorized as a quaternary ammonium parasympatholytic and more specifically a carboxylate ester antimuscarinic, built on the classic amino alcohol/aryl ester antispasmodic scaffold seen in older gastrointestinal anticholinergics. Similar drugs include propantheline, methantheline, glycopyrrolate, clidinium, and other atropine-like peripheral muscarinic antagonists. Its principal pharmacologic targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially M1 and M3 receptors in the gastrointestinal tract and exocrine glands, producing reduced gastric secretion, diminished gut motility, and antispasmodic effects. After oral administration, absorption is limited and variable because the quaternary cation reduces membrane permeability; distribution is largely peripheral with minimal blood-brain barrier entry, metabolism appears limited to partial ester hydrolysis and hepatic biotransformation, and elimination occurs through both renal and biliary/fecal routes, with unchanged drug and metabolites recoverable in urine. Toxicity reflects exaggerated antimuscarinic effects, including severe xerostomia, constipation, urinary retention, tachycardia, blurred vision, reduced sweating, and possible paralytic ileus, with heightened risk in elderly patients and in glaucoma, prostatic hypertrophy, or obstructive uropathy. Clinically, isopropamide has been used as an adjunct in peptic ulcer disease, gastritis, hyperacidity, and functional gastrointestinal spasm, and for symptom relief of abdominal cramping and motility-related discomfort.

Name: Pargyline
Description: Pargyline (DB01626) is an older, irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor built on a small propargylamine structure consisting of a tertiary amine bearing a benzyl-substituted alkynyl side chain, with a phenyl-alkynyl-amine motif that confers mechanism-based MAO inhibition; chemically it is classified as a nonhydrazine propargylamine MAOI, and its core scaffold is the aryl-propargylamine/phenylylpropynylamine scaffold shared conceptually with other acetylenic MAO inhibitors. Similar drugs include tranylcypromine, selegiline, and rasagiline as irreversible MAO inhibitors, and older antihypertensive MAOIs such as phenelzine and isocarboxazid, although those differ by hydrazine chemistry. Its principal targets are mitochondrial monoamine oxidase enzymes, especially MAO-B and at higher exposure MAO-A, causing reduced oxidative deamination of catecholamines and other biogenic amines. It was used primarily as an antihypertensive agent for essential hypertension, with occasional historical interest in depressive disorders because of MAO inhibition. Pargyline is orally absorbed, distributes systemically including into the CNS, undergoes substantial hepatic metabolism with irreversible enzyme binding contributing to prolonged pharmacodynamic effects beyond plasma persistence, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine. Toxicity reflects excessive monoaminergic potentiation and MAO inhibition, including tyramine-induced hypertensive crisis, hyperpyrexia, agitation, and possible intracranial hemorrhage; overdose may produce severe hypertension followed by cardiovascular collapse or CNS complications. Adverse effects include orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, insomnia, dry mouth, constipation, sexual dysfunction, edema, and weight gain. Clinically, its use required strict dietary and drug-interaction precautions, particularly avoidance of sympathomimetics, serotonergic agents, and tyramine-rich foods.

Name: Roflumilast
Description: Roflumilast (DrugBank DB01656) is a selective, nonsteroidal phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor built on a substituted benzamide/anilide-like aromatic scaffold featuring a dichloropyridyl ring linked through an ether bridge to a methoxy-substituted phenyl system, a compact heteroaromatic lipophilic framework that places it in the chlorinated small-molecule PDE4 inhibitor class; its core scaffold is closely related to other PDE4 inhibitors such as rolipram, cilomilast, and the structurally distinct but pharmacologically similar apremilast. Its principal targets are PDE4 isoenzymes, especially PDE4B and PDE4D, leading to increased intracellular cAMP and suppression of inflammatory cell signaling. After oral administration it is well absorbed, with high bioavailability, extensive tissue distribution, and clinically important hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 and CYP1A2 to the active N-oxide metabolite, followed by further oxidative biotransformation and predominantly urinary excretion of metabolites with some fecal elimination; the parent drug and metabolite together account for sustained PDE4 inhibition. It is indicated primarily to reduce risk of exacerbations in severe COPD associated with chronic bronchitis and a history of exacerbations, and it is also used topically for inflammatory dermatoses such as plaque psoriasis and seborrheic dermatitis. Adverse effects commonly include diarrhea, nausea, decreased appetite, weight loss, abdominal pain, headache, insomnia, and dizziness; clinically important toxicities include excessive weight loss, psychiatric reactions such as anxiety, depression, and rare suicidal ideation, plus intolerance from gastrointestinal toxicity. In practice it is used as an anti-inflammatory maintenance therapy rather than a bronchodilator, often as add-on treatment in COPD patients with recurrent exacerbations.

Name: Fumaric acid
Description: Fumaric acid (DrugBank DB01677) is a small, unsaturated dicarboxylic acid composed of a trans-alkene core bearing two terminal carboxyl groups, giving a rigid, planar trans-butenedioic acid framework with strong acidity and ready participation in conjugation and esterification chemistry; it is therefore classified as an aliphatic dicarboxylic acid and more specifically an unsaturated carboxylic acid, with the fumarate scaffold serving as the key chemical motif also found in related agents such as dimethyl fumarate, diroximel fumarate, monomethyl fumarate, and the geometric isomer maleic acid. Pharmacologically, fumaric acid itself is an endogenous tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediate and is generally handled through normal intermediary metabolism: oral fumarates are typically absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, distributed largely in body water, rapidly hydrolyzed if administered as esters, metabolized through fumarase-dependent conversion to malate and downstream carbon flux, and eliminated mainly as exhaled carbon dioxide with minor renal excretion of metabolites. Known biological targets are indirect rather than highly selective and include modulation of the KEAP1-NRF2 oxidative stress response pathway through electrophilic fumarate esters, with downstream immunologic effects on pathways involving HCAR2 and NF-kappaB reported for fumarate derivatives. Toxicity is usually low for fumaric acid at modest exposure but can include mucosal and skin irritation, gastrointestinal pain, nausea, metabolic disturbance at excessive doses, and rare renal or hepatic injury in the broader fumarate class. Clinically, fumaric acid is used mainly as a precursor, excipient, acidifier, or nutraceutical-related intermediate rather than a major standalone drug, while fumarate-based therapy is associated with psoriasis and multiple sclerosis treatment; adverse effects seen with fumarate exposure include flushing, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, lymphopenia, and elevated liver enzymes.

Name: Topiroxostat
Description: Topiroxostat (DrugBank DB01685) is a non-purine xanthine oxidoreductase inhibitor whose structure is centered on a compact heteroaromatic pyrazine-derived scaffold bearing nitrile and substituted phenyl functionalities, giving a planar, electron-deficient aza-heterocycle designed to bind tightly within the molybdenum-pterin active site channel of xanthine oxidase; chemically it is classified as a small-molecule heteroaryl urate-lowering agent, with a pyrazine/carbonitrile aromatic scaffold that distinguishes it from purine analog inhibitors. Similar drugs include allopurinol and its active metabolite oxypurinol, the non-purine inhibitor febuxostat, and other xanthine oxidase inhibitors used in hyperuricemia and gout. Its principal target protein is xanthine oxidoreductase/xanthine oxidase, leading to reduced uric acid formation. Pharmacokinetically, topiroxostat is orally active, absorbed sufficiently for chronic once- or twice-daily use, is moderately protein bound, undergoes extensive hepatic biotransformation including glucuronidation and oxidative pathways to inactive or weakly active metabolites, and is eliminated by both renal and fecal routes, with parent drug and metabolites appearing in urine. It is indicated primarily for hyperuricemia, particularly in patients with gout or asymptomatic hyperuricemia, and has been used clinically to lower serum urate and potentially reduce renal urate burden in patients with chronic kidney disease. Adverse effects include hepatic enzyme elevation, rash, gastrointestinal discomfort, nausea, arthralgia, and gout flares during urate mobilization; toxicity concerns include liver dysfunction, hypersensitivity, and possible renal-related laboratory changes, so liver and renal function monitoring are typically advised during clinical use.

Name: Rutin
Description: Rutin (DrugBank DB01698), also called rutoside or quercetin-3-O-rutinoside, is a polyphenolic flavonoid glycoside whose structure consists of the flavonol aglycone quercetin bearing multiple phenolic hydroxyl groups and a disaccharide rutinoside moiety attached at the 3-position, giving a planar benzopyranone-based aromatic system with extensive hydrogen-bonding capacity and limited lipophilicity; chemically it belongs to the flavonoids, specifically flavonol O-glycosides, and its core scaffold is the quercetin flavonol scaffold linked to a rutinose sugar. Similar drugs or closely related natural products include quercetin, hesperidin, diosmin, troxerutin, and other hydroxyethylrutosides used as vasoprotective agents. Orally, rutin has relatively poor absorption in intact form, undergoes deglycosylation by intestinal microbiota and enteric enzymes to quercetin and phenolic metabolites, shows limited systemic bioavailability of parent compound, distributes mainly as conjugated metabolites, and is eliminated predominantly in urine and bile after glucuronidation, sulfation, and methylation. Its pharmacology is largely attributed to antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, capillary-protective, and venotonic effects, with reported interactions affecting xanthine oxidase, cyclooxygenases, lipoxygenases, NF-kB-related signaling, VEGF-associated pathways, and occasionally protein disulfide isomerase in antithrombotic research. Toxicity is generally low, but high doses may cause gastrointestinal irritation, headache, or rare hypersensitivity; experimental concerns include pro-oxidant effects under some conditions and potential interactions with anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs. Clinically, rutin has been used mainly for chronic venous insufficiency, hemorrhoids, varicose veins, capillary fragility, edema, and bruising, and also as an adjunct in symptomatic management of vascular and inflammatory disorders.

Name: Prasterone
Description: Prasterone (dehydroepiandrosterone, DHEA; DrugBank DB01708) is an endogenous adrenal and gonadal steroid characterized structurally as a C19 androstane derivative with the classic fused four-ring cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene nucleus, a 3β-hydroxyl group, a 17-keto group, and a double bond at C5–C6, placing it in the steroid hormone/androgen precursor class and more specifically within the androstene steroid scaffold. It is closely related to and functionally similar to other endogenous sex-steroid precursors and metabolites such as dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate, androstenedione, testosterone, estradiol precursors, and synthetic or semisynthetic vaginal prasterone products. Pharmacokinetically, prasterone is absorbed after oral or intravaginal administration, distributes widely with extensive protein binding and rapid tissue uptake, and undergoes substantial first-pass and peripheral metabolism to DHEA sulfate via SULT2A1 and to active androgens and estrogens through 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, 17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, aromatase/CYP19A1, and steroid sulfatase pathways; elimination occurs mainly as sulfate and glucuronide metabolites in urine. Its biological targets are therefore indirect and include the androgen receptor, estrogen receptors ESR1 and ESR2, and steroidogenic enzymes rather than a single primary receptor. Toxicity is generally low at therapeutic doses but may include androgenic and estrogenic effects, hepatically altered steroid metabolism, and theoretical risks of stimulating hormone-sensitive malignancies; overdose may cause acne, hirsutism, seborrhea, mood change, or endocrine disturbance. Clinically, prasterone is used mainly for dyspareunia and vulvovaginal atrophy in postmenopausal women and has also been studied for adrenal insufficiency, sexual dysfunction, aging-related symptoms, mood disorders, and lupus-related fatigue, with common adverse effects including vaginal discharge, abnormal Pap smear findings, local irritation, acne, oily skin, and unwanted hair growth.

Name: Dalfopristin
Description: Dalfopristin (DrugBank DB01764) is a semisynthetic streptogramin A antibacterial derived from pristinamycin, characterized structurally as a highly oxygenated, lipophilic 23-membered polyunsaturated macrocyclic depsipeptide/lactone bearing multiple ester, hydroxyl, ketone, and conjugated alkene functionalities; chemically it belongs to the streptogramin class of macrolide-like polyketide-peptide antibiotics, and its core scaffold is the pristinamycin II A-type macrocyclic depsipeptide. It is most closely related to other streptogramins, especially quinupristin, with which it is coformulated, and to pristinamycin, virginiamycin M, and madumycin. Its principal target is the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit, binding the 23S rRNA peptidyl transferase region; dalfopristin induces a conformational change that enhances quinupristin binding, producing synergistic inhibition of protein synthesis and bactericidal activity in combination against many Gram-positive pathogens. Pharmacokinetically, it is administered intravenously because oral bioavailability is poor, distributes widely into tissues but has limited cerebrospinal fluid penetration, is highly protein bound, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism including conjugation and hydrolysis to active and inactive metabolites, and is eliminated predominantly via biliary/fecal excretion with relatively minor renal clearance. Toxicity is chiefly hepatic and infusion related, with examples including hyperbilirubinemia, transaminase elevation, arthralgia-myalgia syndrome, and local venous irritation; adverse effects also include nausea, rash, headache, and phlebitis. Clinically, dalfopristin is used only with quinupristin for serious infections due to susceptible Gram-positive organisms, especially vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium bacteremia and complicated skin and soft-tissue infections caused by methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes.

Name: Pantothenic acid
Description: Pantothenic acid (DrugBank DB01783), also known as vitamin B5, is a small, highly water-soluble aliphatic carboxylic acid composed of pantoic acid linked by an amide bond to beta-alanine, giving a flexible, nonaromatic structure with terminal hydroxyl and carboxyl functionalities; chemically it is classified as a B-complex vitamin and essential nutrient, and its core scaffold is a pantoyl-beta-alanine vitamin scaffold that serves as the biosynthetic precursor of 4-phosphopantetheine and coenzyme A. Closely related agents include dexpanthenol, pantethine, pantethine-derived supplements, and coenzyme A precursors, which share the same pantothenate backbone or immediate metabolic lineage. After oral administration, pantothenic acid is efficiently absorbed mainly in the small intestine by a saturable sodium-dependent multivitamin transporter and by passive diffusion at higher doses, distributed widely in plasma and tissues with highest functional demand in liver, adrenal glands, kidney, and rapidly proliferating cells, minimally protein bound, converted intracellularly through phosphorylation and subsequent enzymatic steps into coenzyme A and acyl carrier protein cofactors, and excreted largely unchanged in urine with limited fecal loss. Its principal biological targets are indirect metabolic enzymes that require coenzyme A or 4-phosphopantetheine, while the uptake target is SLC5A6; no classic high-affinity drug receptor is central to its action. It is indicated for prevention and treatment of pantothenate deficiency, including deficiency-associated paresthesias, fatigue, irritability, gastrointestinal complaints, and rare malnutrition-related states, and is also used clinically in vitamin supplementation, parenteral nutrition formulations, and occasionally as dexpanthenol-related mucocutaneous support. Toxicity is low, with no well-defined severe overdose syndrome, but high doses may cause diarrhea, abdominal cramping, nausea, heartburn, or fluid retention, and hypersensitivity reactions are uncommon.

Name: Taurine
Description: Taurine (DB01956) is a small, highly polar sulfur-containing amino acid analog whose structure is defined by a two-carbon ethane scaffold bearing a terminal primary amine and a sulfonic acid group, existing predominantly as a zwitterion at physiologic pH; chemically it is classified as an amino sulfonic acid rather than a true proteinogenic amino acid, with a simple 2-aminoethanesulfonic acid scaffold shared conceptually with related osmolytes and sulfonate-containing compounds. Similar agents include homotaurine (tramiprosate), acamprosate, hypotaurine, and the bile acid conjugates taurocholate and taurodeoxycholate, which preserve the taurine sulfonate pharmacophore. Pharmacokinetically, taurine is absorbed in the small intestine by carrier-mediated transport, distributes widely to excitable and secretory tissues including retina, myocardium, skeletal muscle, brain, and leukocytes, undergoes minimal biotransformation because it is largely an endogenous nutrient, participates in bile acid conjugation and cellular osmolyte pools, and is eliminated mainly unchanged by the kidney with active tubular reabsorption regulating plasma levels. Toxicity is generally low, but excessive intake may cause gastrointestinal discomfort, headache, dizziness, hypotension, or electrolyte/osmotic disturbances, and very high exposures or use in stimulant-containing energy products have raised concerns in patients with cardiac or renal disease. Known targets and functional effectors include the taurine transporter SLC6A6, glycine and GABAA receptor systems, NMDA-modulatory pathways, bile acid handling proteins, and ion-transport processes affecting calcium homeostasis. Clinically, taurine has been used as a nutritional supplement or adjunct in deficiency states, cardiomyopathy or heart failure, retinal degeneration, mitochondrial disease, cholestatic liver disorders, cystic fibrosis, diabetes-related complications, and fatigue or muscle cramping, with side effects usually mild and use largely supportive rather than as a conventional high-potency receptor-selective drug.

Name: Flufenamic acid
Description: Flufenamic acid (DrugBank DB02266) is an anthranilic acid derivative of the fenamate class of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, structurally characterized as an N-arylanthranilic acid bearing a trifluoromethyl-substituted aniline ring linked through a secondary anilide-like nitrogen to a benzoic acid core, giving a relatively lipophilic, twisted biaryl scaffold typical of fenamates. Its core chemical scaffold is the fenamate or N-phenylanthranilic acid framework, and structurally related drugs include mefenamic acid, meclofenamate, tolfenamic acid, and niflumic acid, which share similar arylamino benzoic acid motifs and NSAID pharmacology. Pharmacologically, flufenamic acid primarily inhibits cyclooxygenase enzymes PTGS1 and PTGS2, reducing prostaglandin synthesis; it is also reported to modulate several ion channels and aldo-keto reductase family members in experimental systems. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed, is highly plasma protein bound, distributes into inflamed tissues, undergoes hepatic metabolism mainly by oxidation and conjugation, and is eliminated through renal and biliary routes as metabolites. Its principal indication has been symptomatic treatment of pain and inflammation, including musculoskeletal pain, rheumatoid and osteoarthritis symptoms, dysmenorrhea, and other mild-to-moderate inflammatory painful states. Adverse effects are typical of NSAIDs and include dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, edema, and rash. Toxicity includes gastrointestinal ulceration or bleeding, renal impairment, fluid retention, hypersensitivity reactions, and less commonly hepatotoxicity; overdose or high exposure may provoke severe GI irritation, CNS symptoms, and metabolic disturbance. Clinically it has been used as an analgesic and anti-inflammatory agent where a fenamate NSAID is considered appropriate.

Name: Calcipotriol
Description: Calcipotriol (calcipotriene; DrugBank DB02300) is a synthetic vitamin D3 analog whose structure retains the secosteroid/cholecalciferol framework of calcitriol, featuring a broken B-ring steroid nucleus, a conjugated triene system, 1α- and 3β-hydroxyl groups, and a modified lipophilic side chain containing cyclopropyl-related substitution that reduces calcemic activity while preserving receptor binding; chemically it is classified as a secosteroidal vitamin D analog built on the vitamin D/scaled sterol scaffold. Closely related drugs include calcitriol, tacalcitol, maxacalcitol, doxercalciferol, and paricalcitol, which share the vitamin D receptor agonist pharmacophore. Its principal target is the vitamin D receptor, a nuclear receptor that heterodimerizes with retinoid X receptors and modulates transcription of genes controlling keratinocyte proliferation, differentiation, and immune signaling. After topical administration, systemic absorption is usually low and formulation-, site-, and surface area-dependent; absorbed drug is highly protein bound, distributes into lipid-rich tissues, undergoes rapid hepatic and extrahepatic metabolism to less active metabolites, and is eliminated mainly via the biliary/fecal route with limited renal excretion. Toxicity is dominated by excessive vitamin D activity, especially hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria, more likely with overuse, large treatment areas, occlusion, or combination therapy; local irritation can also be dose limiting. It is indicated primarily for plaque psoriasis, including scalp psoriasis, to reduce scaling, thickness, and erythema, and is used clinically as cream, ointment, solution, or foam, often alone or with topical corticosteroids such as betamethasone. Common adverse effects include burning, pruritus, erythema, irritation, dryness, dermatitis, and occasional worsening of psoriasis.

Name: Carbenoxolone
Description: Carbenoxolone (DrugBank DB02329) is a semisynthetic triterpenoid derivative of glycyrrhetinic acid in which the oleanane pentacyclic ring system is retained and functionalized by a hemisuccinate/carboxylated side chain, giving an amphipathic acidic structure; chemically it is classified as a glycyrrhetinic acid analog, triterpenoid saponin-related antiulcer agent, and mineralocorticoid-active compound, with an oleanolic/ursane-like pentacyclic triterpene scaffold. Closely related compounds include glycyrrhizin, glycyrrhetinic acid, enoxolone, and other antiulcer cytoprotective agents such as sucralfate, although the latter are mechanistically distinct. Carbenoxolone is absorbed orally but variably, is highly protein bound in plasma, distributes to gastrointestinal and renal tissues, undergoes hepatic biotransformation with hydrolysis/reduction and conjugative metabolism, and is excreted mainly in bile and feces with some renal elimination; enterohepatic recycling likely contributes to persistence. Its best-known targets are 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (HSD11B2), which it inhibits to enhance cortisol-mediated mineralocorticoid receptor activation, and connexin gap-junction proteins including GJA1/connexin-43 and pannexin channels, which it functionally blocks; modulation of epithelial repair and mucus production has also been described. It has been used mainly for peptic ulcer disease, aphthous or oral ulceration, esophagitis, and mucosal inflammation. Toxicity is dominated by pseudohyperaldosteronism, with sodium and water retention, hypertension, edema, metabolic alkalosis, hypokalemia, myopathy, and arrhythmias; headache, dizziness, gastrointestinal upset, and worsening heart failure are recognized adverse effects. Clinically, it has been administered orally or topically as an ulcer-healing and mucosal protective drug, though use has been limited by mineralocorticoid-related toxicity.

Name: Aminobenzoic acid
Description: Aminobenzoic acid, usually referring to para-aminobenzoic acid or PABA, is a small aromatic aminocarboxylic acid composed of a benzene ring bearing an amino group and a carboxylic acid in the para position, making it a simple aniline-substituted benzoic acid; chemically it belongs to the aminobenzoic acid family within aromatic carboxylic acids and aniline derivatives, and its core scaffold is a substituted benzoic acid/para-aniline pharmacophore. It is structurally related to other folate-pathway ligands and PABA-derived drugs, including sulfonamides such as sulfamethoxazole and sulfadiazine, as well as ester local anesthetics such as benzocaine, procaine, and tetracaine, which contain a PABA-like motif. Pharmacologically, PABA is best known as a bacterial metabolite and substrate for dihydropteroate synthase in folate biosynthesis rather than a high-affinity human drug target; in humans, oral absorption is generally good, distribution is expected to be mainly in extracellular fluids, metabolism occurs largely by hepatic conjugation including acetylation and glycine conjugation, and urinary renal excretion is the major elimination route. Toxicity is usually low at modest exposure but overdose or prolonged use can cause nausea, vomiting, fever, rash, hepatotoxicity, and rarely methemoglobinemia or hypersensitivity; contact allergy has also been reported historically with sunscreen exposure. Human target proteins are not well established for therapeutic action, although bacterial dihydropteroate synthase is the key biologic interaction relevant to its analogs. Clinically, PABA has been used as a nutritional supplement and historically for fibrotic dermatoses such as Peyronie disease and scleroderma-related conditions, while adverse effects include gastrointestinal upset, anorexia, pruritus, and allergic dermatitis.

Name: Tolrestat
Description: Tolrestat (DB02383) is a synthetic aldose reductase inhibitor characterized structurally as an aromatic heterocycle-rich carboxylic acid containing a lipophilic fused-ring/aryl system linked to a polar acidic terminus, a design that supports high-affinity binding in the hydrophobic and anion-binding regions of aldo-keto reductase family 1 member B1; chemically it is classified as a carboxylic acid aldose reductase inhibitor, and its core scaffold is best described as an aryl-heterocyclic hydrophobic pharmacophore appended to an acidic headgroup typical of early diabetic complication modulators. It is closely related pharmacologically to other aldose reductase inhibitors such as sorbinil, epalrestat, ponalrestat, zopolrestat, and ranirestat, which share the goal of suppressing sorbitol pathway flux. Its principal target is aldose reductase (AKR1B1), with possible lesser interaction within the broader aldo-keto reductase family. Tolrestat was developed for chronic diabetic complications, especially diabetic peripheral neuropathy, and was also explored for retinopathy and nephropathy by reducing intracellular sorbitol accumulation under hyperglycemic conditions. After oral administration it is absorbed systemically, is highly protein bound, distributes mainly in plasma and peripheral tissues, undergoes hepatic biotransformation with subsequent renal and likely biliary elimination of metabolites, and was intended for repeated dosing. Its clinical use was limited and ultimately curtailed because toxicity, particularly serious idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity with marked transaminase elevation, hepatitis, jaundice, and rare liver failure, outweighed benefit; other adverse effects included gastrointestinal upset, headache, dizziness, rash, and fatigue. Thus, although tolrestat showed mechanistically rational activity against diabetic neuropathic symptoms, its clinical role became largely historical because of safety concerns.

Name: Vorinostat
Description: Vorinostat (DrugBank DB02546), also known as suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid, is a small-molecule hydroxamic acid histone deacetylase inhibitor built from a linear aliphatic octanoyl linker connecting a terminal hydroxamic acid zinc-binding group to an anilide cap; chemically it is categorized as a hydroxamate, HDAC inhibitor, and substituted aromatic amide, with a classic HDAC inhibitor pharmacophore scaffold consisting of cap group, hydrophobic linker, and metal-chelating hydroxamic acid. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other HDAC inhibitors such as panobinostat, belinostat, trichostatin A, and to a lesser extent romidepsin, though the latter is a cyclic depsipeptide rather than a hydroxamate. Vorinostat primarily targets class I and II HDAC enzymes, including HDAC1, HDAC2, HDAC3, HDAC6, and related isoforms, increasing histone and nonhistone protein acetylation and thereby altering transcription, cell-cycle control, differentiation, and apoptosis. Orally administered vorinostat is absorbed with moderate bioavailability, is widely distributed, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism by glucuronidation and hydrolysis followed by beta-oxidation rather than major CYP-dependent oxidation, and is excreted mainly in urine as metabolites with a relatively short plasma half-life. Its major indication is treatment of refractory, persistent, or progressive cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, especially with skin manifestations such as plaques, pruritus, and tumors; it has also been used clinically and investigationally in other hematologic malignancies and solid tumors. Toxicities include dose-related thrombocytopenia, anemia, fatigue, gastrointestinal toxicity, dehydration, hyperglycemia, and occasional QT prolongation or thromboembolic events; common adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, anorexia, weight loss, dysgeusia, and asthenia. In practice, vorinostat is used as an oral epigenetic anticancer agent, particularly in previously treated CTCL patients requiring systemic therapy.

Name: Oseltamivir acid
Description: Oseltamivir acid (DB02600) is the active carboxylate metabolite of oseltamivir and a polar cyclohexene-based antiviral characterized structurally by a highly functionalized unsaturated six-membered ring bearing a carboxylate group, an amino substituent, and an ether-linked alkyl side chain arranged to mimic the transition state of sialic acid cleavage; chemically it is classified as a neuraminidase inhibitor and more broadly as a sialic-acid-mimetic amino acid derivative, with a cyclohexene carboxylate scaffold. Closely related drugs include oseltamivir phosphate as the oral prodrug, zanamivir, peramivir, and laninamivir, all sharing influenza neuraminidase inhibition as the core mechanism. Its principal targets are influenza virus neuraminidase proteins from influenza A and B, including N1 and N2 subtype enzymes, where binding blocks virion release and viral spread. Pharmacokinetically, oseltamivir acid itself is the systemically active species generated rapidly from the prodrug by hepatic and intestinal esterases; it has good systemic distribution into respiratory tract secretions, minimal further metabolism, low protein binding, and is eliminated largely unchanged by renal excretion through glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, with exposure increased in renal impairment. Toxicity is generally low but can include dose-related gastrointestinal intolerance and, rarely, neuropsychiatric events, hypersensitivity, or serious cutaneous reactions; overdose experience suggests nausea, vomiting, dizziness, and agitation as examples. It is indicated for treatment and post-exposure or seasonal prophylaxis of influenza A and B, especially acute uncomplicated influenza with fever, cough, myalgia, and malaise, and is used clinically in adults and children, ideally within 48 hours of symptom onset, as well as in high-risk patients and outbreak-control settings.

Name: Cholic Acid
Description: Cholic acid (DrugBank DB02659) is a primary endogenous bile acid with a rigid cholane steroid nucleus composed of four fused rings, a C24 side chain terminating in a carboxylic acid, and characteristic 3α,7α,12α-trihydroxy substitution that creates a facially amphipathic structure important for micelle formation; chemically it belongs to the bile acids/bile salts and more broadly to steroidal carboxylic acids, with a 5β-cholane scaffold. Closely related drugs and analogues include chenodeoxycholic acid, deoxycholic acid, ursodeoxycholic acid, and semisynthetic obeticholic acid. Its pharmacology reflects both detergent and signaling functions: after oral administration it is absorbed mainly in the small intestine, undergoes extensive enterohepatic circulation, is highly extracted by the liver, conjugated chiefly with glycine or taurine, secreted into bile via transporters such as ABCB11/BSEP, metabolized further by intestinal microbiota to secondary bile acids, and excreted predominantly in feces with limited urinary elimination. Relevant targets and regulated proteins include FXR/NR1H4, GPBAR1/TGR5, CYP7A1 through feedback regulation, and bile acid transport systems including SLC10A2/ASBT, SLC10A1/NTCP, and ABCB11. Clinically, cholic acid is indicated for bile acid synthesis disorders due to single-enzyme defects and for peroxisomal disorders including Zellweger spectrum disorders, where it suppresses toxic atypical bile acid production and improves bile flow. Adverse effects include diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea, reflux, jaundice, skin lesions, and peripheral neuropathy; toxicity is chiefly hepatobiliary, with excessive exposure potentially worsening cholestasis, elevating transaminases, and causing bile acid-mediated liver injury.

Name: Fusidic acid
Description: Fusidic acid (DrugBank DB02703) is a steroid-like fusidane antibiotic characterized by a highly lipophilic tetracyclic triterpenoid nucleus resembling a partially unsaturated steroid scaffold, bearing multiple methyl substituents, a carboxylic acid side chain, and hydroxyl/acetoxy-type oxygenation that confer amphipathic behavior and are central to its antibacterial activity. Chemically, it is classified as a fusidane steroid antibiotic and its core scaffold is the fusidane tetracyclic ring system; structurally and mechanistically related agents include sodium fusidate, and more distantly other steroidal antimicrobials or protein-synthesis inhibitors such as mupirocin, although the latter is not scaffold-similar. Its principal target is bacterial elongation factor G, encoded by fusA, with binding that blocks EF-G turnover on the ribosome and inhibits translocation, especially in Staphylococcus aureus. After oral administration fusidic acid is generally well absorbed, is highly protein bound, distributes well into skin, soft tissue, bone, and purulent material, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism with biliary excretion, and has minimal renal elimination, making dose adjustment less dependent on kidney function. Toxicity is chiefly hepatobiliary, with examples including cholestatic jaundice, elevated transaminases, and rare severe hepatic injury; resistance-associated target alteration in EF-G is microbiologic rather than host toxicity. Adverse effects include gastrointestinal upset, rash, pruritus, jaundice, and occasional hematologic abnormalities. Clinically it is used topically and systemically for susceptible staphylococcal infections, including impetigo, infected dermatitis, wound infections, osteomyelitis, and prosthetic or deep soft-tissue infections, often in combination therapy to reduce emergence of resistance.

Name: Uridine
Description: Uridine (DrugBank DB02745) is a naturally occurring pyrimidine nucleoside composed of the nucleobase uracil linked through a β-N1-glycosidic bond to a ribofuranose sugar bearing multiple hydroxyl groups, giving a polar, hydrogen-bonding structure typical of endogenous RNA precursors; chemically it belongs to the pyrimidine ribonucleoside class, and its core scaffold is the uracil-ribose nucleoside framework. Closely related compounds include cytidine, thymidine, uracil, uridine triacetate, and the uridine prodrug uridine monophosphate, as well as functionally adjacent pyrimidine analogs such as fluorouracil rescue agents. Pharmacokinetically, oral uridine is absorbed in the intestine via nucleoside transport processes, distributed widely into plasma and tissues including liver and central nervous system, enters endogenous pyrimidine pools, and is metabolized through salvage pathways by uridine-cytidine kinase and by catabolic enzymes such as uridine phosphorylase to uracil and downstream metabolites, with renal excretion of parent compound and metabolites. Its main pharmacologic targets are not classic receptors but metabolic enzymes and transport systems involved in pyrimidine homeostasis, including uridine-cytidine kinase, uridine phosphorylase, equilibrative and concentrative nucleoside transporters, and indirectly RNA and phospholipid biosynthetic pathways. Clinically, uridine and especially uridine triacetate are used to treat hereditary orotic aciduria and as antidotal therapy for fluorouracil or capecitabine overdose or severe early toxicity; investigational and supplemental uses have included mitochondrial disorders, neuropathy, and support of membrane phospholipid synthesis. Toxicity is generally low because uridine is endogenous, but excessive exposure can cause gastrointestinal intolerance such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, and in rescue settings adverse effects may include abdominal discomfort; theoretical metabolic effects include perturbation of nucleotide balance, while severe toxicity is far less prominent than with cytotoxic pyrimidine analogs.

Name: Stanolone
Description: Stanolone (DrugBank DB02901), also known as dihydrotestosterone, is a naturally occurring 5α-reduced androgen with the classic steroid tetracyclic cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene nucleus, bearing a 3-keto group and a 17β-hydroxyl group in the androstane series; chemically it belongs to the androgenic anabolic steroid and steroid hormone class, and its core scaffold is the saturated androstane steroid framework. It is closely related to testosterone, from which it is formed by 5α-reductase, and has pharmacologic similarity to other androgens such as methyltestosterone, testosterone propionate, fluoxymesterone, and topical androgen preparations. Its principal target is the androgen receptor, with biologic effects mediated by high-affinity receptor binding and transcriptional activation in androgen-responsive tissues. Pharmacokinetically, stanolone has limited oral usefulness because of extensive first-pass metabolism, so it has mainly been used topically or parenterally; it distributes into skin, prostate, genital tissue, muscle, and other steroid-responsive compartments, is highly protein bound in plasma, undergoes hepatic metabolism to less active androgen metabolites and conjugates, and is excreted primarily in urine with some fecal elimination. Toxicity is broadly androgen-related and may include virilization, prostate enlargement, suppression of gonadotropins, polycythemia, edema, lipid changes, and hepatic strain with some formulations; examples include premature sexual development in children and worsening of androgen-sensitive prostate disease in men. Adverse effects include acne, seborrhea, hirsutism, alopecia, mood changes, reduced fertility, gynecomastia via hormonal imbalance, and menstrual disturbance in women. Clinically, stanolone has been used as androgen replacement or anabolic support in male hypogonadism, micropenis or delayed sexual development, and selected catabolic or deficiency states, though modern use is limited and highly indication-specific.

Name: Piretanide
Description: Piretanide (DrugBank DB02925) is a loop diuretic with a benzoic acid–sulfonamide architecture characterized by an aromatic carboxylic acid linked to a sulfamoyl group and a lipophilic heterocyclic/aryl substituent, a motif that confers strong activity at the thick ascending limb of Henle; chemically it is categorized as a sulfonamide-containing loop diuretic and its core scaffold is best described as an anthranilic/benzoic acid diuretic scaffold functionally analogous to other high-ceiling diuretics. Closely related drugs include furosemide, bumetanide, and torsemide, which share inhibition of the apical Na+/K+/2Cl− cotransporter NKCC2 encoded by SLC12A1, the principal known target protein; downstream effects on renal electrolyte handling also secondarily influence ROMK and tubular transport processes. After oral administration, piretanide is generally rapidly absorbed, moderately protein bound, distributed mainly in extracellular fluid, undergoes limited hepatic biotransformation relative to many xenobiotics, and is eliminated predominantly by the kidney via filtration and tubular secretion, with a relatively short duration of action typical of loop diuretics. Toxicity is chiefly an extension of pharmacology and includes volume depletion, hypotension, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, prerenal azotemia, hyperuricemia with gout precipitation, and less commonly ototoxicity or sulfonamide hypersensitivity. It is indicated for edema associated with congestive heart failure, renal disease, or hepatic cirrhosis, and for hypertension, especially when rapid natriuresis is desired. In clinical use it has been employed to mobilize fluid overload, relieve peripheral or pulmonary edema, and augment blood-pressure control, while common adverse effects include dizziness, thirst, polyuria, muscle cramps, weakness, and dehydration.

Name: Acetylcholine
Description: Acetylcholine (DrugBank DB03128) is a small endogenous choline ester composed of a quaternary ammonium headgroup linked through a two-carbon chain to an acetate ester, giving a permanently charged, highly polar structure with minimal membrane permeability; chemically it belongs to the cholinergic agonists and, more specifically, the acetylcholine ester/neurotransmitter class, built on a simple choline-ester scaffold that is closely related to other direct-acting cholinomimetics such as methacholine, carbachol, bethanechol, and the naturally occurring alkaloid muscarine in functional similarity. Its principal targets are cholinergic receptors, including muscarinic GPCRs CHRM1, CHRM2, CHRM3, CHRM4, and CHRM5, and nicotinic ligand-gated ion channels composed of neuronal and neuromuscular subunits such as CHRNA and CHRNB family members. Pharmacokinetically, acetylcholine has negligible oral bioavailability, does not meaningfully cross the blood-brain barrier, acts extremely briefly when administered locally or systemically, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid, and is rapidly hydrolyzed by acetylcholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase to choline and acetate, with metabolites subsequently recycled or renally eliminated. Toxicity reflects excessive cholinergic stimulation, producing bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm, bronchorrhea, diarrhea, abdominal cramping, salivation, lacrimation, miosis, sweating, muscle fasciculations, weakness, and at high exposure potentially respiratory failure or cardiac arrest. Clinically, acetylcholine is used primarily as an ophthalmic miotic to induce rapid intraoperative miosis during cataract and other anterior segment surgery, rather than for chronic systemic indications, although physiologically it mediates parasympathetic signaling relevant to glaucoma, gastrointestinal atony, and urinary retention paradigms.

Name: Acetic acid
Description: Acetic acid (DrugBank DB03166) is the simplest monocarboxylic organic acid, consisting of a two-carbon framework with a terminal carbonyl and hydroxyl forming a carboxyl group attached to a methyl substituent; chemically it is a small aliphatic saturated carboxylic acid and its core scaffold is the C2 alkyl-carboxylic acid motif that also underlies homologous short-chain fatty acids. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other low-molecular-weight acids such as propionic acid, butyric acid, formic acid, and topical acidifying antiseptics. Pharmacokinetically, when ingested or generated endogenously it is rapidly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, distributes widely in total body water, readily enters intermediary metabolism after conversion to acetyl-coenzyme A, and is ultimately eliminated mainly as carbon dioxide in expired air and water, with only minor renal excretion of unchanged acetate; topical use produces primarily local exposure. Toxicity is concentration dependent: dilute preparations are generally well tolerated, whereas concentrated acetic acid is corrosive and can cause chemical burns, ocular injury, mucosal necrosis, metabolic acidosis, hemolysis, and gastrointestinal perforation after ingestion. Its relevant biological targets are not highly selective drug receptors but include pH-sensitive microbial and host proteins; antimicrobial effects arise largely from intracellular acidification, membrane disruption, and protein denaturation rather than single-target binding. Clinically, it is indicated mainly as a topical acidifying antimicrobial or otic anti-infective, for example in otitis externa and in wound care against susceptible bacteria including Pseudomonas species. Adverse effects include burning, stinging, irritation, erythema, pain, tissue damage, and, in the ear, transient discomfort or inflammation. In practice it is used in dilute topical or otic solutions and occasionally as an acidity-modifying agent or procedural reagent rather than as a systemic therapeutic.

Name: Oteracil
Description: Oteracil (DrugBank DB03209), commonly used as the potassium salt oteracil potassium, is a fluoropyrimidine-modulating antineoplastic agent structurally characterized as a highly polar substituted pyridine bearing a carboxylate and hydroxymethyl functionality, giving it a heteroaromatic acidic framework designed for limited systemic uptake; chemically it is classified as a pyridinecarboxylic acid derivative and more broadly as an antimetabolite adjunct, with a simple aza-aromatic carboxylate scaffold distinct from the uracil nucleus but functionally related to fluoropyrimidine biochemistry. It is most similar pharmacologically to other modulators of 5-fluorouracil toxicity used in combination therapy, especially gimeracil and tegafur within the S-1 regimen, and more broadly to fluoropyrimidines such as 5-fluorouracil and capecitabine. Its principal target is orotate phosphoribosyltransferase, which it inhibits predominantly in gastrointestinal tissues, thereby reducing local conversion of 5-fluorouracil to cytotoxic nucleotides and attenuating GI injury rather than exerting major direct antitumor activity. Pharmacokinetically, oteracil has poor oral absorption, low systemic distribution, minimal metabolism of clinical relevance, and is eliminated largely unchanged in urine and feces, properties that support gut-selective action. Toxicity is generally related to combination fluoropyrimidine therapy; oteracil is intended to reduce severe diarrhea, mucositis, enteritis, and abdominal toxicity, though adverse effects in S-1-treated patients can still include nausea, vomiting, myelosuppression, anorexia, stomatitis, and fatigue. Clinically, it is used as part of S-1 with tegafur and gimeracil for gastric cancer and other solid tumors including colorectal, pancreatic, and head and neck cancers, chiefly to preserve antitumor efficacy while improving gastrointestinal tolerability.

Name: Phenol
Description: Phenol (DrugBank DB03255) is the prototypical monohydric phenolic compound, consisting of a planar aromatic benzene ring bearing a single hydroxyl substituent, which confers weak acidity, hydrogen-bonding capacity, and substantial protein-denaturing and membrane-disrupting reactivity; chemically it belongs to the simple phenols, within the broader aromatic alcohol and antiseptic/disinfectant class, and its core scaffold is a hydroxybenzene or phenyl-OH motif. Structurally and pharmacologically related compounds include cresols, resorcinol, catechol, hydroquinone, chloroxylenol, and guaiacol-derived antiseptics, which share aromatic hydroxyl functionality and caustic antimicrobial behavior. Phenol is absorbed rapidly through skin, mucosa, the gastrointestinal tract, and by inhalation, distributes widely into well-perfused tissues, including the central nervous system, undergoes predominant hepatic phase II metabolism to phenyl sulfate and phenyl glucuronide with minor oxidative catechol/hydroquinone pathways, and is excreted mainly in urine as conjugates. Its pharmacologic effects are largely nonspecific, mediated by protein coagulation, lipid membrane disruption, and local neurolysis rather than high-affinity receptor pharmacology, so no single canonical therapeutic target protein is established, although broad interactions with membrane proteins and ion channels are implicated. Clinically, phenol has been used as a topical antiseptic, disinfectant, local anesthetic/analgesic, sclerosing and cauterizing agent, and neurolytic agent, for example in sore throat preparations, chemical matricectomy, hemorrhoid therapy, and spasticity or pain procedures. Toxicity is substantial and includes corrosive burns, systemic CNS depression or seizures, arrhythmias, methemoglobinemia, hemolysis, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, and death after significant exposure; adverse effects include local irritation, whitening/eschar formation, ulceration, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, and chemical burns.

Name: Deoxycholic acid
Description: Deoxycholic acid (DrugBank DB03619) is a naturally occurring secondary bile acid with a rigid cholane steroid nucleus, a 5β-configured fused four-ring bile acid framework bearing hydroxyl groups at C3 and C12 and a terminal C24 carboxylic acid on a short aliphatic side chain, giving an amphipathic facial structure responsible for its detergent properties. Chemically it belongs to the bile acids/bile salts class, and its core scaffold is the steroidal cholanic acid (5β-cholan-24-oic acid) framework. Closely related and pharmacologically similar compounds include cholic acid, chenodeoxycholic acid, ursodeoxycholic acid, and semisynthetic bile acid derivatives such as obeticholic acid. After oral exposure, deoxycholic acid is absorbed in the intestine, undergoes extensive enterohepatic recirculation, is highly associated with bile acid transport pathways in the liver and gut, and is metabolized mainly by hepatic conjugation with glycine or taurine; it is excreted predominantly in bile with minor fecal loss and limited renal elimination. Its biological targets and signaling interactors include bile acid receptors and transport-linked proteins such as FXR/NR1H4, GPBAR1/TGR5, and bile acid transport systems including SLC10A1 and SLC10A2. Toxicity is dominated by membrane-disruptive and cytolytic effects, with dose-dependent local tissue necrosis, inflammation, hepatobiliary irritation, and at excess exposure gastrointestinal injury; for example, injection can damage adjacent nerves or skin and intraluminal bile acid excess may promote mucosal injury. It is indicated primarily for reduction of submental fullness by adipocytolysis, and clinically used as injectable deoxycholic acid for cosmetic treatment of visible submental fat. Common adverse effects include injection-site pain, edema, bruising, induration, numbness, erythema, dysphagia, and less commonly marginal mandibular nerve paresis or ulceration.

Name: Tromethamine
Description: Tromethamine (tris, THAM; DrugBank DB03754) is a small, highly polar alkanolamine buffer composed of a central tetrahedral carbon bearing one primary amine and three hydroxymethyl substituents, giving it a compact aminopolyol architecture with strong proton-accepting capacity. Chemically it belongs to the amino alcohol/alkanolamine class and is best described by a tris(hydroxymethyl)aminomethane scaffold, a simple nonaromatic polyol-amine framework shared conceptually with other systemic alkalinizing agents and buffering amines; clinically similar drugs include sodium bicarbonate and, in some acid-base contexts, acetate- or lactate-generating alkalinizers, although these differ structurally. Its pharmacologic action is largely physicochemical rather than receptor-mediated: it acts as a proton acceptor in body fluids and urine, so no single canonical target protein is established, though its effects functionally intersect acid-base handling proteins in renal tubular physiology and carbonic acid/bicarbonate systems. After intravenous administration it distributes mainly in extracellular water, has negligible protein binding, is not extensively metabolized, and is eliminated primarily unchanged by the kidneys, where urinary excretion contributes to alkalinization; oral systemic use is limited, while ophthalmic tromethamine serves mainly as a formulation excipient and pH adjuster. Toxicity relates to overalkalinization and osmotic/ionic disturbances, with examples including metabolic alkalosis, hypoglycemia, hyperkalemia or local tissue injury from extravasation, respiratory depression from rapid correction of acidosis, and renal stress in impaired kidney function. Adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, headache, irritability, hypotension, phlebitis, and electrolyte abnormalities. Clinically, tromethamine is used to treat metabolic acidosis, including acidosis associated with cardiac bypass, renal insufficiency, or severe systemic illness, and as the tromethamine salt in products such as ketorolac tromethamine to improve pharmaceutical handling and administration.

Name: Doconexent
Description: Doconexent (DrugBank DB03756) is docosahexaenoic acid, a long-chain omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid built on a linear 22-carbon carboxylic acid framework containing six cis double bonds, giving it a highly flexible, kinked lipid structure; chemically it belongs to the fatty acids, specifically the omega-3 PUFA/eicosanoid precursor class, and its core scaffold is a polyunsaturated aliphatic carboxylate chain. It is closely related to other therapeutic or nutritional omega-3 lipids such as eicosapentaenoic acid, omega-3-acid ethyl esters, icosapent ethyl, and fish-oil-derived mixtures. Pharmacokinetically, doconexent is absorbed in the small intestine with dietary lipids, incorporated into chylomicrons, distributed extensively into plasma lipoproteins, erythrocyte membranes, neural tissue, and retinal phospholipids, then metabolized mainly by esterification into complex lipids and by beta-oxidation, while also serving as a precursor to specialized pro-resolving mediators including resolvins and protectins; excretion occurs predominantly after oxidative metabolism as carbon dioxide, with minor fecal loss. Known biological targets are not limited to a single receptor but include modulation of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors, effects on membrane-associated signaling proteins, and indirect regulation of inflammatory pathways. Doconexent is used mainly for nutritional supplementation and for conditions linked to omega-3 deficiency or altered lipid/inflammatory homeostasis, with examples including hypertriglyceridemia support, cardiovascular risk modification, infant neurodevelopment support, and ocular or neurologic health. Toxicity is generally low, but excessive exposure may increase bleeding tendency, gastrointestinal intolerance, lipid peroxidation risk, and rarely immune or glycemic effects; side effects commonly include fishy aftertaste, dyspepsia, nausea, diarrhea, and loose stools. Clinically, it is used in dietary supplements, enteral formulations, and omega-3-based therapeutic regimens, often as adjunctive care rather than as a classic single-target drug.

Name: Benzoic acid
Description: Benzoic acid (DrugBank DB03793) is the simplest aromatic carboxylic acid, consisting of a planar benzene ring directly substituted by a single carboxyl group, giving a compact, weakly acidic, lipophilicity-modulated structure whose core scaffold is the benzenecarboxylic acid or phenylcarboxylic acid motif. Chemically it belongs to the benzoic acids, a subclass of aromatic monocarboxylic acids, and it is structurally related to drugs and excipients such as sodium benzoate, benzyl benzoate, salicylic acid, para-aminobenzoic acid derivatives, and various substituted benzoates that retain the same aromatic acid framework. Its pharmacology is largely nonspecific rather than receptor-selective: no single high-affinity therapeutic human protein target is classically assigned, although antimicrobial effects are linked to pH-dependent disruption of microbial membrane function and intracellular acid-base homeostasis; at a biochemical level it is also handled by mitochondrial glycine N-acyltransferase following activation to benzoyl-CoA. After oral exposure it is readily absorbed, distributed mainly in extracellular water with limited tissue accumulation, extensively metabolized in the liver by glycine conjugation to hippuric acid, and rapidly excreted in urine, with renal clearance enhanced by urinary alkalinization. Benzoic acid is used primarily as an antimicrobial preservative in foods, topical formulations, and some pharmaceutical preparations, and benzoate-related therapy has been used in hyperammonemia, though usually as sodium benzoate rather than the free acid. Toxicity is dose dependent and includes mucosal and skin irritation, eye irritation, gastrointestinal upset, nausea, vomiting, and occasional hypersensitivity or pseudoallergic reactions; large exposures may cause metabolic acidosis and CNS symptoms. Clinically, its direct medicinal use is limited but it appears in topical antifungal or keratolytic combinations and in preservative roles intended to suppress microbial contamination.

Name: Formaldehyde
Description: Formaldehyde (DrugBank DB03843) is the simplest aldehyde, a highly reactive one-carbon carbonyl compound with a trigonal-planar formyl center consisting of a terminal aldehydic carbon double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to hydrogen, placing it in the aldehyde class of volatile organic compounds and, more specifically, the small aliphatic carbonyl/oxo-methane scaffold rather than a complex heterocyclic framework. Closely related agents include glutaraldehyde, paraformaldehyde, methanol as a metabolic precursor, and formic acid as a downstream metabolite. Pharmacokinetically, exogenous formaldehyde is rapidly absorbed by inhalation, ingestion, or mucosal/dermal exposure, but because it is intensely reactive it remains largely at the site of contact, forms reversible and irreversible adducts with proteins and nucleic acids, distributes poorly as free parent compound, and is swiftly metabolized mainly by glutathione-dependent formaldehyde dehydrogenase/alcohol dehydrogenase 5 to S-formylglutathione and then by esterases and aldehyde dehydrogenases to formate, with further oxidation to carbon dioxide and urinary excretion of formate-derived carbon. Known biological targets are therefore not classic receptors but cellular macromolecules and enzymes involved in detoxification, especially ADH5, ALDH family enzymes, and glutathione pathways. Its principal uses are as a tissue fixative, embalming and disinfecting agent, and historically in topical wart preparations or formalin-based preservation rather than routine systemic therapy. Toxicity is dominated by corrosive local injury, protein cross-linking, cytotoxicity, genotoxicity, and carcinogenicity, with examples including eye and airway irritation, bronchospasm, chemical burns, nausea, vomiting, metabolic acidosis after ingestion, and increased nasopharyngeal malignancy risk with chronic exposure.

Name: Urea
Description: Urea (DrugBank DB03904) is the simplest carbamide, consisting of a planar carbonyl flanked by two amino groups, a highly polar, strongly hydrogen-bonding structure that underlies its exceptional water solubility and keratolytic and osmotic behavior; chemically it belongs to the organic amide/carbamide class, and its core scaffold is the unsubstituted urea moiety, a motif shared across many medicinal and industrial compounds. Similar drugs or related agents include other osmotic or keratolytic therapies such as mannitol, glycerol, ammonium lactate, salicylic acid, and substituted urea derivatives, although these differ materially in mechanism and therapeutic context. Pharmacokinetically, urea is readily absorbed across skin when formulated topically to a degree dependent on concentration and barrier integrity, distributes rapidly in total body water when given systemically, is produced endogenously in the liver via the urea cycle rather than being extensively metabolized as a drug, and is eliminated mainly by renal excretion with filtration and partial tubular reabsorption. Its toxicity is concentration- and route-dependent: topical use may cause local irritation, burning, stinging, erythema, or maceration, whereas excessive systemic exposure can contribute to osmotic shifts, nausea, headache, confusion, or azotemia-like burden, particularly in renal impairment. Urea has no conventional high-affinity drug target proteins; its effects are largely physicochemical, though biological handling involves urea transporters such as SLC14A1 and SLC14A2 and skin barrier modulation. Indications include xerosis, ichthyosis, hyperkeratotic dermatoses, calluses, corns, nail dystrophies, and cerumen softening, and clinically it is used in creams, lotions, foams, nail preparations, and otic products to hydrate, soften, and debride thickened keratin.

Name: Nicotinyl alcohol
Description: Nicotinyl alcohol (pyridine-3-methanol) is a small heteroaromatic nicotinic acid-related compound whose structure consists of a six-membered pyridine ring bearing a ring nitrogen and a hydroxymethyl substituent at the 3-position, making it the reduced alcohol analog of nicotinic acid and a relatively polar aromatic primary alcohol. Chemically it is classified as a pyridyl alcohol and niacin derivative, with a simple nicotinyl/pyridine scaffold shared with related vasoactive or vitamin B3-associated molecules such as nicotinic acid, nicotinamide, and esterified nicotinyl alcohol derivatives including inositol nicotinate. Its pharmacology has historically been linked more to peripheral vasodilatory activity than to a highly specific receptor-mediated mechanism; no well-validated canonical human target proteins are firmly established, although effects may overlap indirectly with pathways engaged by niacin, including prostaglandin-dependent vasomotor responses. Pharmacokinetic data are limited, but as a low-molecular-weight hydrophilic alcohol it is expected to be absorbed after oral or topical exposure, distributed mainly in extracellular water, oxidized hepatically to nicotinic acid and related pyridine metabolites, and excreted predominantly in urine as parent compound and oxidative metabolites. Toxicity is generally low at therapeutic exposure but can include dose-related vasodilatory intolerance such as flushing, warmth, headache, dizziness, hypotension, and local irritation; excessive exposure could plausibly increase gastrointestinal upset or hepatic metabolic burden, analogous to other niacin-related agents. Clinically, nicotinyl alcohol has mainly been used as a peripheral vasodilator, particularly in topical rubefacient or circulation-enhancing preparations, for symptoms associated with poor peripheral blood flow, cold extremities, mild muscular pain, or localized ischemic discomfort rather than as a mainstream systemic therapy.

Name: Citric acid
Description: Citric acid (DrugBank DB04272) is a small, highly polar tricarboxylic alpha-hydroxy acid built on a saturated propane backbone bearing three carboxyl groups and one tertiary alcohol, giving it a compact citrate scaffold that is conformationally simple, strongly acidic, and an excellent metal chelator; it belongs chemically to the carboxylic acid/citrate class and is closely related to similar agents such as sodium citrate, potassium citrate, calcium citrate, and the anticoagulant citrate dextrose solutions. Pharmacologically, citric acid has no classic selective receptor-based drug action, but citrate is a central endogenous metabolite and can interact functionally with calcium through chelation and with transport/metabolic proteins involved in the tricarboxylic acid cycle, including aconitase and citrate transport systems, rather than serving as a conventional high-affinity drug ligand. After oral exposure it is readily absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, distributed mainly in total body water, enters normal intermediary metabolism, is rapidly converted through the Krebs cycle to carbon dioxide and water, and only a minor fraction is excreted unchanged in urine. Toxicity is generally low at therapeutic or dietary exposures, but concentrated preparations can cause local irritation, dental enamel erosion, nausea, abdominal pain, vomiting, and in large systemic citrate loads may contribute to metabolic disturbances such as hypocalcemia or alkalosis, particularly during massive transfusion or renal impairment. Clinically it is used primarily as a urinary alkalinizing and citrate-replacement component, as an excipient, acidifying/flavoring agent, and in some formulations for prevention of calcium-containing nephrolithiasis or relief of dyspeptic symptoms, with adverse effects most often limited to gastrointestinal irritation, sour taste, mucosal burning, and rarely electrolyte imbalance.

Name: Lactic acid
Description: Lactic acid (DrugBank DB04398) is a small endogenous alpha-hydroxy carboxylic acid composed of a three-carbon propionic acid backbone bearing a terminal carboxyl group and a secondary hydroxyl at C2, creating a chiral center and existing as L- and D-enantiomers, with the biologically predominant form being L-lactic acid; chemically it belongs to the hydroxy acid and organic acid class, and its core scaffold is the simple 2-hydroxypropanoic acid motif shared with related alpha-hydroxy acids. Similar drugs or comparators include glycolic acid, citric acid, malic acid, salicylic acid, and the lactate salts such as sodium lactate or Ringer’s lactate used systemically. Pharmacokinetically, lactic acid is readily absorbed from topical or mucosal surfaces and, when introduced systemically as lactate, distributes rapidly in total body water, enters intermediary metabolism via monocarboxylate transporters, and is converted by lactate dehydrogenase to pyruvate for oxidation in the tricarboxylic acid cycle or for gluconeogenesis, with renal excretion of unchanged compound being limited except in overload states or renal dysfunction. Its known biological targets are not classic high-affinity drug receptors but include lactate dehydrogenase isoenzymes, monocarboxylate transporters such as SLC16 family members, and the hydroxycarboxylic acid receptor HCAR1/GPR81. Toxicity is mainly concentration and exposure dependent, with excessive systemic accumulation causing lactic acidosis, acid-base disturbance, and tissue injury, while topical exposure may cause burning, erythema, desquamation, and irritation. Indications and clinical use include topical keratolysis and moisturization in xerosis, ichthyosis, calluses, and hyperkeratotic dermatoses, pH adjustment and antimicrobial acidification in selected formulations, and use of lactate-containing solutions in fluid and electrolyte replacement; adverse effects include stinging, peeling, contact sensitivity, and, rarely, worsening irritation on compromised skin.

Name: Lactose
Description: Lactose (DrugBank DB04465) is a naturally occurring reducing disaccharide composed of one D-galactose and one D-glucose unit linked by a β-(1→4) glycosidic bond, giving a highly polar, polyhydroxylated carbohydrate structure that exists in α- and β-anomeric forms at the glucose residue; chemically it belongs to the carbohydrate class, specifically disaccharides, and its core scaffold is a galactopyranosyl-glucopyranose sugar framework. Closely related or similar agents include other saccharides and excipient sugars such as lactulose, sucrose, glucose, galactose, and maltose, with lactulose being a notable semisynthetic analog used therapeutically. Pharmacokinetically, orally administered lactose is ordinarily hydrolyzed at the intestinal brush border by lactase-phlorizin hydrolase (LCT) into glucose and galactose, which are then absorbed via intestinal monosaccharide transport pathways; intact systemic distribution of lactose is negligible, metabolism is effectively presystemic, and excretion of unhydrolyzed lactose occurs mainly in feces, with possible colonic bacterial fermentation to short-chain fatty acids and gas in lactase deficiency. Toxicity is low and largely gastrointestinal rather than systemic, but excessive exposure in lactose-intolerant individuals can cause osmotic diarrhea, abdominal cramping, bloating, borborygmi, and flatulence; rare risks include worsening symptoms in congenital lactase deficiency or galactose-related metabolic disorders when lactose contributes to galactose burden. The principal known biological target relevant to disposition is LCT rather than a classical pharmacologic receptor. Lactose is used mainly as a pharmaceutical excipient and nutrient sugar, including as a tablet and capsule filler, powder diluent, carrier in dry-powder inhalers, and component of infant formulas or nutritional products, while adverse effects clinically are chiefly intolerance-associated gastrointestinal symptoms rather than direct drug-like toxicities.

Name: Gluconolactone
