Description: Gluconolactone (DrugBank DB04564) is a small, highly polar carbohydrate-derived polyhydroxy acid lactone, specifically the cyclic ester of D-gluconic acid, with a six-membered 1,5-lactone ring bearing multiple secondary alcohol groups that confer strong hydrogen-bonding capacity, high water solubility after ring opening, and ready interconversion with gluconate in aqueous media; chemically it belongs to the aldonic acid lactones and broader sugar-acid derivatives, and its core scaffold is a glucono-1,5-lactone carbohydrate lactone framework. Structurally and functionally similar agents include gluconic acid, calcium gluconate, sodium gluconate, glucuronolactone, and other polyhydroxy carboxylate/lactone compounds used as excipients, chelators, or metabolic intermediates. Pharmacokinetic data in humans are limited, but orally administered gluconolactone is expected to be readily dissolved, hydrolyzed nonenzymatically and enzymatically to gluconate in the gastrointestinal tract and plasma, distributed largely within extracellular water, incorporated into intermediary carbohydrate metabolism, and eliminated mainly in urine as gluconate or downstream metabolites; significant protein binding, bioaccumulation, or CYP-mediated biotransformation are not established. No specific high-affinity drug target proteins are well validated; its biological effects are better viewed as physicochemical and metabolic, although gluconate can participate in endogenous oxidative carbohydrate pathways. Toxicity is generally low at customary exposure levels, but excessive intake may cause gastrointestinal discomfort, osmotic diarrhea, bloating, or rare metabolic intolerance; serious organ toxicity is not well documented. Clinically, gluconolactone has mainly nontraditional drug use as a formulation ingredient, chelating/acidifying agent, and in dermatologic or cosmetic applications as a polyhydroxy acid for mild keratolysis, moisturization, and treatment of photoaging, acne-prone skin, or dyschromia, with adverse effects typically limited to transient irritation, stinging, erythema, or peeling.

Name: Trioxsalen
Description: Trioxsalen (DrugBank DB04571), also known as trimethylpsoralen, is a tricyclic furocoumarin composed of a planar psoralen core in which a furan ring is fused to a coumarin (benzopyrone) system and substituted with methyl groups that increase lipophilicity and photoreactivity; chemically it belongs to the psoralen/linear furanocoumarin class and is built on the classic psoralen scaffold. Closely related drugs include methoxsalen (8-methoxypsoralen), bergapten (5-methoxypsoralen), and aminolevulinic acid-based photosensitizers used in different photomedical contexts. Its pharmacology is dominated by UVA-dependent intercalation into nucleic acids followed by covalent photoadduct formation, especially with pyrimidine bases in DNA, producing mono-adducts and interstrand crosslinks that suppress keratinocyte proliferation and alter local immune responses; therefore its main functional target is DNA rather than a conventional protein receptor, although downstream effects involve cell-cycle and inflammatory signaling pathways. After oral or topical administration it is absorbed variably, distributes preferentially to skin and other tissues exposed to light, undergoes hepatic oxidative metabolism, and is eliminated mainly as urinary metabolites with some biliary/fecal excretion; like other psoralens, exposure is influenced by formulation and light timing. Clinically, trioxsalen has been used as a photosensitizer in PUVA-type therapy for vitiligo, psoriasis, and selected eczematous or pigmentary disorders. Adverse effects include nausea, pruritus, erythema, blistering, hyperpigmentation, phototoxic burns, headache, and ocular photosensitivity, while toxicity concerns include dose-related phototoxic injury, mutagenicity/genotoxicity from DNA crosslinking, cataract risk without eye protection, and a long-term increased risk of photoaging and nonmelanoma skin cancer with repeated UVA exposure.

Name: Thiotepa
Description: Thiotepa (DB04572) is a small, highly strained trifunctional alkylating agent built on a thiophosphoramide core in which a phosphoryl sulfur center is bound to three aziridine rings, giving a compact polyaziridinyl scaffold that serves as the defining chemical motif for this ethyleneimine antineoplastic class. It is closely related to other aziridine or alkylating drugs such as triethylenemelamine, altretamine, and mechanistically to nitrogen mustards including cyclophosphamide and melphalan, all of which generate electrophiles that damage DNA. Thiotepa is used primarily in ovarian and breast cancer, superficial bladder cancer by intravesical administration, and as part of high-dose conditioning regimens before hematopoietic stem cell transplantation; it has also been used in leptomeningeal malignancy and regional cavity therapy. Its pharmacologic action is largely nonselective DNA alkylation with interstrand cross-linking after aziridine ring opening, so there is no single dominant protein target, although genomic DNA is the functional target and metabolism depends mainly on hepatic CYP3A4 and CYP2B6, which convert it to the active metabolite tepa. It is usually given parenterally, distributes widely with penetration into cerebrospinal fluid, is moderately protein bound, undergoes extensive hepatic biotransformation, and is excreted mainly in urine as metabolites with a relatively short parent half-life. Dose-limiting toxicity is profound myelosuppression, with leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, infection, and bleeding; additional toxicities include mucositis, nausea, vomiting, neurotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, infertility, and secondary malignancy risk, while common adverse effects include fatigue, alopecia, and local irritative effects such as chemical cystitis in bladder use.

Name: Estrone sulfate
Description: Estrone sulfate (DrugBank DB04574) is the sulfate ester conjugate of estrone, characterized by the classical steroidal cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene nucleus with an aromatic A ring, a 17-ketone, and a polar sulfate group esterified at the 3-hydroxyl position, making it a water-soluble endogenous estrogen metabolite and reservoir form. Chemically, it belongs to the estrogen steroids, specifically conjugated steroid sulfates, and its core scaffold is the estrane steroid framework. Closely related compounds include estrone, estradiol, estriol, and the clinically used esterified or conjugated estrogen mixtures such as conjugated estrogens and estradiol sulfate analogs. Pharmacokinetically, estrone sulfate is relatively hydrophilic compared with unconjugated estrogens, circulates extensively bound to albumin, serves as a large peripheral pool convertible to estrone by steroid sulfatase, and can then be reduced to estradiol by 17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases; it is formed largely in liver and peripheral tissues, undergoes enterohepatic recirculation, and is eliminated mainly in urine as sulfate and glucuronide conjugates. Its pharmacology is mediated indirectly and directly through estrogen receptor targets ESR1 and ESR2 after desulfation and interconversion, with transport involving organic anion transporters such as SLCO family members. Toxicity resembles estrogen excess, including endometrial hyperplasia, thromboembolic risk, cholestatic effects, and potential stimulation of estrogen-sensitive malignancies such as breast or endometrial cancer. Adverse effects include breast tenderness, nausea, fluid retention, headache, and uterine bleeding. Clinically, estrone sulfate is primarily a biomarker and endogenous metabolite rather than a common standalone drug, but it is relevant to menopausal hormone therapy, hypoestrogenic states, and estrogen-responsive conditions through its role in conjugated estrogen preparations and steroid sulfatase-dependent estrogen replacement physiology.

Name: Quinestrol
Description: Quinestrol (DB04575) is a synthetic, long-acting steroidal estrogen structurally derived from estradiol, characterized by the classic estrane tetracyclic nucleus with an aromatic A-ring and a 3-cyclopentyl ether substitution that markedly increases lipophilicity and duration of action; chemically, it belongs to the semisynthetic estrogen and estradiol ether class, with an estrane/phenanthrene steroid scaffold closely related to ethinyl estradiol, mestranol, and especially estradiol valerate and other estrogenic prodrugs, although its closest analogs are quinestrol-containing estrogen formulations and natural estradiol itself. Its principal pharmacologic targets are estrogen receptors ESR1 and ESR2, through which it exerts genomic estrogenic effects on reproductive tissues, bone, pituitary feedback pathways, and vaginal epithelium. After oral administration, quinestrol is well absorbed, extensively distributed into adipose and other tissues because of high lipophilicity, slowly hydrolyzed and metabolized in the liver to active estrogenic metabolites including ethinyl estradiol-like species, and eliminated gradually via hepatic biotransformation with biliary and urinary excretion, accounting for its prolonged action. It has been used as an estrogen replacement agent and in gynecologic practice for menopausal symptoms, hypoestrogenic states, menstrual disorders, atrophic vaginitis, and occasionally suppression-related reproductive indications. Adverse effects resemble those of other estrogens and include nausea, breast tenderness, edema, headache, uterine bleeding, and fluid retention, while important toxicities include thromboembolic events, hypertension, cholestatic jaundice, endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma with unopposed exposure, and potential worsening of estrogen-sensitive malignancies; overdose or chronic excess may produce marked feminizing and uterotrophic effects.

Name: Benoxaprofen
Description: Benoxaprofen (DB04812) is a lipophilic arylpropionic acid nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug characterized structurally by a 2-arylpropionic acid framework in which a propionic acid side chain is attached to a benzoxazole-containing aromatic system bearing a para-chlorophenyl substituent; thus, its chemical category is the profen subclass of NSAIDs and its core chemical scaffold is a benzoxazole-linked arylpropionic acid. It is chemically and pharmacologically related to other profens and anti-inflammatory arylacetic/arylpropionic agents such as ibuprofen, naproxen, ketoprofen, fenoprofen, and to some extent suprofen and diclofenac by shared cyclooxygenase-directed anti-inflammatory activity. Its principal known targets are cyclooxygenase enzymes, especially PTGS1 and PTGS2, with suppression of prostaglandin synthesis accounting for analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antipyretic effects; additional photobiologic and hepatic liabilities likely reflect off-target oxidative and phototoxic processes rather than a unique therapeutic target. Benoxaprofen was used clinically for rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, and musculoskeletal pain and stiffness, particularly inflammatory arthropathies in older adults. After oral administration it is well absorbed, highly plasma-protein bound, distributes extensively into tissues, and has an unusually long elimination half-life for an NSAID, favoring accumulation; metabolism is limited relative to many comparators, with hepatic biotransformation and substantial biliary/fecal elimination alongside renal excretion of drug-related material. Its major toxicities include cholestatic or mixed hepatotoxicity, prolonged jaundice, severe photosensitivity and photo-onycholysis, and enhanced risk in the elderly due to accumulation; other adverse effects include dyspepsia, nausea, diarrhea, rash, pruritus, edema, headache, and typical NSAID gastrointestinal intolerance. Because of serious hepatic and cutaneous toxicity, including fatal liver injury in some patients, its clinical use was abandoned and it was withdrawn from the market.

Name: Clioquinol
Description: Clioquinol (DrugBank DB04815) is a halogenated 8-hydroxyquinoline characterized by a bicyclic quinoline aromatic system bearing a phenolic hydroxyl at the 8-position and halogen substituents, classically iodine and chlorine, that confer marked lipophilicity and metal-chelating capacity; thus it belongs to the hydroxyquinoline antifungal/antiprotozoal class and is built on the 8-hydroxyquinoline scaffold. Structurally and pharmacologically related drugs include other hydroxyquinolines such as iodoquinol, chlorquinaldol, nitroxoline, and broader quinoline derivatives with antimicrobial activity. Its activity is attributed less to a single high-affinity receptor than to chelation of transition metals such as copper and zinc, disruption of metal-dependent microbial processes, and effects on amyloid handling; reported protein-level associations include amyloid precursor protein, matrix metalloproteinases, and metal-dependent enzymes, although no uniquely validated canonical target fully explains all actions. After oral or topical administration, absorption is variable but can be substantial, distribution is favored into lipid-rich tissues with some CNS penetration, metabolism occurs mainly by hepatic glucuronidation and sulfation, and excretion is primarily urinary as conjugates with limited unchanged drug. Indications have historically included topical treatment of fungal and eczematous dermatoses and oral treatment of intestinal amoebiasis or nonspecific infectious diarrhea; it has also been studied experimentally in Alzheimer disease and cancer. Adverse effects include gastrointestinal upset, rash, pruritus, and iodism-like reactions, while major toxicity includes dose- and duration-related neurotoxicity, especially subacute myelo-optic neuropathy, peripheral neuropathy, visual impairment, and rare myelopathy, which severely curtailed systemic clinical use in many countries.

Name: Dantron
Description: Dantron (DrugBank DB04816), also known as chrysazin or 1,8-dihydroxyanthraquinone, is a small planar aromatic molecule built on an anthracene-9,10-dione core bearing two phenolic hydroxyl groups at the 1 and 8 positions, giving it a rigid, highly conjugated, weakly acidic polycyclic quinone structure; chemically it belongs to the hydroxyanthraquinone/anthracenedione class, and its defining scaffold is the anthraquinone nucleus shared with stimulant laxatives and related quinonoid compounds. Similar drugs include anthraquinone laxatives such as senna derivatives (sennosides, which yield active anthrones), cascara constituents, aloe-emodin derivatives, and the diphenylmethane laxative bisacodyl as a mechanistically related stimulant cathartic comparator. Dantron is poorly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, acts mainly locally in the colon, undergoes limited systemic distribution, may be reduced by intestinal flora to active anthrone-like metabolites, and is eliminated primarily in feces with some urinary excretion of metabolites. Its pharmacologic effect is thought to reflect direct stimulation of colonic motility and secretion rather than a well-defined single protein target, and no highly validated specific target protein is generally established. It has been used for constipation, especially opioid-associated constipation and severe chronic constipation, often in palliative-care settings and sometimes in combination products such as co-danthramer. Toxicity is important: chronic exposure has been linked to abdominal cramping, diarrhea, electrolyte depletion, melanosis coli, skin irritation from fecal contact, and notably genotoxicity and carcinogenicity concerns, including associations with gastrointestinal and urinary tract tumors in animal studies, which led to major restrictions or withdrawal in many jurisdictions. Clinically, its use has therefore become limited and largely historical despite efficacy as a stimulant laxative.

Name: Iproniazid
Description: Iproniazid (DrugBank DB04818) is an isonicotinic acid hydrazide derivative structurally characterized by a pyridine ring bearing a carboxylic acid hydrazide that is N-isopropyl substituted, making it a hydrazine-containing aromatic heterocycle and placing it in the monoamine oxidase inhibitor and hydrazide chemical categories; its core scaffold is the isonicotinoyl hydrazine, closely related to isoniazid, with similar drugs including other nonselective irreversible MAO inhibitors such as phenelzine, isocarboxazid, and tranylcypromine, as well as the antitubercular hydrazide isoniazid. Pharmacokinetically, iproniazid is orally absorbed, distributes systemically including into the central nervous system, undergoes extensive hepatic biotransformation with hydrolytic and oxidative metabolism generating reactive hydrazine intermediates, and is eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites. Its principal pharmacologic targets are monoamine oxidase A and monoamine oxidase B, which it inhibits irreversibly, increasing synaptic serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine; it has also been associated with interactions affecting pyridoxine-dependent pathways and hepatic enzymes. Historically it was indicated for major depressive disorder, especially psychomotor retardation, anergic depression, and some cases of treatment-resistant depression, after initial observation of mood elevation in tuberculosis patients. Clinical use was largely abandoned because of toxicity, notably severe hepatotoxicity ranging from asymptomatic transaminase elevation to fulminant hepatitis and hepatic necrosis, plus hypertensive crisis with tyramine, serotonin toxicity in combinations, orthostatic hypotension, weight gain, insomnia, agitation, dry mouth, constipation, dizziness, and peripheral neuropathy.

Name: Methapyrilene
Description: Methapyrilene (DrugBank DB04819) is a first-generation H1-antihistamine characterized structurally as an ethylenediamine derivative bearing a 2-pyridylaryl antihistamine pharmacophore, with a flexible diamine linker connecting heteroaromatic and lipophilic substituents that support histamine H1 receptor antagonism; chemically it belongs to the ethylenediamine antihistamine class, and its core scaffold is the classic diaryl/heteroaryl-substituted ethylenediamine motif seen in early sedating antiallergics. Similar drugs include other first-generation H1 blockers such as tripelennamine, pyrilamine, antazoline, and mepyramine, which share related aromatic-amine scaffolds and central nervous system penetration. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor (HRH1), with likely ancillary anticholinergic and sedative off-target effects typical of the class. Methapyrilene was historically used for symptomatic relief of allergic rhinitis, urticaria, pruritus, and other histamine-mediated symptoms, and in some settings as a nighttime cold or allergy remedy because of its sedative properties. Pharmacokinetically, it is expected to be well absorbed orally, widely distributed, cross the blood-brain barrier, undergo extensive hepatic biotransformation including oxidative metabolism, and be eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine. Adverse effects are typical of older antihistamines and include drowsiness, impaired psychomotor performance, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention. Toxicity is notable because methapyrilene became a classic experimental hepatotoxicant and rodent hepatocarcinogen, producing liver injury with chronic exposure, which led to abandonment of routine clinical use; overdose or excessive exposure may also exacerbate CNS depression and anticholinergic toxicity.

Name: Oxeladin
Description: Oxeladin (DrugBank DB04822) is a centrally acting, non-opioid antitussive whose structure is characterized by a lipophilic aromatic ether–ester framework built around a substituted phenyl ring linked through an alkoxy chain to an aminoalcohol-derived ester, giving it the properties of a basic, membrane-permeable tertiary amine; chemically it is generally classified as a synthetic cough suppressant within the arylalkylamine/antitussive ester class, with a scaffold that can be described as an aromatic ether connected to a dialkylaminoalkyl side chain. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to older non-narcotic antitussives such as cloperastine, levodropropizine, tipepidine, and in broad therapeutic intent to dextromethorphan, although it lacks the classic opioid scaffold. Its principal pharmacologic effect is suppression of the medullary cough center, but specific high-confidence molecular target proteins are not well established in modern target-based databases, so no definitive receptor or enzyme target can be assigned. After oral administration, oxeladin is understood to be absorbed adequately, distributed widely including likely CNS penetration because of its lipophilicity, metabolized predominantly in the liver by ester hydrolysis and oxidative biotransformation, and excreted mainly as metabolites in urine. It is indicated for symptomatic relief of nonproductive cough, for example cough associated with upper respiratory tract infections, bronchitic irritation, or inflammatory airway states. Adverse effects are usually mild and include drowsiness, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, dry mouth, and gastrointestinal discomfort; excessive exposure may produce CNS depression, agitation, or anticholinergic-like effects. Clinical use has therefore been as short-term symptomatic cough suppression in adults and children where an opioid antitussive is undesirable.

Name: Oxyphenisatin
Description: Oxyphenisatin (DrugBank DB04823) is a triarylmethane-derived diphenylmethane laxative characterized structurally by a rigid aromatic core bearing two para-hydroxylated phenyl rings linked to a carbonyl-containing heterocyclic or phenolic framework, giving it a planar, highly conjugated bis-aryl scaffold typical of stimulant cathartics; chemically, it is classified as a phenolphthalein-related stimulant laxative and more broadly as a synthetic polyaromatic phenolic compound, with a scaffold most closely related to diaryl/triarylmethane cathartics. Similar drugs include phenolphthalein, bisacodyl, sodium picosulfate, and older anthraquinone or diphenylmethane stimulant laxatives that promote colonic evacuation. Its pharmacokinetics were never extensively modernized, but historical use suggests limited systemic absorption after oral administration, predominant action within the intestine, some hepatic uptake and biotransformation likely via phase II conjugation of phenolic groups, biliary contribution to elimination, and fecal excretion as the major route with minor urinary elimination of absorbed metabolites. Oxyphenisatin is notable for clinically important hepatotoxicity, including cholestatic and hepatocellular hepatitis, jaundice, elevated transaminases, and rare severe liver injury after repeated use, which led to withdrawal or abandonment in many markets; GI toxicity such as cramping and diarrhea also occurs. No specific high-affinity molecular target protein is well established, and its effect is generally attributed to direct stimulation of enteric mucosa and colonic motility with altered fluid secretion rather than a defined receptor. It was indicated for constipation and bowel evacuation, used historically for short-term relief of refractory constipation or as a cathartic, but adverse effects including abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, electrolyte loss, dependence with chronic use, and especially hepatotoxicity severely limited clinical use.

Name: Buformin
Description: Buformin (DrugBank DB04830) is a synthetic biguanide antihyperglycemic agent whose structure consists of a substituted biguanide core bearing a butyl side chain, giving a small, strongly basic, highly polar cationic molecule at physiological pH; chemically it belongs to the biguanide class and is built on the aminoguanidine/biguanide scaffold shared with metformin and phenformin, its closest analogues, with antidiabetic similarity also extending mechanistically to other insulin-sensitizing agents though not structurally to sulfonylureas or thiazolidinediones. Buformin is absorbed orally, distributes mainly into hydrophilic tissues with limited protein binding, enters cells through organic cation transport systems, undergoes little or no significant hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by the kidney, so accumulation is promoted by renal impairment and states of hypoxia. Its principal pharmacologic targets are not a single high-affinity receptor but cellular energy-sensing pathways, especially mitochondrial respiratory-chain complex I as a functional site of action, with downstream activation of AMP-activated protein kinase; transport-related proteins likely relevant to disposition include OCT1, OCT2, and MATE transporters. It was used for type 2 diabetes mellitus, particularly hyperglycemia associated with insulin resistance and obesity, to reduce hepatic glucose output and improve peripheral glucose utilization. Major toxicities include lactic acidosis, sometimes fatal, especially in renal failure, cardiovascular collapse, sepsis, liver disease, or alcohol excess; other adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, anorexia, weakness, and possible weight loss or vitamin B12 deficiency with chronic use. Clinically, buformin saw historical use as an oral antidiabetic but was largely withdrawn or restricted in many markets because its risk-benefit profile, particularly regarding lactic acidosis, was less favorable than metformin.

Name: Tienilic acid
Description: Tienilic acid (DrugBank DB04831) is a thiophene-containing arylacetic acid diuretic structurally characterized by a chlorinated thiophene ring linked to a thenoyl-substituted phenoxy/acetic acid framework, giving an acidic, lipophilic heteroaromatic molecule that behaves as a halogenated thiophene carboxylic acid derivative; chemically it is classified among uricosuric thiazide-like diuretic agents, with a thiophene-acetic acid/aryloxy acid scaffold related functionally, though not identically, to other diuretics such as indapamide, chlorthalidone, hydrochlorothiazide, and the uricosuric diuretic/antihypertensive class more broadly. It was developed for hypertension because it promoted natriuresis and lowered serum urate, likely through inhibition of renal tubular electrolyte reabsorption, with the kidney as the principal site of action; specific target assignment has historically been limited, but functional interaction with renal electrolyte transport systems and urate handling pathways is recognized, and cytochrome P450 2C9 is an important bioactivation-related protein rather than a therapeutic target. After oral administration it is absorbed systemically, distributed with substantial plasma protein binding, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism including oxidation of the thiophene ring to reactive intermediates, and is eliminated through renal excretion of parent drug and metabolites. Its major clinical limitation was severe hepatotoxicity, including hepatitis, cholestatic injury, fulminant liver failure, and formation of anti-liver/kidney microsomal autoantibodies linked to CYP2C9-centered immune reactions; other adverse effects included typical diuretic events such as dizziness, polyuria, electrolyte disturbances, hypotension, hyperuricemia-related fluctuations despite uricosuric action, and gastrointestinal intolerance. Clinically, it was used as an antihypertensive and diuretic in edema-associated states, but was withdrawn because idiosyncratic hepatic toxicity outweighed benefit.

Name: Amineptine
Description: Amineptine (DrugBank DB04836) is a tricyclic antidepressant distinguished structurally from classical dibenzazepine or dibenzocycloheptene agents by a dibenzoazepine-like tricyclic core bearing a seven-membered nitrogen-containing central ring and a substituted aminoacyl side chain that confers relatively selective dopaminergic activity; chemically it is categorized as an atypical tricyclic antidepressant, with a tricyclic aminoketone/amino acid-derived scaffold closely related in overall ring architecture to imipramine, clomipramine, and tianeptine, although pharmacologically it more closely resembles dopamine reuptake inhibitors such as bupropion in part of its action profile. Its principal known target is the dopamine transporter SLC6A3, with weaker effects on norepinephrine uptake and minimal direct serotonergic activity. It was indicated for major depressive episodes, especially depression with psychomotor retardation, anergia, or low motivation, and was used clinically as an oral antidepressant in some European countries. After oral administration it is absorbed reasonably well, distributes systemically with likely high tissue and protein binding typical of lipophilic tricyclics, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism including beta-oxidation and side-chain biotransformation to active and inactive metabolites, and is eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites with some biliary/fecal excretion. Its adverse-effect profile included insomnia, agitation, anxiety, palpitations, nausea, dry mouth, and dizziness, while toxicity was notable for abuse and dependence liability, stimulant-like behavioral effects, hepatotoxicity including cytolytic or cholestatic hepatitis, and dermatologic reactions such as severe acneiform eruptions; overdose or misuse could produce neuropsychiatric excitation and cardiovascular complications. Because of these safety concerns, especially hepatotoxicity and misuse potential, its clinical use became highly restricted or withdrawn despite antidepressant efficacy.

Name: Clofedanol
Description: Clofedanol (DrugBank DB04837) is a centrally acting non-opioid antitussive whose structure is characterized by a lipophilic triaryl tertiary carbinol framework, typically described as a substituted diphenyl/propanol-type alcohol bearing an aminoalkyl side chain, placing it in the broader chemical category of amino alcohol antitussives and giving it a benzhydryl-alkanol scaffold related to other cough suppressants with diaryl hydrophobic cores. Structurally and pharmacologically it resembles agents such as diphenhydramine, cloperastine, and to some extent dextromethorphan in antitussive use, although it is not an opioid and is more closely aligned by scaffold to benzhydryl ether/alcohol antihistamine-like compounds. Its mechanism is incompletely defined; no single high-confidence molecular target is universally established, but antitussive activity is generally attributed to central suppression of the medullary cough center, with possible weak interactions at histaminergic, muscarinic, or sigma-related pathways rather than a canonical opioid receptor mechanism. After oral administration, it is believed to be reasonably well absorbed, distributed into tissues including the central nervous system because of high lipophilicity, metabolized hepatically by oxidative and conjugative pathways, and excreted mainly in urine as metabolites with limited unchanged drug. It has been used for symptomatic treatment of nonproductive cough in upper respiratory tract infection, bronchitis, pharyngitis, and irritative cough states. Adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, dry mouth, nausea, and gastrointestinal discomfort; overdose or heightened sensitivity may produce marked sedation, confusion, anticholinergic-type effects, or impaired psychomotor performance. Toxicity data are limited, but caution is warranted in children, the elderly, and in combination with alcohol or other CNS depressants. Clinically, it has historically been used as an oral cough suppressant, particularly when reduction of cough reflex without narcotic exposure is desired.

Name: Fluspirilene
Description: Fluspirilene (DB04842) is a long-acting diphenylbutylpiperidine antipsychotic whose structure is characterized by a lipophilic bis(aryl)-substituted butyl chain linked to a piperidine nitrogen and bearing fluorinated aromatic rings, giving a highly hydrophobic, conformationally flexible neuroleptic framework; chemically it belongs to the diphenylbutylpiperidine class, and its core scaffold is the piperidine–butyl–diaryl motif shared with related butyrophenone-like dopamine antagonists. Similar drugs include pimozide, penfluridol, and to a lesser extent haloperidol, which overlap in dopamine receptor blockade and antipsychotic profile. Its principal known target is dopamine D2 receptor antagonism, with additional affinity reported for D1, D3, D4, 5-HT2A, and possibly alpha-adrenergic receptors, consistent with suppression of mesolimbic dopaminergic signaling. Fluspirilene has been used primarily as a depot antipsychotic for chronic schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders, especially in patients with poor adherence, and can reduce hallucinations, delusions, agitation, and behavioral disorganization. After intramuscular depot administration it is absorbed slowly, distributes extensively into lipid-rich tissues and the CNS, shows prolonged apparent half-life due to depot release and tissue sequestration, undergoes hepatic oxidative metabolism, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in feces and urine. Toxicity is typical of potent D2 antagonists and includes dose-related extrapyramidal toxicity, tardive dyskinesia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, QT-related arrhythmogenic risk, sedation, and hypotension. Common adverse effects include parkinsonism, akathisia, dystonia, tremor, hyperprolactinemia, weight gain, anticholinergic complaints, and injection-site reactions. Clinically, it has been used mainly in maintenance treatment rather than acute sedation because of its slow onset and prolonged action.

Name: Mepenzolate
Description: Mepenzolate bromide (DB04843) is a synthetic quaternary ammonium antimuscarinic built as a substituted glycolate ester in which a tertiary carbinol-like carbon bears phenyl and cyclopentyl groups and is esterified to a piperidinium alcohol, giving a permanently charged bromide salt that limits membrane and CNS penetration; chemically it belongs to the anticholinergic/parasympatholytic amino alcohol ester class, and its core scaffold is the mepenzolate/glycopyrrolate-like cationic antimuscarinic ester scaffold linking a bulky hydrophobic acyl moiety to a quaternized heterocycle. Similar drugs include glycopyrrolate, propantheline, clidinium, oxybutynin, ipratropium, and atropine, which share muscarinic antagonism but differ in tertiary versus quaternary amine character and tissue penetration. Its principal pharmacologic targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially peripheral CHRM1, CHRM2, and CHRM3, with clinically relevant inhibition of CHRM3-mediated gastrointestinal smooth muscle contraction and glandular secretion. After oral administration it is variably and incompletely absorbed, distributes mainly extracellularly, shows poor blood-brain barrier entry, undergoes limited ester hydrolysis and hepatic biotransformation relative to tertiary amines, and is eliminated by renal and fecal routes largely as unchanged drug and metabolites. It has been used mainly for peptic ulcer disease, abdominal cramping, irritable bowel symptoms, and other gastrointestinal hypermotility or hypersecretory states. Adverse effects and toxicity are typical of antimuscarinics, including dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, tachycardia, urinary retention, reduced sweating, and precipitation of angle-closure glaucoma; overdose may cause severe ileus, hyperthermia, confusion or agitation despite low CNS entry, especially in older adults. Clinically, it has served as an adjunctive antisecretory and antispasmodic agent rather than definitive ulcer therapy.

Name: Ixabepilone
Description: Ixabepilone (DB04845) is a semisynthetic epothilone B analog characterized by a 16-membered macrocyclic lactone bearing multiple hydroxyl substituents, a ketone, defined alkene geometry, and a distinctive thiazole-containing side chain; structurally, replacement of the epothilone epoxide with an aza-modified moiety improves metabolic stability while preserving tubulin binding. It belongs to the epothilone class of antineoplastic microtubule inhibitors, with an epothilone macrolide scaffold closely related to natural products such as epothilone B and pharmacologically similar to taxanes including paclitaxel and docetaxel, although it can retain activity in some taxane-resistant settings. Its principal target is beta-tubulin within the alpha/beta-tubulin microtubule polymer, promoting microtubule stabilization, mitotic arrest, and apoptosis. Clinically, it is indicated for metastatic or locally advanced breast cancer, particularly after failure of anthracyclines, taxanes, and capecitabine, and has been used as monotherapy or in combination with capecitabine. Pharmacokinetically, it is given intravenously, is extensively distributed with high tissue uptake and substantial protein binding, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism via CYP3A4, and is eliminated mainly through biliary/fecal excretion with limited renal clearance; dose reduction is required in hepatic impairment and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors or inducers can alter exposure. Major toxicities include dose-limiting peripheral sensory neuropathy and myelosuppression, especially neutropenia, with increased risk of severe toxicity in liver dysfunction; other adverse effects include fatigue, alopecia, nausea, vomiting, mucositis, diarrhea, arthralgia, myalgia, and infusion-related hypersensitivity due partly to formulation excipients.

Name: Celiprolol
Description: Celiprolol (DrugBank DB04846) is a cardioselective vasodilating beta-adrenoceptor ligand built on the aryloxypropanolamine chemotype, with a substituted phenoxypropanolamine core bearing a para-acetyl-substituted aromatic ring and a bulky polar amino side chain that confers amphiphilic character; chemically it is classified as a beta-blocker and more specifically a phenoxypropanolamine derivative, with the classic beta-adrenergic antagonist scaffold shared by related agents such as atenolol, betaxolol, metoprolol, propranolol, and acebutolol. Pharmacologically, celiprolol acts primarily at beta-1 adrenergic receptors with beta-2 agonist or partial agonist vasodilatory activity and little membrane-stabilizing effect, and reported targets include ADRB1 and ADRB2. After oral administration it is absorbed incompletely and variably, with bioavailability limited partly by intestinal transport effects and reduced by food; protein binding is low to moderate, tissue distribution is modest, metabolism is limited compared with many lipophilic beta-blockers, and elimination occurs predominantly as unchanged drug in feces and urine with a terminal half-life that supports once- or twice-daily dosing. It is indicated mainly for hypertension, with clinical use also in chronic stable angina and situations where beta-blockade with less bronchoconstrictive liability is desired. Adverse effects resemble those of other beta-blockers and include bradycardia, hypotension, fatigue, dizziness, headache, gastrointestinal upset, and cold extremities, while important toxicities include excessive beta-blockade causing conduction disturbance, heart failure exacerbation, bronchospasm in susceptible patients, and masking of hypoglycemia; overdose may produce severe bradycardia, shock, and syncope.

Name: Roxadustat
Description: Roxadustat (DrugBank DB04847) is an orally active small-molecule hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor built around a heteroaromatic glycinamide-type scaffold featuring a substituted pyridine core linked to an amide/acid-derived metal-chelating pharmacophore and lipophilic aryl substitution, a design characteristic of 2-oxoglutarate mimetics that bind the catalytic iron center of prolyl hydroxylase domain enzymes; chemically it is classified as a HIF stabilizer, PHD enzyme inhibitor, and N-heteroaromatic carboxamide-like agent, with related drugs in the same class including daprodustat, vadadustat, molidustat, and enarodustat. Its principal targets are EGLN1/PHD2, EGLN2/PHD1, and EGLN3/PHD3, leading to stabilization of HIF-1 alpha and HIF-2 alpha and downstream induction of erythropoietin, transferrin handling, and iron-utilization genes. Roxadustat is indicated primarily for anemia associated with chronic kidney disease, including dialysis-dependent and non-dialysis CKD, and has been used clinically to raise hemoglobin and reduce need for exogenous erythropoiesis-stimulating agents or transfusions. After oral administration it is absorbed systemically with moderate bioavailability, is highly protein bound, distributes mainly in plasma and extracellular compartments, undergoes predominant phase II metabolism including glucuronidation and sulfation with limited oxidative biotransformation, and is eliminated through both fecal and urinary routes largely as metabolites. Important toxicities include excessive erythropoiesis, hypertension, thromboembolic and cardiovascular events, hyperkalemia, and possible hepatic injury; common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, headache, fatigue, edema, increased blood pressure, and access thrombosis in dialysis patients.

Name: Febuxostat
Description: Febuxostat (DrugBank DB04854) is a nonpurine, small-molecule xanthine oxidoreductase inhibitor whose structure is centered on a substituted thiazole scaffold bearing a nitrile group and an isobutoxy-substituted phenyl ring, giving a lipophilic heteroaryl carboxylic acid architecture that distinguishes it from purine analogs. Chemically it is classified as a thiazole-containing aromatic carboxylic acid and a nonpurine antihyperuricemic agent; its core scaffold is best described as an aryl-thiazole carboxylic acid. Similar drugs include allopurinol and its active metabolite oxypurinol, which also lower uric acid but are purine-like xanthine oxidase inhibitors, and uricosurics such as probenecid that act by a different mechanism. Febuxostat selectively inhibits xanthine oxidase/xanthine oxidoreductase, the principal known target protein, thereby reducing conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid. It is orally well absorbed, highly protein bound, reaches peak concentrations within hours, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly by glucuronidation and oxidation involving UGT enzymes and CYP pathways including CYP1A2, CYP2C8, and CYP2C9, and is eliminated through both urine and feces as parent drug and metabolites, with a terminal half-life that supports once-daily dosing. It is indicated for chronic hyperuricemia in gout, including prevention of recurrent gout flares, tophi formation, and urate nephropathy risk, and is used clinically in patients intolerant of allopurinol or with inadequate urate control. Important adverse effects include gout flare on initiation, liver enzyme elevations, nausea, arthralgia, rash, and diarrhea; notable toxicities include hepatotoxicity, hypersensitivity reactions, and a recognized cardiovascular safety concern with increased risk of cardiovascular death in some high-risk populations.

Name: Dronedarone
Description: Dronedarone (DB04855) is a noniodinated benzofuran-derived antiarrhythmic structurally related to amiodarone, characterized by a dibutyl-substituted benzofuran scaffold linked to a methanesulfonamide-bearing phenoxy side chain, a design that reduces iodine-associated tissue toxicity while preserving broad ion-channel blocking activity; chemically it is classified as a multichannel class III antiarrhythmic with additional class I, II, and IV properties, and its core scaffold is the benzofuran diaryl ether framework. Similar drugs include amiodarone as the closest structural and pharmacologic analogue, and mechanistically related antiarrhythmics such as sotalol, dofetilide, flecainide, and propafenone. Its principal targets include cardiac potassium channels underlying IKr and IKs currents, sodium channels such as SCN5A, L-type calcium channels including CACNA1C-containing complexes, and antiadrenergic pathways via beta-adrenergic receptor antagonism, resulting in prolonged action potential duration, slowed conduction, and reduced automaticity. Orally administered dronedarone has low to moderate bioavailability that increases with food, is highly protein bound, distributes extensively, undergoes major hepatic metabolism predominantly by CYP3A4 with contributions from CYP2D6-related interactions, and is excreted mainly in feces with limited renal elimination; its half-life is markedly shorter than that of amiodarone. It is indicated to reduce hospitalization in patients with paroxysmal or persistent atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter in sinus rhythm, but is not for permanent atrial fibrillation. Important toxicities include hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation, bradycardia, worsening heart failure, pulmonary toxicity, and clinically significant drug-drug interactions; adverse effects commonly include diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, rash, fatigue, and serum creatinine increases. Clinically, it is used for rhythm control and maintenance of sinus rhythm in selected atrial fibrillation patients, particularly when a less tissue-accumulative alternative to amiodarone is desired.

Name: Omacetaxine mepesuccinate
Description: Omacetaxine mepesuccinate (DB04865) is a semisynthetic ester salt of homoharringtonine, a cephalotaxine-derived plant alkaloid characterized by a highly oxygenated pentacyclic cephalotaxine core bearing multiple fused rings, several stereocenters, methoxy and hydroxyl substituents, and an esterified side chain presented as the mepesuccinate salt to improve formulation; chemically it belongs to the cephalotaxine alkaloids and functionally to small-molecule antineoplastics/protein synthesis inhibitors, with a cephalotaxine alkaloid scaffold distinct from kinase inhibitors. Closely related or similar agents include homoharringtonine itself and other cephalotaxine esters such as harringtonine, while mechanistically it contrasts with BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitors like imatinib, dasatinib, and nilotinib that are used in similar disease settings. Omacetaxine binds the A-site cleft of the large ribosomal subunit and inhibits elongation during translation, thereby depleting short-lived oncoproteins such as BCR-ABL and MCL1; its primary molecular target is the eukaryotic ribosome rather than a single classic protein enzyme. After subcutaneous administration it is systemically absorbed, distributes beyond plasma with moderate protein binding, undergoes hydrolysis and esterase-mediated metabolism with additional minor hepatic biotransformation, and is eliminated through both urinary and nonrenal routes with a short terminal half-life on the order of hours. Its major toxicities are dose-limiting myelosuppression, including thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, and anemia, with infection and bleeding risk; other adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, fatigue, pyrexia, injection-site reactions, hyperglycemia, and asthenia. Clinically it is indicated for chronic or accelerated phase chronic myeloid leukemia resistant to or intolerant of at least two tyrosine kinase inhibitors, particularly in patients with refractory disease or T315I-associated treatment failure.

Name: Lorcaserin
Description: Lorcaserin (DrugBank DB04871) is a small-molecule, orally active substituted arylalkylamine built around a rigid benzazepine/tetrahydro-1H-benzoazepine scaffold bearing a chlorophenyl substituent and a primary amine, a structure that places it within serotonergic anorectic agents and conformationally restricted phenethylamine-like compounds; its closest pharmacologic analogs are other centrally acting anti-obesity drugs and serotonergic appetite suppressants such as fenfluramine, dexfenfluramine, sibutramine, and to a lesser extent phentermine, although lorcaserin is distinguished by greater selectivity for the 5-HT2C receptor. Its principal target is the serotonin 5-HT2C receptor (HTR2C), with weaker activity at 5-HT2A and 5-HT2B, and appetite suppression is mediated through hypothalamic pro-opiomelanocortin pathway activation. It was indicated for chronic weight management in adults with obesity or overweight with comorbidities such as type 2 diabetes, hypertension, or dyslipidemia, and was clinically used as an adjunct to calorie restriction and exercise to reduce body weight and improve metabolic parameters. After oral administration it is well absorbed, reaches peak concentrations in roughly 1.5 to 2 hours, distributes systemically with moderate protein binding, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism through multiple pathways including oxidation and conjugation rather than reliance on a single CYP isozyme, and is eliminated predominantly in urine as metabolites with an elimination half-life of about 11 hours. Adverse effects commonly included headache, dizziness, fatigue, nausea, dry mouth, constipation, and hypoglycemia in diabetic patients; important toxicities included serotonin syndrome with serotonergic co-medications, psychiatric effects, cognitive slowing, rare valvulopathy concerns from serotonergic cross-reactivity, and a later signal for increased cancer risk that led to market withdrawal in the United States.

Name: Vildagliptin
Description: Vildagliptin (DrugBank DB04876) is a small-molecule oral antihyperglycemic agent of the dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor, or gliptin, class, structurally characterized by a cyanopyrrolidine core linked through an amino substituent to a substituted adamantane-like hydroxyadamantyl moiety, with the nitrile-bearing pyrrolidine serving as the key pharmacophore for reversible covalent interaction with its enzyme target; thus, its principal chemical scaffold is a cyanopyrrolidine peptidomimetic DPP-4 inhibitor scaffold. It is chemically and pharmacologically similar to other DPP-4 inhibitors such as sitagliptin, saxagliptin, alogliptin, and linagliptin, although these differ in heterocyclic and lipophilic substituent patterns. Its primary target is DPP-4/CD26, leading to prolonged incretin activity, especially GLP-1 and GIP, with consequent glucose-dependent enhancement of insulin secretion and suppression of glucagon. Vildagliptin is indicated for type 2 diabetes mellitus, particularly for improving glycemic control as monotherapy when metformin is unsuitable or in combination with metformin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones, or insulin. It is generally well absorbed orally, has moderate bioavailability, low plasma protein binding, distributes systemically without major tissue sequestration, undergoes predominantly non-CYP hydrolytic metabolism to inactive metabolites, and is eliminated mainly in urine as parent drug and metabolites, with a relatively short half-life but durable DPP-4 inhibition. Adverse effects include headache, dizziness, nasopharyngitis, constipation, nausea, peripheral edema, and hypoglycemia when combined with insulin secretagogues; important toxicities include hepatic enzyme elevations, rare hepatitis, pancreatitis, hypersensitivity reactions including angioedema, and infrequent severe arthralgia, so clinical use commonly includes periodic liver function monitoring and dose adjustment in renal impairment.

Name: Voglibose
Description: Voglibose (DrugBank DB04878) is a highly polar pseudo-carbohydrate alpha-glucosidase inhibitor built on a valiolamine/aminocyclitol core that mimics the oxocarbenium ion-like transition state of oligosaccharide hydrolysis; structurally it is a polyhydroxylated substituted cyclohexane bearing multiple vicinal hydroxyl groups and a nitrogen-containing sugar mimic, placing it in the iminosugar/aminocyclitol antidiabetic class with a carbohydrate-mimetic scaffold closely related to other intestinal alpha-glucosidase inhibitors such as acarbose and miglitol. Its principal targets are brush-border alpha-glucosidases in the small intestine, particularly maltase-glucoamylase and sucrase-isomaltase activities, with consequent delay of complex carbohydrate digestion and blunting of postprandial glucose excursions. Voglibose is indicated for type 2 diabetes mellitus, especially postprandial hyperglycemia, and has also been used clinically in impaired glucose tolerance or as add-on therapy to diet, metformin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones, DPP-4 inhibitors, or insulin when meal-related glucose control is inadequate. Pharmacokinetically, systemic absorption is minimal after oral dosing, distribution is therefore limited, circulating concentrations are very low, metabolism is negligible to limited, and elimination is mainly via feces with little renal excretion of absorbed drug, so its action is largely local within the gut lumen. Toxicity is dominated by exaggerated gastrointestinal carbohydrate fermentation rather than systemic organ toxicity, with flatulence, abdominal distension, borborygmi, soft stools, and diarrhea being common; abdominal pain, nausea, constipation, and rare hepatic enzyme elevations or ileus-like complications have been reported, and hypoglycemia may occur when combined with insulin secretagogues or insulin.

Name: Dapoxetine
Description: Dapoxetine (DrugBank DB04884) is a short-acting arylalkylamine antidepressant derivative developed as a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, structurally characterized by a chiral propylamine backbone bearing a naphthyl ether linked to a dimethylphenyl group, placing it in the phenoxy/aryloxy-propanamine class and specifically within the SSRI-related naphthalene-containing aryloxypropylamine scaffold; it is chemically and pharmacologically similar to other SSRIs such as fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline, citalopram, and especially the related agent duloxetine in its aryl ether motif, although dapoxetine is distinguished by rapid onset and short half-life. Its principal target is the serotonin transporter SLC6A4, with lesser activity reported at norepinephrine and dopamine transport processes, and its therapeutic indication is premature ejaculation in adult men, where it increases intravaginal ejaculatory latency time and improves perceived control and distress. After oral administration it is rapidly absorbed, reaches peak plasma concentrations in about 1-2 hours, is widely distributed, is highly protein bound, and undergoes extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism mainly via CYP2D6 and CYP3A4, with contributions from flavin-containing monooxygenase pathways, to inactive and weakly active metabolites that are excreted largely in urine; its brief effective half-life supports on-demand dosing. Toxicity is generally SSRI-like and dose-related, including nausea, dizziness, headache, insomnia, diarrhea, fatigue, orthostatic symptoms, syncope, and rare serotonin syndrome, seizures, or mood destabilization, with increased risk in overdose or when combined with MAO inhibitors, thioridazine, potent CYP3A4 inhibitors, alcohol, or other serotonergic drugs. Clinically it is used as needed before sexual activity rather than as a chronic antidepressant, particularly in men with lifelong or acquired premature ejaculation.

Name: Bepotastine
Description: Bepotastine (DrugBank DB04890) is a second-generation antiallergic agent structurally characterized as a zwitterionic piperidine-containing benzoic acid derivative, featuring an aromatic diaryl ether-like framework linked to a basic tertiary amine and a terminal carboxylic acid, a design that confers potent peripheral H1-antihistamine activity with limited central nervous system penetration; chemically it is classified as an antihistamine within the piperidine/carboxylated aryl ether class, and its core scaffold can be viewed as a substituted piperidine attached to a diphenyl-ether/arylpropionic acid-like motif. It is broadly similar to other second-generation H1 antagonists such as fexofenadine, epinastine, cetirizine, olopatadine, and loratadine analogs in being peripherally selective and minimally sedating. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor (HRH1), with additional reported mast-cell stabilizing and anti-eosinophilic effects that may reduce mediator release and eosinophil migration. After oral administration, bepotastine is absorbed relatively rapidly, reaches peak plasma concentrations within a few hours, shows modest protein binding, distributes mainly peripherally, undergoes limited metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged in urine, making renal excretion the major clearance pathway and renal impairment a consideration. Toxicity is generally low, with overdose or heightened exposure potentially producing somnolence, dry mouth, gastrointestinal discomfort, headache, or anticholinergic-like symptoms, while serious cardiotoxicity appears uncommon compared with older antihistamines. It is indicated for allergic rhinitis, urticaria, pruritus, and allergic conjunctivitis; clinically it is used orally for seasonal allergy symptoms such as sneezing, rhinorrhea, and itching, and ophthalmically for itching associated with allergic conjunctival disease.

Name: Milnacipran
Description: Milnacipran (DrugBank DB04896) is a small-molecule aminomethyl cyclopropane antidepressant characterized structurally by a constrained cyclopropane core bearing an aryl substituent and a dialkylamino-containing side chain, typically described as a phenyl-substituted cyclopropane derivative with a primary carboxamide-related amino alcohol motif in its resolved stereochemical form; chemically it is classified as a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor and more broadly as a phenylcyclopropylamine-related central nervous system agent, with a rigid cyclopropane scaffold that distinguishes it from more flexible SNRI chemotypes. Similar drugs include levomilnacipran, its more active enantiomer, and other SNRIs such as duloxetine, venlafaxine, and desvenlafaxine. Its principal targets are the norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2 and serotonin transporter SLC6A4, with greater relative inhibition of norepinephrine reuptake than serotonin reuptake. Orally administered milnacipran is well absorbed, has high bioavailability, limited plasma protein binding, distributes systemically without marked tissue sequestration, undergoes relatively modest hepatic metabolism mainly by conjugative pathways rather than extensive CYP oxidation, and is excreted predominantly unchanged in urine, making renal function a key determinant of exposure. Toxicity is consistent with SNRI pharmacology and includes dose-related tachycardia, hypertension, agitation, seizures in overdose, hepatotoxicity reported rarely, hyponatremia, serotonin syndrome when combined with serotonergic agents, and suicidality risk typical of antidepressants. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, constipation, headache, dizziness, insomnia, hyperhidrosis, palpitations, dry mouth, and urinary hesitancy. Clinically, milnacipran is used primarily for fibromyalgia to reduce chronic widespread pain, fatigue, and functional impairment, and in some regions has also been used as an antidepressant for major depressive disorder.

Name: Flibanserin
Description: Flibanserin (DB04908) is a centrally acting, nonhormonal serotonergic agent whose structure is a substituted benzimidazole linked through an ethyl spacer to a piperazine ring bearing a 3-trifluoromethylphenyl group, making it a lipophilic arylpiperazine; chemically it is categorized as a heteroaryl piperazine/benzimidazole derivative, with an arylpiperazine scaffold that is shared with several CNS-active ligands. Related drugs by chemotype or receptor pharmacology include buspirone, trazodone, nefazodone, and certain serotonin receptor modulators such as tandospirone. Its principal targets are serotonin 5-HT1A receptors, where it acts predominantly as an agonist or partial agonist, and 5-HT2A receptors, where it acts as an antagonist, with reported activity also at 5-HT2B and 5-HT2C receptors and downstream effects that increase dopamine and norepinephrine while reducing serotonin signaling in selected brain regions. Pharmacokinetically, flibanserin is orally administered, absorbed with moderate bioavailability limited by first-pass metabolism, highly protein bound, distributed into the CNS, extensively metabolized in the liver mainly by CYP3A4 and to a lesser extent CYP2C19, and excreted primarily as metabolites in urine and feces; exposure rises with hepatic impairment or strong CYP3A4 inhibition. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related CNS depression and cardiovascular effects, notably sedation, dizziness, fatigue, hypotension, and syncope, with marked risk when combined with alcohol, azole antifungals, macrolides, protease inhibitors, or grapefruit products. Clinically it is indicated for acquired, generalized hypoactive sexual desire disorder in premenopausal women, where it is used chronically at bedtime to reduce low sexual desire and associated distress rather than for situational sexual dysfunction.

Name: Oritavancin
Description: Oritavancin (DrugBank DB04911) is a semisynthetic lipoglycopeptide antibiotic structurally derived from the vancomycin/chloroeremomycin family, consisting of a heavily cross-linked glycopeptide heptapeptide core decorated with aromatic residues, chlorinated substituents, sugar moieties, and a characteristic hydrophobic lipophilic side chain that enhances membrane anchoring and potency against resistant Gram-positive organisms. Chemically, it belongs to the glycopeptide/lipoglycopeptide class and retains the vancomycin-like rigid macrocyclic glycopeptide scaffold. Closely related or mechanistically similar drugs include vancomycin, telavancin, dalbavancin, and teicoplanin. Its antibacterial activity is mediated primarily by binding the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of peptidoglycan precursors, with additional disruption of cell wall transglycosylation/transpeptidation and bacterial membrane integrity; thus its functional target is lipid II and related peptidoglycan biosynthetic intermediates rather than a human protein target. After intravenous administration, absorption is complete by infusion only, distribution is extensive with a very large apparent volume and prolonged tissue persistence, protein binding is high, metabolism is minimal, and elimination is slow with a terminal half-life on the order of many days, permitting single-dose therapy; excretion occurs mainly unchanged via reticuloendothelial handling and, to a lesser extent, renal and fecal routes. Toxicities include infusion-related reactions, hypersensitivity, osteomyelitis signal in trials, and laboratory interference with coagulation assays; adverse effects commonly include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, limb or infusion-site reactions, and pruritus. Clinically, it is indicated for acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections caused by susceptible Gram-positive pathogens such as Staphylococcus aureus including MRSA, Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus agalactiae, Streptococcus anginosus group, and Enterococcus faecalis, and is used as a long-acting outpatient intravenous option when adherence or prolonged daily dosing is problematic.

Name: Itopride
Description: Itopride (DrugBank DB04924) is a substituted benzamide gastroprokinetic composed of an anisamide-like aromatic ring bearing methoxy substitution and linked through an amide to a short alkyl chain terminating in a tertiary dimethylamino functionality; this places it in the benzamide/prokinetic chemical category with a para-substituted benzamide scaffold closely related to other dopamine-modulating prokinetics such as metoclopramide, domperidone, levosulpiride, and to some extent cisapride by therapeutic similarity rather than core chemistry. Its principal targets are dopamine D2 receptor antagonism and acetylcholinesterase inhibition, increasing acetylcholine availability in the enteric nervous system and enhancing upper gastrointestinal motility. It is indicated mainly for functional dyspepsia, postprandial fullness, early satiety, bloating, epigastric discomfort, nausea, vomiting, and other symptoms associated with delayed gastric emptying or mild gastroparesis. After oral administration it is rapidly absorbed, has moderate bioavailability limited partly by first-pass metabolism, distributes mainly in extracellular fluids with relatively limited central nervous system penetration, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism largely via flavin-containing monooxygenase 3 to inactive or less active metabolites rather than heavy CYP dependence, and is excreted chiefly in urine as parent drug and metabolites. Toxicity is generally modest but includes cholinergic and antidopaminergic effects; examples include diarrhea, abdominal cramping, headache, dizziness, and hyperprolactinemia with galactorrhea or menstrual disturbance, while serious toxicity may rarely involve hepatic enzyme elevations or leukopenia. Clinically, it is used in several Asian countries as an oral prokinetic for chronic dyspeptic symptoms and motility disorders, especially when improved gastric accommodation and emptying are desired without major extrapyramidal liability.

Name: Permethrin
Description: Permethrin (DrugBank DB04930) is a synthetic type I pyrethroid composed of a cyclopropane carboxylate ester linking a dichlorovinyl-substituted cyclopropyl moiety to a 3-phenoxybenzyl alcohol fragment, giving a lipophilic aryl ether–cyclopropane ester architecture with cis/trans stereoisomerism; chemically it belongs to the pyrethroid insecticides, and its core scaffold is the chrysanthemate-like cyclopropane carboxylate ester shared across many ectoparasiticides. Closely related drugs include pyrethrins, deltamethrin, cypermethrin, phenothrin, and allethrin, which share voltage-gated sodium channel activity but differ in substituents and kinetic behavior. Permethrin acts primarily on arthropod voltage-gated sodium channels, prolonging channel opening and causing repetitive firing, paralysis, and death; mammalian sodium channels are less sensitive, contributing to its therapeutic selectivity. After topical use, systemic absorption is usually low but increases with disrupted skin; distribution is mainly into superficial skin and hair, metabolism occurs rapidly via ester hydrolysis and hepatic oxidation to inactive metabolites, and excretion is chiefly urinary with some fecal elimination. Toxicity is generally low in humans but includes paresthesia, burning, pruritus, erythema, and irritant dermatitis, while excessive exposure may cause nausea, tremor, or neuroexcitation; cats are notably susceptible to pyrethroid toxicity. Its principal indications are scabies and pediculosis capitis, with clinical use as 5% cream for Sarcoptes scabiei infestation and 1% lotion or rinse for head lice, and it is also used in impregnated clothing and bed nets for arthropod-borne disease prevention.

Name: Afamelanotide
Description: Afamelanotide (DrugBank DB04931) is a synthetic melanocortin peptide analog structurally derived from alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone, designed as a short linear oligopeptide with strategic substitutions including norleucine and D-phenylalanine that increase receptor potency and markedly improve resistance to rapid enzymatic degradation; chemically it is classified as a melanocortin receptor agonist peptide and more broadly as a synthetic peptide hormone analog, built on the alpha-MSH melanocortin scaffold. Closely related agents include melanotan I, melanotan II, and the endogenous ligand alpha-MSH, as well as other melanocortin agonists such as setmelanotide. Its principal target is melanocortin 1 receptor, with lesser activity reported at other melanocortin receptors, leading to stimulation of eumelanin synthesis and photoprotective pigmentation. Clinically, afamelanotide is used primarily for prevention of phototoxicity in erythropoietic protoporphyria, where it reduces light-induced pain and increases sunlight tolerance; it has also been explored in pigmentary and photodermatosis-related conditions such as vitiligo and polymorphous light eruption. After subcutaneous implantation it is slowly absorbed, distributed systemically as a peptide, cleared mainly by proteolytic metabolism to smaller peptides and amino acids rather than CYP-dependent biotransformation, and eliminated predominantly as metabolic fragments via renal routes; terminal exposure is limited but prolonged relative to native alpha-MSH because of depot delivery and peptide stabilization. Adverse effects are usually mild to moderate and include nausea, headache, fatigue, flushing, implant-site reactions, hyperpigmentation, and darkening of nevi or skin. Toxicity is generally low, but excessive melanocortin stimulation can produce diffuse pigmentation changes and warrants caution in patients with significant pigmentary lesions or melanoma risk.

Name: Lofexidine
Description: Lofexidine (DrugBank DB04948) is a centrally acting imidazoline-derived sympatholytic whose structure consists of a substituted phenoxyethyl framework linked to an imidazoline ring, specifically an aryl-oxyethyl imidazoline bearing dichloro substitution on the phenyl ring, placing it in the chemical category of alpha-adrenergic agonists and more specifically imidazoline antihypertensive or anti-withdrawal agents; its core scaffold is closely related to clonidine-like arylalkyl imidazolines, and similar drugs include clonidine, guanfacine, tizanidine, and xylazine, with clonidine being the most pharmacologically analogous. Its principal targets are alpha-2 adrenergic receptor subtypes, especially ADRA2A, ADRA2B, and ADRA2C, with central presynaptic agonism reducing norepinephrine release and sympathetic outflow. Pharmacokinetically, lofexidine is orally active, absorbed with moderate bioavailability, distributed systemically with central nervous system penetration sufficient for autonomic effects, metabolized predominantly in the liver to inactive or less active metabolites, and eliminated mainly in urine with a terminal half-life generally in the low-to-mid teens of hours. It is indicated primarily for mitigation of opioid withdrawal symptoms such as tachycardia, sweating, anxiety, agitation, and gastrointestinal distress, and has also been used historically as an antihypertensive. Adverse effects commonly include hypotension, bradycardia, dry mouth, dizziness, sedation, somnolence, orthostasis, and insomnia; important toxicities include excessive CNS depression, syncope, rebound hypertension after abrupt discontinuation, and QT prolongation risk, particularly in overdose or when combined with other hypotensive, sedative, or QT-prolonging drugs. Clinically, it is used as a non-opioid adjunct in supervised opioid detoxification and withdrawal management to blunt autonomic hyperactivity without treating opioid craving directly.

Name: Pirfenidone
Description: Pirfenidone (DB04951) is a small, orally active synthetic antifibrotic built on a simple heteroaromatic scaffold consisting of a substituted pyridone ring, specifically 5-methyl-1-phenyl-2(1H)-pyridone, placing it in the pyridone/lactam class of aromatic antifibrotic agents; its core chemical scaffold is a phenyl-substituted 2-pyridone, a relatively planar lipophilic ring system that supports tissue penetration and oral bioavailability. It is chemically and pharmacologically similar in broad antifibrotic intent, though not close in structure, to agents such as nintedanib, and has also been compared with experimental TGF-beta-modulating or collagen-suppressing compounds. Its mechanism is pleiotropic rather than defined by a single high-affinity receptor, with reported effects on TGF-beta1, TNF-alpha, PDGF-related signaling, collagen synthesis pathways, and fibroblast proliferation; no single canonical target fully explains activity, but transforming growth factor beta pathways are central. After oral administration it is rapidly absorbed, reaches peak plasma levels in hours, is moderately distributed, extensively metabolized in the liver predominantly by CYP1A2 with lesser roles for other CYP enzymes, and is excreted mainly in urine as metabolites, especially the 5-carboxy derivative; food reduces peak-related intolerance. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related gastrointestinal and constitutional effects, hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevation, and photosensitivity or phototoxic rash, with overdose or susceptibility potentially worsening nausea, dizziness, and liver injury. Clinically it is indicated primarily for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis to slow decline in forced vital capacity and disease progression, and it has been used or studied in other fibrosing interstitial lung diseases. Common adverse effects include nausea, dyspepsia, anorexia, fatigue, diarrhea, rash, and dizziness, and routine use involves oral chronic therapy with liver-function and sun-exposure monitoring.

Name: Belinostat
Description: Belinostat (DB05015) is a hydroxamic acid–based antineoplastic agent structurally characterized by a terminal hydroxamate zinc-binding group linked through an alkene-containing amide spacer to a substituted aromatic sulfonamide system, placing it in the histone deacetylase inhibitor class and more specifically within the hydroxamate pan-HDAC inhibitor chemotype built on an aryl-sulfonamide/hydroxamate scaffold. It is chemically and pharmacologically similar to other HDAC inhibitors such as vorinostat, panobinostat, givinostat, and to a lesser extent romidepsin, although romidepsin is a cyclic peptide prodrug with a distinct scaffold. Belinostat targets class I and II HDAC enzymes, including HDAC1, HDAC2, HDAC3, HDAC6, and related isoforms, increasing histone and non-histone protein acetylation and thereby altering transcription, cell-cycle control, apoptosis, and differentiation. Clinically, it is indicated primarily for relapsed or refractory peripheral T-cell lymphoma, with broader investigational use in other hematologic malignancies and selected solid tumors. It is administered intravenously, achieving systemic exposure rapidly; distribution is moderate and likely includes substantial tissue uptake; metabolism is predominantly hepatic, especially by UGT1A1-mediated glucuronidation with minor oxidative CYP contributions; and elimination occurs mainly as metabolites in urine, with a short terminal half-life supporting intermittent infusion schedules. Toxicities include myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity, fatigue, gastrointestinal intolerance, and QT-related cardiac risk; severe examples include anemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, serious infection, and liver enzyme elevation. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fatigue, pyrexia, and infusion-related weakness. In practice, belinostat is used as single-agent salvage therapy in PTCL, particularly when rapid disease control is needed after prior systemic treatment failure.

Name: Ataluren
Description: Ataluren (DB05016) is a small orally active heteroaromatic carboxylic acid whose structure is centered on a substituted 1,2,4-oxadiazole linked to multiple phenyl rings, giving a lipophilic diaryl/triaryl-like scaffold terminated by a benzoic acid moiety; chemically it is classified as an oxadiazole-containing aromatic carboxylic acid and more broadly as a nonsense-mutation readthrough agent, with a biaryl-heterocycle scaffold distinct from aminoglycosides but functionally analogous to other premature stop-codon suppressors such as gentamicin, G418, and investigational readthrough compounds including RTC13/RTC14-like series. Its pharmacology is attributed not to a single canonical protein target but to modulation of the eukaryotic ribosomal translation machinery, promoting selective ribosomal readthrough of premature termination codons while preserving most normal stop-codon recognition; direct high-confidence protein targets are therefore not well defined, though the ribosome and release factor-dependent translation termination process are the operative molecular systems. After oral administration it is absorbed with measurable systemic exposure, is highly plasma protein bound, distributed systemically, undergoes predominant hepatic phase II glucuronidation to ataluren acyl glucuronide with minor oxidative metabolism, and is excreted mainly in urine as metabolites. Toxicity is generally moderate, with nonclinical concerns including gastrointestinal and hepatic effects at high exposure and interaction-related attenuation of effect with some aminoglycosides. Clinically it is indicated for nonsense mutation Duchenne muscular dystrophy, aiming to restore dystrophin production in ambulatory patients with nonsense mutations; adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, decreased appetite, abdominal pain, hypertension, and renal laboratory abnormalities. Its clinical use is mutation-specific rather than symptom-based, serving as a precision therapy for genetic diseases caused by premature stop codons, most prominently nmDMD and historically explored in cystic fibrosis and other nonsense-mutation disorders.

Name: Migalastat
Description: Migalastat (DrugBank DB05018) is a small iminosugar pharmacological chaperone structurally characterized as a polyhydroxylated piperidine, specifically a 1-deoxygalactonojirimycin analog, in which a six-membered nitrogen-containing sugar mimic presents multiple hydroxyl substituents that emulate the galactose transition-state binding geometry; chemically it belongs to the aza-sugar/iminosugar class and is built on a nojirimycin-like piperidine scaffold. Similar drugs include other iminosugars and lysosomal modulators such as miglustat, eliglustat, and substrate-mimicking glycosidase inhibitors like acarbose, although migalastat is distinguished by selective binding to amenable mutant alpha-galactosidase A. Its principal target protein is alpha-galactosidase A encoded by GLA, which it binds reversibly in the endoplasmic reticulum to stabilize misfolded amenable variants, promote lysosomal trafficking, and increase catabolism of globotriaosylceramide and related substrates in Fabry disease. After oral administration it is absorbed with moderate bioavailability, reaches systemic circulation widely including kidney and other relevant tissues, shows low protein binding, undergoes minimal metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged in urine with a terminal half-life on the order of several hours; food reduces absorption, supporting dosing in a fasting state. Toxicity is generally limited compared with cytotoxic agents, but adverse findings include gastrointestinal intolerance, headache, dizziness, pyrexia, nasopharyngitis, urinary tract infection, and occasional paresthesia or palpitations, with caution in significant renal impairment where exposure-effect relationships may change. Clinically, it is used as oral precision therapy for adults with Fabry disease carrying amenable GLA variants, aiming to reduce lysosomal glycolipid accumulation and stabilize renal, cardiac, and systemic manifestations.

Name: Erdosteine
Description: Erdosteine (DrugBank DB05057) is a synthetic thiol prodrug mucolytic whose structure is characterized by a small sulfur-containing heterocyclic scaffold, specifically a substituted tetrahydrothiazole/carbothioate framework bearing blocked sulfhydryl functionality that is converted in vivo to reactive free-thiol metabolites; chemically it is classified as an organosulfur mucolytic and thiol derivative, with a scaffold related to cysteine-inspired sulfur heterocycles. It is pharmacologically similar to other mucolytics and thiol drugs such as N-acetylcysteine, carbocisteine, and to some extent ambroxol in clinical positioning, although erdosteine is distinguished by its prodrug thiol-release design.
