After oral administration it is well absorbed, undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism to active metabolites including Metabolite I with a free sulfhydryl group, distributes systemically with modest protein binding, and is eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites with a relatively short plasma half-life that supports repeated daily dosing. Its principal targets are not a single canonical receptor but airway mucus glycoprotein disulfide bonds, which it reduces, and it also appears to modulate oxidative stress and inflammatory signaling, with reported effects on reactive oxygen species pathways and mucus hypersecretion. It is indicated for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic bronchitis, and other respiratory disorders with viscous secretions, where it is used to reduce sputum viscosity, improve expectoration, and lessen exacerbation burden. Adverse effects are usually mild and gastrointestinal, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, epigastric pain, and dyspepsia, with headache, rash, urticaria, and rarely hypersensitivity reported; toxicity is generally low at therapeutic doses, while overdose is expected to accentuate gastrointestinal intolerance and possibly systemic thiol-related adverse reactions.

Name: Ganaxolone
Description: Ganaxolone (DB05087) is a synthetic neuroactive steroid and 3β-methylated analog of allopregnanolone built on the pregnane steroid nucleus, retaining the tetracyclic cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene scaffold with a 3α-hydroxyl, 20-ketone, and a 3β-methyl substituent that increases metabolic stability by limiting oxidation at C3; chemically it is classified as a GABAergic steroid modulator within the broader class of steroidal anticonvulsants and shares a neurosteroid scaffold with allopregnanolone, brexanolone, and related positive GABAA receptor modulators such as alphaxalone. Its principal targets are GABAA receptor complexes, where it acts as a positive allosteric modulator at synaptic and extrasynaptic receptor isoforms, including receptors containing δ subunits, thereby enhancing inhibitory chloride currents. Ganaxolone is indicated for seizure disorders, especially cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 deficiency disorder, and has also been studied in refractory epilepsy, status epilepticus, tuberous sclerosis complex, and fragile X syndrome. After oral administration, especially as suspension, absorption is improved with food but bioavailability is limited by poor aqueous solubility; it is highly lipophilic, extensively distributed, highly protein bound, metabolized mainly by hepatic CYP3A4-mediated oxidation and reduction pathways, and excreted predominantly as metabolites in feces and urine, with a terminal half-life compatible with repeated daily dosing. Dose-limiting toxicity is chiefly central nervous system depression, with somnolence, dizziness, fatigue, ataxia, and sedation most common; examples of more serious risks include excessive sedation, respiratory compromise when combined with other CNS depressants, falls, and potential suicidal ideation typical of antiseizure drugs. Clinically, it is used as an adjunctive antiseizure therapy, particularly in pediatric and rare genetic epilepsies, where reduction of convulsive and nonconvulsive seizure burden is the primary therapeutic goal.

Name: Trabectedin
Description: Trabectedin (DB05109) is a complex marine-derived tetrahydroisoquinoline alkaloid antineoplastic agent originally isolated from Ecteinascidia turbinata and now produced semisynthetically; structurally it is a highly oxygenated, polycyclic tri-subunit ecteinascidin framework composed of fused tetrahydroisoquinoline rings, multiple ether and ester functionalities, and a carbinolamine-containing DNA-reactive core that defines its ecteinascidin scaffold. It belongs to the natural product DNA-binding alkaloid class, with related or mechanistically similar agents including lurbinectedin, the closely related synthetic analog, and more distantly other minor-groove binders such as duocarmycins. Trabectedin binds the DNA minor groove, alkylating guanine N2 residues and bending DNA, thereby perturbing transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair and modulating the activity of repair proteins and transcription factors; reported protein-level associations include RNA polymerase II/XPB-containing TFIIH pathways and DNA repair components such as ERCC5/XPG and ERCC1-XPF rather than a single classic receptor target. It is given intravenously with essentially complete systemic availability, exhibits extensive tissue distribution and very high protein binding, undergoes predominant hepatic CYP3A4-mediated metabolism, and is eliminated mainly via the biliary-fecal route with limited renal excretion and a prolonged terminal half-life. Major toxicities include dose-limiting neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, transaminase elevation, rhabdomyolysis, and hepatotoxicity, with adverse effects such as nausea, vomiting, fatigue, anemia, anorexia, constipation, and infusion-related complications. Clinically, it is used for advanced soft tissue sarcoma, especially liposarcoma and leiomyosarcoma after anthracycline failure, and in combination with pegylated liposomal doxorubicin for relapsed platinum-sensitive ovarian cancer.

Name: Pretomanid
Description: Pretomanid (DB05154) is a nitroimidazo-oxazine antitubercular agent whose structure is defined by a bicyclic 4-nitroimidazo[2,1-b][1,3]oxazine core bearing lipophilic aryl and heterocyclic substituents that confer oral activity and intracellular penetration; chemically it belongs to the bicyclic nitroimidazole class, with a nitroimidazo-oxazine scaffold closely related to other nitroimidazole antimycobacterials such as delamanid and, more distantly, metronidazole and PA-824 analogs. It is a prodrug selectively activated within Mycobacterium tuberculosis by the deazaflavin-dependent nitroreductase Ddn using the F420 cofactor system, with resistance linked to Ddn and F420-biosynthetic proteins including Fgd1, FbiA, FbiB, and FbiC; activation leads to respiratory poisoning via nitric oxide release under anaerobic conditions and inhibition of mycolic acid biosynthesis under aerobic growth. After oral administration with food, absorption is improved; the drug is moderately protein bound, distributes into tissues including pulmonary lesions, undergoes predominantly hepatic metabolism with limited major circulating active metabolites, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine and feces, with a terminal half-life on the order of many hours permitting once-daily dosing. Toxicity concerns include hepatotoxicity, QT-interval prolongation risk in multidrug regimens, peripheral and optic neuropathy, myelosuppression-related effects when coadministered with linezolid, and reproductive toxicity seen in animal studies. Its indication is treatment of highly drug-resistant pulmonary tuberculosis, especially extensively drug-resistant or treatment-intolerant/nonresponsive multidrug-resistant disease, and clinically it is used in combination regimens such as BPaL or BPaLM with bedaquiline and linezolid, where common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, headache, acne or rash, transaminase elevations, anemia, and neuropathic symptoms.

Name: Vintafolide
Description: Vintafolide (DB05168) is a folate-targeted small-molecule drug conjugate built from a pteroate/folic acid core linked through a peptide-containing, hydrophilic spacer to a vinca alkaloid cytotoxic payload, specifically desacetylvinblastine hydrazide, giving a modular structure in which the folate ligand preserves high-affinity receptor recognition while the vinca-derived warhead confers microtubule inhibition; chemically it is best categorized as a folate-conjugated antineoplastic agent and targeted drug conjugate, with a folate scaffold fused to a vinca alkaloid pharmacophore. Related agents include other folate receptor-targeted conjugates and imaging compounds such as etarfolatide, as well as payload-related vinca drugs including vinblastine and vinorelbine. Its principal target protein is folate receptor alpha (FOLR1/FR-alpha), which mediates endocytic uptake into receptor-overexpressing tumor cells, after which the vinca moiety acts on tubulin to disrupt microtubule dynamics and induce mitotic arrest. Pharmacokinetically, it is administered intravenously, remains largely in the vascular/extracellular compartment because of its polar conjugate character, is distributed preferentially to FR-positive tumors and kidneys, undergoes linker- and hydrazide-related biotransformation with limited classic CYP dependence, and is cleared mainly by renal excretion of parent- and metabolite-related material. Toxicity reflects both targeted uptake and vinca-like cytotoxicity, with reported or expected adverse effects including constipation, nausea, fatigue, sensory neuropathy, abdominal pain, leukopenia, and infusion-related reactions; renal accumulation may contribute to concern for kidney exposure. Clinically, it was developed for folate receptor-positive malignancies, especially platinum-resistant ovarian cancer, and was also explored in non-small cell lung cancer, typically in biomarker-selected patients identified as FR-positive.

Name: Sofalcone
Description: Sofalcone (DB05197) is a synthetic antiulcer gastroprotective agent structurally characterized as a lipophilic chalcone derivative built on an aromatic ketone scaffold in which two substituted phenyl rings are linked by an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl system; the molecule bears isoprenyloxy and related alkoxy substituents that increase membrane affinity and are typical of cytoprotective chalcones. Chemically it belongs to the flavonoid-related chalcone/retinoid-like aryl enone class, and its core scaffold is the substituted diarylpropenone framework. Similar drugs in therapeutic concept include other mucosal protective antiulcer agents such as rebamipide, teprenone (geranylgeranylacetone), sucralfate, and gefarnate, although these are not close structural analogs; among structural analogs, other prenylated chalcones are the most relevant comparators. Sofalcone is used mainly for gastritis and gastric or duodenal ulcer disease, including dyspepsia, epigastric pain, mucosal erosion, and prevention or treatment of NSAID-associated gastric mucosal injury. Its pharmacology is driven less by a single high-affinity receptor than by cytoprotective actions involving enhancement of gastric mucosal blood flow, stimulation of endogenous prostaglandin production, increased mucus secretion, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, inhibition of Helicobacter pylori growth, and reported modulation of targets such as H+,K+-ATPase, cyclooxygenase-related prostaglandin pathways, and inflammatory mediators including TNF-α and NF-κB signaling. It is orally administered, absorbed to a limited-to-moderate extent because of lipophilicity, distributed preferentially to gastrointestinal tissues, hepatically metabolized largely by oxidative and conjugative pathways, and excreted mainly in bile/feces with some urinary metabolites. Toxicity is generally low, but adverse effects can include constipation or diarrhea, nausea, abdominal discomfort, rash, and transient liver enzyme elevation; overdose data are limited, though excessive exposure would be expected to amplify gastrointestinal and hepatic intolerance.

Name: Crisaborole
Description: Crisaborole (DB05219) is a small, nonsteroidal boron-containing anti-inflammatory agent whose structure is centered on a benzoxaborole scaffold, a bicyclic fused aromatic system in which a boronic acid-like boron is embedded within an oxaborole ring and substituted with a para-cyanophenoxy group that increases lipophilicity and topical skin penetration; chemically it is classified as a boron-based heteroaryl phosphodiesterase inhibitor, specifically a benzoxaborole derivative. Its closest similar drugs are other boron-containing benzoxaboroles such as tavaborole, and more broadly topical anti-inflammatory comparators include calcineurin inhibitors like tacrolimus and pimecrolimus, although these are mechanistically distinct. Crisaborole primarily targets phosphodiesterase 4 isoenzymes, reducing intracellular cAMP degradation and thereby suppressing proinflammatory cytokine signaling in skin. After topical administration, systemic absorption is low but measurable, with distribution largely limited by dermal delivery, moderate plasma protein binding, oxidative metabolism mainly via hydrolysis and subsequent conversion to inactive metabolites including boron-containing biotransformation products, and urinary excretion of metabolites as the major elimination route. Toxicity is generally low relative to systemic immunomodulators, with no major organ toxicity expected at therapeutic topical exposure, though local intolerance and occasional hypersensitivity reactions have been described; excessive exposure would be expected to accentuate irritation rather than produce severe systemic poisoning. It is indicated for mild to moderate atopic dermatitis, particularly eczema-associated pruritus, erythema, and inflammation in pediatric and adult patients. Common adverse effects include application-site pain, burning, stinging, irritation, and rarely contact urticaria or allergic dermatitis. Clinically, it is used as a topical steroid-sparing therapy for chronic inflammatory eczema, especially on sensitive areas where long-term corticosteroid use is undesirable.

Name: Beraprost
Description: Beraprost (DB05229) is an orally active, chemically stable prostacyclin analogue in the eicosanoid class, built on a modified prostaglandin/prostacyclin scaffold consisting of a substituted cyclopentane core bearing a carboxylic acid side chain, hydroxyl functionality, and lipophilic aryl-alkenyl substituents that mimic endogenous PGI2 while improving oral bioavailability and metabolic stability. It is categorized as an antiplatelet and vasodilatory prostanoid, and is structurally related to other prostacyclin-pathway drugs such as epoprostenol, iloprost, treprostinil, and selexipag as a nonprostanoid IP receptor agonist comparator. Its principal target is the prostacyclin receptor PTGIR on vascular smooth muscle cells and platelets, activating Gs, increasing intracellular cAMP, inhibiting platelet aggregation, and promoting vasodilation; downstream effects may also influence endothelial function and vascular remodeling. After oral administration, beraprost is absorbed relatively rapidly, undergoes distribution consistent with a moderately lipophilic acidic prostanoid, is extensively metabolized hepatically mainly by beta-oxidation and related side-chain oxidation pathways to less active metabolites, and is excreted predominantly in urine with some fecal elimination; it has a short plasma half-life, necessitating repeated daily dosing. Toxicity is largely extension-of-pharmacology, including dose-related hypotension, flushing, headache, tachycardia, dizziness, and increased bleeding tendency, with gastrointestinal intolerance such as nausea and diarrhea also reported. It is indicated primarily for pulmonary arterial hypertension and peripheral arterial occlusive disease, including symptoms such as ischemic ulcers, intermittent claudication, and cold extremities, and has been used clinically to improve exercise tolerance, peripheral circulation, and platelet hyperreactivity in selected vascular disorders.

Name: Cobimetinib
Description: Cobimetinib (DrugBank DB05239) is an orally active, small-molecule antineoplastic with a highly substituted aromatic heterocyclic structure built around a kinase-binding azaheteroaryl carboxamide scaffold, commonly described as a chlorinated fluorinated benzimidazole-like or related fused heteroaromatic MEK-inhibitor chemotype bearing amide and ether functionality that supports selective allosteric binding to MAP2K1/MEK1 and MAP2K2/MEK2; chemically it is categorized as a targeted protein kinase inhibitor, specifically a mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway inhibitor, and it is structurally and pharmacologically related to other MEK inhibitors such as trametinib, binimetinib, and selumetinib. Its principal targets are MEK1 and MEK2 in the RAF-MEK-ERK signaling cascade, leading to suppression of ERK phosphorylation and reduced proliferation in MAPK-driven tumors. Clinically, cobimetinib is indicated primarily for unresectable or metastatic melanoma with BRAF V600E or V600K mutation in combination with vemurafenib, and it has also been used in BRAF-mutant histiocytic neoplasms in some settings. After oral administration it is absorbed with moderate bioavailability, is highly protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A-mediated oxidation, and is eliminated chiefly in feces with a terminal half-life supporting once-daily intermittent dosing. Toxicities include dose-limiting serous retinopathy, cardiomyopathy with reduced ejection fraction, hepatotoxicity, severe rash, photosensitivity, hemorrhage, and rhabdomyolysis or creatine phosphokinase elevation. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, pyrexia, acneiform or maculopapular rash, edema, and elevated liver enzymes, and in practice it is used as precision combination therapy to improve progression-free control in BRAF-mutant melanoma while requiring monitoring of ocular, cardiac, hepatic, and muscular safety.

Name: Methsuximide
Description: Methsuximide (DrugBank DB05246) is an anticonvulsant of the succinimide class built on a 2,5-pyrrolidinedione, or cyclic imide, scaffold in which the succinimide ring is substituted to increase lipophilicity, a structural motif shared with related agents such as ethosuximide and phensuximide. Chemically, it is best categorized as a dicarboximide/imidic anticonvulsant, with the succinimide nucleus serving as the core pharmacophore associated with anti-absence activity. Its principal pharmacologic target is not fully defined, but the class is associated with reduction of thalamocortical low-threshold T-type calcium currents, particularly through Cav3 family calcium channels, thereby suppressing absence-seizure oscillatory activity. Methsuximide is administered orally and is generally well absorbed, distributes into the central nervous system because of adequate lipophilicity, undergoes extensive hepatic biotransformation to the active metabolite N-desmethylmethsuximide, and is eliminated largely by renal excretion of metabolites; the metabolite has a substantially longer half-life and contributes importantly to steady-state efficacy and toxicity. It is indicated primarily for refractory absence seizures, especially petit mal epilepsy not adequately controlled by first-line therapy, and has been used clinically as adjunctive or alternative therapy in mixed seizure disorders with absence components. Adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, ataxia, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, and hiccups, with more serious toxicity including behavioral changes, leukopenia, rash, lupus-like reactions, and rare severe blood dyscrasias or hepatotoxicity; overdose or accumulation may produce marked CNS depression and gastrointestinal intolerance.

Name: Ecabet
Description: Ecabet (DrugBank DB05265), commonly used as the sodium salt ecabet sodium, is a non-systemic gastroprotective antiulcer agent characterized chemically as a highly polar aromatic sulfonate-bearing dicarboxylic acid derivative with multiple acidic functionalities appended to a substituted naphthalene-like aryl scaffold, giving it strong anionic character and high water solubility but minimal membrane permeability; thus, it is best categorized as a mucosal protective agent rather than a classic acid-suppressive drug, and its core scaffold is an aryl polyacid/sulfonated aromatic gastroprotective framework related in functional behavior, though not close structural identity, to other mucosal protectants such as sucralfate, rebamipide, and to some extent bismuth-based antiulcer therapies. Pharmacokinetically, ecabet is very poorly absorbed after oral administration, acts mainly locally in the stomach, shows negligible systemic distribution, undergoes little meaningful hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged in feces, with any absorbed fraction excreted largely in urine. Its pharmacology is attributed to binding to damaged gastric mucosa, enhancement of endogenous mucus and bicarbonate defense, interference with pepsin activity, and cytoprotective effects; no single canonical high-affinity target protein is firmly established, although interactions with gastric mucin, pepsin, and mucosal prostaglandin-linked protective pathways are implicated. It is indicated for gastritis, gastric ulcer, and dyspeptic symptoms associated with mucosal injury, including adjunctive use in peptic ulcer disease. Adverse effects are usually mild and gastrointestinal, such as constipation, diarrhea, nausea, abdominal discomfort, and rarely hypersensitivity or laboratory abnormalities. Toxicity is generally low because of poor systemic exposure, though excessive use may worsen GI intolerance, and clinical use has principally been as an oral mucosal protective therapy in ulcer healing and gastritis management.

Name: Ibudilast
Description: Ibudilast (DrugBank DB05266) is a small, lipophilic synthetic heteroaromatic agent built around a substituted pyrazolo-pyridine bicyclic scaffold, specifically a 3-isobutyryl-2-isopropyl pyrazolo[1,5-a]pyridine core, placing it in the nonselective phosphodiesterase inhibitor and glial modulator chemical category; this fused nitrogen-containing scaffold is shared conceptually with other PDE-active heterocycles, and pharmacologically it is often compared with cilostazol, pentoxifylline, roflumilast, apremilast, and the methylxanthine-like neuroimmune modulator propentofylline. Its known targets include multiple cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterases, especially PDE3, PDE4, PDE10, and PDE11, with additional reported suppression of macrophage migration inhibitory factor and attenuation of Toll-like receptor 4-linked glial activation, thereby reducing proinflammatory mediators such as TNF-alpha, IL-1 beta, and IL-6. After oral administration it is reasonably well absorbed, distributed systemically with CNS penetration consistent with its neuroactive use, metabolized predominantly in the liver by oxidative biotransformation to inactive or less active metabolites, and eliminated mainly in urine with some fecal excretion; reported half-life is short enough to require repeated daily dosing. Toxicity is generally modest at therapeutic exposure, but dose-related gastrointestinal upset, CNS effects, and hepatic laboratory abnormalities have been described, while overdose concerns include exaggerated vasodilatory and neuropsychiatric effects. Indications and clinical use include bronchial asthma, post-stroke dizziness, allergic ocular disease, and investigational use in neuropathic pain, multiple sclerosis, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and substance use disorders. Common adverse effects include nausea, dyspepsia, headache, dizziness, flushing, palpitations, and fatigue.

Name: Rotigotine
Description: Rotigotine (DB05271) is a non-ergoline dopaminergic agonist built on an aminotetralin scaffold, specifically a substituted 2-aminotetralin with a thiophene-containing side chain and phenolic hydroxyl functionality that confers dopamine-receptor-binding mimicry; chemically it is categorized as a small-molecule aminotetralin dopamine agonist and is structurally related to other non-ergot antiparkinsonian agents such as pramipexole, ropinirole, and apomorphine by shared dopaminergic pharmacology rather than identical core chemistry. Its principal targets are dopamine receptors DRD3, DRD2, and DRD1, with activity also reported at DRD4 and DRD5 and some interaction with selected adrenergic and serotonergic receptors, supporting continuous dopaminergic stimulation. Rotigotine is used mainly for Parkinson disease, including early-stage monotherapy and adjunctive treatment of advanced disease with motor fluctuations, and for moderate-to-severe restless legs syndrome, improving bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor, nocturnal symptoms, and sleep disruption. Clinically it is administered as a transdermal patch, providing slow, sustained absorption over 24 hours, avoiding extensive first-pass effects, achieving broad tissue distribution due to lipophilicity, undergoing extensive hepatic conjugation and N-dealkylation with CYP-independent metabolism predominating, and being excreted mainly in urine as inactive metabolites with a smaller fecal component. Adverse effects commonly include application-site reactions, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, somnolence, headache, insomnia, orthostatic hypotension, and peripheral edema; more serious toxicities include hallucinations, confusion, dyskinesia, impulse-control disorders, sudden sleep attacks, and rare neuroleptic malignant syndrome-like withdrawal phenomena, with overdose expected to exaggerate dopaminergic and cardiovascular effects.

Name: Vandetanib
Description: Vandetanib (DB05294) is an orally active small-molecule anilinoquinazoline tyrosine kinase inhibitor whose structure is centered on a substituted 4-anilinoquinazoline core bearing methoxy and bromofluorophenyl features with a dimethylaminoethoxy side chain, placing it in the quinazoline-based heteroaromatic anticancer kinase inhibitor class and specifically within the EGFR/VEGFR inhibitor scaffold family; it is chemically and pharmacologically related to other quinazoline kinase inhibitors such as gefitinib and erlotinib, while sharing multi-kinase antiangiogenic features with agents such as cabozantinib and lenvatinib. Its principal targets are VEGFR2/KDR, VEGFR3/FLT4, EGFR/ERBB1, and RET proto-oncogene, with additional activity reported against VEGFR1/FLT1, thereby suppressing tumor cell signaling and angiogenesis. Vandetanib is indicated primarily for unresectable, locally advanced, or metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma, especially RET-driven disease, and has also been used clinically for symptomatic control and disease stabilization in progressive thyroid cancer. After oral administration it is well absorbed, has a very large distribution volume and extensive tissue penetration, is highly protein bound, reaches steady state slowly because of a long terminal half-life of roughly 19 days, undergoes hepatic metabolism predominantly via CYP3A4 to N-desmethyl vandetanib with flavin-containing monooxygenase contribution to N-oxide formation, and is eliminated in both feces and urine. Its toxicology is notable for dose-related QT prolongation and risk of torsades de pointes, severe diarrhea, hypertension, rash, interstitial lung disease, hepatotoxicity, and embryo-fetal toxicity; common adverse effects include diarrhea, acneiform eruption, nausea, fatigue, decreased appetite, abdominal pain, and photosensitivity. Clinically, its use requires ECG and electrolyte monitoring, attention to drug interactions that prolong QT or alter CYP3A4 activity, and careful patient selection because the benefit in medullary thyroid carcinoma must be balanced against potentially serious cardiopulmonary and gastrointestinal toxicity.

Name: Eldecalcitol
Description: Eldecalcitol (DB05295) is a synthetic active vitamin D analog structurally derived from calcitriol, retaining the secosteroid vitamin D triene core and fused steroid-like A, C, and D ring system but distinguished by a hydroxypropyloxy substituent at the 2 beta position and hydroxyl groups that preserve high vitamin D receptor activity; chemically it is a vitamin D3 derivative, secosteroid, and vitamin D receptor agonist built on the calcitriol/secocalciferol scaffold. Closely related drugs include calcitriol, alfacalcidol, paricalcitol, doxercalciferol, and maxacalcitol, all sharing the vitamin D endocrine axis but differing in side-chain or ring substitutions that alter calcemic potency and tissue selectivity. Its primary target is the vitamin D receptor, with downstream modulation of intestinal calcium transport proteins, osteoblast and osteoclast regulatory pathways, and parathyroid hormone signaling. After oral administration, eldecalcitol is absorbed systemically, is highly bound in plasma largely to vitamin D-binding protein, distributes to liver, bone, and other vitamin D-responsive tissues, undergoes limited hepatic oxidative metabolism relative to native vitamin D compounds, and is eliminated mainly via biliary/fecal routes with a comparatively prolonged half-life that supports once-daily dosing. It is indicated principally for osteoporosis, especially postmenopausal osteoporosis, to improve bone mineral density and reduce vertebral and other fragility fractures, and is used clinically alone or with calcium or antiresorptives. Toxicity is dominated by exaggerated vitamin D effects such as hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, nephrolithiasis, renal dysfunction, soft-tissue or vascular calcification, and overdose-related gastrointestinal and neuropsychiatric symptoms. Common adverse effects include increased serum or urinary calcium, constipation, nausea, abdominal discomfort, thirst, and reduced renal tolerance in susceptible patients.

Name: Dexlansoprazole
Description: Dexlansoprazole (DrugBank DB05351) is the R-enantiomer of lansoprazole, a substituted benzimidazole proton-pump inhibitor characterized structurally by a chiral sulfoxide linking a benzimidazole ring to a substituted pyridine, with electron-withdrawing and lipophilic substituents that enable acid-activated conversion to a reactive sulfenamide; chemically it belongs to the benzimidazole sulfoxide class, and its core scaffold is the benzimidazole–pyridine PPI framework shared with related agents such as lansoprazole, omeprazole, esomeprazole, pantoprazole, and rabeprazole. Its principal target is the gastric H+/K+-ATPase proton pump, primarily ATP4A with functional inhibition of the ATP4A/ATP4B complex in parietal cells, where covalent binding to cysteine residues suppresses final-step acid secretion. Dexlansoprazole is indicated for gastroesophageal reflux disease, healing and maintenance of erosive esophagitis, and relief of heartburn and other acid-related symptoms. Orally administered as a dual delayed-release formulation, it is absorbed in two phases to prolong plasma exposure, is highly protein bound, widely distributed, extensively metabolized hepatically mainly by CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 to inactive metabolites, and excreted predominantly in urine with some fecal elimination. Toxicity is generally low but includes risks associated with chronic acid suppression such as hypomagnesemia, vitamin B12 deficiency, Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea, acute interstitial nephritis, bone fracture, and rare cutaneous or systemic lupus-like reactions; overdose usually causes limited nonspecific symptoms. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, flatulence, and upper respiratory tract symptoms. Clinically, it is used as maintenance antisecretory therapy in patients with persistent reflux symptoms, nocturnal heartburn, or healed erosive esophagitis requiring durable acid control.

Name: Histamine
Description: Histamine (DrugBank DB05381) is a small endogenous biogenic amine structurally characterized by an aromatic five-membered imidazole heterocycle linked through a two-carbon ethyl chain to a terminal primary amine, making it a flexible, highly polar, protonatable mediator that exists in cationic forms at physiologic pH; chemically it belongs to the imidazole-containing monoamines and more specifically the histaminergic autacoid class, with an imidazole-ethylamine scaffold shared conceptually with related histaminergic ligands and analogs such as betahistine, 2-methylhistamine, dimaprit, and impromidine. Its principal targets are the histamine receptors HRH1, HRH2, HRH3, and HRH4, all GPCRs mediating vasodilation, bronchial and gastrointestinal smooth-muscle effects, gastric acid secretion, neurotransmission, and immune-cell chemotaxis. Pharmacokinetically, exogenous histamine is poorly suited to sustained systemic use because it is rapidly absorbed only locally or parenterally, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid, does not persist because it is swiftly metabolized by histamine N-methyltransferase and diamine oxidase to inactive metabolites such as N-methylhistamine and imidazole acetic acid derivatives, and is excreted largely in urine as metabolites. Toxicity reflects exaggerated receptor activation and includes flushing, headache, hypotension, tachycardia, bronchospasm, pruritus, urticaria, abdominal cramping, diarrhea, and in severe exposure circulatory collapse; histamine excess is clinically relevant in anaphylaxis, mast-cell disorders, and scombroid poisoning. Therapeutically, histamine has had limited clinical use mainly as a provocative or diagnostic agent, for example in gastric acid secretion testing, bronchial reactivity studies, and, historically, in combination regimens such as histamine dihydrochloride with interleukin-2 in acute myeloid leukemia.

Name: Telaprevir
Description: Telaprevir (DrugBank DB05521) is a first-generation, peptidomimetic direct-acting antiviral whose structure is built around a linear ketoamide-derived tripeptidic framework with multiple stereocenters, a key alpha-ketoamide warhead, hydrophobic cyclopropyl and substituted heterocyclic/carbamate-containing elements, and a conformationally constrained protease-binding motif designed to mimic hepatitis C virus substrate cleavage intermediates; chemically it is classified as an NS3/4A serine protease inhibitor and more broadly as a peptide-like ketoamide antiviral, with a peptidomimetic protease-inhibitor scaffold related to other HCV protease inhibitors such as boceprevir, simeprevir, faldaprevir, grazoprevir, and paritaprevir. Its principal target is the HCV nonstructural serine protease complex NS3/4A, inhibition of which blocks viral polyprotein processing and replication. Clinically, telaprevir was indicated for chronic hepatitis C, especially genotype 1 infection, in combination with peginterferon alfa and ribavirin for treatment-naive patients and some treatment-experienced patients, including relapsers and partial responders. Orally administered, it is absorbed better with food, is highly protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 with additional hydrolysis/reduction pathways, acts as a CYP3A inhibitor, and is eliminated predominantly in feces with limited renal excretion. Major toxicities include severe rash, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and DRESS, anemia, and anorectal discomfort; common adverse effects include pruritus, nausea, diarrhea, fatigue, hemorrhoidal/anorectal symptoms, dysgeusia, and insomnia. Its clinical use was historically as part of triple therapy to improve sustained virologic response in genotype 1 HCV, but it was largely displaced by newer, safer interferon-free regimens with broader activity and fewer drug-drug interactions.

Name: Brivaracetam
Description: Brivaracetam (DrugBank DB05541) is a chiral pyrrolidone-derived antiepileptic whose structure is defined by a 2-oxo-pyrrolidineacetamide core bearing an n-propyl substituent and a stereochemically defined side chain, placing it in the racetam/synaptic vesicle protein ligand class and more specifically within the levetiracetam-like pyrrolidone acetamide scaffold; closely related drugs include levetiracetam as the principal analogue, with mechanistic similarity but higher SV2A affinity for brivaracetam, while other antiseizure comparators include perampanel and lacosamide. Its primary target is synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A), with limited evidence for weak modulatory effects on voltage-gated sodium channels at higher concentrations. Pharmacokinetically, it is rapidly and almost completely absorbed after oral administration, has high oral bioavailability, low plasma protein binding, good blood-brain barrier penetration, and an apparent volume of distribution approximating total body water; it undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly by amide hydrolysis and CYP2C19-mediated hydroxylation to inactive metabolites, with elimination largely via the urine as metabolites and a terminal half-life of roughly 7 to 9 hours. Toxicity is generally dose-related and CNS-predominant, with somnolence, sedation, dizziness, fatigue, and ataxia most typical; irritability, anxiety, depression, aggression, and rare suicidal ideation or psychotic reactions exemplify important neuropsychiatric toxicity, and overdose usually causes marked CNS depression rather than major organ failure. Clinically, it is indicated chiefly for focal-onset seizures in epilepsy, including partial seizures with or without secondary generalization, and is used as adjunctive or monotherapy in adolescents and adults, particularly when rapid titration, oral or intravenous transition, and SV2A-directed seizure control are desired.

Name: Faropenem medoxomil
Description: Faropenem medoxomil (DrugBank DB05659) is an orally active ester prodrug of faropenem, a penem beta-lactam antibiotic whose structure features the fused beta-lactam and five-membered unsaturated sulfur-containing ring typical of penems, with a hydroxyethyl substituent and a medoxomil promoiety that increases lipophilicity and oral absorption before enzymatic cleavage to active faropenem; chemically it belongs to the beta-lactam antibacterial class, more specifically the penem subclass, and its core scaffold is the bicyclic penem nucleus closely related to carbapenem-like beta-lactam frameworks. Similar drugs include other beta-lactams such as imipenem, meropenem, ertapenem, and oral cephalosporins, although faropenem is distinguished by oral bioavailability and relative stability to many common beta-lactamases. Its antibacterial targets are penicillin-binding proteins, especially transpeptidases involved in peptidoglycan cross-linking, leading to inhibition of bacterial cell-wall synthesis. After oral administration, the prodrug is absorbed and hydrolyzed in the gut wall and/or plasma to faropenem; the active drug distributes mainly into respiratory and urinary tract tissues, undergoes limited further metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly by renal excretion, with a relatively short half-life requiring repeated dosing. Toxicity is generally low but includes class-related hypersensitivity reactions, gastrointestinal intolerance, and rare hepatic or hematologic abnormalities; overdose would be expected to accentuate CNS or GI effects, especially in renal impairment. Indications and clinical use include mild to moderate community-acquired infections such as acute bacterial sinusitis, pharyngotonsillitis, bronchitis exacerbations, pneumonia, skin and soft-tissue infections, and uncomplicated urinary tract infections; common adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, abdominal discomfort, rash, and candidiasis.

Name: Apremilast
Description: Apremilast (DB05676) is a small-molecule, orally active phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor built on a substituted phthalimide/glutarimide-like immunomodulatory scaffold closely related to thalidomide analog chemistry, featuring a methoxy-substituted aromatic isoindoline-dione core linked to a chiral side chain that helps confer PDE4 affinity and oral bioavailability; chemically it is classified as a synthetic immunomodulatory anti-inflammatory agent and PDE4 inhibitor, with structurally and mechanistically similar drugs including roflumilast, crisaborole, and the broader IMiD-related agents thalidomide and lenalidomide as distant scaffold analogs. Its principal target is PDE4, especially PDE4B and PDE4D isoforms, leading to increased intracellular cAMP and downstream suppression of proinflammatory mediators such as TNF-α, IL-17, IL-23, and other cytokine networks relevant to psoriatic disease. After oral administration, apremilast is well absorbed with moderate to good bioavailability, reaches peak plasma levels within a few hours, distributes systemically with moderate protein binding, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism through CYP3A4 with lesser contributions from CYP1A2 and CYP2A6 plus non-CYP hydrolysis, and is eliminated as metabolites in both urine and feces with a terminal half-life of roughly several hours, making strong CYP3A4 inducers clinically important interaction risks. Toxicity is generally dose-limiting rather than organ-destructive, with notable examples including severe diarrhea, nausea, dehydration, weight loss, and rare mood changes or depression; common adverse effects include gastrointestinal upset, headache, upper respiratory symptoms, and insomnia. Clinically, apremilast is used as an oral systemic therapy for plaque psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, and oral ulcers associated with Behçet disease, particularly when a nonbiologic option is preferred for chronic inflammatory disease control.

Name: Obeticholic acid
Description: Obeticholic acid (DB05990) is a semisynthetic bile acid analogue structurally derived from chenodeoxycholic acid, featuring the rigid steroidal cholane nucleus with a 6α-ethyl substitution and retained 3α- and 7α-hydroxyl groups plus the terminal C24 carboxylic acid typical of bile acids; chemically it belongs to the steroidal bile acid/farnesoid X receptor agonist class and is built on a chenodeoxycholate bile acid scaffold. Closely related or pharmacologically similar agents include chenodeoxycholic acid itself, ursodeoxycholic acid, cholic acid, and investigational non-bile-acid FXR agonists such as tropifexor or cilofexor. Its principal target is the nuclear receptor FXR (NR1H4), with downstream modulation of CYP7A1, FGF19 signaling, bile acid transporters such as BSEP/ABCB11, and broader effects on hepatic and intestinal bile acid homeostasis. After oral administration it is absorbed and undergoes extensive glycine and taurine conjugation, enterohepatic recirculation, high hepatic exposure, limited renal elimination, and predominantly fecal excretion as conjugated or deconjugated bile acid species. It is indicated primarily for primary biliary cholangitis, especially in patients with inadequate response or intolerance to ursodeoxycholic acid, and has also been used or studied in cholestatic liver disease and nonalcoholic steatohepatitis. Major adverse effects include dose-related pruritus, fatigue, abdominal discomfort, dyslipidemia with reduced HDL and possible LDL increase, rash, constipation, and dizziness. Toxicity is centered on worsening hepatic decompensation, jaundice, ascites, and liver failure risk in patients with moderate to severe cirrhosis or portal hypertension, making careful dose adjustment and monitoring essential in clinical use.

Name: Cariprazine
Description: Cariprazine (DB06016) is a lipophilic arylpiperazine antipsychotic whose structure consists of a dichlorophenyl-substituted piperazine linked through an alkyl urea/carbamate-like spacer to a cyclohexyl group, placing it in the atypical antipsychotic and dopamine-serotonin partial agonist chemical category; its core scaffold is best described as a substituted piperazine/aryl-urea framework related to other D2/D3 partial agonists. Similar drugs include aripiprazole, brexpiprazole, and to a lesser extent quetiapine and risperidone in therapeutic class, although cariprazine is distinguished by preferential high-affinity binding at dopamine D3 over D2 receptors. Its known targets include DRD3, DRD2, HTR1A, HTR2B, and HTR2A, with clinically relevant activity characterized mainly by partial agonism at D3/D2 and 5-HT1A receptors and antagonism at 5-HT2A-family sites. Pharmacokinetically, it is orally active, well absorbed, highly protein bound, widely distributed, extensively metabolized in the liver primarily by CYP3A4 and to a lesser extent CYP2D6 to active metabolites desmethyl-cariprazine and didesmethyl-cariprazine, and eliminated slowly through fecal and renal routes, with an especially prolonged effective half-life due to persistent active metabolites. Toxicity is broadly consistent with dopamine-modulating antipsychotics and includes dose-related extrapyramidal symptoms, akathisia, tremor, restlessness, sedation, nausea, and potential metabolic, orthostatic, and class-labeled risks such as tardive dyskinesia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis. It is indicated for schizophrenia, acute manic or mixed episodes of bipolar I disorder, bipolar depression, and as adjunctive therapy in major depressive disorder, and in clinical use it is prescribed to reduce psychosis, mood elevation, irritability, anhedonia, and depressive symptoms while requiring slow dose adjustment and monitoring for delayed adverse effects because of its long-lived metabolites.

Name: Lumateperone
Description: Lumateperone (DrugBank DB06077) is an atypical antipsychotic of the butyrophenone-derived, heterotricyclic small-molecule class whose structure is characterized by a lipophilic polycyclic fused-ring scaffold bearing a ketone-containing butanone linker and a basic tertiary amine, giving it the cationic amphiphilic properties typical of CNS monoaminergic ligands; its core scaffold is commonly described as a substituted tetrahydrocyclopenta-indole/pyridone-like tricyclic antipsychotic framework rather than the benzisoxazole or dibenzothiazepine motifs seen in some comparators. Chemically and pharmacologically it is related to other dopamine-serotonin modulating antipsychotics such as risperidone, paliperidone, quetiapine, olanzapine, clozapine, and lurasidone, although it is distinguished by multimodal activity with prominent serotonin 5-HT2A antagonism, dopamine D2 receptor presynaptic partial agonist/postsynaptic antagonist behavior, and effects on dopamine, serotonin, and glutamatergic signaling; reported target proteins include DRD2, HTR2A, the serotonin transporter SLC6A4, and dopamine transporter SLC6A3. It is indicated primarily for schizophrenia and bipolar depression, including depressive episodes associated with bipolar I or II disorder, and is used clinically to reduce psychosis, hallucinations, delusions, disorganized thought, depressed mood, anhedonia, and functional impairment. After oral administration it is absorbed with peak levels in roughly 1 to 2 hours, is highly protein bound, widely distributed, extensively metabolized by CYP3A4, UGT, and other pathways to multiple metabolites, and is eliminated in both urine and feces with an effective terminal half-life on the order of about 13 to 18 hours. Adverse effects commonly include somnolence, sedation, dry mouth, dizziness, fatigue, nausea, and constipation; toxicities of concern include orthostatic hypotension, falls, extrapyramidal symptoms such as akathisia though generally at relatively low rates, metabolic changes such as weight gain or hyperglycemia, leukopenia, and class-labeled risks of tardive dyskinesia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis.

Name: Cenobamate
Description: Cenobamate (DB06119) is a small, lipophilic, fluorinated carbamate anticonvulsant built around a substituted phenoxybenzyl motif in which a chlorophenyl ring and a fluorophenyl-containing ether linkage are connected to a carbamate functionality, placing it chemically in the aryl ether/carbamate class with a biaryl-oxy-alkyl scaffold related to other modern antiseizure agents but not a classic dibenzazepine, hydantoin, or succinimide core; in a broad pharmacologic sense it has similarities to felbamate, lacosamide, lamotrigine, and retigabine as a sodium-current-modulating antiseizure drug, though it is structurally distinct. Its principal targets are voltage-gated sodium channels, where it preferentially enhances inactivation and reduces persistent sodium current, and GABAA receptor systems, where it positively modulates inhibitory neurotransmission. After oral administration, cenobamate is well absorbed, with generally dose-proportional exposure, moderate protein binding, a distribution profile consistent with CNS penetration, and a relatively long half-life permitting once-daily use; it is metabolized mainly by glucuronidation and oxidation involving UGT2B7, UGT2B4, CYP2E1, CYP2A6, and CYP2B6, with clinically relevant inhibition of CYP2C19 and induction of CYP3A4/CYP2B6, and metabolites are eliminated primarily in urine. It is indicated for focal-onset seizures in adults, including drug-resistant partial epilepsy. Toxicities include dose-related CNS depression, dizziness, somnolence, ataxia, diplopia, and fatigue, plus potentially serious DRESS/hypersensitivity, suicidal ideation risk, and QT-interval shortening. Clinically it is used as adjunctive therapy and, in some settings, maintenance monotherapy for refractory focal seizures, with examples including patients uncontrolled on levetiracetam, lamotrigine, or carbamazepine, while monitoring for sedation, rash, and pharmacokinetic drug interactions.

Name: Tirbanibulin
Description: Tirbanibulin (DrugBank DB06137) is a synthetic, nonpeptide small-molecule antiproliferative agent structurally characterized as a heteroaromatic benzyl-substituted inhibitor built around an indole-based, highly conjugated aromatic scaffold with a tertiary amide/urea-like linkage that supports lipophilicity and tubulin-binding activity; chemically it is best categorized as a tubulin polymerization inhibitor and Src signaling modulator, and its core scaffold is commonly described as an N-benzyl substituted indole derivative. It is not closely analogous to classic taxanes or vinca alkaloids by structure, but it is pharmacologically similar to other microtubule-targeting agents such as colchicine-site binders, combretastatin analogues, vinblastine, paclitaxel, and to some extent kinase-directed antiproliferative agents that suppress Src-family signaling. Known targets include tubulin/microtubules and downstream Src family kinase signaling pathways, leading to inhibition of cell proliferation and induction of apoptosis. Tirbanibulin is approved for topical treatment of actinic keratosis on the face or scalp, particularly localized field disease caused by chronic ultraviolet damage and premalignant keratinocytic dysplasia. After topical administration, systemic absorption is minimal, plasma exposure is very low, distribution is therefore limited, and metabolism and excretion have not shown clinically important systemic burdens in routine use, with elimination presumed to follow minor hepatic biotransformation and biliary/renal clearance of absorbed trace drug. Toxicity is predominantly local rather than systemic, with dose-limiting examples including application-site erythema, flaking/scaling, crusting, pruritus, pain, edema, and occasional erosions or ulcerative dermatitis; systemic toxicities typical of intravenous antimitotics are not expected at labeled exposure. Clinical use is a short-course 1% ointment regimen applied once daily for 5 days to contiguous lesions or treatment fields, valued for convenience and low systemic risk, while adverse effects most often include localized irritation, burning, tenderness, and contact dermatitis-like reactions.

Name: Aminoimidazole carboxamide
Description: Aminoimidazole carboxamide, DrugBank ID DB06143, is a small, highly polar imidazole-derived antimetabolite/nucleoside-precursor characterized structurally by a 5-aminoimidazole ring bearing a carboxamide substituent, a scaffold that mimics purine biosynthetic intermediates and underlies its classification as an aminoimidazole carboxamide ribotide-related purine analog. Its core chemical scaffold is the amino-substituted imidazole-4-carboxamide pharmacophore, closely related to endogenous AICAR and to mechanistically similar purine antimetabolites and AMP-mimetic agents such as acadesine and, more distantly, azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine in the broader class of purine-pathway modulators. Pharmacologically, aminoimidazole carboxamide is chiefly linked to intracellular conversion to phosphorylated ribotide species that activate AMP-activated protein kinase and perturb de novo purine synthesis; reported protein-level targets therefore include AMPK heterotrimers, with downstream effects on mTOR signaling and cellular energy-sensing networks, while adenosine-regulating pathways may contribute secondarily. As a very hydrophilic compound, oral bioavailability is expected to be limited or variable, tissue distribution largely extracellular unless transporter-mediated uptake occurs, metabolism depends on cellular phosphorylation and further incorporation into purine-intermediate pathways, and renal elimination of parent drug and polar metabolites is expected to predominate. Toxicities are consistent with metabolic and antiproliferative stress, including cytopenias, hepatocellular enzyme elevations, gastrointestinal intolerance, lactic acidosis or hypoglycemia in susceptible settings, and potential cardiac or hemodynamic effects; side effects may include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fatigue, headache, flushing, and transient hypotension. Clinically, it has been investigated rather than routinely used, mainly in oncology, ischemia-reperfusion, and metabolic research contexts, with examples including experimental use in leukemia and solid-tumor studies, cardioprotection models, and disorders where AMPK activation or purine-pathway modulation may be beneficial.

Name: Sertindole
Description: Sertindole (DrugBank DB06144) is an atypical antipsychotic of the phenylindole/piperidine class built around a substituted indole nucleus linked through a flexible alkyl chain to a piperidine ring and bearing halogenated aryl substitution, giving a lipophilic multiring scaffold often described as a phenylindole antipsychotic pharmacophore. It is chemically and pharmacologically related to other second-generation antipsychotics with prominent serotonin-dopamine antagonism, with similarities to risperidone, ziprasidone, iloperidone, and to some extent haloperidol in D2-directed activity, although its scaffold is distinct. Its principal targets are dopamine D2 receptors, serotonin 5-HT2A receptors, serotonin 5-HT2C receptors, and alpha1-adrenergic receptors, with relatively low muscarinic cholinergic affinity and modest histaminergic activity, a profile associated with antipsychotic efficacy and comparatively limited extrapyramidal liability. After oral administration it is well absorbed, extensively distributed because of high lipophilicity and protein binding, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 to less active metabolites, and is eliminated predominantly after biotransformation in feces with a smaller urinary component; it has a long elimination half-life that supports once-daily dosing. The main indication is schizophrenia, especially maintenance treatment of chronic psychosis with positive and negative symptoms such as hallucinations, delusions, thought disorder, and social withdrawal. Important toxicities include dose-related QT prolongation and risk of torsades de pointes or sudden cardiac death, as well as orthostatic hypotension, and common adverse effects include dizziness, sedation, dry mouth, rhinitis, weight gain, sexual dysfunction, and peripheral edema. Clinically, its use has been restricted or carefully monitored, typically reserved for patients needing an alternative atypical antipsychotic when ECG surveillance and electrolyte management are feasible.

Name: Sulfathiazole
Description: Sulfathiazole (DrugBank DB06147) is a classic short-acting sulfonamide antibacterial whose structure consists of a p-aminobenzenesulfonamide core in which the sulfonamide nitrogen is linked to a thiazole ring, giving an aniline-sulfonamide heteroaryl architecture that defines both its reactivity and antimicrobial profile. Chemically, it belongs to the sulfonamide antibiotics, and its central scaffold is the sulfanilamide pharmacophore appended to a five-membered thiazole heterocycle; closely related drugs include sulfamethoxazole, sulfadiazine, sulfisoxazole, and sulfadoxine, which share the same para-aminobenzenesulfonamide motif but differ in heteroaryl substitution and pharmacokinetic behavior. Its principal target is bacterial dihydropteroate synthase, which it inhibits as a para-aminobenzoic acid mimic, thereby blocking folate biosynthesis and suppressing growth of susceptible organisms such as streptococci, pneumococci, staphylococci, Escherichia coli, and some other Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. After administration, sulfathiazole is absorbed variably from the gastrointestinal tract, distributed widely into extracellular fluids and some tissues, exhibits modest protein binding, undergoes limited hepatic biotransformation including N4-acetylation, and is excreted primarily by the kidney through glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, with urinary pH influencing solubility and clearance. Toxicities are typical of older sulfonamides and include crystalluria, hematuria, obstructive nephropathy, hypersensitivity reactions, fever, rash, urticaria, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, hepatotoxicity, and hematologic effects such as hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and methemoglobinemia, especially in predisposed patients including those with G6PD deficiency. Historically, it was indicated for susceptible bacterial infections including urinary tract infections, skin and soft-tissue infections, and streptococcal infections, and it has also seen topical or local clinical use in infected wounds or vaginal preparations, although modern systemic use is limited by resistance and safety concerns.

Name: Mianserin
Description: Mianserin (DrugBank DB06148) is a tetracyclic piperazino-azepine antidepressant whose structure consists of a rigid dibenzazepine-like fused tricyclic aromatic system linked to a piperazine-containing ring, giving a compact polycyclic scaffold closely related to the mianserin/mirtazapine class; chemically it is categorized as a tetracyclic antidepressant with a dibenzoazepine-derived scaffold. Similar drugs include mirtazapine, maprotiline, and to a lesser extent tricyclic agents such as amitriptyline that share sedating antidepressant properties but differ in receptor-binding profiles. Its pharmacology is driven primarily by antagonism at central alpha-2 adrenergic autoreceptors and heteroreceptors, with additional high-affinity blockade of serotonin 5-HT2 and 5-HT3 receptors and histamine H1 receptors; reported target proteins include ADRA2A, ADRA2B, ADRA2C, HTR2A, HTR2C, HTR3A, and HRH1. After oral administration it is well absorbed, undergoes substantial hepatic first-pass metabolism, is widely distributed due to lipophilicity and protein binding, is metabolized mainly by CYP2D6- and CYP1A2-mediated oxidation and N-demethylation to active and inactive metabolites, and is excreted predominantly in urine with some fecal elimination. Clinically it has been used for major depressive disorder, especially depression with anxiety, insomnia, agitation, or weight loss, and sometimes in older adults when a sedating antidepressant is desired. Common adverse effects include somnolence, dry mouth, constipation, dizziness, increased appetite, and weight gain; important toxicities include orthostatic hypotension, impaired psychomotor performance, rare seizures, hepatotoxicity, blood dyscrasias such as agranulocytosis, and overdose-related CNS depression and cardiac conduction abnormalities.

Name: Acetylcysteine
Description: Acetylcysteine (DrugBank DB06151) is the N-acetyl derivative of the natural amino acid L-cysteine, structurally characterized as a small, highly polar aliphatic aminothiol bearing a carboxylic acid, an acetamido-substituted alpha-amino center, and a free sulfhydryl group responsible for its reducing and nucleophilic reactivity; chemically it belongs to the cysteine analogs and aminothiol/mucolytic class, with a simple acetylated amino acid scaffold based on an N-acetyl-L-cysteine backbone. Similar drugs include carbocisteine, erdosteine, cysteamine, and the related thiol donor glutathione. Its principal pharmacology reflects cleavage of disulfide bonds in mucoproteins and replenishment of intracellular glutathione, with functional relevance to oxidative stress pathways and detoxification; rather than a single high-affinity receptor, recognized biological targets include glutathione-dependent systems and indirect modulation of enzymes such as glutathione S-transferases, antioxidant redox pathways, and the acetaminophen-toxic metabolite NAPQI through chemical conjugation. After oral administration it is absorbed but undergoes substantial first-pass metabolism, giving low bioavailability; it distributes widely, including to liver and lung, is deacetylated to cysteine and further metabolized to glutathione, disulfides, and sulfate, and is eliminated mainly in urine as inorganic sulfate and other metabolites. It is indicated for acetaminophen overdose, where it limits hepatotoxicity, and as a mucolytic in bronchitis, COPD, cystic fibrosis, and viscous airway secretions. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, unpleasant sulfur odor, rash, and bronchospasm, while toxicity is usually low but overdose or rapid intravenous infusion can cause anaphylactoid reactions, hypotension, tachycardia, and rarely severe respiratory compromise; clinically it is used orally or intravenously for paracetamol poisoning and by inhalation or oral routes to facilitate mucus clearance.

Name: Nylidrin
Description: Nylidrin (DrugBank DB06152) is a synthetic sympathomimetic vasodilator and bronchodilator in the aryloxypropanolamine/phenylaminoethanol family, structurally characterized by a substituted aromatic ring linked through an ether-containing side chain to a secondary amino alcohol, giving it the classic β-adrenergic agonist pharmacophore built on a phenoxypropanolamine-like scaffold. Chemically it is best classified as a phenylethanolamine-related adrenergic agent, with similarity to other β-agonists such as isoxsuprine, ritodrine, terbutaline, and to a lesser extent epinephrine-like sympathomimetics that share a protonatable amine and hydroxylated side chain important for receptor binding. Its principal targets are β-adrenergic receptors, predominantly ADRB2 in vascular and bronchial smooth muscle, with possible lesser activity at ADRB1 contributing to cardiac effects. Pharmacokinetic data are limited, but like older catecholamine-related oral agents it is absorbed after oral administration, distributed systemically to smooth-muscle-rich tissues, undergoes substantial hepatic biotransformation including oxidative and conjugative metabolism, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine. Clinically, it has been used primarily as a peripheral vasodilator for disorders involving compromised blood flow, such as peripheral vascular disease, intermittent claudication, acrocyanosis, and vasospastic symptoms, and historically also for bronchodilation. Toxicity is typical of sympathomimetics and dose related, including tachycardia, palpitations, hypotension, flushing, tremor, nervousness, headache, nausea, and dizziness; excessive exposure may provoke arrhythmias, angina, or marked cardiovascular instability, especially in patients with ischemic heart disease or hyperthyroidism. Its clinical use has therefore been limited and largely historical, with careful titration required when used for symptomatic relief of peripheral ischemic complaints.

Name: Rimonabant
Description: Rimonabant (DrugBank DB06155) is a lipophilic, orally active diaryl pyrazole derivative characterized structurally by a 1,5-diaryl-substituted pyrazole core bearing a carboxamide functionality and halogenated aryl groups, features that confer high cannabinoid receptor affinity; chemically it belongs to the cannabinoid receptor antagonist/inverse agonist class, with a pyrazole carboxamide scaffold that is shared across several first-generation CB1 ligands. Similar drugs include other CB1 antagonists such as taranabant, otenabant, and surinabant, as well as the related pyrazole analog AM251 used experimentally. Its principal target is the cannabinoid receptor 1, encoded by CNR1, with much lower activity at cannabinoid receptor 2, and its pharmacology reflects inverse agonism at central and peripheral CB1 signaling pathways involved in appetite, reward, and metabolic regulation. Rimonabant was developed for obesity and cardiometabolic risk reduction, including overweight or obesity associated with type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, abdominal adiposity, and smoking cessation support in some studies. After oral administration it is absorbed reasonably well but undergoes variable bioavailability, distributes extensively because of high lipophilicity and strong protein binding, is metabolized predominantly in the liver, mainly via CYP3A4 and amide hydrolysis pathways, and is excreted chiefly as metabolites in feces with a smaller urinary component; its terminal half-life is prolonged. Major toxicities are neuropsychiatric, including depression, anxiety, irritability, insomnia, and suicidal ideation, with other adverse effects such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness, and headache. Although clinically used in some regions for weight management and metabolic improvement, its marketing was withdrawn because psychiatric risk outweighed benefit.

Name: Garenoxacin
Description: Garenoxacin (DB06160) is a des-fluoro quinolone antibacterial built on a 1,8-naphthyridone/quinolone-like fused bicyclic heteroaromatic core bearing the canonical 3-carboxyl and 4-keto pharmacophore required for type II topoisomerase inhibition, with lipophilicity and substituent pattern optimized to enhance Gram-positive and atypical respiratory pathogen activity; chemically it is categorized as a synthetic quinolone, more specifically a des-F(6) fluoroquinolone-related agent, and its central scaffold is the naphthyridone topoisomerase-poisoning pharmacophore shared with other quinolones. Similar drugs include levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, ciprofloxacin, gemifloxacin, and trovafloxacin, which act through closely related enzyme binding. Its principal targets are bacterial DNA gyrase subunits GyrA/GyrB and topoisomerase IV subunits ParC/ParE, causing inhibition of DNA replication and lethal double-strand break accumulation. Pharmacokinetically, garenoxacin is orally active with good absorption and clinically useful tissue penetration, especially into respiratory tissues and epithelial lining fluid; protein binding is moderate, metabolism appears limited relative to extensively biotransformed agents, and elimination occurs through mixed renal and nonrenal pathways, supporting once-daily dosing in studies. Toxicities are broadly quinolone-like, including GI intolerance, CNS effects such as dizziness or headache, hepatotoxicity signal, dysglycemia risk, QT-related concern considered lower than some comparators, hypersensitivity, tendinopathy, and potential cartilage toxicity seen as a class example. It has been investigated and used mainly for community-acquired respiratory and skin infections, including community-acquired pneumonia, acute bacterial sinusitis, acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, and uncomplicated skin and soft tissue infections; common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, headache, insomnia, and rash, and clinical use has centered on empiric treatment of susceptible multidrug-resistant respiratory pathogens when a broad-spectrum oral quinolone option is desired.

Name: Romidepsin
Description: Romidepsin (DB06176) is a natural product-derived bicyclic depsipeptide and antineoplastic epigenetic agent whose structure is characterized by a strained macrocyclic peptide–ester scaffold containing a disulfide bond; intracellular reduction generates a free thiol that is critical for activity, making its core scaffold a disulfide-bridged cyclic depsipeptide closely related to other histone deacetylase inhibitors such as belinostat, vorinostat, panobinostat, and the cyclic peptide/depsipeptide natural product trapoxin. Chemically, it belongs to the class of HDAC-inhibiting depsipeptides, with a compact macrocycle that functions as a prodrug for a zinc-binding thiol warhead. Its principal targets are class I histone deacetylases, especially HDAC1, HDAC2, HDAC3, and HDAC8, with resultant histone hyperacetylation, altered gene expression, cell-cycle arrest, and apoptosis. Pharmacokinetically, romidepsin is administered intravenously, is highly protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes extensive hepatic biotransformation primarily via CYP3A4 with additional non-CYP pathways and reduction of its disulfide moiety, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in bile/feces with a smaller urinary component; the parent drug has a short plasma half-life but durable pharmacodynamic effects. Toxicities include dose-limiting myelosuppression, infection risk, QT-interval prolongation and other ECG changes, electrolyte-sensitive arrhythmia risk, hepatotoxicity, and embryo-fetal toxicity. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, fatigue, anorexia, dysgeusia, diarrhea or constipation, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, anemia, and infections. Clinically, it is used for relapsed or refractory cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and peripheral T-cell lymphoma, for example in mycosis fungoides, Sézary syndrome, and previously treated PTCL after prior systemic therapy.

Name: Forodesine
Description: Forodesine (DB06185) is a transition-state analogue purine nucleoside drug characterized structurally as a halogenated deoxyribose-like iminosugar/nitrogen-substituted sugar linked to a hypoxanthine-related purine base, giving a rigid hydroxyl-rich heterocyclic framework that mimics the substrate of purine nucleoside phosphorylase; chemically it is categorized as a purine nucleoside antimetabolite and enzyme inhibitor, with a deaza/imino-ribose nucleoside scaffold. It is closely related pharmacologically to other purine antimetabolites or PNP-directed agents, although not structurally identical, such as nelarabine, fludarabine, cladribine, pentostatin, and immucillin-derived analogues. Its principal target is purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP), inhibition of which causes accumulation of deoxyguanosine and intracellular dGTP, especially in T lymphocytes, leading to apoptosis. Pharmacokinetically, forodesine is orally active, absorbed sufficiently for systemic exposure, distributes into plasma and lymphoid compartments, undergoes limited oxidative biotransformation because it is designed to resist phosphorolysis, and is eliminated largely unchanged by the kidney, so exposure may increase with renal dysfunction. Toxicity is dominated by exaggerated immunosuppressive and myelosuppressive effects, with examples including lymphopenia, neutropenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and heightened susceptibility to serious bacterial, viral, and fungal infections; hyperuricemia, hepatic enzyme elevations, and rare severe systemic toxicities have also been reported. Its main indication has been relapsed or refractory T-cell malignancies, particularly peripheral T-cell lymphoma and T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, with investigation in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and other lymphoid neoplasms. Common adverse effects include fatigue, nausea, fever, edema, diarrhea, headache, insomnia, upper respiratory infection, and cytopenias. Clinically, it has been used primarily as an oral targeted antineoplastic agent in heavily pretreated T-cell cancers, sometimes within trial settings or region-specific approvals, especially where selective depletion of malignant T cells is desired.

Name: Pixantrone
Description: Pixantrone (DrugBank DB06193) is a synthetic aza-anthracenedione antineoplastic agent structurally related to anthracenediones, built on a planar tricyclic aromatic quinone-like core in which nitrogen incorporation into the ring system and two terminal hydroxyethylamino side chains distinguish it from classical anthracyclines and are intended to reduce iron binding and free-radical cardiotoxicity; chemically it is categorized as an aza-anthracenedione/anthracenedione DNA-interactive cytotoxic, with an aza-anthracenedione scaffold. Similar drugs include mitoxantrone, doxorubicin, daunorubicin, and other DNA intercalating topoisomerase II-targeting agents, although pixantrone is designed to be less cardiotoxic than anthracyclines. Its principal pharmacologic targets are DNA and topoisomerase II, especially TOP2A and TOP2B, with activity involving DNA intercalation, disruption of replication and mitosis, and formation of DNA strand breaks. Pharmacokinetically, it is given intravenously, so absorption is complete by infusion; it distributes widely into tissues, shows substantial plasma protein binding, undergoes limited hepatic biotransformation including side-chain modification, and is eliminated by both biliary/fecal and renal routes, with a terminal half-life on the order of many hours. Toxicity is dominated by dose-limiting myelosuppression, especially neutropenia and leukopenia, with infection risk; clinically relevant examples also include cumulative cardiac toxicity, QT prolongation, hepatotoxicity, and tissue injury with extravasation. Indications and clinical use center on relapsed or refractory aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma, particularly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma after multiple prior regimens, where it has been used as monotherapy salvage treatment. Common adverse effects include neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, alopecia, blue-green discoloration of skin or urine, and edema.

Name: Icatibant
Description: Icatibant (DrugBank DB06196) is a synthetic, peptidomimetic bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist built on a modified linear oligopeptide scaffold in which noncanonical amino acids and conformationally constraining aromatic/cycloaliphatic residues replace native bradykinin elements to confer receptor affinity, proteolytic stability, and subcutaneous activity; chemically it is best classified as a peptide analog, peptidomimetic, and selective kinin receptor blocker, with a scaffold closely related to rationally engineered bradykinin antagonists rather than small-molecule GPCR ligands. Similar drugs in the broader hereditary angioedema space include the plasma kallikrein inhibitors ecallantide and lanadelumab and C1 esterase inhibitor concentrates, although these act upstream rather than directly at BDKRB2, its principal and clinically relevant target protein. After subcutaneous administration, icatibant is rapidly absorbed, reaches peak concentrations within about an hour, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid with moderate plasma protein binding, undergoes extensive proteolytic metabolism to inactive peptide fragments, and is eliminated predominantly as metabolites in urine, with a short terminal half-life of roughly 1 to 2 hours. Toxicity is generally low and dominated by local tolerability issues; severe systemic toxicity is uncommon, but caution is warranted in ischemic heart disease or acute stroke because bradykinin blockade could theoretically alter vascular homeostasis. Its approved indication is treatment of acute attacks of hereditary angioedema due to C1 inhibitor deficiency or dysfunction, including cutaneous, abdominal, and laryngeal symptoms. Common adverse effects are injection-site pain, erythema, swelling, burning, pruritus, nausea, headache, dizziness, pyrexia, and transient transaminase elevations. Clinically it is used as on-demand rescue therapy, often self-administered subcutaneously, to shorten attack duration and relieve pain, swelling, and airway-threatening edema.

Name: Rufinamide
Description: Rufinamide (DrugBank DB06201) is a synthetic antiepileptic with a relatively simple aromatic-triazole architecture consisting of a 1,2,3-triazole ring bearing a carboxamide and linked to a difluorobenzyl substituent, placing it in the triazole-carboxamide class and giving it a benzyl-substituted triazole scaffold distinct from classic dibenzazepine or succinimide anticonvulsants. It is chemically and pharmacologically related in broad function, though not close structure, to other sodium channel-modulating antiseizure drugs such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, lacosamide, and phenytoin. Its principal target is believed to be voltage-gated sodium channels, particularly by prolonging the inactive state and limiting repetitive neuronal firing; no single protein isoform is uniquely established as its exclusive clinical target. Rufinamide is indicated mainly for adjunctive treatment of seizures associated with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, including tonic-atonic, tonic, and atypical absence seizures, and is also used clinically in refractory focal or generalized epilepsies in selected patients. Oral absorption is enhanced by food, bioavailability is good, protein binding is low, and distribution is moderate; it undergoes minimal CYP-mediated biotransformation, being metabolized mainly by carboxylesterase-mediated hydrolysis of the carboxamide to an inactive acid, with metabolites and some unchanged drug excreted predominantly in urine and an elimination half-life typically around 6-10 hours. Adverse effects commonly include somnolence, dizziness, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, diplopia, and headache, while important toxicities include QT interval shortening, hypersensitivity reactions such as rash or DRESS, and CNS depression or ataxia in overdose; clinically it is used as chronic oral adjunctive therapy, often with valproate dose adjustment considerations and careful monitoring for tolerability and seizure response.

Name: Alogliptin
Description: Alogliptin (DrugBank DB06203) is an orally active, highly selective dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor built around a compact aminopiperidine-containing cyanobenzyl/xanthine-like heteroaromatic framework, typically described structurally as a substituted pyrimidinedione-derived scaffold linked to a chiral aminopiperidine moiety and a nitrile-bearing aryl group that supports potent DPP-4 binding through hydrogen-bonding and hydrophobic interactions. Chemically, it belongs to the gliptin class of antihyperglycemic agents, with a heterocyclic peptidomimetic scaffold related pharmacologically to sitagliptin, saxagliptin, linagliptin, and vildagliptin, which are similar drugs used for the same mechanism-based purpose. Its principal target protein is DPP-4, also known as CD26; inhibition increases endogenous incretin activity, especially GLP-1 and GIP signaling, thereby enhancing glucose-dependent insulin secretion and reducing glucagon output in type 2 diabetes mellitus. Pharmacokinetically, alogliptin is well absorbed after oral dosing, has high bioavailability, low to moderate protein binding, limited tissue distribution, minimal hepatic metabolism with minor CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 contribution, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged in urine, giving it a relatively long half-life that supports once-daily dosing; renal impairment increases exposure and motivates dose adjustment. Toxicity is generally modest but includes risk of hypoglycemia when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas, postmarketing pancreatitis, severe hypersensitivity reactions such as anaphylaxis, angioedema, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, hepatotoxicity, and possible worsening heart failure in susceptible patients. Common adverse effects include nasopharyngitis, upper respiratory tract infection, headache, gastrointestinal discomfort, rash, and pruritus.
