Clinically, it is used as an adjunct to diet and exercise, alone or in combination regimens such as with metformin or pioglitazone, for glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes, but it is not indicated for type 1 diabetes or diabetic ketoacidosis.

Name: Tapentadol
Description: Tapentadol (DrugBank DB06204) is a centrally acting synthetic analgesic whose structure is a substituted phenol linked to a branched pentan-1-ol chain bearing a tertiary dimethylamino group, creating a chiral, flexible amino-alcohol architecture that combines opioid pharmacophoric and monoaminergic features; chemically it is an aminophenol/tertiary amine analgesic, and its core scaffold is commonly described as a phenolic propyl- or pentyl-amino alcohol related to the tramadol-type arylalkylamine scaffold, although it is structurally simpler and not a prodrug. Similar drugs include tramadol, which also combines opioid and monoaminergic actions, and classical opioids such as morphine, oxycodone, and hydromorphone, though tapentadol differs by prominent norepinephrine reuptake inhibition. Its principal targets are the mu-opioid receptor and the norepinephrine transporter, with minimal clinically relevant serotonin reuptake inhibition. After oral administration it is rapidly absorbed, has moderate bioavailability limited by first-pass metabolism, is distributed systemically with relatively low protein binding, undergoes extensive hepatic phase II glucuronidation with lesser CYP-mediated metabolism, and is excreted predominantly in urine as conjugated metabolites with a short elimination half-life requiring repeated or extended-release dosing. It is indicated for moderate to severe acute pain, chronic pain, and neuropathic pain associated with diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, dizziness, somnolence, constipation, headache, and pruritus; serious toxicities include respiratory depression, CNS depression, dependence, abuse, withdrawal, hypotension, seizures, and possible serotonin or adrenergic interaction toxicity in overdoses or combinations. Clinically, it is used as immediate- and extended-release oral therapy in postoperative pain, musculoskeletal pain, osteoarthritis-related pain, low back pain, and painful diabetic neuropathy.

Name: Silodosin
Description: Silodosin (DrugBank DB06207) is a highly uroselective α1-adrenoceptor antagonist whose structure comprises a substituted indoline/benzene-derived aromatic system linked through a propyl side chain bearing a secondary alcohol to a urea-like carboxamide functionality, with fluorinated and methoxy-substituted aryl features that increase lipophilicity and receptor affinity; chemically it is best categorized as an arylpropylamine-like benzenesulfonamide/carboxamide-containing small molecule, and its core scaffold is commonly described as a substituted indoline-arylpropyl alcohol amide scaffold. It is closely related pharmacologically to other α1 blockers used for lower urinary tract symptoms, including tamsulosin, alfuzosin, doxazosin, terazosin, and naftopidil, though silodosin is distinguished by particularly high selectivity for ADRA1A over ADRA1B/ADRA1D. After oral administration it is well absorbed, with food modestly affecting rate more than extent; it is substantially protein bound, distributed systemically but acts predominantly at prostatic and bladder-neck smooth muscle, metabolized mainly by UGT2B7, alcohol/aldehyde dehydrogenase pathways, and CYP3A4 to active and inactive metabolites, and excreted through both urine and feces. Its principal target protein is the α1A-adrenergic receptor, with lesser activity at α1B and α1D. The main indication is treatment of signs and symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia, such as weak stream, hesitancy, incomplete emptying, and urinary frequency. Adverse effects commonly include abnormal or retrograde ejaculation, dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, nasal congestion, and diarrhea; toxicities are chiefly extensions of α1 blockade, including syncope and hypotension, especially with antihypertensives or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, and caution is warranted in renal or hepatic impairment and in patients undergoing cataract surgery because of intraoperative floppy iris syndrome. Clinically, silodosin is used as a once-daily oral agent to improve urinary flow and lower urinary tract symptoms in men with BPH, particularly when receptor selectivity and minimized blood-pressure effects are desired.

Name: Doripenem
Description: Doripenem (DrugBank DB06211) is a parenteral carbapenem beta-lactam antibiotic whose structure is defined by the bicyclic carbapenem nucleus, a highly strained beta-lactam fused to a five-membered unsaturated ring, with a trans-1-hydroxyethyl substituent typical of carbapenems and a distinctive C-2 thio side chain containing a sulfamoylaminomethyl-substituted pyrrolidine that enhances broad-spectrum antibacterial activity and relative stability to many beta-lactamases. Chemically it belongs to the beta-lactam/carbapenem class and is built on the penem-like carbapenem scaffold. Similar drugs include imipenem, meropenem, ertapenem, and biapenem, which share the same core but differ in side-chain features and spectrum. Doripenem acts by binding bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, especially PBPs involved in peptidoglycan cross-linking such as PBP2 and PBP3 in susceptible Gram-negative organisms, thereby inhibiting cell-wall synthesis and causing bactericidal lysis. It is administered intravenously, has essentially complete systemic bioavailability by infusion, low to moderate protein binding, distributes well into extracellular fluids and urine, undergoes minimal hepatic metabolism, and is primarily eliminated unchanged by the kidneys, with a short half-life requiring dose adjustment in renal impairment. Its main toxicities are class-related hypersensitivity and neurotoxicity, including rare seizures, with added risk in renal dysfunction; gastrointestinal effects and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea may occur. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, diarrhea, headache, rash, phlebitis, and transaminase elevations. Clinically, doripenem has been used for complicated intra-abdominal infection, complicated urinary tract infection including pyelonephritis, and serious nosocomial infections caused by susceptible organisms such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacterales, and anaerobes.

Name: Tolvaptan
Description: Tolvaptan (DrugBank DB06212) is an orally active, nonpeptide vasopressin receptor antagonist built on a diaryl benzazepine-like scaffold featuring a substituted benzoazepine core linked to hydrophobic aryl groups and an amide functionality, giving a lipophilic small-molecule architecture optimized for selective receptor binding; chemically it is classified as a benzazepine-derived aquaretic and vasopressin antagonist. Its closest similar drugs are other vasopressin receptor antagonists, especially conivaptan, lixivaptan, mozavaptan, and satavaptan, which share nonpeptide lipophilic scaffolds and promote free-water excretion. Tolvaptan primarily targets arginine vasopressin receptor 2 (AVPR2) and, with lower affinity, vasopressin receptor 1A (AVPR1A), thereby reducing vasopressin-mediated aquaporin-2 trafficking in the renal collecting duct. Pharmacokinetically, it is well absorbed after oral dosing, highly protein bound, hepatically metabolized predominantly by CYP3A4, has minimal unchanged renal excretion, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in feces with a terminal half-life that supports once- or twice-daily use depending on indication. Its major indications are clinically significant euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia, including that associated with heart failure or syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, and slowing kidney volume growth and renal function decline in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. Toxicities include idiosyncratic liver injury, excessive aquaresis causing dehydration, hypernatremia, hypotension, and overly rapid sodium correction with risk of osmotic demyelination. Common adverse effects include thirst, polyuria, nocturia, dry mouth, fatigue, dizziness, and urinary frequency. Clinically, it is used under careful sodium and liver-function monitoring to induce aquaresis without major natriuresis, for example in hospitalized hyponatremic patients and in selected adults with rapidly progressive ADPKD.

Name: Asenapine
Description: Asenapine (DB06216) is a dibenzo-oxepino pyrrole atypical antipsychotic with a rigid tricyclic, highly lipophilic tetracyclic-like framework composed of fused aromatic rings and a central heterocyclic oxepine/pyrrole-containing scaffold, placing it within the multireceptor serotonin-dopamine antagonist class related structurally and pharmacologically to clozapine, olanzapine, quetiapine, and loxapine. Its core scaffold is often described as a dibenzoxepinopyrrole system that supports high-affinity binding to multiple aminergic GPCRs, notably serotonin 5-HT2A, 5-HT2C, 5-HT7, 5-HT2B, 5-HT6, dopamine D2, D3, D4, and D1 receptors, as well as adrenergic alpha1 and alpha2 and histamine H1 receptors, with minimal muscarinic activity. Clinically, it is indicated for schizophrenia and for acute manic or mixed episodes associated with bipolar I disorder, for example agitation, mood elevation, and psychosis; it is used mainly as a sublingual or transdermal antipsychotic when broad receptor antagonism and avoidance of strong anticholinergic effects are desired. Oral swallowing gives very low bioavailability because of extensive first-pass metabolism, whereas sublingual absorption is clinically effective; distribution is extensive with high protein binding, metabolism occurs predominantly via direct glucuronidation by UGT1A4 and oxidative pathways including CYP1A2, and elimination is mainly as metabolites in urine and feces with an elimination half-life on the order of about 24 hours. Adverse effects commonly include somnolence, dizziness, akathisia, extrapyramidal symptoms, oral hypoesthesia with sublingual dosing, weight gain, and orthostatic hypotension; important toxicities include QT prolongation, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, tardive dyskinesia, leukopenia/neutropenia, seizures, metabolic disturbances, and increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis.

Name: Vernakalant
Description: Vernakalant (DrugBank DB06217) is an atrial-selective antiarrhythmic small molecule with a substituted aminopropoxy aromatic structure characterized by a para-methoxyphenyl ring linked through an ether-containing propanol/amine side chain to a heteroaryl moiety, giving it the profile of a lipophilic phenoxyalkylamine derivative; chemically it is usually classified as a class III antiarrhythmic with mixed ion-channel blocking properties, and its core scaffold can be described as an aryloxypropanolamine/aryl-alkylamine framework related in broad medicinal-chemistry terms to other aromatic cationic channel modulators. Similar drugs from a therapeutic standpoint include ibutilide, amiodarone, flecainide, propafenone, and dofetilide, although Vernakalant is distinguished by greater atrial selectivity. Its principal targets are cardiac ion channels, especially potassium channels mediating IKur and Ito such as KCNA5 and KCND3-associated currents, with additional blockade of sodium channels including SCN5A/Nav1.5, producing frequency- and voltage-dependent slowing of atrial conduction and prolongation of atrial refractoriness. It is used for rapid pharmacologic cardioversion of recent-onset atrial fibrillation, including postoperative AF after cardiac surgery. Given intravenously, it has rapid systemic availability, fast onset within minutes, moderate distribution, extensive hepatic metabolism primarily via CYP2D6 with some phase II conjugation, and elimination mainly as metabolites in urine; the terminal half-life is short, on the order of hours. Toxicities include hypotension, ventricular arrhythmia risk, atrial flutter with 1:1 conduction, and bradycardia, with contraindication in severe aortic stenosis, recent acute coronary syndrome, severe heart failure, or marked QT prolongation. Common adverse effects include dysgeusia, sneezing, paresthesia, nausea, and transient hypotension. Clinically, it is administered under ECG and hemodynamic monitoring in monitored hospital settings for adults with hemodynamically stable recent AF when rapid conversion to sinus rhythm is desired.

Name: Rivaroxaban
Description: Rivaroxaban (DrugBank DB06228) is an orally active, small-molecule direct factor Xa inhibitor built on an oxazolidinone-based heteroaromatic architecture featuring a chlorothiophene moiety linked to a morpholinone-containing aromatic core, giving a rigid, lipophilic scaffold optimized for high-affinity binding in the S1 and S4 pockets of factor Xa; chemically it is classified as an oxazolidinone derivative and, more broadly, a direct oral anticoagulant, with a diaryl-heterocycle/oxazolidinone scaffold shared conceptually with related factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban, edoxaban, betrixaban, and the older parenteral agent fondaparinux as a mechanistically similar anticoagulant comparator. Its principal target protein is coagulation factor Xa (F10), with consequent suppression of thrombin generation. Oral bioavailability is high, especially with food at higher doses, peak concentrations occur within a few hours, protein binding is high, volume of distribution is moderate, and elimination is mediated by mixed hepatic metabolism and renal excretion; CYP3A4/3A5, CYP2J2, and transporter systems including P-glycoprotein and BCRP contribute to disposition, with excretion occurring as both unchanged drug in urine and inactive metabolites in urine and feces. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related bleeding, including gastrointestinal hemorrhage, epistaxis, hematuria, wound-site bleeding, and rare intracranial hemorrhage, with increased risk in renal impairment, hepatic disease, advanced age, or interacting drugs. Indications and clinical use include prevention of stroke and systemic embolism in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, treatment and secondary prevention of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, postoperative venous thromboembolism prophylaxis after hip or knee replacement, and reduction of major cardiovascular or limb events in selected patients with coronary or peripheral artery disease; common adverse effects include bleeding, anemia, nausea, dizziness, bruising, and elevated liver enzymes.

Name: Nalmefene
Description: Nalmefene (DrugBank DB06230) is a semisynthetic opioid antagonist structurally derived from the morphinan series, closely related to naltrexone and oxymorphone, and characterized by a rigid polycyclic phenanthrene-like morphinan core bearing a 4,5-epoxy bridge, a 6-methylene substitution, a 14-hydroxyl group, and an N-cyclopropylmethyl moiety that confers potent antagonist activity at opioid receptors; accordingly, it is classified as an opioid receptor modulator, specifically a morphinan opioid antagonist, with a 4,5-epoxymorphinan scaffold. Similar drugs include naloxone and naltrexone, as well as older antagonists such as nalorphine, all sharing related opioid antagonist pharmacophores. Nalmefene targets the mu-opioid receptor (OPRM1), kappa-opioid receptor (OPRK1), and delta-opioid receptor (OPRD1), acting predominantly as an antagonist at mu and delta receptors and as an antagonist or weak partial agonist at kappa receptors depending on assay context. It is used for reversal of opioid effects and, in some regions, for reduction of alcohol consumption in alcohol dependence. Pharmacokinetically, it is well absorbed after oral administration, distributes systemically with moderate protein binding, undergoes primarily hepatic phase II metabolism, especially glucuronidation with limited CYP involvement, and is eliminated mainly in urine as conjugated metabolites, with a longer half-life than naloxone that supports sustained receptor blockade. Toxicity is generally related to precipitation of acute opioid withdrawal, with agitation, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, hypertension, pain, and rarely arrhythmias or pulmonary complications; other adverse effects include dizziness, insomnia, headache, fatigue, decreased appetite, and anxiety. Clinically, it has been used in opioid overdose management and in alcohol use disorder to reduce heavy drinking in patients who can take it on an as-needed basis.

Name: Avanafil
Description: Avanafil (DrugBank DB06237) is a selective phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor built on a heteroaromatic pyrimidine-carboxamide core linked to a substituted piperazine and other nitrogen-rich ring features, giving it a compact, moderately lipophilic small-molecule structure optimized for rapid oral activity; chemically it belongs to the PDE5 inhibitor class and more broadly to synthetic nitrogen-containing heterocyclic carboxamides, with a scaffold related to the pyrazolopyrimidine/pyrimidinone-like erectile dysfunction agents, and it is pharmacologically similar to sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil, and udenafil. Its principal target is PDE5 (PDE5A), whose inhibition increases cGMP signaling in corpus cavernosum smooth muscle and enhances nitric oxide-mediated vasodilation. Avanafil is indicated for erectile dysfunction, including difficulty achieving or maintaining erections sufficient for sexual activity, and is used clinically as an on-demand oral therapy because of its relatively rapid onset. After oral administration it is rapidly absorbed, reaching peak plasma concentrations in roughly 30 to 45 minutes, is extensively distributed with high plasma protein binding, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism via CYP3A4 with minor CYP2C contributions to active and inactive metabolites, and is eliminated mainly in feces with a smaller urinary fraction; terminal half-life is on the order of several hours. Toxicity is chiefly extension of its vasodilatory pharmacology, with headache, flushing, nasal congestion, dizziness, dyspepsia, and back pain common, while more serious risks include symptomatic hypotension, syncope, priapism, sudden hearing loss, non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, and major interactions with nitrates, riociguat, strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, and excess alcohol; overdose would be expected to intensify cardiovascular and visual adverse effects.

Name: Incadronic acid
Description: Incadronic acid (DrugBank DB06255) is a nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate characterized structurally by a geminal P-C-P backbone in which two phosphonate groups are attached to the same carbon and linked to a heterocyclic amino side chain, giving a highly polar, strongly calcium-chelating molecule with high affinity for hydroxyapatite; chemically it belongs to the bisphosphonate class, specifically the aminobisphosphonates, and its core scaffold is the nonhydrolyzable pyrophosphate-mimetic bisphosphonate pharmacophore bearing a basic nitrogen-containing cyclic substituent. Similar drugs include pamidronate, alendronate, risedronate, ibandronate, and zoledronic acid, which share the same antiresorptive class and related bone-targeting motif. Like other bisphosphonates, oral absorption is expected to be very poor and markedly reduced by food or divalent cations, distribution is rapid to mineralized bone with prolonged skeletal retention and minimal soft-tissue penetration, metabolism is negligible because the compound is not appreciably biotransformed, and elimination occurs largely by renal excretion of unchanged drug, with the remainder sequestered in bone and released slowly during remodeling. Its principal molecular target is farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway of osteoclasts, leading to impaired protein prenylation and osteoclast apoptosis. It has been used as an antiresorptive agent for disorders such as osteoporosis, cancer-associated osteolysis, hypercalcemia of malignancy, and bone metastasis-related skeletal complications. Adverse effects and toxicities include upper gastrointestinal irritation with oral exposure, nausea, fever, hypocalcemia, musculoskeletal pain, renal toxicity with excessive parenteral dosing, and class-associated osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femoral fracture during prolonged use.

Name: Droxidopa
Description: Droxidopa (L-threo-3,4-dihydroxyphenylserine; DB06262) is a small-molecule aromatic amino acid that structurally resembles L-DOPA but carries a β-hydroxylated phenylserine framework, consisting of a catechol ring linked to an α-amino acid side chain with an additional β-hydroxyl group; chemically it is classified as a catecholamine precursor and nonproteinogenic amino acid, with a catechol amino-acid scaffold shared conceptually with norepinephrine precursors and related sympathomimetic bioprecursors such as levodopa and methyldopa. Its principal pharmacologic target is indirect: it is converted by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (DDC/AADC) to norepinephrine, thereby augmenting signaling at endogenous adrenergic targets, especially alpha-1, alpha-2, and beta-1 adrenergic receptors; transport across tissues may involve large neutral amino acid transport systems. After oral administration, droxidopa is absorbed systemically, distributed to peripheral tissues and to some extent the CNS, undergoes enzymatic decarboxylation to norepinephrine and other minor catechol-related metabolism including O-methylation/deamination pathways, and is eliminated mainly in urine as parent drug and metabolites; its half-life is short, supporting divided dosing. Toxicity is largely an extension of catecholaminergic activity, with clinically important supine hypertension, headache, tachycardia, arrhythmia risk, and possible precipitation of ischemic cardiovascular or cerebrovascular events, while nausea may also occur. It is indicated primarily for symptomatic neurogenic orthostatic hypotension in disorders such as Parkinson disease, multiple system atrophy, pure autonomic failure, and dopamine beta-hydroxylase deficiency, and is used clinically to improve dizziness, lightheadedness, visual blurring, fatigue, and risk of syncope in such autonomic failure states.

Name: Tolperisone
Description: Tolperisone (DrugBank DB06264) is a centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant whose structure is characterized by an aryl ketone containing a para-methyl-substituted phenyl ring linked through a propanone side chain to a tertiary piperidine nitrogen, placing it in the piperidine-containing amino ketone class and giving it an aryl-alkyl-ketone scaffold related to other centrally acting spasmolytics. Its closest pharmacologic analog is eperisone, with broader functional similarity to agents such as tizanidine, baclofen, and methocarbamol, although tolperisone is chemically distinct from these. The drug appears to act mainly through membrane-stabilizing and antispastic effects, with inhibition of voltage-gated sodium and calcium currents and suppression of spinal reflex transmission; no single canonical target protein is universally established, but proposed targets include voltage-gated sodium channels and L-type or other voltage-dependent calcium channels in neurons. After oral administration it is absorbed variably and undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, yielding relatively low and variable bioavailability; it distributes systemically, is extensively metabolized in the liver and possibly kidney via hydroxylation and conjugative pathways, and is excreted predominantly in urine as metabolites with minimal unchanged drug. It is indicated for painful muscle spasm, spasticity, and increased muscle tone, for example after stroke, in multiple sclerosis, and in degenerative or inflammatory musculoskeletal disorders such as low back pain or cervical syndromes. Adverse effects are usually mild and include dizziness, somnolence, कमजitude, headache, nausea, abdominal discomfort, and hypotension, while toxicity may present with marked CNS depression, ataxia, cardiorespiratory instability, or hypersensitivity reactions, including rare serious allergic events; clinically, it is used as an oral antispastic and muscle relaxant to improve mobility, reduce painful contracture, and facilitate rehabilitation.

Name: Lonidamine
Description: Lonidamine (DB06266) is a substituted indazole-3-carboxylic acid derivative whose structure is centered on an indazole bicyclic heteroaromatic scaffold bearing a 2,4-dichlorobenzyl substituent and a terminal carboxylic acid, placing it in the chemical category of halogenated heteroaromatic antineoplastic and metabolic-modulating agents; its core scaffold is therefore an indazole carboxylic acid linked to a dichlorobenzyl pharmacophore. It is chemically and mechanistically related to other tumor-energy metabolism modifiers rather than a large established class, with partially analogous antitumor metabolic inhibitors including 3-bromopyruvate and dichloroacetate as functional comparators. Lonidamine is absorbed after oral administration, distributes into tissues including tumors and testes, shows substantial protein binding, undergoes limited hepatic biotransformation with conjugative pathways reported, and is eliminated slowly through both biliary/fecal and renal routes, giving a relatively prolonged half-life. Its main pharmacologic targets are not classically selective receptors but mitochondrial and glycolytic functions, with reported interaction or inhibition involving hexokinase 2, monocarboxylate transporters such as SLC16A1/MCT1, the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier, and mitochondria-associated energy metabolism, thereby suppressing aerobic glycolysis and lactate handling in cancer cells. It has been investigated primarily as an antineoplastic sensitizer in solid tumors including breast, lung, ovarian, brain, and prostate cancers, often combined with radiotherapy, cisplatin, doxorubicin, or other chemotherapy to enhance response. Toxicities and adverse effects include myalgia, asthenia, somnolence, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, testicular pain, reversible hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevation, and occasional neuropathic or gastrointestinal intolerance; dose-limiting toxicity has often been muscular and constitutional rather than severe myelosuppression, shaping its mainly investigational and adjuvant clinical usage rather than routine standalone therapy.

Name: Udenafil
Description: Udenafil (DrugBank DB06267) is a synthetic small-molecule phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor built on a pyrazolopyrimidinone heteroaromatic core, bearing alkoxy-substituted phenyl and piperazine-containing side chains that confer sildenafil-like cGMP-potentiating activity; chemically it is classified as a PDE5 inhibitor and more broadly as a nitrogen-rich heterocyclic vasoactive agent, with a scaffold closely related to the pyrazolopyrimidinone class exemplified by sildenafil and sharing functional similarity with other erectile dysfunction agents such as tadalafil, vardenafil, and avanafil. Its principal target is PDE5A, with lesser off-target inhibition reported for other phosphodiesterase isoenzymes in some studies, accounting for vascular and occasional visual or systemic effects. Pharmacokinetically, udenafil is orally absorbed with relatively rapid onset, moderate bioavailability, substantial plasma protein binding, hepatic metabolism predominantly via CYP3A4 to active and inactive metabolites, and elimination mainly through feces with a smaller urinary component; its terminal half-life is longer than sildenafil but shorter than tadalafil, supporting on-demand and, in some settings, once-daily use. It is indicated primarily for erectile dysfunction, improving penile erection in men with vasculogenic, diabetic, psychogenic, or mixed etiologies, and has also been investigated in lower urinary tract symptoms and pulmonary vascular disorders. Adverse effects are typical of PDE5 inhibition and include headache, flushing, nasal congestion, dyspepsia, dizziness, and back pain, while toxicities of concern include symptomatic hypotension, especially with nitrates or alpha-blockers, rare priapism, and uncommon visual or cardiovascular events; clinically, it is used as an oral therapy for erectile dysfunction, particularly where an intermediate duration of action is desired.

Name: Sitaxentan
Description: Sitaxentan (DrugBank DB06268) is a small-molecule, orally active endothelin receptor antagonist characterized structurally by a sulfonamide-containing aromatic heterocyclic framework built around a substituted pyrazine-linked diaryl scaffold, with electron-withdrawing substituents that support high potency and marked ETA selectivity; chemically it is categorized as a non-peptide endothelin antagonist and more specifically an aryl sulfonamide/heteroaryl vasomodulator. Its core scaffold is closely related to other endothelin receptor antagonists such as ambrisentan, bosentan, and the later dual antagonist macitentan, although sitaxentan is distinguished by its stronger preference for endothelin receptor type A over type B. Its principal target protein is endothelin-1 receptor type A encoded by EDNRA, with much weaker activity at endothelin receptor type B encoded by EDNRB. Pharmacokinetically, sitaxentan is well absorbed after oral administration, is highly protein bound in plasma, distributes mainly within the vascular compartment, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism largely via cytochrome P450 pathways with clinically important drug-drug interactions, and is eliminated predominantly as metabolites in bile and feces with a smaller renal component. It was developed for pulmonary arterial hypertension, where it lowers pulmonary vascular resistance and improves exercise capacity and symptoms such as dyspnea and fatigue. Adverse effects include headache, peripheral edema, nasal congestion, dizziness, anemia, and elevated hepatic transaminases. Its major toxicity is hepatotoxicity, ranging from asymptomatic liver enzyme elevation to severe liver injury and rare fatal hepatic failure, and it can also potentiate warfarin exposure. Clinically, it was used as an oral therapy for PAH, particularly WHO functional class II-III disease, but marketing was withdrawn in multiple regions because liver toxicity outweighed its therapeutic benefit.

Name: Maxacalcitol
Description: Maxacalcitol (DB06272) is a synthetic vitamin D3 analog built on a secosteroid framework derived from the cholecalciferol/calcitriol scaffold, characterized by the opened B-ring triene system typical of vitamin D compounds, a sterol-like hydrophobic core, a 1alpha,25-dihydroxy-like pharmacophore, and a distinctive 22-oxa modification in the side chain that alters receptor interaction and calcium-mobilizing activity; chemically it is classified as a secosteroidal vitamin D receptor agonist and belongs to the broader class of vitamin D analogs used in calcium-phosphate and parathyroid regulation. Closely related drugs include calcitriol, alfacalcidol, paricalcitol, doxercalciferol, and falecalcitriol. Its principal target is the vitamin D receptor, a ligand-activated nuclear receptor that heterodimerizes with retinoid X receptors to regulate transcription of genes involved in parathyroid hormone suppression, keratinocyte differentiation, and mineral homeostasis. Maxacalcitol is used mainly for secondary hyperparathyroidism, especially in dialysis-associated chronic kidney disease, and topically for psoriasis, where it reduces epidermal hyperproliferation and inflammation. After parenteral or topical administration it is absorbed systemically to a limited to moderate extent depending on route, is highly protein bound in circulation, distributes to liver and target tissues, undergoes hepatic oxidative metabolism and side-chain degradation with subsequent biliary and renal elimination, and generally has a shorter or more controllable calcemic effect than calcitriol. Its major toxicity is hypercalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, with examples including nausea, anorexia, constipation, weakness, pruritus, confusion, nephrocalcinosis, and soft-tissue or vascular calcification; clinically reported adverse effects also include elevated calcium-phosphate product, headache, gastrointestinal upset, and local irritation with topical use.

Name: Alvimopan
Description: Alvimopan (DB06274) is a peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonist structurally derived from the trans-3,4-dimethyl-4-(3-hydroxyphenyl)piperidine opioid pharmacophore, bearing a substituted piperidine core with a phenolic aryl group and a bulky side chain that increases polarity and limits central nervous system penetration; chemically it is classified as an opioid receptor antagonist, more specifically a quaternary-like, peripherally selective MOR antagonist, with a piperidine/arylpropyl scaffold related to other PAMORAs. Similar drugs include methylnaltrexone, naloxegol, naldemedine, and the less peripherally restricted antagonists naloxone and naltrexone. Its principal target is the mu-opioid receptor OPRM1, with much lower activity at other opioid receptors and minimal clinically relevant central antagonism. Alvimopan is indicated primarily to accelerate recovery of gastrointestinal function after partial large or small bowel resection with primary anastomosis by preventing postoperative opioid-induced gut hypomotility and is also mechanistically relevant to opioid-induced bowel dysfunction and postoperative ileus. After oral administration, absorption is limited to moderate, systemic bioavailability is low, protein binding is substantial, distribution is largely peripheral, and CNS exposure is minimal; it undergoes limited hepatic biotransformation, with formation of an active metabolite by intestinal flora, and is eliminated mainly through feces with lesser renal excretion. Adverse effects include dyspepsia, constipation, anemia, back pain, urinary retention, and hypokalemia, while toxicity concerns include abdominal cramping and possible precipitation of opioid withdrawal in susceptible patients; long-term exposure has raised concern for increased myocardial infarction risk, which is why clinical use is restricted to short-term in-hospital administration under a REMS-style program.

Name: Levocetirizine
Description: Levocetirizine (DrugBank DB06282) is the active R-enantiomer of cetirizine and is a second-generation piperazine-derived antihistamine whose structure consists of a substituted piperazine core linked to a diaryl system bearing a chlorophenyl ring and a phenyl ring terminated by a carboxylic acid-containing side chain, giving it amphoteric character and limited central nervous system penetration relative to older antihistamines. Chemically it is classified as a piperazine antihistamine and arylalkyl carboxylic acid derivative, with a cetirizine/hydroxyzine-like piperazine-diaryl scaffold; similar drugs include cetirizine, hydroxyzine, fexofenadine, loratadine, and desloratadine. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, encoded by HRH1, at which it acts as a potent peripheral antagonist or inverse agonist. After oral administration it is rapidly and extensively absorbed, with high bioavailability, peak plasma concentrations typically within about 1 hour, low first-pass metabolism, moderate protein binding, limited hepatic biotransformation, and predominant renal excretion largely as unchanged drug, giving an elimination half-life of roughly 7 to 10 hours that is prolonged in renal impairment. It is indicated for allergic rhinitis, including seasonal and perennial forms, and chronic spontaneous urticaria, improving sneezing, rhinorrhea, nasal and ocular pruritus, and wheals. Adverse effects are usually mild and include somnolence, fatigue, dry mouth, headache, and nasopharyngitis; toxicity is generally low, but overdose may cause marked sedation in adults or agitation followed by drowsiness in children, and dose adjustment is important in renal dysfunction to reduce accumulation. Clinically, it is widely used as an oral once-daily symptomatic antiallergic agent in adults and children when sustained H1 blockade with relatively low sedation burden is desired.

Name: Ziconotide
Description: Ziconotide (DB06283) is a synthetic peptide analgesic corresponding to ω-conotoxin MVIIA, a compact 25-residue, highly disulfide-constrained polypeptide whose structure is defined by a cysteine-rich inhibitory cystine-knot-like conotoxin fold that confers marked conformational rigidity and high selectivity; chemically it belongs to the conopeptide/neuropeptide toxin class, with a disulfide-bridged peptide scaffold typical of ω-conotoxins. It is mechanistically related to other conotoxin-derived or calcium-channel-modulating analgesic concepts, although no close marketed structural analog exists; pharmacologically similar comparators include intrathecal analgesics such as morphine and calcium-channel ligands such as gabapentin or pregabalin, though these are chemically distinct. Its principal target is the Cav2.2 N-type voltage-gated calcium channel alpha-1B subunit encoded by CACNA1B, producing potent inhibition of presynaptic neurotransmitter release in the dorsal horn. Ziconotide is indicated for severe chronic refractory pain, especially neuropathic pain, cancer pain, or failed back surgery syndrome, when intrathecal therapy is warranted. Because it is not orally bioavailable and does not meaningfully cross the blood-brain barrier systemically, it is administered only by continuous intrathecal infusion; distribution is largely within cerebrospinal fluid with limited peripheral exposure, metabolism occurs by ubiquitous proteolytic peptide degradation rather than CYP-mediated biotransformation, and elimination is principally via CSF turnover and peptide catabolism. Toxicity is predominantly dose-related neurotoxicity, including severe dizziness, ataxia, confusion, hallucinations, cognitive impairment, mood changes, and rarely suicidality, with additional adverse effects such as nausea, nystagmus, urinary retention, blurred vision, and somnolence; clinically, it is used as a non-opioid intrathecal option in carefully titrated pain-pump regimens for patients intolerant of or refractory to opioids.

Name: Temsirolimus
Description: Temsirolimus (DrugBank DB06287) is a semisynthetic ester analog of sirolimus in the rapamycin class, structurally characterized as a large, highly lipophilic 31-membered triene macrolide lactone bearing multiple hydroxyl, methoxy, ketone, and ester functionalities, with a distinctive 42-O-(2,2-bis(hydroxymethyl)propionic acid) substitution that differentiates it from sirolimus and supports its prodrug behavior. Chemically it is categorized as a macrocyclic polyketide natural product derivative and mTOR inhibitor, with a rapamycin/macrolide scaffold shared by related drugs such as sirolimus and everolimus. Its principal pharmacologic target is mechanistic target of rapamycin kinase complex 1 through initial high-affinity binding to FKBP12 (FKBP1A), forming an inhibitory FKBP12-temsirolimus complex; downstream effects include reduced signaling through p70S6K and 4E-BP1. Temsirolimus is administered intravenously, is extensively distributed and highly protein bound, undergoes predominant hepatic CYP3A4 metabolism to sirolimus and other metabolites, and is eliminated mainly via feces with limited renal excretion; exposure can therefore be altered by hepatic impairment or CYP3A4 inhibitors and inducers. Toxicities include dose-related myelosuppression, metabolic derangements such as hyperglycemia and hyperlipidemia, hepatotoxicity, mucositis, immunosuppression-related infection risk, interstitial pneumonitis, impaired wound healing, and occasional hypersensitivity reactions. Common adverse effects include rash, asthenia, nausea, diarrhea, anorexia, edema, thrombocytopenia, anemia, and elevated transaminases. Clinically, it is used primarily for advanced renal cell carcinoma, especially poor-prognosis disease, and has also been explored in mantle cell lymphoma and other solid tumors where PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway activation is relevant.

Name: Amisulpride
Description: Amisulpride (DrugBank DB06288) is a substituted benzamide antipsychotic whose structure is centered on a salicylamide-like benzamide core bearing electron-donating methoxy and sulfonamide substituents and a pyrrolidine-containing side chain, placing it within the benzamide/sulfonamide class and more specifically the aminobenzamide scaffold shared with several dopamine-selective neuroleptics. Closely related or pharmacologically similar drugs include sulpiride, levosulpiride, tiapride, and metoclopramide, which also exploit substituted benzamide chemistry, although amisulpride is more CNS-directed than the latter. Its principal targets are dopamine D2 receptor and dopamine D3 receptor, where it acts predominantly as an antagonist; at low doses it is often described as preferentially modulating presynaptic dopaminergic transmission, whereas at higher doses it blocks postsynaptic receptors. Orally administered amisulpride has moderate bioavailability, relatively limited hepatic metabolism, low protein binding, modest distribution, a half-life of roughly half a day, and is eliminated largely unchanged by the kidney, so renal impairment can substantially increase exposure. It is indicated for schizophrenia, especially acute psychosis and predominant negative symptoms, and in some regions has also been used for dysthymia or depressive symptoms and, intravenously at lower doses, for prevention of postoperative nausea and vomiting. Toxicities include dose-related extrapyramidal symptoms, marked hyperprolactinemia with galactorrhea, amenorrhea or sexual dysfunction, QT prolongation and rare arrhythmia, sedation, weight gain, and overdose manifestations such as somnolence, hypotension, and movement disorders; clinically it is used as monotherapy or adjunctive antipsychotic treatment with dose selection guided by symptom profile and renal function.

Name: Dapagliflozin
Description: Dapagliflozin (DrugBank DB06292) is a synthetic, orally active C-aryl glucoside belonging to the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor class, structurally characterized by a β-D-glucopyranose core linked through a metabolically stable carbon-carbon bond to a substituted diarylmethylene/benzyl aryl system bearing lipophilic chloro- and ethoxy-substituted phenyl rings; its key chemical scaffold is therefore a C-glucoside arylpropyl biaryl motif designed to resist hydrolysis relative to older O-glucosides such as phlorizin. Closely related drugs include other gliflozins such as empagliflozin, canagliflozin, ertugliflozin, and sotagliflozin, which share the C-glycoside SGLT inhibitory pharmacophore. Its principal target is SLC5A2/SGLT2 in the renal proximal tubule, with much weaker activity at SLC5A1/SGLT1, producing glucosuria and thereby lowering plasma glucose independent of insulin; clinically it is indicated for type 2 diabetes mellitus and is also used to reduce hospitalization for heart failure and slow progression of chronic kidney disease, including patients with reduced ejection fraction or albuminuric renal disease. Oral absorption is good, bioavailability is high, protein binding is moderate to high, distribution is systemic, metabolism occurs predominantly via UGT1A9-mediated glucuronidation to inactive metabolites, and excretion is mainly renal as metabolites with a smaller fecal component; the terminal half-life supports once-daily dosing. Toxicities and adverse effects reflect osmotic diuresis and glycosuria, including volume depletion, hypotension, dehydration, genital mycotic infections, urinary tract infection, polyuria, and rare euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis, acute kidney injury, Fournier gangrene, and hypersensitivity; in practice it is used alone or with metformin, insulin, or other antihyperglycemics for glycemic control and cardiorenal risk reduction.

Name: Tucidinostat
Description: Tucidinostat (DB06334, also known as chidamide) is a synthetic benzamide-class histone deacetylase inhibitor built on an aromatic benzamide scaffold featuring a substituted anilide linked to a heteroaromatic cap group and a zinc-binding amide pharmacophore, a structural motif shared with other class I-selective HDAC inhibitors. Chemically, it is categorized as an epigenetic modulator and hydroxamate-sparing HDAC inhibitor, with closest analogic relationships to entinostat and, more broadly, to vorinostat, panobinostat, and romidepsin, although tucidinostat is more structurally aligned with benzamide inhibitors than hydroxamates or cyclic peptides. Its principal targets are HDAC1, HDAC2, HDAC3, and HDAC10, producing increased histone acetylation, transcriptional reprogramming, cell-cycle arrest, apoptosis, and immune modulation. After oral administration it is absorbed with clinically useful bioavailability, distributes systemically with moderate protein binding, undergoes predominantly hepatic metabolism involving oxidative and conjugative pathways rather than extensive unchanged renal clearance, and is eliminated through both fecal and urinary routes with a half-life compatible with intermittent dosing. Toxicity is dominated by dose-dependent myelosuppression, especially thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, leukopenia, and anemia; examples of other toxicities include hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevation, fatigue, gastrointestinal upset, and occasional infectious complications secondary to cytopenias. Its main indications are relapsed or refractory peripheral T-cell lymphoma and other T-cell lymphoid malignancies, with clinical use also explored in breast cancer, adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and combination regimens with endocrine therapy or immunotherapy. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, decreased appetite, pyrexia, asthenia, and laboratory evidence of liver dysfunction.

Name: Saxagliptin
Description: Saxagliptin (DrugBank DB06335) is a small-molecule cyanopyrrolidine antidiabetic agent structurally characterized by a substituted pyrrolidine core bearing a nitrile warhead and a hydroxyadamantyl substituent, features that confer potent, reversible covalent inhibition of dipeptidyl peptidase-4; chemically it belongs to the gliptin class of DPP-4 inhibitors and is built on a cyanopyrrolidine scaffold related to other incretin enhancers such as vildagliptin, sitagliptin, linagliptin, and alogliptin, although the hydroxyadamantane-containing framework helps distinguish it. Its principal target is DPP4/CD26, with much weaker activity against related serine proteases such as DPP8 and DPP9 at therapeutic exposure. Pharmacokinetically, saxagliptin is orally absorbed with good bioavailability, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, shows limited protein binding and broad tissue distribution, undergoes hepatic CYP3A4/5-mediated metabolism to an active hydroxylated metabolite, and is eliminated through both renal and fecal routes, with parent drug and metabolite contributing to activity. Toxicity is generally modest at approved doses but includes dose-related hypoglycemia when combined with sulfonylureas or insulin, hypersensitivity reactions such as angioedema or rash, rare pancreatitis, severe arthralgia, and a noted signal for heart failure hospitalization in susceptible patients, especially those with prior cardiovascular or renal disease. It is indicated for type 2 diabetes mellitus to improve glycemic control by enhancing endogenous incretin action, thereby lowering fasting and postprandial glucose; common adverse effects include upper respiratory tract infection, urinary tract infection, headache, nasopharyngitis, and peripheral edema. Clinically, it is used as an adjunct to diet and exercise, either as monotherapy when metformin is unsuitable or more often in combination regimens with metformin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones, insulin, or an SGLT2 inhibitor-containing strategy.

Name: Bazedoxifene
Description: Bazedoxifene (DB06401) is a third-generation selective estrogen receptor modulator with a nonsteroidal indole-based triaryl framework, characterized structurally by a substituted indole core bearing para-hydroxylated aryl groups and a basic aminoethyl side chain that supports high-affinity estrogen receptor binding and tissue-selective agonist/antagonist behavior; chemically it belongs to the SERM class and more specifically to the indole/triarylethylene-like antiestrogen pharmacophore family, with a scaffold related functionally, though not identically, to raloxifene, tamoxifen, lasofoxifene, ospemifene, and clomiphene. Its principal targets are estrogen receptor alpha and estrogen receptor beta (ESR1 and ESR2), where it acts predominantly as an antagonist in uterine and breast tissue and as an agonist or partial agonist in bone, reducing osteoclast-mediated bone resorption. After oral administration, bazedoxifene is absorbed with relatively low absolute bioavailability due to extensive first-pass metabolism, is highly protein bound, widely distributed, undergoes minimal CYP-mediated oxidation with predominant phase II glucuronidation by UGT enzymes, and is eliminated mainly via feces with limited renal excretion and an elimination half-life supportive of once-daily dosing. It is indicated primarily for prevention and treatment of postmenopausal osteoporosis and, in combination with conjugated estrogens, for menopausal vasomotor symptoms and vulvovaginal atrophy prevention of endometrial hyperplasia. Important toxicities and adverse effects include class-associated venous thromboembolism, possible stroke risk in predisposed patients, leg cramps, nausea, abdominal pain, dyspepsia, dizziness, headache, neck pain, and hot flushes, while clinical use focuses on postmenopausal women needing bone protection with reduced uterine stimulatory effects relative to conventional estrogen therapy.

Name: Telavancin
Description: Telavancin (DrugBank DB06402) is a semisynthetic lipoglycopeptide antibiotic derived from the vancomycin class, built on a rigid heptapeptide glycopeptide core bearing multiple aromatic residues, chlorinated substituents, carbohydrate moieties, and a characteristic lipophilic decylaminoethyl side chain that increases membrane affinity; thus, its chemical category is lipoglycopeptide/glycopeptide antibacterial and its core scaffold is the vancomycin-type glycosylated heptapeptide. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to vancomycin, teicoplanin, dalbavancin, oritavancin, and to a lesser extent the investigational lipoglycopeptide telavancin congeners designed to enhance membrane interaction. Its principal target is the peptidoglycan precursor lipid II, specifically the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of cell wall intermediates, with secondary functional disruption of the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane causing depolarization and increased permeability, making it active against Gram-positive pathogens such as Staphylococcus aureus including MRSA, Streptococcus spp., and Enterococcus faecalis with vancomycin-susceptible phenotypes. Pharmacokinetically, telavancin is administered intravenously because oral absorption is negligible, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid with moderate protein binding and clinically relevant penetration into skin, soft tissue, and lung compartments, undergoes minimal hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by the kidney with a terminal half-life permitting once-daily dosing. Major toxicities include nephrotoxicity, QT interval prolongation risk, embryo-fetal toxicity, and interference with coagulation laboratory assays; adverse effects commonly include taste disturbance, nausea, vomiting, foamy urine, headache, infusion-related reactions, and elevated serum creatinine. Clinically it is used for complicated skin and skin structure infections and hospital-acquired or ventilator-associated bacterial pneumonia caused by susceptible Gram-positive organisms, particularly when MRSA is suspected or when alternatives such as vancomycin are unsuitable.

Name: Oxymetholone
Description: Oxymetholone (DB06412) is a synthetic orally active anabolic-androgenic steroid structurally derived from the androstane nucleus, characterized by a 17α-methyl substitution that confers oral bioavailability, a 2-hydroxymethylene substituent, and a 3-keto, 17β-hydroxyl steroid framework; chemically it belongs to the 17α-alkylated anabolic steroid class and is built on the testosterone/dihydrotestosterone-like cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene steroid scaffold. It is closely related to other anabolic steroids such as methandrostenolone, oxandrolone, stanozolol, nandrolone, and testosterone derivatives, which share androgen receptor-mediated anabolic activity with differing androgenic and hepatotoxic profiles. Its principal target is the androgen receptor, with downstream effects on erythropoiesis and protein synthesis; hematologic benefit may also reflect indirect stimulation of erythropoietin-responsive pathways. After oral administration it is well absorbed, highly protein bound in plasma, distributed systemically, extensively metabolized hepatically through steroid biotransformation pathways, and excreted mainly in urine as metabolites, with 17α-alkylation prolonging exposure but increasing hepatic burden. Oxymetholone is indicated primarily for refractory or hypoproliferative anemias, including aplastic anemia, myelofibrosis-associated anemia, and anemia due to deficient red cell production, and has also been used to counter catabolic states or weight loss in selected historical settings. Toxicity is dominated by cholestatic hepatitis, jaundice, peliosis hepatis, hepatic adenoma or carcinoma risk, fluid retention, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and thrombotic or cardiovascular complications. Common adverse effects include virilization, acne, edema, nausea, altered libido, menstrual irregularities, gynecomastia, and growth suppression in children. Clinically, it has been used as an oral anabolic agent to raise hemoglobin and improve body mass, but modern use is limited by its substantial hepatic and endocrine toxicity.

Name: Armodafinil
Description: Armodafinil (DB06413) is the R-enantiomer of modafinil, a wake-promoting benzhydryl sulfinyl compound whose structure consists of a diphenylmethyl group linked through a chiral sulfoxide to an acetamide moiety; chemically it is classified as a eugeroic and more specifically a diphenylmethyl-sulfinyl acetamide, built on a modafinil-like benzhydryl sulfoxide scaffold. Closely related drugs include racemic modafinil and the modafinil metabolite modafinilic acid, while other clinically similar wake-promoting agents such as solriamfetol or pitolisant are pharmacologically analogous rather than close structural congeners. Its principal molecular target is the dopamine transporter SLC6A3, which it inhibits to increase extracellular dopamine; lesser or indirect effects have been described on norepinephrine, orexin/hypocretin, histamine, glutamate, and GABA signaling systems, but no single additional primary target is firmly established. After oral administration it is well absorbed, with peak concentrations typically reached in about 2 hours fasting and delayed by food; it distributes systemically with moderate plasma protein binding, undergoes mainly hepatic metabolism by amide hydrolysis and S-oxidation, with CYP3A4 contributing and CYP2C19/CYP2C9 affecting exposure in some patients, and is eliminated predominantly in urine as inactive metabolites, with a terminal half-life of roughly 12-15 hours. It is indicated for excessive sleepiness associated with narcolepsy, obstructive sleep apnea, and shift work disorder. Common adverse effects include headache, nausea, dizziness, insomnia, anxiety, and dry mouth; important toxicities include hypertension, tachycardia, psychiatric activation such as mania or hallucinations, hypersensitivity reactions including rash and rare Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and reduced effectiveness of steroidal contraceptives via enzyme induction. Clinically, it is used as a once-daily wakefulness-promoting therapy to improve alertness, vigilance, and functional performance in patients with pathological daytime somnolence.

Name: Etravirine
Description: Etravirine (DB06414) is a second-generation non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor characterized structurally as a highly substituted diarylpyrimidine bearing brominated and nitrile-substituted aromatic rings linked to a central pyrimidine core through an ether and an amino bridge, a flexible conformation that allows adaptive binding within mutated HIV-1 reverse transcriptase; chemically it belongs to the aryl heterocyclic NNRTI class and specifically the diarylpyrimidine scaffold, closely related to other NNRTIs such as rilpivirine, delavirdine, efavirenz, nevirapine, and doravirine, though it is most scaffold-similar to rilpivirine. Its principal target protein is HIV-1 reverse transcriptase, at the allosteric NNRTI-binding pocket, where it inhibits viral DNA polymerization. It is indicated for treatment of HIV-1 infection, especially in treatment-experienced patients with resistance to first-generation NNRTIs, and is used in combination antiretroviral therapy for multidrug-resistant disease. Orally administered etravirine shows improved absorption with food, is highly protein bound in plasma, distributes systemically, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4, CYP2C9, and CYP2C19 followed by glucuronidation, and is eliminated predominantly in feces with limited renal excretion. Toxicity is dominated by cutaneous and hypersensitivity reactions, including severe rash, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, erythema multiforme, and rare toxic epidermal necrolysis, with hepatotoxicity and laboratory liver enzyme elevations also reported. Common adverse effects include rash, nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, fatigue, peripheral neuropathy, and headache. Clinically, it is used with agents such as boosted protease inhibitors, integrase inhibitors, and nucleoside analogs in salvage or resistance-guided HIV regimens.

Name: Clomethiazole
Description: Clomethiazole (DrugBank DB06470), also known as chlormethiazole, is a thiazole-derived sedative-hypnotic whose structure consists of a substituted 1,3-thiazole heteroaromatic ring bearing a 4-methyl group and a 5-(2-chloroethyl) side chain, making it a small lipophilic sulfur- and nitrogen-containing heterocycle; chemically it is classified as a thiazole CNS depressant, and its core scaffold is a simple alkyl-substituted thiazole ring. It is pharmacologically related to other GABAergic sedative agents such as benzodiazepines, barbiturates, and older hypnotics, although it is structurally distinct from diazepam, phenobarbital, and paraldehyde. Its principal molecular action is positive allosteric modulation of GABAA receptor complexes, with no single uniquely established protein target beyond GABAA receptor subunits. After oral administration it is rapidly absorbed, undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism with relatively short duration of action, distributes into the CNS because of its lipophilicity, is metabolized mainly by hepatic oxidative pathways including CYP-mediated biotransformation, and is excreted predominantly as metabolites in urine. Clinically it has been used mainly for alcohol withdrawal states, including delirium tremens and agitation, and as a sedative in acute confusion, insomnia, or geriatric agitation in some settings. Adverse effects include drowsiness, nasal irritation, headache, ataxia, confusion, excess sedation, and hypotension. Toxicity is chiefly dose-related CNS and respiratory depression, especially in overdose or when combined with ethanol, opioids, or other sedatives, with examples including coma, aspiration risk, cardiovascular collapse, and enhanced danger in hepatic impairment or frail elderly patients.

Name: Prucalopride
Description: Prucalopride (DrugBank DB06480) is a highly selective, substituted dihydrobenzofuran-carboxamide serotonin receptor agonist whose structure is built around a benzofuran-like bicyclic aromatic scaffold bearing a carboxamide and a basic heterocyclic side chain, with halogen substitution that helps confer receptor affinity and metabolic stability; chemically it is classified as a serotonergic prokinetic agent and aryl carboxamide, and its core scaffold is distinct from but pharmacologically related to other 5-HT4 agonists such as cisapride, tegaserod, mosapride, and velusetrag. Its principal target is the 5-hydroxytryptamine receptor 4, encoded by HTR4, with minimal off-target activity relative to earlier agents. Pharmacokinetically, prucalopride is well absorbed orally, has high bioavailability, low to moderate plasma protein binding, broad tissue distribution, limited hepatic metabolism, a relatively long elimination half-life of about 1 day, and is cleared predominantly unchanged in urine with lesser fecal excretion, making clinically important CYP-mediated interactions uncommon. Toxicologically, it is generally better tolerated and less arrhythmogenic than older nonselective prokinetics, though overdose or heightened sensitivity may accentuate gastrointestinal and autonomic effects; preclinical concerns have included class-related cardiovascular and reproductive observations, but major QT liability is low at therapeutic exposure. It is indicated primarily for chronic idiopathic constipation, especially in patients with inadequate response to laxatives, and is used clinically to improve bowel movement frequency, colonic transit, stool consistency, and symptoms such as straining, bloating, and incomplete evacuation. Common adverse effects include headache, nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, dizziness, and sometimes fatigue, particularly early in treatment.

Name: Minodronic acid
Description: Minodronic acid (DrugBank DB06548) is a potent nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate whose structure is defined by a geminal bisphosphonate P-C-P core attached to an imidazo[1,2-a]pyridine-containing side chain, a heteroaromatic nitrogen-rich motif that confers high antiresorptive potency and strong hydroxyapatite affinity; chemically it belongs to the aminobisphosphonate class, with a bisphosphonate scaffold linked to a fused imidazole-pyridine heteroaryl substituent. It is closely related pharmacologically to other nitrogenous bisphosphonates such as zoledronic acid, risedronate, alendronate, ibandronate, and pamidronate, all of which inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone resorption. Its principal target is farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway of osteoclasts, leading to impaired prenylation of small GTPases and osteoclast apoptosis. After oral administration, absorption is low and markedly reduced by food, calcium, and polyvalent cations; absorbed drug distributes selectively to mineralized bone surfaces, shows negligible biotransformation, and is eliminated largely unchanged by renal excretion, while the skeletal fraction persists for prolonged periods because of tight bone binding. Toxicity is largely class-related and includes upper gastrointestinal irritation, hypocalcemia, renal toxicity with excessive exposure or predisposition, severe suppression of bone turnover, osteonecrosis of the jaw, and atypical femoral fractures during long-term use. Adverse effects include dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, esophagitis, musculoskeletal pain, headache, and decreased serum calcium. Clinically, minodronic acid is used primarily for osteoporosis, particularly postmenopausal osteoporosis and other high-fracture-risk states, to increase bone mineral density and reduce vertebral and nonvertebral fracture risk.

Name: Cetilistat
Description: Cetilistat (DrugBank DB06586) is a lipophilic small-molecule anti-obesity agent structurally characterized as a substituted benzoxazinone-derived ester/lactone-like compound bearing long hydrophobic aromatic and aliphatic features that favor partitioning into the gastrointestinal lumen; chemically it is classified as a gastrointestinal lipase inhibitor and more broadly as an enzyme-directed serine hydrolase inhibitor, with a benzoxazinone-centered scaffold related functionally, though not closely identical, to the beta-lactone lipase inhibitor scaffold exemplified by orlistat. Similar drugs include orlistat as the closest marketed comparator and, mechanistically, older pancreatic lipase-directed fat absorption inhibitors. Its principal targets are gastric lipase and pancreatic lipase, likely through covalent or tightly reversible interaction with the active-site serine, thereby reducing hydrolysis and absorption of dietary triglycerides. Pharmacokinetically, cetilistat shows minimal systemic absorption after oral administration, acts mainly locally in the gut, has limited distribution beyond the intestinal compartment, undergoes little clinically relevant systemic metabolism because of poor bioavailability, and is eliminated predominantly in feces, largely as unchanged drug and unabsorbed fat, with urinary excretion expected to be minor. Toxicity is driven mainly by exaggerated pharmacology rather than systemic organ toxicity, with examples including steatorrhea, fecal urgency, oily spotting, diarrhea, abdominal cramping, and potential reduction in absorption of fat-soluble vitamins; severe toxicity is uncommon but malabsorption-related nutritional issues may occur. It is indicated for obesity and weight management, especially in patients with elevated body mass index, including obesity associated with type 2 diabetes or dyslipidemia, and clinically it has been used as an adjunct to calorie restriction to promote weight loss and improve metabolic parameters.

Name: Pazopanib
Description: Pazopanib (DB06589) is an orally active small-molecule, multikinase inhibitor built on a heteroaromatic indazole-pyrimidine framework with an aniline linkage and sulfonamide-substituted side chain, giving a planar ATP-mimetic architecture optimized for receptor tyrosine kinase binding; chemically it is classified as a synthetic aromatic heterocyclic tyrosine kinase inhibitor, and its core scaffold is closely related to other VEGFR-directed kinase inhibitors such as sunitinib, sorafenib, axitinib, and cediranib, with partial mechanistic similarity to regorafenib. Its principal targets include VEGFR1, VEGFR2, VEGFR3, PDGFR-alpha, PDGFR-beta, FGFR1, FGFR3, and KIT, producing predominantly antiangiogenic and antiproliferative effects. After oral administration, absorption is variable and pH dependent, food increases exposure, protein binding is very high, distribution is extensive, metabolism occurs mainly in the liver via CYP3A4 with lesser CYP1A2 and CYP2C8 contributions, and elimination is predominantly fecal with minimal renal excretion; the terminal half-life is roughly about 30 hours, supporting once-daily dosing. Clinically, pazopanib is indicated for advanced renal cell carcinoma and advanced soft tissue sarcoma after prior chemotherapy, and it has also been used in angiogenesis-driven malignancy settings. Toxicity is notable for hepatotoxicity with transaminase and bilirubin elevation, hypertension, QT prolongation, cardiac dysfunction, hemorrhage, thromboembolism, proteinuria, gastrointestinal perforation or fistula, impaired wound healing, and rare posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, fatigue, hair depigmentation, anorexia, weight loss, stomatitis, hypothyroidism, and hand-foot skin reaction. In practice it is used as an oral targeted therapy in metastatic RCC and selected non-adipocytic soft tissue sarcomas, particularly when antiangiogenic disease control is desired.

Name: Ceftaroline fosamil
Description: Ceftaroline fosamil (DB06590) is a water-soluble N-phosphono prodrug of ceftaroline, a fifth-generation cephalosporin beta-lactam whose structure contains the cephem bicyclic core fused beta-lactam and dihydrothiazine ring system, with oxyimino/acylamino side-chain features that enhance stability to many beta-lactamases and a phosphono promoiety that improves intravenous formulation; chemically it belongs to the cephalosporin subclass of beta-lactam antibacterials and is built on the classic cepham/cephem scaffold. It is most similar to other advanced cephalosporins such as ceftobiprole, ceftriaxone, cefepime, and cefotaxime, although ceftaroline is distinguished by potent anti-MRSA activity through high-affinity binding to altered penicillin-binding protein PBP2a, as well as binding to other PBPs including PBP1a, PBP2b, PBP2x, and related staphylococcal and pneumococcal transpeptidases. After intravenous administration, ceftaroline fosamil is rapidly converted by plasma phosphatases to active ceftaroline; oral absorption is not clinically relevant, protein binding is low to moderate, distribution is mainly into extracellular fluid including skin and lung tissues, metabolism is limited, and elimination is primarily renal as unchanged ceftaroline, with dose adjustment in renal impairment. Toxicity is generally typical of cephalosporins, including hypersensitivity reactions up to anaphylaxis, positive Coombs test, hematologic abnormalities such as neutropenia with prolonged therapy, CNS excitation or seizures in severe renal dysfunction, and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea. Indications and clinical use include acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections and community-acquired bacterial pneumonia caused by susceptible organisms, particularly MRSA, methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and certain Enterobacterales; common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, rash, pruritus, headache, infusion-site reactions, and vulvovaginal candidiasis.

Name: Agomelatine
Description: Agomelatine (DB06594) is a synthetic naphthalene analog antidepressant whose structure is characterized by a substituted naphthalene bicyclic aromatic core bearing a methoxy group and an acetamide side chain, placing it in the arylalkylamide/naftylacetamide chemical category and giving it a melatonin-mimetic scaffold closely related to other melatonergic ligands. Its core scaffold can be described as a methoxy-substituted naphthalene linked to an ethyl-acetamide motif, and structurally or pharmacologically similar drugs include melatonin, ramelteon, tasimelteon, and to a lesser extent other antidepressants with multimodal circadian effects. Agomelatine acts primarily as an agonist at melatonin receptors MT1 and MT2 (MTNR1A and MTNR1B) and as an antagonist at serotonin 5-HT2C and 5-HT2B receptors (HTR2C, HTR2B), supporting resynchronization of circadian rhythms and enhancement of frontal cortical dopaminergic and noradrenergic transmission. It is indicated mainly for major depressive disorder, particularly when insomnia, circadian disruption, anhedonia, or anxiety symptoms are prominent. After oral administration it is rapidly absorbed but has low absolute bioavailability because of extensive first-pass metabolism; it is highly protein bound, distributed systemically, metabolized predominantly in the liver via CYP1A2 with contributions from CYP2C9 and CYP2C19, and excreted mainly as metabolites in urine. Major toxicological concern is hepatotoxicity, ranging from asymptomatic transaminase elevations to rare serious liver injury, with risk increased by hepatic impairment or CYP1A2 inhibitors such as fluvoxamine. Common adverse effects include nausea, dizziness, somnolence, headache, insomnia, fatigue, dry mouth, abdominal discomfort, and sweating. Clinically, it is used as an antidepressant with sleep-normalizing properties, often when sexual dysfunction, weight gain, or discontinuation symptoms from conventional monoaminergic antidepressants are concerns.

Name: Midostaurin
Description: Midostaurin (DB06595) is a semisynthetic staurosporine-derived small molecule multikinase inhibitor whose structure is characterized by a rigid fused indolocarbazole core with a lactam-containing macrocyclic-like framework and appended substituted aromatic/alkyl functionalities that preserve the ATP-competitive kinase-binding pharmacophore; chemically it is classified as an indolocarbazole alkaloid analogue and its central scaffold is the staurosporine/indolocarbazole nucleus. Closely related or mechanistically similar drugs include staurosporine, lestaurtinib, crenolanib, gilteritinib, quizartinib, and other FLT3-directed kinase inhibitors. Its principal targets include FLT3, KIT, PDGFRA, PDGFRB, VEGFR2/KDR, PKC isoforms, SYK, and additional class III receptor tyrosine kinases, accounting for antileukemic and anti-mast-cell activity. Orally administered midostaurin is absorbed with measurable systemic exposure, is highly protein bound, distributes extensively, undergoes predominant hepatic CYP3A4 metabolism to active metabolites including CGP62221 and CGP52421, and is eliminated mainly via feces with relatively limited renal excretion and a terminal half-life prolonged by active metabolite persistence. Toxicity is typical of targeted antineoplastics and includes myelosuppression, severe neutropenia, hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation, interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis, and embryo-fetal toxicity; overdose or interaction with strong CYP3A4 modulators can increase exposure and adverse effects. Indications include FLT3-mutated acute myeloid leukemia in combination with standard induction and consolidation chemotherapy, and advanced systemic mastocytosis, aggressive systemic mastocytosis, or mast cell leukemia, sometimes with an associated hematologic neoplasm. Common side effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, mucositis, rash, edema, febrile neutropenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, headache, and fatigue. Clinically, it is used as precision therapy in FLT3-driven AML and KIT-dependent mast cell disorders, often as part of combination regimens and with monitoring of blood counts, liver function, pulmonary symptoms, and drug-drug interactions.

Name: Nemonoxacin
Description: Nemonoxacin (DrugBank DB06600) is a non-fluorinated quinolone antibacterial built on a 1,8-naphthyridone/quinolone-like fused bicyclic aromatic core bearing the canonical 3-carboxyl and 4-keto pharmacophore required for bacterial topoisomerase inhibition, with additional heterocyclic substitution that enhances Gram-positive potency; chemically it is classified as a novel non-fluorinated quinolone, and its central scaffold is the naphthyridone fluoroquinolone-mimetic nucleus. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, ciprofloxacin, and gemifloxacin, although it lacks the fluorine atom typical of that class. Its principal targets are bacterial DNA gyrase, especially GyrA/GyrB, and topoisomerase IV, especially ParC/ParE, producing bactericidal inhibition of DNA replication and segregation. After oral administration it is absorbed efficiently with clinically useful bioavailability, reaches peak plasma concentrations within a few hours, distributes into respiratory tissues and epithelial lining fluid, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged via renal and, to a lesser extent, fecal pathways, supporting once-daily dosing. Toxicity is generally similar to other quinolones but appears comparatively moderate; concerns include dose-related gastrointestinal and central nervous system effects, hepatic enzyme elevations, hypersensitivity, QT-interval prolongation risk, and class-related warnings for tendinopathy, dysglycemia, and selection of resistant organisms. It is indicated primarily for community-acquired pneumonia and other susceptible respiratory tract infections caused by organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and atypical pathogens, and clinically it has been used as an oral monotherapy option for mild to moderate bacterial pneumonia, acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, and selected skin or soft-tissue infections where active local susceptibility data support use.

Name: Apixaban
Description: Apixaban (DrugBank DB06605) is a small-molecule, orally active direct factor Xa inhibitor built on a substituted pyrazole-containing carboxamide scaffold fused functionally to a lactam-like pyridinone motif and decorated with anisidine and piperidine-derived aryl substituents, giving a rigid, heteroaromatic, highly target-selective architecture typical of oxopiperidine/pyrazole anticoagulants. Chemically, it is classified as a synthetic heteroaromatic anticoagulant and belongs to the direct oral anticoagulant class, with a scaffold and pharmacology similar to other factor Xa inhibitors such as rivaroxaban, edoxaban, betrixaban, and the parenteral analog fondaparinux in terms of pathway inhibition, though fondaparinux acts indirectly via antithrombin. Its principal target is coagulation factor Xa, inhibiting both free and prothrombinase-bound Xa and thereby reducing thrombin generation and fibrin clot formation. Apixaban is indicated for stroke and systemic embolism prevention in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, treatment of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, reduction of recurrent venous thromboembolism, and thromboprophylaxis after hip or knee replacement surgery. Oral absorption is good, bioavailability is roughly 50%, peak concentrations occur in 3 to 4 hours, protein binding is high, volume of distribution is moderate, metabolism occurs mainly through CYP3A4/5 with minor contributions from other CYP pathways, and elimination is via mixed fecal/biliary and renal routes, with a half-life of about 12 hours. Major toxicity is bleeding, including gastrointestinal, postoperative, traumatic, and rare intracranial hemorrhage; anemia, elevated transaminases, nausea, and contusion are recognized adverse effects. Clinically, it is used as a fixed-dose anticoagulant without routine coagulation monitoring, but caution is required with strong CYP3A4 or P-glycoprotein inhibitors or inducers, renal or hepatic impairment, and situations of active bleeding.

Name: Tafenoquine
Description: Tafenoquine (DB06608) is a synthetic 8-aminoquinoline antimalarial characterized by a quinoline aromatic heterobicycle bearing a methoxy substituent, an aryl ether linkage, and a substituted aminoalkyl side chain that confers marked lipophilicity and prolonged tissue persistence; chemically it belongs to the aminoquinoline class, specifically the 8-aminoquinoline family, and its core scaffold is the primaquine-like 8-aminoquinoline pharmacophore. Structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include primaquine as the closest analogue, with broader antimalarial class relationships to chloroquine and mefloquine, although these latter agents are not 8-aminoquinolines. Tafenoquine is orally absorbed, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, is extensively distributed into tissues, is highly protein bound, and has an unusually long terminal half-life of about two to three weeks, supporting single-dose or weekly regimens; metabolism appears limited relative to primaquine, with hepatic biotransformation contributing but not dominating clearance, and excretion occurs slowly via renal and biliary routes. Its antiplasmodial activity is associated with bioactivation-dependent oxidative stress and mitochondrial disruption in Plasmodium species rather than a single validated human protein target, though parasite targets linked to redox homeostasis are implicated. It is indicated for radical cure and relapse prevention of Plasmodium vivax malaria and for malaria prophylaxis.
