Major toxicities include hemolytic anemia in patients with G6PD deficiency, methemoglobinemia, and potential embryofetal risk, with additional concerns for neuropsychiatric and ocular toxicity. Common adverse effects include headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, insomnia, back pain, and transient corneal deposits. Clinically, tafenoquine is used as a single-dose antirelapse therapy with blood-schizonticidal treatment for P. vivax and as once-weekly prophylaxis in selected adults after G6PD screening.

Name: Bosutinib
Description: Bosutinib (DrugBank DB06616) is an orally active, small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor built on a substituted 4-anilino-3-quinolinecarbonitrile/quinoline heteroaromatic scaffold, featuring a planar bicyclic nitrogen-containing ring system with an aniline linkage, a nitrile substituent, and methoxy/chloro-patterned aryl functionality that supports ATP-site binding; chemically it is categorized as a quinoline-based antineoplastic kinase inhibitor and more specifically a Src/Abl inhibitor. Its scaffold and mechanism place it near other BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib, and ponatinib, although bosutinib is distinguished by strong Src family kinase inhibition and relatively limited activity against KIT and PDGFR. Pharmacokinetically, bosutinib is absorbed orally with increased exposure when taken with food, is highly protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism predominantly via CYP3A4 to less active metabolites, and is eliminated mainly in feces with a minor renal contribution; acid-reducing agents can lower absorption and CYP3A inhibitors or inducers substantially alter exposure. Its principal targets include BCR-ABL1 and Src family kinases such as SRC, LYN, and HCK. It is indicated primarily for Philadelphia chromosome-positive chronic myeloid leukemia, including chronic, accelerated, or blast phase disease, especially after resistance or intolerance to prior therapy, and is also used in some newly diagnosed chronic-phase patients. Toxicities include myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevations, severe diarrhea, fluid retention, QT-related cardiac concerns, and embryo-fetal risk; common adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, rash, fatigue, abdominal pain, thrombocytopenia, anemia, and neutropenia. Clinically, bosutinib is used as a targeted oral therapy for CML requiring BCR-ABL suppression, with dose adjustment and monitoring guided by hepatic function, drug interactions, blood counts, and gastrointestinal tolerance.

Name: Axitinib
Description: Axitinib (DrugBank DB06626) is a small-molecule, orally active indazole-derived tyrosine kinase inhibitor whose structure features a substituted indazole core linked through a vinyl spacer to a pyridine carboxamide and bearing sulfur-containing substitution, giving a relatively planar, heteroaromatic, lipophilic pharmacophore optimized for ATP-site binding in receptor kinases. Chemically it is classified as a targeted antineoplastic agent and heteroaryl kinase inhibitor, with an indazole-based VEGFR inhibitor scaffold closely related in function, though not identical in structure, to other antiangiogenic TKIs such as sunitinib, sorafenib, pazopanib, cabozantinib, and tivozanib. Its principal targets are vascular endothelial growth factor receptors VEGFR-1/FLT1, VEGFR-2/KDR, and VEGFR-3/FLT4, with lesser activity reported against PDGFR and c-KIT in some systems; its therapeutic effect is predominantly antiangiogenic. After oral administration, axitinib is rapidly absorbed, reaches peak plasma concentrations within a few hours, shows high protein binding, distributes systemically, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism primarily by CYP3A4/5 with contributions from CYP1A2, CYP2C19, and UGT1A1, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in feces with a smaller urinary component; exposure is altered by strong CYP3A modulators and by hepatic impairment. Toxicities reflect on-target VEGF pathway blockade and include hypertension, arterial and venous thromboembolic events, hemorrhage, gastrointestinal perforation, impaired wound healing, proteinuria, hepatotoxicity, and reversible posterior leukoencephalopathy syndrome. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, fatigue, decreased appetite, nausea, dysphonia, palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia, weight loss, hypothyroidism, and mucositis. Clinically, axitinib is used mainly for advanced renal cell carcinoma, especially after prior systemic therapy, and also in combination regimens such as with immune checkpoint inhibitors for first-line treatment of advanced or metastatic clear cell kidney cancer.

Name: Isavuconazonium
Description: Isavuconazonium (DB06636) is a water-soluble azole antifungal prodrug, administered clinically as the sulfate salt, that is rapidly cleaved by plasma esterases to the active moiety isavuconazole; structurally, it is a triazolium-containing prodrug built on the triazole antifungal pharmacophore with fluorinated aromatic rings and a thiazole-containing side chain, while the prodrug portion incorporates an ionizable N-linked promoiety designed to enhance intravenous and oral delivery. Chemically it belongs to triazole antifungals, with a substituted triazole-diaryl/thiazolyl scaffold closely related to other broad-spectrum azoles such as voriconazole, posaconazole, fluconazole, and itraconazole. Its principal target is fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase, encoded by CYP51/Erg11, thereby inhibiting ergosterol biosynthesis and disrupting fungal membrane integrity. Isavuconazole shows excellent oral bioavailability, low food effect, extensive tissue distribution, high protein binding, a long terminal half-life suitable for once-daily maintenance dosing, predominant hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 and CYP3A5, and elimination chiefly as inactive metabolites in feces and urine with minimal unchanged drug excretion. Toxicity is generally lower than that of some older azoles but includes hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevations, infusion-related reactions, gastrointestinal intolerance, hypokalemia, and important CYP3A-mediated drug interactions; unlike several azoles, it can shorten rather than prolong the QT interval. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, peripheral edema, dyspnea, rash, and elevated liver enzymes. Clinically, it is indicated for invasive aspergillosis and invasive mucormycosis, for example pulmonary or disseminated Aspergillus infections and Mucorales disease in immunocompromised patients, and is used in both intravenous and oral step-down therapy when broad-spectrum mold-active treatment is required.

Name: Safinamide
Description: Safinamide (DB06654) is a small, orally active α-aminoamide built around an aryl ether benzylamine-derived scaffold, specifically a substituted propanamide featuring a fluorobenzyl moiety linked through an ether to a methoxybenzene ring and bearing a chiral aminamide center; chemically it is classified as a phenylpropylaminoamide and multifunctional central nervous system agent, with a scaffold related to other MAO-B–directed antiparkinsonian drugs but structurally distinct from the propargylamine scaffold of selegiline and rasagiline. Similar drugs include the MAO-B inhibitors rasagiline and selegiline and, by therapeutic context, COMT inhibitors such as entacapone and opicapone used as levodopa adjuncts. Its main targets are monoamine oxidase B as a potent, selective, reversible inhibitor, and voltage-gated sodium channels and abnormal glutamate release pathways, which support both dopaminergic enhancement and non-dopaminergic modulation. Safinamide is indicated as add-on therapy to levodopa, alone or with other antiparkinsonian drugs, for idiopathic Parkinson disease with wearing-off fluctuations, helping reduce OFF time and improve motor control. It is well absorbed orally, has high bioavailability, moderate protein binding, wide tissue distribution including CNS penetration, and a relatively long half-life permitting once-daily dosing; metabolism occurs largely via non-CYP amidase-mediated hydrolytic and oxidative pathways to inactive metabolites, with minimal CYP interaction, and elimination is predominantly renal as metabolites. Toxicities include excessive dopaminergic effects, potential worsening dyskinesia, serotonergic risk when combined with serotonergic drugs, hypertensive reactions with sympathomimetics or tyramine excess, and caution in severe hepatic impairment or retinal disease. Common adverse effects include dyskinesia, nausea, insomnia, dizziness, falls, headache, orthostatic symptoms, and hallucinations, and clinically it is used chiefly in fluctuating mid- to late-stage Parkinson disease to smooth levodopa response and reduce motor complications.

Name: Clevudine
Description: Clevudine (DB06683) is a synthetic pyrimidine nucleoside analogue of the thymidine family, structurally characterized by a uracil/thymine-like base linked to an unusual 2-fluoro-substituted arabinofuranose/deoxyribose-like sugar, giving it the classic antiviral nucleoside scaffold shared by L- or modified D-nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitors; chemically it is categorized as a fluorinated heterocyclic antimetabolite and antiviral nucleoside, with a scaffold closely related to other anti-hepadnaviral nucleosides such as telbivudine, lamivudine, emtricitabine, entecavir, and, more distantly, adefovir and tenofovir. Its principal target is hepatitis B virus polymerase/reverse transcriptase, after intracellular phosphorylation to active nucleotide forms that inhibit viral DNA synthesis. It has been used primarily for chronic hepatitis B, especially suppression of HBV replication, reduction of serum HBV DNA, and improvement of hepatic inflammation in patients with active viral hepatitis. Pharmacokinetically, clevudine is orally absorbed, distributes systemically including to hepatocytes, undergoes limited CYP-dependent metabolism with activation mainly by host kinases, and is eliminated predominantly by renal excretion of parent drug and metabolites; a notable feature is sustained antiviral effect that may persist after dosing cessation, consistent with prolonged intracellular active metabolite retention. Toxicity is dominated by mitochondrial-related myopathy with creatine kinase elevation, proximal muscle weakness, and occasional severe neuromuscular toxicity after prolonged therapy; other adverse effects include fatigue, nausea, headache, abdominal discomfort, and potential hepatobiliary laboratory abnormalities. Clinically, it has been used as an oral anti-HBV agent in chronic hepatitis B management, but long-term use has been limited by safety concerns, particularly delayed skeletal muscle toxicity.

Name: Vilazodone
Description: Vilazodone (DrugBank DB06684) is a serotonergic antidepressant with a compact arylpiperazine-derived structure characterized by an indole-like bicyclic aromatic system linked through a butyl chain to a piperazine ring and terminated by a benzofuran moiety, placing it in the phenylpiperazine/arylpiperazine class and giving it an indole-alkyl-piperazine scaffold related to mixed serotonin reuptake inhibitors and 5-HT1A ligands. It is most often compared with trazodone, nefazodone, buspirone, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors such as fluoxetine or sertraline because it combines serotonin transporter inhibition with partial agonism at the serotonin 5-HT1A receptor; its principal known targets are SLC6A4 and HTR1A. After oral administration, vilazodone is absorbed better with food, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, is highly protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism predominantly via CYP3A4 with lesser contributions from CYP2C19 and CYP2D6, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in feces and urine with a terminal half-life of about one day. Its toxicity profile is typical of serotonergic agents: overdose may produce lethargy, agitation, tachycardia, and vomiting, and important risks include serotonin syndrome, suicidality in younger patients, and bleeding or hyponatremia, especially when combined with NSAIDs, anticoagulants, MAO inhibitors, or other serotonergic drugs. It is indicated primarily for major depressive disorder, including depressive symptoms such as low mood, anhedonia, and anxiety, and is used clinically as an oral daily antidepressant, often when an SSRI-like drug with 5-HT1A activity is desired; common adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, dizziness, headache, dry mouth, and sexual dysfunction, though sexual adverse effects may be less prominent than with some conventional SSRIs.

Name: Laquinimod
Description: Laquinimod (DB06685) is an orally active, synthetic quinoline-3-carboxamide immunomodulator structurally characterized by a substituted quinoline aromatic bicyclic heterocycle bearing a carboxamide at the 3-position and halogenated/methoxy-substituted anilide features, placing it in the quinoline carboxamide class and giving it a concise quinoline-carboxamide scaffold closely related to other aryl carboxamide immunomodulators. It is considered a safer, second-generation analogue in the linomide/laquinimod series, with similar drugs or mechanistically related comparators including linomide, tasquinimod, and broader multiple-sclerosis agents such as dimethyl fumarate and fingolimod. Its pharmacology appears pleiotropic rather than dependent on a single high-affinity receptor, with reported effects on S100A9, antigen-presenting cells, NF-kB-related inflammatory signaling, astrocytes, and microglial pathways, leading to reduced proinflammatory cytokine output and promotion of regulatory immune phenotypes; no single definitive canonical target fully explains its activity. After oral administration it is well absorbed, highly protein bound, distributed systemically including access to inflammatory CNS compartments, metabolized predominantly by hepatic CYP3A4 to inactive metabolites, and eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine with a terminal half-life supporting once-daily dosing. It was developed primarily for relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, with investigation also in Huntington disease and other neuroinflammatory conditions, aiming to reduce relapse activity, MRI lesion burden, and disability progression. Adverse effects reported in trials include headache, back pain, arthralgia, abdominal pain, cough, nausea, diarrhea, and transient liver enzyme elevations; important toxicities include hepatotoxicity, inflammatory or infectious complications, and potential embryofetal risk, while earlier quinoline carboxamides raised concerns about serositis and cardiopulmonary toxicity, underscoring cautious clinical use mainly as an investigational or regionally limited oral immunomodulatory therapy rather than a widely established standard treatment.

Name: Mepyramine
Description: Mepyramine (DrugBank DB06691), also known as pyrilamine, is a first-generation H1-antihistamine of the ethylenediamine class characterized by a diaryl-substituted ethylenediamine framework in which a 2-pyridyl ring and a para-methoxybenzyl/anisyl aromatic moiety are linked to a tertiary diamine, giving a flexible, lipophilic cationic scaffold typical of classical sedating antihistamines; its core chemical scaffold is therefore an aryl-heteroaryl ethylenediamine. It is chemically and pharmacologically similar to other older H1 blockers such as tripelennamine, antazoline, chlorpheniramine, diphenhydramine, and doxylamine, although the scaffold differs somewhat across these examples. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, where it acts as an inverse agonist/antagonist; ancillary antimuscarinic activity may contribute to some adverse effects. Mepyramine has been used for symptomatic relief of allergic rhinitis, urticaria, pruritus, insect bites, and minor allergic skin reactions, and historically in some cough, cold, and topical antipruritic preparations. It is generally well absorbed after oral administration, distributes widely including into the central nervous system because of blood-brain barrier penetration, undergoes hepatic biotransformation likely via oxidative N-dealkylation and related pathways, and is excreted mainly in urine as metabolites and some unchanged drug. Toxicity resembles that of other sedating antihistamines, with overdose producing marked CNS depression or paradoxical excitation, anticholinergic effects, tachycardia, and rarely seizures. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, impaired psychomotor performance, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, and dizziness, which have limited modern systemic use mainly to short-term allergy symptom control or topical antipruritic applications.

Name: Xylometazoline
Description: Xylometazoline (DrugBank DB06694) is a topical sympathomimetic imidazoline derivative whose structure consists of an imidazoline ring linked to a substituted benzyl group bearing a para-tert-butyl-like alkyl substituent and ortho methyl groups, giving a lipophilic aryl-imidazoline architecture characteristic of direct-acting nasal vasoconstrictors. Chemically it is classified as an alpha-adrenergic agonist and decongestant, built on the aryl-imidazoline scaffold shared with related agents such as oxymetazoline, naphazoline, tetrahydrozoline, and to some extent clonidine-like imidazoline-containing sympathomimetics. Its principal targets are alpha-adrenergic receptors, predominantly ADRA1A, ADRA1B, ADRA1D, and possibly alpha-2 receptor subtypes in nasal mucosal vasculature, producing vasoconstriction that reduces edema and secretions. It is indicated for symptomatic relief of nasal congestion in common cold, allergic rhinitis, sinusitis, and hay fever, and is also used in some formulations for nasopharyngeal mucosal decongestion. After intranasal administration, local absorption is rapid with onset within minutes and duration often up to 8-10 hours; systemic bioavailability is usually low at recommended doses but increases with excessive dosing or damaged mucosa. Distribution is expected to favor well-perfused tissues; metabolism is incompletely characterized but likely involves hepatic biotransformation after systemic absorption, with renal excretion of metabolites and some unchanged drug. Toxicity includes excessive sympathomimetic and CNS effects such as hypertension, reflex bradycardia or tachycardia, agitation, sedation, and in children severe poisoning with respiratory depression or coma; chronic use can cause rhinitis medicamentosa and rebound congestion. Common adverse effects include nasal dryness, burning, stinging, छींकना, irritation, headache, and palpitations. Clinically, it is used short term, typically as drops or spray, to improve nasal airflow before sleep, during upper respiratory infections, or adjunctively before nasal examination or minor ENT procedures.

Name: Betahistine
Description: Betahistine (DrugBank DB06698) is a small, synthetic histamine analog whose structure consists of a substituted pyridine ring bearing a two-carbon side chain terminating in a primary amine, making it a basic, nitrogen-containing heteroaromatic compound that is commonly handled clinically as the dihydrochloride salt; chemically it is classified as an aminopyridine and more broadly as a histaminergic agent, with a pyridyl-ethylamine scaffold that mimics key pharmacophoric features of histamine. Similar drugs include histamine itself and other antivertigo or histaminergic agents such as cinnarizine and dimenhydrinate, although these are pharmacologically distinct. Its principal known targets are histamine H1 and H3 receptors, acting mainly as a weak H1 agonist and more importantly as an H3 receptor antagonist or inverse agonist, thereby enhancing histaminergic neurotransmission and vestibular microcirculation. Betahistine is used primarily for Ménière disease and related vestibular disorders, including recurrent vertigo, tinnitus, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, and aural fullness, and is also used clinically for symptomatic treatment of peripheral vertigo. It is generally well absorbed orally but undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism, yielding the major inactive metabolite 2-pyridylacetic acid; distribution data are limited, protein binding is low, and elimination occurs predominantly by renal excretion of metabolites with a relatively short parent-drug half-life. Toxicity is usually mild, with overdose associated with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, tachycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm, or seizures in severe cases. Common adverse effects include dyspepsia, headache, nausea, and cutaneous hypersensitivity, and caution is advised in asthma, peptic ulcer disease, and pheochromocytoma.

Name: Desvenlafaxine
Description: Desvenlafaxine (DB06700) is a bicyclic aryloxyalkylamine phenethylamine antidepressant and the major active O-desmethyl metabolite of venlafaxine, structurally characterized by a cyclohexanol core bearing a 4-hydroxyphenyl group and a 2-dimethylaminoethyl substituent, giving a phenolic, tertiary amine-containing framework; chemically it is classified as a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI), with a venlafaxine/tramadol-like aryloxypropanamine-related scaffold centered on a substituted cyclohexanol diaryl motif. Closely related drugs include venlafaxine, levomilnacipran, duloxetine, and milnacipran, with venlafaxine being the most direct analogue. Its principal targets are the serotonin transporter SLC6A4 and norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, with much weaker functional effect at the dopamine transporter SLC6A3 and minimal affinity for muscarinic, histaminergic, or adrenergic receptors. After oral administration it is well absorbed, has moderate absolute bioavailability, low-to-moderate protein binding, broad tissue distribution, and a terminal half-life of roughly 11 hours; metabolism is limited compared with venlafaxine, occurring mainly by UGT-mediated conjugation and minor CYP3A4 oxidation, and elimination is predominantly renal as unchanged drug and glucuronide metabolites. It is indicated primarily for major depressive disorder, including depressed mood, anhedonia, and associated anxiety symptoms, and is used clinically as a once-daily extended-release antidepressant, especially when serotonergic-noradrenergic dual action is desired. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, dizziness, insomnia, somnolence, dry mouth, sweating, constipation, decreased appetite, and sexual dysfunction; clinically important toxicities include dose-related hypertension and tachycardia, serotonin syndrome, mydriasis, hyponatremia, abnormal bleeding, seizure risk, hepatotoxicity infrequently, and discontinuation symptoms, while overdose may produce agitation, ECG changes, and CNS depression.

Name: Dexmethylphenidate
Description: Dexmethylphenidate (DrugBank DB06701) is the pharmacologically more active d-threo enantiomer of methylphenidate, a piperidine-based central nervous system stimulant whose structure consists of a substituted phenyl ring linked through a chiral acetate ester side chain to a 2-piperidyl moiety; chemically it is an arylalkylamine/piperidine ester and is best described as built on a phenyl-piperidine stimulant scaffold closely related to methylphenidate, ethylphenidate, and other catecholamine reuptake inhibitors, with broader pharmacologic similarity to amphetamine-class ADHD therapies such as lisdexamfetamine and mixed amphetamine salts despite a distinct scaffold. Its principal targets are the dopamine transporter SLC6A3 and norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, which it inhibits to raise synaptic dopamine and norepinephrine, especially in frontostriatal circuits. After oral administration it is rapidly absorbed, with immediate-release products reaching peak concentrations in about 1 to 1.5 hours and extended-release formulations prolonging exposure; it distributes systemically with modest protein binding, undergoes extensive first-pass hydrolysis primarily by carboxylesterase 1 to inactive ritalinic acid, and is excreted mainly in urine as metabolites, with a short plasma half-life of roughly 2 to 4 hours for the active moiety. It is indicated mainly for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, improving inattention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity in children, adolescents, and adults. Adverse effects commonly include decreased appetite, insomnia, abdominal pain, anxiety, irritability, tachycardia, and weight loss; toxicity may involve agitation, tremor, hypertension, arrhythmias, psychosis, seizures, and abuse dependence liability, and clinical use centers on individualized ADHD titration, often when lower total stimulant exposure than racemic methylphenidate is desired.

Name: Fesoterodine
Description: Fesoterodine (DB06702) is a synthetic tertiary amine antimuscarinic urinary antispasmodic structurally characterized as an isobutyrate ester prodrug of 5-hydroxymethyl tolterodine, containing a substituted diphenylpropanol-like core with a phenyl ring and an isopropyl-substituted phenyl ring attached to a chiral alcohol center and linked to a diisopropylamino side chain; chemically it is an arylalkyl tertiary amino alcohol ester, and its principal scaffold is the tolterodine/diaryl tertiary alcohol antimuscarinic scaffold. Closely related or pharmacologically similar drugs include tolterodine, oxybutynin, solifenacin, darifenacin, and trospium. After oral administration, fesoterodine is well absorbed and rapidly hydrolyzed by nonspecific plasma esterases to the active metabolite 5-hydroxymethyl tolterodine, thereby avoiding major dependence on CYP2D6 for activation; the active metabolite is moderately protein bound, distributed systemically, further metabolized mainly by CYP2D6 and CYP3A4, and eliminated in urine with some fecal excretion. Its pharmacologic targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially M2 and M3 receptor subtypes in the bladder detrusor, reducing involuntary contractions and urgency. It is indicated for overactive bladder, particularly urinary urgency, increased frequency, and urge urinary incontinence. Adverse effects are typical of anticholinergics, including dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, dyspepsia, urinary retention, and tachycardia, with CNS effects such as dizziness or insomnia occurring less commonly. Toxicity reflects excessive muscarinic blockade, for example severe urinary retention, decreased sweating, confusion, or precipitated angle-closure glaucoma, and caution is warranted in bladder outlet obstruction, gastrointestinal obstructive disorders, hepatic impairment, and with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. Clinically, it is used as once-daily extended-release therapy in adults with symptomatic overactive bladder when behavioral measures alone are inadequate.

Name: Lumefantrine
Description: Lumefantrine (DB06708) is a highly lipophilic aryl amino alcohol antimalarial built around a fluorene-derived polycyclic aromatic scaffold bearing a chlorobenzyl substituent and a dibutylamino side chain attached through a secondary alcohol, placing it in the class of fluorene antimalarials and aligning it structurally with other quinoline- or aryl-amino alcohol partner drugs such as mefloquine, halofantrine, quinine, and related blood-schizonticidal agents. Its scaffold is often described as a fluorene/aryl amino alcohol framework optimized for membrane partitioning and prolonged parasite exposure. Although no single validated human target defines its action, lumefantrine is believed to act within the Plasmodium digestive vacuole by interfering with toxic heme detoxification to hemozoin, and resistance associations have been reported with parasite transport proteins including PfMDR1 and PfCRT rather than a classic mammalian receptor target. It is indicated for uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria, especially as fixed-dose artemether-lumefantrine, and is used clinically for acute symptomatic malaria with fever, chills, headache, and parasitemia. Oral absorption is variable but markedly enhanced by fat-containing food; distribution is extensive with high protein binding; metabolism occurs mainly via CYP3A4 to desbutyl-lumefantrine, an active metabolite; and elimination is slow, predominantly biliary/fecal, with a terminal half-life of several days that supports post-artemisinin parasite clearance. Toxicities include dose-related QT prolongation and other cardiac conduction concerns, hepatotoxicity risk, and potential embryo-fetal toxicity; common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, anorexia, dizziness, asthenia, myalgia, arthralgia, palpitations, rash, and headache.

Name: Methyltestosterone
Description: Methyltestosterone (DrugBank DB06710) is a synthetic orally active androgen and anabolic steroid derived from testosterone, characterized structurally as a 17alpha-methylated androstane steroid bearing the classic four-ring cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene nucleus, a 3-keto group, and a 17beta-hydroxyl substituent; chemically it belongs to the 17alpha-alkylated androgen class, with an androst-4-en-3-one scaffold shared across many testosterone analogs. Closely related drugs include testosterone, fluoxymesterone, oxandrolone, danazol, and nandrolone, which share the steroidal androgen framework but differ in substitutions affecting potency, oral bioavailability, and anabolic-androgenic balance. Its principal target is the androgen receptor (AR/NR3C4), with downstream genomic effects on protein synthesis, virilization, erythropoiesis, and sexual development; weak interactions with sex hormone-binding globulin and indirect modulation after aromatization or 5alpha-reduction may also contribute. Orally absorbed, methyltestosterone has enhanced first-pass stability from 17alpha-methylation, distributes widely into androgen-responsive tissues, is hepatically metabolized by reduction, oxidation, conjugation, and partial aromatization to estrogenic metabolites, and is excreted mainly in urine as conjugated metabolites. Major toxicities include dose-related hepatotoxicity such as cholestatic jaundice, elevated transaminases, peliosis hepatis, and rarely hepatic neoplasms, as well as dyslipidemia, polycythemia, edema, and cardiovascular risk. Adverse effects include acne, hirsutism, virilization in women, menstrual irregularities, gynecomastia, reduced spermatogenesis, testicular atrophy, mood changes, and premature epiphyseal closure in children. Clinically it has been used for male hypogonadism, delayed puberty, androgen deficiency, palliation of metastatic breast cancer in selected women, and occasionally symptoms such as low libido or constitutional androgen deficiency.

Name: Naphazoline
Description: Naphazoline (DrugBank DB06711) is a sympathomimetic imidazoline derivative whose structure consists of a naphthalene ring system linked through a methylene bridge to a 4,5-dihydro-1H-imidazole moiety, giving a compact aromatic-heterocyclic vasoconstrictor pharmacophore; chemically it is classified as a direct-acting adrenergic agonist, specifically an imidazoline decongestant, built on the arylmethyl-imidazoline scaffold shared with related agents such as tetrahydrozoline, xylometazoline, oxymetazoline, and to a lesser extent clonidine-like imidazoline-containing sympathomimetics. Its principal targets are alpha-adrenergic receptors, predominantly ADRA1 family receptors with some activity at ADRA2 receptors, producing vasoconstriction in conjunctival and nasal mucosal vessels. After topical ocular or intranasal administration, systemic absorption is usually limited but can become clinically significant with frequent dosing, damaged mucosa, or pediatric exposure; distribution is sufficient to produce central and cardiovascular effects in overdose, hepatic biotransformation is presumed but incompletely characterized, and metabolites plus parent drug are eliminated mainly via the kidney. It is indicated for temporary relief of eye redness and nasal congestion, for example in allergic conjunctival hyperemia, minor ocular irritation, rhinitis, and common cold-related nasal stuffiness. Adverse effects commonly include transient burning, stinging, blurred vision, rebound hyperemia or congestion, dryness, and mydriasis; toxicity, especially after accidental ingestion or excessive topical use, may include hypertension followed by hypotension, bradycardia, CNS depression, sedation, agitation, and respiratory depression, with children particularly vulnerable. Clinically, naphazoline is used in ophthalmic and nasal preparations for short-term symptomatic vasoconstriction rather than disease modification.

Name: Potassium Iodide
Description: Potassium iodide (DrugBank DB06715) is a simple inorganic ionic salt composed of a monovalent potassium cation electrostatically paired with an iodide anion, giving it a minimal noncovalent crystal-lattice structure rather than a complex organic framework; chemically it belongs to the alkali metal halides and its scaffold is best described as the potassium-halide ion pair. Closely related or pharmacologically similar agents include sodium iodide, Lugol’s solution, strong iodine solution, radioactive iodine isotopes such as iodine-131, and iodinated expectorant preparations. After oral administration it is rapidly and efficiently absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid, and is selectively concentrated by the thyroid via the sodium/iodide symporter SLC5A5, with additional uptake in salivary glands, gastric mucosa, and lactating breast; it is not metabolized in the usual xenobiotic sense, as iodide is incorporated into thyroid hormone biosynthesis through thyroid peroxidase-mediated organification and excess is excreted primarily in urine, with minor fecal, sweat, and salivary elimination. Known protein targets relevant to its effects include SLC5A5 and thyroid peroxidase, with indirect modulation of thyroglobulin iodination and thyroid hormone synthesis/release. Clinically, potassium iodide is used for thyroid blockade after radioactive iodine exposure, short-term preoperative management of hyperthyroidism and thyrotoxic crisis, and as an expectorant; it is also used in some cases of cutaneous sporotrichosis and erythema nodosum. Toxicity includes iodism, thyroid dysfunction such as hypo- or hyperthyroidism, goiter, fetal/neonatal thyroid suppression, hyperkalemia in predisposed patients, and severe hypersensitivity reactions. Common adverse effects include metallic taste, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, salivary gland swelling, acneiform rash, urticaria, and mucosal irritation.

Name: Fosaprepitant
Description: Fosaprepitant (DrugBank DB06717) is a water-soluble phosphorylated prodrug of aprepitant characterized structurally as an N-phosphoryloxymethyl derivative built on a highly lipophilic morpholine-containing, trifluoromethyl-substituted diaryl core with a fluorophenyl ring and a 1,2,4-triazolinone moiety; chemically it is best classified as a neurokinin-1 receptor antagonist prodrug, and its central scaffold is the aprepitant diaryl-triazolinone/morpholine framework modified with a phosphate ester to enable intravenous administration. Closely related drugs include aprepitant itself, the oral active moiety, and other NK1 antagonists such as rolapitant and netupitant. After IV infusion, fosaprepitant is rapidly and extensively converted by phosphatases to aprepitant, so absorption is not relevant in the oral sense; the active drug is widely distributed, highly protein bound, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism predominantly via CYP3A4 with minor CYP1A2 and CYP2C19 contributions, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in feces with a smaller urinary component. Its principal target is TACR1, the substance P/neurokinin-1 receptor, through which it prevents central and peripheral emetic signaling. Clinically it is indicated for prevention of acute and delayed chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, including highly emetogenic cisplatin-based regimens, and for prevention of postoperative nausea and vomiting in selected settings. Toxicity is generally moderate but includes clinically important CYP3A4-mediated drug interactions, infusion-site pain, erythema, thrombophlebitis, hypersensitivity or anaphylactoid reactions, and potential hepatotoxicity; common adverse effects include fatigue, hiccups, constipation, diarrhea, headache, and transient transaminase elevations. In practice it is used in combination with a 5-HT3 antagonist and dexamethasone as part of modern antiemetic prophylaxis.

Name: Stanozolol
Description: Stanozolol (DrugBank DB06718) is a synthetic 17alpha-alkylated anabolic-androgenic steroid structurally derived from dihydrotestosterone, characterized by the fused cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene steroid nucleus bearing a 17alpha-methyl group that confers oral activity and a distinctive pyrazole ring annelated to the A-ring, giving a pyrazolosteroid framework. Chemically it belongs to the androgen/anabolic steroid class, with a DHT-like steroid scaffold modified into a heterocyclic pyrazole-fused scaffold; similar drugs include oxandrolone, methandienone, nandrolone, testosterone derivatives, and other 17alpha-alkylated anabolic agents such as oxymetholone. Its principal pharmacologic target is the androgen receptor, with downstream modulation of androgen-responsive gene transcription; it also suppresses sex hormone-binding globulin and alters hepatic synthesis of proteins involved in coagulation and lipoprotein handling. Stanozolol is well absorbed orally and can also be given intramuscularly as an aqueous suspension; it distributes widely into tissues, undergoes extensive hepatic biotransformation by steroid-reducing and hydroxylating enzymes with conjugative metabolism, and is eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites, with a terminal half-life prolonged by 17alpha-alkylation. Historically it has been indicated for hereditary angioedema prophylaxis and has also been used for catabolic states, delayed growth, osteoporosis, and anemia in some settings. Toxicity is dominated by hepatotoxicity, including cholestatic jaundice, transaminase elevation, peliosis hepatis, and rare hepatic neoplasms, plus endocrine and cardiovascular harms such as virilization, menstrual irregularity, testicular atrophy, infertility, dyslipidemia, hypertension, thrombosis, and adverse behavioral effects. Clinical use has therefore been limited and often discontinued in many markets, though it remains notable for hereditary angioedema and as a widely misused performance-enhancing agent.

Name: Aluminum hydroxide
Description: Aluminum hydroxide (DrugBank DB06723) is an inorganic, poorly water-soluble hydrated aluminum oxide hydroxide material composed of trivalent aluminum centers coordinated by hydroxide and oxide ligands in an amorphous or microcrystalline polymeric lattice rather than a discrete small organic molecule; chemically it belongs to the aluminum salts and inorganic hydroxide antacid/phosphate-binder class, and its scaffold can be viewed as a layered metal-hydroxide network related to other basic aluminum minerals. Similar drugs include magnesium hydroxide, calcium carbonate, sodium bicarbonate, and the phosphate binders lanthanum carbonate and sevelamer, with aluminum-containing relatives such as aluminum carbonate gels. Its pharmacokinetics are dominated by local gastrointestinal action: oral absorption is minimal, most of the dose remains intraluminal, small absorbed amounts distribute largely bound to transferrin and albumin with deposition possible in bone and CNS, it is not metabolized enzymatically, and elimination is mainly fecal for unabsorbed drug and renal for absorbed aluminum. Toxicity is usually limited at standard doses but can include phosphate depletion, osteomalacia, proximal myopathy, microcytic anemia, and encephalopathy in patients with renal failure or prolonged exposure. It has no classic selective protein target; instead it neutralizes gastric hydrochloric acid and binds dietary phosphate, with minor adsorption of bile acids and other luminal constituents. Indications include symptomatic relief of dyspepsia, heartburn, acid indigestion, adjunctive management of gastroesophageal reflux and peptic ulcer disease, and control of hyperphosphatemia in chronic kidney disease. Common adverse effects are constipation, nausea, fecal impaction, hypophosphatemia, and reduced absorption of coadministered drugs such as tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, levothyroxine, and iron. Clinically it is used orally alone or in combination antacid products, and historically as a phosphate binder in dialysis patients, although chronic use has declined because of aluminum accumulation risk.

Name: Calcium carbonate
Description: Calcium carbonate (DrugBank DB06724) is an inorganic ionic salt composed of divalent calcium cations coordinated to planar trigonal carbonate anions in a highly crystalline lattice, most commonly encountered in calcite or aragonite forms; chemically it belongs to the alkaline-earth metal carbonates and its scaffold is best described as a simple mineral carbonate ion pair rather than an organic pharmacophore. Closely related or therapeutically similar agents include other oral calcium salts and antacids such as calcium citrate, calcium acetate, calcium gluconate, magnesium carbonate, magnesium hydroxide, and aluminum hydroxide. Its pharmacologic effects are mediated primarily by local physicochemical action rather than selective receptor binding, although the relevant physiological target space includes calcium-sensing pathways and phosphate handling systems, with no canonical high-affinity drug target protein typically assigned; in phosphate binding, it acts in the gastrointestinal lumen to form insoluble calcium phosphate, and in antacid use it neutralizes gastric hydrochloric acid. Oral absorption of elemental calcium is incomplete and variable, enhanced by vitamin D and gastric acidity, with distribution into extracellular fluid, bone, and teeth, essentially no metabolic biotransformation beyond dissociation and participation in endogenous calcium homeostasis, and fecal excretion predominating for unabsorbed drug with renal elimination of absorbed calcium under endocrine control. It is indicated for calcium supplementation in deficiency states, osteoporosis prevention or adjunctive treatment, hypocalcemia, dyspepsia, gastroesophageal reflux symptoms, and hyperphosphatemia in chronic kidney disease. Adverse effects commonly include constipation, bloating, eructation, and nausea, while excessive use can cause hypercalcemia, nephrolithiasis, milk-alkali syndrome, arrhythmias, confusion, and renal impairment. Clinically, it is widely used as an over-the-counter antacid, a dietary calcium supplement in pregnancy or elderly patients, and a phosphate binder in dialysis or advanced renal disease.

Name: Lornoxicam
Description: Lornoxicam (DrugBank DB06725) is an oxicam-class nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug built on a 4-hydroxy-1,2-benzothiazine 1,1-dioxide scaffold bearing a carboxamide substituent and a chlorinated pyridyl ring, a heteroaryl-enriched enolic acid framework that supports potent cyclooxygenase inhibition; chemically it is a thienothiazine-related enolamide/sulfonamide-like anti-inflammatory agent within the broader NSAID family. Its closest analogs are other oxicams such as piroxicam, tenoxicam, and meloxicam, which share the benzothiazine dioxide core and similar COX-mediated pharmacology. Lornoxicam targets prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthase 1 and 2, namely COX-1 and COX-2, reducing prostaglandin synthesis and thereby producing analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antipyretic effects. It is used for acute and chronic painful inflammatory states including osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, postoperative pain, acute sciatica, and musculoskeletal or dental pain. After oral administration it is well absorbed with relatively high bioavailability, is highly plasma protein bound, distributes mainly in the vascular/extracellular compartment, undergoes extensive hepatic biotransformation largely via CYP2C9 to inactive hydroxylated metabolites, and is eliminated by both renal and biliary/fecal routes with a relatively short elimination half-life compared with several other oxicams. Toxicity is typical of nonselective NSAIDs and includes dose-related gastrointestinal irritation, ulceration, bleeding, renal impairment, fluid retention, hypertension, and rare hepatotoxicity or hypersensitivity, with overdose potentially causing nausea, vomiting, CNS symptoms, or GI hemorrhage. Common adverse effects include dyspepsia, abdominal pain, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, rash, and edema. Clinically, it is used as an oral or parenteral analgesic/anti-inflammatory drug when a relatively fast-onset, short-acting oxicam is desired for perioperative pain control or symptomatic management of rheumatic disease.

Name: Aceclofenac
Description: Aceclofenac (DrugBank DB06736) is a phenylacetic acid–derived nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug structurally characterized as a dichloroaniline-substituted diarylamine bearing a phenylacetic acid core esterified as a glycolic acid derivative, making it a close analog and prodrug-like relative of diclofenac; chemically it belongs to the arylacetic acid NSAID class, with a diclofenac-like diphenylamine scaffold as its central pharmacophore. Similar drugs include diclofenac, which is its principal structural and metabolic comparator, as well as other NSAIDs such as ketoprofen, indomethacin, and naproxen by therapeutic class. Its main targets are cyclooxygenase enzymes PTGS1 and PTGS2, with functional anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antipyretic effects attributed largely to inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis, and some activity may reflect biotransformation to diclofenac. Orally, aceclofenac is well absorbed, highly protein bound, distributed systemically including inflamed tissues, metabolized extensively in the liver via hydrolysis and oxidative pathways, notably involving CYP2C9, to diclofenac and hydroxylated metabolites, and excreted mainly in urine as metabolites with limited unchanged drug. It is indicated for pain and inflammation in osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, and other musculoskeletal or dental pain states. Adverse effects resemble other NSAIDs, including dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, dizziness, edema, and rash. Important toxicities include peptic ulceration, gastrointestinal bleeding, hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevations, renal impairment, fluid retention, hypertension, and rare hypersensitivity or bronchospasm, particularly in susceptible patients. Clinically, it is used as an oral anti-inflammatory analgesic for chronic arthritic disorders and short-term treatment of painful inflammatory conditions.

Name: Ambroxol
Description: Ambroxol (DrugBank DB06742) is a brominated aniline-derived mucolytic whose structure is characterized by a substituted cyclohexanol linked through a methylene bridge to a 2-amino-3,5-dibromobenzylamine moiety, giving an aromatic dibromophenyl aminoalcohol architecture; chemically it is classified as a secretolytic/expectorant and more specifically a brominated benzylamine derivative, with a scaffold closely related to the vasicine-inspired bromhexine family. Similar drugs include bromhexine, its parent prodrug-like analog, as well as other mucoactive agents such as N-acetylcysteine and carbocisteine, though these differ structurally. Ambroxol is generally well absorbed orally, undergoes moderate first-pass hepatic metabolism, distributes კარგად into lung tissue and bronchial secretions, is substantially protein bound, and is metabolized mainly by hepatic biotransformation including CYP3A4-mediated pathways to dibromoanthranilic acid and glucuronide conjugates, with renal excretion of metabolites and a terminal half-life on the order of about 10 hours. Pharmacologically it enhances mucus clearance, stimulates surfactant production, and has local anesthetic-like sodium channel blocking effects; reported targets/mechanistic proteins include voltage-gated sodium channels, surfactant regulatory pathways in type II pneumocytes, and in pharmacologic repurposing literature glucocerebrosidase/GBA1. It is indicated for productive cough and disorders with tenacious mucus such as acute and chronic bronchitis, COPD, and other respiratory tract diseases with impaired expectoration. Adverse effects are usually mild and gastrointestinal, including nausea, vomiting, dyspepsia, diarrhea, and dry mouth, with rash, urticaria, dysgeusia, and rare severe hypersensitivity reactions such as anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, or toxic epidermal necrolysis; toxicity is generally low in routine use but overdose may cause GI irritation, restlessness, or transient neurologic symptoms. Clinically, Ambroxol is used orally, by syrup, lozenge, or inhaled formulations as a mucokinetic and expectorant to reduce sputum viscosity, facilitate clearance in infectious and obstructive airway disease, and sometimes to relieve sore throat because of its local anesthetic effect.

Name: Betaine
Description: Betaine (DB06756), also called trimethylglycine, is a small, highly polar zwitterionic quaternary ammonium compound structurally derived from glycine, consisting of a carboxylate linked to a permanently charged N,N,N-trimethylammonium group; chemically it belongs to the amino acid derivative and methyl-donor/osmolyte class, and its core scaffold is a substituted glycine betaine backbone shared with related methylamine osmoprotectants. Similar agents include choline, carnitine, dimethylglycine, methionine-cycle modulators such as folic acid and vitamin B12 in functional context, and other betaines such as L-carnitine analogs. Pharmacokinetically, oral betaine is readily absorbed, distributed mainly in total body water, taken up into liver and kidney where it participates in one-carbon metabolism and osmoprotection, minimally transformed except through demethylation pathways linked to methionine/homocysteine metabolism, and eliminated primarily by renal excretion with dose-related urinary recovery. Its principal pharmacologic target is betaine-homocysteine S-methyltransferase, which uses betaine as a methyl donor to remethylate homocysteine to methionine; it also functionally influences osmotic stress pathways rather than acting through classic receptor pharmacology. It is indicated mainly for treatment of homocystinuria, particularly forms with elevated homocysteine such as cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency and certain remethylation defects, to reduce plasma homocysteine and related thromboembolic risk. Adverse effects are usually gastrointestinal, including nausea, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, and body odor, while toxicity is generally low but may include hypermethioninemia and rare cerebral edema, especially in susceptible homocystinuria patients. Clinically, it is used as adjunctive metabolic therapy alongside pyridoxine, folate, vitamin B12, methionine restriction, and specialist dietary management.

Name: Pinacidil
Description: Pinacidil (DrugBank DB06762) is a cyanoguanidine potassium-channel opener characterized structurally by a substituted pyridyl moiety linked through an amino bridge to a cyanoguanidine/guanidine-like pharmacophore, with a lipophilic aromatic component that supports membrane penetration and ATP-sensitive potassium channel activity; chemically it belongs to the vasodilatory KATP channel openers, and its core scaffold is best described as an N-cyano-N′-heteroaryl-N″-substituted guanidine. It is closely related pharmacologically to other KATP openers such as minoxidil, nicorandil, cromakalim, and diazoxide, although these differ in scaffold while converging on smooth-muscle hyperpolarization. Its principal targets are ATP-sensitive potassium channels, especially complexes containing inward-rectifier potassium channel Kir6.x subunits and sulfonylurea receptor regulatory subunits, notably ABCC8/SUR1 and ABCC9/SUR2, with vascular effects mainly attributed to SUR2-containing channels. Pinacidil is absorbed sufficiently for systemic hemodynamic activity, distributes into vascular tissues, undergoes hepatic biotransformation with metabolite formation, and is eliminated primarily via renal excretion of metabolites; like many older vasodilators, detailed human ADME characterization is limited relative to modern agents. Toxicity is dominated by exaggerated pharmacology, including profound hypotension, reflex tachycardia, dizziness, headache, fluid retention, and potential myocardial ischemia in susceptible patients; experimental overdose or excessive vasodilation can impair organ perfusion. Adverse effects similarly include flushing, palpitations, edema, nausea, and orthostatic symptoms. Clinically, pinacidil was investigated and used primarily as an antihypertensive and arterial vasodilator for hypertension and related high-resistance states, with additional experimental use in angina, heart failure, and vascular spasm settings, though its routine clinical adoption remained limited.

Name: Tetryzoline
Description: Tetryzoline (DrugBank DB06764) is a sympathomimetic imidazoline derivative characterized structurally by an imidazoline ring linked to a substituted benzyl/aryl moiety, giving a compact basic heteroaromatic vasoconstrictor pharmacophore typical of topical decongestants; chemically it is classified as an imidazoline alpha-adrenergic agonist, and its core scaffold is the aryl-imidazoline motif shared with related ophthalmic and nasal vasoconstrictors. Similar drugs include naphazoline, oxymetazoline, xylometazoline, and tetrahydrozoline-containing formulations, all of which act primarily through alpha-adrenergic receptor stimulation. Its principal targets are alpha-1 adrenergic receptors and, to a lesser extent, alpha-2 adrenergic receptors on vascular smooth muscle, producing local vasoconstriction and reduced hyperemia. Tetryzoline is used mainly topically in ophthalmology for temporary relief of conjunctival redness and irritation due to minor eye irritants, and in some settings as a nasal decongestant for rhinitis-related mucosal congestion. Systemic pharmacokinetic data are limited because intended use is local; after ocular or nasal administration absorption is usually low but can become clinically significant with frequent dosing or ingestion, distribution then becoming systemic, with presumed hepatic metabolism and renal excretion of metabolites as for related imidazolines. Adverse effects include transient burning, stinging, blurred vision, mydriasis, rebound redness, and local irritation; excessive exposure may cause hypertension or reflex bradycardia, whereas overdose, especially in children, can produce CNS depression, hypotension, bradycardia, respiratory depression, and coma. Clinically, it is used short term in over-the-counter eye-whitening or decongestant preparations, with toxicity risk increased by misuse, chronic administration, or accidental oral ingestion.

Name: Alcaftadine
Description: Alcaftadine (DrugBank DB06766) is a tricyclic piperidine-derived small molecule ophthalmic antiallergic agent whose structure consists of a dibenzocycloheptene-like hydrophobic tricyclic ring system linked through an exocyclic double bond to a substituted piperidine side chain bearing a tertiary alcohol, placing it within the antihistamine class and more specifically among H1-receptor antagonist/mast cell-stabilizing agents built on a tricyclic aryl-heterocyclic scaffold. This scaffold is chemically and pharmacologically related to other ophthalmic antiallergy drugs and systemic antihistamines with polycyclic amine frameworks, with useful comparators including ketotifen, olopatadine, azelastine, epinastine, and bepotastine. Its principal targets are the histamine H1 receptor and, with additional reported activity, H2 and H4 histamine receptors, consistent with suppression of allergen-induced itching and reduced conjunctival inflammatory signaling. Alcaftadine is indicated for prevention of ocular pruritus associated with allergic conjunctivitis and is used clinically as a once-daily topical ophthalmic solution for seasonal or perennial allergic eye symptoms such as itching, redness, tearing, and conjunctival irritation. After ocular administration, systemic absorption is low; distribution is largely local to ocular tissues with limited plasma exposure; metabolism appears predominantly hepatic when absorbed, including oxidation and conjugative pathways typical of lipophilic amine antihistamines; and excretion is expected mainly via renal elimination of metabolites. Toxicity is generally low at therapeutic ophthalmic doses, with serious systemic toxicity uncommon, although exaggerated exposure could plausibly produce antihistaminic adverse effects such as somnolence, dry mouth, or tachycardia. Common side effects include transient eye irritation, burning or stinging, աչular redness, instillation-site discomfort, and headache.

Name: Bendamustine
Description: Bendamustine (DrugBank DB06769) is a bifunctional alkylating antineoplastic agent with a distinctive structure that combines a bis(2-chloroethyl) nitrogen mustard moiety linked through a butyric acid side chain to a benzimidazole ring, giving it hybrid features of a classical mechlorethamine-like mustard and a purine-analog-like heteroaromatic system; chemically it is categorized as a nitrogen mustard alkylating agent, and its core scaffold is best described as a benzimidazole-alkylamine mustard. Structurally and pharmacologically related drugs include chlorambucil, cyclophosphamide, melphalan, mechlorethamine, and ifosfamide, although bendamustine shows a partially distinct DNA-damage response profile. Its principal targets are not discrete receptors but genomic DNA, where it forms intra- and interstrand crosslinks; proteins implicated in response include TP53 pathway components, DNA damage and repair machinery, and apoptosis regulators rather than a single canonical target. After intravenous administration, absorption is complete by definition, plasma protein binding is high, distribution is moderate, metabolism occurs mainly by hydrolysis to less active metabolites with a minor CYP1A2 contribution to active gamma-hydroxy and N-desmethyl metabolites, and elimination is predominantly fecal with partial renal excretion; the terminal half-life is short, but cytotoxic effects persist due to irreversible DNA injury. It is indicated for chronic lymphocytic leukemia, indolent B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma refractory to rituximab, and commonly used in mantle cell lymphoma and other lymphoid malignancies, often alone or with rituximab. Major toxicities include dose-limiting myelosuppression, severe lymphopenia, infection risk, infusion reactions, hepatotoxicity, rash including severe cutaneous reactions, secondary malignancy potential, and teratogenicity; common adverse effects include neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, fever, diarrhea, constipation, mucositis, and alopecia.

Name: Benzyl alcohol
Description: Benzyl alcohol (DrugBank DB06770) is a simple aromatic primary alcohol consisting of a monosubstituted benzene ring bearing a benzylic hydroxymethyl group, placing it in the aralkyl alcohol and aromatic alcohol class, with a benzene–methylene–alcohol scaffold that is shared by related benzylic compounds such as benzaldehyde, benzoic acid, benzyl benzoate, and structurally similar preservatives or local anesthetic excipients including phenethyl alcohol and chlorobutanol. It is used mainly as an antimicrobial preservative and solvent/excipient rather than a classic receptor-directed drug, and no highly specific human target protein is generally assigned; its activity is thought to reflect nonspecific membrane and protein perturbation that inhibits microbial growth, while local anesthetic-like effects have also been described. Pharmacokinetically, benzyl alcohol can be absorbed after parenteral, topical, inhalational, or oral exposure, distributes widely in body water, is rapidly oxidized in the liver by alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenase pathways to benzaldehyde and then benzoic acid, conjugated with glycine to hippuric acid, and excreted predominantly in urine. Toxicity is dose dependent and especially important in neonates with immature conjugation capacity, where accumulation has caused the potentially fatal gasping syndrome with metabolic acidosis, respiratory distress, CNS depression, hypotension, and cardiovascular collapse; irritation and systemic toxicity can also follow excessive exposure. Clinically, it is used as a preservative in injectable products and as a topical agent, for example in formulations for pediculosis, while adverse effects include local pain, burning, contact dermatitis, hypersensitivity, nausea, dizziness, and, at high systemic doses, neurotoxicity and respiratory depression.

Name: Besifloxacin
Description: Besifloxacin (DrugBank DB06771) is a fourth-generation fluoroquinolone antibacterial formulated primarily for topical ophthalmic use; structurally it is a chlorinated, fluorinated quinolone-3-carboxylic acid bearing the classic 4-oxo-1,4-dihydroquinoline core, with a C6 fluorine, C7 amino-azepinyl heterocycle, and an N1 cyclopropyl substituent that enhance potency and broad-spectrum activity. Chemically it belongs to the fluoroquinolone carboxylic acids, and its core scaffold is the 4-quinolone/fluoroquinolone nucleus shared with related agents such as moxifloxacin, gatifloxacin, ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, and ofloxacin, although besifloxacin was developed specifically for ophthalmic infection. Its principal targets are bacterial DNA gyrase subunits GyrA/GyrB and topoisomerase IV subunits ParC/ParE, causing inhibition of DNA replication and transcription in susceptible Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens. Clinically it is indicated for bacterial conjunctivitis, especially infections due to organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis, and is used as topical eye-drop therapy in acute conjunctival infection with purulent discharge, hyperemia, and irritation. Systemic pharmacokinetic exposure is minimal after ocular administration, with low absorption into plasma, distribution largely confined to ocular surface tissues and tears, limited clinically relevant metabolism, and negligible systemic excretion burden; this restricted exposure contributes to a favorable safety profile. Toxicity is mainly local, including conjunctival redness, blurred vision, eye pain, irritation, pruritus, and dysgeusia, while serious systemic fluoroquinolone toxicities are theoretically possible but uncommon with ophthalmic dosing; hypersensitivity and selection of resistant organisms remain important precautions in clinical use.

Name: Capsaicin
Description: Capsaicin (DrugBank DB06774) is a naturally occurring vanilloid alkaloid/phenolic amide from Capsicum species characterized structurally by a 4-hydroxy-3-methoxybenzyl vanillyl head group linked through an amide bond to a երկարated hydrophobic branched alkenyl acyl chain, giving an amphiphilic architecture typical of capsaicinoids; chemically it is classified as a capsaicinoid, a vanilloid phenol, and an aromatic fatty acid amide, with a vanillamide scaffold that it shares with related agents such as nonivamide, dihydrocapsaicin, nordihydrocapsaicin, resiniferatoxin, and the ultra-potent TRPV1 agonist analogs used experimentally. Its principal pharmacologic target is transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1), with downstream effects on substance P-containing nociceptive neurons and functional defunctionalization of peripheral C fibers after repeated exposure. Following topical administration, systemic absorption is generally low but increases with dose, surface area, and skin integrity; distribution is mainly local to epidermal and dermal sensory nerve endings, while absorbed drug undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism by CYP450 enzymes to hydroxy- and dehydro-metabolites and is eliminated primarily in urine as metabolites. Toxicity is dominated by intense local neurogenic irritation, burning pain, erythema, cough or bronchospasm after inhalation, gastrointestinal irritation if ingested, and rare severe eye or mucosal injury; high exposures can produce reversible epidermal degeneration and marked nociceptor activation. Clinically, capsaicin is used as a topical analgesic for neuropathic and musculoskeletal pain, including postherpetic neuralgia, diabetic peripheral neuropathy, osteoarthritis, and minor aches, with adverse effects commonly including burning, stinging, pruritus, erythema, and transient treatment-related pain exacerbation.

Name: Chenodeoxycholic acid
Description: Chenodeoxycholic acid (DrugBank DB06777) is a naturally occurring primary bile acid with a cholanic steroid nucleus characterized by the rigid cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene scaffold, a C24 5β-cholane framework bearing hydroxyl groups at the 3α and 7α positions and a terminal carboxylic acid side chain, placing it in the bile acids/bile salts and steroid acid chemical category; its core scaffold is closely related to other endogenous and therapeutic bile acids such as cholic acid, ursodeoxycholic acid, deoxycholic acid, and obeticholic acid. Pharmacologically, it acts mainly through bile acid signaling and detergent effects, with known targets including the nuclear bile acid receptor FXR/NR1H4 and the membrane receptor GPBAR1/TGR5, and it also modulates cholesterol homeostasis and biliary lipid secretion. After oral administration it is absorbed in the small intestine, extensively protein bound, distributed predominantly within the enterohepatic circulation and liver, conjugated with glycine or taurine in hepatocytes, partially transformed by intestinal microbiota to lithocholic acid and other secondary bile acids, then excreted mainly in bile with minor fecal and minimal renal loss. Clinically it has been used to dissolve radiolucent cholesterol gallstones and as replacement therapy in cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis, where it suppresses abnormal bile acid synthesis and lowers cholestanol accumulation. Adverse effects commonly include diarrhea, abdominal cramping, nausea, and dose-related elevations in hepatic transaminases; toxicity concerns include hepatocellular injury, worsening cholestasis, and lithocholic acid-associated hepatotoxicity, especially with excessive dosing or preexisting liver disease.

Name: Dimercaprol
Description: Dimercaprol (DrugBank DB06782), also known as British anti-Lewisite, is a small vicinal dithiol with a three-carbon propane backbone bearing two adjacent sulfhydryl groups and one hydroxyl substituent, making it a lipophilic metal-chelating alcohol-thiol; chemically it belongs to the organosulfur antidotes and chelating agents, and its core scaffold is 2,3-dimercapto-1-propanol, closely related to other sulfhydryl chelators such as succimer, unithiol/dimercaptopropane sulfonate, and more distantly penicillamine. Its pharmacologic action is not mediated by a classical receptor but by direct coordination of soft metal ions, especially arsenic, mercury, and gold, thereby protecting cellular sulfhydryl-dependent enzymes such as the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and other lipoamide-containing proteins from irreversible metal binding. After deep intramuscular administration in peanut oil, absorption is fairly rapid, distribution is widespread including partial tissue and central nervous system penetration, metabolism occurs largely by hepatic biotransformation to inactive conjugates, and excretion is predominantly renal as metabolites and metal-chelate complexes. Toxicity is clinically important because dimercaprol itself has a narrow therapeutic window and may redistribute arsenic to the brain, exacerbate cadmium nephrotoxicity, and cause dose-related hypertension, tachycardia, nausea, vomiting, fever, lacrimation, salivation, chest or abdominal pain, anxiety, and painful injections; hemolysis may occur in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. It is indicated for acute arsenic, inorganic mercury, and gold poisoning, and is used clinically, often with calcium disodium edetate, in severe lead encephalopathy and other life-threatening heavy-metal intoxications.

Name: Halcinonide
Description: Halcinonide (DrugBank DB06786) is a highly potent synthetic fluorinated corticosteroid built on the pregnane glucocorticoid nucleus, specifically a 9-fluoro, 16,17-acetonide-substituted corticosteroid bearing multiple hydroxyl and ketone functionalities that increase topical anti-inflammatory potency and lipophilicity; chemically it belongs to the class of halogenated topical glucocorticoids and uses the classic steroidal cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene scaffold of corticosteroids. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other potent topical steroids such as fluocinonide, fluocinolone acetonide, betamethasone valerate, clobetasol propionate, and triamcinolone acetonide. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor, encoded by NR3C1, with downstream repression of proinflammatory mediators including cytokines, prostaglandins, and leukotrienes, and reduced activity of phospholipase A2 through lipocortin induction. After topical administration, absorption is usually limited but rises with inflamed skin, occlusion, prolonged use, or large treatment area; the absorbed fraction distributes systemically bound to corticosteroid-binding proteins, undergoes mainly hepatic steroid metabolism, and is eliminated as metabolites in urine and to a lesser extent bile/feces. Toxicity reflects local and systemic corticosteroid excess: skin atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, delayed wound healing, secondary infection, and with excessive exposure HPA-axis suppression, hyperglycemia, glucosuria, and iatrogenic Cushingoid features, particularly in children. Adverse effects include burning, stinging, dryness, irritation, folliculitis, acneiform eruption, hypopigmentation, and allergic contact dermatitis. Clinically, halcinonide is used topically for corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses such as eczema, atopic dermatitis, contact dermatitis, lichen simplex chronicus, psoriasis, and seborrheic or inflammatory pruritic eruptions when a high-potency anti-inflammatory agent is needed.

Name: Lanreotide
Description: Lanreotide (DrugBank DB06791) is a synthetic long-acting cyclic octapeptide somatostatin analog whose structure contains a conformationally constrained peptide macrocycle with a disulfide bridge and key aromatic and D-amino-acid substitutions that increase metabolic stability and receptor affinity relative to native somatostatin; chemically it belongs to the peptide hormone analog class, with a somatostatin-derived cyclic peptide scaffold. Closely related drugs include octreotide and pasireotide, which share the somatostatin-mimetic pharmacophore but differ in receptor subtype selectivity and dosing characteristics. Lanreotide acts primarily at somatostatin receptors SSTR2 and SSTR5, with additional lower-affinity interactions at other SSTR subtypes, thereby inhibiting growth hormone release and reducing secretion of serotonin, chromogranin A, insulin, glucagon, vasoactive intestinal peptide, and other peptides. After deep subcutaneous administration in prolonged-release depot formulations, absorption is slow and sustained, bioavailability is prolonged over weeks, distribution is limited as expected for a peptide, metabolism occurs largely through peptide hydrolysis/proteolysis rather than CYP pathways, and elimination is mainly via biliary/fecal routes with some renal contribution. Its principal indications are acromegaly, symptoms from gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors such as carcinoid syndrome, and antiproliferative treatment of unresectable or metastatic well- or moderately differentiated enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. Adverse effects commonly include diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea, steatorrhea, cholelithiasis, injection-site reactions, bradycardia, and dysglycemia; toxicities reflect endocrine and gastrointestinal suppression, with examples including gallbladder sludge/stones, altered glucose homeostasis, pancreatitis, and rare hypersensitivity. Clinically, lanreotide is used as a long-interval depot therapy to normalize IGF-1 and growth hormone in acromegaly and to control flushing and secretory diarrhea in neuroendocrine tumor patients.

Name: Lodoxamide
Description: Lodoxamide (DrugBank DB06794) is a topical antiallergic ophthalmic agent whose structure is characterized by a highly polar aromatic dicarboxylic acid framework built on a salicylate-like benzene scaffold bearing amide-linked substituents and multiple hydrogen-bonding functionalities, features that confer strong acidity, low lipophilicity, and poor membrane permeability; chemically it is classified as a mast-cell stabilizer and aromatic dicarboxylate derivative, with a substituted isophthalic/salicylamide-type scaffold related to other cromone-free antiallergic agents. Similar drugs include cromolyn sodium, nedocromil, pemirolast, and olopatadine, which share mast-cell inhibitory or antiallergic ophthalmic activity. Its principal pharmacologic action is inhibition of antigen-induced mast-cell degranulation with reduced release of histamine, leukotrienes, and other inflammatory mediators; no single high-affinity target protein is definitively established, but functional effects involve mast cells and suppression of mediator release pathways rather than classic receptor antagonism. After ocular administration, systemic absorption is minimal, ocular tissue exposure is localized, plasma concentrations are typically very low, metabolism is limited, and absorbed drug is thought to be cleared largely unchanged by renal excretion. Toxicity is generally low because of limited systemic exposure, though local intolerance can occur; overdoses would be expected mainly to increase ocular irritation rather than cause major systemic poisoning. It is indicated for allergic conjunctivitis, especially vernal keratoconjunctivitis and chronic allergic ocular itching, tearing, and redness. Common adverse effects include transient burning or stinging, discomfort, blurred vision, dry eyes, pruritus, and foreign-body sensation. Clinically, it is used as ophthalmic drops for prophylactic and maintenance control of allergic eye disease rather than rapid rescue of acute symptoms.

Name: Methylnaltrexone
Description: Methylnaltrexone (DrugBank DB06800) is a peripherally acting opioid receptor antagonist structurally derived from naltrexone as a quaternary N-methyl analog of the morphinan nucleus, retaining the rigid polycyclic phenanthrene-like opioid scaffold with key hydroxylated functionality but carrying a permanently charged tertiary-to-quaternary ammonium center that markedly limits blood-brain barrier penetration. Chemically, it is a semisynthetic morphinan opioid antagonist and fits the broader class of quaternary ammonium opioid antagonists; its core scaffold is closely related to naltrexone, naloxone, and nalmefene, with methylnaltrexone most similar to naltrexone but distinguished by restricted central nervous system access. Its principal targets are the peripheral mu-opioid receptor, with lesser activity at kappa- and delta-opioid receptors. After subcutaneous or oral administration, absorption is adequate for peripheral antagonism; distribution is limited centrally because of low lipid permeability and ionic charge; metabolism is minimal to modest, with some conversion to methyl-6-naltrexol isomers; and elimination occurs largely via renal excretion with additional fecal clearance, giving a relatively short half-life that supports once-daily or every-other-day use depending on formulation. It is indicated for opioid-induced constipation, particularly in adults with chronic non-cancer pain or advanced illness receiving palliative care when response to laxatives is inadequate. Adverse effects commonly include abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, flatulence, and hyperhidrosis, while clinically important toxicities include gastrointestinal perforation risk in patients with compromised gut integrity, severe diarrhea, orthostatic symptoms, and precipitation of opioid withdrawal with cramping, anxiety, yawning, and chills. Clinically, it is used to restore bowel function without substantially reversing opioid analgesia, for example in refractory constipation during chronic opioid therapy.

Name: Plerixafor
Description: Plerixafor (DB06809) is a small-molecule bicyclam hematopoietic stem-cell mobilizer composed of two macrocyclic tetraazacyclotetradecane-like cyclam rings linked through an aromatic xylyl spacer, yielding a highly polycationic, metal-chelating amine-rich structure; chemically it is classified as a polyamine macrocycle and CXCR4 antagonist, with a bicyclam scaffold that distinguishes it from other stem-cell mobilizers. Closely related or mechanistically similar agents include the bicyclam analogue AMD3465 and the CXCR4-directed peptide antagonist motixafortide, while granulocyte colony-stimulating factor is clinically similar in use though structurally unrelated. Its principal target is C-X-C chemokine receptor type 4 (CXCR4), functionally disrupting CXCL12/SDF-1 binding and thereby releasing CD34+ hematopoietic stem cells from bone marrow niches. After subcutaneous administration, plerixafor is rapidly absorbed, reaches peak plasma concentrations within about 0.5 to 1 hour, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid with limited metabolism, shows low protein binding, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by the kidney, with a terminal half-life of roughly 3 to 5 hours and increased exposure in renal impairment. Toxicity is usually mild to moderate, but includes leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, splenic enlargement or rare rupture, hypersensitivity, vasovagal reactions, and potential embryo-fetal risk; gastrointestinal toxicity such as diarrhea, nausea, and abdominal cramps is common. Approved indications center on mobilization of hematopoietic stem cells for autologous transplantation in multiple myeloma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, typically in combination with G-CSF, especially in poor mobilizers; adverse effects commonly include injection-site reactions, fatigue, headache, arthralgia, dizziness, and transient elevations in white blood cell counts.

Name: Polidocanol
Description: Polidocanol (DrugBank DB06811), also known as lauromacrogol 400, is a nonionic surfactant sclerosing agent chemically characterized as a dodecyl alcohol core bearing a short polyoxyethylene chain terminated by a hydroxyl group, giving an amphiphilic fatty alcohol ethoxylate structure; thus it belongs to the macrogol ether/surfactant class and is built on a simple aliphatic alkyl-ether ethoxylate scaffold rather than a heterocyclic pharmacophore. Structurally and functionally related drugs include other detergent sclerosants such as sodium tetradecyl sulfate and older sclerosing agents like ethanolamine oleate, although polidocanol is generally regarded as less painful on injection.
