Its pharmacology is primarily local: after intravascular or topical administration it partitions into lipid membranes and denatures endothelial cell surface proteins, causing membrane disruption, endothelial necrosis, platelet adhesion, thrombosis, and eventual fibrosis of treated vessels; no single canonical target protein is established, though membrane proteins and endothelial lipid bilayers are the relevant biological targets. Systemic pharmacokinetic data are limited because intended action is local, but absorbed drug is expected to distribute briefly in extracellular fluids and undergo hepatic oxidative metabolism of the fatty alcohol/polyether moiety with renal excretion of metabolites. Toxicity is dose- and concentration-dependent and includes local tissue necrosis after extravasation, intravascular thrombosis, hemoglobinuria, and rare cardiopulmonary or neurologic events such as arrhythmia, chest tightness, visual disturbance, migraine, or stroke-like reactions. It is indicated for sclerotherapy of varicose veins, reticular veins, spider veins, and some hemorrhoidal or venous malformation settings, and clinically is used as injectable liquid or foam to obliterate incompetent superficial veins; common adverse effects include injection-site pain, burning, hyperpigmentation, urticaria, edema, superficial thrombophlebitis, and rare anaphylaxis.

Name: Pyrithione
Description: Pyrithione (DB06815) is a metal-chelating heteroaromatic antimicrobial built on a 1-hydroxypyridine-2-thione nucleus that exists in thione-thiol tautomeric forms and commonly functions as a bidentate ligand, especially in clinically used zinc pyrithione complexes; chemically it belongs to the pyridinethione family of organosulfur antifungal and antibacterial agents, with a compact hydroxypyridine-thione scaffold that underlies its membrane-active, ionophoric behavior. Closely related agents include zinc pyrithione itself, sodium pyrithione, and mechanistically comparable topical antifungals such as selenium sulfide or azole agents used for dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis. Its pharmacology is dominated by topical exposure: dermal absorption is generally low from rinse-off products, distribution is largely confined to the stratum corneum and hair-bearing skin, systemic metabolism and excretion are limited after normal use but absorbed material is expected to undergo hepatic biotransformation and renal elimination of metabolites. Pyrithione has broad antimicrobial activity against Malassezia species, dermatophytes, and various bacteria; rather than a single selective receptor, reported targets and effects include disruption of membrane transport, collapse of transmembrane ion gradients, metal homeostasis perturbation, and inhibition of proton pumping and energy metabolism. Indications center on dandruff, seborrheic dermatitis, and related scalp pruritus and scaling, with some use in topical antiseptic or preservative contexts. Toxicity is primarily irritant and dose dependent, with examples including ocular irritation, contact dermatitis, burning, dryness, and erythema; significant systemic exposure may pose neurotoxic or cytotoxic risk in experimental settings. Clinically, pyrithione is used mainly in shampoos and washes, especially as zinc pyrithione, to reduce scalp flaking, itching, and fungal burden.

Name: Raltegravir
Description: Raltegravir (DB06817) is an antiretroviral HIV-1 integrase strand-transfer inhibitor built around a hydroxypyrimidinone-like metal-chelating pharmacophore linked to a fluorobenzyl-substituted oxadiazole/carboxamide-rich heteroaromatic framework; chemically it is a diketo acid mimic within the pyrimidinone carboxamide class, and its core scaffold is the integrase-binding chelating heterocycle that coordinates the catalytic Mg2+ ions in the viral enzyme active site. It is most similar to other HIV integrase inhibitors such as elvitegravir, dolutegravir, bictegravir, and cabotegravir, which share metal-chelation-based integrase inhibition but differ in scaffold rigidity, resistance profile, and pharmacokinetics. Raltegravir is administered orally, is absorbed relatively rapidly, reaches peak plasma concentrations in a few hours, is moderately protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes limited CYP-mediated metabolism and is cleared primarily by UGT1A1-mediated glucuronidation to an inactive metabolite, with elimination via feces and urine and a relatively short half-life necessitating standard twice-daily dosing for the original formulation, although an HD once-daily formulation exists. Its principal target is HIV-1 integrase, with activity also against HIV-2 integrase. It is indicated for treatment of HIV-1 infection, including use in treatment-naive and treatment-experienced patients and in combination regimens for pediatric and adult populations. Toxicities are generally mild to moderate but include creatine kinase elevation, myopathy, rare rhabdomyolysis, hypersensitivity, hepatotoxicity, and severe cutaneous reactions. Common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, headache, insomnia, dizziness, fatigue, and rash. Clinically, it is used as part of combination antiretroviral therapy to suppress viral load, improve CD4 counts, and manage resistant or drug-interaction-sensitive HIV cases.

Name: Phenylbutyric acid
Description: Phenylbutyric acid (4-phenylbutyric acid; DrugBank DB06819) is a small aromatic fatty-acid derivative structurally defined by a terminal carboxylic acid linked through a flexible four-carbon aliphatic chain to a phenyl ring, giving a hydrophobic phenethyl-like aryl-alkyl scaffold capped by an acidic headgroup; chemically it is classified as a phenyl-substituted short-chain carboxylic acid and aromatic fatty acid, with a simple phenylbutyrate scaffold related to other short-chain acid therapeutics. Similar drugs include sodium phenylbutyrate, glycerol phenylbutyrate, sodium benzoate, and to a mechanistic extent histone deacetylase inhibitors such as valproic acid and butyrate. Its pharmacology is best known from the phenylbutyrate salt/prodrug forms: oral absorption is generally good, distribution is systemic with hepatic uptake, metabolism occurs predominantly by mitochondrial beta-oxidation to phenylacetate, which conjugates with glutamine to form phenylacetylglutamine, and renal excretion of this conjugate provides an alternative nitrogen-disposal pathway. Known targets are relatively pleiotropic rather than highly selective, including histone deacetylases, molecular chaperone/protein-folding pathways, and indirect modulation of ammonia and glutamine handling. Clinically it is indicated mainly for urea-cycle disorders with hyperammonemia, and has also been explored in cystic fibrosis, sickle-cell disease, cancer, and neurodegenerative or protein-misfolding disorders. Toxicities include gastrointestinal intolerance, sodium load with edema in salt forms, neurocognitive symptoms at higher exposure, menstrual irregularities, reduced appetite, fatigue, and laboratory abnormalities; phenylacetate-related accumulation may contribute to nausea, vomiting, headache, confusion, or metabolic stress. In practice, its major clinical use is chronic nitrogen scavenging in patients with carbamyl phosphate synthetase, ornithine transcarbamylase, or argininosuccinate synthetase pathway defects.

Name: Sulconazole
Description: Sulconazole (DrugBank DB06820) is a topical imidazole antifungal whose structure is defined by an azole pharmacophore linked through a thioether-containing, lipophilic aryl-alkyl framework bearing chlorinated phenyl substituents, giving it a halogenated aromatic imidazole architecture optimized for membrane partitioning and antifungal activity. Chemically, it belongs to the imidazole class of azole antifungals, with an aryl thioether imidazole scaffold closely related to other topical imidazoles such as miconazole, econazole, oxiconazole, and tioconazole. Its principal pharmacologic target is fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase, the CYP51 enzyme, leading to inhibition of ergosterol biosynthesis, disruption of fungal membrane integrity, and growth arrest; broader membrane effects may also contribute. After topical administration, systemic absorption is generally low, with activity concentrated in the stratum corneum and superficial epidermis; distribution is therefore mainly local, while any absorbed fraction is expected to undergo hepatic oxidative metabolism and biliary or renal elimination, although detailed human ADME data are limited. Sulconazole is used for superficial dermatophyte and yeast infections including tinea pedis, tinea cruris, tinea corporis, and cutaneous candidiasis, and clinically it is applied as a cream or solution for localized inflammatory or pruritic fungal dermatoses. Toxicity is usually mild and local rather than systemic, with reported adverse effects including burning, stinging, irritation, erythema, pruritus, dryness, and contact dermatitis; examples of more significant toxicity include allergic sensitization or worsening inflammation at the application site, while serious systemic toxicity is uncommon because of minimal absorption.

Name: Tiopronin
Description: Tiopronin (DB06823) is a small-molecule thiol drug chemically described as N-(2-mercaptopropionyl)glycine, consisting of a carboxylic acid and amide-linked glycine attached to a 2-mercaptopropionyl moiety; its defining structural feature is a free sulfhydryl group on an acylated amino acid framework, placing it in the aminothiol/thiol-containing carboxylic acid class and giving it a simple mercaptoacyl-glycine scaffold closely related to other sulfhydryl drugs such as D-penicillamine, captopril, and mesna, all of which exploit thiol chemistry for disulfide exchange or metal/cystine binding. Its principal pharmacologic target is not a classical receptor but urinary cystine, with which it forms a more soluble mixed disulfide; broader thiol reactivity may also affect cysteine-rich proteins and redox pathways. Orally administered tiopronin is absorbed systemically, distributes largely in extracellular fluid with substantial reversible protein disulfide binding, undergoes limited biotransformation dominated by thiol-disulfide interchange and formation of mixed disulfides and conjugates, and is excreted mainly in urine as parent drug and disulfide metabolites. It is indicated primarily for prevention of cystine nephrolithiasis in severe homozygous cystinuria when hydration, alkalinization, and diet are inadequate, thereby reducing recurrent stone formation, renal colic, and obstructive complications. Toxicities resemble other thiol agents and include proteinuria or membranous nephropathy, hypersensitivity reactions, hepatotoxicity, hematologic suppression such as thrombocytopenia or leukopenia, and occasional severe mucocutaneous reactions. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, fatigue, fever, arthralgia, rash, oral ulcers, and altered taste. Clinically, it is used as a second-line or adjunctive chronic stone-prevention therapy with urine monitoring and periodic renal, hepatic, and hematologic surveillance.

Name: Triethylenetetramine
Description: Triethylenetetramine, DrugBank DB06824, is a small, flexible linear polyamine composed of a tetraamine chain with four basic nitrogen atoms linked by ethylene units, giving it a highly protonatable, strongly metal-chelating structure; chemically it belongs to the aliphatic polyamine and chelating-agent class, and its core scaffold is an acyclic ethylenediamine-repeat backbone closely related to other polyvalent amine chelators. Similar drugs include penicillamine, dimercaprol, succimer, and edetate, although trientine is most closely aligned with copper chelators used in Wilson disease. Its principal pharmacologic action is not mediated by a classic receptor but by coordination of copper to form stable complexes, reducing free copper and promoting urinary excretion; no single canonical target protein is established, though its therapeutic effect functionally intersects copper-binding systems such as albumin, ceruloplasmin, and intracellular metalloprotein pools. Oral absorption is variable and incomplete, food reduces bioavailability, distribution is mainly in extracellular water with metal-binding in plasma, metabolism is limited with formation of acetylated metabolites, and elimination occurs predominantly via the urine as parent drug and copper complexes. It is indicated primarily for Wilson disease, especially in patients intolerant of penicillamine, to treat pathological copper accumulation affecting liver, brain, and other tissues. Adverse effects include nausea, abdominal pain, gastritis, rash, arthralgia, iron deficiency, anemia, and occasional neurologic worsening early in decoppering therapy. Toxicity is generally lower than penicillamine but may include excessive copper depletion, sideroblastic anemia, and hypersensitivity; clinically it is used for chronic maintenance or initial chelation in symptomatic or hepatic Wilson disease, often with monitoring of urinary copper and hematologic indices.

Name: Azapropazone
Description: Azapropazone (DrugBank DB07402) is a pyrazolidinedione-derived nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug characterized structurally by a 4,5-dihydro-1H-pyrazole-3,5-dione core bearing bulky aryl substituents, including a propyl-linked aromatic moiety and a pyridyl ring, giving it a lipophilic diaryl heterocyclic architecture typical of older acidic anti-inflammatory agents; chemically it is classified as a pyrazolone/pyrazolidinedione NSAID, and its key scaffold is the substituted pyrazolidinedione ring system. It is broadly similar to phenylbutazone and, more distantly, oxyphenbutazone and other older cyclooxygenase-inhibiting anti-inflammatory analgesics. Its principal pharmacologic targets are cyclooxygenase enzymes, especially PTGS1 and PTGS2, with consequent suppression of prostaglandin synthesis. After oral administration it is well absorbed, is highly bound to plasma proteins, distributes mainly within the vascular/extracellular compartment, undergoes hepatic biotransformation with formation of oxidative metabolites, and is eliminated slowly via renal and biliary routes, giving a relatively prolonged half-life and potential for drug interactions. It has been used for symptomatic treatment of inflammatory and painful musculoskeletal disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, gout, and acute pain with stiffness and swelling. Adverse effects resemble those of other NSAIDs and include dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, fluid retention, dizziness, rash, and headache, while important toxicities include peptic ulceration, gastrointestinal bleeding, renal impairment, hepatotoxicity, hypersensitivity reactions, and rare but serious hematologic events such as agranulocytosis or thrombocytopenia. Clinically, it was used as an anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antipyretic agent, particularly in chronic rheumatic disease and acute gouty exacerbations, but its use became limited by safety concerns and the availability of better-tolerated NSAIDs.

Name: Felbinac
Description: Felbinac (DrugBank DB07477) is a topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug structurally characterized as a biphenyl-4-acetic acid derivative, consisting of a biaryl scaffold in which two phenyl rings are directly linked and one ring bears an acetic acid side chain; chemically it belongs to the arylacetic acid NSAID class and more specifically the biphenylacetic acid scaffold, closely related to agents such as diclofenac, felbinac trometamol formulations, and other peripheral cyclooxygenase-inhibiting topical NSAIDs, with broader mechanistic similarity to ibuprofen, ketoprofen, and flurbiprofen. Its principal pharmacologic targets are cyclooxygenase enzymes PTGS1 (COX-1) and PTGS2 (COX-2), leading to reduced prostaglandin synthesis and consequent anti-inflammatory and analgesic effects. Felbinac is used mainly for local relief of musculoskeletal pain and inflammation, including osteoarthritis, periarthritis, tendinitis, sprains, strains, back pain, and traumatic soft-tissue injury. After topical administration, systemic absorption is limited relative to oral NSAIDs, with drug penetration into inflamed superficial tissues favored; distribution is therefore primarily local, plasma exposure generally low, hepatic biotransformation likely occurs through oxidative and conjugative pathways typical of NSAIDs, and renal excretion of metabolites is expected to predominate. Toxicity is usually low when used topically, but excessive application or damaged skin may increase systemic exposure and NSAID-type risks such as gastrointestinal irritation, renal impairment, or hypersensitivity. Common adverse effects are local rash, erythema, pruritus, burning, contact dermatitis, and occasional photosensitivity, while clinical use is generally short-term symptomatic treatment in gels, creams, or patches for localized inflammatory pain.

Name: Chloramphenicol succinate
Description: Chloramphenicol succinate (DrugBank DB07565) is the water-soluble sodium succinate ester prodrug of chloramphenicol, built on the chloramphenicol scaffold consisting of a p-nitrophenyl ring linked to a dichloroacetamide-bearing 1,3-propanediol core, with succinyl esterification of a primary hydroxyl to enhance parenteral formulation; chemically it is classified as an amphenicol antibiotic and more specifically an esterified prodrug of a nitroaromatic dichloroacetamide. Its closest analogs and related drugs are chloramphenicol, thiamphenicol, and florfenicol, which share the amphenicol pharmacophore but differ in substituents affecting toxicity and resistance. After intravenous or intramuscular administration, chloramphenicol succinate is variably hydrolyzed by esterases to active chloramphenicol; distribution is wide, including cerebrospinal fluid, eye, and intracellular compartments, protein binding is moderate, metabolism of liberated chloramphenicol occurs predominantly in the liver via glucuronidation, and elimination is primarily renal as inactive metabolites and, with incomplete hydrolysis, some unchanged succinate ester. The principal molecular target is the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit, especially 23S rRNA within the peptidyl transferase center, inhibiting peptide bond formation and protein synthesis. It has been used for serious susceptible infections such as meningitis, typhoid fever, rickettsial disease, brain abscess, and anaerobic infections when safer agents are unsuitable. Major toxicities include dose-related reversible bone marrow suppression, rare idiosyncratic aplastic anemia, gray baby syndrome in neonates from impaired glucuronidation, and neurotoxicity such as optic neuritis; adverse effects also include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, candidiasis, rash, and superinfection. Clinically, it is mainly reserved for severe systemic infections requiring parenteral therapy when alternatives are ineffective, contraindicated, or unavailable.

Name: Tranilast
Description: Tranilast (DB07615) is a small-molecule antiallergic and antifibrotic agent whose structure is best described as an anthranilic acid derivative bearing a substituted cinnamoyl side chain, specifically a 3,4-dimethoxycinnamoyl amide linked to an o-aminobenzoic acid core; chemically it belongs to aromatic carboxylic acids and cinnamamide-like anti-inflammatory agents, with a scaffold centered on an N-cinnamoyl anthranilic acid framework related in a broad medicinal-chemistry sense to other anthranilic acid drugs and to antiallergic mast-cell stabilizing agents, with partially similar therapeutic space to cromolyn, ketotifen, and repirinast, though it is structurally distinct. Pharmacokinetically, tranilast is orally active, absorbed to a clinically useful extent, circulates substantially protein bound, distributes mainly in extracellular fluids, undergoes hepatic biotransformation including O-demethylation and conjugative metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly in urine as parent drug and metabolites, with a terminal half-life generally compatible with multiple-daily dosing. Its pharmacology is pleiotropic rather than highly selective, with reported effects on mast-cell mediator release and fibrosis signaling involving TGF-β-related pathways, and literature has implicated modulation of targets or pathways including TGFB1, collagen synthesis programs, histamine release processes, aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling, and transient receptor potential channel TRPV2 in some experimental settings. Clinically, it has been used for bronchial asthma, allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis, keloids, hypertrophic scars, and other fibroproliferative or allergic symptoms such as pruritus. Adverse effects include gastrointestinal upset, nausea, abdominal discomfort, dizziness, rash, edema, and hepatic enzyme elevation, while important toxicities include drug-induced liver injury and rarer renal or hematologic abnormalities, warranting liver-function monitoring during clinical use.

Name: Dibromotyrosine
Description: Dibromotyrosine (DrugBank DB07637) is a brominated halogenated amino-acid derivative structurally characterized as an L-tyrosine scaffold bearing two bromine substituents on the aromatic phenyl ring together with the canonical amino acid side chain containing a phenolic hydroxyl, an alpha-amino group, and a carboxylate; chemically it belongs to the bromophenol/halogenated amino acid class and is most appropriately described as a substituted tyrosine or phenylalanine-like aromatic amino acid scaffold. It is more a biochemical metabolite and probe-like small molecule than a therapeutic agent, and structurally related compounds include monobromotyrosine, iodotyrosines such as monoiodotyrosine and diiodotyrosine, tyrosine itself, and other halogenated phenolic amino acids generated during eosinophil or peroxidase-mediated oxidative chemistry. No well-validated human drug target proteins are established for dibromotyrosine, although its formation is linked to eosinophil peroxidase- and myeloperoxidase-driven bromination reactions and it is therefore better viewed as a biomarker of brominative oxidative stress than a target-directed medicine. Pharmacokinetic data in humans are sparse; as a polar amino-acid analogue it would be expected to have limited passive diffusion, potential uptake by amino acid transport processes, distribution largely in extracellular fluids, metabolism through amino acid catabolic pathways or further conjugation, and predominant renal excretion of parent compound or metabolites. Toxicity data are limited, but excessive exposure to halogenated tyrosines may reflect or contribute to oxidative protein injury, inflammatory tissue damage, and possible interference with normal amino acid handling; specific adverse effects and routine clinical side effects are not established because dibromotyrosine is not a standard approved therapeutic. Accordingly, there is no recognized clinical indication or routine clinical use, though it has research and potential diagnostic utility as a marker in eosinophilic asthma, atopic disease, parasitic inflammation, and other disorders marked by eosinophil activation.

Name: Fasudil
Description: Fasudil (DB08162) is a synthetic isoquinoline sulfonamide vasodilator characterized structurally by an isoquinoline aromatic bicyclic heterocycle linked through a sulfonyl group to a terminal homopiperazine ring, giving a basic, cationic nitrogen-containing scaffold optimized for kinase binding; chemically it is classified as a small-molecule protein kinase inhibitor, specifically an isoquinoline sulfonamide, and its core scaffold is the fasudil/HA-1077-type isoquinoline-sulfonyl-homopiperazine motif shared with related Rho kinase inhibitors and vasoactive kinase inhibitors. Similar drugs include ripasudil, another ROCK inhibitor used ophthalmically, and more distantly belumosudil and Y-27632 as ROCK-pathway comparators. Fasudil primarily targets ROCK1 and ROCK2, with additional activity reported against PRKACA, PRKCG, PRKG1, and myosin light-chain phosphorylation pathways, thereby reducing calcium sensitization and vascular smooth-muscle contraction. Pharmacokinetically, it is typically administered intravenously, producing rapid systemic exposure, broad vascular tissue distribution, hepatic metabolism mainly by aldehyde oxidase to the active metabolite hydroxyfasudil, and predominantly renal excretion of metabolites with a relatively short parent half-life. Clinically, it is used chiefly for prevention and treatment of cerebral vasospasm after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, and has been explored in pulmonary hypertension, angina, ischemic stroke, vasospastic disorders, and neurovascular dysfunction. Adverse effects include hypotension, headache, flushing, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, fever, and local injection-site reactions. Toxicity is generally related to excessive vasodilation and cardiovascular effects such as blood-pressure reduction, but liver enzyme elevations and systemic intolerance have also been reported, especially with high exposure or prolonged use.

Name: Parecoxib
Description: Parecoxib (DrugBank DB08439) is a parenteral, water-soluble amide prodrug of valdecoxib built on a diaryl-substituted pyrazole scaffold, structurally characterized by a 1,5-diaryl pyrazole core bearing a sulfonamide functionality and an N-acyl side chain that enhances injectable formulation; chemically it belongs to the coxib class of selective cyclooxygenase-2 nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, with close analogs including valdecoxib, celecoxib, etoricoxib, and rofecoxib, all sharing related heteroaryl-diaryl COX-2-selective motifs. After intravenous or intramuscular administration, parecoxib is rapidly and extensively converted hepatically to the active moiety valdecoxib, producing analgesic effects without oral absorption considerations; valdecoxib distributes systemically with substantial protein binding, undergoes hepatic metabolism primarily via CYP3A4 and CYP2C9 with additional non-CYP pathways, and is eliminated largely as metabolites in urine and feces, with a parent parecoxib short half-life but longer effective half-life for valdecoxib. Its principal targets are PTGS2 as the intended high-affinity target and, to a lesser extent, PTGS1. Clinically it is indicated for short-term management of acute pain, especially postoperative pain and reduction of opioid requirements after orthopedic, dental, gynecologic, or abdominal surgery, and it has also been used for perioperative dysmenorrhea-type pain. Toxicities reflect the NSAID/coxib class and valdecoxib-related liabilities, including serious cardiovascular thrombotic events, renal impairment, sodium and fluid retention, gastrointestinal ulceration or bleeding, severe cutaneous hypersensitivity such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, anaphylactoid reactions in sulfonamide-sensitive patients, and hepatotoxicity; common adverse effects include nausea, dyspepsia, headache, dizziness, injection-site reactions, edema, hypertension, and reduced renal function.

Name: Thiorphan
Description: Thiorphan (DB08626) is a small-molecule thiol-containing peptidomimetic best known as the active metabolite of racecadotril and is structurally characterized by a mercaptoacyl moiety attached to a glycine-derived backbone and a terminal benzyl group, giving a compact aromatic thiol amide architecture optimized for zinc binding in metalloproteases. Chemically, it is classified as a neutral endopeptidase inhibitor, specifically a thiol-based metalloprotease inhibitor, with a mercaptoamide/arylalkyl-glycine scaffold. Closely related agents include racecadotril, its prodrug precursor, and other neprilysin inhibitors such as sacubitrilat and candoxatrilat, although these differ in zinc-binding groups and scaffold topology. Thiorphan inhibits neprilysin, also known as membrane metalloendopeptidase or MME/CD10/enkephalinase, thereby reducing degradation of enkephalins and certain secretory-regulating peptides; neprilysin is its principal validated target. After oral administration of racecadotril, thiorphan is generated rapidly by esterase-mediated hydrolysis, reaches systemic circulation, distributes mainly extracellularly with limited central nervous system penetration, undergoes further biotransformation including disulfide formation and conjugative pathways, and is eliminated through renal and fecal routes. Toxicity is generally modest at therapeutic exposure but can include excessive secretory modulation, gastrointestinal discomfort, rash, and hypersensitivity; overdose or high exposure could theoretically potentiate peptide-mediated effects without marked opioid-like respiratory depression. Its main indication is symptomatic treatment of acute diarrhea, especially secretory diarrhea, where it reduces intestinal hypersecretion without substantially altering transit. Reported adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, constipation, headache, and cutaneous reactions such as erythema or urticaria. Clinically, it is used chiefly via the prodrug racecadotril in adults and children with acute diarrheal illness, often alongside oral rehydration therapy.

Name: Zofenoprilat
Description: Zofenoprilat (DrugBank DB08766) is the pharmacologically active de-esterified metabolite of zofenopril and is a sulfur-containing dicarboxylate angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor characterized structurally by a proline-like amino acid core bearing a free thiol group and carboxylate functionalities linked to a lipophilic phenyl-substituted bicyclic moiety; chemically it is classified as a thiol ACE inhibitor, with a peptidomimetic proline-derived scaffold related to other sulfhydryl-containing ACE inhibitors. Similar drugs include captopril, which also contains a thiol zinc-binding group, and non-thiol ACE inhibitors such as enalaprilat, lisinopril, ramiprilat, and quinaprilat, which share the general diacid peptidomimetic ACE-inhibitor framework. Zofenoprilat inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme, also known as ACE or kininase II, thereby reducing angiotensin II formation and limiting bradykinin degradation. Pharmacokinetically, it is formed after oral administration of the prodrug zofenopril, distributes to vascular and cardiac tissues with substantial protein binding, undergoes limited further metabolism relative to the parent ester, and is eliminated by both renal and biliary/fecal routes, with exposure prolonged in renal impairment. Its therapeutic indication is principally hypertension and post-myocardial-infarction cardiovascular risk reduction, particularly in patients with left ventricular dysfunction or high ischemic burden. Adverse effects and toxicity are consistent with ACE inhibition and include hypotension, dizziness, cough, hyperkalemia, renal function worsening, and, more rarely, angioedema; overdose may cause marked hypotension and renal hypoperfusion. Clinically, zofenoprilat exposure underlies the use of zofenopril for blood-pressure control, cardioprotection after acute MI, and adjunctive management in patients with concomitant cardiovascular disease.

Name: Azidocillin
Description: Azidocillin (DrugBank DB08795) is a semisynthetic penicillin characterized structurally by the conserved penam nucleus, a bicyclic beta-lactam fused to a thiazolidine ring, bearing an azido-substituted acyl side chain that distinguishes it from benzylpenicillin and contributes to its antibacterial profile; chemically it belongs to the beta-lactam antibiotics, specifically the penicillins, and its core scaffold is the 6-aminopenicillanic acid framework. It is most similar to other narrow-spectrum penicillins and acid-labile penicillinase-sensitive agents such as penicillin G, pheneticillin, propicillin, and azlocillin in the broader ureido/acyl side-chain-modified penicillin family, although azidocillin is classically grouped with antistaphylococcal or antistreptococcal penicillin derivatives depending on source context. Its antibacterial action is mediated by covalent inhibition of bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, including transpeptidases such as PBP1, PBP2, and PBP3, thereby blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking and causing cell-wall lysis. Pharmacokinetically, like many older penicillins it is expected to have limited oral stability with clinical use favoring parenteral exposure, low to moderate plasma protein binding, broad extracellular distribution, poor intracellular penetration, minimal metabolism, and predominant renal excretion via glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, with dose adjustment in renal impairment. Toxicity is generally that of the penicillin class, notably hypersensitivity reactions ranging from rash and urticaria to anaphylaxis, gastrointestinal intolerance, antibiotic-associated diarrhea, and rarely interstitial nephritis, hemolytic reactions, neurotoxicity or seizures at high concentrations. It has been used for susceptible Gram-positive bacterial infections, especially streptococcal and pneumococcal infections and other penicillin-sensitive infections such as respiratory tract, skin/soft tissue, and ENT infections; adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, candidiasis, injection-site reactions, and allergic dermatitis, and clinical use has historically centered on treatment of infections caused by penicillin-susceptible organisms when a narrow-spectrum beta-lactam is appropriate.

Name: Salicylamide
Description: Salicylamide (DrugBank DB08797) is a simple salicylate-derived aromatic hydroxybenzamide whose structure consists of a benzene ring bearing an ortho-phenolic hydroxyl group and a carboxamide, a substitution pattern that enables intramolecular hydrogen bonding and places it within the phenolic amide, salicylamide, and non-opioid analgesic/antipyretic chemical categories; its core scaffold is the salicylamide or 2-hydroxybenzamide nucleus, closely related to salicylic acid, acetylsalicylic acid, diflunisal, and the para-aminophenol analgesics such as paracetamol by functional analogy rather than identical structure. Pharmacologically, it has been used as an analgesic and antipyretic for mild pain, headache, myalgia, arthralgia, fever, and common cold or influenza-associated symptoms, with effects generally attributed to weak inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis and central analgesic mechanisms, although no single highly selective target protein is firmly established; reported or inferred targets include cyclooxygenase enzymes PTGS1 and PTGS2. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed, distributed systemically, extensively metabolized in the liver primarily by conjugation pathways including glucuronidation and sulfation with limited unchanged renal elimination, and excreted mainly in urine as metabolites, giving a relatively short duration of action. Toxicity resembles other salicylate-like agents and may include nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, dizziness, tinnitus, sweating, and, in overdose, metabolic acidosis, CNS symptoms, and salicylate intoxication; hypersensitivity reactions and hepatic or renal stress are possible but uncommon. Clinically, salicylamide has mainly served as an older symptomatic relief agent, often in combination cold and pain preparations, rather than a modern first-line standalone drug.

Name: Antazoline
Description: Antazoline (DrugBank DB08799) is a first-generation antihistamine characterized structurally by a benzhydryl-substituted imidazoline/ethylenediamine-like motif in which lipophilic diaryl functionality is linked to a basic nitrogen-containing heterocycle, giving the molecule the amphipathic cationic profile typical of older H1 antagonists; chemically it is classified as an antihistaminic imidazoline derivative, and its core scaffold can be described as a diarylmethyl-imidazoline pharmacophore related to other classical H1 blockers. Similar drugs include antazoline analogs and other first-generation antihistamines such as diphenhydramine, tripelennamine, antazoline-containing ophthalmic combinations, and to some extent promethazine, which share lipophilic aromatic domains and protonatable amines. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, where it acts as an inverse agonist/antagonist; older literature also supports ancillary anticholinergic and local anesthetic-like membrane effects that contribute to both efficacy and adverse reactions. Antazoline is used mainly for symptomatic relief of allergic conditions, especially allergic conjunctivitis and ocular itching, redness, and irritation, and historically for rhinitis and urticaria-related symptoms. After topical ocular or oral administration it is absorbed to a variable extent, distributes into tissues with some CNS penetration expected for a first-generation agent, undergoes hepatic biotransformation, and is eliminated primarily as metabolites in urine. Toxicity is consistent with this class and includes dose-related sedation, confusion, antimuscarinic effects, and, in overdose, agitation, arrhythmia, or seizures. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, blurred vision, dry mouth, tachycardia, urinary retention, and local ocular irritation. Clinically, it is most often used in ophthalmic practice, frequently combined with a vasoconstrictor such as naphazoline for short-term treatment of allergic eye symptoms.

Name: Roxatidine acetate
Description: Roxatidine acetate (DrugBank DB08806) is an orally active acetate ester prodrug of roxatidine, a histamine H2-receptor antagonist characterized structurally by a substituted aromatic ether–alkylamine framework bearing an O-acetylated oxime/carbamate-type functionality that is rapidly converted in vivo to the active desacetyl metabolite; chemically it belongs to the H2 antihistamine/antiulcer class and is built on the non-imidazole H2-blocker scaffold that distinguishes it from earlier imidazole-containing agents. Similar drugs include ranitidine, famotidine, nizatidine, and the older cimetidine, all of which reduce gastric acid secretion through antagonism of the histamine H2 receptor, encoded by HRH2 on gastric parietal cells. After oral administration, roxatidine acetate is generally well absorbed, undergoes presystemic and systemic deacetylation to active roxatidine, distributes mainly in extracellular fluids with limited central penetration, and is eliminated predominantly by renal excretion of parent drug and metabolites, so exposure may increase in renal impairment; hepatic biotransformation is relatively limited compared with some earlier H2 blockers. Its principal indication is acid-related upper gastrointestinal disease, including gastric ulcer, duodenal ulcer, reflux esophagitis, gastritis-associated hyperacidity, epigastric pain, heartburn, and nocturnal acid breakthrough. Adverse effects are usually mild and include constipation, diarrhea, nausea, abdominal discomfort, headache, dizziness, fatigue, rash, and transient liver enzyme elevations; uncommon but clinically relevant toxicities reported for H2 antagonists include confusion in elderly or renally impaired patients, hypersensitivity reactions, hematologic abnormalities, and rare hepatic dysfunction. Clinically, it has been used for ulcer healing, maintenance therapy to prevent ulcer recurrence, and symptomatic control of acid-peptic disorders, particularly when oral once- or twice-daily acid suppression is desired.

Name: Bupranolol
Description: Bupranolol (DrugBank DB08808) is a lipophilic aryloxypropanolamine beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist whose structure consists of the classic beta-blocker pharmacophore, a protonatable secondary alcohol-containing propanolamine side chain linked through an ether to a substituted aromatic ring system, giving it the characteristic nonselective beta-blocker scaffold shared by propranolol-like agents. Chemically it is categorized as a nonselective beta-adrenergic antagonist in the aryloxypropanolamine class, with a propranolol-related scaffold and similarity to propranolol, timolol, nadolol, carteolol, and pindolol. Its principal targets are beta-1 adrenergic receptor and beta-2 adrenergic receptor, with pharmacology consistent with reduction of sympathetic stimulation in cardiac tissue and aqueous humor production in the eye. Bupranolol has been used mainly as an ophthalmic and, in some regions, systemic beta-blocker for glaucoma or ocular hypertension and for cardiovascular indications such as hypertension, tachyarrhythmia, or angina-related symptoms. After administration, especially topical ocular dosing, systemic absorption can still occur through conjunctival and nasolacrimal routes; distribution is expected to favor well-perfused tissues, metabolism is largely hepatic as with related lipophilic beta-blockers, and excretion occurs predominantly as metabolites in urine. Toxicity reflects exaggerated beta-blockade, including bradycardia, hypotension, atrioventricular conduction delay, bronchospasm, and possible worsening of heart failure; overdose may produce severe cardiovascular depression or hypoglycemia masking. Adverse effects include ocular irritation, dry eye, blurred vision, fatigue, dizziness, cold extremities, and bronchoconstriction. Clinically, it has been used to lower intraocular pressure in open-angle glaucoma and to manage sympathetic cardiovascular symptoms where nonselective beta-blockade is desired.

Name: Dichloroacetic acid
Description: Dichloroacetic acid (DrugBank DB08809) is a small halogenated aliphatic carboxylic acid structurally characterized by a two-carbon acetic acid scaffold bearing two chlorine substituents on the alpha carbon, creating a simple dichlorinated acetate framework that places it within the haloacetic acid and organochlorine compound categories; its core chemical scaffold is therefore an alpha,alpha-dichloro-substituted acetate, and related or chemically similar agents include monochloroacetic acid, trichloroacetic acid, sodium dichloroacetate, and the mechanistically analogous pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase inhibitor pyruvate. Pharmacologically, dichloroacetic acid is best known as a metabolic modulator that inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase kinases, especially PDK isoforms regulating the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, thereby promoting mitochondrial glucose oxidation and lowering lactate production; additional downstream effects involve metabolic reprogramming relevant to mitochondrial disease, lactic acidosis, pulmonary hypertension, and experimental oncology. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed, distributes widely in body water and mitochondria-rich tissues, undergoes predominant hepatic biotransformation via glutathione transferase zeta-1/maleylacetoacetate isomerase, shows nonlinear and genotype-dependent kinetics with potential accumulation during repeated dosing, and is excreted mainly as urinary metabolites with limited unchanged renal elimination. Its major toxicities include dose- and duration-related peripheral neuropathy, hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevation, CNS effects such as sedation or confusion, and gastrointestinal irritation; animal studies also raise concerns for developmental toxicity and hepatocarcinogenicity at high chronic exposures. Clinically, it has been used mainly investigationally or off-label for congenital and acquired lactic acidosis, mitochondrial cytopathies such as MELAS, and selected metabolic disorders, while adverse effects commonly include paresthesias, weakness, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, and reversible liver enzyme abnormalities.

Name: Lurasidone
Description: Lurasidone (DrugBank DB08815) is an atypical antipsychotic of the benzisothiazole-derived piperazine class, structurally characterized by a chlorinated benzoisothiazole ring linked through a piperazine moiety to a bicyclic isoindole-like imide-containing system, giving a rigid, lipophilic, heteroaryl-piperazine scaffold typical of serotonin-dopamine antagonists; its core scaffold and receptor-binding profile make it chemically and pharmacologically similar to other second-generation antipsychotics such as ziprasidone, risperidone, paliperidone, and to a lesser extent aripiprazole. Its principal targets are dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors as antagonistic sites, with high affinity also reported for 5-HT7 and 5-HT1A receptors, plus activity at adrenergic alpha2 receptor subtypes and minimal affinity for histamine H1 and muscarinic receptors, a profile relevant to lower anticholinergic burden. Orally administered lurasidone is absorbed better with food, is highly protein bound, reaches peak concentrations within hours, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly by CYP3A4 to active and inactive metabolites, and is eliminated through both feces and urine with a terminal half-life supporting once-daily dosing. It is indicated for schizophrenia and bipolar depression, including depressive episodes in bipolar I disorder, and is used clinically to reduce hallucinations, delusions, disorganized thought, and depressive symptoms. Adverse effects commonly include akathisia, somnolence, nausea, parkinsonism, dystonia, agitation, and modest weight gain, while toxicities of concern include extrapyramidal symptoms, tardive dyskinesia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, hyperprolactinemia, orthostatic hypotension, leukopenia, and metabolic effects that are generally less pronounced than with olanzapine or quetiapine.

Name: Ticagrelor
Description: Ticagrelor (DrugBank DB08816) is a small-molecule, orally active cyclopentyl-triazolo-pyrimidine antiplatelet agent whose structure consists of a densely substituted fused triazolopyrimidine heterobicyclic core linked to a cyclopropylamino group, a fluorophenyl substituent, and a polyhydroxylated cyclopentane side chain, giving a nucleoside-mimetic but non-thienopyridine architecture; chemically it is classified as a reversible direct-acting P2Y12 receptor antagonist, with a triazolopyrimidine scaffold distinct from the thienopyridine scaffold of clopidogrel and prasugrel, though pharmacologically similar to cangrelor and more broadly to other ADP-pathway platelet inhibitors. Its principal target is the platelet purinergic receptor P2RY12, producing inhibition of ADP-mediated platelet activation and aggregation. Ticagrelor is indicated to reduce thrombotic cardiovascular events in acute coronary syndrome, prior myocardial infarction, and selected high-risk coronary artery disease settings, and is used clinically with aspirin in unstable angina, NSTEMI, STEMI, post-percutaneous coronary intervention, and in some secondary stroke or transient ischemic attack prevention strategies. It is rapidly absorbed orally, has moderate bioavailability, reaches peak concentrations within hours, is highly protein bound, undergoes hepatic metabolism mainly by CYP3A4/5 to an active metabolite with similar P2Y12 antagonism, and is eliminated largely via biliary/fecal routes with limited renal clearance. Toxicity is dominated by bleeding, including gastrointestinal, procedural, and intracranial hemorrhage, with dyspnea, bradyarrhythmias or ventricular pauses, hyperuricemia, and creatinine increases also recognized; common adverse effects include epistaxis, bruising, hematuria, GI bleeding, and shortness of breath, while overdose or combination with anticoagulants or strong CYP3A modulators can intensify bleeding risk or alter exposure.

Name: Tafluprost
Description: Tafluprost (DrugBank DB08819) is a fluorinated prostaglandin F2α analog used as an ocular hypotensive agent; structurally it is an isopropyl ester prodrug with the classic prostanoid cyclopentane core, two aliphatic side chains, defined hydroxyl substituents, and a characteristic 15,15-difluoro modification that increases metabolic stability and receptor potency. Chemically, it belongs to the eicosanoid/prostanoid class, specifically prostaglandin analog antiglaucoma agents, and its principal scaffold is the PGF2α prostane framework. Closely related drugs include latanoprost, travoprost, bimatoprost, and unoprostone, which share ocular hypotensive use and broadly similar lipidic prostanoid architectures. After topical ophthalmic administration, tafluprost is absorbed through the cornea and rapidly hydrolyzed by ocular esterases to tafluprost acid, the active metabolite; systemic exposure is typically very low, distribution is largely local to anterior ocular tissues, metabolism proceeds further by β-oxidation and phase II conjugative pathways, and elimination occurs mainly as inactive metabolites in urine and feces. Its main target is the prostaglandin F receptor, PTGFR, activation of which increases uveoscleral, and to some extent trabecular, aqueous humor outflow. It is indicated for reduction of elevated intraocular pressure in open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension. Adverse effects are mainly local and include conjunctival hyperemia, eye irritation, pruritus, foreign-body sensation, eyelash growth, periocular skin pigmentation, iris pigmentation, dry eye, and blurred vision. Toxicity is generally low because of minimal systemic exposure, but class-related concerns include irreversible iris color change, prostaglandin-associated periorbitopathy, and caution in aphakia, uveitis, or macular edema risk states. Clinically, it is used as once-daily topical therapy, including preservative-free formulations for patients intolerant of benzalkonium chloride.

Name: Ivacaftor
Description: Ivacaftor (DB08820) is a small-molecule cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator modulator with a lipophilic heteroaryl aromatic structure characterized by a quinolinone-based core linked to substituted phenyl and tert-butyl-containing moieties through amide functionality, placing it in the biaryl/heteroaryl amide class and more specifically within the quinolone-like CFTR potentiator chemotype; its principal scaffold is a substituted 4-oxo-1,4-dihydroquinoline (quinolinone) framework, and structurally or mechanistically similar drugs include other CFTR modulators such as lumacaftor, tezacaftor, elexacaftor, and the related potentiator class prototype itself in combination regimens. Ivacaftor targets CFTR/ABCC7 directly, increasing channel opening probability at the epithelial cell surface, and is indicated for cystic fibrosis in patients with responsive CFTR gating, residual-function, or selected splice/conductance mutations, with clinical use in disorders such as G551D mutation-associated disease and in combination therapy for broader genotypes including F508del-containing cystic fibrosis. It is orally administered, better absorbed with fat-containing food, highly protein bound, extensively distributed, and metabolized predominantly by CYP3A4 and CYP3A5 to active and inactive metabolites, with elimination chiefly via the feces and minimal renal excretion; dose adjustment and interaction management are important with strong CYP3A modulators. Toxicity is dominated by hepatotoxicity risk with transaminase elevations, potential cataracts observed in pediatric monitoring, and embryo-fetal risk considerations, while adverse effects commonly include headache, upper respiratory symptoms, abdominal pain, diarrhea, rash, dizziness, nausea, and elevated liver enzymes. In practice, ivacaftor is used both as monotherapy for eligible gating mutations and in fixed combinations such as ivacaftor/lumacaftor, ivacaftor/tezacaftor, and ivacaftor/tezacaftor/elexacaftor to improve lung function, reduce pulmonary exacerbations, and enhance weight gain and quality of life.

Name: Azilsartan medoxomil
Description: Azilsartan medoxomil (DB08822) is an orally administered prodrug angiotensin II receptor blocker in which a lipophilic medoxomil ester masks the active acid azilsartan; structurally it is a biphenyl-tetrazole/oxadiazole-containing antihypertensive built on the classic sartanoid scaffold, with a substituted biphenyl core, tetrazole bioisostere, and heteroaromatic ring system that confers high affinity for the angiotensin II type 1 receptor. Chemically it belongs to the tetrazole-containing biphenyl ARB class, and it is closely related to candesartan cilexetil, olmesartan medoxomil, valsartan, irbesartan, losartan, and telmisartan, which share overlapping receptor pharmacology but differ in scaffold substitutions and pharmacokinetics. After oral administration, azilsartan medoxomil is rapidly hydrolyzed in the gastrointestinal tract to active azilsartan; bioavailability is moderate, peak concentrations occur within a few hours, protein binding is high, distribution is largely extracellular, metabolism occurs mainly via CYP2C9 to inactive metabolites, and elimination is through both renal and fecal routes with a terminal half-life permitting once-daily dosing. Its primary target is AGTR1, with functional blockade of angiotensin II signaling leading to reduced vasoconstriction and aldosterone effects. It is indicated principally for hypertension, including essential hypertension requiring long-term blood-pressure control, sometimes in combination regimens. Adverse effects include dizziness, hypotension, fatigue, diarrhea, and increases in serum creatinine; clinically important toxicities include renal impairment, hyperkalemia, and fetal toxicity in pregnancy, with risk accentuated in volume-depleted patients or those with renal artery stenosis. Clinically, it is used as a once-daily antihypertensive alone or with agents such as chlorthalidone or amlodipine to reduce elevated blood pressure and associated cardiovascular risk.

Name: Deferiprone
Description: Deferiprone (DrugBank DB08826) is a small, orally active bidentate iron chelator built on a simple 3-hydroxypyridin-4-one heteroaromatic ring scaffold, specifically a 1,2-dimethyl-substituted hydroxypyridone whose adjacent carbonyl and hydroxyl functionalities create the metal-binding pharmacophore; chemically it belongs to the hydroxypyridinone class of chelators and is structurally related to other iron-chelating drugs such as deferoxamine and deferasirox, although it is distinguished by its compact pyridinone scaffold and neutral lipophilic character that facilitates tissue penetration. Its principal pharmacologic target is ferric iron rather than a classical receptor, forming stable 3:1 deferiprone-Fe3+ complexes and thereby lowering toxic non-transferrin-bound and labile iron pools; direct protein targets are not central, though clinically relevant iron-handling proteins include transferrin and ferritin as iron sources. Deferiprone is rapidly absorbed after oral administration, reaches peak plasma concentrations within about 1 hour, is moderately distributed including access to intracellular and cardiac iron compartments, undergoes predominant hepatic glucuronidation to an inactive 3-O-glucuronide, and is eliminated mainly in urine as metabolite with a shorter elimination half-life requiring thrice-daily dosing in many regimens. It is indicated primarily for transfusional iron overload, especially in thalassemia syndromes, and is also used in selected patients with sickle cell disease or other chronic anemias requiring repeated transfusion, including cases with cardiac iron loading. Important toxicities include agranulocytosis and neutropenia, hepatotoxicity, zinc deficiency, arthropathy, and iron deficiency with overchelation; common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, elevated transaminases, reddish-brown urine, and musculoskeletal pain. Clinically, it is used as monotherapy or in combination with deferoxamine for patients inadequately controlled on other chelators or needing enhanced cardiac iron removal.

Name: Vismodegib
Description: Vismodegib (DB08828) is a small-molecule Hedgehog pathway inhibitor with a halogenated aromatic amide-like architecture characterized by multiple substituted phenyl/pyridyl rings, including chlorophenyl and pyridyl motifs linked through a rigid, lipophilic scaffold containing sulfonyl/carbamoyl functionality; chemically it is best classified as a synthetic aromatic heterocyclic antineoplastic agent, and its core scaffold is commonly described as a diaryl/heteroaryl Hedgehog-pathway-binding framework optimized for Smoothened antagonism. Structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include sonidegib and glasdegib, which also target Smoothened, although with distinct heteroaromatic scaffolds. Its principal target protein is Smoothened homolog (SMO), thereby suppressing aberrant Hedgehog signaling and downstream GLI-mediated transcription. Pharmacokinetically, vismodegib is orally administered, has concentration-limited absorption and very high protein binding, distributes extensively in plasma with prolonged persistence, is metabolized mainly by oxidation, glucuronidation, and uncommon pyridine-ring cleavage pathways involving CYP enzymes such as CYP2C9 and CYP3A4/5, and is eliminated slowly predominantly via the feces with a lesser urinary component, yielding an unusually long apparent half-life. It is indicated primarily for adults with metastatic basal cell carcinoma or locally advanced basal cell carcinoma not amenable to surgery or radiotherapy, and has also been explored in other Hedgehog-driven malignancies. Toxicities include marked embryo-fetal toxicity and teratogenicity, class-related developmental toxicity, and less commonly severe cutaneous or systemic intolerance. Common adverse effects include muscle spasms, alopecia, dysgeusia or ageusia, weight loss, fatigue, nausea, diarrhea, decreased appetite, constipation, and arthralgia. Clinically, it is used as an oral targeted therapy in advanced basal cell carcinoma to shrink tumors, palliate disease burden, and provide a non-surgical option in patients with recurrent, inoperable, or metastatic disease.

Name: Tyramine
Description: Tyramine (DrugBank DB08841) is a small biogenic trace amine structurally characterized as a para-hydroxylated phenethylamine, consisting of a benzene ring bearing a phenolic hydroxyl group and a two-carbon side chain terminating in a primary amine; chemically it belongs to the monoamine, phenethylamine, and trace amine classes, and its core scaffold is the tyramine/phenethylamine aromatic-ethylamine framework shared with related sympathomimetic or endogenous amines such as phenethylamine, octopamine, dopamine, and indirectly epinephrine-like pressor agents. Pharmacologically, tyramine is best known as an indirectly acting adrenergic agonist and endogenous trace amine that can interact with trace amine-associated receptor 1 and promote norepinephrine release via uptake through the norepinephrine transporter, with functional relevance also to vesicular monoamine transport processes and adrenergic signaling. It is well absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract but normally undergoes extensive first-pass oxidative deamination by monoamine oxidase, especially MAO-A, in the gut and liver, limiting systemic bioavailability; distribution is expected to favor highly perfused tissues, metabolism yields p-hydroxyphenylacetic acid and related metabolites, and urinary excretion occurs mainly as metabolites. Toxicity is dominated by hypertensive pressor reactions, particularly in patients receiving monoamine oxidase inhibitors, with examples including severe hypertension, headache, intracranial hemorrhage risk, palpitations, and arrhythmias after ingestion of tyramine-rich foods. Adverse effects therefore include headache, flushing, diaphoresis, nausea, chest pain, and blood pressure elevation. Tyramine has little routine therapeutic use as a modern drug but is used experimentally as a pharmacologic probe of catecholamine release and autonomic function; clinically, its main relevance is as a dietary and drug-interaction hazard in MAOI-treated patients and in provoking migraine or hypertensive symptoms in susceptible individuals.

Name: Acetylcarnitine
Description: Acetylcarnitine (DrugBank DB08842), usually referring to the endogenous ester L-acetylcarnitine, is a small zwitterionic quaternary ammonium compound consisting of the carnitine backbone bearing a β-hydroxyl group, a terminal carboxylate, and an acetyl ester on the hydroxyl, placing it in the carnitine/acylcarnitine class of amino acid-derived metabolites with a trimethylammonium hydroxycarboxylate scaffold. It is closely related to L-carnitine and other acylcarnitines such as propionyl-L-carnitine, which are pharmacologically similar mitochondrial substrate carriers. Its principal biological role is not classic receptor agonism but participation in mitochondrial acetyl-group trafficking via the carnitine shuttle; relevant protein interactors include carnitine acetyltransferase, carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 and 2, the organic cation/carnitine transporter SLC22A5 (OCTN2), and the mitochondrial carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase SLC25A20. Orally it is absorbed variably and incompletely, distributed to plasma, skeletal muscle, heart, liver, and CNS with some blood-brain barrier penetration, undergoes reversible interconversion with carnitine and acetyl-CoA, and is eliminated mainly by renal excretion with substantial tubular reabsorption. Toxicity is generally low; adverse effects are usually dose-related and include nausea, abdominal cramping, diarrhea, agitation, headache, insomnia, and fishy body odor from trimethylamine production, while rare concerns include seizure exacerbation in predisposed patients. Clinically it has been used for carnitine deficiency states, neuropathic pain, diabetic peripheral neuropathy, cognitive symptoms, fatigue, and as an adjunct in mitochondrial dysfunction, ischemia, or male infertility, although efficacy varies by indication.

Name: Pitavastatin
Description: Pitavastatin (DrugBank DB08860) is a synthetic lipid-lowering agent of the statin class, specifically a heptenoic acid HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor, structurally characterized by the statin pharmacophore consisting of a dihydroxyheptenoic acid side chain linked to a lipophilic aromatic core containing a fluorophenyl group, a cyclopropyl substituent, and a quinoline-like heteroaromatic system that together define its compact, highly hydrophobic scaffold; chemically it is categorized as a synthetic aromatic hydroxy acid statin, and its core scaffold is closely related to other type II statins such as atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, fluvastatin, and to a lesser extent pravastatin. Its principal target is 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase, with downstream effects including upregulation of hepatic LDL receptor expression and reduction of circulating LDL cholesterol, total cholesterol, and triglycerides. Pitavastatin is indicated for primary hypercholesterolemia, mixed dyslipidemia, and prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk in patients requiring LDL lowering. It is orally absorbed with moderate bioavailability, reaches peak plasma concentrations within about 1 hour, is highly protein bound, undergoes limited CYP-mediated metabolism with glucuronidation and lactonization as major pathways, and is excreted predominantly via the bile with minor renal elimination, giving it relatively low susceptibility to CYP3A4 drug interactions. Toxicity is broadly similar to other statins and includes dose-related myalgia, myopathy, rare rhabdomyolysis, transaminase elevations, and uncommon hepatotoxicity, with risk increased by interacting transport inhibitors or severe renal impairment. Common adverse effects include muscle pain, arthralgia, constipation, diarrhea, headache, and abdominal discomfort. Clinically, it is used as adjunctive therapy to diet and lifestyle modification, either alone or in selected combination lipid-lowering regimens, particularly when potent LDL reduction with relatively limited CYP interaction liability is desired.

Name: Fingolimod
Description: Fingolimod (DB08868) is a synthetic sphingosine analog and aminodiol prodrug whose structure consists of a lipophilic para-substituted phenyl ring attached to a flexible octyl side chain bearing a primary alcohol and a 2-amino-1,3-propanediol-like polar headgroup; chemically it is categorized as an immunomodulatory lipid-like small molecule, with a sphingoid base scaffold that mimics endogenous sphingosine and is closely related to other sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulators such as siponimod, ozanimod, ponesimod, and ceralifimod. After oral administration it is well absorbed with high bioavailability, reaches peak levels over hours, distributes extensively into tissues and erythrocytes, crosses the blood-brain barrier, and is phosphorylated mainly by sphingosine kinase 2 to the active metabolite fingolimod-phosphate; it has a long terminal half-life of roughly 6-9 days, undergoes slow oxidative biotransformation largely via CYP4F2 and related pathways plus fatty acid-like degradation, and is eliminated predominantly as inactive metabolites in urine with minor fecal excretion. Its principal targets are sphingosine-1-phosphate receptors S1PR1, S1PR3, S1PR4, and S1PR5, with functional antagonism at S1PR1 causing lymphocyte sequestration in lymph nodes. It is indicated primarily for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis, including relapsing-remitting and active secondary progressive disease, to reduce relapse frequency and MRI lesion activity. Important toxicities and adverse effects include first-dose bradycardia, atrioventricular block, hypertension, macular edema, elevated hepatic enzymes, lymphopenia with serious opportunistic infections such as varicella-zoster and cryptococcosis, reduced pulmonary function, teratogenic risk, posterior reversible encephalopathy, and possible skin cancer risk; common side effects include headache, cough, diarrhea, back pain, influenza, and abnormal liver tests. Clinically, it is used as an oral disease-modifying therapy in adults and some pediatric patients with multiple sclerosis, particularly when sustained suppression of inflammatory relapses is desired.

Name: Tesamorelin
Description: Tesamorelin (DB08869) is a synthetic peptide analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone, structurally a modified 44-amino-acid GHRH sequence with strategic substitutions and an N-terminal trans-3-hexenoic acid group that increase resistance to dipeptidyl peptidase degradation while preserving receptor agonism; chemically it belongs to the peptidomimetic endocrine hormone class, and its core scaffold is the linear GHRH peptide backbone. It is most similar to other GHRH agonists or growth hormone secretagogic peptides such as sermorelin and CJC-1295, and is pharmacologically related, though mechanistically distinct, from ghrelin-receptor agonists like macimorelin. Its principal target is the growth hormone-releasing hormone receptor (GHRHR) on pituitary somatotrophs, leading to pulsatile growth hormone release and downstream insulin-like growth factor 1 elevation. After subcutaneous administration, tesamorelin is absorbed systemically, has limited distribution beyond extracellular fluid typical of peptides, undergoes proteolytic catabolism to smaller peptides and amino acids rather than CYP-mediated metabolism, and is cleared mainly through peptide degradation with renal elimination of metabolites; its terminal half-life is short but pharmacodynamic IGF-1 effects persist longer. The approved indication is reduction of excess visceral abdominal adipose tissue in HIV-associated lipodystrophy, for example in patients with prominent central fat accumulation. Adverse effects commonly include injection-site reactions, arthralgia, myalgia, peripheral edema, nausea, pruritus, and headache, with clinically relevant risks of glucose intolerance or diabetes worsening, fluid retention, and hypersensitivity. Toxicity is driven largely by excessive GH/IGF-1 axis stimulation, with examples including hyperglycemia, edema, and theoretical promotion of neoplastic growth, so clinical use requires monitoring of IGF-1, metabolic status, and contraindications such as active malignancy.

Name: Eribulin
Description: Eribulin (DB08871) is a non-taxane microtubule dynamics inhibitor and a fully synthetic analog of the marine natural product halichondrin B, characterized structurally by a highly oxygenated, conformationally constrained polyether macrolide-like ketone framework with multiple fused ether rings, numerous hydroxyl substituents, and a distinctive truncated macrocyclic polycyclic scaffold that preserves the pharmacophore required for tubulin binding; chemically it is classified as an antineoplastic macrocyclic ketone/polyether natural-product analog, and its core scaffold is the halichondrin-derived polycyclic ether system. Closely related or mechanistically similar drugs include halichondrin B, vinorelbine, vinblastine, paclitaxel, ixabepilone, and other tubulin-targeting antimitotics, although eribulin is distinguished by binding predominantly to the plus ends of microtubules and inhibiting polymerization without promoting depolymerization; its principal target is tubulin, especially β-tubulin within microtubule assemblies. Pharmacokinetically, eribulin is administered intravenously, shows rapid distribution with a large volume of distribution and extensive tissue uptake, is highly but not completely plasma protein bound, undergoes minimal oxidative metabolism with limited CYP3A4 involvement, and is eliminated mainly unchanged via biliary/fecal excretion with a smaller renal contribution and a prolonged terminal half-life. Major toxicities include dose-limiting neutropenia, leukopenia, peripheral neuropathy, QT prolongation risk, hepatotoxicity, and embryo-fetal toxicity. It is indicated for metastatic breast cancer previously treated with anthracycline- and taxane-based regimens and for unresectable or metastatic liposarcoma after prior anthracycline therapy. Common adverse effects include fatigue, alopecia, nausea, constipation, anemia, febrile neutropenia, and sensory neuropathy, and clinically it is used as monotherapy in heavily pretreated advanced breast cancer and selected soft-tissue sarcoma settings.

Name: Gabapentin enacarbil
Description: Gabapentin enacarbil (DB08872) is an orally administered acyloxyalkyl carbamate prodrug of gabapentin in which the parent 1-aminomethyl cyclohexane acetic acid scaffold is masked as an enacarbil ester to enhance intestinal transport and bioavailability; chemically it is a gabapentinoid, amino acid related small molecule, and prodrug built on a cyclohexaneacetic acid scaffold closely related to gabapentin and, more distantly, pregabalin as a similar alpha2delta ligand. Unlike gabapentin, it is designed for high-capacity uptake through intestinal nutrient transporters, particularly monocarboxylate transporter 1 and sodium-dependent multivitamin transporter, after which it is rapidly hydrolyzed by nonspecific esterases to gabapentin, carbon dioxide, acetaldehyde, and isobutyric acid. Systemic exposure to active gabapentin is dose proportional over its therapeutic range, absorption is improved and more predictable than immediate-release gabapentin, plasma protein binding is low, distribution is similar to gabapentin, metabolism of released gabapentin is negligible, and elimination occurs primarily as unchanged gabapentin in urine, so renal impairment increases exposure and prolongs half-life. Its principal pharmacologic target is the alpha2delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, especially CACNA2D1 and CACNA2D2, reducing excitatory neurotransmitter release. It is indicated clinically for moderate-to-severe primary restless legs syndrome and for postherpetic neuralgia, with use aimed at symptoms such as urge to move the legs, nocturnal discomfort, and neuropathic pain. Adverse effects commonly include somnolence, dizziness, sedation, fatigue, and headache; clinically important toxicities include CNS depression, impaired coordination, falls, suicidal ideation warnings, hypersensitivity, and enhanced respiratory depression when combined with opioids or other sedatives.

Name: Boceprevir
Description: Boceprevir (DB08873) is a first-generation, orally active direct-acting antiviral designed as a linear peptidomimetic ketoamide featuring a reversible covalent α-ketoamide warhead, multiple amide bonds, a hydrophobic tert-butyl/alkyl-rich peptide-like backbone, and a constrained proline-derived element that mimics the natural hepatitis C virus protease substrate; chemically it is classified as a peptidomimetic serine protease inhibitor, with a ketoamide protease-inhibitor scaffold closely related to other early HCV NS3/4A inhibitors such as telaprevir and, more distantly, later agents including simeprevir, paritaprevir, grazoprevir, and voxilaprevir. Its principal target is the HCV NS3/4A serine protease, whose inhibition blocks viral polyprotein processing and suppresses replication, particularly in chronic hepatitis C virus genotype 1 infection, where it was used with peginterferon alfa and ribavirin in treatment-naive patients and some previously treated relapsers or partial responders. Pharmacokinetically, boceprevir is absorbed orally with improved exposure when taken with food, is highly protein bound, distributes systemically without unusual tissue sequestration, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism primarily by aldo-keto reductases with additional CYP3A4/5 involvement, and is eliminated mainly in feces with a smaller urinary component; it is also a strong CYP3A4/5 inhibitor, creating clinically important interaction potential. Toxicity is dominated by additive hematologic and constitutional effects in combination therapy, especially anemia, neutropenia, and fatigue, with dysgeusia, nausea, headache, and rash also common; examples of more serious concerns include worsened ribavirin-associated anemia, hepatic impairment-related exposure changes, and substantial drug-drug interactions with CYP3A substrates. Clinically, boceprevir was used as part of response-guided triple therapy for chronic HCV rather than for symptom palliation, but has largely been superseded by newer interferon-free regimens with superior efficacy and tolerability.

Name: Fidaxomicin
Description: Fidaxomicin (DB08874) is a narrow-spectrum macrocyclic antibiotic structurally characterized by a large 18-membered macrolactone-based ring with multiple hydroxyl substituents, conjugated unsaturation, aromatic moieties, and glycosidic sugar appendages, giving it a highly oxygenated lipophilic macrocycle; chemically it belongs to the macrocyclic antibacterial class, specifically the tiacumicin/lipiarmycin family, and its core scaffold is a glycosylated macrocyclic lactone. It is most closely related to other RNA polymerase-inhibiting macrocycles such as lipiarmycin A3 and tiacumicin B, and is sometimes discussed alongside oral agents used for Clostridioides difficile infection such as vancomycin, although those are mechanistically and structurally distinct. Fidaxomicin acts primarily on the bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase sigma-subunit initiation complex, with rpoB-associated polymerase components considered the functional target, thereby blocking transcription initiation. Pharmacokinetically, oral absorption is minimal, systemic exposure is low, intraluminal fecal concentrations are very high, plasma protein binding of absorbed drug/metabolite is substantial, metabolism occurs mainly by hydrolysis to the active metabolite OP-1118, and excretion is predominantly fecal with negligible renal elimination. Toxicity is generally limited because of poor absorption, though nonclinical and clinical experience supports gastrointestinal intolerance and occasional hepatic enzyme elevations; serious systemic toxicity is uncommon. It is indicated for treatment of C. difficile-associated diarrhea and recurrent or nonsevere-to-severe C. difficile infection in adults and selected pediatric patients. Adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, constipation, gastrointestinal bleeding, anemia, neutropenia, and hypersensitivity reactions. Clinically, it is used orally to achieve microbiota-sparing eradication of C. difficile and to reduce recurrence risk, for example in initial CDI episodes or recurrence-prone patients.

Name: Cabozantinib
Description: Cabozantinib (DrugBank DB08875) is an orally active small-molecule multikinase inhibitor built on a substituted quinoline/quinazoline-like heteroaromatic kinase-binding scaffold linked through an ether bridge to a fluorophenyl group and bearing a carboxamide-containing cyclopropane moiety, a structure typical of lipophilic ATP-competitive receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Chemically, it is best categorized as a heteroaryl urea-/amide-like targeted anticancer agent within the class of small-molecule RTK inhibitors, with a scaffold and pharmacophore broadly similar to other VEGFR/MET-directed agents such as vandetanib, lenvatinib, sorafenib, regorafenib, and sunitinib. Its principal targets include MET, VEGFR2/KDR, AXL, RET, ROS1, TYRO3, MER, KIT, FLT3, TIE2/TEK, and TRKB/NTRK2, supporting antiangiogenic and antitumor activity. Clinically, it is indicated for advanced renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma after prior sorafenib, differentiated thyroid cancer refractory to radioactive iodine, and medullary thyroid cancer, and is also used in combinations such as with nivolumab in renal cell carcinoma. Oral absorption is adequate but variable, protein binding is high, distribution is extensive, metabolism occurs predominantly via hepatic CYP3A4 oxidation, and elimination is mainly fecal with a long terminal half-life that supports once-daily dosing. Toxicities reflect potent anti-VEGF and multikinase effects and include hypertension, diarrhea, palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia, fatigue, mucositis, anorexia, weight loss, proteinuria, hepatotoxicity, hemorrhage, thromboembolism, impaired wound healing, gastrointestinal perforation or fistula, osteonecrosis of the jaw, and reversible posterior leukoencephalopathy; common adverse effects also include nausea, dysphonia, constipation, and hypothyroidism.

Name: Ruxolitinib
Description: Ruxolitinib (DrugBank DB08877) is an orally active small-molecule Janus kinase inhibitor whose structure is centered on a substituted pyrazole linked to a deazapurine-like pyrrolopyrimidine heteroaromatic system, with a nitrile-bearing side chain and cyclopentyl substitution that optimize ATP-site binding and kinase selectivity. Chemically, it is classified as a heteroaryl kinase inhibitor, specifically a targeted antineoplastic and immunomodulatory agent, built on a pyrazole–pyrrolopyrimidine scaffold typical of ATP-competitive JAK inhibitors. Structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include tofacitinib, baricitinib, fedratinib, and upadacitinib, which also inhibit JAK-family signaling with differing selectivity profiles. Ruxolitinib primarily targets JAK1 and JAK2, with downstream suppression of STAT-mediated cytokine signaling. It is well absorbed orally, reaches peak plasma concentrations within a few hours, is moderately protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 with a lesser contribution from CYP2C9, and is eliminated predominantly as metabolites in urine with a relatively short terminal half-life requiring twice-daily dosing in many settings. Its major toxicities are dose-related myelosuppression, especially anemia and thrombocytopenia, along with neutropenia, immunosuppression, infection risk including herpes zoster and opportunistic infections, and occasional nonmelanoma skin cancer signals.
