Approved and common clinical uses include myelofibrosis, polycythemia vera intolerant of or resistant to hydroxyurea, and steroid-refractory acute or chronic graft-versus-host disease, where it reduces splenomegaly, constitutional symptoms, pruritus, cytokine-driven inflammation, and transfusion burden in selected patients.

Name: Aminopterin
Description: Aminopterin (DrugBank DB08878) is a classical antifolate antimetabolite built on a pteridine-based folate mimic scaffold consisting of a substituted pteridine ring linked through a p-aminobenzoyl moiety to a terminal glutamate residue; structurally, it is the 4-amino analog of folic acid and is closely related to the dihydrofolate reductase inhibitors methotrexate, trimetrexate, and pralatrexate, with methotrexate being the most clinically analogous agent. Chemically it belongs to the antineoplastic and immunosuppressive folate analog class, with a pterin-p-aminobenzoate-glutamate scaffold characteristic of classical antifolates. Its principal target is dihydrofolate reductase, leading to depletion of reduced folates and secondary inhibition of thymidylate and purine synthesis; intracellular polyglutamation may enhance retention and pathway inhibition. Aminopterin has been used in leukemia, especially acute lymphoblastic leukemia, and has also seen historical or limited use in psoriasis and other proliferative disorders. Pharmacokinetically, it is variably absorbed orally, can be given parenterally, distributes into proliferative tissues with limited CNS penetration unless administered intrathecally or at high exposure, undergoes intracellular polyglutamation with relatively limited oxidative metabolism, and is cleared predominantly unchanged by the kidney, so renal dysfunction increases exposure. Toxicity is typical of potent antifolates and includes severe myelosuppression, mucositis, stomatitis, nausea, diarrhea, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, dermatitis, and profound teratogenic and embryotoxic effects; examples include pancytopenia, opportunistic infection, gastrointestinal ulceration, and fatal marrow aplasia in overdose. Clinically, its use is now largely historical or highly specialized, often supplanted by methotrexate, but it remains an important prototype antifolate in oncologic and pharmacologic practice.

Name: Teriflunomide
Description: Teriflunomide (DB08880) is a small-molecule immunomodulator that is the active metabolite of leflunomide, structurally characterized as an isoxazole-derived aromatic enone bearing a trifluoromethyl-substituted phenyl ring and a cyano-enol/amide-like pharmacophore; it belongs to the isoxazole and fluorinated aromatic nitrile class and is commonly described as having a leflunomide/teriflunomide isoxazolyl-anilide scaffold. Closely related drugs include leflunomide, its prodrug precursor, and by mechanistic analogy other antiproliferative immunomodulators used in autoimmune disease such as dimethyl fumarate and cladribine, though these are not close structural analogs. Its principal target is dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH), causing inhibition of de novo pyrimidine synthesis and thereby limiting proliferation of activated T and B lymphocytes; reported ancillary effects include reduced tyrosine kinase-dependent signaling. After oral administration it is well absorbed, highly protein bound, has a small apparent distribution volume, undergoes limited further metabolism with enterohepatic recycling, and displays a very long elimination half-life; excretion occurs via both feces and urine, and accelerated elimination can be achieved with cholestyramine or activated charcoal. Toxicity is dominated by hepatotoxicity, embryo-fetal toxicity, peripheral neuropathy, hypertension, cytopenias, infection risk, and rare severe cutaneous or interstitial lung reactions. Adverse effects commonly include diarrhea, nausea, alopecia, elevated transaminases, headache, and paresthesias. It is indicated primarily for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis, where it is used clinically to reduce relapse frequency and slow disability progression in conditions such as relapsing-remitting disease and active secondary progressive presentations.

Name: Vemurafenib
Description: Vemurafenib (DB08881) is an orally active, small-molecule antineoplastic of the biaryl sulfonamide class built on a substituted azaindole/7-azaindole kinase-inhibitor scaffold, with halogenated aryl and propyl-sulfonamide features that promote selective binding to the ATP pocket of mutant BRAF; it is therefore chemically related to other RAF-directed agents such as dabrafenib and encorafenib, and more broadly to multikinase or MAPK-pathway inhibitors used in BRAF-driven cancers. Its principal target is BRAF, especially the activating BRAF V600E mutant, with activity also reported against BRAF V600K and downstream MAPK signaling, while paradoxical ERK activation can occur in BRAF wild-type cells. Pharmacokinetically, vemurafenib is administered orally, has relatively slow but meaningful absorption, high plasma protein binding and extensive tissue distribution, reaches steady state after repeated dosing, undergoes predominantly hepatic metabolism with CYP3A4 involvement plus conjugative pathways, and is eliminated mainly via the feces with minimal renal excretion. Clinically, it is indicated for unresectable or metastatic melanoma harboring BRAF V600 mutations and has also been used in Erdheim-Chester disease and other histiocytic neoplasms with BRAF V600 alterations. Toxicities include hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation, severe photosensitivity, dermatologic toxicity, arthralgia, fatigue, and secondary cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma or keratoacanthoma related to paradoxical MAPK activation; common adverse effects include rash, alopecia, pruritus, nausea, diarrhea, and palmar-plantar reactions. In practice, it is used as precision therapy after molecular confirmation of a BRAF V600 mutation, either alone or in modern settings alongside MEK-pathway strategies to improve disease control and mitigate resistance.

Name: Linagliptin
Description: Linagliptin (DrugBank DB08882) is an orally active xanthine-based dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor whose structure is defined by a purine-2,6-dione/xanthine core elaborated with a quinazoline-containing aromatic substituent and a butynyl side chain, giving a rigid, heteroaromatic, nitrogen-rich small molecule optimized for high-affinity binding to the DPP-4 catalytic site; chemically it is classified as a synthetic xanthine derivative and antidiabetic incretin enhancer, and its key scaffold can be described as a substituted xanthine fused functionally to a quinazoline-like heteroaryl pharmacophore. Similar drugs include other gliptins such as sitagliptin, saxagliptin, alogliptin, and vildagliptin, which share DPP-4 inhibition but differ in scaffold and elimination. Linagliptin targets DPP4/CD26 primarily, increasing endogenous GLP-1 and GIP activity to improve glucose-dependent insulin secretion and reduce glucagon release in type 2 diabetes mellitus. It has rapid oral absorption, high potency, extensive target-mediated and protein-associated distribution, minimal CYP-mediated metabolism, a long terminal half-life supporting once-daily dosing, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged via biliary/fecal routes with relatively little renal excretion, making dose adjustment in renal impairment generally unnecessary. Toxicity is usually low but includes rare hypersensitivity reactions, severe arthralgia, bullous pemphigoid, pancreatitis, and possible hepatic enzyme elevations; overdose experience suggests limited acute toxicity. Common adverse effects include nasopharyngitis, cough, diarrhea, and, especially with sulfonylureas or insulin, hypoglycemia. Clinically, it is used as monotherapy or in combination regimens for glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes, particularly in patients needing a renally sparing oral antihyperglycemic agent.

Name: Carfilzomib
Description: Carfilzomib (DrugBank DB08889) is a synthetic, tetrapeptide-derived epoxyketone proteasome inhibitor whose structure consists of a short peptidomimetic backbone capped by a highly electrophilic epoxyketone warhead, with hydrophobic amino acid side chains and morpholine-containing substituents that promote selective binding to the proteasome; chemically, it belongs to the epoxyketone peptide antineoplastic class and is built on a leucine-based peptide epoxyketone scaffold related to the natural-product lead epoxomicin. Similar drugs include other proteasome inhibitors such as bortezomib, ixazomib, and oprozomib, although carfilzomib is distinguished by its irreversible covalent inhibition. Its principal targets are the 20S proteasome catalytic beta subunits, especially PSMB5 (chymotrypsin-like), with activity also against PSMB8 and related immunoproteasome subunits, causing accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins, proteotoxic stress, and apoptosis in malignant plasma cells. Pharmacokinetically, carfilzomib is administered intravenously, has rapid systemic clearance, a very short plasma half-life, limited reliance on cytochrome P450 metabolism, extensive extrahepatic peptide hydrolysis and epoxide hydrolysis to inactive metabolites, broad tissue distribution, and elimination mainly as metabolites in urine. It is indicated primarily for relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma, including use in combination regimens with dexamethasone, lenalidomide, or daratumumab. Clinically important toxicities include cardiotoxicity with heart failure and ischemia, hypertension, renal injury, hepatotoxicity, infusion reactions, thrombocytopenia, anemia, dyspnea, fatigue, diarrhea, and peripheral edema; rare but serious events include thrombotic microangiopathy, tumor lysis syndrome, and posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome.

Name: Linaclotide
Description: Linaclotide (DB08890) is a synthetic 14-amino-acid peptide enteric secretagogue structurally modeled on the heat-stable enterotoxin peptide family, with a compact cystine-rich architecture containing three intramolecular disulfide bonds that constrain a guanylin-like peptide fold; chemically it is classified as a disulfide-bonded peptide agonist of intestinal guanylate cyclase, and its scaffold is best described as an STa/guanylin-uroguanylin-inspired cyclic-like cysteine-rich oligopeptide motif. Closely related or mechanistically similar drugs include plecanatide, another guanylate cyclase-C agonist peptide, while more distantly similar constipation therapies include lubiprostone, which differs chemically as a prostaglandin derivative. Its principal target is guanylate cyclase-C (GUCY2C) on the luminal surface of intestinal epithelial cells, increasing intracellular cGMP, stimulating CFTR-mediated chloride and bicarbonate secretion, reducing sodium absorption, accelerating transit, and diminishing visceral pain signaling. Pharmacokinetically, linaclotide has negligible oral systemic bioavailability, acts locally in the gastrointestinal lumen, is minimally distributed systemically, and is metabolized within the intestine by proteolytic loss of a terminal tyrosine to an active metabolite followed by further peptide degradation to small fragments and amino acids; plasma concentrations are generally unquantifiable and excretion is predominantly fecal as degraded peptide products. Its major dose-limiting toxicity is diarrhea, which can be severe enough to cause dehydration, hypotension, electrolyte disturbances, syncope, or hospitalization; pediatric toxicity concerns underlie a contraindication in very young children. Adverse effects include diarrhea, abdominal pain, flatulence, abdominal distension, fecal urgency, and headache. Clinically, it is used for irritable bowel syndrome with constipation and chronic idiopathic constipation, particularly in adults with hard stools, infrequent bowel movements, straining, bloating, and abdominal discomfort.

Name: Tofacitinib
Description: Tofacitinib (DrugBank DB08895) is a synthetic, orally active small-molecule Janus kinase inhibitor built around a substituted pyrrolo[2,3-d]pyrimidine heteroaromatic core bearing a piperidine-linked nitrile-containing side chain and a methyl substituent, a structure that places it in the aminopyrimidine-like kinase inhibitor class and more specifically among JAK-targeted immunomodulatory heterocycles; its key scaffold is the ATP-competitive fused bicyclic pyrrolopyrimidine pharmacophore, shared conceptually with related kinase inhibitors, and it is most similar therapeutically and mechanistically to other JAK inhibitors such as baricitinib, upadacitinib, ruxolitinib, and filgotinib. It primarily targets JAK1 and JAK3, with lesser activity against JAK2 and TYK2, thereby suppressing cytokine signaling through STAT pathways. Pharmacokinetically, it is well absorbed orally, reaches peak plasma concentrations within about 1 hour, has moderate protein binding, distributes systemically without extreme tissue sequestration, is metabolized predominantly by CYP3A4 and to a lesser extent CYP2C19, and is eliminated through both hepatic metabolism and renal excretion, with a short terminal half-life supporting once- or twice-daily use depending on formulation. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related immunosuppression, including serious infections such as herpes zoster, tuberculosis, and opportunistic fungal disease, as well as cytopenias, transaminase elevation, lipid increases, gastrointestinal perforation, major adverse cardiovascular events, thrombosis, and malignancy risk including lymphoma and non-melanoma skin cancer. Clinically, it is used for rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ulcerative colitis, polyarticular-course juvenile idiopathic arthritis, and in some regions ankylosing spondylitis, improving joint inflammation, pain, stiffness, and bowel symptoms; common adverse effects include upper respiratory infection, headache, diarrhea, nausea, hypertension, acneiform eruption, and laboratory abnormalities such as lymphopenia and anemia.

Name: Regorafenib
Description: Regorafenib (DrugBank DB08896) is an orally active halogenated biaryl urea multikinase inhibitor whose structure is centered on a diphenylurea scaffold linking two substituted aromatic rings, notably a fluorinated phenoxy pyridine-type ring system and a chlorinated trifluoromethyl-bearing phenyl moiety, a chemotype closely related to sorafenib and representative of the diaryl/biaryl urea kinase inhibitor class; similar drugs include sorafenib, lenvatinib, cabozantinib, and sunitinib, although regorafenib is particularly characterized by broad antiangiogenic, stromal, and oncogenic kinase inhibition. Its known targets include VEGFR1/FLT1, VEGFR2/KDR, VEGFR3/FLT4, TIE2/TEK, PDGFR, FGFR, KIT, RET, RAF1, BRAF including mutant forms, and CSF1R, supporting both anti-proliferative and anti-vascular activity. After oral administration it is absorbed with moderate bioavailability, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, is highly protein bound, distributes extensively, undergoes hepatic metabolism primarily via CYP3A4 oxidation and UGT1A9 glucuronidation to active metabolites including the N-oxide and N-desmethyl N-oxide species, and is eliminated mainly in feces with limited renal excretion and an effective half-life permitting once-daily dosing. Toxicity is clinically significant and includes hepatotoxicity with severe liver injury, hypertension, hemorrhage, gastrointestinal perforation, impaired wound healing, myocardial ischemia, and severe dermatologic toxicity such as hand-foot skin reaction. Approved clinical use includes metastatic colorectal cancer, advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumor after failure of imatinib and sunitinib, and previously treated hepatocellular carcinoma, with common adverse effects including fatigue, diarrhea, mucositis, anorexia, weight loss, dysphonia, rash, and palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia.

Name: Aclidinium
Description: Aclidinium bromide (DB08897) is a synthetic quaternary ammonium antimuscarinic bronchodilator whose structure is built around a substituted quinuclidine/tropane-like bicyclic cationic core linked through an ester to a hydroxy-diphenylacetate-type aromatic moiety, giving a permanently charged, lipophilic muscarinic antagonist optimized for inhalation; chemically it belongs to the long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) class and more broadly to quaternary ammonium anticholinergics, with a scaffold closely related to other inhaled bronchodilators such as tiotropium, ipratropium, umeclidinium, and glycopyrronium. Its principal targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially M3 (CHRM3) in airway smooth muscle, with additional binding to M1 (CHRM1) and M2 (CHRM2), producing prolonged bronchodilation by blocking vagally mediated bronchoconstriction. After oral inhalation, pulmonary deposition drives local activity while systemic absorption is limited; any absorbed drug is rapidly hydrolyzed in plasma to inactive alcohol and carboxylic acid metabolites, resulting in low bioavailability, modest distribution because of its permanent positive charge, minimal CYP involvement, and elimination mainly as metabolites in urine and feces with a short systemic half-life despite sustained receptor residence in the lung. It is indicated for maintenance treatment of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, including chronic bronchitis and emphysema, improving airflow limitation, dyspnea, and exacerbation-related symptom burden, but it is not intended for acute bronchospasm relief. Toxicity is primarily anticholinergic and usually mild because of low systemic exposure, but overdose or susceptible patients may develop dry mouth, tachycardia, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation, angle-closure glaucoma precipitation, or paradoxical bronchospasm; common adverse effects include dry mouth, nasopharyngitis, headache, cough, diarrhea, and sinusitis. Clinically, aclidinium is used as a twice-daily maintenance inhaler, often in patients needing durable symptom control or in fixed combinations with long-acting beta2-agonists for persistent COPD symptoms.

Name: Enzalutamide
Description: Enzalutamide (DB08899) is a nonsteroidal second-generation antiandrogen characterized structurally by a diaryl thiohydantoin-derived architecture centered on a 2-thioxo-imidazolidin-4-one core bearing substituted aryl groups, notably a fluorobenzamide-like aryl system and a dimethyl-substituted heteroaryl moiety that together create a rigid, lipophilic androgen-receptor-binding pharmacophore; chemically it is classified as an androgen receptor antagonist and aryl thiohydantoin derivative, with a thiohydantoin/diaryl scaffold shared conceptually with other androgen-signaling inhibitors. Similar drugs include apalutamide, which is closely related structurally and mechanistically, darolutamide, and older antiandrogens such as bicalutamide, flutamide, and nilutamide. Its principal target is the androgen receptor (NR3C4), which it inhibits by blocking androgen binding, receptor nuclear translocation, DNA binding, and coactivator recruitment. Orally administered enzalutamide is well absorbed, highly protein bound, widely distributed, penetrates the CNS, is metabolized mainly by CYP2C8 and CYP3A4 to the active metabolite N-desmethyl enzalutamide and an inactive carboxylic acid metabolite, has a long terminal half-life permitting once-daily dosing, and is eliminated predominantly in urine as metabolites with minor fecal excretion. It is indicated for metastatic and nonmetastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer. Clinically, it is used alone with ongoing androgen-deprivation therapy in patients with biochemical progression, radiographic progression, or metastatic burden. Toxicities include dose-related fatigue, hypertension, falls, fractures, cognitive effects, and a recognized seizure risk likely related to CNS exposure; additional adverse effects include hot flushes, asthenia, diarrhea, musculoskeletal pain, headache, and rare posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome or major cardiovascular events.

Name: Ponatinib
Description: Ponatinib (DrugBank DB08901) is a synthetic, orally active small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor built on a rigid diaryl-ethynyl scaffold featuring an imidazo[1,2-b]pyridazine heteroaromatic core linked through a carbon-carbon triple bond to a substituted methylpiperazine-containing aniline, a design that enables high-affinity binding to the ATP pocket of kinases including sterically hindered mutants. Chemically, it is best classified as a multitarget aminopyridazine/heteroaryl ethynyl kinase inhibitor, and its scaffold is closely related in concept to other BCR-ABL TKIs, with functionally similar drugs including imatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib, bosutinib, and asciminib, although ponatinib is particularly notable for activity against the T315I gatekeeper mutation. Its principal targets are BCR-ABL1 and mutant ABL1 variants, and it also inhibits VEGFR2/KDR, FGFR1-4, PDGFR, KIT, FLT3, RET, SRC-family kinases, and others. It is indicated primarily for resistant or intolerant chronic myeloid leukemia and Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia, especially in T315I-positive disease. After oral administration, absorption is adequate, distribution is extensive with high protein binding, metabolism occurs predominantly via hepatic CYP3A4 with lesser contributions from other CYPs and esterases, and elimination is mainly fecal with limited renal excretion and a terminal half-life supporting once-daily dosing. Its major toxicities include arterial occlusive events, venous thromboembolism, hypertension, heart failure, hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, hemorrhage, and myelosuppression. Common adverse effects include rash, abdominal pain, nausea, constipation, fatigue, headache, elevated lipase, thrombocytopenia, anemia, and neutropenia. Clinically, ponatinib is used as a later-line precision TKI in molecularly defined leukemias, often after failure of prior TKIs or when mutation-driven resistance necessitates potent pan-BCR-ABL inhibition.

Name: Bedaquiline
Description: Bedaquiline (DB08903) is a lipophilic diarylquinoline antimycobacterial agent whose structure is centered on a substituted quinoline ring linked to a phenyl-containing tertiary alcohol framework and a dimethylamino side chain, giving a rigid aromatic, cationic, amphiphilic architecture associated with high tissue penetration and prolonged retention; chemically it belongs to the quinoline/diarylquinoline class, with a diarylquinoline scaffold distinct from rifamycins, fluoroquinolones, and oxazolidinones, although functionally it is used alongside similar anti-tubercular drugs such as linezolid, clofazimine, delamanid, pretomanid, moxifloxacin, and rifampin in resistant disease settings. Its principal target is mycobacterial ATP synthase, specifically the c subunit of the proton pump rotor encoded by atpE, leading to collapse of energy production in Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Pharmacokinetically, oral absorption is enhanced by food, distribution is extensive with high protein binding and a very large apparent volume of distribution, metabolism occurs mainly through CYP3A4 to the less active N-monodesmethyl metabolite M2, and elimination is predominantly fecal with an exceptionally long terminal half-life reflecting slow tissue release. Toxicity is notable for QT-interval prolongation, hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevation, and increased risk when combined with other QT-prolonging or CYP3A4-modulating drugs; examples include arrhythmia risk with clofazimine or fluoroquinolones and altered exposure with rifamycins or azoles. Adverse effects include nausea, arthralgia, headache, dizziness, hemoptysis, and hepatic enzyme abnormalities. Clinically, bedaquiline is indicated for multidrug-resistant and extensively drug-resistant pulmonary tuberculosis, and is used as part of combination regimens such as bedaquiline-linezolid-pretomanid or longer WHO-based background regimens for refractory mycobacterial disease.

Name: Formestane
Description: Formestane (DrugBank DB08905) is a steroidal aromatase inhibitor built on an androstane nucleus, structurally characterized as 4-hydroxyandrost-4-ene-3,17-dione, with a rigid four-ring cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene scaffold, a 3,17-dione functionality, and a 4-hydroxyl substitution that supports high affinity for the aromatase active site; chemically it belongs to the steroidal endocrine antineoplastic agents and is often grouped with type I, irreversible aromatase inactivators. Its core scaffold and mechanism make it closely related to other steroidal aromatase inhibitors such as exemestane, and pharmacologically analogous though not structurally identical to nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitors including anastrozole and letrozole. Its principal target protein is aromatase, the cytochrome P450 enzyme CYP19A1, leading to suppression of peripheral conversion of androstenedione and testosterone to estrogens. Formestane has historically been administered mainly by intramuscular depot injection, with systemic absorption from the injection site, distribution expected to favor lipophilic tissues and plasma protein binding typical of steroids, hepatic metabolism to steroid metabolites including 4-hydroxytestosterone, and excretion primarily via urine with some fecal elimination. Toxicity is largely endocrine and steroid-related rather than acutely cytotoxic, with examples including hypoestrogenism, androgenic effects, and potential hepatic enzyme abnormalities. Adverse effects include hot flashes, sweating, nausea, fatigue, injection-site reactions, acne, hirsutism, menstrual disturbance, and decreased libido. Clinically, it has been used mainly for estrogen-dependent breast cancer in postmenopausal women, especially advanced or recurrent disease, and has also been explored in settings where estrogen suppression is therapeutically desirable.

Name: Fluticasone furoate
Description: Fluticasone furoate (DB08906) is a highly lipophilic synthetic trifluorinated corticosteroid ester characterized by the classical pregnane steroid nucleus with fused four-ring corticosteroid scaffold, a 6α-fluoro substituent, 9α-fluoro functionality, 11β-hydroxyl, 16α-methyl group, 17β-thioester side chain, and a bulky furoate ester at C17 that increases glucocorticoid receptor affinity and tissue retention; chemically it is a halogenated corticosteroid, specifically an inhaled and intranasal glucocorticoid, built on the corticosteroid/pregnane scaffold and closely related to fluticasone propionate, mometasone furoate, budesonide, beclomethasone dipropionate, and ciclesonide. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, with downstream transrepression of NF-κB- and AP-1-driven inflammatory signaling and reduced production of cytokines, eosinophil mediators, and chemokines. After intranasal or inhaled administration, systemic absorption is low because of limited gastrointestinal bioavailability and marked first-pass metabolism; distribution is extensive with high plasma protein binding, metabolism occurs predominantly via CYP3A4 to inactive metabolites, and excretion is mainly in feces with minimal renal elimination. Toxicity is largely class-related and dose dependent: local irritation, epistaxis, dysphonia, and oropharyngeal candidiasis are common examples, while excessive systemic exposure may cause adrenal suppression, growth suppression in children, reduced bone mineral density, cataracts, glaucoma, hypercorticism, and increased infection risk. It is indicated for allergic rhinitis, nonallergic rhinitis, asthma maintenance therapy, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in combination products; clinically it is used as intranasal monotherapy for nasal congestion, sneezing, and rhinorrhea, and as inhaled therapy, often with vilanterol, for persistent asthma or COPD symptom control.

Name: Canagliflozin
Description: Canagliflozin (DrugBank DB08907) is a small-molecule C-aryl glucoside antidiabetic agent whose structure consists of a β-D-glucopyranose core linked through a carbon-carbon bond to a lipophilic substituted phenyl/thiophene-containing aryl system, a design that confers resistance to enzymatic cleavage compared with O-glucosides; chemically it is classified as a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor within the broader class of glycosides and diarylmethane-like aryl-glucosides, and its core scaffold is a C-glucoside attached to a heteroaryl-substituted aromatic ring. Similar drugs include other SGLT2 inhibitors such as dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, ertugliflozin, and sotagliflozin, which share glucoside-based scaffolds and promote urinary glucose excretion. Its primary targets are SLC5A2 (SGLT2) in the renal proximal tubule and, with lower potency, SLC5A1 (SGLT1). After oral administration, canagliflozin is well absorbed, reaches peak concentrations within a few hours, is highly protein bound, undergoes limited oxidative metabolism but predominantly UGT1A9- and UGT2B4-mediated O-glucuronidation to inactive metabolites, and is eliminated through both fecal and renal routes with a terminal half-life supporting once-daily dosing. It is indicated for type 2 diabetes mellitus to improve glycemic control and is also used to reduce risk of major cardiovascular events and slow diabetic kidney disease progression in appropriate patients. Adverse effects include genital mycotic infections, urinary tract infections, polyuria, volume depletion, hypotension, and increased LDL cholesterol; important toxicities include euglycemic ketoacidosis, acute kidney injury, hyperkalemia, bone fracture risk, and the historically noted increased risk of lower-limb amputation. Clinically, it is used as monotherapy or in combination with metformin, insulin, or other antihyperglycemics, particularly in patients needing glucose lowering with added cardiorenal benefit.

Name: Dimethyl fumarate
Description: Dimethyl fumarate (DrugBank DB08908) is a small, symmetrical methyl ester of fumaric acid characterized structurally by an electron-deficient trans-alkene flanked by two ester groups, making it a reactive alpha,beta-unsaturated dicarboxylic acid ester and a classic Michael acceptor; chemically it belongs to the fumaric acid ester class, with a simple fumarate scaffold that is shared with related agents such as monomethyl fumarate, diroximel fumarate, and older mixed fumaric acid ester formulations used in psoriasis. After oral administration, dimethyl fumarate is rapidly presystemically hydrolyzed by esterases to the active metabolite monomethyl fumarate, so parent drug exposure is low; absorption is oral, distribution is systemic with no major plasma accumulation of parent compound, metabolism proceeds mainly through the tricarboxylic acid pathway rather than CYP-dependent oxidation, and elimination occurs predominantly as exhaled carbon dioxide with minor renal and fecal excretion of metabolites. Its pharmacology is linked to covalent modification of cysteine-containing proteins and activation of the NFE2L2/NRF2 antioxidant pathway via KEAP1, with additional immunomodulatory effects involving HCAR2, NF-kappaB-related signaling, and reduced proinflammatory lymphocyte activity. Clinically, it is indicated for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis and is also used in some regions for plaque psoriasis. Important adverse effects include flushing, abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, rash, and lymphopenia; notable toxicities include hepatotoxicity, proteinuria, rare progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in the setting of prolonged lymphopenia, hypersensitivity, and opportunistic infection risk. In practice, it is used as an oral disease-modifying therapy to reduce relapse frequency and MRI lesion activity in multiple sclerosis and to improve inflammatory skin disease burden in psoriasis.

Name: Glycerol phenylbutyrate
Description: Glycerol phenylbutyrate (DrugBank DB08909) is an orally administered triglyceride-like prodrug in which all three hydroxyl groups of glycerol are esterified with phenylbutyric acid residues, giving a neutral, lipophilic triester built on a glycerol backbone with terminal phenyl rings and flexible aliphatic linkers; chemically it is classified as an aromatic fatty acid ester and specifically a nitrogen-scavenging prodrug, with a glycerol triester/phenyl-substituted short-chain fatty acid scaffold. It is closely related to sodium phenylbutyrate and sodium benzoate, and mechanistically to other ammonia-lowering agents such as carglumic acid, although glycerol phenylbutyrate itself acts mainly as a prodrug rather than a receptor ligand. After oral administration it is hydrolyzed by pancreatic lipases to phenylbutyrate, absorbed enterally, extensively converted by mitochondrial beta-oxidation to phenylacetate, and then conjugated primarily with glutamine via glycine N-acyltransferase–associated nitrogen disposal pathways to form phenylacetylglutamine, which is excreted in urine; distribution is largely systemic through its metabolites, and renal elimination of the conjugate is the major excretory route. Its principal functional target is excess systemic ammonia and glutamine handling rather than a classical high-affinity protein target, though pancreatic triglyceride lipase and conjugation enzymes are relevant to disposition. It is indicated for chronic management of urea cycle disorders, including ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency, and argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency, to reduce recurrent hyperammonemia. Adverse effects commonly include diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, decreased appetite, fatigue, and headache, while important toxicities include neurotoxicity from phenylacetate accumulation, worsening hyperammonemia if underdosed, and caution in pancreatic insufficiency, hepatic impairment, or overdose; clinically it is used as long-term maintenance therapy with dietary protein restriction and amino acid supplementation in patients requiring ongoing ammonia control.

Name: Trametinib
Description: Trametinib (DB08911) is a small-molecule, orally active, allosteric mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase inhibitor whose structure is characterized by a highly halogenated heteroaromatic core incorporating a pyridopyrimidinone-like fused aza-heterocycle linked through an anilide-type connector to substituted aromatic and heterocyclic moieties, giving a rigid, lipophilic kinase-directed pharmacophore; chemically it is best categorized as a targeted antineoplastic heteroaryl amide/urea-like kinase inhibitor, and its scaffold is most usefully described as a fused aza-heterocyclic MEK-inhibitor scaffold related to other MAPK-pathway agents. Similar drugs include other MEK inhibitors such as cobimetinib, binimetinib, and selumetinib, and it is commonly paired mechanistically with BRAF inhibitors such as dabrafenib. Its principal targets are MAP2K1/MEK1 and MAP2K2/MEK2, suppressing ERK-pathway signaling in RAS/RAF-driven tumors. Pharmacokinetically, trametinib is orally absorbed, reaches peak concentrations in hours, has high protein binding and a large apparent distribution, undergoes predominantly deacetylation with secondary conjugative biotransformation rather than major CYP-dependent oxidation, and is eliminated slowly with a terminal half-life of about 4 to 5 days, with excretion mainly via feces and lesser urinary recovery. It is indicated for BRAF V600-mutant unresectable or metastatic melanoma, adjuvant melanoma, BRAF V600E-mutant metastatic non-small cell lung cancer, and anaplastic thyroid cancer, among other MAPK-driven settings, usually with dabrafenib. Toxicities include cardiomyopathy, retinal pigment epithelial detachment, interstitial lung disease, severe rash, hemorrhage, colitis, hepatotoxicity, and pyrexia; common adverse effects include acneiform dermatitis, diarrhea, edema, fatigue, hypertension, stomatitis, and nail toxicity. Clinically, it is used as precision therapy to inhibit MAPK signaling alone or, more often, in combination regimens to improve response durability and delay resistance.

Name: Dabrafenib
Description: Dabrafenib (DB08912) is an orally active, ATP-competitive small-molecule kinase inhibitor whose structure is defined by a substituted aminopyrimidine core linked to a thiazole-containing heteroaromatic system and a sulfonamide-bearing aryl region, giving a lipophilic, heteroatom-rich architecture optimized for mutant BRAF binding; chemically it is a synthetic heteroaryl sulfonamide and aminopyrimidine antineoplastic agent, and its dominant scaffold is the 2-aminopyrimidine kinase-inhibitor pharmacophore. It is closely related in therapeutic class to other BRAF inhibitors such as vemurafenib and encorafenib, and is often discussed alongside MEK inhibitors such as trametinib because of combination use. Its principal targets are mutant BRAF serine/threonine kinase, especially BRAF V600E and V600K, with lesser activity against wild-type BRAF and CRAF/RAF1 in some contexts, thereby suppressing MAPK/ERK signaling. After oral administration it is absorbed with peak concentrations in about 2 hours, food reduces exposure, it is highly protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP2C8 and CYP3A4 to active metabolites including hydroxy- and desmethyl-dabrafenib, and is eliminated predominantly in feces with a smaller urinary fraction; the terminal half-life is roughly 8 hours. Toxicities include pyrexia, cutaneous toxicity, hyperglycemia, hepatotoxicity, uveitis, QT-related concern, and paradoxical MAPK activation causing secondary cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. Clinically it is used for BRAF V600-mutant unresectable or metastatic melanoma, adjuvant melanoma, metastatic non-small cell lung cancer, anaplastic thyroid cancer, and certain solid tumors such as low-grade glioma, commonly in combination with trametinib; frequent adverse effects include fever, fatigue, rash, arthralgia, headache, nausea, diarrhea, alopecia, and palmar-plantar reactions.

Name: Radium Ra 223 dichloride
Description: Radium Ra 223 dichloride (DB08913) is a radiopharmaceutical consisting of the divalent alkaline-earth metal radionuclide radium-223 paired with two chloride counterions in a simple ionic salt; structurally it is best understood not through an organic pharmacophore but as a calcium-mimetic alpha-emitting metal complex precursor that dissociates in vivo to Ra2+, placing it in the chemical category of therapeutic radiometals and bone-seeking radiopharmaceuticals, with an inorganic radionuclide scaffold rather than a classical small-molecule scaffold. Similar agents include other bone-targeted radiopharmaceuticals such as strontium-89 chloride, samarium-153 lexidronam, phosphorus-32 sodium phosphate, and the beta-emitter lutetium-177-based targeted radiotherapies by therapeutic analogy. After intravenous administration, it is not orally bioavailable; it rapidly clears from blood, distributes predominantly to areas of increased osteoblastic activity by incorporation into hydroxyapatite at bone metastasis surfaces, undergoes no enzymatic metabolism, and is eliminated mainly unchanged through the intestine and feces with relatively limited renal excretion. Its pharmacologic effect is mediated by high-linear-energy-transfer alpha particle emission causing localized irreparable double-strand DNA damage and tumor cell death in the bone microenvironment rather than binding a conventional protein target, so no specific target protein is established, though the functional target compartment is mineralized bone adjacent to metastatic cells. It is indicated for castration-resistant prostate cancer with symptomatic bone metastases and no known visceral metastatic disease, and clinically used to reduce skeletal tumor burden and improve survival. Key toxicities include myelosuppression such as anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia, along with gastrointestinal toxicity including nausea, diarrhea, and vomiting; adverse effects also include bone pain, peripheral edema, and less commonly severe marrow failure or increased fracture risk, especially when combined with certain hormonal agents.

Name: Afatinib
Description: Afatinib (DrugBank DB08916) is an orally active, small-molecule anilino-quinazoline derivative whose structure features a 4-anilinoquinazoline heteroaromatic core, dimethylamino-substituted side chain, and a reactive crotonamide-based Michael acceptor that enables covalent target engagement; chemically it is classified as a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, specifically an irreversible ErbB family blocker, built on the classic quinazoline EGFR-inhibitor scaffold. Similar drugs include other EGFR/ErbB inhibitors such as gefitinib, erlotinib, dacomitinib, osimertinib, and the dual EGFR/HER2 agent lapatinib, with dacomitinib being especially close in irreversible pan-ErbB design. Afatinib targets EGFR/ERBB1, HER2/ERBB2, and HER4/ERBB4 directly, and also suppresses signaling from transphosphorylated HER3/ERBB3-containing dimers. After oral administration it is absorbed with peak concentrations typically within a few hours, has moderate bioavailability limited somewhat by transporter effects and food, is highly protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes minimal CYP-mediated metabolism because much of its chemistry reflects covalent adduct formation rather than oxidative biotransformation, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged via feces with lesser renal excretion; its terminal half-life supports once-daily dosing. Toxicity is dominated by mechanism-based epithelial injury, particularly severe diarrhea, acneiform rash, stomatitis, paronychia, dehydration, renal impairment secondary to fluid loss, and less commonly interstitial lung disease, hepatotoxicity, and ocular toxicity. It is indicated mainly for EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer, including metastatic tumors with exon 19 deletions or L858R substitutions, and has also been used in squamous NSCLC. Clinically, afatinib is used as first-line or subsequent targeted therapy to inhibit oncogenic ErbB signaling, shrink tumors, and delay progression, with common adverse effects including rash, diarrhea, mucositis, decreased appetite, and nail changes.

Name: Levomilnacipran
Description: Levomilnacipran (DrugBank DB08918) is the levorotatory enantiomer of milnacipran and is a small, conformationally restricted phenethylamine antidepressant built around a cyclopropane-containing carboxamide scaffold, specifically a 1-phenyl-1-carbamoylmethyl-2-aminomethylcyclopropane framework bearing a dimethylamino side chain; chemically it is classified as a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor and more broadly as an aminomethyl cyclopropane derivative. Its scaffold and pharmacology resemble those of milnacipran most closely, with broader mechanistic similarity to other SNRIs such as venlafaxine, desvenlafaxine, duloxetine, and sibutramine-like monoamine uptake inhibitors, although levomilnacipran is relatively more noradrenergically selective than many comparators. Its principal targets are the norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2 and serotonin transporter SLC6A4, with negligible clinically relevant activity at muscarinic, histaminergic, or adrenergic receptors, helping limit off-target receptor burden. After oral administration it is well absorbed with high bioavailability, reaches peak concentrations within hours, shows low to moderate protein binding and broad tissue distribution, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4-mediated pathways including desethylation, and is excreted predominantly in urine as unchanged drug and metabolites, giving a half-life compatible with once-daily extended-release dosing. It is indicated for major depressive disorder, especially episodes marked by low energy, impaired concentration, and anhedonia. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, constipation, hyperhidrosis, tachycardia, palpitations, urinary hesitation, erectile or ejaculatory dysfunction, insomnia, and increased blood pressure; serious toxicity can include serotonin syndrome, suicidality in younger patients, angle-closure glaucoma precipitation, hepatically modest but possible overdose-related CNS and cardiovascular effects, and discontinuation symptoms if abruptly stopped. Clinically, it is used as an extended-release oral antidepressant in adults, particularly when a noradrenergic emphasis is desired or when other first-line antidepressants are ineffective or poorly tolerated.

Name: Perospirone
Description: Perospirone (DrugBank DB08922) is an atypical antipsychotic of the arylpiperazine/azaspirodecanedione class whose structure features a rigid spiro-fused cyclic imide-like core linked through a butyl chain to a substituted piperazine, yielding a serotonin-dopamine antagonist framework characteristic of several modern psychotropics; its principal scaffold is an arylpiperazine tethered to a spirocyclic lactam-dione nucleus. It is chemically and pharmacologically related to other serotonin-dopamine modulators such as buspirone, gepirone, tandospirone, and atypical antipsychotics including risperidone and ziprasidone by virtue of shared piperazine-containing recognition elements and high serotonergic affinity. Perospirone is administered orally, is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, undergoes hepatic first-pass metabolism, distributes systemically with central nervous system penetration, is metabolized mainly by CYP3A4 to active and inactive metabolites including 1-(2-pyrimidinyl)piperazine, and is eliminated largely as urinary metabolites with lesser fecal excretion. Its major targets include serotonin 5-HT2A, 5-HT1A, dopamine D2, and alpha1-adrenergic receptors, with antipsychotic efficacy attributed primarily to 5-HT2A/D2 antagonism and partial 5-HT1A agonist activity. It is indicated chiefly for schizophrenia, especially positive symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions, and may also help anxiety, agitation, and affective symptoms. Adverse effects include akathisia, tremor, parkinsonism, somnolence, dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, dry mouth, constipation, and weight gain; toxicities include extrapyramidal symptoms, hyperprolactinemia, QT-related cardiac risk, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, seizures, and overdose-related CNS depression. Clinically, it has been used in Japan as an oral antipsychotic for acute and maintenance treatment of schizophrenia, particularly when a serotonin-dopamine antagonist with anxiolytic 5-HT1A activity is desired.

Name: Riociguat
Description: Riociguat (DrugBank DB08931) is a small-molecule soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator built around a nitrogen-rich fused heteroaromatic pyrazolo[3,4-b]pyridine core linked through an amino substituent to a fluorobenzyl moiety and a methyl carbamate-containing side chain, giving a lipophilic, weakly basic heterocycle optimized for oral activity. Chemically it is categorized as an sGC stimulator and heteroaromatic carbamate; its principal scaffold is the aminopyrazolopyridine pharmacophore. Related drugs include the sGC stimulator vericiguat and, mechanistically though not structurally, phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil and tadalafil used in overlapping pulmonary vascular disease settings. Riociguat is orally absorbed with high bioavailability, reaches peak plasma levels in roughly 1-2 hours, is moderately to highly protein bound, distributes systemically to vascular tissues, and undergoes hepatic metabolism primarily via CYP1A1, CYP3A4, CYP2C8, and CYP2J2 to an active N-demethylated metabolite, with elimination through both renal and biliary/fecal routes and a terminal half-life of about 7 hours in healthy subjects and longer in patients. Its main toxicity is extension of pharmacologic vasodilation, causing dose-dependent hypotension, syncope, headache, dizziness, and bleeding risk including hemoptysis; embryo-fetal toxicity is a major concern, and it is contraindicated with nitrates or nitric oxide donors because of profound hypotension. The key target is soluble guanylate cyclase, stimulating cGMP generation independently of and synergistically with nitric oxide. Clinically it is indicated for pulmonary arterial hypertension and chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension to improve exercise capacity, functional class, and hemodynamics, with common adverse effects including dyspepsia, gastroesophageal reflux, nausea, diarrhea, peripheral edema, and nasal congestion.

Name: Macitentan
Description: Macitentan (DrugBank DB08932) is an orally active dual endothelin receptor antagonist whose structure is characterized by a lipophilic sulfamide-substituted heteroaromatic framework containing a substituted pyrimidine core linked to a bromophenyl group and an alkoxy side chain, giving a compact, conformationally restricted small molecule optimized for tissue penetration and sustained receptor binding. Chemically, it belongs to the endothelin receptor antagonist class and more broadly to aryl-sulfamide heterocyclic agents; its key scaffold is a substituted diaryl-heteroaryl sulfamide/pharmacophore related to other endothelin antagonists. Similar drugs include bosentan, ambrisentan, and sitaxsentan, although macitentan is distinguished by slower receptor dissociation and active metabolite formation. It targets endothelin receptor type A and type B, encoded by EDNRA and EDNRB, thereby reducing endothelin-1-mediated vasoconstriction and vascular remodeling. Pharmacokinetically, it is well absorbed after oral administration, highly protein bound, distributes into tissues effectively, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 with lesser CYP2C8, CYP2C9, and CYP2C19 contribution to form the active metabolite aprocitentan, and is eliminated through both fecal and renal routes, with a parent half-life of roughly 16 hours and a longer metabolite half-life. It is indicated for pulmonary arterial hypertension, including idiopathic, heritable, and connective-tissue-disease-associated PAH, to reduce morbidity and delay clinical worsening. Major toxicities include embryo-fetal toxicity, hepatotoxic potential, anemia, hypotension, and fluid retention; adverse effects commonly include headache, nasopharyngitis, bronchitis, anemia, urinary tract infection, and edema. Clinically, it is used as chronic oral PAH therapy either alone or in combination with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors or prostacyclin-pathway agents in patients with symptomatic WHO group 1 pulmonary arterial hypertension.

Name: Luliconazole
Description: Luliconazole (DrugBank DB08933) is a topical imidazole-derived antifungal whose structure is characterized by a chiral dithioacetal-linked aromatic system containing a 1,3-dithiolane scaffold attached to a substituted phenyl ring and an imidazole moiety, a design that confers high lipophilicity and strong affinity for fungal sterol biosynthetic enzymes; chemically it is classified as an azole antifungal, more specifically an imidazole, built on an imidazole–dithioacetal aryl scaffold related to other topical azoles such as lanoconazole, efinaconazole, ketoconazole, clotrimazole, miconazole, and luliconazole’s parent stereochemical series. Its principal target is fungal lanosterol 14alpha-demethylase, the CYP51 enzyme encoded by ERG11/CYP51, leading to inhibition of ergosterol synthesis, disruption of membrane integrity, and potent activity against dermatophytes including Trichophyton rubrum and Trichophyton mentagrophytes. It is indicated primarily for superficial dermatophyte infections such as interdigital tinea pedis, tinea cruris, and tinea corporis, and clinically is used as a once-daily topical cream with examples including short-course treatment of athlete’s foot, jock itch, and ringworm. Pharmacokinetically, systemic absorption after topical administration is low but measurable, with drug concentrating in the stratum corneum and superficial epidermis, minimal distribution beyond skin under usual use, hepatic metabolism expected for absorbed fractions via oxidative pathways typical of azoles, and excretion presumed mainly as metabolites through biliary/fecal and urinary routes. Toxicity is generally limited to local intolerance rather than systemic azole toxicity, with examples including application-site dermatitis, erythema, pruritus, burning, pain, vesiculation, and rare hypersensitivity or irritant contact reactions.

Name: Sofosbuvir
Description: Sofosbuvir (DrugBank DB08934) is a uridine nucleotide analog prodrug built on a modified ribofuranose nucleoside framework bearing a 2-fluoro-2-C-methyl substitution and a phosphoramidate ProTide moiety that masks the monophosphate with ester and amino acid-derived groups to enhance intracellular delivery; chemically, it is an antiviral direct-acting agent in the nucleoside/nucleotide analog class, with a phosphoramidate pyrimidine scaffold related to other HCV polymerase inhibitors. Similar drugs include other NS5B-directed antivirals such as dasabuvir, as well as nucleotide or nucleoside analog antivirals like remdesivir and ribavirin in broader mechanistic analogy. After oral administration, sofosbuvir is well absorbed, undergoes extensive first-pass and intracellular activation by sequential hydrolysis and phosphorylation to the active uridine triphosphate analog GS-461203, is distributed systemically with plasma predominance of the inactive circulating metabolite GS-331007, shows limited intact-parent persistence, and is eliminated mainly renally as GS-331007, with a shorter parent half-life and longer metabolite half-life; severe renal impairment increases exposure to metabolites. Its principal target is the hepatitis C virus NS5B RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, which incorporates the analog and causes chain termination of viral RNA synthesis. It is indicated for chronic hepatitis C infection across multiple genotypes, including use in genotype 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6 disease in combination regimens, for example with velpatasvir or ledipasvir. Toxicity is generally modest but includes fatigue, headache, nausea, insomnia, anemia in ribavirin-containing regimens, and clinically important bradycardia when coadministered with amiodarone; clinical use centers on curative oral combination therapy for chronic HCV, including compensated cirrhosis and selected post-transplant or HIV/HCV-coinfected patients.

Name: Chlorcyclizine
Description: Chlorcyclizine (DrugBank DB08936) is a first-generation H1-antihistamine of the piperazine class whose structure is characterized by a diarylmethyl-substituted piperazine scaffold, specifically a benzhydryl center bearing chlorinated aryl substituents linked to a tertiary piperazine nitrogen, a motif that confers lipophilicity, central nervous system penetration, and anticholinergic activity; chemically it belongs to the ethanolamine/piperazine-like sedating antihistamine family and is closely related to cyclizine, meclizine, hydroxyzine, and buclizine, which share the same antihistaminic diaryl-substituted amine pharmacophore. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor (HRH1), with additional clinically relevant off-target muscarinic cholinergic receptor antagonism that contributes to antiemetic and vestibular-suppressant effects. Chlorcyclizine is used for symptomatic relief of allergic disorders such as seasonal allergic rhinitis, urticaria, pruritus, and other histamine-mediated upper respiratory symptoms, and has also been used for nausea, vomiting, and motion sickness. After oral administration it is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, distributes widely into tissues including the brain because of its lipophilic tertiary amine character, undergoes hepatic biotransformation with first-pass metabolism likely involving cytochrome P450-mediated oxidation and conjugation, and is eliminated predominantly as metabolites in urine with some biliary/fecal excretion. Toxicity is typical of sedating antihistamines and includes dose-related CNS depression, impaired psychomotor performance, confusion, anticholinergic toxicity with dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention, while overdose may cause marked somnolence, agitation, tachycardia, and rarely seizures or cardiac conduction effects. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, xerostomia, gastrointestinal discomfort, and reduced alertness; clinically it has been used as an oral antiallergic and antiemetic agent when sedation is acceptable or beneficial.

Name: Isoxsuprine
Description: Isoxsuprine (DrugBank DB08941) is a synthetic phenoxyethylamine vasodilator structurally characterized by a substituted aromatic ring linked through an ether bond to a beta-amino alcohol side chain, giving it a flexible aryl-oxy-propanolamine/phenethylamine-like architecture with a secondary amine and hydroxyl functionality that support adrenergic receptor interactions; chemically it is classified as a sympathomimetic peripheral vasodilator and uterine relaxant, and its core scaffold is best described as a phenoxyalkanolamine related to beta-adrenergic agonist pharmacophores. Similar drugs include other beta-adrenergic or vasodilatory agents such as ritodrine, terbutaline, nylidrin, and to some extent isoxylsuprine-like peripheral vasodilators historically used in vascular insufficiency. Its pharmacology is attributed mainly to beta-adrenergic agonist activity, with functional effects at beta-2 adrenergic receptor pathways and possible smooth-muscle relaxation involving ADRB2 and related downstream cAMP signaling systems; alpha-adrenergic antagonistic or direct myometrial/vascular smooth-muscle relaxant effects have also been described. Oral absorption is generally adequate but variable, distribution is systemic with access to vascular and uterine smooth muscle, metabolism is predominantly hepatic, likely via oxidative and conjugative pathways, and excretion occurs mainly in urine as metabolites. Adverse effects and toxicity reflect sympathomimetic vasodilation, including tachycardia, palpitations, hypotension, flushing, dizziness, tremor, nausea, and weakness, while overdose may produce marked cardiovascular instability or arrhythmia. Clinically, it has been used for peripheral vascular disease such as cerebral or peripheral arterial insufficiency, Raynaud-like vasospasm, and as a tocolytic to suppress premature uterine contractions, although its modern use is limited.

Name: Inositol nicotinate
Description: Inositol nicotinate (DrugBank DB08949) is a niacin ester prodrug consisting of a cyclohexane-like myo-inositol core whose six hydroxyl groups are esterified with nicotinic acid moieties, giving a highly substituted polyol hexanicotinate structure that is more lipophilic and less acutely vasodilatory than free niacin; chemically it is classified as a vitamin B3 derivative, nicotinate ester, and vasoactive peripheral vasodilator, with a scaffold best described as a myo-inositol polyol platform decorated by pyridine-3-carboxylate esters. Similar agents include nicotinic acid itself, acipimox, xanthinol nicotinate, and other niacin esters used to improve peripheral blood flow. Its pharmacokinetics are characterized by oral administration with relatively slow gastrointestinal absorption, gradual esterase-mediated hydrolysis to nicotinic acid and inositol, systemic distribution without a well-defined high-affinity tissue target, hepatic conversion of released niacin to NAD/NADP-related metabolites and conjugates, and mainly renal excretion of metabolites. Toxicity is generally low at therapeutic doses but may include niacin-like effects such as cutaneous vasodilation, flushing, headache, dizziness, gastrointestinal upset, and rarely hepatotoxicity or worsened glycemic control with excessive exposure. No single definitive target protein is established for the intact ester; pharmacology is usually attributed to release of nicotinic acid, which can engage hydroxycarboxylic acid receptor 2, and to downstream vascular effects on peripheral microcirculation. It is used mainly for symptomatic treatment of peripheral vascular insufficiency, including intermittent claudication, Raynaud-type symptoms, acrocyanosis, chilblains, and other disorders with impaired peripheral perfusion, with clinical use as an oral adjunct intended to improve limb blood flow and reduce coldness, pain, or paresthesia.

Name: Azosemide
Description: Azosemide (DrugBank DB08961) is a non-thiazide sulfonamide loop diuretic built around a chlorinated aromatic sulfonamide framework linked to a nitrogen-containing heteroaromatic ring, giving a compact arylsulfonamide structure with both acidic and hydrogen-bonding functionality important for renal transporter binding; chemically it is categorized as a sulfonamide high-ceiling diuretic, and its scaffold is best described as an aromatic sulfonamide/heteroaryl diuretic core related in pharmacophoric terms to other loop diuretics. Similar drugs include furosemide, bumetanide, piretanide, torsemide, and ethacrynic acid, although azosemide is structurally closest to sulfonamide-containing loop diuretics. Its principal target is the Na+/K+/2Cl− cotransporter NKCC2 encoded by SLC12A1 in the thick ascending limb of Henle, producing natriuresis, chloruresis, and diuresis with secondary kaliuresis. After oral administration it is absorbed to a clinically useful extent, distributes largely within extracellular fluid with meaningful plasma protein binding, undergoes limited to moderate hepatic biotransformation, and is eliminated predominantly by the kidney via urinary excretion of parent drug and metabolites, with a duration of action often longer than furosemide. Toxicities are those typical of loop diuretics and include dehydration, volume depletion, hypotension, prerenal azotemia, electrolyte disturbances such as hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, hyperuricemia with gout, and occasional ototoxicity or sulfonamide hypersensitivity. Adverse effects commonly include dizziness, thirst, weakness, polyuria, rash, and renal function worsening. Clinically, azosemide is used to treat edema associated with congestive heart failure, renal disease, and hepatic disease, and it is also used as an antihypertensive diuretic, particularly when prolonged loop diuresis is desired.

Name: Etofenamate
Description: Etofenamate (DrugBank DB08984) is a topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug of the anthranilic acid, or fenamate, class characterized structurally as an aromatic ester linking a glycolic acid-derived oxyethyl moiety to a fenamate nucleus, with two substituted phenyl rings joined through an anilide-like nitrogen-containing diaryl scaffold that confers high lipophilicity and good tissue penetration; its core chemical scaffold is therefore the diarylamine/fenamate framework seen in related NSAIDs such as mefenamic acid, flufenamic acid, tolfenamic acid, and meclofenamate. Pharmacologically, etofenamate primarily inhibits cyclooxygenase enzymes PTGS1 and PTGS2, reducing peripheral prostaglandin synthesis and thereby suppressing inflammation, pain, and local edema. It is used mainly for topical treatment of musculoskeletal and soft-tissue disorders including sprains, strains, contusions, tendinitis, bursitis, low back pain, osteoarthritis, and other localized rheumatic pain states. After dermal administration, absorption is limited relative to oral NSAIDs but sufficient to generate high local concentrations in inflamed tissues; distribution favors underlying soft tissues and synovial structures, systemic protein binding is expected to be high for absorbed drug, hepatic biotransformation occurs largely by ester cleavage and oxidative conjugative pathways, and metabolites are eliminated predominantly in urine with some biliary/fecal excretion. Toxicity is generally lower systemically than with oral NSAIDs, but excessive exposure may still produce class effects such as gastrointestinal irritation, renal dysfunction, hypersensitivity, or bronchospasm in aspirin-sensitive patients; more commonly, adverse effects are local erythema, pruritus, burning, dermatitis, and photosensitivity. Clinically, it is used as gels, creams, or lotions for localized symptomatic relief when anti-inflammatory efficacy is desired with reduced systemic NSAID burden.

Name: Enviomycin
Description: Enviomycin (DrugBank DB08993) is a complex basic peptide antibiotic of the tuberactinomycin family, structurally characterized as a highly polar cyclic depsipeptide/oligopeptide containing multiple unusual amino acid residues, several amide linkages, hydroxylated functionalities, and a guanidino-rich cationic surface that supports tight binding to mycobacterial ribosomal RNA; chemically it is classified as a nonribosomal peptide antitubercular antibiotic, and its core scaffold is the tuberactinomycin cyclic peptide framework closely related to viomycin and capreomycin. Similar drugs include viomycin, capreomycin, and, more distantly by therapeutic role rather than scaffold, the aminoglycosides kanamycin and amikacin used in resistant tuberculosis. Its principal molecular target is the mycobacterial 70S ribosome, especially the 16S and 23S rRNA interface within the 30S/50S subunit interaction region, where binding inhibits translocation and protein synthesis. Enviomycin has historically been used as a second-line agent for tuberculosis, particularly multidrug-resistant pulmonary tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Pharmacokinetically, like other highly polar peptide antibiotics, it is poorly absorbed orally and therefore administered parenterally, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid with limited intracellular and CNS penetration except when meninges are inflamed, undergoes minimal metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by glomerular filtration, so accumulation occurs in renal impairment. Major toxicities include nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity with vestibular or auditory injury, and neuromuscular blockade; adverse effects can include dizziness, tinnitus, hearing loss, proteinuria, rising serum creatinine, electrolyte disturbances, and injection-site pain. Clinically, its use has been largely restricted to refractory or resistant tuberculosis regimens when better-tolerated alternatives are unavailable.

Name: Dexetimide
Description: Dexetimide (DrugBank DB08997) is a centrally acting antimuscarinic agent of the synthetic tertiary amine class, structurally characterized by a lipophilic aromatic ester architecture built around a glycolate-like anticholinergic pharmacophore bearing bulky hydrophobic aryl and cyclic amine substituents that favor blood-brain barrier penetration; chemically it is best categorized as an anticholinergic/parasympatholytic compound, and its core scaffold is related to the diaryl or aryl-cycloalkyl tertiary amino ester framework seen in potent central muscarinic antagonists. It is broadly similar to agents such as benztropine, trihexyphenidyl, biperiden, and procyclidine, which share CNS-penetrant antimuscarinic properties. Its principal known pharmacologic targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially M1-class central receptors, though older compounds in this class are often relatively nonselective across CHRM1-CHRM5. Dexetimide has been investigated for antiparkinsonian and anti-extrapyramidal use, particularly for parkinsonian rigidity, tremor, and drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms. Like other tertiary antimuscarinics, it is expected to be well absorbed orally, widely distributed with significant CNS exposure, metabolized hepatically by oxidative and hydrolytic pathways, and excreted mainly as metabolites in urine, with limited unchanged drug recovery. Its toxicity profile is that of central and peripheral anticholinergic excess, including confusion, agitation, delirium, mydriasis, tachycardia, urinary retention, decreased sweating, hyperthermia, and constipation; overdose may cause hallucinations and severe CNS dysfunction. Common adverse effects include dry mouth, blurred vision, cognitive slowing, dizziness, and constipation. Clinically, its use has historically centered on symptomatic management of Parkinson disease and antipsychotic-associated movement disorders rather than disease modification.

Name: Demexiptiline
Description: Demexiptiline (DrugBank DB08998) is a tricyclic antidepressant characterized structurally by a dibenzazepine-like tricyclic aromatic core bearing a three-carbon side chain terminated by a tertiary amine, a motif that confers high lipophilicity, central nervous system penetration, and cationic amphiphilic behavior; chemically it is classified among tricyclic antidepressants, with a scaffold closely related to iminodibenzyl/dibenzazepine antidepressant frameworks. Similar drugs include amitriptyline, imipramine, clomipramine, and doxepin, which share the same broad polycyclic amine pharmacophore and comparable monoamine reuptake-blocking properties. Its principal targets are believed to be the serotonin transporter SLC6A4 and norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, with additional lower-selectivity interactions commonly described for tricyclics at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, histamine H1 receptors, and alpha1-adrenergic receptors. Pharmacokinetically, demexiptiline is expected to be well absorbed orally, extensively distributed into tissues with high protein binding, to undergo substantial hepatic metabolism including oxidative biotransformation and possible demethylation/hydroxylation via cytochrome P450 enzymes, and to be excreted mainly in urine as metabolites. It has been used as an antidepressant for depressive disorders, especially major depression with anxiety, insomnia, or psychomotor retardation. Adverse effects are consistent with the class and include sedation, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention, orthostatic hypotension, tachycardia, weight gain, and sexual dysfunction. Toxicity in overdose can be serious, with anticholinergic delirium, seizures, coma, and potentially fatal cardiac conduction abnormalities or ventricular arrhythmias, limiting use largely to supervised clinical treatment of refractory or severe depressive states.

Name: Clobutinol
Description: Clobutinol (DrugBank DB09004) is a centrally acting, non-opioid antitussive built on a substituted benzhydrol/aminoalcohol framework, characterized by a lipophilic diaryl tertiary carbinol-like core bearing a chlorinated aromatic ring and an aliphatic tertiary amino side chain, placing it within the synthetic cough-suppressant class of arylalkanolamine-related agents; its core scaffold is best described as a chlorophenyl-substituted benzhydrol linked to a dialkylaminoalkyl moiety, a motif shared broadly with older antitussives and antihistamine-like cough remedies. Similar drugs include dextromethorphan, cloperastine, pentoxyverine, and codeine as pharmacologic comparators, although clobutinol is chemically distinct from opioids. It was used for symptomatic treatment of nonproductive cough, irritative cough, and cough associated with upper respiratory tract infections or bronchitis. Pharmacokinetically, it is orally absorbed, distributes systemically with expected central nervous system penetration due to substantial lipophilicity, undergoes hepatic biotransformation likely involving oxidative and conjugative pathways, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine. Its molecular target profile has not been sharply defined, but antitussive action is generally attributed to suppression of the medullary cough center rather than a single validated receptor; no widely accepted high-affinity target protein is firmly established. Adverse effects include dizziness, sedation, fatigue, nausea, dry mouth, and gastrointestinal discomfort. The major toxicity concern is dose-related QT interval prolongation with risk of ventricular arrhythmias including torsades de pointes and sudden cardiac death, particularly in overdose or susceptible patients, which led to withdrawal or severe restriction in several markets. Clinically, it was historically used as an oral cough suppressant in adults and children, but its practical use became obsolete because cardiac risk outweighed benefit for routine symptomatic cough treatment.

Name: Carmofur
Description: Carmofur (DB09010) is a lipophilic antineoplastic fluoropyrimidine consisting of a 5-fluorouracil uracil ring bearing a carbamoyl linkage to a hexyl chain, making it an N-hexylcarbamoyl derivative of 5-fluorouracil; chemically it is classified as a pyrimidine analog and antimetabolite, and its core scaffold is the fluorinated uracil/5-fluoropyrimidine scaffold with a urea-like carbamoyl substituent that increases membrane permeability relative to 5-FU. Similar drugs include 5-fluorouracil itself, tegafur, capecitabine, doxifluridine, and other fluoropyrimidine prodrugs or congeners used in gastrointestinal malignancies. Carmofur is orally active, absorbed through the gastrointestinal tract, distributes relatively broadly because of its lipophilicity and has been reported to penetrate the central nervous system better than 5-FU; it undergoes metabolic conversion releasing 5-FU and downstream active fluoronucleotides, with catabolism influenced by dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase-mediated fluoropyrimidine clearance, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine. Its principal pharmacologic targets are thymidylate synthase after bioactivation to FdUMP and, more broadly, RNA- and DNA-synthetic pathways via FUTP and FdUTP metabolites; carmofur has also been described as an inhibitor of acid ceramidase. Indications and clinical use have included colorectal and other gastrointestinal cancers, particularly postoperative adjuvant treatment or palliative therapy for colorectal, gastric, and occasionally breast or CNS-associated malignancies. Toxicities and adverse effects resemble fluoropyrimidines, including myelosuppression, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, mucositis, anorexia, hepatotoxicity, neurotoxicity, and dermatitis, with severe toxicity possible in patients with impaired fluoropyrimidine metabolism.

Name: Befunolol
Description: Befunolol (DrugBank DB09013) is an aryloxypropanolamine beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist whose structure consists of a lipophilic fused aromatic ring system linked through an ether to a 2-hydroxy-3-isopropylaminopropyl side chain, the classic pharmacophore of many beta blockers; chemically it is categorized as a synthetic beta-blocker and more specifically an aromatic ether amino alcohol, with an aryloxypropanolamine scaffold closely related to those of propranolol, timolol, carteolol, levobunolol, and other ophthalmic beta antagonists. Its principal targets are beta-1 adrenergic receptor and beta-2 adrenergic receptor, with ocular hypotensive activity attributed to blockade of beta receptors in the ciliary epithelium, reducing aqueous humor production. Befunolol has been used primarily as an antiglaucoma agent, especially for open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension, and clinically as topical ophthalmic drops to lower intraocular pressure. As an ophthalmic drug, systemic pharmacokinetic data are limited, but it is expected to undergo local ocular absorption with some nasolacrimal and conjunctival systemic uptake, moderate tissue distribution, hepatic oxidative metabolism typical of lipophilic beta blockers, and renal excretion of metabolites and some unchanged drug. Toxicity is generally consistent with the beta-blocker class: excessive exposure may cause bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm, atrioventricular conduction delay, fatigue, or worsening heart failure, while local toxicity includes eye irritation and corneal discomfort. Adverse effects reported or expected in clinical use include burning or stinging on instillation, blurred vision, dry eye, conjunctival hyperemia, headache, dizziness, and rare systemic beta-blockade effects, particularly in patients with asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes, or cardiac conduction disease.

Name: Captodiame
Description: Captodiame (DrugBank DB09014) is a centrally acting psychotropic agent classed as an anxiolytic and atypical antidepressant with antihistaminic and sedative properties; chemically it is a diphenylmethane-derived tertiary amine bearing a thioether-linked dimethylaminoethyl side chain, giving it a lipophilic aryl-alkyl-amine architecture typical of older sedative anxiolytics. Its core scaffold is best described as a substituted diarylmethane/sulfide-containing aminoalkyl framework, and it shows structural and pharmacological similarity to other first-generation sedative anxiolytic or antihistamine-like agents such as hydroxyzine, diphenhydramine, and related H1-antagonist-type diaryl compounds, although captodiame is distinct in being developed primarily for anxiety and mood symptoms. Its pharmacology is not completely defined, but reported targets and mechanisms include central histaminergic signaling, sigma receptor interactions, and modulation of dopaminergic and serotonergic neurotransmission; specific molecular targets have been proposed rather than firmly established, with H1 histamine receptor and sigma sites most often cited. After oral administration it is absorbed adequately, distributes widely into the CNS because of high lipophilicity, undergoes hepatic biotransformation likely via oxidative and N-dealkylation pathways, and is eliminated predominantly as metabolites in urine. Adverse effects are mainly those of sedating anticholinergic psychotropics, including drowsiness, fatigue, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, and impaired concentration; overdose or excessive exposure may cause marked CNS depression, confusion, agitation, or cardiovascular effects. Clinically, it has been used for anxiety states, stress-related symptoms, mild depressive presentations, sleep disturbance, and psychosomatic complaints, particularly where sedation is therapeutically useful.

Name: Bisacodyl
Description: Bisacodyl (DrugBank DB09020) is a diphenylmethane-derived stimulant laxative whose structure consists of a substituted triarylmethane-like bis(4-hydroxyphenyl)pyridylmethane core masked as a diacetate prodrug, with two acetylated phenolic groups that increase stability until deacetylation in the gut; chemically it is categorized as a diphenylmethane laxative and its key scaffold is the bisphenolic pyridylmethane framework, closely related in pharmacologic behavior to sodium picosulfate and historically to phenolphthalein-like stimulant cathartics. After oral or rectal administration, systemic absorption of parent drug is low; it is converted in the intestine by deacetylation to the active metabolite bis-(p-hydroxyphenyl)-pyridyl-2-methane, which acts locally in the colon, with minimal distribution, limited systemic exposure, hepatic conjugation of absorbed metabolite mainly to glucuronides, and excretion primarily in feces with a smaller urinary fraction as metabolites. Its pharmacologic target is not a single well-defined receptor, but it functionally stimulates enteric neurons and colonic smooth muscle, increasing peristalsis and secretion while reducing water absorption; direct molecular targets are incompletely characterized, though enteric nerve plexus and epithelial transport processes are implicated. Bisacodyl is indicated for short-term treatment of constipation and for bowel evacuation before colonoscopy, surgery, or radiologic procedures.
