Adverse effects commonly include abdominal cramping, diarrhea, nausea, and rectal irritation with suppositories; excessive use may cause dehydration, hypokalemia, weakness, and laxative dependence, while overdose can produce severe fluid and electrolyte loss. Clinically, it is used orally for overnight relief of episodic constipation and rectally when rapid colonic emptying is desired.

Name: Aliskiren
Description: Aliskiren (DrugBank DB09026) is a small-molecule, nonpeptide direct renin inhibitor whose structure is a conformationally flexible, highly functionalized hydroxyethylene-like transition-state mimetic bearing multiple aliphatic chains, ether and alcohol functionalities, and a substituted aromatic moiety, designed to engage the catalytic aspartyl protease active site of renin; chemically it is best classified as a peptidomimetic antihypertensive and its core scaffold is a hydrophobic hydroxyethylene/alkanolamine renin-binding framework rather than a true peptide backbone. Similar drugs include other renin-pathway modulators such as enalkiren, remikiren, and zankiren, although these are less widely used, and it is mechanistically related, though not structurally identical, to ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers. Its principal target protein is renin, encoded by REN, leading to suppression of angiotensin I and downstream angiotensin II generation. Pharmacokinetically, aliskiren has low oral bioavailability, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, shows moderate protein binding and substantial tissue distribution, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism with only a minor CYP3A4 contribution, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged via the hepatobiliary-fecal route with a relatively long terminal half-life that supports once-daily dosing. It is indicated primarily for essential hypertension, including blood-pressure reduction in adults requiring renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system blockade. Adverse effects include diarrhea, headache, dizziness, fatigue, cough less commonly than ACE inhibitors, hyperkalemia, renal function deterioration, and hypotension; important toxicities include angioedema, fetal toxicity in pregnancy, and increased risk of renal impairment, hypotension, and hyperkalemia when combined with ACE inhibitors or ARBs, especially in patients with diabetes or chronic kidney disease. Clinically, it has been used as monotherapy or in combination with other antihypertensives such as thiazides or calcium channel blockers for patients with uncomplicated or treatment-resistant hypertension.

Name: Ledipasvir
Description: Ledipasvir (DrugBank DB09027) is a direct-acting antiviral for hepatitis C virus characterized by a large, highly lipophilic, nonpeptidic small-molecule structure containing multiple fused aromatic and heteroaromatic ring systems, fluorinated phenyl motifs, imidazole- and carbamate-like functionalities, and a conformationally constrained polycyclic core that supports high-affinity viral protein binding. Chemically, it is best classified as an HCV NS5A inhibitor and more broadly as a fluorinated aromatic antiviral; its scaffold is the symmetric or pseudosymmetric diimidazole-linked NS5A inhibitor chemotype shared across this drug class. Similar drugs include daclatasvir, velpatasvir, elbasvir, ombitasvir, and pibrentasvir, which also target NS5A with related aromatic, conformationally restricted scaffolds. Ledipasvir acts primarily on the HCV nonstructural protein 5A, disrupting replication complex assembly and virion production. It is indicated for chronic hepatitis C infection, especially genotype 1, and in fixed-dose combination with sofosbuvir has also been used for genotypes 4, 5, and 6, including patients with compensated liver disease and some treatment-experienced populations. Orally administered ledipasvir has limited aqueous solubility and pH-dependent absorption, high protein binding, minimal CYP-mediated metabolism, and is transported by P-glycoprotein and breast cancer resistance protein; elimination is predominantly biliary-fecal with little renal excretion. Toxicity is generally low but includes potential hepatotoxicity risk when combined with interacting drugs, severe bradycardia reported with concomitant amiodarone and sofosbuvir, and embryo-fetal risk mainly inferred from combination regimens. Common adverse effects include fatigue, headache, nausea, diarrhea, insomnia, and asthenia. Clinically, it is used chiefly as the once-daily ledipasvir-sofosbuvir combination for curative interferon-sparing treatment of chronic HCV infection.

Name: Miltefosine
Description: Miltefosine (DB09031) is a synthetic alkylphosphocholine antiprotozoal composed of a linear hexadecyl lipophilic chain attached through an ether linkage to a phosphocholine headgroup, giving an amphiphilic lysophospholipid-like structure that lacks a glycerol backbone and behaves as a membrane-active cationic phospholipid analog. Chemically it belongs to the alkylphosphocholine and ether lipid class, with an alkylphosphocholine scaffold related to other membrane-targeting lipids such as perifosine and edelfosine. Its activity is not mediated by a single canonical target; rather, it perturbs parasite membrane lipid composition and signaling, with implicated targets or pathways including phospholipid and sterol metabolism, glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchor biosynthesis, mitochondrial membrane function, cytochrome c oxidase-associated processes, and parasite transport proteins involved in uptake and resistance such as the miltefosine transporter complex MT and Ros3. Orally administered miltefosine is well absorbed, widely distributed into tissues, highly membrane associated, has a long terminal half-life measured in days, undergoes limited oxidative metabolism with substantial persistence as parent compound, and is eliminated slowly by metabolic degradation and minor renal and fecal routes. It is indicated primarily for leishmaniasis, including visceral leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania donovani and selected cases of cutaneous and mucosal disease, and has also been used for free-living amoebic infections such as Naegleria fowleri. Toxicity is notable for dose-limiting gastrointestinal injury, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, hemolytic and reproductive toxicity, and marked teratogenicity and embryofetal toxicity. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, transaminase elevation, increased creatinine, headache, dizziness, pruritus, and rash. Clinically, it is valued as an oral alternative to amphotericin B or antimonials, especially in endemic settings and combination regimens.

Name: Suvorexant
Description: Suvorexant (DrugBank DB09034) is an orally active small-molecule dual orexin receptor antagonist characterized by a densely functionalized diazabicyclic core linked to multiple lipophilic aryl and heteroaryl substituents, giving a rigid polycyclic, amide-containing architecture optimized for central nervous system penetration; chemically it is classified as a heteroaryl-substituted diazabicyclic orexin antagonist, with a diaryl/diazabicyclononane-like scaffold that distinguishes it from classical benzodiazepine or nonbenzodiazepine hypnotics. Structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include other dual orexin receptor antagonists such as lemborexant, daridorexant, and almorexant, which share orexin pathway inhibition but differ in half-life and receptor-binding kinetics. Its principal targets are orexin receptor type 1 and orexin receptor type 2, where antagonism suppresses wake-drive signaling mediated by endogenous orexin A and orexin B. Suvorexant is indicated for insomnia, particularly difficulty with sleep onset and sleep maintenance, and is used clinically in chronic insomnia disorder in adults, including patients with fragmented nocturnal sleep. After oral administration it is absorbed with peak concentrations typically reached in a few hours, shows high plasma protein binding and broad tissue distribution, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism predominantly via CYP3A with a minor contribution from CYP2C19, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in feces with lesser urinary excretion; its effective half-life supports nighttime dosing but can contribute to next-day effects. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related CNS depression, somnolence, impaired driving performance, balance disturbance, and complex sleep behaviors, with greater risk in obesity, hepatic impairment, or concomitant CYP3A inhibitors; other adverse effects include fatigue, abnormal dreams, dry mouth, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations, and cataplexy-like symptoms, making caution important in patients with narcolepsy, respiratory compromise, substance misuse vulnerability, or use with other sedatives.

Name: Empagliflozin
Description: Empagliflozin (DrugBank DB09038) is an orally active C-aryl glucoside antidiabetic agent whose structure consists of a β-D-glucopyranose-like polyhydroxylated sugar core linked through a metabolically stable carbon-carbon bond to a substituted diaryl aglycone containing chlorophenyl and tetrahydrofuran-derived aryl elements; chemically it belongs to the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor class and more broadly to C-glucoside glycosuric agents, with a core scaffold closely related to the aryl C-glucoside/phlorizin-mimetic motif. Similar drugs include dapagliflozin, canagliflozin, ertugliflozin, and the dual SGLT1/2 inhibitor sotagliflozin. Its principal target is SLC5A2 (SGLT2) in the renal proximal tubule, with much weaker activity at SLC5A1 (SGLT1), producing reduced renal glucose reabsorption, glycosuria, mild natriuresis, and osmotic diuresis. After oral administration it is well absorbed, reaches peak plasma concentrations in roughly 1 to 2 hours, shows moderate protein binding and broad systemic distribution, undergoes limited oxidative metabolism with predominant phase II glucuronidation to inactive metabolites, and is eliminated by both urine and feces, with a terminal half-life supporting once-daily dosing. It is indicated for type 2 diabetes mellitus, and clinically used to improve glycemic control and to reduce cardiovascular death and hospitalization for heart failure, including in patients with heart failure or chronic kidney disease. Important adverse effects include genital mycotic infections, urinary tract infection, polyuria, volume depletion, hypotension, and increased LDL cholesterol; notable toxicities include euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis, acute kidney injury in susceptible patients, and rare Fournier gangrene, while hypoglycemia is uncommon unless combined with insulin or sulfonylureas.

Name: Eliglustat
Description: Eliglustat (DrugBank DB09039) is an orally active small-molecule glucosylceramide synthase inhibitor used as substrate reduction therapy for Gaucher disease type 1; structurally, it is a ceramide-mimetic amino alcohol built around a substituted phenyl-containing hydroxy-pyrrolidine scaffold with lipophilic aryl and alkoxy features that enable high-affinity interaction with the glycosphingolipid biosynthetic machinery. Chemically, it is classified as a glycosphingolipid synthesis inhibitor and iminosugar-like/ceramide-analog pharmacophore, with a nitrogen-containing heterocyclic scaffold related conceptually to other substrate reduction agents. Similar drugs include miglustat, another glucosylceramide synthase-directed substrate reduction therapy, and enzyme replacement agents such as imiglucerase, velaglucerase alfa, and taliglucerase alfa, which are mechanistically different but used in the same disease setting. Its principal target is UDP-glucose:ceramide glucosyltransferase, also called glucosylceramide synthase or UGCG, thereby reducing formation of glucosylceramide and downstream glycosphingolipid accumulation in macrophages. Eliglustat is well absorbed orally, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism predominantly by CYP2D6 and CYP3A4, has pharmacokinetics highly dependent on CYP2D6 metabolizer status, is distributed systemically with limited central nervous system penetration, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine and feces. Toxicity concerns include exposure-related cardiac conduction abnormalities such as PR, QTc, or QRS prolongation, especially in poor metabolizers or with strong CYP2D6/CYP3A inhibitors; overdose or interacting co-medications may increase dizziness, bradyarrhythmic risk, and syncope. Adverse effects commonly include fatigue, headache, nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, arthralgia, back pain, and extremity pain. Clinically, it is indicated for long-term treatment of adults with Gaucher disease type 1 who are CYP2D6 extensive, intermediate, or certain poor metabolizers, with use aimed at reducing hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and skeletal disease burden.

Name: Efinaconazole
Description: Efinaconazole (DrugBank DB09040) is a topical triazole antifungal whose structure is characterized by a fluorinated phenyl-substituted azole framework containing a 1,2,4-triazole ring linked to a chiral alcohol center and an extended methylene-piperidine side chain, giving a lipophilic yet nail-penetrant profile; chemically it belongs to the azole, specifically triazole, class and is built on a triazole-alcohol antifungal scaffold related to other ergosterol biosynthesis inhibitors such as itraconazole, voriconazole, ravuconazole, and fluconazole, although it is optimized for topical ungual delivery. Its principal pharmacologic target is fungal lanosterol 14alpha-demethylase, the cytochrome P450 enzyme CYP51/Erg11, leading to impaired ergosterol synthesis and disruption of fungal membrane integrity, particularly in dermatophytes such as Trichophyton rubrum and Trichophyton mentagrophytes. Pharmacokinetically, topical nail application produces low systemic absorption, high transungual penetration, limited systemic distribution, minimal circulating exposure, hepatic oxidative metabolism if absorbed, and excretion expected mainly via feces and urine as metabolites rather than unchanged drug. Toxicity is generally low because of limited systemic exposure, with no major systemic azole toxicities typically seen in clinical use, though local irritation has been observed and class-related concerns at higher exposure would include hepatotoxicity or CYP-mediated drug interactions. It is indicated for onychomycosis of the toenails, especially distal lateral subungual disease caused by dermatophytes, and is used clinically as a once-daily topical solution for prolonged courses to improve mycologic cure and nail clearing. Common adverse effects include application-site dermatitis, erythema, vesiculation, pain, ingrown toenail, and local burning or pruritus.

Name: Tavaborole
Description: Tavaborole (DB09041) is a small, boron-containing oxaborole antifungal whose structure is defined by a compact benzoxaborole/oxaborole bicyclic scaffold consisting of a fused aromatic ring and a five-membered boron-oxygen heterocycle, with fluorine substitution that increases lipophilicity and nail penetration; chemically it belongs to the boronic acid-derived oxaborole class and is scaffold-related to other boron-based anti-infectives such as crisaborole and investigational oxaboroles including AN2690 analogs. Its primary molecular target is fungal leucyl-tRNA synthetase, which it inhibits through the oxaborole tRNA-trapping mechanism, blocking protein synthesis in dermatophytes such as Trichophyton rubrum and Trichophyton mentagrophytes. Tavaborole is indicated for topical treatment of onychomycosis of the toenails, especially distal subungual disease caused by susceptible dermatophytes, and in clinical use it is applied as a nail solution for prolonged courses to achieve transungual drug delivery. Pharmacokinetically, systemic absorption after topical administration is low but measurable, distribution is primarily local within the nail plate and periungual tissues, metabolism appears limited with no major clinically important biotransformation issues reported, and elimination of absorbed drug is predominantly renal as parent drug and minor metabolites. Toxicity is generally mild and localized rather than systemic; preclinical concerns are low relative to oral antifungals, though excessive exposure could theoretically reflect boron-associated developmental toxicity. Common adverse effects include application-site exfoliation, erythema, dermatitis, ingrown toenail, and local irritation or pain. Clinically, tavaborole is valued as a non-oral option when avoidance of systemic azole or terbinafine toxicity, drug interactions, or hepatic monitoring is desirable.

Name: Tedizolid phosphate
Description: Tedizolid phosphate (DrugBank DB09042) is a phosphate prodrug of tedizolid, a synthetic oxazolidinone antibacterial whose structure features the characteristic 2-oxazolidinone ring attached to a fluorophenyl system and a heteroaryl D-ring, with the phosphate moiety appended to enhance aqueous solubility and enable rapid in vivo conversion to the active alcohol tedizolid; chemically it is classified as an oxazolidinone prodrug and more broadly a synthetic antibacterial, built on the oxazolidinone scaffold shared with related agents such as linezolid, radezolid, and sutezolid. Its principal target is the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit, specifically the 23S rRNA peptidyl transferase region, where tedizolid inhibits formation of the 70S initiation complex and suppresses protein synthesis, with activity against many Gram-positive pathogens including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus agalactiae, Enterococcus faecalis, and Enterococcus faecium. After oral administration tedizolid phosphate is well absorbed with high bioavailability, rapidly dephosphorylated by endogenous phosphatases, minimally affected by food, highly protein bound, widely distributed into tissues including skin and soft tissue, only minimally metabolized by CYP pathways, converted largely to inactive sulfate conjugates, and eliminated mainly in feces with a smaller urinary component; its terminal half-life supports once-daily dosing. It is indicated primarily for acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections such as cellulitis, wound infection, and major cutaneous abscess caused by susceptible Gram-positive organisms. Adverse effects are usually mild and include nausea, diarrhea, headache, vomiting, and dizziness, while toxicities of concern include thrombocytopenia or other myelosuppressive effects, peripheral or optic neuropathy with prolonged exposure, lactic acidosis risk, and potentially less pronounced monoamine oxidase interaction than linezolid, though serotonergic caution remains clinically relevant.

Name: Finafloxacin
Description: Finafloxacin (DrugBank DB09047) is a fifth-generation fluoroquinolone antibacterial built on the classical 4-quinolone-3-carboxylic acid scaffold, bearing the quinolone bicyclic core with a fluorine substituent that enhances Gram-negative activity and a heterocyclic amine-rich side chain that contributes to potency, tissue penetration, and retention of activity in acidic environments; chemically it belongs to the fluoroquinolone carboxylic acid class and shares a quinolone scaffold closely related to ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, delafloxacin, and besifloxacin. Its principal targets are bacterial DNA gyrase, especially GyrA/GyrB, and topoisomerase IV, through which it inhibits DNA supercoiling and chromosome segregation. Finafloxacin has been developed mainly as a topical anti-infective, particularly in otic formulations, so systemic pharmacokinetic exposure is limited after local administration, with low absorption from the ear, minimal distribution beyond local tissues, little clinically relevant metabolism expected at topical doses, and elimination of absorbed drug presumed primarily renal as with other quinolones. It is indicated for acute otitis externa, including infections caused by susceptible organisms such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus, and has also been investigated more broadly for complicated urinary tract and respiratory infections because of its unusual activity at low pH. Adverse effects are mainly local and mild, including ear pruritus, discomfort, pain, erythema, dysgeusia, or nausea, whereas serious fluoroquinolone-class toxicities such as tendinopathy, CNS effects, QT prolongation, dysglycemia, hypersensitivity, and cartilage toxicity remain theoretical or uncommon with topical use; accordingly, clinical use is chiefly as otic therapy for bacterial ear infection when targeted local quinolone treatment is desired.

Name: Naloxegol
Description: Naloxegol (DrugBank DB09049) is a semisynthetic PEGylated morphinan derived from naloxone, in which the opioid antagonist core retains the rigid pentacyclic phenanthrene/morphinan scaffold with a 4,5-epoxy bridge, tertiary amine, aromatic hydroxyl functionality, and a polyethylene glycol ether substituent that increases polarity and limits central nervous system penetration; chemically it is classified as a peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonist and more specifically a PEGylated opioid antagonist. Its closest analogs and pharmacologic comparators include naloxone, naltrexone, methylnaltrexone, and alvimopan, all sharing opioid antagonist activity but differing in scaffold substitution and peripheral restriction. Naloxegol targets the mu-opioid receptor encoded by OPRM1, with functional antagonism at peripheral opioid receptors in the gastrointestinal tract to reverse opioid-induced suppression of motility, secretion, and transit. It is indicated for opioid-induced constipation in adults with chronic non-cancer pain, for example in patients receiving long-term oxycodone or morphine therapy. After oral administration it is absorbed systemically, with exposure increased by high-fat food; it is moderately distributed but has limited brain entry due to PEGylation and P-glycoprotein-mediated efflux, undergoes predominantly CYP3A-mediated oxidative metabolism, and is eliminated in both feces and urine mainly as parent drug and metabolites. Toxicity is chiefly gastrointestinal and mechanism-based, including abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, flatulence, vomiting, and possible opioid withdrawal-like symptoms; serious risks include gastrointestinal perforation in susceptible patients with structural gut disease and increased exposure with strong CYP3A inhibitors. Clinically it is used as an oral once-daily laxation-restoring therapy when conventional laxatives are inadequate.

Name: Ceftolozane
Description: Ceftolozane (DrugBank DB09050) is a parenteral antipseudomonal cephalosporin characterized by a cephem nucleus containing the strained beta-lactam fused to a dihydrothiazine ring, with an aminothiadiazole oxime-containing acyl side chain and a substituted pyrazolium moiety that enhance stability to some beta-lactamases and improve activity against Gram-negative pathogens, especially Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Chemically it belongs to the beta-lactam antibiotic class, specifically the cephalosporins, and its core scaffold is the 7-aminocephalosporanic acid/cephem scaffold. Structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include ceftazidime, cefepime, cefiderocol, and other advanced cephalosporins; in practice it is commonly paired with the beta-lactamase inhibitor tazobactam in the marketed combination. Its antibacterial effect is mediated by binding penicillin-binding proteins involved in peptidoglycan cross-linking, notably PBP1b, PBP1c, PBP2, and PBP3 in susceptible organisms. Pharmacokinetically, ceftolozane is administered intravenously, has essentially complete systemic bioavailability by infusion, low-to-moderate protein binding, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid with useful epithelial lining fluid and urinary exposure, undergoes minimal metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by the kidneys, so dose reduction is required in renal impairment. Toxicity is typical of cephalosporins and includes hypersensitivity reactions, positive Coombs test, neurotoxicity such as encephalopathy or seizures in predisposed patients with renal dysfunction, and risk of Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea. Indications include complicated urinary tract infection, pyelonephritis, complicated intra-abdominal infection when combined with metronidazole, and hospital-acquired or ventilator-associated bacterial pneumonia, particularly when multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacilli are suspected. Common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, headache, pyrexia, constipation, infusion-site reactions, and transaminase elevation. Clinically, it is used for serious infections caused by susceptible Enterobacterales and difficult-to-treat P. aeruginosa, especially in nosocomial settings and when resistance limits use of older cephalosporins.

Name: Ibrutinib
Description: Ibrutinib (DB09053) is an orally active small-molecule antineoplastic agent chemically classified as a targeted covalent kinase inhibitor, specifically a Bruton's tyrosine kinase inhibitor, built on a substituted pyrazolo-pyrimidine heteroaromatic scaffold bearing a pendant phenoxyphenyl group and an electrophilic acrylamide Michael acceptor that enables irreversible bond formation with a cysteine residue in the ATP-binding site; this scaffold is shared conceptually with other covalent BTK inhibitors, and clinically similar drugs include acalabrutinib, zanubrutinib, tirabrutinib, and the noncovalent BTK inhibitor pirtobrutinib. Its principal target is BTK, but it also inhibits other kinases containing a homologous cysteine, including TEC, BMX, ITK, EGFR, ERBB2/HER2, and JAK3, contributing to both efficacy and off-target effects. Pharmacokinetically, ibrutinib is rapidly absorbed after oral administration, exhibits low-to-moderate bioavailability limited by extensive first-pass metabolism, is highly protein bound, distributes widely, is metabolized predominantly by CYP3A4 with minor CYP2D6 contribution to active and inactive metabolites, and is eliminated mainly in feces with minimal renal excretion; exposure rises with CYP3A inhibitors and falls with CYP3A inducers. Clinically it is used in B-cell malignancies such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma, mantle cell lymphoma, Waldenström macroglobulinemia, marginal zone lymphoma, and chronic graft-versus-host disease. Toxicities include bleeding, atrial fibrillation, hypertension, serious infection, cytopenias, and rare ventricular arrhythmias; common adverse effects include diarrhea, fatigue, rash, musculoskeletal pain, bruising, nausea, stomatitis, and neutropenia.

Name: Idelalisib
Description: Idelalisib (DrugBank DB09054) is an orally active, small-molecule phosphoinositide 3-kinase inhibitor with a purine-like heteroaromatic core, specifically a substituted adenine/quinazoline-like scaffold bearing fluorinated aryl and alkynyl features that confer ATP-pocket binding selectivity; chemically it is categorized as a targeted antineoplastic kinase inhibitor and more specifically a selective PI3K delta inhibitor, built on a purine-derived kinase-binding scaffold similar in pharmacologic intent, though not identical in structure, to other PI3K-pathway agents such as duvelisib, copanlisib, and umbralisib. Its principal target is PI3K delta, encoded by PIK3CD, with downstream suppression of AKT signaling in malignant B cells. After oral administration, absorption is adequate with peak plasma levels typically within a few hours; distribution is moderate and highly protein bound; metabolism occurs mainly via aldehyde oxidase with a lesser CYP3A contribution to an inactive major metabolite; excretion is predominantly fecal with limited renal elimination, and the terminal half-life supports twice-daily dosing. Idelalisib is indicated for relapsed hematologic malignancies, especially chronic lymphocytic leukemia in combination with rituximab, follicular lymphoma, and small lymphocytic lymphoma after prior therapy. Toxicity is clinically significant and includes severe hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevation, serious diarrhea or colitis, pneumonitis, intestinal perforation, severe cutaneous reactions, and opportunistic or fatal infections such as Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia or CMV reactivation. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, fatigue, nausea, pyrexia, cough, rash, abdominal pain, and neutropenia. In clinical use it serves as a precision B-cell malignancy therapy, particularly in patients unsuitable for conventional chemoimmunotherapy or with relapsed indolent lymphoma.

Name: Avibactam
Description: Avibactam (DB09060) is a synthetic non-β-lactam β-lactamase inhibitor with a compact diazabicyclooctane core bearing a sulfate/sulfate-like oxyanion functionality and carboxamide substitution, giving a highly polar, conformationally constrained structure designed to reversibly acylate serine β-lactamases without itself being a β-lactam antibiotic. Chemically it belongs to the diazabicyclooctane class, and its key scaffold is the bridged bicyclic DBO ring system; related agents include other DBO inhibitors such as relebactam and durlobactam, and more distantly the boronate inhibitor vaborbactam and older β-lactam-based inhibitors such as clavulanate, sulbactam, and tazobactam. Its principal targets are bacterial serine β-lactamases, especially Ambler class A enzymes including KPC and CTX-M, class C AmpC enzymes, and some class D enzymes such as OXA-48-like carbapenemases, thereby protecting partner β-lactams rather than exerting substantial standalone antibacterial activity. Pharmacokinetically, avibactam is given intravenously, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid with low protein binding, undergoes negligible metabolism, and is eliminated largely unchanged by the kidney with dose adjustment in renal impairment. Toxicity is generally limited and resembles that of combination products, though accumulation in renal dysfunction may increase adverse effects; serious concerns include hypersensitivity, Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea, and seizures reported rarely in predisposed patients receiving β-lactam combinations. Clinically it is used with ceftazidime for complicated urinary tract infection, complicated intra-abdominal infection with metronidazole, hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia, and other serious infections caused by multidrug-resistant Enterobacterales or Pseudomonas aeruginosa; common side effects include nausea, diarrhea, constipation, vomiting, transaminase elevations, rash, infusion-site reactions, and positive direct Coombs test.

Name: Cannabidiol
Description: Cannabidiol (DrugBank DB09061) is a plant-derived phytocannabinoid characterized by a resorcinol aromatic ring bearing two phenolic hydroxyl groups, a lipophilic pentyl side chain, and a terpene-derived cyclohexene moiety linked through a flexible carbon bridge, giving a non-nitrogenous, highly hydrophobic dibenzopyran-related cannabinoid architecture without the psychoactive ring closure typical of tetrahydrocannabinol; chemically it is a terpenophenolic meroterpenoid in the cannabinoid class, built on a cannabidiol/cyclohexenyl-resorcinol scaffold. Similar drugs include delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, dronabinol, nabilone, nabiximols, and other phytocannabinoids such as cannabigerol. Oral cannabidiol shows variable and generally low bioavailability because of poor aqueous solubility and extensive first-pass metabolism, with improved exposure when taken with high-fat food; it is highly protein bound, widely distributed into lipid-rich tissues including the CNS, metabolized predominantly by CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 with additional UGT-mediated conjugation to active and inactive hydroxylated and carboxylated metabolites, and eliminated mainly in feces with a smaller urinary fraction. Its pharmacology is pleiotropic, with reported targets including CNR1 and CNR2 modulation, TRPV1, GPR55, HTR1A, adenosine transport-related pathways, and voltage-gated ion channel effects. Clinically, it is used primarily for seizures in Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, Dravet syndrome, and tuberous sclerosis complex, and is also used in some settings for spasticity, pain, and anxiety-spectrum symptoms. Toxicities include dose-related somnolence, diarrhea, decreased appetite, fatigue, transaminase elevation and hepatocellular injury risk, especially with valproate, plus important CYP-mediated drug interactions and occasional rash or infection-related adverse events.

Name: Ceritinib
Description: Ceritinib (DB09063) is an orally active, small-molecule aminopyrimidine-based tyrosine kinase inhibitor whose structure is centered on a substituted chlorinated pyrimidine/anilino heteroaromatic core linked to a piperidinyl and sulfonyl-containing aryl system, giving a lipophilic, basic, ATP-competitive kinase-binding architecture; chemically it is best classified as a heteroaryl kinase inhibitor, and its principal scaffold is an anilinopyrimidine/aminopyrimidine scaffold. It is closely related pharmacologically to other ALK inhibitors such as crizotinib, alectinib, brigatinib, lorlatinib, and to a lesser extent ROS1-directed kinase inhibitors. Ceritinib targets anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) as its main protein target and also inhibits ROS1 and insulin receptor family kinases including IGF1R and INSR in some settings, explaining both efficacy and some off-target toxicity. It is indicated primarily for ALK-positive metastatic non-small cell lung cancer, including tumors with ALK rearrangements and in patients progressing after or intolerant to earlier ALK inhibitors. After oral administration, absorption is variable but increases with food; it is highly protein bound, widely distributed, extensively metabolized in the liver predominantly by CYP3A, and excreted mainly via the feces with minimal renal elimination. Toxicities include dose-limiting gastrointestinal injury, hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevation, hyperglycemia, interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis, bradycardia, pancreatitis, and QT prolongation. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fatigue, decreased appetite, weight loss, constipation, rash, and laboratory abnormalities such as elevated ALT, AST, lipase, and glucose. Clinically, ceritinib is used as targeted therapy for ALK-driven lung cancer, including systemic disease and selected patients with central nervous system involvement.

Name: Ciprofibrate
Description: Ciprofibrate (DrugBank DB09064) is a phenoxyisobutyric acid derivative in the fibrate class of antihyperlipidemic agents, structurally characterized by an aryloxy linkage connecting a substituted chlorophenyl ring to an alpha-methylpropionic acid moiety, with a cyclopropyl-containing lipophilic aryl substituent that helps define its receptor-binding properties; its core chemical scaffold is the fibrate/aryloxyisobutyric acid scaffold shared with related agents such as bezafibrate, fenofibrate, gemfibrozil, and clofibrate, although ciprofibrate is generally considered a more potent peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha agonist. Its principal known target is PPARA, leading to increased lipoprotein lipase activity, enhanced catabolism of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, reduced hepatic very-low-density lipoprotein production, and moderate increases in high-density lipoprotein cholesterol. Clinically it is indicated for primary hypertriglyceridemia, mixed dyslipidemia, and hyperlipoproteinemias marked by elevated triglycerides, particularly when dietary measures are insufficient, and it has been used in patients at risk of pancreatitis from severe triglyceride elevation. Orally administered ciprofibrate is well absorbed, is highly plasma protein bound, distributes mainly within the vascular compartment, undergoes limited hepatic biotransformation relative to some other fibrates, and is eliminated slowly, largely in urine as unchanged drug and conjugated metabolites, giving a relatively long duration of action. Toxicities and adverse effects resemble those of other fibrates and include dose-related hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevation, myalgia, myopathy or rare rhabdomyolysis, cholelithiasis from altered biliary lipid composition, dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, headache, rash, and fatigue, with risk increased in renal impairment or when combined with statins or anticoagulants.

Name: Cobicistat
Description: Cobicistat (DrugBank DB09065) is a synthetic, nonpeptidic pharmacoenhancer built around a substituted thiazolyl-carbamate/urea-like scaffold with multiple heteroatoms, a bulky lipophilic backbone, and stereodefined secondary alcohol functionality that confers high affinity for drug-metabolizing enzymes rather than direct antiviral activity; chemically it is best classified as a cytochrome P450 inhibitor, specifically a mechanism-based CYP3A inhibitor, and it is structurally and functionally related to ritonavir, with ritonavir being the prototypical similar booster, while other pharmacokinetic enhancers such as pharmaceutically boosted protease inhibitor regimens are analogous in use. Its principal target protein is CYP3A4, with inhibition also affecting CYP3A5 and transporters including P-glycoprotein; it also inhibits intestinal CYP3A, thereby increasing oral exposure of coadministered substrates. After oral administration, cobicistat is absorbed and used in fixed-dose antiretroviral combinations; it is highly protein bound, hepatically metabolized mainly by CYP3A with minor CYP2D6 contribution, has minimal renal elimination of unchanged drug, and is excreted predominantly in feces. Clinically, it is indicated as a boosting agent in HIV-1 therapy, for example with elvitegravir, darunavir, or atazanavir, to enhance systemic concentrations and prolong half-life. Toxicity is dominated by drug-drug interactions, hepatotoxicity risk, and benign increases in serum creatinine from inhibition of tubular creatinine secretion rather than true glomerular injury, although renal adverse outcomes can occur in susceptible patients, especially with tenofovir-containing regimens. Common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, jaundice or hyperbilirubinemia in some combinations, rash, and fatigue. In practice, cobicistat is used not as an antiretroviral effector itself but as a metabolic inhibitor to optimize HIV combination therapy and simplify once-daily dosing.

Name: Vortioxetine
Description: Vortioxetine (DrugBank DB09068) is a centrally active serotonergic antidepressant with a compact, lipophilic aryl-piperazine–like architecture built around a substituted piperazine core linking two aromatic rings, one being a dimethylphenyl group and the other a thioether-connected anisole-type ring; chemically it is classified as a multimodal antidepressant and more specifically a piperazine derivative with a diaryl sulfide scaffold. It is structurally and pharmacologically related to other serotonergic antidepressants, especially SSRIs and mixed serotonin modulators such as fluoxetine, paroxetine, vilazodone, and trazodone, although its multimodal receptor profile is distinctive. Its principal targets include the serotonin transporter SLC6A4, which it inhibits, and several serotonin receptors, functioning as a 5-HT1A agonist, 5-HT1B partial agonist, 5-HT3 antagonist, 5-HT7 antagonist, and 5-HT1D antagonist. After oral administration it is well absorbed, has high bioavailability, reaches peak plasma levels in hours, is extensively distributed with high protein binding, undergoes hepatic oxidative metabolism mainly via CYP2D6 with contributions from CYP3A4/5, CYP2A6, CYP2C9, and CYP2C19, and is eliminated largely as inactive metabolites in urine and feces with a long half-life permitting once-daily dosing. Toxicity is generally moderate but includes dose-related nausea, vomiting, dizziness, serotonin syndrome, hyponatremia, abnormal bleeding risk, and overdose manifestations such as seizures or CNS depression; like other antidepressants it carries a suicidality warning in younger patients. It is indicated for major depressive disorder, including depressed mood, anhedonia, cognitive symptoms, and anxiety-associated depressive states, and is used clinically as an oral maintenance or acute-phase antidepressant, particularly when tolerability, sexual side-effect burden, or cognitive dysfunction are relevant treatment considerations.

Name: Tibolone
Description: Tibolone (DrugBank DB09070) is a synthetic steroidal tissue-selective hormone replacement agent built on a 19-nortestosterone-derived gonane framework, characterized by the tetracyclic cyclopentanophenanthrene steroid nucleus with a 3-keto group, a 7α-methyl substituent, and a 17β-hydroxyl functionality with unsaturation that enables formation of active metabolites; chemically it is categorized as a synthetic estrogenic-progestogenic-androgenic steroid, with a norethisterone-like steroid scaffold. Similar drugs include other menopausal hormone therapies and related steroidal agents such as norethisterone, levonorgestrel, estradiol, conjugated estrogens, and selective tissue estrogenic compounds such as raloxifene in the broader therapeutic landscape. After oral administration tibolone is rapidly absorbed and undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism, with low parent-drug exposure and conversion primarily to the 3α-hydroxy and 3β-hydroxy metabolites, which show estrogen receptor activity, and the Δ4-isomer, which has progestogenic and androgenic activity; distribution is consistent with a lipophilic steroid, metabolism is mainly hepatic via hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase and conjugative pathways, and excretion occurs predominantly as sulfate and glucuronide metabolites in urine and feces. Its principal targets are estrogen receptor alpha, estrogen receptor beta, progesterone receptor, and androgen receptor through metabolite-dependent binding. Tibolone is indicated for relief of menopausal symptoms such as vasomotor instability, night sweats, vaginal dryness, and prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis. Adverse effects include vaginal bleeding or spotting, abdominal pain, breast tenderness, weight gain, edema, headache, dizziness, and dermatologic effects; important toxicities include increased risk of stroke in older women, possible stimulation of hormone-sensitive malignancy, and concern for endometrial and breast effects, making its clinical use mainly postmenopausal symptom control and bone protection in selected women when individualized risk-benefit assessment supports therapy.

Name: Sodium oxybate
Description: Sodium oxybate (DB09072) is the sodium salt of gamma-hydroxybutyric acid, a small endogenous short-chain hydroxy carboxylate whose structure consists of a four-carbon aliphatic backbone bearing a terminal carboxylate and a gamma-position hydroxyl group; chemically it is classified as a fatty-acid-like hydroxy acid salt and its core scaffold is the simple GHB/butanoate hydroxy-acid framework. Closely related or similar drugs include gamma-hydroxybutyric acid itself, the precursor gamma-butyrolactone, 1,4-butanediol, and the mixed-cation oxybate products such as calcium/magnesium/potassium/sodium oxybates; pharmacodynamically it also overlaps with sedative-hypnotics that enhance inhibitory neurotransmission, such as benzodiazepines, though by a distinct mechanism. Its known targets include GABAB receptor subunits GABBR1 and GABBR2, with additional interaction reported at putative specific GHB binding sites. After oral administration, sodium oxybate is rapidly absorbed, shows dose-dependent and saturable pharmacokinetics, distributes mainly in total body water, crosses the blood-brain barrier, undergoes extensive hepatic and extrahepatic metabolism largely through conversion to succinic semialdehyde and then succinate entering the Krebs cycle, and is eliminated predominantly as carbon dioxide with minimal unchanged renal excretion. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related CNS and respiratory depression, coma, bradycardia, seizures, confusion, abuse and dependence potential, and dangerous interactions with alcohol, opioids, or other sedatives. It is indicated mainly for narcolepsy, especially cataplexy and excessive daytime sleepiness, and in some regions for idiopathic hypersomnia; adverse effects include nausea, dizziness, enuresis, headache, somnolence, vomiting, anxiety, parasomnias, and depression. Clinically, it is used as a tightly regulated nocturnal therapy to consolidate sleep and improve daytime alertness in narcoleptic patients.

Name: Palbociclib
Description: Palbociclib (DrugBank DB09073) is an orally active, small-molecule cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor whose structure is centered on a substituted pyrido[2,3-d]pyrimidin-7-one–type fused heteroaromatic core bearing piperazine and acetyl substituents that confer kinase-binding affinity and suitable physicochemical properties; chemically it is a heterocyclic nitrogen-rich targeted anticancer agent, and its principal scaffold is the aminopyridopyrimidinone CDK-inhibitor pharmacophore. It is closely related to other selective CDK4/6 inhibitors such as ribociclib and abemaciclib, and more distantly to older pan-CDK inhibitors. Its primary targets are CDK4 and CDK6, thereby inhibiting RB phosphorylation and G1-to-S cell-cycle progression in hormone receptor-positive breast cancer cells. Clinically, palbociclib is indicated mainly for HR-positive, HER2-negative advanced or metastatic breast cancer, typically in combination with endocrine therapy such as letrozole, anastrozole, or fulvestrant, including postmenopausal first-line use and endocrine-resistant disease. After oral administration it is absorbed with a median time to peak of several hours, shows moderate bioavailability with food reducing variability, is highly protein bound and extensively distributed, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A and sulfotransferase pathways, and is eliminated chiefly in feces with a minor urinary component; its terminal half-life supports once-daily dosing on a 21-days-on/7-days-off schedule. Dose-limiting toxicity is mainly myelosuppression, especially neutropenia and leukopenia, with anemia and thrombocytopenia also reported; other adverse effects include fatigue, nausea, stomatitis, diarrhea, alopecia, decreased appetite, infections, and transaminase elevations, while clinically important risks include febrile neutropenia and drug interactions with strong CYP3A inhibitors or inducers.

Name: Olaparib
Description: Olaparib (DB09074) is a small-molecule antineoplastic agent in the poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitor class, structurally characterized by a fused phthalazinone-based heteroaromatic core bearing a fluorobenzyl substituent and a piperazine-containing amide side chain, giving a compact, nitrogen-rich, lipophilic PARP-binding pharmacophore; its principal chemical scaffold is the phthalazinone PARP-inhibitor scaffold that mimics nicotinamide interactions in the catalytic site. Similar drugs include other PARP inhibitors such as niraparib, rucaparib, talazoparib, and veliparib, which share target class overlap but differ in trapping potency and pharmacokinetic behavior. Olaparib selectively inhibits PARP1, PARP2, and to a lesser extent PARP3, blocking DNA single-strand break repair and promoting synthetic lethality in homologous recombination-deficient tumors, especially those with BRCA1 or BRCA2 alterations. It is orally active, with moderate bioavailability, peak plasma concentrations typically within a few hours, wide tissue distribution, high protein binding, extensive hepatic metabolism predominantly via CYP3A4/5, and elimination through both urine and feces mainly as metabolites; dose adjustment or caution is warranted with strong CYP3A inhibitors or inducers and in renal impairment. Toxicities include class-related myelosuppression and gastrointestinal effects, with clinically important anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, and decreased appetite; rare but serious events include myelodysplastic syndrome, acute myeloid leukemia, and pneumonitis. Clinically, it is used for maintenance or treatment of BRCA-mutated or homologous recombination-deficient ovarian, fallopian tube, primary peritoneal, breast, pancreatic, and prostate cancers, including platinum-sensitive recurrent ovarian cancer and metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer with homologous recombination repair gene mutations.

Name: Edoxaban
Description: Edoxaban (DrugBank DB09075) is a small-molecule, orally active direct factor Xa inhibitor built on a compact heteroaromatic carboxamide scaffold featuring a chloropyridinyl ring linked to a substituted pyrazine/piperidine-containing framework, giving an amphiphilic, highly protein-binding anticoagulant chemotype optimized for selective engagement of the factor Xa active site; chemically it is classified as a synthetic oxamidine- and carboxamide-containing antithrombotic in the direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) class, with a heteroaryl-piperidine amide scaffold related in function, though not identical in structure, to other Xa inhibitors such as apixaban, rivaroxaban, betrixaban, and the parenteral agent fondaparinux as a mechanistically similar but structurally distinct comparator. Its principal target is coagulation factor X, specifically activated factor Xa (F10), producing reduced thrombin generation and fibrin clot formation. After oral administration, absorption is moderate with bioavailability around 60% and peak concentrations in 1-2 hours; distribution is characterized by moderate volume of distribution and roughly 55% plasma protein binding; metabolism is limited, with hydrolysis, conjugation, and minor CYP3A4-mediated oxidation; excretion occurs through both renal and biliary/fecal routes, with about half eliminated unchanged in urine and a terminal half-life generally about 10-14 hours. Clinically, edoxaban is indicated for prevention of stroke and systemic embolism in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation and for treatment and secondary prevention of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, typically after initial parenteral anticoagulation. Its major toxicity is bleeding, including gastrointestinal, genitourinary, postoperative, and life-threatening intracranial hemorrhage; other adverse effects include anemia, rash, elevated liver enzymes, and less commonly hypotension or thrombocytopenia, and clinical use requires dose adjustment in renal impairment, caution with P-glycoprotein inhibitors, and avoidance in situations with high bleeding risk or mechanical heart valves.

Name: Umeclidinium
Description: Umeclidinium (DrugBank DB09076) is a synthetic quaternary ammonium antimuscarinic bronchodilator built on a conformationally restricted biaryl and substituted quinuclidine-like/tropane-related cationic scaffold, incorporating ester and ether functionality that confer high affinity for airway muscarinic receptors while limiting systemic penetration; chemically it is classified as a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) and belongs to the inhaled anticholinergic bronchodilator class. Its scaffold and pharmacology are closely related to other quaternary antimuscarinics such as tiotropium, aclidinium, glycopyrrolate, and ipratropium. The principal targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially M3 (CHRM3) on airway smooth muscle, with activity also at M1 (CHRM1) and M2 (CHRM2), producing sustained bronchodilation by inhibiting acetylcholine-mediated bronchoconstriction. After oral inhalation, systemic absorption is low to moderate but measurable, time to peak plasma levels is rapid, distribution is limited by permanent cationic character, protein binding is moderate, metabolism occurs mainly via CYP2D6-mediated oxidation with additional substrate recognition by P-glycoprotein, and elimination is through combined hepatic metabolism with fecal and urinary excretion of parent drug and metabolites; the effective pulmonary duration supports once-daily dosing. It is indicated for maintenance treatment of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, including chronic bronchitis and emphysema, and is also used in fixed-dose combinations such as umeclidinium/vilanterol for persistent airflow limitation. Adverse effects reflect anticholinergic action and include dry mouth, constipation, tachycardia, urinary retention, blurred vision, and paradoxical bronchospasm, while common clinical side effects include nasopharyngitis, cough, upper respiratory tract infection, arthralgia, and headache. Toxicity is generally low at therapeutic inhaled doses, but overdose or susceptible patients may develop pronounced antimuscarinic effects, precipitation of narrow-angle glaucoma, worsening bladder outlet obstruction, or cardiovascular symptoms.

Name: Lenvatinib
Description: Lenvatinib (DrugBank DB09078) is an orally active small-molecule multikinase inhibitor built on a substituted quinoline/quinazoline-like heteroaromatic urea scaffold, featuring a halogenated aromatic ether and cyclopropyl-containing framework that supports high-affinity ATP-site binding to receptor tyrosine kinases; chemically it is categorized as a synthetic heteroaryl kinase inhibitor, with a diaryl ether–urea pharmacophore and scaffold features broadly similar to other antiangiogenic tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as sorafenib, regorafenib, pazopanib, sunitinib, and axitinib. Its principal targets include VEGFR1/FLT1, VEGFR2/KDR, VEGFR3/FLT4, FGFR1-4, PDGFRα, RET, and KIT, explaining its antiangiogenic and antiproliferative effects. After oral administration, lenvatinib is well absorbed, reaches peak concentrations within hours, is highly protein bound, distributes systemically, is metabolized predominantly by CYP3A4 and nonenzymatic pathways including aldehyde oxidase with minor contributions from glutathione-related processes, and is eliminated through both fecal and renal routes with a terminal half-life that supports once-daily dosing. Clinically, it is used for radioactive iodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer, unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma, advanced renal cell carcinoma in combination with everolimus, and advanced endometrial carcinoma in combination with pembrolizumab. Toxicities reflect potent VEGF-pathway blockade and include hypertension, proteinuria, hemorrhage, arterial thromboembolic events, hepatotoxicity, renal dysfunction, impaired wound healing, gastrointestinal perforation, and embryo-fetal toxicity; common adverse effects include fatigue, diarrhea, decreased appetite, weight loss, nausea, stomatitis, palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia, dysphonia, and hypothyroidism. In practice, it is used as a targeted systemic antineoplastic agent requiring blood pressure, renal, hepatic, and urine protein monitoring, dose interruption, and reduction for intolerance.

Name: Nintedanib
Description: Nintedanib (DB09079) is an orally active small-molecule indolinone-derived tyrosine kinase inhibitor whose structure is centered on a substituted 1H-indole/indolinone-like aromatic core linked through a methylene bridge to a dimethyl-substituted amino phenyl ring and bearing a methyl ester and polar carbonyl functionalities, features that support ATP-pocket binding in receptor kinases; chemically it is categorized as a multikinase angiokinase inhibitor, and its key scaffold is the 6-methoxy indolinone/indole-type heteroaromatic kinase-inhibitor framework. Similar drugs include other antiangiogenic kinase inhibitors such as sunitinib, sorafenib, pazopanib, and axitinib, although nintedanib is particularly distinguished by combined inhibition of fibroblast growth factor, platelet-derived growth factor, and vascular endothelial growth factor receptor families. Its major targets include VEGFR1/FLT1, VEGFR2/KDR, VEGFR3/FLT4, FGFR1-3, PDGFR-alpha and PDGFR-beta, with additional activity reported against kinases such as LCK, LYN, and SRC family-related enzymes. Pharmacokinetically, it is orally absorbed with low-to-moderate bioavailability limited by first-pass handling, is highly protein bound, distributes mainly within plasma and tissues relevant to fibrotic and tumor disease, undergoes predominant esterase-mediated hydrolysis followed by glucuronidation with relatively minor CYP3A4 contribution, and is eliminated chiefly via the biliary-fecal route with limited renal excretion. It is indicated for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, other progressive fibrosing interstitial lung diseases, systemic sclerosis-associated interstitial lung disease, and in combination with docetaxel for previously treated non-small cell lung adenocarcinoma. Toxicities are dominated by gastrointestinal and hepatic effects, including diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, transaminase elevations, and drug-induced liver injury; clinically important examples also include bleeding, hypertension, arterial thromboembolic events, impaired wound healing, gastrointestinal perforation, and embryo-fetal toxicity. In practice, nintedanib is used as an antifibrotic and antiangiogenic agent to slow forced vital capacity decline in fibrosing lung disease and to provide adjunct antitumor benefit in advanced lung cancer, with common side effects including diarrhea, decreased appetite, weight loss, fatigue,

Name: Olodaterol
Description: Olodaterol (DrugBank DB09080) is a synthetic long-acting sympathomimetic bronchodilator whose structure is characterized by an aryloxyalkanolamine beta-agonist pharmacophore containing a substituted phenyl ring linked through an ether side chain to a chiral ethanolamine-like moiety and appended aromatic/heteroaromatic functionality that confers high β2-adrenoceptor affinity and prolonged receptor residence time; chemically it is classified as a phenethylamine-derived adrenergic agonist, more specifically a long-acting β2-adrenergic receptor agonist, built on the classic aryloxypropanolamine/arylethanolamine bronchodilator scaffold seen in related agents. Similar drugs include formoterol, salmeterol, indacaterol, vilanterol, and short-acting congeners such as albuterol (salbutamol). Its principal target is the β2-adrenergic receptor encoded by ADRB2 on airway smooth muscle, where receptor activation increases adenylate cyclase signaling and cAMP to produce sustained bronchodilation. After oral inhalation, systemic absorption is relatively low to moderate but measurable, pulmonary uptake is rapid, distribution is consistent with a lipophilic LABA, metabolism occurs predominantly by direct glucuronidation and O-demethylation with CYP involvement including CYP2C8 and CYP2C9, and elimination is via both renal and fecal routes with a terminal half-life supporting once-daily dosing. Toxicity is typical of β2-agonists and includes dose-related tachycardia, palpitations, tremor, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, and potential QT-related or other arrhythmic risk in overdose or susceptible patients. It is indicated as maintenance bronchodilator therapy for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, including chronic bronchitis and emphysema, improving dyspnea, airflow limitation, exercise tolerance, and rescue-medication use; clinically it is used once daily, often as an inhaled combination with tiotropium, and common adverse effects include nasopharyngitis, cough, dizziness, back pain, arthralgia, and upper respiratory symptoms.

Name: Idebenone
Description: Idebenone (DrugBank DB09081) is a short-chain benzoquinone structurally characterized by a 1,4-benzoquinone ring bearing methoxy substituents and a terminal hydroxylated decyl side chain, making it a synthetic analog of coenzyme Q10; chemically it belongs to the quinone/ubiquinone-related antioxidant class and is built on a para-benzoquinone redox scaffold. Similar drugs include coenzyme Q10 itself, ubidecarenone, and other mitochondrial redox-active quinones such as menadione, although idebenone is distinguished by its shorter, more polar side chain and improved oral bioavailability. Pharmacokinetically, it is orally administered, absorbed variably but better with food, is highly lipophilic yet sufficiently amphipathic to distribute into tissues including the CNS, undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism mainly by side-chain oxidation and quinone reduction/conjugation to inactive sulfate and glucuronide metabolites, and is eliminated predominantly in urine as metabolites with a lesser fecal component; parent drug exposure is generally low and half-life is relatively short. Its principal pharmacology involves antioxidant and electron-carrier effects in mitochondrial bioenergetics, with reported functional interactions involving components of the electron transport chain, especially NQO1-mediated reduction and modulation of complex III-related electron flow rather than a single classical receptor target. It is indicated mainly for Leber hereditary optic neuropathy and has been studied in Friedreich ataxia, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, and other mitochondrial or neurodegenerative disorders. Adverse effects are usually mild, including diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, headache, cough, and nasopharyngitis; toxicity is generally low, but excessive exposure may theoretically promote redox cycling, hepatic burden, or quinone-related oxidative injury. Clinically, idebenone has been used as an oral neuroprotective and mitochondrial support agent to preserve or improve vision in LHON and to investigate symptomatic benefit in disorders marked by oxidative stress, fatigue, exercise intolerance, or neurologic dysfunction.

Name: Vilanterol
Description: Vilanterol (DrugBank DB09082) is a long-acting inhaled sympathomimetic bronchodilator structurally characterized as an aryloxyalkylamino ethanol derivative bearing a substituted phenethylamine/beta-amino alcohol core with a lipophilic aromatic ether region and hydroxylated side chains that support high beta2-adrenoceptor affinity and prolonged receptor residency; chemically it is a long-acting beta2-adrenergic receptor agonist within the phenethanolamine class, built on the classic saligenin/arylethanolamine bronchodilator scaffold modified for ultra-long activity. It is closely related to other LABAs such as salmeterol, formoterol, indacaterol, and olodaterol, which share beta2-selective bronchodilatory pharmacology. Its principal target is the beta2-adrenergic receptor encoded by ADRB2, activation of which increases adenylate cyclase signaling and airway smooth-muscle relaxation. After oral inhalation, systemic absorption is limited but measurable, with rapid pulmonary uptake, extensive tissue distribution, high plasma protein binding, predominant hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 to less active metabolites, and elimination chiefly as metabolites in urine and feces; the effective bronchodilator duration supports once-daily dosing. Toxicity is consistent with beta-agonist excess and may include tachycardia, palpitations, tremor, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, QT-related arrhythmic risk, and paradoxical bronchospasm, with overdose potentially causing clinically significant cardiovascular stimulation. Vilanterol is indicated for maintenance treatment of airflow obstruction in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and, in fixed-dose combinations with inhaled corticosteroids such as fluticasone furoate, for maintenance treatment of asthma; clinically it is used in products such as fluticasone furoate/vilanterol and umeclidinium/vilanterol to improve lung function, reduce dyspnea and wheeze, and decrease exacerbation burden, while common adverse effects include nasopharyngitis, headache, cough, oropharyngeal irritation, and, in combination regimens, pneumonia risk in susceptible COPD patients.

Name: Ivabradine
Description: Ivabradine (DB09083) is a small, lipophilic, orally active benzazepinone-derived bradycardic agent whose structure is centered on a fused bicyclic benzocyclobutane/benzazepinone-like aromatic heterocyclic scaffold bearing methoxy substituents and a tertiary amine-containing side chain, a motif that supports selective binding within hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated channels; chemically it is classified as a cardioselective funny current inhibitor and more broadly as a heterocyclic amine. Its principal scaffold is the substituted benzazepine/benzocyclobutane pharmacophore seen in other heart-rate-lowering agents, although true close analogs are limited; mechanistically similar drugs include beta blockers such as metoprolol and calcium-channel blockers such as verapamil, while alinidine is a historical example of another sinus-node rate-reducing agent. Ivabradine is absorbed orally with good bioavailability that increases with food, reaches peak plasma concentrations in about 1 hour, is moderately protein bound, distributes systemically to cardiac tissue, undergoes extensive hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4-mediated oxidation to an active N-desmethyl metabolite, and is eliminated through both feces and urine with an effective half-life of about 6 hours. Its main target is HCN4 in the sinoatrial node, with lesser activity at related HCN channel isoforms and retinal Ih channels that explain visual phenomena. It is indicated for chronic stable angina and chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction in patients in sinus rhythm, particularly when heart rate remains elevated despite beta-blocker therapy or beta blockers are not tolerated. Toxicity is dominated by exaggerated pharmacology, including sinus bradycardia, conduction disturbances, hypotension, atrial fibrillation, and overdose-associated profound bradyarrhythmia; luminous phenomena or phosphenes are characteristic adverse effects, alongside headache, dizziness, fatigue, and occasional QT-related proarrhythmic concern secondary to marked bradycardia. Clinically, ivabradine is used to lower heart rate without reducing myocardial contractility, for example to improve angina symptoms and reduce heart-failure hospitalization risk in selected patients.

Name: Benzydamine
Description: Benzydamine (DrugBank DB09084) is a locally acting nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug with analgesic, local anesthetic, and antiseptic properties, structurally characterized as an indazole derivative bearing a substituted benzyl group and a dimethylaminoalkoxy side chain, giving it an amphiphilic aromatic tertiary-amine architecture; chemically it is classified among indazole-based NSAID-like anti-inflammatory agents, and its core scaffold is best described as an indazole heteroaromatic system linked to a benzyloxyethyl dimethylamine motif. It is broadly similar in therapeutic intent, though not necessarily close in structure, to topical anti-inflammatory and oral mucosal agents such as flurbiprofen, difflam formulations of benzydamine itself, and to some extent topical ketoprofen or phenol-containing throat preparations. Benzydamine is mainly used topically on the oral, pharyngeal, or vaginal mucosa, where systemic absorption is limited but measurable; absorbed drug distributes into inflamed tissues, undergoes hepatic metabolism including oxidative and conjugative pathways, and is excreted primarily in urine as metabolites with a smaller fraction as unchanged drug. Its pharmacology is attributed less to classic cyclooxygenase inhibition than to suppression of pro-inflammatory cytokine production and membrane-stabilizing/local anesthetic effects; no single definitive high-affinity human target protein is universally established, although interactions affecting inflammatory mediators such as TNF-alpha, IL-1 beta, and prostaglandin-related pathways are implicated. Indications include symptomatic relief of sore throat, oral mucositis, gingivitis, stomatitis, post-dental or post-tonsillectomy pain, and inflammatory vaginal conditions. Adverse effects are usually local and mild, including burning, stinging, numbness, dry mouth, taste disturbance, nausea, and hypersensitivity reactions; toxicity is uncommon at therapeutic topical doses but overdose, especially oral ingestion, may cause agitation, hallucinations, vomiting, CNS excitation, or seizures. Clinically, it is used as mouthwash, gargle, spray, lozenge, or vaginal preparation for short-term relief of pain and inflammation in ENT, dental, oncology supportive care, and gynecologic practice.

Name: Tetracaine
Description: Tetracaine (DrugBank DB09085) is a potent ester-type local anesthetic whose structure consists of a para-aminobenzoic acid–derived aromatic ring linked through an ester bond to a 2-dimethylaminoethyl side chain, with a butyl substituent on the aniline nitrogen that increases lipophilicity and topical potency; chemically it belongs to the amino ester local anesthetics, and its core scaffold is the p-aminobenzoate ester pharmacophore shared by several classic surface anesthetics. Closely related drugs include procaine, chloroprocaine, benzocaine, and cocaine, with tetracaine generally being more lipophilic and longer acting than procaine. Its principal target proteins are voltage-gated sodium channels, especially neuronal Nav channel isoforms, which it blocks in a state-dependent manner to inhibit action potential initiation and conduction. Tetracaine is used primarily for topical and regional anesthesia, including ophthalmic anesthesia, spinal anesthesia, and relief of pain or pruritus on mucosal or cutaneous surfaces, for example before eye procedures, lumbar puncture, or minor dermatologic interventions. Systemic absorption depends on dose, formulation, and site of application, increasing across mucosa or damaged skin; distribution is rapid to highly perfused tissues, protein binding is moderate to high, metabolism occurs mainly by plasma pseudocholinesterases and other esterases to para-aminobenzoic acid-related metabolites, and excretion is chiefly renal as metabolites. Toxicity reflects excessive sodium channel blockade and CNS or cardiovascular exposure, causing agitation, tinnitus, circumoral numbness, seizures, hypotension, arrhythmias, respiratory depression, or cardiac arrest, while local adverse effects include burning, erythema, corneal injury, and allergic reactions, particularly ester-anesthetic hypersensitivity related to PABA metabolites.

Name: Chlortetracycline
Description: Chlortetracycline (DrugBank DB09093) is a first-generation tetracycline antibiotic characterized by a rigid, linearly fused four-ring naphthacene core bearing multiple keto-enol and phenolic hydroxyl functionalities, a C4 dimethylamino group essential for antibacterial activity, and a distinctive chlorine substituent that differentiates it from tetracycline; chemically it belongs to the polyketide-derived tetracycline class, with the classic tetracycline scaffold serving as its central chemophore. Closely related drugs include tetracycline, oxytetracycline, doxycycline, demeclocycline, and minocycline, which share the same 30S ribosomal inhibition mechanism but differ in substitution pattern and pharmacokinetic behavior. Its principal target is the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit, especially 16S rRNA within the A-site region, where it blocks aminoacyl-tRNA binding and suppresses protein synthesis. Orally absorbed incompletely and variably, its bioavailability is reduced by food and markedly by divalent or trivalent cations; it distributes widely to tissues, accumulates in bone and teeth, crosses the placenta, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated mainly unchanged by renal and biliary/fecal routes. Toxicities include dose-related gastrointestinal irritation, hepatotoxicity, phototoxicity, superinfection, and permanent tooth discoloration or impaired skeletal growth in fetuses and children; adverse effects commonly include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, esophagitis, rash, and photosensitivity. Clinically, chlortetracycline has been used for susceptible bacterial infections such as respiratory, skin, ocular, and genitourinary infections, acneiform disorders, and some veterinary indications, although modern human use is limited by resistance, tolerability, and the availability of better-characterized tetracyclines.

Name: Benzoyl peroxide
Description: Benzoyl peroxide (DrugBank DB09096) is a symmetric diacyl peroxide composed of two benzoyl aromatic rings linked through a peroxide bond, making it a highly oxidizing, lipophilic organic peroxide; chemically it is classified as a peroxide antiseborrheic/anti-acne agent, and its core scaffold is the dibenzoyl peroxide motif, an aromatic acyl-peroxide framework shared conceptually with other peroxide oxidants. Similar drugs include topical anti-acne oxidizing or keratolytic agents such as hydrogen peroxide, adapalene, tretinoin, salicylic acid, and azelaic acid, although these differ structurally and mechanistically. After topical administration, systemic absorption is low; the drug penetrates the stratum corneum and pilosebaceous unit, where it is rapidly reduced in skin to benzoic acid, with minimal distribution beyond cutaneous tissues, little unchanged parent detectable systemically, hepatic-independent local biotransformation, and urinary excretion mainly as benzoate/hippurate-related metabolites. Its pharmacologic action is largely non-receptor mediated: it generates reactive oxygen species that kill Cutibacterium acnes and has mild comedolytic and keratolytic effects; no single high-affinity human target protein is established, though microbial membrane and protein oxidation are central. It is indicated primarily for acne vulgaris, including inflammatory papules, pustules, and comedonal disease, and is also used in combination regimens for truncal acne or rosacea-like follicular eruptions. Toxicity is predominantly local and dose dependent, with irritant dermatitis, erythema, peeling, burning, edema, and rare allergic contact dermatitis; ocular or mucosal exposure causes marked irritation, and ingestion can irritate the gastrointestinal tract. Clinical use is mainly topical gels, creams, washes, and fixed-dose combinations with clindamycin, erythromycin, or adapalene to reduce bacterial burden, limit antibiotic resistance, and improve mild-to-moderate acne outcomes.

Name: Magnesium hydroxide
Description: Magnesium hydroxide (DrugBank DB09104) is a simple inorganic alkaline earth metal hydroxide composed of divalent magnesium coordinated to hydroxide ions in a brucite-like ionic lattice, forming a poorly water-soluble basic solid rather than a discrete organic pharmacophore; chemically it belongs to the mineral hydroxides and saline antacids/laxatives, and its scaffold is best described as a magnesium-centered metal hydroxide framework. Closely related or functionally similar drugs include aluminum hydroxide, calcium carbonate, sodium bicarbonate, magnesium carbonate, magnesium oxide, and the osmotic saline cathartic magnesium citrate. Its pharmacological action is largely physicochemical rather than receptor-mediated: in the stomach it neutralizes hydrochloric acid to form magnesium chloride and water, while in the intestine unabsorbed magnesium salts retain water osmotically and may stimulate cholecystokinin-mediated motility; therefore no specific target protein is firmly established, though gastrointestinal acid and fluid balance are the relevant biological systems. Oral absorption of magnesium is limited and variable, distribution follows systemic magnesium handling when absorbed, it is not metabolized, and absorbed magnesium is eliminated mainly by the kidney whereas unabsorbed material is excreted in feces. It is indicated for symptomatic relief of dyspepsia, heartburn, sour stomach, and as a laxative for constipation, including occasional bowel evacuation. Adverse effects include diarrhea, abdominal cramping, nausea, and electrolyte disturbances. Toxicity is usually low in patients with normal renal function but excessive dosing or renal impairment can cause hypermagnesemia with lethargy, hypotension, diminished reflexes, bradycardia, respiratory depression, and rarely cardiac arrest. Clinically it is used alone or in combination antacid products and in milk of magnesia formulations for short-term treatment of acid-related symptoms and constipation.

Name: Colfosceril palmitate
Description: Colfosceril palmitate (DrugBank DB09114), also known as dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine, is a synthetic or purified phospholipid composed of a glycerophosphocholine backbone esterified with two saturated palmitic acid chains, giving an amphipathic structure with a zwitterionic phosphocholine headgroup and a diacylglycerol lipid scaffold characteristic of phosphatidylcholines; chemically it is a glycerophospholipid, specifically a saturated phosphatidylcholine, and its core scaffold is the 1,2-diacyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine framework. It is closely related to endogenous pulmonary surfactant lipids and to exogenous surfactant drugs such as beractant, calfactant, poractant alfa, and lucinactant, although those preparations are multicomponent mixtures rather than single-molecule phospholipids. Its pharmacologic action is primarily biophysical rather than receptor-mediated, with no single well-defined protein target; instead it integrates into the alveolar air-liquid interface to reduce surface tension, though surfactant-associated proteins such as SFTPB and SFTPC are biologically relevant comparators in native surfactant systems. Administered intratracheally or by inhalation, it acts locally in the lung with minimal systemic absorption; distributed across alveolar surfaces, it is turned over by alveolar type II pneumocytes and macrophages, metabolized by phospholipases to lysophospholipids, choline, glycerol derivatives, and palmitate, and its components are recycled or cleared through normal lipid metabolic pathways rather than renal excretion as intact drug. It is indicated for prevention or treatment of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome due to surfactant deficiency, and has been used clinically in premature infants and investigated in other surfactant-deficient pulmonary states. Toxicity is generally low and largely procedure- or formulation-related, with examples including transient hypoxia, bradycardia, airway obstruction, reflux of instilled material, pulmonary hemorrhage, and alterations in ventilation; adverse effects similarly include endotracheal tube blockage, desaturation, and hemodynamic instability during administration. In practice, colfosceril palmitate has been used as an exogenous surfactant replacement therapy in neonatal intensive care to improve lung compliance, oxygenation, and survival in preterm infants with established or

Name: Stiripentol
Description: Stiripentol (DB09118) is a chiral aromatic allylic alcohol anticonvulsant whose structure is centered on a substituted pentenol backbone bearing a tertiary alcohol, a 3,4-methylenedioxyphenyl ring, and a trifluoromethyl group, giving a lipophilic, electron-rich phenyl-alkenol framework; chemically it is best classified as a methylenedioxy-substituted aromatic alcohol and fluorinated anticonvulsant, with a phenyl-alkenol scaffold related in broad medicinal-chemistry terms to other aromatic antiseizure agents and to methylenedioxy-containing compounds such as carbamazepine-like anticonvulsants in therapeutic space, though not by close structural identity, and it is sometimes discussed alongside clobazam, valproate, and cannabidiol as functionally similar combination therapies in severe epilepsies.
