Its principal targets are not a single canonical receptor but include positive allosteric enhancement of GABAA receptor-mediated neurotransmission and inhibition of several cytochrome P450 enzymes, notably CYP3A4, CYP1A2, and CYP2C19, thereby increasing concentrations of coadministered agents such as clobazam and norclobazam. Oral absorption is substantial, food can affect exposure, protein binding is high, distribution is systemic with CNS penetration, metabolism is extensive hepatic biotransformation, and excretion occurs mainly as metabolites in urine. It is indicated primarily for Dravet syndrome, especially as adjunctive therapy with clobazam and valproate for refractory generalized tonic-clonic or clonic seizures. Adverse effects commonly include somnolence, sedation, ataxia, irritability, anorexia, weight loss, nausea, neutropenia, and elevated liver enzymes; toxicity is dominated by CNS depression, feeding difficulty, and drug-drug interactions from enzyme inhibition, with increased risk of excessive benzodiazepine exposure. Clinically, it is used in pediatric and specialist epilepsy practice for pharmacoresistant epileptic encephalopathies when seizure reduction justifies careful monitoring of sedation, hematologic parameters, hepatic function, and interacting antiseizure drugs.

Name: Eslicarbazepine acetate
Description: Eslicarbazepine acetate (DrugBank DB09119) is a dibenzazepine-derived anticonvulsant prodrug structurally characterized by a tricyclic iminostilbene-like framework bearing a 10,11-dihydrocarboxamide core and an O-acetylated hydroxyl substituent that is rapidly converted in vivo to eslicarbazepine; chemically it is a carboxamide and acetate ester, and its core scaffold is the dibenz[b,f]azepine system shared with several voltage-gated sodium channel modulators. Closely related drugs include carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and the active metabolite licarbazepine, all of which belong to the same broader anticonvulsant chemical family. Its principal pharmacologic target is voltage-gated sodium channels, especially neuronal sodium channel alpha subunits such as SCN1A, SCN2A, and SCN8A, with functional preference for stabilization of the inactivated state and reduction of repetitive neuronal firing. After oral administration it is well absorbed, extensively and rapidly hydrolyzed by first-pass esterases to eslicarbazepine, minimally protein bound to a moderate degree, distributed systemically, and eliminated mainly by renal excretion as unchanged eslicarbazepine and glucuronide conjugates; oxidative CYP metabolism is limited, supporting a relatively predictable interaction profile, although enzyme induction effects can occur. It is indicated primarily for focal-onset seizures in epilepsy, including partial seizures with or without secondary generalization, and is used clinically as once-daily monotherapy or adjunctive therapy. Adverse effects commonly include dizziness, somnolence, diplopia, nausea, vomiting, headache, ataxia, and fatigue, while notable toxicities include hyponatremia, rash or rare severe hypersensitivity, hepatic dysfunction, suicidal ideation, and dose-related CNS depression; overdose may produce marked sedation, vertigo, and coordination impairment.

Name: Aurothioglucose
Description: Aurothioglucose (DrugBank DB09121) is a parenteral gold(I) coordination compound in which monovalent gold is linearly bound to a thiolate sulfur derived from thioglucose, giving an organogold, sulfur-containing carbohydrate structure best viewed as a gold-thiosugar complex rather than a classical small heterocycle; chemically it belongs to the antirheumatic gold salts, and its core scaffold is the gold(I)-thiolate motif shared with other chrysotherapeutic agents. Closely related drugs include sodium aurothiomalate and auranofin, which likewise deliver gold to biologic nucleophiles, although auranofin is more lipophilic and orally active. After intramuscular administration, aurothioglucose is absorbed slowly, distributes extensively to plasma proteins and tissues of the reticuloendothelial system including synovium, liver, kidney, skin, and bone marrow, undergoes limited classic biotransformation with ligand exchange and persistent tissue binding to sulfhydryl-rich macromolecules, and is eliminated slowly via urine and feces with marked tissue retention and a long terminal persistence. Its pharmacology is linked to protein thiol binding and inhibition of inflammatory and immune pathways; reported targets are not highly selective but include thioredoxin reductase and other cysteine-dependent redox or lysosomal enzymes in immune cells. It was used mainly for rheumatoid arthritis and occasionally other inflammatory arthropathies when disease-modifying therapy was needed. Toxicity is important and includes dermatitis, stomatitis, pruritus, proteinuria and gold nephropathy, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, aplastic anemia, hepatotoxicity, and rare interstitial pneumonitis; adverse effects commonly include rash, mucosal ulceration, diarrhea, and injection-site reactions, which limited clinical use and led to decline in favor of safer modern DMARDs.

Name: Dienogest
Description: Dienogest (DrugBank DB09123) is a synthetic progestin derived from the 19-nortestosterone series, structurally characterized as a steroidal gonane with the classic four-ring cyclopenta[a]phenanthrene nucleus, a 17α-cyanomethyl substituent, a 17β-hydroxyl group, and an additional double bond that contributes to its distinctive pharmacology; chemically it is classified as a nortestosterone-derived progestogen, and its core scaffold is the estrane/gonane steroid framework. It is pharmacologically similar to other progestins such as norethindrone, levonorgestrel, desogestrel metabolites, and the antiandrogenic progestin drospirenone, although dienogest is notable for relatively strong progestational and antiandrogenic activity with minimal glucocorticoid or mineralocorticoid effects. Its principal target is the progesterone receptor, with functional suppression of gonadotropin release and indirect reduction of estradiol-driven endometrial proliferation; lower-affinity interactions affecting androgenic pathways help explain its antiandrogenic profile. Orally, dienogest is well absorbed with high bioavailability, moderate plasma protein binding mainly to albumin rather than sex hormone-binding globulin, wide tissue distribution, extensive hepatic metabolism largely via CYP3A4-mediated hydroxylation and conjugation, and urinary plus fecal excretion of metabolites with a terminal half-life compatible with once-daily dosing. Toxicity is generally that of a hormonal agent, including embryo-fetal risk in pregnancy, potential hepatic dysfunction, abnormal uterine bleeding, and uncommon thromboembolic or mood-related adverse outcomes. Clinically it is used for endometriosis, dysmenorrhea, chronic pelvic pain, and as a component of some oral contraceptive regimens; common adverse effects include irregular bleeding, headache, breast discomfort, nausea, acne, decreased libido, and depressive symptoms.

Name: Potassium citrate
Description: Potassium citrate (DrugBank DB09125) is an orally administered potassium salt of citric acid in which three potassium cations are associated with the tricarboxylate form of citrate, a small, highly polar aliphatic hydroxycarboxylate characterized by a three-carbon backbone bearing three carboxylate groups and one secondary hydroxyl group; chemically it belongs to mineral supplements, urinary alkalinizers, and citrate salts, with a citrate/hydroxytricarboxylate scaffold that is shared across related agents such as sodium citrate, citric acid, potassium bicarbonate/citrate combinations, and calcium citrate. After oral administration it is well absorbed and dissociates in the gastrointestinal tract into potassium and citrate; citrate is distributed in extracellular fluid, enters intermediary metabolism, and is largely oxidized to bicarbonate, thereby increasing systemic alkali load and urinary pH, while potassium distributes according to total body stores and renal handling; elimination occurs mainly through renal excretion of potassium, with urinary citrate rising as a pharmacodynamic effect rather than extensive unchanged drug excretion. Its principal pharmacologic targets are physiological rather than receptor-specific, involving modulation of urinary hydrogen ion balance and ionic interactions that reduce calcium stone formation; no single canonical protein target is usually assigned, though effects depend on renal transport processes handling citrate and potassium. It is indicated for hypocitraturia, uric acid nephrolithiasis, calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis, and renal tubular acidosis, and is used clinically to prevent recurrent kidney stones and alkalinize urine. Toxicity is dominated by hyperkalemia and metabolic alkalosis, particularly in renal impairment or with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or potassium-sparing diuretics, with examples including arrhythmias, muscle weakness, and cardiac conduction disturbances; common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, and esophageal or gastric irritation, especially with inadequate dilution or prolonged tablet contact.

Name: Uridine triacetate
Description: Uridine triacetate (DB09144) is the tri-O-acetylated prodrug of the endogenous pyrimidine nucleoside uridine, consisting of a uracil base linked to a ribofuranose ring in which the 2′, 3′, and 5′ hydroxyl groups are esterified with acetate moieties, making it a lipophilic nucleoside ester and chemically a pyrimidine nucleoside derivative; its core scaffold is the uridine or ribosyl-uracil scaffold, and structurally or mechanistically related agents include uridine itself, uridine monophosphate preparations, and the antidotal pyrimidine rescue analogue leucovorin only in the broad sense of metabolic rescue, although leucovorin is not a nucleoside. After oral administration, uridine triacetate is absorbed and rapidly deacetylated by nonspecific esterases to uridine, producing plasma uridine concentrations well above endogenous levels; uridine distributes systemically, enters salvage pathways, is phosphorylated intracellularly to UMP, UDP, and UTP, and is ultimately catabolized through normal pyrimidine metabolism with renal excretion of metabolites. Its principal pharmacologic target is not a single high-affinity protein receptor but the metabolic network of pyrimidine salvage enzymes, and in hereditary orotic aciduria it functionally bypasses deficient uridine monophosphate synthase. Clinically, it is indicated as an antidote for 5-fluorouracil or capecitabine overdose or early severe toxicity, where excess uridine competes with toxic FUTP incorporation into RNA, and for hereditary orotic aciduria to correct pyrimidine deficiency. Toxicity is generally low relative to cytotoxic antidotes, but adverse effects include vomiting, nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and occasionally headache; serious toxicity is uncommon, though delayed treatment after fluoropyrimidine poisoning may fail to prevent life-threatening myelosuppression, mucositis, neurotoxicity, or cardiotoxicity from the parent exposure.

Name: Nitrogen
Description: Nitrogen (DrugBank DB09152) is the elemental diatomic gas N2, consisting of two identical nitrogen atoms joined by a very strong nonpolar triple bond in a linear, highly symmetric structure that is chemically inert under physiological conditions; it belongs to the inorganic medicinal gas class and its scaffold is best described simply as a homonuclear diatomic small-molecule gas rather than an organic pharmacophore. Similar drugs are other medical gases and cryogenic agents, especially argon, helium, xenon, oxygen, nitrous oxide, and carbon dioxide, although nitrogen is distinguished by minimal intrinsic receptor-mediated pharmacology. Pharmacokinetically, nitrogen is not meaningfully absorbed as a reactive solute but equilibrates by inhalation across alveoli according to partial-pressure gradients, distributes rapidly in blood and tissues with greater retention in enclosed gas spaces, undergoes no metabolism, and is eliminated unchanged via exhalation; as a compressed or liquid gas, exposure kinetics depend strongly on ambient concentration and pressure. Toxicity is primarily physical and environmental rather than biochemical, with simple asphyxiation from oxygen displacement, decompression-related bubble effects under pressure, and severe cold injury or frostbite with liquid nitrogen; examples include hypoxic syncope, nitrogen narcosis in divers, and cryogenic tissue damage. No specific target proteins are established for therapeutic action. Its principal indication is as a pharmaceutical excipient, inert atmosphere, and cryogen for preservation and procedural cooling, including storage of reproductive cells, tissues, blood products, and laboratory specimens. Adverse effects in exposure settings include dizziness, confusion, headache, loss of consciousness, frostbite, and rarely death from hypoxia. Clinically, nitrogen is used mainly in gas mixtures, device systems, cryopreservation, and procedural cryogenic applications rather than as a conventional systemic drug.

Name: Sodium citrate
Description: Sodium citrate (DrugBank DB09154) is the trisodium salt of citric acid, a small, highly water-soluble aliphatic hydroxytricarboxylate composed of a three-carbon citrate scaffold bearing one hydroxyl and three carboxylate groups that are extensively ionized at physiologic pH; it is therefore classified as an organic sodium salt, citrate salt, and systemic/urinary alkalinizing agent. Its core chemical scaffold is the citrate backbone shared with related agents such as citric acid, potassium citrate, sodium citrate/citric acid combinations, and anticoagulant citrate dextrose solutions. Pharmacologically, sodium citrate acts mainly through physicochemical buffering and calcium chelation rather than selective receptor binding; accordingly, no canonical high-affinity drug target proteins are usually assigned, although citrate is handled by endogenous transport and metabolic systems including sodium-dependent citrate transporters such as SLC13 family members. After oral administration it is readily absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, distributed largely within extracellular fluid, metabolized predominantly in the liver and other tissues through the tricarboxylic acid cycle to bicarbonate, and excreted mainly as bicarbonate/carbon dioxide and, depending on dose and urine pH, partially in urine as citrate. Clinically it is used to alkalinize urine in metabolic acidosis, renal tubular acidosis, uric acid or cystine nephrolithiasis, and dysuria associated with acidic urine, and as an anticoagulant in extracorporeal circuits and blood products by lowering ionized calcium. Toxicity is usually related to sodium load, metabolic alkalosis, hypernatremia, and citrate-induced hypocalcemia, with manifestations including tetany, paresthesias, arrhythmias, and seizures, especially in renal or hepatic impairment or massive transfusion. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, belching, and electrolyte disturbances.

Name: Etizolam
Description: Etizolam (DrugBank DB09166) is a thienotriazolodiazepine anxiolytic-hypnotic whose structure consists of a benzodiazepine-like fused heteroaromatic system in which a thiophene ring replaces the benzene ring of classical benzodiazepines and a triazole ring is annelated onto the diazepine core, with a chlorophenyl substituent that contributes to high lipophilicity and receptor affinity; chemically it is classified as a benzodiazepine-related GABAergic sedative, with a thienodiazepine/thienotriazolodiazepine scaffold. It is closely related pharmacologically to alprazolam, triazolam, diazepam, and clotiazepam, sharing positive allosteric modulation of GABAA receptors at the benzodiazepine site, principally on receptor complexes containing alpha, gamma2, and related subunits rather than a single unique protein target. After oral administration it is rapidly absorbed, reaches peak plasma concentrations within a few hours, distributes well into the CNS because of lipophilicity, undergoes extensive hepatic biotransformation mainly via CYP3A4 to alpha-hydroxyethyl and 8-hydroxy metabolites, and is excreted predominantly in urine as metabolites, with an elimination half-life generally shorter than many classical benzodiazepines. Its main indications are anxiety disorders, panic symptoms, insomnia, and short-term management of psychosomatic tension states. Adverse effects include drowsiness, sedation, psychomotor impairment, ataxia, anterograde amnesia, dizziness, cognitive slowing, and less commonly paradoxical disinhibition. Toxicity resembles other benzodiazepine-like agents, with overdose causing profound CNS depression, slurred speech, respiratory compromise especially with opioids or alcohol, tolerance, dependence, and withdrawal phenomena including rebound anxiety, insomnia, tremor, and seizures. Clinically, it has been used as a short-term anxiolytic and hypnotic for generalized anxiety, acute stress-related insomnia, and panic-associated autonomic symptoms.

Name: Dosulepin
Description: Dosulepin (dothiepin; DrugBank DB09167) is a tricyclic antidepressant built on a dibenzothiepin nucleus, consisting of two fused benzene rings linked through a sulfur-containing seven-membered ring and bearing a three-carbon side chain terminating in a tertiary dimethylamino group, a structural motif that confers lipophilicity and amine basicity typical of monoamine reuptake inhibitors. Chemically it is a tertiary amine TCA, and its scaffold is the dibenzothiepin/tricyclic ring system closely related to other TCAs such as amitriptyline, imipramine, doxepin, and trimipramine, with thiothixene-like sulfur-containing tricyclic resemblance at the scaffold level but antidepressant pharmacology. It is generally well absorbed orally, undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, is highly protein bound and widely distributed including CNS penetration, and is metabolized mainly by CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 to active metabolites including northiaden, with elimination occurring predominantly as urinary metabolites and a relatively long half-life that supports once- or divided-daily dosing. Its principal targets are the serotonin transporter SLC6A4 and norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, with additional antagonism at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, histamine H1 receptors, and alpha1-adrenergic receptors that shape tolerability. It is indicated mainly for major depressive disorder, especially depression with anxiety, insomnia, or psychomotor agitation, and has also been used for some chronic pain syndromes. Adverse effects commonly include sedation, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention, orthostatic hypotension, tachycardia, weight gain, and cognitive impairment. Toxicity is clinically important because overdose can cause seizures, coma, marked anticholinergic delirium, QRS widening, ventricular arrhythmias, and death, making it a higher-risk TCA whose clinical use has become more restricted, generally reserved for selected patients when safer antidepressants are unsuitable.

Name: Dasabuvir
Description: Dasabuvir (DB09183) is a direct-acting antiviral built as a non-nucleoside inhibitor of hepatitis C virus replication, chemically characterized as a highly substituted benzamide-like small molecule containing multiple aromatic/heteroaromatic rings, a carboxamide linkage, and lipophilic alkoxy and halogenated aryl features that promote binding to an allosteric pocket rather than acting as a nucleoside mimic; thus, it belongs to the non-nucleoside polymerase inhibitor class and is commonly described as having a diaryl amide/aryl-imidazole-type scaffold. It is structurally and therapeutically similar to other HCV direct-acting antivirals, especially NS5B inhibitors such as deleobuvir and beclabuvir, while used clinically alongside mechanistically distinct agents such as ombitasvir and paritaprevir/ritonavir. Its principal target is the HCV NS5B RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, to which it binds at a noncatalytic allosteric site, inhibiting viral RNA synthesis, particularly in genotype 1 infection. After oral administration, dasabuvir is absorbed with improved exposure when taken with food, is highly protein bound, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism predominantly via CYP2C8 with a lesser CYP3A contribution, and is eliminated mainly in feces with limited renal excretion; its terminal half-life is on the order of several hours. Toxicity is driven largely by hepatic risk and drug-drug interactions, with clinically relevant concern for elevated transaminases, bilirubin abnormalities when combined regimens are used, and increased exposure with strong CYP2C8 inhibitors such as gemfibrozil. Common adverse effects include nausea, pruritus, insomnia, fatigue, asthenia, and rash. Clinically, dasabuvir was used in combination regimens for chronic hepatitis C, especially genotype 1a and 1b infection, including compensated liver disease, to achieve sustained virologic response and reduce progression to cirrhosis and hepatic complications.

Name: Viloxazine
Description: Viloxazine (DrugBank DB09185) is a bicyclic aryloxyalkylamine antidepressant and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor whose structure is centered on a substituted phenoxyethyl scaffold incorporated into a morpholine ring system, specifically a 2-(2-ethoxyphenoxy)methyl morpholine framework that confers moderate lipophilicity and central nervous system penetration; chemically it is classified as a phenoxy-morpholine and more broadly as a non-stimulant catecholaminergic CNS agent, with a scaffold related to aryloxypropanolamine/aryloxyethylamine motifs seen in older antidepressant chemistry. Similar drugs include atomoxetine and reboxetine as norepinephrine transporter inhibitors, and historically some functional resemblance to tricyclic antidepressants despite a distinct scaffold. Its principal target is the norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, with lesser indirect effects on serotonergic signaling reported. Orally administered viloxazine is well absorbed, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism predominantly via CYP2D6 and UGT-mediated pathways to inactive or weakly active hydroxylated and glucuronidated metabolites, distributes systemically with CNS access, and is eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites with a relatively short half-life that supports daily dosing in extended-release form. Clinically it was used as an antidepressant and is now used as viloxazine extended release for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, improving inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity in pediatric patients. Adverse effects include somnolence, decreased appetite, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, headache, irritability, insomnia, and increased heart rate or blood pressure. Toxicity is generally moderate but includes risk of suicidal ideation, hepatic enzyme elevations, CNS depression or agitation in overdose, and potential interactions with other noradrenergic or serotonergic drugs.

Name: Lobeglitazone
Description: Lobeglitazone (DrugBank DB09198) is a synthetic thiazolidinedione antidiabetic agent whose structure is centered on the characteristic 1,3-thiazolidine-2,4-dione ring linked through a benzyl spacer to a substituted aromatic/heteroaromatic lipophilic system, a design that preserves the acidic TZD headgroup needed for receptor binding while increasing hydrophobic interactions; chemically it belongs to the glitazone class of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma agonists, with a thiazolidinedione scaffold as its defining pharmacophore. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to pioglitazone and rosiglitazone, and more distantly to earlier TZDs such as troglitazone. Its principal known target is PPARG, with downstream modulation of insulin-sensitive gene transcription in adipose tissue, liver, and skeletal muscle. Clinically it is indicated for type 2 diabetes mellitus, particularly for improving glycemic control in patients with insulin resistance, and is used alone or in combination with agents such as metformin, DPP-4 inhibitors, or sulfonylureas. After oral administration it is absorbed systemically, is highly protein bound in distribution, undergoes predominantly hepatic metabolism likely involving CYP-mediated oxidative biotransformation, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites through biliary/fecal and to a lesser extent renal pathways. Adverse effects are broadly class-consistent with TZDs, including weight gain, edema, fluid retention, and possible worsening of congestive heart failure; other reported effects include headache, upper respiratory symptoms, and hypoglycemia when combined with insulin secretagogues. Toxicity concerns include hepatobiliary laboratory abnormalities, bone-fracture risk, and dose-related cardiovascular fluid overload rather than prominent direct cytotoxicity.

Name: Synephrine
Description: Synephrine (DrugBank DB09203) is a naturally occurring phenylethanolamine protoalkaloid, most commonly the p-synephrine isomer, whose structure consists of a benzene ring bearing a para-phenolic hydroxyl group attached to a β-hydroxylated, N-methylated ethylamine side chain; chemically it belongs to the adrenergic amine/trace amine family and is built on a substituted phenethylamine, specifically phenylethanolamine, scaffold closely related to ephedrine, norepinephrine, octopamine, phenylephrine, and other sympathomimetic amines. Pharmacologically, synephrine acts mainly as a relatively weak adrenergic agonist with reported activity at α1-adrenergic receptors and possibly β3-adrenergic receptors, while also being discussed in relation to trace amine-associated receptor 1 and indirect sympathomimetic pathways, although target selectivity is incompletely defined. After oral intake, such as from Citrus aurantium extracts, it is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, distributed systemically with limited central penetration compared with amphetamine-like agents, metabolized predominantly by oxidative deamination and phase II conjugation, and excreted mainly in urine as metabolites and conjugates. It has been used or marketed for weight management, appetite suppression, and nasal decongestion, and historically for hypotension or bronchial symptoms, but clinical evidence is limited. Toxicity is chiefly cardiovascular and dose dependent, with examples including hypertension, tachycardia, palpitations, vasospasm, headache, anxiety, and rare reports of arrhythmia, ischemic events, and stroke, especially when combined with caffeine or other stimulants. Accordingly, adverse effects include insomnia, tremor, restlessness, gastrointestinal upset, and elevated blood pressure, and present clinical use is largely restricted to dietary supplement contexts rather than well-established prescription therapeutics.

Name: Moxisylyte
Description: Moxisylyte (thymoxamine; DrugBank DB09205) is a small-molecule aryloxypropanolamine-related vasodilator built around a substituted anisole/phenoxyethyl scaffold bearing a tertiary amine, with methoxy-substituted aromatic and ether functionalities that confer moderate lipophilicity and support adrenergic receptor binding; chemically it is classified as a selective alpha-1 adrenergic receptor antagonist and can be viewed within the broader phenoxyethylamine/aryloxyalkylamine class. Its scaffold and pharmacology make it similar to other peripheral alpha-blockers such as prazosin, indoramin, phentolamine, and to some extent alfuzosin and doxazosin, although it is structurally less quinazoline-like than the latter agents. The principal known targets are alpha-1 adrenergic receptor subtypes, especially ADRA1A, ADRA1B, and ADRA1D, leading to reduced sympathetic vasoconstriction and improved peripheral and ocular blood flow. It has been used clinically for peripheral vascular disorders such as Raynaud phenomenon and acrocyanosis, and historically in ophthalmology to provoke mydriasis or aid diagnosis of Horner syndrome by blocking iris dilator responses. After oral administration it is absorbed variably, distributes mainly in extracellular and vascular compartments, undergoes hepatic biotransformation including oxidative and conjugative metabolism, and is excreted predominantly as metabolites in urine with limited unchanged drug. Toxicity is mainly an extension of alpha-blockade, with orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, syncope, reflex tachycardia, flushing, and headache; overdose may produce marked hypotension and cardiovascular instability. Adverse effects reported in routine use include nausea, palpitations, nasal congestion, weakness, and occasional gastrointestinal upset, so clinical use has generally been limited to selected vasospastic conditions and niche ophthalmic applications rather than broad long-term cardiovascular therapy.

Name: Trimazosin
Description: Trimazosin (DrugBank DB09206) is a quinazoline-derived antihypertensive belonging to the class of selective peripheral alpha-1 adrenergic receptor antagonists; structurally, it contains the characteristic substituted quinazoline nucleus linked through a piperazine-containing side chain to aromatic ether functionality, a motif typical of vasodilatory alpha-blockers and central to its receptor-binding profile. Its core chemical scaffold is therefore best described as a 4-amino-6,7-dimethoxyquinazoline-like alpha-blocker scaffold, closely related to other quinazoline/piperazine agents such as prazosin, terazosin, and doxazosin, which are the most relevant similar drugs from both structural and pharmacologic perspectives. Pharmacologically, trimazosin lowers blood pressure by antagonizing alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, primarily ADRA1A, ADRA1B, and ADRA1D, thereby reducing peripheral vascular resistance; like related agents, it is expected to be orally absorbed, distributed systemically with meaningful plasma protein binding, metabolized predominantly in the liver by oxidative and conjugative pathways, and excreted as parent drug and metabolites mainly via renal and possibly biliary routes, although published PK data are limited compared with marketed congeners. Its principal indication is hypertension, especially essential hypertension, with clinical use as an oral vasodilatory antihypertensive in patients needing alpha-blockade. Toxicity is broadly consistent with the class and includes exaggerated pharmacodynamic hypotension, first-dose syncope, dizziness, reflex tachycardia, headache, weakness, and orthostatic intolerance; overdose would be expected to produce marked vasodilatory collapse. Adverse effects similarly include postural hypotension, fatigue, palpitations, nasal congestion, and occasional gastrointestinal complaints, making it most suitable for monitored blood-pressure control rather than first-line use in all patients.

Name: Limaprost
Description: Limaprost (DrugBank DB09211) is a synthetic prostaglandin E1 analogue characterized by the classic eicosanoid/prostanoid framework: a substituted cyclopentane core bearing hydroxyl functionality and two aliphatic side chains, one incorporating unsaturation and the other terminating in a carboxylic acid, with modifications that increase oral stability relative to endogenous alprostadil; chemically it belongs to the prostaglandins, specifically prostaglandin E1 analogues, and its core scaffold is the prostanoic acid cyclopentane lipid mediator scaffold. Closely related drugs include alprostadil, misoprostol, gemeprost, and other prostanoid analogues such as beraprost and iloprost, which share eicosanoid-inspired architectures but differ in ring and side-chain substitutions. Limaprost acts primarily at prostaglandin E receptors, especially EP receptor subtypes including PTGER2 and PTGER4, promoting vasodilation, inhibition of platelet aggregation, and improved microcirculatory flow. After oral administration it is absorbed and undergoes first-pass biotransformation, with distribution expected to be moderate and partly albumin-associated, metabolism occurring mainly through oxidation and beta-oxidation-like degradation of the side chains to less active metabolites, and excretion proceeding predominantly in urine as metabolites. Its main indications are improvement of ischemic symptoms in peripheral arterial occlusive disease and treatment of lumbar spinal canal stenosis, particularly lower-limb pain, numbness, coldness, rest pain, and ulcer-related circulatory insufficiency. Adverse effects are usually mild and include flushing, headache, nausea, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, palpitations, dizziness, rash, and hypotension; toxicity is largely an extension of prostaglandin pharmacology, with excessive vasodilation, syncope, gastrointestinal intolerance, and bleeding tendency as notable risks, especially in vulnerable patients or with antiplatelet/anticoagulant co-therapy.

Name: Loxoprofen
Description: Loxoprofen (DrugBank DB09212) is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug of the arylpropionic acid, or profen, class whose structure consists of a substituted phenyl ring bearing a 2-oxocyclopentyl group and a propionic acid side chain, giving it the characteristic acidic arylaliphatic scaffold shared with many cyclooxygenase inhibitors; its core scaffold is therefore best described as an arylpropionic acid linked to a cyclic ketone-containing hydrophobic moiety. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other propionic acid NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, ketoprofen, flurbiprofen, and naproxen, although loxoprofen is notable as a ketone-containing prodrug that is converted after absorption to the pharmacologically active trans-alcohol metabolite. After oral administration it is rapidly absorbed, achieves good systemic exposure, is moderately protein bound in plasma, distributes to inflamed tissues and synovial compartments, undergoes carbonyl reduction mainly in the liver to active and inactive alcohol metabolites, and is eliminated predominantly in urine as metabolites with a relatively short plasma half-life. Its principal targets are cyclooxygenase enzymes PTGS1 and PTGS2, reducing prostaglandin synthesis and thereby producing analgesic, antipyretic, and anti-inflammatory effects. Clinically it is used for pain and inflammation in osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, low back pain, postoperative pain, dental pain, dysmenorrhea, and fever. Adverse effects resemble other NSAIDs and include dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, gastritis, peptic ulceration, gastrointestinal bleeding, rash, edema, renal dysfunction, and elevated liver enzymes; overdose or susceptible patients may develop severe GI hemorrhage, acute kidney injury, bronchospasm, or hypersensitivity reactions.

Name: Dexibuprofen
Description: Dexibuprofen (DrugBank DB09213) is the pharmacologically active S-(+)-enantiomer of ibuprofen, structurally an arylpropionic acid bearing a para-isobutyl-substituted phenyl ring attached to a chiral propionic acid side chain; this places it in the nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug class, specifically the profen subgroup of 2-arylpropionic acids, with an arylpropionic acid scaffold. Closely related drugs include racemic ibuprofen, ketoprofen, flurbiprofen, naproxen, and loxoprofen, which share similar acidic aryl scaffolds and cyclooxygenase inhibition. Its principal targets are cyclooxygenase-1 and cyclooxygenase-2, with consequent reduction in prostaglandin synthesis underlying analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antipyretic effects. Dexibuprofen is generally well absorbed orally, reaches peak plasma concentrations within a few hours, is highly albumin bound, distributes mainly within extracellular fluids and inflamed tissues, undergoes extensive hepatic oxidation and conjugation primarily via CYP2C9-dependent and glucuronidation pathways, and is excreted mainly in urine as inactive metabolites with minimal unchanged drug. It is indicated for symptomatic treatment of pain and inflammation such as osteoarthritis, rheumatoid disorders, musculoskeletal pain, dysmenorrhea, dental pain, postoperative pain, and fever. Typical adverse effects include dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, heartburn, headache, dizziness, edema, and rash. Important toxicities mirror other NSAIDs: dose-related gastritis, peptic ulceration, gastrointestinal bleeding, renal hypoperfusion or acute kidney injury, fluid retention, hypertension, rare hepatotoxicity, and hypersensitivity including bronchospasm in aspirin-sensitive patients. Clinically, it is used as an oral NSAID when a lower milligram dose than racemic ibuprofen is desired for arthritis flares, soft-tissue injury, menstrual pain, and other mild-to-moderate painful inflammatory states.

Name: Nicorandil
Description: Nicorandil (DrugBank DB09220) is a hybrid antianginal small molecule structurally defined as a nicotinamide derivative bearing an N-(2-hydroxyethyl) substituent and a nitrate ester, so it combines a pyridine carboxamide core with an organic nitrate pharmacophore; chemically it is categorized as a nicotinamide nitrate ester, vasodilator, and potassium-channel opener, with a simple heteroaromatic pyridine-carboxamide scaffold linked to a hydroxyethyl nitrate side chain. It is most similar to other nitric oxide-donating antianginals and KATP-active vasodilators, with partial pharmacologic resemblance to nitrates such as nitroglycerin and isosorbide dinitrate and mechanistic overlap with potassium-channel openers such as pinacidil or cromakalim. Its principal targets are ATP-sensitive potassium channels, particularly SUR2-containing vascular KATP channel complexes with Kir6.x pore-forming subunits, and it also acts functionally through nitric oxide signaling with activation of soluble guanylate cyclase. Nicorandil is used mainly for chronic stable angina and symptomatic ischemic heart disease, including effort-induced chest pain refractory to first-line therapy. It is generally well absorbed orally, distributed systemically with modest protein binding, undergoes limited CYP-dependent biotransformation with predominant denitration and amide-related metabolism, and is eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites. Adverse effects reflect vasodilation and include headache, flushing, dizziness, hypotension, palpitations, and nausea. Important toxicities include excessive hypotension, syncope, and a characteristic risk of severe oral, gastrointestinal, perianal, genital, or skin ulceration, especially in predisposed patients; overdose may cause profound vasodilatory collapse. Clinically, it is used as an add-on or alternative antianginal agent when beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, or traditional nitrates are inadequate or poorly tolerated.

Name: Blonanserin
Description: Blonanserin (DrugBank DB09223) is an atypical antipsychotic of the benzoisoxazole/piperazine class characterized by a rigid tricyclic-like aromatic heterocyclic core containing a benzoisoxazole ring linked through a butyl chain to a tertiary amine within a piperazine-derived framework, a motif that supports high-affinity aminergic receptor binding; its central chemical scaffold is therefore a benzoisoxazole tethered alkyl-piperazine pharmacophore, closely related in medicinal-chemistry terms to other dopamine-serotonin antagonists such as risperidone and ziprasidone, with broader similarity to aripiprazole and perospirone as multi-receptor antipsychotics. Pharmacologically, blonanserin acts primarily at dopamine D2 and D3 receptors and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors, with lower activity at targets such as 5-HT2C, 5-HT6, and alpha1-adrenergic receptors, a profile relevant to antipsychotic efficacy with comparatively limited histaminergic and muscarinic burden. It is used mainly for schizophrenia, particularly positive symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions, and in some settings for negative symptoms and related psychotic disorders. After oral administration it is absorbed moderately, undergoes hepatic first-pass metabolism predominantly via CYP3A4 to inactive or less active metabolites, is distributed systemically with meaningful protein binding, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine and feces. Toxicities include dose-related extrapyramidal toxicity, hyperprolactinemia, sedation, orthostatic symptoms, and potential QT-related or neuroleptic malignant syndrome risks, while common adverse effects include akathisia, tremor, rigidity, dystonia, insomnia, anxiety, dry mouth, constipation, dizziness, weight gain, and prolactin elevation. Clinically, it is prescribed as an oral or transdermal antipsychotic for maintenance and acute treatment of schizophrenia in adults, especially when control of dopaminergic psychosis is desired with relatively modest metabolic liability.

Name: Aranidipine
Description: Aranidipine (DB09229) is a lipophilic dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker characterized structurally by a 1,4-dihydropyridine core bearing the typical ester-substituted C3 and C5 positions and aryl substitution that confers potent vascular L-type calcium-channel antagonism; chemically it belongs to the dihydropyridine antihypertensive class, and its central scaffold is the 1,4-dihydropyridine ring system shared by related agents such as amlodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine, felodipine, and benidipine. Its principal molecular targets are voltage-dependent L-type calcium channel subunits in vascular smooth muscle, particularly CaV1.2 channels encoded by CACNA1C, leading to inhibition of transmembrane calcium influx, arterial vasodilation, and reduced peripheral vascular resistance. Pharmacokinetically, aranidipine is expected to be orally absorbed as a highly lipophilic agent, to undergo substantial tissue distribution with strong membrane partitioning, extensive hepatic oxidative metabolism likely involving CYP3A-family enzymes, and elimination mainly as inactive metabolites via biliary and urinary routes rather than unchanged renal excretion. Toxicity is consistent with the dihydropyridine class and includes exaggerated vasodilatory and cardiovascular effects in overdose, such as hypotension, reflex tachycardia, dizziness, flushing, and possible myocardial ischemia in susceptible patients; severe poisoning may cause profound shock. Adverse effects in routine use likewise include headache, palpitations, ankle edema, flushing, lightheadedness, and fatigue. Clinically, aranidipine has been investigated or used as an antihypertensive and antianginal vasodilator for conditions such as essential hypertension, elevated blood pressure with vascular stiffness, and chronic stable angina symptoms, where it serves as a long-acting vascular-selective calcium antagonist similar to other drugs in its class.

Name: Efonidipine
Description: Efonidipine (DB09235) is a lipophilic dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker characterized structurally by a 1,4-dihydropyridine core bearing ester functionalities and an aryl substituent, with a distinctive phosphonate-containing side chain that helps differentiate it from simpler dihydropyridines; chemically it is classified as a dihydropyridine antihypertensive and more broadly as a calcium antagonist, and its principal scaffold is the 1,4-dihydropyridine ring system shared by many vasoselective calcium-channel blockers. Similar drugs include amlodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine, felodipine, and cilnidipine, although efonidipine is notable for dual L-type and T-type calcium channel inhibition. Its key targets are voltage-dependent calcium channels, especially Cav1.x L-type channels and Cav3.x T-type channels in vascular smooth muscle, myocardium, and renal tissue, producing vasodilation, reduction in peripheral resistance, and slowing of heart rate. It is used mainly for essential hypertension, and in some settings angina or hypertension with tachycardic tendency, with clinical use including blood-pressure control in adults and possible renoprotective benefit in hypertensive patients with kidney disease. After oral administration it is absorbed with first-pass hepatic metabolism, is highly protein bound, distributes into vascular tissues, undergoes extensive hepatic biotransformation likely involving CYP-mediated oxidation and ester hydrolysis, and is excreted predominantly as metabolites in bile/feces and urine. Adverse effects and dose-related toxicity are typical of calcium antagonists, including headache, flushing, dizziness, palpitations, edema, hypotension, gingival hyperplasia, and occasionally bradycardia or conduction slowing; overdose may cause marked hypotension and cardiovascular depression.

Name: Moxonidine
Description: Moxonidine (DrugBank DB09242) is a centrally acting antihypertensive with an imidazoline-derived structure characterized by a substituted imidazoline/amidine-like heterocyclic core linked to a chlorinated, methoxy-substituted aromatic ring, placing it in the imidazoline receptor agonist class and giving it an aryl-imidazoline scaffold closely related to other sympatholytic agents such as clonidine, rilmenidine, and to a lesser extent guanfacine. Its principal pharmacologic targets are imidazoline I1 receptors in the rostral ventrolateral medulla, where it reduces central sympathetic outflow; it also shows weaker agonist activity at alpha2-adrenergic receptors, a property that helps distinguish it from clonidine by producing less sedation and xerostomia in many patients. After oral administration, moxonidine is rapidly and well absorbed with high bioavailability, low protein binding, relatively limited metabolism, and predominant renal excretion of unchanged drug, yielding a short elimination half-life that can be prolonged in renal impairment. Clinically it is indicated mainly for essential hypertension, particularly when reduction of sympathetic tone is desirable, and has been used in patients with metabolic syndrome, obesity-associated hypertension, or diabetes-related hypertension. Adverse effects are usually dose-related and include dry mouth, dizziness, somnolence, headache, fatigue, nausea, and occasionally bradycardia or orthostatic symptoms. Toxicity is generally an extension of its pharmacology, with overdose potentially causing marked hypotension, bradycardia, CNS depression, and weakness; caution is warranted in renal dysfunction, conduction disease, and when combined with other antihypertensives or sedatives.

Name: Pirlindole
Description: Pirlindole (DrugBank DB09244) is an antidepressant with a compact tetracyclic/bridged heteroaromatic structure centered on a pyrroloindole-type system, typically described as a rigid aza-polycyclic amine in which a fused indole-like aromatic domain is joined to a saturated nitrogen-containing ring, creating a conformationally constrained basic scaffold; chemically it is classified as a reversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor, more specifically a heterocyclic antidepressant of the RIMA class, and its core scaffold is closely related to other indole- or bicyclic MAO-inhibitor frameworks. Similar drugs include moclobemide, toloxatone, and befloxatone as reversible MAO-A inhibitors, and more distantly older irreversible MAO inhibitors such as phenelzine and tranylcypromine. Its principal target is monoamine oxidase A, with functional elevation of synaptic serotonin, norepinephrine, and to a lesser extent dopamine. After oral administration it is reportedly absorbed reasonably well, distributes into the CNS because of sufficient lipophilicity, undergoes hepatic biotransformation with metabolite formation typical of heterocyclic amines, and is eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites; detailed modern PK data are limited, but MAO-A reversibility implies a shorter functional effect than classic irreversible MAO inhibitors. It has been used for depressive disorders, especially mild to moderate depression with asthenia, anxiety, or psychovegetative symptoms. Adverse effects can include insomnia, agitation, dry mouth, dizziness, headache, nausea, constipation, orthostatic symptoms, and less commonly hypertensive reactions or serotonergic toxicity when combined with serotonergic agents; overdose may produce CNS and cardiovascular toxicity. Clinically, pirlindole has been used as an oral antidepressant where a reversible MAO-A inhibitor is preferred, particularly when lower dietary tyramine risk and better tolerability than older MAO inhibitors are desired.

Name: Toloxatone
Description: Toloxatone (DrugBank DB09245) is a synthetic oxazolidinone-derived monoamine oxidase inhibitor characterized structurally by a 2-oxazolidinone heterocycle bearing aryl substitution, giving a compact, moderately lipophilic aromatic carbamate-like framework; chemically it is classified as a reversible inhibitor of monoamine oxidase type A within the broader phenethylamine-modulating antidepressant class, and its core scaffold is the aryl-substituted oxazolidinone ring system rather than the hydrazine or cyclopropylamine motifs seen in older MAO inhibitors. Similar drugs include other MAO-A or reversible MAO inhibitors such as moclobemide, befloxatone, brofaromine, and, more distantly, irreversible MAO inhibitors like phenelzine and tranylcypromine. Its principal target protein is MAOA, with functional consequences including reduced oxidative deamination of serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine and consequent enhancement of central monoaminergic neurotransmission. Toloxatone is orally active, absorbed reasonably well, distributed systemically with CNS penetration, undergoes predominantly hepatic biotransformation to inactive metabolites, and is eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites, with a relatively short half-life consistent with reversible MAO-A inhibition. Toxicity is generally lower than that of older irreversible MAO inhibitors but can include overdose-related agitation, hypertension or hypotension, insomnia, and risk of serotonin toxicity when combined with serotonergic agents; tyramine interactions are possible but typically less pronounced. Adverse effects reported for clinical use include nausea, dry mouth, dizziness, headache, sleep disturbance, anxiety, and orthostatic symptoms. Clinically, it has been used as an antidepressant, particularly for major depressive episodes, anxiety-depressive states, psychomotor inhibition, and related mood symptoms, especially where a reversible MAO-A inhibitor is preferred over classical nonselective MAO inhibitors.

Name: Iproclozide
Description: Iproclozide (DrugBank DB09247) is a first-generation antidepressant built on a substituted benzyl hydrazide/hydrazine architecture, specifically an isopropyl-substituted chlorophenoxyacetyl hydrazide motif, placing it in the hydrazine monoamine oxidase inhibitor class and giving it an aryloxyacyl-hydrazine scaffold related to other irreversible MAO inhibitors. Chemically and pharmacologically it is most similar to iproniazid, isocarboxazid, phenelzine, nialamide, and other older nonselective MAO inhibitors, although its precise scaffold is closer to hydrazide-derived agents than to cyclopropylamines such as tranylcypromine. Its principal known targets are mitochondrial monoamine oxidase A and monoamine oxidase B, which it inhibits irreversibly, increasing synaptic serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine. It was indicated for depressive illness, particularly severe, endogenous, or treatment-resistant depression, sometimes with anxiety, psychomotor retardation, or anergic symptoms. After oral administration it is absorbed systemically, distributed widely including to the central nervous system, and undergoes extensive hepatic biotransformation typical of hydrazine MAO inhibitors, with formation of reactive metabolites thought to contribute to toxicity; elimination occurs mainly as metabolites in urine, while pharmacodynamic recovery depends on de novo MAO resynthesis rather than plasma clearance alone. Its major limitation was severe hepatotoxicity, including hepatitis, cholestatic jaundice, fulminant hepatic necrosis, and fatal liver failure; additional toxicities include hypertensive crisis with tyramine, serotonin toxicity with serotonergic drugs, and CNS or autonomic adverse effects. Common side effects included orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, insomnia, agitation, dry mouth, constipation, weight gain, and sexual dysfunction. Clinically, despite antidepressant efficacy, use became obsolete or withdrawn because the toxicity profile outweighed benefit relative to safer antidepressants.

Name: Mebanazine
Description: Mebanazine (DrugBank DB09248) is an older hydrazine-derived monoamine oxidase inhibitor characterized structurally as a substituted benzylhydrazine/aralkyl hydrazine containing a simple aromatic ring linked through a short alkyl spacer to a hydrazine functional group, placing it in the hydrazine antidepressant class and giving it a relatively compact phenethyl- or benzylhydrazine-like scaffold; this scaffold is closely related to other early irreversible MAO inhibitors such as phenelzine, isocarboxazid, iproniazid, and nialamide, which share hydrazine or hydrazide-based motifs and similar enzyme-inactivating chemistry. Its principal known targets are monoamine oxidase enzymes, especially MAO-A and MAO-B, with antidepressant activity arising from inhibition of oxidative deamination of serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine in central and peripheral tissues. Pharmacokinetically, mebanazine is orally active, absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, distributed systemically including CNS penetration, metabolized largely hepatically through oxidative and conjugative pathways with probable hydrazine-derived reactive intermediates, and excreted mainly in urine as metabolites, although detailed modern human ADME parameters are limited. It was used clinically as an antidepressant for depressive illness, particularly severe or treatment-resistant depression with psychomotor retardation or anxiety symptoms. Adverse effects are typical of classical MAO inhibitors and include orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, insomnia, agitation, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, weight gain, and sexual dysfunction. Important toxicities include hepatotoxicity, hypertensive crisis after tyramine exposure, and potentially severe drug interactions causing serotonin toxicity or exaggerated sympathomimetic responses, which ultimately limited routine clinical use.

Name: Gimeracil
Description: Gimeracil (DrugBank DB09257) is a small, fluorinated heteroaromatic antimetabolite characterized structurally as a substituted pyridinedione bearing a fluorine atom and a hydroxymethyl side chain, giving it a uracil-like electronic profile despite its non-nucleoside pyridine scaffold; chemically it is classified as a dihydropyridone/pyridinedione fluoropyrimidine-modulating agent, with a compact aza-uracil mimic scaffold related functionally to pyrimidine catabolism inhibitors. Its closest analogs in use are fluoropyrimidine biochemical modulators such as uracil and eniluracil, and it is specifically partnered with tegafur and oteracil in the oral combination product S-1. Gimeracil’s principal target is dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase, the rate-limiting enzyme in 5-fluorouracil degradation, which it potently inhibits, thereby increasing systemic and intratumoral exposure to 5-fluorouracil generated from tegafur. After oral administration in S-1, it is absorbed systemically, distributes sufficiently to inhibit peripheral and hepatic DPD, undergoes limited biotransformation relative to tegafur, and is cleared predominantly by renal excretion; renal impairment can therefore increase exposure and toxicity. Its toxicology is largely mechanism-based through enhancement of fluoropyrimidine effects, including severe myelosuppression, diarrhea, mucositis, nausea, vomiting, and risk of life-threatening toxicity when 5-FU exposure becomes excessive, especially in patients with renal dysfunction or altered fluoropyrimidine handling. Clinically, it is used not as a standalone cytotoxic but as a pharmacokinetic enhancer in S-1 for cancers such as gastric, colorectal, pancreatic, biliary tract, breast, and head and neck malignancies, where it improves oral fluoropyrimidine efficacy while enabling sustained 5-FU exposure.

Name: Imidafenacin
Description: Imidafenacin (DrugBank DB09262) is a synthetic small-molecule antimuscarinic agent structurally characterized as a lipophilic tertiary amine bearing a substituted aromatic heterocycle linked to an amide-containing side chain, a design that supports high affinity for bladder muscarinic receptors while limiting prolonged systemic exposure; chemically it is classified as a quaternary-ammonium–like bladder antispasmodic/anticholinergic in therapeutic use, though structurally it is more precisely a tertiary amine muscarinic receptor antagonist with an aromatic amide scaffold. Its core scaffold is related to other overactive bladder antimuscarinics, and similar drugs include solifenacin, tolterodine, fesoterodine, oxybutynin, trospium, darifenacin, and propiverine, all sharing pharmacologic antagonism at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors despite differing chemotypes. Imidafenacin primarily targets CHRM3 and CHRM1, with clinically relevant activity also at CHRM2; inhibition of detrusor muscarinic signaling reduces involuntary bladder contractions. It is indicated mainly for overactive bladder, including urinary urgency, urge incontinence, frequency, and nocturia. After oral administration it is absorbed relatively rapidly, reaches low-to-moderate systemic exposure, distributes sufficiently to bladder tissue, undergoes hepatic metabolism involving CYP3A4 and UGT pathways, and is eliminated through both renal and fecal routes, with a comparatively short half-life that can lessen persistent adverse effects. Toxicity is typical of anticholinergics and includes dose-related xerostomia, constipation, blurred vision, tachycardia, urinary retention, and potential heat intolerance; overdose may produce central and peripheral antimuscarinic effects such as agitation or marked retention. In clinical use it is prescribed orally, especially in adults with overactive bladder who require symptom control with relatively bladder-selective antimuscarinic therapy.

Name: Strontium ranelate
Description: Strontium ranelate (DB09267) is an oral anti-osteoporotic agent composed of two divalent strontium cations complexed with ranelic acid, a polyanionic heteroaromatic dicarboxylate bearing a substituted thiophene core with nitrile and carboxymethyl functionalities, giving a metal-organic salt architecture rather than a classical small neutral molecule; chemically it is categorized as a strontium salt and bone-active mineral agent, with a ranelic acid thiophene-dicarboxylate scaffold. It is often discussed alongside other osteoporosis drugs such as bisphosphonates including alendronate and risedronate, denosumab, teriparatide, and calcium/vitamin D supplementation, although its chemistry is distinct from these classes. Its pharmacology is characterized by modest oral absorption that is reduced by food, milk, and calcium, low protein binding of strontium, preferential distribution to mineralized bone with incorporation onto hydroxyapatite crystal surfaces, minimal metabolic biotransformation because the organic moiety is largely not oxidatively metabolized, and predominantly renal elimination of absorbed strontium with fecal elimination of unabsorbed drug. Mechanistically, no single canonical high-affinity protein target is definitive, but effects are linked to the calcium-sensing receptor, osteoblast activation, reduced osteoclast differentiation, and modulation of the OPG/RANKL axis. It is indicated for osteoporosis, especially severe postmenopausal osteoporosis and fracture-risk reduction, including vertebral and some nonvertebral fractures. Adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, headache, dermatitis, eczema, and venous thromboembolism, while major toxicities include DRESS/hypersensitivity, myocardial infarction signal, seizure risk in predisposed patients, and caution in severe renal impairment. Clinically, it has been used when other osteoporosis therapies are unsuitable, particularly in postmenopausal women and sometimes men at high fracture risk.

Name: Ubidecarenone
Description: Ubidecarenone (coenzyme Q10, DB09270) is a highly lipophilic benzoquinone composed of a redox-active 1,4-benzoquinone headgroup bearing methoxy substituents and a long polyisoprenoid side chain of ten isoprene units, placing it in the quinone/isoprenoid lipid class and more specifically among ubiquinones; its core scaffold is therefore a substituted benzoquinone linked to a decaprenyl tail, a motif shared with related agents such as idebenone, ubiquinol, menaquinones, and shorter-chain ubiquinone analogs. Pharmacologically, it functions primarily as an endogenous electron carrier in the mitochondrial respiratory chain, shuttling electrons between complexes I/II and complex III, and also acts as a membrane antioxidant; relevant protein-level associations include NADH dehydrogenase (complex I), succinate dehydrogenase (complex II), the cytochrome bc1 complex (complex III), and broader interactions with mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation systems rather than a single high-affinity receptor target. Oral absorption is variable and dissolution-limited, improved by lipid-based formulations and food; distribution is extensive to lipoproteins, heart, skeletal muscle, liver, and mitochondria; it undergoes reduction to ubiquinol and limited hepatic metabolism with biliary/fecal elimination predominating and minimal renal excretion. Toxicity is generally low, but high doses may cause gastrointestinal intolerance, headache, insomnia, rash, and occasional transaminase elevation, and it may reduce warfarin effect in some patients. Clinically, it is used as supplementation or adjunctive therapy in primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency, mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, heart failure, statin-associated myalgia, migraine prophylaxis, and sometimes Parkinson disease or male infertility, with adverse effects usually mild and dose related.

Name: Artesunate
Description: Artesunate (DrugBank DB09274) is a semisynthetic artemisinin derivative whose structure is defined by a sesquiterpene lactone endoperoxide built on the trioxane-containing artemisinin scaffold, with conversion of dihydroartemisinin to a hemisuccinate ester that increases water solubility for oral, rectal, and especially intravenous use; chemically it is an endoperoxide antimalarial and belongs to the artemisinin class, with close analogs and similar drugs including artemisinin, dihydroartemisinin, artemether, and arteether. Its pharmacologically critical scaffold is the peroxide bridge, which upon activation by ferrous heme released during parasite hemoglobin digestion generates reactive radicals that damage parasite proteins and membranes; proposed protein targets include Plasmodium falciparum sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase PfATP6, heme, and multiple promiscuously alkylated parasite proteins. Artesunate is rapidly absorbed and extensively converted by plasma esterases to the active metabolite dihydroartemisinin, which distributes widely, is highly protein bound to a moderate extent, undergoes hepatic glucuronidation mainly via UGT1A9 and UGT2B7, and is eliminated largely as inactive metabolites in urine and bile with a short parent half-life and brief but potent exposure to dihydroartemisinin. It is indicated primarily for severe falciparum malaria and is also used in uncomplicated malaria as part of artemisinin-based combination therapy, including cerebral malaria, high-parasitemia infection, and multidrug-resistant malaria. Adverse effects are usually mild and include nausea, vomiting, dizziness, abdominal pain, transient bradycardia, rash, and liver enzyme elevation, while important toxicities include post-artesunate delayed hemolysis, neutropenia, hypersensitivity, rare hepatotoxicity, and embryotoxicity seen in animal studies, guiding cautious clinical use in parenteral rescue therapy followed by combination antimalarial treatment.

Name: Fimasartan
Description: Fimasartan (DB09279) is a nonpeptide angiotensin II receptor blocker whose structure is characterized by a biphenyl-tetrazole pharmacophore linked to a substituted imidazole/heteroaryl core and lipophilic aromatic substituents, a design that mimics the acidic and hydrophobic recognition elements required for high-affinity antagonism at the angiotensin II type 1 receptor; chemically it belongs to the biphenyl-tetrazole ARB class, and its core scaffold is closely related to the losartan-type sartan framework. Similar drugs include losartan, valsartan, irbesartan, candesartan, olmesartan, azilsartan, and telmisartan, all sharing AT1 receptor antagonism with differing heteroaryl and acidic substituent patterns. Its principal target is the angiotensin II receptor type 1, encoded by AGTR1, with therapeutic effects deriving from blockade of vasoconstrictive and aldosterone-secreting actions of angiotensin II. Fimasartan is used primarily for essential hypertension and has been studied or used clinically where blood-pressure lowering and renin-angiotensin system inhibition are desired, including patients at cardiovascular risk. Orally administered, it is absorbed reasonably rapidly, reaches peak plasma levels within hours, is highly protein bound, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism with a substantial fraction remaining as parent drug, and is eliminated mainly via hepatobiliary/fecal routes with lesser renal excretion; food may reduce exposure modestly without abolishing effect. Toxicities and adverse effects are generally class-typical and include hypotension, dizziness, headache, fatigue, hyperkalemia, increases in serum creatinine, and renal function worsening, especially in renal artery stenosis, volume depletion, or combination therapy with other renin-angiotensin system blockers; fetal toxicity is a key risk, so it is contraindicated in pregnancy. Clinically, it is prescribed as an antihypertensive monotherapy or in combination regimens, for example with diuretics or calcium-channel blockers, to achieve sustained blood-pressure control.

Name: Lumacaftor
Description: Lumacaftor (DB09280) is a small-molecule CFTR corrector used in cystic fibrosis, characterized structurally as a heavily halogenated, lipophilic aromatic amide containing a substituted benzo[d][1,3]dioxole/biaryl-like system linked through an amide to a carboxamide-bearing aromatic framework, a design that confers high membrane affinity and activity on misfolded CFTR; chemically it is best classified as an aromatic carboxamide and CFTR modulator, with a halogenated polyaromatic scaffold that is distinct from potentiators but related functionally to other CFTR correctors. Similar drugs include tezacaftor and elexacaftor, which also improve folding and trafficking of mutant CFTR, and ivacaftor, which is often coadministered although it acts primarily as a channel potentiator rather than a corrector. Its principal target is the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator protein, especially F508del-CFTR, where lumacaftor promotes conformational stabilization, processing, and delivery of the protein to the cell surface. After oral administration with fat-containing food, absorption is improved; the drug is highly protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes limited oxidative metabolism with substantial disposition as parent compound, can induce CYP3A and other enzymes/transport pathways, and is eliminated predominantly in feces with minimal renal excretion. Indicated for cystic fibrosis in patients with homozygous F508del CFTR mutations, it is used clinically mainly in fixed combination with ivacaftor to improve lung function, reduce pulmonary exacerbations, and support weight or respiratory symptom control. Important adverse effects include dyspnea, chest tightness, nausea, diarrhea, increased sputum, fatigue, rash, menstrual abnormalities, elevated transaminases, and blood pressure increases; toxicity concerns include hepatotoxicity, bronchospasm or acute respiratory events particularly at initiation, and clinically significant drug interactions due to enzyme induction, for example reduced exposure to hormonal contraceptives or azole antifungals.

Name: Molsidomine
Description: Molsidomine (DrugBank DB09282) is a mesoionic sydnonimine nitric oxide donor whose structure consists of a 1,2,3-oxadiazolium-5-olate ring system bearing an imino functionality and a morpholine-substituted ethyl side chain, making it a heterocyclic vasodilator in the sydnonimine/NO-donor class; its core scaffold is the sydnonimine mesoionic heterocycle, chemically and pharmacologically related to other nitrovasodilators and NO-releasing antianginal agents such as linsidomine, nitroglycerin, isosorbide dinitrate, and isosorbide mononitrate, although unlike organic nitrates it does not require thiol-dependent bioactivation and tends to show less tolerance. After oral administration it is well absorbed, undergoes first-pass hepatic conversion to the active metabolite linsidomine (SIN-1), which then spontaneously releases nitric oxide, with distribution typical of a moderately lipophilic small molecule, metabolism largely hepatic, and elimination occurring mainly as metabolites in urine with a relatively short parent half-life but longer pharmacodynamic effect due to active metabolite formation. Its principal functional target is the soluble guanylate cyclase pathway activated by NO, increasing cGMP in vascular smooth muscle; no single high-affinity receptor target is primary. Clinically it is used for prophylaxis of angina pectoris, especially chronic stable angina and ischemic symptoms due to coronary artery disease, and has also been used as an adjunct vasodilator in some heart failure or pulmonary vascular settings. Adverse effects and toxicity are extensions of excessive vasodilation, including headache, flushing, dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, reflex tachycardia, nausea, and syncope, with overdose causing marked hypotension and circulatory collapse; caution is warranted with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors and other antihypertensives because of potentially profound blood-pressure reduction.

Name: Imolamine
Description: Imolamine (DrugBank DB09284) is a synthetic small-molecule amino alcohol best described as a lipophilic aryl-substituted alkanolamine containing a tertiary amine linked through a short carbon chain to a hydroxyl-bearing center, placing it in the broader chemical category of amphiphilic amine vasoactive agents; its core scaffold is an ethanolamine/propanolamine-like amino alcohol framework appended to hydrophobic aromatic substituents, a motif shared with several vasoactive and smooth-muscle–active compounds. Structurally and pharmacologically, it has been compared with older peripheral vasodilators and antianginal amino alcohols such as prenylamine and related coronary vasodilating agents, although it is not widely used in modern practice. The drug has been investigated primarily as a peripheral and coronary vasodilator for ischemic symptoms, including angina pectoris, cerebrovascular insufficiency, and peripheral vascular disease with manifestations such as intermittent claudication. Its molecular targets have not been definitively established; reported activity is consistent with nonspecific smooth-muscle relaxation and possible modulation of calcium handling or adrenergic tone rather than a single validated protein target. Pharmacokinetic data are limited, but available descriptions suggest oral absorption, extensive tissue distribution driven by lipophilicity, hepatic biotransformation of the amine/alcohol functionalities, and renal excretion of metabolites. Adverse effects are those expected for vasodilatory amino alcohols, including hypotension, dizziness, flushing, headache, palpitations, and gastrointestinal intolerance, while toxicity at higher exposure may include excessive vasodilation, orthostatic symptoms, and cardiovascular instability. Clinically, imolamine has been used historically as a symptomatic vasodilator rather than a disease-modifying therapy.

Name: Rolapitant
Description: Rolapitant (DrugBank DB09291) is a highly lipophilic, small-molecule neurokinin-1 receptor antagonist built around a substituted piperidine-containing, diaryl/heteroaryl scaffold with multiple fluorinated aryl groups that confer metabolic stability and prolonged receptor occupancy; chemically it is categorized as an antiemetic substance P antagonist within the NK1 receptor blocker class, and its scaffold is broadly related to other centrally active NK1 antagonists such as aprepitant, fosaprepitant, netupitant, and casopitant. Its principal target is the human tachykinin receptor 1, NK1R, encoded by TACR1, through which it inhibits substance P-mediated emetic signaling in the central nervous system. Pharmacokinetically, rolapitant is orally absorbed with clinically useful bioavailability, reaches peak concentrations within hours, is extensively distributed with high protein binding, undergoes hepatic oxidative metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 to an active metabolite, and is eliminated slowly through fecal and, to a lesser extent, renal pathways, with an unusually long terminal half-life of about 7 days that supports single-dose per chemotherapy cycle administration. Unlike some NK1 antagonists, it is not a significant CYP3A4 inhibitor or inducer, but it inhibits CYP2D6 and transporters such as BCRP and P-glycoprotein, creating interaction risks. Its indication is prevention of delayed nausea and vomiting associated with emetogenic cancer chemotherapy, for example cisplatin- or anthracycline/cyclophosphamide-based regimens, typically combined with a 5-HT3 antagonist and dexamethasone. Adverse effects include neutropenia, headache, constipation, fatigue, decreased appetite, dyspepsia, hiccups, dizziness, and stomatitis; toxicity concerns center on drug-drug interactions and possible increased exposure to sensitive CYP2D6, BCRP, or P-gp substrates rather than prominent intrinsic organ toxicity.

Name: Sacubitril
Description: Sacubitril (DB09292) is a small-molecule neprilysin inhibitor used clinically as the ethyl ester prodrug component of sacubitril/valsartan; structurally it is a peptidomimetic carboxylate ester bearing a substituted biphenyl group, an amide linkage, and a chiral hydroxy-acid precursor motif that is hydrolyzed to the active metabolite LBQ657, placing it in the aryloxy/arylalkyl peptidomimetic neutral endopeptidase inhibitor class with a biphenyl-amino-acid-like scaffold. It is chemically and mechanistically similar to other neprilysin inhibitors or vasopeptidase-related agents such as racecadotril, thiorphan, candoxatril, and omapatrilat, although sacubitril is optimized for use with angiotensin receptor blockade rather than ACE inhibition. Its principal target is neprilysin, also known as membrane metalloendopeptidase or MME/NEP/CD10, leading to reduced degradation of natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, adrenomedullin, and related vasoactive peptides. After oral administration in the fixed-dose combination, sacubitril is rapidly absorbed and extensively converted by esterases to LBQ657, with limited parent exposure, moderate protein binding, minimal CYP-dependent metabolism, and elimination primarily as active metabolite through renal excretion with some fecal clearance. Toxicity is dominated by exaggerated hemodynamic and renal effects, including hypotension, hyperkalemia, and renal impairment; clinically important examples include angioedema risk, especially with prior ACE inhibitor exposure, and embryo-fetal toxicity through RAAS blockade from the combination product. Indications and clinical use center on chronic heart failure, especially symptomatic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, to reduce cardiovascular death and heart-failure hospitalization, and in some settings pediatric heart failure or selected heart-failure populations. Common adverse effects include dizziness, cough, syncope, renal dysfunction, nausea, and elevated potassium.

Name: Ombitasvir
Description: Ombitasvir (DrugBank DB09296) is a direct-acting antiviral for hepatitis C virus and is chemically a highly functionalized peptidomimetic small molecule of the NS5A inhibitor class, built around a symmetric or near-symmetric aromatic core linked through amide/carbamate-type connections to rigid proline-derived and heteroatom-rich side chains that create a bivalent scaffold optimized for high-affinity binding to HCV NS5A; thus its chemical category is an antiviral peptidomimetic, and its scaffold is closely related to the dimeric NS5A-inhibitor motif seen in drugs such as daclatasvir, ledipasvir, elbasvir, velpatasvir, and pibrentasvir. Its principal known target protein is the HCV nonstructural protein 5A replication complex, through which it disrupts viral RNA replication and virion assembly. Pharmacokinetically, ombitasvir is orally administered in fixed-dose combination regimens, exhibits absorption sufficient for once-daily dosing, is highly protein bound, has a relatively limited apparent distribution volume, undergoes minimal oxidative metabolism compared with many small molecules, and is eliminated predominantly via biliary/fecal excretion with negligible renal clearance; exposure can rise in hepatic impairment. Clinically it has been used mainly with paritaprevir/ritonavir and dasabuvir, with or without ribavirin, for chronic HCV infection, particularly genotype 1 and genotype 4 infection. Adverse effects in combination therapy commonly include fatigue, nausea, pruritus, insomnia, asthenia, and anemia when ribavirin is included; toxicity concerns include elevations of alanine aminotransferase, hyperbilirubinemia in multidrug regimens, and risk of hepatic decompensation in patients with advanced cirrhosis, while intrinsic acute toxicity appears low at therapeutic exposure.

Name: Tenofovir alafenamide
Description: Tenofovir alafenamide (DB09299) is a lipophilic phosphonamidate prodrug of the acyclic adenine nucleotide analog tenofovir, structurally characterized by an adenine base linked to an open-chain propyl phosphonate and masked by an L-alanine isopropyl ester aryl phosphoramidate ProTide moiety that enhances intracellular delivery; chemically it belongs to the nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor class and, more specifically, to phosphoramidate ester prodrugs of acyclic nucleoside phosphonates, with an adenine acyclic nucleoside phosphonate scaffold. Closely related drugs include tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, the older tenofovir prodrug, as well as mechanistically similar NRTIs such as adefovir dipivoxil, emtricitabine, lamivudine, and entecavir. After oral administration, tenofovir alafenamide is efficiently absorbed, is relatively stable in plasma, and is taken up into hepatocytes and lymphoid cells where cathepsin A and carboxylesterase 1 hydrolyze it to tenofovir, which is then phosphorylated to the active metabolite tenofovir diphosphate; systemic tenofovir exposure is markedly lower than with tenofovir disoproxil, distribution is intracellularly favored, metabolism is primarily via enzymatic activation rather than CYP oxidation, and elimination occurs mainly as renally excreted tenofovir with minor fecal contribution. Its principal pharmacologic target is HIV-1 reverse transcriptase and, in hepatitis B, HBV polymerase/reverse transcriptase, where tenofovir diphosphate causes competitive inhibition and chain termination.
