It is indicated for HIV-1 infection in combination antiretroviral therapy and chronic hepatitis B, including virologic suppression in adults and selected adolescents. Toxicities include renal tubular injury, reduced bone mineral density, lactic acidosis, hepatomegaly with steatosis, and HBV flare after discontinuation, although renal and bone toxicity are generally less frequent than with tenofovir disoproxil. Common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, headache, fatigue, abdominal pain, cough, and rash. Clinically, it is used in fixed-dose HIV regimens such as with emtricitabine plus integrase inhibitors or rilpivirine, and as a component of oral therapy for chronic

Name: Butylscopolamine
Description: Butylscopolamine (hyoscine butylbromide; DrugBank DB09300) is a semisynthetic quaternary ammonium derivative of scopolamine built on a rigid tropane alkaloid framework with a bicyclic 8-azabicyclo[3.2.1]octane core, an epoxide bridge characteristic of scopine/scopoline-type antimuscarinics, an ester linkage to tropic acid, and N-butyl quaternization that confers a permanent positive charge and limits central nervous system penetration; chemically it belongs to the belladonna-type anticholinergic/antispasmodic alkaloids, with a tropane ester scaffold. Closely related drugs include scopolamine, atropine, homatropine, methscopolamine, ipratropium, and tiotropium, which share muscarinic antagonism but differ in quaternization, receptor kinetics, and tissue selectivity. Its principal targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially CHRM1, CHRM2, and CHRM3 on gastrointestinal, biliary, genitourinary, and smooth muscle tissues, where competitive antagonism reduces spasm and secretory tone. Oral absorption is generally poor and erratic because of low membrane permeability; systemic bioavailability is low, distribution is largely extracellular with minimal blood-brain barrier entry, metabolism appears limited to partial ester hydrolysis/hepatic biotransformation, and elimination occurs through fecal and renal routes with excretion of unchanged drug and metabolites. It is indicated for abdominal and pelvic smooth-muscle spasm, including irritable bowel syndrome, intestinal colic, biliary colic, renal colic, dysmenorrhea, and as an antispasmodic during endoscopic or radiologic procedures. Adverse effects reflect peripheral antimuscarinic activity, including dry mouth, tachycardia, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, reduced sweating, and occasionally confusion only rarely because CNS entry is minimal. Toxicity is usually anticholinergic, with overdose causing marked tachyarrhythmia, ileus, urinary obstruction, hyperthermia, and precipitation of angle-closure glaucoma, so clinical use is primarily short-term symptomatic spasm relief in gastrointestinal and genitourinary practice.

Name: Carindacillin
Description: Carindacillin (DrugBank DB09319) is a semisynthetic carboxypenicillin β-lactam antibiotic structurally characterized by the penam nucleus, comprising a strained fused β-lactam and thiazolidine ring system, bearing a carboxy-substituted side chain that increases activity against certain Gram-negative bacilli and confers acid lability relative to more oral-stable penicillins; chemically it belongs to the penicillin family, specifically the antipseudomonal/carboxypenicillin class, and its core scaffold is the 6-aminopenicillanic acid penam framework. It is closely related to carbenicillin and ticarcillin, with broader family analogs including ampicillin and piperacillin as other extended-spectrum penicillins. Like other β-lactams, it targets bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, particularly transpeptidases involved in peptidoglycan cross-linking, leading to inhibition of cell-wall synthesis and bacterial lysis; no human protein target is therapeutically relevant. Carindacillin has been used primarily for urinary tract infections caused by susceptible organisms such as Escherichia coli, Proteus species, Enterobacter, and some Pseudomonas strains, historically as an orally active prodrug approach to carbenicillin exposure. After oral administration it is absorbed and converted to active carbenicillin, distributed mainly in extracellular fluid with renal tissue and urinary concentrations of clinical importance, undergoes minimal further metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly by renal excretion via glomerular filtration and tubular secretion, giving high urine levels. Toxicities and adverse effects resemble those of carbenicillin and related penicillins, including hypersensitivity reactions, rash, urticaria, anaphylaxis, gastrointestinal upset, diarrhea, candidiasis, and less commonly electrolyte disturbances, platelet dysfunction, or superinfection; clinical use was chiefly in susceptible urinary infections rather than severe systemic disease.

Name: Procaine benzylpenicillin
Description: Procaine benzylpenicillin (DrugBank DB09320) is a depot intramuscular formulation consisting of the procaine salt of benzylpenicillin (penicillin G), in which the active penam nucleus contains a strained bicyclic scaffold formed by a beta-lactam ring fused to a thiazolidine ring and bearing a benzyl acyl side chain; chemically it is classified as a natural penicillin, beta-lactam antibiotic, and carboxylate salt with the local anesthetic procaine. Its core scaffold is the 6-aminopenicillanic acid penam framework, shared with related agents such as benzylpenicillin potassium/sodium, benzathine benzylpenicillin, phenoxymethylpenicillin, ampicillin, and cloxacillin. After deep intramuscular injection, absorption is slow because of low aqueous solubility, producing prolonged but relatively low serum penicillin concentrations; distribution is mainly into extracellular fluid with variable penetration into inflamed tissues and limited CNS entry unless meninges are inflamed; benzylpenicillin undergoes minimal metabolism and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by renal tubular secretion and glomerular filtration, while procaine is hydrolyzed by esterases. Its antibacterial targets are bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, especially transpeptidases involved in peptidoglycan cross-linking, leading to cell-wall synthesis inhibition and lysis in susceptible organisms. It is indicated for penicillin-sensitive infections such as streptococcal upper respiratory infection, pneumococcal infection, susceptible staphylococcal soft-tissue infection, syphilis, and some treponemal or skin infections. Toxicity is dominated by hypersensitivity reactions ranging from rash and urticaria to anaphylaxis, plus procaine-related neuropsychiatric reactions, rare hemolytic anemia, interstitial nephritis, seizures at high exposure, and antibiotic-associated colitis. Common adverse effects include injection-site pain, fever, nausea, diarrhea, candidiasis, and allergic exanthems. Clinically, it has been used when sustained low-level penicillin exposure is desired, especially for outpatient treatment of mild-to-moderate susceptible infections and selected treponemal diseases.

Name: Sulbactam
Description: Sulbactam (DrugBank DB09324) is a semisynthetic beta-lactamase inhibitor built on a penicillanic acid sulfone framework, featuring the strained bicyclic beta-lactam fused to a thiazolidine-like ring with oxidation of the sulfur to a sulfone, a structure that preserves beta-lactam reactivity while favoring irreversible enzyme inhibition rather than strong direct antibacterial activity; chemically it belongs to the beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor class, with a penam sulfone scaffold closely related to clavulanic acid, tazobactam, and durlobactam, and often compared clinically with amoxicillin-clavulanate or piperacillin-tazobactam combinations. Its principal targets are bacterial serine beta-lactamases, especially class A enzymes such as TEM-type and some SHV enzymes, with additional intrinsic activity against Acinetobacter baumannii through binding to penicillin-binding proteins, notably PBP1 and PBP3. Pharmacokinetically, sulbactam is administered parenterally or as the orally absorbed prodrug sultamicillin, distributes largely in extracellular fluid with penetration into tissues and inflammatory exudates, shows low protein binding, undergoes minimal metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged in urine with a short half-life that is prolonged in renal impairment. Toxicity is generally low but includes hypersensitivity typical of beta-lactams, neurotoxicity or seizures at high exposures or in renal dysfunction, and superinfection risk such as Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea. Indications center on restoring activity of beta-lactam partners, for example in skin and soft-tissue, intra-abdominal, gynecologic, respiratory, and polymicrobial infections, including beta-lactamase-producing Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, and anaerobes when used as ampicillin-sulbactam. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, rash, injection-site reactions, transaminase elevation, and candidiasis. Clinically, it is used mainly in fixed combinations, especially ampicillin-sulbactam, and in some settings high-dose sulbactam-containing regimens are used for multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter infections.

Name: Sodium fluoride
Description: Sodium fluoride (DrugBank DB09325) is a simple inorganic ionic salt composed of dissociated sodium cations and fluoride anions, lacking a complex covalent framework and therefore best described structurally as a monatomic halide scaffold rather than an organic pharmacophore-bearing molecule; chemically it belongs to the alkali metal fluorides and more broadly to inorganic fluoride salts, with close analogs and therapeutically similar agents including stannous fluoride, sodium monofluorophosphate, acidulated phosphate fluoride, and, outside dentistry, other fluoride salts such as potassium fluoride. Its pharmacologic activity is mediated primarily by fluoride ion rather than binding to a single classic receptor, although relevant biological targets include hydroxyapatite in enamel and bone, bacterial glycolytic enzymes such as enolase, proton-translocating ATPases in cariogenic bacteria, and mineralizing osteoblast/osteoclast-associated processes. After oral ingestion it is generally well absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, distributes rapidly in extracellular water with marked uptake into calcified tissues and teeth, crosses the placenta, shows minimal true metabolism because it remains largely as fluoride ion, and is excreted predominantly by the kidney with urinary clearance influenced by urine pH and renal function. Clinically it is used to prevent dental caries, promote enamel remineralization, reduce dentinal hypersensitivity, and historically as a supplement in children with low-fluoride water exposure. Toxicity is dose dependent: acute overdose may cause nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, hypersalivation, hypocalcemia, arrhythmias, seizures, and potentially fatal cardiotoxicity, whereas chronic excess can produce dental fluorosis, skeletal fluorosis, osteosclerosis, and joint pain. Common adverse effects in routine use are usually local and mild, including oral irritation, unpleasant taste, and occasional gastrointestinal upset with swallowed preparations.

Name: Osimertinib
Description: Osimertinib (DB09330) is a third-generation, orally active epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitor built on a substituted anilino-pyrimidine/quinazoline-like heteroaromatic kinase-inhibitor framework, featuring a planar aza-heterocyclic core linked to lipophilic aryl and tertiary amine-containing substituents and, critically, an acrylamide Michael acceptor that enables covalent binding to cysteine in mutant EGFR; chemically it is best categorized as a covalent, small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor, and its core scaffold is closely related to other EGFR inhibitors such as gefitinib, erlotinib, afatinib, dacomitinib, and the mutant-selective rociletinib. Its principal targets are EGFR/ERBB1, especially activating exon 19 deletion and L858R mutants and the resistance mutation T790M, with weaker activity against wild-type EGFR; limited activity on other ERBB family kinases may occur. After oral administration it is well absorbed, reaches peak concentrations within hours, is highly distributed into tissues, is extensively protein bound, and is metabolized mainly by CYP3A-mediated oxidation and dealkylation to active metabolites including AZ5104 and AZ7550; elimination is predominantly via feces, with a terminal half-life of roughly 2 days supporting once-daily dosing. Clinically, it is indicated for EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer, including first-line metastatic disease, T790M-positive disease after prior EGFR TKI exposure, and adjuvant treatment after resection. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, rash, dry skin, paronychia, stomatitis, decreased appetite, and fatigue, while important toxicities include interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis, QT prolongation, cardiomyopathy, keratitis, myelosuppression, and embryo-fetal toxicity. In practice it is used as a targeted therapy for molecularly selected lung adenocarcinoma patients, including those with central nervous system metastases because of clinically meaningful CNS penetration.

Name: Tipiracil
Description: Tipiracil (DrugBank DB09343) is a halogenated pyrimidine-based antimetabolite analogue structurally characterized by a substituted uracil/thymine-like heteroaromatic ring bearing carbonyl functionality and a brominated side chain motif, placing it in the class of thymidine phosphorylase inhibitors and fluoropyrimidine-modulating agents; its core scaffold is a brominated pyrimidinedione closely related to uracil derivatives, and chemically or mechanistically similar agents include trifluridine, fluorouracil, capecitabine, and other pyrimidine analogues used in colorectal cancer therapy. Its principal target is thymidine phosphorylase, which it inhibits to prevent rapid degradation of trifluridine, thereby increasing systemic trifluridine exposure rather than acting primarily as a standalone cytotoxin. Clinically, tipiracil is used in fixed combination with trifluridine for metastatic colorectal cancer and also gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma after prior standard therapies, for example in refractory metastatic disease. After oral administration as the trifluridine/tipiracil combination, tipiracil is absorbed enterally, has limited protein binding, distributes systemically but mainly serves a peripheral enzyme-inhibitory role, undergoes relatively limited hepatic biotransformation compared with many cytotoxics, and is eliminated largely in urine as parent drug and metabolites. Toxicity is dominated by combination-related myelosuppression, especially neutropenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and infection risk, with gastrointestinal toxicity such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and fatigue also common; serious examples include febrile neutropenia and severe sepsis. Its adverse-effect profile in practice therefore reflects both pharmacokinetic enhancement of trifluridine and the expected hematologic and gastrointestinal toxicities of fluoropyrimidine-based antineoplastic treatment.

Name: Pramocaine
Description: Pramocaine (DrugBank DB09345), also known as pramoxine, is a topical local anesthetic built on a non-amide, non-ester ether architecture featuring a lipophilic aryl-alkoxy side linked through a morpholine ring, giving it a distinctive morpholine ether scaffold that differentiates it from classical benzoate-ester or anilide local anesthetics. Chemically it is categorized as a morpholine-derived topical anesthetic and is most similar functionally to agents such as lidocaine, benzocaine, dibucaine, and tetracaine, although its scaffold is closer to other nontraditional ether anesthetics than to ester or amide classes. Its pharmacologic action is attributed to reversible blockade of neuronal voltage-gated sodium channels, reducing initiation and propagation of action potentials in peripheral sensory nerves; specific protein targets are not always individually assigned in product labeling, but Nav channel isoforms such as SCN9A, SCN10A, and related peripheral sodium channels are the relevant mechanistic targets. Systemic pharmacokinetic data are limited because it is intended for topical use and generally exhibits low percutaneous absorption when applied to intact skin, with distribution and metabolism presumed minimal at recommended doses, likely involving hepatic biotransformation of any absorbed fraction and renal excretion of metabolites. Toxicity is usually low but can include local irritation, burning, stinging, allergic or contact dermatitis, and with excessive application, damaged skin, or mucosal exposure, systemic local-anesthetic toxicity such as CNS excitation or depression and rare cardiac effects may occur. Clinically it is used for temporary relief of pain, pruritus, and burning associated with hemorrhoids, insect bites, minor cuts, sunburn, poison ivy, eczema, rashes, and other superficial dermatoses.

Name: Piperonyl butoxide
Description: Piperonyl butoxide (DrugBank DB09350) is a synthetic methylenedioxyphenyl insecticide synergist characterized structurally by a 1,3-benzodioxole aromatic ring linked through an ether-containing pentyl chain to a bulky butoxyethoxy side chain, giving a lipophilic aryl ether architecture; chemically it is classified as a methylenedioxyphenyl synergist and broadly as an aromatic ether/acetal-like benzodioxole derivative, with a benzodioxole scaffold closely related to other cytochrome P450-inhibiting synergists such as sesamex, piperonyl cyclonene, and to the natural-product motif found in safrole-like methylenedioxyphenyl compounds. Its pharmacological activity is not based on direct insecticidal action but on inhibition of xenobiotic-metabolizing enzymes, especially insect microsomal cytochrome P450s, with additional effects reported on esterases and mixed-function oxidases; specific human target assignment is limited, but CYP-family inhibition underlies its mechanism. After exposure, absorption can occur by inhalation, ingestion, and dermal routes; distribution is favored into lipid-rich tissues, metabolism occurs mainly in the liver via oxidative O-dealkylation and side-chain oxidation to more polar metabolites, and excretion is primarily urinary with some fecal elimination. Toxicity is generally low to moderate acutely but increases with dose and chronic exposure, with hepatic enlargement, enzyme induction or inhibition, gastrointestinal irritation, CNS depression, and in experimental animals developmental or carcinogenicity signals at high doses. It is indicated and clinically used not as a therapeutic drug but as a pesticide adjuvant in formulations for pediculosis and ectoparasite control and in agricultural or household pyrethrin/pyrethroid products to enhance efficacy against lice, mosquitoes, flies, fleas, and resistant insects. Adverse effects in exposed humans include skin and eye irritation, cough, nausea, headache, dizziness, and rarely sensitization or respiratory irritation.

Name: Levobetaxolol
Description: Levobetaxolol (DrugBank DB09351) is the levorotatory active enantiomer of betaxolol, an aryloxypropanolamine beta-adrenergic antagonist whose structure features a para-substituted phenoxypropanolamine core bearing a secondary alcohol, a protonatable secondary amine, and a cyclopropyl-containing alkyl substituent that contributes lipophilicity and receptor affinity; chemically it belongs to the beta-blocker class, specifically the phenoxypropanolamine/aryloxypropanolamine family, with an archetypal propranolol-like beta-blocker scaffold. Similar drugs include betaxolol, timolol, levobunolol, carteolol, metipranolol, and propranolol, which share beta-adrenergic receptor antagonism and related ocular hypotensive use. Its principal targets are beta-1 adrenergic receptor and, to a lesser extent, beta-2 adrenergic receptor, with lowering of intraocular pressure attributed to reduced aqueous humor production in the ciliary epithelium. Pharmacokinetically, ophthalmic levobetaxolol is absorbed through the cornea and conjunctiva with some systemic absorption via nasolacrimal drainage, distributes locally to anterior ocular tissues, undergoes predominantly hepatic metabolism similar to racemic betaxolol, likely involving oxidative pathways, and is excreted mainly as metabolites in urine. It is indicated primarily for open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension, including chronic pressure lowering in patients intolerant of less beta-1-selective agents. Adverse effects include ocular burning, stinging, blurred vision, tearing, dry eye, and foreign-body sensation, while systemic beta-blockade may cause bradycardia, hypotension, fatigue, depression, bronchospasm, or masking of hypoglycemia. Toxicity is generally an extension of beta-blockade, with overdose potentially producing severe bradyarrhythmia, heart block, heart failure, and respiratory compromise, warranting caution in asthma, COPD, conduction disease, and patients receiving other rate-limiting drugs.

Name: Hydroxyamphetamine
Description: Hydroxyamphetamine (DrugBank DB09352) is a sympathomimetic phenethylamine and substituted amphetamine whose structure consists of the classic amphetamine backbone, alpha-methylphenethylamine, bearing a para-hydroxyl substituent on the aromatic ring; this makes it a phenylethanolamine-related aralkylamine with an amphetamine scaffold characterized by a lipophilic phenyl ring linked to a two-carbon side chain and terminal primary amine, with the alpha-methyl group conferring resistance to metabolism and central/peripheral adrenergic activity. It is chemically related to other indirect-acting adrenergic agents and amphetamine-like drugs such as amphetamine, methamphetamine, ephedrine, tyramine, and pholedrine. Its principal pharmacology is promotion of norepinephrine release from sympathetic nerve terminals, with functional interaction at the norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2 and downstream activation of alpha-1 adrenergic receptors in the iris dilator muscle; it may also weakly affect dopamine transport processes. After topical ophthalmic administration, systemic absorption is usually limited but can occur via conjunctival and nasolacrimal routes; distribution is expected to favor sympathetic tissues, metabolism occurs at least partly by oxidative deamination and related hepatic pathways, and renal excretion eliminates parent drug and metabolites. Toxicity reflects excessive sympathomimetic exposure, including hypertension, tachycardia, arrhythmia, mydriasis, headache, agitation, and rare cardiovascular or CNS overstimulation, with greater risk in children or overdose. Clinically, hydroxyamphetamine is used mainly as an ophthalmic mydriatic and diagnostically in Horner syndrome to distinguish preganglionic or central lesions from postganglionic sympathetic denervation; adverse effects include transient աչքի irritation, blurred vision, photophobia, increased intraocular pressure, palpitations, and nervousness.

Name: Sulfabenzamide
Description: Sulfabenzamide (DrugBank DB09355) is a classic sulfonamide antibacterial whose structure consists of a para-aminobenzenesulfonamide core in which the sulfonamide nitrogen is substituted by a benzamide-containing aryl group, giving an aniline-sulfonamide linked to a benzoyl-substituted aromatic scaffold; chemically it belongs to the sulfonamide anti-infectives and more specifically the p-aminobenzenesulfonamide family, with a sulfanilamide-like scaffold decorated by a benzamide moiety that increases lipophilicity. It is structurally and pharmacologically related to other older sulfonamides such as sulfanilamide, sulfacetamide, sulfadiazine, sulfathiazole, and sulfamethoxazole. Like other agents in this class, it acts by competitively inhibiting bacterial dihydropteroate synthase, thereby blocking folate biosynthesis; this enzyme is the principal known target protein. Sulfabenzamide has mainly been used as a topical or poorly absorbed local antibacterial rather than a modern systemic agent, so oral absorption is limited or variable, tissue distribution is correspondingly modest when given locally, hepatic biotransformation may include N-acetylation typical of sulfonamides, and elimination is expected to occur predominantly by renal excretion of parent drug and metabolites. Toxicities resemble those of other sulfonamides and include hypersensitivity reactions, rash, fever, urticaria, rare Stevens-Johnson syndrome, crystalluria, hemolysis in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, and occasional hepatic or hematologic injury. Adverse effects include local irritation, gastrointestinal upset if absorbed, and allergic dermatitis. Clinically, it has been used for superficial bacterial infections, especially topical treatment of infected wounds, burns, and certain skin or mucosal infections, often in combination products for local antimicrobial coverage.

Name: Dexpanthenol
Description: Dexpanthenol (DrugBank DB09357) is the alcohol analog and dextrorotatory provitamin of pantothenic acid, structurally characterized as a small, highly polar aliphatic pantothenyl derivative bearing multiple hydroxyl groups and a terminal primary alcohol, with a flexible open-chain scaffold rather than a fused ring system; chemically it is classified as a water-soluble vitamin derivative and polyol amide, built on the pantothenic acid/pantoate–beta-alanine scaffold. Closely related agents include pantothenic acid itself, calcium pantothenate, and mechanistically similar epithelial repair adjuvants such as allantoin. After oral or topical administration, dexpanthenol is readily absorbed and rapidly oxidized to pantothenic acid, distributes widely in extracellular fluids and tissues, and enters intermediary metabolism as a precursor of coenzyme A; specific plasma protein binding is not usually emphasized, metabolism is dominated by conversion to pantothenate, and renal excretion of pantothenate and unchanged small fractions is the principal elimination route. Its pharmacology is therefore mediated less by high-affinity receptor binding than by replenishment of pantothenate-dependent pathways; no definitive single drug target protein is established, although downstream biochemical dependence includes pantothenate kinase and coenzyme A-utilizing enzymes. Toxicity is generally low, with wide tolerability in topical, oral, and parenteral use, but examples of adverse effects include skin irritation, contact dermatitis, pruritus, erythema, and occasional gastrointestinal upset such as nausea or diarrhea. Clinically, it is used to support wound healing and skin or mucosal barrier repair, including minor burns, abrasions, dermatitis, xerosis, diaper rash, postoperative or radiation-associated mucosal irritation, and as a component of hair, ocular, nasal, and oral care formulations.

Name: Norethynodrel
Description: Norethynodrel (DB09371) is a first-generation synthetic progestin and orally active steroidal 19-nor pregnane derivative whose structure is based on the estrane/gonane steroid nucleus with a 17α-ethynyl substituent, a 3-keto function, and a 5(10)-ene unsaturation, features that support oral bioavailability and progestational activity; chemically it is classified as a steroid hormone analogue, specifically an estrane-type progestogen, and its core scaffold is closely related to nortestosterone-derived oral contraceptive steroids. Similar drugs include norethindrone, ethynodiol diacetate, lynestrenol, levonorgestrel, and medroxyprogesterone acetate, which share steroidal progestin pharmacology but differ in androgenic, estrogenic, and metabolic profiles. Norethynodrel acts primarily via the progesterone receptor, with biologically relevant interactions also involving the estrogen receptor through metabolic conversion and downstream hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis suppression, thereby inhibiting ovulation and altering cervical mucus and endometrium. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed, distributed extensively in plasma bound to albumin and sex hormone-binding proteins to a limited extent, metabolized hepatically by steroid-transforming enzymes to active and inactive metabolites including estrogenic products such as ethinyl estradiol, and excreted mainly in urine with some fecal elimination. Toxicities and adverse effects resemble those of older combined oral contraceptive progestins, including nausea, headache, breast tenderness, breakthrough bleeding, edema, weight change, mood effects, cholestatic jaundice, and rare thromboembolic or cardiovascular events, with overdose usually causing limited acute toxicity. Clinically it was used mainly in oral contraception and menstrual regulation, including suppression of ovulation, treatment of dysfunctional uterine bleeding, and cycle control, historically often in combination with mestranol.

Name: Norgestrel
Description: Norgestrel (DrugBank DB09389) is a synthetic orally active progestin composed of a hydrophobic steroid nucleus built on an estrane/gonane framework, specifically a 19-nortestosterone-derived tetracyclic cyclopenta[a]phenanthrene core bearing a 3-keto group, a 17β-hydroxyl substituent, and a characteristic 13-ethyl plus 17α-ethynyl pattern; it is marketed as a racemate, with levonorgestrel representing the active levo isomer. Chemically it belongs to the progestogens and more specifically the estrane/gonane anabolic-androgenic steroid-related contraceptive progestins; its core scaffold is the norethindrone-like 17α-ethynyl-19-nortestosterone steroid scaffold. Similar drugs include levonorgestrel, norethindrone, desogestrel, gestodene, norgestimate, and medroxyprogesterone acetate. Its principal target is the progesterone receptor, with weaker off-target androgen receptor activity and suppression of hypothalamic-pituitary gonadotropin signaling. After oral administration it is well absorbed, highly protein bound mainly to sex hormone-binding globulin and albumin, widely distributed, hepatically metabolized largely by reduction and conjugation with CYP3A4 participation, and eliminated as urinary and fecal metabolites with an elimination half-life typically in the roughly 16- to 24-hour range. Toxicity is generally low in therapeutic use but includes dose-related endocrine and vascular risk, such as cholestatic jaundice, hypertension, venous thromboembolism risk when combined with estrogens, and fetal virilization concerns with inappropriate pregnancy exposure. Adverse effects include nausea, breast tenderness, headache, mood change, acne, weight change, irregular bleeding, amenorrhea, and decreased libido. Clinically, norgestrel is used chiefly in combined oral contraception, menstrual cycle regulation, treatment of abnormal uterine bleeding or dysmenorrhea, and other situations where reliable ovulation suppression and progestational endometrial control are desired.

Name: Isosorbide
Description: Isosorbide (DrugBank DB09401) is a rigid, bicyclic dianhydro sugar alcohol derived from sorbitol, structurally characterized by a fused 2,5:3,6-dianhydrohexitol scaffold bearing two secondary hydroxyl groups in a V-shaped, conformationally constrained ring system; chemically it belongs to the polyol and carbohydrate-derived cyclic diether class, with the isosorbide core serving as its defining scaffold. It is structurally related to other alditol-derived cyclic compounds and nitrate ester analogs such as isosorbide mononitrate and isosorbide dinitrate, although the parent isosorbide itself lacks the nitrate functionalities responsible for classic antianginal nitric oxide donation. Pharmacokinetically, isosorbide is orally absorbed, distributed largely in total body water, undergoes limited biotransformation relative to nitrate esters, and is eliminated mainly in urine as unchanged compound or simple metabolites, with a generally short to moderate residence time and low protein binding. Toxicity is usually low, but excessive exposure may cause osmotic gastrointestinal intolerance, dehydration, headache, dizziness, or renal stress; in formulation or excipient contexts, high doses can provoke diarrhea or electrolyte imbalance. No highly specific canonical pharmacologic target protein is established for the parent compound, and it is often better regarded as a chemical intermediate, excipient, or platform molecule rather than a receptor-directed therapeutic, though downstream derivatives act via soluble guanylate cyclase signaling secondary to nitric oxide release. Clinically, isosorbide has limited direct therapeutic use compared with its nitrate derivatives; its principal relevance is in pharmaceutical manufacturing, polymer and excipient applications, and as a precursor to antianginal drugs used for angina pectoris, ischemic heart disease, and relief of chest pain, where related agents commonly cause headache, flushing, hypotension, reflex tachycardia, and dizziness.

Name: Sodium phosphate, monobasic
Description: Sodium phosphate, monobasic (DrugBank DB09449) is an inorganic sodium acid phosphate salt composed of a monovalent sodium cation paired with the dihydrogen phosphate anion, featuring a tetrahedral phosphorus center bound to four oxygens, two bearing acidic hydrogens, placing it in the phosphate mineral/electrolyte class and more specifically among inorganic acid salts; its core scaffold is therefore a simple monophosphate oxyanion rather than an organic carbon-based framework. Closely related drugs include sodium phosphate, dibasic, potassium phosphate salts, phosphoric acid preparations, and combination sodium phosphate bowel-cleansing products. Pharmacokinetically, oral phosphate is absorbed mainly in the small intestine through passive diffusion and sodium-dependent phosphate transporters such as SLC34A2, distributes predominantly in extracellular fluid with major physiological incorporation into bone and intracellular phosphate pools, is not metabolized in the classical hepatic sense because it enters endogenous phosphate homeostasis, and is excreted largely by the kidney under regulation by PTH, FGF23, and vitamin D. Pharmacologically it acts primarily as a phosphate and sodium replacement agent and osmotic cathartic, without a single canonical receptor target, though transport and homeostatic proteins including SLC34 family transporters, PTH1R-regulated renal pathways, and FGF receptor/Klotho signaling are relevant. Indications include prevention or treatment of hypophosphatemia, urinary acidification in some settings, and bowel evacuation before colonoscopy or surgery. Toxicity is dominated by hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, dehydration, hypernatremia, metastatic calcification, acute phosphate nephropathy, arrhythmia, seizure, and renal failure, particularly in elderly patients or those with kidney disease. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramping, diarrhea, bloating, dizziness, and electrolyte disturbances. Clinically it is used as oral or parenteral phosphate replacement and in selected cathartic or bowel-preparation regimens, with careful electrolyte and renal monitoring.

Name: Glycerin
Description: Glycerin (glycerol; DrugBank DB09462) is a small, highly polar trihydric alcohol whose structure consists of a linear three-carbon propane backbone bearing one hydroxyl group on each carbon, yielding a symmetric polyol with extensive hydrogen-bonding capacity, high water miscibility, viscosity, and humectant behavior; chemically it belongs to the alcohol/polyol class, and its core scaffold is a simple propane-1,2,3-triol backbone. Closely related or functionally similar agents include other osmotic or lubricating polyols and hyperosmotic agents such as propylene glycol, sorbitol, mannitol, and lactulose, depending on indication. Pharmacokinetically, glycerin is readily absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract and across mucosal surfaces, distributes mainly in total body water, and when administered rectally acts largely locally by osmotic water retention; systemically absorbed glycerol is rapidly taken up by liver and kidney, phosphorylated by glycerol kinase to glycerol-3-phosphate, entering glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, and triglyceride synthesis, with renal excretion of unchanged drug typically limited unless doses are high. Its pharmacology is mediated more by physicochemical effects than selective receptor binding, although glycerol kinase and aquaporin-facilitated transport are relevant biological interactors; no canonical high-affinity drug target protein is central to use. Clinically it is used as an osmotic laxative for constipation, as a hyperosmotic agent to transiently reduce intraocular pressure in glaucoma, and as a demulcent, lubricant, humectant, and solvent in topical, oral, rectal, ophthalmic, and pharmaceutical formulations. Adverse effects include abdominal cramping, diarrhea, rectal irritation, nausea, thirst, headache, dehydration, and electrolyte disturbance, while excessive systemic exposure may contribute to hyperglycemia, osmotic shifts, or rarely renal and neurologic complications in susceptible patients.

Name: Sodium sulfate
Description: Sodium sulfate (DrugBank DB09472) is a simple inorganic ionic salt composed of two sodium cations electrostatically associated with a tetrahedral sulfate dianion, in which a central sulfur atom is fully oxidized and bonded to four oxygen atoms; structurally it lacks a complex organic pharmacophore and is best classified as an alkali metal sulfate, with the sulfate oxyanion serving as its minimal chemical scaffold. It is chemically and functionally related to other saline cathartics and osmotic agents such as magnesium sulfate, sodium phosphate, potassium sulfate, and sulfate-containing bowel-cleansing combinations. Pharmacokinetically, oral sodium sulfate is poorly absorbed to variably absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, remains largely in the intestinal lumen where it exerts osmotic activity by retaining water, has negligible tissue distribution beyond extracellular ionic compartments for the absorbed fraction, undergoes no metabolic biotransformation, and is eliminated primarily unchanged in feces with absorbed sulfate excreted renally. Its pharmacology is largely physicochemical rather than receptor-mediated, so no specific high-affinity target proteins are generally assigned; its effect derives from osmotic water retention and promotion of intestinal motility. Clinically it is used mainly as a laxative and bowel-cleansing agent, for example before colonoscopy or other colorectal procedures and for relief of constipation. Adverse effects commonly include diarrhea, abdominal cramping, nausea, vomiting, bloating, and dehydration. Toxicity is mainly related to excessive fluid and electrolyte shifts, with examples including hypernatremia, sulfate-related osmotic diarrhea, hypovolemia, renal stress, and in susceptible patients electrolyte disturbances that may contribute to weakness, confusion, or arrhythmia.

Name: Enalaprilat
Description: Enalaprilat (DB09477) is the active diacid metabolite of enalapril and a dicarboxylate angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor built on a substituted L-alanyl-L-proline/2-methylpropanoyl-proline peptidomimetic framework, with a proline-derived bicyclic/heterocyclic peptide-like scaffold bearing two carboxylate groups and a secondary amine that enable tight coordination within the zinc-containing catalytic site of ACE; chemically it belongs to the peptide-mimetic dicarboxylate class of ACE inhibitors, and its scaffold is closely related to enalapril, lisinopril, ramiprilat, quinaprilat, perindoprilat, and captopril as mechanistically similar antihypertensives. Its principal target protein is angiotensin-converting enzyme, especially somatic ACE, leading to reduced angiotensin II formation and decreased bradykinin degradation. Pharmacokinetically, enalaprilat is poorly absorbed orally and is therefore mainly used intravenously; it distributes largely in extracellular fluid with limited CNS penetration, exhibits relatively low protein binding, undergoes little to no further metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by the kidney, so clearance is prolonged in renal impairment. Toxicity is dominated by exaggerated pharmacology, notably profound hypotension, azotemia or acute kidney injury, hyperkalemia, and rare but serious angioedema; fetal toxicity in pregnancy is a major class risk, and overdose may produce marked blood-pressure reduction and renal dysfunction. It is indicated for hypertension and hypertensive urgency when parenteral ACE inhibition is needed, and may also be used in heart failure settings requiring afterload reduction. Adverse effects include cough, dizziness, headache, syncope, nausea, renal function deterioration, hyperkalemia, rash, and angioedema. Clinically, enalaprilat is used as an intravenous inpatient agent when oral therapy is not feasible, such as perioperative hypertension, severe uncontrolled blood pressure, or temporary conversion from oral ACE inhibitor therapy.

Name: Magnesium carbonate
Description: Magnesium carbonate (DrugBank DB09481) is an inorganic magnesium salt composed of divalent magnesium cations associated with planar trigonal carbonate anions in an ionic crystal lattice, often encountered in basic or hydrated forms rather than as a discrete covalent small-molecule architecture; chemically it belongs to the alkaline earth metal carbonates, and its scaffold is best described as a simple metal-carbonate ionic framework. Similar drugs include other magnesium salts and antacid/laxative agents such as magnesium hydroxide, magnesium oxide, magnesium citrate, calcium carbonate, and sodium bicarbonate. After oral administration, magnesium carbonate reacts with gastric acid to form soluble magnesium chloride, water, and carbon dioxide, with only a fraction of liberated magnesium absorbed mainly in the small intestine; absorbed magnesium distributes largely to bone and intracellular compartments, is not metabolized, and is excreted primarily by the kidney, while unabsorbed material is eliminated in feces. Its pharmacology is largely physicochemical rather than receptor-selective, and no highly specific canonical protein target is usually assigned, although systemic magnesium can modulate ion channels and transport systems including calcium channels and NMDA receptor-associated signaling. Clinically it is used as an antacid for dyspepsia, heartburn, and acid indigestion, and in some formulations as a magnesium supplement for hypomagnesemia. Adverse effects commonly include diarrhea, abdominal cramping, nausea, belching, and flatulence; excessive exposure, especially in renal impairment, can cause hypermagnesemia with कमजोरी, hypotension, bradycardia, lethargy, diminished reflexes, and rarely respiratory or cardiac depression. Toxicity is therefore most relevant in overdose or reduced renal clearance, and clinical use favors short-term symptomatic relief or supplementation with caution in patients with kidney disease.

Name: Acrivastine
Description: Acrivastine (DrugBank DB09488) is a second-generation H1-antihistamine characterized structurally as a substituted acrylate/propionic acid derivative bearing a triprolidine-like aryl-alkenyl scaffold, with a carboxylated side chain linked to a pyridyl ring and a p-methylphenyl group across a constrained unsaturated framework; chemically it is classified as a non-sedating alkylamine antihistamine and can be viewed as an acrylate-containing analog within the triprolidine-related scaffold family. Similar drugs include triprolidine, from which it is structurally derived, and other peripheral H1 antagonists such as cetirizine, loratadine, and fexofenadine, although these differ in core scaffold. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, where it acts functionally as a peripheral antagonist or inverse agonist to reduce histamine-mediated capillary permeability, pruritus, sneezing, and rhinorrhea. Pharmacokinetically, acrivastine is rapidly absorbed after oral administration, producing a relatively fast onset of action; distribution is moderate with limited central nervous system penetration compared with older antihistamines; metabolism is limited, and elimination occurs predominantly via renal excretion of unchanged drug, giving it a relatively short half-life and favoring multiple daily dosing. It is indicated for symptomatic relief of seasonal allergic rhinitis, urticaria, and related allergic symptoms such as itching, tearing, and nasal congestion. Adverse effects are usually mild and include drowsiness, dizziness, dry mouth, nausea, and headache, while toxicity in overdose may produce enhanced CNS depression or anticholinergic-like symptoms, though serious cardiotoxicity is not a defining feature. Clinically, it has been used alone or with a decongestant such as pseudoephedrine for hay fever and other acute allergic conditions requiring rapid but comparatively short-acting antihistaminic control.

Name: Cetyl alcohol
Description: Cetyl alcohol (DrugBank DB09494), also called 1-hexadecanol, is a straight-chain, saturated 16-carbon primary fatty alcohol with a terminal hydroxyl group appended to a long hydrophobic alkyl chain, placing it in the long-chain aliphatic alcohol and fatty alcohol chemical category; its core scaffold is a linear hexadecyl hydrocarbon backbone bearing a single primary alcohol functionality, a motif shared with similar excipient-type lipophilic alcohols such as stearyl alcohol, cetearyl alcohol, lauryl alcohol, and myristyl alcohol. It is used predominantly as a pharmaceutical excipient rather than a classic active drug, functioning as an emollient, stiffening agent, viscosity enhancer, and nonionic emulsion stabilizer in topical creams, ointments, lotions, suppositories, and some oral formulations; thus it has no well-established therapeutic target proteins and no specific receptor-mediated pharmacology, although it can influence barrier properties and formulation-dependent drug release. Pharmacokinetically, systemic exposure is usually low after topical use because percutaneous absorption is limited; if ingested, it is expected to partition into lipid compartments, undergo oxidation by alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenase pathways to palmitic acid, enter normal fatty acid metabolism, and be eliminated largely as carbon dioxide after beta-oxidation, with minor incorporation into endogenous lipids. Toxicity is generally low at pharmaceutical exposure levels, but excessive ingestion may cause gastrointestinal irritation, and occupational or formulation-related exposure can rarely provoke skin or eye irritation. Adverse effects are usually local and uncommon, including contact dermatitis, erythema, pruritus, burning, follicular irritation, or acneiform reactions, especially in sensitive patients. Clinically, cetyl alcohol is used to support treatment of xerosis, eczema, dermatitis, and other conditions requiring moisturization or stable topical drug delivery, for example in corticosteroid creams, antifungal preparations, barrier creams, and cosmetic dermatology products.

Name: Octinoxate
Description: Octinoxate (DrugBank DB09496), also known as octyl methoxycinnamate or ethylhexyl methoxycinnamate, is a lipophilic cinnamate ester composed of a para-methoxy-substituted phenyl ring linked through an E-configured alkene to an octyl ester, giving a conjugated aromatic acrylate-like chromophore that efficiently absorbs UVB radiation; chemically it belongs to the cinnamate ester and organic UV filter class, with a methoxycinnamate scaffold. It is structurally related to other sunscreen agents such as cinoxate, amiloxate, and to broader aromatic UV filters including octocrylene and padimate O, which share hydrophobic esterified aromatic photophores. Its principal pharmacologic role is physical-chemical rather than receptor-mediated, with no established therapeutic protein target central to efficacy, although in vitro interactions have been reported with steroid hormone receptors including estrogen receptor ESR1, androgen receptor, and progesterone receptor, underpinning endocrine-disruption concerns. After topical administration, dermal absorption is generally low but measurable and increases with damaged skin, formulation effects, occlusion, or repeated use; distributed into the stratum corneum and superficial epidermis, a small absorbed fraction can enter systemic circulation, undergo hepatic ester hydrolysis and oxidative conjugative metabolism, and be excreted mainly in urine with some biliary/fecal elimination. Indications and clinical use are as a sunscreen active in creams, lotions, lip balms, and cosmetic products for prevention of UVB-induced sunburn, photodamage, and photosensitivity exacerbation in disorders such as melasma or lupus-related photosensitivity. Adverse effects are usually local, including irritant or allergic contact dermatitis, stinging, erythema, and rare photoallergy; toxicology highlights aquatic ecotoxicity and possible endocrine activity, with high-dose experimental data suggesting reproductive or developmental concerns, while acute human systemic toxicity at labeled topical exposure is generally low.

Name: Hydroquinone
Description: Hydroquinone (DrugBank DB09526) is a simple aromatic benzenediol composed of a benzene ring bearing two hydroxyl groups in the para 1,4-relationship, giving a small, planar, redox-active phenolic structure; chemically it is classified as a dihydroxybenzene, phenol, and reducing agent, with a para-substituted hydroquinone/benzoquinone redox scaffold that is shared with related compounds such as resorcinol derivatives, catechol analogs, mequinol, arbutin, and the oxidation product p-benzoquinone. Pharmacologically, its best characterized functional targets are melanogenic pathways rather than a single high-affinity receptor, particularly inhibition of tyrosinase and interference with melanosome formation and melanocyte metabolic processes, accounting for its depigmenting activity. After topical administration, percutaneous absorption is limited but increases with concentration, damaged skin, occlusion, or large surface area exposure; absorbed drug distributes locally and systemically, undergoes hepatic and cutaneous phase II metabolism mainly to glucuronide and sulfate conjugates, with some oxidation-reduction cycling to quinone species, and is eliminated predominantly in urine as conjugated metabolites. Hydroquinone is indicated primarily for hyperpigmentary disorders such as melasma, chloasma, solar lentigines, ephelides, and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and is used clinically in topical creams or combination regimens with retinoids and corticosteroids for localized dyschromia. Toxicities include local irritation, irritant or allergic contact dermatitis, erythema, burning, xerosis, and paradoxical ochronosis with prolonged high-dose use, especially in darker skin; excessive exposure can also raise concern for oxidative cytotoxicity, corneal injury, and rare systemic toxicity such as methemoglobin-related effects.

Name: Methyl salicylate
Description: Methyl salicylate (DrugBank DB09543), commonly known as oil of wintergreen, is a small aromatic ester consisting of a salicylic acid core in which the carboxyl group is methyl-esterified while the ortho phenolic hydroxyl is retained, giving a lipophilic o-hydroxybenzoate structure that readily penetrates skin; chemically it belongs to the salicylates and more specifically the hydroxybenzoate ester class, with a salicylate/benzoate aromatic scaffold. Structurally and pharmacologically related drugs include salicylic acid, acetylsalicylic acid, diflunisal, and topical counterirritants such as trolamine salicylate. After topical administration it is absorbed through intact skin, with absorption increasing with heat, occlusion, large treated surface area, damaged skin, or repeated dosing; it distributes systemically after hydrolysis to salicylate, is metabolized mainly in the liver by esterases and subsequent glycine and glucuronide conjugation pathways, and is excreted predominantly in urine, with renal clearance enhanced by alkaline urine. Its principal pharmacologic targets are functionally shared with salicylates, especially cyclooxygenase enzymes PTGS1 and PTGS2, reducing prostaglandin synthesis, although much of its topical effect also reflects counterirritant action. It is indicated for temporary relief of minor muscle and joint pain such as backache, sprains, strains, arthritis, and sports injuries. Common adverse effects are local burning, erythema, irritation, and contact dermatitis, whereas toxicity includes salicylism, metabolic acidosis, tinnitus, vomiting, hyperpnea, CNS dysfunction, and potentially fatal poisoning after excessive topical exposure or ingestion, particularly in children. Clinically it is used mainly in topical creams, gels, liniments, and patches, often combined with menthol or camphor, for short-term symptomatic analgesia in musculoskeletal pain.

Name: Dexchlorpheniramine maleate
Description: Dexchlorpheniramine maleate (DrugBank DB09555) is the maleate salt of dexchlorpheniramine, the dextrorotatory active enantiomer of chlorpheniramine, and is a classic first-generation alkylamine antihistamine built on a propylamine scaffold linking a substituted pyridine ring and a para-chlorophenyl ring to a tertiary dimethylamino side chain; chemically it belongs to the arylalkylamine H1-antihistamines, with a chlorpheniramine-like diarylpropylamine scaffold shared by related agents such as chlorpheniramine, brompheniramine, pheniramine, and triprolidine. Its principal pharmacologic target is the histamine H1 receptor, where it acts as an inverse agonist/antagonist, and it may also show weak antimuscarinic activity that contributes to its adverse-effect profile. After oral administration it is well absorbed, undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, distributes broadly including into the central nervous system, is metabolized mainly by hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes, particularly CYP2D6, to demethylated metabolites, and is eliminated primarily in urine as parent drug and metabolites, with duration of action often exceeding its plasma half-life. It is indicated for symptomatic relief of allergic rhinitis, urticaria, conjunctival itching, pruritus, common cold rhinorrhea, and other histamine-mediated symptoms. Typical clinical use includes oral tablets, syrups, and combination cold-allergy products for hay fever, hives, and allergic skin reactions. Toxicity is characterized chiefly by dose-related CNS depression or paradoxical excitation, anticholinergic effects, and in overdose agitation, hallucinations, seizures, arrhythmias, and respiratory compromise, especially in children and older adults. Common side effects include drowsiness, dizziness, impaired psychomotor performance, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention.

Name: Levmetamfetamine
Description: Levmetamfetamine (DrugBank DB09571) is the levorotatory enantiomer of methamphetamine, a phenethylamine/amphetamine-class sympathomimetic amine characterized structurally by a benzene ring linked through a two-carbon side chain to a chiral alpha-methylated secondary amine, giving an alpha-methylphenethylamine scaffold; chemically it is an arylalkylamine and more specifically a substituted amphetamine built on the phenethylamine core. Its closest analogs include dextromethamphetamine, amphetamine, lisdexamfetamine, phentermine, ephedrine, and pseudoephedrine, which share related sympathomimetic pharmacology to varying degrees. Levmetamfetamine primarily acts indirectly by promoting release of norepinephrine and, less prominently than the dextro isomer, dopamine via interaction with monoamine transporters, especially the norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2 and dopamine transporter SLC6A3, with weaker functional effects at SLC6A4; trace amine-associated receptor 1 is also a plausible mechanistic target in line with the class. Clinically it has been used mainly as an over-the-counter nasal decongestant for temporary relief of nasal congestion associated with common cold, allergic rhinitis, and sinus irritation. Systemic absorption from inhalation is generally limited at recommended use, distribution is expected to favor well-perfused tissues including CNS to a lesser extent than dextromethamphetamine, hepatic CYP2D6-mediated oxidative metabolism contributes to amphetamine-related metabolites, and renal excretion of parent drug and metabolites is enhanced in acidic urine. Toxicity reflects sympathomimetic excess, including hypertension, tachycardia, agitation, insomnia, mydriasis, tremor, and risk of arrhythmia; excessive exposure or misuse may cause CNS stimulation, ischemic events, or psychotoxicity. Adverse effects in routine use include local nasal irritation, rebound congestion with overuse, nervousness, dizziness, and palpitations.

Name: Aluminum chloride
Description: Aluminum chloride (DrugBank DB11081) is a simple inorganic Lewis-acidic aluminum salt composed of a trivalent aluminum center coordinated by three chloride ligands, existing as anhydrous trigonal-planar AlCl3 and, in aqueous or hydrated environments, as hydrolyzed octahedral chloro-aqua complexes; chemically it belongs to the metal halide class, specifically an aluminum salt, and its scaffold is best described as a minimal mononuclear Al(III)-chloride framework rather than an organic pharmacophore. Similar drugs include other topical aluminum salts such as aluminum chlorohydrate, aluminum sesquichlorohydrate, aluminum acetate, and aluminum sulfate, which share astringent or antiperspirant uses. Pharmacokinetically, topical aluminum chloride has limited intact dermal absorption, reacts locally with water and proteins in eccrine ducts to form precipitated proteinaceous-metal plugs, shows minimal systemic distribution under normal use, undergoes no enzymatic metabolism, and any absorbed aluminum is handled as endogenous aluminum burden with predominant renal excretion. Its pharmacologic action is not mediated by a defined receptor target, and no specific canonical target proteins are established; rather, it acts through nonspecific protein precipitation and ductal obstruction, with secondary reduction of sweat output and local antibacterial effects. It is indicated primarily for hyperhidrosis, especially axillary, palmar, plantar, and craniofacial sweating, and is also used to control bromhidrosis. Toxicity is mainly local and concentration dependent, with irritant dermatitis, burning, pruritus, erythema, scaling, and occasional erosions as examples; systemic aluminum toxicity is unlikely with proper topical use but is a theoretical concern with excessive exposure, damaged skin, or renal impairment. Clinically, high-strength topical solutions are applied intermittently, often overnight, for refractory excessive sweating.

Name: Resorcinol
Description: Resorcinol (DrugBank DB11085) is a small aromatic dihydroxybenzene characterized structurally as benzene-1,3-diol, with two hydroxyl groups in the meta position on a simple phenyl ring, placing it in the phenol and benzenediol chemical class and giving it a compact resorcinol scaffold that recurs in medicinal chemistry and dye intermediates. It is chemically and pharmacologically related to other dihydroxybenzenes and topical phenolics such as catechol, hydroquinone, phenol, and sulfur-resorcinol combinations used in dermatology. Its activity is largely local rather than receptor-selective: it acts as a keratolytic, weak antiseptic, and protein-denaturing agent, so no single high-affinity therapeutic target protein is typically emphasized, although nonspecific interactions with keratins and microbial proteins are relevant. After topical administration, absorption is limited through intact skin but increases across damaged, inflamed, or extensively treated skin; once absorbed it distributes systemically, undergoes hepatic phase II conjugation mainly to sulfate and glucuronide metabolites, and is excreted predominantly in urine. Resorcinol is indicated chiefly for hyperkeratotic and inflammatory skin disorders, including acne, seborrheic dermatitis, eczema, psoriasis, corns, calluses, warts, and some dandruff formulations. Clinical use is therefore primarily topical in low-concentration creams, lotions, peels, and compounded preparations, often combined with sulfur for acne or seborrhea. Adverse effects are usually local irritation, burning, erythema, peeling, and allergic dermatitis, whereas excessive exposure can cause systemic toxicity including methemoglobinemia, thyroid dysfunction or goitrogenic effects, CNS symptoms, hemolysis, and renal or hepatic injury, particularly in children or with prolonged application to large body surface areas.

Name: Docusate
Description: Docusate (DrugBank DB11089), commonly used as docusate sodium or calcium, is an anionic surfactant stool softener built on a dioctyl sulfosuccinate structure: a sulfosuccinic acid core bearing two branched 2-ethylhexyl ester chains and a terminal sulfonate salt, giving a strongly amphiphilic architecture that underlies its detergent-like behavior; chemically it is classified as a sulfosuccinate ester and surfactant laxative, with a sulfosuccinate scaffold linked to lipophilic alkyl esters. Closely related or pharmacologically similar agents include other emollient laxatives such as docusate calcium and docusate potassium, and mechanistically adjacent constipation therapies such as mineral oil, glycerin, senna, bisacodyl, lactulose, and polyethylene glycol. Its principal action is local rather than receptor-mediated, lowering stool surface tension to promote water and lipid penetration into fecal material; no specific human target protein is well established. Oral absorption is limited and variable, distribution is therefore minimal systemically, metabolism is incompletely characterized but appears limited with some hepatic biotransformation possible, and elimination occurs mainly in feces with little clinically relevant renal excretion. Docusate is generally low in acute toxicity, but excessive use may cause diarrhea, fluid loss, electrolyte disturbance, and rarely hepatotoxicity or intestinal mucosal injury; chronic coadministration with mineral oil may increase systemic absorption of the oil. It is indicated for constipation, especially when straining should be minimized, such as after myocardial infarction, anorectal surgery, hemorrhoids, or postpartum. Adverse effects include abdominal cramping, diarrhea, nausea, bitter taste, throat irritation with liquid forms, and rare rash; clinically it is used primarily for short-term prevention or treatment of hard stools rather than for severe refractory constipation.

Name: Calcium citrate
Description: Calcium citrate (DrugBank DB11093) is an inorganic-organic calcium salt composed of divalent calcium cations coordinated to citrate, the tricarboxylate anion of citric acid, forming an ionic metal-carboxylate complex in which calcium interacts with multiple carboxylate and hydroxyl oxygen donors; chemically it is classified as a mineral supplement, calcium salt, and citrate salt, with a simple citrate-based polycarboxylate scaffold rather than a classic drug-like heterocyclic framework. It is closely related to other oral calcium replacement agents such as calcium carbonate, calcium acetate, calcium lactate, calcium gluconate, and calcium phosphate, which share the therapeutic goal of calcium repletion but differ in elemental calcium content, solubility, and acid dependence. After oral administration, calcium citrate is relatively well absorbed and is less dependent on gastric acidity than calcium carbonate, making it useful in achlorhydria or proton-pump inhibitor use; absorbed calcium distributes mainly to bone, teeth, and extracellular fluid, is not metabolized in the conventional xenobiotic sense, and is eliminated primarily through feces with smaller urinary losses, while citrate enters normal intermediary metabolism. Its pharmacologic targets are physiologic rather than selective and include calcium-sensing receptor pathways and the broader network of calcium-dependent proteins involved in neuromuscular transmission, bone mineralization, and parathyroid regulation. It is indicated for prevention and treatment of hypocalcemia, calcium deficiency, osteoporosis support, osteopenia, rickets or osteomalacia adjunctive care, and supplementation in pregnancy or postmenopausal states. Adverse effects are usually gastrointestinal, including constipation, bloating, nausea, flatulence, and abdominal discomfort; excessive use may cause hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, nephrolithiasis, milk-alkali syndrome, arrhythmia, or confusion, particularly in renal impairment or with high-dose vitamin D. Clinically, it is widely used as an oral supplement when better tolerability or absorption in low-acid conditions is desired, including in older adults, patients after bariatric surgery, and individuals requiring chronic calcium replacement.

Name: Allantoin
Description: Allantoin (DrugBank DB11100) is a small, highly polar diureide of glyoxylic acid characterized structurally by a substituted imidazolidine-2,4-dione/ureide core bearing carbonyl-rich functionality and strong hydrogen-bonding capacity, placing it within the heterocyclic ureides and oxidation products of uric acid; its principal chemical scaffold is the allantoin hydantoin-like ring system, which is closely related to hydantoin and other cyclic ureides, and it is therefore chemically similar to compounds such as hydantoin, allantoin derivatives used in dermatology, and the anti-irritant/keratoplastic agent aluminum chlorohydroxy allantoinate. Pharmacokinetically, topical allantoin is believed to have minimal systemic absorption through intact skin, with distribution largely confined to the stratum corneum and superficial epidermis; if absorbed, it would be expected to distribute in total body water, undergo little or no significant biotransformation because it is itself an endogenous or naturally occurring metabolite in many species, and be eliminated mainly renally. Its molecular pharmacology is not defined by a single high-affinity canonical target protein, and no well-established human target proteins are typically assigned; instead, its effects are attributed to local moisturizing, desquamation-promoting, barrier-protective, and wound-healing supportive actions. Clinically, it is used as a topical skin protectant in minor cuts, abrasions, burns, chapped skin, xerosis, diaper rash, irritant dermatitis, and in cosmetic or oral formulations for mucosal soothing. Toxicity is generally low, though excessive exposure may cause local irritation, stinging, erythema, rash, or hypersensitivity reactions; systemic toxicity is uncommon due to poor absorption. In practice, allantoin is widely included in creams, ointments, lotions, lip products, shampoos, anti-acne preparations, and oral care products to reduce irritation and promote skin comfort and epithelial recovery.

Name: Magnesium citrate
Description: Magnesium citrate (DrugBank DB11110) is an inorganic-organic magnesium salt complex in which divalent magnesium is coordinated by citrate, the tricarboxylate conjugate base of citric acid, giving a small, highly polar, polycarboxylate chelate structure with a citrate scaffold built on a 2-hydroxypropane-1,2,3-tricarboxylate backbone; chemically it belongs to mineral supplements, saline laxatives, and electrolyte replacement agents. It is structurally and therapeutically similar to other magnesium salts and osmotic cathartics such as magnesium hydroxide, magnesium sulfate, magnesium oxide, sodium phosphate preparations, and polyethylene glycol-based bowel cleansers. Its pharmacokinetics are dominated by partial gastrointestinal absorption of magnesium, which is greater in deficiency states and occurs through passive paracellular uptake and channels including TRPM6/TRPM7; the citrate moiety enters normal intermediary metabolism, while absorbed magnesium distributes mainly to bone, muscle, and extracellular fluid, is not metabolized, and is eliminated renally, so accumulation may occur in renal impairment. Toxicity is chiefly hypermagnesemia, with examples including nausea, flushing, lethargy, hypotension, bradycardia, loss of deep tendon reflexes, respiratory depression, cardiac conduction abnormalities, and in severe overdose cardiac arrest; excessive catharsis can also cause dehydration and electrolyte disturbances. Relevant molecular targets are not classical drug receptors but physiological transport systems and effectors, including TRPM6, TRPM7, and calcium-sensing-related magnesium homeostatic pathways. Clinically, magnesium citrate is indicated for occasional constipation, bowel evacuation before procedures such as colonoscopy, and magnesium replacement in mild deficiency states; common adverse effects include diarrhea, abdominal cramping, bloating, and nausea, and its use is standard as an oral saline laxative and supplement, particularly when rapid bowel emptying is desired.

Name: Undecylenic acid
Description: Undecylenic acid (DrugBank DB11117) is an 11-carbon, terminally unsaturated fatty acid characterized structurally as a medium-chain alkenyl carboxylic acid with a linear hydrocarbon chain, a distal double bond, and a polar carboxylic acid headgroup; chemically it belongs to the class of unsaturated fatty acids and more specifically antifungal fatty-acid derivatives, with a simple monounsaturated aliphatic acid scaffold. It is closely related to other topical antifungal fatty acids and derivatives such as propionic acid, caprylic acid, and zinc undecylenate, the latter often used in similar formulations. Its pharmacologic activity is attributed less to a highly specific receptor interaction than to disruption of fungal cell membrane function and inhibition of morphologic transition in susceptible fungi, especially Candida species; no single validated human target protein is established, although fungal membrane-associated processes and possibly enzymes involved in filamentation and adhesion are functionally affected. Pharmacokinetically, undecylenic acid is used primarily topically, where systemic absorption is limited through intact skin; any absorbed fraction would be expected to distribute like endogenous fatty acids, undergo hepatic and mitochondrial beta-oxidation, and be eliminated largely as carbon dioxide and common fatty-acid metabolites rather than unchanged drug. Toxicity is generally low when used externally but includes local irritation, burning, erythema, dermatitis, and ocular or mucosal irritation; ingestion may cause gastrointestinal irritation. It is indicated for superficial fungal infections such as tinea pedis, tinea cruris, tinea corporis, and some candidal intertriginous eruptions, and clinically it is used in creams, powders, sprays, and solutions to reduce scaling, itching, burning, and recurrence in athlete’s foot and related dermatomycoses.

Name: Benzethonium
Description: Benzethonium (DrugBank DB11125) is a synthetic quaternary ammonium antiseptic whose structure is characterized by a permanently charged benzyldimethylammonium headgroup linked to a bulky lipophilic framework containing aryl and tert-alkyl-substituted ether motifs, giving it the amphiphilic cationic architecture typical of membrane-active surfactants. Chemically, it belongs to the quaternary ammonium compound class, specifically a cationic surfactant/disinfectant, and its core scaffold is best described as a benzyltrialkylammonium pharmacophore embedded in a diaryl ether-like hydrophobic domain; related drugs include benzalkonium chloride, cetylpyridinium chloride, cetrimonium, dequalinium, and other topical cationic antiseptics. Its pharmacological activity is largely nonspecific rather than receptor-selective: it interacts with microbial cell envelopes, causing membrane disruption, leakage of intracellular contents, protein denaturation, and loss of osmotic integrity; no single validated human target protein is central to its action, though membrane phospholipids and microbial envelope components are the functional targets. Pharmacokinetically, systemic use is not intended: dermal or mucosal absorption is generally low when used topically, distribution is therefore limited, metabolism is poorly characterized, and any absorbed fraction is expected to undergo limited biotransformation with biliary or renal elimination, but robust human ADME datasets are sparse. Benzethonium is indicated for topical antisepsis and preservation, for example in minor wound cleansers, first-aid preparations, skin disinfectants, and some oral or personal-care products. Toxicity includes local irritation, corrosive injury at high concentrations, ocular damage, and gastrointestinal toxicity if ingested, with poisoning potentially causing nausea, vomiting, mucosal burns, CNS depression, or respiratory compromise. Adverse effects in clinical use are mainly burning, stinging, erythema, contact dermatitis, and hypersensitivity reactions, and its practical clinical role is limited to external antimicrobial cleansing and prevention of superficial infection rather than systemic anti-infective therapy.

Name: Calcium gluconate
Description: Calcium gluconate (DrugBank DB11126) is an inorganic-organic calcium salt composed of a divalent calcium cation coordinated by two gluconate anions, each derived from the oxidation of glucose to an aldonic acid and characterized by a linear six-carbon polyhydroxycarboxylate framework rich in hydroxyl groups that confer high aqueous solubility; chemically it belongs to the mineral supplements and electrolyte replacement agents, with a simple calcium–carboxylate scaffold based on the gluconate sugar-acid backbone rather than a complex heterocycle or lipophilic pharmacophore. Similar drugs include calcium chloride, calcium carbonate, calcium citrate, and calcium lactate, which differ mainly in calcium content, ionization, tolerability, and route-dependent utility. Its pharmacokinetics depend strongly on route: oral calcium is variably absorbed in the small intestine by vitamin D-dependent active transport and passive diffusion, distributed largely to extracellular fluid and bone, not metabolized in the conventional xenobiotic sense because gluconate enters normal carbohydrate metabolism, and eliminated primarily via feces with smaller renal losses of calcium; intravenous administration provides immediate bioavailable ionized calcium. Pharmacologically, it acts mainly by restoring extracellular calcium concentrations rather than through a classic receptor, though physiologic effects involve calcium-sensing receptor signaling and calcium-dependent ion channels in myocardium, nerve, and muscle. It is indicated for acute symptomatic hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia with membrane instability, hypermagnesemia, calcium channel blocker overdose, and local treatment of hydrofluoric acid burns. Toxicity includes hypercalcemia, milk-alkali syndrome, arrhythmias, bradycardia, vasodilation, nausea, constipation, and tissue necrosis with extravasation; adverse effects include flushing, injection-site pain, hypotension, and rebound electrolyte disturbances. Clinically, it is used orally for calcium supplementation and intravenously in emergency medicine for ECG changes from hyperkalemia, tetany, severe hypocalcemia, and selected toxicologic emergencies.

Name: Silicon dioxide
Description: Silicon dioxide (DrugBank DB11132) is an inorganic oxide of silicon composed of an extended three-dimensional network of tetrahedral silicon atoms each covalently bound to oxygen atoms, most commonly represented as a polymeric SiO2 lattice that may occur in amorphous, colloidal, hydrated, or crystalline forms; chemically it belongs to the mineral oxide and silica class, and its core scaffold is best described as a cross-linked siloxane/quartz-like framework rather than a discrete small-molecule pharmacophore. Similar pharmaceutical excipients and functionally related materials include colloidal silicon dioxide, silicic acid derivatives, talc, kaolin, magnesium trisilicate, and other adsorbent or glidant mineral excipients. Pharmacokinetically, silicon dioxide is essentially pharmacologically inert when used orally or topically: gastrointestinal absorption is negligible for particulate forms, systemic distribution is minimal, it is not metabolized by human enzymes, and any small absorbed soluble silica fraction is handled as silicic acid and excreted mainly in urine, while unabsorbed material is eliminated in feces. It has no established therapeutic target proteins and acts primarily through physicochemical excipient functions such as flow promotion, anti-caking, adsorption, and tablet stabilization. Toxicity is formulation- and route-dependent: oral excipient exposure is generally low risk, but chronic inhalation of respirable crystalline silica is associated with pulmonary inflammation, fibrosis, silicosis, and increased lung cancer risk; irritation of eyes, skin, and airways can also occur. Its main indication is not as an active drug but as a pharmaceutical aid in tablets, capsules, powders, topical products, and some medical or nutritional preparations, with adverse effects in routine clinical use being uncommon aside from local irritation or hypersensitivity-like intolerance in susceptible individuals.

Name: Butamben
Description: Butamben (DrugBank DB11148) is a benzoate ester local anesthetic structurally characterized as the butyl ester of p-aminobenzoic acid, containing a para-amino-substituted aromatic ring linked through an ester bond to a straight-chain butyl group; chemically it belongs to the amino ester class of local anesthetics, and its core scaffold is the p-aminobenzoate or aniline-benzoate ester motif shared with related agents. Similar drugs include benzocaine, procaine, tetracaine, chloroprocaine, and proparacaine, which retain the same aromatic amino ester pharmacophore but differ in lipophilic substituents and duration of action. Pharmacologically, butamben acts primarily by reversible blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels in peripheral neuronal membranes, especially Nav channel isoforms such as SCN9A, SCN10A, and SCN11A, thereby preventing action potential initiation and conduction. It is used as a topical or mucosal anesthetic for relief of pain and irritation in conditions involving the oropharynx, skin, anorectal region, or superficial wounds and ulcers, and has also been used in some otic and hemorrhoidal preparations. Absorption is limited after topical use but increases on damaged or highly vascular mucosa; distribution is mainly local, with systemic exposure generally low. Like other ester anesthetics, it is expected to undergo hydrolysis by plasma and tissue esterases to p-aminobenzoic acid derivatives and butanol, with metabolites excreted renally. Toxicity is usually related to excessive systemic absorption or hypersensitivity, with examples including CNS excitation or depression, cardiovascular toxicity, and allergic reactions linked to PABA formation; methemoglobinemia is less prominent than with some topical anesthetics but remains a theoretical risk. Common adverse effects include local burning, stinging, contact dermatitis, rash, edema, and rare anaphylactoid reactions.
