Clinically, butamben is mainly employed for short-term symptomatic topical anesthesia rather than prolonged procedural anesthesia, particularly where low aqueous solubility and prolonged surface residence are advantageous.

Name: Pyrantel
Description: Pyrantel (DrugBank DB11156) is a tetrahydropyrimidine anthelmintic structurally characterized by a partially saturated six-membered dihydropyrimidine/tetrahydropyrimidine ring linked through a vinyl bridge to a 2-thiophene moiety, typically formulated clinically as the pamoate salt; chemically it belongs to the nicotinic agonist class of antiparasitic agents and is built on a heteroaromatic thiophene–tetrahydropyrimidine scaffold. Closely related or mechanistically similar drugs include morantel, oxantel, levamisole, and the macrocyclic lactone ivermectin as a broader comparator in nematode therapy. Pyrantel acts primarily at parasite nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subtypes on somatic muscle, producing persistent depolarization, spastic paralysis, and expulsion of susceptible helminths; specific molecular targets are parasite nicotinic acetylcholine receptor channel complexes, with acetylcholinesterase having at most a minor or indirect role. It is indicated for intestinal nematode infections such as enterobiasis due to Enterobius vermicularis, ascariasis due to Ascaris lumbricoides, and hookworm infection caused by Ancylostoma duodenale or Necator americanus. Pharmacokinetically, oral pyrantel pamoate is poorly absorbed, remains largely within the intestinal lumen where it exerts local activity, undergoes limited hepatic metabolism of the absorbed fraction, and is eliminated mainly unchanged in feces with a small urinary component. Toxicity is generally low because systemic exposure is minimal, but overdose or increased absorption may cause cholinergic or neuromuscular symptoms, gastrointestinal irritation, transient aminotransferase elevations, and rarely hepatotoxicity. Common adverse effects include nausea, abdominal cramps, diarrhea, vomiting, headache, dizziness, drowsiness, and rash. Clinically, it is widely used as a single-dose or short-course oral deworming agent in community treatment, household pinworm eradication, and routine management of uncomplicated luminal nematode infections.

Name: Phenyltoloxamine
Description: Phenyltoloxamine (DrugBank DB11160) is a first-generation ethanolamine antihistamine whose structure consists of a diaryl-substituted ether built on a 2-dimethylaminoethyl side chain, typically described as a benzhydryl/aryloxyethylamine arrangement in which lipophilic aromatic rings are linked through an ether oxygen to a tertiary aminoethyl moiety; chemically it belongs to the ethanolamine H1-antihistamine class, with an aryloxyalkyl tertiary amine scaffold closely related to other sedating antihistamines such as diphenhydramine, doxylamine, carbinoxamine, and clemastine. Its principal pharmacologic target is the histamine H1 receptor, where it acts as an inverse agonist/antagonist, and like related agents it may also show clinically relevant antimuscarinic activity. Phenyltoloxamine has been used for symptomatic relief of allergic conditions such as allergic rhinitis, urticaria, pruritus, and other histamine-mediated upper respiratory symptoms, and historically also as an adjunct in analgesic combination products to enhance perceived sedation or comfort. After oral administration it is expected to be reasonably well absorbed, distributed widely including into the central nervous system because of high lipophilicity, metabolized hepatically by oxidative N-dealkylation and related biotransformations, and excreted primarily as metabolites in urine. Toxicity resembles that of other first-generation antihistamines: dose-related CNS depression, psychomotor impairment, and anticholinergic toxicity including dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention, with overdose potentially causing agitation, delirium, seizures, arrhythmias, or coma. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, fatigue, impaired concentration, and paradoxical excitation in children. Clinically, it has mainly been used as an older sedating antiallergic agent and in some combination cough, cold, or pain products.

Name: Homatropine
Description: Homatropine (DrugBank DB11181) is a semisynthetic tropane alkaloid derivative formed as the ester of tropine with mandelic acid, giving a bicyclic 8-azabicyclo[3.2.1]octane tropane core bearing a tertiary alcohol/tertiary amine framework and an aromatic alpha-hydroxy acid ester substituent; chemically it is classified as an antimuscarinic parasympatholytic mydriatic and belongs to the atropine-like belladonna alkaloid family, with a tropane ester scaffold closely related to atropine, scopolamine, and other muscarinic antagonists such as cyclopentolate and tropicamide. Its principal pharmacologic targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially M3 receptors in the iris sphincter and ciliary muscle, with broader antagonism at M1-M5 subtypes accounting for systemic effects. After topical ophthalmic administration, homatropine is absorbed through the cornea and conjunctiva with some systemic absorption via ocular tissues and nasolacrimal drainage; distribution is primarily local to the anterior chamber, while systemically absorbed drug is expected to distribute similarly to other tertiary amine anticholinergics, undergo partial hepatic ester hydrolysis and other metabolism, and be eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites and unchanged drug. Toxicity reflects dose-dependent anticholinergic excess, including mydriasis, cycloplegia, tachycardia, urinary retention, hyperthermia, agitation, hallucinations, and CNS toxicity, with children and older adults particularly susceptible and acute overdose potentially producing an atropine-like toxidrome. It is indicated mainly for diagnostic or therapeutic mydriasis and cycloplegia and for relief of pain and prevention of synechiae in anterior uveitis or iridocyclitis. Common adverse effects include transient stinging, photophobia, blurred vision, increased intraocular pressure, dry mouth, flushing, and tachycardia. Clinically, it is used as ophthalmic drops to facilitate refraction, funduscopic examination, and management of inflammatory eye disease.

Name: Pentoxyverine
Description: Pentoxyverine (DrugBank DB11186), also known as carbetapentane, is a centrally acting antitussive built around a tertiary aminoether structure in which a substituted piperidine ring is linked through an aliphatic chain to a bulky diaryl/carbinol-derived ether motif, placing it within the synthetic non-opioid cough suppressant class and more specifically among piperidine-containing aminoether antitussives; its core scaffold is therefore a lipophilic aryl-alkyl-piperidine framework related in broad medicinal-chemistry terms to other centrally acting antitussives and antihistamine-like agents. Similar drugs include dextromethorphan, cloperastine, benproperine, levodropropizine, and older opioid antitussives such as codeine, although pentoxyverine is structurally distinct from morphinans and phenanthrenes. Its principal pharmacology is suppression of the cough center in the medulla, with no single definitively established high-affinity molecular target in routine references; reported or inferred target space includes central neural pathways involved in cough reflex modulation and possible weak anticholinergic activity rather than a well-validated receptor-selective mechanism. After oral administration it is absorbed adequately, distributes into tissues including the CNS because of its lipophilicity, undergoes hepatic biotransformation, and is eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites with limited unchanged drug excretion. It is indicated for symptomatic relief of nonproductive cough in conditions such as acute viral upper respiratory infection, tracheobronchitis, and irritative cough. Adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, nausea, dry mouth, and occasionally constipation or blurred vision; toxicity is generally characterized by CNS depression, confusion, anticholinergic symptoms, and in overdose agitation or respiratory compromise, so clinical use is typically short-term symptomatic cough suppression in adults and, depending on local labeling, selected pediatric patients.

Name: Dioxybenzone
Description: Dioxybenzone (DrugBank DB11221) is a benzophenone ultraviolet filter characterized structurally by a diaryl ketone core in which two substituted phenyl rings are linked through a central carbonyl, with hydroxyl and methoxy substituents that create a conjugated aromatic chromophore capable of absorbing primarily UVB and part of the UVA spectrum; chemically it belongs to the benzophenone class of sunscreen agents and is built on the classic benzophenone scaffold. Similar drugs include other organic UV filters, especially oxybenzone, sulisobenzone, avobenzone, octinoxate, and homosalate, which share lipophilic aromatic frameworks and photoprotective use. Its pharmacokinetics are mainly relevant after topical administration: dermal absorption is generally limited but measurable, enhanced by damaged skin, repeated application, occlusion, or large body-surface exposure; once absorbed it distributes systemically at low concentrations, undergoes hepatic phase I oxidation and phase II conjugation such as glucuronidation and sulfation, and is excreted predominantly in urine with minor fecal elimination. Dioxybenzone is used as a sunscreen active to prevent sunburn and reduce UV-induced photodamage in settings such as routine sun exposure and photosensitivity disorders. It has no well-established therapeutic protein target in the conventional receptor or enzyme sense, acting instead by photon absorption and dissipation. Toxicity is usually low at approved topical exposures but may include local irritation, stinging, allergic or photoallergic contact dermatitis, and rarely systemic safety concerns typical of benzophenone filters, including endocrine-signaling activity in experimental systems. Clinical use is topical, commonly in sunscreens and protective skin products, often in combination formulations to broaden spectral coverage.

Name: Zinc gluconate
Description: Zinc gluconate (DrugBank DB11248) is an orally and topically used zinc salt consisting of a divalent zinc cation coordinated by gluconate anions derived from gluconic acid, a linear polyhydroxycarboxylate generated by oxidation of glucose; structurally it is best viewed as an inorganic-organic coordination complex in which Zn2+ is chelated by oxygen donors from carboxylate and hydroxyl groups, placing it in the trace-element mineral supplement class with a simple zinc-carboxylate scaffold. Similar drugs include other zinc salts such as zinc sulfate, zinc acetate, and zinc picolinate, as well as nutritionally related mineral preparations. Pharmacologically, zinc gluconate dissociates in the gastrointestinal tract to provide absorbable zinc, with uptake primarily in the small intestine via transporters including SLC39A4/ZIP4 and cellular handling by metallothioneins and efflux transporter SLC30A1/ZnT1; distribution is broad, with high binding in plasma to albumin and accumulation in muscle, bone, liver, and other tissues, while it is not metabolized in the classic sense because zinc is an elemental ion, and elimination occurs mainly through feces with smaller losses in urine, sweat, and desquamation. Its relevant biological targets are therefore zinc transport and binding systems, including ZIP4, ZnT1, metallothioneins, and numerous zinc-dependent enzymes and transcription factors. Clinically it is indicated for prevention and treatment of zinc deficiency, including malnutrition, malabsorption, chronic diarrhea, acrodermatitis enteropathica, and supplementation during increased demand, and it has also been used in cold lozenges and wound-support settings. Adverse effects are usually gastrointestinal, including nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, dyspepsia, diarrhea, and metallic taste; excessive or chronic exposure can cause copper deficiency, anemia, neutropenia, reduced HDL, and, in overdose, significant GI irritation.

Name: Levomefolic acid
Description: Levomefolic acid (L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate; DrugBank DB11256) is the biologically active, reduced, C5-methylated folate stereoisomer, structurally characterized by a pteridine-like heterobicyclic folate headgroup linked through p-aminobenzoate to a glutamate residue, with a tetrahydrofolate core that carries a one-carbon methyl substituent; chemically it belongs to the folate/vitamin B9 class, specifically a reduced folate cofactor, and its scaffold is the classical pteroylglutamate antifolate/folate framework in a reduced methyl-donating form. Closely related agents include folic acid, folinic acid (leucovorin), levoleucovorin, methotrexate, and pemetrexed, although the latter two are antifolates rather than vitamin replacement forms. Pharmacokinetically, levomefolic acid is orally absorbed in the proximal small intestine via folate transport systems including SLC19A1/RFC1, PCFT/SLC46A1, and folate receptors such as FOLR1; it distributes widely to liver, plasma, and tissues, crosses the placenta and blood-brain barrier to a limited but clinically relevant extent, enters one-carbon metabolism without requiring MTHFR reduction, is converted intracellularly to polyglutamated folate cofactors, and is eliminated mainly by renal excretion with some biliary/enterohepatic contribution. Its principal biochemical targets are indirect folate-dependent enzymes, notably methionine synthase (MTR) in concert with MTRR, supporting homocysteine remethylation and nucleotide biosynthesis. Toxicity is generally low, but excessive folate can mask vitamin B12 deficiency and permit progression of neurologic injury; adverse effects are uncommon and usually mild, including gastrointestinal upset, nausea, abdominal discomfort, irritability, insomnia, rash, pruritus, and rare hypersensitivity. Clinically, it is used for folate deficiency states, hyperhomocysteinemia, megaloblastic anemia due to folate deficiency, prenatal supplementation to reduce neural tube defect risk, and as adjunctive therapy in depression, particularly in patients with impaired folate metabolism or SSRI/SNRI partial response.

Name: Dihydroergocornine
Description: Dihydroergocornine (DB11273) is a semisynthetic hydrogenated ergot alkaloid derived from ergot peptide alkaloids, characterized structurally by a rigid tetracyclic ergoline nucleus with an indole-containing lysergic acid-like core in which hydrogenation of the 9,10 double bond yields the dihydroergot framework, amide-linked to a tripeptide-derived moiety that confers high receptor affinity and prolonged vascular activity; it is therefore classified as an ergopeptide ergot alkaloid, with an ergoline scaffold as its defining chemical core. It is closely related to other dihydrogenated ergot derivatives such as dihydroergotamine, dihydroergocristine, dihydroergocryptine, and the mixture dihydroergotoxine/ergoloid mesylates. Pharmacologically, it interacts with alpha-adrenergic receptors and several serotonin and dopamine receptor subtypes, with reported targets including ADRA1, ADRA2, HTR1-family receptors, HTR2 receptors, and dopamine D2-like receptors, producing complex partial agonist/antagonist vasomotor and neuroregulatory effects. Oral absorption is variable and limited by first-pass metabolism; distribution is extensive with substantial tissue binding, metabolism occurs predominantly in the liver via oxidative biotransformation, and elimination is mainly biliary/fecal with lesser renal excretion. Toxicity resembles that of other ergot derivatives and includes dose-related vasospasm, peripheral ischemia, hypertension or paradoxical hypotension, bradycardia, and in overdose ergotism with severe ischemic complications. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, vomiting, dizziness, headache, flushing, nasal congestion, and orthostatic symptoms. Clinically it has been used mainly as a component of ergoloid preparations for cerebrovascular insufficiency, age-related cognitive and behavioral symptoms, and sometimes vascular headache or peripheral circulatory disorders, although such uses are historically variable and often limited by modest efficacy and ergot-related safety concerns.

Name: Epicriptine
Description: Epicriptine (DB11275) is an ergot-derived semisynthetic dopamine agonist whose structure is characterized by the rigid tetracyclic ergoline nucleus with an indole-like bicyclic system, multiple fused rings, and peptide-like amide substitution typical of bromocriptine-related ergot alkaloids; chemically it is classified as an ergoline/ergot alkaloid derivative, and its core scaffold is the lysergic acid–based ergoline framework. It is therefore closely related to bromocriptine, cabergoline, pergolide, lisuride, and other dopaminergic ergot agents. Its principal pharmacology is expected to involve dopamine D2 receptor agonism, with possible interactions at D1-family dopamine receptors and serotonergic and adrenergic GPCRs that are commonly engaged by ergot derivatives; prolactin-regulating pituitary lactotroph pathways are a key functional target context. After oral administration, drugs of this class are generally variably but often incompletely absorbed, undergo extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism, display high protein binding and broad tissue distribution, and are eliminated predominantly via biliary/fecal excretion with limited renal clearance; CYP-mediated oxidative biotransformation is typical. Toxicity is consistent with ergot dopaminergic agents and may include nausea, vomiting, orthostatic hypotension, headache, hallucinations, confusion, vasospasm, digital ischemia, and, with prolonged exposure in some agents, pleuropulmonary, retroperitoneal, or valvular fibrotic complications. Clinically, epicriptine has been associated with use as a prolactin-lowering dopaminergic agent for hyperprolactinemia, galactorrhea, amenorrhea, prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas, and sometimes Parkinsonian symptoms or acromegaly-related endocrine control, with adverse effects such as dizziness, constipation, nasal congestion, fatigue, and syncope reflecting its central dopaminergic and peripheral vasoactive actions.

Name: Methscopolamine
Description: Methscopolamine (DrugBank DB11315) is a quaternary ammonium antimuscarinic derived from the tropane alkaloid scopolamine, structurally characterized by a rigid 8-azabicyclo[3.2.1]octane tropane core bearing the scopic acid ester and a permanently charged methylated nitrogen, which makes it a polar semisynthetic belladonna-type ester with limited membrane permeability; thus, its chemical category is a quaternary ammonium anticholinergic/antispasmodic, and its core scaffold is the substituted tropane ester scaffold shared with related muscarinic antagonists. Similar drugs include scopolamine, atropine, hyoscyamine, glycopyrrolate, propantheline, and ipratropium, all of which reduce parasympathetic cholinergic signaling to varying extents. Its principal targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially peripheral M1, M2, and M3 receptor subtypes, where it acts as a competitive antagonist to decrease gastrointestinal motility, secretions, and smooth-muscle spasm. Pharmacokinetically, methscopolamine is incompletely and variably absorbed orally, distributes mainly to peripheral tissues with poor blood-brain barrier penetration because of its permanent positive charge, undergoes limited hepatic biotransformation relative to tertiary amines, and is eliminated predominantly by renal excretion of unchanged drug and metabolites. It has been used as an adjunct in peptic ulcer disease and for symptomatic treatment of gastrointestinal hypermotility, abdominal cramping, irritable bowel symptoms, and excessive secretions. Adverse effects and toxicity are typical of antimuscarinics and include dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, tachycardia, urinary retention, decreased sweating, and mydriasis; overdose may produce severe ileus, hyperthermia, precipitated angle-closure glaucoma, and pronounced urinary obstruction, although central toxicity is less prominent than with scopolamine.

Name: Tetradecyl hydrogen sulfate (ester)
Description: Tetradecyl hydrogen sulfate (ester) (DrugBank DB11328) is a long-chain alkyl sulfate consisting of a linear tetradecyl (myristyl) C14 hydrocarbon tail linked through an oxygen atom to a sulfate monoester headgroup, giving an amphiphilic surfactant architecture with a hydrophobic alkyl chain and a strongly acidic, anionic sulfate moiety when ionized; chemically it belongs to the alkyl sulfuric acid ester or anionic detergent class, and its core scaffold is the simple fatty alcohol sulfate scaffold shared by related surfactants such as sodium lauryl sulfate, sodium myristyl sulfate, cetyl sulfate, and other sulfated fatty alcohol derivatives. As a detergent-like excipient rather than a classical receptor-directed therapeutic, it has no well-established selective human target proteins in DrugBank-style annotation, and its biological effects are largely mediated by nonspecific interactions with membrane lipids and proteins, causing surface activity, protein denaturation, and barrier disruption at sufficient concentrations. Pharmacokinetic data in humans are limited; systemic absorption is expected to be low after topical or local exposure, distribution would be minimal unless significant absorption occurs, metabolism may involve hydrolytic conversion to tetradecanol and inorganic sulfate or oxidative fatty-chain biotransformation, and excretion would likely occur via urinary sulfate and lipid metabolite pathways. Toxicity is primarily irritant, with concentration-dependent skin, eye, and mucosal injury, hemolysis, and gastrointestinal irritation if ingested; adverse effects therefore include erythema, burning, dryness, contact dermatitis, ocular irritation, and local inflammation. It has no widely recognized standalone therapeutic indication, but alkyl sulfate surfactants are used clinically or pharmaceutically as formulation excipients, cleansing agents, and penetration-enhancing or sclerosing-type local agents in specialized preparations rather than as standard systemic drugs.

Name: Calcium Phosphate
Description: Calcium phosphate (DB11348) is an inorganic calcium salt composed of calcium cations coordinated to orthophosphate anions in ionic, polymeric crystal lattices that may occur in monobasic, dibasic, tribasic, or hydroxyapatite-like forms; chemically it belongs to the mineral electrolyte and phosphate salt class, and its core scaffold is best described as a simple ionic calcium–phosphate framework rather than an organic covalent skeleton. Closely related agents include calcium carbonate, calcium citrate, calcium acetate, calcium gluconate, and phosphate replacement products such as potassium phosphate, as well as the physiologic mineral analog hydroxyapatite. Pharmacokinetically, oral calcium phosphate dissociates partially in the gastrointestinal tract, with calcium absorption occurring mainly in the small intestine through vitamin D-dependent transcellular transport and passive paracellular flux, while phosphate is absorbed efficiently in the intestine via sodium-phosphate cotransport; distribution is predominantly to extracellular fluid and bone, where both ions are incorporated into skeletal mineral, it is not metabolized in the conventional hepatic sense, and excess calcium and phosphate are eliminated largely through feces and, to a variable degree depending on renal function and endocrine status, through urine. Toxicity is principally related to excessive calcium or phosphate load, causing hypercalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, constipation, soft-tissue or vascular calcification, and in severe cases renal impairment or arrhythmia, especially in patients with chronic kidney disease. It has no classic drug-specific protein target, but its biologic handling involves TRPV6, calbindin, PMCA1, SLC34 family phosphate transporters, the calcium-sensing receptor, parathyroid hormone signaling, and vitamin D receptor-regulated pathways. Clinically, it is used as a calcium and phosphate supplement in deficiency states, osteomalacia, rickets, hypocalcemia prevention, osteoporosis support, and in some formulations as a biomaterial or dental/bone graft adjunct; common adverse effects include bloating, constipation, nausea, and, with overuse, hypercalcemic symptoms such as weakness, polyuria, and confusion.

Name: Guaiacol
Description: Guaiacol (DrugBank DB11359) is a small aromatic phenolic ether structurally defined as o-methoxyphenol, consisting of a benzene ring bearing adjacent methoxy and hydroxyl substituents, which confers moderate lipophilicity, weak acidity, hydrogen-bonding capacity, and characteristic phenolic reactivity; it belongs to the methoxyphenol/alkoxyphenol class of simple phenylpropanoid-related natural product derivatives, and its core scaffold is a substituted anisole-phenol, specifically a guaiacyl aromatic nucleus found in lignin-derived compounds. Similar drugs and congeners include creosote constituents and related expectorant or phenolic agents such as guaifenesin, eugenol, vanillin, catechol derivatives, and historically creosote-based preparations. Pharmacokinetically, guaiacol is absorbed through the gastrointestinal tract and also across mucosal surfaces, distributes broadly into well-perfused tissues, undergoes extensive hepatic phase I oxidation and O-demethylation followed by phase II glucuronidation and sulfation, and is excreted mainly in urine as conjugated metabolites with limited unchanged parent compound. Toxicity is typical of phenolics: local irritation to skin and mucosa, gastrointestinal burning, nausea, vomiting, CNS depression at high exposure, methemoglobinemia or hemolytic risk in severe poisoning, and hepatic or renal stress with excessive dosing. No single highly specific therapeutic protein target is firmly established; reported pharmacology involves nonspecific modulation of airway secretions, weak antiseptic activity, and possible interactions with oxidative enzymes and sensory pathways rather than a validated receptor target set. Clinically, guaiacol has been used as an expectorant and respiratory symptom reliever in bronchitis, productive cough, upper respiratory catarrh, and throat irritation, with adverse effects including gastric upset, dizziness, sweating, rash, and mucosal irritation; current use is largely historical or as a precursor/intermediate for guaifenesin and other guaiacol-derived medicinal products.

Name: Dichlorophen
Description: Dichlorophen (DrugBank DB11396) is a halogenated bisphenolic aromatic compound characterized structurally by two phenyl rings linked through a methylene bridge and bearing phenolic hydroxyl groups together with chlorine substituents, giving a lipophilic, weakly acidic disinfectant/anthelmintic profile; chemically it belongs to the chlorinated phenols, more specifically the bisphenol antiseptic/antiparasitic class, and its core scaffold is a diarylmethane bisphenol scaffold related to other halogenated phenolic antiparasitics and antiseptics. Similar drugs include niclosamide, bithionol, hexachlorophene, and related chlorinated or halogenated salicylanilide/bisphenolic agents that share membrane-disruptive or parasite-toxic properties. Its pharmacokinetics are incompletely characterized in modern sources, but after oral administration it is expected to be variably absorbed because of high lipophilicity, distributed preferentially into lipid-rich tissues, extensively protein bound, metabolized mainly by hepatic conjugation of phenolic groups such as glucuronidation and sulfation, and eliminated largely via biliary/fecal excretion with some urinary conjugates. Toxicity is consistent with chlorinated phenols and includes gastrointestinal irritation, CNS depression or neurotoxicity at excessive doses, hepatotoxicity, and local irritant effects; overdose examples include vomiting, diarrhea, weakness, and possible liver injury. No single highly validated human target protein is established; its antiparasitic action is generally attributed to nonspecific disruption of parasite energy metabolism and membrane function rather than selective receptor pharmacology. Clinically, dichlorophen has been used as a veterinary and older human anthelmintic, especially against cestode infections such as Dipylidium caninum or Taenia species and occasionally Fasciola-associated helminth disease, with side effects including nausea, abdominal cramping, diarrhea, anorexia, and lethargy; its practical use has been largely historical or veterinary rather than contemporary first-line therapy.

Name: Moxidectin
Description: Moxidectin (DrugBank DB11431) is a semisynthetic milbemycin macrocyclic lactone endectocide characterized by a large 16-membered highly lipophilic macrolactone ring bearing multiple fused ether/olefinated substituents and a distinctive methoxime side chain, placing it in the macrocyclic lactone antiparasitic class and more specifically the milbemycin/avermectin-related scaffold family. Its closest analogs are other macrocyclic lactones such as ivermectin, abamectin, doramectin, eprinomectin, selamectin, and milbemycin oxime, which share nematocidal and insecticidal pharmacology. The principal pharmacologic targets are parasite glutamate-gated chloride channels, with additional activity at ligand-gated chloride channels including GABA-related channels in invertebrates, causing hyperpolarization, paralysis, and death of susceptible helminths and ectoparasites. Pharmacokinetically, moxidectin is orally bioavailable, slowly absorbed, extensively distributed into adipose and other tissues because of marked lipophilicity, highly protein bound, only limitedly metabolized compared with some related agents, and eliminated predominantly via biliary/fecal excretion with a long terminal half-life that supports prolonged antiparasitic activity. It is indicated for parasitic infections such as onchocerciasis in humans and, in veterinary medicine, heartworm prevention and treatment of gastrointestinal nematodes, mites, lice, and mange. Adverse effects include pruritus, rash, headache, dizziness, nausea, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, fever, myalgia, cough, and edema; reactions may reflect parasite killing, as in Mazzotti-type inflammatory responses. Toxicity is generally related to neurotoxicity at excessive exposure, with ataxia, lethargy, tremor, and coma possible, especially when blood-brain barrier protection is impaired, as in P-glycoprotein-deficient animals. Clinically, it is used as a long-acting antiparasitic agent in oral, topical, and injectable formulations for sustained control of nematode and ectoparasite burdens.

Name: Butacaine
Description: Butacaine (DrugBank DB11502) is an ester-type local anesthetic characterized structurally as a para-aminobenzoic acid derivative in which the aromatic p-aminobenzoate pharmacophore is linked through an ester bond to a lipophilic tertiary aminoalcohol moiety, giving the typical amphiphilic architecture required for membrane penetration and reversible sodium channel blockade; chemically it belongs to the amino ester local anesthetic class, and its core scaffold is the PABA ester scaffold shared with several early topical anesthetics. Closely related drugs include benzocaine, procaine, tetracaine, chloroprocaine, and butamben, which share the same general aryl ester anesthetic motif but differ in lipophilicity, duration, and route suitability. Its principal pharmacologic target is the voltage-gated sodium channel family, especially neuronal sodium channels responsible for impulse initiation and conduction, although historical compounds of this class were not highly subtype-selective. Butacaine has primarily topical or local anesthetic use for transient relief of pain on mucous membranes or superficial tissues, for example in minor procedures involving the oral cavity, throat, or other accessible surfaces. As with other ester anesthetics, systemic absorption depends on formulation, dose, tissue vascularity, and mucosal integrity; once absorbed it distributes into well-perfused tissues, undergoes rapid esterase-mediated hydrolysis in plasma and tissues to para-aminobenzoic acid-related metabolites, and is then excreted mainly in urine. Toxicity is dominated by excessive sodium channel blockade and hypersensitivity: CNS excitation or depression, dizziness, tremor, seizures, cardiovascular depression or arrhythmias, and allergic reactions including rash or contact dermatitis may occur, with ester-derived PABA metabolites increasing allergy risk. Clinically, it has been used as a short-acting surface anesthetic when localized analgesia is desired without deep tissue anesthesia.

Name: Lesinurad
Description: Lesinurad (DrugBank DB11560) is a small-molecule uricosuric agent built on a substituted triazolyl-containing aromatic scaffold, featuring a chlorinated phenyl ring linked to a 1,2,4-triazole/azole-like heteroaromatic system and a thioacetic acid-derived acidic terminus that supports anionic character at physiological pH; chemically it is classified as a heteroaryl carboxylic acid and can be viewed within the broader biaryl/heteroaryl urate transport inhibitor class. Its scaffold and mechanism make it similar to other urate-lowering drugs that modulate renal urate handling, especially probenecid and benzbromarone, although it is more selectively developed for transporter inhibition; xanthine oxidase inhibitors such as allopurinol and febuxostat are clinically related comparators rather than close structural analogues. Lesinurad primarily targets the renal urate reabsorption transporter SLC22A12/URAT1 and also inhibits SLC2A9/GLUT9 and OAT4 to varying degrees, thereby increasing urinary uric acid excretion. It is orally absorbed, reaches peak concentrations within a few hours, is highly protein bound, undergoes predominant hepatic oxidative metabolism mainly via CYP2C9, and is eliminated through both renal and fecal routes with parent drug and metabolites recovered in urine. Its main indication has been treatment of hyperuricemia associated with gout, particularly in patients inadequately controlled on a xanthine oxidase inhibitor alone, and it was used clinically in combination with allopurinol or febuxostat rather than as monotherapy. Important adverse effects include headache, influenza-like illness, gastroesophageal reflux, and elevated creatinine, while major toxicities include nephrotoxicity, acute renal failure risk, nephrolithiasis, and greater cardiovascular safety concern in some studies, especially with higher doses or monotherapy.

Name: Grazoprevir
Description: Grazoprevir (DB11575) is a second-generation, direct-acting hepatitis C antiviral whose structure is a conformationally constrained, macrocyclic peptidomimetic containing multiple heteroaromatic and carbamate/amide functionalities, fluorinated and alkyl-substituted lipophilic regions, and a protease-binding motif engineered to occupy the catalytic cleft of the viral NS3/4A serine protease; chemically it is classified as an HCV NS3/4A protease inhibitor and belongs to the macrocyclic peptidomimetic protease inhibitor scaffold exemplified by related agents such as paritaprevir, glecaprevir, simeprevir, voxilaprevir, and earlier analogs including asunaprevir. Its principal target is the hepatitis C virus NS3/4A protease complex, inhibition of which blocks viral polyprotein processing and replication. Pharmacokinetically, oral absorption is adequate and enhanced by food, plasma protein binding is very high, hepatic uptake and disposition are influenced by transporters including OATP1B1/1B3 and efflux systems such as P-glycoprotein, metabolism occurs predominantly via CYP3A-mediated oxidation with limited renal clearance, and excretion is mainly fecal through biliary routes; exposure rises substantially with strong CYP3A inhibitors or OATP inhibitors and is increased in moderate to severe hepatic impairment. Toxicologically, the major concern is hepatotoxicity, including clinically significant ALT elevations and worsening liver function in susceptible patients, with increased risk in advanced liver disease; common adverse effects include fatigue, headache, nausea, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, and asthenia. Clinically, grazoprevir is used with elbasvir as a fixed-dose oral regimen for chronic hepatitis C, especially genotype 1 and 4 infection, including in patients with compensated liver disease, chronic kidney disease, or prior treatment experience, to achieve sustained virologic response and reduce progression to cirrhosis and hepatic complications.

Name: Venetoclax
Description: Venetoclax (DrugBank DB11581) is an orally active, highly lipophilic small-molecule antineoplastic agent built as a rationally designed BH3-mimetic that contains a rigid polyaromatic, heterocycle-rich structure with chlorinated phenyl motifs, a piperazine-linked side chain, and strategically placed hydrogen-bonding and hydrophobic substituents that mimic pro-apoptotic BH3-domain interactions. Chemically, it is classified as a targeted synthetic organic antineoplastic and apoptosis regulator, and its core scaffold is best described as a fused/aromatic BH3-mimetic pharmacophore optimized for high-affinity BCL-2 binding. Similar drugs include other BCL-2 family inhibitors and BH3 mimetics such as navitoclax, as well as the more selective experimental or newer agents lisaftoclax and sonrotoclax. Venetoclax is absorbed orally, with food increasing exposure; it is highly protein bound, distributes extensively into tissues, is metabolized predominantly by CYP3A4/5, and is eliminated mainly via feces with minimal renal clearance, giving it clinically important interactions with strong CYP3A inhibitors or inducers. Its principal target protein is B-cell lymphoma 2 (BCL2), with consequent displacement of pro-apoptotic proteins and induction of mitochondrial apoptosis in BCL-2-dependent malignancies. It is indicated chiefly for chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma and acute myeloid leukemia, particularly in combination regimens such as with obinutuzumab, rituximab, azacitidine, decitabine, or low-dose cytarabine. Major toxicities include tumor lysis syndrome, severe neutropenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and serious infections including sepsis and pneumonia; common adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, fatigue, upper respiratory infection, and musculoskeletal pain. Clinically, it is used with dose ramp-up and laboratory prophylaxis in high-burden CLL and in older or unfit AML patients as a chemotherapy-sparing, biomarker-informed targeted therapy.

Name: Thiocolchicoside
Description: Thiocolchicoside (DrugBank DB11582) is a semisynthetic sulfur-containing glucoside derivative of colchicoside, structurally characterized by a tropolone-containing tricyclic colchicine-like framework bearing methoxy substituents and a thiomethyl-linked sugar moiety, placing it in the alkaloid-derived glycoside and colchicine congener class with a colchicine/tropolone scaffold. It is chemically and pharmacologically related to colchicine, colchicoside, and more distantly other muscle relaxant agents used for painful spasm, although its mechanism differs from classical neuromuscular blockers. Its principal known targets are inhibitory neurotransmitter receptors, especially GABAA receptor and glycine receptor binding sites, where it behaves as a functional modulator linked to centrally acting muscle-relaxant effects rather than direct anti-inflammatory activity. After oral or intramuscular administration, absorption is moderate, systemic exposure is influenced by first-pass metabolism, distribution is mainly extracellular with limited data on protein binding, metabolism is extensive in the intestine and liver to active and inactive metabolites including 3-demethylthiocolchicine, and elimination occurs through biliary/fecal and urinary routes. It is indicated as an adjunctive treatment for painful muscle contractures and acute musculoskeletal spasm, such as low back pain, cervicalgia, torticollis, and postoperative or traumatic muscle spasm. Clinical use is typically short term and often combined with NSAIDs or analgesics. Major adverse effects include diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea, somnolence, and hypersensitivity, while important toxicities include dose-related convulsions, genotoxicity/aneugenicity concerns from metabolites, embryo-fetal risk, and possible hepatotoxicity, supporting restrictions in pregnancy, epilepsy, and prolonged high-dose use.

Name: Asunaprevir
Description: Asunaprevir (DB11586) is a direct-acting antiviral designed as a conformationally constrained, peptidomimetic small molecule HCV NS3/4A serine protease inhibitor, featuring a macrocyclic scaffold with multiple amide linkages, hydrophobic aromatic substituents, and heterocyclic elements that optimize binding in the viral protease active site; chemically it is categorized as a macrocyclic peptidomimetic protease inhibitor, with a scaffold closely related to other HCV NS3/4A inhibitors such as simeprevir, paritaprevir, grazoprevir, and earlier linear or macrocyclic ketoamide-like protease inhibitor designs including telaprevir and boceprevir. Its principal target protein is the hepatitis C virus NS3/4A protease complex, whose inhibition blocks cleavage of the viral polyprotein and suppresses replication. Pharmacokinetically, asunaprevir is orally administered, absorbed with moderate bioavailability, extensively bound to plasma proteins, concentrated in the liver, and metabolized predominantly by CYP3A-mediated oxidation with transporter involvement including OATP and P-glycoprotein; excretion occurs mainly through the feces with minimal renal elimination. Toxicologically, the major concern is hepatotoxicity, including clinically significant transaminase elevations and rare severe hepatic injury, with increased exposure possible in hepatic impairment and in the setting of CYP3A inhibitors. It is indicated for chronic hepatitis C, especially genotype 1 and in some regions genotype 4, commonly in combination regimens such as with daclatasvir for genotype 1b infection. Adverse effects include fatigue, headache, diarrhea, nausea, pyrexia, and elevations in ALT, AST, and bilirubin. Clinically, it has been used as an interferon-free component of combination antiviral therapy in patients with compensated liver disease, including some who are treatment-experienced or interferon-ineligible.

Name: Bilastine
Description: Bilastine (DrugBank DB11591) is a second-generation, non-sedating antihistamine whose structure is characterized by a substituted piperidine linked to a biaryl/arylalkyl framework bearing polar functionality including a carboxylate-containing side chain, giving a zwitterion-like, peripherally restricted profile with low central nervous system penetration; chemically it is classified as a piperidine antihistamine and more broadly as an H1-receptor inverse agonist/antagonist, with a benzhydryl-biaryl piperidine scaffold related to other modern antihistamines. Similar drugs include fexofenadine, loratadine, desloratadine, cetirizine, levocetirizine, rupatadine, and ebastine, especially other peripherally selective H1 blockers used for allergic disease. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor encoded by HRH1, with little meaningful activity at muscarinic or other off-target receptors at therapeutic exposure. Bilastine is orally administered, rapidly absorbed with peak concentrations typically within about 1 to 1.5 hours, but food and fruit juice can reduce absorption; it shows low-to-moderate protein binding, limited blood-brain barrier penetration, minimal metabolism with little CYP involvement, and is eliminated largely unchanged in feces and urine, making drug-drug interaction liability relatively low. Toxicity is generally mild, with no major cardiotoxic QT liability at standard doses, though overdose or high exposure may increase dizziness, somnolence, or headache; caution is reasonable in severe renal impairment and with potent transporter inhibitors. It is indicated for allergic rhinitis, including seasonal and perennial forms, and chronic spontaneous urticaria, improving sneezing, rhinorrhea, nasal itching, conjunctival symptoms, pruritus, and wheals. Common adverse effects include headache, somnolence, fatigue, dizziness, and less often dry mouth or gastrointestinal discomfort. Clinically, it is used as once-daily symptomatic therapy in adolescents and adults with pollen allergy, dust-mite rhinitis, or chronic hives when a low-sedation antihistamine is preferred.

Name: Levoleucovorin
Description: Levoleucovorin, DrugBank DB11596, is the pharmacologically active levo isomer of folinic acid, a reduced folate composed of a pteridine ring linked through p-aminobenzoate to an L-glutamate residue with a 5-formyl tetrahydrofolate framework; chemically it is an antifolate rescue agent within the reduced folate/vitamin B9 analog class, built on the classical folate scaffold of pterin-p-aminobenzoyl-glutamate. Closely related drugs include racemic leucovorin, folic acid, and methotrexate-pathway modulators such as pemetrexed in terms of folate biology, although levoleucovorin itself functions as a reduced folate donor rather than a cytotoxic antifolate. It is administered mainly intravenously, with distribution into extracellular fluids and uptake into cells via reduced folate carriers such as SLC19A1 and folate transport systems; intracellular polyglutamation can enhance retention and metabolic function, while hepatic and tissue interconversion to other reduced folates, including 5-methyltetrahydrofolate, supports its activity, and elimination occurs largely through renal excretion of parent and metabolites. Its principal targets are indirect and pathway based, notably thymidylate synthase TYMS, which it stabilizes in the ternary complex with fluorouracil, and folate-dependent biosynthetic enzymes functionally bypassed during methotrexate toxicity. Clinically, it is indicated for rescue after high-dose methotrexate in osteosarcoma and other malignancies and for combination treatment with 5-fluorouracil in colorectal cancer. Toxicity is generally limited but may include hypersensitivity, gastrointestinal intolerance, and rarely seizures or enhanced fluoropyrimidine toxicity such as severe mucositis, diarrhea, and myelosuppression; common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, stomatitis, rash, fatigue, and infusion-related reactions.

Name: Velpatasvir
Description: Velpatasvir (DrugBank DB11613) is a direct-acting antiviral with a highly lipophilic, conformationally constrained polyheterocyclic structure characterized by multiple fused aromatic/azaaromatic ring systems, carbamate functionality, and fluorinated substituents that support potent binding to hepatitis C virus replication machinery; chemically it is categorized as a small-molecule NS5A inhibitor and its scaffold is best described as a symmetric-like diimidazole/azaheteroaromatic-linked macrostructure typical of second-generation HCV NS5A antagonists. Closely related drugs include other NS5A inhibitors such as ledipasvir, elbasvir, ombitasvir, pibrentasvir, and daclatasvir, which share extended aromatic heterocyclic scaffolds and very high antiviral potency. Its principal target is HCV nonstructural protein 5A, a multifunctional phosphoprotein required for replication complex assembly and virion production. Velpatasvir is indicated for chronic hepatitis C infection across genotypes 1-6, most commonly in fixed-dose combination with sofosbuvir for uncomplicated infection, compensated cirrhosis, and, with ribavirin in some settings, decompensated cirrhosis. Orally administered velpatasvir is absorbed with pH-dependent solubility, reaches peak concentrations in a few hours, is highly protein bound, distributes extensively, undergoes limited oxidative metabolism with CYP2B6, CYP2C8, and CYP3A4 involvement, and is eliminated predominantly via biliary-fecal excretion with minimal renal clearance. Toxicity is generally low but includes clinically important hepatotoxicity risk from drug interactions and serious bradycardia when combined with sofosbuvir and amiodarone. Common adverse effects include headache, fatigue, nausea, insomnia, and asthenia. Clinically, it is used as a pan-genotypic backbone therapy because of its high barrier to resistance, convenience, and strong efficacy in patients with prior treatment exposure or cirrhosis.

Name: Rupatadine
Description: Rupatadine (DrugBank DB11614) is a second-generation antiallergic agent structurally characterized as a lipophilic tricyclic/pyridine-containing piperidine derivative bearing an aromatic chlorophenyl substituent and a basic tertiary amine, features typical of amphiphilic H1-antihistamines that support high receptor affinity and oral activity. Chemically, it is classified as an antihistamine and platelet-activating factor antagonist, with a piperidine-based tricyclic scaffold related to other modern H1 blockers. Similar drugs include loratadine, desloratadine, ketotifen, and ebastine, which share bulky aromatic antihistamine pharmacophores, although rupatadine is distinguished by dual H1 and PAF antagonism. After oral administration it is well absorbed, undergoes significant first-pass hepatic metabolism, is highly protein bound, and distributes systemically with limited central nervous system penetration relative to first-generation antihistamines; metabolism occurs mainly via CYP3A4 to active metabolites such as desloratadine-like derivatives, and elimination is through fecal and urinary routes as metabolites. Toxicity is generally low at therapeutic doses, but overdose or interaction with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors may increase sedation, anticholinergic-like effects, tachycardia, or QT-related cardiovascular risk, and hepatic impairment can increase exposure. Its principal targets are the histamine H1 receptor and the platelet-activating factor receptor. Rupatadine is indicated for allergic rhinitis and chronic spontaneous urticaria, improving sneezing, rhinorrhea, nasal itching, conjunctival symptoms, wheals, and pruritus. Common adverse effects include somnolence, headache, fatigue, dizziness, and dry mouth. Clinically, it is used as an oral once-daily symptomatic treatment in seasonal or perennial allergic rhinitis and urticaria, particularly when both histaminergic and inflammatory mediator blockade are desirable.

Name: Aclarubicin
Description: Aclarubicin (DrugBank DB11617) is an anthracycline antineoplastic antibiotic characterized by a planar tetracyclic anthraquinone/anthracenedione-like aromatic aglycone core, aklavinone, bearing quinone and hydroquinone functionalities and linked glycosidically to a trisaccharide chain of amino deoxy sugars, a structural feature that modulates DNA binding and cellular uptake; chemically it belongs to the anthracycline glycosides, with an anthracycline chromophore scaffold closely related to other DNA-intercalating topoisomerase-active agents such as daunorubicin, doxorubicin, epirubicin, idarubicin, and pirarubicin. Its principal pharmacologic targets are DNA and topoisomerase II, with secondary effects on nucleic acid synthesis and chromatin function; unlike some anthracyclines, it is often described as strongly inhibiting RNA synthesis in addition to causing DNA intercalation. After intravenous administration, aclarubicin shows rapid tissue distribution, extensive cellular uptake, high protein and tissue binding, predominant hepatic metabolism to less active metabolites, biliary/fecal elimination as the major route, and limited renal excretion, with exposure influenced by liver function. Toxicity is typical of anthracyclines and includes dose-related myelosuppression, mucositis, hepatotoxicity, and cumulative cardiotoxicity such as arrhythmia or cardiomyopathy, although its cardiac risk has sometimes been considered somewhat lower than doxorubicin in some settings; local tissue injury can occur with extravasation. Adverse effects include leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, nausea, vomiting, stomatitis, alopecia, fever, and infection risk. Clinically, aclarubicin has been used mainly in leukemia regimens, especially acute myeloid leukemia and acute lymphoblastic leukemia, and in some regions for myelodysplastic syndromes or lymphoma-containing combination chemotherapy protocols.

Name: Neridronic Acid
Description: Neridronic acid (DrugBank DB11620) is a non-nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate characterized structurally by a geminal P-C-P bisphosphonate motif attached to a short aliphatic aminoalkyl side chain, specifically an aminobutyl scaffold that confers high affinity for hydroxyapatite in bone; chemically it belongs to the aminobisphosphonate-adjacent class of antiresorptive pyrophosphate analogs, with a simple alkyl-bisphosphonate scaffold related to other bone-seeking bisphosphonates such as clodronate, etidronate, pamidronate, alendronate, and ibandronate. Its principal pharmacology is osteoclast inhibition after selective adsorption to mineralized bone, with intracellular effects in osteoclasts linked to disruption of energy-dependent pathways and suppression of bone resorption; no single high-affinity protein target is universally assigned, but functionally relevant targets include osteoclast-associated pathways and, for the class, enzymes in the mevalonate pathway such as farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase. Pharmacokinetically, neridronic acid is poorly absorbed orally, is therefore commonly administered parenterally, distributes rapidly to bone and extracellular fluid, undergoes negligible metabolism, and is eliminated largely unchanged by the kidney, with prolonged skeletal retention but a shorter plasma half-life. Toxicity is typical of bisphosphonates and includes dose-related renal intolerance, hypocalcemia, local injection reactions, and rare class events such as osteonecrosis of the jaw or atypical femoral fracture after prolonged exposure. Adverse effects commonly include fever, arthralgia, myalgia, bone pain, gastrointestinal upset, and transient flu-like symptoms. Clinically it is used as an antiresorptive agent in disorders such as osteogenesis imperfecta, Paget disease of bone, osteoporosis, complex regional pain syndrome, and other conditions with increased bone turnover or bone pain.

Name: Dehydrocholic acid
Description: Dehydrocholic acid (DrugBank DB11622) is a semisynthetic oxidized bile acid derived from the cholane nucleus of cholic acid, characterized by a rigid tetracyclic steroid framework with a C24 side chain terminating in a carboxylic acid and carbonyl substitutions at the 3, 7, and 12 positions in place of the parent hydroxyl groups; chemically it belongs to the bile acids and bile acid derivatives, with a cholanic acid or steroidal bile acid scaffold. It is structurally and pharmacologically related to other choleretic or bile acid agents such as cholic acid, ursodeoxycholic acid, chenodeoxycholic acid, and to some extent obeticholic acid as a more modern bile acid analog. Its pharmacokinetics are incompletely characterized by modern standards, but oral absorption appears limited to moderate, followed by hepatic uptake and prominent enterohepatic handling; unlike naturally occurring bile acids, it is less extensively conjugated and may undergo reduction to hydroxy bile acid metabolites in the liver and intestine, with elimination mainly in bile and feces and a smaller urinary fraction. Its pharmacologic action is largely choleretic rather than receptor-selective, and no single definitive target protein is well established, though bile acid transport and signaling systems such as FXR, TGR5, NTCP, BSEP, and related hepatic transport pathways are potentially relevant. Clinically, it has been used to stimulate bile flow in biliary insufficiency, dyspepsia, constipation associated with reduced bile secretion, and some hepatobiliary disorders. Adverse effects are primarily gastrointestinal, including abdominal cramping, diarrhea, nausea, and irritation of the gastric or intestinal mucosa; excessive exposure may worsen fluid loss or electrolyte imbalance, and use in obstructive jaundice or severe hepatic dysfunction may increase intolerance or toxicity.

Name: Laropiprant
Description: Laropiprant (DB11629) is a small-molecule nicotinic acid derivative designed as a selective prostaglandin D2 receptor antagonist, structurally characterized by a substituted pyridine carboxylic acid core bearing lipophilic aryl/heteroaryl features that confer high affinity for the prostaglandin D2 receptor subtype 1; chemically it is best classified as a heteroaromatic carboxylic acid and its principal scaffold is a functionalized pyridyl benzoic acid-like anti-inflammatory receptor-antagonist framework. It is most closely related pharmacologically to other DP1 antagonists such as asapiprant, fevipiprant, and setipiprant, although those agents are structurally distinct and were developed mainly for allergic or inflammatory indications. Laropiprant targets PTGDR, the human DP1 receptor, thereby blocking prostaglandin D2-mediated vasodilation and flushing rather than directly altering lipid metabolism. It was developed for use with extended-release niacin to reduce niacin-induced cutaneous flushing in dyslipidemia, including hypercholesterolemia and mixed dyslipidemia, as exemplified by the niacin/laropiprant combination previously marketed in some regions. After oral administration it is absorbed systemically, achieves plasma exposure sufficient for receptor blockade, is distributed predominantly in the extracellular compartment with moderate protein binding, undergoes hepatic biotransformation with oxidative and conjugative pathways, and is eliminated through both biliary/fecal and renal routes. Reported adverse effects include headache, gastrointestinal upset, diarrhea, nausea, pruritus, and dizziness; toxicity concerns arose largely in combination therapy, with examples including increased rates of myopathy, hepatic adverse events, infection, bleeding, and worsened glycemic control when paired with niacin and statins, which limited its clinical utility and contributed to withdrawal from routine use.

Name: Isavuconazole
Description: Isavuconazole (DrugBank DB11633) is a broad-spectrum triazole antifungal administered clinically as the water-soluble prodrug isavuconazonium sulfate; the active moiety contains a substituted 1,2,4-triazole pharmacophore linked to a halogenated aromatic system and a flexible ether-containing side chain, placing it in the azole antifungal class and more specifically the triazole subclass, with a scaffold closely related to other mold-active triazoles such as voriconazole, posaconazole, fluconazole, and itraconazole. Its antifungal activity is mediated primarily by inhibition of fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase, the CYP51 enzyme encoded in many fungi by ERG11/CYP51, leading to impaired ergosterol biosynthesis and membrane dysfunction. After oral or intravenous dosing, bioavailability is high, absorption is reliable and not strongly food- or acid-dependent, protein binding is extensive, tissue distribution is broad, and the terminal half-life is long; metabolism occurs mainly via CYP3A4 and CYP3A5 with inactive metabolites, and elimination is predominantly metabolic with fecal and lesser renal excretion. It is indicated for invasive aspergillosis and invasive mucormycosis, including severe pulmonary or disseminated disease in immunocompromised patients. Adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, headache, hypokalemia, peripheral edema, dyspnea, elevated hepatic enzymes, and infusion-related reactions; important toxicities include hepatotoxicity, hypersensitivity, embryo-fetal risk, and clinically significant CYP3A4-mediated drug interactions, although unlike many azoles it may shorten rather than prolong the QT interval. In practice it is used for step-down or primary therapy of invasive mold infections, especially when prolonged treatment, oral transition, or avoidance of cyclodextrin-associated renal concerns is desirable.

Name: Delamanid
Description: Delamanid (DB11637) is a lipophilic nitro-dihydro-imidazooxazole antimycobacterial agent whose structure is defined by a fused imidazooxazole bicyclic core bearing a nitro substituent and extended with halogenated aromatic and ether-linked hydrophobic moieties, placing it in the nitroimidazole-related antitubercular chemical category with an imidazooxazole scaffold closely related in function, though not identical in ring system, to other nitroimidazole antimycobacterial drugs such as pretomanid and metronidazole-derived bioreductive agents. It is used primarily for multidrug-resistant pulmonary tuberculosis, especially as part of combination regimens when resistance or intolerance limits standard therapy. Its principal pharmacologic action depends on activation within Mycobacterium tuberculosis by the deazaflavin-dependent nitroreductase Ddn, with involvement of the F420 biosynthetic/activation system including Fgd1, FbiA, FbiB, and FbiC; this bioreductive process inhibits mycolic acid synthesis, particularly methoxy- and keto-mycolates, impairing mycobacterial cell wall formation. Oral absorption is improved with food, protein binding is very high, tissue distribution is broad, metabolism occurs predominantly via albumin-mediated and other non-CYP transformation with minor CYP3A4 contribution, and elimination is mainly as metabolites in feces with limited renal excretion; the terminal half-life is prolonged, supporting twice-daily dosing. Major toxicities include QT prolongation and cardiotoxicity risk, especially with other QT-prolonging agents, plus hepatotoxicity and metabolic concerns such as hypoalbuminemia-associated exposure increases. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, dizziness, headache, insomnia, anxiety, paresthesia, and palpitations. Clinically, it is used in MDR-TB regimens with drugs such as linezolid, fluoroquinolones, clofazimine, and bedaquiline, with ECG and hepatic monitoring guiding safe use.

Name: Artenimol
Description: Artenimol (dihydroartemisinin; DrugBank DB11638) is a semisynthetic artemisinin derivative whose structure is defined by a sesquiterpene lactone endoperoxide built on a compact, highly oxygenated trioxane-containing polycyclic framework, with the unusual 1,2,4-trioxane peroxide bridge serving as the critical pharmacophore; chemically it belongs to the artemisinin class of peroxide antimalarials and is scaffolded on the artemisinin/dihydroartemisinin tetracyclic sesquiterpene core. Closely related drugs include artemisinin itself and the derivatives artesunate, artemether, and arteether, which act as prodrugs or analogs of the same peroxide-bearing scaffold. Artenimol is rapidly absorbed after oral administration, although it has limited aqueous solubility and variable bioavailability; it distributes widely, shows moderate plasma protein binding, undergoes hepatic phase II metabolism predominantly by glucuronidation after interconversion from related derivatives, and is cleared relatively quickly with a short elimination half-life, with metabolites excreted mainly in urine and bile. Its antimalarial activity is linked primarily to activation by heme or ferrous iron in Plasmodium-infected erythrocytes, generating reactive radicals that damage parasite proteins and membranes; proposed molecular targets include Plasmodium falciparum ATPase 6 and multiple parasite redox and metabolic proteins rather than a single validated human target. It is indicated for uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria and is used in artemisinin-based combination therapies, for example with piperaquine, to reduce parasitemia and fever rapidly. Adverse effects are usually mild and include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, dizziness, headache, rash, and transient transaminase elevation, while toxicity concerns include embryotoxicity in animal studies, rare hypersensitivity, occasional neutropenia or reticulocytopenia, and potential delayed hemolysis noted more often with severe malaria treatment using related artemisinin derivatives.

Name: Amifampridine
Description: Amifampridine (3,4-diaminopyridine; DrugBank DB11640) is a small, basic, aromatic heterocycle consisting of a pyridine ring bearing adjacent amino substituents at the 3 and 4 positions, giving a compact, highly polar, weakly basic diamino-azaaryl structure; chemically it belongs to the aminopyridine class and is built on a simple pyridine scaffold, specifically a diaminosubstituted pyridyl pharmacophore related to other potassium-channel blocking aminopyridines such as fampridine (4-aminopyridine/dalfampridine) and less commonly 3,4-diaminopyridine phosphate formulations. Its principal pharmacologic action is blockade of presynaptic voltage-gated potassium channels, prolonging depolarization and increasing calcium-dependent acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction; relevant target space therefore includes neuronal Kv channel subtypes rather than a single highly selective protein, with functional effects linked to presynaptic calcium entry and neuromuscular transmission. Amifampridine is used primarily for Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome to improve muscle strength and symptoms such as proximal weakness, autonomic dysfunction, and reduced reflexes, and it has also been used in congenital myasthenic syndromes and selected neuromuscular transmission disorders. Orally administered, it is generally well absorbed, distributes modestly with limited protein binding, undergoes substantial N-acetylation mainly via NAT2 with pharmacogenetic variability in exposure, and is excreted predominantly in urine as parent drug and metabolites. Toxicity is dose related and dominated by neurologic hyperexcitability, with seizures the major serious risk, especially at high exposure or in predisposed patients; common adverse effects include paresthesia, perioral tingling, abdominal pain, nausea, dyspepsia, headache, dizziness, insomnia, and elevated blood pressure, while clinical use centers on individualized oral titration to symptomatic benefit with monitoring for seizure risk and tolerability.

Name: Vinflunine
Description: Vinflunine (DrugBank DB11641) is a semisynthetic fluorinated vinca alkaloid derived from the catharanthine-vindoline family, characterized by a complex polycyclic bisindole framework with multiple fused and bridged rings, tertiary nitrogen functionality, oxygenated substituents, and strategically introduced fluorine atoms that distinguish it from earlier vinca agents and modulate lipophilicity, tubulin affinity, and metabolic behavior; chemically it belongs to the antimitotic vinca alkaloid class and is built on the classic vindoline-catharanthine bisindole scaffold shared with vinorelbine, vinblastine, vincristine, and vindesine, which are its closest structural and pharmacologic analogues. Its principal targets are tubulin and microtubule polymers, with binding at the vinca domain of beta-tubulin to inhibit microtubule assembly, disrupt mitotic spindle formation, and induce G2/M arrest and apoptosis in rapidly proliferating cells. Pharmacokinetically, vinflunine is administered intravenously, exhibits extensive tissue distribution and high protein binding, undergoes predominantly hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 to active and inactive metabolites, and is eliminated through both fecal/biliary and renal routes with a relatively long terminal half-life. Clinically it is used as an antineoplastic agent, especially for advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma after platinum failure, and has also been studied in non-small cell lung cancer and breast cancer. Dose-limiting and clinically important toxicities include severe neutropenia, febrile neutropenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, constipation or ileus, mucositis, fatigue, abdominal pain, and peripheral neuropathy, with caution warranted in hepatic impairment, myelosuppression, infection risk, and gastrointestinal obstruction.

Name: Tafamidis
Description: Tafamidis (DB11644) is a small-molecule transthyretin stabilizer built on a halogenated biaryl ether scaffold, chemically described as a benzoxazole-derived aromatic carboxylic acid in which a substituted phenoxy/heteroaryl system and a terminal carboxyl group confer high-affinity binding within the thyroxine-binding channels of transthyretin; thus it is categorized as an amyloidogenesis inhibitor and kinetic stabilizer of a transport protein rather than a classic receptor agonist or enzyme inhibitor. Its core scaffold is an aryl-heteroaryl ether linked to a planar benzoxazole-type framework, and structurally or mechanistically similar drugs include diflunisal, acoramidis, and related TTR tetramer stabilizers. The principal and essentially unique target protein is transthyretin, including wild-type and variant forms associated with amyloidosis. Pharmacokinetically, tafamidis is orally bioavailable, absorbed with predictable exposure, highly plasma protein bound, distributed mainly in the vascular compartment, undergoes limited oxidative metabolism with predominant glucuronidation, and is eliminated mainly in feces with a smaller urinary component; it has a relatively long half-life that supports once-daily dosing. Toxicity is generally modest, with no dominant dose-limiting organ toxicity in routine use, but adverse findings can include elevations in hepatic enzymes, urinary tract infection, vaginal infection, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and rare hypersensitivity or intolerance, while reproductive risk remains a caution because of retinoid-related transport biology. Clinically, tafamidis is indicated for transthyretin amyloidosis, especially hereditary transthyretin amyloid polyneuropathy and transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy, where it is used to slow neurologic decline, reduce cardiovascular hospitalization, and preserve functional status in patients with symptoms such as peripheral neuropathy, autonomic dysfunction, heart failure, and exercise limitation.

Name: Bremelanotide
Description: Bremelanotide (DrugBank DB11653) is a synthetic melanocortin receptor agonist built as a conformationally constrained cyclic peptide analog of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone, featuring a short peptide macrocycle with aromatic and basic residues and designed to enhance receptor affinity and metabolic stability relative to the endogenous ligand; chemically it belongs to the melanocortin peptide therapeutics class, and its core scaffold is the cyclic heptapeptide/bioactive melanocortin pharmacophore exemplified by MT-II-like analogs. Closely related or mechanistically similar drugs include melanotan II, afamelanotide, and the older investigational melanocortin agonist melanotan I. Its principal targets are melanocortin receptors, especially MC4R, with activity also reported at MC1R and MC3R, and sexual-response effects are mainly attributed to central melanocortin signaling. After subcutaneous administration, bremelanotide is absorbed relatively rapidly, reaches systemic circulation without oral bioavailability, distributes in extracellular fluid with peptide-like tissue penetration, undergoes proteolytic peptide metabolism rather than major CYP-dependent biotransformation, and is cleared through metabolic degradation with renal excretion of peptide fragments as the main elimination route. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related nausea, vomiting, flushing, headache, and transient increases in blood pressure with reductions in heart rate; caution is warranted in patients with uncontrolled hypertension or cardiovascular disease, and melanocortin-related hyperpigmentation or focal gum/skin darkening can occur. It is indicated for acquired, generalized hypoactive sexual desire disorder in premenopausal women, particularly low sexual desire causing distress. Clinically, it is used as an on-demand subcutaneous treatment before anticipated sexual activity, with common adverse effects including nausea, injection-site reactions, headache, and flushing.

Name: Rebamipide
Description: Rebamipide (DB11656) is a gastroprotective small molecule built on a quinolinone-based aromatic carboxylic acid framework, specifically a 2(1H)-quinolinone scaffold bearing a 4-chlorobenzoylamino substituent and an acetic acid side chain, placing it in the category of mucosal protective antiulcer agents and acidic quinolinone derivatives; its core scaffold is therefore best described as a substituted quinolinone linked to a haloaryl amide. Structurally and pharmacologically related drugs include other gastric cytoprotective agents such as teprenone, sucralfate, irsogladine, and to some extent prostaglandin-enhancing antiulcer therapies, although rebamipide is chemically distinct from proton pump inhibitors and H2 antagonists. It is used mainly for gastric ulcer, gastritis, NSAID-associated gastropathy, dyspepsia, and protection of gastric and occasionally ocular mucosa, including dry eye formulations in some regions. Its mechanism is pleiotropic rather than single-target driven, with reported effects on PTGS1 and PTGS2 signaling, enhancement of endogenous prostaglandins, increased mucin production, free-radical scavenging, suppression of inflammatory cytokines such as TNF and IL8 pathways, and modulation of neutrophil adhesion molecules and epithelial repair processes rather than a highly selective receptor interaction. Oral absorption is modest, distribution is systemic but limited by moderate protein binding, metabolism occurs mainly in the liver with limited biotransformation, and elimination is primarily renal as unchanged drug and minor metabolites. Toxicity is generally low, with animal and clinical experience suggesting a wide therapeutic margin; adverse effects are usually mild and include constipation, diarrhea, nausea, abdominal discomfort, rash, pruritus, dizziness, headache, and rare hepatic enzyme elevations or hypersensitivity. Clinically, rebamipide is used as an adjunct or alternative mucosal protective therapy, especially in peptic ulcer disease, chronic gastritis, and prevention or mitigation of NSAID-induced mucosal injury.

Name: Latanoprostene bunod
Description: Latanoprostene bunod (DB11660) is a nitric oxide-donating prostaglandin F2α analog designed as an ophthalmic ester prodrug that structurally combines a latanoprost acid-like prostanoid core with an aromatic ester side chain and a butanediol mononitrate-derived nitric oxide-releasing moiety; chemically it is categorized as a prostaglandin analog and nitrate ester, with a prostanoid eicosanoid scaffold closely related to isopropyl ester glaucoma agents. Its closest similar drugs include latanoprost, travoprost, bimatoprost, tafluprost, and unoprostone, especially latanoprost because latanoprostene bunod is metabolically converted to latanoprost acid plus a nitric oxide-donating fragment. After topical ocular administration, corneal esterases rapidly hydrolyze it in the eye; systemic absorption is low, distribution is largely local to anterior ocular tissues, metabolism yields latanoprost acid and butanediol mononitrate with subsequent nitric oxide generation and further oxidative degradation, and elimination of metabolites occurs predominantly via systemic biotransformation and renal excretion. Pharmacologically, latanoprost acid acts at the prostanoid FP receptor, encoded by PTGFR, to increase uveoscleral outflow, while nitric oxide functionally relaxes trabecular meshwork and Schlemm canal tissue through soluble guanylate cyclase signaling, principally involving GUCY1A1 and GUCY1B1. It is indicated for reduction of elevated intraocular pressure in open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension. Adverse effects are mainly ocular and include conjunctival hyperemia, eye irritation, instillation-site pain, blurred vision, eyelash growth, iris pigmentation, and periocular skin darkening. Toxicity is generally low and localized, but class-related concerns include intraocular inflammation, cystoid macular edema in susceptible patients, and rare exacerbation of herpetic keratitis; clinically it is used as once-daily topical therapy, particularly when enhanced pressure lowering beyond standard prostaglandin analog monotherapy is desired.

Name: Triheptanoin
Description: Triheptanoin (DB11677) is a medium odd-chain triglyceride composed of glycerol esterified at all three hydroxyls with heptanoic acid, giving a neutral, highly lipophilic triacylglycerol structure; chemically it belongs to the fatty acid ester and triglyceride class, and its core scaffold is a glycerol triester bearing three linear C7 aliphatic chains. It is closely related to other medical nutritional lipids and medium-chain triglyceride preparations, including trioctanoin, tricaprylin/caprylic triglyceride, and mixed MCT oils, although triheptanoin is distinguished by its anaplerotic odd-chain metabolism. After oral administration it is absorbed as a dietary fat following pancreatic lipase hydrolysis to heptanoate and glycerol, distributed largely via chylomicron-associated lipid handling and portal uptake of liberated medium-chain fatty acid, extensively metabolized by mitochondrial beta-oxidation to acetyl-CoA and propionyl-CoA with hepatic generation of C5 ketone bodies such as beta-hydroxypentanoate and beta-ketopentanoate, and excreted mainly as oxidized carbon products rather than unchanged drug, with minimal renal elimination of parent compound. Its pharmacologic effect is not mediated by a classic receptor target, and no definitive target proteins are established, though functional dependence on pancreatic lipase, fatty acid transport systems, carnitine-independent mitochondrial entry typical of medium-chain fatty acids, and beta-oxidation enzymes is central. It is indicated for long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorders such as VLCAD, LCHAD, trifunctional protein deficiency, and CPT II-related energy deficiency states, where it is used chronically to reduce cardiomyopathy, rhabdomyolysis, hypoglycemia, and exercise intolerance. Toxicity is predominantly gastrointestinal and dose related, with abdominal pain, diarrhea, vomiting, nausea, and bloating most common; excessive use may worsen malabsorption, contribute to weight gain, and in susceptible patients has been associated with feeding intolerance or alteration in essential fatty acid balance, so clinical use is as a specialized metabolic energy substrate under expert dietary supervision.

Name: Daprodustat
Description: Daprodustat (DrugBank DB11682) is an orally active small-molecule hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor built around a compact heteroaromatic glycinamide-like scaffold, featuring a substituted fused aza-aromatic ring system linked to polar amide functionality and lipophilic aryl substitution that supports metal-chelating interactions within the prolyl hydroxylase catalytic site; chemically it is best classified as a heteroaryl amide, and its core scaffold is related to other HIF-prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors used for renal anemia, including roxadustat, vadadustat, molidustat, and enarodustat. Its principal targets are HIF prolyl hydroxylase domain proteins EGLN1/PHD2, EGLN2/PHD1, and EGLN3/PHD3, leading to stabilization of HIF-α, increased endogenous erythropoietin signaling, and modulation of iron-handling genes.
