It is indicated primarily for anemia associated with chronic kidney disease, especially symptomatic anemia in dialysis-dependent or non-dialysis CKD patients, where it is used to raise hemoglobin and reduce transfusion or exogenous erythropoiesis-stimulating agent requirements. After oral administration it is absorbed systemically with hepatic metabolism predominating, largely through CYP2C8 with contribution from CYP3A4, and metabolites are eliminated by renal and fecal routes; distribution is consistent with a moderately protein-bound, nonbiologic oral agent. Toxicity concerns include excessive hemoglobin rise, hypertension, thromboembolic and other major adverse cardiovascular events, and potential hepatic laboratory abnormalities. Common adverse effects include nausea, headache, hypertension, diarrhea, dizziness, and vascular access thrombosis or edema in susceptible patients. Clinically, daprodustat is used as a chronic oral anemia therapy in CKD, particularly when an oral alternative to injectable erythropoiesis-stimulating therapy is desired.

Name: Selumetinib
Description: Selumetinib (DrugBank DB11689) is a small-molecule, orally active, ATP-independent allosteric inhibitor of mitogen-activated protein kinase kinases MEK1 and MEK2, chemically characterized by a substituted benzimidazole-based heteroaromatic structure bearing halogenated and oxygen-containing aryl substituents that confer lipophilicity and kinase-pocket selectivity; it is generally classified as an antineoplastic kinase inhibitor, specifically a MAPK/ERK pathway inhibitor, with a benzimidazole/heteroaryl scaffold typical of allosteric MEK inhibitors. Closely related or mechanistically similar drugs include trametinib, cobimetinib, binimetinib, and refametinib, which share MEK-targeted activity but differ in scaffold and pharmacokinetic behavior. After oral administration, selumetinib is absorbed with moderate bioavailability, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, is substantially protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism primarily via CYP3A4 with contributions from phase II pathways such as glucuronidation, and is eliminated through both fecal and urinary routes mainly as metabolites; exposure can be altered by hepatic impairment and strong CYP modulators. Its principal targets are MAP2K1 and MAP2K2, leading to suppression of ERK phosphorylation and downstream proliferative signaling. Clinically, it is indicated most prominently for neurofibromatosis type 1-associated symptomatic, inoperable plexiform neurofibromas, and has also been studied in BRAF- or RAS-driven malignancies such as melanoma, thyroid cancer, and pediatric low-grade glioma. Toxicities include class-related cardiomyopathy, ocular toxicity including retinal pigment epithelial detachment, hepatotoxicity, creatine phosphokinase elevation, and embryo-fetal toxicity; common adverse effects include rash, acneiform dermatitis, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, edema, stomatitis, paronychia, and elevated transaminases. In practice, selumetinib is used as precision MAPK-pathway therapy, especially in pediatric NF1, with monitoring of cardiac, ophthalmic, hepatic, and dermatologic safety.

Name: Naldemedine
Description: Naldemedine (DrugBank DB11691) is a peripherally acting opioid receptor antagonist structurally derived from the morphinan opioid scaffold of naltrexone, retaining the rigid fused polycyclic phenanthrene-like core and 4,5-epoxy morphinan architecture while incorporating a polar side chain that increases hydrophilicity and limits blood-brain barrier penetration; chemically it is classified as an opioid antagonist, specifically a peripheral mu-opioid receptor antagonist, within the morphinan/semisynthetic opiate derivative class. Its core scaffold and pharmacology make it similar to other PAMORAs such as naloxegol and methylnaltrexone, and more broadly to centrally active antagonists like naltrexone and naloxone. Its principal targets are the mu-opioid receptor with additional antagonist activity at delta- and kappa-opioid receptors. After oral administration, naldemedine is absorbed systemically with clinically useful bioavailability, reaches peak concentrations within hours, is substantially protein bound, distributes predominantly peripherally, undergoes hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A-mediated oxidation with contribution from UGT1A3 glucuronidation, and is eliminated through both urine and feces, with a terminal half-life supporting once-daily dosing. It is indicated for opioid-induced constipation in adults, particularly in patients with chronic non-cancer pain and also in some patients receiving opioids for chronic pain syndromes. Toxicity is largely mechanism-based and gastrointestinal, including severe abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and rare gastrointestinal perforation risk in susceptible patients with structural gut disease; opioid withdrawal symptoms can occur. Common adverse effects include abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, and gastroenteritis. Clinically, it is used as a daily oral agent to restore bowel function without meaningfully reversing central analgesia in patients maintained on opioid therapy.

Name: Voclosporin
Description: Voclosporin (DB11693) is a semisynthetic cyclic undecapeptide immunosuppressant structurally derived from the calcineurin inhibitor cyclosporine, distinguished by a highly lipophilic macrocyclic peptide framework containing multiple N-methylated amino acid residues and a modified side chain at the first amino acid that increases potency and alters metabolism; chemically, it belongs to the cyclosporine-class calcineurin inhibitors and its core scaffold is the cyclic peptide/macrocyclic polypeptide scaffold characteristic of fungal peptide immunosuppressants. Similar drugs include cyclosporine and tacrolimus, with pimecrolimus as a related calcineurin-pathway agent. Voclosporin binds cyclophilin, and the drug-cyclophilin complex inhibits calcineurin phosphatase, suppressing NFAT activation and downstream T-cell cytokine transcription; relevant targets therefore include cyclophilin family proteins, calcineurin catalytic subunits PPP3CA/PPP3CB, and the NFAT signaling axis. Orally administered voclosporin is absorbed with measurable bioavailability, is highly protein and erythrocyte associated, undergoes extensive hepatic CYP3A-mediated metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly via the biliary/fecal route with minimal renal excretion of unchanged drug. Toxicity is broadly consistent with calcineurin inhibition and includes nephrotoxicity with reduced glomerular filtration, hypertension, hyperkalemia, neurotoxicity, infection risk, and possible hepatotoxicity; overdose or interacting CYP3A inhibitors may increase these risks. Its principal indication is lupus nephritis in combination with background immunosuppression, where it is used to reduce proteinuria and improve renal response in active systemic lupus erythematosus with kidney involvement. Common adverse effects include decreased renal function, hypertension, diarrhea, headache, anemia, cough, urinary tract infection, and upper respiratory infection, and clinically it is used as an oral steroid-sparing immunomodulator requiring renal function, blood pressure, potassium, and drug-interaction monitoring.

Name: Racecadotril
Description: Racecadotril (DB11696) is an orally active antidiarrheal prodrug whose structure is a small lipophilic acetylated thioester featuring a glycine-derived backbone, an amide linkage, a terminal carboxyl function, and a phenylpropyl substituent; chemically it is best classified as an enkephalinase inhibitor prodrug within the peptidomimetic amino acid derivative class, built on a thioester/amide-substituted glycine scaffold related to enkephalinase inhibitory mercaptoacyl frameworks. It is most similar pharmacologically and structurally to its active metabolite thiorphan and to other neprilysin inhibitors such as acetorphan analogs, although it is distinct from opioid agonist antidiarrheals like loperamide. After oral administration, racecadotril is rapidly absorbed and extensively converted by esterases to thiorphan, the active metabolite; systemic distribution of thiorphan is moderate with appreciable plasma protein binding, central nervous system penetration is minimal, metabolism proceeds largely through biotransformation of the thiol-containing metabolite to inactive disulfide and conjugated products, and excretion occurs mainly in urine with a smaller fecal component. Its principal target protein is neprilysin, also called neutral endopeptidase or membrane metalloendopeptidase, whose inhibition reduces degradation of endogenous enkephalins in the intestinal mucosa and thereby suppresses hypersecretion without markedly slowing transit. Clinically it is indicated for symptomatic treatment of acute diarrhea, including infectious or nonspecific secretory diarrhea in adults and children, often alongside oral rehydration. Adverse effects are usually mild and include headache, nausea, abdominal discomfort, constipation, and rash; rarer toxicities include hypersensitivity reactions such as urticaria, erythema multiforme, or angioedema, while overdose experience suggests relatively low acute toxicity but warrants supportive management.

Name: Ipragliflozin
Description: Ipragliflozin (DrugBank DB11698) is a small-molecule antidiabetic agent of the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor class, structurally characterized as a C-aryl glucoside in which a glucose-like sugar moiety is linked through a carbon-carbon bond to a lipophilic aromatic aglycone bearing substituted phenyl and heteroaromatic features, a design that confers high metabolic stability relative to O-glucosides; its core scaffold is the C-glucoside SGLT2-inhibitor pharmacophore shared with related drugs such as dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, canagliflozin, ertugliflozin, and luseogliflozin. Its principal target is SLC5A2/SGLT2 in the renal proximal tubule, with functional selectivity over SLC5A1/SGLT1, thereby reducing renal glucose reabsorption, increasing urinary glucose excretion, and lowering plasma glucose in type 2 diabetes mellitus, including patients with inadequate glycemic control on diet, exercise, metformin, DPP-4 inhibitors, or other oral agents. After oral administration it is absorbed with clinically useful bioavailability, reaches peak concentrations within hours, is substantially protein bound, distributes systemically without unusual tissue sequestration, undergoes predominant hepatic biotransformation mainly by glucuronidation with lesser oxidative metabolism, and is eliminated through both urine and feces chiefly as metabolites. Adverse effects and toxicity reflect glucosuria and volume loss, including genital mycotic infection, urinary tract infection, polyuria, dehydration, hypotension, and occasional renal function worsening; class-associated serious risks include euglycemic ketoacidosis and rare severe urogenital infection, while hypoglycemia is uncommon unless combined with insulin or sulfonylureas. Clinically, ipragliflozin is used as an oral once-daily antihyperglycemic drug to improve glycemic control, reduce fasting and postprandial glucose, and promote modest weight and blood pressure reduction in adults with type 2 diabetes.

Name: Tropisetron
Description: Tropisetron (DrugBank DB11699) is an indole-derived, conformationally restricted heterocyclic antiemetic whose structure consists of a substituted indole nucleus linked through an ester functionality to a rigid bicyclic tropane-like framework, giving a serotonin-mimetic aromatic system appended to a basic nitrogen-containing cage; chemically it is classified as a selective 5-hydroxytryptamine-3 (5-HT3) receptor antagonist within the setron class, and its core scaffold is commonly described as an indole-carboxylate/tropane hybrid. Closely related drugs include ondansetron, granisetron, dolasetron, palonosetron, and ramosetron, which share 5-HT3 antagonism but differ in aromatic heterocycle and pharmacokinetic behavior. Its principal target is the 5-HT3 receptor, particularly the ionotropic receptor subunits encoded by HTR3A and associated HTR3 family members on vagal afferents and in the area postrema; tropisetron has also been reported to interact with nicotinic acetylcholine receptor systems, especially alpha7 nAChR, though this is not its primary clinical mechanism. After oral administration it is well absorbed, undergoes substantial hepatic first-pass metabolism largely via CYP2D6-mediated oxidation and conjugative pathways, distributes systemically with moderate protein binding, and is eliminated as metabolites in urine with a smaller fecal component; exposure varies with CYP2D6 phenotype. It is indicated mainly for prevention and treatment of chemotherapy-induced and postoperative nausea and vomiting, for example in patients receiving emetogenic cytotoxic regimens or recovering from anesthesia. Adverse effects are usually mild and include headache, constipation, dizziness, fatigue, and abdominal discomfort; less commonly diarrhea, hypersensitivity, blood pressure changes, or QT-related cardiac effects may occur. Toxicity is generally low at therapeutic doses, but overdose or susceptible patients may show CNS symptoms, gastrointestinal disturbance, or clinically relevant arrhythmia risk. In practice, tropisetron is used as a supportive-care antiemetic, often peri-chemotherapy or perioperatively, sometimes in combination with corticosteroids such as dexamethasone to improve control of acute emesis.

Name: Setmelanotide
Description: Setmelanotide (DrugBank DB11700) is a synthetic melanocortin receptor agonist in the peptide/peptidomimetic class, structurally characterized as a short conformationally constrained cyclic peptide built on an α-melanocyte-stimulating hormone–derived pharmacophore, with a lactam-bridged melanocortin scaffold that preserves the key receptor-binding motif while enhancing potency and selectivity; chemically it belongs to melanocortin analogs, and its closest similar drugs include the nonselective melanocortin agonists melanotan I, melanotan II, and afamelanotide, although setmelanotide is distinguished by preferential activation of melanocortin-4 receptor. Its principal target is MC4R, with much weaker activity at other melanocortin receptors such as MC1R, MC3R, and MC5R, supporting restoration of hypothalamic satiety signaling and increased energy expenditure. Pharmacokinetically, it is administered subcutaneously, reaches systemic circulation with peptide-like absorption kinetics, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid, undergoes proteolytic peptide catabolism rather than major CYP-mediated biotransformation, and is eliminated largely as inactive metabolites through renal and possibly minor fecal pathways; the terminal half-life is compatible with once-daily dosing. It is indicated for chronic weight management in patients with obesity due to genetically defined POMC, PCSK1, or leptin receptor deficiency, and certain Bardet-Biedl syndrome patients, with clinical use focused on reducing hyperphagia and body weight. Adverse effects commonly include injection-site reactions, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, headache, spontaneous penile erection, sexual arousal disturbances, skin hyperpigmentation, and darkening of nevi, reflecting melanocortin pathway activity. Toxicity is generally dominated by dose-related gastrointestinal and pigmentary effects, but monitoring is warranted for hypersensitivity, mood changes including depression or suicidal ideation, and persistent erection-related events.

Name: Amenamevir
Description: Amenamevir (DB11701) is an orally active antiherpes antiviral distinguished chemically as a non-nucleoside helicase-primase inhibitor built around a heteroaryl amide-like small-molecule framework, with a compact polycyclic/aromatic scaffold incorporating halogenated and nitrogen-containing ring elements that confer high lipophilicity and potent protein-binding interactions; it is generally categorized within the thiazolyl/heteroaromatic antiviral class and is structurally and mechanistically related to other herpesvirus helicase-primase inhibitors such as pritelivir, while differing fundamentally from nucleoside analogs like acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir. Its principal targets are the herpesvirus helicase-primase complex, especially the viral proteins UL5 helicase, UL52 primase, and the accessory factor UL8 in varicella-zoster virus and herpes simplex virus, thereby blocking viral DNA replication without requiring initial phosphorylation by viral thymidine kinase. Pharmacokinetically, amenamevir is orally absorbed, reaches systemic circulation adequately for once-daily use, distributes broadly with meaningful plasma protein binding, undergoes predominantly hepatic metabolism largely via CYP3A-mediated oxidative pathways, and is eliminated mainly in feces with a lesser renal contribution. Toxicity is generally manageable at therapeutic doses, but exposure may rise with strong CYP3A inhibitors or hepatic impairment; nonclinical concerns are typical of small-molecule antivirals and may include hepatic enzyme elevations and drug interaction liability. Clinically, it is used primarily for herpes zoster, including shingles with acute dermatomal rash and pain, and has been studied for herpes simplex infections. Reported adverse effects include nasopharyngitis, headache, gastrointestinal upset, nausea, diarrhea, and occasional liver function test abnormalities, supporting its practical use as an oral alternative when standard nucleoside antiherpetics are unsuitable or resistance/intolerance is a concern.

Name: Tezacaftor
Description: Tezacaftor (DrugBank DB11712) is a small-molecule cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) modulator with a lipophilic, conformationally restricted structure featuring multiple aromatic/heteroaromatic rings, fluorinated aryl substitution, and amide/carbamate-type functionality that supports high membrane permeability and binding to misfolded CFTR; chemically it is classified as a CFTR corrector and more broadly as a heteroaryl aromatic carboxamide-like therapeutic agent built on a polycyclic bis-aryl heterocyclic scaffold. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other CFTR modulators, especially lumacaftor as a first-generation corrector, and is commonly paired with potentiators such as ivacaftor; it is also related in therapeutic context to elexacaftor in triple-combination regimens. Its principal target is CFTR (ABCC7), where it improves folding, intracellular processing, and trafficking of F508del-CFTR to the cell surface. After oral administration, especially with fat-containing food, absorption is improved; the drug is highly protein bound, widely distributed, metabolized predominantly by CYP3A-mediated oxidation to less active metabolites, and eliminated mainly in feces with a minor renal component, supporting twice-daily combination use. Toxicity is generally moderate but includes transaminase elevation, potential drug-drug interactions with strong CYP3A inducers or inhibitors, and embryo-fetal risk concerns based on class labeling considerations. It is indicated for cystic fibrosis caused by responsive CFTR mutations, particularly F508del-containing genotypes, to improve chloride transport, lung function, and pulmonary symptom burden. Common adverse effects include headache, nausea, sinus congestion, dizziness, and elevations in liver enzymes, while clinical use is primarily in fixed-dose tezacaftor/ivacaftor and elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor regimens for chronic management of mutation-specific cystic fibrosis.

Name: Encorafenib
Description: Encorafenib (DB11718) is a small-molecule, orally active ATP-competitive serine/threonine kinase inhibitor chemically classified as a substituted azaindole/aryl urea-like targeted antineoplastic agent, built around a compact heteroaromatic scaffold featuring a chlorinated phenyl ring linked to a nitrogen-rich bicyclic core and additional carbamate/amide-type functionality that optimizes binding within the RAF kinase ATP pocket; its medicinal chemistry places it among type I BRAF inhibitors with a heteroaryl kinase-inhibitor scaffold related pharmacologically to vemurafenib, dabrafenib, and to some extent the multikinase RAF inhibitor sorafenib. Its principal target is mutant BRAF, especially BRAF V600E and V600K, with activity in the RAF/MEK/ERK MAPK pathway and pharmacodynamic suppression of downstream ERK signaling; off-target RAF family interactions may contribute to both efficacy and toxicity. Clinically it is indicated for BRAF V600-mutant unresectable or metastatic melanoma, commonly in combination with binimetinib, for metastatic colorectal cancer with cetuximab, and in some settings for other BRAF V600E-positive solid tumors. After oral administration it is well absorbed, reaches peak concentrations within hours, is highly protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism primarily via CYP3A4 with contributions from CYP2C19 and CYP2D6, and is eliminated through both feces and urine predominantly as metabolites; its half-life is relatively short compared with some other BRAF inhibitors. Important toxicities include dose-related hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation, hemorrhage, dermatologic toxicity including palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia and secondary cutaneous neoplasms, ocular toxicity such as uveitis, and embryo-fetal toxicity. Common adverse effects include fatigue, nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, arthralgia, myalgia, rash, pyrexia, headache, and elevated liver enzymes. In practice, encorafenib is used as precision oncology therapy for molecularly defined BRAF-driven cancers, often in rational combinations that improve response durability and reduce paradoxical MAPK reactivation.

Name: Ribociclib
Description: Ribociclib (DrugBank DB11730) is an orally active, selective small-molecule cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor built on a heteroaromatic aminopyrimidine-containing bicyclic core, with substituted piperazine and lipophilic aryl functionality that support kinase hinge binding and physicochemical properties suitable for oral dosing; chemically it is classified as a synthetic targeted antineoplastic, specifically a CDK4/6 inhibitor, and its dominant scaffold is a substituted pyrrolo- or fused aza-heterocyclic aminopyrimidine kinase-inhibitor framework closely related to other CDK4/6 inhibitors such as palbociclib and abemaciclib. Its principal targets are CDK4 and CDK6, thereby reducing retinoblastoma protein phosphorylation and arresting hormone receptor-positive tumor cells in G1. Pharmacokinetically, ribociclib is well absorbed after oral administration, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, is extensively distributed with substantial protein binding, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 with minor phase I/II biotransformation, and is eliminated through both feces and urine, with fecal excretion predominating and a terminal half-life that supports once-daily dosing on an intermittent schedule. Toxicity is characterized by dose-dependent myelosuppression, especially neutropenia and leukopenia, plus hepatotoxicity and QT interval prolongation; overdose or high exposure may increase risks of severe infection, transaminase elevation, and arrhythmia. Common adverse effects include neutropenia, nausea, fatigue, diarrhea, alopecia, anemia, vomiting, constipation, and elevated liver enzymes. Clinically, ribociclib is used primarily in HR-positive, HER2-negative advanced or metastatic breast cancer, typically combined with an aromatase inhibitor or fulvestrant in postmenopausal, premenopausal, or perimenopausal patients, including endocrine-sensitive and selected endocrine-resistant disease settings.

Name: Lasmiditan
Description: Lasmiditan (DB11732) is a centrally acting, non-vasoconstrictive antimigraine small molecule whose structure is defined by a pyridinoyl-piperidine core bearing a trifluoromethyl-substituted pyridine ring and other heteroaryl functionality, giving a lipophilic, nitrogen-rich arylpiperidine architecture optimized for high 5-HT1F receptor affinity and blood-brain barrier penetration. Chemically it is best categorized as a selective serotonin receptor agonist, specifically a ditan, and its principal scaffold is an aryl-substituted piperidine linked to a heteroaromatic carboxamide-like framework rather than the indole/tryptamine-derived triptan scaffold. Similar drugs include the triptans such as sumatriptan, rizatriptan, and eletriptan, which are also acute antimigraine agents but primarily target 5-HT1B/1D receptors and cause vasoconstriction, unlike lasmiditan. Its main known pharmacologic target is HTR1F (5-hydroxytryptamine receptor 1F). After oral administration it is rapidly absorbed, with peak concentrations typically reached in about 1.5 to 2.5 hours; distribution includes CNS exposure; metabolism occurs predominantly through non-CYP pathways with hepatic and extrahepatic biotransformation; and excretion is mainly renal as metabolites, with a terminal half-life of roughly 5 to 6 hours. It is indicated for the acute treatment of migraine with or without aura in adults, such as disabling episodic migraine attacks with photophobia, phonophobia, nausea, or throbbing unilateral headache, but not for preventive therapy. Toxicity is chiefly CNS-depressant in nature, with dose-related dizziness, somnolence, fatigue, paresthesia, sedation, and impaired driving ability; serotonin syndrome is a potential risk with serotonergic co-medications, and overdose may accentuate neurologic depression and cardiovascular symptoms such as bradycardia or blood pressure changes. Clinically, lasmiditan is used when rapid abortive treatment is needed, particularly in patients who may not tolerate or should avoid vasoconstrictive agents because of cardiovascular risk factors or triptan contraindications.

Name: Rilmenidine
Description: Rilmenidine (DrugBank DB11738) is a centrally acting antihypertensive built on a substituted imidazoline/oxazoline-type heterocyclic framework linked to a halogenated aromatic ring, giving a compact, lipophilic aryl-heterocycle optimized for central nervous system penetration; chemically it is classified as an imidazoline receptor agonist and more broadly as a sympatholytic antihypertensive, with an aryl-imidazoline scaffold related to other centrally acting agents such as moxonidine and, more distantly, clonidine and guanfacine. Its principal pharmacology is agonism at imidazoline I1 binding sites, thought to involve nischarin/IRAS-associated imidazoline-responsive systems, with weaker activity at central alpha-2 adrenergic receptors than clonidine, a feature associated with somewhat improved tolerability. After oral administration it is well absorbed, has good bioavailability, distributes sufficiently to access brainstem cardiovascular regulatory centers, undergoes limited hepatic biotransformation relative to many antihypertensives, and is eliminated predominantly in urine as unchanged drug and minor metabolites, with a clinically useful dosing interval compatible with once-daily use in many patients. Rilmenidine is indicated for essential hypertension, particularly when reduction of sympathetic tone is desired, and has been used in mild to moderate high blood pressure, including patients with metabolic comorbidity. Adverse effects and toxicity are generally dose-related and include asthenia, somnolence, insomnia, dry mouth, palpitations, gastrointestinal upset, cold extremities, and less commonly orthostatic hypotension or bradycardia; overdose may produce excessive hypotension, sedation, and cardiovascular depression. Clinically, it is used as monotherapy or in combination with diuretics, calcium-channel blockers, or renin-angiotensin system inhibitors when central sympatholysis is appropriate.

Name: Vonoprazan
Description: Vonoprazan (DB11739) is an orally active potassium-competitive acid blocker with a compact heteroaromatic structure built around a substituted pyridine linked to a methylmethanamine center and an imidazo-fused aromatic ring bearing fluorinated substituents, giving it a basic, lipophilic architecture that concentrates in the acidic canaliculi of gastric parietal cells; chemically it is classified as a P-CAB rather than a proton-pump inhibitor, and its core scaffold is an imidazopyridine/aza-heteroaryl acid-suppression pharmacophore. Similar drugs include other P-CABs such as tegoprazan, fexuprazan, and revaprazan, while functionally related comparators include proton-pump inhibitors like lansoprazole and esomeprazole. Its principal target is the gastric H+/K+-ATPase proton pump, encoded by ATP4A and ATP4B, which it inhibits reversibly at the potassium-binding site to produce rapid, potent, and sustained suppression of gastric acid secretion. After oral administration, vonoprazan is well absorbed, reaches peak concentrations within hours, is distributed systemically with meaningful protein binding, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 with lesser contributions from other CYP pathways, and is eliminated as metabolites in urine and feces; unlike many PPIs, its activity is less dependent on acid activation or CYP2C19 phenotype. It is indicated for acid-related disorders including erosive esophagitis, gastroesophageal reflux disease, peptic ulcer disease, prevention of NSAID- or aspirin-associated ulcers, and Helicobacter pylori eradication regimens. Adverse effects are usually gastrointestinal or mild systemic events such as diarrhea, constipation, nausea, abdominal discomfort, headache, and nasopharyngitis, while toxicities of concern include hypergastrinemia, reduced absorption of acid-dependent nutrients or drugs, possible hepatic enzyme elevations, and with prolonged profound acid suppression, theoretical increased risk of enteric infection and gastric mucosal endocrine-cell changes.

Name: Ebastine
Description: Ebastine (DrugBank DB11742) is a second-generation H1-antihistamine characterized structurally by a highly lipophilic diarylbutanone/piperidine architecture, containing a para-substituted diphenyl motif linked through a flexible aliphatic chain to a tertiary piperidine nitrogen and a butanone functionality; chemically it is classified as a piperidine-based antihistamine and its core scaffold is closely related to the butyrophenone-like aryl-alkyl-piperidine framework seen in other non-sedating antiallergics. Similar drugs include loratadine, desloratadine, fexofenadine, cetirizine, and mizolastine, which share peripheral H1 receptor selectivity and reduced CNS penetration. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor encoded by HRH1, where it acts as a peripheral inverse agonist/antagonist to suppress histamine-mediated wheal, flare, pruritus, rhinorrhea, and sneezing. After oral administration, ebastine is well absorbed but undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism to the active carboxylic acid metabolite carebastine, with distribution favored into peripheral tissues, relatively limited brain entry, metabolism mediated mainly by CYP3A4, and elimination occurring largely as metabolites in urine and feces. Toxicity is generally low at therapeutic doses, but overdose or interacting CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ketoconazole, itraconazole, erythromycin, or clarithromycin may increase exposure and raise concern for QT prolongation or other cardiac electrophysiologic effects, alongside anticholinergic-like symptoms such as dry mouth or somnolence. Clinically, it is indicated for allergic rhinitis, seasonal pollinosis, and chronic idiopathic urticaria, and is used to relieve itching, nasal congestion-related symptoms, sneezing, and hives; common adverse effects include headache, dry mouth, drowsiness, dyspepsia, and fatigue.

Name: Clobetasol
Description: Clobetasol (DrugBank DB11750, generally referring clinically to clobetasol propionate) is a super-high-potency halogenated synthetic corticosteroid built on the pregnane steroid nucleus, with the classic four-ring cyclopenta[a]phenanthrene glucocorticoid scaffold and distinguishing structural features that include 9-fluoro substitution, 21-chlorination in clobetasol, an 11β-hydroxyl group, a 17α-hydroxyl/side-chain region, 3-keto and 20-keto functionalities, and in the marketed propionate ester a 17-propionate group that increases lipophilicity and topical potency. Chemically it belongs to corticosteroids, specifically topical glucocorticoids; structurally and pharmacologically similar agents include betamethasone dipropionate, diflorasone diacetate, fluocinonide, halobetasol propionate, and desoximetasone. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, with downstream transrepression of proinflammatory mediators such as NF-κB- and AP-1-regulated cytokines, reduced phospholipase A2 activity via lipocortin induction, and secondary vasoconstrictive, antiproliferative, and immunosuppressive effects. After topical administration, absorption is usually limited but rises substantially with inflamed skin, large treated surface area, prolonged use, occlusion, or damaged epidermis; distribution after systemic uptake is expected to involve plasma protein binding and tissue partitioning typical of lipophilic steroids; metabolism occurs mainly hepatically through ester hydrolysis and oxidative/reductive steroid biotransformation; excretion is primarily renal as metabolites with some biliary/fecal elimination. It is indicated for corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses such as plaque psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, lichen planus, discoid lupus erythematosus, and severe eczema, and is used clinically as short-course topical therapy for refractory pruritic, erythematous, hyperkeratotic inflammatory skin disease. Toxicity is dominated by excessive local and systemic glucocorticoid exposure, including skin atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, acneiform eruption, perioral dermatitis, delayed wound healing, secondary infection, and, with overuse, HPA-axis suppression, hyperglycemia, Cushingoid

Name: Cabotegravir
Description: Cabotegravir (DrugBank DB11751) is a second-generation antiretroviral built on a polycyclic integrase inhibitor chemotype featuring a halogenated, highly functionalized tricyclic carbamoyl pyridone/oxoazepine-like core with diketo acid bioisosteric metal-chelating elements and lipophilic aryl substitution that supports strong binding in the HIV integrase active site; chemically it is classified as an HIV-1 integrase strand transfer inhibitor, and its scaffold is closely related to the dolutegravir/bictegravir family, with dolutegravir the most obvious structural and pharmacologic analogue and raltegravir and elvitegravir representing earlier mechanistically similar INSTIs. Its principal target is HIV-1 integrase, inhibiting strand transfer by chelating the catalytic Mg2+ ions in the integrase-DNA complex. Cabotegravir is indicated, in combination with rilpivirine, for maintenance treatment of HIV-1 infection in virologically suppressed adults and adolescents, and as long-acting pre-exposure prophylaxis for prevention of sexually acquired HIV-1 infection in at-risk individuals. Pharmacokinetically, oral absorption is adequate, while the long-acting nanosuspension intramuscular formulation provides very slow absorption and prolonged exposure over weeks to months; it is highly protein bound, distributes well systemically, undergoes minimal CYP-mediated metabolism with primary glucuronidation via UGT1A1 and to a lesser extent UGT1A9, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in feces and urine, with a long apparent terminal half-life after depot injection. Toxicity is generally manageable but includes hepatotoxicity, hypersensitivity, depressive disorders, and embryo-fetal risk signals; common adverse effects include injection-site pain, fever, fatigue, headache, nausea, dizziness, diarrhea, rash, and sleep disturbance. Clinically, it is used as oral lead-in or direct-to-inject therapy with rilpivirine for maintenance HIV care and as extended-interval injectable prophylaxis when adherence to daily oral prevention is difficult.

Name: Rifamycin
Description: Rifamycin (DrugBank DB11753) is an ansamycin antibacterial of the rifamycin class characterized by a rigid naphthohydroquinone or naphthalene-like aromatic core bridged by a long aliphatic ansa chain containing multiple hydroxyl, acetyl, methoxy, and conjugated carbonyl functionalities, a structure that defines the rifamycin scaffold and supports high-affinity binding to bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Chemically it belongs to macrocyclic polyketide natural products, and it is closely related to rifampin, rifabutin, rifapentine, and rifaximin, which share the same rifamycin ansa scaffold with substitutions that alter potency, oral bioavailability, tissue penetration, and enzyme induction. Its principal target is the bacterial RNA polymerase beta subunit encoded by rpoB, leading to inhibition of transcription initiation; no therapeutically relevant human protein target is intended. Pharmacokinetically, rifamycin derivatives vary, but rifamycin used clinically for intestinal indications is minimally absorbed after oral administration, remains largely within the gastrointestinal lumen, shows negligible systemic distribution, undergoes limited metabolism, and is excreted predominantly in feces. Toxicity is generally lower than with systemically absorbed rifamycins, but class effects include hepatotoxicity, hypersensitivity, orange-red discoloration of body fluids, and selection of resistant mutants via rpoB alterations; gastrointestinal intolerance such as abdominal pain and nausea may occur. Indications and clinical use center on susceptible bacterial infections, especially noninvasive intestinal disease such as traveler’s diarrhea caused by noninvasive Escherichia coli, with related rifamycins also used in tuberculosis, leprosy, and mycobacterial infections. Common side effects include nausea, flatulence, constipation, abdominal cramping, headache, and occasionally rash or liver enzyme elevations.

Name: Istradefylline
Description: Istradefylline (DB11757) is a synthetic xanthine-derived, non-methylxanthine heteroaromatic small molecule built on a fused purinedione-like/xanthine core, specifically a tricyclic xanthine-related scaffold bearing lipophilic aryl and alkyl substitutions that increase adenosine receptor affinity and central nervous system penetration; chemically it is classified as an adenosine receptor antagonist and more broadly as a substituted xanthine derivative, with a scaffold related to other adenosinergic antagonists such as caffeine, theophylline, and preladenant, although istradefylline is markedly more selective for the adenosine A2A receptor. Its principal target protein is the adenosine A2A receptor encoded by ADORA2A, with functional modulation of indirect basal ganglia pathways relevant to dopaminergic motor control in Parkinson disease. After oral administration it is absorbed with moderate time to peak, is highly protein bound, widely distributed, and undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism predominantly via CYP3A4, with minor contributions from other oxidative pathways; elimination is mainly as metabolites in feces, with limited renal excretion of unchanged drug and a relatively long terminal half-life supporting once-daily dosing. Toxicity is generally consistent with CNS and neuropsychiatric stimulation, and overdosing or susceptible patients may show dyskinesia worsening, hallucinations, insomnia, agitation, or impulse-control symptoms; nonclinical concerns have included class-related hepatic metabolic liability rather than prominent organotoxicity. It is indicated as adjunctive therapy to levodopa/carbidopa in adults with Parkinson disease experiencing off episodes, and in clinical use it is added to existing dopaminergic regimens to reduce off time and improve motor fluctuations, with common adverse effects including dyskinesia, dizziness, constipation, nausea, insomnia, and hallucinations.

Name: Talazoparib
Description: Talazoparib (DrugBank DB11760) is a potent orally active poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitor whose structure is a rigid, fused heteroaromatic tricyclic system containing a phthalazinone-like PARP-binding core with additional nitrogen-rich ring fusion and a fluorophenyl substituent, features that support high-affinity catalytic inhibition and exceptional PARP-trapping activity; chemically it is a small-molecule heterocyclic antineoplastic agent in the PARP inhibitor class, built on a bicyclic/tricyclic nicotinamide-mimetic phthalazinone-related scaffold similar to other DNA damage response drugs such as olaparib, niraparib, rucaparib, and pamiparib. Its principal targets are PARP1 and PARP2, with cytotoxicity driven by inhibition of single-strand break repair and trapping of PARP-DNA complexes, creating synthetic lethality in homologous recombination-deficient tumors, especially those with BRCA1 or BRCA2 alterations. Talazoparib is indicated primarily for germline BRCA-mutated, HER2-negative locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer and is also used in selected homologous recombination repair-deficient solid tumors, including in combination regimens for prostate cancer. After oral administration it is well absorbed, shows moderate distribution, limited hepatic metabolism, minimal CYP involvement, and is eliminated largely unchanged through renal excretion with some fecal clearance, supporting once-daily dosing. Dose-limiting toxicity is mainly myelosuppression, with anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and occasional pancytopenia; other adverse effects include fatigue, nausea, vomiting, decreased appetite, alopecia, headache, and diarrhea, while rare severe risks include transfusion requirement, persistent marrow suppression, and possible myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukemia. Clinically, it is used as a precision oncology agent in biomarker-selected patients, either as monotherapy or in combination strategies designed to exploit DNA repair defects.

Name: Tenapanor
Description: Tenapanor (DrugBank DB11761) is a minimally absorbed, small-molecule intestinal sodium/hydrogen exchanger 3 inhibitor built as a conformationally constrained, polycyclic, highly polar aryl-benzimidazole/heteroaryl-linked scaffold with multiple amine-rich and halogenated aromatic features that favor local gastrointestinal activity over systemic exposure; chemically it is best classified as a gut-restricted ion-transport modulator, and its scaffold is distinct from classical laxatives but functionally resembles other locally acting intestinal secretory or transport-targeting agents such as linaclotide, plecanatide, lubiprostone, and the phosphate-lowering NHE3 inhibitor class more broadly. Its principal target is SLC9A3/NHE3 on the apical surface of enterocytes, where inhibition reduces intestinal sodium absorption, increases luminal water content, softens stool, accelerates transit, and also decreases paracellular phosphate uptake. Pharmacokinetically, oral absorption is negligible, plasma concentrations are typically very low or unquantifiable, distribution is therefore largely confined to the gut lumen and intestinal epithelium, metabolism appears limited with no major systemic biotransformation burden identified, and excretion occurs predominantly in feces as parent-related material. Toxicity is driven mainly by exaggerated pharmacology rather than systemic organ toxicity, with diarrhea that may become severe, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, dizziness, and occasional treatment discontinuation; juvenile animal findings underpin a contraindication in children under 6 years because of dehydration risk. Adverse effects include diarrhea, abdominal distension, flatulence, and abdominal discomfort. Clinically, tenapanor is used for irritable bowel syndrome with constipation to improve bowel movement frequency and abdominal symptoms, and has also been used to reduce serum phosphorus in adults with chronic kidney disease receiving dialysis.

Name: Talinolol
Description: Talinolol (DrugBank DB11770) is a cardioselective beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist of the aryloxypropanolamine class, structurally characterized by the canonical beta-blocker scaffold of a 2-hydroxy-3-aminopropoxy linker attached to an aromatic ring system and a bulky substituted amino side chain, features that confer beta1-receptor preference while limiting central nervous system penetration because of relatively hydrophilic, polar functionality. Its chemical scaffold is therefore best described as an aryloxypropanolamine beta-blocker pharmacophore, closely related to agents such as atenolol, metoprolol, bisoprolol, and celiprolol, with which it shares beta-adrenergic antagonism but differs somewhat in transporter interactions and disposition. Talinolol primarily targets beta1-adrenergic receptors in the heart, with lesser activity at beta2 receptors; it is also widely recognized as a probe substrate of P-glycoprotein/ABCB1, which influences intestinal absorption and biliary or renal handling. Pharmacokinetically, it is absorbed orally with incomplete and variable bioavailability, shows limited tissue and brain distribution, low protein binding relative to more lipophilic beta-blockers, minimal hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated largely unchanged via renal and biliary/fecal routes, making transporter effects clinically relevant. It is indicated for hypertension and other cardiovascular states in which beta-blockade is useful, including symptomatic tachycardia or chronic ischemic heart disease/angina control in some settings. Adverse effects and toxicity are typical of beta-blockers, including bradycardia, hypotension, fatigue, dizziness, exercise intolerance, cold extremities, and possible bronchospasm in susceptible patients; overdose may produce severe bradycardia, atrioventricular block, cardiogenic shock, and hypoglycemia masking. Clinically, talinolol has been used chiefly as an oral antihypertensive and antianginal agent and also as a pharmacokinetic probe in drug-transporter interaction studies.

Name: Pazufloxacin
Description: Pazufloxacin (DB11774) is a synthetic fluoroquinolone antibacterial built on the canonical 4-quinolone-3-carboxylic acid scaffold, featuring the bicyclic quinolone core with a 4-oxo group, a 3-carboxylate required for metal-ion-mediated enzyme binding, a fluorine substituent that enhances potency, and a basic nitrogen-containing heterocyclic side chain that modulates Gram-negative activity and pharmacokinetic behavior; chemically it is categorized as a fluoroquinolone and more specifically a quinolone carboxylic acid, with a scaffold closely related to ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, ofloxacin, moxifloxacin, and tosufloxacin. Its principal targets are bacterial DNA gyrase, especially GyrA/GyrB, and topoisomerase IV, leading to inhibition of DNA replication and cell division. Pazufloxacin has been used mainly as a parenteral agent for susceptible bacterial infections such as pneumonia, urinary tract infection, intra-abdominal infection, gynecologic infection, skin and soft tissue infection, and sepsis or febrile states caused by Gram-negative organisms including Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Pharmacokinetically, intravenous administration provides complete systemic availability, with moderate extracellular distribution, clinically useful penetration into urine and inflamed tissues, limited biotransformation, and predominant renal excretion of unchanged drug, so clearance is reduced in renal impairment. Toxicities are broadly class-typical and include dose-related CNS stimulation or seizures, QT-interval prolongation, dysglycemia, hepatotoxicity, phototoxicity, tendinopathy or tendon rupture, cartilage toxicity in juveniles, and risk of Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea; adverse effects commonly include nausea, diarrhea, rash, infusion-site reactions, headache, dizziness, and laboratory liver enzyme elevations. Clinically, pazufloxacin has been used when broad Gram-negative coverage is needed, particularly in hospitalized patients requiring injectable quinolone therapy.

Name: Imidapril
Description: Imidapril (DrugBank DB11783) is an orally active angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor of the dicarboxylate, prodrug class, structurally characterized by a peptidomimetic dipeptide-like framework containing a fused bicyclic octahydrocyclopenta[b]pyrrole/proline-derived core, an esterified carboxyl group that enhances oral absorption, and an amide-linked side chain that is hydrolyzed in vivo to the active diacid metabolite imidaprilat; its chemical scaffold is therefore closely related to the proline-based ACE-inhibitor scaffold seen in other ester prodrugs. Similar drugs include enalapril, ramipril, quinapril, benazepril, perindopril, and trandolapril, which share conversion to active ACE-inhibiting diacids. Its principal target is angiotensin-converting enzyme, ACE/ACE1, leading to reduced angiotensin II formation and decreased aldosterone signaling, with secondary enhancement of bradykinin activity. Pharmacokinetically, imidapril is absorbed after oral administration, undergoes first-pass ester hydrolysis to imidaprilat, distributes systemically with meaningful tissue ACE binding, and is eliminated through both renal and, to a lesser extent, biliary/fecal pathways; impaired renal function can increase exposure to the active metabolite. It is indicated primarily for hypertension, including essential hypertension and blood-pressure reduction in patients at cardiovascular risk, and is used clinically as chronic oral antihypertensive therapy alone or with diuretics or calcium-channel blockers. Toxicities and adverse effects are typical of ACE inhibitors and include dose-related hypotension, dizziness, cough, hyperkalemia, renal function deterioration, and rare but serious angioedema; examples of clinically important toxicity include acute kidney injury in renovascular disease and fetotoxicity in pregnancy, making it contraindicated during gestation.

Name: Capmatinib
Description: Capmatinib (DB11791) is a small-molecule, orally active ATP-competitive tyrosine kinase inhibitor whose structure is characterized by a heteroaromatic, kinase-directed chemotype built around a substituted quinoline/triazine-like fused aza-heterocyclic core linked to polar nitrogen-containing substituents and fluorinated aryl features that optimize MET binding, lipophilicity, and oral bioavailability; chemically it is best classified as a targeted antineoplastic aminopyridine/aza-heteroaryl kinase inhibitor, with a compact type I MET-inhibitor scaffold typical of hinge-binding receptor tyrosine kinase drugs. Closely related or pharmacologically similar MET-directed agents include tepotinib, savolitinib, crizotinib, and cabozantinib, although capmatinib is more selectively developed for MET dysregulation. Its principal target protein is the hepatocyte growth factor receptor MET proto-oncogene receptor tyrosine kinase, with downstream suppression of MAPK, PI3K-AKT, and STAT signaling in MET-driven tumors. Clinically, it is indicated primarily for metastatic non-small cell lung cancer harboring MET exon 14 skipping alterations, and has also been studied in other MET-amplified solid tumors. After oral administration, absorption is adequate with peak levels in a few hours; distribution is moderate with meaningful tissue penetration, metabolism occurs predominantly via CYP3A4 and aldehyde oxidase, and elimination proceeds through both fecal and urinary routes, largely as metabolites, with a terminal half-life supporting twice-daily dosing. Toxicities include hepatotoxicity with elevated ALT/AST, interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis, embryo-fetal toxicity, and photosensitivity; common adverse effects include peripheral edema, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, decreased appetite, dyspnea, and creatinine elevation. In practice, capmatinib is used as precision therapy in molecularly selected NSCLC patients, including those requiring systemic treatment for advanced or metastatic MET exon 14-skipping disease.

Name: Mirodenafil
Description: Mirodenafil (DrugBank DB11792) is a synthetic small-molecule phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor built around a heteroaromatic, sildenafil-like pyrazolopyrimidinone core bearing a piperazine-containing sulfonamide side chain and additional alkoxy/aryl substitution that confer high PDE5 affinity and oral activity; chemically it is categorized as a PDE5-inhibiting erectogenic agent within the pyrazolopyrimidinone/heterocyclic sulfonamide class, and its principal scaffold is closely related to the fused nitrogen-rich bicyclic scaffold seen in other PDE5 inhibitors. Similar drugs include sildenafil, vardenafil, udenafil, tadalafil, and avanafil, with greatest structural resemblance to sildenafil and vardenafil. Its primary target protein is cGMP-specific phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5A), inhibition of which augments nitric oxide-mediated cGMP signaling and promotes cavernosal smooth-muscle relaxation. It is indicated mainly for erectile dysfunction, particularly difficulty achieving or maintaining penile erection sufficient for sexual activity, and has been used clinically as an oral on-demand therapy in adult men. Pharmacokinetically, mirodenafil is orally absorbed, reaches systemic circulation relatively rapidly, is distributed systemically with expected protein binding typical of lipophilic PDE5 inhibitors, undergoes extensive hepatic biotransformation predominantly via cytochrome P450 pathways, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites through fecal and, to a lesser extent, urinary excretion. Toxicity is generally mechanism-based and dose related, including vasodilatory hypotension, especially with nitrates or nitric oxide donors, and caution is warranted in cardiovascular disease or hepatic impairment. Common adverse effects include headache, flushing, nasal congestion, dyspepsia, dizziness, and visual or facial vasodilatory symptoms; serious but uncommon risks include marked hypotension, priapism, and cardiovascular events in susceptible patients.

Name: Niraparib
Description: Niraparib (DrugBank DB11793) is an orally active small-molecule antineoplastic agent of the poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitor class, structurally characterized by a substituted benzo[h][1,6]naphthyridine/aza-fused bicyclic aromatic core bearing a carboxamide and a basic piperidine side chain, a heteroaromatic lactam-like scaffold that supports high-affinity binding in the nicotinamide pocket of PARP enzymes. Its chemical scaffold is closely related to other PARP inhibitors, with mechanistically similar drugs including olaparib, rucaparib, talazoparib, and pamiparib, although niraparib is distinguished by its specific fused bicyclic carboxamide framework and prominent PARP-trapping activity. The principal targets are PARP1 and PARP2, with inhibition of PARP-mediated DNA repair and trapping of PARP-DNA complexes producing synthetic lethality in homologous recombination-deficient tumors, especially BRCA1/2-altered cancers. Pharmacokinetically, niraparib is well absorbed after oral administration, has high bioavailability, broad tissue distribution, moderate protein binding, a relatively long terminal half-life permitting once-daily dosing, and is cleared through both hepatic and extrahepatic pathways, with metabolism occurring mainly via carboxylesterase-mediated hydrolysis and subsequent conjugation rather than dominant CYP oxidation, followed by elimination in urine and feces. It is indicated mainly for maintenance treatment of epithelial ovarian, fallopian tube, and primary peritoneal cancers, including recurrent platinum-sensitive disease and selected first-line settings, and has also been used in biomarker-defined homologous recombination deficiency contexts. Dose-limiting and clinically important toxicities include thrombocytopenia, anemia, neutropenia, hypertension, and rare myelodysplastic syndrome/acute myeloid leukemia; common adverse effects include nausea, fatigue, constipation, vomiting, insomnia, headache, and palpitations. Clinically, it is used as oral maintenance therapy after platinum response, with individualized dosing based on body weight and baseline platelet count to mitigate hematologic toxicity.

Name: Bictegravir
Description: Bictegravir (DB11799) is a second-generation HIV-1 integrase strand transfer inhibitor characterized by a conformationally constrained, polyheterocyclic small-molecule structure built around a metal-chelating diketo acid bioisostere within a bicyclic nitrogen-containing core, appended to halogenated aryl and lipophilic substituents that optimize binding in the integrase active site; chemically it belongs to the antiretroviral integrase inhibitor class, and its scaffold is closely related to other INSTIs, especially dolutegravir and cabotegravir, with broader class similarity to raltegravir and elvitegravir. It targets HIV-1 integrase by chelating the catalytic Mg2+ ions in the integrase-DNA complex and blocking strand transfer; no major human pharmacologic target is intended. Bictegravir is indicated for treatment of HIV-1 infection, most commonly as part of the fixed-dose combination bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide for initial therapy and for switching virologically suppressed adults or adolescents without known resistance to the components. Orally administered, it is well absorbed, reaches peak concentrations within hours, is highly protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes dual metabolism primarily by CYP3A and UGT1A1, and is eliminated through both fecal and urinary routes mainly as metabolites, supporting once-daily dosing without pharmacokinetic boosting. Toxicity is generally low relative to older antiretrovirals, but clinically relevant concerns include transaminase elevation, worsening hepatitis B if the combination regimen is stopped, renal laboratory changes related to tubular secretion markers, and rare hypersensitivity; adverse effects commonly include diarrhea, nausea, headache, fatigue, insomnia, and abnormal dreams. Clinically, it is widely used in durable, high-barrier combination antiretroviral therapy because of potent viral suppression, activity against many integrase inhibitor-resistant patterns being more limited than dolutegravir in some settings, and a favorable interaction and tolerability profile.

Name: Tivozanib
Description: Tivozanib (DB11800) is an oral, small-molecule quinoline-urea antiangiogenic agent whose structure is defined by a substituted benzoquinoline/quinoline aromatic system linked through a urea pharmacophore to a chlorophenyl-type hydrophobic aryl ring, a motif that supports high-affinity binding in the ATP pocket of vascular endothelial growth factor receptors; chemically it is best classified as a heteroaromatic tyrosine kinase inhibitor, with a quinoline-urea scaffold closely related in design logic to other VEGFR-directed multikinase inhibitors such as axitinib, sunitinib, sorafenib, pazopanib, lenvatinib, and cabozantinib, although tivozanib is distinguished by marked selectivity for VEGFR signaling. Its principal targets are VEGFR-1 (FLT1), VEGFR-2 (KDR), and VEGFR-3 (FLT4), leading to suppression of tumor angiogenesis. It is indicated primarily for relapsed or refractory renal cell carcinoma, especially advanced clear-cell RCC after prior systemic therapy, and is used clinically as a later-line oral VEGFR TKI to delay progression and reduce tumor vascularity. Pharmacokinetically, tivozanib is orally absorbed, highly protein bound, has a large apparent distribution, undergoes limited oxidative biotransformation with CYP3A4 contribution and predominately parent-drug systemic exposure, exhibits a long terminal half-life permitting once-daily dosing schedules, and is eliminated mainly via feces with lesser renal excretion. Toxicities are class-consistent and include dose-related hypertension, proteinuria, renal dysfunction, hepatotoxicity, hemorrhage, arterial and venous thromboembolic events, impaired wound healing, and reversible posterior leukoencephalopathy in rare cases. Common adverse effects include hypertension, dysphonia, fatigue, diarrhea, decreased appetite, stomatitis, nausea, hypothyroidism, and palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia.

Name: Talaporfin
Description: Talaporfin (DrugBank DB11812) is a second-generation porphyrin-based photosensitizer, chemically a chlorin derivative known as mono-L-aspartyl chlorin e6, built on a reduced tetrapyrrolic macrocycle with an extended conjugated aromatic system and peripheral carboxylate functionality that confers amphiphilic behavior; its chemical category is photodynamic antineoplastic and diagnostic agent, and its core scaffold is the chlorin/chlorophyll-related porphyrinoid ring system. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other porphyrin-class photosensitizers such as porfimer sodium, verteporfin, temoporfin, and chlorin e6 derivatives, although talaporfin is generally designed for stronger absorption in the red region and faster clearance than first-generation agents. After intravenous administration, it distributes into plasma, tumor tissue, vascular endothelium, and inflamed or dysplastic tissues, with photoactive accumulation influenced by lipoprotein binding and tissue perfusion; it undergoes limited classical CYP-mediated biotransformation, and elimination is thought to occur mainly via hepatic and biliary routes with relatively lower prolonged cutaneous retention than porfimer. Its pharmacologic target is not a single receptor protein; rather, upon laser activation it transfers energy to molecular oxygen to generate singlet oxygen and related reactive oxygen species that damage membranes, mitochondria, lysosomes, and tumor microvasculature, with apoptosis, necrosis, and vascular shutdown as downstream effects; no unique high-affinity target protein is firmly established, though photodamage can involve albumin- and lipoprotein-associated distribution compartments. Clinically it is used in photodynamic therapy for early lung cancer, superficial or centrally located bronchial malignancies, recurrent esophageal lesions, and selected brain tumors such as malignant glioma, with adverse effects and toxicity dominated by photosensitivity reactions, local edema, pain, fever, transient liver test abnormalities, inflammation, mucosal necrosis, airway swelling, and tissue injury to illuminated normal structures.

Name: Baricitinib
Description: Baricitinib (DrugBank DB11817) is a small-molecule, orally active Janus kinase inhibitor built on a heteroaromatic pyrazolopyrimidine-like kinase-binding core linked to a substituted azetidine/acetonitrile side chain and an ethylsulfonyl group, a structure designed to mimic ATP-pocket interactions in tyrosine kinases; chemically it is best classified as a synthetic targeted immunomodulatory aza-heterocycle and nitrile-containing sulfone, with a JAK-inhibitor scaffold closely related to other ATP-competitive kinase inhibitors. Similar drugs include other JAK inhibitors such as tofacitinib, upadacitinib, ruxolitinib, filgotinib, and abrocitinib, which share kinase-directed heterocyclic pharmacophores but differ in selectivity. Its principal targets are JAK1 and JAK2, with weaker activity at TYK2 and JAK3, thereby suppressing downstream STAT signaling from cytokines including IL-6, interferons, GM-CSF, and others. Baricitinib is indicated primarily for moderate-to-severe rheumatoid arthritis, and is also used in atopic dermatitis, alopecia areata, and in selected settings of hospitalized COVID-19 requiring anti-inflammatory therapy. Pharmacokinetically, it is well absorbed orally, has relatively rapid Tmax, moderate protein binding, distributes systemically without extensive tissue sequestration, undergoes minimal hepatic metabolism with limited CYP3A4 contribution, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged in urine with a smaller fecal component; renal function is therefore a major determinant of exposure. Toxicities and adverse effects include serious infections such as herpes zoster, pneumonia, and opportunistic infections, cytopenias, elevated transaminases, creatine kinase and lipids, nausea, acne, upper respiratory infection, and headache, with clinically important risks of venous thromboembolism, major adverse cardiovascular events, and malignancy in susceptible patients. In practice it is used as an oral disease-modifying therapy, either after methotrexate inadequacy in rheumatoid arthritis or as a targeted systemic option when topical or conventional immunosuppressive treatments are insufficient.

Name: Nifurtimox
Description: Nifurtimox (DrugBank DB11820) is a nitrofuran antiprotozoal whose structure consists of a 5-nitrofuran heteroaromatic ring linked through an imine/hydrazone-like side chain to a substituted tetrahydrothiazine dioxide moiety, making it a nitroheterocyclic small molecule with a redox-active nitro group that is central to bioactivation. Chemically it belongs to the nitrofuran class, and its core scaffold is best described as a 5-nitrofuran Schiff-base-like framework appended to a sulfone-containing saturated thiazine ring; related nitroheterocyclic antiparasitics include benznidazole, nitrofurantoin, furazolidone, and the antitrypanosomal nitroimidazole fexinidazole. Its activity is attributed to intracellular nitroreduction in Trypanosoma cruzi and Trypanosoma brucei, generating reactive nitro-anion and oxygen radical species that damage nucleic acids, proteins, and membranes; no single dominant human target protein is established, but parasite type I nitroreductases are important activation enzymes. Orally administered nifurtimox is reasonably absorbed, widely distributed, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism with relatively short plasma persistence, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine. Toxicity reflects oxidative stress and off-target reactivity, with dose-limiting anorexia, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, insomnia, irritability, peripheral neuropathy, tremor, and less commonly psychosis or seizures. It is indicated primarily for Chagas disease, especially acute, congenital, or early chronic T. cruzi infection, and has also been used in African trypanosomiasis in combination regimens such as nifurtimox-eflornithine combination therapy for second-stage T. b. gambiense infection.

Name: Esketamine
Description: Esketamine (DB11823) is the S-enantiomer of ketamine, a chiral arylcyclohexylamine anesthetic characterized structurally by a cyclohexanone core bearing a 2-chlorophenyl ring and a methylamino substituent, placing it in the dissociative anesthetic class and more specifically the arylcyclohexylamine scaffold; its rigid chlorophenyl-cyclohexanone framework is closely related to ketamine itself and to similar NMDA receptor antagonists such as arketamine, norketamine, phencyclidine, and tiletamine. Pharmacologically, esketamine acts primarily as a noncompetitive antagonist of the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor, especially on GRIN-containing NMDA receptor complexes, with additional interactions reported at opioid receptors, sigma receptors, and monoaminergic transport-related systems that may contribute to antidepressant and dissociative effects. After intranasal administration it is rapidly absorbed, reaches peak plasma concentrations within minutes to under an hour, distributes extensively into the CNS owing to high lipophilicity, undergoes hepatic metabolism mainly by CYP2B6 and CYP3A4 with contributions from CYP2C9 and CYP2C19 to form norketamine and hydroxynorketamine metabolites, and is excreted largely in urine as metabolites. Toxicity includes dose-related sedation, dissociation, perceptual disturbance, hypertension, tachycardia, cognitive and psychomotor impairment, abuse liability, and in overdose profound CNS depression; chronic ketamine-class toxicity includes ulcerative cystitis and hepatobiliary injury. Esketamine is indicated for treatment-resistant major depressive disorder and depressive symptoms in adults with major depressive disorder and acute suicidal ideation or behavior, and clinically is used as supervised intranasal therapy with an oral antidepressant, with common adverse effects including dizziness, nausea, somnolence, dysgeusia, vertigo, increased blood pressure, anxiety, and dissociation.

Name: Tofogliflozin
Description: Tofogliflozin (DB11824) is an orally active C-aryl glucoside sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor characterized structurally by a glucose-like polyhydroxylated pyranose linked through a metabolically stable carbon-carbon bond to a substituted aromatic aglycone bearing a fused heteroaromatic ring system, a design that confers high selectivity and resistance to glycosidic hydrolysis; chemically it belongs to the SGLT2 inhibitor, or gliflozin, class and is built on the canonical C-glucoside diaryl/heteroaryl scaffold shared by related agents such as dapagliflozin, canagliflozin, empagliflozin, and luseogliflozin. Its principal target protein is SLC5A2 (SGLT2) in the renal proximal tubule, with much weaker activity at SLC5A1 (SGLT1), leading to reduced renal glucose reabsorption and increased urinary glucose excretion. Pharmacokinetically, tofogliflozin is well absorbed after oral dosing, reaches peak plasma concentrations within a few hours, is moderately protein bound, distributes systemically without unusual tissue sequestration, undergoes predominant hepatic biotransformation mainly by glucuronidation with minor oxidative pathways, and is eliminated in urine and feces largely as metabolites with a terminal half-life compatible with once-daily dosing. It is indicated for type 2 diabetes mellitus, particularly to improve glycemic control in patients with hyperglycemia inadequately controlled by diet, exercise, or other antihyperglycemics, and is used clinically as monotherapy or combined with agents such as metformin, DPP-4 inhibitors, or insulin. Adverse effects and toxicities are largely mechanism based and include osmotic diuresis, polyuria, volume depletion, hypotension, genital mycotic and urinary tract infections, thirst, and occasional hypoglycemia when combined with insulin secretagogues or insulin; rarer but important class-associated risks include euglycemic ketoacidosis, renal function decline in susceptible patients, and dehydration-related events, especially in elderly or renally impaired individuals.

Name: Mirogabalin
Description: Mirogabalin (DrugBank DB11825) is a small-molecule gabapentinoid built around a substituted cyclohexane-acetic acid framework bearing a chiral aminomethyl side chain and a carboxylic acid, giving it the general topological features of a polar amino acid mimetic designed to engage voltage-gated calcium channel auxiliary subunits. Chemically, it is categorized as a gabapentinoid and more broadly as a GABA-analog–derived analgesic, although it does not act directly at GABA receptors; its core scaffold is most closely described as a constrained cyclohexyl amino acid scaffold related to pregabalin and gabapentin. Similar drugs include pregabalin and gabapentin, and more distantly mirogabalin shares mechanistic space with other alpha2delta ligands used for neuropathic pain. Its principal targets are the alpha2delta-1 and alpha2delta-2 auxiliary subunits of voltage-gated calcium channels, with analgesic benefit attributed mainly to high-affinity binding with relatively sustained occupancy at alpha2delta-1. Pharmacokinetically, mirogabalin is orally absorbed, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, shows low to moderate protein binding, limited oxidative metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by the kidney, so exposure increases in renal impairment and dose adjustment is required. Toxicity is generally consistent with CNS depressant-type gabapentinoids, with dose-related dizziness, somnolence, gait disturbance, fatigue, and edema; overdose or coadministration with sedatives may increase risk of excessive sedation and falls. It is indicated for peripheral neuropathic pain, including diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain and postherpetic neuralgia, and clinically is used as an oral analgesic in these chronic neuropathic pain syndromes, particularly when burning pain, allodynia, paresthesias, or sleep-disrupting neuropathic symptoms are prominent.

Name: Ertugliflozin
Description: Ertugliflozin (DrugBank DB11827) is a synthetic C-aryl glucoside antidiabetic agent in the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor class, structurally characterized by a glucose-like polyhydroxylated sugar core linked through a metabolically stable carbon-carbon bond to a chlorinated aromatic/heteroaromatic aglycone containing a tetrahydrofuran-substituted phenyl motif; this places it within the C-glucoside diarylmethane-like scaffold family shared by related gliflozins. Close structural and pharmacological analogs include canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, and sotagliflozin, all designed to reduce renal glucose reabsorption. Its principal target is SLC5A2/SGLT2 in the proximal renal tubule, with much weaker activity at SLC5A1/SGLT1. After oral administration, ertugliflozin is well absorbed, reaches peak concentrations in about 1 hour, has high oral bioavailability, moderate protein binding, and a half-life of roughly 16-17 hours supporting once-daily dosing; it undergoes limited CYP-mediated oxidation and is cleared predominantly by UGT1A9- and UGT2B7-mediated O-glucuronidation to inactive metabolites, with elimination via urine and feces. It is indicated for type 2 diabetes mellitus to improve glycemic control, including use alone or with metformin, sitagliptin, or insulin, and has also been used for cardiovascular and renal risk reduction within the SGLT2 inhibitor class context. Adverse effects commonly include female genital mycotic infections, vulvovaginal candidiasis, balanitis, polyuria, thirst, urinary tract infection, volume depletion, hypotension, and modest LDL elevation; important toxicities include euglycemic ketoacidosis, acute kidney injury, hypoglycemia when combined with insulin or secretagogues, rare urosepsis/pyelonephritis, and class-associated concern for lower-limb amputation risk observed more prominently with some analogs.

Name: Neratinib
Description: Neratinib (DrugBank DB11828) is an orally active, small-molecule 4-anilinoquinoline-derived tyrosine kinase inhibitor whose structure is characterized by a substituted quinoline/quinazoline-like heteroaromatic core linked to an aniline moiety and bearing an electrophilic Michael acceptor crotonamide side chain that enables covalent bond formation with kinase cysteine residues; chemically it is categorized as a synthetic aromatic heterocyclic antineoplastic agent and more specifically an irreversible pan-HER ErbB family inhibitor built on the anilino-heteroaryl kinase-inhibitor scaffold. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other HER-family TKIs such as afatinib, lapatinib, tucatinib, and gefitinib/erlotinib analogously, though neratinib is distinguished by irreversible HER2-directed covalent binding. Its principal targets are EGFR/ERBB1, HER2/ERBB2, and HER4/ERBB4, with inhibition of downstream MAPK and PI3K/AKT signaling. After oral administration, absorption is variable and enhanced by food, distribution is extensive with high protein binding, metabolism occurs predominantly via CYP3A4 with minor flavin-containing monooxygenase contribution, and excretion is mainly fecal with limited renal elimination. Dose-limiting toxicity is chiefly gastrointestinal, especially severe diarrhea that may cause dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, and hepatotoxicity; other adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fatigue, rash, stomatitis, decreased appetite, and transaminase elevations. Clinically, neratinib is indicated mainly for HER2-positive breast cancer, especially extended adjuvant treatment after trastuzumab-based therapy and in some metastatic settings, often combined with capecitabine, to reduce recurrence risk and control progressive HER2-driven disease.

Name: Osilodrostat
Description: Osilodrostat (DrugBank DB11837) is a small, orally active, nonsteroidal steroidogenesis inhibitor whose structure is centered on a compact nitrogen-rich heteroaromatic scaffold bearing azole functionality and lipophilic aryl substitution, a design that enables coordination to the heme iron of cytochrome P450 enzymes; chemically it is best classified as a heterocyclic azole-like CYP inhibitor, with an imidazole/pyridine-type fused pharmacophore serving as its key scaffold. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other adrenal steroidogenesis inhibitors such as metyrapone, ketoconazole, levoketoconazole, and etomidate, although osilodrostat is generally more potent and selective for cortisol synthesis blockade. Its principal targets are 11beta-hydroxylase CYP11B1 and, to a lesser extent, aldosterone synthase CYP11B2, producing reduced cortisol biosynthesis with compensatory ACTH and steroid precursor increases. After oral administration it is well absorbed, reaches peak concentrations within hours, has moderate protein binding, distributes systemically, undergoes hepatic metabolism through multiple CYP and non-CYP pathways with limited reliance on a single enzyme, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine with a terminal half-life supportive of twice-daily dosing. Toxicities reflect adrenal blockade and precursor accumulation, including adrenal insufficiency, hypocortisolism, nausea, fatigue, dizziness, hypokalemia, edema, hypertension, androgenic effects such as acne or hirsutism, and QT prolongation; liver test abnormalities may occur. Clinically it is indicated for endogenous hypercortisolemia in Cushing disease, especially persistent or recurrent disease after pituitary surgery or when surgery is not feasible, and is used to control symptoms and complications such as hyperglycemia, weight gain, proximal myopathy, and difficult-to-treat hypertension.

Name: Relugolix
Description: Relugolix (DrugBank DB11853) is an orally active, nonpeptide small-molecule gonadotropin-releasing hormone receptor antagonist built around a heteroaromatic, highly substituted urea-like/polar pharmacophore linked to fluorinated aromatic and alkoxy fragments, giving a compact, lipophilic medicinal-chemistry design optimized for potent pituitary GnRH receptor binding; chemically it is categorized as a synthetic nonsteroidal hormonal modulator, and its scaffold is commonly described as a diaryl/heteroaryl GnRH antagonist chemotype related to other small-molecule GnRH antagonists. Similar drugs include elagolix and linzagolix, which share the oral nonpeptide GnRH antagonist concept, whereas degarelix is mechanistically similar but peptide-based and parenteral. Its principal target is the gonadotropin-releasing hormone receptor, also called GNRHR or LHRHR, on anterior pituitary gonadotrophs, where antagonism rapidly suppresses luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone and thereby lowers testosterone in men or estradiol/progesterone in women. Pharmacokinetically, relugolix is orally absorbed, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, is highly protein bound, undergoes predominantly hepatic metabolism including CYP3A and CYP2C8 with transporter effects such as P-glycoprotein relevance, and is eliminated mainly in feces with a smaller urinary component; the terminal half-life supports once-daily dosing.
