Toxicity is largely an extension of profound sex-hormone suppression, including hot flushes, decreased libido, bone mineral density loss, amenorrhea, and potential embryo-fetal harm, with possible hepatic enzyme elevations and cardiovascular risk considerations in susceptible patients. Clinically it is used for advanced prostate cancer and, in some regions or combinations, for uterine fibroids and endometriosis-associated pain, with common adverse effects including hot flashes, fatigue, arthralgia, constipation or diarrhea, headache, mood changes, and musculoskeletal symptoms.

Name: Revefenacin
Description: Revefenacin (DB11855) is a long-acting inhaled muscarinic antagonist designed as a nonester, tertiary amide-containing bronchodilator with a biphenyl-carbamate–piperidine-like framework linked to a quaternary ammonium-containing pharmacophore, giving it the cationic antimuscarinic character typical of airway-selective bronchodilators; chemically it is categorized as a synthetic anticholinergic bronchodilator and more specifically a long-acting muscarinic antagonist, with a scaffold related conceptually to other quaternary ammonium bronchodilators built around bulky aromatic and amino-heterocyclic motifs. Similar drugs include tiotropium, umeclidinium, aclidinium, glycopyrrolate, and ipratropium, which share muscarinic receptor antagonism but differ in duration and structural details. Its principal targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially M3 (CHRM3) in airway smooth muscle, with additional binding to M1 (CHRM1) and M2 (CHRM2). After nebulized inhalation, systemic absorption is relatively limited, pulmonary residence is prolonged, protein binding is high, distribution is largely peripheral, metabolism occurs mainly via hepatic hydrolysis and oxidative biotransformation to an active metabolite and then further inactive metabolites, and elimination occurs through both fecal and renal routes with low unchanged urinary recovery. Toxicity is dominated by antimuscarinic effects; overdose or high exposure may cause tachycardia, urinary retention, blurred vision, constipation, dry mouth, or worsening narrow-angle glaucoma, while nonclinical concern also includes class-related cardiovascular effects. It is indicated for maintenance treatment of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, including chronic bronchitis and emphysema, to improve airflow limitation and reduce dyspnea, but not for acute bronchospasm. Common adverse effects include cough, nasopharyngitis, upper respiratory tract infection, headache, and back pain, with less common paradoxical bronchospasm or hypersensitivity. Clinically, it is used as once-daily nebulized maintenance therapy, particularly in COPD patients who benefit from nebulizer delivery because of poor inhaler coordination or low inspiratory flow.

Name: Laninamivir octanoate
Description: Laninamivir octanoate (DB11888) is a long-acting inhaled neuraminidase inhibitor prodrug structurally derived from laninamivir, consisting of a highly polar sialic acid/N-acetylneuraminic acid mimetic bearing a guanidino-substituted cyclohexene-like core and multiple hydroxyl groups, with an octanoyl ester promoiety that increases lipophilicity and pulmonary retention before enzymatic conversion to the active drug; chemically it is classified as an antiviral neuraminidase inhibitor prodrug and more specifically as an esterified zanamivir/laninamivir-related sialic acid analogue, with the core scaffold being a polyhydroxylated unsaturated cyclohexene carboxylate typical of influenza neuraminidase binders. Similar drugs include zanamivir, oseltamivir, and peramivir, all of which target influenza virus neuraminidase, although laninamivir octanoate is distinguished by prolonged airway residence and single-dose use. Its principal target proteins are influenza A and B viral neuraminidases, including N1 and N2 subtypes, where active laninamivir inhibits cleavage of terminal sialic acid residues and blocks virion release. After oral administration it is not used systemically; after inhalation, absorption from the respiratory tract is followed by local hydrolysis to laninamivir, low systemic exposure, limited distribution outside respiratory tissues, minimal further metabolism, and predominantly renal excretion of active laninamivir. Toxicity is generally low, but class-related concerns include bronchospasm, hypersensitivity, and rare neuropsychiatric or hepatic adverse events; overdose experience is limited. Indications include treatment and prophylaxis of influenza A and B, especially uncomplicated seasonal influenza with fever, cough, sore throat, and malaise. Common side effects include cough, nasal symptoms, diarrhea, headache, and nausea. Clinically, it is used as a single inhaled dose in adults and children in some countries, particularly when adherence to multi-dose neuraminidase inhibitor regimens is a concern.

Name: Prulifloxacin
Description: Prulifloxacin (DrugBank DB11892) is an oral fluoroquinolone antibacterial developed as a lipophilic prodrug of ulifloxacin, featuring the canonical quinolone core with a 6-fluoro substituent, a 7-piperazinyl-type heterocyclic side chain important for gram-negative activity, and an esterified promoiety that enhances oral delivery before conversion to the active carboxylic acid metabolite; chemically it belongs to the fluoroquinolone/quinolone carboxylic acid class and is built on the 4-quinolone scaffold shared with related agents such as ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, ofloxacin, norfloxacin, and ulifloxacin. Its antibacterial targets are bacterial DNA gyrase, especially GyrA/GyrB, and topoisomerase IV, especially ParC/ParE, leading to inhibition of DNA replication and bacterial cell death. After oral administration, prulifloxacin is well absorbed and rapidly hydrolyzed during first-pass metabolism to ulifloxacin; food has limited clinical impact, distribution is broad with penetration into urine, respiratory tissues, and prostate, protein binding is moderate, metabolism beyond prodrug activation is limited, and elimination occurs predominantly as unchanged ulifloxacin via renal excretion with some biliary/fecal contribution, supporting once-daily dosing in many settings. It is used for susceptible bacterial infections including acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, community respiratory infections, uncomplicated and complicated urinary tract infections, and prostatitis. Adverse effects are typical of fluoroquinolones, including nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, rash, photosensitivity, and less commonly QT prolongation, dysglycemia, hepatotoxicity, seizures, peripheral neuropathy, tendinopathy, and tendon rupture; toxicity concerns also include class warnings for CNS effects, Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea, and risk amplification in older adults, corticosteroid users, and patients with renal impairment.

Name: Apalutamide
Description: Apalutamide (DB11901) is a small-molecule, nonsteroidal antiandrogen built around a diaryl thiohydantoin-like scaffold featuring a substituted imidazolidine-2-thione core linked to fluorinated aryl groups and a nitrile-containing heteroaryl substituent, a structure designed to enhance high-affinity antagonism of the androgen receptor; chemically it belongs to the second-generation androgen receptor inhibitors, with a scaffold closely related to other aryl thiohydantoin/diaryl antiandrogens such as enzalutamide and, more distantly, darolutamide. Its principal target protein is the androgen receptor (nuclear receptor subfamily 3 group C member 4, NR3C4), where it inhibits androgen binding, receptor nuclear translocation, DNA binding, and transcriptional activation. After oral administration, apalutamide is well absorbed, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, is highly protein bound, distributes systemically, and undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP2C8 and CYP3A4 to the active metabolite N-desmethyl apalutamide; elimination is prolonged, supporting once-daily dosing, with excretion occurring through both urine and feces predominantly as metabolites. Toxicity is characterized mainly by dose-related class effects rather than acute organotoxicity, including seizure risk, falls, fractures, hypothyroidism, rash, and rare severe cutaneous reactions; embryo-fetal toxicity is expected from androgen-axis blockade. Adverse effects commonly include fatigue, hypertension, diarrhea, weight loss, arthralgia, hot flushes, peripheral edema, and decreased appetite. Clinically, apalutamide is used in prostate cancer, especially nonmetastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer, typically in combination with ongoing androgen-deprivation therapy to delay metastasis, prolong progression-free intervals, and improve survival-related outcomes.

Name: Valbenazine
Description: Valbenazine (DB11915) is a small-molecule vesicular monoamine transporter 2 inhibitor built as a highly substituted piperidine-containing valine ester prodrug of the active metabolite dihydrotetrabenazine; structurally it features an aryl-alkyl piperidine framework with methoxy-substituted aromatic elements and an isobutyl amino acid-derived promoiety, placing it in the central nervous system monoamine-depleting agents and piperidine/benzylic amine derivative category, with a tetrabenazine-like VMAT2 inhibitor scaffold. Closely related drugs include tetrabenazine and deutetrabenazine, as well as the active valbenazine metabolite [+]-alpha-dihydrotetrabenazine. Its principal target is SLC18A2/VMAT2, with functional reduction of presynaptic monoamine packaging, especially dopamine. After oral administration valbenazine is well absorbed, suitable for once-daily dosing, distributed systemically with substantial protein binding, and undergoes hydrolysis and oxidative metabolism, chiefly via CYP3A4/5 and CYP2D6, to active dihydrotetrabenazine metabolites; elimination occurs through both urine and feces with an effective half-life supporting steady-state maintenance. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related CNS depression and monoaminergic effects, including somnolence, fatigue, anticholinergic-like dry mouth, balance impairment, and potential QT prolongation; caution is warranted in hepatic impairment, poor CYP2D6 metabolizers, and with strong CYP inhibitors. It is indicated primarily for tardive dyskinesia and also used for chorea associated with Huntington disease, improving involuntary oro-buccal-lingual movements, limb choreiform activity, and functional motor burden. Common adverse effects include somnolence, akathisia, sedation, headache, constipation, and urinary retention, while clinical use emphasizes gradual titration, medication-interaction review, and monitoring for parkinsonism, depression or suicidality risk, and cardiac conduction effects in vulnerable patients.

Name: Deflazacort
Description: Deflazacort (DrugBank DB11921) is a synthetic oxazoline-containing glucocorticoid prodrug structurally derived from prednisolone, built on the pregnane corticosteroid tetracyclic steroid nucleus with characteristic 3-keto and 20-ketone functionality, a 1,4-diene A-ring, 11β- and 21-hydroxyl groups, and a fused 21-oxazoline/acetate-related substituent that distinguishes it from older corticosteroids; chemically it belongs to the corticosteroid, specifically glucocorticoid, class and uses the classic pregnane steroid scaffold. Similar drugs include prednisone, prednisolone, methylprednisolone, dexamethasone, and hydrocortisone, which share glucocorticoid receptor-mediated anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive actions. After oral administration, deflazacort is rapidly absorbed and extensively converted by plasma esterases to the active metabolite 21-desacetyldeflazacort; this metabolite distributes systemically with moderate protein binding, undergoes further hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites, with a relatively short parent half-life but pharmacologic activity determined by the active metabolite. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, with downstream transrepression of NF-κB- and AP-1-regulated inflammatory pathways and reduced cytokine production. It is indicated for inflammatory, autoimmune, allergic, and neuromuscular disorders, notably Duchenne muscular dystrophy, asthma exacerbations, rheumatoid conditions, nephrotic syndrome, and other steroid-responsive diseases. Toxicities reflect systemic corticosteroid exposure, including adrenal suppression, infection risk, hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, growth retardation, cataracts, glaucoma, mood changes, myopathy, hypertension, and Cushingoid effects; common side effects include weight gain, increased appetite, dyspepsia, behavioral change, edema, and sleep disturbance. Clinically it is used as an oral corticosteroid when chronic glucocorticoid therapy is needed, sometimes favored for a potentially somewhat reduced impact on bone and carbohydrate metabolism relative to some comparators.

Name: Vaniprevir
Description: Vaniprevir (DB11929) is a macrocyclic, peptidomimetic direct-acting antiviral designed as an inhibitor of the hepatitis C virus NS3/4A serine protease; structurally, it is a conformationally constrained acylsulfonamide-containing inhibitor with a densely functionalized macrocycle, multiple amide and heterocyclic features, and lipophilic substituents that optimize occupancy of the viral protease substrate-binding cleft. Chemically it belongs to the HCV NS3/4A protease inhibitor class, and its core scaffold is the macrocyclic ketoamide/acylsulfonamide peptidomimetic motif characteristic of second-generation HCV protease inhibitors. Similar drugs include telaprevir, boceprevir, simeprevir, paritaprevir, grazoprevir, and asunaprevir, with greatest structural and pharmacologic resemblance to other macrocyclic NS3/4A inhibitors. Its principal target is the HCV NS3/4A protease complex, thereby blocking viral polyprotein processing and replication. Pharmacokinetically, vaniprevir is orally administered, absorbed with moderate bioavailability, highly protein bound, distributed predominantly to the liver, metabolized mainly hepatically via CYP3A-mediated oxidation with transporter involvement, and eliminated chiefly through the biliary-fecal route with minimal renal excretion; exposure may increase in hepatic impairment or with strong CYP3A inhibitors. Toxicity is dominated by hepatic and gastrointestinal effects, with reported concerns including elevated transaminases, bilirubin abnormalities, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fatigue, pruritus, and headache; as with the class, drug-drug interactions can potentiate adverse events. Clinically, vaniprevir was developed for chronic hepatitis C, especially genotype 1 infection, typically in combination with peginterferon alfa and ribavirin to improve sustained virologic response in treatment-naive or treatment-experienced patients, but its use became limited as newer interferon-free regimens with broader coverage and better tolerability emerged.

Name: Abametapir
Description: Abametapir (DrugBank DB11932) is a small, lipophilic heteroaromatic pediculicide built around a substituted pyridine core bearing adjacent hydroxyl functionality and aryl substitution, giving a metal-chelating nitrosoxidative pharmacophore often described as a hydroxypyridine/aryl pyridinol structure; chemically it is classified as a heteroaryl anti-infective ectoparasiticide, and its principal scaffold is a halogenated biaryl pyridine related to other metalloproteinase-inhibitory hydroxypyridine chemotypes. Similar drugs are not close structural congeners in routine clinical use, but mechanistically and therapeutically it can be grouped with topical pediculicides such as ivermectin, malathion, permethrin, spinosad, and benzyl alcohol, which treat the same condition by different mechanisms. Its known pharmacologic target space is believed to involve metalloproteinases critical for louse egg development and survival, with broad inhibition of metal-dependent enzymes rather than one fully validated human protein target. Clinically, it is indicated for topical treatment of head louse infestation, Pediculus humanus capitis, including eradication of lice and ova in affected patients. Systemic pharmacokinetic exposure after topical administration is low but measurable, with limited dermal absorption, distribution expected to favor lipid-rich compartments, hepatic metabolism likely involving oxidative and conjugative pathways, and elimination presumed mainly through urinary and possibly fecal excretion as metabolites. Toxicity is chiefly local and exposure-related: skin or scalp irritation, erythema, burning sensation, rash, and ocular irritation can occur, while excessive ingestion or broad exposure could theoretically increase systemic toxicity. Reported adverse effects are generally mild, including application-site erythema, rash, burning, and contact irritation. In practice, abametapir is used as a single topical lotion treatment for head lice, particularly when ovicidal activity is desired to reduce retreatment needs and improve adherence.

Name: Bempedoic acid
Description: Bempedoic acid (DB11936) is a small-molecule, nonstatin antihyperlipidemic agent structurally characterized as a substituted dicarboxylic fatty-acid derivative with a long aliphatic chain, terminal carboxylic acid functionality, and an aryl-ether-linked ketoacid motif; chemically it is an ACL inhibitor prodrug within the class of synthetic lipid-lowering carboxylic acids, built on a lipophilic fatty-acid/ketoacid scaffold that functionally resembles intermediary metabolites upstream of cholesterol biosynthesis. It is most similar pharmacologically to other LDL-C lowering drugs such as statins, ezetimibe, and PCSK9-pathway inhibitors, although structurally it is closer to fatty-acid-like small molecules than to HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors. After oral administration it is well absorbed, highly protein bound, activated mainly in the liver by very-long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase 1 (SLC27A2/ACSVL1) to bempedoyl-CoA, distributed predominantly to hepatic tissue with minimal skeletal muscle activation, metabolized further by conjugation including glucuronidation and reversible conversion to an active metabolite, and excreted primarily in urine as metabolites with a lesser fecal component. Its principal target is ATP-citrate lyase (ACLY), reducing hepatic cholesterol synthesis and upregulating LDL receptors; liver-selective activation helps limit myotoxicity relative to statins. It is indicated for hypercholesterolemia, including heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia and established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease requiring additional LDL-C reduction, often with maximally tolerated statins or when statins are inadequate or poorly tolerated. Important adverse effects and toxicities include hyperuricemia and gout, mild reversible increases in hepatic enzymes and creatinine, tendon injury or rupture, abdominal pain, upper respiratory symptoms, muscle spasms, back or extremity pain, and occasional anemia; clinically it is used alone or in fixed combination with ezetimibe to lower LDL-C and reduce cardiovascular risk in high-risk patients.

Name: Difelikefalin
Description: Difelikefalin (DrugBank DB11938) is a synthetic, peripherally restricted opioid tetrapeptide designed as a selective kappa opioid receptor agonist; structurally it is a highly polar peptide-like small molecule built on a short D-amino-acid-rich peptide framework with a modified Tyr/D-Phe/D-Leu/Lys-derived arrangement and terminal functionalization that enhances metabolic stability, limits passive blood-brain barrier penetration, and favors peripheral receptor engagement. Chemically, it belongs to the peptide opioid class, more specifically a kappa-opioid agonist peptidomimetic, and its core scaffold is a constrained hydrophilic tetrapeptide opioid pharmacophore related conceptually to other kappa agonists. Similar drugs include nalfurafine, U50,488, spiradoline, and the mixed opioid peptide analogs that share kappa-preferring activity, although difelikefalin is distinguished by its peripheral selectivity and peptide character. Its principal known target is OPRK1, the kappa opioid receptor, with clinically relevant antipruritic signaling attributed to peripheral neuronal and possibly immune-cell receptor activation. Pharmacokinetically, it is administered intravenously or orally depending on formulation context, has limited CNS distribution, low protein binding, minimal CYP-mediated metabolism, and is cleared predominantly unchanged by the kidney, with exposure increased in renal impairment. Toxicity is generally consistent with opioid-class and kappa-agonist effects but is comparatively limited in central dysphoria or hallucinations because of restricted brain entry; overdose or high exposure may increase sedation, dizziness, or impaired mental status. It is indicated primarily for moderate-to-severe pruritus, especially chronic kidney disease-associated pruritus in hemodialysis patients, and is used clinically to reduce itching burden and improve quality of life, with common adverse effects including diarrhea, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, gait disturbance, headache, somnolence, and occasional hyperkalemia or confusion.

Name: Selinexor
Description: Selinexor (DB11942) is a small-molecule, orally active selective inhibitor of nuclear export characterized structurally by a highly substituted, drug-like heteroaromatic framework containing a Michael-acceptor alkenyl linkage attached to a trifluoromethyl-substituted pyrazine-bearing scaffold and lipophilic aryl functionality; chemically it is best classified as a synthetic heteroaryl antineoplastic agent and covalent exportin inhibitor, with a scaffold related to the SINE class built around a substituted pyazine/alkenyl pharmacophore rather than a natural-product core. Its closest similar drugs are other XPO1/exportin-1 inhibitors, especially eltanexor and the earlier tool compound verdinexor, which share the same mechanistic class. Selinexor targets XPO1/CRM1, forming a slowly reversible covalent interaction with the cargo-binding cysteine and thereby retaining tumor suppressor proteins such as TP53, RB1, FOXO, IKB, and regulators of glucocorticoid signaling in the nucleus, while indirectly modulating NF-kB and oncogenic protein translation pathways. After oral administration it is absorbed with peak concentrations in a few hours, is widely distributed, is highly protein bound, undergoes predominantly hepatic biotransformation including glucuronidation and oxidative metabolism with only limited unchanged renal elimination, and has a terminal half-life on the order of several hours supporting intermittent dosing. It is indicated for relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma, including use with dexamethasone and in combination regimens such as bortezomib-based therapy, and for relapsed or refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Its toxicity profile is clinically distinctive, with dose-limiting thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, anemia, severe nausea, vomiting, anorexia, weight loss, fatigue, hyponatremia, dehydration, and infection risk; neurocognitive effects, dizziness, cataract, and hepatobiliary laboratory abnormalities may also occur. In practice, clinical use requires antiemetic prophylaxis, close blood count and electrolyte monitoring, nutritional support, dose interruption or reduction, and careful management of frail or heavily pretreated patients.

Name: Delafloxacin
Description: Delafloxacin (DB11943) is an anionic fluoroquinolone antibacterial built on the quinolone-3-carboxylic acid core, bearing the characteristic 4-oxo motif, a fluorinated heteroaromatic system, and a bulky heterocyclic substituent that differentiates it from older zwitterionic quinolones and enhances activity in acidic environments; chemically it is classified as a fluoroquinolone antibiotic, with a quinolone/pyridone bicyclic scaffold closely related to other DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV inhibitors such as ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, and besifloxacin. Its principal targets are bacterial DNA gyrase subunits GyrA and GyrB and topoisomerase IV subunits ParC and ParE, leading to inhibition of DNA replication and cell death. Delafloxacin is indicated for acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections and community-acquired bacterial pneumonia, including infections caused by susceptible Gram-positive organisms such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and selected Gram-negative pathogens. Pharmacokinetically, it is available intravenously and orally, has moderate oral bioavailability, broad tissue distribution with clinically useful penetration into skin, soft tissue, and lung, modest protein binding, limited oxidative metabolism with substantial recovery of parent drug and conjugated metabolites, and elimination predominantly via renal excretion with a smaller fecal component, supporting dose adjustment in significant renal impairment for intravenous use. Class-related toxicities include tendinopathy and tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, central nervous system effects, dysglycemia, hypersensitivity, Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea, and selection of resistant organisms; common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, headache, transaminase elevation, and infusion-site reactions. Clinically, it is used as empiric or directed monotherapy when a broad-spectrum fluoroquinolone active against resistant skin or respiratory pathogens is needed.

Name: Teneligliptin
Description: Teneligliptin (DrugBank DB11950) is a synthetic, orally active dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor characterized by a rigid, J-shaped heteroaromatic structure containing a pyrrolidine-linked piperazine core attached to a thiazolidine/thiazoline-like sulfur-containing ring system and substituted phenyl and pyrazolyl moieties, a design that supports high-affinity binding within the extended S1, S2, and S2 extensive pockets of DPP-4; chemically it is a small-molecule nitrogen- and sulfur-containing heterocycle, and its core scaffold is commonly described as a piperazine-pyrrolidine DPP-4 inhibitor chemotype. Similar drugs include other gliptins such as sitagliptin, vildagliptin, saxagliptin, linagliptin, alogliptin, and anagliptin, which share incretin-enhancing pharmacology despite distinct scaffolds. Its principal target is DPP4/CD26, leading to reduced degradation of GLP-1 and GIP, increased glucose-dependent insulin secretion, and suppression of glucagon. Teneligliptin is used for type 2 diabetes mellitus, particularly for improvement of glycemic control as monotherapy or in combination with agents such as metformin, sulfonylureas, pioglitazone, insulin, or SGLT2 inhibitors. Oral absorption is generally good, protein binding is moderate, distribution is systemic, metabolism occurs through both CYP3A4-dependent and flavin monooxygenase-mediated pathways with some unchanged drug persisting, and elimination is mixed renal and fecal, giving a relatively long half-life that supports once-daily dosing. Adverse effects are usually mild and include hypoglycemia when combined with insulin secretagogues, constipation, nausea, dizziness, headache, and nasopharyngitis; important toxicities include rare hepatic dysfunction, pancreatitis, severe hypersensitivity, skin reactions, and QT-interval prolongation risk at high exposure or in predisposed patients.

Name: Lemborexant
Description: Lemborexant (DrugBank DB11951) is a small-molecule dual orexin receptor antagonist whose structure is defined by a compact, conformationally restricted heteroaromatic scaffold containing oxygen- and nitrogen-bearing ring systems linked to substituted aromatic elements, giving a lipophilic, CNS-penetrant chemotype optimized for high-affinity antagonism at orexin receptors; chemically it is categorized as a diazepane/heteroaryl insomnia therapeutic within the broader class of orexin antagonists, with a fused or semi-rigid heterocyclic scaffold distinct from classical benzodiazepines and Z-drugs. Similar agents include suvorexant and daridorexant, which share dual OX1R/OX2R antagonism, although lemborexant shows particularly strong functional activity at orexin-mediated wake signaling. Its known targets are orexin receptor type 1 and orexin receptor type 2, with clinically relevant hypnotic efficacy largely attributed to suppression of orexin-driven arousal pathways, especially via OX2R. Pharmacokinetically, it is orally active, absorbed with a time to peak of roughly 1 to 3 hours, highly protein bound, distributed sufficiently to reach the brain, extensively metabolized hepatically mainly by CYP3A-mediated oxidation, and eliminated predominantly as metabolites in feces with a smaller urinary component; exposure rises with CYP3A inhibitors and falls with inducers. It is indicated for insomnia, particularly sleep-onset and sleep-maintenance difficulties, and is used clinically in adults with chronic insomnia characterized by difficulty falling asleep, frequent nocturnal awakening, or nonrestorative sleep. Adverse effects and toxicity are chiefly CNS depressant-related, including somnolence, fatigue, dizziness, headache, abnormal dreams, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations, complex sleep behaviors, and next-day impairment, with greater concern in overdose, hepatic impairment, or combination with alcohol, opioids, or other sedatives.

Name: Duvelisib
Description: Duvelisib (DB11952) is an orally active small-molecule phosphoinositide 3-kinase inhibitor built on a fused bicyclic heteroaryl kinase-inhibitor framework, commonly described as a purine-like or azaindole/heteroaromatic scaffold bearing substituted aryl and lipophilic amine-containing motifs that support ATP-site binding; chemically, it belongs to the class of targeted antineoplastic kinase inhibitors, more specifically PI3K inhibitors, with a scaffold and mechanism broadly similar to other PI3K-pathway drugs such as idelalisib, copanlisib, alpelisib, and the dual PI3K/mTOR agent dactolisib. Its principal targets are the class I PI3K isoforms p110-delta (PIK3CD) and p110-gamma (PIK3CG), producing inhibition of malignant B-cell signaling and modulation of the tumor microenvironment. Duvelisib is indicated mainly for relapsed or refractory chronic lymphocytic leukemia, small lymphocytic lymphoma, and follicular lymphoma after prior therapies, and in clinical use it has been administered as an oral therapy for heavily pretreated indolent B-cell malignancies. Pharmacokinetically, it is orally absorbed, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, is moderately protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4, and is eliminated through both fecal and urinary routes, with fecal excretion generally predominant and a terminal half-life supporting twice-daily dosing. Toxicity is clinically significant and includes serious infections, opportunistic pneumonia, hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevation, severe diarrhea or colitis, cutaneous reactions, and pneumonitis; common adverse effects include neutropenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, fatigue, nausea, cough, pyrexia, rash, and transaminitis, necessitating monitoring, dose interruption, antimicrobial prophylaxis in selected patients, and careful risk-benefit assessment in routine oncology practice.

Name: Dacomitinib
Description: Dacomitinib (DB11963) is an orally active, small-molecule 4-anilinoquinazoline derivative whose structure features a quinazoline heteroaromatic core substituted with an aniline-linked electrophilic moiety that enables irreversible receptor binding, along with ether and piperidine-containing side-chain functionality that modulates lipophilicity and kinase affinity; chemically it is classified as an anilinoquinazoline tyrosine kinase inhibitor, and its core scaffold is the covalent EGFR/HER-family inhibitor pharmacophore exemplified by quinazoline-based ErbB antagonists. Closely related drugs include afatinib, gefitinib, erlotinib, and osimertinib, especially other EGFR-directed kinase inhibitors, with afatinib being the most mechanistically similar irreversible pan-HER inhibitor. Its principal targets are EGFR/ERBB1, HER2/ERBB2, and HER4/ERBB4, with inhibition of ATP-site signaling leading to suppression of MAPK and PI3K/AKT pathways. Clinically, it is indicated for metastatic non-small cell lung cancer harboring EGFR-activating mutations such as exon 19 deletions or exon 21 L858R substitution, and is used as first-line targeted therapy in appropriate molecularly selected patients. Pharmacokinetically, it is orally absorbed with a relatively long half-life permitting once-daily dosing, is highly protein bound, widely distributed, metabolized mainly by oxidative and glutathione-related pathways with CYP2D6 involvement but limited dependence on CYP-mediated clearance overall, and is excreted predominantly in feces with lesser urinary elimination. Toxicity is dominated by mechanism-based epithelial injury, including severe diarrhea, rash, stomatitis, paronychia, dehydration, interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis, and hepatotoxicity; common adverse effects include acneiform dermatitis, dry skin, mucositis, decreased appetite, and weight loss, and dose reduction or interruption is often required in routine oncology practice.

Name: Ilaprazole
Description: Ilaprazole (DrugBank DB11964) is a substituted benzimidazole proton-pump inhibitor characterized by the classic acid-labile PPI architecture of a benzimidazole ring linked through a sulfoxide bridge to a substituted pyridine, with additional lipophilic ring substitution that increases potency and duration relative to some earlier agents. Chemically it belongs to the benzimidazole sulfoxide class of antisecretory agents, and its core scaffold is the omeprazole-like benzimidazole–sulfoxide–pyridine pharmacophore shared by related PPIs such as omeprazole, esomeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole, and rabeprazole. After oral administration, ilaprazole is absorbed in the small intestine, reaches systemic circulation as a prodrug, distributes sufficiently to gastric parietal cells, and becomes protonated and activated in the acidic canaliculus, where it forms reactive sulfenamide intermediates that covalently inhibit the gastric H+/K+-ATPase, principally ATP4A/ATP4B. It undergoes hepatic biotransformation, reportedly with less dependence on CYP2C19 polymorphism than some PPIs and contribution from CYP3A-mediated pathways, with metabolites excreted mainly in urine and feces. Its principal indication is acid-related disease, especially gastroesophageal reflux disease, erosive esophagitis, duodenal ulcer, gastric ulcer, dyspepsia, and prevention or treatment of peptic injury associated with hypersecretory states. Adverse effects are generally similar to other PPIs and include headache, diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea, constipation, dizziness, and rash; longer-term class toxicities may include hypergastrinemia, vitamin B12 or magnesium deficiency, fracture risk, enteric infection, and interstitial nephritis. Clinically, ilaprazole is used for symptomatic reflux control, ulcer healing, maintenance therapy, and as part of antiulcer regimens where durable acid suppression is desired.

Name: Binimetinib
Description: Binimetinib (DB11967) is a small-molecule, orally active, ATP-noncompetitive allosteric inhibitor of MAPK/ERK kinase 1 and 2, structurally characterized by a substituted heteroaromatic amide architecture containing a halogenated aromatic ring linked to a nitrogen-rich bicyclic/aza-heterocyclic core and polar hydrogen-bonding groups that support selective MEK binding; chemically it is best categorized as a targeted antineoplastic kinase inhibitor, more specifically a heteroaryl amide MEK inhibitor, built on the aryl-heterocycle carboxamide scaffold typical of allosteric MEK inhibitors. Closely related drugs include trametinib, cobimetinib, and selumetinib, which share MEK1/2 pathway inhibition despite differing peripheral ring substitutions and physicochemical properties. Its principal targets are MAP2K1/MEK1 and MAP2K2/MEK2, suppressing downstream ERK signaling in tumors with MAPK pathway activation. Binimetinib is indicated primarily, in combination with encorafenib, for unresectable or metastatic melanoma with BRAF V600E or V600K mutations, and has also been clinically explored in other RAS/RAF-driven malignancies such as colorectal and ovarian cancers. After oral administration it is absorbed with moderate bioavailability, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, is moderately protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes predominant metabolic clearance via glucuronidation and other phase I/II biotransformation pathways, and is eliminated through both fecal and urinary routes with a relatively short terminal half-life requiring twice-daily dosing. Toxicities include cardiomyopathy with reduced ejection fraction, retinal pigment epithelial detachment and other ocular events, hepatotoxicity, creatine phosphokinase elevation, interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis, and embryo-fetal toxicity; common adverse effects include fatigue, nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, abdominal pain, rash, peripheral edema, acneiform dermatitis, and visual disturbance. In clinical practice it is used as precision therapy in BRAF-mutant melanoma, especially to enhance pathway suppression and delay resistance when paired with a BRAF inhibitor.

Name: Glasdegib
Description: Glasdegib (DB11978) is an orally active small-molecule hedgehog-pathway inhibitor built on a substituted pyridine/heteroaryl scaffold in which a central aromatic nitrogen-containing ring system is linked to additional lipophilic aryl and amine-bearing motifs, giving a compact, drug-like heterocycle-rich structure optimized for Smoothened binding; chemically it is best classified as a synthetic heteroaromatic antineoplastic agent and more specifically a Smoothened antagonist, with a scaffold related pharmacologically to other hedgehog inhibitors such as vismodegib and sonidegib, although its exact chemotype is distinct. Its principal target protein is Smoothened (SMO), thereby suppressing downstream GLI-mediated hedgehog signaling implicated in leukemic stem-cell maintenance. After oral administration, glasdegib is absorbed with moderate bioavailability, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, shows a large apparent volume of distribution and meaningful plasma protein binding, and is cleared primarily by hepatic metabolism, predominantly via CYP3A4 with minor renal excretion of unchanged drug; its terminal half-life supports once-daily dosing. Toxicologically, it carries embryo-fetal toxicity risk consistent with hedgehog-pathway inhibition, can prolong the QT interval, and may cause clinically relevant myelosuppression and hepatic laboratory abnormalities. The approved indication is newly diagnosed acute myeloid leukemia in older adults or patients with substantial comorbidity who are unsuitable for intensive induction chemotherapy, specifically in combination with low-dose cytarabine; clinically it is used in frail AML populations to reduce leukemic burden and improve survival endpoints. Common adverse effects include anemia, thrombocytopenia, febrile neutropenia, fatigue, nausea, decreased appetite, dysgeusia, constipation, diarrhea, mucositis, edema, muscle spasms, dyspnea, and rash.

Name: Entrectinib
Description: Entrectinib (DrugBank DB11986) is an orally active, small-molecule, ATP-competitive multikinase inhibitor with a compact heteroaromatic structure built around a substituted aza/heterobiaryl aromatic core linked to lipophilic aryl and nitrogen-containing functionalities that promote kinase hinge binding and central nervous system penetration; chemically it is classified as a targeted antineoplastic tyrosine kinase inhibitor, and its scaffold is commonly described as a substituted aminopyridine/heteroaryl kinase-inhibitor framework. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other TRK/ROS1-directed agents such as larotrectinib, repotrectinib, crizotinib, and to some extent ceritinib. Its principal targets are TRKA/NTRK1, TRKB/NTRK2, TRKC/NTRK3, ROS1, and ALK, with antitumor activity driven mainly by inhibition of constitutively activated fusion kinases. After oral administration, entrectinib is absorbed systemically, reaches meaningful tissue and intracranial exposure, is highly protein bound, is metabolized predominantly by CYP3A4 to the active metabolite M5, and is eliminated mainly via feces with limited renal excretion; exposure can increase with strong CYP3A modulators. Clinically, it is indicated for NTRK gene fusion-positive solid tumors, including salivary gland, thyroid, sarcoma, and lung cancers, and for ROS1-positive non-small cell lung cancer, especially when brain metastases are present. Adverse effects commonly include fatigue, dysgeusia, dizziness, constipation, diarrhea, nausea, edema, weight gain, cognitive disturbance, and anemia. Important toxicities include congestive heart failure, QT prolongation, hepatotoxicity, hyperuricemia, skeletal fractures, and CNS effects such as ataxia or confusion, so clinical use requires molecular selection, monitoring of hepatic and cardiac function, and management of drug-drug interactions.

Name: Omarigliptin
Description: Omarigliptin (DB11992) is a long-acting, orally active dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor built as a small, highly substituted heteroaromatic amine containing a fluorinated piperidine-linked scaffold and polar nitrogen-rich ring system that confers potent, selective, once-weekly DPP-4 binding; chemically it is categorized as an antidiabetic gliptin and more specifically a fluorinated aminopiperidine-based DPP-4 inhibitor, with a scaffold broadly related to other class members such as sitagliptin, alogliptin, linagliptin, saxagliptin, vildagliptin, and trelagliptin, although omarigliptin is distinguished by its extended duration of action. Its principal target protein is DPP4/CD26, and inhibition increases endogenous incretin activity, especially GLP-1 and GIP signaling, thereby improving glucose-dependent insulin secretion and suppressing glucagon. Pharmacokinetically, omarigliptin is orally absorbed with a long elimination half-life compatible with once-weekly dosing, relatively limited biotransformation, low-to-moderate protein binding, and elimination predominantly as unchanged drug through renal excretion, making kidney function relevant to exposure and dose selection. Toxicity is generally modest and class-consistent, with low intrinsic hypoglycemia risk when used alone, but higher risk in combination with insulin or sulfonylureas; postmarketing or class-associated concerns include hypersensitivity reactions, severe arthralgia, pancreatitis, hepatic enzyme elevation, and possible bullous pemphigoid. It is indicated for type 2 diabetes mellitus to improve glycemic control, particularly elevated fasting glucose and HbA1c, and is used clinically as monotherapy when metformin is unsuitable or in combination regimens with metformin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones, insulin, or SGLT2 inhibitors; common adverse effects include nasopharyngitis, upper respiratory symptoms, headache, gastrointestinal discomfort, and sometimes peripheral edema or rash.

Name: Avatrombopag
Description: Avatrombopag (DrugBank DB11995) is an orally active, nonpeptide small-molecule thrombopoietin receptor agonist built around a highly lipophilic heteroaryl biaryl scaffold containing substituted aromatic rings and nitrogen-bearing heterocycles with a terminal carboxylic acid functionality, placing it in the chemical category of thrombopoietic agents and synthetic TPO-receptor agonists; its scaffold is broadly related to other small-molecule c-Mpl agonists such as eltrombopag and lusutrombopag, although it is structurally distinct from peptide agonists like romiplostim. Its principal target protein is the thrombopoietin receptor MPL (CD110, c-Mpl), with downstream activation of JAK2/STAT signaling that promotes megakaryocyte proliferation and platelet production. Pharmacokinetically, avatrombopag is orally absorbed, with exposure increased by food and generally suitable for once-daily dosing; it is highly protein bound, distributed systemically, metabolized predominantly in the liver via CYP2C9 and CYP3A-mediated oxidation, and eliminated mainly through feces with limited renal excretion. Clinically, it is indicated for thrombocytopenia in adults with chronic liver disease undergoing procedures and for chronic immune thrombocytopenia, where it is used to raise platelet counts and reduce bleeding risk or the need for rescue therapy. Toxicity is dominated by exaggerated pharmacology, especially thrombocytosis and thromboembolic complications such as portal vein thrombosis or venous thromboembolism, with additional concerns including hepatobiliary laboratory abnormalities and potential drug interactions from CYP modulation. Common adverse effects include headache, fatigue, nausea, pyrexia, abdominal pain, arthralgia, edema, and upper respiratory symptoms.

Name: Abemaciclib
Description: Abemaciclib (DB12001) is an orally active, small-molecule antineoplastic agent of the targeted kinase inhibitor class, specifically a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor with selectivity for CDK4 and CDK6; structurally, it is a substituted 2-aminopyrimidine/pyridine-rich heteroaromatic compound bearing halogenated aryl and piperazine-like basic features that support ATP-site binding and oral bioavailability, and its core chemical scaffold is commonly described as an aminopyrimidine-based kinase-inhibitor scaffold. It is closely related pharmacologically to other CDK4/6 inhibitors such as palbociclib and ribociclib, which share ATP-competitive inhibition of cell-cycle kinases, although abemaciclib is often considered somewhat more CDK4-selective and more continuously dosed. Its principal targets are CDK4 and CDK6, with downstream suppression of retinoblastoma protein phosphorylation and G1-to-S cell-cycle progression; weaker activity against other kinases including CDK9 has been reported. Pharmacokinetically, it is well absorbed orally, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, is highly protein bound, distributes broadly into tissues, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism predominantly via CYP3A4 to active metabolites, and is eliminated mainly in feces with limited renal excretion; the terminal half-life supports twice-daily dosing. Clinically, it is indicated primarily for hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced or metastatic breast cancer, including use with endocrine therapy such as fulvestrant or aromatase inhibitors and as monotherapy in selected previously treated patients. Major toxicities include dose-limiting diarrhea, neutropenia, leukopenia, anemia, fatigue, nausea, hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevation, venous thromboembolism, and less commonly interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis, so monitoring of blood counts, liver function, and gastrointestinal toxicity is central to safe use.

Name: Fostamatinib
Description: Fostamatinib (DB12010) is an orally available small-molecule kinase inhibitor administered as a phosphate prodrug that is rapidly converted to the active metabolite R406; structurally it is a heteroaryl-substituted aminopyrimidine/azaindole-like system bearing a phosphated hydroxyl functionality to enhance solubility, and it is best classified as a synthetic tyrosine kinase inhibitor, specifically a spleen tyrosine kinase inhibitor, built on a fused nitrogen-containing aromatic kinase-binding scaffold typical of ATP-competitive inhibitors. It is chemically and pharmacologically related to other multi-kinase or immunomodulatory tyrosine kinase inhibitors, with mechanistic similarities often noted to SYK-pathway inhibitors and broader kinase inhibitors such as entospletinib, cerdulatinib, and to some extent multitarget agents like dasatinib, although fostamatinib is distinguished by its prodrug design and SYK emphasis. Its principal target is SYK, but R406 also inhibits kinases including FLT3, JAK-family members, LYN, and VEGFR-related pathways at varying potencies, contributing to both efficacy and off-target effects. After oral dosing, fostamatinib is absorbed and extensively converted in the gut to R406, which is systemically distributed with high protein binding, metabolized mainly by CYP3A4-mediated oxidation and UGT1A9 glucuronidation, and excreted primarily in feces with lesser urinary elimination. Clinically it is used mainly for chronic immune thrombocytopenia in adults refractory to prior therapy, improving platelet counts by reducing Fc receptor-mediated platelet destruction; it has also been explored in autoimmune and inflammatory disorders. Important adverse effects and toxicities include diarrhea, hypertension, hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevation, neutropenia, dizziness, nausea, rash, and infection risk, with examples of severe toxicity including hypertensive urgency, significant liver enzyme abnormalities, and embryo-fetal harm, so clinical use requires blood pressure, liver function, and hematologic monitoring.

Name: Alpelisib
Description: Alpelisib (DrugBank DB12015) is an orally active, small-molecule phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase inhibitor whose structure is built around a substituted aminothiazole-pyridine/pyrimidine-like heteroaromatic core linked to lipophilic aryl and ether functionalities, creating an ATP-competitive kinase-binding pharmacophore; chemically, it is classified as a targeted antineoplastic aminothiazole-containing heteroaryl kinase inhibitor, with a scaffold characteristic of class I PI3K inhibitors and closest in medicinal chemistry space to other PI3K-pathway drugs such as idelalisib, copanlisib, duvelisib, and the dual PI3K/mTOR inhibitor dactolisib, although alpelisib is distinguished by its relative selectivity for the p110alpha catalytic isoform. Its principal target is phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate 3-kinase catalytic subunit alpha, encoded by PIK3CA, with downstream suppression of AKT/mTOR signaling. After oral administration, absorption is adequate and improved with food, peak concentrations occur within hours, protein binding is moderate to high, tissue distribution is sufficient for solid-tumor exposure, metabolism occurs mainly through chemical and enzymatic amide hydrolysis with lesser CYP3A4 contribution, and elimination is primarily via feces with a smaller urinary component; the terminal half-life supports once-daily dosing. Clinically, it is indicated for PIK3CA-mutated, hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced or metastatic breast cancer, typically combined with fulvestrant after endocrine resistance, and has also been used in PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum. Toxicities reflect on-target pathway inhibition and include marked hyperglycemia, rash, diarrhea, stomatitis, nausea, fatigue, decreased appetite, weight loss, and less commonly severe cutaneous reactions, pneumonitis, colitis, and embryo-fetal toxicity, so clinical use requires mutation selection, glucose monitoring, rash management, and dose interruption or reduction when adverse effects emerge.

Name: Ozagrel
Description: Ozagrel (DB12017) is a small synthetic antiplatelet agent structurally characterized as an aromatic heterocycle-bearing acrylic acid derivative, consisting of an imidazole ring linked through a styryl/vinyl spacer to a benzoic acid-like acidic terminus; chemically it is classified as a thromboxane A2 synthase inhibitor within the broader class of eicosanoid-modulating agents, and its core scaffold can be summarized as an imidazolyl-substituted unsaturated aryl carboxylic acid. It is chemically and pharmacologically related to other antithrombotic drugs that interfere with thromboxane signaling, including dazoxiben and, more broadly by pathway similarity rather than structure, aspirin and thromboxane receptor antagonists such as ifetroban. Its principal target is thromboxane-A synthase, encoded by CYP5A1, leading to suppression of thromboxane A2 generation, reduced platelet aggregation, and attenuation of vasoconstriction. Clinically, ozagrel has been used mainly in cerebrovascular settings, particularly for improvement of cerebral vasospasm and ischemic symptoms after subarachnoid hemorrhage surgery, and for acute thrombotic or ischemic cerebrovascular disorders such as cerebral thrombosis-associated motor deficits. Pharmacokinetically, it is typically administered parenterally in clinical practice, producing rapid systemic exposure, limited distribution largely in extracellular fluid, hepatic metabolism with formation of inactive metabolites, and predominantly renal urinary excretion; elimination is relatively short, supporting infusion-based dosing. Adverse effects reflect antiplatelet activity and include bleeding, hemorrhagic transformation of stroke, gastrointestinal symptoms, rash, and liver enzyme elevation, while toxicity concerns center on serious intracranial, gastrointestinal, or postoperative bleeding, hepatic dysfunction, and caution in patients with active bleeding risk or severe hepatic impairment.

Name: Tecovirimat
Description: Tecovirimat (DrugBank DB12020) is a small-molecule antiviral with a highly lipophilic, polycyclic aromatic structure built around a substituted tricyclononene-related hydrophobic core linked to an amide-containing side chain and additional electron-withdrawing/heteroatom-bearing substituents that support target binding and oral bioavailability; chemically it is best classified as a synthetic orthopoxvirus egress inhibitor within the broader amide-containing antiviral class, and its key scaffold is a rigid fused carbocyclic cage-like aryl system rather than a nucleoside analogue framework. It is structurally and mechanistically distinct from older anti-orthopox agents such as cidofovir and brincidofovir, which are nucleotide/nucleoside phosphonate DNA polymerase inhibitors, but these drugs are often considered therapeutically similar comparators in smallpox or mpox management. Tecovirimat targets the orthopoxvirus VP37 envelope wrapping protein, encoded by F13L in vaccinia and homologous proteins in variola and monkeypox viruses, thereby blocking formation of extracellular enveloped virions and viral dissemination. It is indicated for treatment of smallpox and has been used clinically and under expanded-access protocols for mpox and other serious orthopoxvirus infections. Oral absorption is improved with food, distribution is systemic with substantial protein binding, metabolism occurs mainly through hydrolysis and glucuronidation with limited CYP involvement, and elimination is primarily via urinary metabolites with some fecal excretion. Toxicity is generally low relative to alternative antivirals; nonclinical concerns have included reversible gastrointestinal and hepatic findings at high exposures, while resistance can arise through VP37 mutations. Common adverse effects include headache, nausea, abdominal pain, and vomiting, and clinical use includes oral or intravenous treatment of adults and children with confirmed or suspected orthopoxvirus disease, especially severe, disseminated, ocular, or immunocompromised-host infection.

Name: Voxilaprevir
Description: Voxilaprevir (DB12026) is a direct-acting antiviral for hepatitis C virus and is chemically a complex, lipophilic peptidomimetic NS3/4A protease inhibitor built around a conformationally constrained macrocyclic scaffold with multiple fused or linked heterocyclic and carbamate/amide functionalities, designed to mimic protease substrate geometry while improving potency against resistant variants; thus, its chemical category is a macrocyclic antiviral protease inhibitor and its scaffold is closely related to the ketoamide-derived, macrocycle-rich HCV NS3/4A inhibitor chemotype seen in agents such as grazoprevir, glecaprevir, simeprevir, paritaprevir, and voxilaprevir’s broader class analogs. Its principal target is the HCV NS3/4A serine protease, whose inhibition blocks viral polyprotein cleavage and replication across multiple genotypes. Clinically, voxilaprevir is used in combination therapy, most notably with sofosbuvir and velpatasvir, for chronic hepatitis C infection including genotype-diverse disease and salvage treatment in patients previously exposed to NS5A inhibitor-containing regimens. Pharmacokinetically, it is orally absorbed, reaches peak concentrations within hours, is highly protein bound, has limited distribution outside plasma, undergoes predominantly hepatic metabolism with minor CYP-mediated biotransformation, and is eliminated mainly via biliary/fecal excretion with minimal renal clearance, making hepatic function more clinically relevant than kidney function. Toxicity is generally dominated by hepatobiliary risk, including transaminase elevations and increased exposure in moderate to severe hepatic impairment, with examples of worsened liver-related adverse outcomes in advanced liver disease; common side effects in combination regimens include headache, fatigue, diarrhea, and nausea. Overall, its clinical usage centers on resistant or previously treated HCV infection where potent NS3/4A inhibition complements nucleotide and NS5A inhibitors to improve sustained virologic response.

Name: Sarecycline
Description: Sarecycline (DB12035) is a third-generation, narrow-spectrum tetracycline-class antibiotic built on the classic tetracyclic naphthacene carboxamide scaffold of tetracyclines, with a distinctive extended C7 side chain on the D ring that increases lipophilicity and helps differentiate it from older congeners; chemically it is an aminomethylcycline-related tetracycline derivative and is structurally and pharmacologically similar to doxycycline, minocycline, and tetracycline, while also showing conceptual similarity to other modern tetracycline-family agents such as omadacycline and eravacycline. Its primary target is the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit, especially 16S rRNA within the decoding region, where it inhibits aminoacyl-tRNA accommodation and suppresses protein synthesis, with activity against Cutibacterium acnes and selected Gram-positive organisms. Orally administered sarecycline is absorbed systemically with peak concentrations reached within a few hours; food, especially dairy or multivalent cations, can reduce or delay absorption, distribution is moderate with protein binding typical of tetracyclines, metabolism is limited, and elimination occurs through both fecal and renal pathways with a terminal half-life supporting once-daily dosing. It is indicated primarily for inflammatory lesions of non-nodular moderate to severe acne vulgaris, for example facial and truncal acne in patients aged 9 years and older, and in practice is used as an oral acne-directed systemic antibiotic when topical therapy is inadequate. Adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, vulvovaginal candidiasis, photosensitivity, and dizziness, while toxicities of concern include tetracycline-class tooth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia in developing teeth, inhibition of bone growth in children, pseudotumor cerebri, hypersensitivity, hepatotoxicity, and rare severe cutaneous or esophageal reactions.

Name: Letermovir
Description: Letermovir (DB12070) is a small-molecule anti-cytomegalovirus agent with a highly functionalized heteroaromatic structure characterized by a non-nucleoside 3,4-dihydroquinazoline-based core bearing multiple fluorinated aryl substituents and polar heterocyclic functionality, giving it a lipophilic but conformationally constrained architecture optimized for selective viral protein binding; chemically it is best categorized as a quinazoline-derived antiviral and its central scaffold is a substituted dihydroquinazoline/heterobiaryl framework rather than a nucleoside analog. It is most similar pharmacologically to other CMV antivirals such as ganciclovir, valganciclovir, foscarnet, cidofovir, and maribavir, although it is structurally distinct and notable for targeting the CMV terminase complex rather than viral DNA polymerase. Its principal known target is the CMV terminase subunit pUL56, with effects on the pUL51/pUL89-associated DNA processing-packaging machinery. Letermovir is indicated primarily for prophylaxis of cytomegalovirus infection and disease in CMV-seropositive adult allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients, and it is also used in high-risk transplant settings to prevent CMV viremia, CMV syndrome, and end-organ disease such as pneumonitis or gastrointestinal CMV. Pharmacokinetically, it is orally active and also available intravenously, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, is highly protein bound, undergoes limited oxidative metabolism with glucuronidation and transporter-mediated disposition, and is eliminated mainly via the feces with minimal renal clearance; exposure increases with cyclosporine because of OATP1B1/3 interactions. Toxicity is generally lower than with older anti-CMV drugs, lacking the prominent myelosuppression or nephrotoxicity typical of ganciclovir or foscarnet, but clinically important adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, peripheral edema, headache, fatigue, abdominal pain, and occasional atrial arrhythmias or hepatic enzyme elevations. In practice, it is used as CMV prophylaxis initiated early after transplant, often when avoidance of marrow suppression is especially desirable, with monitoring for drug interactions involving CYP3A and hepatic transporters.

Name: Vaborbactam
Description: Vaborbactam (DB12107) is a cyclic boronic acid beta-lactamase inhibitor whose structure is defined by a monocyclic boronate pharmacophore containing a boron-centered, tetrahedral transition-state mimic linked to a substituted carboxylated side chain, giving a compact, highly polar, non-beta-lactam architecture optimized for serine beta-lactamase binding. Chemically, it belongs to the boronic acid antibacterial adjuvant class, and its core scaffold is a cyclic boronate similar in concept to other boron-based beta-lactamase inhibitors such as taniborbactam, while functionally resembling diazabicyclooctane inhibitors like avibactam and relebactam despite a distinct scaffold. Its principal targets are bacterial class A and class C serine beta-lactamases, especially Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase enzymes including KPC-2 and KPC-3, with activity also against some ESBLs and AmpC enzymes, but limited activity against metallo-beta-lactamases and many class D carbapenemases. Clinically it is used only in combination with meropenem for complicated urinary tract infection, including pyelonephritis, caused by susceptible Enterobacterales, particularly carbapenem-resistant KPC-producing strains. Pharmacokinetically, vaborbactam is administered intravenously, displays low protein binding, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid, achieves therapeutic urinary and plasma concentrations, undergoes minimal metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by the kidney, so exposure rises in renal impairment and dose adjustment is required. Toxicity is generally consistent with combination beta-lactam therapy; important concerns include hypersensitivity reactions, infusion-related effects, renal function considerations, and risk of Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea, while common adverse effects include headache, phlebitis, diarrhea, and nausea. In practice, meropenem-vaborbactam is used for multidrug-resistant Gram-negative infections when restoration of carbapenem activity against KPC-producing Enterobacterales is desired.

Name: Lorlatinib
Description: Lorlatinib (DrugBank DB12130) is a macrocyclic, small-molecule aminopyridine tyrosine kinase inhibitor designed to penetrate the central nervous system; structurally, it contains a compact heteroaryl-rich macrocycle with substituted pyridine/pyridazine-like ring elements and a fluorinated aryl motif that constrains conformation for potent kinase binding and brain exposure. It is classified as an antineoplastic kinase inhibitor, specifically a third-generation ALK/ROS1 inhibitor, and its core scaffold is a conformationally restricted macrocyclic aminopyridine framework. Similar drugs include other ALK inhibitors such as crizotinib, ceritinib, alectinib, brigatinib, and ensartinib, although lorlatinib was optimized to retain activity against many resistance mutations and CNS disease. Its principal targets are anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) and ROS1 receptor tyrosine kinase, with inhibitory activity against multiple mutant ALK variants. Orally administered lorlatinib is well absorbed, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, is widely distributed including across the blood-brain barrier, is extensively metabolized mainly by CYP3A4 and UGT1A4, and is eliminated through both feces and urine predominantly as metabolites; exposure is altered by strong CYP3A modulators. Clinically, it is indicated for ALK-positive metastatic non-small cell lung cancer and is also used in ROS1-rearranged NSCLC in some settings, particularly after progression on prior TKIs or with brain metastases. Toxicities include hyperlipidemia, CNS effects such as cognitive or mood changes, peripheral neuropathy, edema, hepatotoxicity, and less commonly interstitial lung disease or atrioventricular block. Common adverse effects include increased cholesterol and triglycerides, weight gain, fatigue, diarrhea, arthralgia, speech effects, and edema, and clinical use often includes lipid monitoring, neuropsychiatric assessment, and management of drug-drug interactions.

Name: Vinpocetine
Description: Vinpocetine (DB12131) is a semisynthetic ethyl ester derivative of the indole alkaloid apovincamine, characterized by a compact polycyclic eburnane/vinca-like framework containing an indole-fused bicyclic nitrogenous core and an ester substituent that increases lipophilicity and supports central nervous system penetration. Chemically it is classified as a synthetic vinca alkaloid-related cerebroactive alkaloid derivative, with an apovincamine or eburnamine scaffold; structurally and pharmacologically similar compounds include vincamine, apovincaminic acid derivatives, and more distantly other cerebral vasomodulators/nootropics such as nicergoline or nimodipine. Its pharmacology is linked mainly to inhibition of phosphodiesterase 1, modulation of voltage-gated sodium channels, and reduction of calcium-dependent neuronal injury, with reported effects on IKBKB/NF-kappaB signaling, cerebral blood flow, and neuroinflammation; PDE1A, PDE1B, and PDE1C are the most commonly cited target proteins. After oral administration, vinpocetine is absorbed reasonably well, undergoes first-pass hydrolysis to apovincaminic acid as a major circulating metabolite, is widely distributed including to brain, is metabolized primarily by ester cleavage and subsequent hepatic biotransformation, and is excreted mainly in urine with some fecal elimination. Toxicity is generally low at therapeutic doses but includes dose-related hypotension, tachycardia, gastrointestinal upset, dizziness, and headache; embryo-fetal toxicity and possible increased miscarriage risk have been reported, making use in pregnancy inappropriate. Adverse effects include flushing, dry mouth, insomnia, nausea, and blood pressure changes. Clinically, it has been used in some countries for cerebrovascular insufficiency, cognitive impairment, post-stroke deficits, vertigo, tinnitus, and vascular dementia symptoms, although evidence quality and regulatory acceptance vary.

Name: Erdafitinib
Description: Erdafitinib (DrugBank DB12147) is a small-molecule, orally active fibroblast growth factor receptor inhibitor built on a heteroaromatic kinase-inhibitor framework featuring a chlorinated azaindole-like core linked to substituted aromatic and alkoxy side groups that support ATP-pocket binding; chemically it is best categorized as a targeted antineoplastic tyrosine kinase inhibitor, and its scaffold is consistent with compact fused nitrogen-containing bicyclic kinase-binding motifs seen in FGFR-directed agents. Closely related or mechanistically similar drugs include pemigatinib, infigratinib, futibatinib, derazantinib, and broader multikinase FGFR-active inhibitors such as ponatinib. Its principal targets are FGFR1, FGFR2, FGFR3, and FGFR4, with greatest clinical relevance in tumors harboring FGFR2 or FGFR3 activating mutations or fusions. Erdafitinib is indicated primarily for locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma with susceptible FGFR3 or FGFR2 alterations after prior platinum-based therapy, and it has also been explored in FGFR-altered cholangiocarcinoma and other solid tumors. Pharmacokinetically, it is well absorbed orally, reaches steady state within about two weeks, is highly protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP2C9 and CYP3A4, and is eliminated through both feces and urine, with a terminal half-life on the order of tens of hours allowing once-daily dosing. Toxicities reflect on-target FGFR inhibition and include hyperphosphatemia, central serous retinopathy or retinal pigment epithelial detachment, stomatitis, nail and skin toxicity, diarrhea, dry mouth, and hand-foot syndrome; serious examples include ocular toxicity, severe electrolyte disturbances, and embryo-fetal harm. In clinical use, serum phosphate-guided dose escalation and ophthalmologic monitoring are characteristic features of therapy.

Name: Deutetrabenazine
Description: Deutetrabenazine (DB12161) is a deuterium-substituted benzoquinolizine derivative structurally derived from tetrabenazine, retaining the reserpine-like tetrahydroisoquinoline/benzo[a]quinolizine scaffold with methoxy-substituted aromatic functionality and strategically incorporated deuterium at metabolically labile positions to slow biotransformation; chemically it is classified as a vesicular monoamine transporter inhibitor within the monoamine-depleting tetrabenazine analog class, and its closest similar drugs include tetrabenazine itself and valbenazine, as well as the VMAT inhibitor reserpine as a more distant mechanistic analogue. Its principal pharmacologic target is vesicular monoamine transporter 2 encoded by SLC18A2, with therapeutic activity mediated largely by active reduced metabolites that reversibly inhibit VMAT2 and thereby reduce presynaptic packaging of dopamine, and to a lesser extent other monoamines. After oral administration, deutetrabenazine is well absorbed and rapidly converted by carbonyl reductase to active alpha- and beta-dihydrometabolites; deuteration prolongs metabolite half-life and reduces peak-trough fluctuation relative to tetrabenazine, while subsequent metabolism depends importantly on CYP2D6, with wide distribution and mainly urinary excretion of metabolites after hepatic clearance. Clinically it is indicated for chorea associated with Huntington disease and tardive dyskinesia, for example involuntary facial, lingual, truncal, or limb movements. Toxicity is dominated by excessive monoamine depletion and exposure-related CNS effects, including somnolence, parkinsonism, akathisia, depression, suicidality risk in Huntington disease, QT prolongation, and potential neuroleptic malignant syndrome; adverse effects commonly include sedation, fatigue, diarrhea, dry mouth, insomnia, anxiety, and balance disturbance. In practice it is used as a dose-titrated oral symptomatic therapy, with CYP2D6 status, concomitant strong CYP2D6 inhibitors, hepatic impairment, and psychiatric history informing safe use.

Name: Gepirone
Description: Gepirone (DB12184) is an azapirone anxiolytic/antidepressant structurally characterized as an arylpiperazine with a piperazine core linked through an alkyl spacer to a cyclic imide/lactam-like heterocycle, placing it in the serotonin receptor ligand class and giving it the classic buspirone-like arylpiperazine scaffold seen in related compounds such as buspirone, tandospirone, and ipsapirone. Pharmacologically, it acts primarily as a partial agonist at the serotonin 5-HT1A receptor, with much lower affinity at other serotonergic and dopaminergic sites than older azapirones; the principal target protein is HTR1A, while off-target interactions may include other serotonin receptor subtypes and limited binding to dopamine D2-family receptors. It has been developed mainly for major depressive disorder and anxiety-spectrum symptoms, including psychic anxiety, tension, and anxious depression. After oral administration, gepirone is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract but undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, producing active metabolites including 1-(2-pyrimidinyl)piperazine; distribution is expected to be moderate with central nervous system penetration, metabolism occurs largely via CYP3A4-mediated oxidative biotransformation, and elimination is primarily renal as metabolites with some fecal excretion. Adverse effects are broadly consistent with serotonergic azapirones and include dizziness, nausea, headache, somnolence, insomnia, dry mouth, asthenia, and gastrointestinal upset. Toxicity is generally lower than that of benzodiazepines with less abuse liability and minimal respiratory depression, but overdose or drug interactions may increase CNS effects, orthostasis, or serotonin-related adverse reactions. Clinically, gepirone has been used as an oral non-benzodiazepine option for depressive illness with prominent anxiety and for patients in whom sedation, dependence, or cognitive impairment are undesirable.

Name: Faropenem
Description: Faropenem (DrugBank DB12190) is an orally active beta-lactam antibacterial of the penem class, structurally characterized by a fused bicyclic beta-lactam-thiazoline-like core typical of penems, with a trans-hydroxyethyl substituent and sulfur-containing unsaturation that confers stability to many beta-lactamases and broad antibacterial activity; its chemical category is therefore a penem/beta-lactam antibiotic, and its core scaffold is the carbapenem-like penem bicyclic nucleus. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other beta-lactams, especially oral penems and carbapenem-related agents such as tebipenem, imipenem, meropenem, and ertapenem, though faropenem is distinguished by oral bioavailability. Its antibacterial targets are bacterial penicillin-binding proteins, particularly transpeptidases involved in peptidoglycan cross-linking, leading to inhibition of cell-wall synthesis and bacterial death. Pharmacokinetically, faropenem is absorbed orally as the active drug or prodrug form depending on formulation, achieves useful plasma and tissue levels in respiratory and urinary compartments, shows modest protein binding, undergoes limited metabolism with hydrolytic opening of the beta-lactam ring, and is eliminated primarily via renal excretion of parent drug and metabolites. It is indicated for susceptible community-acquired infections such as acute bacterial sinusitis, otitis media, pharyngotonsillitis, bronchitis, pneumonia, skin and soft-tissue infection, and urinary tract infection. Adverse effects are similar to other beta-lactams and include diarrhea, nausea, abdominal discomfort, rash, candidiasis, and transient liver enzyme elevations; toxicities include hypersensitivity reactions up to anaphylaxis, Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea, rare seizures in predisposed patients or renal impairment, and selection of resistant organisms. Clinically, it has been used as an oral step-down or outpatient option for respiratory, urogenital, and skin infections caused by susceptible streptococci, staphylococci, Enterobacterales, and some anaerobes.

Name: Landiolol
Description: Landiolol (DB12212) is an ultra-short-acting, highly cardioselective beta-adrenergic receptor antagonist whose structure is built on the classic aryloxypropanolamine beta-blocker pharmacophore, featuring an aromatic ether linked to a chiral propanolamine side chain and an ester-containing substituent that confers rapid hydrolysis; chemically it is categorized as an esterified phenoxypropanolamine and its core scaffold is closely related to esmolol-like short-acting beta-blockers. Similar drugs include esmolol, another ultra-short-acting intravenous beta1-selective blocker, as well as more conventional beta1-selective agents such as metoprolol and bisoprolol, though landiolol is generally more beta1-selective and shorter acting. Its principal targets are beta1-adrenergic receptors in the heart, with much weaker activity at beta2 receptors, producing negative chronotropic and modest negative inotropic effects. Pharmacokinetically, landiolol is administered intravenously because it is intended for rapid titration in acute care; it has immediate systemic availability, a very small effective half-life of only a few minutes, limited tissue persistence, and is rapidly metabolized mainly by plasma and hepatic esterases to inactive metabolites that are then excreted predominantly in urine. Toxicity is largely an extension of pharmacology and includes excessive bradycardia, hypotension, atrioventricular block, reduced cardiac output, and potential worsening of acute heart failure or shock, with bronchospasm possible but less prominent than with nonselective beta-blockers. Clinically, it is used for rapid rate control in supraventricular tachyarrhythmias, especially atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, perioperative tachycardia, and critical-care tachyarrhythmias, where adverse effects commonly include bradycardia, hypotension, dizziness, and injection-site reactions.

Name: Luseogliflozin
Description: Luseogliflozin (DB12214) is an orally active C-aryl glucoside sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor characterized structurally by a glucose-like polyhydroxylated sugar core linked through a metabolically stable carbon-carbon bond to a substituted aromatic heterocyclic aglycone, giving it the typical SGLT2-inhibitor pharmacophore of a hydrophilic glucoside headgroup and lipophilic aryl scaffold; chemically it belongs to the antidiabetic gliflozin class, and its core scaffold is a C-glucoside biaryl/heteroaryl motif closely related to other SGLT2 inhibitors such as dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, canagliflozin, tofogliflozin, and ipragliflozin. Its principal target protein is SLC5A2, the renal SGLT2 transporter in the proximal tubule, with much weaker activity at SLC5A1/SGLT1, leading to reduced renal glucose reabsorption, increased urinary glucose excretion, and improvement in hyperglycemia in type 2 diabetes mellitus. After oral administration it is well absorbed, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, is substantially protein bound, distributes systemically without unusual tissue sequestration, undergoes mainly hepatic biotransformation including oxidation and conjugative pathways, and is eliminated via both urine and feces as parent drug and metabolites, with a half-life compatible with once-daily dosing. Toxicities and adverse effects are broadly class-related and include osmotic diuresis, volume depletion, hypotension, genital mycotic infection, urinary tract infection, pollakiuria, thirst, mild renal function changes, and occasional hypoglycemia when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas; rare but important risks include ketoacidosis and dehydration.
