Clinically, luseogliflozin is used as monotherapy or in combination regimens for type 2 diabetes, especially in patients with inadequate glycemic control, and may be particularly useful when reduction in fasting glucose, HbA1c, body weight, or blood pressure is desired.

Name: Bunazosin
Description: Bunazosin (DrugBank DB12230) is a quinazoline-based antihypertensive and ophthalmic alpha-adrenergic antagonist whose structure is centered on a 6,7-dimethoxyquinazoline aromatic heterobicycle linked through a piperazine spacer to a benzyl-type lipophilic moiety, placing it in the arylpiperazine/quinazoline class and giving it the same core scaffold seen in selective alpha1-adrenoceptor blockers such as prazosin, terazosin, doxazosin, and related congeners including alfuzosin. Its principal known targets are alpha1-adrenergic receptor subtypes, especially ADRA1A, ADRA1B, and ADRA1D, where antagonism reduces sympathetic vasoconstriction and can also lower intraocular pressure. Pharmacokinetically, bunazosin is administered orally and topically, is absorbed sufficiently to produce systemic alpha-blockade after oral use, distributes into vascular smooth muscle and ocular tissues, is expected to show moderate protein binding and hepatic biotransformation typical of quinazoline alpha1-blockers, and is eliminated through combined biliary/fecal and renal routes as parent drug and metabolites, although detailed human ADME datasets are limited in the open literature. Toxicity is dominated by exaggerated pharmacology, including orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, syncope, reflex tachycardia, headache, nasal congestion, and fatigue, with overdose potentially causing profound hypotension. Therapeutically it has been used mainly for hypertension and in ophthalmology for glaucoma or ocular hypertension, with clinical use exemplified by blood-pressure reduction through peripheral vasodilation and topical reduction of elevated intraocular pressure. Adverse effects also include palpitations, weakness, and occasional gastrointestinal discomfort, consistent with the alpha1-blocker class.

Name: Iguratimod
Description: Iguratimod (DB12233) is a synthetic small-molecule antirheumatic drug built around a substituted benzamide/methanesulfonanilide-like framework, characterized structurally by an aromatic amide linked to a heteroaromatic ring and further decorated with a sulfonyl-substituted phenyl moiety, giving a relatively rigid, lipophilic, nonbiologic scaffold suited to oral immunomodulation; chemically it is generally classified as a conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drug and anti-inflammatory aromatic sulfonamide-related compound, with a central diaryl amide scaffold that distinguishes it from biologic DMARDs but places it conceptually near other synthetic immunomodulators such as leflunomide, methotrexate, sulfasalazine, tofacitinib, and other csDMARD or targeted synthetic DMARD comparators used in rheumatoid arthritis. Pharmacologically, iguratimod suppresses inflammatory cytokine production and immunoglobulin synthesis, with reported effects on NF-kappaB-related signaling and downstream mediators including IL6, TNF, IL1beta, COX-2/PTGS2, and RANKL/TNFSF11-associated osteoclastogenic pathways rather than a single highly selective receptor target. After oral administration it is absorbed systemically, shows moderate protein binding, distributes into inflamed synovial compartments, undergoes predominantly hepatic metabolism including oxidation and conjugative pathways, and is eliminated through both urine and feces with a half-life compatible with chronic twice-daily dosing in some regimens. It is indicated mainly for rheumatoid arthritis, especially active disease with joint pain, swelling, stiffness, and progressive structural damage, and has also been studied in other autoimmune or inflammatory disorders. Adverse effects commonly include gastrointestinal upset, nausea, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, dizziness, rash, stomatitis, and liver enzyme elevation, while important toxicities include hepatotoxicity, leukopenia or other cytopenias, proteinuria, and rare serious hypersensitivity or interstitial lung events, so clinical use centers on monitored long-term oral DMARD therapy, often alone or combined with methotrexate or other antirheumatic agents in patients needing steroid-sparing control of synovitis and inhibition of radiographic progression.

Name: Estetrol
Description: Estetrol (DrugBank DB12235) is a native human fetal estrogen characterized structurally as a steroidal estrane with the classical four-ring cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene nucleus and multiple hydroxyl substituents, notably a phenolic A-ring hydroxyl and additional hydroxylation on the D-ring side of the scaffold, giving a polyhydroxylated estrogen profile distinct from estradiol and ethinyl estradiol; chemically it belongs to the natural estrogen class and more specifically a fetal steroid hormone, built on an estrane estrogen scaffold. Similar drugs include estradiol, estriol, conjugated estrogens, and ethinyl estradiol, although estetrol is differentiated by high oral bioavailability, relative metabolic stability, and weaker hepatic stimulation. Its principal targets are estrogen receptor alpha and estrogen receptor beta, through which it exerts tissue-selective estrogenic effects. Pharmacokinetically, estetrol is orally active, absorbed efficiently, shows limited cytochrome P450 involvement, relatively low plasma protein binding compared with some estrogens, metabolism mainly by phase II conjugation to glucuronides and sulfates, and elimination predominantly in urine with a terminal half-life supportive of once-daily dosing. Toxicity is broadly estrogen-related; major concerns include venous thromboembolism risk, cholestatic or hepatic effects, endometrial stimulation when inadequately opposed, and potential reproductive or developmental hazards in inappropriate populations, though available data suggest a comparatively modest hepatic coagulation impact versus ethinyl estradiol. It is used mainly in combined oral contraception, for example with drospirenone, and has also been investigated for menopausal symptoms such as vasomotor instability and vulvovaginal atrophy. Common adverse effects include irregular uterine bleeding, headache, nausea, breast tenderness, dysmenorrhea, mood changes, and acne, while clinical use centers on oral contraceptive therapy and potentially estrogen replacement settings.

Name: Edaravone
Description: Edaravone (DB12243) is a small, lipophilic synthetic antioxidant built on a 2-pyrazolin-5-one/pyrazolone core, specifically a substituted five-membered diazolone ring bearing a phenyl group and keto-enol tautomerism that supports facile electron donation and free-radical trapping; chemically it is classified as a pyrazolone derivative and free-radical scavenger, with a phenyl-pyrazolone scaffold shared in a broad sense with other pyrazolone drugs, while functionally similar neuroprotective or antioxidant comparators include riluzole, tirilazad, N-acetylcysteine, and dexpramipexole. Its pharmacology is driven less by a single high-affinity receptor than by quenching hydroxyl radical, peroxyl radical, and lipid peroxide species, thereby reducing oxidative injury to membranes, endothelium, and neurons; reported pathway-level targets affected include myeloperoxidase, lipoxygenase-linked lipid peroxidation systems, and oxidative stress signaling rather than a uniquely defined canonical protein target. After intravenous administration, absorption is complete, distribution is rapid into extracellular fluids and tissues including the CNS, protein binding is moderate, metabolism occurs mainly by hepatic and extrahepatic conjugation to sulfate and glucuronide metabolites, and elimination is predominantly renal as metabolites with a short parent half-life. Toxicities include hypersensitivity and anaphylactoid reactions, sulfite-associated bronchospasm in susceptible patients, hepatic enzyme elevation, renal dysfunction, and infusion-related effects. Approved and established clinical use includes amyotrophic lateral sclerosis to slow functional decline and acute ischemic stroke in some markets to limit oxidative neuronal damage; common adverse effects include contusion, gait disturbance, headache, dermatitis, eczema, fatigue, and abnormal liver tests.

Name: Triclabendazole
Description: Triclabendazole (DrugBank DB12245) is a halogenated benzimidazole anthelmintic whose structure consists of a benzimidazole core bearing a thioether-linked chlorophenoxy substituent and additional chloro substitution, giving a lipophilic aromatic heterocycle optimized for trematode activity; chemically it belongs to the benzimidazole carbamate-related flukicidal class, although it is structurally distinguished from many nematocidal benzimidazoles by its substituted phenoxy methylthio scaffold, with the benzimidazole nucleus serving as the key pharmacophore. Similar drugs include albendazole, mebendazole, fenbendazole, thiabendazole, and other flukicides such as bithionol, though triclabendazole is notably more active against Fasciola species. After oral administration it is absorbed better with food, widely distributed, and rapidly oxidized in the liver to the pharmacologically important sulfoxide and sulfone metabolites; elimination is primarily biliary and fecal, with limited renal excretion. Its precise targets are not fully resolved, but benzimidazole-sensitive beta-tubulin and other parasite cytoskeletal or tegumental processes are implicated, with disruption of microtubule-dependent function proposed. It is indicated mainly for fascioliasis caused by Fasciola hepatica and Fasciola gigantica, including hepatic and biliary disease manifestations such as abdominal pain, fever, eosinophilia, and obstructive symptoms, and has also been used for other susceptible trematode infections. Adverse effects are often mild and partly disease-related, including biliary colic, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, headache, dizziness, pruritus, urticaria, and transient liver enzyme elevations; toxicity is generally limited at therapeutic doses, but hepatobiliary reactions and inflammatory responses from dying parasites can occur, so clinical use centers on oral treatment of confirmed or suspected fascioliasis in adults and children, often as a short-course regimen with follow-up parasitologic and hepatic assessment.

Name: Tulobuterol
Description: Tulobuterol (DrugBank DB12248) is a phenethylamine-derived adrenergic bronchodilator with a substituted aryl-ethanolamine structure characterized by a chlorinated aromatic ring linked to a 2-amino-1-ol side chain bearing a tert-butyl-substituted amino group, placing it in the selective β2-adrenergic receptor agonist class; its core scaffold is the aryloxy- or aryl-substituted ethanolamine/beta-amino alcohol motif shared by sympathomimetic bronchodilators. Structurally and pharmacologically it is related to other β2-agonists such as terbutaline, salbutamol (albuterol), clenbuterol, mabuterol, and procaterol. Its principal target is the β2-adrenergic receptor encoded by ADRB2, with lesser activity at other beta-adrenergic receptors at higher exposures, leading to bronchial smooth-muscle relaxation via cyclic AMP signaling. Tulobuterol is used for asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysematous airway obstruction, and other reversible obstructive airway symptoms such as wheeze, dyspnea, and nocturnal bronchospasm; clinically it has been used orally and especially as a transdermal patch to provide sustained bronchodilation and improve adherence in pediatric and elderly patients. Pharmacokinetically, it is absorbed systemically after oral or transdermal administration, with transdermal delivery producing slower onset, prolonged plasma exposure, reduced peak-trough fluctuation, broad tissue distribution, hepatic biotransformation including oxidative and conjugative pathways, and renal excretion of parent drug and metabolites. Toxicity is typical of sympathomimetics and includes dose-related tachycardia, palpitations, tremor, nervousness, headache, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, and rarely arrhythmia or paradoxical bronchospasm; overdose may provoke marked beta-adrenergic stimulation, chest discomfort, vomiting, and ECG changes. Common adverse effects in routine use include tremor, insomnia, nausea, dizziness, rash or patch-site erythema, and mild cardiovascular stimulation.

Name: Vadadustat
Description: Vadadustat (DB12255) is an orally active small-molecule hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor built around a heteroaromatic carboxylic acid scaffold, commonly described as a pyridine-containing or related aza-heterocyclic aromatic system bearing polar substituents that mimic 2-oxoglutarate interactions within the catalytic pocket of prolyl hydroxylase domain enzymes; chemically it is categorized as a HIF stabilizer and 2-oxoglutarate analog-type enzyme inhibitor, with a compact heteroaryl acid scaffold comparable in therapeutic concept and mechanistic class to roxadustat, daprodustat, desidustat, and molidustat. Its principal targets are EGLN1/PHD2, EGLN2/PHD1, and EGLN3/PHD3, leading to reduced HIF-alpha hydroxylation, stabilization of HIF transcription factors, and increased endogenous erythropoietin signaling with downstream effects on iron metabolism genes. Pharmacokinetically, vadadustat is administered orally, is systemically absorbed, circulates with meaningful plasma protein binding, undergoes predominant phase II biotransformation including glucuronidation with limited oxidative metabolism, and is eliminated through both renal and fecal routes, largely as metabolites rather than unchanged drug. It is indicated for anemia associated with chronic kidney disease, especially anemia due to inadequate erythropoietin production in dialysis-dependent and non-dialysis CKD settings. Adverse effects reported or anticipated in its class include hypertension, diarrhea, nausea, headache, thromboembolic events, hyperkalemia, and potential cardiovascular complications; toxicity concerns include excessive erythropoiesis, increased blood pressure, major adverse cardiovascular events, vascular access thrombosis, hepatic laboratory abnormalities, and possible theoretical risks related to pathological HIF activation such as tumor progression or retinopathy. Clinically, it is used as an oral alternative to erythropoiesis-stimulating agents to raise hemoglobin, reduce transfusion requirements, and manage symptomatic fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance in CKD-associated anemia.

Name: Fexinidazole
Description: Fexinidazole (DrugBank DB12265) is an orally active 5-nitroimidazole antiprotozoal whose structure consists of a nitro-substituted imidazole ring bearing a methyl group and a thioether-linked para-methylsulfonyl phenyl substituent, placing it in the nitroheterocyclic anti-infective class and more specifically within the 2-substituted 5-nitroimidazole scaffold shared with other bioreductively activated antiparasitic agents. It is chemically and pharmacologically related to nitroimidazoles such as metronidazole, benznidazole, and to some extent nifurtimox by virtue of reductive bioactivation and generation of toxic intermediates in susceptible parasites. Its principal known molecular targets are not a single human protein but parasite macromolecular systems damaged after activation by type I nitroreductases, especially the trypanosomal nitroreductase NTR1, leading to reactive metabolites that injure DNA, proteins, and redox pathways. After oral administration with food, fexinidazole is absorbed systemically, distributed widely, and undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism to the pharmacologically important sulfoxide and sulfone metabolites, which contribute substantially to activity; elimination is predominantly as metabolites via urine and feces, with parent drug exposure lower than metabolite exposure. It is indicated for human African trypanosomiasis caused by Trypanosoma brucei gambiense, including hemolymphatic and certain meningoencephalitic stages, enabling simplified treatment of sleeping sickness. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, decreased appetite, headache, dizziness, asthenia, insomnia, tremor, and reversible transaminase elevations; clinically relevant toxicities include hepatotoxicity, gastrointestinal intolerance, weight loss, neuropsychiatric effects, and potential embryo-fetal risk. In practice it is used as a finite oral regimen, especially in ambulatory management of gambiense HAT where it can reduce reliance on parenteral therapies such as NECT.

Name: Doravirine
Description: Doravirine (DrugBank DB12301) is a synthetic non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor with a compact heteroaromatic structure built around a chlorinated pyridone-based scaffold linked to substituted phenyl and triazolinone-like aryl-heterocyclic features that confer high affinity for the allosteric NNRTI pocket of HIV-1 reverse transcriptase; chemically it is categorized as an antiviral small molecule, specifically an NNRTI, and its scaffold is distinct from but pharmacologically related to diarylpyrimidine and other heteroaryl NNRTI frameworks. Similar drugs include efavirenz, rilpivirine, etravirine, nevirapine, and delavirdine, although doravirine was designed to retain activity against several common NNRTI resistance-associated variants. It targets HIV-1 reverse transcriptase as its principal protein target, inhibiting viral DNA synthesis by noncompetitive allosteric modulation. After oral administration it is well absorbed, can be taken with or without food, is moderately protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes predominant hepatic oxidative metabolism via CYP3A4, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in feces with a lesser urinary component; its terminal half-life supports once-daily dosing. Toxicity is generally low relative to older NNRTIs, but clinically relevant concerns include transaminase elevations, rash, hypersensitivity, neuropsychiatric effects such as abnormal dreams or insomnia, and reduced exposure with strong CYP3A inducers such as rifampin. Adverse effects commonly include nausea, dizziness, headache, fatigue, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, and sleep disturbance. Clinically, doravirine is indicated for treatment of HIV-1 infection, typically in combination antiretroviral therapy, for example as oral doravirine-containing regimens in treatment-naive adults or selected virologically suppressed patients requiring a switch strategy.

Name: Benzbromarone
Description: Benzbromarone (DrugBank DB12319) is a highly lipophilic uricosuric agent built on a substituted benzofuran scaffold, structurally characterized as a 3-benzoylbenzofuran bearing brominated aryl rings and a phenolic hydroxyl group that contributes to protein binding and transporter interaction; chemically it is classified as a halogenated benzofuran derivative and aromatic ketone. Its closest pharmacologic analogs are other urate-lowering drugs, especially uricosurics such as probenecid, sulfinpyrazone, and lesinurad, although xanthine oxidase inhibitors such as allopurinol and febuxostat are used for similar clinical goals rather than close structural similarity. Benzbromarone is well absorbed orally, extensively bound to plasma proteins, distributed predominantly in the vascular/hepatic compartment, and undergoes substantial hepatic metabolism, mainly via CYP2C9, to active hydroxylated metabolites; elimination is chiefly biliary/fecal with some renal excretion of metabolites, and its half-life supports once-daily use. The principal known target is the renal urate transporter URAT1/SLC22A12, with inhibitory effects also described on GLUT9/SLC2A9 and possibly OAT-family urate handling pathways, producing increased renal uric acid excretion. It is indicated for chronic hyperuricemia and gout, particularly underexcretors or patients refractory or intolerant to allopurinol. Toxicity is dominated by idiosyncratic but potentially severe hepatotoxicity, including hepatitis and rare fulminant liver failure, with additional concerns of nephrolithiasis from uricosuria and occasional gastrointestinal intolerance. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, rash, and transaminase elevations. Clinically, it has been used as a second-line or alternative urate-lowering therapy for gout with tophi, recurrent gout flares, or asymptomatic hyperuricemia in selected settings, but its use has been restricted or withdrawn in some markets because hepatic risk can outweigh benefit.

Name: Eravacycline
Description: Eravacycline (DrugBank DB12329) is a fully synthetic fluorocycline antibiotic in the tetracycline class, built on the classic four linearly fused-ring naphthacene/tetracycline scaffold with characteristic diketone, phenolic, amide, and dimethylamino-related functionality, but distinguished by strategic C7 fluorine substitution and a C9 pyrrolidinoacetamido side chain that broaden antibacterial potency and help overcome common tetracycline resistance mechanisms. Chemically, it is categorized as a next-generation fluorinated glycylcycline-like tetracycline derivative, and it is structurally similar to tigecycline, tetracycline, doxycycline, minocycline, and omadacycline. Its primary target is the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit, specifically 16S rRNA-associated binding sites, where it inhibits aminoacyl-tRNA accommodation and suppresses protein synthesis; this confers activity against many Gram-positive, Gram-negative, anaerobic, and atypical pathogens, including resistant organisms. Pharmacokinetically, eravacycline is administered intravenously because oral bioavailability is not clinically used; it shows linear exposure, substantial tissue distribution, moderate plasma protein binding, hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4-mediated oxidation, and elimination through both fecal/biliary and renal routes, with fecal excretion predominating. It is indicated for complicated intra-abdominal infections, for example polymicrobial peritonitis or intra-abdominal abscess caused by susceptible Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Enterococcus faecalis, Bacteroides species, and other mixed flora. Adverse effects are mainly gastrointestinal, especially nausea and vomiting, with infusion-site reactions, diarrhea, hypersensitivity, dizziness, and transaminase elevations also reported. Toxicities class-wide include tooth discoloration, inhibition of bone growth in the fetus or child, photosensitivity, hepatotoxicity, and rare intracranial hypertension; accordingly, clinical use is primarily in adults with serious multidrug-resistant intra-abdominal infections when broad-spectrum tetracycline-class coverage is desired.

Name: Imrecoxib
Description: Imrecoxib (DrugBank DB12354) is an orally active selective cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitor whose structure is characterized by a diaryl heteroaromatic framework bearing a methyl-substituted furanone/lactone core linked to halogenated and methoxy-substituted aryl groups, a motif that confers COX-2 selectivity through a coxib-like spatial arrangement rather than the classic acidic NSAID pharmacophore. Chemically, it is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug in the coxib-related diaryl heterocycle class, with a scaffold broadly analogous to other selective COX-2 inhibitors such as celecoxib, rofecoxib, valdecoxib, etoricoxib, and lumiracoxib, although it is structurally distinct from each. Its principal target proteins are PTGS2 (COX-2), which it inhibits preferentially, and to a lesser extent PTGS1 (COX-1). After oral administration it is absorbed adequately, reaches systemic circulation without a need for parenteral delivery, is distributed sufficiently for anti-inflammatory and analgesic activity, undergoes extensive hepatic biotransformation to active and inactive metabolites, likely involving oxidative pathways including CYP-mediated metabolism, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites through renal and biliary/fecal routes. Toxicity resembles that of other selective COX-2 inhibitors: generally reduced upper gastrointestinal injury relative to nonselective NSAIDs but persistent risks of dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, edema, hypertension, renal function impairment, hepatotoxicity, hypersensitivity, and potentially thrombotic cardiovascular events with prolonged or high-dose exposure. Clinically it is used mainly for osteoarthritis and other musculoskeletal pain/inflammatory states, providing symptomatic relief of joint pain, stiffness, and functional limitation, with adverse effects most often including gastrointestinal discomfort, dizziness, rash, and peripheral swelling.

Name: Betrixaban
Description: Betrixaban (DrugBank DB12364) is a small-molecule, orally active direct factor Xa inhibitor built on a nonpeptidic aromatic heterocycle-rich structure that includes a substituted benzo-fused heteroaromatic core linked to additional aryl and heteroatom-containing functionality, giving a rigid, lipophilic, hydrogen-bond-capable architecture optimized for S1 and S4 pocket binding within factor Xa; chemically it is categorized as an oxomorpholine-containing anticoagulant and belongs to the direct oral anticoagulant class, with a scaffold broadly related to the anthranilamide/heteroaryl factor Xa inhibitor chemotype seen across this therapeutic area. Similar drugs include rivaroxaban, apixaban, and edoxaban, which share selective Xa inhibition but differ in scaffold, clearance, and dosing. Its principal target is coagulation factor X, specifically activated factor Xa (F10), leading to reduced thrombin generation. Betrixaban is indicated for prevention of venous thromboembolism, especially extended prophylaxis in acutely ill hospitalized adults at risk for deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. After oral administration it is absorbed with moderate bioavailability, reaches peak levels in hours, is highly protein bound, has a relatively long half-life permitting once-daily dosing, undergoes minimal CYP-mediated metabolism, and is eliminated largely unchanged through hepatobiliary and intestinal routes with a smaller renal contribution, making it comparatively less dependent on kidney clearance than some other DOACs. Toxicity is dominated by bleeding, ranging from epistaxis and gastrointestinal hemorrhage to major or fatal intracranial or retroperitoneal bleeding, with increased risk in renal impairment, interacting drugs, or invasive procedures. Common adverse effects include bleeding, anemia, nausea, and urinary tract bleeding; clinically it has been used chiefly as extended thromboprophylaxis rather than broad-spectrum anticoagulation across all thromboembolic settings.

Name: Siponimod
Description: Siponimod (DB12371) is an orally active, synthetic sphingosine 1-phosphate receptor modulator with a lipophilic small-molecule structure built around a substituted aromatic/heteroaromatic scaffold bearing trifluoromethyl and alkoxy-type functionality and a terminal carboxylic acid, giving it features of an amphipathic S1P-mimetic but not a peptide or nucleotide analogue; chemically it is categorized as an immunomodulatory aminocarboxylic acid derivative and is often described as a next-generation selective S1P receptor modulator with a biaryl-like scaffold related to fingolimod-class agents. Similar drugs include fingolimod, ozanimod, ponesimod, and etrasimod, which share S1P receptor targeting but differ in receptor selectivity and pharmacokinetics. Siponimod primarily targets S1PR1 and S1PR5, with little meaningful activity at S1PR2 and S1PR3, functionally antagonizing lymphocyte egress through receptor internalization and potentially affecting oligodendrocytes and astrocyte signaling in the CNS. It is indicated for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis, especially active secondary progressive multiple sclerosis, as well as clinically isolated syndrome and relapsing-remitting disease in some jurisdictions. Oral absorption is good, bioavailability is high, protein binding is extensive, tissue distribution includes CNS penetration, metabolism is predominantly hepatic via CYP2C9 with contribution from CYP3A4, and elimination occurs mainly as metabolites in feces with lesser renal excretion; CYP2C9 genotype strongly influences exposure and dosing. Toxicities include dose-dependent bradyarrhythmia and atrioventricular conduction delay at initiation, elevated transaminases, hypertension, macular edema, lymphopenia with infection risk including herpes zoster, reduced pulmonary function, fetal risk, and rare posterior reversible encephalopathy; common adverse effects include headache, hypertension, peripheral edema, liver enzyme elevation, and infections. Clinically it is used as a disease-modifying therapy to reduce relapse activity, inflammatory lesion burden on MRI, and disability progression in appropriately selected multiple sclerosis patients.

Name: Relebactam
Description: Relebactam (DrugBank DB12377) is a non-β-lactam diazabicyclooctane β-lactamase inhibitor whose structure is centered on a rigid bicyclic amidine/urea-like diazabicyclooctane core bearing polar amide/carbamate functionality and a basic piperidine substituent, features that confer high aqueous solubility and enable reversible covalent acylation of serine β-lactamases; chemically it belongs to the diazabicyclooctane antibacterial adjuvant class, with a DBO scaffold closely related to avibactam and other next-generation β-lactamase inhibitors such as nacubactam and zidebactam. Its principal targets are class A and class C serine β-lactamases, including Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase and AmpC cephalosporinases, with activity against some class D enzymes but not metallo-β-lactamases; clinically it is used not as monotherapy but in fixed combination with imipenem and cilastatin to restore imipenem activity against susceptible resistant Gram-negative pathogens. Indications include complicated urinary tract infection, complicated intra-abdominal infection when combined with appropriate additional agents, and hospital-acquired or ventilator-associated bacterial pneumonia caused by organisms such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa or Enterobacterales with relevant resistance mechanisms. Pharmacokinetically, relebactam is given intravenously, has limited protein binding, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid, undergoes minimal metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by the kidney, so exposure rises in renal impairment and dose reduction is required. Toxicity is generally low and largely reflects combination-product experience, but adverse effects include gastrointestinal upset, diarrhea, nausea, transaminase elevations, infusion-site reactions, headache, and positive Coombs test, while serious examples include hypersensitivity reactions, seizures risk in predisposed patients receiving imipenem, and superinfection including Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea.

Name: Evocalcet
Description: Evocalcet (DB12388) is a small-molecule calcimimetic designed as an orally active allosteric modulator of the calcium-sensing receptor, with a compact nonpeptidic structure built around an aromatic hydrophobic scaffold linked to a basic amine-containing side chain that mimics key features required for CaSR activation; chemically it is best categorized as a synthetic phenylalkylamine-like calcimimetic, and its scaffold is closely related conceptually to other type II calcimimetics that combine a lipophilic aryl domain with a protonatable nitrogen for receptor binding. The most similar approved drug is cinacalcet, and structurally related investigational or regionally used agents include other CaSR-positive allosteric modulators such as etelcalcetide, although the latter is a peptide and therefore chemically distinct. Its principal target protein is the calcium-sensing receptor encoded by CASR on parathyroid chief cells, where activation suppresses parathyroid hormone secretion and lowers serum calcium-phosphate burden. Clinically, evocalcet is indicated for secondary hyperparathyroidism, especially in patients with chronic kidney disease on dialysis, and has also been used for hypercalcemia associated with parathyroid disorders. After oral administration it is absorbed with clinically useful bioavailability, distributes systemically with moderate protein binding, undergoes hepatic biotransformation with less problematic CYP-mediated interaction potential than cinacalcet, and is eliminated through both metabolic and excretory pathways, mainly as metabolites in urine and feces. Its main toxicities reflect exaggerated pharmacology, particularly hypocalcemia, which may cause paresthesias, muscle cramps, tetany, QT prolongation, or seizures; common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, decreased appetite, abdominal discomfort, and dizziness. In practice, it is used to reduce PTH concentrations while often improving gastrointestinal tolerability relative to cinacalcet in dialysis-associated secondary hyperparathyroidism.

Name: Polmacoxib
Description: Polmacoxib (DrugBank DB12399) is an orally active, small-molecule nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug built on a diaryl heteroaromatic coxib-like framework in which substituted aryl rings are appended to a pyrazole-based core, conferring strong lipophilicity and cyclooxygenase-2 selectivity; chemically it is best classified as a selective COX-2 inhibitor within the aryl-heterocycle NSAID class, and its scaffold is closely related to the diarylpyrazole motif exemplified by celecoxib, with similarity also to other coxibs such as etoricoxib and valdecoxib. Its principal pharmacologic targets are cyclooxygenase-2 (PTGS2) and, with substantially weaker activity, cyclooxygenase-1 (PTGS1), leading to reduced prostaglandin synthesis and consequent anti-inflammatory and analgesic effects. It is indicated primarily for symptomatic treatment of osteoarthritis and other painful inflammatory musculoskeletal conditions, especially relief of joint pain, stiffness, and functional limitation. After oral administration it is absorbed systemically, reaches therapeutically relevant plasma concentrations consistent with once-daily use, is distributed as a protein-bound lipophilic agent, undergoes predominantly hepatic biotransformation likely involving oxidative metabolism and conjugative pathways, and is eliminated through combined biliary/fecal and renal routes as metabolites. Toxicity is broadly NSAID-like, including gastrointestinal irritation, ulceration or bleeding, renal function impairment, edema, hypertension, and potential thrombotic cardiovascular risk, although COX-2 selectivity may lessen but not abolish upper gastrointestinal toxicity. Common adverse effects include dyspepsia, abdominal discomfort, nausea, diarrhea, dizziness, headache, peripheral edema, and blood pressure elevation. Clinically, it is used as an anti-inflammatory analgesic when sustained symptom control is needed and when a COX-2 selective agent is preferred over a nonselective NSAID in patients at concern for gastrointestinal tolerability.

Name: Gemigliptin
Description: Gemigliptin (DB12412) is an orally active antidiabetic agent of the dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitor class, structurally characterized as a fluorinated, heteroaromatic small molecule built around a pyrimidine-containing core linked to a piperidine/piperidinone-like basic ring system and substituted with trifluoromethyl and other lipophilicity-modulating groups that promote high affinity for the DPP-4 catalytic site; thus its chemical category is a synthetic aminopiperidine-derived gliptin, and its principal scaffold is a substituted pyrimidino-piperidine DPP-4 inhibitory framework. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other gliptins such as sitagliptin, linagliptin, saxagliptin, vildagliptin, and alogliptin, all of which enhance incretin signaling by preventing degradation of GLP-1 and GIP. After oral administration, gemigliptin is well absorbed, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, shows moderate protein binding and broad tissue distribution, undergoes limited to moderate hepatic metabolism largely involving CYP3A4, and is eliminated by mixed biliary/fecal and renal routes, supporting use without extreme dependence on kidney clearance relative to some peers. Its main target protein is DPP4/CD26; off-target pharmacology is limited but related enzymes such as DPP8 and DPP9 are generally considered in selectivity assessments. It is indicated for type 2 diabetes mellitus, particularly to improve glycemic control as monotherapy or in combination with metformin, sulfonylureas, or insulin. Adverse effects are usually mild and include nasopharyngitis, upper respiratory infection, headache, dizziness, gastrointestinal discomfort, and hypoglycemia mainly when combined with insulin secretagogues; uncommon but clinically important toxicities include hypersensitivity reactions, hepatic enzyme elevations, pancreatitis concerns shared across the class, and rare severe joint pain. Clinically, gemigliptin is used as a once-daily glucose-lowering therapy in adults with type 2 diabetes, especially when a weight-neutral, low-hypoglycemia oral incretin-based option is desired.

Name: Anagliptin
Description: Anagliptin (DrugBank DB12417) is an orally active, small-molecule dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitor with a nitrogen-rich heterocyclic structure characterized by a cyanopyrrolidine-derived pharmacophore linked to amide/urea-like polar functionality and additional substituted cyclic amine features that confer high aqueous compatibility and enzyme-binding specificity; chemically it belongs to the gliptin class of antidiabetic agents, and its core scaffold is best described as a peptidomimetic cyanopyrrolidine DPP-4-inhibitor scaffold. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other DPP-4 inhibitors such as vildagliptin, saxagliptin, sitagliptin, linagliptin, and alogliptin, although anagliptin is relatively more polar than some congeners. Its principal target is DPP4/CD26, producing prolongation of endogenous incretin activity, especially GLP-1 and GIP signaling, thereby enhancing glucose-dependent insulin secretion and suppressing glucagon. After oral administration it is absorbed with clinically useful bioavailability, shows limited tissue distribution and low to moderate protein binding, undergoes relatively modest hepatic metabolism with much of the dose remaining unchanged, and is eliminated predominantly by renal excretion, so kidney function can influence exposure. Toxicity is generally low but includes class-related risks such as hypoglycemia when combined with sulfonylureas or insulin, hepatic enzyme elevations, renal exposure-related accumulation, hypersensitivity reactions, and rare pancreatitis. Adverse effects reported with clinical use include constipation, nausea, abdominal discomfort, dizziness, headache, rash, edema, and upper respiratory symptoms. Clinically, anagliptin is used for type 2 diabetes mellitus, particularly in patients requiring HbA1c reduction through oral incretin-based therapy, either as monotherapy or in combination with agents such as metformin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones, or insulin.

Name: Nadifloxacin
Description: Nadifloxacin (DrugBank DB12447) is a topical fluoroquinolone antibacterial built on the 4-quinolone/1,8-naphthyridone-related bicyclic scaffold, characterized by a fluorinated quinolone core bearing the canonical 3-carboxyl and 4-oxo pharmacophore required for bacterial enzyme binding, with additional substituents that enhance lipophilicity and cutaneous penetration; chemically it is classified as a fluoroquinolone and more specifically a topical quinolone anti-infective. Its closest analogs are other quinolone antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin, ofloxacin, levofloxacin, and topical agents including ozenoxacin, although nadifloxacin is primarily optimized for dermatologic use. The principal targets are bacterial DNA gyrase (gyrA/gyrB) and topoisomerase IV (parC/parE), leading to inhibition of DNA replication and rapid bactericidal activity against organisms relevant to acne and superficial skin infection, notably Cutibacterium acnes, Staphylococcus aureus, and some Gram-negative bacteria. Pharmacokinetically, after topical administration systemic absorption is generally low, with drug concentrating in the epidermis, follicles, and sebum-rich skin; distribution is therefore mainly local, systemic protein binding and tissue distribution are not usually clinically important, metabolism appears limited at therapeutic topical exposure, and any absorbed fraction is expected to undergo hepatic biotransformation and renal/biliary elimination similar to other quinolones. Toxicity is usually mild and localized, with low risk of systemic quinolone toxicities, though irritation, erythema, burning, pruritus, dryness, and contact dermatitis can occur; rare concerns include hypersensitivity and promotion of bacterial resistance with prolonged use. Clinically, nadifloxacin is used mainly for acne vulgaris and other mild superficial bacterial dermatoses, especially inflammatory acne lesions, folliculitis, impetiginized eruptions, and infected eczema where topical antibacterial therapy is appropriate.

Name: Omadacycline
Description: Omadacycline (DB12455) is a semisynthetic aminomethylcycline antibiotic structurally derived from the tetracycline family, built on the rigid four linearly fused-ring naphthacene/tetracycline core bearing the characteristic keto-enol and phenolic functionalities for metal chelation, with a C9 aminomethyl substitution that helps overcome common tetracycline resistance mechanisms; thus it is classified as a modern tetracycline-class antibacterial, specifically an aminomethylcycline, with the classic tetracycline scaffold as its chemotype. Closely related or mechanistically similar drugs include tetracycline, doxycycline, minocycline, tigecycline, and eravacycline. Its antibacterial effect is mediated by binding the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit, especially 16S rRNA within the decoding region, thereby inhibiting aminoacyl-tRNA accommodation and suppressing protein synthesis. Omadacycline is used for acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections and community-acquired bacterial pneumonia, including infections caused by susceptible Staphylococcus aureus including some MRSA isolates, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and atypical respiratory pathogens. Pharmacokinetically, it is available intravenously and orally; oral absorption is moderate and reduced by food, dairy, and multivalent cations, distribution is extensive into tissues including lung, plasma protein binding is modest, metabolism is minimal, and elimination occurs largely as unchanged drug in feces with a lesser renal component, supporting once-daily dosing. Toxicities resemble those of tetracyclines and include gastrointestinal intolerance, infusion-site reactions, transaminase elevation, tooth discoloration and inhibition of bone growth in fetuses and children, and potential class warnings for hypersensitivity, intracranial hypertension, and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, and headache, and clinically it is used as a broad-spectrum option when oral or IV treatment is needed for susceptible gram-positive, gram-negative, and atypical bacterial infections.

Name: Belotecan
Description: Belotecan (DB12459) is a semisynthetic camptothecin analogue whose structure retains the hallmark pentacyclic fused quinoline-pyranoindolizino core and the essential E-ring α-hydroxylactone required for topoisomerase I poisoning, with a water-solubilizing basic side-chain modification that distinguishes it from parent camptothecin and improves pharmaceutical handling; chemically it is an antineoplastic topoisomerase inhibitor within the camptothecin alkaloid family, and its scaffold is the camptothecin lactone pharmacophore shared with irinotecan, topotecan, exatecan, and 10-hydroxycamptothecin. Its principal target is DNA topoisomerase I (TOP1), which it stabilizes in the cleavable TOP1-DNA complex, causing replication-associated DNA strand breaks and apoptosis. Belotecan has been developed primarily for solid tumors, especially small cell lung cancer and ovarian or cervical malignancies, and has also been explored in combination regimens for recurrent or platinum-treated disease. Pharmacokinetically, it is administered intravenously, distributes into plasma and tissues with lactone-carboxylate interconversion influenced by physiologic pH and protein binding, undergoes limited metabolic transformation relative to irinotecan, and is cleared by both renal and biliary routes, with exposure increased in organ dysfunction. Toxicity is typical of camptothecins and is dose-limiting for bone marrow, with neutropenia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and anemia commonly reported; nonhematologic adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, mucositis, fatigue, alopecia, and transient hepatic laboratory abnormalities, while severe examples can include febrile neutropenia, infection, dehydration, and treatment delay or dose reduction. In clinical use, belotecan serves as a cytotoxic second-line or combination chemotherapy option where TOP1-directed therapy is desired.

Name: Favipiravir
Description: Favipiravir (DB12466) is a small, fluorinated pyrazinecarboxamide antiviral built on a 6-fluoro-3-hydroxypyrazine-2-carboxamide core, making it a heteroaromatic N-heterocyclic carboxamide and a pyrazine analog; its key scaffold is the substituted pyrazine ring, which functionally mimics purine nucleobase substrates after intracellular activation. It is chemically and mechanistically related to broad-spectrum RNA antiviral nucleoside or nucleobase analogs such as ribavirin, molnupiravir, remdesivir, and T-1105/T-1106 analog series, although favipiravir itself is not a classical nucleoside. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed, distributed systemically with moderate protein binding, and converted intracellularly by phosphoribosylation to favipiravir-ribofuranosyl-5′-triphosphate, the active metabolite that targets viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerases; it undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism mainly via aldehyde oxidase, with xanthine oxidase contributing, to an inactive hydroxylated metabolite that is eliminated largely in urine. Toxicity is notable for teratogenicity and embryotoxicity in animals, hyperuricemia from interference with urate handling, and potential liver enzyme elevations; overdose or susceptible patients may show worsening hepatic dysfunction or metabolic abnormalities. Its principal target is viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase from influenza and other RNA viruses, with no major intended human protein target. Clinically it is indicated primarily for influenza and has been used or studied for Ebola virus disease and COVID-19. Common adverse effects include increased uric acid, elevated transaminases, gastrointestinal upset, neutropenia, and rash. In practice it has been used as an oral antiviral for uncomplicated or refractory influenza and in investigational or regional protocols for emerging RNA viral infections.

Name: Ibrexafungerp
Description: Ibrexafungerp (DrugBank DB12471) is a semisynthetic triterpenoid antifungal structurally derived from the enfumafungin natural-product series, characterized by a rigid polycyclic terpene-like core appended to a lipophilic aromatic side chain and multiple oxygenated substituents that support potent glucan synthase inhibition; chemically it is classified as a glucan synthase inhibitor within the triterpenoid antifungal class, and its core scaffold is the enfumafungin-derived pentacyclic triterpene pharmacophore rather than the lipopeptide scaffold of echinocandins. Similar drugs include echinocandins such as caspofungin, micafungin, and anidulafungin, which share the same fungal cell-wall pathway target but differ structurally and in oral bioavailability. Its principal target is the fungal 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase complex, particularly Fks subunits, causing impaired cell-wall biosynthesis and fungicidal or growth-inhibitory activity against Candida species, including some azole- and echinocandin-resistant isolates. Pharmacokinetically, ibrexafungerp is orally active, absorbed with improved exposure when taken with food, highly protein bound, broadly distributed, metabolized predominantly by CYP3A4, and eliminated mainly via feces with limited renal excretion and a terminal half-life compatible with twice-daily short-course therapy. Toxicity is generally manageable, with animal developmental toxicity and embryo-fetal risk prompting pregnancy precautions; overdose-like or exposure-related toxicities mainly involve gastrointestinal intolerance and hepatic enzyme elevations. Approved and studied uses include vulvovaginal candidiasis and recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis, with clinical use also extending to difficult mucosal or invasive candidiasis settings when oral non-azole therapy is desirable. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, vomiting, dizziness, and transient transaminase elevations.

Name: Acotiamide
Description: Acotiamide (DrugBank DB12482) is a small-molecule gastroprokinetic agent structurally characterized as a substituted benzamide bearing a salicylamide-like aromatic core with amide and carboxyl functionalities linked to a basic cyclic amine side chain, giving it amphoteric properties and placing it in the acetylcholine-modulating prokinetic drug class; its principal chemical scaffold is an aromatic carboxamide/benzoic acid framework related in a broad medicinal-chemistry sense to other prokinetics and benzamide-derived gastrointestinal agents, although it is pharmacologically distinct from examples such as mosapride, itopride, domperidone, metoclopramide, and cisapride. Its best-described targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially antagonism at presynaptic M1 and M2 autoregulatory receptors in the enteric nervous system, thereby enhancing acetylcholine release and improving gastric accommodation and emptying, with additional reported interactions affecting acetylcholinesterase only weakly or indirectly depending on the assay system. Pharmacokinetically, acotiamide is orally active, absorbed to clinically useful systemic concentrations, distributed mainly in extracellular fluids with moderate protein binding, metabolized predominantly in the liver through phase II conjugative pathways and lesser oxidative biotransformation, and excreted mainly in urine as metabolites with a smaller fecal component; accumulation is generally limited at therapeutic dosing. It is indicated primarily for functional dyspepsia, particularly the postprandial distress syndrome subtype, improving symptoms such as postprandial fullness, early satiety, upper abdominal bloating, and epigastric discomfort. Adverse effects are usually mild and include diarrhea, constipation, nausea, headache, dizziness, and transient elevations in hepatic enzymes; toxicity is generally low, with no defining dose-limiting organ toxicity in routine use, though overdose or susceptible patients could plausibly experience exaggerated cholinergic gastrointestinal effects or liver test abnormalities. Clinically, it is used as an oral symptomatic therapy in patients with meal-related dyspeptic symptoms, especially when impaired gastric motility or accommodation is suspected.

Name: Elobixibat
Description: Elobixibat (DB12486) is a minimally absorbed, locally acting ileal bile acid transporter inhibitor whose structure is characterized by a bulky, highly lipophilic aromatic framework bearing a carboxylic acid and polar substituents arranged to mimic features of bile acid recognition while remaining nonsteroidal; chemically it is best classified as a synthetic small-molecule bile acid transporter inhibitor, and its core scaffold is generally described as an aryl/heteroaryl carboxylic acid pharmacophore built on a rigid hydrophobic polyaromatic platform. It is pharmacologically similar to other ASBT/IBAT inhibitors such as odevixibat and maralixibat, although those agents are used mainly in cholestatic liver disease, whereas elobixibat has been developed primarily for constipation. Its principal target is SLC10A2, the apical sodium-dependent bile acid transporter in the terminal ileum, with inhibition increasing colonic bile acid delivery, thereby stimulating secretion and motility. After oral administration, systemic absorption is very low, distribution is correspondingly limited, metabolism appears minimal because most activity is intraluminal, and elimination occurs predominantly via fecal excretion with little renal clearance. Toxicity is generally gastrointestinal and mechanism-based rather than systemic, with dose-related diarrhea, abdominal pain, cramping, fecal urgency, and occasional dehydration or electrolyte disturbance; excessive bile acid exposure may also raise concern for worsening diarrhea-predominant states. Clinically, it is indicated for chronic constipation, especially chronic idiopathic constipation and constipation in patients with impaired bowel motility, and is used to improve spontaneous bowel movements, stool consistency, straining, and bloating, particularly in patients inadequately controlled with conventional laxatives.

Name: Clascoterone
Description: Clascoterone (DB12499) is a synthetic steroidal antiandrogen structurally derived from cortexolone, bearing the classic cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene steroid nucleus with ketone functionality and an esterified 17-position that increases lipophilicity for topical delivery; chemically it is best classified as a corticosteroid-related steroidal androgen receptor antagonist, built on a pregnane/cortexolone steroid scaffold. It is most similar to other antiandrogenic agents used in androgen-driven dermatoses, including spironolactone, cyproterone acetate, flutamide, bicalutamide, and topical androgen-modulating approaches, although clascoterone is distinctive in being designed for predominantly local cutaneous action. Its primary known target is the androgen receptor, where it acts as a competitive antagonist and thereby reduces androgen-stimulated transcription in sebocytes and follicular units. After topical administration, systemic absorption is limited under normal use, with most pharmacologic activity occurring in the skin; absorbed drug is rapidly hydrolyzed to cortexolone and further metabolized by hepatic and extrahepatic steroid-metabolizing pathways, with excretion expected mainly as urinary metabolites and, to a lesser extent, biliary/fecal products. Toxicity is generally low in topical use, but excessive exposure could theoretically produce local irritation and limited systemic steroid-related or endocrine effects; animal and nonclinical assessments have not suggested the cytotoxic profile seen with classic oral antiandrogens. It is indicated primarily for acne vulgaris, particularly androgen-influenced inflammatory and noninflammatory facial lesions. Common adverse effects include erythema, pruritus, dryness, burning, scaling, and local edema, with occasional irritation at the application site. Clinically, it is used as topical cream therapy for acne in adolescents and adults, especially when reduction of sebum production and androgen signaling in skin is desired without the broader systemic exposure associated with oral antiandrogens.

Name: Fedratinib
Description: Fedratinib (DrugBank DB12500) is an orally active small-molecule antineoplastic built around a nitrogen-rich heteroaromatic kinase-inhibitor framework, featuring a substituted pyrimidine core linked to additional aromatic/heterocyclic moieties that confer ATP-competitive binding; chemically it is categorized as a targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitor, more specifically a Janus kinase inhibitor, with a pyrimidine-based kinase-binding scaffold closely related to other ATP-site directed myeloproliferative neoplasm agents. Similar drugs include ruxolitinib, momelotinib, and pacritinib, which also target JAK-STAT signaling in myelofibrosis. Its principal target protein is JAK2, including constitutively active JAK2V617F, with lesser activity reported against FLT3 and related kinases, thereby suppressing pathological cytokine signaling and myeloproliferation. Fedratinib is indicated primarily for intermediate-2 or high-risk primary or secondary myelofibrosis, including post-polycythemia vera and post-essential thrombocythemia myelofibrosis, where it is used to reduce splenomegaly and constitutional symptoms such as night sweats, pruritus, bone pain, and weight loss. Pharmacokinetically, it is orally absorbed, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, is highly protein bound, has a large apparent distribution, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 with minor contributions from CYP2C19 and flavin-containing monooxygenases, and is eliminated largely in feces with a terminal half-life supporting once-daily dosing. Important toxicities include serious gastrointestinal toxicity, myelosuppression with anemia and thrombocytopenia, hepatic enzyme elevation, and rare but clinically critical thiamine-deficiency-associated encephalopathy including Wernicke’s encephalopathy. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Clinically, it is used as a targeted oral therapy in adults with myelofibrosis, including patients previously treated with ruxolitinib or those needing spleen and symptom control through selective JAK2 inhibition.

Name: Mizolastine
Description: Mizolastine (DrugBank DB12523) is a second-generation antihistamine whose structure is characterized by a lipophilic polycyclic aromatic system linked through a short spacer to a basic nitrogen-containing heterocycle, giving an amphiphilic molecule with a cationizable amine and features typical of peripherally selective H1 antagonists; chemically it is classified as a benzimidazole- or related heteroaromatic-based piperidine antihistamine, with a scaffold centered on an aryl-heterocycle–piperidine pharmacophore seen across modern non-sedating antiallergics. Similar drugs include loratadine, ebastine, cetirizine, desloratadine, and fexofenadine, which share peripheral H1 receptor selectivity and reduced CNS penetration. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, where it acts as an antagonist/inverse agonist; limited ancillary effects on cardiac repolarization have been noted through hERG potassium channel interaction at higher exposure. Mizolastine is used for symptomatic treatment of seasonal or perennial allergic rhinitis and chronic idiopathic urticaria, improving sneezing, rhinorrhea, nasal and ocular pruritus, and wheal-and-flare symptoms. It is generally well absorbed orally, reaches peak plasma concentrations within a few hours, is highly protein bound, distributes mainly peripherally with limited blood-brain barrier entry, undergoes hepatic metabolism with CYP-mediated biotransformation, and is eliminated by combined biliary/fecal and renal routes with a half-life compatible with once-daily dosing. Toxicity is usually mild but includes dose-related somnolence, headache, dry mouth, fatigue, and dyspepsia; more serious concerns involve QT prolongation and ventricular arrhythmia risk, especially in overdose, hepatic impairment, electrolyte disturbance, or coadministration with CYP inhibitors such as macrolides or azole antifungals. Clinically, it has been used as a once-daily oral antiallergic when a relatively non-sedating H1 blocker is desired.

Name: Samidorphan
Description: Samidorphan (DB12543) is a semisynthetic morphinan-derived opioid receptor modulator whose structure is best described as a rigid pentacyclic 4,5-epoxymorphinan scaffold closely related to naltrexone, incorporating the classic phenanthrene-like fused ring system with a tertiary amine and oxygenated substituents that confer high opioid receptor affinity; chemically it belongs to the opioid antagonist/partial agonist class and specifically to the morphinan scaffold family. Closely related drugs include naltrexone, naloxone, nalmefene, and the mixed agonist-antagonist buprenorphine, all sharing overlapping opioid-receptor pharmacology and core opioid scaffolds. Samidorphan targets the mu opioid receptor primarily as an antagonist, while also interacting with kappa and delta opioid receptors with antagonist or weak partial agonist properties depending on assay context. After oral administration it is absorbed systemically and used clinically in fixed-dose combination products; distribution is consistent with a lipophilic CNS-penetrant small molecule, hepatic metabolism appears to be the dominant clearance route with oxidative and conjugative biotransformation, and elimination occurs via renal and fecal excretion of metabolites, with a clinically useful half-life allowing once-daily administration. Toxicity is generally consistent with opioid antagonists and combination-product exposure, including potential precipitation of acute opioid withdrawal in opioid-dependent individuals, reduced opioid analgesic efficacy, and possible CNS or gastrointestinal adverse effects; overdose concerns are more related to withdrawal, agitation, nausea, and cardiovascular stress than classic opioid respiratory depression. Approved clinical use is as the opioid antagonist component of olanzapine/samidorphan for schizophrenia and bipolar I disorder, primarily to preserve antipsychotic efficacy while mitigating olanzapine-associated weight gain; adverse effects reported in practice include somnolence, dry mouth, increased appetite, dizziness, constipation, and metabolic or extrapyramidal effects largely attributable to the olanzapine-containing regimen.

Name: Fluocinolone
Description: Fluocinolone (DrugBank DB12553) is a synthetic fluorinated corticosteroid built on the pregnane steroid nucleus, specifically a hydrocortisone-like 3-keto-Δ1,4 steroid framework bearing the characteristic 11β-hydroxyl, 17α-hydroxyl, 21-hydroxyl, 9α-fluoro, and 16α,17α-acetonide features that increase topical anti-inflammatory potency and lipophilicity; chemically it belongs to the glucocorticoid corticosteroid class, with a corticosteroid cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene scaffold. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other topical corticosteroids such as triamcinolone acetonide, fluocinonide, fluocortolone, and hydrocortisone derivatives. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor encoded by NR3C1, through which it modulates transcription of anti-inflammatory proteins and suppresses proinflammatory cytokines, prostaglandins, and leukotrienes; indirect downstream effects include reduced activity of PLA2/arachidonic acid pathways and inflammatory transcription programs. Fluocinolone is used mainly for corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses and inflammatory disorders, including eczema, atopic dermatitis, seborrheic dermatitis, psoriasis, otic inflammation, and in intravitreal implant form for chronic noninfectious uveitis or diabetic macular edema. Systemic exposure is usually low after topical or otic administration but increases with damaged skin, occlusion, prolonged use, or large treated areas; the absorbed drug is distributed systemically, hepatically metabolized by steroid-transforming enzymes including CYP3A-mediated pathways, and excreted mainly as urinary metabolites with some biliary/fecal elimination. Toxicity reflects corticosteroid excess: skin atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, delayed wound healing, secondary infection, ocular hypertension, cataract, hyperglycemia, HPA-axis suppression, and Cushingoid features, while common adverse effects include burning, irritation, dryness, folliculitis, acneiform eruption, hypopigmentation, and pruritus; clinically it is used as creams, ointments, solutions, scalp oils, otic preparations, and sustained-release intravitreal implants tailored to site and severity of inflammation.

Name: Nafamostat
Description: Nafamostat (DB12598) is a synthetic small-molecule serine protease inhibitor built around an amidino-substituted aromatic ester, classed chemically as a guanidine/amidine-containing ester and more specifically as an arginine-mimetic trypsin-like protease inhibitor; its core scaffold is a p-guanidinobenzoate-type aromatic ester linked to a substituted naphthalene ring, a motif that confers strong interaction with the acidic S1 pocket of trypsin-like enzymes. It is closely related to other synthetic serine protease inhibitors such as camostat and gabexate, which share cationic amidine/guanidine pharmacophores and are used in overlapping pancreatitis or anticoagulation settings. Pharmacokinetically, nafamostat is administered intravenously because it is not meaningfully orally bioavailable, distributes mainly within plasma and extracellular fluid, is highly short-acting due to rapid hydrolysis by blood and hepatic esterases to less active metabolites including 6-amidino-2-naphthol, and is eliminated predominantly as metabolites in urine. Its major targets include thrombin, plasmin, kallikrein, trypsin, factors XIIa and Xa, complement-associated proteases, and TMPRSS2, supporting anticoagulant, antifibrinolytic, anti-inflammatory, and antiviral interest. Clinically it is used mainly in Japan and Korea for acute pancreatitis, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and as an anticoagulant during extracorporeal circulation or hemodialysis, with investigated use in COVID-19. Toxicity includes bleeding risk, hyperkalemia, agranulocytosis, anaphylactoid reactions, hepatic dysfunction, and coagulation abnormalities; common adverse effects include nausea, rash, fever, hypotension, injection-site reactions, thrombocytopenia, and laboratory electrolyte disturbances.

Name: Urapidil
Description: Urapidil (DrugBank DB12661) is a piperazine-containing antihypertensive built around a substituted uracil/pyrimidinedione-like aromatic heterocyclic core linked through an alkyl chain to a phenylpiperazine moiety, giving an arylpiperazine scaffold characteristic of centrally and peripherally active adrenergic modulators; chemically it is classified as an arylpiperazine antihypertensive and alpha-adrenergic antagonist, with structural and pharmacologic similarity to other alpha1-blocking or phenylpiperazine agents such as prazosin, doxazosin, terazosin, and to some extent 5-HT1A-active arylpiperazines like buspirone in scaffold terms. Its principal targets are the alpha1-adrenergic receptor, which it antagonizes to reduce peripheral vascular resistance, and central serotonin 5-HT1A receptors, where agonist-like activity contributes to sympatholytic effects and limited reflex tachycardia. After intravenous use and oral administration, urapidil is absorbed reasonably well, distributes into vascular and extravascular compartments with moderate protein binding, undergoes substantial hepatic metabolism mainly by hydroxylation and conjugation to less active metabolites, and is eliminated predominantly in urine with a smaller fecal component; its half-life is relatively short, supporting titrated acute use. It is indicated for essential hypertension, hypertensive urgencies or emergencies, and perioperative blood-pressure control, including severe blood pressure elevation during surgery, eclampsia-related hypertension, or catecholamine-associated crises. Adverse effects and dose-related toxicity reflect vasodilation and CNS effects, including hypotension, orthostatic dizziness, headache, fatigue, nausea, flushing, palpitations, and occasional bradycardia or syncope; overdose may produce profound hypotension and circulatory collapse. Clinically, it is used especially in Europe as an intravenous agent for rapid but controllable BP reduction and as an oral option for chronic hypertension.

Name: Lurbinectedin
Description: Lurbinectedin (DB12674) is a synthetic tetrahydroisoquinoline alkaloid antineoplastic agent structurally derived from the trabectedin family, featuring a complex fused polycyclic ecteinascidin-like scaffold with multiple oxygenated rings, bridged tetrahydroisoquinoline subunits, and a reactive carbinolamine/lactone-containing architecture that enables covalent interaction with DNA; chemically it is classified as a marine natural product-inspired DNA-binding alkaloid and belongs to the ecteinascidin scaffold class. Closely related drugs include trabectedin, its prototypical analogue, and more broadly other DNA minor-groove-directed cytotoxics such as doxorubicin or platinum agents by functional similarity rather than close structure. Lurbinectedin binds preferentially to guanine residues in the DNA minor groove, causing DNA adduct formation, transcriptional stalling, double-strand breaks, and modulation of the tumor microenvironment; relevant molecular targets include DNA itself, elongating RNA polymerase II, and downstream DNA damage response machinery. It is administered intravenously, so absorption is complete by infusion; it shows extensive tissue distribution and high plasma protein binding, undergoes predominant hepatic CYP3A4-mediated metabolism, and is eliminated mainly via feces with limited renal excretion and a terminal half-life on the order of days. Dose-limiting toxicity is chiefly myelosuppression, especially neutropenia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and anemia, with hepatotoxicity, creatine phosphokinase elevation, and occasional sepsis or rhabdomyolysis as serious examples. Common adverse effects include fatigue, nausea, decreased appetite, constipation, vomiting, dyspnea, and elevated transaminases. Its principal indication and clinical use is metastatic small cell lung cancer progressing after platinum-based chemotherapy, where it is used as single-agent salvage therapy, and it has also been investigated in other solid tumors such as ovarian, endometrial, breast, and sarcoma settings.

Name: Perazine
Description: Perazine (DrugBank DB12710) is a typical antipsychotic of the phenothiazine class, structurally characterized by a tricyclic phenothiazine core containing sulfur and nitrogen heteroatoms and a ring-substituted side chain terminating in a tertiary piperazine nitrogen, a motif that places it within the piperazine-substituted phenothiazine scaffold associated with relatively potent dopamine receptor antagonism. Chemically and pharmacologically it is closely related to other piperazine phenothiazines such as prochlorperazine, perphenazine, trifluoperazine, and fluphenazine, which share the same antipsychotic/antiemetic chemotype. Its principal targets are dopamine D2 receptors, with additional activity likely at D1, 5-HT2, histamine H1, muscarinic cholinergic, and alpha1-adrenergic receptors, explaining both efficacy and adverse effects. Perazine has been used mainly for schizophrenia, psychotic agitation, paranoid states, and severe behavioral disturbance, and in practice may also reduce anxiety, tension, and nausea in selected settings. After oral administration it is absorbed variably, undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, is widely distributed into lipid-rich tissues including brain, is highly protein bound, and is eliminated predominantly as hepatic metabolites in urine and bile; like related phenothiazines, metabolism is thought to involve oxidative pathways including CYP enzymes. Toxicity resembles that of other typical antipsychotics and includes dose-related extrapyramidal syndromes, tardive dyskinesia, sedation, anticholinergic burden, orthostatic hypotension, hyperprolactinemia, QT prolongation, seizures, hepatotoxicity, and the rare but serious neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Clinically, it has been used as a conventional antipsychotic for acute and chronic psychoses, particularly when calming sedation and control of hallucinations, delusions, and agitation are required.

Name: Pilsicainide
Description: Pilsicainide (DrugBank DB12712) is a class Ic antiarrhythmic with a relatively simple aromatic amide structure built around a substituted anisidine-derived benzene ring linked through a carboxamide to a saturated nitrogen-containing heterocycle, giving it the chemical character of a basic amide and aromatic ether; its core scaffold is therefore an anilide/benzamide-like framework appended to a pyrrolidine ring. It is commonly grouped with potent sodium channel blockers and is pharmacologically similar to other class Ic agents such as flecainide, propafenone, and, more distantly, encainide, although pilsicainide is structurally less bulky and is often considered a pure Na+ channel blocker. Its principal target is the cardiac voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.5 encoded by SCN5A, with use-dependent blockade of fast inward sodium current and consequent slowing of impulse conduction in atrial and ventricular myocardium. Clinically it is used mainly for supraventricular tachyarrhythmias, especially paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, and other symptomatic premature atrial or ventricular beats, and in some settings for pharmacologic cardioversion. Orally administered, it is generally well absorbed, exhibits limited protein binding and modest distribution, undergoes relatively little hepatic metabolism compared with many antiarrhythmics, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged in urine, so exposure increases in renal impairment and dosage adjustment is important. Toxicity reflects excessive sodium channel blockade, with QRS widening, PR prolongation, proarrhythmia including ventricular tachycardia, worsening heart failure, dizziness, tremor, visual disturbance, nausea, and hypotension; overdose or accumulation, particularly in renal dysfunction or structural heart disease, can precipitate severe conduction block, bradyarrhythmia, or malignant ventricular arrhythmias.

Name: Sotagliflozin
Description: Sotagliflozin (DrugBank DB12713) is a small-molecule C-aryl glucoside antidiabetic agent whose structure consists of a glucose-derived polyhydroxylated sugar head group linked through a metabolically stable carbon-carbon bond to a substituted aromatic aglycone bearing lipophilic aryl/heteroaryl features, a motif characteristic of modern sodium-glucose cotransporter inhibitors; chemically it is classified as an SGLT inhibitor, more specifically a dual SGLT1/SGLT2 inhibitor, built on the C-glucoside diaryl scaffold seen across the gliflozin class. Closely related drugs include dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, canagliflozin, and ertugliflozin, although sotagliflozin is distinguished by meaningful intestinal SGLT1 inhibition in addition to renal SGLT2 blockade. Its main targets are SLC5A2 (SGLT2) in the renal proximal tubule and SLC5A1 (SGLT1) in the small intestine and kidney, lowering plasma glucose by increasing urinary glucose excretion and delaying intestinal glucose absorption. After oral administration it is absorbed systemically, is moderately protein bound, undergoes predominant phase II metabolism including glucuronidation with limited oxidative biotransformation, and is eliminated via both fecal and renal routes as parent drug and metabolites. Toxicities reflect its mechanism and class, including osmotic diuresis, volume depletion, hypotension, acute kidney injury risk, genital mycotic infections, urinary tract infection, diarrhea from SGLT1 inhibition, and euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis, especially in insulin-treated patients; severe hypoglycemia is uncommon unless combined with insulin or secretagogues. Clinically it has been used for type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus and for reduction of cardiovascular and heart-failure events in appropriate adults, with practical use as an adjunct to diet, exercise, and standard cardiometabolic therapy.

Name: Lafutidine
Description: Lafutidine (DrugBank DB12770) is a second-generation histamine H2-receptor antagonist with a heteroaromatic, non-imidazole structure characterized by a substituted furan core linked through a thioether/aminomethyl-type spacer to a basic amidine- or guanidine-like terminal functionality and an additional aromatic nitrogen-containing ring, giving an amphiphilic scaffold optimized for potent gastric antisecretory activity and mucosal protection; chemically it is classified as an H2 antihistamine and antiulcer agent, and its core scaffold is best viewed as a furfuryl-sulfur-linked heteroaryl amidine pharmacophore. It is structurally and pharmacologically related to other H2 blockers such as famotidine, nizatidine, ranitidine, and cimetidine, although lafutidine is distinguished by stronger gastroprotective effects, including capsaicin-sensitive sensory neuron activation and enhancement of mucosal blood flow and mucus secretion in addition to H2 receptor blockade. Its principal target is the histamine H2 receptor, with downstream suppression of gastric acid secretion; additional functional interactions are inferred in sensory afferent pathways relevant to mucosal defense. After oral administration it is absorbed adequately, used clinically as an oral agent, distributed systemically at modest levels, undergoes limited to moderate hepatic biotransformation, and is eliminated through both renal and biliary/fecal routes, with a relatively short elimination half-life consistent with once- or twice-daily dosing. Toxicity is generally low at therapeutic exposure, but excessive dosing may increase CNS and gastrointestinal intolerance; serious organ toxicity is uncommon. Indications include gastric ulcer, duodenal ulcer, reflux esophagitis, gastritis-associated lesions, heartburn, epigastric pain, and acid-related dyspepsia. Adverse effects are usually mild and include constipation, diarrhea, nausea, abdominal discomfort, headache, dizziness, rash, and transient liver enzyme elevation. Clinically, it is used for healing and maintenance therapy in peptic ulcer disease and for symptomatic control of acid hypersecretion, particularly where both acid suppression and reinforcement of gastric mucosal defense are desired.

Name: Dinoprost
Description: Dinoprost (DrugBank DB12789) is prostaglandin F2alpha, a naturally occurring eicosanoid derived from arachidonic acid and structurally characterized by a 20-carbon prostanoic acid framework bearing a cyclopentane core, an alpha-chain terminating in a carboxylic acid, an omega-chain with a terminal hydroxyl, and multiple defined stereocenters with hydroxyl substituents and cis/trans alkene geometry that are critical for receptor recognition; chemically it belongs to the prostaglandins, specifically the PGF series of fatty-acid autacoids, and its core scaffold is the prostane/prostanoid cyclopentyl-heptenoic acid skeleton. Similar drugs include other prostaglandin analogs such as carboprost, latanoprost, travoprost, bimatoprost, and dinoprostone, which share related lipid mediator scaffolds but differ in receptor selectivity and stability. Dinoprost acts primarily at the prostaglandin F receptor PTGFR to stimulate uterine and smooth-muscle contraction. After parenteral administration it is rapidly distributed, extensively and quickly metabolized mainly in lung and liver by oxidation of the 15-hydroxyl group and beta- and omega-oxidative pathways to less active metabolites, and eliminated largely in urine as metabolites; oral bioavailability is poor because of rapid first-pass metabolism.
