Toxicity reflects exaggerated prostaglandin activity, including severe uterine hyperstimulation, bronchoconstriction, hypertension or hypotension, cardiovascular stress, gastrointestinal toxicity, and rare anaphylactoid reactions; overdose may cause intense myometrial contraction and fetal distress. Adverse effects commonly include abdominal cramping, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fever, flushing, headache, chest tightness, and bronchospasm. Clinically, dinoprost is used to induce abortion, evacuate missed abortion, manage intrauterine fetal death, and promote uterine evacuation in selected obstetric and gynecologic settings.

Name: Laninamivir
Description: Laninamivir (DB12791) is a neuraminidase inhibitor built on a highly polar sialic-acid-like cyclohexene scaffold, structurally characterized by a polyhydroxylated unsaturated ring bearing a carboxylate and guanidino functionality that mimic the transition state of influenza neuraminidase cleavage; chemically it is a zanamivir-related antiviral belonging to the neuraminic acid analog class, with the core scaffold best described as a modified 4-guanidino DANA-type influenza neuraminidase inhibitor. Similar drugs include zanamivir, oseltamivir, peramivir, and the related long-acting prodrug laninamivir octanoate. Its principal targets are influenza virus neuraminidase proteins from influenza A and B strains, including N1 and N2 subtype enzymes. Pharmacokinetically, active laninamivir is poorly absorbed orally and is therefore administered by inhalation, producing high and prolonged respiratory tract concentrations with relatively low systemic exposure; it distributes mainly within airway mucosa, undergoes minimal metabolism, and is eliminated largely unchanged in urine when systemically absorbed, while the octanoate prodrug is hydrolyzed in the lung to active drug. It is indicated for treatment and, in some settings, prophylaxis of uncomplicated influenza A and B, especially early symptomatic seasonal influenza. Toxicity is generally low because of limited systemic exposure, but bronchospasm, hypersensitivity, and rare neuropsychiatric or severe allergic events are concerns, particularly in patients with reactive airway disease. Common adverse effects include cough, nasal symptoms, diarrhea, headache, and throat irritation. Clinically, it is used as a single-inhalation long-acting anti-influenza therapy, especially in outpatient management of acute influenza and post-exposure prophylaxis where adherence to multi-dose regimens is problematic.

Name: Trifarotene
Description: Trifarotene (DrugBank DB12808) is a fourth-generation topical retinoid whose structure is characterized by a rigid polyaromatic terphenyl-like scaffold bearing a carboxylic acid retinoid pharmacophore and chlorinated aryl substitution, features that confer high receptor selectivity and lipophilicity; chemically it belongs to the aromatic retinoic acid derivatives and more specifically the arotinoid/terphenyl retinoid class. Its core scaffold and pharmacology make it similar to other topical retinoids such as tretinoin, adapalene, tazarotene, and bexarotene, although trifarotene is distinguished by marked selectivity for retinoic acid receptor gamma. The principal known target protein is RAR-gamma, with much weaker activity at RAR-alpha and RAR-beta, leading to modulation of retinoid-responsive gene transcription, normalization of keratinocyte differentiation, and anti-inflammatory effects. It is indicated primarily for acne vulgaris, including facial and truncal acne with comedones, papules, and pustules. Clinically it is used as a once-daily topical treatment in patients requiring field therapy over larger surface areas such as the chest, shoulders, and back. Systemic pharmacokinetic exposure after topical administration is low; absorption through skin is limited but can increase with extensive application, distribution is expected to favor skin with minimal plasma levels, metabolism is predominantly hepatic via CYP-mediated oxidation, especially CYP2C9, CYP3A4, CYP2C8, and to a lesser extent CYP2B6, and excretion occurs mainly as metabolites via biliary/fecal and renal routes. Toxicity is mainly local and dose-related, with erythema, scaling, dryness, burning, and irritant dermatitis; class-related concerns include photosensitivity, teratogenic risk if significant systemic exposure were to occur, and caution in eczema or sunburned skin. Common adverse effects include application-site irritation, pruritus, pain, and sun sensitivity.

Name: Lefamulin
Description: Lefamulin (DB12825) is a semisynthetic pleuromutilin antibacterial characterized by a tricyclic mutilin diterpene core bearing a C14 glycolic-acid-derived side chain with strategically placed heteroatoms that enhance binding to the bacterial ribosome; chemically it belongs to the pleuromutilin class and retains the classic pleuromutilin scaffold shared with related agents such as retapamulin, tiamulin, and valnemulin. Its antibacterial activity derives from selective binding to the peptidyl transferase center of the 50S bacterial ribosomal subunit, primarily interacting with 23S rRNA and associated ribosomal protein elements, thereby inhibiting protein synthesis. Lefamulin is indicated mainly for community-acquired bacterial pneumonia, including infections caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus including methicillin-susceptible strains, Haemophilus influenzae, Legionella pneumophila, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and Chlamydophila pneumoniae, and is used clinically as intravenous or oral step-down therapy in adults. Oral absorption is moderate but clinically useful, distribution is extensive with good penetration into pulmonary epithelial lining fluid and alveolar macrophages, protein binding is high, metabolism occurs predominantly via hepatic CYP3A4-mediated pathways with additional unchanged drug present, and excretion occurs through both fecal/biliary and urinary routes, with a terminal half-life supporting twice-daily dosing. Toxicities of concern include QT interval prolongation, hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevations, embryo-fetal risk, and increased exposure in severe hepatic impairment. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, infusion-site reactions, and elevated liver enzymes. Its clinical utility lies in treating adult CABP when a ribosome-targeting agent with activity against typical and atypical respiratory pathogens is desired.

Name: Amithiozone
Description: Amithiozone (DrugBank DB12829), also known as thiacetazone, is a small synthetic thiosemicarbazone antitubercular agent characterized structurally by an aromatic aldehyde-derived thiosemicarbazone framework, typically described as a para-acetamidobenzaldehyde thiosemicarbazone with a conjugated aryl-imine-thioamide system that imparts planarity and metal-binding reactivity; chemically it belongs to the thiosemicarbazone class and more broadly to aromatic hydrazine/thioamide-containing antimycobacterial compounds, with a core scaffold consisting of a substituted phenyl ring linked through an azomethine C=N bond to a thiosemicarbazide moiety. Similar drugs include other older antitubercular thiosemicarbazones and mechanistically related mycolic-acid-pathway inhibitors, with ethionamide, prothionamide, and isoniazid often cited as therapeutic comparators, though they are not close structural analogs. Its best-characterized targets are mycobacterial cell-envelope biosynthesis proteins in the HadAB/HadBC dehydratase system after bioactivation by the monooxygenase EthA, leading to inhibition of mycolic acid synthesis and activity against Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Pharmacokinetic data are limited but indicate oral absorption, systemic distribution, probable hepatic metabolism with bioactivation and detoxification, and predominantly renal excretion of metabolites. Toxicity is significant, notably severe cutaneous hypersensitivity, mucosal injury, gastrointestinal intolerance, hepatotoxicity, and potentially fatal Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis, especially in patients with HIV infection. Adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, anorexia, dizziness, rash, dermatitis, conjunctivitis, and hematologic intolerance. Clinically, amithiozone was used as a second-line or companion drug for tuberculosis, including pulmonary TB in resource-limited settings, but its use has largely been abandoned because of poor tolerability and safer alternatives.

Name: Tandospirone
Description: Tandospirone (DB12833) is an azapirone anxiolytic with a nonbenzodiazepine serotonergic structure built around an arylpiperazine motif linked by a butyl chain to a cyclic imide-like heterocycle, giving it a lipophilic buspirone-like architecture typical of 5-HT1A receptor ligands; chemically it is categorized as an anxiolytic psychotropic agent within the azaspirodecanedione/arylpiperazine-related serotonin receptor modulator class, and its core scaffold is best described as an arylpiperazine tethered to a constrained cyclic carbonyl-containing heterocycle. Similar drugs include buspirone, gepirone, and ipsapirone, which share the azapirone scaffold and partial agonism at serotonin 5-HT1A receptors. Tandospirone is absorbed orally, undergoes significant first-pass hepatic metabolism, distributes into the central nervous system sufficiently to produce anxiolytic effects, and is eliminated mainly after oxidative biotransformation, principally via CYP3A4, with urinary excretion of metabolites and limited unchanged drug recovery. Its principal target is HTR1A, where it acts as a partial agonist at presynaptic and postsynaptic 5-HT1A receptors; weaker interactions with dopamine D2 or other monoaminergic sites have been described but are not primary. It is indicated mainly for anxiety disorders, especially generalized anxiety states, tension, autonomic symptoms, and anxiety associated with depression or psychosomatic illness. Adverse effects are usually mild to moderate and include dizziness, drowsiness, headache, nausea, gastrointestinal discomfort, fatigue, and insomnia; toxicity is generally lower than with benzodiazepines, with relatively little respiratory depression, dependence, or withdrawal liability, though overdose may still cause marked sedation, emesis, and impaired psychomotor function. Clinically, tandospirone has been used as an oral anxiolytic in Japan and parts of Asia for neurosis, anxiety with depressive symptoms, and stress-related somatic complaints, and it has also been explored as an adjunct in schizophrenia, mood disorders, and functional gastrointestinal syndromes where serotonergic anxiolysis is desirable.

Name: Secnidazole
Description: Secnidazole (DrugBank DB12834) is a 5-nitroimidazole antimicrobial whose structure consists of a nitro-substituted imidazole heteroaromatic ring bearing a 2-methyl group and a hydroxypropyl side chain, placing it in the nitroimidazole class and on the metronidazole-like 5-nitroimidazole scaffold shared with metronidazole, tinidazole, ornidazole, and benznidazole. As with related agents, its activity depends on reductive bioactivation in susceptible anaerobic protozoa and bacteria, where low-redox electron transport proteins such as pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase-linked systems and ferredoxin-like nitroreductive pathways convert the nitro group to reactive intermediates that damage DNA and other macromolecules; therefore no single human protein target is primary, and microbial nitroreductases are the key functional targets. Secnidazole is used mainly for bacterial vaginosis and protozoal infections such as trichomoniasis, giardiasis, and intestinal or hepatic amebiasis. It is well absorbed orally, reaches high systemic exposure after single-dose administration, distributes broadly into tissues and vaginal secretions, undergoes relatively limited hepatic biotransformation compared with some shorter-acting congeners, and is eliminated through both renal excretion of parent drug and metabolites and, to a lesser extent, fecal routes; its prolonged elimination half-life supports one-dose regimens. Adverse effects are usually mild and include nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, dysgeusia or metallic taste, headache, dizziness, and vulvovaginal candidiasis, while toxicity concerns include hypersensitivity, peripheral neuropathy or other neurotoxicity with prolonged nitroimidazole exposure, possible leukopenia, and disulfiram-like reactions with alcohol. Clinically, it is valued for simplified adherence, especially as single-dose oral therapy for bacterial vaginosis and selected anaerobic or protozoal infections.

Name: Reproterol
Description: Reproterol (DrugBank DB12846) is a short-acting sympathomimetic bronchodilator whose structure is that of a substituted phenethylamine/arylethanolamine bearing a resorcinol-type aromatic ring and a beta-hydroxylated amino side chain with a bulky N-substituent, features that confer beta2-adrenoceptor selectivity and resistance to rapid catechol-O-methyltransferase degradation; chemically it is classified as a phenylaminoethanol beta2-adrenergic agonist and belongs to the arylethanolamine scaffold shared with other inhaled bronchodilators. Closely related or pharmacologically similar drugs include terbutaline, fenoterol, salbutamol (albuterol), ritodrine, and metaproterenol, all of which act through beta2-adrenergic receptor stimulation. Its principal target is the beta2-adrenergic receptor encoded by ADRB2, with lesser activity at beta1 receptors at higher exposure, leading to activation of adenylate cyclase, increased cAMP, and relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle. Reproterol has mainly been used by inhalation for rapid relief of reversible bronchospasm in bronchial asthma and chronic obstructive airway disease, including acute wheeze, exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, and symptomatic airflow limitation. After inhalation, pulmonary absorption is rapid, swallowed drug undergoes first-pass metabolism, distribution is largely extracellular with limited CNS penetration, metabolism occurs predominantly by phase II conjugation such as sulfation or glucuronidation rather than extensive oxidative catechol metabolism, and excretion is mainly renal as parent drug and conjugates. Toxicity is typical of beta-agonists and dose related, including tachycardia, palpitations, tremor, nervousness, headache, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, and rarely arrhythmias or myocardial ischemia, especially with overdose or concomitant xanthines; accordingly, clinical use has focused on as-needed bronchodilation, sometimes in fixed combinations, while monitoring cardiovascular tolerance.

Name: Sivelestat
Description: Sivelestat (DB12863) is a small-molecule synthetic neutrophil elastase inhibitor characterized structurally as a low-molecular-weight aryl sulfonyl compound bearing a benzene sulfonyl core linked through an amide/carbamoyl-type connector to a substituted heteroaromatic moiety and commonly formulated clinically as the sodium hydrate salt; chemically it falls within sulfonamides/sulfonylated enzyme inhibitors, with a benzenesulfonyl-anilide-like scaffold optimized to occupy the elastase substrate-binding pocket. It is most similar pharmacologically to other serine protease inhibitors that target neutrophil elastase or related inflammatory proteases, such as alvelestat, AZD9668, and older elastase-directed agents including alpha-1 proteinase inhibitor replacement strategies, although its chemistry is distinct from peptide inhibitors. Its principal known target is neutrophil elastase, with possible activity against closely related serine proteases at higher concentrations. Sivelestat is used mainly for acute lung injury and acute respiratory distress syndrome associated with systemic inflammatory response, sepsis, severe pneumonia, trauma, burns, or post-operative inflammation, where suppression of elastase-mediated endothelial and alveolar damage is desired. Given intravenously, it has rapid systemic availability, limited oral relevance, distribution largely in extracellular fluid, hepatic metabolism including hydrolytic/phase II pathways, and predominantly renal excretion of metabolites, with a relatively short elimination half-life requiring continuous infusion or repeated dosing. Adverse effects include hepatic enzyme elevation, bilirubin increase, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, rash, gastrointestinal upset, and infusion-related reactions; toxicity concerns center on hepatotoxicity, renal dysfunction, bleeding tendency, and hypersensitivity, especially in critically ill patients. Clinically, it has been used in Japan as adjunctive therapy to improve pulmonary inflammation, oxygenation, and ventilatory outcomes in elastase-driven lung injury.

Name: Etelcalcetide
Description: Etelcalcetide (DB12865) is a synthetic peptide-derived calcimimetic composed of a short linear oligopeptide built around multiple D-amino acid residues and a terminal cysteine-like thiol functionality that forms a reversible disulfide interaction with its receptor, making its structure more accurately described as a small peptidomimetic disulfide-containing oligopeptide than a classical small molecule. Chemically it belongs to the calcimimetic class and to peptide/peptidomimetic therapeutics, with a scaffold defined by a linear D-amino acid chain linked to a reactive disulfide-capable cysteine motif. Its closest similar drug is cinacalcet, another calcium-sensing receptor agonist used for secondary hyperparathyroidism, although cinacalcet is orally active and structurally a nonpeptide allosteric modulator; evocalcet is another related calcimimetic example. Etelcalcetide targets the calcium-sensing receptor CASR on parathyroid chief cells, lowering parathyroid hormone secretion and thereby reducing serum calcium and phosphate abnormalities in chronic kidney disease. It is indicated primarily for secondary hyperparathyroidism in adult patients with CKD receiving hemodialysis. Because it is administered intravenously at the end of hemodialysis, absorption is complete by infusion; distribution is largely extracellular with extensive reversible covalent exchange with circulating thiols such as albumin; metabolism occurs mainly through disulfide exchange and biotransformation rather than CYP-mediated pathways; and elimination is predominantly renal, with hemodialysis contributing importantly to clearance. Major toxicities reflect exaggerated pharmacology, especially hypocalcemia, which may cause QT prolongation, ventricular arrhythmia, seizures, paresthesias, muscle spasms, and worsening heart failure; common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, hypocalcemia, and headache. Clinically, it is used in dialysis units to suppress persistently elevated PTH when vitamin D analogs or phosphate-control measures alone are inadequate.

Name: Benperidol
Description: Benperidol (DrugBank DB12867) is a potent first-generation antipsychotic of the butyrophenone class, structurally characterized by a para-fluorobutyrophenone pharmacophore linked through a tertiary alcohol center to a piperidine ring and an additional para-chlorophenyl substituent, giving a highly lipophilic halogenated aryl-ketone architecture typical of high-potency dopamine antagonists. Its core chemical scaffold is therefore the fluorobutyrophenone–piperidinol framework, closely related to other butyrophenones such as haloperidol, droperidol, trifluperidol, and bromperidol, which are considered its nearest structural and pharmacologic analogues. Benperidol primarily targets dopamine D2 receptors, with additional activity reported at D1-like and possibly sigma and serotonergic sites, and its antipsychotic efficacy is attributed mainly to strong central D2 blockade in mesolimbic pathways. It has been used in schizophrenia, acute psychosis, severe agitation, mania, and behavioral disturbance, especially where marked antipsychotic potency is desired. Pharmacokinetically, it is absorbed after oral administration, distributes widely into the CNS because of high lipophilicity, undergoes substantial hepatic biotransformation including carbonyl reduction and oxidative pathways, and is eliminated as metabolites in urine and feces; like related agents, it likely has moderate oral bioavailability, extensive tissue distribution, and a clinically relevant half-life permitting repeated daily dosing. Toxicity resembles other high-potency typical antipsychotics and includes dose-related extrapyramidal toxicity, akathisia, parkinsonism, dystonia, hyperprolactinemia, sedation, autonomic effects, and risk of tardive dyskinesia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, seizures, and QT-related ventricular arrhythmias in overdose or susceptible patients. Clinically, benperidol has mainly served as a specialist antipsychotic for chronic schizophrenia and severe refractory psychotic states, but its use is limited by its narrow tolerability profile and high burden of neurologic adverse effects.

Name: Quizartinib
Description: Quizartinib (DrugBank DB12874) is an orally active, small-molecule type II receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor whose structure is characterized by a lipophilic, highly substituted aromatic heterocyclic framework built around a bis-aryl urea-like pharmacophore linked to nitrogen-containing heteroaromatic rings and halogenated phenyl elements that stabilize binding to the inactive DFG-out kinase conformation; chemically it is best classified as a heteroaryl kinase inhibitor, with a diaryl/heteroaryl urea-related scaffold typical of FLT3-directed agents. It is most similar pharmacologically to other FLT3 inhibitors such as midostaurin, gilteritinib, crenolanib, and sorafenib, although quizartinib is especially potent against FLT3 internal tandem duplication-mutant disease. Its principal target is FLT3 (CD135, FLT3 receptor tyrosine kinase), with additional activity reported against KIT, PDGFR, and CSF1R at varying potency. After oral administration it is absorbed systemically with a relatively long half-life permitting once-daily dosing, is extensively distributed and highly protein bound, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism via CYP3A4 to an active metabolite, and is eliminated mainly in feces with lesser renal excretion. Clinically, it is used for relapsed or refractory acute myeloid leukemia with FLT3-ITD mutations and has been studied in other FLT3-driven myeloid malignancies. Major toxicities include QT prolongation and ventricular arrhythmia risk, myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity, gastrointestinal toxicity, and embryo-fetal toxicity; common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fatigue, febrile neutropenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, edema, mucositis, and electrolyte disturbances. In practice it is used as targeted monotherapy in molecularly selected AML, with ECG and CYP3A-interaction monitoring central to safe use.

Name: Tazemetostat
Description: Tazemetostat (DB12887) is a selective, orally active small-molecule epigenetic anticancer agent that inhibits the histone-lysine N-methyltransferase enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2), the catalytic subunit of the polycomb repressive complex 2; structurally, it is a synthetic heteroaromatic amide-containing compound built around a compact aza-heterocyclic, SAM-competitive methyltransferase-inhibitor architecture with a substituted aromatic/heterobicyclic core that supports high affinity binding in the EZH2 catalytic pocket. Chemically it is categorized as a targeted antineoplastic methyltransferase inhibitor, and its scaffold is generally described as a fused nitrogen-rich heteroaryl epigenetic-inhibitor scaffold related to other SAM-competitive EZH2 inhibitors. Similar drugs include valemetostat, pinometostat in the broader epigenetic enzyme inhibitor space, and investigational EZH2 inhibitors such as GSK126 and CPI-1205. After oral administration, tazemetostat is absorbed systemically, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, is moderately distributed, is highly protein bound, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism primarily via CYP3A to inactive metabolites, and is eliminated mainly in feces with a smaller urinary component; strong CYP3A modulators can materially alter exposure. Toxicity is generally manageable but includes embryo-fetal toxicity, secondary malignancy risk such as myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukemia, and dose-limiting constitutional and hematologic effects. Its principal target is EZH2, including gain-of-function mutant forms seen in cancer. It is indicated for epithelioid sarcoma and for relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma with EZH2 mutation or, when no satisfactory alternatives exist, even without mutation in some settings. Common adverse effects include fatigue, nausea, decreased appetite, abdominal pain, constipation, musculoskeletal pain, and cytopenias. Clinically, it is used as an oral precision oncology therapy in molecularly selected or otherwise treatment-limited patients, particularly those with EZH2-driven lymphoid malignancy or advanced epithelioid sarcoma.

Name: Ozenoxacin
Description: Ozenoxacin (DB12924) is a nonfluorinated quinolone antibacterial whose structure is built on a bicyclic quinolone-3-carboxylic acid core with a ketone, aromatic substitution pattern, and lipophilic heteroaryl functionality that enhance Gram-positive antibacterial potency while avoiding the fluorine present in many older quinolones; chemically it is categorized as a topical quinolone antibiotic, and its core scaffold is the quinolone/naphthyridone-like DNA gyrase inhibitor framework. It is most similar to other quinolone antibacterials such as ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, nadifloxacin, and besifloxacin, although it is distinguished by nonfluinated design and topical dermatologic use. Its pharmacology is driven by inhibition of bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, with target proteins corresponding to the bacterial GyrA/GyrB and ParC/ParE enzyme complexes; activity is especially relevant against Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes, including some resistant strains. Pharmacokinetically, ozenoxacin is formulated for topical administration, shows minimal systemic absorption through intact or affected skin, limited distribution beyond the application site, negligible clinically relevant metabolism because circulating levels are extremely low, and excretion is not a major determinant of use due to near-absent systemic exposure. Toxicity is therefore low in routine use, with no meaningful phototoxicity or fluorquinolone-class systemic toxicities expected at topical exposures, though local intolerance can occur. It is indicated for impetigo, particularly nonbullous impetigo caused by S. aureus or S. pyogenes, and is used clinically as a short-course topical treatment for localized superficial bacterial skin infection. Adverse effects are usually mild and application-site limited, including pruritus, erythema, seborrheic dermatitis-like irritation, and discomfort.

Name: Opipramol
Description: Opipramol (DrugBank DB12930) is a dibenzazepine-derived tricyclic psychotropic agent structurally characterized by a tricyclic aromatic ring system linked through a short side chain to a piperazine-containing propyl moiety, giving it a close topological resemblance to tricyclic antidepressants while conferring a distinct receptor-binding profile; chemically it is classified as a tricyclic anxiolytic/antidepressant, and its core scaffold is the dibenzazepine-tricyclic nucleus with a terminal piperazine side chain. Similar drugs include other tricyclics such as imipramine, desipramine, doxepin, and amitriptyline, although opipramol differs pharmacologically by acting predominantly at sigma receptors rather than as a classic monoamine reuptake inhibitor. Its known targets include sigma-1 and sigma-2 receptors, with additional moderate antagonistic activity at histamine H1, dopamine D2, and serotonergic receptors, which contributes to its sedative and anxiolytic effects. After oral administration it is well absorbed, undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, is widely distributed including into the central nervous system, is metabolized mainly by oxidative biotransformation to active and inactive metabolites, and is excreted primarily in urine with some fecal elimination. It is indicated chiefly for generalized anxiety states, somatoform disorders, tension, agitation, and depressive symptoms with prominent anxiety. Adverse effects commonly include sedation, dry mouth, dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, constipation, fatigue, and weight gain; toxic effects in overdose may include marked CNS depression, anticholinergic symptoms, cardiac conduction abnormalities, arrhythmias, and seizures. Clinically, it is used mainly in parts of Europe for anxiety disorders, mixed anxious-depressive states, and psychosomatic complaints where a calming, sleep-promoting tricyclic agent is desired.

Name: Darolutamide
Description: Darolutamide (DrugBank DB12941) is a nonsteroidal androgen receptor antagonist built around a densely functionalized, conformationally constrained aromatic-heterocyclic framework containing a substituted pyrazole-linked carboxamide/amide motif and polar substituents that distinguish it from earlier antiandrogens; chemically, it is categorized as a second-generation nonsteroidal antiandrogen, and its core scaffold is best described as a diaryl-heteroaryl pyrazole-amide pharmacophore optimized for high-affinity androgen receptor binding and limited blood-brain barrier penetration. Structurally and mechanistically similar drugs include enzalutamide, apalutamide, and, more distantly, bicalutamide and nilutamide, although darolutamide has a distinct scaffold and lower CNS exposure. Its principal target protein is the androgen receptor, including clinically relevant mutant forms, where it inhibits androgen-induced receptor signaling, nuclear translocation, and transcriptional activation. After oral administration, absorption is improved with food; the drug shows moderate protein binding and systemic distribution with relatively low CNS penetration, is metabolized mainly by CYP3A4 and UGT pathways to the active metabolite keto-darolutamide, and is eliminated through both urine and feces. Toxicity is generally manageable compared with some related agents, but fatigue, asthenia, rash, hypertension, falls, and liver enzyme elevations have been reported; embryo-fetal toxicity is a theoretical and labeled concern based on mechanism, and serious adverse events may include ischemic heart disease or fractures in susceptible patients. Clinically, darolutamide is indicated for prostate cancer, especially nonmetastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, where it is used with androgen deprivation therapy, and in some settings with docetaxel, to delay metastasis, prolong survival, and control disease progression.

Name: Lactitol
Description: Lactitol (DrugBank DB12942) is a synthetic sugar alcohol disaccharide derived by reduction of lactose, consisting of a galactose unit linked to sorbitol through a glycosidic bond, giving a highly hydroxylated, flexible polyol structure with a lactose-like carbohydrate scaffold and placing it in the chemical category of disaccharide osmotic laxatives and low-digestible polyols; its core scaffold is therefore a galactosyl-sorbitol saccharide framework. Similar drugs include lactulose, sorbitol, mannitol, and polyethylene glycol as osmotic cathartics, with lactulose being the closest mechanistic analogue in hepatic encephalopathy and constipation. Pharmacokinetically, lactitol is minimally absorbed in the small intestine, has negligible systemic distribution, undergoes no meaningful host metabolism, and is fermented by colonic bacteria to short-chain organic acids that increase osmotic water retention and acidify the colonic lumen; absorbed fractions, if any, are excreted largely unchanged in urine, while most of the dose is eliminated in feces as parent compound or bacterial metabolites. Its known pharmacologic action is largely non-protein-target-based, so no specific human target proteins are established; instead, it acts through luminal osmotic effects and microbiome-mediated acidification that reduces intestinal ammonia absorption. Indications include chronic constipation and portal-systemic encephalopathy or hepatic encephalopathy, where it helps lower ammonia and improve neuropsychiatric symptoms. Toxicity is usually dose related and gastrointestinal, including abdominal cramping, flatulence, bloating, and osmotic diarrhea, with excessive use potentially causing dehydration and electrolyte disturbances such as hypokalemia or hypernatremia. Clinically, it is used orally as a powder or solution for bowel regulation and as an ammonia-lowering agent in cirrhotic patients with encephalopathy.

Name: Doxifluridine
Description: Doxifluridine (5′-deoxy-5-fluorouridine; DrugBank DB12947) is an orally active fluorinated pyrimidine antimetabolite whose structure consists of a 5-fluorouracil base linked to a 2-deoxyribose-like furanose sugar lacking the 5′-hydroxymethyl oxygen, making it a nucleoside analog and prodrug of 5-fluorouracil; chemically it belongs to the fluoropyrimidine class and is built on a pyrimidine nucleoside scaffold closely related to uridine, floxuridine, capecitabine, tegafur, and 5-fluorouracil itself. It is absorbed enterally after oral administration, distributed to systemic tissues including tumors, and is converted mainly by thymidine phosphorylase, often enriched in malignant tissue, to 5-fluorouracil, which then undergoes intracellular activation to fluorodeoxyuridine monophosphate and fluorouridine triphosphate; catabolism is driven largely by dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase with further hepatic metabolism and urinary excretion of metabolites. Its pharmacologic targets are therefore principally thymidylate synthase, with downstream disruption of DNA synthesis, and RNA-processing pathways through misincorporated fluorinated nucleotides; enzymes governing activation and breakdown, including thymidine phosphorylase and DPD, are clinically relevant determinants of response and toxicity. Doxifluridine has been used for gastrointestinal malignancies, especially gastric and colorectal cancer, and sometimes breast or other solid tumors, either alone or in combination regimens. Major adverse effects mirror fluoropyrimidines and include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, stomatitis, mucositis, myelosuppression, anorexia, fatigue, and hand-foot syndrome, while serious toxicity can include severe enterocolitis, neutropenia, infection, neurotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, and potentially fatal reactions in DPD-deficient patients.

Name: Pyronaridine
Description: Pyronaridine (DrugBank DB12975) is a synthetic benzonaphthyridine-derived antimalarial built around a planar tricyclic aza-aromatic scaffold, specifically a substituted benzo[b][1,5]naphthyridine/chloro-anilino core bearing pyrrolidinylmethyl side chains that confer cationic, amphiphilic, heme-binding properties; chemically it is classified as a Mannich-base antimalarial and weakly basic heteroaromatic blood schizontocide, with structural and pharmacologic similarity to other quinoline- or acridine-like hematin-interfering agents such as chloroquine, amodiaquine, mepacrine, and quinacrine. Its principal antiplasmodial target is not a single parasite protein but the heme detoxification pathway in the Plasmodium digestive vacuole, where it accumulates by pH trapping and inhibits conversion of toxic ferriprotoporphyrin IX to hemozoin; additional activity against parasite nucleic acid processes has been proposed. Orally administered pyronaridine is absorbed adequately, commonly given with artesunate, displays extensive tissue and erythrocyte distribution, high protein/cellular binding, and a long terminal half-life on the order of days to weeks, supporting sustained post-treatment exposure; metabolism is predominantly hepatic, likely involving oxidative biotransformation and biliary/fecal elimination, with limited renal clearance. It is indicated for uncomplicated malaria, especially Plasmodium falciparum and also P. vivax in some settings, and is used clinically as the fixed-dose combination pyronaridine-artesunate for acute malaria treatment. Important adverse effects include headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and asymptomatic or clinically significant transaminase elevations; toxicity concerns center on hepatotoxicity, potential QT effects that appear limited relative to some antimalarials, and caution in patients with pre-existing liver disease or repeated dosing exposure.

Name: Pexidartinib
Description: Pexidartinib (DB12978) is an orally active small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor built around a substituted heteroaromatic azaindole/pyridine-rich framework with halogenated and amino side-chain features that support high-affinity binding in kinase ATP pockets; chemically it is best categorized as a targeted antineoplastic kinase inhibitor, and its core scaffold is commonly described as an azaindole-like CSF1R-directed kinase-binding motif. It is structurally and pharmacologically related to other multitargeted kinase inhibitors, particularly colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor and KIT inhibitors such as imatinib, nilotinib, sorafenib, and quizartinib, although pexidartinib is distinguished by strong CSF1R inhibition. Its principal targets are CSF1R, KIT, and FLT3, with downstream suppression of macrophage-driven and proliferative signaling. After oral administration it is absorbed systemically, with exposure influenced by food and gastric conditions; it is highly protein bound, distributes broadly, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 and UGT1A4, and is eliminated through both fecal and urinary routes largely as metabolites. The major toxicity concern is serious hepatotoxicity, including mixed or cholestatic liver injury and clinically significant transaminase, bilirubin, and alkaline phosphatase elevations, which has necessitated intensive liver monitoring and restricted-distribution prescribing; embryo-fetal toxicity is also a concern. Adverse effects commonly include fatigue, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, decreased appetite, dysgeusia, periorbital edema, hair color changes, anemia, and increased liver enzymes. Clinically, it is used primarily for symptomatic tenosynovial giant cell tumor, especially unresectable or surgery-morbid disease, where CSF1R blockade can reduce tumor burden, pain, stiffness, and impaired joint function.

Name: Tinoridine
Description: Tinoridine (DrugBank DB13001) is a small-molecule nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug of the basic anti-inflammatory/analgesic class, structurally characterized by a heteroaromatic sulfur-containing scaffold centered on a thiophene-derived ring system bearing amidine/guanidine-like basic functionality and aryl substitution, a motif that confers cationic character and distinguishes it from acidic arylacetic or propionic acid NSAIDs; thus, its chemical scaffold is best described as an amidino-substituted thiophene anti-inflammatory pharmacophore. It is chemically related in therapeutic intent, though not identical in scaffold, to other older NSAIDs and anti-inflammatory analgesics such as indomethacin, diclofenac, ibuprofen, and tiaprofenic acid, but it is more closely grouped with older basic anti-inflammatory agents developed for rheumatic disease. Its precise molecular targets are not fully defined, but pharmacology is generally consistent with inhibition of inflammatory mediator generation, including cyclooxygenase-linked prostaglandin synthesis, with downstream effects on pain and inflammation pathways rather than a highly selective single-protein mechanism. Tinoridine has been used clinically for inflammatory and painful disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, periarthritis, low back pain, and postoperative or musculoskeletal pain. After oral administration it is absorbed systemically, distributed to inflamed tissues, undergoes hepatic biotransformation, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine with some biliary/fecal excretion; detailed modern ADME parameters are limited. Adverse effects resemble those of older NSAIDs and include gastrointestinal discomfort, nausea, dyspepsia, rash, dizziness, and headache, while toxicity may include peptic ulceration, gastrointestinal bleeding, hepatic enzyme elevation, hypersensitivity, and renal functional impairment, particularly with prolonged use or in susceptible patients.

Name: Ramatroban
Description: Ramatroban (DrugBank DB13036) is a small-molecule eicosanoid receptor antagonist built around an aromatic carboxylic acid-containing anti-inflammatory pharmacophore, with a lipophilic diaryl/aryl-heteroaryl framework linked to a propionic acid-like acidic terminus that supports high-affinity binding to prostanoid receptors; chemically it is generally classified as a synthetic thromboxane A2 receptor antagonist and antiallergic agent, and its scaffold is commonly described as an arylalkanoic acid-derived prostanoid antagonist scaffold. It is structurally and pharmacologically related to other thromboxane pathway modulators and TP antagonists such as seratrodast, terutroban, ifetroban, and ozagrel, although ozagrel acts by thromboxane synthase inhibition rather than direct receptor blockade. Ramatroban primarily targets the thromboxane prostanoid receptor TP, encoded by TBXA2R, and has also been reported to antagonize the prostaglandin D2 receptor CRTH2/DP2, contributing to anti-inflammatory and antiallergic effects. After oral administration it is absorbed adequately, is substantially protein bound, distributes mainly within the vascular and extracellular compartment, undergoes hepatic biotransformation with oxidative and conjugative metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly as metabolites in urine and feces with a relatively short clinical half-life requiring repeated dosing. Toxicity is generally modest at therapeutic doses but may include gastrointestinal intolerance, hepatic enzyme elevation, headache, dizziness, and potential bleeding-related concerns from interference with thromboxane signaling; overdose would be expected to intensify these effects. Clinically, it has been used mainly for allergic rhinitis, especially nasal obstruction, rhinorrhea, and sneezing, and has also been explored in asthma and other eosinophilic or platelet-driven inflammatory conditions.

Name: Oteseconazole
Description: Oteseconazole (DrugBank DB13055) is a novel oral tetrazole antifungal whose structure is characterized by a highly lipophilic, fluorinated azole pharmacophore built around a tetrazole ring linked to substituted aromatic/heteroaromatic groups, a design that preserves fungal CYP51 binding while reducing affinity for human steroidogenic cytochrome P450 enzymes; chemically it belongs to the azole-derived sterol biosynthesis inhibitors, with a tetrazole-containing triazole-like scaffold related to other lanosterol 14α-demethylase inhibitors. Similar drugs include fluconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, and isavuconazole, although oteseconazole is distinguished by greater selectivity for fungal CYP51. Its principal target protein is fungal lanosterol 14α-demethylase, encoded by CYP51/ERG11, leading to inhibition of ergosterol synthesis and disruption of fungal membrane integrity, especially in Candida species. Pharmacokinetically, it is orally bioavailable, reaches systemic circulation with a long terminal half-life, is extensively distributed into tissues, is highly protein bound, undergoes limited oxidative metabolism compared with older azoles, and is eliminated slowly through combined hepatic/biliary and minor renal routes, supporting intermittent or loading/maintenance regimens. Toxicity is generally milder than with less selective azoles, but class-relevant concerns include hepatotoxicity, embryo-fetal risk, and potential QT-interval effects, with adverse findings from reproductive toxicology prompting contraindication in pregnancy and in females of reproductive potential. Clinically, it is indicated for recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis, particularly to reduce episodes caused by Candida albicans, and is used in patients with repeated vulvovaginal itching, burning, irritation, and discharge. Common adverse effects include headache, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, dysmenorrhea, and vulvovaginal symptoms, while serious events are uncommon but may include hepatic enzyme elevations and hypersensitivity.

Name: Tramazoline
Description: Tramazoline (DrugBank DB13064) is an imidazoline-derived sympathomimetic nasal decongestant whose structure is characterized by a substituted aromatic ring linked through a benzyl-type carbon to a cyclic imidazoline/amidine moiety, giving a basic, cationizable alpha-adrenergic agonist pharmacophore optimized for topical vasoconstrictor activity. Chemically it is classified as an imidazoline decongestant and more broadly as a direct-acting adrenergic agonist; its core scaffold is the aryl-alkyl-imidazoline motif shared with related topical vasoconstrictors. Similar drugs include xylometazoline, oxymetazoline, naphazoline, and tetrahydrozoline, which have comparable alpha-adrenergic receptor agonist properties and local decongestant uses. Its principal targets are alpha-adrenergic receptors, especially ADRA1A, ADRA1B, ADRA1D, and possibly alpha-2 receptor subtypes, producing constriction of nasal mucosal capacitance vessels and reduction of edema and secretions. After intranasal administration, tramazoline is intended for predominantly local action, with limited but clinically relevant systemic absorption, distribution expected to favor well-perfused tissues if absorbed, hepatic biotransformation likely contributing to clearance, and renal excretion of metabolites; precise human ADME parameters are not extensively characterized. It is indicated for symptomatic relief of nasal congestion in common cold, acute rhinitis, allergic rhinitis, and sinusitis. Clinical use is as a short-course topical nasal spray or drops. Adverse effects include nasal dryness, burning, irritation, sneezing, headache, and less commonly palpitations, hypertension, tachycardia, insomnia, or restlessness from systemic sympathomimetic exposure. Toxicity is usually related to overdose or prolonged use, with risks of rebound congestion, rhinitis medicamentosa, and in severe exposures cardiovascular or CNS effects, especially in children.

Name: Meclocycline
Description: Meclocycline (DrugBank DB13092) is a semisynthetic tetracycline antibiotic whose structure consists of the characteristic linearly fused four-ring naphthacene core bearing multiple keto, phenolic, and enolic hydroxyl functionalities with a dimethylamino substituent typical of tetracyclines and additional halogenation that contributes to its lipophilicity; chemically it belongs to the polyketide-derived tetracycline class, with the classic tetracycline/naphthacene scaffold as its defining chemotype. It is closely related to other tetracyclines such as tetracycline, demeclocycline, doxycycline, minocycline, and chlortetracycline, which share a broadly similar antibacterial mechanism. Like other members of the class, meclocycline acts by binding the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit, principally interacting with 16S rRNA within the ribosome to block aminoacyl-tRNA accommodation and inhibit protein synthesis; this is its primary known target system rather than a human protein target. Meclocycline has mainly been used topically, so systemic pharmacokinetic data are limited, but topical administration is intended to minimize absorption, with any absorbed fraction expected to distribute similarly to tetracyclines, undergo limited hepatic biotransformation, and be eliminated via renal and biliary routes. Its indications have included superficial bacterial skin infections and acneiform conditions, especially infections involving susceptible gram-positive or gram-negative organisms. Adverse effects and toxicities resemble those of tetracyclines, including local irritation, erythema, burning, photosensitivity, superinfection, and, if systemically absorbed, gastrointestinal upset, hepatotoxicity, tooth discoloration, and effects on bone growth; clinically it has been used in dermatologic preparations for infected dermatoses and acne where a topical antibacterial tetracycline is desired.

Name: Saroglitazar
Description: Saroglitazar (DB13115) is a small-molecule glitazar and dual peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor agonist with predominant PPARα activity and moderate PPARγ activity; structurally, it is an aryl-substituted phenoxy/benzyl ether–type acidic ligand built around the fibrate/thiazolidinedione-like PPAR-binding pharmacophore, bearing a lipophilic aromatic scaffold linked to a polar acidic headgroup that supports nuclear receptor binding, and it is therefore classified within antidiabetic, antihyperlipidemic PPAR modulators with a glitazar scaffold related mechanistically and chemically to pioglitazone, rosiglitazone, muraglitazar, tesaglitazar, and to some extent the fibrate class such as fenofibrate. Its known target proteins are PPARA and PPARG, with downstream transcriptional effects on genes regulating fatty-acid oxidation, triglyceride metabolism, insulin sensitivity, and hepatic lipid handling. Clinically, it is used primarily for diabetic dyslipidemia and hypertriglyceridemia in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus, and has also been used in practice for mixed dyslipidemia and explored in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease or steatohepatitis contexts because of effects on triglycerides and liver enzymes. After oral administration it is absorbed systemically, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, is highly protein bound, distributes mainly within the vascular/extracellular compartment, undergoes limited hepatic biotransformation relative to some other PPAR ligands, and is eliminated largely via hepatobiliary/fecal routes with lesser renal excretion. Adverse effects are generally mild and include dyspepsia, gastritis, कमजोरी/fatigue, peripheral edema, weight gain, and headache; important toxicities of concern for the class include fluid retention, worsening heart failure risk, hepatic enzyme elevations, myalgia or creatine kinase increase, and renal function changes, although saroglitazar has been developed to reduce the excess edema and cardiovascular toxicity seen with earlier glitazars.

Name: Lusutrombopag
Description: Lusutrombopag (DrugBank DB13125) is a small-molecule, orally active thrombopoietin receptor agonist built as a nonpeptide, highly aromatic heterocyclic compound containing multiple fused and substituted ring systems, including a carboxylic acid-bearing biaryl/heterobiaryl framework that confers lipophilicity and receptor-binding specificity; chemically it is categorized as a thrombopoietin mimetic and thrombopoiesis-stimulating agent, and its core scaffold is a synthetic heteroaromatic biaryl small-molecule scaffold broadly related to other nonpeptide TPO receptor agonists. Similar drugs include avatrombopag and eltrombopag, which share the same therapeutic concept though differ structurally, while romiplostim is a mechanistically similar peptide agonist. Its principal target is the thrombopoietin receptor MPL (CD110; gene MPL) on megakaryocyte lineage cells, activating downstream JAK2/STAT and related proliferative signaling to increase platelet production. Lusutrombopag is indicated primarily for thrombocytopenia in adults with chronic liver disease undergoing invasive procedures, where it is used to reduce the need for platelet transfusion and rescue treatment for bleeding; clinically, it is given as a short oral preprocedural course before interventions such as ablation, endoscopy, or surgery. Pharmacokinetically, it is orally absorbed, reaches peak concentrations within hours, is highly protein bound, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism including CYP4-mediated oxidation with contributions from transport processes, and is eliminated mainly via feces with limited renal excretion; its half-life supports once-daily dosing. Important toxicities include thromboembolic events, especially portal vein thrombosis in susceptible liver disease patients, hepatobiliary laboratory abnormalities, and excessive platelet elevation. Common adverse effects include headache, nausea, abdominal discomfort, pyrexia, and procedure-related events, with overall use requiring platelet monitoring and attention to thrombotic risk.

Name: Artemisinin
Description: Artemisinin (DrugBank DB13132) is a sesquiterpene lactone endoperoxide natural product isolated from Artemisia annua, characterized by a compact, highly oxygenated tricyclic framework containing a distinctive 1,2,4-trioxane ring with an essential peroxide bridge fused to a lactone-bearing sesquiterpene scaffold; chemically it belongs to the terpene peroxide/antimalarial endoperoxide class, and its core scaffold is the artemisinin trioxane endoperoxide, which is shared or semisynthetically elaborated in related drugs such as dihydroartemisinin, artesunate, artemether, and arteether. Its antimalarial activity is linked primarily to heme- or ferrous iron-mediated cleavage of the endoperoxide within Plasmodium-infected erythrocytes, generating reactive intermediates that damage multiple parasite proteins and membranes; proposed molecular targets include heme, PfATP6, translationally controlled tumor protein, and numerous alkylated parasite proteins involved in redox balance and metabolism. Orally absorbed but variably bioavailable, artemisinin is widely distributed, rapidly metabolized in the liver mainly by CYP2B6 and CYP3A4 with autoinduction that lowers repeated-dose exposure, and eliminated predominantly as inactive metabolites in urine and bile, giving a short half-life of only a few hours. It is indicated for malaria, especially uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum infection, but in practice is mainly used through derivatives in artemisinin-based combination therapies for multidrug-resistant malaria. Toxicity is generally limited at therapeutic doses, though high-dose or animal data show potential neurotoxicity, embryotoxicity, and hematologic effects; adverse effects can include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, dizziness, fever, rash, transient bradycardia, and liver enzyme elevation. Clinically, artemisinin itself has seen limited direct use because of poor pharmacokinetic properties, whereas its derivatives are standard components of combination regimens for acute malaria and severe disease management strategies.

Name: Levosalbutamol
Description: Levosalbutamol (DrugBank DB13139) is the pharmacologically active R-enantiomer of salbutamol/albuterol, a chiral phenethylamine bronchodilator built on a substituted resorcinol-ethanolamine framework with an aromatic ring bearing hydroxyl groups and a side chain containing a β-hydroxyl and tert-butylamino moiety; chemically it is classified as a short-acting β2-adrenergic receptor agonist within the sympathomimetic phenylaminoethanol class, and its core scaffold is the arylethanolamine/β-phenylethanolamine scaffold typical of bronchodilating β-agonists. Closely related drugs include racemic salbutamol, terbutaline, fenoterol, metaproterenol, and longer-acting congeners such as salmeterol and formoterol. Its principal target is the β2-adrenergic receptor encoded by ADRB2, with minor off-target β1/β3 activity at higher exposures. After inhalation it is rapidly absorbed from the airways, with a swallowed fraction undergoing variable gastrointestinal absorption; distribution is moderate with limited protein binding, metabolism occurs mainly by sulfate conjugation and other phase II pathways with less contribution from oxidative metabolism, and excretion is primarily renal as unchanged drug and conjugates, producing a short duration of action of about 4–6 hours. Toxicity reflects exaggerated β-adrenergic stimulation, including dose-related tachycardia, tremor, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, QT-related arrhythmic risk, and rare paradoxical bronchospasm; overdose may cause palpitations, chest pain, or lactic acidosis. It is indicated for relief and prevention of reversible bronchospasm in asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, including exercise-induced bronchospasm, and is used clinically as inhaled rescue therapy via metered-dose inhaler or nebulization, with common adverse effects including tremor, nervousness, headache, dizziness, cough, throat irritation, and palpitations.

Name: Clobetasone
Description: Clobetasone (DrugBank DB13158) is a synthetic halogenated corticosteroid built on the pregnane steroid nucleus, specifically a 21-carbon glucocorticoid framework with the characteristic four fused rings, a 3-keto-4-ene A-ring, 11β-hydroxyl, 20-ketone, 21-hydroxyl side chain, and halogen/substituent pattern that increases topical anti-inflammatory potency while limiting systemic activity; chemically it is categorized as a corticosteroid, more specifically a topical glucocorticoid, and its core scaffold is the hydrocortisone/prednisolone-like steroid scaffold. Similar drugs include hydrocortisone, desonide, prednisolone, betamethasone, and clobetasol, which share the same corticosteroid pharmacophore but differ in potency and substitution. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, with downstream suppression of phospholipase A2 activity, NF-κB- and AP-1-mediated cytokine transcription, and reduced prostaglandin, leukotriene, and inflammatory mediator production. After topical administration, absorption is limited but increases on inflamed, abraded, occluded, or thin skin; distributed largely within skin and, if systemically absorbed, is highly protein bound, hepatically metabolized by steroid-reducing and conjugative pathways, and excreted mainly in urine with some biliary/fecal elimination. It is indicated for corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses such as eczema, dermatitis, and inflammatory pruritic rashes, and in ophthalmic use for steroid-responsive ocular inflammation. Toxicity is predominantly local, including skin atrophy, telangiectasia, striae, delayed wound healing, acneiform eruptions, perioral dermatitis, and secondary infection, while excessive or prolonged exposure can cause HPA-axis suppression, hyperglycemia, Cushingoid features, glaucoma, or cataract. Clinically, it is used as a lower-to-moderate potency topical steroid when anti-inflammatory benefit is needed with less risk than very potent agents, for example in atopic eczema, seborrheic dermatitis, contact dermatitis, and selected eyelid or facial inflammatory conditions under careful supervision.

Name: Ripasudil
Description: Ripasudil (DB13165) is a small-molecule ophthalmic Rho-associated coiled-coil containing protein kinase inhibitor whose structure is characterized by a heteroaromatic isoquinoline-based core linked through a flexible amino-containing spacer to a lipophilic cyclopentyl-substituted amide-like/basic side chain, giving an amphiphilic, cationic ROCK-binding pharmacophore optimized for topical ocular delivery; chemically it is best classified as a synthetic heteroaryl amine/amide-like kinase inhibitor, and its key scaffold is the isoquinoline ROCK-inhibitor motif seen across this drug class. Similar drugs include netarsudil and fasudil, with fasudil being a prototypic earlier ROCK inhibitor and netarsudil a more recent ophthalmic analogue with overlapping pressure-lowering pharmacology. Ripasudil acts primarily on ROCK1 and ROCK2, reducing actomyosin contraction in the trabecular meshwork and Schlemm canal to enhance conventional aqueous humor outflow; secondary vascular and anti-fibrotic effects have also been described. After topical instillation, ocular absorption is rapid with predominantly local anterior-segment exposure, limited systemic distribution, hepatic and ocular metabolism including conversion to an active metabolite, and elimination mainly through systemic metabolic clearance with urinary excretion of metabolites rather than unchanged parent drug. Toxicity is generally dominated by local ocular effects rather than systemic toxicity; examples include transient conjunctival hyperemia, irritation, blepharitis, allergic conjunctivitis, and corneal epithelial changes, while serious systemic adverse effects are uncommon at ophthalmic doses. Clinically, ripasudil is indicated for glaucoma and ocular hypertension, especially primary open-angle glaucoma, and is used alone or adjunctively with prostaglandin analogues, beta-blockers, or carbonic anhydrase inhibitors when further intraocular-pressure reduction is needed.

Name: Zofenopril
Description: Zofenopril (DrugBank DB13166) is a sulfhydryl-containing angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor administered as a lipophilic ester prodrug whose structure is characterized by a proline-like bicyclic/peptidomimetic ACE-inhibitor framework bearing a thioacetyl-derived mercapto functionality that, after bioactivation, chelates the catalytic zinc of ACE; chemically it belongs to the carboxylate-containing, sulfur-substituted ACE inhibitor class, with a proline-based peptidomimetic scaffold closely related to captopril, enalapril, ramipril, quinapril, benazepril, and trandolapril. It is absorbed orally and undergoes extensive first-pass hydrolysis to the active metabolite zofenoprilat, with good tissue penetration due to lipophilicity, substantial plasma protein binding, distribution to vascular and cardiac tissues, hepatic conversion as the main metabolic step, and elimination of parent drug/metabolite by both renal and biliary-fecal routes, with exposure prolonged in renal or hepatic impairment. Its principal target is angiotensin-converting enzyme/kininase II, reducing angiotensin II formation and aldosterone secretion while increasing bradykinin. Indications include essential hypertension, particularly mild to moderate disease, and post-acute myocardial infarction management with preserved hemodynamic stability, where it is used to reduce afterload, improve ventricular remodeling, and limit cardiovascular risk. Adverse effects resemble other ACE inhibitors and include cough, dizziness, hypotension, headache, fatigue, nausea, hyperkalemia, and renal function worsening; important toxicities include first-dose syncope, acute kidney injury in renovascular disease, angioedema, and fetotoxicity in pregnancy, with overdose causing marked hypotension. Clinically, it is used as monotherapy or with thiazide diuretics or other antihypertensives in patients needing renin-angiotensin system blockade.

Name: Alclofenac
Description: Alclofenac (DrugBank DB13167) is an arylacetic acid nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug characterized structurally by a chlorinated phenyl ring linked through an amino bridge to a phenylacetic acid motif, giving it an anilide-like, lipophilic acidic framework typical of peripheral cyclooxygenase inhibitors; its chemical category is therefore the phenylacetic acid/aromatic acetic acid NSAID class, and its core scaffold is a substituted anilino-phenylacetic acid. It is chemically and pharmacologically related to other arylacetic acid NSAIDs such as diclofenac, fenclofenac, alclofenac analogs, and more broadly to indomethacin and tolmetin as anti-inflammatory comparators. Like older NSAIDs, it is understood to act mainly through inhibition of prostaglandin biosynthesis via cyclooxygenase targets, especially PTGS1 and PTGS2, although older literature may describe this mechanism less selectively. It was used for symptomatic treatment of rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, and other painful inflammatory musculoskeletal conditions, including joint pain, stiffness, and swelling. Pharmacokinetically, alclofenac appears to be orally absorbed, distributed systemically with expected plasma protein binding typical of acidic NSAIDs, hepatically metabolized by aromatic oxidation and conjugative pathways, and excreted predominantly in urine with some biliary or fecal elimination. Its toxicity profile resembles that of other nonselective NSAIDs, with gastrointestinal irritation, dyspepsia, nausea, peptic ulceration, and gastrointestinal bleeding as principal dose-limiting risks, plus possible rash, dizziness, fluid retention, renal function impairment, and rare hypersensitivity or hepatotoxic reactions. Clinically, it was used as an oral anti-inflammatory and analgesic agent in chronic rheumatic disease, but like many older NSAIDs its use has been limited by tolerability and safety concerns.

Name: Plecanatide
Description: Plecanatide (DrugBank DB13170) is a synthetic peptide analog of the endogenous intestinal hormone uroguanylin, structurally characterized as a short, acid-sensitive, disulfide-bonded peptide with a compact cystine-constrained conformation that preserves the pharmacophore required for guanylate cyclase-C activation; chemically it belongs to the peptide therapeutic and secretagogue class, and its core scaffold is a uroguanylin-like bicyclic/cystine-stabilized peptide motif. Closely related drugs include linaclotide, another guanylate cyclase-C agonist used for constipation-predominant disorders, and more distantly uroguanylin and guanylin as endogenous homologs. Its principal known target protein is guanylate cyclase-C (GUCY2C) on the luminal surface of intestinal epithelial cells, leading to increased intracellular cyclic GMP, enhanced chloride and bicarbonate secretion via CFTR, increased intestinal fluid, and accelerated transit, with possible reduction in visceral pain signaling. Pharmacokinetically, plecanatide acts locally in the gastrointestinal tract after oral administration, has minimal systemic absorption, limited distribution beyond the gut, is expected to undergo proteolytic degradation within the intestinal lumen to smaller peptides and amino acids, and is eliminated predominantly in feces with negligible renal excretion of parent drug. Toxicity is mainly an extension of pharmacology, especially diarrhea that may become severe and cause dehydration or electrolyte disturbance; this underlies the major contraindication in patients with known or suspected mechanical gastrointestinal obstruction and the warning against pediatric use due to dehydration risk. It is indicated for chronic idiopathic constipation and irritable bowel syndrome with constipation, and in clinical use it is prescribed to improve stool frequency, stool consistency, straining, and abdominal discomfort, with common adverse effects including diarrhea, abdominal distension, flatulence, abdominal tenderness, and occasional dizziness or dehydration-related symptoms.

Name: Inositol
Description: Inositol (DrugBank DB13178) is a naturally occurring cyclitol, most commonly the myo-inositol stereoisomer, characterized structurally by a saturated six-membered carbocyclic ring bearing six hydroxyl groups in a defined stereochemical arrangement that mimics a sugar alcohol yet lacks a ring oxygen; chemically it belongs to the polyol/cyclitol class and has an inositane hexol scaffold that also underlies second-messenger lipids such as phosphatidylinositol and inositol phosphates. Closely related or similar agents include D-chiro-inositol, scyllo-inositol, and the inositol-derived signaling molecules inositol trisphosphate and phosphatidylinositol phosphates; mechanistically relevant comparators in supplementation practice include folate and metformin in polycystic ovary syndrome. Pharmacokinetically, oral inositol is generally well absorbed in the small intestine via sodium-dependent myo-inositol transporters, distributes widely to brain, kidney, liver, and reproductive tissues, participates extensively in endogenous biosynthetic and phosphoinositide pathways rather than classical xenobiotic metabolism, and is eliminated largely unchanged or after limited catabolic conversion in urine, with renal handling influencing exposure. Known molecular targets are not conventional high-affinity drug receptors but include the transporters SLC5A3 and SLC2A13 and downstream phosphoinositide-linked signaling systems involving phospholipase C, IP3 receptors, and protein kinase C pathways. It is used clinically or as a nutraceutical for insulin resistance and ovulatory dysfunction in polycystic ovary syndrome, and has been studied in metabolic syndrome, gestational diabetes prevention, panic disorder, depression, and neonatal respiratory support. Toxicity is generally low, with high doses mainly causing gastrointestinal intolerance such as nausea, flatulence, diarrhea, and abdominal discomfort; headache, dizziness, fatigue, and sleep disturbance are reported, while rare examples of mood activation or mania have been described in susceptible psychiatric patients.

Name: Piperidione
Description: Piperidione (DrugBank DB13224) is best described as a small cyclic diketone built on a six-membered saturated nitrogen-containing heterocycle in which the piperidine ring bears two ketone functionalities, giving a compact, polar piperidinedione or imide-like structure with hydrogen-bond-accepting carbonyl groups and a conformationally restricted heteroalicyclic scaffold. Chemically it falls within the piperidinedione/heterocyclic ketone class, and its core scaffold is related to other medicinally relevant cyclic imides and diones; accordingly, structurally similar drugs or analog classes include glutarimide- and piperidinedione-containing compounds such as thalidomide-related cereblon binders and older sedative-hypnotic cyclic imides, although Piperidione itself is not a well-established therapeutic agent. Publicly available pharmacology for DB13224 is sparse, and no definitive, validated human target protein profile has been clearly established; it is therefore best regarded as an experimental or minimally characterized compound without a confirmed mechanism, though nonspecific interactions with carbonyl-recognizing enzymes or CNS-relevant receptors would be chemically plausible. Likewise, pharmacokinetic data are limited, but based on size and polarity it would be expected to show at least moderate oral absorption, distribution largely to aqueous tissues with limited protein binding, hepatic phase I/II biotransformation via carbonyl reduction or ring oxidation followed by conjugation, and predominantly renal excretion of metabolites. Toxicity data are also limited; as with related cyclic imides, potential concerns include CNS depression, irritation, hepatotoxicity, and dose-related neurotoxicity. No approved indication, routine clinical usage, or well-defined adverse-effect profile has been established, and any use would mainly be historical, investigational, or as a chemical intermediate rather than standard treatment for specific diseases or symptoms.

Name: Calcium lactate
Description: Calcium lactate (DrugBank DB13231) is an organic calcium salt composed of divalent calcium coordinated by two lactate anions, each derived from 2-hydroxypropionic acid and containing a carboxylate plus adjacent secondary hydroxyl group, giving a small, highly polar aliphatic hydroxycarboxylate structure that is typically handled as a hydrated ionic solid. Chemically it belongs to mineral supplements/electrolyte replacements and specifically the calcium salts of alpha-hydroxy carboxylic acids; its scaffold is best described as a simple lactate hydroxyacid framework paired with Ca2+. Similar drugs include other oral calcium supplements such as calcium carbonate, calcium citrate, calcium gluconate, and calcium phosphate, which differ mainly in anion, elemental calcium content, and gastrointestinal tolerability. After oral administration, calcium is absorbed in the small intestine by vitamin D-dependent transcellular transport involving TRPV6, calbindin, and PMCA1b and by passive paracellular flux; absorbed calcium distributes largely to extracellular fluid and bone, while the lactate moiety enters normal intermediary metabolism and is converted to pyruvate. Calcium is not metabolized per se and is excreted mainly in feces from unabsorbed drug and via renal urinary elimination for the absorbed fraction. Toxicity is chiefly related to excessive calcium exposure, causing hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, nephrolithiasis, constipation, milk-alkali syndrome, renal impairment, and, in severe overdose, arrhythmias or confusion. It does not act through a classic drug receptor, but physiologic targets include calcium-sensing pathways and downstream systems dependent on ionized calcium. Clinically it is used to prevent or treat hypocalcemia and as supplementation in calcium deficiency states such as osteoporosis, osteomalacia, rickets, pregnancy, lactation, and malabsorption; adverse effects commonly include bloating, nausea, abdominal discomfort, and constipation.

Name: Pramiracetam
Description: Pramiracetam (DrugBank DB13247) is a lipophilic racetam nootropic built on the 2-pyrrolidone nucleus, specifically a substituted pyrrolidinone acetamide in which the racetam core bears a dipropan-2-ylaminoethyl side chain that increases membrane permeability relative to piracetam; chemically it is classified as a pyrrolidone derivative and central nervous system agent, with the classical racetam scaffold serving as its defining chemotype. Similar drugs include piracetam, aniracetam, oxiracetam, levetiracetam, and phenylpiracetam, which share the same core heterocycle but differ in side-chain substitution and CNS profile. Its mechanism is not fully resolved, and no single validated high-affinity target protein is established, but reported pharmacology includes enhancement of high-affinity choline uptake in hippocampal neurons, modulation of cholinergic neurotransmission, and downstream effects on neuronal membrane function; thus direct target assignment remains uncertain. Pramiracetam is orally active, generally well absorbed, penetrates the CNS because of greater lipophilicity than piracetam, shows limited known biotransformation, and is thought to be eliminated largely unchanged by renal excretion, with a moderate plasma half-life consistent with divided daily dosing. Toxicity appears relatively low in therapeutic use, though excessive exposure may produce CNS overstimulation, irritability, insomnia, nausea, abdominal discomfort, headache, tremor, or agitation; caution is warranted in renal impairment and with other neuroactive agents. It has been investigated or used clinically for cognitive impairment, memory deficits, reduced attention, and post-traumatic or cerebrovascular cognitive symptoms, with examples including age-related cognitive decline and rehabilitation settings after brain injury, although regulatory approval and routine clinical adoption have been limited.

Name: Acetarsol
Description: Acetarsol (DrugBank DB13268) is an organoarsenic anti-infective whose structure is characterized by a pentavalent arsenic center in an arsonic acid functionality directly attached to an aromatic phenyl ring bearing an acetamido substituent, giving a relatively simple arsanilic-acid–like architecture with an acetanilide-related aromatic scaffold; chemically it belongs to aromatic arsenicals and more specifically amino/acetamido phenyl arsonic acids, with close analogues including arsanilic acid, carbarsone, tryparsamide, and other historical arsenical antiparasitic or antiamoebic agents. Its pharmacologic action is not linked to a single well-defined modern protein target, but is thought to reflect nonspecific interaction of arsenical species with essential sulfhydryl-containing parasitic and microbial enzymes, impairing cellular respiration and metabolism; no validated human target protein is typically assigned. Acetarsol has been used mainly topically or locally, particularly in suppositories or pessaries, so systemic absorption is generally limited but can increase across inflamed mucosa; after absorption, arsenicals distribute into tissues with potential accumulation in liver, kidney, skin, and keratin-rich compartments, undergo limited biotransformation with possible reduction/methylation of arsenic species, and are excreted predominantly in urine. Toxicity is that of arsenicals, including local irritation and potentially systemic arsenic poisoning with gastrointestinal distress, neuropathy, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, dermatitis, and bone marrow effects if absorbed excessively. Indications have included refractory vaginitis, vaginal discharge, trichomonal or nonspecific genital infections, and historically some protozoal intestinal disease. Adverse effects include burning, irritation, ulceration, rash, nausea, abdominal pain, headache, and rarely systemic arsenic toxicity. Clinically, it has been used chiefly as a topical vaginal anti-infective when other options were unavailable or ineffective, but modern use is limited because safer agents have largely replaced arsenical therapy.

Name: Benzododecinium
Description: Benzododecinium (DrugBank DB13282) is a quaternary ammonium antiseptic whose structure is characterized by a permanently charged benzyldimethylammonium headgroup linked to a linear dodecyl hydrophobic chain, giving it the amphiphilic architecture typical of membrane-active cationic surfactants; chemically it belongs to the quaternary ammonium compound class, with a benzalkonium-type scaffold consisting of an aromatic benzyl substituent on a trialkylammonium center plus a C12 alkyl tail. It is closely related to other cationic disinfectants such as benzalkonium chloride congeners, cetrimonium, cetylpyridinium, and domiphen. Its pharmacology is largely nonspecific, with no single validated human target protein; instead, it interacts with negatively charged microbial cell envelopes and lipid bilayers, causing membrane disruption, leakage of intracellular contents, protein denaturation, and rapid microbicidal activity, although broad binding to membrane phospholipids and surface proteins is expected. Because it is mainly used topically, systemic absorption is generally minimal across intact skin or mucosa; distribution, metabolism, and excretion in humans are poorly defined but likely limited, with any absorbed fraction expected to partition into tissues and undergo slow hepatic biotransformation and biliary or renal elimination. Benzododecinium has been used as a local antiseptic or preservative for disinfection of skin, wounds, and mucosal surfaces and in formulations for minor infections or hygiene applications. Adverse effects are chiefly local irritation, burning, dryness, contact dermatitis, and ocular or mucosal injury, while excessive exposure can produce corrosive toxicity, gastrointestinal injury if ingested, and, rarely, systemic neuromuscular or respiratory complications typical of quaternary ammonium poisoning.

Name: Meticrane
Description: Meticrane (DrugBank DB13284) is a thiazide-like sulfonamide diuretic whose structure is characterized by an aromatic chlorinated benzene ring bearing a sulfamyl group and incorporated into a heterocyclic sulfur-containing scaffold, giving it the physicochemical features typical of saluretic carbonic-anhydrase–related sulfonamides while remaining distinct from classical benzothiadiazine thiazides; chemically it is categorized as a sulfonamide diuretic and its core scaffold is best described as a chlorinated aryl-sulfonamide linked to a sulfur-containing heterocycle.
