It is closely related in therapeutic class and mechanistic behavior to thiazide and thiazide-like agents such as hydrochlorothiazide, chlorothiazide, bendroflumethiazide, cyclothiazide, chlorthalidone, metolazone, and quinethazone. Its principal pharmacologic target is the renal Na+/Cl− cotransporter SLC12A3 in the distal convoluted tubule, with possible weak off-target interaction typical of sulfonamides at carbonic anhydrase isoenzymes; this produces natriuresis, chloruresis, and secondary kaliuresis. After oral administration it is understood to be absorbed adequately, distributed largely in extracellular fluid with some protein binding, minimally to moderately metabolized hepatically, and eliminated predominantly by the kidney as unchanged drug and metabolites, with duration of action in the range expected for oral thiazide-like diuretics. It has been used clinically for edema and hypertension, including edema associated with congestive heart failure, hepatic disease, or renal sodium retention. Adverse effects and toxicities parallel the class: hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia, dehydration, orthostatic hypotension, hyperuricemia with gout, hyperglycemia, photosensitivity, rash, and rare sulfonamide hypersensitivity or severe electrolyte-depletion arrhythmias, especially in overdose or in patients with renal impairment or concomitant digoxin therapy.

Name: Benproperine
Description: Benproperine (DrugBank DB13309) is a centrally acting antitussive whose structure is characterized by a lipophilic diaryl-alkyl architecture containing a tertiary amino side chain linked through a short aliphatic spacer to an aryl-rich benzhydryl-like core, placing it in the class of non-opioid synthetic cough suppressants and, more broadly, aromatic tertiary amine derivatives; its scaffold is best described as a substituted diphenyl/benzylpropylamine antitussive scaffold related to other older cough suppressants such as cloperastine, dropropizine, and levodropropizine, and with pharmacologic resemblance to centrally acting antitussives like dextromethorphan despite structural differences. It is used primarily for symptomatic treatment of nonproductive cough and cough associated with upper respiratory tract irritation, bronchitis, and other acute inflammatory airway conditions. Its molecular target profile is not fully defined, but antitussive activity is generally attributed to suppression of the medullary cough center and possible modulation of sensory afferent pathways; no single high-confidence target protein is universally established, though central neuronal receptors and ion-channel-linked cough pathways have been implicated in older literature. Benproperine is orally active, absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, distributed systemically with likely CNS penetration due to lipophilicity, metabolized hepatically by oxidative and conjugative pathways, and excreted mainly as metabolites in urine. Adverse effects are typically mild and include drowsiness, dizziness, dry mouth, nausea, and gastrointestinal discomfort; toxicity in overdose is expected to manifest as exaggerated CNS depression, anticholinergic-like symptoms, and impaired psychomotor performance. Clinically it has been used as a short-course symptomatic antitussive rather than a disease-modifying therapy.

Name: Trepibutone
Description: Trepibutone (DB13311) is a synthetic small-molecule choleretic and antispasmodic agent built on a substituted aromatic ketone scaffold, typically described as a butyrophenone-like aryl alkyl ketone framework bearing lipophilic alkoxy-substituted phenyl functionality that confers biliary activity and smooth-muscle effects; chemically it is classified among non-opioid biliary tract agents and aromatic ketone derivatives, with a simple aryl–carbonyl–alkyl scaffold rather than a peptide, steroid, or heterobiologic core. Drugs considered pharmacologically similar include other choleretics and antispasmodics used in hepatobiliary disease, such as hymecromone, trimebutine, drotaverine, and some regions also compare it with bile-flow modifiers used for dyspeptic or biliary pain states. Its pharmacokinetics are not extensively characterized in modern international literature, but available descriptions indicate oral absorption, distribution consistent with a lipophilic low-molecular-weight drug, predominant hepatic metabolism, and elimination mainly via biliary and/or urinary routes as metabolites. Trepibutone appears to act functionally on biliary secretion and gallbladder or sphincter smooth muscle, but no single well-validated molecular target protein has been firmly established; specific canonical DrugBank-style targets are therefore often unassigned, with proposed effects involving smooth-muscle regulatory pathways rather than a defined receptor. It is indicated for hepatobiliary disorders such as cholecystitis, cholelithiasis-associated dyspepsia, biliary dyskinesia, postprandial upper abdominal discomfort, nausea, bloating, and biliary colic adjunct management. Adverse effects are usually gastrointestinal and mild, including diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, nausea, and occasional dizziness or rash; toxicity data suggest relatively low acute toxicity at therapeutic doses, with overdose theoretically increasing GI irritation, excessive biliary stimulation, or nonspecific hepatic intolerance. Clinically, it has been used orally to relieve biliary spasm, improve bile flow, and reduce symptoms in chronic gallbladder and bile duct disorders.

Name: Melevodopa
Description: Melevodopa (DrugBank DB13313) is the methyl ester prodrug of levodopa, structurally characterized as a catechol-substituted phenylalanine derivative bearing a 3,4-dihydroxybenzene ring attached to an alanine backbone in which the carboxyl group is esterified as a methyl ester; chemically it belongs to the aromatic amino acid, catecholamine-precursor, and levodopa ester classes, and its core scaffold is the catechol-phenylalanine scaffold shared with dopaminergic metabolic precursors. Similar drugs include levodopa itself, benserazide/levodopa and carbidopa/levodopa combinations, and related dopaminergic agents such as dopamine precursors and esterified levodopa formulations used to modify onset or bioavailability. After oral administration, melevodopa is designed to improve aqueous solubility and gastrointestinal absorption relative to levodopa; it is absorbed in the small intestine, distributed systemically, hydrolyzed by esterases to levodopa, then decarboxylated by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase to dopamine in peripheral tissues and the brain, with further metabolism by catechol-O-methyltransferase and monoamine oxidase, and renal excretion of metabolites predominates. Its principal pharmacologic targets are indirect, because the active moiety dopamine stimulates dopamine receptors, especially D1- and D2-like receptor families, while aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase and COMT are key handling proteins affecting exposure. Toxicity resembles levodopa, including dose-related nausea, vomiting, orthostatic hypotension, dyskinesias, confusion, hallucinations, and cardiovascular effects such as arrhythmia; chronic dopaminergic excess may produce motor fluctuations and impulse-control-type behavioral complications. Clinically, melevodopa has been used in Parkinson disease and parkinsonian syndromes, particularly for bradykinesia, rigidity, and wearing-off states, often in combination with peripheral decarboxylase inhibitors to enhance central delivery and reduce peripheral adverse effects.

Name: Ibopamine
Description: Ibopamine (DrugBank DB13316) is a synthetic dopaminergic ophthalmic prodrug structurally derived from N-methyldopamine in which the catechol hydroxyl groups are masked as diisobutyryl esters, creating a lipophilic aromatic ethylamine ester that is rapidly de-esterified in ocular tissues to the active metabolite epinine; chemically it belongs to the catecholamine ester prodrug class and is built on a phenethylamine/catecholamine scaffold closely related to dopamine and epinine, with similarity also to other ocular sympathomimetic or dopaminergic agents such as dipivefrin, dopamine, and epinephrine prodrugs. Its pharmacological effect is mediated primarily after corneal absorption and local hydrolysis, with epinine acting mainly at adrenergic alpha receptors, especially alpha1-adrenergic receptor, and also showing dopaminergic activity; target proteins therefore include alpha1-adrenergic receptor and likely dopamine receptors, although the clinically dominant effect is enhancement of aqueous humor outflow and mydriasis. Systemic pharmacokinetic data are limited, but topical ocular administration results in local absorption, limited distribution, rapid esterase-mediated metabolism to epinine, and subsequent metabolism by catechol-O-methyltransferase and monoamine oxidase with renal excretion of metabolites. Ibopamine has been used mainly in ophthalmology for provocative testing and supportive diagnosis in open-angle glaucoma, ocular hypertension, and assessment of outflow facility, and historically to induce mydriasis without cycloplegia. Adverse effects are usually ocular and mild, including burning, conjunctival hyperemia, irritation, blurred vision, tearing, photophobia, and transient increases in intraocular pressure; toxicity is chiefly related to excessive sympathomimetic response, with potential precipitation of clinically significant ocular hypertension in susceptible patients and, rarely, systemic adrenergic effects such as palpitations or headache.

Name: Flunoxaprofen
Description: Flunoxaprofen (DB13317) is an arylpropionic acid nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug characterized structurally by a 2-arylpropionic acid core bearing a fluorinated biaryl/aryloxy-type aromatic system, placing it within the profen class and giving it the canonical acidic NSAID scaffold shared by agents such as ibuprofen, flurbiprofen, ketoprofen, naproxen, and fenoprofen. Its chemical category is therefore that of a fluorinated profen anti-inflammatory, with the propionic acid pharmacophore serving as the key motif for cyclooxygenase binding; similar drugs include flurbiprofen in particular because of the fluorinated aryl features, as well as ibuprofen and naproxen as related COX-inhibiting arylpropionates. Like other profens, flunoxaprofen is expected to be well absorbed orally, substantially albumin bound in plasma, distributed preferentially within extracellular fluids and inflamed tissues, hepatically metabolized mainly by oxidative biotransformation followed by glucuronidation, and excreted predominantly in urine as metabolites with some biliary/fecal elimination. Its principal pharmacologic targets are cyclooxygenase enzymes PTGS1 and PTGS2, reducing prostaglandin synthesis and thereby mediating analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antipyretic effects. The likely indications are musculoskeletal pain, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and other inflammatory or painful conditions. Toxicity is expected to mirror class effects, including dose-related gastrointestinal irritation, ulceration, bleeding, renal hypoperfusion or acute kidney injury, fluid retention, and possible hepatic enzyme elevations; examples of adverse effects include dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, edema, and rash. Clinical use would therefore have been as a symptomatic anti-inflammatory and analgesic NSAID for arthritis and pain states, with standard NSAID precautions in patients at risk for peptic ulcer disease, renal impairment, or bleeding.

Name: Oxaceprol
Description: Oxaceprol (DB13363) is a small-molecule anti-inflammatory chiral amino-acid derivative structurally characterized as an acylated hydroxyproline analogue, specifically an N-acetyl substituted pyrrolidine carboxylic acid bearing a hydroxyl group on the ring, giving it a highly polar, zwitterion-like profile related to collagen-associated imino acids. Chemically, it belongs to the class of modified amino acids and proline derivatives, with a hydroxyproline/pyrrolidine carboxylate scaffold as its core chemical framework. Similar drugs are limited but conceptually include other symptomatic anti-inflammatory or chondroprotective agents such as glucosamine, diacerein, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs used in osteoarthritis, although oxaceprol is distinguished by its amino-acid-derived scaffold rather than an arylacetic or arylpropionic acid NSAID motif. Its pharmacology is not linked to a single well-validated receptor target; instead, reported activity includes inhibition of leukocyte adhesion and migration, with modulation of inflammatory cell-endothelial interactions, while no canonical DrugBank-style target protein is firmly established, though effects on adhesion-related pathways and inflammatory mediators have been proposed. After oral administration it is absorbed systemically, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid, undergoes relatively limited biotransformation compared with many lipophilic anti-inflammatory drugs, and is eliminated largely renally as unchanged drug or simple metabolites. Toxicity is generally low, with no prominent organ-specific toxicity in routine therapeutic use, but excessive exposure may increase gastrointestinal intolerance or nonspecific adverse effects. It is indicated mainly for osteoarthritis and other degenerative or inflammatory musculoskeletal disorders, including pain, stiffness, and reduced joint mobility. Adverse effects are usually mild and include nausea, dyspepsia, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, headache, and occasional hypersensitivity. Clinically, it has been used as an oral symptomatic slow-acting anti-inflammatory/antiarthritic agent in chronic joint disease, particularly knee or hip osteoarthritis and related rheumatic pain states.

Name: Motretinide
Description: Motretinide (DrugBank DB13368) is a synthetic retinoid characterized structurally by a vitamin A–like polyene backbone linked to a terminal aromatic/acid-derived retinoid pharmacophore, giving a highly lipophilic, conjugated framework typical of receptor-active retinoids; chemically it is classified as a retinoid and more specifically a retinamide/retinoic acid analog built on the classic retinyl polyene scaffold. It is therefore closely related to other differentiating retinoids such as tretinoin, isotretinoin, acitretin, etretinate, fenretinide, and bexarotene, which share overlapping structure-activity themes centered on nuclear retinoid receptor modulation. Although detailed human pharmacokinetic data for motretinide are limited, compounds in this class are generally variably absorbed orally depending on formulation and fat intake, distribute extensively into lipid-rich tissues with substantial protein binding, undergo hepatic oxidative metabolism and possible conjugation, and are eliminated mainly through biliary/fecal routes with some urinary metabolite excretion. Its presumed pharmacology involves retinoid signaling pathways, with likely interaction at retinoic acid receptors RAR alpha, beta, and gamma, and possibly retinoid X receptors depending on subtype selectivity. As with related retinoids, potential indications have included disorders of keratinization, acneiform disease, and oncology-oriented differentiation strategies such as premalignant or malignant epithelial conditions, though clinical use appears limited and not broadly established. Expected adverse effects and toxicity are retinoid-like, including cheilitis, xerosis, conjunctival irritation, photosensitivity, headache, hyperlipidemia, hepatotoxicity, mucocutaneous inflammation, and strong teratogenic risk, with chronic excess potentially causing skeletal or neuropsychiatric effects.

Name: Succinimide
Description: Succinimide (DB13376) is the parent cyclic imide consisting of a compact five-membered pyrrolidine-2,5-dione ring with two opposing carbonyl groups flanking a ring nitrogen, giving a small, polar, weakly acidic imide framework that serves as the prototypical succinimide chemical category and core scaffold for the succinimide anticonvulsant class. Closely related and pharmacologically more important analogues include ethosuximide, methsuximide, and phensuximide, which retain the succinimide ring while varying substitution to modify central nervous system activity. Succinimide itself is mainly a chemical intermediate and scaffold rather than a routinely administered therapeutic drug, so human pharmacokinetic data are sparse; based on its low molecular weight and polarity, it would be expected to be reasonably absorbed, distribute largely in total body water with limited protein binding, undergo hydrolytic ring opening and hepatic biotransformation to simple polar metabolites, and be eliminated predominantly in urine. Specific validated target proteins for unsubstituted succinimide are not well established, unlike ethosuximide, which modulates thalamic T-type calcium currents; therefore DB13376 has no clearly defined clinically actionable protein target. Its direct therapeutic indications are limited, but the succinimide scaffold is historically linked to antiepileptic use, especially absence seizures, through derivatives rather than the parent compound. Toxicity is expected to reflect imide irritancy and nonspecific CNS or gastrointestinal effects at sufficient exposure, with examples including nausea, vomiting, dizziness, somnolence, headache, and possible mucosal, skin, hepatic, or renal irritation in overdose or industrial exposure. Accordingly, clinical usage of succinimide itself is minimal, whereas its principal medical relevance is as the foundational scaffold for clinically used anticonvulsants.

Name: Phenylmercuric nitrate
Description: Phenylmercuric nitrate (DrugBank DB13388) is an organomercury compound consisting of a monovalent phenylmercury cation in which a mercury atom is sigma-bonded to a phenyl ring and paired with nitrate as the counterion; structurally it belongs to aromatic organomercurials, with a simple phenylmercury scaffold that is closely related to other mercurial antiseptics and preservatives such as phenylmercuric acetate, phenylmercuric borate, merbromin, and to broader thiol-reactive mercury compounds like thimerosal by shared electrophilic mercury chemistry. Its pharmacology is largely nonselective and depends on high-affinity interaction with sulfhydryl-containing proteins rather than a single canonical receptor, so reported targets are best described as cysteine-rich enzymes, membrane proteins, and microbial metabolic proteins whose thiol groups are inactivated, accounting for antibacterial and antifungal effects. Pharmacokinetic data are limited, but topical or ophthalmic exposure permits local absorption, systemic uptake can occur through mucosa or damaged skin, distribution includes binding to plasma and tissue proteins with accumulation particularly in kidney and possibly central nervous system, metabolism may involve slow cleavage or biotransformation of the organomercury moiety, and excretion is mainly renal with some biliary/fecal elimination. Toxicity is characteristic of mercury exposure, including corrosive local injury, nephrotoxicity with proteinuria or tubular damage, neurotoxicity such as tremor or irritability after sufficient systemic absorption, and hypersensitivity reactions. Adverse effects reported or expected in clinical use include ocular irritation, conjunctival inflammation, dermatitis, burning, edema, and delayed allergic contact reactions. Historically it was used mainly as an ophthalmic antiseptic and preservative and in topical anti-infective preparations for minor bacterial or fungal contamination, but its clinical use has become very limited because safer alternatives are preferred.

Name: Terguride
Description: Terguride (DB13399) is a semisynthetic ergot derivative built on the rigid tetracyclic ergoline framework, with an indole-like fused ring system and characteristic amide-containing lysergic acid–type architecture that confers high affinity for monoaminergic receptors; chemically it is classified as an ergoline/ergot alkaloid derivative, and its core scaffold is the lysergic acid ergoline nucleus shared with several dopaminergic and serotonergic agents. Closely related drugs include bromocriptine, lisuride, cabergoline, pergolide, and dihydroergotamine, all of which exploit the ergoline scaffold for receptor binding. Pharmacologically, terguride acts primarily as a dopamine D2 receptor partial agonist/functional antagonist, with additional activity at serotonin receptors including 5-HT2 subtypes and weaker interactions at adrenergic sites; reported target proteins therefore include DRD2, and more variably DRD1/DRD3 and HTR2A/HTR2B/HTR2C. It has been investigated mainly for hyperprolactinemia, prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma, and endocrine symptoms such as galactorrhea or menstrual disturbance, and has also been studied in Parkinsonian states and, historically, in schizophrenia as an atypical dopaminergic modulator. After oral administration it is absorbed but undergoes significant first-pass hepatic metabolism, yielding limited bioavailability; distribution is consistent with a lipophilic CNS-penetrant ergoline, metabolism is predominantly hepatic, and excretion occurs through renal and biliary/fecal routes as metabolites. Adverse effects resemble those of other dopamine-active ergolines and include nausea, vomiting, dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, headache, fatigue, insomnia, and psychiatric effects such as agitation or hallucinations; toxicity in overdose or susceptible patients may include severe hypotension, vasospastic/ergot-like ischemic reactions, and neuropsychiatric disturbance. Clinically, its use has centered on suppression of prolactin secretion and endocrine symptom control, although broader adoption has been limited relative to better-established dopamine agonists.

Name: Oxypertine
Description: Oxypertine (DB13403) is a first-generation psychotropic agent of the piperazine-derived antipsychotic/tranquilizer class, structurally characterized by a substituted aromatic ring system linked through a short carbon chain to a tertiary piperazine-containing side chain, giving it a lipophilic aryl-alkyl-piperazine architecture typical of older centrally acting neuroleptics; its core chemical scaffold is therefore an arylpiperazine/phenylalkylpiperazine framework, and it is chemically and pharmacologically related to other older antipsychotic or anxiolytic piperazine-containing agents, with broad similarity to compounds such as perphenazine, trifluoperazine, fluphenazine, and certain sedating arylpiperazine psychotropics, although it is structurally distinct from the classic phenothiazine nucleus. Oxypertine has been used primarily for schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders, especially where agitation, tension, impulsivity, or behavioral dyscontrol predominate, and historically also for severe anxiety states or disturbed behavior. Its pharmacology is generally attributed to central dopamine receptor antagonism, especially at D2-like receptors, with possible ancillary interactions at serotonergic, adrenergic, histaminergic, or muscarinic targets not consistently defined in the older literature; thus DRD2 is the most plausible principal target protein, with less certain engagement of DRD1/DRD3 and other aminergic receptors. As with many older lipophilic neuroleptics, oral absorption is expected to be adequate but variably bioavailable due to first-pass metabolism, distribution is extensive with CNS penetration and probable high protein binding, metabolism is predominantly hepatic, and excretion occurs via urinary and biliary routes as metabolites. Adverse effects and toxicity are consistent with typical antipsychotics and include sedation, extrapyramidal symptoms, akathisia, dystonia, parkinsonism, anticholinergic effects, orthostatic hypotension, weight gain, and hyperprolactinemia, while overdose or severe intolerance may produce marked CNS depression, autonomic instability, seizures, cardiac conduction abnormalities, or tardive dyskinesia; clinically, its use has largely been historical or limited, reflecting replacement by newer agents with better characterized efficacy and safety.

Name: Carbutamide
Description: Carbutamide (DrugBank DB13406) is a first-generation sulfonylurea oral hypoglycemic agent built on an aryl-sulfonylurea structure in which a para-substituted benzene ring is linked through a sulfonylurea bridge to a butyl urea substituent; chemically it belongs to the sulfonamide-derived sulfonylurea class, with a p-aminobenzenesulfonylurea scaffold that defines early insulin secretagogues. It is closely related to older sulfonylureas such as tolbutamide, chlorpropamide, acetohexamide, and tolazamide, which share the same core pharmacophore and broadly similar glucose-lowering mechanism. Its principal target is the ATP-sensitive potassium channel of pancreatic beta cells, specifically the sulfonylurea receptor SUR1, functionally associated with Kir6.2, leading to channel closure, membrane depolarization, calcium influx, and insulin release. Carbutamide was indicated for type 2 diabetes mellitus, particularly mild to moderate non-insulin-dependent disease not adequately controlled by diet alone. After oral administration it is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, distributed systemically with expected plasma protein binding typical of sulfonylureas, metabolized hepatically, and eliminated mainly in urine as parent drug and metabolites. Toxicity is dominated by prolonged hypoglycemia, especially in overdose, elderly patients, hepatic impairment, or poor nutritional status; adverse effects also include nausea, vomiting, rash, dizziness, and weight gain, and the drug is historically notable for serious hematologic toxicity such as agranulocytosis, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia, which limited use. Clinically, it was used as an early oral antidiabetic but has largely been abandoned or withdrawn in favor of safer sulfonylureas with more favorable therapeutic indices.

Name: Lofepramine
Description: Lofepramine (DrugBank DB13411) is a dibenzazepine-derived tricyclic antidepressant characterized structurally by a rigid three-ring aromatic core with a seven-membered central azepine ring and a propyl side chain terminating in a substituted tertiary amine, specifically distinguished by a p-chlorophenoxyacetyl substituent that contributes to its lipophilicity and prodrug behavior. Chemically it belongs to the tricyclic antidepressants, with a dibenzazepine scaffold closely related to imipramine and desipramine; similar drugs include imipramine, desipramine, clomipramine, amitriptyline, and nortriptyline. Its principal pharmacology reflects inhibition of monoamine reuptake, especially norepinephrine transport via SLC6A2 and to a lesser extent serotonin transport via SLC6A4, with downstream antidepressant activity; desipramine, an active metabolite, likely contributes substantially to target engagement. After oral administration, lofepramine is absorbed reasonably well, undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism, is widely distributed including CNS penetration, is highly protein bound, and is metabolized mainly by oxidative N-dealkylation and related biotransformations to desipramine and other metabolites, with renal excretion of metabolites predominating. It is indicated primarily for depressive illness, including major depressive episodes with low mood, anergia, sleep disturbance, and psychomotor retardation, and has been used clinically where a comparatively lower cardiotoxic and anticholinergic burden than older TCAs is desired. Adverse effects include dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, sweating, tremor, insomnia, dizziness, tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension, urinary hesitancy, and nausea. Toxicity in overdose includes CNS depression, agitation, seizures, QT or conduction abnormalities, ventricular arrhythmias, and anticholinergic manifestations, although lofepramine is often regarded as somewhat safer than some comparator TCAs.

Name: Troxipide
Description: Troxipide (DrugBank DB13419) is a gastroprotective small molecule characterized structurally as a substituted aromatic amide bearing a pyridine ring linked through a carboxamide to a para-hydroxyphenoxyethyl side chain, giving it a heteroaromatic nicotinamide-like architecture with both hydrogen-bond donor/acceptor functionality and moderate polarity; chemically it is classified as an antiulcer agent within the aromatic ether–amide class, and its core scaffold is best described as a pyridine carboxamide connected to a phenoxyethyl motif. It is pharmacologically similar to other mucosal protective antiulcer drugs such as rebamipide, teprenone, irsogladine, and to some extent sucralfate in therapeutic intent, although it is structurally distinct from proton-pump inhibitors and H2-receptor antagonists. Troxipide is used primarily for gastritis, gastric ulcer, dyspepsia, epigastric pain, nausea, bloating, and mucosal injury associated with acid-peptic disease, where its clinical use centers on enhancement of gastric mucosal defense, suppression of inflammatory cell infiltration, improvement of mucus secretion and microcirculation, and promotion of ulcer healing rather than direct acid suppression. Absorption after oral dosing appears adequate for local and systemic mucosal effects, distribution is expected to favor gastrointestinal tissues, metabolism is thought to occur mainly hepatically with conjugative and/or oxidative biotransformation, and excretion likely proceeds predominantly in urine with some biliary/fecal elimination, although detailed human ADME datasets are limited. No single canonical target protein is firmly established; reported mechanistic associations include modulation of gastric mucin, prostaglandin-linked cytoprotection, inhibition of neutrophil-mediated inflammation, and effects on inflammatory mediators rather than high-affinity receptor antagonism. Toxicity is generally low in therapeutic use, with adverse effects usually mild and including constipation, diarrhea, nausea, abdominal discomfort, headache, dizziness, rash, and transient liver-enzyme elevation; serious toxicity appears uncommon but hypersensitivity and clinically significant hepatic intolerance are plausible rare examples.

Name: Endralazine
Description: Endralazine (DB13435) is a small-molecule vasodilator of the hydrazinophthalazine/heteroaromatic hydrazine class, characterized structurally by a fused aza-aromatic ring system bearing a terminal hydrazino functionality that confers basicity, redox reactivity, and smooth-muscle relaxant activity; its core scaffold is therefore best described as a phthalazine-like bicyclic nitrogen-containing aromatic scaffold substituted with a hydrazine moiety. It is chemically and pharmacologically related to direct vasodilators such as hydralazine and, more distantly, other antihypertensive vasodilators including dihydralazine and cadralazine, which share hydrazine-linked aromatic frameworks. Although the precise molecular target profile has not been fully defined, endralazine is generally regarded as a direct arterial smooth-muscle relaxant, with functional effects likely involving reduced peripheral vascular resistance and possible modulation of intracellular calcium handling; no single validated high-affinity protein target is firmly established, though vascular smooth-muscle signaling proteins are implicated. Pharmacokinetically, it is expected to be orally absorbed, distributed systemically to vascular tissues, hepatically metabolized through oxidative and conjugative pathways analogous to related hydrazines, and excreted mainly as metabolites in urine. Toxicity is consistent with its class and includes dose-related hypotension, reflex sympathetic activation, headache, dizziness, flushing, palpitations, and fluid retention, with rarer concerns such as hepatotoxicity, peripheral neuropathic symptoms, or lupus-like immune phenomena described for related hydrazine vasodilators. Its principal indication is hypertension, especially essential or resistant hypertension, and clinical use has historically been as an antihypertensive, often in combination regimens when lowering elevated blood pressure and reducing vascular resistance are required.

Name: Nepinalone
Description: Nepinalone (DrugBank DB13445) is described as a small, lipophilic synthetic analgesic–anti-inflammatory agent built around an aryl ketone scaffold, specifically a propiophenone-like framework in which a substituted phenyl ring is linked to a short alkanone side chain, placing it within the broader class of non-opioid aromatic ketone analgesics and making it chemically reminiscent of other simple arylalkanones and older nonsteroidal pain-relieving drugs; structurally and pharmacologically it has been compared with agents such as phenylbutazone, suprofen, and other historically used non-opioid antipyretic or anti-inflammatory compounds, although it is less widely characterized than modern NSAIDs. Its pharmacology is thought to involve inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis through cyclooxygenase pathway suppression, but specific, well-validated molecular target proteins have not been clearly established in public sources, so COX-1 and COX-2 are best regarded as putative rather than definitively confirmed targets. Nepinalone has been used for symptomatic treatment of pain, fever, and inflammatory conditions such as musculoskeletal pain, arthralgia, and minor rheumatic complaints. Expected pharmacokinetics are consistent with an orally active lipophilic aryl ketone: gastrointestinal absorption, moderate tissue distribution with probable plasma-protein binding, hepatic biotransformation by carbonyl reduction and/or oxidative conjugative metabolism, and predominantly renal excretion of metabolites. Adverse effects likely resemble those of older analgesic anti-inflammatory drugs, including nausea, dyspepsia, abdominal discomfort, dizziness, headache, rash, and somnolence, while toxicity may include gastrointestinal irritation or ulceration, hypersensitivity reactions, and with excessive exposure possible hepatic or renal dysfunction. Clinically, its use has historically been as a symptomatic oral analgesic and antipyretic rather than a disease-modifying therapy.

Name: Oxaflozane
Description: Oxaflozane (DrugBank DB13457) is a small-molecule psychoactive agent described as an aromatic heterocyclic compound built around a substituted anisole/aryl-ether framework linked to a nitrogen-containing side chain, giving it the overall character of a lipophilic CNS-active base; chemically it is generally grouped with older anxiolytic-antidepressant agents and can be viewed as fitting a phenoxyalkylamine-like scaffold rather than a modern SSRI, benzodiazepine, or tricyclic template. Structurally and pharmacologically it has been compared with other legacy sedative-anxiolytic or antidepressant drugs that combine an aryl ether motif with a basic amine, although it does not map cleanly onto a major contemporary class; examples of broadly similar CNS drugs include etifoxine, meprobamate, and certain sedating tricyclic-like agents in terms of therapeutic niche rather than exact chemistry. Available pharmacokinetic information is limited, but oxaflozane is expected to be orally absorbed, distributed into the CNS because of substantial lipophilicity, metabolized hepatically by oxidative biotransformation and conjugation, and excreted mainly in urine as metabolites. Specific validated molecular targets are not well established in standard sources, and its mechanism has historically been described only broadly as central psychotropic modulation. It has been used for anxiety, depressive symptoms, psychovegetative complaints, agitation, and stress-related insomnia. Adverse effects are consistent with sedating psychotropics, including drowsiness, dizziness, impaired concentration, dry mouth, orthostatic symptoms, and gastrointestinal upset; overdose or excessive exposure could plausibly produce marked CNS depression. Toxicology data are sparse, but caution is warranted in hepatic impairment, with alcohol or other sedatives, and where psychomotor performance is critical.

Name: Oxetorone
Description: Oxetorone (DrugBank DB13463) is a centrally acting antimigraine agent of the piperazine-derived serotonin-antagonist/antihistamine class, built around an aryl-substituted piperazine scaffold linked to lipophilic aromatic and carbonyl-containing substituents that confer high CNS penetration and receptor-binding promiscuity; chemically it is best viewed as a diaryl-piperazine-like scaffold related to older H1-antihistaminic and antiserotonergic drugs, with pharmacologic similarity to pizotifen, cyproheptadine, methysergide, and in broader antimigraine prophylaxis practice to flunarizine. Its principal targets are reported to include serotonin receptors, especially 5-HT2-family sites, and histamine H1 receptors, with possible ancillary anticholinergic activity that may contribute to clinical and adverse effects. Oxetorone has been used mainly for migraine prophylaxis and related vascular headache syndromes, particularly recurrent migraine with or without aura, where it is intended to reduce attack frequency rather than abort acute attacks. After oral administration it is absorbed sufficiently for chronic use, distributes widely with likely substantial tissue and CNS uptake owing to lipophilicity, undergoes hepatic biotransformation, and is eliminated as metabolites by renal and possibly biliary routes; however, detailed modern ADME parameters are not well characterized in public sources. Toxicity is dominated by CNS depression and autonomic adverse effects, with examples including somnolence, fatigue, dizziness, dry mouth, constipation, and weight gain; overdose or susceptible patients may develop marked sedation, confusion, or cardiovascular effects such as hypotension. Clinically, oxetorone has been used as a preventive migraine therapy in adults, especially when sedation is acceptable or when older serotonin-antagonist strategies are preferred.

Name: Nepinalone
Description: Nepinalone (DrugBank DB13475) is a small-molecule central nervous system agent described chemically as an aryl ketone with a relatively simple nonpolycyclic framework in which a lipophilic aromatic ring is linked through a carbonyl-containing side chain to a short aliphatic amine-bearing moiety, placing it in the broad category of synthetic neuroactive ketones and giving it a propiophenone-like or arylalkanone scaffold; on structural grounds it is often considered analogous to older centrally acting sedative-analgesic or muscle relaxant chemotypes, with loose similarity to other simple aromatic ketone CNS drugs such as methyprylon-like sedatives and certain arylketone analgesic prototypes, although it is not a major modern therapeutic standard. Its pharmacology has historically been characterized more by functional CNS depressant activity than by a precisely defined molecular mechanism, and no firmly established high-affinity target protein has been consistently validated, though nonspecific modulation of neuronal excitability and possible indirect effects on GABAergic signaling have been proposed. Pharmacokinetic data are limited; available descriptions suggest oral absorption, systemic distribution into well-perfused tissues including the CNS because of moderate lipophilicity, hepatic biotransformation likely via carbonyl reduction and oxidative pathways, and renal excretion of metabolites. Reported or expected adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, impaired coordination, confusion, nausea, and dose-related psychomotor slowing, while toxicity is consistent with CNS depressant overdose, including profound sedation, respiratory depression, hypotension, and coma, especially with alcohol or other sedatives. Clinically, nepinalone has been used historically as a symptomatic agent for pain, muscle spasm, tension states, and related discomfort, but its use appears limited and largely superseded by better-characterized alternatives.

Name: Meptazinol
Description: Meptazinol (DrugBank DB13478) is a synthetic opioid analgesic built on a compact phenolic azabicyclic/aminocyclohexane-like framework, characterized by a tertiary amine embedded in a constrained ring system and an aryl-phenol moiety that supports opioid receptor recognition; chemically it is classified as an opioid analgesic and more specifically a phenolic opioid, with a meptazinol-specific bridged aminoalcohol scaffold distinct from morphine’s pentacyclic nucleus but functionally analogous to other mixed agonist-type analgesics. Structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include pentazocine, tramadol, buprenorphine, codeine, and morphine, although meptazinol is generally considered a relatively short-acting, lower-potency opioid with partial agonist properties, acting primarily at the mu-opioid receptor; opioid receptor proteins such as OPRM1 are the main recognized targets, with less certain or weaker activity at other opioid receptor subtypes. It is used for moderate to severe pain, including postoperative pain, obstetric analgesia, trauma-related pain, and occasionally musculoskeletal or visceral pain. After oral or parenteral administration it is absorbed fairly rapidly, distributes systemically with CNS penetration sufficient for analgesia, undergoes substantial hepatic metabolism mainly by conjugative pathways such as glucuronidation, and is eliminated predominantly in urine as metabolites, giving a relatively short duration of action and supporting repeated dosing when needed. Adverse effects resemble those of other opioids and include nausea, vomiting, dizziness, sweating, sedation, constipation, and dry mouth; toxicity may present with excessive CNS depression, hypotension, confusion, and respiratory depression, though this may be somewhat less pronounced than with full mu agonists, while overdose risk increases with alcohol or other sedatives. Clinically, meptazinol has been used as an alternative opioid when effective short-term analgesia is needed with a potentially lower burden of respiratory suppression or dependence than conventional strong opioids, although opioid-class cautions, abuse liability, and use restrictions in hepatic impairment or susceptible patients remain important.

Name: Tenidap
Description: Tenidap (DB13481) is a synthetic anti-inflammatory small molecule built around an indole/indene-like heteroaromatic acidic scaffold with a planar, lipophilic aryl system and a carboxylic acid-containing pharmacophore that supports protein binding and tissue penetration; it is generally classified as a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory and disease-modifying antirheumatic candidate, with a heteroaryl acetic acid–type scaffold related functionally, though not identically, to other acidic anti-inflammatory agents. Similar drugs in therapeutic space include NSAIDs and antirheumatic agents such as diclofenac, indomethacin, piroxicam, and disease-modifying comparators such as sulfasalazine or methotrexate, although tenidap was distinguished by broader cytokine-modulating effects. Its pharmacology was linked to inhibition of cyclooxygenase-dependent prostaglandin synthesis and suppression of inflammatory cytokines, particularly IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-associated pathways; reported target associations therefore include cyclooxygenase enzymes, with broader modulation of cytokine signaling rather than a single highly selective receptor target. Pharmacokinetically, tenidap was orally active, absorbed systemically, highly protein bound, distributed into inflamed tissues, metabolized hepatically with oxidative and conjugative pathways, and eliminated through both renal and biliary routes; accumulation risk would be greater in hepatic dysfunction. It was developed mainly for rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory arthropathies to reduce pain, swelling, stiffness, and inflammatory markers, but clinical use was limited and ultimately abandoned because of toxicity, notably hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, proteinuria, edema, hematologic abnormalities, and occasional serious hypersensitivity; common adverse effects also included gastrointestinal upset, headache, rash, and fluid retention.

Name: Bencyclane
Description: Bencyclane (also known as bencyclane fumarate or halidor) is a synthetic vasodilatory antispasmodic built around a lipophilic benzhydryl–thioether scaffold linked through a propyl chain to a tertiary amine-containing saturated heterocycle, giving it the character of a basic aralkyl sulfide with spasmolytic activity; chemically it is classified as a vasoactive peripheral smooth-muscle relaxant and antispasmodic, and its core scaffold places it near other older peripheral vasodilators and spasmolytics such as papaverine, drotaverine, cinnarizine, and naftidrofuryl, which share smooth-muscle-relaxing or circulation-improving properties despite structural differences. Pharmacologically, bencyclane is reported to inhibit calcium-dependent smooth-muscle contraction, reduce vasospasm, and interfere with platelet aggregation and phosphodiesterase-linked signaling, although no single highly selective canonical target protein is firmly established; proposed target systems include voltage-sensitive calcium handling pathways, calmodulin-related contractile mechanisms, phosphodiesterases, and platelet activation pathways. It is used mainly for peripheral vascular disease and vasospastic states, including intermittent claudication, acrocyanosis, Raynaud-type symptoms, cerebrovascular insufficiency, and visceral smooth-muscle spasm such as biliary or urinary tract spasm. After oral administration it is absorbed reasonably well, distributes widely into tissues because of its lipophilicity, undergoes substantial hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated chiefly as metabolites in urine with a moderate duration of action. Adverse effects include dizziness, headache, nausea, epigastric discomfort, dry mouth, tachycardia, flushing, hypotension, and occasional CNS excitation or confusion; toxicity is dominated by neurotoxicity and cardiovascular effects, with overdose potentially causing agitation, seizures, arrhythmias, and circulatory instability, so clinical use has generally been as an older symptomatic agent for vasospasm and peripheral circulation disorders rather than a first-line modern therapy.

Name: Bamipine
Description: Bamipine (DrugBank DB13489) is a first-generation H1-antihistamine of the ethanolamine/tertiary amine anticholinergic class, structurally characterized by a lipophilic diaryl- or aryl-substituted aminoalkyl framework built around a basic tertiary amine linked through a short flexible alkyl/ether-like spacer to hydrophobic aromatic moieties, a motif typical of classic sedating antihistamines; its core chemical scaffold is therefore an aminoalkyl-diaryl antihistamine scaffold related to agents such as diphenhydramine, doxylamine, carbinoxamine, clemastine, and dimenhydrinate. Pharmacologically, bamipine acts primarily as an antagonist or inverse agonist at the histamine H1 receptor (HRH1), with clinically relevant off-target antimuscarinic activity likely contributing to both efficacy and adverse effects. It has been used mainly for symptomatic relief of allergic conditions and pruritic dermatoses, including urticaria, insect bites, allergic skin reactions, and itch associated with contact dermatitis, and in some markets as a topical antipruritic preparation. Like other older H1 blockers, bamipine is expected to be absorbed after local or systemic administration, distribute widely into tissues, and, because of its lipophilicity and tertiary amine character, penetrate the central nervous system; it is presumed to undergo hepatic oxidative metabolism followed by urinary excretion of metabolites and a smaller fraction of unchanged drug. Toxicity is broadly consistent with first-generation antihistamines, with overdose or excessive exposure potentially causing marked sedation, confusion, anticholinergic syndrome, tachycardia, urinary retention, dry mucosa, and, especially in children, paradoxical excitation. Common side effects include drowsiness, dizziness, blurred vision, dry mouth, constipation, and local irritation with topical use, so clinical use has generally been limited to short-term treatment of itch and minor allergic symptoms rather than chronic systemic therapy.

Name: Poldine
Description: Poldine (DrugBank DB13507) is a synthetic antimuscarinic agent of the quaternary ammonium anticholinergic class, structurally characterized by a permanently charged nitrogen center embedded in a substituted aminoalcohol/ester-like framework with bulky hydrophobic aryl and cycloalkyl features that restrict central nervous system penetration; its medicinal-chemistry scaffold is best viewed as a quaternary ammonium parasympatholytic scaffold related to classic atropine-like peripheral anticholinergics. Similar drugs include propantheline, glycopyrronium, methantheline, hyoscine butylbromide, and to some extent atropine analogues used for gastrointestinal spasm and antisecretory effects. Its principal pharmacologic targets are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially peripheral M1 and M3 receptor populations in gastrointestinal smooth muscle and exocrine glands, producing reduced motility, diminished spasm, and decreased gastric and intestinal secretions. Poldine has historically been used for peptic ulcer disease, pylorospasm, irritable or spastic colon states, and other hypermotility or hypersecretory gastrointestinal symptoms. As a quaternary ammonium compound, oral absorption is generally incomplete, distribution is largely peripheral with poor blood-brain barrier entry, metabolism appears limited or variable, and elimination is expected to occur through renal and possibly biliary routes, partly as unchanged drug. Toxicity is dominated by excessive anticholinergic effects, with examples including severe xerostomia, constipation, urinary retention, tachycardia, blurred vision, precipitated angle-closure glaucoma, and reduced sweating with heat intolerance; overdose may cause ileus and marked autonomic blockade. Common adverse effects include dry mouth, nausea, abdominal distension, constipation, palpitations, and difficulty micturating. Clinically, it has been used as an adjunctive peripheral antispasmodic and antisecretory drug rather than a disease-modifying therapy.

Name: Levomethadone
Description: Levomethadone (DrugBank DB13515) is the levorotatory, pharmacologically dominant enantiomer of methadone, a synthetic diphenylheptanone opioid characterized by a flexible 6-(dimethylamino)-4,4-diphenylheptan-3-one framework containing a tertiary amine, a central ketone, and two phenyl rings; chemically it belongs to the diphenylpropylamine/diphenylheptanone class and is built on the methadone acyclic diarylalkylamine scaffold. Closely related drugs include racemic methadone, dextromethadone, and other strong opioids such as morphine, fentanyl, and levorphanol, although the scaffold is distinct from morphinans and anilidopiperidines. Its principal target is the mu-opioid receptor encoded by OPRM1, with lesser activity reported at delta and kappa opioid receptors and possible interaction with NMDA signaling and monoamine transport systems that may contribute to analgesic effects. Levomethadone is well absorbed orally, highly lipophilic, extensively distributed into tissues, strongly protein bound, and subject to hepatic N-demethylation mainly by CYP2B6, CYP3A4, and CYP2D6 to inactive metabolites such as EDDP, followed by renal and fecal excretion; it has a long and variable half-life supporting once-daily maintenance in some settings. It is indicated for severe chronic pain and opioid dependence or withdrawal management, including heroin-use disorder substitution therapy. Adverse effects and toxicity are typical of potent opioids and include sedation, constipation, nausea, sweating, miosis, respiratory depression, overdose coma, dependence, withdrawal, and clinically important QT prolongation with torsades de pointes risk, particularly at high doses or with interacting drugs. In clinical use it serves as an analgesic and as maintenance or detoxification therapy where the single active enantiomer may offer more predictable opioid effects than the racemate.

Name: Angiotensinamide
Description: Angiotensinamide (DrugBank DB13517) is a synthetic peptide pressor agent structurally derived from the angiotensin family and characterized by a short oligopeptide framework bearing the aromatic, basic, and amide-functional residues required for potent vasoconstrictor activity; chemically it is classified as a vasoactive oligopeptide and specifically an angiotensin analog, with a scaffold consisting of the conserved angiotensin peptide backbone terminated by an amide group that enhances receptor activity and distinguishes it from some endogenous counterparts. Similar drugs include angiotensin II, other angiotensin analogs, and vasopressor peptides used in shock states, such as synthetic hypertensin-like agents, although catecholamine vasopressors are only pharmacodynamically analogous rather than structurally similar. Its primary targets are angiotensin receptors, predominantly AGTR1 and to a lesser extent AGTR2, mediating arteriolar vasoconstriction, increased systemic vascular resistance, and blood pressure elevation. Pharmacokinetically, like other small peptides, it is not orally bioavailable, is administered parenterally, distributes mainly within the vascular and extracellular space, undergoes rapid enzymatic degradation by circulating and tissue peptidases, and has a very short duration of action with metabolites cleared largely by renal mechanisms after peptide hydrolysis. Toxicity is chiefly an extension of its pharmacology, including excessive hypertension, reflex bradycardia, reduced organ perfusion, arrhythmogenic risk, and ischemic complications such as myocardial or peripheral ischemia at high exposure. Adverse effects can include headache, chest discomfort, palpitations, nausea, vasoconstriction-related pallor, and blood pressure lability. Clinically, angiotensinamide has been used primarily as a diagnostic or therapeutic vasopressor in hypotensive states, especially acute shock or refractory hypotension, and historically in settings where rapid restoration of vascular tone was desired.

Name: Proglumetacin
Description: Proglumetacin (DB13527) is an ester prodrug that covalently links the indoleacetic acid NSAID indomethacin to the antiulcer agent proglumide, giving a hybrid structure with an indole nucleus bearing a p-chlorobenzoyl substituent and methoxy group joined through an amide/ester-containing linker to a substituted glutaramic acid derivative; chemically it is best classified as an indomethacin-derived nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory prodrug and, more broadly, an aromatic carboxylic acid derivative. Its dominant scaffold is the indomethacin indole-aryl acetic acid pharmacophore masked within a mutual prodrug framework, and it is similar to indomethacin itself as well as other acidic NSAIDs such as acemetacin, sulindac, diclofenac, and ketoprofen, especially agents designed to reduce gastrointestinal irritation. After oral administration, proglumetacin is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract and undergoes presystemic and systemic hydrolysis to release indomethacin and proglumide; distribution is expected to mirror indomethacin, with high plasma protein binding and penetration into inflamed synovial tissues, metabolism occurring mainly through hepatic deacylation, demethylation, and conjugation of released indomethacin, followed by renal and biliary excretion of parent-derived metabolites. Its principal targets are cyclooxygenase enzymes PTGS1 and PTGS2 via released indomethacin, reducing prostaglandin synthesis. It is indicated for painful inflammatory disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, and other musculoskeletal pain states. Toxicity is typical of NSAIDs, including gastrointestinal ulceration or bleeding, renal impairment, fluid retention, hepatotoxicity, and hypersensitivity; side effects include dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, headache, dizziness, edema, and occasional CNS effects. Clinically, it has been used when anti-inflammatory efficacy comparable to indomethacin is desired with the aim of improved gastric tolerability in chronic rheumatic disease management.

Name: Chlormadinone
Description: Chlormadinone (DrugBank DB13528) is a synthetic steroidal progestin and antiandrogen built on the pregnane/progesterone nucleus, characterized structurally as a halogenated 17α-acetoxy, 6-chloro substituted pregna-diene ketone that preserves the fused four-ring cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene steroid framework typical of progesterone analogues. Chemically it belongs to the 17α-hydroxyprogesterone-derived progestogens, with a pregnane steroid scaffold; similar drugs include cyproterone acetate, medroxyprogesterone acetate, megestrol acetate, nomegestrol acetate, and progesterone itself, particularly among agents combining progestational and antiandrogenic properties. Its principal targets are the progesterone receptor and androgen receptor, acting mainly as a potent PR agonist and AR antagonist, with limited interaction at glucocorticoid-related pathways compared with some related steroids. After oral administration, chlormadinone acetate is absorbed reasonably well, is highly plasma protein bound, distributes into lipid-rich tissues, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism including reduction, hydroxylation, and deacetylation to active and inactive metabolites, and is eliminated through both biliary/fecal and renal routes, with a terminal half-life sufficient for once-daily use. Toxicities reflect hormonal steroid exposure and may include cholestatic liver dysfunction, thromboembolic risk, adverse lipid changes, weight gain, and rare mood or glucose effects; reproductive toxicity would be expected in pregnancy because of endocrine activity. Clinically it is used in oral contraception and for androgen-dependent conditions such as acne, seborrhea, hirsutism, menstrual disorders, endometriosis-related symptoms, and benign prostatic hyperplasia in some regions. Common adverse effects include breakthrough bleeding, amenorrhea, breast tenderness, headache, nausea, edema, decreased libido, and fatigue.

Name: Bifemelane
Description: Bifemelane (DB13550) is a centrally acting arylalkylamine nootropic and cerebral metabolic enhancer characterized structurally by a diphenylmethyl ether framework linked through a short alkoxy chain to a dimethylamino moiety, making it a lipophilic tertiary amine with a cationic center at physiological pH; chemically it is classified as a neuroactive diphenyl ether/phenoxyalkylamine derivative, and its core scaffold is best described as a benzhydryl-oxyethyl-dimethylamine pharmacophore. It is structurally and pharmacologically related to older cognition-oriented cerebroactive agents and monoaminergic modulators, with partial resemblance to compounds such as amantadine-like CNS stimulants, indeloxazine, idebenone, and other anti-dementia cerebral activators used in Japan. Its pharmacokinetics are reported to involve oral absorption with CNS penetration due to substantial lipophilicity, wide tissue distribution including brain, hepatic metabolism likely via oxidative N-dealkylation and aromatic/side-chain hydroxylation followed by conjugation, and predominantly renal excretion of metabolites. Bifemelane has been associated with relatively low acute toxicity at therapeutic doses, but overdose or susceptible elderly patients may develop agitation, insomnia, tremor, confusion, gastrointestinal upset, or hepatic dysfunction; rare serious events include seizures or marked neuropsychiatric activation. Its molecular targets have not been fully defined, but reported actions include inhibition of monoamine oxidase, enhancement of cholinergic and monoaminergic neurotransmission, and possible interaction with muscarinic cholinergic, dopaminergic, and adrenergic signaling pathways rather than a single high-affinity target protein. Clinically it has been used for cognitive impairment, apathy, reduced spontaneity, emotional disturbance, and memory deficits associated with cerebrovascular disease, senile dementia, post-stroke states, and chronic cerebral circulation insufficiency, with adverse effects including nausea, anorexia, dizziness, headache, sleep disturbance, palpitations, and rash.

Name: Zipeprol
Description: Zipeprol (DrugBank DB13564) is a centrally acting non-opioid antitussive whose structure is characterized by an aryloxy-alkylamine architecture built around a piperazine-containing scaffold linked through a short aliphatic chain to substituted aromatic rings, giving it physicochemical similarity to lipophilic cough suppressants and some first-generation antihistamine-like agents; chemically it is generally classified as a piperazine derivative and more broadly as an aryl ether/tertiary amine antitussive, with a scaffold related to other centrally active cough suppressants such as cloperastine and, more distantly by therapeutic role rather than exact chemotype, dextromethorphan and benproperine. Its pharmacology appears to involve depression of the medullary cough center and central sedative actions, but no single validated high-affinity target protein is firmly established; reported or proposed target-level interactions include sigma-site and other CNS receptor interactions, while classic opioid receptors are not considered the primary mechanism. It was used for symptomatic treatment of nonproductive cough in upper respiratory infections, bronchitis, pharyngitis, and irritative cough states. Pharmacokinetic data are limited, but it is orally absorbed, distributes into the CNS because of sufficient lipophilicity, undergoes hepatic biotransformation likely via oxidative N-dealkylation and conjugative pathways, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine. Toxicity is clinically important: misuse and overdose have been associated with hallucinations, agitation, seizures, respiratory depression, coma, and deaths, particularly in adolescents and in combination with alcohol or other CNS depressants. Common adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, nausea, dry mouth, confusion, and ataxia. Because of abuse liability and neurotoxicity concerns, its clinical use as an antitussive has been restricted or withdrawn in several markets.

Name: Acefylline
Description: Acefylline (DrugBank DB13573) is a xanthine-derived bronchodilator in which the core purine-2,6-dione/theophylline-like bicyclic heteroaromatic scaffold is substituted to increase hydrophilicity and modify tolerability, placing it within the methylxanthine chemical category and specifically among theophylline-related respiratory stimulants; its scaffold is therefore best described as a substituted xanthine nucleus closely related to the purine dione framework found in theophylline, aminophylline, doxofylline, and etofylline. By analogy with other xanthines, its pharmacology is thought to involve weak nonselective phosphodiesterase inhibition and adenosine receptor antagonism, with relevant target proteins including adenosine A1 and A2A receptors and multiple PDE isoenzymes, although specific high-confidence human target annotation for acefylline itself is limited. It has been used primarily for symptomatic treatment of bronchospasm, asthma, chronic bronchitis, and chronic obstructive airway disease, and in some settings as an adjunct mucoregulating or bronchodilating agent for cough with airway obstruction. Pharmacokinetic data are sparse, but xanthine-like behavior suggests oral absorption, distribution into total body water with limited protein binding, hepatic biotransformation, and predominantly renal excretion of metabolites and some unchanged drug; elimination may be prolonged in hepatic impairment, older age, or heart failure. Toxicity is expected to resemble other methylxanthines, including dose-related gastrointestinal irritation, nausea, vomiting, tremor, insomnia, agitation, tachycardia, and, at high exposure, hypokalemia, arrhythmias, and seizures. Clinical use has therefore generally been as a secondary or adjunct bronchodilator rather than a first-line modern controller therapy, especially in chronic reactive or obstructive airway conditions where symptomatic relief is needed.

Name: Naftidrofuryl
Description: Naftidrofuryl (DrugBank DB13588) is a synthetic vasoactive agent built around a 2-(diethylamino)ethyl ester linked to a substituted aromatic system containing a tetrahydrofuran moiety and a naphthalene-derived carboxylate framework, giving it an amphiphilic structure with both lipophilic aromatic and basic tertiary amine features; chemically it is classified as a vasodilatory serotonin antagonist, often grouped among peripheral vasoactive or hemorheologic drugs, and its core scaffold can be described as a naftidrofurylate ester of a diethylaminoethanol side chain fused conceptually to an aryl-tetrahydrofuran motif. Structurally and pharmacologically related drugs include other peripheral vasodilators and serotonergic antagonists such as cinnarizine, nicergoline, pentoxifylline, and buflomedil, although they differ in primary scaffold. Its principal target is generally considered the serotonin 5-HT2 receptor family, especially 5-HT2A-mediated vascular actions, with downstream improvement in peripheral blood flow and cellular oxygen utilization. After oral administration it is absorbed variably, undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism to inactive or less active metabolites, is widely distributed, and is eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites, with a relatively short parent-plasma half-life. It is indicated mainly for symptomatic treatment of peripheral arterial occlusive disease, particularly intermittent claudication, and has also been used in cerebrovascular insufficiency or ischemic symptoms in some settings. Adverse effects are usually gastrointestinal, including nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea, with headache, dizziness, and rash also reported. Toxicity is generally low at therapeutic doses but overdose may cause marked GI intolerance or CNS symptoms; prolonged use has rarely been associated with hepatic injury or calcium oxalate urolithiasis. Clinically, it is used to improve walking distance, reduce ischemic limb discomfort, and support management of chronic peripheral circulatory disorders.

Name: Tiocarlide
Description: Tiocarlide (DrugBank DB13608) is a thiocarbanilide-derived antimycobacterial agent whose structure is characterized by a substituted diaryl thiourea/thioamide motif, with two aromatic rings linked through a sulfur-containing urea-like core that confers marked lipophilicity and underlies its classification as a thiourea, specifically within the thiocarbanilide chemical class; its core scaffold is therefore a diaryl thiourea (thiocarbanilide) framework, closely related to older antitubercular thiocarlide analogs and structurally similar lipophilic antimycobacterial agents such as isoxyl and other thiourea-based compounds. Pharmacologically, it has been used as a second-line antitubercular drug active against Mycobacterium tuberculosis, historically in pulmonary tuberculosis and in some multidrug-resistant settings, with activity linked to inhibition of mycolic-acid biosynthesis; EthA, the mycobacterial monooxygenase involved in prodrug activation, and downstream fatty-acid/mycolic-acid synthesis proteins are the most commonly cited functional target pathway components, although a single definitive protein target has not been fully established in all sources. Like other highly lipophilic thiocarbamides, tiocarlide is thought to be orally absorbed variably, distribute extensively into tissues, undergo hepatic biotransformation, and be eliminated mainly via biliary/fecal routes with some renal excretion of metabolites. Its adverse-effect profile includes gastrointestinal intolerance, dizziness, weakness, and rash, while dose-limiting toxicity has included hepatotoxicity and dermatologic hypersensitivity; examples of serious toxicity reported for related use include hepatitis and severe intolerance. Clinically, tiocarlide has had limited modern use because of toxicity, variable efficacy, and replacement by better-tolerated tuberculosis regimens.

Name: Umifenovir
Description: Umifenovir (DrugBank DB13609, also known as arbidol) is a small-molecule indole-derived antiviral built on a substituted indole scaffold, specifically a highly functionalized 1H-indole core bearing bromine, hydroxy, dimethylaminomethyl, methyl, and a thioether-linked carboxylate ester side chain, placing it within the indole antivirals and lipophilic heteroaromatic fusion inhibitors. Its closest pharmacologic analogs are other direct-acting influenza entry inhibitors or membrane-fusion blockers, although it is structurally distinct from neuraminidase inhibitors such as oseltamivir and zanamivir and from the cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitor baloxavir; broader mechanistic similarity is sometimes drawn to fusion-targeting antivirals used for enveloped viruses. Umifenovir is absorbed orally with moderate bioavailability, reaches peak plasma levels within hours, shows substantial tissue distribution and protein binding, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism including phase I oxidation and phase II conjugative pathways, and is eliminated mainly via biliary/fecal routes with limited renal clearance. It is generally considered to have relatively low acute toxicity at therapeutic doses, but overdose or susceptible patients may experience gastrointestinal intolerance, hepatic enzyme elevations, or hypersensitivity-type reactions; reproductive and chronic toxicity concerns are less well characterized outside regional use. The best-described target is influenza virus hemagglutinin, where it stabilizes the prefusion state and inhibits viral-endosomal membrane fusion, while proposed host-related effects include interference with clathrin-mediated uptake and immunomodulatory signaling. Clinically, it has been used for treatment and prophylaxis of influenza A and B, acute respiratory viral infections, and in some settings investigated for coronavirus infections. Adverse effects include nausea, dyspepsia, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, rash, and transient transaminase increases, and its clinical use has been most prominent in Russia and parts of Asia for seasonal influenza, post-exposure prophylaxis, and adjunctive management of viral respiratory syndromes.

Name: Metizoline
Description: Metizoline (DB13614) is an imidazoline-derived sympathomimetic nasal decongestant whose structure is characterized by an aromatic lipophilic ring system linked through a short spacer to a protonatable imidazoline moiety, placing it in the imidazoline/arylimidazoline class and giving it the same core scaffold seen in topical α-adrenergic agonists. Structurally and pharmacologically it is similar to xylometazoline, oxymetazoline, naphazoline, and tetrahydrozoline, all of which share an aryl-substituted imidazoline vasoconstrictor pharmacophore. Its principal targets are adrenergic α-receptors, predominantly α1-adrenergic receptors with possible contribution from α2-adrenergic receptor signaling in nasal mucosal vessels, producing local vasoconstriction and reduced mucosal edema. It is indicated for symptomatic relief of nasal congestion, especially in rhinitis, common cold, allergic rhinitis, and sinusitis-related obstruction, and has been used clinically as a topical intranasal decongestant for short-term reduction of rhinorrhea and swelling. Pharmacokinetic data are limited, but like related agents it is intended for local intranasal absorption with low systemic exposure at therapeutic doses, distribution largely confined to mucosal tissues, probable hepatic oxidative metabolism if absorbed, and renal excretion of metabolites and small amounts of unchanged drug. Toxicity is mainly due to excessive systemic α-adrenergic stimulation or rebound congestion after prolonged use; examples include hypertension, reflex bradycardia, CNS depression or agitation in overdose, and rhinitis medicamentosa with chronic administration. Common adverse effects include nasal dryness, burning, irritation, sneezing, headache, and palpitations, with pediatric ingestion posing particular risk of serious poisoning.

Name: Tenitramine
Description: Tenitramine (DrugBank DB13637) is best described as a small synthetic aromatic amine with a nitro-substituted heteroaryl/arylamine architecture, featuring a planar, electron-poor ring system linked to a basic amine functionality; on this basis it falls within the broad chemical category of nitroaromatic amines and can be summarized structurally by an aniline-like pharmacophore embedded in a compact heteroaromatic scaffold. Its closest conceptual analogs are older nitroaromatic anti-infective or trypanocidal agents such as nifurtimox, benznidazole, and related redox-active aromatic amines, although Tenitramine itself is not widely characterized in modern clinical pharmacology sources. The likely scaffold-driven pharmacology is redox cycling or bioactivation-dependent cytotoxicity rather than highly selective receptor pharmacology, and no definitively established human target proteins are well validated in the public domain; if active, the relevant targets are more plausibly microbial or parasite-associated reductases and downstream macromolecular damage pathways than a single host protein. Pharmacokinetic data are sparse, but such molecules are generally expected to be orally absorbed to a variable extent, distribute moderately into perfused tissues, undergo hepatic reduction and oxidative biotransformation with possible conjugation, and be excreted mainly in urine as metabolites. Toxicologically, nitroaromatic amines are often associated with dose-limiting gastrointestinal intolerance, dizziness, headache, hepatotoxicity, neuropathy, methemoglobinemia, and possible mutagenic or genotoxic liability. Consequently, reported or anticipated indications and clinical use have historically centered on anti-infective or antiparasitic contexts rather than chronic therapy, with adverse effects and safety concerns limiting broad contemporary use.

Name: Ethacizine
Description: Ethacizine (DrugBank DB13645) is a class Ic antiarrhythmic built on a phenothiazine-related tricyclic aromatic scaffold in which the dibenzothiazine core is functionally adapted with basic aminoalkyl substituents, giving a lipophilic, cationic molecule optimized for membrane penetration and sodium-channel blockade; chemically it is generally categorized as a phenothiazine-derived antiarrhythmic rather than a neuroleptic, with a rigid tricyclic heteroaromatic scaffold that places it in the same broad structural space as other membrane-active antiarrhythmics and certain phenothiazine congeners. Similar drugs by pharmacologic behavior include flecainide, propafenone, encainide, and to some extent ajmaline and procainamide, although ethacizine is structurally closer to phenothiazine-derived agents than to those scaffolds. Its principal targets are cardiac voltage-gated sodium channels, especially SCN5A/Nav1.5, with resulting depression of phase 0 depolarization and slowed atrial, nodal, His-Purkinje, and ventricular conduction; ancillary effects on other cardiac ion currents may contribute. It is used for supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmias, including premature atrial or ventricular beats, paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, atrial tachyarrhythmias, and selected ventricular tachyarrhythmias. Pharmacokinetically, it is administered orally, absorbed systemically, distributed extensively into tissues including myocardium, undergoes hepatic biotransformation to active or inactive metabolites, and is eliminated through combined renal and biliary routes; like other class I agents, exposure may rise in hepatic dysfunction. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related proarrhythmia, QRS widening, AV block, sinus node suppression, negative inotropy, hypotension, and CNS effects such as dizziness or tremor; adverse effects can also include nausea, dry mouth, weakness, visual disturbance, and rarely severe ventricular arrhythmia or conduction collapse. Clinically, it has been used mainly when rhythm suppression is specifically required and with ECG monitoring, particularly in symptomatic ectopy or recurrent tachyarrhythmias where benefit outweighs proarrhythmic risk.

Name: Tenonitrozole
Description: Tenonitrozole (DrugBank DB13659) is a nitroimidazole-derived anti-infective whose structure is centered on a 5-nitroimidazole heteroaromatic ring bearing a thioether-linked side chain with lipophilic substitution, a motif that supports redox activation in anaerobic organisms; chemically it is classified as a nitroimidazole antimicrobial, and its core scaffold is the 5-nitroimidazole pharmacophore shared with related agents such as metronidazole, tinidazole, ornidazole, secnidazole, and nimorazole. Like other members of this class, it is thought to undergo intracellular reductive activation by low-redox-potential electron transport proteins in susceptible protozoa and anaerobic bacteria, generating reactive nitro radical intermediates that damage DNA and other macromolecules; no highly specific human protein target is established, and the relevant microbial targets are generally ferredoxin-linked nitroreductive systems and DNA as the ultimate site of injury. Pharmacokinetic data are limited, but it is expected to be orally absorbed, to distribute widely into tissues and possibly genital and gastrointestinal compartments relevant to protozoal infection, to undergo hepatic biotransformation including oxidative and conjugative pathways, and to be eliminated mainly in urine with some biliary or fecal excretion. Toxicity is presumed to parallel other nitroimidazoles, with dose-related gastrointestinal intolerance, metallic taste, headache, dizziness, and less commonly peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects, hypersensitivity, and possible disulfiram-like reactions with alcohol; mutagenicity concerns arise from the nitro group in preclinical systems. Tenonitrozole has been used primarily as an antiprotozoal, especially for trichomoniasis and related urogenital infections, and more broadly for anaerobe-associated or protozoal syndromes where nitroimidazole therapy is appropriate, although modern clinical use appears limited and largely supplanted by better-characterized congeners.

Name: Ipidacrine
Description: Ipidacrine (DrugBank DB13668) is a synthetic cholinergic agent structurally characterized as a substituted tetrahydroacridine derivative, specifically a partially hydrogenated acridine tricyclic aza-aromatic system bearing methyl substitution, which places it in the broader class of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors and potassium-channel-blocking neuroactive compounds; its core scaffold is the tacrine-like aminoacridine/narrowly defined tetrahydroacridine framework, and it is therefore chemically similar to other centrally active cholinesterase inhibitors such as tacrine, donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine, and the related post-Soviet agent amiridine.
