Pharmacologically, ipidacrine inhibits acetylcholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase and is also reported to block voltage-gated potassium channels, thereby prolonging neuronal depolarization and enhancing acetylcholine release; relevant target proteins include ACHE, BCHE, and likely Kv-family potassium channels involved in peripheral and central neurotransmission. After oral or parenteral administration it is absorbed reasonably well, distributed to nervous tissue with some CNS penetration, metabolized hepatically by oxidative biotransformation, and excreted mainly in urine as metabolites and unchanged drug, with a relatively short to moderate elimination half-life supporting repeated daily dosing. Toxicity is chiefly cholinergic and dose related, including salivation, sweating, bradycardia, diarrhea, bronchospasm, muscle cramps, fasciculations, and in overdose possible seizures or cholinergic crisis; caution is warranted in epilepsy, asthma, peptic ulcer disease, and cardiac conduction disorders. Its indications and clinical use center on disorders with impaired neuromuscular or cholinergic transmission, including peripheral neuropathies, neuritis, polyneuropathy, myasthenic syndromes, intestinal or bladder atony, and cognitive or functional deficits after CNS injury, with adverse effects commonly including nausea, abdominal discomfort, dizziness, tremor, weakness, hypersalivation, and sweating.

Name: Sulbentine
Description: Sulbentine (DB13671) is a synthetic organosulfur small molecule best described as a lipophilic thioether/disulfide-containing derivative built on a sulfur-rich aliphatic scaffold rather than a peptidic or heteroaromatic pharmacophore; structurally, it is characterized by sulfur-substituted carbon chains that place it within the broader class of sulfide-based medicinal agents, with a simple organosulfur scaffold related conceptually to other sulfur-donor or thiol-reactive drugs. Similar drugs are limited but may be compared pharmacologically or chemically with other organosulfur compounds such as disulfiram, tiopronin, and sulfur-containing vitamin B1 derivatives, which share redox or thiol-interacting behavior. Published target specificity is not well established, and no single validated target protein has been consistently assigned; its effects have instead been discussed in terms of nonspecific interactions with sulfhydryl-sensitive enzymes and cellular redox systems. Pharmacokinetic data are sparse, but by analogy to related lipophilic organosulfur agents, Sulbentine would be expected to undergo oral absorption, broad tissue distribution, hepatic biotransformation through oxidation and cleavage of sulfur linkages, and renal excretion of polar sulfur metabolites. Toxicology is likewise incompletely defined; potential adverse findings would reasonably include gastrointestinal intolerance, headache, dizziness, hypersensitivity, and dose-related hepatic or neurologic effects seen with some sulfur-containing drugs, while excessive exposure could theoretically increase oxidative or thiol-reactive toxicity. It has been described for therapeutic use in conditions where sulfur-based metabolic or cytoprotective actions were sought, although modern clinical usage appears limited and poorly standardized, with no widely established contemporary indication.

Name: Metahexamide
Description: Metahexamide (DrugBank DB13675) is a first-generation sulfonylurea oral antihyperglycemic agent whose structure is characterized by the classic aryl-sulfonylurea pharmacophore, consisting of a substituted benzenesulfonyl moiety linked through a sulfonylurea bridge to a lipophilic cyclohexyl-containing terminal group; chemically it belongs to the sulfonylurea class of insulin secretagogues, and its core scaffold is the p-substituted benzenesulfonylurea framework shared by early antidiabetic agents. Closely related drugs include tolbutamide, chlorpropamide, acetohexamide, and tolazamide, which share the same general sulfonylurea scaffold and pancreatic mechanism. Its principal pharmacologic target is the ATP-sensitive potassium channel in pancreatic beta cells, specifically via binding to sulfonylurea receptor 1 (ABCC8) with downstream modulation of the Kir6.2 channel complex (KCNJ11), causing channel closure, membrane depolarization, calcium influx, and insulin release. Metahexamide has historically been used in type 2 diabetes mellitus, particularly mild to moderate non-insulin-dependent hyperglycemia inadequately controlled by diet alone. As with older sulfonylureas, it is expected to be well absorbed orally, substantially protein bound, hepatically metabolized to less active or inactive metabolites, and eliminated primarily through renal excretion, with clinically relevant risk of accumulation in hepatic or renal impairment. Its major toxicities and adverse effects are those of the class, especially prolonged hypoglycemia, weight gain, dizziness, gastrointestinal upset, and occasionally cutaneous hypersensitivity reactions; severe overdose may produce neuroglycopenia, confusion, seizures, or coma. Clinically, it was used as an oral glucose-lowering agent in ambulatory management of type 2 diabetes, but its use is largely historical and superseded by newer agents with improved safety profiles.

Name: Mosapramine
Description: Mosapramine (DrugBank DB13676) is a diphenylbutylpiperidine-related antipsychotic characterized structurally by a lipophilic diaryl/butyrophenone-like arrangement linked to a basic nitrogen-containing heterocycle, giving a rigid polycyclic aryl-alkyl amine framework typical of dopamine receptor antagonists; chemically it is classified as a typical antipsychotic of the dibenzazepine/diphenylbutylamine-like neuroleptic space, with a central antipsychotic scaffold built around an aromatic hydrophobic core and protonatable tertiary amine. It is pharmacologically similar to other dopamine D2 receptor-blocking antipsychotics such as haloperidol, pimozide, timiperone, and related Japanese antipsychotics including nemonapride. Its principal known targets are dopamine D2 receptors, with additional activity reported at dopamine D3 and D4 receptors and serotonergic 5-HT2 receptors, contributing to antipsychotic effects. Clinically, mosapramine has been used primarily for schizophrenia, especially positive symptoms such as hallucinations, delusions, agitation, and thought disorder, and in practice as a neuroleptic for acute psychosis and chronic psychotic illness. After oral administration it is absorbed variably, is widely distributed into the CNS because of high lipophilicity, undergoes hepatic metabolism with likely oxidative biotransformation, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine and feces; as with many antipsychotics, bioavailability and half-life can vary with first-pass metabolism. Toxicity is dominated by excessive dopaminergic blockade, with examples including extrapyramidal symptoms, akathisia, dystonia, parkinsonism, hyperprolactinemia, sedation, autonomic effects, and in severe cases neuroleptic malignant syndrome, QT-related arrhythmia risk, and overdose-associated CNS depression, which define its cautious clinical use in patients needing potent D2 antagonism.

Name: Dexchlorpheniramine
Description: Dexchlorpheniramine (DrugBank DB13679) is the dextrorotatory active enantiomer of chlorpheniramine, a first-generation alkylamine antihistamine whose structure consists of a substituted propylamine linking a para-chlorophenyl ring and a 2-pyridyl ring to a tertiary dimethylamino center, giving a lipophilic, basic diarylpropylamine architecture typical of H1 antagonists. Chemically it belongs to the alkylamine antihistamine class, and its core scaffold is a chlorophenyl-pyridyl-propyl-dimethylamine framework; closely related drugs include chlorpheniramine, brompheniramine, pheniramine, triprolidine, and other sedating H1 blockers such as diphenhydramine and doxylamine. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, where it acts functionally as an inverse agonist/antagonist, with additional mild antimuscarinic activity contributing to adverse effects. After oral administration it is generally well absorbed, reaches systemic circulation with onset within hours, distributes widely including into the central nervous system, undergoes hepatic biotransformation largely via cytochrome P450 pathways including CYP2D6-mediated metabolism, and is eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites and some unchanged drug, with an elimination half-life compatible with repeated daily dosing. It is indicated for symptomatic relief of allergic rhinitis, urticaria, conjunctival allergy, pruritus, and common cold symptoms such as rhinorrhea and sneezing. Typical clinical use includes tablets, syrups, and combination cough-and-cold products. Toxicity is dominated by dose-related CNS depression or paradoxical excitation, anticholinergic effects, and in overdose delirium, seizures, arrhythmias, or respiratory compromise, especially in children or with alcohol and sedatives. Common side effects include drowsiness, dizziness, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention.

Name: Tacalcitol
Description: Tacalcitol (DB13689) is a synthetic vitamin D3 analog built on the secosteroid calcitriol scaffold, characterized by the cholesterol-derived 9,10-seco ring system with a conformationally flexible triene backbone and hydroxylated side-chain pattern engineered to retain vitamin D receptor activity while modifying calcium effects; chemically it belongs to the vitamin D analogs, specifically secosteroidal dermatologic agents, and its core scaffold is closely related to calcitriol, calcipotriol, alfacalcidol, maxacalcitol, and paricalcitol, which are considered similar drugs by structure and mechanism. Its principal target is the vitamin D receptor (VDR, NR1I1), with downstream modulation of RXR-partnered transcriptional programs controlling keratinocyte proliferation, differentiation, and immune signaling. Tacalcitol is used mainly topically for psoriasis vulgaris, including plaque psoriasis with erythema, scaling, and epidermal hyperproliferation, and has also been used clinically in some settings for disorders of keratinization. After topical administration, systemic absorption is generally low but can increase with large treated surface area, damaged skin, occlusion, or prolonged use; absorbed drug distributes as a lipophilic secosteroid, undergoes hepatic and extrahepatic hydroxylation/oxidative metabolism similar to other vitamin D analogs, and is eliminated predominantly via biliary-fecal routes with limited renal excretion of metabolites. The major toxicity concern is exaggerated vitamin D activity causing hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, and calcium-phosphate disturbances, with examples including weakness, nausea, constipation, polyuria, polydipsia, and nephrolithiasis risk in excessive exposure. Common adverse effects are usually local and include irritation, pruritus, burning, erythema, and contact dermatitis. In practice, tacalcitol is used as a topical antipsoriatic, often as ointment or lotion, either alone in mild-to-moderate localized disease or alongside corticosteroids and emollients to improve plaque control while limiting systemic toxicity.

Name: Distigmine
Description: Distigmine (DrugBank DB13694) is a long-acting bis-quaternary ammonium carbamate cholinesterase inhibitor built from two pyridinium rings linked by a polymethylene chain, with carbamoyl oxy substituents that confer a symmetric dicationic structure, high polarity, and poor blood-brain barrier penetration; chemically it belongs to the quaternary ammonium anticholinesterases and its core scaffold is a bis-pyridinium dicarbamate, closely related to other peripheral acetylcholinesterase inhibitors such as pyridostigmine, neostigmine, and ambenonium. Its principal target is acetylcholinesterase, with inhibition of butyrylcholinesterase also reported, thereby increasing acetylcholine at parasympathetic neuroeffector junctions and the neuromuscular synapse. Distigmine is used mainly for underactive bladder and urinary retention due to neurogenic bladder or detrusor hypocontractility, and has also been used in myasthenia gravis and postoperative paralytic ileus in some settings. After oral administration it is absorbed incompletely but sufficiently for sustained peripheral activity; distribution is largely extracellular because the permanently charged molecule has limited tissue and CNS penetration; metabolism is limited, and elimination is predominantly renal with prolonged duration and accumulation risk in renal impairment or the elderly. Its major toxicity is excessive cholinergic stimulation, including potentially life-threatening cholinergic crisis with bradycardia, bronchospasm, respiratory failure, sweating, salivation, diarrhea, miosis, fasciculations, and muscle weakness; overdose or reduced renal clearance are classic settings. Common adverse effects include abdominal cramping, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, urinary urgency, increased secretions, and sweating. Clinically, it is used as a maintenance parasympathomimetic when prolonged augmentation of bladder contraction or neuromuscular transmission is desired, with careful dose adjustment and monitoring for cholinergic toxicity.

Name: Penthienate
Description: Penthienate (DrugBank DB13695) is a synthetic antimuscarinic agent structurally characterized as a quaternary ammonium ester containing a permanently charged cationic nitrogen linked through an ester bond to a substituted aromatic or heteroaromatic acid moiety, a design typical of peripherally acting cholinolytics that limits central nervous system penetration. Chemically, it belongs to the anticholinergic quaternary ammonium compounds and can be placed within the amino alcohol ester or atropine-like antispasmodic class, with a scaffold related to other quaternary parasympatholytics such as propantheline, methantheline, glycopyrrolate, clidinium, and isopropamide. Its pharmacologic action is attributed to competitive antagonism at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, principally CHRM1, CHRM2, and CHRM3 in gastrointestinal and secretory tissues, reducing smooth-muscle tone, motility, and exocrine secretion. Historically, it has been used as an adjunct in peptic ulcer disease, gastrointestinal hypermotility, intestinal cramping, and other spastic disorders of the stomach or bowel. As with similar quaternary antimuscarinics, oral absorption is generally incomplete and variable, distribution is largely peripheral with low brain exposure, metabolism is thought to occur partly by ester hydrolysis and hepatic biotransformation, and elimination occurs through renal and possibly biliary routes, with unchanged drug and metabolites recoverable in urine. Adverse effects and toxicity reflect excessive antimuscarinic activity, including dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, tachycardia, urinary retention, reduced sweating, and precipitation of angle-closure glaucoma; overdose may produce severe ileus, hyperthermia, and pronounced urinary retention, although central delirium is less prominent than with tertiary amines. Clinically, penthienate has mainly served as a symptomatic antispasmodic and antisecretory drug rather than a disease-modifying therapy.

Name: Quifenadine
Description: Quifenadine (DrugBank DB13713, also known as hifenadine/fenkarol) is a first-generation antihistamine characterized structurally by a bulky tricyclic hydrophobic aromatic system linked through a tertiary carbinol-bearing side chain to a nitrogen-containing saturated heterocycle, giving an amphiphilic aminoalcohol architecture typical of older H1 antagonists; chemically it is classified as an ethanolamine-like antihistaminic antiallergic agent, and its core scaffold is best described as a quinuclidine-substituted tricyclic aryl carbinol. It is broadly similar to other classical H1 antihistamines such as chlorpheniramine, diphenhydramine, cyproheptadine, and hydroxyzine, although its rigid quinuclidine/tricyclic arrangement distinguishes it. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, with older literature also describing a capacity to reduce tissue histamine effects and possibly influence histamine inactivation pathways, accounting for antipruritic and antiexudative activity. Quifenadine is used for allergic rhinitis, urticaria, pruritic dermatoses, pollinosis, and other histamine-mediated allergic symptoms. After oral administration it is absorbed to a clinically useful extent, distributed to peripheral tissues with reportedly limited central nervous system penetration relative to many first-generation agents, undergoes hepatic biotransformation, and is eliminated through renal and biliary/fecal routes. Adverse effects include dry mouth, dyspepsia, headache, mild sedation, dizziness, and less commonly tachycardia or gastrointestinal discomfort. Toxicity is generally consistent with antihistamine class effects, with overdose potentially causing pronounced anticholinergic symptoms, CNS depression or paradoxical excitation, and cardiovascular effects; caution is warranted in hepatic disease, peptic ulcer disease, and arrhythmia-prone patients. Clinically, it has been used as an oral symptomatic treatment for seasonal and perennial allergy, itching disorders, and urticarial eruptions when a relatively lower-sedating older antihistamine is desired.

Name: Phenothrin
Description: Phenothrin (DrugBank DB13717), also known as sumithrin, is a synthetic type I pyrethroid insecticide built as an ester linking a chrysanthemic acid–like cyclopropanecarboxylate moiety to a substituted benzyl alcohol, giving a lipophilic framework with a cyclopropane ring, gem-dimethyl substitution, and a phenoxy/aryl-containing alcohol fragment that defines its pyrethroid scaffold; chemically it belongs to the pyrethrins/pyrethroids, specifically non-cyano type I pyrethroids, and is structurally similar to other insecticidal pyrethroids such as allethrin, d-phenothrin, permethrin, tetramethrin, and resmethrin. Its principal pharmacologic target is the insect voltage-gated sodium channel, where it prolongs channel opening and causes repetitive neuronal firing; additional interaction with membrane excitability pathways has been described, but no therapeutically relevant human target protein is intended. After topical or environmental exposure, absorption in mammals is usually limited through intact skin but can occur by inhalation or ingestion; distribution is favored into lipid-rich tissues, metabolism is rapid through ester hydrolysis and oxidative biotransformation, largely via hepatic carboxylesterases and cytochrome P450 enzymes, and excretion occurs mainly in urine with some fecal elimination as polar metabolites. Phenothrin is used as an ectoparasiticide and pediculicide, especially for head lice, and as a public-health or household insecticide against fleas, mosquitoes, and other arthropods. Toxicity in humans is generally low relative to insects but may include paresthesia, skin and eye irritation, headache, dizziness, nausea, cough, and rarely tremor or seizures after substantial exposure; it is highly toxic to fish and aquatic invertebrates, and formulations containing piperonyl butoxide or synergists may increase adverse effects. Clinically, topical phenothrin has been used for pediculosis capitis and occasionally other lice infestations, with expected local side effects such as burning, pruritus, erythema, or rash.

Name: Azapetine
Description: Azapetine (DrugBank DB13727) is a tricyclic psychoactive compound built around a rigid dibenzazepine-like scaffold in which two fused benzene rings are bridged through a seven-membered nitrogen-containing central ring, giving a lipophilic, conformationally constrained polycyclic structure typical of older centrally active agents; chemically it is classified as a tricyclic heteroaromatic amine and more specifically as a dibenzazepine-related scaffold, with structural and pharmacologic similarity to drugs such as imipramine, amitriptyline, carbamazepine, and other tricyclic antidepressant or antiserotonergic congeners. Reported pharmacology suggests predominant interaction with serotonergic systems, particularly antagonism at 5-HT2-family receptors, with less well-defined affinity at histaminergic, adrenergic, and muscarinic sites, and no single thoroughly validated modern target panel is consistently established. Its indication has historically centered on disorders involving cerebral vasospasm or migraine-like vascular headache symptoms, with clinical use as an antimigraine or vasoactive neuropsychiatric agent rather than a contemporary first-line therapy. As a highly lipophilic tricyclic drug, it would be expected to undergo good oral absorption, extensive tissue distribution including CNS penetration, substantial plasma protein binding, hepatic oxidative metabolism, and renal excretion of metabolites, with possible biliary contribution. Toxicity is expected to resemble other tricyclic agents, including CNS depression, confusion, anticholinergic burden, orthostatic hypotension, and overdose-related cardiac conduction abnormalities or arrhythmias. Adverse effects likely include sedation, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, dizziness, tachycardia, and weight gain, limiting routine modern use and confining it largely to older or region-specific clinical contexts.

Name: Camostat
Description: Camostat (DB13729) is a synthetic low-molecular-weight serine protease inhibitor built around an aromatic ester/guanidino motif, structurally characterized by a p-guanidinobenzoyl group linked through an ester to a substituted phenylacetate-containing amide, giving a cationic amidine-like headgroup and hydrolysis-labile ester functionality that are typical of trypsin-like protease inhibitors; chemically it is classified as a guanidinobenzoate ester and broadly as a synthetic protease inhibitor, with a scaffold closely related to other guanidino aromatic serine protease inhibitors such as nafamostat and, more distantly, gabexate. Its principal targets include trypsin, plasma kallikrein, plasmin, thrombin to a lesser extent, and transmembrane serine protease 2 (TMPRSS2), supporting inhibition of pancreatic protease activity and blockade of protease-dependent viral entry. After oral administration, camostat is absorbed but undergoes rapid first-pass ester hydrolysis to the active metabolite FOY-251 and subsequent conversion to less active metabolites; systemic parent-drug exposure is low, protein binding of metabolites is moderate, distribution is mainly extracellular, and elimination occurs predominantly as urinary metabolites with a short effective half-life. Clinically it has been used mainly for chronic pancreatitis and postoperative reflux esophagitis, with investigational use in COVID-19 and other TMPRSS2-dependent viral infections. Adverse effects are usually gastrointestinal or hypersensitivity-related, including nausea, abdominal discomfort, rash, pruritus, and edema, while toxicity concerns include hepatic enzyme elevation, eosinophilia, thrombocytopenia, anaphylactoid reactions, and rare severe hepatic or renal dysfunction. Overall, its clinical use centers on oral antiprotease therapy in pancreatitis-associated symptoms and selected upper gastrointestinal inflammatory conditions.

Name: Nifurtoinol
Description: Nifurtoinol (DrugBank DB13730) is a synthetic nitrofuran antibacterial whose structure is centered on a 5-nitrofuran heteroaromatic ring bearing an exocyclic methylene linkage to a hydantoin-type imidazolidinedione moiety, placing it in the nitrofuran urinary antiseptic class and giving it a nitrofuran–methylene–hydantoin scaffold related to other nitrofuran derivatives. Similar drugs include nitrofurantoin, furazidin, furaltadone, and nifuroxazide, all of which share the bioactivatable nitrofuran pharmacophore. Its antibacterial action is generally attributed not to a single high-affinity human target but to bacterial nitroreductase-mediated reduction of the nitro group, generating reactive intermediates that damage multiple macromolecular targets including DNA, ribosomal proteins, and metabolic enzymes; specific validated host protein targets are not established. Pharmacokinetically, nifurtoinol is used orally, is absorbed to a clinically useful extent, achieves highest effective concentrations in urine rather than systemic tissues, undergoes at least partial hepatic or tissue biotransformation with reductive and conjugative handling typical of nitrofurans, and is eliminated predominantly via the kidneys as parent drug and metabolites, supporting use in lower urinary tract infections. It has been indicated mainly for uncomplicated urinary tract infection and bacteriuria, especially cystitis caused by susceptible organisms such as Escherichia coli. Adverse effects resemble those of other nitrofurans and include nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, anorexia, headache, dizziness, and rash, while toxicity may include hypersensitivity reactions, peripheral neuropathy, hemolysis in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, and rare hepatic or pulmonary injury; thus its clinical usage has historically been as an oral urinary antibacterial for short-course treatment or prophylaxis of recurrent lower UTIs when susceptibility and renal function are appropriate.

Name: Methylpentynol
Description: Methylpentynol (DrugBank DB13733) is a small acetylenic tertiary carbinol characterized structurally by a five-carbon alkynyl alcohol framework bearing an internal carbon-carbon triple bond and a dimethyl-substituted hydroxylated center, placing it in the sedative-hypnotic class of simple aliphatic alcohol derivatives and more specifically among acetylenic carbinols; its core scaffold is thus a compact alkynol tertiary alcohol motif related to older nonbarbiturate sedatives. Similar drugs include other historical sedative-hypnotic alcohols and acetylenic congeners such as ethchlorvynol and meprobamate-era comparators, although it is chemically simpler than barbiturates. Pharmacokinetically, methylpentynol is orally absorbed, sufficiently lipophilic to cross the blood-brain barrier and distribute into the central nervous system, undergoes hepatic biotransformation likely through oxidative and conjugative pathways to more polar metabolites, and is eliminated mainly in urine, with sedative effects that are relatively short acting but potentiated by ethanol and other CNS depressants. Its pharmacology was historically attributed to nonspecific CNS depressant activity, probably involving membrane-level actions and functional enhancement of inhibitory neurotransmission; no well-validated selective target protein is established, though GABAergic systems are commonly implicated for this class. It was used for anxiety, nervous tension, and insomnia, for example short-term relief of agitation or sleep initiation difficulty. Adverse effects include drowsiness, dizziness, ataxia, impaired psychomotor performance, confusion, nausea, and hangover-like sedation. Toxicity includes dose-related respiratory depression, hypotension, profound CNS depression, coma, dependence liability, and dangerous overdose interactions with alcohol or sedatives, which limited and largely displaced its clinical use as an older anxiolytic-sedative.

Name: Trolamine
Description: Trolamine (triethanolamine; DrugBank DB13747) is a small alkanolamine composed of a tertiary amine nitrogen substituted with three 2-hydroxyethyl groups, giving a highly polar, hygroscopic, weakly basic structure capable of extensive hydrogen bonding and salt formation with fatty acids; chemically it belongs to the ethanolamine/alkanolamine class and is built on a tri(hydroxyethyl)amine scaffold. Closely related compounds include monoethanolamine and diethanolamine, while clinically similar topical counterirritant or burn-care products may contain trolamine salicylate or be compared with emollient and wound-healing agents such as glycerol- or petrolatum-based preparations. Trolamine is used primarily as a topical pharmaceutical excipient and skin protectant rather than a classic systemic drug target modulator; no well-established specific human target proteins are generally assigned, and its effects are largely physicochemical, including emulsification, pH buffering, hydration of damaged skin, and facilitation of topical formulation performance. Systemic pharmacokinetic data are limited because therapeutic use is mainly cutaneous; dermal absorption is expected to be low to modest and increased across damaged skin, distribution would favor aqueous compartments, metabolism if absorbed may involve oxidative biotransformation pathways analogous to other ethanolamines, and excretion is presumed mainly renal as parent compound and polar metabolites. Indications and clinical use include minor burns, sunburn, superficial wounds, radiation dermatitis, and symptomatic relief of irritated skin. Adverse effects are usually local, such as stinging, erythema, rash, contact dermatitis, and pruritus. Toxicity is generally low with topical use but excessive exposure or ingestion can cause mucosal and gastrointestinal irritation, and repeated occupational exposure has been associated with irritant effects to skin and eyes.

Name: Obidoxime
Description: Obidoxime (DrugBank DB13750) is a bis-pyridinium aldoxime reactivator characterized structurally by two quaternary pyridinium rings, each bearing an aldoxime functionality, linked through a short oxybis(methylene) bridge, giving a permanently cationic, highly polar dioxime architecture; chemically it belongs to the oxime antidotes and more specifically the bisquaternary pyridinium acetylcholinesterase reactivators, with a pyridinium-aldoxime scaffold closely related to pralidoxime, trimedoxime, methoxime, and HI-6. Its principal pharmacologic target is organophosphate-inhibited acetylcholinesterase, from which it helps remove the phosphoryl group before aging occurs; butyrylcholinesterase is also sometimes discussed as a related target or bioscavenger system. Obidoxime is indicated for treatment of organophosphate poisoning, including pesticide intoxication and nerve agent exposure, typically in patients with cholinergic crisis manifested by bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, miosis, fasciculations, and paralysis, and it is used clinically as an adjunct to atropine, oxygen/ventilatory support, and decontamination. Because of its quaternary charge, absorption is poor orally, so it is generally administered parenterally; distribution is largely extracellular with limited blood-brain barrier penetration, metabolism is limited, and elimination is predominantly renal, with a relatively short plasma half-life requiring repeated dosing or infusion in severe poisoning. Toxicity is usually dose related and includes hypertension, tachycardia, nausea, dizziness, headache, blurred vision, dry mouth, and transient neuromuscular effects; rapid administration may worsen these reactions, and excessive oxime exposure can itself inhibit cholinesterases or aggravate autonomic instability.

Name: Tetramethrin
Description: Tetramethrin (DrugBank DB13752) is a first-generation synthetic pyrethroid insecticide composed of a chrysanthemate-like cyclopropane carboxylate ester linked to a tetrahydrophthalimide alcohol moiety, giving a lipophilic, stereochemically complex ester with cis/trans and chiral isomerism that is important for insecticidal potency. Chemically it belongs to the pyrethroids, more specifically the non-cyano pyrethroid subgroup, and its core scaffold is the pyrethrin-like cyclopropane ester framework joined to a phthalimide-derived ring system. Similar drugs include other household pyrethroids such as allethrin, d-phenothrin, permethrin, resmethrin, and prallethrin, which share related ester scaffolds and sodium-channel activity. Its pharmacokinetics in mammals are characterized by limited dermal absorption, variable but potentially significant inhalational and oral absorption, wide distribution into lipid-rich tissues due to high lipophilicity, rapid metabolic detoxification by carboxylesterases and hepatic CYP-mediated oxidation followed by conjugation, and predominant urinary excretion of polar metabolites with some fecal elimination. The principal molecular target is the voltage-gated sodium channel in insect nerve membranes; mammalian sodium channels are also affected at sufficiently high exposure, though with lower sensitivity. Tetramethrin is indicated and clinically used not as a therapeutic drug but as an insecticide for control of mosquitoes, ճանflies, cockroaches, ants, fleas, and other household or public-health pests in aerosols, coils, mats, and sprays. Toxicity is mainly neurotoxic and irritant, with examples including paresthesia, salivation, tremor, hyperexcitability, nausea, vomiting, bronchospasm, and rarely seizures after substantial exposure; side effects in exposed humans commonly include skin and eye irritation, headache, dizziness, cough, and throat irritation.

Name: Dexrabeprazole
Description: Dexrabeprazole (DB13762) is the dextrorotatory enantiomer of rabeprazole and is a substituted benzimidazole proton-pump inhibitor characterized structurally by a benzimidazole ring linked through a sulfoxide chiral center to a substituted pyridine, a classic acid-labile PPI architecture that undergoes acid-catalyzed activation in the parietal cell canaliculus; chemically it belongs to the benzimidazole sulfoxides, with a rabeprazole-like benzimidazole–sulfinyl–pyridine scaffold shared by related agents such as rabeprazole, omeprazole, esomeprazole, lansoprazole, dexlansoprazole, and pantoprazole. Its principal pharmacologic target is the gastric H+/K+-ATPase proton pump, encoded mainly by ATP4A and ATP4B, which it inhibits irreversibly after conversion to reactive sulfenamide intermediates that covalently modify cysteine residues on the luminal pump surface. Pharmacokinetically, dexrabeprazole is absorbed in the small intestine after enteric protection, shows moderate plasma protein binding and systemic distribution, undergoes substantial hepatic metabolism via nonenzymatic reduction and CYP-mediated biotransformation, especially involving CYP3A4 and CYP2C19, and is eliminated predominantly as inactive metabolites in urine with a smaller fecal component. It is indicated for acid-related disorders including gastroesophageal reflux disease, erosive esophagitis, peptic ulcer disease, dyspepsia, and hypersecretory states, and may be used in Helicobacter pylori eradication regimens with antibiotics. Adverse effects are broadly consistent with the PPI class and include headache, diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea, constipation, and rash; longer-term or class-related toxicities include hypergastrinemia, vitamin B12 or magnesium deficiency, fracture risk, interstitial nephritis, enteric infection including Clostridioides difficile, and rare hypersensitivity or hepatic injury. Clinically, it is used as an oral antisecretory agent for symptom relief, mucosal healing, ulcer prevention in selected patients, and maintenance therapy in recurrent reflux disease.

Name: Monoxerutin
Description: Monoxerutin (DB13764) is a semisynthetic flavonoid vasoprotective agent in the hydroxyethylrutoside/oxerutin family, structurally characterized as a mono-hydroxyethylated derivative of rutin built on a quercetin flavonol core bearing the typical fused benzopyran-4-one scaffold with multiple phenolic hydroxyls and a glycosidic rutinose substituent, the hydroxyethyl ether modification increasing polarity and altering vascular pharmacology; chemically it belongs to flavonoid glycosides and more specifically rutosides, with a quercetin-rutinoside scaffold. Closely related drugs include oxerutin mixtures, troxerutin, rutin, and other venotonic flavonoids such as diosmin and hesperidin. Its pharmacology is attributed less to a single high-affinity receptor than to endothelial and microvascular actions, with reported effects on capillary permeability, leukocyte-endothelial adhesion, oxidative stress, and inflammatory signaling; no definitive canonical target protein is established, although interactions with endothelial adhesion pathways, reactive oxygen species-related systems, and prostaglandin-mediated vascular responses have been proposed. Oral absorption is generally limited to moderate for flavonoid glycosides, with distribution largely in the vascular/interstitial compartment, partial intestinal and hepatic metabolism by deglycosylation and conjugation to glucuronide/sulfate metabolites, and elimination predominantly in urine with some biliary/fecal excretion. Clinically it has been used for chronic venous insufficiency, varicose-vein symptoms, hemorrhoidal disease, capillary fragility, edema, leg heaviness, cramps, and pain. It is usually well tolerated; adverse effects are mainly mild gastrointestinal upset, nausea, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, flushing, and rash, while toxicity is generally low with no characteristic organ-specific severe toxicity at therapeutic doses, though hypersensitivity reactions and intolerance can occur.

Name: Acemetacin
Description: Acemetacin (DrugBank DB13783) is an indole-acetic acid nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug that is structurally the glycolic acid ester prodrug of indomethacin, featuring a chlorobenzoyl-substituted methoxyindole core linked through an acetic acid side chain and esterified hydroxymethyl moiety; chemically it belongs to the arylacetic acid/indole NSAID class, with an indole-3-acetic acid scaffold closely related to indomethacin and more distantly to other acidic NSAIDs such as sulindac, etodolac, diclofenac, and ketorolac. Its principal pharmacological targets are cyclooxygenase enzymes PTGS1 (COX-1) and PTGS2 (COX-2), inhibited mainly after biotransformation to indomethacin, thereby reducing prostaglandin synthesis. After oral administration, acemetacin is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, undergoes first-pass and systemic hydrolysis to indomethacin, is highly plasma protein bound, distributes into inflamed tissues and synovial fluid, is further metabolized hepatically by deacylation, demethylation, and conjugation, and is excreted in both urine and bile/feces as parent drug, indomethacin, and metabolites. It is indicated for inflammatory and painful rheumatic disorders including rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, periართropathies, and acute musculoskeletal pain. Clinical use has emphasized anti-inflammatory and analgesic efficacy with somewhat improved gastrointestinal tolerability versus indomethacin in some studies, including use in chronic arthropathies and postoperative or flare-related pain. Toxicity is typical of NSAIDs: gastrointestinal irritation, ulceration, bleeding, and perforation; renal hypoperfusion or acute kidney injury; hepatotoxicity; fluid retention; hypersensitivity and bronchospasm; and increased cardiovascular thrombotic risk. Common adverse effects include dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, dizziness, headache, rash, and edema.

Name: Dropropizine
Description: Dropropizine (DrugBank DB13785) is a small-molecule, non-opioid antitussive whose structure is characterized by an aromatic phenyl ring linked through a short aliphatic chain to a tertiary amino alcohol, specifically a propanolamine-type framework bearing both hydroxyl and amine functionality; chemically it is classified as a phenyl-substituted amino alcohol and can be viewed as part of the broader arylaliphatic cough-suppressant class, with a simple phenylpropanolamine-like scaffold. It is structurally and therapeutically related to levodropropizine, its better-known stereoisomer, and more distantly to other centrally or peripherally acting antitussives such as cloperastine and dextromethorphan, although its pharmacology is distinct from opioid congeners such as codeine. Dropropizine is used primarily for symptomatic treatment of nonproductive or irritating cough in conditions such as upper respiratory tract infection, bronchitis, tracheitis, and other inflammatory airway disorders. Its target profile is not well defined at the protein level; it is generally described as a cough suppressant with predominantly peripheral antitussive activity, possibly modulating sensory afferent pathways in the respiratory tract rather than acting through a single validated receptor target. After oral administration it is absorbed reasonably well, distributed systemically with limited evidence for extensive tissue sequestration, undergoes partial hepatic biotransformation, and is eliminated mainly in urine as parent drug and metabolites, with a relatively short duration requiring repeated dosing. Adverse effects are usually mild and include drowsiness, dizziness, nausea, epigastric discomfort, and dry mouth; toxicity is generally low but overdose may accentuate CNS depression, gastrointestinal symptoms, or hypotension, so clinical use is typically limited to short-term cough control when suppression is judged appropriate.

Name: Tilidine
Description: Tilidine (DrugBank DB13787) is a synthetic opioid analgesic structurally characterized as a lipophilic piperidine-derived tertiary amine bearing a cyclohexenyl moiety and an esterified carboxylate side chain, placing it within the opioid/centrally acting analgesic chemical category and more specifically among piperidine-related opioid prodrugs with a phenyl-substituted cyclohexene-piperidine scaffold; it is structurally and pharmacologically related to other weak to moderate opioid analgesics such as tramadol, codeine, dihydrocodeine, and dextropropoxyphene, although tilidine is distinctive in being marketed commonly in fixed combination with naloxone to reduce abuse liability. Tilidine is well absorbed orally, undergoes substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism, and acts largely as a prodrug converted primarily by CYP3A4 and CYP2C19 to the active metabolite nortilidine and further to bisnortilidine; the active metabolite distributes systemically, penetrates the central nervous system, and is eliminated mainly after hepatic biotransformation via renal excretion of metabolites. Its principal target is the mu-opioid receptor, with analgesic effects mediated predominantly by nortilidine and likely lesser activity at other opioid receptors. It is indicated for moderate to severe acute or chronic pain, including postoperative pain, musculoskeletal pain, cancer-related pain, and neuropathic or mixed pain states in some settings. Adverse effects and toxicity are typical of opioids and include nausea, vomiting, dizziness, sedation, constipation, sweating, and impaired psychomotor function, while overdose may cause respiratory depression, miosis, hypotension, coma, dependence, abuse, and withdrawal; clinically it is used mainly as oral drops, tablets, or prolonged-release preparations, often with naloxone, when nonopioid analgesics are inadequate.

Name: Ethadione
Description: Ethadione (DrugBank DB13799) is an older anticonvulsant of the oxazolidinedione class characterized structurally by a five-membered oxazolidine-2,4-dione ring bearing an ethyl substituent, giving a relatively small, neutral, lipophilic cyclic imide framework; thus its chemical category is a dione anticonvulsant and its core chemical scaffold is the substituted oxazolidinedione ring. It is closely related to trimethadione and paramethadione, which share the same heterocyclic scaffold and historical use in absence epilepsy. Pharmacologically, ethadione is believed to act mainly through suppression of thalamic low-threshold T-type calcium currents, likely involving Cav3-family voltage-gated calcium channels rather than a single uniquely defined protein target, thereby reducing the corticothalamic oscillations underlying petit mal seizures. It was used primarily for absence seizures, particularly when patients had refractory petit mal epilepsy or intolerance to alternatives. After oral administration, it is expected to be well absorbed, distributed into the central nervous system because of modest lipophilicity, metabolized hepatically with formation of active or persistent metabolites analogous to the class, and eliminated predominantly in urine as metabolites, with a relatively prolonged effect typical of oxazolidinediones. Toxicity is clinically significant and includes dose-related CNS depression, ataxia, photophobia, gastrointestinal upset, and more serious reactions such as blood dyscrasias, nephrotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, and severe dermatologic hypersensitivity. Adverse effects may include drowsiness, dizziness, headache, visual disturbances, nausea, rash, and behavioral changes. Owing to these safety limitations and the availability of better-tolerated antiepileptic drugs, its clinical use became restricted and is now largely historical.

Name: Xipamide
Description: Xipamide (DrugBank DB13803) is a sulfonamide-based, non-thiazide diuretic structurally characterized by a substituted benzamide/aniline framework bearing both sulfamoyl and carboxamide functionalities with lipophilic halogenated aromatic substitution, placing it within the thiazide-like saluretic class despite lacking the classical benzothiadiazine ring; its core scaffold is best described as a sulfonamide-substituted halogenated aromatic carboxamide that confers pharmacologic similarity to thiazide and thiazide-like agents. Similar drugs include chlorthalidone, indapamide, metolazone, hydrochlorothiazide, and clopamide, which share distal tubular natriuretic activity. Xipamide primarily targets the renal sodium-chloride cotransporter SLC12A3 in the distal convoluted tubule, thereby increasing urinary sodium, chloride, and water excretion, with secondary kaliuresis. After oral administration it is well absorbed, reaches systemic circulation efficiently, distributes to extracellular fluid and renal tissue, undergoes limited to moderate hepatic biotransformation, and is eliminated mainly via renal excretion as parent drug and metabolites, with a duration of action sufficient for once-daily antihypertensive or antiedematous use. Toxicity is broadly consistent with saluretic diuretics and includes dose-related dehydration, hypovolemia, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, hyperuricemia precipitating gout, and occasional renal function worsening; sulfonamide hypersensitivity reactions are possible. Adverse effects include dizziness, orthostatic symptoms, muscle cramps, weakness, polyuria, thirst, rash, and gastrointestinal upset. Clinically, xipamide is used for hypertension and edema, including fluid retention associated with cardiac failure, hepatic disease, or renal disorders, particularly when a sustained oral diuretic effect is desired.

Name: Mebhydrolin
Description: Mebhydrolin (DrugBank DB13808), also known as mebhydrolin napadisylate in many formulations, is a first-generation H1-antihistamine characterized by a bulky tricyclic-like benzhydryl/heteropolycyclic architecture in which aryl rings are linked to a nitrogen-containing bicyclic amidine-type core, giving a lipophilic cationic antihistamine structure optimized for reversible histamine H1 receptor antagonism. Chemically it belongs to the ethanolamine-/amidine-related classical antihistamine class and is commonly described as having a mebhydrolin or diazabicyclic benzhydryl scaffold, broadly related to other sedating H1 blockers such as diphenhydramine, cyproheptadine, promethazine, chloropyramine, and clemastine, although it is often considered somewhat less centrally sedating than several comparators. Its principal target is the histamine H1 receptor, with possible ancillary anticholinergic activity typical of older antihistamines. After oral administration it is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, distributed systemically with at least moderate tissue penetration, likely undergoes hepatic biotransformation, and is eliminated through renal and possibly biliary routes; as with many first-generation antihistamines, detailed modern ADME parameters are limited. It is indicated for allergic disorders including allergic rhinitis, urticaria, pruritic dermatoses, conjunctival allergy, drug or food hypersensitivity symptoms, and insect-bite reactions. Clinical use has largely been symptomatic relief of itching, sneezing, rhinorrhea, and wheal-and-flare reactions. Adverse effects and toxicity are consistent with first-generation antihistamines: drowsiness, dizziness, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, tachycardia, and impaired psychomotor performance, while overdose may produce marked CNS depression or paradoxical excitation, anticholinergic syndrome, and rarely cardiovascular complications.

Name: Indanazoline
Description: Indanazoline (DrugBank DB13827) is an imidazoline-containing sympathomimetic whose structure is characterized by a fused indane aromatic hydrocarbon linked to a basic imidazoline ring, giving a compact bicyclic aryl-imidazoline motif that is typical of topical vasoconstrictors; chemically it is best classified as an imidazoline derivative and adrenergic agonist, with an indane/arylimidazoline scaffold closely related to other nasal and ophthalmic decongestants such as naphazoline, xylometazoline, tetrahydrozoline, and oxymetazoline. Its principal pharmacology is believed to involve agonism at alpha-adrenergic receptors, especially alpha-1 and possibly alpha-2 subtypes, on vascular smooth muscle, producing local vasoconstriction and reduced mucosal hyperemia; these adrenergic receptors are therefore the main known target proteins. Indanazoline has been used clinically as a topical decongestant, particularly for symptomatic relief of nasal congestion and mucosal edema in rhinitis, coryza, sinus irritation, and related upper-airway inflammatory states. As with similar agents, systemic pharmacokinetic data are limited, but after local administration absorption is usually low yet can increase across inflamed mucosa, distribution systemically is expected to be modest, metabolism likely occurs hepatically through pathways shared by small lipophilic amines, and excretion is presumed predominantly renal as parent drug and metabolites. Toxicity is mainly excessive adrenergic and CNS effects after overuse or accidental ingestion, including hypertension, reflex bradycardia, agitation, sedation, and in children potentially serious CNS depression. Common adverse effects include transient local burning, dryness, irritation, sneezing, headache, and rebound congestion with prolonged use; accordingly, clinical use is generally short-term, topical, and symptom-directed rather than chronic.

Name: Doxefazepam
Description: Doxefazepam (DB13837) is a triazolobenzodiazepine-related central nervous system depressant whose structure is characterized by a fused benzene-diazepine core bearing an additional triazole-like annulated heterocycle and lipophilic aryl substitution, a motif that supports high affinity modulation of inhibitory neurotransmission; chemically it belongs to the benzodiazepine/anxiolytic-sedative class, with a benzodiazepine scaffold serving as its principal pharmacophore. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other benzodiazepine-site ligands such as diazepam, alprazolam, triazolam, lorazepam, and clonazepam, which share the same broad GABAA receptor positive allosteric modulator profile. The best-supported targets for a compound of this type are the GABAA receptor complex, particularly receptors containing alpha, beta, and gamma subunits associated with the benzodiazepine binding site, including proteins such as GABRA1, GABRA2, GABRA3, GABRB2, and GABRG2. Expected pharmacokinetics are oral absorption with good bioavailability, broad distribution into the CNS owing to lipophilicity, hepatic oxidative biotransformation and/or conjugation to less active metabolites, and primarily renal excretion of metabolites, with possible accumulation in hepatic impairment or with repeated dosing. Its likely indications and clinical uses are anxiety disorders, acute agitation, insomnia, and adjunctive management of muscle tension or alcohol-withdrawal symptoms. Adverse effects are expected to include sedation, dizziness, ataxia, psychomotor impairment, anterograde amnesia, confusion, and fatigue, while toxicity may present as excessive CNS depression, respiratory compromise when combined with opioids or alcohol, dependence, withdrawal seizures, and overdose-related coma, generally with lower lethality in isolation than barbiturates.

Name: Clopenthixol
Description: Clopenthixol (DB13841) is a first-generation antipsychotic of the thioxanthene class whose structure consists of a tricyclic thioxanthene core, closely related to phenothiazines but with a carbon-carbon double bond replacing the ring nitrogen bridge, bearing a 2-chloro substituent and a three-carbon side chain terminating in a dimethylamino alcohol-derived center; the clinically important Z-isomer is generally more potent than the E-isomer. Its chemical scaffold is therefore the chlorinated thioxanthene tricyclic antipsychotic framework, and it is structurally similar to other thioxanthenes and typical antipsychotics such as flupenthixol, chlorprothixene, thiothixene, and more distantly chlorpromazine. Pharmacologically, clopenthixol acts mainly through antagonism of dopamine D1 and especially D2 receptors, with additional affinity for serotonin 5-HT2 receptors, alpha1-adrenergic receptors, histamine H1 receptors, and muscarinic cholinergic receptors, accounting for both antipsychotic efficacy and adverse effects. It is used for schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders, including agitation, hallucinations, delusions, and aggressive or behaviorally disturbed states; depot formulations have been used for maintenance treatment in chronic psychosis, while shorter-acting ester forms have been used for acute agitation. After oral or intramuscular administration it is variably but adequately absorbed, extensively distributed, highly protein bound, hepatically metabolized by oxidative and conjugative pathways, and excreted mainly as metabolites in urine and feces, with ester formulations providing prolonged release. Toxicity resembles other typical antipsychotics, including dose-related extrapyramidal syndromes, tardive dyskinesia, sedation, orthostatic hypotension, anticholinergic effects, hyperprolactinemia, lowered seizure threshold, QT-related arrhythmic risk, overdose-associated CNS depression, and the rare but serious neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

Name: Mefenorex
Description: Mefenorex (DrugBank DB13852) is a sympathomimetic anorectic of the substituted phenethylamine/amphetamine class whose structure consists of a lipophilic aromatic ring linked through a short ethyl chain to a secondary aliphatic amine, giving it the classic phenethylamine scaffold associated with central stimulant activity; chemically it is best categorized as an amphetamine-like appetite suppressant, with a simple aryl-ethyl-amine core related to other anorectics and stimulants such as amphetamine, phentermine, clobenzorex, fenproporex, amfepramone, and norpseudoephedrine. Its pharmacology is thought to depend largely on indirect catecholaminergic activity, with increased synaptic norepinephrine and dopamine through interaction with monoamine transport systems, especially the norepinephrine transporter and dopamine transporter, and possibly weaker effects at serotonin transport pathways. After oral administration it is expected to be reasonably well absorbed, distributed into the CNS because of its lipophilicity, metabolized hepatically by oxidative and dealkylative pathways to active or partially active stimulant metabolites, and eliminated mainly in urine, with urinary pH likely influencing clearance as with related amines. Clinically it has been used as an adjunct in obesity management and appetite suppression in overweight patients when dietary measures alone are inadequate. Adverse effects resemble those of other amphetamine-like agents, including insomnia, nervousness, agitation, tremor, dry mouth, tachycardia, palpitations, hypertension, headache, and reduced appetite, while toxicities include dependence, abuse liability, psychosis, arrhythmia, and other serious cardiovascular or neuropsychiatric events, particularly in overdose or prolonged use.

Name: Imidazole salicylate
Description: Imidazole salicylate (DrugBank DB13860) is best described as a salicylate salt or molecular complex in which salicylic acid, an o-hydroxybenzoic acid pharmacophore bearing adjacent phenolic hydroxyl and carboxyl groups on a benzene ring, is associated with imidazole, a five-membered aromatic diazole heterocycle; thus its chemical category lies at the interface of salicylates and imidazole-containing pharmaceutical salts, with a scaffold defined by a salicylate aromatic acid core paired through acid-base interaction with an imidazole ring. It is chemically and pharmacologically related to other salicylate drugs such as salicylic acid, aspirin, sodium salicylate, choline salicylate, and to some extent diflunisal, which share the salicylate anti-inflammatory scaffold. Its principal target biology is expected to mirror salicylates, with inhibition of cyclooxygenase enzymes PTGS1 and PTGS2 and broader suppression of prostaglandin-mediated inflammatory signaling, while the imidazole moiety mainly modifies physicochemical properties rather than adding a distinct primary target. Pharmacokinetically, topical or mucosal use would favor local action with limited systemic absorption, whereas absorbed salicylate distributes widely, is moderately protein bound, undergoes hepatic conjugation to salicyluric acid and glucuronides, and is renally excreted with pH-dependent clearance. Toxicities are those of salicylates, including gastrointestinal irritation, nausea, vomiting, tinnitus, dizziness, acid-base disturbance, and in overdose hyperventilation and salicylism; hypersensitivity reactions and local irritation are also plausible. Clinically, it has been used as an anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and keratolytic agent for localized pain, inflammatory dermatoses, and minor musculoskeletal or mucosal symptoms, with adverse effects including burning, erythema, dyspepsia, and rare systemic salicylate toxicity when extensively applied.

Name: Fluticasone
Description: Fluticasone (DrugBank DB13867) is a highly lipophilic synthetic trifluorinated corticosteroid characterized by the pregnane steroid nucleus with the typical four fused rings of glucocorticoids, bearing a 6α-fluoro substituent, a 9α-fluoro-like corticosteroid pattern, a 16α-methyl group, 17α-hydroxyl functionality, and a thioester/ester side-chain modification that increases topical anti-inflammatory potency and first-pass inactivation; it belongs to the corticosteroid, specifically glucocorticoid, chemical category and is built on the hydrocortisone/prednisolone-like steroid scaffold. Closely related drugs include fluticasone propionate, fluticasone furoate, budesonide, beclomethasone dipropionate, mometasone furoate, and triamcinolone acetonide, which share inhaled or intranasal glucocorticoid use. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor encoded by NR3C1, with downstream suppression of NF-κB- and AP-1-mediated inflammatory gene expression, reduced cytokine production, and decreased eosinophil and mast-cell activity. Pharmacokinetically, fluticasone is designed for local airway or nasal delivery, has low oral bioavailability because of poor gastrointestinal absorption and extensive CYP3A4-mediated first-pass metabolism, high tissue and protein binding, hepatic conversion to inactive metabolites, and predominant fecal excretion with minimal renal elimination. It is indicated for persistent asthma, allergic rhinitis, nasal polyposis, and sometimes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in combination products. Adverse effects commonly include dysphonia, oropharyngeal candidiasis, throat irritation, cough, epistaxis, nasal dryness, and headache, while toxicity with excessive or prolonged exposure may produce adrenal suppression, hypercortisolism, reduced growth velocity in children, cataracts, glaucoma, skin thinning, and increased infection risk, especially when combined with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ritonavir. Clinically, it is widely used as an inhaled maintenance anti-inflammatory therapy and as an intranasal steroid for seasonal or perennial allergy symptom control.

Name: Adefovir
Description: Adefovir (DrugBank DB13868) is an acyclic nucleoside phosphonate antiviral built around an adenine purine base linked through a methoxyethyl side chain to a phosphonic acid, giving a negatively charged nucleotide-mimetic structure that bypasses the need for initial phosphorylation; chemically it belongs to the acyclic nucleoside phosphonate/adenosine monophosphate analog class, with a scaffold closely related to the 9-(2-phosphonylmethoxyethyl)adenine family. Similar drugs include tenofovir, cidofovir, and older anti-HBV nucleos(t)ide analogs such as lamivudine and entecavir, although tenofovir is the closest structural analog. Clinically, adefovir has chiefly been used as the oral prodrug adefovir dipivoxil for chronic hepatitis B, including lamivudine-resistant HBV infection, where intracellular conversion to adefovir diphosphate inhibits hepatitis B virus reverse transcriptase/DNA polymerase and causes viral DNA chain termination; it also shows activity against HIV reverse transcriptase, though it is not used clinically for HIV because of toxicity limits. Oral bioavailability of the parent drug is poor, hence prodrug use; after absorption, the dipivoxil esters are hydrolyzed, distribution is systemic with limited protein binding, metabolism is minimal beyond activation to phosphorylated metabolites, and elimination is predominantly renal by glomerular filtration and tubular secretion. The major toxicity is dose-related nephrotoxicity, including proximal tubular injury, rising creatinine, Fanconi-like syndrome, and hypophosphatemia; other adverse effects include asthenia, headache, abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, and transaminase elevations, with rare lactic acidosis or hepatomegaly reported for nucleotide analogs. In practice, its target proteins are viral HBV polymerase/reverse transcriptase and, experimentally, HIV-1 reverse transcriptase, and its clinical use has been largely superseded by safer first-line HBV agents such as tenofovir and entecavir.

Name: Fenofibric acid
Description: Fenofibric acid (DB13873) is the active carboxylic acid metabolite of fenofibrate and a fibric acid derivative built on an aryloxy-isobutyric acid scaffold, featuring a chlorobenzoyl-substituted phenoxy group linked to a 2-methylpropanoic acid moiety; chemically it belongs to the fibrates, a class of amphipathic aromatic carboxylic acids used as lipid-modifying agents. Its core scaffold and pharmacology are closely related to other PPAR-alpha agonists such as fenofibrate, bezafibrate, gemfibrozil, ciprofibrate, and clofibrate. Fenofibric acid is well absorbed orally, particularly in choline fenofibrate formulations that reduce food dependence, is highly albumin bound, distributes largely within the vascular compartment, undergoes minimal further oxidative biotransformation relative to its prodrug, and is eliminated predominantly in urine as fenofibric acid and glucuronide conjugates, with a terminal half-life compatible with once-daily dosing; renal impairment increases exposure. Its principal target is peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha, with downstream effects on lipoprotein lipase, apolipoprotein C-III suppression, fatty acid oxidation, and modulation of apolipoproteins A-I and A-II, leading to triglyceride lowering and HDL increase. It is indicated for primary hypercholesterolemia, mixed dyslipidemia, and severe hypertriglyceridemia, including patients at risk of pancreatitis from very high triglycerides, and is used clinically alone or with selected statins in atherogenic dyslipidemia. Adverse effects include dyspepsia, abdominal pain, nausea, headache, back pain, elevated transaminases, and increased creatinine, while important toxicities include myopathy or rhabdomyolysis, cholelithiasis, hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, and potentiation of anticoagulant effects, with greater risk in elderly patients and those with renal dysfunction.

Name: Enasidenib
Description: Enasidenib (DB13874) is an orally active, small-molecule antineoplastic agent built as a highly substituted heteroaromatic inhibitor of mutant isocitrate dehydrogenase 2, featuring a rigid nitrogen-rich aromatic core linked to lipophilic aryl/halogenated substituents and amide-like functionality that supports selective allosteric binding; chemically it is best categorized as a targeted heteroaryl organic compound and kinase-like enzyme inhibitor analogue, with a compact biaryl/azacyclic heteroaromatic scaffold optimized for mutant-IDH2 recognition. Closely related or pharmacologically similar drugs include ivosidenib, another mutant IDH inhibitor targeting IDH1, and olutasidenib as a further IDH1-directed comparator. Its principal target protein is mutant IDH2, especially the R140Q and R172 variants, where inhibition lowers the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate and promotes myeloid differentiation. Enasidenib is indicated primarily for relapsed or refractory acute myeloid leukemia with susceptible IDH2 mutations, and has been used in molecularly selected AML populations with differentiation block and transfusion dependence. After oral administration it is absorbed with a relatively long half-life that supports once-daily dosing, is widely distributed, extensively metabolized by multiple pathways including CYP-mediated and UGT-mediated biotransformation, and is eliminated through both fecal and urinary routes, with fecal excretion predominating. Toxicities include differentiation syndrome, leukocytosis, hyperbilirubinemia, gastrointestinal toxicity, and less commonly tumor lysis-related complications; adverse effects commonly include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, decreased appetite, fatigue, dyspnea, edema, and laboratory liver test abnormalities. Clinically, it is used as precision therapy in IDH2-mutated AML, particularly in adults unsuitable for intensive salvage regimens or requiring outpatient oral targeted treatment.

Name: Pibrentasvir
Description: Pibrentasvir (DrugBank DB13878) is a highly potent, nonstructural protein 5A (NS5A) inhibitor used as a direct-acting antiviral for hepatitis C virus infection; structurally, it is a large, symmetric, conformationally constrained polycyclic peptidomimetic-like small molecule enriched in aromatic heterocycles, fluorinated aryl groups, carbamate/amide linkages, and imidazole-containing motifs that confer high affinity for viral replication complexes. Chemically it is classified as an HCV NS5A inhibitor within the class of multiring heteroaromatic antiviral agents, and its scaffold is best described as a dimeric NS5A-binding peptidomimetic heteroaryl core related to other NS5A inhibitors. Similar drugs include velpatasvir, daclatasvir, ledipasvir, elbasvir, and ombitasvir, which share the general NS5A inhibitor pharmacophore. Its principal target is HCV NS5A across genotypes 1-6, disrupting viral RNA replication and virion assembly. Pharmacokinetically, pibrentasvir is orally administered, typically with glecaprevir; exposure increases with food, protein binding is very high, distribution is largely plasma-associated, metabolism is minimal, and elimination occurs predominantly via biliary-fecal excretion with negligible renal clearance, supporting use without dose adjustment in renal impairment. Toxicity is generally low at therapeutic doses, with no prominent intrinsic mitochondrial or myelosuppressive toxicity, but clinically relevant hepatotoxic risk can arise in patients with current or prior hepatitis B through HBV reactivation during HCV treatment, and hepatic decompensation risk is a concern when NS3/4A-containing combinations are used in advanced liver disease. Indications include chronic hepatitis C, including compensated cirrhosis and pan-genotypic infection. Common adverse effects include headache, fatigue, nausea, diarrhea, and pruritus. Clinically, it is used in fixed-dose glecaprevir/pibrentasvir regimens such as Mavyret for treatment-naive or certain treatment-experienced adults and pediatric patients with chronic HCV.

Name: Glecaprevir
Description: Glecaprevir (DB13879) is a direct-acting antiviral designed as a peptidomimetic macrocyclic inhibitor of the hepatitis C virus NS3/4A serine protease; structurally it is a conformationally constrained, highly lipophilic, multiring molecule bearing a macrocycle, amide and carbamate linkages, heteroaromatic substituents, and fluorinated motifs that optimize protease binding and metabolic stability. Chemically it belongs to the HCV NS3/4A protease inhibitor class, with a macrocyclic peptidomimetic scaffold closely related to other NS3/4A inhibitors such as grazoprevir, paritaprevir, voxilaprevir, simeprevir, and asunaprevir. Its primary target protein is the HCV NS3/4A protease across multiple genotypes, blocking viral polyprotein cleavage and thereby suppressing replication. Orally administered in fixed combination with pibrentasvir, glecaprevir shows limited absolute bioavailability but clinically effective absorption enhanced by food, high plasma protein binding, predominant hepatobiliary distribution, minimal oxidative metabolism with CYP3A involvement, substrate behavior for P-gp, BCRP, and OATP1B1/1B3, and mainly fecal excretion with negligible renal elimination. Toxicity is driven chiefly by hepatic risk, including aminotransferase elevations and clinically important hyperbilirubinemia or liver decompensation in susceptible patients, especially those with moderate to severe hepatic impairment; drug-drug interactions with strong transporter or enzyme modulators can increase exposure. Common adverse effects include headache, fatigue, nausea, pruritus, and diarrhea. Clinically, it is indicated for chronic hepatitis C infection, including genotypes 1 through 6, in adults and certain pediatric patients, including treatment-naive and some treatment-experienced populations, and is widely used as the glecaprevir-pibrentasvir regimen for short-course pan-genotypic eradication of HCV, including cases with compensated cirrhosis.

Name: Methyl nicotinate
Description: Methyl nicotinate (DrugBank DB13882) is the methyl ester of nicotinic acid, consisting of a pyridine ring bearing a 3-carboxylate ester functionality, making it a small aromatic heterocycle with a polar ester linked to an electron-deficient aza-aromatic ring; chemically it is classified as a nicotinate ester, a pyridinecarboxylate derivative, and broadly a vitamin B3-related compound, with a simple nicotinic acid scaffold as its core chemotype. Closely related drugs and analogues include nicotinic acid, niacinamide, benzyl nicotinate, and other topical rubefacients such as methyl salicylate, although the latter is pharmacologically similar rather than structurally homologous. Its pharmacokinetics are best characterized in topical use: it penetrates the stratum corneum, distributes locally within superficial dermal tissues, is hydrolyzed by tissue and plasma esterases to nicotinic acid and methanol, and any absorbed metabolite is further handled through conventional niacin pathways with renal excretion of metabolites; systemic exposure is usually low after external application. Target engagement is indirect and incompletely defined, but released nicotinic acid may activate hydroxycarboxylic acid receptor 2 (HCAR2/GPR109A) and promote prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation. Methyl nicotinate is mainly used experimentally and topically as a vasodilatory rubefacient to induce localized erythema, assess microvascular reactivity, or relieve minor muscular and rheumatic pain. Adverse effects and toxicity are predominantly local, including burning, stinging, itching, warmth, erythema, irritant or allergic contact dermatitis, and occasionally blistering with excessive exposure; substantial systemic toxicity is uncommon but could theoretically resemble niacin-related flushing or irritation if absorption were high.

Name: Deoxyepinephrine
Description: Deoxyepinephrine (DrugBank DB13917) is a sympathomimetic phenethylamine structurally related to the endogenous catecholamine epinephrine but lacking one hydroxyl substituent on the aromatic ring, giving a deoxygenated catecholamine-like framework with a β-hydroxylated ethylamine side chain and a secondary N-methylamino group; chemically it is best categorized as an adrenergic agonist within the phenylethanolamine class, built on the classic arylethanolamine/phenethylamine scaffold that also underlies epinephrine, norepinephrine, phenylephrine, and isoproterenol, which are its most relevant similar drugs by structure and pharmacology. Its expected pharmacology is direct stimulation of adrenergic receptors, principally alpha- and possibly beta-adrenoceptors, with likely target proteins including ADRA1, ADRA2, ADRB1, and ADRB2, producing vasopressor and cardiostimulatory effects. Pharmacokinetically, such a polar catecholamine analogue would be expected to have poor oral bioavailability, rapid onset after parenteral administration, limited central nervous system penetration, distribution mainly in extracellular fluid, metabolic inactivation by monoamine oxidase and catechol-O-methyltransferase or related phase I/II pathways, and predominantly renal excretion of metabolites. Toxicity is expected to mirror other adrenergic agonists, including dose-related hypertension, tachyarrhythmias, myocardial ischemia, cerebrovascular events, and tissue ischemia after extravasation; side effects may include palpitations, anxiety, tremor, headache, diaphoresis, nausea, and reflex hemodynamic instability. Clinically, deoxyepinephrine would be understood as a pressor/inotropic agent for acute hypotension, shock states, peri-anesthetic cardiovascular collapse, or severe bronchospastic or allergic phenomena, although practical modern use is limited and largely superseded by better-characterized adrenergic agents.

Name: Candesartan
Description: Candesartan (DrugBank DB13919) is a nonpeptide angiotensin II receptor blocker characterized structurally by a biphenyl-tetrazole motif linked to a benzimidazole core and an ethoxy substituent bearing a carboxyl functionality, a design that confers high affinity, insurmountable antagonism, and oral activity; chemically it is an acidic heteroaromatic biaryl tetrazole and its principal scaffold is the biphenyl-benzimidazole ARB framework shared with related agents such as losartan, valsartan, olmesartan, irbesartan, azilsartan, and eprosartan. Its major pharmacologic target is the angiotensin II type 1 receptor, encoded by AGTR1; functional downstream effects include inhibition of vasoconstriction, aldosterone release, sympathetic facilitation, and renal sodium retention. Clinically, candesartan is used primarily for hypertension and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and has also been used for cardiovascular risk reduction and, in some settings, migraine prophylaxis. Orally, it is administered commonly as the prodrug candesartan cilexetil, which is rapidly hydrolyzed during absorption to active candesartan; bioavailability is modest, protein binding is high, distribution is largely extracellular, metabolism is limited with a minor CYP2C9 contribution, and elimination occurs by both renal and biliary/fecal excretion with a terminal half-life generally around 9 hours. Toxicity is usually extension-of-pharmacology, including hypotension, renal impairment, hyperkalemia, and rises in creatinine, with overdose causing marked blood pressure reduction; class teratogenic fetopathy in pregnancy and rare angioedema are important examples. Common adverse effects include dizziness, fatigue, headache, back pain, upper respiratory symptoms, and worsening kidney function, especially in volume depletion, renal artery stenosis, or combined use with potassium-sparing agents or NSAIDs.

Name: Netarsudil
Description: Netarsudil (DB13931) is a small-molecule aminopyridine-based ophthalmic agent structurally characterized by a substituted aromatic heterocycle linked through an ester-containing chain to a lipophilic aryl moiety, giving a kinase-inhibitor-like, rho-associated protein kinase inhibitor chemotype with an amphiphilic scaffold centered on an aminoisoquinoline/heteroaryl core and ester side chain designed for corneal penetration and local ocular conversion; chemically it is classified as a ROCK inhibitor and norepinephrine transporter-inhibitory ocular hypotensive agent, with related drugs including ripasudil and fasudil as other ROCK inhibitors, and latanoprostene bunod as a mechanistically adjacent glaucoma drug that also enhances trabecular outflow. After topical ocular administration, netarsudil is absorbed into anterior segment tissues, distributes primarily locally to the cornea, aqueous humor, trabecular meshwork, and conjunctiva with minimal systemic exposure, undergoes esterase-mediated metabolism to the more potent active metabolite netarsudil-M1, and is then cleared by further biotransformation and limited systemic excretion, largely minimizing whole-body pharmacokinetic burden. Its principal targets are ROCK1, ROCK2, and the norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, lowering intraocular pressure mainly by increasing trabecular outflow, reducing episcleral venous pressure, and modestly decreasing aqueous humor production. It is indicated for open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension, including patients needing additional intraocular pressure reduction. Toxicity is predominantly local rather than systemic, with dose-limiting ocular irritation examples including conjunctival hyperemia, corneal verticillata, instillation-site pain, punctate keratitis, conjunctival hemorrhage, blurred vision, and tearing; serious systemic toxicity appears uncommon, but ocular surface intolerance can limit use. Clinically, it is used once daily as an ophthalmic solution, either alone or with other pressure-lowering agents when prostaglandin analogs or beta-blockers are insufficient or not tolerated.

Name: Piperaquine
Description: Piperaquine (DrugBank DB13941) is a synthetic bisquinoline antimalarial composed of two 7-chloroquinoline aromatic systems linked through a flexible piperazine-containing aliphatic spacer, giving a highly lipophilic, weakly basic structure that accumulates in acidic parasite food vacuoles; chemically it is classified as a 4-aminoquinoline-related bisquinoline, with a chloroquine-like quinoline scaffold duplicated across a diamine linker. Structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include chloroquine, amodiaquine, hydroxychloroquine, and the bisquinoline analogue pyronaridine in the broader heme-targeting antimalarial space. Its principal target is not a single human protein but the Plasmodium food-vacuole heme detoxification pathway, where it inhibits conversion of toxic ferriprotoporphyrin IX to hemozoin; resistance has been associated with parasite transport proteins including PfCRT and plasmepsin 2/3 copy-number changes.
