After oral administration, especially in fixed-dose combination with dihydroartemisinin, absorption is substantial but variable and enhanced with food; distribution is extensive with very large tissue sequestration and an exceptionally long terminal half-life measured in weeks, metabolism is limited but involves hepatic CYP3A4 to lesser extents, and excretion is slow, predominantly biliary/fecal with minor renal elimination. It is indicated for uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria and mixed malaria infections, and used clinically mainly as dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine for treatment and in some settings intermittent preventive therapy. Major adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, cough, asthenia, and pruritus, while important toxicities include dose-related QT-interval prolongation, rare arrhythmia risk, and potential hepatotoxicity; overdose may cause severe cardiotoxicity and CNS toxicity.

Name: Testosterone cypionate
Description: Testosterone cypionate (DrugBank DB13943) is a long-acting injectable androgen ester consisting of the natural testosterone steroid nucleus, an androst-4-en-3-one framework with a 17beta-hydroxyl group esterified by cyclopentylpropionate (cypionate), which increases lipophilicity and slows release from the intramuscular depot; chemically it is an androgenic anabolic steroid, specifically a testosterone ester, built on the classic cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene steroid scaffold. Closely related drugs include testosterone enanthate, testosterone undecanoate, testosterone propionate, and mixed testosterone esters, as well as other anabolic-androgenic steroids such as nandrolone esters. Its principal target is the androgen receptor (NR3C4), with many effects mediated after intracellular conversion to dihydrotestosterone by steroid 5-alpha-reductase and aromatization to estradiol via CYP19A1. After intramuscular administration it is slowly absorbed, extensively distributed with high binding to sex hormone-binding globulin and albumin, hydrolyzed to testosterone, hepatically metabolized mainly by reduction and conjugation, and excreted predominantly in urine as glucuronide and sulfate metabolites, with only minor fecal elimination. It is indicated for male hypogonadism, delayed puberty in selected males, and gender-affirming masculinizing hormone therapy, improving symptoms such as low libido, fatigue, reduced muscle mass, and impaired secondary sexual characteristics. Adverse effects include acne, edema, polycythemia, gynecomastia, mood changes, infertility, testicular atrophy, and suppression of gonadotropins; important toxicities include hypertension, dyslipidemia, thromboembolic risk, worsening sleep apnea, hepatic strain less than with oral 17alpha-ალკylated agents, virilization in women or children, and potential stimulation of prostate disease.

Name: Testosterone enanthate
Description: Testosterone enanthate (DrugBank DB13944) is a long-acting esterified androgen consisting of the natural steroid testosterone with the 17β-hydroxyl group esterified by heptanoic acid, preserving the classic androstane four-ring cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene steroid nucleus with a 3-keto and Δ4 double bond; chemically it is an androgen ester, anabolic-androgenic steroid, and prodrug of testosterone built on the testosterone/androst-4-en-3-one scaffold. Closely related drugs include testosterone cypionate, testosterone undecanoate, testosterone propionate, and mixed testosterone esters, as well as other anabolic steroids such as nandrolone esters. After deep intramuscular injection in oil, absorption is slow from the depot because of high lipophilicity, distribution is extensive with strong binding to sex hormone-binding globulin and albumin, hydrolysis releases active testosterone, metabolism occurs mainly in liver and peripheral tissues to dihydrotestosterone via 5α-reductase and estradiol via aromatase with further reduction/conjugation, and excretion is primarily urinary as glucuronide and sulfate metabolites with minor fecal elimination. Its principal target is the androgen receptor, with downstream effects influenced by SRD5A1/SRD5A2 and CYP19A1. It is indicated for male hypogonadism, delayed puberty in selected males, and gender-affirming masculinizing hormone therapy, and has also been used palliatively in some breast cancers. Toxicities include polycythemia, edema, hypertension, dyslipidemia, hepatotoxicity less often than 17α-alkylated agents, suppression of spermatogenesis and infertility, virilization, and potential worsening of prostate disease or sleep apnea. Common adverse effects include acne, oily skin, injection-site pain, mood changes, gynecomastia, weight gain, alopecia, and increased hematocrit. Clinically it is used as an intramuscular depot testosterone replacement to restore libido, energy, muscle mass, bone density, and secondary sexual characteristics in androgen-deficient states.

Name: Testosterone undecanoate
Description: Testosterone undecanoate (DrugBank DB13946) is a long-chain fatty acid ester prodrug of testosterone in which the 17 beta-hydroxyl group of the androst-4-en-3-one steroid nucleus is esterified with undecanoic acid, preserving the classical androgenic cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene scaffold and placing it within the androgen, anabolic steroid, and steroid ester chemical categories. Its closest structural and therapeutic analogs are other testosterone esters and androgen formulations such as testosterone enanthate, cypionate, propionate, and testosterone itself, as well as related anabolic-androgenic steroids with differing ester side chains that modulate release and exposure. After oral administration, the highly lipophilic undecanoate ester is absorbed mainly via the intestinal lymphatic route with dietary fat, partially bypassing first-pass hepatic metabolism, whereas intramuscular depot formulations are slowly released from the injection site; in circulation it is extensively protein bound after hydrolysis to testosterone, distributes broadly to androgen-responsive tissues, is metabolized by esterases to testosterone and then further by hepatic pathways to active dihydrotestosterone via SRD5A enzymes and estradiol via aromatase CYP19A1, with subsequent conjugation and urinary predominance of excretion. Its principal target is the androgen receptor, with indirect engagement of pathways involving sex hormone-binding globulin, 5-alpha-reductase, and aromatase. It is indicated for male hypogonadism and testosterone deficiency syndromes, including delayed puberty or symptoms such as low libido, fatigue, and reduced muscle mass. Adverse effects include acne, edema, polycythemia, hypertension, gynecomastia, infertility, mood changes, and prostate-related effects; major toxicities include virilization, hepatic dysfunction less commonly than 17-alpha-alkylated steroids, thromboembolic or cardiovascular risk, and pulmonary oil microembolism or anaphylactoid reactions with some injectable products. Clinically it is used as long-acting oral or intramuscular testosterone replacement to restore serum androgen levels, sexual function, bone density, erythropoiesis, and body composition in appropriately selected patients.

Name: Estradiol cypionate
Description: Estradiol cypionate (DrugBank DB13954) is a long-acting esterified natural estrogen in which 17β-estradiol retains the rigid cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene steroid nucleus and aromatic A-ring with phenolic 3-hydroxyl, while the 17β-hydroxyl is esterified with cyclopentylpropionate (cypionate), increasing lipophilicity and depot duration; it is therefore classified as a steroid estrogen, specifically an estradiol ester prodrug, built on the estrane/estradiol steroid scaffold. Closely related drugs include estradiol valerate, estradiol benzoate, estradiol acetate, estradiol enanthate, and the nonesterified parent estradiol, as well as other estrogenic agents such as conjugated estrogens and ethinyl estradiol. After intramuscular administration in oil, absorption is slow from the depot, distribution is extensive with high plasma protein binding mainly to albumin and sex hormone-binding globulin after hydrolysis, metabolism occurs primarily via ester cleavage to estradiol followed by hepatic interconversion with estrone and phase II conjugation to glucuronides and sulfates, and excretion is mainly renal with some biliary/fecal elimination. Its principal targets are estrogen receptor alpha ESR1 and estrogen receptor beta ESR2, with downstream regulation of gonadotropin secretion and estrogen-responsive gene transcription. Clinically it has been used for menopausal symptoms, hypoestrogenism, female hypogonadism, dysfunctional uterine bleeding, palliative treatment of selected androgen-dependent prostate cancers, and gender-affirming hormone therapy. Adverse effects and toxicity reflect estrogen excess and include nausea, breast tenderness, edema, headache, melasma, breakthrough bleeding, hypertension, cholestatic effects, and serious risks such as venous thromboembolism, stroke, and endometrial hyperplasia/carcinoma when unopposed in women with a uterus.

Name: Estradiol valerate
Description: Estradiol valerate (DrugBank DB13956) is a semisynthetic fatty-acid ester prodrug of 17β-estradiol in which the 17β-hydroxyl group of the natural estrogenic steroid nucleus is esterified with valeric acid, preserving the aromatic A ring and classic cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene scaffold characteristic of C18 steroid estrogens; chemically it belongs to the estrogen ester, steroid hormone, and estradiol derivative classes, with a scaffold closely related to estradiol, estradiol cypionate, estrone, ethinyl estradiol, and conjugated estrogens. After oral or intramuscular administration it is absorbed and rapidly hydrolyzed by esterases to estradiol and valerate, with the ester increasing lipophilicity and, for depot injection, prolonging release; estradiol is widely distributed, highly protein bound mainly to albumin and sex hormone-binding globulin, metabolized primarily in the liver to estrone, estriol, and their sulfate/glucuronide conjugates via hydroxylation and interconversion pathways, and excreted mainly in urine with some biliary/fecal elimination. Its principal targets are estrogen receptor alpha and beta (ESR1, ESR2), producing genomic estrogenic effects on reproductive tissues, bone, liver, and the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. Clinically it is used for menopausal hormone therapy, treatment of hypoestrogenism or ovarian failure, menstrual disorders, palliative therapy in selected prostate cancer settings, and gender-affirming feminizing hormone therapy. Adverse effects include nausea, breast tenderness, edema, headache, breakthrough bleeding, melasma, and mood changes, while serious toxicity includes endometrial hyperplasia/carcinoma risk without progestin opposition, venous thromboembolism, stroke, hypertension, cholestatic jaundice, and possible promotion of estrogen-sensitive malignancies; overdose is usually characterized by nausea, vomiting, and vaginal bleeding.

Name: Choline salicylate
Description: Choline salicylate (DrugBank DB14006) is the choline salt of salicylic acid, structurally comprising a salicylate anion built on an o-hydroxybenzoic acid aromatic ring paired ionically with a quaternary ammonium choline cation bearing a hydroxyethyl substituent; it is therefore classified as a salicylate, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug and topical analgesic, with a simple salicylic acid/benzoate scaffold. It is chemically and pharmacologically related to other salicylates and NSAID-like agents such as aspirin, sodium salicylate, magnesium salicylate, methyl salicylate, and diflunisal. Its main pharmacologic effect is attributed to salicylate-mediated inhibition of cyclooxygenase enzymes, especially PTGS1 and PTGS2, leading to reduced prostaglandin synthesis, with secondary anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antipyretic actions. After local oral or mucosal administration it is absorbed through inflamed mucosa to a variable extent; systemically absorbed salicylate distributes widely, is moderately protein bound, undergoes hepatic conjugation mainly to salicyluric acid and phenolic/acyl glucuronides, and is excreted renally with pH-dependent clearance. Toxicity resembles that of other salicylates and includes mucosal irritation, nausea, vomiting, tinnitus, dizziness, metabolic acidosis, hyperventilation, and in severe overdose CNS toxicity or salicylism, with heightened concern in children and aspirin-sensitive patients. It is used primarily for symptomatic relief of painful inflammatory conditions of the mouth and throat, including aphthous ulcers, gingivitis, denture irritation, sore throat, and oral mucositis, and clinically appears in gels, paints, mouth preparations, and other topical formulations where common adverse effects include transient burning, local irritation, hypersensitivity reactions, and occasional gastrointestinal symptoms if appreciable systemic absorption occurs.

Name: Benzoin
Description: Benzoin (DB14020) is an aromatic α-hydroxy ketone characterized structurally as 2-hydroxy-1,2-diphenylethanone, with two phenyl rings flanking a vicinal hydroxy-ketone center; chemically it belongs to the benzoins, a subclass of aromatic ketols/acyloins, and its core scaffold is the diphenyl α-hydroxy ketone framework. It is chemically related to other aromatic carbonyl or resin-associated topical agents, with similarities often noted to benzaldehyde-derived compounds such as benzil, benzoic acid derivatives, and compound tincture of benzoin constituents including styrax-like balsamic resins. Benzoin itself is used primarily as a topical protectant, adhesive adjunct, and fragrance/flavoring ingredient rather than a systemic therapeutic, so pharmacokinetic data are limited: when applied to intact skin or mucosa, systemic absorption is expected to be minimal, distribution correspondingly low, and any absorbed fraction would likely undergo hepatic oxidation/reduction and conjugation with urinary excretion of metabolites; inhalational or oral exposure is uncommon in medical use. Toxicity is mainly local and exposure-dependent, including skin and mucosal irritation, allergic contact dermatitis, burning, erythema, and rare respiratory irritation if vapors are inhaled; substantial systemic toxicity is not well established at therapeutic topical exposures. No validated, specific human target proteins are established, and its clinical effects are largely physicochemical, forming a protective film that improves adhesion of surgical dressings and canker sore preparations. Indications include topical skin protection, enhancement of bandage adhesion, and symptomatic management of minor oral or cutaneous irritation, while side effects in practice include stinging, rash, hypersensitivity, and dryness. Clinically, benzoin is used in tincture form on small wounds, around ostomy or dressing sites, and on oral lesions where a protective coating is desired.

Name: Thiosalicylic acid
Description: Thiosalicylic acid (DrugBank DB14026), also known as 2-mercaptobenzoic acid, is a small aromatic organosulfur compound consisting of a benzoic acid core bearing an ortho thiol substituent, giving a compact bifunctional structure with adjacent carboxylic acid and sulfhydryl groups capable of redox chemistry, metal coordination, and thioester formation; it is therefore classified as a thiobenzoic acid/aryl thiol and more broadly as an organosulfur carboxylic acid, built on a salicylic acid-like benzenoid scaffold in which the phenolic oxygen is replaced by sulfur. Closely related compounds include salicylic acid, 3-mercaptobenzoic acid, 4-mercaptobenzoic acid, and medicinal chemistry derivatives such as S-farnesylthiosalicylic acid (salirasib), which exploits the same scaffold for Ras pathway modulation. Thiosalicylic acid itself is mainly a chemical intermediate and pharmacologic tool rather than an established therapeutic drug; accordingly, definitive human pharmacokinetic data are limited, but by analogy it would be expected to show at least partial gastrointestinal absorption, plasma protein binding through its aromatic acid functionality, hepatic oxidation and thiol conjugation or disulfide formation, and predominantly renal excretion of parent and conjugated metabolites. Its toxicity is consistent with thiol-containing aromatic acids, including skin and eye irritation, mucosal irritation, possible oxidative stress, and at higher exposures hepatotoxic or nephrotoxic risk; adverse effects would be expected to include gastrointestinal upset, dermatitis, and irritation-related symptoms. No well-validated clinical target protein is established for thiosalicylic acid itself, although the scaffold can interact with prenyl-binding proteins and thiol-reactive enzymes. There is no standard approved indication or routine clinical use; instead, it is used primarily in synthesis and research, while derivatives have been investigated in oncology, especially Ras-driven cancers.

Name: Tretamine
Description: Tretamine (DB14031) is a classical antineoplastic alkylating agent of the ethylenimine/aziridine class, structurally characterized by a triazine core substituted with three highly strained aziridine rings, giving a compact polyfunctional electrophile built on a triethylene-melamine scaffold; chemically it is therefore a tri-aziridinyl s-triazine derivative, closely related to other aziridine alkylators such as triethylenemelamine, triethylenephosphoramide, and related historical DNA-crosslinking agents. Its pharmacologic activity arises not from selective high-affinity protein binding but from direct covalent alkylation of nucleophilic sites in DNA, especially guanine residues, producing interstrand crosslinks, inhibition of DNA replication and transcription, and consequent cytotoxicity in rapidly proliferating cells; no single canonical target protein is typically assigned, although the functional biomolecular target is genomic DNA and downstream DNA damage response pathways. Pharmacokinetic data are limited and largely historical, but it is understood to be systemically absorbed when administered therapeutically, to distribute broadly into proliferative tissues, to undergo chemical and hepatic inactivation through aziridine ring opening and hydrolytic/metabolic transformation, and to be eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine. Toxicity is characteristic of potent alkylators, with dose-limiting myelosuppression, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, mucosal injury, nausea, vomiting, and potential gonadal toxicity, mutagenicity, teratogenicity, and carcinogenicity. Tretamine was used primarily in oncology, especially for ovarian carcinoma and other disseminated solid tumors, with clinical use now largely obsolete because of severe toxicity and replacement by safer, better-characterized modern cytotoxics.

Name: Menthol
Description: Menthol (DrugBank DB14123) is a small, lipophilic monoterpenoid alcohol, classically the cyclohexanol derivative 2-isopropyl-5-methylcyclohexan-1-ol, most commonly used as the naturally occurring l-menthol stereoisomer; structurally it belongs to the terpene alcohol/monocyclic monoterpene class and is built on a p-menthane cyclohexane scaffold shared with related cooling agents and terpenes. Similar drugs or analogues include peppermint oil constituents, menthone, eucalyptol, camphor, thymol, and synthetic cooling agents such as icilin and WS-3/WS-23, which overlap in sensory pharmacology. Menthol is absorbed through skin and mucosa and after oral exposure is also gastrointestinally absorbed; its distribution is favored into lipid-rich tissues, while metabolism occurs predominantly in the liver by phase I oxidation and extensive glucuronidation, producing menthol glucuronide and other hydroxylated metabolites that are eliminated mainly in urine, with minor biliary or exhalational clearance. Its principal targets include TRPM8, which mediates cooling sensation and mild analgesia, with additional activity reported at TRPA1, voltage-gated sodium channels, kappa-opioid signaling pathways, and GABAergic systems depending on concentration and preparation. Clinically, menthol is used as a topical counterirritant, antipruritic, mild local analgesic, decongestant, cough suppressant adjunct, and flavoring agent in products for myalgia, arthralgia, pruritus, sore throat, nasal congestion, and minor cough. Adverse effects are usually local irritation, burning, contact dermatitis, lacrimation, and mucosal discomfort; toxicity at excessive doses can include nausea, abdominal pain, dizziness, ataxia, CNS depression, and rarely seizures, especially in children or after concentrated ingestion or inhalation.

Name: Benazeprilat
Description: Benazeprilat (DrugBank DB14125) is the active diacid metabolite of benazepril and is a dicarboxylate angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor whose structure features a proline-like amino acid core linked to a lipophilic bicyclic/benzazepine-derived moiety and terminating carboxylate groups that chelate the catalytic zinc in ACE; chemically it belongs to the non-sulfhydryl, carboxylate-containing ACE inhibitor class, with a proline-based peptidomimetic scaffold typical of zinc metallopeptidase inhibitors. It is closely related to other active diacid ACE inhibitors such as enalaprilat, ramiprilat, perindoprilat, quinaprilat, and trandolaprilat, which share the same general mechanism and similar structure-activity relationships. Its principal target is angiotensin-converting enzyme, especially somatic ACE/ACE1, leading to reduced angiotensin II formation and decreased bradykinin degradation. Pharmacokinetically, benazeprilat is formed by hepatic esterase hydrolysis of the orally administered prodrug benazepril; the active metabolite itself is poorly orally absorbed, distributes largely in extracellular fluid with high, saturable ACE binding, undergoes little further metabolism, and is eliminated mainly unchanged by renal excretion with a contribution from biliary/fecal pathways, producing a prolonged effective half-life because of tight tissue ACE binding. It is indicated for hypertension and is used clinically to lower blood pressure, reduce afterload, and in some settings decrease proteinuric renal disease progression. Toxicity and adverse effects are those of ACE inhibition, including hypotension, dizziness, cough, hyperkalemia, renal function worsening, and rare but important angioedema; examples of serious toxicity include acute kidney injury in bilateral renal artery stenosis and fetotoxicity when exposure occurs during pregnancy.

Name: Tenofovir
Description: Tenofovir (DrugBank DB14126) is an acyclic nucleoside phosphonate analog of adenosine monophosphate characterized structurally by a purine adenine base linked to a flexible aliphatic side chain terminating in a phosphonic acid, giving it a negatively charged, hydrolysis-resistant nucleotide mimic; chemically it is classified as an antiviral nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor and more specifically an acyclic adenine phosphonate, built on the phosphonomethoxypropyl scaffold shared with related agents such as adefovir and cidofovir, while clinically similar drugs also include other anti-HIV or anti-HBV nucleos(t)ide analogs such as emtricitabine, lamivudine, entecavir, and abacavir. After oral administration as the prodrugs tenofovir disoproxil or tenofovir alafenamide, tenofovir is systemically absorbed, distributed widely into plasma and intracellular compartments, undergoes minimal CYP-mediated metabolism, is phosphorylated intracellularly to the active diphosphate, and is eliminated primarily unchanged by the kidney through glomerular filtration and active tubular secretion, with tenofovir alafenamide producing lower plasma tenofovir exposure and greater lymphoid cell delivery than tenofovir disoproxil. Its principal targets are HIV-1 reverse transcriptase, HIV-2 reverse transcriptase, and hepatitis B virus polymerase, with antiviral action mediated by competitive incorporation into viral DNA and chain termination. Indications include HIV-1 treatment and pre-exposure prophylaxis, and chronic hepatitis B. Important toxicities include proximal renal tubulopathy, acute kidney injury, Fanconi syndrome, and reduced bone mineral density; common adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, fatigue, and laboratory renal abnormalities. In practice it is widely used in combination antiretroviral regimens and HBV therapy, for example with emtricitabine in HIV treatment or PrEP, and as long-term suppression therapy in chronic hepatitis B.

Name: Aripiprazole lauroxil
Description: Aripiprazole lauroxil (DB14185) is a long-acting injectable antipsychotic prodrug consisting of aripiprazole esterified through a hydroxymethyl linker to lauric acid, yielding a lipophilic N-acyloxymethyl derivative that masks the active quinolinone-piperazine pharmacophore and slows release after intramuscular administration; chemically it is a fatty-acid ester prodrug and is best classified within atypical antipsychotic prodrugs, while its core scaffold is that of aripiprazole, a dihydroquinolin-2-one linked to a piperazine and dichlorophenyl moiety. Similar drugs include aripiprazole itself, aripiprazole monohydrate long-acting injection, brexpiprazole, cariprazine, and other depot atypical antipsychotics such as paliperidone palmitate. After intramuscular injection, absorption is prolonged by slow dissolution and enzymatic hydrolysis to N-hydroxymethyl aripiprazole and then aripiprazole, with delayed systemic appearance, extensive tissue distribution, high protein binding, hepatic metabolism mainly by CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 to dehydro-aripiprazole, and elimination predominantly as metabolites in urine and feces. Its principal targets are dopamine D2 and D3 receptors and serotonin 5-HT1A and 5-HT2A receptors, acting broadly as a D2/5-HT1A partial agonist and 5-HT2A antagonist. It is indicated for schizophrenia, particularly maintenance treatment in adults requiring improved adherence, and has been used clinically as monthly or longer-interval depot therapy in patients with chronic psychosis, relapse risk, or poor oral compliance. Adverse effects include akathisia, insomnia, anxiety, injection-site pain, weight gain, headache, and extrapyramidal symptoms; important toxicities include tardive dyskinesia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, orthostatic hypotension, metabolic disturbance, leukopenia, impulse-control problems, seizures, and increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis.

Name: Fosinoprilat
Description: Fosinoprilat (DrugBank DB14207) is the active diacid metabolite of fosinopril and is a phosphorus-containing angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor characterized structurally by a proline-like heterocyclic amino acid framework linked to a hydroxyphosphinyl or phosphinate zinc-binding group and a lipophilic alkoxy side chain, placing it in the peptidomimetic organophosphorus ACE inhibitor class with a phosphinic acid scaffold analogous to transition-state mimics of peptide hydrolysis. Its closest related drugs are other ACE inhibitors such as fosinopril, enalaprilat, lisinopril, ramiprilat, benazeprilat, and captopril, which share renin-angiotensin system blockade but differ in zinc-binding chemistry and lipophilicity. Fosinoprilat inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme, primarily the somatic ACE protein, thereby reducing angiotensin II formation and aldosterone secretion while increasing bradykinin. Pharmacokinetically, it is formed from fosinopril after ester hydrolysis; the active metabolite itself has limited oral relevance, distributes to ACE-rich tissues, shows substantial protein binding, undergoes little further metabolism, and is eliminated by both renal and hepatobiliary routes, a clinically useful dual pathway in renal impairment. Toxicity is typical of ACE inhibition and includes excessive hypotension, azotemia, hyperkalemia, and worsening renal function, with rarer serious examples including angioedema and fetal toxicity in pregnancy. Therapeutically it is indicated for hypertension and heart failure, including blood pressure reduction and afterload lowering in symptomatic left ventricular dysfunction. Adverse effects include cough, dizziness, fatigue, headache, nausea, syncope, rash, elevated creatinine, and hyperkalemia. Clinically, fosinopril is administered as the prodrug, with fosinoprilat mediating the pharmacologic effect in chronic antihypertensive and adjunct heart-failure management.

Name: Ramiprilat
Description: Ramiprilat (DrugBank DB14208) is the active diacid metabolite of ramipril and is a peptidomimetic angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor characterized structurally by a substituted proline-like bicyclic/condensed pyrrolidine carboxylate framework bearing two carboxylic acid groups and a hydrophobic side chain that supports high-affinity zinc-dependent binding within the ACE catalytic site; chemically it belongs to the dicarboxylate class of ACE inhibitors, with a proline-derived amino acid mimic scaffold closely related to other carboxylate ACE inhibitors. Similar drugs include ramipril, enalaprilat, lisinopril, benazeprilat, perindoprilat, quinaprilat, and trandolaprilat, which share the same general ACE-inhibitory pharmacophore. Ramiprilat inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme, primarily the somatic ACE isoform encoded by ACE, thereby reducing angiotensin II formation and aldosterone secretion while increasing bradykinin. Pharmacokinetically, ramiprilat is formed hepatically from the prodrug ramipril; as a polar active metabolite it has limited oral absorption itself, distributes to ACE-rich tissues, shows high but partly saturable ACE binding, undergoes minimal further metabolism, and is eliminated mainly by the kidney with a prolonged terminal phase reflecting tight tissue/enzyme binding. Toxicity is principally an extension of pharmacology and includes excessive hypotension, renal dysfunction or acute kidney injury, hyperkalemia, and rare but serious angioedema; fetotoxicity in pregnancy and worsened renal failure in bilateral renal artery stenosis are classic examples. Adverse effects include cough, dizziness, syncope, headache, nausea, rash, and creatinine elevation. Clinically, via the ramipril prodrug, it is used for hypertension, heart failure, post-myocardial-infarction ventricular dysfunction, and cardiovascular risk reduction, and it may also be used to slow proteinuric chronic kidney disease or diabetic nephropathy progression.

Name: Perindoprilat
Description: Perindoprilat (DrugBank DB14213) is the active diacid metabolite of the prodrug perindopril and is a small peptidomimetic angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor characterized structurally by a proline-like bicyclic/heterocyclic amino acid core linked to a substituted aliphatic side chain bearing two carboxylate groups that chelate the catalytic zinc ion of ACE; chemically it belongs to the dicarboxylate, non-sulfhydryl ACE inhibitor class, with a scaffold closely related to other proline-derived ACE inhibitor pharmacophores. Similar drugs include enalaprilat, ramiprilat, lisinopril, quinaprilat, trandolaprilat, and benazeprilat, which share the same zinc-binding, peptide-mimetic antihypertensive design. Its principal target protein is angiotensin-converting enzyme, especially somatic ACE, leading to reduced conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II and reduced bradykinin degradation. Pharmacokinetically, perindoprilat itself has poor oral absorption and is therefore usually generated in vivo after oral perindopril administration; it distributes into plasma and ACE-rich tissues, exhibits substantial protein and tissue ACE binding, undergoes minimal further metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by the kidneys, with a prolonged effective half-life due to tight enzyme binding and accumulation in renal impairment. Toxicity is largely an extension of pharmacology, including dose-related hypotension, azotemia, hyperkalemia, and rare but serious angioedema; fetal toxicity in pregnancy and acute kidney injury in bilateral renal artery stenosis are important examples. Adverse effects include cough, dizziness, headache, syncope, renal dysfunction, rash, and gastrointestinal upset. Clinically, the perindopril/perindoprilat system is used for hypertension, chronic heart failure, and reduction of cardiovascular risk in patients with stable coronary or vascular disease, for example in blood-pressure control, post-myocardial-infarction remodeling prevention, and adjunctive treatment of symptomatic left ventricular dysfunction.

Name: Quinaprilat
Description: Quinaprilat (DrugBank DB14217) is the active diacid metabolite of quinapril and is a peptidomimetic angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor built around a substituted tetrahydroisoquinoline/proline-like dicarboxylate framework, with a compact bicyclic amino-acid-mimetic scaffold bearing carboxylate groups that support high-affinity zinc-dependent ACE binding; chemically it belongs to the dicarboxylate class of ACE inhibitors, and its scaffold and pharmacology are closely related to quinapril, enalaprilat, ramiprilat, benazeprilat, lisinopril, and perindoprilat. Its principal target is angiotensin-converting enzyme, with secondary pharmacodynamic consequences including reduced angiotensin II formation and aldosterone secretion and increased bradykinin exposure. Quinaprilat itself is poorly absorbed orally and is more relevant as the circulating active form generated by hepatic de-esterification of the prodrug quinapril; after formation it distributes mainly in extracellular fluid, shows substantial ACE/tissue binding, limited CNS penetration, minimal further metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly by the kidney, with prolonged exposure in renal impairment. Therapeutically it is used through quinapril administration for hypertension, congestive heart failure, and related cardiovascular risk reduction, for example blood-pressure control in essential hypertension or adjunctive therapy in systolic heart failure. Adverse effects and toxicities are characteristic of ACE inhibition and include hypotension, dizziness, cough, hyperkalemia, renal function deterioration, and less commonly angioedema; overdose may produce marked hypotension and electrolyte disturbances, while fetotoxicity in pregnancy and risk of acute kidney injury in renal artery stenosis are important serious examples.

Name: Monomethyl fumarate
Description: Monomethyl fumarate (DB14219) is a small, unsaturated aliphatic dicarboxylate ester consisting of a fumaric acid scaffold with a trans carbon-carbon double bond bearing one methyl ester and one free carboxylic acid, making it an electrophilic fumarate derivative in the broader class of fumaric acid esters and an α,β-unsaturated carboxylic acid ester; this simple fumarate scaffold is shared with related agents such as dimethyl fumarate, diroximel fumarate, and other medicinal or industrial fumarates. Pharmacologically, monomethyl fumarate is the major active metabolite of dimethyl fumarate and has immunomodulatory and cytoprotective activity mediated chiefly through covalent modification of KEAP1, with downstream activation of the NFE2L2/NRF2 antioxidant pathway, and it also affects HCAR2/GPR109A, contributing to anti-inflammatory signaling. After oral administration as the active moiety generated from fumarate ester prodrugs, it is well absorbed, appears systemically after presystemic esterase cleavage of precursor drugs, shows limited protein binding and broad tissue distribution, undergoes further metabolism through the tricarboxylic acid cycle rather than CYP-dependent biotransformation, and is eliminated predominantly as exhaled carbon dioxide with lesser renal and fecal excretion of metabolites. Its principal indication is relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis, where it is used to reduce relapse frequency and inflammatory disease activity; gastrointestinal toxicity and flushing are common, including abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, and erythema or warmth, while more serious toxicities include lymphopenia, transaminase elevation, proteinuria, hypersensitivity, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy risk in severe prolonged immunosuppression, and opportunistic infection susceptibility.

Name: Sodium ascorbate
Description: Sodium ascorbate (DrugBank DB14482) is the sodium salt of ascorbic acid, structurally characterized as an ionized enediol-lactone built on a five-membered furanone-like ring with multiple hydroxyl substituents that confer strong water solubility and reducing capacity; chemically it belongs to the vitamin C/ascorbate class of carbohydrate-derived antioxidants, and its core scaffold is the ascorbate butenolide-enediol framework. Closely related drugs and analogs include ascorbic acid, calcium ascorbate, potassium ascorbate, and other vitamin C formulations used interchangeably for supplementation. After oral administration it is absorbed in the small intestine mainly via sodium-dependent vitamin C transporters SVCT1 and SVCT2, with saturable uptake, wide distribution into plasma and tissues such as adrenal gland, leukocytes, and liver, limited biotransformation to dehydroascorbic acid and oxalate-related metabolites, and predominant renal excretion with urinary elimination increasing sharply at high plasma concentrations. Its principal molecular targets are not classic receptors but transporter proteins SLC23A1 and SLC23A2, while pharmacologic effects also relate to redox interactions and cofactor roles for Fe2+/2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases such as prolyl hydroxylases. It is indicated for prevention and treatment of vitamin C deficiency including scurvy, and is used clinically in nutritional supplementation, wound healing support, and states of increased vitamin C requirement. Toxicity is generally low but high doses may cause gastrointestinal upset, osmotic diarrhea, hyperoxaluria, calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis, and rarely hemolysis in susceptible patients such as those with G6PD deficiency; common side effects include nausea, abdominal cramps, and diarrhea.

Name: Zinc acetate
Description: Zinc acetate, DrugBank DB14487, is a simple inorganic zinc salt composed of a divalent zinc cation coordinated by two acetate anions, typically forming an ionically bound, highly water-soluble complex in which Zn2+ serves as the pharmacologically active species; it belongs to the metal acetate and zinc salt class, with a minimal scaffold defined by a central zinc ion paired with small carboxylate ligands rather than a complex organic pharmacophore. Similar drugs include other medicinal zinc salts such as zinc sulfate, zinc gluconate, and zinc chloride, which likewise function as zinc donors but differ in tolerability, elemental zinc content, and formulation. After oral administration, zinc acetate dissociates in the gastrointestinal tract, with zinc absorbed mainly in the small intestine via transporters including SLC39A4 ZIP4 and exported by SLC30A1 ZnT1; it distributes broadly bound to albumin, alpha-2-macroglobulin, and intracellular metallothioneins, undergoes no metabolic biotransformation, and is eliminated predominantly in feces with smaller urinary losses. Its major pharmacologic target system is copper handling in enterocytes, where zinc induces metallothionein, a metal-binding protein that sequesters copper and reduces systemic copper absorption, supporting its use in Wilson disease; zinc also nutritionally treats zinc deficiency and has been used in supplementation settings. Toxicity is usually dose related and includes gastric irritation, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and chronic high-dose copper deficiency with anemia, neutropenia, and neurologic complications; adverse effects commonly include dyspepsia and metallic taste. Clinically, zinc acetate is used long term as maintenance or first-line decoppering therapy in Wilson disease, particularly presymptomatic patients, children, pregnancy, or after chelation induction.

Name: Sodium phosphate, dibasic
Description: Sodium phosphate, dibasic (disodium hydrogen phosphate; DrugBank DB14502) is a simple inorganic phosphate salt composed of a hydrogen phosphate tetrahedron with phosphorus centrally coordinated to four oxygens, carrying two sodium counterions; structurally it is a small ionic oxyanion rather than an organic molecule, placing it in the class of inorganic mineral salts/electrolytes with a phosphate salt scaffold shared by hydrogen phosphate and related sodium or potassium phosphates. Similar drugs include sodium phosphate monobasic, tribasic sodium phosphate, potassium phosphate salts, and phosphate-containing bowel preparations such as oral sodium phosphate combinations. Its pharmacologic behavior reflects endogenous phosphate handling: oral absorption occurs in the small intestine by passive and sodium-dependent mechanisms, distribution is mainly to extracellular fluid with rapid exchange into bone and intracellular phosphate pools, there is no metabolic biotransformation, and elimination is primarily renal under regulation by PTH, FGF23, and vitamin D. Toxicity is dominated by electrolyte and acid-base disturbances, especially hyperphosphatemia, secondary hypocalcemia, hypernatremia, volume depletion, metastatic calcification, and acute phosphate nephropathy, with greater risk in older adults and patients with chronic kidney disease, dehydration, bowel obstruction, or concomitant diuretics/RAAS inhibitors. It has no single classic drug target; relevant physiologic targets include intestinal and renal sodium-phosphate cotransporters such as SLC34A1, SLC34A2, and SLC20 family transporters. Clinically it is used as a phosphate supplement to treat or prevent hypophosphatemia and, in some formulations, as an osmotic saline laxative or bowel-cleansing agent before colonoscopy; common adverse effects include diarrhea, abdominal cramping, nausea, vomiting, bloating, thirst, and dizziness, while serious use-limiting events include arrhythmia, tetany, seizures, and renal injury.

Name: Lithium citrate
Description: Lithium citrate (DrugBank DB14507) is an inorganic-organic lithium salt composed of lithium cations ionically paired with citrate, the tricarboxylate conjugate base of citric acid; structurally it is a small, highly polar, nonvolatile coordination salt in which lithium associates with a hydroxytricarboxylate scaffold rather than a lipophilic carbon-rich pharmacophore. It belongs to the chemical category of lithium salts and metal citrates, and its core scaffold is the citrate backbone shared with citric acid and other citrate salts. Similar drugs include other therapeutic lithium formulations such as lithium carbonate and lithium acetate, which deliver the same active moiety, Li+. After oral administration, lithium citrate is well absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, dissociates in body fluids, distributes largely in total body water with gradual entry into the brain, does not undergo metabolic biotransformation, is not protein bound to a major extent, and is excreted almost entirely unchanged by the kidney, where clearance parallels sodium handling; its narrow therapeutic index makes serum-level monitoring essential. Toxicity includes dose-related tremor, vomiting, diarrhea, ataxia, confusion, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy, hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, ECG changes, seizures, and coma in overdose, with risk increased by dehydration, renal impairment, and thiazides, ACE inhibitors, or NSAIDs. No single canonical protein target fully explains its actions, but implicated targets include glycogen synthase kinase-3 alpha and beta, inositol monophosphatase 1, inositol polyphosphate 1-phosphatase, and related phosphomonoesterases. Clinically it is used primarily as a mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder, especially acute mania and maintenance to reduce manic relapse and suicidality, and sometimes for augmentation in refractory major depressive disorder; common adverse effects include fine tremor, polyuria, polydipsia, nausea, weight gain, edema, cognitive dulling, and acne.

Name: Lithium carbonate
Description: Lithium carbonate (DB14509) is a simple inorganic salt composed of two monovalent lithium cations ionically paired with a planar carbonate dianion featuring trigonal carbon-oxygen geometry and resonance-delocalized negative charge; it belongs to the alkali metal carbonate class and has an elemental ionic scaffold rather than a classical organic pharmacophore. Similar drugs include other lithium salts such as lithium citrate and, more broadly by therapeutic use rather than structure, mood stabilizers such as valproate, carbamazepine, and lamotrigine. After oral administration, lithium carbonate is generally well absorbed, dissociates completely, is not protein bound to any major extent, distributes largely in total body water with slower entry into the brain, is not metabolized, and is eliminated almost entirely by the kidney through glomerular filtration with substantial tubular reabsorption paralleling sodium handling; its half-life is commonly about 18-36 hours but is prolonged in renal impairment and the elderly. Its pharmacology is pleiotropic, with reported targets or functionally relevant effectors including glycogen synthase kinase-3 alpha and beta, inositol monophosphatase 1, inositol polyphosphate 1-phosphatase, and downstream signaling systems affecting second-messenger turnover and circadian or neurotrophic pathways. It is indicated primarily for bipolar disorder, especially acute mania and long-term relapse prevention, and is also used to reduce suicidal behavior and sometimes as augmentation in refractory major depressive disorder. Toxicity is concentration-dependent and includes narrow-therapeutic-index neurotoxicity, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy, hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, and teratogenic risk such as Ebstein anomaly; adverse effects commonly include tremor, nausea, diarrhea, polyuria, polydipsia, weight gain, edema, cognitive dulling, acne, and ataxia, while severe overdose can produce confusion, seizures, arrhythmias, and coma.

Name: Mometasone furoate
Description: Mometasone furoate (DrugBank DB14512) is a highly lipophilic synthetic corticosteroid built on the pregnane steroid nucleus, characterized by the classic four-ring glucocorticoid scaffold with a 3-keto-4-ene system, 11β- and 17-hydroxyl functionality, 21-chloro substitution, 9α-halogenation, and a 17-furoate ester that markedly enhances topical anti-inflammatory potency and receptor affinity; chemically it is a halogenated corticosteroid ester and fits the glucocorticoid steroid scaffold closely related to agents such as fluticasone, beclomethasone, budesonide, triamcinolone, and dexamethasone. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, with downstream repression of proinflammatory transcription factors including NF-κB and AP-1 and reduced expression of cytokines, chemokines, cyclooxygenase-2, and adhesion molecules. Pharmacokinetically, systemic absorption is low after intranasal or inhaled use and limited but formulation-dependent after topical administration; absorbed drug is highly protein bound, widely distributed into tissues, and undergoes extensive first-pass and hepatic CYP3A4-mediated metabolism to multiple inactive metabolites, with predominant biliary/fecal excretion and minimal renal elimination. It is indicated for allergic rhinitis, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, asthma maintenance therapy, and corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses such as atopic dermatitis, eczema, and psoriasis. Adverse effects are usually local and include epistaxis, nasal irritation, pharyngitis, headache, oral candidiasis, dysphonia, burning, pruritus, skin atrophy, and acneiform eruption; toxicity from excessive or prolonged exposure can include hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal suppression, hypercortisolism, impaired growth in children, glaucoma, cataracts, delayed wound healing, and increased infection risk, although systemic toxicity is comparatively uncommon at recommended clinical doses.

Name: Hydrocortisone acetate
Description: Hydrocortisone acetate (DrugBank DB14539) is the 21-acetate ester prodrug/derivative of hydrocortisone, a naturally occurring corticosteroid, built on the pregnane steroid nucleus with the characteristic fused four-ring cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene scaffold, a 3-keto-4-ene A-ring, 11beta-, 17alpha-, and 21-hydroxyl functionality, and esterification of the primary 21-hydroxyl as an acetate that increases lipophilicity relative to hydrocortisone. Chemically it is a glucocorticoid corticosteroid ester, closely related to hydrocortisone, cortisone acetate, prednisolone, methylprednisolone, and dexamethasone, which share the same steroidal scaffold but differ in oxidation state, unsaturation, halogenation, or ester substitution. Its principal targets are the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1 and, with weaker but clinically relevant activity, the mineralocorticoid receptor NR3C2; anti-inflammatory effects arise from receptor-mediated transcriptional repression of cytokines and induction of anti-inflammatory proteins. After topical, rectal, intra-articular, or intramuscular administration, local absorption varies with formulation, tissue integrity, and occlusion; absorbed ester is hydrolyzed to hydrocortisone, distributed widely with plasma protein binding mainly to corticosteroid-binding globulin and albumin, metabolized hepatically by reduction and conjugation, and excreted primarily in urine as inactive metabolites. Indications include corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses, pruritus, eczema, dermatitis, hemorrhoidal inflammation, ulcerative proctitis, adrenal insufficiency replacement in some settings, and inflammatory joint disease. Toxicity mirrors systemic corticosteroids: HPA-axis suppression, hyperglycemia, hypertension, infection risk, skin atrophy, poor wound healing, osteoporosis, mood changes, cataracts, and glaucoma, while common adverse effects include local irritation, burning, acneiform eruptions, edema, and Cushingoid features with prolonged or high-exposure use. Clinically, hydrocortisone acetate is used in creams, ointments, suppositories, enemas, and injectable suspensions for localized inflammatory and allergic conditions when a relatively short-acting steroid with both glucocorticoid and modest mineralocorticoid activity is desired.

Name: Hydrocortisone succinate
Description: Hydrocortisone succinate (DrugBank DB14545) is a water-soluble ester prodrug/salt form of hydrocortisone in which the endogenous corticosteroid nucleus bears a succinate moiety, typically at the 21-hydroxyl position, while retaining the classic pregnane steroid framework with a fused four-ring cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene scaffold, 3-keto-4-ene functionality, and 11β, 17α, and 21 hydroxyl groups characteristic of glucocorticoids; chemically it belongs to corticosteroids, specifically glucocorticoid corticosteroid esters, and its core scaffold is the hydrocortisone/cortisol steroid nucleus. Similar drugs include hydrocortisone sodium succinate, prednisone, prednisolone, methylprednisolone sodium succinate, dexamethasone, and cortisone acetate. After parenteral administration it is rapidly bioavailable and hydrolyzed by esterases to active hydrocortisone, distributes widely with substantial plasma protein binding mainly to corticosteroid-binding globulin and albumin, penetrates most tissues, undergoes hepatic reduction and conjugation, and is excreted predominantly in urine as glucuronide and sulfate metabolites with a relatively short plasma half-life but longer biologic effects. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, with some mineralocorticoid receptor activity at NR3C2. Indications include adrenal insufficiency, adrenal crisis, severe allergic reactions, asthma or COPD exacerbations, septic shock adjunctive therapy, autoimmune and inflammatory disorders, and cerebral edema-related inflammation. Toxicity reflects dose and duration, including hyperglycemia, hypertension, sodium and fluid retention, hypokalemia, infection risk, gastrointestinal bleeding, myopathy, osteoporosis, mood changes, psychosis, cataracts, glaucoma, HPA-axis suppression, and growth suppression in children; common adverse effects include edema, insomnia, dyspepsia, acne, and impaired wound healing. Clinically it is used intravenously or intramuscularly for rapid corticosteroid replacement or anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive therapy in acute settings such as anaphylaxis, status asthmaticus, lupus flares, ulcerative colitis flares, and perioperative stress dosing.

Name: Ivosidenib
Description: Ivosidenib (DB14568) is an orally active, small-molecule targeted antineoplastic built around a substituted heteroaromatic biaryl scaffold with fluorinated aryl elements and amide/carbamate-type functionality, giving a lipophilic, conformationally constrained structure optimized for mutant-enzyme binding; chemically, it is best classified as a synthetic heteroaryl aromatic anticancer agent and more specifically a mutant isocitrate dehydrogenase-1 inhibitor, with a scaffold related pharmacologically, though not identically, to other IDH inhibitors such as enasidenib and olutasidenib. Its principal target protein is neomorphic mutant IDH1, including common variants such as R132H and R132C, through which it lowers the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate and promotes cellular differentiation. Pharmacokinetically, ivosidenib is orally absorbed with a relatively long half-life that supports once-daily dosing, is highly protein bound, widely distributed, metabolized predominantly by CYP3A4 with potential for drug-drug interactions and autoinduction effects, and is eliminated mainly in feces with a smaller urinary component. Toxicologically, clinically important risks include QT-interval prolongation, hepatotoxicity or transaminase elevation, leukocytosis, and differentiation syndrome, which can be life-threatening in myeloid malignancies; embryo-fetal toxicity is also a concern. Adverse effects commonly include fatigue, nausea, diarrhea, decreased appetite, arthralgia, edema, rash, electrolyte abnormalities, dyspnea, and ECG changes. Clinically, it is used for IDH1-mutated acute myeloid leukemia, including newly diagnosed patients unfit for intensive therapy and relapsed or refractory disease, and for previously treated IDH1-mutated cholangiocarcinoma, exemplifying precision oncology directed by molecular testing.

Name: Tedizolid
Description: Tedizolid (DrugBank DB14569) is a synthetic oxazolidinone antibacterial administered clinically as the phosphate prodrug tedizolid phosphate and converted in vivo to the active moiety tedizolid, whose structure features a 2-oxazolidinone core bearing the characteristic aryl-oxazolidinone pharmacophore, including a fluorinated phenyl ring and a heteroaromatic D-ring that enhances potency against resistant Gram-positive organisms; chemically it belongs to the oxazolidinone class, with an aryl-substituted oxazolidinone scaffold closely related to linezolid and, more broadly, to other protein synthesis inhibitors active against resistant staphylococci and enterococci. Similar drugs include linezolid, contezolid, and radezolid analogs. Tedizolid selectively targets the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit, binding to 23S rRNA within the peptidyl transferase center and inhibiting formation of the 70S initiation complex, thereby blocking protein synthesis; its target is therefore the bacterial ribosome, especially 23S rRNA-containing 50S particles. It is indicated primarily for acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections caused by susceptible Gram-positive pathogens such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus agalactiae, Streptococcus anginosus group, and Enterococcus faecalis. Pharmacokinetically, oral bioavailability is high, allowing IV-to-oral switch, distribution is extensive into soft tissues, protein binding is high, metabolism occurs mainly by hepatic sulfation rather than CYP-dependent oxidation, and elimination is predominantly as inactive sulfate conjugates in feces and urine, with a terminal half-life permitting once-daily dosing. Toxicities and adverse effects include nausea, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, vomiting, and less commonly thrombocytopenia or other myelosuppressive effects, generally less pronounced than with prolonged linezolid exposure; peripheral neuropathy, optic neuropathy, and serotonergic interactions are considered possible class-related risks but appear uncommon with short-course use. Clinically, tedizolid is used as a once-daily short-course agent for complicated or resistant Gram-positive skin infections, especially when oral step-down therapy, MRSA coverage, or improved tolerability relative to older oxazolidinones is desired.

Name: Eslicarbazepine
Description: Eslicarbazepine (DrugBank DB14575) is a dibenzazepine-carboxamide anticonvulsant and the major active metabolite of eslicarbazepine acetate, structurally characterized by a tricyclic iminostilbene-like 10,11-dihydrodibenzazepine core bearing a 5-carboxamide and a 10-hydroxyl substituent, placing it in the same chemical family as carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine and defining its central dibenzazepine scaffold; closely related drugs include carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and licarbazepine enantiomers, which share sodium-channel-modulating antiepileptic pharmacology. Its principal targets are voltage-gated sodium channels, especially neuronal channel states associated with repetitive firing, with functional effects reported on SCN-family channels and weaker effects on T-type calcium currents. After oral administration of the prodrug, exposure to active eslicarbazepine is high, absorption is substantial, protein binding is modest, distribution is consistent with a small lipophilic CNS-active agent, metabolism is dominated by first-pass hydrolysis of eslicarbazepine acetate to eslicarbazepine with limited CYP involvement, and elimination occurs mainly by renal excretion of unchanged drug and glucuronide conjugates, supporting once-daily dosing. It is indicated primarily for focal-onset seizures in epilepsy, including partial seizures with or without secondary generalization, and is used as monotherapy or adjunctive therapy in adults and, in some settings, pediatric patients. Adverse effects commonly include dizziness, somnolence, diplopia, headache, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, and ataxia, while important toxicities include dose-related CNS depression, hyponatremia, rash or rare severe hypersensitivity reactions, hepatic enzyme elevations, and suicidal ideation risk; overdose may accentuate neurologic impairment and electrolyte disturbance.

Name: Loteprednol etabonate
Description: Loteprednol etabonate (DrugBank DB14596) is a soft corticosteroid built on the pregnane glucocorticoid steroid nucleus, specifically a prednisolone-related 17α-hydroxylated corticosteroid scaffold engineered as a 17β-chloromethyl ester and 17α-etabonate derivative with ketone and hydroxyl substituents that preserve glucocorticoid receptor activity while promoting rapid inactivation after action; chemically it is categorized as a halogenated corticosteroid anti-inflammatory ophthalmic agent, and its core scaffold is closely related to prednisolone and loteprednol analogs, with similar drugs including prednisolone acetate, fluorometholone, dexamethasone, rimexolone, and difluprednate. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor encoded by NR3C1, leading to transcriptional suppression of phospholipase A2-derived inflammatory mediators, cytokines, prostaglandins, and leukocyte trafficking. After topical ophthalmic administration, systemic absorption is typically low, ocular tissue penetration is adequate for anterior segment inflammation, protein binding is expected to be high as with related corticosteroids, metabolism occurs rapidly by ocular and systemic esterases to inactive carboxylic acid metabolites such as PJ-91, and elimination is mainly as inactive metabolites via renal and possibly biliary routes. It is indicated for steroid-responsive inflammatory conditions of the eye, including postoperative ocular inflammation and pain, allergic conjunctivitis, giant papillary conjunctivitis, anterior uveitis, keratitis, and dry eye-associated inflammation. Adverse effects include transient burning, stinging, blurred vision, foreign-body sensation, delayed wound healing, elevated intraocular pressure, glaucoma risk, cataract formation, and secondary bacterial, fungal, or herpetic infection; toxicity is dominated by class steroid effects, especially with prolonged or intensive use, although loteprednol generally shows less intraocular pressure elevation than some conventional ophthalmic steroids.

Name: Prednisolone phosphate
Description: Prednisolone phosphate (DrugBank DB14631) is a water-soluble phosphate ester prodrug of prednisolone, built on the pregnane corticosteroid framework with the classic four-ring cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene steroid nucleus, oxygenation at key glucocorticoid positions, a 1,4-diene-3-ketone A-ring, and a phosphate ester typically attached at the 21-hydroxyl to enhance aqueous solubility for parenteral or ophthalmic use; chemically it belongs to the glucocorticoid corticosteroids and more specifically to synthetic anti-inflammatory steroid phosphate esters, with a prednisolone scaffold closely related to prednisone, methylprednisolone, hydrocortisone, dexamethasone, betamethasone, and prednisolone sodium phosphate. After administration it is rapidly hydrolyzed by phosphatases to active prednisolone; systemic absorption is efficient after oral or injectable dosing and can occur from topical ophthalmic use, distribution is wide with substantial plasma protein binding mainly to albumin and corticosteroid-binding globulin, metabolism occurs predominantly in the liver via reduction and conjugation pathways with contributions from CYP3A-mediated biotransformation, and metabolites plus unchanged drug are excreted mainly in urine. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, with downstream transrepression of NF-kB and AP-1 signaling and broad suppression of cytokine production; mineralocorticoid receptor activity is comparatively weak. Indications include acute allergic reactions, asthma or COPD exacerbations, autoimmune and rheumatic disorders, inflammatory eye disease, dermatologic inflammation, inflammatory bowel disease, nephrotic syndrome, and hematologic malignancy-associated inflammation. Toxicities mirror systemic corticosteroids: hyperglycemia, hypertension, infection risk, adrenal suppression, osteoporosis, psychosis, cataracts, glaucoma, peptic injury, myopathy, growth suppression, and fluid retention, while common adverse effects include dyspepsia, mood change, insomnia, weight gain, edema, and delayed wound healing. Clinically it is used when rapid anti-inflammatory or immunosuppressive glucocorticoid exposure and improved formulation solubility are desired, such as intravenous treatment of severe inflammation, oral therapy for steroid-responsive disease, and ophthalmic treatment of postoperative or uveitic inflammation.

Name: Diloxanide furoate
Description: Diloxanide furoate (DrugBank DB14638) is a dichloroacetamide-derived luminal amebicide whose structure consists of a substituted acetanilide-like aromatic core bearing a dichloroacetamide moiety and esterification with furoic acid, giving a lipophilic aryl amide-ester framework; chemically it is best classified as a halogenated aromatic amide and furoate ester, built on a simple anilide/dichloroacetanilide scaffold rather than a complex heteropolycycle. It is often discussed alongside other antiamoebic agents with related therapeutic use, including diloxanide, metronidazole, tinidazole, paromomycin, and iodoquinol, although these are not close structural analogs. Its pharmacokinetics are characterized by oral administration with partial intestinal absorption, intraluminal persistence that supports activity against Entamoeba histolytica cysts in the bowel, hydrolysis to diloxanide, limited tissue penetration relative to nitroimidazoles, hepatic metabolism with conjugative biotransformation, and predominantly urinary excretion of absorbed metabolites with some fecal elimination of unabsorbed drug. The precise molecular target proteins are not well established, and its effect is generally described as direct luminal antiamoebic activity rather than a defined single-protein mechanism. Clinically, it is indicated for asymptomatic intestinal amebiasis and eradication of the carrier state, and it has also been used after metronidazole or tinidazole for invasive disease to clear residual colonic infection. Toxicity is usually mild, with gastrointestinal irritation, flatulence, nausea, abdominal cramps, and pruritus or urticaria reported; more serious toxicity is uncommon, but use is generally avoided in very young infants and approached cautiously in pregnancy.

Name: Isoflupredone acetate
Description: Isoflupredone acetate (DB14640) is a fluorinated synthetic corticosteroid built on the pregnane steroid nucleus, specifically a hydrocortisone/prednisolone-like four-ring cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene scaffold bearing the characteristic 3-keto-4-ene A-ring, 11beta-, 17alpha-, and 21-hydroxyl functionality, a 9alpha-fluoro substituent that enhances glucocorticoid potency, and a 21-acetate ester that increases lipophilicity and formulation utility; chemically it is classified as a glucocorticoid corticosteroid ester and more broadly as a halogenated steroid anti-inflammatory agent. Structurally and pharmacologically it resembles prednisolone acetate, dexamethasone, fludrocortisone, triamcinolone, and hydrocortisone derivatives. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor, NR3C1, with downstream transrepression of proinflammatory mediators such as NF-kappaB- and AP-1-regulated cytokines; like related steroids it may also show some mineralocorticoid activity. Pharmacokinetic data are limited, but after parenteral veterinary administration it is expected to be absorbed systemically, distributed widely with plasma protein binding, hydrolyzed from the acetate ester, metabolized hepatically by steroid-reduction and conjugation pathways, and excreted mainly in urine with some biliary/fecal elimination. Toxicity is consistent with corticosteroid excess, including dose-related immunosuppression, hyperglycemia, muscle wasting, delayed wound healing, gastrointestinal ulceration, adrenal suppression, and increased infection risk; severe examples include iatrogenic hyperadrenocorticism or laminitis in susceptible animals. Adverse effects include polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, behavioral change, edema, and electrolyte disturbances. Clinically, isoflupredone acetate has been used primarily in veterinary medicine as an anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive agent, for example in bovine ketosis adjunctive therapy, musculoskeletal inflammation, allergic conditions, and other steroid-responsive inflammatory disorders.

Name: Chlorphenesin carbamate
Description: Chlorphenesin carbamate (DrugBank DB14656) is a centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant derived from chlorphenesin in which a chlorinated phenoxypropanediol core is functionalized as a carbamate, giving an aryl ether–propane-1,2-diol–carbamate architecture that places it in the carbamate and phenoxy alcohol chemical categories and on a chlorinated phenoxypropanol scaffold closely related to mephenesin-type relaxants. Structurally and pharmacologically it is similar to chlorphenesin, mephenesin, methocarbamol, and other older centrally acting muscle relaxants, with activity generally attributed to depression of polysynaptic transmission in the spinal cord and brainstem rather than a highly selective receptor interaction; accordingly, no single validated molecular target protein is firmly established, though functional effects are consistent with CNS interneuronal inhibition, and specific high-confidence human target proteins are not well defined. After oral administration it is understood to be absorbed systemically, distributed into well-perfused tissues including the CNS, metabolized mainly in the liver by carbamate hydrolysis and conjugative pathways to more polar metabolites, and excreted predominantly in urine, with older agents in this class typically showing relatively short to moderate duration of action. Its indication and clinical use have been for relief of acute painful musculoskeletal spasm, muscle hypertonicity, and related symptoms such as low back pain, strain, sprain, and tension-associated stiffness. Adverse effects commonly include drowsiness, dizziness, weakness, ataxia, blurred vision, and gastrointestinal upset, while toxicity is dominated by dose-related CNS depression, impaired coordination, confusion, hypotension, and in overdose potentially respiratory depression or coma, with risk amplified by alcohol, sedatives, or other CNS depressants.

Name: Larotrectinib
Description: Larotrectinib (DrugBank DB14723) is a small-molecule, orally active tropomyosin receptor kinase inhibitor built around a compact heteroaromatic kinase-binding scaffold featuring a substituted pyrazolo/pyrrolopyrimidine-like core linked to aromatic amide and hydroxypyrrolidine-containing motifs that support ATP-site binding and kinase selectivity; chemically, it is best classified as a targeted antineoplastic, heteroaryl amide, and TRK-directed kinase inhibitor, with a scaffold broadly related to other neurotrophic tyrosine receptor kinase inhibitors such as entrectinib and the second-generation TRK inhibitor selitrectinib, although larotrectinib is distinguished by high potency and relative selectivity for TRKA, TRKB, and TRKC, encoded by NTRK1, NTRK2, and NTRK3. It is indicated for solid tumors harboring NTRK gene fusions regardless of histology, including infantile fibrosarcoma, secretory breast carcinoma, salivary gland secretory carcinoma, thyroid cancer, lung cancer, and other advanced or metastatic fusion-positive cancers. After oral administration it is rapidly absorbed, reaches peak concentrations in roughly 1 hour, shows moderate protein binding and broad tissue distribution, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4/5, and is eliminated through both feces and urine primarily as metabolites, with a relatively short half-life that supports twice-daily dosing. Toxicity is generally manageable but includes hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevations, neurotoxicity such as dizziness or ataxia, and occasional embryo-fetal risk; common adverse effects include fatigue, nausea, vomiting, constipation, diarrhea, anemia, cough, weight gain, and increased AST/ALT. Clinically, it is used as precision therapy in unresectable, metastatic, or surgery-morbid NTRK fusion cancers, often producing rapid and durable responses across adult and pediatric populations.

Name: Solriamfetol
Description: Solriamfetol (DB14754) is a small, chiral phenylpropylamine-derived central nervous system stimulant whose structure is characterized by a para-hydroxylated phenyl ring attached to a three-carbon side chain bearing a terminal primary amine and a secondary alcohol, giving an aminophenyl alcohol motif that resembles substituted amphetamine-like wake-promoting agents while remaining distinct from classical catecholamines; chemically it is categorized as a phenylalaninol/phenylpropylamine norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor, with a simple aryl-alkanolamine scaffold. Similar drugs include bupropion, modafinil, armodafinil, methylphenidate, and amphetamine, which share stimulant or wake-promoting pharmacology but differ in scaffold and transporter selectivity. Its principal known targets are the dopamine transporter SLC6A3 and norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2, at which it functions primarily as a reuptake inhibitor with minimal direct monoamine releasing activity. After oral administration, solriamfetol is well absorbed, has high bioavailability, reaches peak plasma concentrations in about 2 hours, exhibits limited protein binding, distributes systemically without extensive tissue sequestration, undergoes minimal metabolism, and is eliminated largely unchanged in urine with a terminal half-life of roughly 7 hours, making renal function a major determinant of exposure. It is indicated to improve wakefulness in adults with excessive daytime sleepiness associated with narcolepsy or obstructive sleep apnea, for example persistent sleepiness despite primary OSA therapy. Adverse effects commonly include headache, nausea, decreased appetite, anxiety, insomnia, dry mouth, palpitations, and dose-related increases in blood pressure and heart rate. Toxicity is chiefly sympathomimetic and neuropsychiatric, with overdose or susceptible patients potentially developing marked hypertension, tachycardia, agitation, or insomnia; clinically it is used as a once-daily wake-promoting agent, especially when residual hypersomnolence limits daytime functioning.

Name: Rivoceranib
Description: Rivoceranib (also known as apatinib; DrugBank DB14765) is an orally active small-molecule antineoplastic tyrosine kinase inhibitor whose structure is built around a substituted heteroaromatic scaffold, commonly described as a diaryl urea-like/pyridyl-amide kinase-binding chemotype with lipophilic aryl substituents and basic heterocyclic functionality that supports ATP-pocket binding; chemically it is categorized as a synthetic VEGFR-directed receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor, and its core scaffold is most closely aligned with the class of VEGFR/PDGFR inhibitor pharmacophores seen in agents such as sorafenib, axitinib, sunitinib, pazopanib, and regorafenib, although rivoceranib is particularly notable for potent VEGFR2 selectivity. Its principal target protein is vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2, also known as KDR/FLK1, with weaker reported activity against related kinases including RET, c-KIT, SRC, and PDGFR-family members in some profiling systems. Pharmacokinetically, it is orally absorbed, distributed systemically with substantial tissue penetration and moderate to high protein binding, metabolized predominantly in the liver via oxidative biotransformation, including CYP3A4-mediated pathways, and excreted through both fecal and urinary routes as parent drug and metabolites. Toxicity is largely class-related and antiangiogenic, including dose-limiting hypertension, proteinuria, hemorrhage, gastrointestinal toxicity, hepatotoxicity, delayed wound healing, and rare thromboembolic or gastrointestinal perforation events. Common adverse effects include hand-foot syndrome, fatigue, diarrhea, anorexia, nausea, mucositis, and myelosuppression. Clinically, rivoceranib is used as an antiangiogenic therapy in advanced malignancy, especially gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma after chemotherapy, and has also been investigated or used in hepatocellular carcinoma, breast cancer, lung cancer, sarcoma, and other refractory solid tumors.

Name: Diroximel fumarate
Description: Diroximel fumarate (DB14783) is an orally active small-molecule fumaric acid ester prodrug structurally characterized by an activated fumarate alkene bearing ester functionality and a substituted carbamate/alkoxyethyl promoiety designed to improve gastrointestinal tolerability while delivering the electrophilic monomethyl fumarate metabolite; chemically it belongs to the fumarate ester class and is built on a fumarate scaffold closely related to dimethyl fumarate and other Nrf2-activating Michael acceptors, with similar drugs including dimethyl fumarate and monomethyl fumarate, and more distantly other multiple-sclerosis disease-modifying agents such as fingolimod or teriflunomide by indication rather than structure. After oral administration it is rapidly presystemically hydrolyzed by esterases to monomethyl fumarate, with low parent-drug systemic exposure, absorption sufficient for twice-daily dosing, distribution of the active metabolite into the systemic circulation, further metabolism through the tricarboxylic acid pathway, and elimination predominantly as exhaled carbon dioxide with minor renal and fecal excretion. Its pharmacology is driven mainly by covalent electrophilic modulation of KEAP1 leading to NFE2L2/Nrf2 activation and downstream antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and immunomodulatory signaling, with additional effects reported on HCAR2 and suppression of NF-kB-related pathways. It is indicated for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis, including clinically isolated syndrome, relapsing-remitting disease, and active secondary progressive disease, and is used clinically to reduce relapse frequency and new MRI lesion formation. Important adverse effects and toxicities include flushing, abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, elevated hepatic enzymes, lymphopenia, proteinuria, hypersensitivity, opportunistic infection risk including progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in severely immunosuppressed patients, and potential hepatotoxicity, so monitoring of blood counts, liver tests, and infection risk is standard in practice.

Name: Ripretinib
Description: Ripretinib (DB14840) is an orally active small-molecule type II switch-control kinase inhibitor built around a heteroaromatic urea-containing scaffold that links substituted aromatic/heteroaryl rings into a conformationally flexible ATP-site binder; chemically it is best classified as a multikinase inhibitor within the broader class of diaryl/heteroaryl urea antineoplastic agents, and its core scaffold is designed to engage both the switch pocket and activation loop of class III receptor tyrosine kinases. It is structurally and pharmacologically related to other KIT/PDGFRA-directed tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib, sunitinib, regorafenib, and avapritinib, although ripretinib is distinguished by broad activity against activation-loop and ATP-binding-pocket resistance mutations. Its principal targets are KIT and PDGFRA, with additional activity reported against kinases including PDGFRB, CSF1R, TIE2/TEK, VEGFR2/KDR, and BRAF in some profiling systems. Clinically, it is indicated primarily for advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumor, especially after progression on multiple prior TKIs, including disease driven by KIT exon 11, exon 13, exon 17, or PDGFRA mutant tumors. After oral administration it is absorbed with a time to peak of a few hours, is highly protein bound, widely distributed, metabolized mainly by CYP3A4 to an active metabolite, and eliminated predominantly in feces with a terminal half-life on the order of roughly 15 hours for parent and active metabolite. Toxicities include palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia, hypertension, cardiomyopathy, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, hepatotoxicity, and embryo-fetal toxicity; common adverse effects include alopecia, fatigue, myalgia, nausea, abdominal pain, constipation, and diarrhea. In practice it is used as chronic oral targeted therapy for refractory or metastatic GIST to prolong progression-free survival and provide disease control in heavily pretreated patients.

Name: Filgotinib
