Description: Filgotinib (DB14845) is an orally active, small-molecule aminopyrimidine-based heteroaromatic anti-inflammatory agent whose structure is centered on a substituted pyrrolidine linked to a fluorinated aromatic/heteroaromatic system and a pyrimidine-like kinase-binding motif, placing it in the Janus kinase inhibitor class and more specifically within the targeted synthetic DMARD category; its key scaffold is a JAK-binding aza-heterocycle appended to a conformationally constrained nitrogen-containing ring system, broadly similar to other ATP-competitive JAK inhibitors such as tofacitinib, upadacitinib, baricitinib, and peficitinib, though filgotinib is relatively JAK1-selective. Its principal target protein is JAK1, with weaker activity at JAK2, JAK3, and TYK2, thereby modulating downstream STAT signaling and cytokine pathways including IL-6, interferons, and other inflammatory mediators. Clinically, it has been developed and used for inflammatory disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis and ulcerative colitis, especially in patients with inadequate response to conventional DMARDs or biologics. After oral administration it is well absorbed, reaches peak concentrations within hours, distributes systemically, and undergoes prominent carboxylesterase-mediated metabolism to an active major metabolite with a long half-life that materially contributes to efficacy; elimination is mainly renal as parent drug and metabolites, supporting once-daily dosing. Toxicity concerns are broadly class-related and include serious infection risk, herpes zoster, opportunistic infections, laboratory abnormalities, possible venous thromboembolism signal, embryo-fetal risk, and concern for effects on spermatogenesis seen in nonclinical and dedicated reproductive safety evaluation. Common adverse effects include nausea, upper respiratory infection, urinary tract infection, dizziness, and elevated liver enzymes.

Name: Cefiderocol
Description: Cefiderocol (DB14879) is a synthetic siderophore cephalosporin antibiotic whose structure combines a cephalosporin beta-lactam core fused to a dihydrothiazine ring with distinctive side chains, including a catechol-containing chlorinated oxyiminoacyl moiety that chelates ferric iron and a pyrrolidinium substituent that enhances Gram-negative penetration and beta-lactam stability; chemically it is a beta-lactam, specifically an advanced parenteral cephalosporin, built on the cephalosporin/cephem scaffold and mechanistically related to antipseudomonal cephalosporins such as ceftazidime and cefepime, with broader resemblance to other siderophore-inspired agents though it is structurally unique. It enters bacteria via iron transport systems and inhibits cell-wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins, especially PBP3, with activity against multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, and Enterobacterales. Pharmacokinetically, cefiderocol is given intravenously, has linear exposure, low-to-moderate protein binding, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid with therapeutic pulmonary and urinary penetration, undergoes minimal metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by the kidney, requiring dose adjustment in renal impairment and augmented clearance states. Toxicities and adverse effects are broadly cephalosporin-like and include hypersensitivity reactions, infusion-site reactions, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, rash, elevated hepatic enzymes, candidiasis, and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea, with neurotoxicity or seizures possible in predisposed patients and a reported mortality imbalance in some critically ill carbapenem-resistant infection cohorts. Clinically it is used for complicated urinary tract infection, hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated bacterial pneumonia, and serious infections caused by aerobic Gram-negative organisms when limited alternatives exist, particularly carbapenem-resistant infections.

Name: Oliceridine
Description: Oliceridine (DrugBank DB14881) is a small-molecule, centrally acting opioid analgesic with a synthetic aromatic amine structure characterized by a substituted piperidine-containing, phenyl-linked framework bearing tertiary amine functionality and methoxy-substituted aryl features that confer high lipophilicity and rapid CNS penetration; chemically it is categorized as a biased mu-opioid receptor agonist within the opioid/anilidopiperidine-related analgesic space, and its core scaffold is best described as a functionalized piperidine arylalkyl amine scaffold. It is pharmacologically similar to other strong MOR agonists such as morphine, fentanyl, sufentanil, and hydromorphone, although it was developed to favor G-protein signaling over beta-arrestin recruitment. Its principal target is the mu-opioid receptor encoded by OPRM1, with no clinically central secondary targets established. Oliceridine is indicated for the management of acute severe pain in adults when intravenous opioid therapy is needed, for example postoperative pain after orthopedic, abdominal, or gynecologic surgery, especially when alternative treatments are inadequate. After IV administration it has rapid onset, broad tissue distribution, hepatic metabolism predominantly via CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 to largely inactive metabolites, and elimination mainly in urine with some fecal excretion; exposure can increase in hepatic impairment or with CYP inhibitors. Toxicities are opioid-typical and dose related, notably respiratory depression, profound sedation, hypoxia, bradycardia, hypotension, abuse liability, dependence, and possible serotonin-related risk with interacting drugs. Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, constipation, dizziness, somnolence, headache, pruritus, and oxygen desaturation. Clinically, it is used in monitored settings as intermittent IV bolus or patient-controlled analgesia for short-term treatment of moderate-to-severe acute pain.

Name: Enarodustat
Description: Enarodustat (DB14985) is an orally active small-molecule hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor characterized by a compact heteroaromatic, nitrogen-rich structure containing fused aza-heterocyclic/aromatic ring elements and polar carbonyl- and heteroatom-bearing substituents that support iron-chelating interaction within the prolyl hydroxylase catalytic site; chemically it is best categorized as a synthetic HIF-prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor and more broadly as a heteroaromatic enzyme inhibitor, with a scaffold related to other non-erythropoietin oral anti-anemia agents built around an aromatic/azaheterocyclic PHD-binding core. Similar drugs include roxadustat, daprodustat, vadadustat, molidustat, and desidustat, all of which stabilize HIF by inhibiting EGLN/PHD enzymes. Its principal known targets are HIF prolyl hydroxylase domain proteins EGLN1/PHD2, EGLN2/PHD1, and EGLN3/PHD3, leading to reduced HIF-alpha hydroxylation, HIF stabilization, increased endogenous erythropoietin signaling, and modulation of iron-handling genes. Enarodustat is used for anemia, especially anemia associated with chronic kidney disease, including patients not adequately managed with erythropoiesis-stimulating strategies. Pharmacokinetically, it is orally absorbed, systemically distributed with expected moderate protein binding, metabolized primarily hepatically through oxidative and conjugative pathways, and eliminated via both renal and fecal routes as parent drug and metabolites; exposure may vary with hepatic or renal impairment. Adverse effects reported or expected for the class include hypertension, thromboembolic risk, headache, gastrointestinal upset, edema, and increases in hemoglobin if overcorrected; toxicity concerns include excessive erythropoiesis, cardiovascular events, and possible class concerns regarding tumor progression or retinopathy under prolonged HIF activation. Clinically, it is used as a chronic oral therapy to raise hemoglobin, reduce transfusion requirements, and improve anemia-related fatigue in CKD populations.

Name: Difamilast
Description: Difamilast (DB14987) is a small-molecule boron-containing topical anti-inflammatory agent structurally characterized by a low-molecular-weight heteroaromatic framework bearing a boronic acid pharmacophore linked to an amide-containing aromatic system, a motif designed to support potent phosphodiesterase inhibition while maintaining suitable skin penetration; chemically it is classified as a boronic acid derivative and, pharmacologically, as a topical phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor, with a boron-centered PDE4-inhibitor scaffold distinct from the catechol- or fused-heteroaryl-rich cores seen in some older agents. Similar drugs include other PDE4 inhibitors such as crisaborole, apremilast, roflumilast, and topical roflumilast formulations, although difamilast is most closely aligned with crisaborole by topical anti-inflammatory use. Its principal known targets are PDE4 isoforms, especially PDE4B and PDE4D, leading to increased intracellular cAMP and downstream suppression of proinflammatory cytokine signaling. Difamilast is indicated primarily for atopic dermatitis, particularly mild to moderate eczema with pruritus, erythema, and chronic relapsing inflammatory lesions, and clinically it is used as a nonsteroidal topical option for pediatric and adult patients, including sensitive skin areas where corticosteroid-sparing treatment is desirable. After dermal administration, systemic absorption is generally low, distribution is expected to be limited by low plasma exposure, metabolism appears to occur mainly via hepatic biotransformation pathways with subsequent formation of inactive metabolites, and excretion is presumed to proceed predominantly through renal and biliary routes as metabolites. Toxicity is chiefly local rather than systemic, with low risk of serious organ toxicity at therapeutic exposure; reported or expected adverse effects include application-site burning, stinging, pain, irritation, erythema, pruritus, and occasional contact dermatitis, while serious systemic PDE4-class toxicities such as gastrointestinal or neuropsychiatric effects are considered uncommon because of minimal systemic exposure.

Name: Umbralisib
Description: Umbralisib (DB14989) is an orally active small-molecule kinase inhibitor with a heteroaromatic, polycyclic structure built around a substituted quinazoline/quinazolinone-like fused nitrogen-containing aromatic scaffold linked to additional aryl and polar heterocyclic substituents that optimize phosphoinositide 3-kinase binding; chemically, it is best classified as a targeted antineoplastic kinase inhibitor, specifically a PI3K inhibitor, with a scaffold related to other ATP-competitive heteroaryl kinase inhibitors. It is most similar pharmacologically to other PI3K-pathway drugs such as idelalisib, duvelisib, copanlisib, and to some extent the dual CK1 epsilon/PI3K-directed inhibitor class, although umbralisib is distinguished by relative selectivity for PI3K-delta and inhibition of casein kinase 1 epsilon (CSNK1E). Its principal targets are PI3K-delta (PIK3CD) and CSNK1E, suppressing B-cell receptor signaling and malignant B-cell survival. Clinically it has been used for relapsed or refractory marginal zone lymphoma after prior anti-CD20-based therapy and relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma after multiple prior systemic regimens, with utility in indolent B-cell malignancies characterized by lymphadenopathy and marrow involvement. After oral administration it is absorbed systemically with a time to peak in the low-hour range, is highly protein bound, distributed into tissues, metabolized mainly hepatically through oxidative and conjugative pathways involving CYP3A4 and related enzymes, and excreted predominantly in feces with a lesser urinary component; its half-life supports once-daily dosing. Toxicities include hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevation, severe diarrhea/colitis, opportunistic and serious infections, neutropenia, rash, and less commonly pneumonitis, while common adverse effects include diarrhea, nausea, fatigue, elevated liver enzymes, cytopenias, and infections; accordingly, clinical use has required monitoring of liver tests, blood counts, gastrointestinal toxicity, and infectious complications.

Name: Avacopan
Description: Avacopan (DrugBank DB15011) is a small-molecule, orally active complement-pathway modulator built as a lipophilic heteroaromatic amide/urea-like drug with multiple fused and substituted ring systems, including nitrogen-containing aromatic/partially saturated heterocycles and halogenated hydrophobic motifs that optimize potency and oral exposure; chemically it is best classified as a synthetic heteroaryl anti-inflammatory/immunomodulatory agent, and its scaffold is commonly described as a substituted polycyclic heteroaromatic complement C5a receptor antagonist framework. It is most similar pharmacologically to other C5a-axis inhibitors such as vilobelimab and other experimental C5aR1 antagonists, although these may differ structurally and in route of administration. Its principal target is complement C5a receptor 1, also called C5AR1 or CD88, on neutrophils and other myeloid cells, where it blocks C5a-driven chemotaxis, activation, endothelial injury, and amplification of small-vessel inflammation. Clinically, avacopan is indicated as an adjunctive treatment for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-associated vasculitis, especially granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis, as a steroid-sparing agent used with rituximab or cyclophosphamide-based regimens. It is orally absorbed, highly protein bound, hepatically metabolized predominantly by CYP3A4, and eliminated mainly through biliary/fecal routes with limited renal clearance; exposure is therefore affected by strong CYP3A4 inhibitors or inducers and by hepatic impairment. Toxicity concerns include hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevations, possible increased susceptibility to infection, and hypersensitivity; common adverse effects include nausea, headache, diarrhea, fatigue, vomiting, rash, pyrexia, nasopharyngitis, and upper respiratory tract infection.

Name: Daridorexant
Description: Daridorexant (DrugBank DB15031) is a small-molecule dual orexin receptor antagonist characterized structurally by a compact, lipophilic heteroaromatic architecture containing substituted aromatic/heterocyclic rings linked through amide-like functionality and chiral elements that support high-affinity CNS receptor binding; chemically it is categorized as an orexin receptor antagonist and more broadly as a centrally acting sedative-hypnotic, with a scaffold distinct from benzodiazepines and built around a diaryl/heteroaryl amide-like insomnia-drug framework optimized for OX1R/OX2R antagonism. Similar drugs include other dual orexin receptor antagonists such as suvorexant and lemborexant, and more distantly almorexant, which share the same mechanistic class but differ in scaffold and pharmacokinetic behavior. Its known targets are orexin receptor type 1 and orexin receptor type 2, through which it suppresses wake-promoting orexin signaling. After oral administration daridorexant is absorbed adequately for once-nightly dosing, reaches peak concentrations within a few hours, distributes systemically with substantial protein binding, undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism predominantly via CYP3A4 to inactive metabolites, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in feces with a lesser renal contribution; its terminal half-life is relatively short compared with some class peers, limiting next-day residual effects. Toxicity is principally pharmacodynamic, including excessive CNS depression, next-day somnolence, impaired driving or psychomotor performance, falls, and potential worsening with alcohol or other sedatives; overdose would be expected to produce marked sedation. It is indicated for insomnia, especially difficulty with sleep onset and sleep maintenance, and is used clinically in adults with chronic insomnia symptoms to improve total sleep time and reduce nocturnal awakenings. Common adverse effects include somnolence, fatigue, dizziness, headache, and rarely complex sleep behaviors, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic phenomena, or worsening depression/suicidal ideation in susceptible patients.

Name: Omidenepag isopropyl
Description: Omidenepag isopropyl (DB15071) is a small-molecule ocular hypotensive agent designed as an isopropyl ester prodrug of omidenepag, featuring a lipophilic aromatic prostanoid-mimetic architecture built around a substituted benzoic/aryl core linked to a heteroaryl-containing side chain rather than the classic prostaglandin F2α carbocyclic skeleton; accordingly, it is classified as a selective prostanoid EP2 receptor agonist and more broadly as an antiglaucoma prostaglandin-related agent, with a non-prostanoid prostanoid-receptor agonist scaffold. Similar drugs include FP-receptor prostaglandin analogs such as latanoprost, travoprost, tafluprost, and bimatoprost, although omidenepag differs mechanistically by targeting PTGER2 rather than FP. After topical ophthalmic administration, the isopropyl ester enhances corneal penetration and is rapidly hydrolyzed by ocular esterases to active omidenepag; systemic exposure is generally low, distribution is largely confined to ocular tissues, metabolism proceeds through further oxidative and conjugative pathways, and elimination occurs predominantly as metabolites via renal and/or biliary routes. Its principal target protein is the prostaglandin E receptor 2, activation of which increases aqueous humor outflow, particularly through the conventional and uveoscleral pathways, lowering intraocular pressure. It is indicated for glaucoma and ocular hypertension, for example primary open-angle glaucoma and patients requiring monotherapy IOP reduction. Adverse effects are mainly local, including conjunctival hyperemia, eye pain, punctate keratitis, photophobia, blurred vision, and mild inflammation; unlike FP analogs it may show less eyelash growth or iris pigmentation, but it can still cause ocular irritation and rare cystoid macular edema risk in susceptible eyes. Clinically, it is used as once-daily ophthalmic therapy when reduction of elevated intraocular pressure is needed, including in patients intolerant of or insufficiently controlled by other topical hypotensive agents.

Name: Upadacitinib
Description: Upadacitinib (DB15091) is a synthetic small-molecule Janus kinase inhibitor built around a fused azaindole-like bicyclic heteroaromatic scaffold linked to a substituted pyrazole/piperidine-containing side chain, yielding a lipophilic, nitrogen-rich kinase-binding structure optimized for oral activity and relative JAK1 selectivity; chemically it is best classified as a targeted heteroaryl kinase inhibitor and functionally belongs to the jakinib class. Its scaffold and ATP-competitive mechanism make it structurally and pharmacologically related to other JAK inhibitors such as tofacitinib, baricitinib, filgotinib, and abrocitinib, although it is generally described as more JAK1-selective than earlier agents. The principal target protein is JAK1, with lesser inhibitory activity against JAK2, JAK3, and TYK2 at higher exposures, thereby modulating cytokine signaling through pathways involving interleukins, interferons, and other inflammatory mediators. After oral administration it is well absorbed, reaches peak plasma concentrations within a few hours, displays moderate protein binding, and is metabolized predominantly by CYP3A4 with a minor contribution from CYP2D6; elimination occurs through both metabolism and renal/fecal excretion, with a terminal half-life supporting once-daily dosing. Toxicities reflect immunomodulation and include serious infections such as herpes zoster, opportunistic infection, pneumonia, malignancy risk, major adverse cardiovascular events, venous thromboembolism, laboratory abnormalities including lymphopenia, neutropenia, anemia, transaminase elevation, and lipid increases. Approved and common clinical uses include moderate-to-severe rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, atopic dermatitis, ulcerative colitis, ankylosing spondylitis, and non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis, where it is used to reduce pain, swelling, stiffness, skin inflammation, and other manifestations of immune-mediated disease.

Name: Gefapixant
Description: Gefapixant (DB15097) is a small-molecule, non-opioid sensory-neuron modulator structurally characterized as a substituted heteroaryl amide containing a compact nitrogen-rich bicyclic/heteroaromatic core linked to lipophilic aryl functionality, placing it in the chemical category of synthetic P2X purinergic receptor antagonists; its scaffold is best described as a medicinal-chemistry-optimized fused aza-heterocyclic antagonist framework designed for oral activity and P2X3 selectivity. Similar drugs include other P2X3 antagonists such as eliapixant, sivopixant, and BLU-5937, which were developed for chronic cough and related hypersensitization disorders. Its principal known target protein is the ATP-gated purinergic receptor P2X3, with functional activity also discussed at heteromeric P2X2/3 receptors on vagal afferent sensory fibers, thereby reducing pathologic cough reflex signaling. Pharmacokinetically, gefapixant is orally absorbed, reaches systemic circulation adequately for twice-daily dosing, shows moderate plasma protein binding and broad tissue distribution without extreme accumulation, undergoes limited oxidative biotransformation with a meaningful fraction eliminated as unchanged drug, and is cleared through combined renal and metabolic routes, making renal function relevant to exposure. Toxicity is generally dominated by mechanism-related sensory adverse effects rather than major organ toxicity; dose-limiting examples include dysgeusia, hypogeusia, ageusia, and occasional nausea, while severe hepatotoxicity or cardiotoxicity has not been a defining signal in trials. Clinically, it is indicated for refractory or unexplained chronic cough, including patients with persistent cough despite treatment of contributory conditions such as asthma, gastroesophageal reflux, or upper airway cough syndrome, and its practical use is as an oral antitussive for symptom reduction and quality-of-life improvement in chronic cough populations.

Name: Pemigatinib
Description: Pemigatinib (DB15102) is a synthetic, orally active small-molecule antineoplastic that functions as a selective fibroblast growth factor receptor inhibitor, chemically characterized as a heteroaromatic kinase inhibitor containing a substituted triazine/pyrrolopyridine-like fused aza-heterocyclic core linked through aryl ether/amine-type connections to fluorinated and methoxy-substituted aromatic rings, a design typical of ATP-competitive tyrosine kinase inhibitors; thus it falls within the chemical category of targeted anticancer kinase inhibitors and more specifically the scaffold class of FGFR-directed aza-heteroaryl ATP mimetics. Similar drugs include other FGFR inhibitors such as infigratinib, futibatinib, erdafitinib, and derazantinib, as well as broader multikinase inhibitors with FGFR activity such as lenvatinib and pazopanib. Its principal targets are FGFR1, FGFR2, and FGFR3, with particular clinical relevance for oncogenic FGFR2 fusions/rearrangements. Pharmacokinetically, pemigatinib is orally absorbed with clinically useful bioavailability, reaches systemic distribution with moderate protein binding, is metabolized predominantly by CYP3A4, and is eliminated through both fecal and urinary routes, with dose adjustment or interaction concern when strong CYP3A modulators are coadministered. Toxicities are largely mechanism-based and include hyperphosphatemia from FGFR blockade, retinal pigment epithelial detachment/serous retinopathy, nail and skin toxicity, and embryo-fetal risk; common adverse effects include stomatitis, diarrhea, fatigue, alopecia, dry mouth, dysgeusia, arthralgia, constipation, abdominal pain, and ocular symptoms. Clinically, it is used primarily for previously treated, unresectable or metastatic cholangiocarcinoma harboring FGFR2 fusions or rearrangements, and has also been used in myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with FGFR1 rearrangement, exemplifying precision oncology use in biomarker-selected tumors.

Name: Tepotinib
Description: Tepotinib (DB15133) is an orally active, small-molecule, type Ib MET receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor built on a heteroaromatic kinase-inhibitor framework featuring a substituted benzimidazole/pyridazine-like fused aza-heterocyclic core linked to lipophilic aryl and nitrogen-containing substituents that optimize ATP-pocket binding, placing it in the chemical category of targeted antineoplastic aminopyridine/aza-heteroaryl kinase inhibitors and giving it the canonical c-MET inhibitor scaffold seen across selective MET TKIs. Structurally and pharmacologically similar drugs include capmatinib, savolitinib, and the multikinase inhibitor crizotinib, all used in MET-driven malignancies. Its principal target is the hepatocyte growth factor receptor MET, with antitumor activity driven by blockade of aberrant MET signaling in tumors harboring MET exon 14 skipping alterations and, in some settings, MET amplification or overexpression. Tepotinib is indicated primarily for metastatic non-small cell lung cancer with MET exon 14 skipping, for example advanced lung adenocarcinoma progressing after standard therapy, and is used clinically as precision oral monotherapy in biomarker-selected patients. Pharmacokinetically, it is orally absorbed with a relatively long half-life permitting once-daily dosing, is highly protein bound, distributes systemically, undergoes limited oxidative biotransformation with CYP3A4 participation and substantial unchanged parent drug exposure, and is eliminated predominantly via feces with minor renal excretion. Toxicities are characteristic of MET inhibition and include peripheral edema, pleural effusion, hypoalbuminemia, nausea, diarrhea, fatigue, and increased transaminases; clinically important adverse reactions include interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis, hepatotoxicity, and embryo-fetal toxicity, with dose interruption or reduction used for severe edema, liver enzyme elevations, or pulmonary symptoms.

Name: Pemafibrate
Description: Pemafibrate (DB15212) is a selective peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha modulator, or SPPARMα, structurally characterized as an aromatic carboxylic acid–containing fibrate derivative with a phenoxyalkyl/benzyl ether-rich, highly lipophilic framework designed to optimize receptor binding; chemically it falls within the fibrate-related amphipathic carboxylic acid hypolipidemic agents, and its core scaffold is best described as a substituted aryloxy-benzyl carboxylic acid pharmacophore rather than the simpler phenoxyisobutyric acid motif of older fibrates. Closely related or pharmacologically similar drugs include fenofibrate, bezafibrate, ciprofibrate, and gemfibrozil, although pemafibrate is more potent and selective for PPARα. Its principal target is PPARα (NR1C1), with downstream regulation of genes involved in triglyceride-rich lipoprotein catabolism, fatty acid β-oxidation, apolipoprotein metabolism, and HDL remodeling. Clinically it is indicated for hypertriglyceridemia and mixed dyslipidemia, particularly in patients with elevated triglycerides, low HDL cholesterol, remnant lipoproteinemia, diabetic dyslipidemia, or residual atherogenic risk despite statin therapy. After oral administration it is well absorbed, highly protein bound, distributed primarily in plasma and liver, metabolized predominantly hepatically by oxidation and conjugative pathways with minimal renal elimination of unchanged drug, and excreted mainly via biliary/fecal routes, making it comparatively suitable in mild to moderate renal dysfunction. Adverse effects include elevations in hepatic enzymes, creatine kinase increase, myalgia, dyspepsia, constipation, nausea, rash, and cholelithiasis; important toxicities include hepatotoxicity, myopathy or rhabdomyolysis risk especially with statins, and possible renal laboratory abnormalities, though overall it has shown a relatively favorable hepatic and renal safety profile versus conventional fibrates in routine clinical use.

Name: Tirabrutinib
Description: Tirabrutinib (DB15227) is a small-molecule, orally active covalent Bruton's tyrosine kinase inhibitor built on a heteroaromatic kinase-inhibitor framework that contains a fused aza/aromatic core linked to a Michael acceptor acrylamide warhead, the latter enabling irreversible bond formation with the conserved cysteine in the BTK ATP-binding site; chemically it is best categorized as a targeted antineoplastic, tyrosine kinase inhibitor, and more specifically a second-generation covalent BTK inhibitor with a compact aza-heterocyclic scaffold related conceptually to other irreversible BTK inhibitors such as ibrutinib, acalabrutinib, and zanubrutinib. Its principal target is BTK, a key mediator of B-cell receptor signaling, with reduced but still possible activity on selected TEC-family kinases compared with less selective predecessors. Pharmacokinetically, tirabrutinib is administered orally, is absorbed sufficiently for systemic BTK inhibition, distributes into blood and lymphoid tissues, undergoes predominantly hepatic oxidative biotransformation largely via CYP3A-mediated pathways, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in feces with a smaller renal contribution; like related agents it has a relatively short plasma half-life but prolonged pharmacodynamic effect because of irreversible target engagement. Toxicities include class-related cytopenias, infections, hepatotoxicity, bleeding tendency, rash, and gastrointestinal toxicity, with examples such as neutropenia, pneumonia, transaminase elevation, diarrhea, and bruising; headache, fatigue, nausea, fever, and upper respiratory symptoms have also been reported. Clinically, tirabrutinib has been used for B-cell malignancies and lymphoproliferative disorders, especially relapsed or refractory primary central nervous system lymphoma and Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia/lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, where it is employed as targeted monotherapy or in protocol-based combination regimens.

Name: Avapritinib
Description: Avapritinib (DB15233) is an orally active, small-molecule antineoplastic tyrosine kinase inhibitor built around a rigid heteroaromatic pyrrolotriazine-like scaffold linked to substituted aryl and amine-containing moieties, a design that supports high-affinity binding to the ATP pocket of mutant kinases in their active conformation; chemically it is a targeted kinase inhibitor in the broader class of aminopyrimidine/azaheteroaryl-type anticancer agents, with a compact fused nitrogen-rich heterocyclic scaffold that distinguishes it from other KIT/PDGFRA inhibitors. It is most similar pharmacologically to other KIT/PDGFRA-directed tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib, sunitinib, regorafenib, ripretinib, and midostaurin, although avapritinib is especially notable for potent activity against PDGFRA exon 18 mutants, including D842V, and activating KIT mutants such as D816V. Its known targets are PDGFRA and KIT, with activity centered on mutant receptor signaling suppression. After oral administration it is absorbed systemically with a time to peak concentration of a few hours, is highly protein bound, distributes broadly, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4-mediated oxidation, and is excreted chiefly as metabolites in feces with a smaller urinary component; dose adjustment and interaction vigilance are therefore important with strong CYP3A modulators and hepatic impairment. Clinically, it is indicated for unresectable or metastatic gastrointestinal stromal tumor harboring PDGFRA exon 18 mutations, including D842V, and for advanced systemic mastocytosis in selected settings. Important toxicities include cognitive effects, intracranial hemorrhage, myelosuppression, anemia, thrombocytopenia, edema, and hepatotoxicity risk; common adverse effects include nausea, fatigue, periorbital edema, diarrhea, vomiting, decreased appetite, abdominal pain, and memory impairment. In practice, it is used as a precision oncology therapy in molecularly defined GIST and mast cell neoplasms, especially when conventional TKIs are ineffective against resistant activation-loop mutations.

Name: Epalrestat
Description: Epalrestat (DrugBank DB15293) is a small-molecule carboxylic acid aldose reductase inhibitor built around a conjugated heteroaromatic scaffold, classically described as a rhodanine/thiazolidinone-derived system bearing an exocyclic alkene linked to a substituted phenyl ring and terminated by a polar acrylic acid-like moiety, a structure that combines aromatic hydrophobicity with an acidic metal- and hydrogen-bonding pharmacophore; chemically it is categorized as an aldo-keto reductase modulator and more specifically a carboxylic acid-containing heterocyclic ARI, with a rhodanine-related scaffold shared conceptually with other aldose reductase inhibitors. Similar drugs include ranirestat, fidarestat, sorbinil, tolrestat, and ponalrestat, which also target the polyol pathway but differ in potency, toxicity, and clinical adoption. Its principal target protein is aldose reductase, now designated AKR1B1, with therapeutic inhibition reducing sorbitol accumulation and downstream oxidative and osmotic injury in hyperglycemic tissues. Epalrestat is used primarily for diabetic peripheral neuropathy, especially symptoms such as numbness, pain, paresthesia, burning feet, and reduced nerve conduction, and has also been explored in diabetic retinopathy and nephropathy. Orally active, it is absorbed reasonably well, is substantially protein bound, distributes mainly in extracellular and tissue compartments relevant to diabetic complications, undergoes hepatic biotransformation including conjugative metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly in urine as metabolites with a relatively short half-life requiring repeated daily dosing. Toxicity is generally mild compared with older ARIs, but hepatic enzyme elevations, gastrointestinal intolerance, rash, and rare clinically significant hepatotoxicity have been reported. Common adverse effects include nausea, anorexia, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, dizziness, headache, and hypersensitivity reactions. Clinically, it is used as adjunctive therapy alongside glycemic control in diabetic patients with neuropathic symptoms, particularly in Japan and parts of Asia.

Name: Risdiplam
Description: Risdiplam (DB15305) is an orally active small-molecule pre-mRNA splicing modifier with a heteroaromatic, fluorinated aromatic-rich structure built around a substituted pyridopyrimidinone-like fused nitrogen-containing scaffold linked to additional aromatic/heterocyclic functionality, placing it in the class of synthetic CNS-active RNA-targeted modulators and more specifically the survival motor neuron 2 splicing modifiers; its core scaffold is distinct from oligonucleotide therapeutics but functionally related to other SMN2-directed agents, with similar drugs including nusinersen, an antisense oligonucleotide that also increases SMN protein, and onasemnogene abeparvovec, a gene-replacement therapy for the same disease area. Pharmacologically, risdiplam promotes inclusion of exon 7 in SMN2 transcripts through interaction with the SMN2 splicing machinery and associated RNA/protein complex, thereby increasing functional SMN protein; direct named target assignment is therefore best described as SMN2 pre-mRNA/spliceosomal complex rather than a classical receptor, enzyme, or ion channel. It is indicated for spinal muscular atrophy, including infantile-onset and later-onset disease, to improve motor function and survival outcomes. After oral administration it is well absorbed, widely distributed systemically with clinically relevant penetration into peripheral tissues and CNS, is metabolized mainly by flavin monooxygenases with lesser CYP-mediated oxidation, and is eliminated predominantly as metabolites in feces with some urinary excretion, supporting once-daily dosing. Toxicity concerns include embryo-fetal toxicity and teratogenic risk, potential effects on male fertility, and retinal or epithelial toxicities seen in preclinical studies; common adverse effects include fever, diarrhea, rash, mouth ulcers, headache, nausea, upper respiratory symptoms, constipation, and laboratory liver enzyme elevations. Clinically, it is used as chronic daily oral therapy across pediatric and adult SMA populations, especially when noninvasive systemic treatment is preferred.

Name: Trelagliptin
Description: Trelagliptin (DB15323) is a long-acting oral dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor built around a fluorinated, nitrogen-rich heteroaromatic small-molecule framework that incorporates a conformationally constrained bicyclic amine and substituted aromatic/heterocyclic elements optimized for high-affinity DPP-4 binding; chemically it is classified as a gliptin antidiabetic agent, and its scaffold is commonly described as a xanthine-like or fused nitrogen-heterocycle-containing DPP-4 inhibitor pharmacophore rather than a peptidomimetic substrate analog. It is structurally and pharmacologically similar to other DPP-4 inhibitors such as sitagliptin, alogliptin, linagliptin, vildagliptin, saxagliptin, and omarigliptin, although trelagliptin is distinguished by once-weekly dosing. Its principal target protein is DPP-4/CD26, with consequent prolongation of endogenous incretins including GLP-1 and GIP, enhancing glucose-dependent insulin secretion and reducing glucagon signaling. It is indicated for type 2 diabetes mellitus, particularly in patients requiring improved glycemic control as monotherapy or in combination with agents such as metformin, sulfonylureas, or insulin. Pharmacokinetically, it is orally absorbed with a prolonged elimination half-life that supports weekly administration, shows limited metabolism relative to total exposure, moderate systemic distribution, and is cleared by both renal and nonrenal pathways with an important renal contribution. Toxicity is generally low and consistent with the class, but examples include hypoglycemia when combined with insulin secretagogues or insulin, hypersensitivity reactions, pancreatitis, hepatic enzyme elevations, and possible renal function-related exposure increases. Common adverse effects include nasopharyngitis, gastrointestinal discomfort, headache, dizziness, constipation, skin eruptions, and laboratory abnormalities; clinically it is used as a convenient once-weekly incretin-based therapy to improve fasting glucose and HbA1c while minimizing weight gain and maintaining a relatively low intrinsic risk of hypoglycemia.

Name: Ubrogepant
Description: Ubrogepant (DrugBank DB15328) is an orally active small-molecule calcitonin gene-related peptide receptor antagonist of the gepant class, built on a highly functionalized, conformationally restricted aza-bicyclic/heterocyclic scaffold bearing multiple aromatic and fluorinated substituents and carbonyl-containing motifs that optimize lipophilicity, receptor affinity, and oral exposure; chemically it is best categorized as a CGRP-receptor–targeted heteroaryl amide-like migraine therapeutic, with a scaffold broadly related to other second-generation gepants such as rimegepant, atogepant, and zavegepant, and more distantly to earlier agents like telcagepant. Its principal pharmacologic target is the CGRP receptor complex, mediated through calcitonin receptor-like receptor and receptor activity-modifying protein 1; antagonism suppresses CGRP-driven trigeminovascular vasodilation and nociceptive signaling. Ubrogepant is indicated for the acute treatment of migraine with or without aura in adults, for example episodic attacks characterized by unilateral throbbing headache, photophobia, phonophobia, or nausea, but it is not intended for migraine prevention. After oral administration it is absorbed with peak concentrations at roughly 1.5 hours, is moderately protein bound, undergoes predominantly CYP3A4-mediated hepatic metabolism, and is eliminated mainly via biliary/fecal excretion with a terminal half-life of about 5 to 7 hours; exposure rises with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors and may fall with inducers. Toxicity is generally favorable relative to older gepants, with no dominant hepatotoxicity signal in routine use, though nausea, somnolence, dry mouth, and fatigue occur, and rare hypersensitivity reactions can occur; clinical use is as an as-needed acute antimigraine agent, including in patients who cannot tolerate or should avoid triptans, with dose adjustment or avoidance in severe hepatic impairment, severe renal impairment, or major CYP3A4 drug-interaction settings.

Name: Trilaciclib
Description: Trilaciclib (DB15442) is a small-molecule cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor chemically characterized as a heteroaromatic, nitrogen-rich ATP-competitive compound built around a substituted triazine-like/pyrrolopyrimidine kinase-binding scaffold with appended amine-containing side chains that confer aqueous formulation suitability and selective CDK4/6 engagement; it belongs to the broader class of targeted antineoplastic cell-cycle inhibitors, and its closest similar drugs are other CDK4/6 inhibitors such as palbociclib, ribociclib, and abemaciclib, although trilaciclib is distinguished by short intravenous use for transient myelopreservation rather than chronic oral antitumor suppression. Its known pharmacologic targets are CDK4 and CDK6, acting upstream of retinoblastoma pathway control to induce temporary G1 arrest in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells. Pharmacokinetically, trilaciclib is administered intravenously before chemotherapy, producing rapid systemic exposure, no absorption phase in the usual oral sense, moderate tissue distribution, hepatic metabolic clearance including cytochrome P450-mediated biotransformation, and elimination through both fecal/biliary and urinary routes, with a relatively short half-life that supports same-day prechemotherapy dosing. Clinically, it is indicated to decrease the incidence of chemotherapy-induced myelosuppression in adults with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer receiving platinum/etoposide-containing regimens or topotecan-containing therapy, thereby reducing severe neutropenia, anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Adverse effects include fatigue, headache, hypocalcemia, hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, elevated transaminases, infusion-site or infusion-related reactions, and occasional serious pulmonary toxicity or severe hypersensitivity; toxicity concerns therefore center on infusion reactions, hepatotoxicity signals, electrolyte disturbances, and the possibility of treatment-emergent interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis, although its principal clinical use remains supportive care myelopreservation rather than direct cytotoxic therapy.

Name: Elexacaftor
Description: Elexacaftor (DB15444) is an orally active small-molecule cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator, or CFTR, corrector characterized by a lipophilic, conformationally complex heteroaromatic structure containing multiple fluorinated aryl groups, amide/carbamate-type linkages, and hydrogen-bonding heterocycles that support binding to misfolded CFTR and stabilization of its processing; chemically it is best classified as a CFTR modulator within the broad class of fluorinated aromatic heterocyclic amide-like drugs, and its scaffold can be described as a polyaryl heterocycle-based corrector framework related to other CFTR correctors. Similar drugs include tezacaftor and lumacaftor, which are also CFTR correctors, and ivacaftor, a CFTR potentiator commonly co-administered for complementary functional rescue. Its principal target protein is CFTR (ABCC7), particularly mutant forms such as F508del-CFTR, where it improves folding, trafficking, and cell-surface expression. Pharmacokinetically, elexacaftor is administered orally, with absorption enhanced by fat-containing food, is highly protein bound, distributed systemically, metabolized predominantly by CYP3A-mediated oxidative pathways to circulating metabolites of lesser activity, and excreted mainly in feces with lesser urinary elimination; dose adjustment and interaction vigilance are important with strong CYP3A inhibitors or inducers. It is indicated, in combination regimens such as elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor, for cystic fibrosis caused by responsive CFTR mutations, especially at least one F508del allele, improving lung function, nutritional status, and reducing pulmonary exacerbations. Adverse effects include rash, headache, upper respiratory symptoms, gastrointestinal upset, elevated transaminases, and occasional creatine phosphokinase elevation; toxicity concerns center on hepatotoxicity, hypersensitivity/rash, drug-drug interactions, and embryo-fetal risk uncertainty, so clinical use requires liver-function monitoring and genotype-guided prescribing.

Name: Vericiguat
Description: Vericiguat (DrugBank DB15456) is an orally active soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator built on a compact fused aza-heteroaromatic scaffold featuring a pyrazolo-pyridine/triazine-like nitrogen-rich core with fluorinated and heteroatom-substituted aromatic functionality that confers potent binding to sGC and favorable oral drug-like properties; chemically it is best categorized as a small-molecule heteroaryl guanylate cyclase stimulator, with a nitrogen-rich bicyclic/condensed azine scaffold related pharmacologically to other sGC stimulators such as riociguat and, more distantly, to the sGC activator cinaciguat. Its primary target is soluble guanylate cyclase, acting in the nitric oxide–sGC–cGMP pathway to increase intracellular cGMP independently of and synergistically with endogenous nitric oxide, thereby improving vascular and myocardial signaling. Vericiguat is indicated for symptomatic chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction after a recent worsening event, particularly to reduce the risk of cardiovascular death and heart-failure hospitalization in adults with persistent high-risk disease. After oral administration it is well absorbed, with enhanced bioavailability when taken with food, reaches peak concentrations within hours, is highly protein bound, undergoes limited oxidative biotransformation with predominant glucuronidation by UGT1A9 and UGT1A1, has a terminal half-life of roughly 20 to 30 hours, and is eliminated through both urine and feces mainly as inactive metabolites. Toxicity is dominated by exaggerated pharmacology, especially hypotension and syncope, with embryo-fetal toxicity risk and theoretical concern for additive blood-pressure lowering with nitrates or PDE5 inhibitors. Common adverse effects include symptomatic hypotension, dizziness, anemia, nausea, and occasional dyspepsia. Clinically, it is used as add-on guideline-directed therapy in recently decompensated HFrEF, for example after hospitalization or need for intravenous diuretics, rather than for acute decompensated heart failure, pulmonary arterial hypertension, or isolated hypertension.

Name: Belzutifan
Description: Belzutifan (DrugBank DB15463) is a small-molecule hypoxia-inducible factor pathway inhibitor whose structure is characterized by a compact, lipophilic, heteroaromatic-rich framework containing substituted nitrogen-bearing ring systems and fluorinated aryl motifs that support selective binding within the HIF-2α ligand pocket; chemically it is best categorized as a targeted antineoplastic heteroaryl aromatic inhibitor, and its core scaffold is commonly described as a substituted fused or linked aza-heterocycle/aryl pharmacophore optimized for HIF-2α antagonism. It is most similar mechanistically to other HIF-2α inhibitors such as PT2385 and PT2977 analog-class compounds, and more broadly to targeted renal cancer agents used in overlapping settings, although those may differ in target class. Belzutifan binds hypoxia-inducible factor 2-alpha, encoded by EPAS1, disrupting HIF-2α/HIF-1β dimerization and downstream transcriptional signaling. After oral administration it is absorbed systemically with peak concentrations typically within a few hours, shows moderate protein binding and broad tissue distribution, is metabolized predominantly by hepatic oxidative pathways including CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 with contribution from UGT2B17, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine and feces with a terminal half-life supporting once-daily dosing. Its principal toxicities reflect on-target erythropoietin suppression and hypoxia pathway modulation, notably anemia and hypoxemia, with fatigue, dizziness, headache, nausea, and dyspnea also common; serious examples include severe anemia requiring transfusion and clinically significant oxygen desaturation. Clinically, it is indicated for von Hippel-Lindau disease-associated renal cell carcinoma, central nervous system hemangioblastomas, and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors not requiring immediate surgery, and it is also used in advanced renal cell carcinoma, especially after prior PD-1/PD-L1 and VEGF-directed therapy.

Name: Cilazaprilat
Description: Cilazaprilat (DrugBank DB15565) is the active diacid metabolite of cilazapril and a peptidomimetic angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor whose structure features a proline-like bicyclic/partially saturated heterocyclic core linked to a dicarboxylate-bearing side chain, creating the classic zinc-binding pharmacophore of dicarboxylate ACE inhibitors; chemically it belongs to the pyridazine- or diazabicyclic-related carboxyalkyl dipeptide mimetic ACE inhibitor class, with a scaffold closely related to other proline-based ACE inhibitor frameworks. Similar drugs include enalaprilat, ramiprilat, lisinopril, perindoprilat, benazeprilat, and quinaprilat, all of which inhibit ACE by coordinating the catalytic zinc site. Its principal target protein is angiotensin-converting enzyme, with downstream suppression of angiotensin II formation and reduced bradykinin degradation. As the active metabolite, cilazaprilat is formed from the oral prodrug cilazapril; it has limited intrinsic oral absorption, distributes mainly in extracellular fluid with significant ACE binding, undergoes minimal further metabolism, and is eliminated predominantly unchanged by the kidney, so exposure is prolonged in renal impairment. Toxicity is largely extension of pharmacology and includes excessive hypotension, renal function deterioration, hyperkalemia, and rare but serious angioedema; class fetotoxicity in pregnancy and risk in bilateral renal artery stenosis are important examples. Adverse effects include cough, dizziness, headache, syncope, nausea, rash, increased creatinine, and rarely neutropenia or severe hypersensitivity. Clinically, through cilazapril administration, it is used for hypertension and chronic heart failure, and in some settings to reduce afterload, improve symptomatic control, and support blood-pressure management in patients requiring renin-angiotensin system blockade.

Name: Prednisolone acetate
Description: Prednisolone acetate (DB15566) is the 21-acetate ester prodrug of prednisolone, a synthetic glucocorticoid corticosteroid built on the pregnane steroid nucleus with the characteristic four fused rings, a 1,4-diene-3,20-dione system, an 11beta-hydroxyl group, a 17alpha-hydroxyl substituent, and acetylation of the C21 hydroxymethyl side chain, features that increase lipophilicity and make it especially useful in ophthalmic suspensions; chemically it belongs to the corticosteroid and specifically glucocorticoid ester class, and its core scaffold is the prednisolone/pregnane corticosteroid scaffold. Similar drugs include prednisolone, prednisone, methylprednisolone, hydrocortisone acetate, dexamethasone, and loteprednol. Its principal target is the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, with downstream transrepression of NF-kappaB- and AP-1-dependent inflammatory signaling and reduced cytokine, prostaglandin, and leukocyte responses. After topical ocular administration, absorption occurs through the cornea and conjunctiva with limited but possible systemic uptake; distribution is largely local into anterior segment tissues, while systemically absorbed drug is protein bound, hydrolyzed by esterases to prednisolone, metabolized mainly hepatically by reduction and conjugation, and excreted predominantly in urine as inactive metabolites. Toxicities reflect corticosteroid effects: ocular hypertension, glaucoma, posterior subcapsular cataract, delayed corneal healing, corneal or scleral thinning, and masking or worsening of bacterial, वायरल, fungal, or herpetic infection; systemic excess may rarely cause hyperglycemia or HPA-axis suppression with prolonged intensive use. Indications and clinical use center on steroid-responsive ocular inflammation such as anterior uveitis, postoperative inflammation, allergic conjunctival inflammation, keratitis without active epithelial herpes, and iritis, with common adverse effects including ocular burning, irritation, blurred vision, increased intraocular pressure, and secondary infection.

Name: Desfesoterodine
Description: Desfesoterodine (DB15578) is best understood as the de-esterified active metabolite related to fesoterodine and closely aligned with 5-hydroxymethyl tolterodine, featuring a tertiary amine antimuscarinic pharmacophore attached to a diaryl-substituted propanol framework with a benzylic hydroxymethyl functionality; chemically it belongs to the synthetic arylalkylamine/tertiary amino alcohol class of anticholinergic agents, and its core scaffold is the tolterodine-type diphenylisobutanol-like muscarinic antagonist motif. Similar drugs include fesoterodine, tolterodine, oxybutynin, solifenacin, darifenacin, and trospium, which share bladder-selective antimuscarinic therapeutic use to varying degrees. Pharmacologically, desfesoterodine targets muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, especially M2 and M3 receptor subtypes in the detrusor, thereby reducing involuntary bladder contraction; systemic off-target antagonism at salivary, ocular, and gastrointestinal muscarinic receptors explains many adverse effects. After oral delivery of the prodrug fesoterodine, the active moiety is rapidly generated by nonspecific esterases, distributed systemically with moderate protein binding, further metabolized mainly by CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 to less active metabolites, and excreted predominantly in urine with some fecal elimination. Toxicity is consistent with antimuscarinic excess and includes dose-related dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention, tachycardia, and CNS effects such as confusion, especially in older adults; overdose may produce severe anticholinergic syndrome. Its principal indication and clinical use are overactive bladder with urgency, frequency, and urge urinary incontinence, including patients requiring symptom control when behavioral therapy alone is inadequate.

Name: Climbazole
Description: Climbazole (DrugBank DB15580) is a topical imidazole antifungal whose structure consists of an imidazole azole ring linked through a ketone-containing aryloxy side chain to a chlorinated aromatic system, giving a lipophilic halogenated azole architecture typical of sterol-biosynthesis inhibitors. Chemically it is classified as an azole, more specifically an imidazole antifungal/antimycotic, and its core scaffold is the substituted imidazole-aryl ether ketone motif found in several topical antifungals. Similar drugs include ketoconazole, miconazole, econazole, bifonazole, and clotrimazole, which share azole-mediated inhibition of fungal sterol synthesis. Its principal target is fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase, the CYP51 enzyme, with consequent depletion of ergosterol and disruption of fungal membrane integrity; secondary activity against Malassezia species is particularly relevant. Pharmacokinetically, climbazole is intended for topical use in shampoos, creams, and cosmetic scalp preparations, where systemic absorption is low under normal conditions, distribution is largely confined to the stratum corneum and hair-bearing skin, hepatic oxidative metabolism would be expected for any absorbed fraction, and excretion is presumed mainly via biliary/fecal and urinary routes after metabolism, although robust human ADME data are limited. It is used for dandruff, seborrheic dermatitis, pityriasis versicolor, and other superficial dermatomycoses associated with Malassezia or dermatophytes. Adverse effects are usually local and mild, including irritation, burning, erythema, dryness, pruritus, and contact dermatitis. Toxicity is generally low at cosmetic concentrations, but excessive exposure may increase skin irritation and, as with other azoles, there is theoretical concern for CYP-related off-target effects if substantial systemic absorption were to occur; clinical use is therefore primarily as a topical anti-dandruff and antifungal agent in rinse-off and leave-on formulations.

Name: N4-Hydroxycytidine
Description: N4-Hydroxycytidine, DrugBank ID DB15660, is a ribonucleoside analog structurally derived from cytidine in which the exocyclic N4 amino group on the uracil-like pyrimidinone base is converted to a hydroxylamino moiety while retaining a β-D-ribofuranose sugar with multiple hydroxyl substituents; chemically it is a hydroxylated pyrimidine nucleoside and belongs to the broader class of antiviral nucleoside analogs, with a cytidine/uridine-like pyrimidine ribonucleoside scaffold. It is closely related to other antiviral nucleoside analogs such as cytarabine, gemcitabine, ribavirin, favipiravir-derived ribonucleoside forms, and especially molnupiravir, the orally bioavailable isopropyl ester prodrug that is rapidly converted to N4-hydroxycytidine in vivo. Its principal pharmacologic target is viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, including SARS-CoV-2 nsp12 and analogous polymerases in other RNA viruses, into whose RNA product the active 5′-triphosphate metabolite is incorporated, driving transition mutagenesis and lethal error catastrophe rather than classic chain termination. After oral molnupiravir dosing, N4-hydroxycytidine is well absorbed systemically, distributed into plasma and tissues, intracellularly phosphorylated to mono-, di-, and triphosphate species, and cleared largely after metabolic turnover with urinary excretion of metabolites. Toxicity concerns center on dose-related mutagenic and genotoxic potential observed in some experimental systems, embryofetal risk, and class-related concerns about host nucleotide pool interactions; adverse effects reported clinically include nausea, diarrhea, dizziness, headache, and rash. Clinically, it is used as the active antiviral species generated from molnupiravir for treatment of mild-to-moderate COVID-19 in high-risk outpatients, and it has also been investigated against influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, and other RNA virus infections.

Name: Molnupiravir
Description: Molnupiravir (DrugBank DB15661) is an orally active prodrug of the ribonucleoside analog N4-hydroxycytidine, structurally characterized as an isopropyl ester appended to a modified pyrimidine nucleoside bearing a ribose-like sugar and an N4-hydroxylated cytosine base; chemically it belongs to synthetic antiviral nucleoside analogs, specifically pyrimidine ribonucleoside prodrugs, with a cytidine-like nucleoside scaffold. Closely related or mechanistically similar drugs include other antiviral nucleos(t)ide analogs such as remdesivir, ribavirin, favipiravir, and cytarabine, although molnupiravir is distinctive in driving viral error catastrophe. After oral administration it is rapidly absorbed and extensively converted by host esterases to N4-hydroxycytidine, which distributes systemically and is intracellularly phosphorylated to the active 5′-triphosphate; this metabolite is incorporated by the SARS-CoV-2 RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, primarily nsp12 within the nsp7/nsp8 replication complex, causing transition mutations during viral RNA synthesis. Elimination occurs mainly after metabolic conversion, with renal excretion of metabolites contributing and a relatively short plasma half-life for parent-derived active nucleoside exposure. Its principal indication is treatment of mild-to-moderate COVID-19 caused by SARS-CoV-2 in nonhospitalized adults at risk for progression to severe disease, for example older patients or those with diabetes, obesity, or cardiovascular disease. Adverse effects are usually mild and include diarrhea, nausea, dizziness, and headache. Toxicity concerns center on embryo-fetal risk and theoretical mutagenic or genotoxic potential based on preclinical findings, so use is avoided in pregnancy and approached cautiously in reproductive populations; clinically, it has been used as an oral early outpatient antiviral when more preferred options are unavailable or inappropriate.

Name: Selpercatinib
Description: Selpercatinib (DrugBank DB15685) is an orally active, highly selective small-molecule receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor whose structure is characterized by a heteroaryl-rich, polyfunctional kinase-binding framework containing pyridine/pyrimidine-like azaheterocycles, aryl ether and alkyne-linked aromatic elements, and polar substituents that support hinge-region binding and RET selectivity; chemically it is best categorized as a targeted antineoplastic aminopyrimidine-type heteroaryl kinase inhibitor built on a compact ATP-competitive RET inhibitor scaffold. It is structurally and mechanistically related to other RET-directed agents such as pralsetinib, while broader multikinase inhibitors with anti-RET activity include vandetanib, cabozantinib, lenvatinib, and sorafenib. Its principal targets are RET kinase, including activating point mutations and RET fusion proteins, with weaker activity against VEGFR2/KDR and FGFR-family kinases reported in some datasets. After oral administration, selpercatinib is absorbed systemically with peak concentrations in the first few hours, distributes widely with substantial protein binding, is metabolized predominantly by CYP3A4, and is eliminated mainly via feces with a lesser urinary component; exposure can increase with CYP3A inhibitors and decrease with inducers, and acid-reducing agents may alter absorption. Toxicities include hepatotoxicity with transaminase elevation, hypertension, QT prolongation, hemorrhagic risk, hypersensitivity, and occasional interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis. Common adverse effects include dry mouth, diarrhea, constipation, nausea, fatigue, edema, rash, abdominal pain, and elevated AST/ALT. Clinically, it is used for RET fusion-positive non-small cell lung cancer, RET-mutant medullary thyroid carcinoma, and RET fusion-positive thyroid cancers, including advanced or metastatic disease requiring systemic therapy.

Name: Cedazuridine
Description: Cedazuridine (DB15694) is a synthetic fluorinated pyrimidine nucleoside analog whose structure closely resembles deoxycytidine, built on a ribofuranose-like sugar linked to a substituted 1,3,5-triazinone/pyrimidinone-type base and bearing fluorine-containing substitution that confers potent enzyme inhibitory activity; chemically it is categorized as a nucleoside analog and more specifically a cytidine/deoxycytidine analog, with a scaffold best described as a modified aza-pyrimidine nucleoside. It is most closely related functionally to other cytidine analogs and cytidine deaminase pathway modulators, and is used in conjunction with decitabine, while structurally or mechanistically comparable agents include decitabine, azacitidine, gemcitabine, and tetrahydrouridine. Its principal target is cytidine deaminase (CDA), which it inhibits in the gastrointestinal tract and systemically, thereby preventing first-pass degradation of decitabine and enabling oral exposure approximating intravenous decitabine. After oral administration with decitabine, cedazuridine is absorbed enterally, acts mainly by increasing decitabine bioavailability, is distributed systemically to tissues expressing CDA, undergoes limited characterization as an active CDA inhibitor rather than a major standalone cytotoxic substrate, and is eliminated largely through renal and metabolic routes. Toxicity is driven mainly by combination therapy and includes myelosuppression with neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, and risk of serious infection or bleeding. Adverse effects commonly include fatigue, nausea, constipation, diarrhea, mucositis, arthralgia, headache, dizziness, and laboratory cytopenias. Clinically, it is indicated with decitabine for adults with myelodysplastic syndromes, including previously treated and untreated de novo or secondary MDS and chronic myelomonocytic leukemia, where it is used as an oral hypomethylating regimen to deliver decitabine exposure without intravenous administration.

Name: Metronidazole benzoate
Description: Metronidazole benzoate (DrugBank DB15759) is the benzoate ester prodrug of metronidazole, structurally characterized by a 5-nitroimidazole heteroaromatic ring bearing a 2-methyl substituent and a hydroxyethyl side chain whose hydroxyl is esterified with benzoic acid, making it more lipophilic and masking the bitter taste of the parent drug; it belongs to the nitroimidazole anti-infective class and retains the classic 5-nitroimidazole scaffold found in related agents such as metronidazole, tinidazole, ornidazole, secnidazole, and dimetridazole. After oral administration, metronidazole benzoate is absorbed and hydrolyzed by esterases to active metronidazole, which distributes widely into saliva, gastrointestinal tissues, vaginal secretions, abscess fluid, and the central nervous system; like metronidazole, it is mainly hepatically metabolized by oxidation and glucuronidation, with renal excretion of parent drug and metabolites and some fecal elimination. Its antimicrobial activity depends on reductive activation of the nitro group in anaerobic bacteria and protozoa by low-redox electron transport proteins such as pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase-linked systems and ferredoxin/flavodoxin, generating reactive intermediates that damage DNA and other macromolecules. It is indicated for anaerobic bacterial and protozoal infections, including amoebiasis, giardiasis, trichomoniasis, and susceptible oral or intestinal anaerobic infections, and is used clinically especially as an oral suspension or pediatric formulation when improved palatability is needed. Toxicities and adverse effects generally mirror metronidazole, including nausea, abdominal discomfort, metallic taste after hydrolysis, headache, dizziness, rash, dark urine, peripheral neuropathy with prolonged exposure, rare seizures or encephalopathy, hepatotoxicity, and a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol; overdose may accentuate neurotoxicity and gastrointestinal intolerance.

Name: Chlormadinone acetate
Description: Chlormadinone acetate (DB15903) is a steroidal progestin and antiandrogen structurally derived from the pregnane/progesterone series, characterized by the classic four-ring cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene steroid nucleus bearing a 3-keto-4,6-diene system, a 17α-acetoxy substituent, and a halogenated 6-chloro feature that enhances progestational potency and antiandrogenic activity; chemically it is classified as a halogenated acetylated pregnadienone, with a progesterone-like steroid scaffold closely related to other steroidal progestins such as cyproterone acetate, megestrol acetate, medroxyprogesterone acetate, and nomegestrol acetate. Its principal target is the progesterone receptor, and it also shows clinically relevant antagonistic activity at the androgen receptor, accounting for endocrine effects in androgen-dependent conditions. After oral administration it is absorbed reasonably well, is highly plasma protein bound, distributes broadly to hormone-responsive tissues, undergoes extensive hepatic biotransformation via reduction, hydroxylation, and conjugation to multiple metabolites, and is eliminated mainly as urinary and fecal metabolites rather than unchanged drug. Toxicity is primarily hormonal rather than acutely cytotoxic, with examples including menstrual irregularity, cholestatic liver dysfunction, thromboembolic risk, adverse lipid changes, and potential fetal harm with exposure in pregnancy. It is indicated for contraception and for treatment of gynecologic and androgen-related disorders such as dysfunctional uterine bleeding, dysmenorrhea, endometriosis-associated symptoms, acne, seborrhea, and hirsutism. Common adverse effects include breast tenderness, nausea, headache, weight gain, mood change, decreased libido, edema, and breakthrough bleeding. Clinically, it has been used alone or in combination with estrogens in oral contraceptives and for antiandrogenic management of hyperandrogenic states.

Name: Parathiazine
Description: Parathiazine (DrugBank DB15978) is a first-generation phenothiazine derivative whose structure is characterized by a rigid tricyclic phenothiazine core containing fused benzene and thiazine rings with a ring nitrogen and sulfur, typically bearing a lipophilic side chain on the ring nitrogen that confers antihistaminic and sedative activity; chemically it falls within the phenothiazine class and more broadly among tricyclic neuroactive antihistamine/antiemetic agents, with the phenothiazine scaffold serving as its defining chemotype. It is structurally and pharmacologically related to other phenothiazines such as promethazine, chlorpromazine, prochlorperazine, and methdilazine, which share varying degrees of H1-histamine receptor, muscarinic, dopaminergic, and alpha-adrenergic antagonism. Available legacy descriptions suggest oral activity with gastrointestinal absorption, extensive tissue distribution due to high lipophilicity and likely central nervous system penetration, predominant hepatic metabolism via oxidative biotransformation and conjugation, and elimination mainly as metabolites in urine and to a lesser extent bile/feces, although precise human pharmacokinetic parameters are not well defined. Its known or inferred target profile centers on HRH1, with possible ancillary antagonism at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, dopamine D2 receptor, and alpha1-adrenergic receptors typical of this scaffold. Historically, such agents have been used for allergic symptoms, pruritus, urticaria, nausea, vomiting, motion sickness, and sedation. Adverse effects are consistent with phenothiazines and include drowsiness, dizziness, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, orthostatic hypotension, and cognitive impairment; toxic effects may include anticholinergic syndrome, excessive CNS depression, QT-related arrhythmia risk, seizures, and extrapyramidal reactions in overdose or susceptible patients. Clinically, parathiazine would therefore be viewed primarily as an older symptomatic antihistamine/antiemetic-sedative agent rather than a modern first-line therapy.

Name: Delgocitinib
Description: Delgocitinib (DB16133) is a small-molecule Janus kinase inhibitor built on a heteroaromatic kinase-binding core, commonly described as a fused azaindole/pyrrolopyridine-like scaffold bearing polar nitrogen-rich ring systems and substituents that optimize ATP-site binding, topical penetration, and balanced lipophilicity; chemically it belongs to the synthetic heterocyclic, targeted immunomodulatory class of tyrosine kinase inhibitors, specifically a pan-JAK inhibitor. Its scaffold and mechanism make it similar to other JAK inhibitors such as tofacitinib, ruxolitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib, and abrocitinib, although delgocitinib is distinguished by development primarily as a topical anti-inflammatory agent. It inhibits JAK family target proteins including JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, and TYK2, thereby suppressing cytokine signaling through pathways relevant to interleukins, interferons, and other inflammatory mediators. Clinically, it is used mainly for inflammatory skin disease, especially atopic dermatitis and chronic hand eczema, with therapeutic intent to reduce pruritus, erythema, lichenification, fissuring, and eczematous inflammation. After topical administration, systemic absorption is generally low but can increase with larger treated surface area or impaired skin barrier; distribution is expected to be limited by the low circulating concentrations achieved, metabolism occurs predominantly via hepatic biotransformation with minimal clinically important systemic accumulation, and excretion is expected through renal and fecal routes as metabolites. Toxicity is usually dominated by local tolerability findings such as application-site irritation, burning, folliculitis, or acneiform reactions, while excessive systemic exposure could theoretically share class risks of infection, hematologic change, lipid alteration, or thrombosis seen with oral JAK inhibitors; in practice, reported adverse effects are mainly mild local skin reactions and occasional nasopharyngitis or headache.

Name: Dotinurad
Description: Dotinurad (DB16145) is a small-molecule urate-lowering agent structurally characterized as a nonpurine aromatic carboxylic acid derivative bearing a rigid, lipophilic heteroaryl/aryl framework linked to an acidic functionality that supports high-affinity interaction with renal urate transport proteins; chemically it is best categorized as a selective uricosuric agent and, at the scaffold level, as a substituted bicyclic heteroaromatic carboxylic-acid-containing scaffold distinct from xanthine oxidase inhibitors. It is most similar pharmacologically to other uricosurics such as lesinurad, benzbromarone, probenecid, and sulfinpyrazone, although dotinurad is generally described as more selective for urate reabsorption pathways. Its principal known target is SLC22A12/URAT1 in the proximal renal tubule, with reduced off-target effects on transporters such as ABCG2 and OAT1/OAT3 relative to older agents. After oral administration, dotinurad is absorbed systemically with clinically useful bioavailability, shows measurable plasma protein binding, is metabolized mainly by hepatic conjugative pathways with limited oxidative biotransformation, and is excreted in urine and feces as parent drug and metabolites. It is indicated for hyperuricemia, including gout and asymptomatic hyperuricemia with elevated serum urate, and is used clinically to lower uric acid in patients inadequately controlled by lifestyle measures or intolerant of xanthine oxidase inhibitors. Adverse effects include gout flares during initiation, arthralgia, mild gastrointestinal symptoms, rash, and laboratory abnormalities such as liver enzyme elevations; toxicity concerns include excessive uricosuria with nephrolithiasis risk, possible renal function worsening in susceptible patients, and hypersensitivity or hepatic adverse reactions, though severe toxicity appears less prominent than with some older uricosurics.

Name: Esflurbiprofen
Description: Esflurbiprofen (DB16159) is the S-enantiomer of flurbiprofen, a chiral arylpropionic acid nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug characterized structurally by a biphenyl system bearing a para-fluoro substituent and a propionic acid side chain at the stereogenic center; chemically it belongs to the 2-arylpropionic acid NSAID class, with a profen scaffold built on a fluorinated biphenyl-propionic acid framework. It is closely related to flurbiprofen itself and to other profen analogs such as ibuprofen, ketoprofen, naproxen, and fenoprofen, which share cyclooxygenase inhibition as a principal pharmacologic theme. Its major known targets are cyclooxygenase-1 and cyclooxygenase-2, through which it suppresses prostaglandin synthesis and thereby mediates analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antipyretic effects. Like other profens, esflurbiprofen is expected to be well absorbed orally, to exhibit high plasma protein binding with broad distribution into inflamed tissues, to undergo predominant hepatic biotransformation including oxidative metabolism and acyl-glucuronidation, and to be eliminated mainly in urine as metabolites with limited unchanged drug excretion. Toxicity is expected to mirror established NSAID liabilities, including dose-related gastrointestinal irritation, ulceration, bleeding, renal perfusion impairment, fluid retention, and possible hepatotoxicity or hypersensitivity; overdose may cause nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, dizziness, and metabolic disturbances. Adverse effects include dyspepsia, nausea, abdominal discomfort, headache, edema, rash, and increases in blood pressure or renal indices. Clinically, esflurbiprofen has been investigated or used as an anti-inflammatory and analgesic agent for painful inflammatory conditions such as osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, musculoskeletal pain, and postoperative or dental pain.

Name: Finerenone
Description: Finerenone (DB16165) is a nonsteroidal dihydropyridine-derived mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist characterized by a compact, lipophilic, heteroaromatic-rich structure containing a substituted dihydronaphthyridine/dihydropyridine-like core linked to amide functionality and electron-withdrawing substituents that optimize high-affinity receptor binding while limiting the steroidal features seen in older agents. Chemically, it belongs to the class of nonsteroidal selective mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, with a heterobicyclic dihydropyridine-like scaffold that distinguishes it from steroidal antimineralocorticoids such as spironolactone and eplerenone; related or similar drugs include spironolactone, eplerenone, and the investigational agent esaxerenone. Its principal target is the mineralocorticoid receptor, encoded by NR3C2, through which it suppresses aldosterone-driven proinflammatory and profibrotic signaling in renal and cardiovascular tissues. Finerenone is orally active, absorbed with clinically useful bioavailability, reaches peak plasma concentrations within hours, is highly protein bound, distributes without marked tissue accumulation, and is metabolized predominantly by CYP3A4 to inactive metabolites that are eliminated mainly in urine with a lesser fecal component; its terminal half-life is short, making exposure sensitive to strong CYP3A4 inhibitors or inducers. Toxicity is dominated by mechanism-based hyperkalemia, which may lead to arrhythmia risk, and by possible worsening renal function, especially in chronic kidney disease or when combined with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium supplements, or potassium-sparing diuretics. Approved use centers on chronic kidney disease associated with type 2 diabetes to reduce sustained eGFR decline, end-stage kidney disease, cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, and heart-failure hospitalization; adverse effects include hyperkalemia, hypotension, hyponatremia, and modest creatinine increases, and clinically it is used as an adjunct to standard renin-angiotensin system blockade in appropriate patients with diabetic kidney and cardiorenal disease.

Name: Maralixibat
