Description: Maralixibat (DB16226) is an orally administered, minimally absorbed small-molecule inhibitor of the ileal bile acid transporter, also called apical sodium-dependent bile acid transporter (ASBT; SLC10A2), designed as a large amphiphilic anionic molecule with a polycyclic aromatic/heteroaromatic-rich scaffold appended to strongly acidic, highly polar functionality that limits systemic exposure and favors luminal activity in the distal intestine; chemically it is categorized as an ileal bile acid transport inhibitor and can be viewed within the broader scaffold family of nonabsorbable bile acid reuptake blockers. Similar drugs include odevixibat and linerixibat, which share the same mechanistic class, and more distantly bile acid sequestrants such as cholestyramine, although those are polymeric binders rather than transporter inhibitors. Its pharmacokinetic profile is defined by very low oral bioavailability, predominant confinement to the gastrointestinal tract, limited distribution, minimal metabolism, and excretion largely in feces, with low plasma concentrations reducing classic systemic drug-drug interaction liability. The principal target protein is SLC10A2/ASBT, and downstream pharmacology includes reduced enterohepatic bile acid recirculation and increased fecal bile acid loss. It is indicated for cholestatic pruritus, especially in Alagille syndrome, and has also been studied in other cholestatic disorders such as progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis. Toxicity is mainly mechanism-based and gastrointestinal, including bile acid diarrhea, abdominal pain, vomiting, and potential dehydration; clinically relevant laboratory concerns include elevations in hepatic transaminases. Common adverse effects include diarrhea, abdominal distension, nausea, and reduced fat-soluble vitamin absorption risk. In practice it is used chronically to reduce pruritus burden and improve quality of life in pediatric cholestatic liver disease, with liver tests, nutritional status, and tolerability monitored during therapy.

Name: Mitapivat
Description: Mitapivat (DrugBank DB16236) is an orally active small-molecule allosteric activator of red-cell pyruvate kinase that is structurally characterized as a substituted aromatic heterocycle-rich compound containing lipophilic aryl rings linked to a nitrogen-containing heteroaromatic core and amide-like/polar functionality that supports high-affinity binding at the pyruvate kinase regulatory site; chemically, it is best classified as a synthetic heteroaryl enzyme activator, and its scaffold can be described broadly as a drug-like biaryl/heteroaryl allosteric modulator framework. Its closest similar drugs are other pyruvate kinase activators, especially etavopivat and investigational PKR activators developed for hemolytic anemias, although mitapivat is the best established in class. The principal target protein is pyruvate kinase PKLR, especially the erythrocyte isoform PKR, with pharmacodynamic consequences including increased ATP production and reduced upstream glycolytic intermediates such as 2,3-diphosphoglycerate. Pharmacokinetically, mitapivat is orally absorbed, reaches systemic circulation efficiently, is distributed systemically with clinically relevant exposure in erythroid tissues, undergoes predominantly hepatic oxidative metabolism mediated largely by CYP3A4 with contribution from other CYP pathways, and is eliminated mainly as metabolites in urine and feces; exposure is altered by strong CYP3A modulators. It is indicated for pyruvate kinase deficiency hemolytic anemia and has also been used clinically or investigated in thalassemia and sickle cell disease to improve anemia and markers of hemolysis. Adverse effects commonly include headache, insomnia, nausea, dizziness, and arthralgia, while toxicity concerns include hepatotoxicity signal, hyperuricemia, hormonal interaction potential, and risk of acute worsening of hemolysis if abruptly discontinued; clinical use therefore centers on chronic oral treatment with monitoring of hemoglobin response, liver tests, and drug-drug interactions.

Name: Revaprazan
Description: Revaprazan (DB16308) is an acid-suppressive small molecule of the potassium-competitive acid blocker class, structurally characterized as a lipophilic heteroaromatic gastric antisecretory agent built around a substituted pyrimidine-linked aromatic scaffold with a basic amine-containing side chain that supports reversible binding in the acidic secretory canaliculus of parietal cells; chemically, it is best grouped with P-CABs rather than benzimidazole proton-pump inhibitors, and its core scaffold is distinct from but pharmacologically similar to other acid inhibitors such as vonoprazan, tegoprazan, fexuprazan, and to a lesser extent PPIs including omeprazole, lansoprazole, and pantoprazole. Its principal known target is the gastric H+/K+-ATPase proton pump, which it inhibits in a reversible, K+-competitive manner. Revaprazan is used primarily for peptic ulcer disease, gastritis-related acid symptoms, gastroesophageal reflux disease, epigastric pain, and mucosal injury associated with excess gastric acid, including ulcer healing and symptom control. Pharmacokinetically, it is orally absorbed, shows systemic distribution sufficient to reach gastric parietal cells, undergoes hepatic biotransformation likely involving CYP-mediated oxidative metabolism, and is eliminated through mixed biliary/fecal and renal routes as metabolites; like related agents, food effects and moderate interindividual metabolic variability may occur. Toxicity is generally consistent with acid suppression therapy, with reported concerns including hepatic enzyme elevation, gastrointestinal intolerance, hypersensitivity, and potential risks of prolonged hypochlorhydria such as hypergastrinemia. Adverse effects include nausea, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, constipation, headache, dizziness, and rash. Clinically, revaprazan has been used as an oral antisecretory drug in ulcer healing, reflux symptom relief, and management of erosive or inflammatory acid-related upper gastrointestinal disorders.

Name: Tetramisole
Description: Tetramisole (DrugBank DB16561) is a synthetic imidazothiazole derivative characterized by a compact bicyclic heteroaromatic scaffold in which an imidazoline-like ring is fused to a thiazole/thiazoline system and bears a substituted phenyl group, placing it in the imidazothiazole class of small-molecule anthelmintics and immunomodulators; its core chemical scaffold is closely related to levamisole, the levorotatory active enantiomer, and it is also pharmacologically similar to older nicotinic anthelmintics such as pyrantel in functional effect, although structurally distinct. Its principal known target is the nematode nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, where agonist-like activation produces sustained depolarization and spastic paralysis of helminths; additional immunologic effects have been described in vertebrates, including modulation of T-cell and macrophage function, but these are less precisely target-defined. Tetramisole is generally orally absorbed, distributed systemically, undergoes hepatic biotransformation to multiple metabolites, and is eliminated through both urinary and fecal routes, with relatively short systemic persistence compared with chronically dosed therapeutics. It has been used primarily for treatment of gastrointestinal helminth infections such as ascariasis and hookworm disease, and historically as an immunomodulatory adjunct in some inflammatory or oncologic settings via levamisole-related use patterns. Toxicity includes dose-related cholinergic and neurotoxic manifestations, with examples including tremor, ataxia, salivation, vomiting, and weakness, while serious adverse reactions reported particularly with levamisole/tetramisole exposure include agranulocytosis, leukopenia, vasculitis, and encephalopathy. Common side effects include nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, rash, and malaise, and clinical use has largely centered on veterinary and older human antihelminthic practice rather than modern first-line therapy.

Name: Fosdenopterin
Description: Fosdenopterin (DB16628) is a synthetic cyclic pyranopterin monophosphate, or cPMP, replacement therapy whose structure consists of a pterin-based bicyclic heteroaromatic core fused to a pyran ring and bearing a phosphate ester, making it a highly polar, anionic pterin-phosphate intermediate and placing it in the broader chemical category of pteridines/pterins and phosphorylated metabolic cofactors; its key scaffold is the cyclic pyranopterin phosphate nucleus that mimics the endogenous first committed intermediate in molybdenum cofactor biosynthesis. It is most similar mechanistically to substrate-replacement therapies rather than to conventional small-molecule enzyme inhibitors, with conceptual analogs including cofactor replacement agents such as sapropterin, although direct structural peers are rare. Its known pharmacologic target is not a receptor but the molybdenum cofactor biosynthetic pathway, functionally bypassing defects in MOCS1 and restoring downstream molybdenum cofactor-dependent enzymes including sulfite oxidase, xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase, and aldehyde oxidase. Clinically, it is indicated for molybdenum cofactor deficiency type A, especially neonatal-onset disease marked by toxic sulfite accumulation, severe encephalopathy, intractable seizures, feeding difficulty, developmental failure, and progressive brain injury. Pharmacokinetic data indicate intravenous administration, immediate systemic availability, extracellular distribution expected for a very hydrophilic phosphate compound, limited passive tissue penetration, metabolic utilization within the cofactor synthesis pathway rather than CYP-mediated biotransformation, and probable renal elimination of drug-related material. Toxicity is generally related to treatment-emergent complications such as catheter or infusion issues and potential photosensitivity or phototoxic injury, with adverse effects reported to include infusion-site reactions, fever, viral infections, otitis media, vomiting, upper respiratory symptoms, and agitation. In practice, fosdenopterin is used as early, chronic disease-modifying replacement therapy in genetically confirmed MoCD type A to reduce mortality and preserve neurodevelopment when started promptly after diagnosis.

Name: Belumosudil
Description: Belumosudil (DrugBank DB16703) is an orally active small-molecule kinase inhibitor whose structure is characterized by a heteroaromatic, polycyclic drug-like framework containing a fused azaindole/quinazoline-like aromatic core linked through substituted aryl and amine functionalities that support ATP-site binding and kinase selectivity; chemically it is best categorized as a targeted synthetic heteroaryl kinase inhibitor, and its central scaffold is commonly described as a ROCK-inhibitor chemotype built around a nitrogen-rich fused aromatic hinge-binding core. It is most similar pharmacologically to other ROCK-pathway inhibitors such as ripasudil and fasudil, although belumosudil is distinguished by greater selectivity for ROCK2 over ROCK1 and by oral systemic use rather than primarily ophthalmic or vasodilator applications. Its principal target protein is Rho-associated coiled-coil-containing protein kinase 2 (ROCK2), with downstream immunomodulatory effects on STAT3/STAT5-, Th17-, Treg-, and profibrotic signaling pathways. Pharmacokinetically, belumosudil is administered orally, achieves systemic absorption with food effects reported, is substantially protein bound, undergoes predominant hepatic metabolism mainly via CYP3A4 with lesser contributions from other oxidative pathways, and is eliminated chiefly as metabolites in feces with a smaller renal component. Toxicity is generally consistent with targeted oral oncology/immunology agents, with reported hepatotoxicity manifested by transaminase elevations, embryo-fetal risk, and potential exposure alterations with strong CYP3A modulators. It is indicated for chronic graft-versus-host disease after failure of at least two prior systemic therapies, particularly for patients with sclerotic skin, oral, hepatic, gastrointestinal, or pulmonary manifestations. Common adverse effects include infections, asthenia or fatigue, nausea, diarrhea, cough, dyspnea, edema, hemorrhage, abdominal pain, hypertension, headache, and laboratory abnormalities such as elevated liver enzymes or lymphopenia. Clinically, it is used as an oral steroid-sparing therapy in refractory chronic GVHD to improve symptoms, organ function, mobility, and fibrotic disease burden.
